Ein starkes Verb der Klasse II, das im Frühneuhochdeutschen schwach wurde: bei seiner Wiedereinführung aus dem Mittel- und Niederdeutschen wurde die starke Konjugation zur schwachen regularisiert. Verwandt mit Niederländisch ~duiken~, Schwedisch ~dyka~; eine niederdeutsche Konsonantenvariante derselben Wurzel ist ~ducken~, verwandt mit Englisch ~duck~.
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~ubar~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Lateinisch ~super~ und Altgriechisch ~hupér~, der Quelle des ~hyper-~ englischer Gelehrtenwörter. ~über-~ drückt Bewegung über eine Grenze hinweg aus.

~Übertauchen~ ist vor allem österreichisch und bedeutet, eine schwierige Zeit zu überstehen, sinnbildlich unter einer Woge hindurch und auf der anderen Seite wieder aufzutauchen.
de.übertragen:
Aus mittelhochdeutsch ~übertragen~, zumindest teilweise eine Lehnübersetzung von lateinisch ~transferre~. Analysierbar als ~über-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: Aus mhd. ~tragen~, aus ahd. ~tragan~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~dragan~, aus urgermanisch *~draganą~ („ziehen, schleppen, tragen“), aus PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ („ziehen, schleppen“). Ein starkes Verb der Klasse VI. Verwandt mit englisch ~draw~ und ~drag~, niederländisch ~dragen~, isländisch ~draga~.
• ~über-~: Aus mhd. ~über~, aus ahd. ~ubari~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~uber~, aus urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Verwandt mit englisch ~over~, niederländisch ~over~, lateinisch ~super~, griechisch ~ὑπέρ~ (~hyper~).

~Übertragen~ ist eine germanische Lehnübersetzung von lateinisch ~transferre~ (~trans-~ + ~ferre~, „hinübertragen“), und die Parallele ist exakt: ~über-~ („über, hinüber“) + ~tragen~ („tragen“) = ~transferre~. Englisch ~transfer~ ist die lateinische Entlehnung; ~übertragen~ ist die einheimische germanische Übersetzung desselben Konzepts. Das Bedeutungsspektrum des Verbs ist breit: Geld überweisen, ein Signal übertragen, eine Krankheit übertragen und (in der Wendung ~im übertragenen Sinne~) eine Bedeutung metaphorisch von einem Bereich in einen anderen tragen. Dieser letzte Gebrauch ist selbst ein Akt des ~Übertragens~: bildliche Sprache trägt ein Wort aus seinem wörtlichen Gebiet hinüber. Verwandt mit englisch ~carry over~ und niederländisch ~overdragen~.
de.übertreffen:
Aus mittelhochdeutsch ~übertreffen~. Zusammensetzung aus ~über-~ + ~treffen~:

• ~treffen~: Aus mittelhochdeutsch ~treffen~, aus althochdeutsch ~treffan~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~drepan~, aus urgermanisch *~drepaną~ („schlagen, treffen“). Verwandt mit englisch ~drub~ („prügeln“). Der Bedeutungswandel von „schlagen, treffen“ zu „begegnen“ (der primären modernen Bedeutung von ~treffen~) vollzog sich, weil man eine Begegnung als ein „Auftreffen“ auf jemanden verstand.
• ~über-~: Aus mittelhochdeutsch ~über~, aus althochdeutsch ~ubar~, aus urgermanisch *~uber~, aus protoindoeuropäisch *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Das Präfix drückt hier ein Übersteigen oder Übertreffen aus.

~Übertreffen~ ist stets untrennbar und bedeutet „übertreffen, übersteigen, überholen“. Die Metapher ist ein Treffen über oder jenseits des Ziels hinaus. Das reflexive ~sich selbst übertreffen~ ist sowohl als Lob als auch als ironische Kritik gebräuchlich.
de.übertreiben:
Untrennbares Kompositum aus ~über-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: Aus Mhd. ~trīben~, aus Ahd. ~trīban~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~drīban~, aus Urgermanisch *~drībaną~. Ein starkes Verb der Klasse I (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~), dessen Ablautmuster die urgermanischen Vokalstufen *ei / *ai / *i direkt spiegelt. Verwandt mit Englisch ~drive~, getrennt nur durch die hochdeutsche Lautverschiebung, sowie Niederländisch ~drijven~, Dänisch ~drive~.
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~ubar~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Lateinisch ~super~ und Altgriechisch ~hupér~, der Quelle des ~hyper-~ englischer Gelehrtenwörter. ~über-~ drückt Übermaß aus: etwas zu sehr oder über eine Grenze hinaus tun.

Wörtlich „zu weit treiben“ (wie Vieh, das man übermäßig antreibt), wurde ~übertreiben~ zum Wort für das Aufbauschen einer Darstellung über das Wahre hinaus.
de.übertreten:
Trennbares Kompositum aus ~über-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: Aus Mhd. ~trëten~, aus Ahd. ~trëtan~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~tredan~, aus Urgermanisch *~trudaną~, aus einem möglichen vorgermanischen *~dret-~, vielleicht einer Erweiterung von PIE *~dr-~ („laufen“). Ein starkes Verb der Klasse V (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~), wahrscheinlich zu einem Wurzelaorist mit alternierendem Vokalismus *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Verwandt mit Englisch ~tread~, Niederländisch ~treden~, Altnordisch ~troða~.
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~uber~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“), einer Erweiterung von *~upo~ („unter, von unten herauf“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Niederländisch ~over~, Schwedisch ~över~, Lateinisch ~super~, Altgriechisch ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Es bezeichnet das Hinübergelangen auf die andere Seite: eines Flusses, einer Straße, einer Grenze.

Trennbar (~ist übergetreten~) heißt ~übertreten~ „zu einer anderen Partei, Konfession oder Seite überwechseln“; untrennbar (~hat übertreten~) dagegen „ein Gesetz oder Gebot verletzen“, die beiden Lesarten trennt allein die Betonung.
de.übertöten:
Untrennbares Kompositum aus ~über-~ + ~töten~:

• ~töten~: Aus mittelhochdeutsch ~tœten~, aus althochdeutsch *~tōten~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~daudijan~ („tot machen, töten“), aus urgermanisch *~daudijaną~, einem Faktitivum zu *~daudaz~ („tot“) + *~-janą~ („X machen“), durchsichtig ~tot~ + ~-en~. Vergleiche englisch ~deaden~. Verwandt mit niederländisch ~doden~, altnordisch ~deyða~, gotisch ~dauþjan~.
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~ubar~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Lateinisch ~super~ und Altgriechisch ~hupér~, der Quelle des ~hyper-~ englischer Gelehrtenwörter. ~über-~ drückt Übermaß aus: etwas zu sehr oder über eine Grenze hinaus tun.

~Übertöten~ überträgt das englische „overkill“: mehr Mittel oder Gewalt aufwenden, als zum Ziel nötig wäre.
de.überwachen:
Zusammensetzung aus ~über-~ + ~wachen~:

• ~wachen~: Aus mhd. ~wachen~, aus ahd. ~wahhēn~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~wakēn~, aus urgermanisch *~wakāną~ („wach sein, wachen“), aus PIE *~weǵ-~ („wachen, stark sein, lebendig sein“). Verwandt mit englisch ~wake~ und ~watch~.
• ~über-~: Aus mhd. ~über-~, aus ahd. ~ubar-~, aus urgermanisch *~uberi-~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Das Präfix fügt den Sinn des Wachens über etwas von oben herab hinzu, was Autorität und Kontrolle impliziert.

Die PIE-Wurzel *~weǵ-~ verbindet Wachheit mit Tatkraft und Stärke und spiegelt das alte Verständnis wider, dass Wachsamkeit an sich eine Form von Macht war. ~Überwachen~ bedeutet „beaufsichtigen, kontrollieren, observieren“, und das Substantiv ~Überwachung~ hat im Deutschen scharfe politische Konnotationen angenommen, besonders angesichts der Erfahrungen des Landes mit staatlicher Überwachung sowohl unter dem NS-Regime als auch unter der ostdeutschen Stasi. Der Begriff ~Überwachungsstaat~ ist eine wirkungsmächtige Zusammensetzung, die im deutschen politischen Diskurs tief nachhallt. Englisch ~watch~ und ~wake~ sind direkte germanische Verwandte, und die Verbindung erstreckt sich bis zu lateinisch ~vigil~ („wachsam“) und ~vigor~ („Lebhaftigkeit“), beide aus derselben PIE-Wurzel. Das verwandte Adjektiv ~wach~ bewahrt die einfachste Form dieses uralten Wortes.
de.überwachsen:
Untrennbares Kompositum aus ~über-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: Aus Mhd. ~wahsen~, aus Ahd. ~wahsan~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~wahsan~, aus urgermanisch *~wahsijaną~, aus PIE *~h₂weg-~ („wachsen, zunehmen“). Ein starkes Verb der Klasse VI (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Verwandt mit englisch ~wax~, niederländisch ~wassen~, dänisch ~vokse~, schwedisch ~växa~, gotisch ~wahsjan~.
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~ubar~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Lateinisch ~super~ und Altgriechisch ~hupér~, der Quelle des ~hyper-~ englischer Gelehrtenwörter. ~über-~ drückt aus, dass etwas gründlich durchgegangen oder vollständig überzogen wird.

~Überwachsen~ bezeichnet Pflanzen, die eine Fläche überziehen und ganz bedecken; das Perfekt bildet es mit ~sein~ (~ist überwachsen~).
de.überwechseln:
Trennbares Kompositum aus ~über-~ + ~wechseln~:

• ~wechseln~: Aus Mhd. ~wëhseln~, aus Ahd. *~wehsalōn~, aus urgermanisch *~wihslōną~, aus PIE *~weyk-~, *~weyḱ-~ („wechseln, biegen, weichen“). Verwandt mit niederländisch ~wisselen~, luxemburgisch ~wiesselen~, englisch ~week~, deutsch ~Woche~ und lateinisch ~vicis~ („Wechsel, Reihe, Abwechslung“).
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~uber~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“), einer Erweiterung von *~upo~ („unter, von unten herauf“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Niederländisch ~over~, Schwedisch ~över~, Lateinisch ~super~, Altgriechisch ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Es bezeichnet das Hinübergelangen auf die andere Seite: eines Flusses, einer Straße, einer Grenze.

~Überwechseln~ heißt, von einer Seite, Spur oder Gruppe auf eine andere zu wechseln, auch vom Wild, das die Straße quert.
de.überweisen:
Untrennbares Kompositum aus ~über-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: Aus Mhd. ~wīsen~, aus Ahd. ~wīsen~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~wīsijan~, aus urgermanisch *~wīsijaną~, einem denominalen Verb zu *~wīsaz~ („weise, wissend“), aus PIE *~weyd-so-s~ („kundig“), aus *~weyd-~ („sehen, wissen“). Ein starkes Verb der Klasse I; die Bedeutungen „zeigen“ und „verweisen“ lenken beide Wissen oder Aufmerksamkeit. Verwandt mit englisch ~wise~, ~wit~, ~wizard~.
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~ubar~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Lateinisch ~super~ und Altgriechisch ~hupér~, der Quelle des ~hyper-~ englischer Gelehrtenwörter. ~über-~ drückt Übertragung oder Übergabe an jemanden aus.

~Überweisen~ vereint drei Übergaben: Geld auf ein Konto ~überweisen~, einen Kranken an einen Facharzt ~überweisen~ und eine Vorlage an einen Ausschuss ~überweisen~.
de.überwerfen:
Trennbares Kompositum aus ~über-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: Aus Mhd. ~wërfen~, aus Ahd. ~werfan~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~werpan~, aus urgermanisch *~werpaną~, aus PIE *~wergʷ-~ („biegen, drehen, verzerren“). Ein starkes Verb der Klasse III (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Verwandt mit englisch ~warp~, niederländisch ~werpen~, altsächsisch ~werpan~, altnordisch ~verpa~, gotisch ~wairpan~.
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~uber~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“), einer Erweiterung von *~upo~ („unter, von unten herauf“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Niederländisch ~over~, Schwedisch ~över~, Lateinisch ~super~, Altgriechisch ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Betont und trennbar ist ~über-~ wörtlich und räumlich: Etwas bewegt sich über etwas anderes hinweg oder darauf.

Trennbar bedeutet ~überwerfen~, sich etwas rasch über die Schultern zu werfen; untrennbar heißt ~sich überwerfen~ dagegen „mit jemandem in Streit geraten“.
de.überwiegen:
Untrennbares Kompositum aus ~über-~ + ~wiegen~:

• ~wiegen~: Zwei verschiedene Verben, beide aus Mhd. ~wigen~. Bedeutung 1 („das Gewicht feststellen“): eine nordwestliche Variante von ~wegen~, die den Präsens-Singular-Stammvokal ~i~ verallgemeinerte, aus Ahd. ~wegan~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~wegan~, aus Urgermanisch *~weganą~ („bewegen, tragen, wiegen“), aus PIE *~weǵʰ-~ („befördern, bewegen“); die alte ~e~-Form überlebt in der Dublette ~wägen~. Bedeutung 2 („schaukeln“): von ~wige~ („Wiege“), aus Ahd. ~wīga~, vermutlich verwandt mit Proto-Westgermanisch *~waggjan~ („in Bewegung versetzen“), aus derselben PIE-Wurzel. Verwandt mit Englisch ~weigh~, Niederländisch ~wegen~, Dänisch ~veje~.
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~ubar~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Lateinisch ~super~ und Altgriechisch ~hupér~, der Quelle des ~hyper-~ englischer Gelehrtenwörter. ~über-~ drückt Übermaß aus: etwas zu sehr oder über eine Grenze hinaus tun.

Vom Wurzelverb ~wiegen~ in der Bedeutung „das Gewicht feststellen“ (nicht „schaukeln“) heißt ~überwiegen~, schwerer zu wiegen und daher vorzuherrschen.
de.überwinden:
Aus mittelhochdeutsch ~überwinden~, aus althochdeutsch ~ubarwintan~, einer ursprünglich oberdeutschen Form neben mitteldeutsch ~überwinnen~, ~ubarwinnan~. Die ~nn~-Form stammt aus proto-westgermanisch *~ubarwinnan~. Zusammensetzung aus ~über-~ + ~winden~ (oder möglicherweise ~winnen~):

• ~winden~: Aus mhd. ~winden~, aus ahd. ~wintan~, aus urgermanisch *~windaną~ („winden, wickeln“), aus PIE *~wendʰ-~ („drehen, winden, flechten“). Verwandt mit englisch ~wind~ (das Verb, „aufspulen“), niederländisch ~winden~, dänisch ~vinde~.
• ~über-~: Aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Das Präfix drückt Meisterung und Überlegenheit aus, über ein Hindernis hinwegzukommen.

Ob ~überwinden~ von ~winden~ („drehen, wickeln“) oder vom heute verlorenen Simplex ~winnen~ („gewinnen“, nur noch in der Zusammensetzung ~gewinnen~ erhalten) abstammt, ist eines der faszinierenderen Rätsel der deutschen Wortgeschichte. Die ~nd~-Form könnte eine bloße lautliche Veränderung der ~nn~-Form sein, oder sie könnte eine echte Umdeutung widerspiegeln, die das Verb mit ~winden~ verknüpft, sich aus dem Griff eines Gegners herauswinden als Metapher für das Überwinden. Vereinzelte mhd. Zusammensetzungen wie ~anewinden~ („angreifen“) und ~widerwinden~ („zurückschlagen“) stützen die Kampfbedeutung von ~winden~. Modernes ~überwinden~ bedeutet „überwinden, hinwegkommen über, bewältigen“: Man überwindet Angst (~Angst überwinden~), bezwingt Hindernisse (~Hindernisse überwinden~) und überwindet Trauer (~Trauer überwinden~). Das reflexive ~sich überwinden~ („sich dazu durchringen, sich zwingen“) fängt den inneren Kampf treffend ein. Verwandt mit niederländisch ~overwinnen~ („besiegen, bezwingen“).
de.überzahlen:
Untrennbares Kompositum aus ~über-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: Aus Mhd. ~zaln~, ~zalen~, aus Ahd. ~zalōn~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~talōn~, aus urgermanisch *~talōną~ („erzählen; zählen, rechnen“). ~Zahlen~ und ~zählen~ sind Geschwister derselben Wurzel: Bezahlung erfordert das Abzählen des richtigen Betrags. Verwandt mit englisch ~tale~ und ~tell~, niederländisch ~betalen~, schwedisch ~tala~.
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~ubar~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Lateinisch ~super~ und Altgriechisch ~hupér~, der Quelle des ~hyper-~ englischer Gelehrtenwörter. ~über-~ drückt Übertragung oder Übergabe an jemanden aus.

In dieser Lesart fasst ~überzahlen~ das Zahlen als Übertragung auf: Der Betrag geht an einen Empfänger über. Gebräuchlicher ist freilich die Übermaß-Lesart „zu viel zahlen“.
de.überzeichnen:
Untrennbares Kompositum aus ~über-~ + ~zeichnen~:

• ~zeichnen~: Abgeleitet vom Substantiv ~Zeichen~, aus Mhd. ~zeichen~, aus Ahd. ~zeihhan~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~taikn~, aus urgermanisch *~taikną~, *~taiknaz~ („Zeichen“), aus PIE *~deyḱ-~ („zeigen, weisen“); ~zeichnen~ heißt etymologisch, ein Zeichen zu machen. Verwandt mit englisch ~token~, niederländisch ~teken~, dänisch ~tegn~, schwedisch ~tecken~.
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~ubar~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Lateinisch ~super~ und Altgriechisch ~hupér~, der Quelle des ~hyper-~ englischer Gelehrtenwörter. ~über-~ drückt Übermaß aus: etwas zu sehr oder über eine Grenze hinaus tun.

~Überzeichnen~ heißt, ein Bild über das rechte Maß hinaus auszuführen, bis es ins Übertriebene oder Karikaturhafte kippt.
de.überzeugen:
Aus ~über-~ + ~zeugen~:

• ~zeugen~: Aus mhd. ~ziugen~, ~geziugen~, aus ahd. ~giziugon~, eine Ableitung von ~Zeug~ („Stoff, Gerät, Ausrüstung, Werkzeug“). ~Zeug~ selbst stammt aus mhd. ~ziuc~, aus ahd. ~giziug~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~teug~, aus urgermanisch *~teugą~. Dies ist die nominale Ableitung von *~teuhaną~ („ziehen, führen“), das auch ~ziehen~ zugrunde liegt, aus PIE *~dewk-~ („ziehen, führen“).
• ~über-~: Aus mhd. ~über~, aus ahd. ~ubari~, ~ubar~, aus urgermanisch *~ubar~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“). Das Präfix trägt hier den Sinn der Überwindung oder des Darüberhinausgehens, jemanden überzeugen, indem man sich über seinen Widerstand erhebt.

Die ursprüngliche Bedeutung von ~zeugen~ war „bezeugen, bestätigen“, selbst abgeleitet von der älteren Bedeutung, sein ~Zeug~ (seine Beweise, seine Ausrüstung) vorzubringen oder vorzuzeigen. ~Überzeugen~ bedeutet daher wörtlich „über-bezeugen“ oder „so gründlich bezeugen, dass man den Zweifel des anderen überwindet“. Das Substantiv ~Zeuge~ („Zeuge“) und das Verb ~zeugen~ („erzeugen, hervorbringen“) sind verwandt, alle teilen die Kernidee, etwas hervorzubringen oder ins Dasein zu ziehen. Eine bemerkenswerte englische Parallele: ~convince~ leitet sich letztlich von lateinisch ~vincere~ („besiegen“) ab und spiegelt dieselbe Metapher wider, Widerstand durch Argumentation überwinden. Verwandt mit niederländisch ~overtuigen~.
de.überziehen:
Trennbares Kompositum aus ~über-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: Aus Mhd. ~ziehen~, aus Ahd. ~ziohan~, aus proto-westgermanisch *~teuhan~, aus urgermanisch *~teuhaną~, aus PIE *~dewk-~ („ziehen, führen“). Ein starkes Verb der Klasse II. Verwandt mit gotisch ~tiuhan~, altenglisch ~tēon~, altnordisch ~toga~, westfriesisch ~tsjen~ und englisch ~tie~.
• ~über-~: Aus Mhd. ~über~, aus Ahd. ~ubar~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~uber~, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upéri~ („über, oberhalb“), einer Erweiterung von *~upo~ („unter, von unten herauf“). Verwandt mit Englisch ~over~, Niederländisch ~over~, Schwedisch ~över~, Lateinisch ~super~, Altgriechisch ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Betont und trennbar ist ~über-~ wörtlich und räumlich: Etwas bewegt sich über etwas anderes hinweg oder darauf.

Betont und trennbar meint ~überziehen~ „etwas über sich ziehen“, ein Kleidungsstück anlegen; unbetont und untrennbar bedeutet dieselbe Schreibung „beschichten, überziehen“ oder ein Konto „überziehen“.
de.übrigbleiben:
Trennbares Kompositum aus ~übrig~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: Aus Mhd. ~blīben~, ~belīben~, aus Ahd. ~bilīban~ („verbleiben“), aus Urgermanisch *~bilībaną~, einer Zusammensetzung aus *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, aus PIE *~leyp-~ („kleben, haften“): Physisches Haften wurde zur Metapher für das Verweilen. Verwandt mit Niederländisch ~blijven~, Englisch ~belive~ („verbleiben, bleiben“).
• ~übrig~: Das Adjektiv ~übrig~, aus Mhd. ~überic~, ~überec~, mit dem Suffix ~-ig~ zur Präposition ~über~ gebildet, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upér~, dieselbe Wurzel wie Englisch ~over~ und, über das Griechische und Lateinische, ~hyper-~ und ~super-~. Gemeint ist, was über das erforderliche Maß hinaus vorhanden ist. Die Bedeutung von ~übrig~ ist hier: mit ~bleiben~ „verbleiben, als Einziges bleiben“.

~Übrigbleiben~ bezeichnet das, was nach allem anderen als Einziges zurückbleibt, der Rest, den niemand weggenommen hat.
de.übrighaben:
Trennbares Kompositum aus ~übrig~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: Aus Mhd. ~haben~, aus Ahd. ~habēn~, aus Proto-Westgermanisch *~habbjan~, aus Urgermanisch *~habjaną~, aus PIE *~keh₂p-~ („greifen, ergreifen“). Trotz des Gleichklangs nicht mit Lateinisch ~habēō~ verwandt, wohl aber mit ~capiō~ („ich ergreife“) und mit Deutsch ~heben~. Verwandt mit Englisch ~have~, Niederländisch ~hebben~, Dänisch ~have~, Gotisch ~haban~.
• ~übrig~: Das Adjektiv ~übrig~, aus Mhd. ~überic~, ~überec~, mit dem Suffix ~-ig~ zur Präposition ~über~ gebildet, aus Urgermanisch *~uber~, aus PIE *~upér~, dieselbe Wurzel wie Englisch ~over~ und, über das Griechische und Lateinische, ~hyper-~ und ~super-~. Gemeint ist, was über das erforderliche Maß hinaus vorhanden ist. Die Bedeutung von ~übrig~ ist hier: prädikativ „übrig, verbleibend“.

Wörtlich heißt ~übrighaben~ „etwas übrig, zur Verfügung haben“; die Redewendung „viel für jemanden übrighaben“, aus der die Bedeutung „sich kümmern“ stammt, überträgt das Erübrigen auf Zuneigung.

en.abarbeiten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The compound covers a literal and a figurative range: a list or a debt is worked off item by item, while reflexive ~sich an etwas abarbeiten~ means to wear oneself out on something.
en.abbauen:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~buwen~, from OHG ~buan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~buan~, from Proto-Germanic *~buanan~, from PIE *~bhuH-~ ("to be, to grow, to dwell"). Cognate with English ~build~ (via a different branch), Dutch ~bouwen~, and, more surprisingly, English ~be~ (from the same PIE root *~bhuH-~, whose basic meaning was "to exist, to grow").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epo~ ("off, away"). This prefix adds a sense of "down, off, away," often implying dismantling or reduction.

The semantic development of ~bauen~ from "to dwell" to "to build" is a natural progression: one builds where one intends to live. The related noun ~Bauer~ ("farmer") preserves the older sense of "dweller, cultivator." The compound ~abbauen~ reverses the constructive sense of ~bauen~: rather than building up, one takes down. It is used in mining ("to extract ore"), in employment ("to lay off workers"), in biology ("to break down substances"), and in general for any process of reduction or dismantling. This versatility makes it one of the most semantically productive ~ab-~ compounds in German.
en.abbehalten:
A compound of the separable ~ab-~, the inseparable ~be-~, and ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The two prefixes pull in opposite directions, and that is the point: ~be-~ holds fast, while ~ab-~ names what is withheld from being handed over, a sum kept back out of a payment.
en.abbeißen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~beißen~:

• ~beißen~: From MHG ~bīzen~, from OHG ~bīzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bītaną~, from PIE *~bʰeyd-~ ("to split"). A class I strong verb (~beißen~, ~biss~, ~gebissen~). Cognate with English ~bite~, Dutch ~bijten~, Swedish ~bita~; ~bitter~ is this verb's old participial adjective, literally "biting."
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Literal throughout: the bite separates a piece, and that piece is what ~ab-~ names. The passage from Grimm turns on exactly this: the poisoned morsel Snow White had bitten off is jolted back out of her throat.
en.abbekommen:
A compound of the separable ~ab-~, the inseparable ~be-~, and ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Bekommen~ already means to receive; ~ab-~ makes the receiving partitive: one gets a share off a larger whole, and in the idiom ~etwas abbekommen~ that share is often damage.
en.abberufen:
A compound of the separable ~ab-~, the inseparable ~be-~, and ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. A parallel weak form in Middle High German explains why the modern present lacks the expected umlaut (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Berufen~ calls someone into an office and ~abberufen~ calls them out of it, so the pair is an exact antonym, which is why the Basic Law can put both verbs side by side in a single clause.
en.abbestellen:
A compound of the separable ~ab-~, the inseparable ~be-~, and ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

~Abbestellen~ undoes ~bestellen~: the order stands until it is called off, so the verb terminates a running arrangement rather than removing a physical thing.
en.abbezahlen:
A compound of the separable ~ab-~, the inseparable ~be-~, and ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

Where ~bezahlen~ merely says that payment was made, ~abbezahlen~ says the debt reached zero: the completive ~ab-~ is the whole difference between paying on a loan and paying it off.
en.abbiegen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~biegen~:

• ~biegen~: From MHG ~biegen~, from OHG ~biogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beuganą~, from PIE *~bʰewgʰ-~ ("to bend"). A class II strong verb (~biegen~, ~bog~, ~gebogen~). Cognate with English ~bow~ and ~elbow~ ("arm-bend"), Dutch ~buigen~, Sanskrit ~bhujáti~ ("to bend, curve").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The literal bend survives only faintly: nothing is bent when a driver turns off at a junction, but the road's own curve away from the straight line is what ~ab-~ + ~biegen~ originally described.
en.abbilden:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~bilden~:

• ~bilden~: From MHG ~bilden~, ~bileden~, a merger of OHG ~biliden~ (from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþijan~) and OHG ~bilidōn~ (from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþōn~), both derived from *~biliþī~ ("image, likeness"), whence modern ~Bild~ ("picture, image"). The deeper origin is Proto-West Germanic *~bil~ ("equal, alike").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)~, from OHG ~ab(a)~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). In this compound, the prefix conveys the sense of reproducing or transferring an image from one medium to another.

The MHG predecessor ~abebilden~, ~abebileden~ is attested, confirming the compound's medieval origin. ~Abbilden~ means "to depict, to portray, to map", to create an image (~Bild~) of something, transferring it "off" (~ab~) the original onto a new surface. The noun ~Abbildung~ ("illustration, figure, mapping") is standard in textbooks, scientific papers, and mathematical discourse. In mathematics, ~Abbildung~ is the formal term for a mapping or function, a precise abstraction from the concrete sense of depicting. Cognate with Dutch ~afbeelden~ ("to depict, to portray"), which uses the same prefix-root combination. The deeper connection to *~bil~ ("equal, alike") is revealing: to depict is to create something equal to the original.
en.abbinden:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~binden~:

• ~binden~: From MHG ~binden~, from OHG ~bintan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bindan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bindaną~, from PIE *~bʰendʰ-~ ("to bind, tie"). A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~i~–~a~–~u~ ablaut (~binden~, ~band~, ~gebunden~). Cognate with English ~bind~, Dutch ~binden~, Gothic ~bindan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Ab-~ can undo as readily as it separates: ~abbinden~ is both untying a bond and, in medicine, tying a limb off, the same prefix read from either side of the knot.
en.abbitten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~bitten~:

• ~bitten~: From MHG ~bitten~, from OHG ~bitten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~biddjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bidjaną~, from PIE *~gʷʰedʰ-~ ("to ask for, beseech"). A class V strong verb; the noun ~Bitte~ and the particle ~bitte~ come from the same root. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bidden~ ("to pray"), Danish ~bede~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The object of ~abbitten~ is the offence, not the pardon: one begs a wrong off the person wronged, which is why the verb takes a dative person alongside an accusative fault.
en.abblasen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~blasen~:

• ~blasen~: From MHG ~blāsen~, from OHG ~blāsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blāsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~blēsaną~, from PIE *~bʰleh₁-~ ("to blow, swell"). A class VII strong verb, its reduplicated preterite worn down to ~blies~ (~blasen~, ~blies~, ~geblasen~). Cognate with English ~blast~, Gothic ~ufblēsan~, Old Norse ~blása~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The literal sense (blowing dust off a surface) is now rarer than the figurative one, which comes from the bugle call that ended a military exercise: to ~abblasen~ an event is to call it off.
en.abbleiben:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Rare and now largely regional, ~abbleiben~ asks after what has stayed away (~wo ist es abgeblieben?~ is still current for what became of a missing thing), and, like the simple verb, it forms its perfect with ~sein~.
en.abbrechen:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"). A class IV strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~brechen~, ~brach~, ~gebrochen~. Cognate with English ~break~, Dutch ~breken~, Old Saxon ~brekan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)~, from OHG ~ab(a)~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys separation, termination, or removal.

The compound means "to break off, to abort, to discontinue"; ~ein Gespräch abbrechen~ ("to break off a conversation"), ~ein Studium abbrechen~ ("to drop out of one's studies"), ~das Programm abbrechen~ ("to abort the program"). Both transitive and intransitive: a branch ~bricht ab~ ("breaks off") and a person ~bricht etwas ab~ ("breaks something off"). The English cognate ~break~ is one of the most transparent Germanic word pairs: the High German consonant shift turned Proto-Germanic *~k~ into the OHG affricate written ~hh~ (later ~ch~), so ~break~ and ~brechen~ differ only by this regular sound change. Someone who ~bricht das Studium ab~ is a ~Studienabbrecher~ ("university dropout"), a compound noun that carries considerably less stigma in German-speaking countries than its English equivalent, partly because the German apprenticeship system (~Ausbildung~) provides respected alternative career paths.
en.abbrennen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~brennen~:

• ~brennen~: From MHG ~brennen~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: transitive ~brennan~ ("to set on fire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~brannijan~, and intransitive ~brinnan~, from *~brinnan~, of which *~brannijan~ was the causative. The intransitive is from PIE *~bʰrewh₁-~ ("to boil, brew"), making ~brennen~ a cousin of English ~brew~. A Rückumlaut verb: ~ich brenne~ but ~brannte~, ~gebrannt~. Cognate with English ~burn~, Dutch ~branden~, Icelandic ~brenna~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The root's old transitive/intransitive pair survives in the compound: a house ~brennt ab~ of its own accord, while arsonists ~brennen~ it ~ab~, and in both, ~ab-~ insists that nothing is left.
en.abbringen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Abbringen~ is used almost always of a person's course or conviction rather than of a physical object, and it governs ~von~: Kafka's court is one that can scarcely be brought away from its certainty of guilt.
en.abbuchen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~buchen~:

• ~buchen~: In its commercial sense ("to book, reserve"), a denominal verb from ~Buch~, modelled on English ~to book~. ~Buch~ is from MHG ~buoch~, OHG ~buoh~, Proto-West Germanic *~bōk~, Proto-Germanic *~bōks~, the same root as English ~beech~, early Germanic writing being scratched onto beech tablets. A separate older ~buchen~ is an adjective, "of the beech tree." Cognate with English ~book~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

The bookkeeping metaphor is doubled: ~buchen~ enters an amount in the book, and ~ab-~ enters it on the side that makes the balance fall.
en.abdanken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~danken~:

• ~danken~: From MHG ~danken~, from OHG ~dankōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankōną~, a denominative of *~þankaz~ ("thought, gratitude"), from PIE *~teng-~ ("to perceive, think, feel"), the same root as ~denken~; to thank was to hold in thought. Cognate with English ~thank~ and ~think~, Dutch ~danken~, Danish ~takke~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The thanks were once literal: to ~abdanken~ a soldier was to dismiss him with thanks for his service. Only later did the verb turn intransitive, so that the departing party (a monarch, a minister) now does the leaving.
en.abdecken:
From Middle High German ~abedecken~, equivalent to ~ab-~ + ~decken~. Cognate with Dutch ~afdekken~ ("to cover"). Compound of ~ab-~ + ~decken~:

• ~decken~: From MHG ~decken~, from OHG ~decchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þakkjan~. Equivalent to ~Dach~ ("roof") + ~-en~. Cognate with Frisian ~dekke~, Dutch ~dekken~, English ~thatch~, Danish ~taekke~, and Swedish ~täcka~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~, from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). This prefix conveys removal or separation.

The verb ~abdecken~ presents a fascinating paradox: it can mean both "to uncover, to remove a covering" (taking the ~ab-~ prefix literally as "away") and "to cover, to protect" (where ~ab-~ implies shielding from above). Context determines which sense applies. English ~thatch~, the cognate of ~decken~, reveals the original Proto-Germanic root *~þak-~ ("roof, covering"), which underwent the High German consonant shift from ~þ~ to ~d~. The same shift turned ~þing~ into ~Ding~, ~þorn~ into ~Dorn~, and ~þank~ into ~Dank~. The PIE root *~(s)teg-~ ("to cover") also produced Latin ~tegere~ ("to cover"), yielding English ~protect~, ~detect~, and ~toga~ (a garment that covers the body).
en.abdrehen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). Cognate with English ~throw~ (a true cognate: Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist," a sense that "throw a pot" still keeps) plus English ~thread~, Dutch ~draaien~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Two everyday senses share the prefix's turning-away: a ship ~dreht ab~ from its course, and a tap or a lamp is ~abgedreht~, turned until the supply is cut off, which is what the quoted sentence asks for.
en.abdreschen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~dreschen~:

• ~dreschen~: From MHG ~dreschen~, from OHG ~dreskan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þreskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þreskaną~, probably from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, turn"). A class III strong verb (~dreschen~, ~drosch~, ~gedroschen~). Cognate with English ~thresh~ and its doublet ~thrash~, Dutch ~dorsen~, Swedish ~tröska~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Threshing already means beating the grain from the stalk, so ~ab-~ names what comes away. The figurative ~abgedroschen~, said of a phrase, follows the same image: beaten so long that nothing is left on it, English ~threadbare~ arrived at by a different picture of the same wear.
en.abdringen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~dringen~:

• ~dringen~: From MHG ~dringen~, from OHG ~dringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þringwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrinhwaną~, from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). A class III strong verb (~dringen~, ~drang~, ~gedrungen~); its causative ~drängen~ carries the expected umlaut. Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~ ("to press") and English ~throng~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The pair ~abdringen~ / ~abdrängen~ preserves the strong-weak split named in the root entry: strong ~dringen~ presses inward, and ~abdringen~ presses something out of another's grip (a confession, a promise), where weak ~abdrängen~ merely shoves a body aside.
en.abdrucken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~drucken~:

• ~drucken~: From MHG ~drucken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~ ("to press"). A doublet of ~drücken~ ("to press, push"), which keeps the expected umlaut; ~drucken~ lacks it because Upper German blocked umlaut before a velar geminate, and the form used by the first, southern printers became the technical term. Polish ~drukować~ was borrowed from it.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys copying from a model: reproducing something by taking it off an original.

The reproductive sense is old and physical: the type was pressed onto the paper, so the copy was literally taken off the form. ~Abdrucken~ still means reproducing an existing text, never composing a new one, which is what keeps it distinct from plain ~drucken~.
en.abdrängen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~drängen~:

• ~drängen~: From a merger of two Middle High German verbs: ~drengen~, from OHG ~drengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangwijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrangwijaną~ (a causative); and the now-obsolete ~drangen~, from OHG ~drangōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangōn~ (a denominative). Both from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). ~drängen~ took the transitive senses, the strong ~dringen~ the intransitive. Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~, English ~throng~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Drängen~ supplies the pressure and ~ab-~ the direction: the object is not merely pushed but pushed off its line, as a vehicle is forced off the road.
en.abdrücken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Drücken~ and ~drucken~ are the doublet described in the root entry, and their compounds went separate ways: ~abdrucken~ reproduces a text, while ~abdrücken~ releases a trigger: the finger presses until the shot comes away.
en.aberkennen:
A compound of the separable ~ab-~, the inseparable ~er-~, and ~kennen~:

• ~kennen~: From MHG ~kennen~, from OHG ~kennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kannijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~ ("to know"), a causative of *~kunnaną~, from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"). A member of the Rückumlaut cohort: the present shows umlaut (~ich kenne~), the preterite does not (~kannte~, ~gekannt~). Cognate with Dutch ~kennen~, Scots and English ~ken~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The legal ~erkennen~ underlies this compound (a court that ~erkennt~ pronounces judgement), so ~aberkennen~ does not mean to stop recognizing something but to adjudge it away from its holder: a title, a medal, a citizenship.
en.abernten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~ernten~:

• ~ernten~: From MHG ~ernen~, from OHG ~arnon~, from Proto-Germanic *~azanōną~, a denominative from the noun *~azaniz~ ("harvest"), from PIE *~seh1-~ ("to sow"). The modern ~-t-~ (first in MHG ~ernde~) arose from a merger with OHG ~arnōt~. Cognate with English ~earn~, which generalized the same Proto-Germanic source to "to gain by labor."
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The prefix does the same work as in ~abdreschen~, but on the field rather than the sheaf: the object of ~abernten~ is what is left bare, one harvests a field, not the wheat.
en.aberziehen:
~Aberziehen~ is a compound of separable ~ab-~, inseparable ~er-~, and ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ preserves its own older spatial sense of upward or outward motion.

Because ~ab-~ and ~er-~ pull in opposite directions, the compound means undoing by training what training put there: one ~erzieht~ a child, and one ~erzieht~ it a habit ~ab~ again. Only ~ab-~ separates (~er-~ never does), so the finite forms run ~erzieht ab~.
en.abfahren:
~Abfahren~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The old sense of ~fahren~ was travel of any kind, and ~abfahren~ began as simply setting out from a place; modern German has narrowed it to vehicular departure and, colloquially, extended it to the enthusiasm of ~auf etwas abfahren~ ("to be really into something").
en.abfallen:
~Abfallen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The physical sense (leaves, plaster, a gently sloping lawn) has an old figurative twin: ~von jemandem abfallen~ is to defect, and Luther uses it exactly so for revolt against a king. Both are the same image of something coming loose from what held it.
en.abfangen:
~Abfangen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~fangen~:

• ~fangen~: From MHG ~vāhen~, from OHG ~fāhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~fanhaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to secure, fasten"). A strong verb, originally ~fāhan~ / ~fieng~ / ~gefangan~; the modern present stem ~fang-~ was taken analogically from the past forms. Cognate with English ~fang~, Dutch ~vangen~, West Frisian ~fange~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Fangen~ supplies the catching and ~ab-~ the interception: whatever is ~abgefangen~ has been taken out of a path it was already on, a letter, a person, a skidding car.
en.abfassen:
~Abfassen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~fassen~:

• ~fassen~: From MHG ~vazzen~, from OHG ~fazzōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fatōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fatōną~ ("to hold, seize"), a weak class 2 verb, from PIE *~pod-néh₂-ti~, from *~pod-~ ("to fetch"). German kept the sense of grasping and holding, English that of going to retrieve. Cognate with English ~fetch~; the noun ~Fass~ ("barrel") shares the root.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The compound has narrowed to writing: to ~abfassen~ a text is to bring it into its final, fixed form, which is why it is the ordinary verb for drafting a law. The root's other descendant, ~Fass~ ("barrel"), keeps the older sense of holding; a text ~abgefasst~ is likewise something given a vessel.
en.abfeiern:
~Abfeiern~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~feiern~:

• ~feiern~: From MHG ~vīren~, from OHG ~fīrōn~, a denominative from OHG ~fīra~ (whence ~Feier~), borrowed from Latin ~fēriae~ ("religious holidays"), from Proto-Italic *~fēsiās~, from PIE *~dʰéh₁s-yo-s~, from *~dʰéh₁s~ ("god, deity"). A ~Feiertag~ was originally a day set aside for the gods. Cognate with Dutch ~vieren~, distantly English ~feast~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

Modern usage runs on two tracks: the workplace ~Überstunden abfeiern~, taking time off until the overtime balance is used up, and the colloquial ~jemanden abfeiern~, celebrating someone to excess. Both take the celebrating to its limit rather than merely doing it.
en.abfertigen:
~Abfertigen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~fertigen~:

• ~fertigen~: From MHG ~vertigen~ ("to prepare, make ready"), equivalent to ~fertig~ + ~-en~. The adjective ~fertig~ (MHG ~fertec~, OHG ~fartīg~) belongs to ~fart~ ("journey"), from Proto-Germanic *~farą~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross"); ~fertig~ originally meant "ready for a journey." Cognate with Dutch ~vaardig~, Low German ~fardig~, Old English ~fierd~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The root's original sense (~fertig~ as "ready for a journey"), is still visible: to ~abfertigen~ is to make something ready and send it off, whether freight, a traveler at a counter, or, brusquely, a person one wants rid of.
en.abfinden:
~Abfinden~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~finden~:

• ~finden~: From MHG ~vinden~, from OHG ~findan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~finþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to go, pass; path, bridge"). The development from "to go, pass" to "to find" parallels shifts in Slavic. Cognate with English ~find~, Dutch ~vinden~, Low German ~finden~, Danish ~finde~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The compound is legal before it is emotional: to ~abfinden~ someone is to settle a claim so that nothing is left open, and the reflexive ~sich abfinden mit~ applies that same finality to whatever cannot be changed.
en.abfliegen:
~Abfliegen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~fliegen~:

• ~fliegen~: From MHG ~vliegen~, from OHG ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"), an extension of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim") that also gave ~fließen~. The vowel path *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of class II strong verbs. Cognate with English ~fly~, Dutch ~vliegen~, Danish ~flyve~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Ab-~ marks the moment of leaving: an aircraft ~fliegt ab~ when it quits the ground. Used transitively (to ~abfliegen~ a route) the sense shifts to covering ground from the air, exactly as it does for ~abfahren~ and ~abgehen~.
en.abfließen:
~Abfließen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~fließen~:

• ~fließen~: From MHG ~vlieȥen~, from OHG ~flioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleutaną~ ("to float, stream, flow"), from PIE *~plewd-~ ("to flow, run, swim"). A class II strong verb (~fließen~, ~floss~, ~geflossen~); the zero grade *~flut-~ gave ~Flut~. Cognate with English ~fleet~, ~float~ and ~flood~, Dutch ~vlieten~, Swedish ~flyta~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Water is the usual subject and money the figurative one: German administrative prose has funds ~abfließen~ from a budget exactly as a river drains a basin. That the root is the same extension of *~plew-~ that also gave ~fliegen~ shows how close flowing and flying once were.
en.abfordern:
~Abfordern~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~fordern~:

• ~fordern~: From MHG ~vodern~, ~vordern~, from OHG ~fordarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ(a)rōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþą~, from PIE *~pŕ̥-to-~, from *~per-~ ("forward, through"); "to push forward" became "to advance a claim." Not to be confused with umlauted ~fördern~ from the same root. Cognate with English ~forth~, ~forward~ and ~further~, Dutch ~vorderen~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Fordern~ is "to push forward, to advance a claim"; ~ab-~ adds the person the claim is pressed against. What is ~abgefordert~ is demanded out of someone, not merely asked for.
en.abfragen:
~Abfragen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~fragen~:

• ~fragen~: From MHG ~vrāgen~, from OHG ~frāgēn~, ~frahēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frāgēn~ (a denominative from *~frāgu~, "question"), from Proto-Germanic *~frēgō~ ("question"), from PIE *~preḱ-~ ("to ask"), which also gave Latin ~precor~ and Sanskrit ~pṛcchāti~. Cognate with English ~frain~ (archaic), Dutch ~vragen~, Swedish ~fråga~, Icelandic ~fregna~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The compound belongs first to the schoolroom: to ~abfragen~ vocabulary is to draw the answers out of the learner. Computing took the word over unchanged; a database is ~abgefragt~ just as a pupil is.
en.abführen:
~Abführen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The compound covers leading a prisoner away, paying taxes over to the state, and, medically, the action of a laxative; all three are the same act of conducting something away. Since ~führen~ is the causative of ~fahren~, ~abführen~ is the exact transitive counterpart of ~abfahren~.
en.abfüllen:
~Abfüllen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~füllen~:

• ~füllen~: From MHG ~vüllen~, from OHG ~fullen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fullijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullijaną~ ("to make full"), the causative of *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pl̥h₁nós~ ("full"). English ~fill~ and ~füllen~ are exact cognates, each the causative of its native word for "full." Cognate with English ~fill~, Dutch ~vullen~, Danish ~fylde~, Swedish ~fylla~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The compound is about decanting: wine or water is ~abgefüllt~ from a larger vessel into bottles, so the filling applies to the smaller container and the taking-off to the larger.
en.abgeben:
~Ab-~ + ~geben~. Compound of ~ab-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give").
• ~ab-~: From PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). The prefix adds the sense of transfer, delivery, or separation from the self.

~Abgeben~ means "to hand in, submit, deliver; to give off (heat, sound); to make (a statement); to play (a role)." The prefix ~ab-~ transforms a generic act of giving into an act of handing something away from oneself: a completed transfer. The reflexive ~sich abgeben mit~ ("to busy oneself with, to associate with") adds another dimension: the self is handed over to a task or person. The range of uses is striking: one ~gibt eine Erklärung ab~ ("makes a statement"), one ~gibt Wärme ab~ ("gives off heat"), one ~gibt ein Paket ab~ ("drops off a package"), all unified by the image of something departing from the agent's sphere. Cognate with Dutch ~afgeven~.
en.abgehen:
~Abgehen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The range is wide (a button ~geht ab~, a train departs, a plan ~geht gut ab~), but Luther's use here is the oldest of them: what ~abgeht~ is what is lacking, taken away from a count that should have been full.
en.abgießen:
~Abgießen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~gießen~:

• ~gießen~: From MHG ~giezen~, from OHG ~giozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geutan~ ("to pour"), from Proto-Germanic *~geutaną~, from PIE *~gʰewd-~ ("to pour"). The sense of casting metal and glass is attested since Old High German (participle ~gigozzan~). Cognate with English ~gush~, Dutch ~gieten~, Old English ~geotan~, Gothic ~giutan~, Swedish ~gjuta~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Two trades share the compound: the kitchen, which pours the water off the potatoes, and the foundry, which casts from a mould, ~gießen~ has denoted the casting of metal since Old High German.
en.abgleichen:
~Abgleichen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~gleichen~:

• ~gleichen~: From MHG ~gelīchen~, from OHG ~gilīhhon~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkōną~ ("to make alike, resemble"), from *~galīkaz~ ("alike, similar"), from *~ga-~ + *~līkam~ ("body, form"), from PIE *~leyg-~ ("image, likeness"). A strong verb (~glich~, ~geglichen~), one of the few built on a deadjectival base. Cognate with English ~like~, Dutch ~gelijken~, Old Norse ~glíkr~, Danish ~ligne~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys copying from a model: reproducing something by taking it off an original.

The comparison sense grows out of measuring: whatever is ~abgeglichen~ is checked against an original. The modern data sense (syncing two copies) is the same act performed with two originals and no model.
en.abgleiten:
~Abgleiten~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~gleiten~:

• ~gleiten~: From MHG ~glīten~, from OHG ~glītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~glīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~glīdaną~, from PIE *~ǵʰleydʰ-~ ("to glide, slide"). A class I strong verb (~gleiten~, ~glitt~, ~geglitten~), though a weak ~gleitete~ turns up in technical prose. Cognate with English ~glide~, Dutch ~glijden~, Low German ~glieden~, Swedish ~glida~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The compound is as much figurative as physical: a hand slips off a railing, but a debate can equally ~ins Polemische abgleiten~, sliding away from where it should have stayed.
en.abgraben:
~Abgraben~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~graben~:

• ~graben~: From MHG ~graben~, from OHG ~graban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from PIE *~gʰrebʰ-~ ("to dig, scratch, bury"). A class VI strong verb (~graben~, ~grub~, ~gegraben~). Cognate with English ~grave~ as a verb (now only in ~engrave~ and ~graven image~), Gothic ~graban~, Dutch ~graven~, Old Norse ~grafa~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Beyond the literal digging away, the compound survives in one fixed idiom, ~jemandem das Wasser abgraben~ ("to cut off a rival's water"), a figure from an age when a mill's water supply really could be diverted with a spade.
en.abhalten:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. The PIE origin is uncertain: possibly from *~ḱel-~ ("to hide, conceal") or *~kel-~ ("to drive"). Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)~, from OHG ~ab(a)~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). The prefix adds a sense of keeping at a distance or conducting away.

The literal sense is "to hold off": to keep something at a distance or to conduct an event. ~Abhalten~ has two distinct modern meanings: "to keep from, to prevent" (~jemanden von etwas abhalten~, "to keep someone from something") and "to hold, to conduct" (a meeting, an exam, a ceremony). These senses connect through the idea of holding in a controlled manner: either holding something back or holding something in place while it runs its course. The English cognate ~hold~ preserves both senses too: "hold back" (prevent) and "hold a meeting" (conduct). The relationship between German ~halten~ and English ~hold~ is direct and unbroken from the Proto-Germanic period.
en.abhandeln:
~Abhandeln~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~handeln~:

• ~handeln~: From MHG ~handeln~, from OHG ~hantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handulōn~, a denominative verb from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~ ("hand") with the frequentative suffix *~-lōną~; the sense broadened from "to handle" to "to act, deal, trade." Cognate with English ~handle~, Dutch ~handelen~, Danish ~handle~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

Two senses run side by side: to ~abhandeln~ a topic is to treat it through to its end, while ~jemandem etwas abhandeln~ is to get it off them by bargaining. The root supports both, its "to act" sense and its "to trade" sense each taking the prefix differently.
en.abhandenkommen:
~Abhandenkommen~ is a separable compound of ~abhanden-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~abhanden-~: A fossilized prepositional phrase, ~ab~ + ~Handen~, the old dative plural of ~Hand~: literally "away from the hands." It is the exact opposite of ~vorhanden~ ("at hand, available"), and the pair preserves a case form the modern language has otherwise lost. The particle is frozen so completely that it survives in only one verb, ~abhandenkommen~. ~Hand~ itself, Proto-Germanic *~handuz~, has no secure further etymology. The sense of ~abhanden-~ here is: the fixed idiom ~abhandenkommen~, "to go missing," said of the thing lost rather than of its owner.

The verb takes the thing lost as its subject: German says the key ~kommt mir abhanden~ rather than that I lost it, leaving the loser a dative bystander at the edge of the clause.
en.abhauen:
~Abhauen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~hauen~:

• ~hauen~: From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). Originally a class VII strong verb (~hauen~, ~hieb~, ~gehauen~), partially weakened colloquially, where ~haute~ competes with ~hieb~. Cognate with English ~hew~, Latin ~cūdere~ ("to strike, forge").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

This reading is the weak one, ~haute ab~, against the simplex's strong ~hieb~; the same weak forms also carry the colloquial sense of clearing out, in which ~hau ab~ tells someone to leave.
en.abheben:
~Abheben~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb: the past ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ continue the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The prefix takes something off a surface: fat off a broth, a card off the deck, money off an account, an aircraft off the runway. The reflexive ~sich abheben~ turns that same motion into standing out against a background.
en.abhelfen:
~Abhelfen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~helfen~:

• ~helfen~: From MHG ~hëlfen~, from OHG ~hëlfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helpaną~, from PIE *~ḱelb-~, *~ḱelp-~. A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~e~-~a~-~o~ ablaut pattern (~helfen~, ~half~, ~geholfen~). Cognate with English ~help~, Dutch ~helpen~, Danish ~hjælpe~, Norwegian ~hjelpe~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

German construes it with the dative of the trouble, not of the sufferer: one ~hilft einem Übel ab~, helping the evil away, and that is precisely what separates ~abhelfen~ from plain ~helfen~.
en.abholen:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~holen~:

• ~holen~: From MHG ~holen~, ~holn~, from OHG ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get, draw"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~halōną~, *~hulōną~ ("to call, fetch, summon"), from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, cry, summon").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)~, from OHG ~ab(a)~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). In this compound it carries a sense of removal or retrieval.

The literal sense is "to fetch away," meaning to pick someone or something up from a location. Unlike simple ~holen~ ("to fetch"), ~abholen~ emphasizes going to a specific place to collect something or someone, you ~holen~ a glass of water from the kitchen, but you ~holen ab~ a friend from the airport. English ~haul~ is a distant cousin: it entered English from Old French ~haler~, which itself was borrowed from Frankish *~halōn~, the same Proto-Germanic root as ~holen~. So ~holen~ and ~haul~ are etymological siblings reunited through a detour via medieval France. The PIE root *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, summon") also appears in Latin ~calāre~ ("to call, proclaim"), whence English ~calendar~ (originally a day for calling out debts) and ~claim~.
en.abhängen:
~Abhängen~ is a separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~hängen~:

• ~hängen~: The merger of three OHG verbs: ~hāhan~ (strong, transitive; past ~hieng~, participle ~gehangan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~hą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~hanhaną~; ~hangēn~ (weak, intransitive); and the causative ~hengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hangijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hangijaną~. The distinction is upheld chiefly in the past tense: intransitive ~hing~/~gehangen~ versus transitive ~hängte~/~gehängt~. Cognate with Dutch ~hangen~, English ~hang~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

This reading belongs to the strong, intransitive branch of the merged root (~hing ab~, ~abgehangen~) not to the weak transitive ~hängte ab~ of taking a picture off a wall.
