The image itself is Latin's: ~dependere~ ("to hang down from") gave English ~depend~, and German built the same figure out of native material.
en.abhören:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix names the source or support the action proceeds from: drawing something out of someone, or hanging from something.

The compound keeps hearing at its core but gives it a direction: what is heard is drawn out of its source, whether that is a pupil reciting a lesson, a chest under a stethoscope, or a tapped telephone line.
en.abjagen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~jagen~:

• ~jagen~: From MHG ~jagen~ ("to hurry, drive, pursue, hunt"), from OHG ~jagōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~jagōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~jakkōną~, a ~nā~-iterative formation, likely rebuilt from PIE *~h₁eyǵʰ-~ ("to strive, chase"). Attested since the eighth century; further pre-Germanic etymology is obscure.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix names the source or support the action proceeds from: drawing something out of someone, or hanging from something.

The dative construction is the point: one does not simply ~abjagen~ a thing but ~jemandem etwas abjagen~, so the quarry is hunted out of another's hands rather than out of a forest.
en.abkaufen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, a denominative verb from *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"), a loanword from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper"). Cognate with English ~cheap~, Dutch ~kopen~, Danish ~købe~, Icelandic ~kaupa~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix names the source or support the action proceeds from: drawing something out of someone, or hanging from something.

Where plain ~kaufen~ names only the goods, ~abkaufen~ names the seller as well (~jemandem etwas abkaufen~), and the same figure survives in the idiom ~das kaufe ich dir nicht ab~, "I don't buy that from you."
en.abkehren:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~kehren~:

• ~kehren~: A homograph concealing two distinct verbs. ~Kehren~ (1) "to turn": from MHG ~kēren~, from OHG ~kēran~, ~chēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kairijaną~ or *~kausijaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly connected to *~gers-~ ("to twist, bend, turn"). ~Kehren~ (2) "to sweep": from MHG ~kern~, ~keren~, from OHG ~kerian~, ~cherian~, from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~ ("to scrape, scratch"), from PIE *~ger-~ ("to scrape"). Etymologically unrelated, merged through phonological convergence.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The root here is ~kehren~ (1) "to turn": ~sich von etwas abkehren~ is to turn away from something, not to sweep it up. The weak conjugation is no help in telling the twins apart, since both branches are weak; only the sense decides.
en.abklingen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~klingen~:

• ~klingen~: From MHG ~klingen~, from OHG ~klingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~klinganą~, almost certainly of onomatopoeic origin. A class III strong verb (~klingt~, ~klang~, ~geklungen~), the same pattern as ~singen~. Cognate with English ~clink~ and ~clang~, Middle Dutch ~klinken~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

An onomatopoeic root that has moved past sound: pain, fever, and the heat of an argument all ~abklingen~ in modern German, a noise-word turned into the general shape of anything that trails off.
en.abklären:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~klären~:

• ~klären~: From MHG ~klæren~, denominal from ~klar~ ("clear, bright"), borrowed from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch ~klār~, from Old French ~cler~, from Latin ~clārus~ ("bright, renowned"). English ~clear~ arrived by the same route: cousins by borrowing rather than inheritance.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The image is a liquid left standing until its sediment drops away, and modern administrative German has kept the shape while losing the liquid: ~etwas abklären~ is to settle a question until nothing is left in suspension.
en.abkochen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~kochen~:

• ~kochen~: From MHG ~kochen~, from OHG ~kohhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kokōn~, borrowed from Late Latin ~cocō~, from Latin ~coquō~ ("I cook, I boil"), from PIE *~pekʷ-~ ("to cook, to ripen"). A loan early enough to have undergone the High German shift of ~k~ to ~ch~. Cognate with English ~cook~, Dutch ~koken~, Danish ~koge~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

The prefix does the reducing: ~kochen~ names the heat and ~ab-~ names what the heat takes away, whether that is water boiled off a sauce or the germs boiled out of drinking water.
en.abkommen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys derivation: leading something away from, or tracing it back to, a source.

Two directions live in the one verb: to ~abkommen~ from a path is to stray from it, and to ~abkommen~ from a source is to descend from it, the same movement away, read forward or backward.
en.abkriegen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~kriegen~:

• ~kriegen~: From MHG ~kriegen~ ("to war, to strive for"), a verbalization of ~Krieg~ ("war"), from OHG ~krig~, from Proto-West Germanic *~krīg~, whose origin is debated. The "obtaining" sense overshadowed the military one; colloquial modern German ~kriegen~ simply means "to get." Cognate with Dutch ~krijgen~ ("to get"), Bavarian ~kriagn~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Colloquial through and through: ~kriegen~ had already traded warfare for getting, and ~ab-~ narrows the getting to a piece taken off a larger whole: a share of the cake, or a share of the blame.
en.abkürzen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~kürzen~:

• ~kürzen~: A deadjectival verb from ~kurz~ ("short"), which descends from MHG ~kurz~, OHG ~kurz~, Proto-West Germanic *~kurt~, borrowed from Latin ~curtus~ ("shortened, cut short"), from PIE *~(s)ker-~ ("to cut"), the same root behind English ~shear~, ~short~, and ~skirt~. English ~curt~ is a doublet of the same Latin source.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

The Latin loan behind ~kurz~ also gave English ~curt~, and the same PIE root gave ~short~; ~abkürzen~ applies the cutting indifferently to a road, a word, or a procedure.
en.abladen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two historically distinct verbs under one infinitive. ~laden~ (strong, "to load"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"); cognate with English ~lade~ and ~laden~, Lithuanian ~klṓti~. ~laden~ (weak, "to invite, summon"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root found only in Germanic and Anatolian (Hittite ~halzai~).
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

The root here is the strong ~laden~ "to load," not its weak homograph "to invite": the strong conjugation of ~abladen~ (~lädt ab~, ~lud ab~, ~abgeladen~) settles the branch, and the sense confirms it.
en.ablagern:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~lagern~:

• ~lagern~: Derived from the noun ~Lager~ ("camp, store, warehouse"), from MHG ~lëger~, from OHG ~lëgar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~legr~, from Proto-Germanic *~legrą~. The modern form with ~-a-~ is of East Central German origin, influenced by ~Lage~ ("position"). Cognate with English ~lair~, Dutch ~leger~, Danish ~lejr~, Swedish ~läger~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

A verb built on a noun that once named a place to lie down: what is ~abgelagert~ has come to rest, whether that is silt settling in a riverbed or wine left to mature in a cellar.
en.ablaufen:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~ ("to run, leap"), from PIE *~klewb-~ ("to spring, stumble"). A class VII strong verb. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)~, from OHG ~ab(a)~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys completion, departure, or expiration.

The compound means "to run off, to expire, to elapse"; time, a contract, or a process ~läuft ab~ ("runs off, expires"). The image is of something running its course until it departs. The range of uses is characteristically broad: a passport ~läuft ab~ ("expires"), water ~läuft ab~ ("drains off"), an event ~läuft ab~ ("proceeds, unfolds"), and shoes ~laufen sich ab~ ("wear down from running"). The root verb ~laufen~ shows an interesting phonological history: OHG ~hloufan~ still had the initial ~hl-~ cluster (like English ~leap~ preserves the ~l-~), which was simplified to ~l-~ in Middle High German. The English cognates ~leap~ and ~lope~ seem semantically distant from "to run," but the original Proto-Germanic sense encompassed any rapid forward movement. The related English ~elope~ ("to run away secretly to marry") entered English from Anglo-French but traces back to the same Germanic root.
en.ableben:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

A euphemism assembled out of its own opposite: the verb for living, closed off by ~ab-~, so that ~ableben~ names dying by saying that the living has been carried through to its end.
en.ablegen:
From Middle High German ~abelegen~, from Old High German *~abaleggen~, from Proto-Germanic *~abalagjaną~. Compound of ~ab-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~, a causative formation from *~legʰ-~ ("to lie"). The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~ ("to lie"): to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with English ~lay~, Dutch ~leggen~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)~, from OHG ~ab(a)~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~, Latin ~ab~ ("from").

The combination of "away" + "to lay" yields the core sense "to lay aside, to put down." From this spatial meaning, ~ablegen~ has developed a rich array of figurative uses: ~eine Prüfung ablegen~ ("to take an exam," literally "to lay down a test"), ~einen Eid ablegen~ ("to take an oath"), ~Rechenschaft ablegen~ ("to give an account"), and ~Gewohnheiten ablegen~ ("to shed habits"). The English causative pair ~lie~/~lay~ mirrors the German ~liegen~/~legen~ perfectly, both descending from the same PIE causative derivation, a grammatical mechanism over five thousand years old that is still productive in both languages.
en.ablehnen:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~lehnen~:

• ~lehnen~: From a merger of two related Middle High German verbs: (1) ~linen~ / ~lenen~ (intransitive "to lean"), from OHG ~hlinēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlinēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlināną~; and (2) ~leinen~ (transitive "to lean something"), from OHG ~hleinen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlainijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlainijaną~, a causative of the former. The merger happened in Central and Low German dialects where the vowels fell together.
• ~ab-~: From PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). This separable prefix adds the sense of turning away, removing, or rejecting.

~Ablehnen~ means "to decline, to reject, to refuse", literally to lean away from something. The physical gesture of leaning back from an unwanted offer is frozen in the word. In formal contexts it carries official weight: ~einen Antrag ablehnen~ ("to reject an application"), ~eine Einladung ablehnen~ ("to decline an invitation"). The root verb ~lehnen~ is cognate with English ~lean~ (from the same Germanic source) and Dutch ~leunen~. An unrelated homograph ~lehnen~ ("to lend"), from OHG ~lēhanōn~, gave rise to Dutch ~lenen~ and English ~lend~, a false friend lurking within the same German dictionary entry.
en.ableisten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~leisten~:

• ~leisten~: From MHG ~leisten~, from OHG ~leisten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laistijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~laistijaną~, a denominative of *~laistaz~ ("track, footprint"), from PIE *~leys-~ ("to track; furrow, trail"). Originally "to track, follow," then "to perform, accomplish." Cognate with English ~last~ (OE ~lǣstan~), Old Saxon ~lēstian~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The root's old sense of following a track suits the compound: what one ~ableistet~ (military service, a probationary year), is a course laid out in advance and followed to its end.
en.ableiten:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~laidijaną~ ("to lead, guide"), a causative of *~līþaną~ ("to pass, to go by"). Cognate with English ~lead~, Old Saxon ~lēdian~, Old Norse ~leiða~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)~, from OHG ~ab(a)~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). The prefix adds the sense of derivation or leading away from a source.

The literal sense is "to lead away from": to derive, to divert, to deduce. ~Ableiten~ covers a remarkable semantic range: in linguistics, it means "to derive" (a word from a root); in mathematics, "to differentiate" (a function); in engineering, "to divert" (water, electricity); in logic, "to deduce" (a conclusion from premises). The noun ~Ableitung~ serves as the standard term for "derivative" in both calculus and linguistics. The connection between "leading" and "learning" runs deep in this word family: Proto-Germanic *~laidijaną~ ("to lead") is the causative of *~līþaną~ ("to go"), so to lead is literally "to make someone go." English ~lead~ is a direct cognate, and the semantic parallel (to lead someone through a derivation) is perfectly preserved.
en.ablenken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~lenken~:

• ~lenken~: From MHG ~lenken~, from OHG ~lanca~ ("hip, flank"), related to ~Gelenk~ ("joint"), from Proto-Germanic *~gahlankiją~, from *~hlankaz~ ("flexible, lank, slender"). The path from "joint" to "to steer, guide" ran through bending and turning at a joint. Cognate with English ~lank~ (and ~link~); OHG ~hlanka~ also gave French ~flanc~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The root's joint is still visible in the compound: to ~ablenken~ is to bend something away at an angle, whether that is a beam of light, a river, or a listener's attention.
en.ablesen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys copying from a model: reproducing something by taking it off an original.

Both halves of the root's history survive in the compound: a vintner ~abliest~ grapes from the vine, gathering them off it, while a speaker ~abliest~ a text from the page, reproducing it off an original. Luther's translation still uses the older, literal harvest.
en.abliefern:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~liefern~:

• ~liefern~: From MHG ~lieveren~ (attested before 1350), probably borrowed via Middle Dutch and Middle Low German ~lēveren~, from Old French ~livrer~, from Latin ~līberō~ ("I free, release, deliver"), from ~līber~ ("free"). The word belonged to the Hanseatic League's trade vocabulary. Cognate with Dutch ~leveren~, English ~deliver~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

A Hanseatic trade word descended from Latin ~līber~ "free": delivering was originally releasing goods, and ~ab-~ marks them as passing out of the deliverer's hands.
en.abliegen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

A stative compound rather than an action: nothing moves, and ~ab-~ only measures the distance at which the subject already lies; a village that ~abliegt~ is simply remote.
en.ablöschen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~löschen~:

• ~löschen~: Two distinct verbs merged under one spelling. "To extinguish": from MHG ~leschen~, OHG ~lescan~, Proto-West Germanic *~leskan~, Proto-Germanic *~leskaną~ ("to go out"), originally intransitive, the causative sense developing later; cognate with Dutch ~lessen~. "To delete, unload (cargo)": borrowed from Low German ~lössen~, ~lossen~, from the ancestor of ~los~ ("free, rid of").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The root here is the ~leschen~ branch "to extinguish," not the Low German ~lossen~ of unloading cargo; ~ab-~ carries the extinguishing through to its end, and the kitchen sense of ~ablöschen~ (pouring liquid into a hot pan) is that same act taken literally.
en.ablösen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~lösen~:

• ~lösen~: From MHG ~lœsen~, ~lōsen~, from OHG ~lōsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lausijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausijaną~, a causative of *~leusaną~ ("to lose, let loose"), denominative via *~lausaz~ ("loose, free"), from PIE *~lewh₁-~ ("to cut, sever, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ (via Old Norse ~lauss~), Dutch ~lozen~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The root already meant loosening, so ~ab-~ contributes only the direction (off and away), which is why one verb covers a label peeled from a jar and a sentry relieved at his post.
en.abmachen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The literal sense is still current (~ein Schild abmachen~ takes a sign down), but the completive reading carried the verb into speech, where ~etwas abmachen~ is to settle a matter so that nothing is left open.
en.abmelden:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~melden~:

• ~melden~: From MHG ~mëlden~, from OHG ~mëldōn~, ~mëldēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~melþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~melþōną~, from PIE *~meldʰ-~ ("to ask, pray, speak"). The original sense was supplicatory speech; ~melden~ keeps only the communicative side: "to report, register." Cognate with Dutch ~melden~, English ~meld~ (partial).
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The verb is the exact mirror of ~anmelden~, and the pair has followed German life from the parish register through the residents' registration office to the login screen.
en.abmelken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~melken~:

• ~melken~: From MHG ~melken~, from OHG ~melchan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~melkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~melkaną~, from PIE *~h₂melǵ-~ ("to milk"). A class III strong verb (~melken~, ~molk~, ~gemolken~), though weak forms (~melkte~, ~gemelkt~) are now common. Cognate with English ~milk~, Danish ~malke~, Latin ~mulgēre~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

One of the oldest verbs in the language (the PIE root is reconstructed for milking itself) and ~ab-~ adds only exhaustiveness: to ~abmelken~ is to milk dry, which is why the figurative sense of milking someone reaches for this compound.
en.abmischen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~mischen~:

• ~mischen~: From MHG ~mischen~, from OHG ~misken~, from Proto-Germanic *~miskijaną~ ("to mix"), from PIE *~meyḱ-~ ("to mix, knead"), via the inchoative present *~miḱ-sḱé-~. Cognate with English ~mix~, Latin ~misceō~, Greek ~mísgo~, Sanskrit ~miśrá~ ("mixed").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

A studio word on an ancient root: ~ab-~ marks the mixing as finished, so an ~abgemischter~ track is one whose channels have been brought to their final balance.
en.abnehmen:
From Middle High German ~abenemen~, from Old High German ~abaneman~, from Proto-Germanic *~abanemaną~. Compound of ~ab-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due, to allot, to assign"). Cognate with English ~nim~ (archaic "to take, filch"), Dutch ~nemen~, Danish ~nemme~ ("to learn, grasp"), Swedish ~förnimma~ ("to perceive").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~, from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Conveys removal or decrease.

~Abnehmen~ means "to take off/away, to decrease, to lose weight, to accept (a delivery), to answer (the phone)." The weight-loss sense (where pounds are "taken off") is the most common in everyday speech. The PIE root *~nem-~ is fascinating for its dual nature: it meant both "to give" and "to take" one's allotted portion, reflecting an ancient concept where distribution and reception were two sides of the same act. This root also gave Greek ~némein~ ("to distribute"), the source of ~Nemesis~, the goddess who deals out what is due. The phone sense (~den Hörer abnehmen~, "to lift the receiver") preserves the most literal meaning: physically taking the handset ~off~ its cradle. Cognate with Dutch ~afnemen~.
en.abneigen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~neigen~:

• ~neigen~: A merger of MHG ~nīgen~ (intransitive, strong) and ~neigen~ (transitive, weak), from OHG ~nīgan~ and ~neigen~, from Proto-Germanic *~hnīganą~ ("to bow, bend") and its causative *~hnaigijaną~, from PIE *~kneygʷʰ-~ ("to bend, droop"). The strong forms vanished by the 16th century: a once-strong verb that went entirely weak. Cognate with Old English ~hnīgan~, Old Norse ~hnīga~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The compound is met today almost only in its participle ~abgeneigt~ "disinclined," so a bodily tilting-away has ended up naming a state of mind, with the physical verb surviving mainly in technical description.
en.abnutzen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~nutzen~:

• ~nutzen~: From MHG ~nutzen~, ~nützen~, from OHG ~nuzzōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~nutōną~, from *~nutō~ ("use"), from *~nutiz~ ("useful"), from *~neutaną~ ("to enjoy, use"), from PIE *~newd-~ ("to acquire, make use of"). ~nützen~ is now a chiefly southern conjugation, ~nutzen~ the standard one.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

What ~abnutzen~ wears away is less the substance of a thing than its usefulness: the same ~nutz-~ stem gives the noun ~Nutzen~ ("benefit"), so the compound is literally to use something until its use is gone. It is most often reflexive: ~die Reifen nutzen sich ab~.
en.abordnen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~ordnen~:

• ~ordnen~: From MHG ~ordenen~, from OHG ~ordinōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ordinōn~ ("to put in order"), borrowed from Latin ~ōrdināre~ ("to arrange"), from ~ōrdō~ ("row, rank, order"), from Proto-Italic *~ordō~, probably from PIE *~h₂er-~ ("to fit together"). Doublet of ~ordinieren~. Cognate with English ~order~, Italian ~ordinare~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The participle of this verb became an ordinary German noun: an ~Abgeordneter~, a member of the Bundestag, is literally "one who has been ordered off", sent away from a body to act on its behalf. The bureaucratic ~abordnen~ still means exactly that, a temporary secondment rather than a permanent transfer.
en.abpassen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~passen~:

• ~passen~: Borrowed from French ~passer~, with Dutch ~passen~ as intermediary, from Old French ~passer~, from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, a denominative of Latin ~passus~ ("step, pace"), from ~pandō~ ("to spread"), from PIE *~pet-~ ("to spread, extend"). A false friend: ~passen~ most often means "to fit, to suit," not "to pass by." Cognate with English ~pass~ and ~pace~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

~Passen~ here keeps its older sense of waiting and watching rather than the modern "to fit," so ~abpassen~ is to let an interval run out until the right moment arrives and then seize it, ~den richtigen Augenblick abpassen~, or, of a person, to waylay them.
en.abpfeifen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~pfeifen~:

• ~pfeifen~: From MHG ~pfīfen~, from OHG ~pfīfōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pīpōn~ ("to play a pipe, to whistle"), an early borrowing from Vulgar Latin *~pīpāre~ ("to chirp, peep"), a word of imitative origin. Originally weak, now a class I strong verb (~pfeifen~, ~pfiff~, ~gepfiffen~). Cognate with English ~pipe~ and ~peep~, French ~piper~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

This is the referee's verb, and its noun ~Abpfiff~ is the final whistle. Note that the compound conjugates strong (~pfiff ab~, ~abgepfiffen~) even though ~pfeifen~ itself began as a weak verb: the compound inherited a strength its Latin-borrowed ancestor did not originally have.
en.abprüfen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~prüfen~:

• ~prüfen~: From MHG ~prüeven~, ultimately from Latin ~probāre~ ("to test, approve, prove"), a denominative of ~probus~ ("good, honest, upright"), from Proto-Italic *~proβwos~, from PIE *~pro-bʰuH-wó-s~ ("being foremost"), from *~pro-~ + *~bʰuH-~ ("to be"). It came via Middle Dutch or Middle Low German, which explains the umlaut. Cognate with English ~prove~, ~probe~, French ~prouver~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

Where plain ~prüfen~ simply tests, ~abprüfen~ implies working down a list until every point on it has been examined. The exhaustiveness is the prefix's contribution, not the root's.
en.abraten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~raten~:

• ~raten~: From MHG ~rāten~, from OHG ~rātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rēdaną~ ("to decide, advise, interpret"), from PIE *~Hreh₁dh-~ ("to think, arrange"). Both senses, "to advise" and "to guess," descend from that sense of deliberation. Cognate with English ~read~ (originally "to counsel, interpret"), archaic ~rede~, Dutch ~raden~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Abraten~ is the mirror image of ~raten~: one advises a person away from a course, the person standing in the dative and the matter in ~von~. Of the root's two inherited senses, "to advise" and "to guess," the compound takes only the first.
en.abrechnen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~rechnen~:

• ~rechnen~: From MHG ~rechenen~, from OHG ~rehhanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rekanōn~ ("to count, explain"), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to make straight or right"), the same root as German ~recht~ and Latin ~rectus~. Cognate with English ~reckon~, Dutch ~rekenen~, Low German ~rekenen~, Danish ~regne~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The reckoning is carried through to its close, which is why ~Abrechnung~ names both the final bill and, figuratively, a settling of scores: ~mit jemandem abrechnen~ is to square accounts in a distinctly unfriendly sense.
en.abregen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~regen~:

• ~regen~: From MHG ~regen~ ("to make protrude, to erect, to excite, to move"), from Proto-Germanic *~hragjaną~ ("to make stand, wake up, incite"); synchronically the causative of MHG ~ragen~ ("to project, to tower"). The verb means "to stir, move, rouse", unrelated to the noun ~Regen~ ("rain"), and is most often reflexive (~sich regen~).
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

Used only reflexively, ~sich abregen~ is the exact counterpart of ~sich aufregen~: where ~auf-~ winds the agitation up, ~ab-~ winds it back down. As the root entry notes, the verb has nothing to do with the noun ~Regen~ ("rain"), a coincidence of spelling that catches out most learners.
en.abreiben:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~reiben~:

• ~reiben~: From MHG ~rīben~, from OHG ~rīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrībaną~ ("to rub"); beyond Germanic uncertain, a PIE *~wreyp-~, labial extension of *~wer-~ ("to turn"), being proposed but not secure. A class I strong verb (~reiben~, ~rieb~, ~gerieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~wrijven~, Old Saxon ~wrīvan~; German dropped the initial ~w-~ before ~r~, as in ~ringen~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The compound is plain abrasion, and its derivatives keep that concreteness: ~Abrieb~ is the material worn away by friction, while ~eine Abreibung~ has drifted from a brisk rubdown to a thrashing.
en.abreisen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Given the root's military origin, ~abreisen~ is almost tautologically "to set out away." It describes the departure itself, not the journey: one ~reist ab~ from a place at a particular hour, whereas ~verreisen~ describes being away as a state.
en.abreißen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The compound reaches from a torn-off button to a demolished building (~ein Haus abreißen~), and intransitively it means simply to cease; ~der Kontakt riss ab~. The participle ~abgerissen~ has additionally hardened into an adjective meaning "ragged, shabby," said of clothes and of the people in them.
en.abrichten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~ ("to straighten, set right, direct"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rihtijaną~, a denominative from the adjective *~rehtaz~ ("straight, right"), from PIE *~h₃reǵtós~ ("right, straightened"), from *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to stretch out, straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~richten~, Gothic ~raihtjan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The oldest use is the joiner's: to ~abrichten~ a board is to plane it true. Applied to animals, it means bringing a creature to a prescribed standard, which is why using it of a person is contemptuous, as Nietzsche does in the sentence below.
en.abringen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~ringen~:

• ~ringen~: From MHG ~ringen~, from OHG ~ringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wringaną~ ("to twist, wring"), from a nasalized form of PIE *~wergʰ-~ ("to turn, twist"). A class III strong verb (~ringen~, ~rang~, ~gerungen~). Despite appearances it has nothing to do with ~Ring~. Cognate with English ~wring~, ~wrong~ (originally "twisted"), Dutch ~wringen~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix names the source or support the action proceeds from: drawing something out of someone, or hanging from something.

The construction makes the source explicit: ~jemandem ein Versprechen abringen~ is to wring a promise out of someone, the person in the dative. And despite the modern spelling, the wringing is literal: the root is English ~wring~, not ~Ring~.
en.abrinnen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~rinnen~:

• ~rinnen~: From MHG ~rinnen~, from OHG ~rinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~ ("to run, flow"); the PIE source is debated, most often given as *~h₃reyH-~ ("to churn, set in motion"). A class III strong verb (~rinnen~, ~rann~, ~geronnen~). German ~rennen~ is its causative, from *~rannijaną~. Cognate with English ~run~, Gothic ~rinnan~, Swedish ~rinna~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

~Abrinnen~ is the chiefly literary and southern relative of everyday ~ablaufen~: water running down off a roof, tears down a face. Its causative twin ~rennen~ took the same root in the opposite direction, from flowing to running.
en.abrollen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~rollen~:

• ~rollen~: From MHG ~rollen~, borrowed from Old French ~roeler~, from Medieval Latin ~rotulāre~ ("to roll"), from Latin ~rotula~ ("small wheel"), diminutive of ~rota~ ("wheel"), from PIE *~ret-~ ("to run, to roll"). Cognate with English ~roll~ (also borrowed from Old French), Dutch ~rollen~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The everyday sense is unwinding something from a spool (a cable, a carpet, a bandage) with the roll itself giving up its material. Figuratively a planned sequence ~rollt ab~, running its course as smoothly as a wheel.
en.abrufen:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~. Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~ ("to call"). The origin of *~hrōpaną~ is uncertain; one theory connects it to *~hrōþiz~ ("glory, fame"), the first element of names like Rudolf.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)~, from OHG ~ab(a)~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). The prefix adds a sense of retrieval or completion.

~Abrufen~ means "to call off, to recall" and, in modern usage, "to retrieve (data)." The computational sense ("to call away from storage") has made this once-ordinary compound a staple of the digital age. German speakers ~rufen Daten ab~ ("retrieve data") and ~rufen E-Mails ab~ ("check email"). The journey from a Proto-Germanic shout (*~hrōpaną~) to silently polling a server is a striking example of semantic adaptation.
en.abrunden:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~runden~:

• ~runden~: From ~rund~ + ~-en~. ~Rund~ descends from MHG ~runt~, borrowed from Old French ~ront~, from Latin ~rotundus~ ("round"), from ~rota~ ("wheel, disk"), from PIE *~Hróth₂o~ (from *~ret-~ "to run, to roll"), one of the few everyday German adjectives that arrived via Latin and French rather than directly from Proto-Germanic. English ~round~ took the same detour.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Roundness is achieved by taking the corners off, and the arithmetic sense keeps that direction: ~abrunden~ rounds a number down, ~aufrunden~ rounds it up. Figuratively the same removal of rough edges gives "to round off, to complete"; ~ein abgerundetes Bild~.
en.abrutschen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~rutschen~:

• ~rutschen~: From MHG ~rutzen~, ~rützen~, an onomatopoeic formation imitating the sound of sliding, with a later shift from ~-tz-~ to ~-tsch-~ (as in ~fletschen~); perhaps related to OHG ~rūtezzen~. The noun ~Rutsche~ ("slide, chute") derives from the verb. English ~rutch~ and ~rutsch~ are borrowed from German or its Low German cognates.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

The prefix supplies the downward direction the onomatopoeic root lacks: a foot slips off a rung, a car off an embankment. The figurative use runs the same way; grades, standards, and moods all ~rutschen ab~.
en.abräumen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~räumen~:

• ~räumen~: From Early New High German ~reumen~, a Central German umlaut variant of ~raumen~, from MHG ~rūmen~, from OHG ~rūmen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rūmijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rūmijaną~, a factitive verb from the adjective *~rūmaz~ ("roomy, spacious"), from PIE *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open"). Etymologically, "to make room." Cognate with English ~room~, the noun ~Raum~, Bavarian ~rama~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Since ~räumen~ is etymologically "to make room," ~abräumen~ makes room by taking things off a surface, a table after a meal, a building site. Colloquially it has also come to mean winning everything on offer, as though sweeping the board clear.
en.abrücken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~rücken~:

• ~rücken~: From MHG ~rücken~, from OHG ~rucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rukkijan~. The verb means "to move, to shift" and is the base of ~verrückt~ ("crazy," literally "shifted, displaced"); the noun ~Rücken~ ("back") is etymologically a separate word. Cognate with English ~rock~, Old Norse ~rykkja~, Old English ~roccian~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Both the literal and the figurative reading are alive: a chair is ~abgerückt~ from the wall, and a politician ~rückt von einer Aussage ab~, distancing himself from something he said. The root's most famous descendant is ~verrückt~, literally "shifted out of place."
en.absagen:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~ab-~: From PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). As a separable prefix, it means "off, away, down."

~Absagen~ means "to cancel, to call off, to decline", literally "to say off," speaking an event or invitation away from existence. The construction works in two directions: one can ~eine Veranstaltung absagen~ ("cancel an event") or ~jemandem absagen~ ("decline someone's invitation"). The pair ~zusagen~/~absagen~ ("to accept"/"to decline") forms a neat antonym based on directional prefixes: ~zu~ ("toward") versus ~ab~ ("away").
en.absaufen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~saufen~:

• ~saufen~: From MHG ~sūfen~ ("to sip, drink"), from OHG ~sūfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sūpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sūpaną~, from PIE *~sewp-~, a labial extension of *~sew-~ ("to take liquid, slurp"). A class II strong verb (~saufen~, ~soff~, ~gesoffen~). The drift from "to sip" to today's "to booze" dates only to the sixteenth century. Cognate with English ~sup~, Dutch ~zuipen~, Old Norse ~súpa~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

The compound inherits the root's coarse register: ~saufen~ is drinking as animals do, so ~absaufen~ is the undignified way to sink or drown. It is also what a flooded engine does, and the transitive counterpart ~absäufen~ is what a miner's water does to a shaft.
en.absaugen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~saugen~:

• ~saugen~: From MHG ~sūgen~, from OHG ~sūgan~ ("to suck"), from Proto-West Germanic *~sūgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sūganą~, from PIE *~sewk-~ ("to suck"). Historically a class II strong verb (~saugen~, ~sog~, ~gesogen~), it now inflects weak (~saugte~, ~gesaugt~) just as readily. Cognate with English ~suck~, Dutch ~zuigen~, Danish ~suge~, Old English ~sūcan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

This is the verb of the vacuum cleaner (the ~Staubsauger~ literally a "dust-sucker"), and of the surgeon's suction tube. As with the simplex, the strong forms (~sog ab~, ~abgesogen~) survive beside the weak ones, and the weak are winning.
en.abschaffen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schaffen~:

• ~schaffen~: Two historically distinct verbs have merged under a single infinitive, distinguished only by their conjugation. The strong ~schaffen~ (~schuf~, ~geschaffen~, "to create") descends from MHG ~schaffen~, OHG ~scaffan~, a byform of ~skephen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skappjan~; the ~-f-~ was chiefly back-formed from the participle ~giscaffan~. The weak ~schaffen~ (~schaffte~, ~geschafft~, "to manage, accomplish") descends from OHG ~skaffōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skapōn~, from the same root. Cognate with Dutch ~scheppen~, English ~shape~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Of the two verbs that fell together as ~schaffen~, this compound descends from the weak one (~schaffte ab~, ~abgeschafft~, from OHG ~skaffōn~ "to manage, arrange"), and not from the strong verb of creation. That is fitting: abolishing a law is an administrative act, not the undoing of a creation.
en.abschalten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schalten~:

• ~schalten~: From MHG ~schalten~, from OHG ~scaltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaldan~ ("to push, shove"); the further etymology is debated, Pokorny deriving it from PIE *~(s)kelH-~ ("to split, separate"), which would relate it to English ~shell~. The physical sense of shoving a lever became the modern "to switch, shift gears, manage." Cognate with Old Saxon ~skaldan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The root's original shoving of a lever is still visible in the gesture: one throws a switch and the current stops. The figurative use is of the mind rather than the machine; ~ich schalte abends einfach ab~, "in the evening I simply switch off."
en.abschauen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys copying from a model: reproducing something by taking it off an original.

The construction names the model in the dative: ~jemandem etwas abschauen~ is to pick something up by watching them do it. Because the root is southern, so is the compound; northern German says ~abgucken~ for the same act, and both carry a faint whiff of copying in school.
en.abscheiden:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~scheiden~:

• ~scheiden~: From MHG ~scheiden~, from OHG ~sceidan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaiþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaiþaną~, from PIE *~skeyt-~ ("to cut, separate"). Cognate with English ~shed~ (originally "to separate"), Dutch ~scheiden~, West Frisian ~skiede~, and Greek ~skhizein~ ("to split," source of ~schism~).
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Modern German keeps two distant descendants of one image: chemistry has a substance ~abscheiden~ out of a solution, while the older sense "to be parted from the living" survives in ~der Abgeschiedene~, the departed.
en.abschicken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schicken~:

• ~schicken~: From MHG ~schicken~ ("to outfit oneself, fit in, arrange appropriately"), from OHG *~skihhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skikkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skikkijaną~ ("to order, send"), the causative of the verb underlying MHG ~geschehen~ ("to happen, rush"). The sense "to send" grew from "to make ready to go." Related to English ~chic~ (via French), ~geschickt~, and ~Schicksal~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Plain ~schicken~ says only that something is on its way; ~ab-~ fixes the point of departure, so ~abschicken~ is the moment the letter leaves the hand, which is why the writer is the ~Absender~, the one who sends it off, not merely the sender.
en.abschieben:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schieben~:

• ~schieben~: From MHG ~schieben~, from OHG ~skioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeubaną~, from PIE *~skewbʰ-~ ("to push, to shove, to thrust"). A class II strong verb (~schieben~, ~schob~, ~geschoben~). Cognate with English ~shove~, Dutch ~schuiven~, Danish ~skubbe~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Literally a shove away from oneself. Officialese narrowed it to deportation, while the figurative ~Verantwortung abschieben~, pushing responsibility onto someone else, preserves the older and wider image.
en.abschießen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb (~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~). Cognate with English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Old Norse ~skjóta~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Abschießen~ covers both ends of the shot: the projectile leaving the weapon and the target brought down by it, so the ~ab-~ migrates from the bullet to whatever it hits. Figuratively one looses off a remark the same way.
en.abschinden:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schinden~:

• ~schinden~: From MHG ~schinden~ ("to flay, peel; torment"), from OHG ~skinten~, a denominal verb on Proto-Germanic *~skinþą~ ("hide, peel"), from PIE *~(s)ken-~ ("to split off"), a nasal extension of *~sek-~ ("to cut"). Originally weak, it took on strong inflection in Middle High German by analogy with ~binden~ and ~finden~, and now runs as a class III strong verb (~schinden~, ~schund~, ~geschunden~). Cognate with Old Norse ~skinn~, English ~skin~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Because the root already means stripping off the hide, ~ab-~ only makes the removal explicit. The everyday survivor is reflexive: ~sich abschinden~, to work oneself raw.
en.abschlagen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Beside the blow that takes something off, ~abschlagen~ carries the everyday sense "to refuse": a request is struck away rather than taken up. Both readings are still live, which is why a head and a favour can equally be ~abgeschlagen~.
en.abschleifen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schleifen~:

• ~schleifen~: Two verbs share this spelling. The strong ~schleifen~ ("to grind, whet, polish") is from MHG ~slīfen~, OHG ~slīfan~, Proto-West Germanic *~slīpan~, Proto-Germanic *~slīpaną~ ("to slide, to whet"): class I, ~schleifen~, ~schliff~, ~geschliffen~, cognate with English ~slip~, Dutch ~slijpen~. The weak ~schleifen~ ("to drag; to raze a fortress") is from MHG ~sleifen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slaipijan~ ("to cause to slide"), the causative of the first, and inflects ~schleifte~, ~geschleift~; a doublet of ~schleppen~, cognate with Dutch ~slepen~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The parent here is the strong ~schleifen~ "to grind, whet," not its weak twin "to drag, to raze"; the reading is strong, and the sense is abrasive. ~Abschleifen~ takes material off a surface and, figuratively, wears the edges off a manner or a dialect.
en.abschließen:
From Middle High German ~abeslieȥen~, equivalent to ~ab-~ + ~schließen~. Compound of ~ab-~ + ~schließen~:

• ~schließen~: From MHG ~slieȥen~, from OHG ~sliozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sleutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slūtaną~, *~sleutaną~ ("to lock, shut"). A class II strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~schließen~, ~schloss~, ~geschlossen~.
• ~ab-~: From OHG ~ab-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab-~, from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). As a separable prefix, ~ab-~ adds a sense of removal, completion, or finality: "locking away" or "closing off."

The compound covers a remarkable semantic range: "to lock" (a door), "to conclude" (a contract), "to complete" (a project), and "to infer" (a logical conclusion), all unified by the metaphor of bringing something to a close or fastening it shut. The last sense (~daraus schließen~, "to conclude from that") shows how physical bolt-sliding became abstract reasoning. Cognate with Dutch ~afsluiten~.
en.abschmecken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schmecken~:

• ~schmecken~: From MHG ~smecken~, from OHG ~smecchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smakkijan~ ("to taste"), from *~smakku~ ("a taste"). In southern and Austrian German ~schmecken~ also means "to smell." Cognate with English ~smack~ (as in "it smacks of"), Dutch ~smaken~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

~Abschmecken~ is not tasting for pleasure but tasting toward an end: the cook samples and seasons until nothing further is wanted, and the dish is finished.
en.abschneiden:
From Middle High German ~abesnīden~. Compound of ~ab-~ + ~schneiden~:

• ~schneiden~: From MHG ~snīden~, from OHG ~snīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~snīþan~ ("to cut"), from Proto-Germanic *~snīþaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sneyt-~ ("to cut"). Cognate with English dialectal ~snithe~ ("to cut"), Swedish ~snida~ ("to carve"), Icelandic ~sníða~ ("to trim").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). This prefix adds a sense of removal or separation to the base verb.

The root is related to English ~snide~, which originally meant "cutting" in a literal sense before acquiring its modern figurative meaning of "derisively critical." Dutch ~snijden~ ("to cut, carve, intersect") is a close cognate. The compound ~abschneiden~ literally means "to cut off" but has developed the idiomatic sense of "to perform" or "to do" (as in ~gut abschneiden~, "to do well"), a semantic leap from the concrete act of cutting to an abstract assessment of results.
en.abschreiben:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys copying from a model: reproducing something by taking it off an original.

One verb serves the schoolroom and the ledger: ~abschreiben~ is copying from a model, and in accounting it is writing an asset down to nothing. A person given up on is ~abgeschrieben~.
en.abschreiten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schreiten~:

• ~schreiten~: From MHG ~schrīten~, from OHG ~skrītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīþan~ ("to step, stride"), from Proto-Germanic *~skrīþaną~ ("to walk, glide, crawl"), from PIE *~(s)kreyt-~ ("to stride"), an extension of *~(s)krey-~ ("to go about"). Cognate with Lithuanian ~skrìsti~ ("to rush, run"), Latvian ~skrìet~ ("to run, fly"). Related to ~Schritt~ ("step").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

~Abschreiten~ measures ground with the body: one covers a stretch from end to end, whether to judge its length or, on parade, to review a line of troops.
en.abschwellen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schwellen~:

• ~schwellen~: From MHG ~swëllen~, from OHG ~swëllan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swellaną~ ("to swell"), perhaps from PIE *~swelH-~, though the root is not securely established. A class III strong verb (~schwellen~, ~schwoll~, ~geschwollen~), beside a weak causative ~schwellen~ ("to make swell") from Proto-Germanic *~swallijaną~. Cognate with English ~swell~, Dutch ~zwellen~, Old Norse ~svella~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

It is the strong intransitive ~schwellen~ that takes ~ab-~, not its weak causative: a swelling goes down of its own accord, and the prefix reads as reduction rather than removal. A noise ~abschwillt~ in exactly the same way.
en.abschwören:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schwören~:

• ~schwören~: From MHG ~swern~, from OHG ~swerien~, from Proto-West Germanic *~swarjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swarjaną~, from PIE *~swer-~ ("to speak, to talk"). A class VI strong verb (~schwören~, ~schwor~, ~geschworen~); the older Präteritum ~schwur~ is now archaic. Cognate with English ~swear~, Dutch ~zweren~, Danish ~sværge~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

To ~abschwören~ is to turn an oath against an earlier commitment: the swearing does not bind but severs. English ~forswear~ and ~abjure~ (Latin ~ab-~ + ~iurare~) build the identical compound out of identical parts.
en.abschätzen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schätzen~:

• ~schätzen~: A denominal verb from ~Schatz~ ("treasure"), from MHG ~schaz~, OHG ~scaz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skatt~ ("cattle, treasure"), an early Germanic word in which cattle served as a measure of wealth. Cognate with Old Norse ~skattr~ (whence Danish ~skat~ and Swedish ~skatt~, both "tax"), Gothic ~skatts~, Old English ~sċeatt~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys derivation: leading something away from, or tracing it back to, a source.

To ~abschätzen~ is to take a value off the thing itself, reading the estimate from the evidence in front of you. The appraiser's stance turns sour in the adjective ~abschätzig~, "disparaging", a valuation that has already decided the answer is low.
en.abschütteln:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~schütteln~:

• ~schütteln~: From MHG ~schütelen~, from OHG ~scutilōn~, an iterative formation from ~schütten~ ("to pour, to shake") marking repeated back-and-forth motion. ~schütten~ derives from OHG ~scuttēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skudjaną~, perhaps from PIE *~(s)kewt-~ ("to shake, jolt"). Cognate with Dutch ~schudden~ ("to shake").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The shaking is the means and ~ab-~ the result: what is shaken must come off, dust, snow, or a pursuer.
en.absehen:
~Ab-~ + ~sehen~. Compound of ~ab-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~ ("to see"), from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice").
• ~ab-~: From PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). The prefix adds the sense of looking away, looking off (from something), or discerning from a distance.

~Absehen~ means "to foresee, to look away from, to refrain from", a verb whose meanings seem to pull in different directions but share the logic of directed visual attention. ~Es ist abzusehen~ ("it is foreseeable") uses the prefix in its "seeing from a distance" sense. ~Von etwas absehen~ ("to refrain from, to disregard") uses it in the "looking away from" sense; one averts one's gaze and therefore one's intention. The derived noun ~Absicht~ ("intention, purpose") crystallizes the "aiming one's gaze" metaphor: an ~Absicht~ is literally where you direct your sight, hence your aim, your plan. The participial adjective ~absehbar~ ("foreseeable") is a mainstay of German political and economic discourse: ~in absehbarer Zeit~ ("in the foreseeable future"). Cognate with Dutch ~afzien~ ("to refrain from; to be able to see from a distance"), which preserves the same dual-meaning structure.
en.absenden:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~senden~:

• ~senden~: From MHG ~senden~, from OHG ~senten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sandijaną~, from PIE *~sont-eye-~, a causative of *~sent-~ ("to walk, travel"), originally "to cause to go." It has a double Präteritum: ~sendete~ for broadcasting, ~sandte~ (a Rückumlaut form) for sending a letter. Cognate with English ~send~, Dutch ~zenden~, Gothic ~sandjan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Absenden~ is the formal counterpart of ~abschicken~, at home on forms and in postal language, and it inherits the root's double Präteritum: ~absandte~ beside ~absendete~.
en.absenken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~senken~:

• ~senken~: From OHG ~senken~, from Proto-Germanic *~sankwijaną~, a causative of *~sinkwaną~ ("to sink"), from PIE *~sengʷ-~ ("to sink, to fall"). ~senken~ is thus the causative partner of ~sinken~: "to cause to sink." The vowel alternation reflects the causative *~-jan-~ suffix, which triggered umlaut. Cognate with Gothic ~sagqjan~, Old Norse ~søkkva~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

~Senken~ already lowers; ~ab-~ supplies the endpoint, so ~absenken~ is a controlled reduction to a target level: of a road bed, a temperature, or a budget line.
en.absetzen:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place"), the causative of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit"), from PIE *~sed-~ ("to sit"). Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)~, from OHG ~ab(a)~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). As a separable prefix, it conveys removal, departure, or setting down.

~Absetzen~ means "to set down, to remove, to depose, to deduct", an extraordinarily versatile verb. One can ~die Brille absetzen~ ("to take off one's glasses"), ~einen König absetzen~ ("to depose a king"), ~Kosten absetzen~ ("to deduct expenses" from taxes), ~ein Medikament absetzen~ ("to discontinue a medication"), or ~ein Theaterstück absetzen~ ("to cancel a play from the repertoire"). The PIE root *~sed-~ ("to sit") is one of the most prolific in Indo-European, producing Latin ~sedēre~ ("to sit"), whence English ~sediment~, ~session~, ~president~ ("one who sits before"), ~reside~, and ~siege~ (via Old French, from Vulgar Latin *~sedicāre~). The causative relationship between ~sitzen~ ("to sit") and ~setzen~ ("to set, to cause to sit") perfectly mirrors that between English ~sit~ and ~set~.
en.absichern:
From ~ab-~ + ~sichern~. Compound of a Germanic prefix and a Latin-derived verb:

• ~sichern~: Derived from the adjective ~sicher~, from MHG ~siher~, from OHG ~sihur~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sikur~ ("secure, sure"), borrowed from Latin ~sēcūrus~ ("free from care, safe"), itself from ~sē-~ ("without") + ~cūra~ ("care, concern").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Here the prefix conveys completeness or thoroughness rather than removal.

The word ~sicher~ is one of German's earliest Latin loanwords, entering Germanic speech during the Roman period when Germanic tribes had extensive contact with the Roman Empire along the ~limes~. Latin ~sēcūrus~ is also the source of English ~secure~ and ~sure~ (the latter via Old French). The prefix ~ab-~ in ~absichern~ intensifies the meaning beyond simple ~sichern~ ("to secure") to suggest a more thorough safeguarding or hedging against risk.
en.absinken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~sinken~:

• ~sinken~: From MHG ~sinken~, from OHG ~sinkan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sinkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sinkwaną~, from PIE *~sengʷ-~ ("to sink, to drop"). A class III strong verb (~sinken~, ~sank~, ~gesunken~); the weak causative ~senken~ is its transitive partner. Cognate with English ~sink~, Dutch ~zinken~, Danish ~synke~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.
