The compound pair mirrors the root pair exactly: ~absinken~ is what a thing does by itself, ~absenken~ what someone does to it. In modern use the sinking is usually figurative: a level, a standard, a ranking slipping.
en.absolvieren:
From Latin ~absolvēre~ ("to set free, to complete, to finish"), composed of ~ab-~ ("from, away from"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"), + ~solvō~ ("to release, loosen, dissolve"), which is itself from ~sē-~ ("apart, aside, away"), from PIE *~s(w)ēd~ (ablative of *~swé~, "self"), + ~luō~ ("to untie, set free"), from PIE *~lewh₃-~ ("to wash, to loosen"). The German suffix ~-ieren~ marks the standard adaptation of Latin verbs.

The Latin original meant "to loosen from, to release, to acquit", hence its theological use: a priest ~absolviert~ a penitent from sin (gives ~Absolution~). But German has developed a second, thoroughly secular meaning: "to complete, to pass" (~eine Prüfung absolvieren~, "to pass an exam"; ~sein Studium absolvieren~, "to finish one's degree"; ~ein Training absolvieren~, "to complete a training course"). This semantic shift from "releasing from obligation" to "completing an obligation" is almost paradoxical, yet both senses share the notion of bringing a process to its end. The derived nouns ~Absolvent~ (male graduate) and ~Absolventin~ (female graduate) are specific to the completionist meaning.
en.abspeisen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~speisen~:

• ~speisen~: From MHG ~spīsen~ ("to feed"), a denominative verb from MHG ~spīse~ ("food"), from Medieval Latin ~spēsa~, from Latin ~expēnsa~ ("money paid out"), from ~expendere~ ("to weigh out, pay out"). A weak verb throughout its history. Cognate with Dutch ~spijzen~; the same Latin source gave English ~expense~ and ~spend~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The literal act (feeding someone and thereby ending the meal) turned into a brush-off: to ~abspeisen~ a person is to serve up just enough to send them away, English "to fob off."
en.absperren:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~sperren~:

• ~sperren~: From MHG ~sperren~, from OHG ~sperran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sparrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sparrijaną~ ("to bar, to block"), a denominative verb from *~sparrô~ ("wooden beam, log"), originally to bar a passage with a beam. Cognate with English ~spar~ ("to bolt, bar"; the noun for a wooden beam), Dutch ~sperren~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The root's beam is still visible in the modern act: ~absperren~ shuts a street or a valve off from whatever lies beyond it. Austrian and Bavarian usage keeps the plainer sense of locking a door.
en.abspielen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

To ~abspielen~ a recording is to let it run through to its end; reflexively, ~sich abspielen~ says the same of an event, which simply runs its course in front of onlookers.
en.absprechen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~sprechen~:

• ~sprechen~: From MHG ~sprëchen~, from OHG ~sprëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sprekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sprekaną~, probably from PIE *~spregʰ-~ ("to crackle"). The sense developed from an onomatopoeic root meaning "to crackle, make noise" to "to speak." Cognate with Dutch ~spreken~, English ~speak~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

Two senses live side by side. Reflexive ~sich absprechen~ is talking a matter through until it is settled, while ~jemandem etwas absprechen~ takes the separative reading of ~ab-~ instead and denies a person some quality outright.
en.abspringen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~springen~:

• ~springen~: From OHG ~springan~, from Proto-Germanic *~springaną~, from PIE *~sprenǵʰ-~, a nasalized form of *~sperǵʰ-~ ("to move energetically, to hasten, to spring"). A class III strong verb (~springen~, ~sprang~, ~gesprungen~). Cognate with English ~spring~, Dutch ~springen~, Danish ~springe~, Greek ~spérkhō~ ("to hasten").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The jump is literal for a parachutist and figurative for a customer who backs out; said of paint or plaster, ~abspringen~ is simply flaking off.
en.abstammen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~stammen~:

• ~stammen~: A denominative verb from ~Stamm~ ("trunk, stem, tribe, stock") with the suffix ~-en~. ~Stamm~ derives from MHG ~stam~, OHG ~stam~, Proto-Germanic *~stamnaz~, *~stamniz~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand, stay"). Cognate with English ~stem~, Dutch ~stam~, Danish ~stamme~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys derivation: leading something away from, or tracing it back to, a source.

~Abstammen~ makes the tree-image grammatical: a family, a word, or a species is traced back down the ~Stamm~ to its source, and the noun ~Abstammung~ serves genealogy and etymology alike.
en.abstechen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~stechen~:

• ~stechen~: From MHG ~stëchen~, from OHG ~stëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stekaną~ ("to stab, prick"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to stick, poke"). Cognate with Dutch ~steken~ ("to stab, sting"), Old Norse ~stinga~, English ~stick~ (originally "to stab, pierce").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The stab performs the separation: peat, turf, or an animal is cut away with a blade. The commonest modern use is the other one: ~gegen etwas abstechen~, to stand out sharply against a background, where the contrast cuts as the knife once did.
en.abstecken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~stecken~:

• ~stecken~: Modern ~stecken~ merges two verbs: the transitive weak one ("to put, stick something in") from MHG ~stecken~, OHG ~steckōn~, a geminate derivative of ~stëhhan~ (the ancestor of ~stechen~), and the strong intransitive one (archaic ~stak~/~gestocken~, "to be stuck"); the two fused in Early Modern German. Both trace to Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stikaną~, from PIE *~(s)teyg-~ ("to be sharp, stab, goad"). Cognate with English ~stick~ and ~steak~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Abstecken~ descends from the root's weak transitive branch, and surveyor and dressmaker do the same thing with it: one marks a boundary with stakes, the other pins a hem to length. In each case ~ab-~ sets the limit that divides inside from out.
en.abstehen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The subject holds a distance instead of closing it: ears ~stehen~ ~ab~ from the head. The older legal use (~von etwas abstehen~, to desist from a claim) is the same standing-away, applied to an intention rather than a body.
en.absteigen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

The compound means literally "to climb down", and it keeps that sense for dismounting a horse or descending a mountain; two idioms grew out of it: putting up at a hotel, where the traveller once climbed down from the coach, and being relegated to a lower league.
en.abstellen:
From Middle High German ~abestellen~. Compound of ~ab-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from Proto-Indo-European *~stel-~ ("to place, put, stand").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Here the prefix conveys cessation or deactivation.

The PIE root *~stel-~ is extraordinarily productive: it yielded not only German ~stellen~ but also English ~stall~, ~still~, ~install~, and Greek ~stēlē~ (an upright stone slab). The compound ~abstellen~ has developed two distinct semantic branches: a concrete sense of "to put down, to park" (as in parking a vehicle) and an abstract sense of "to turn off, to stop" (as in stopping an engine or eliminating an abuse). Both senses derive logically from the idea of placing something away from its active state.
en.absterben:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~sterben~:

• ~sterben~: From MHG ~stërben~, from OHG ~stërban~, from Proto-Germanic *~sterbaną~, from PIE *~(s)terp-~ ("to lose force, become numb") or *~sterbʰ-~ ("to become stiff"), both traceable to *~ster-~ ("stiff, rigid"). A class III strong verb (~stirbt~, ~starb~, ~gestorben~). Cognate with English ~starve~, Dutch ~sterven~, West Frisian ~stjerre~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The terminative prefix turns ~sterben~ into a gradual dying-off: German uses ~absterben~ of tissue, of limbs going numb, and of branches on a tree, while a person simply ~stirbt~.
en.abstimmen:
From ~ab-~ + ~stimmen~. Compound of:

• ~stimmen~: From MHG ~stimmen~, from OHG *~stimmen~ (attested in the compound ~gistimmen~), a denominative verb from ~Stimme~ ("voice, vote"). ~Stimme~ descends from MHG ~stimme~, from OHG ~stimma~ or ~stimna~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stebnu~, from Proto-Germanic *~stebnō~, from PIE *~stomen-~ ("mouth, muzzle"). Cognate with English ~steven~ (archaic "voice"), Old English ~stefn~, and Ancient Greek ~stóma~ ("mouth").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~, from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). As a verbal prefix, it often conveys removal, completion, or adjustment.

The two principal senses of ~abstimmen~ ("to vote" and "to coordinate, tune") both arise from the root meaning of ~Stimme~. The voting sense is literal: casting one's ~voice~ in a poll. The coordination sense derives from the musical meaning of ~stimmen~ ("to tune an instrument"), bringing multiple voices or elements into harmony. The prefix ~ab-~ here suggests finality or settlement, as in reaching a settled result. The connection between ~Stimme~ ("voice") and Ancient Greek ~stóma~ ("mouth") reveals an ancient conceptual link between the organ that produces sound and the sound itself. Modern German ~Abstimmung~ can mean either "vote" or "coordination" depending on context, a homonymy that occasionally produces amusing ambiguities.
en.abstoßen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). Cognate with dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce, ricochet"), Dutch ~stoten~, Old Norse ~stauta~ and ~steyta~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Literally "to push away": a boat shoves off from the bank, like charges repel one another, and figuratively a person repels us; commercially it also means to offload goods one no longer wants.
en.abstreichen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~streichen~:

• ~streichen~: From MHG ~strīchen~, from OHG ~strīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~strīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~strīkaną~ ("to stroke, to rub"), from PIE *~streyg-~ ("to stroke, rub, press"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with English ~strike~, Dutch ~strijken~ ("to iron, to stroke").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Literally "to stroke off", the compound covers wiping mud from one's boots and striking an amount off a bill, the same gesture applied once to a surface and once to a ledger.
en.abstreiten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~streiten~:

• ~streiten~: From MHG ~strīten~, from OHG ~strītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~strīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~strīdaną~, probably from Pre-Germanic *~streydʰh₁-~, a compound of PIE *~strey-~ ("to resist") + *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, place"). Cognate with English ~stride~, Dutch ~strijden~ ("to fight, struggle"), Low German ~striden~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The object of ~abstreiten~ is not the opponent but the claim: one fights an assertion away from the person making it, which is how a verb of combat came to mean "to deny".
en.abstürzen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~stürzen~:

• ~stürzen~: From MHG ~stürzen~, from OHG ~sturzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sturtijan~ ("to fall down, tumble"), of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly from PIE *~ster-~ ("to be stiff") via a dental extension *~sterd-~, though the derivation is debated. Cognate with English ~start~, a doublet from the same Proto-West Germanic source, from which the meanings have diverged radically.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

Literally "to plunge downward", said of aircraft and of climbers; the computing sense (a program crashing) is a twentieth-century metaphor taken straight from aviation.
en.abstützen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~stützen~:

• ~stützen~: Attested as a simplex verb only since the 17th century, probably a back-formation from the inherited compound ~unterstützen~ (MHG ~understüzzen~, OHG ~untarstuzzen~), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *~stuttijan~; related to Proto-Germanic *~stuþs~ ("post, prop"). Cognate with English ~stud~, Dutch ~stutten~, Norwegian ~støtte~, Swedish ~stötta~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

Here the downward orientation is the path of the load rather than any reduction: a wall that is ~abgestützt~ passes its weight down into whatever is braced beneath it.
en.absuchen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~suchen~:

• ~suchen~: From MHG ~suochen~, ~süechen~, from OHG ~suohhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sōkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sōkijaną~, from PIE *~seh₂g-~ ("to seek out"). The modern umlautless form reflects the Upper German dialect, which resisted umlaut of long rounded vowels before velars. Cognate with English ~seek~, Dutch ~zoeken~, Danish ~søge~, Gothic ~sōkjan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The completive prefix changes what the object is: one ~sucht~ for a thing but ~sucht~ the surface ~ab~, covering it end to end without a gap.
en.abtauchen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~tauchen~:

• ~tauchen~: From MHG ~tūchen~, ~touchen~, from OHG *~tūhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dūkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dūkaną~ ("to duck, to dive under"), whose further etymology is uncertain. A class II strong verb that became weak in the early modern period: when it was reintroduced from Central and Low German, the strong conjugation was regularized to weak. Cognate with Dutch ~duiken~, Swedish ~dyka~; a Low German consonant variant of the same root is ~ducken~, cognate with English ~duck~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

Literally "to dive down"; modern German uses it just as readily of a person who disappears from public view, going under not into water but into hiding.
en.abtauschen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~tauschen~:

• ~tauschen~: From MHG ~tiuschen~, derived from ~tūschen~, related to ~täuschen~ ("to deceive"), both of uncertain further origin. The sense ran from "to deceive" to "to trick someone into buying one's goods" to "to trade, exchange, barter"; ~tauschen~ lost the negative connotation along the way while ~täuschen~ retained it.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The separative prefix makes the exchange a removal: in chess ~abtauschen~ takes both pieces off the board, so the trade is defined by what leaves rather than by what is gained.
en.abteilen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~teilen~:

• ~teilen~: From MHG ~teilen~ and OHG ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~ ("to divide, part, deal"), from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, a denominative of *~dailiz~ ("part, share"), from PIE *~dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo-~, tentatively from *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, set, place"), though the precise PIE derivation is uncertain. Cognate with English ~deal~, Dutch ~delen~, Danish ~dele~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Where ~teilen~ divides a whole, ~abteilen~ marks one part off from the rest, the same partitioning that gave German the railway ~Abteil~ ("compartment") and the office ~Abteilung~ ("department").
en.abtippen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~tippen~:

• ~tippen~: From Low German, where the standard High German equivalent would have been ~tüpfen~ ("to dab, dot"). The word has two branches: in the sense "to type, to tap" it derives from the onomatopoeic imitation of light touching, while in the sense "to bet, to guess" (~Lotto tippen~) it comes from the noun ~Tipp~, borrowed from English ~tip~ ("a piece of advice, a hint").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys copying from a model: reproducing something by taking it off an original.

Of the root's two branches the compound takes the onomatopoeic one, tapping at keys, and not the wagering ~Tipp~ borrowed from English; the prefix supplies the copying, which is why ~abtippen~ is always transcription from an existing model.
en.abtragen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb whose semantic range broadened from "to drag, pull" to "to carry, bear, wear." Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

"To carry off" reaches everything that goes piece by piece: a hill levelled by erosion, a coat worn threadbare, a debt paid down in instalments.
en.abtreiben:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The compound covers everything driven away: a boat carried off course, cattle brought down from the alpine pasture, and, the sense that dominates modern usage, the medical termination of a pregnancy.
en.abtrennen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~trennen~:

• ~trennen~: From MHG ~trennen~, from OHG ~trennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~trannijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trannijaną~. The deeper etymology is uncertain: the Proto-Germanic root is not securely connected to any PIE root. Cognate with Low German ~trennen~ and Dutch ~tornen~, which has narrowed to "to unpick stitches."
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Trennen~ separates two things from each other; ~abtrennen~ takes one off a whole it belonged to, which is why it is the verb for detaching a coupon, a limb, or a seam.
en.abtreten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Literally "to step off": a soldier falls out, an actor leaves the stage, a minister stands down, and in law one cedes a right, an ~Abtretung~.
en.abtrinken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~trinken~:

• ~trinken~: From MHG ~trinken~, from OHG ~trinkan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drinkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drinkaną~; no non-Germanic cognate has been securely identified, so the word may be a Germanic innovation. Cognate with English ~drink~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Old Norse ~drekka~ and Gothic ~𐌳𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌺𐌰𐌽~ (drigkan).
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The separative prefix is partitive here: one drinks a little off the top of a glass too full to carry, taking part of the liquid away rather than emptying it.
en.abtrocknen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~trocknen~:

• ~trocknen~: A deadjectival verb from the adjective ~trocken~ ("dry") with the verbal suffix ~-en~. ~Trocken~ traces to MHG ~trucken~, from OHG ~truckan~, ~trokkan~ ("dried out"), from Proto-West Germanic *~drukn~, from Proto-Germanic *~druknaz~ ("dry"), from PIE *~dʰerǵʰ-~ ("to become hard or solid"), an extension of *~dʰer-~ ("to hold, hold fast"). Cognate with Old Saxon ~drokno~ and Old English ~gedrycnan~ ("to dry up").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

What is removed is the water: ~abtrocknen~ takes the wet off a surface, and the same verb serves intransitively for the surface that dries out by itself.
en.abtöten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~töten~:

• ~töten~: From MHG ~tœten~, from OHG *~tōten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~daudijan~ ("to make dead, to kill"), from Proto-Germanic *~daudijaną~, a factitive of *~daudaz~ ("dead") + *~-janą~ ("to make X"), transparently ~tot~ + ~-en~. Compare English ~deaden~. Cognate with Dutch ~doden~, Old Norse ~deyða~, Gothic ~dauþjan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The prefix makes the killing exhaustive rather than personal: German ~tötet~ a person but ~tötet~ germs, nerves and feelings ~ab~, whatever has to be extinguished wholesale.
en.abwandeln:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~wandeln~:

• ~wandeln~: From MHG ~wandeln~, from OHG ~wantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandōną~, from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). It means both "to walk, stroll" and "to change, transform" (~sich wandeln~), both from the root idea of turning. Cognate with English ~wend~ and ~wind~, Dutch ~wandelen~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys derivation: leading something away from, or tracing it back to, a source.

Of the root's two senses (walking and changing) the compound takes the second, and the prefix supplies the model it departs from: a version that is ~abgewandelt~ is always a variant of something already there.
en.abwandern:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~wandern~:

• ~wandern~: From MHG ~wandern~, from OHG *~wantarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandarōn~, formed from *~wandōn~ ("to turn") with the frequentative suffix *~-rōn~ (not a single journey but repeated, meandering motion), from Proto-Germanic *~wandōną~, from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, to wind"). Cognate with English ~wander~, Danish ~vandre~, Swedish ~vandra~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The frequentative root already means repeated, unhurried motion; the prefix gives it a direction away, so ~abwandern~ describes departure as a drift: of people out of a region, of jobs and capital out of a country.
en.abwarten:
Compound of ~ab-~ + ~warten~:

• ~warten~: From MHG ~warten~, from OHG ~wartēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wardēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wardāną~ ("to guard, protect, watch over"), derived from *~warduz~ ("a guard"), ultimately from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, watch, guard"). Cognate with English ~ward~, Swedish ~vårda~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)~, from OHG ~ab(a)~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Here it adds a sense of completion or patient observation from a distance.

~Abwarten~ means "to wait and see, to bide one's time." Where simple ~warten~ is neutral waiting, ~abwarten~ implies patience with an eye on the outcome: watching from above (~ab-~ "down from") until events unfold. The famous German proverb ~Abwarten und Tee trinken~ ("Wait and drink tea") counsels patience, a calmer counterpart to the English "wait and see." The root ~warten~ itself preserves the original sentinel sense: one who ~abwartet~ is, etymologically, a guard watching from a vantage point, waiting for the situation to resolve itself.
en.abwaschen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~waschen~:

• ~waschen~: From MHG ~waschen~, from OHG ~wascan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~waskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waskaną~, from an earlier *~watskaną~, a ~ske~-present formation from PIE *~wed-~ ("wet, water"), hence "to make wet (repeatedly)." Cognate with English ~wash~, ~water~, ~wet~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vaske~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

What comes off is the dirt, not the thing: one washes blood off a wound and sin off a soul, and the everyday sense of doing the dishes (der ~Abwasch~) is the same removal applied to a plate.
en.abwechseln:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~wechseln~:

• ~wechseln~: From MHG ~wëhseln~, from OHG *~wehsalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wihslōną~, from PIE *~weyk-~, *~weyḱ-~ ("to change, bend, yield"). Cognate with Dutch ~wisselen~, Luxembourgish ~wiesselen~, English ~week~, German ~Woche~, and Latin ~vicis~ ("change, turn, alternation").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

In ~abwechseln~ the removal is mutual: each turn relieves the one before it, as in ~ablösen~ or ~abtreten~, so the participants take each other off duty and the verb is normally reciprocal; ~sie wechseln sich ab~.
en.abwehren:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~wehren~:

• ~wehren~: From MHG ~weren~, from OHG ~werien~, from Proto-West Germanic *~warjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~warjaną~ ("to defend, to ward off, to protect"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to close, to cover, to protect"). Most commonly used reflexively: ~sich wehren~ ("to defend oneself"). Cognate with English ~weir~, ~ward~, ~guard~, Dutch ~weren~, Old Norse ~verja~, Gothic ~warjan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Since ~wehren~ already means to ward off, the prefix reinforces a direction the root supplies rather than adding one, the same doubling English performs when it turns ~ward~ into ~ward off~. The noun ~Abwehr~ ("defense") comes from the verb, in football and in counter-intelligence alike.
en.abweichen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~weichen~:

• ~weichen~: From MHG ~wīchen~, from OHG ~wīchan~ ("to yield, give way"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wīkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīkwaną~, from PIE *~h₃weyg-~ ("to start moving, to distance oneself, to bend, wind"). A class I strong verb, "to yield, give way, retreat"; not to be confused with the weak ~weichen~ ("to soften, to soak"), which derives from ~weich~ ("soft"). Cognate with Old English ~wīcan~, Old Norse ~vīkja~, Swedish ~vika~ ("to give way, fold").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Its strong forms (~wich ab~, ~abgewichen~) place ~abweichen~ with the class I verb "to yield, give way," not with the weak homograph "to soak": to deviate is to give way from a line and move off it. Hence ~Abweichung~ ("deviation") in statistics and in law.
en.abweisen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative verb from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from PIE *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know"). A class I strong verb; its senses "to show, point" and "to direct, expel" both direct knowledge or attention. Cognate with English ~wise~, ~wit~, ~wizard~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

~Weisen~ directs attention or movement; with ~ab-~ it directs them away: one turns away a petitioner, a lawsuit, or an application. The courtroom formula ~die Klage wird abgewiesen~ ("the suit is dismissed") preserves the old gesture of pointing inside modern officialese.
en.abwenden:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~wenden~:

• ~wenden~: From MHG ~wenden~, from OHG ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), the causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). It belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort (preterite ~wandte~, participle ~gewandt~) and has a doubled preterite: ~wandte~ for turning the self or one's attention, the regularized ~wendete~ for physical turning. Cognate with English ~wend~, Armenian ~gind~ ("ring").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The root's doubled preterite survives in the compound: ~wandte den Blick ab~ for a gaze or an attention turned away, with ~wendete ab~ preferred where a danger or a loss is averted.
en.abwerben:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~werben~:

• ~werben~: From MHG ~werben~, from OHG ~werban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hwerban~, from Proto-Germanic *~hwerbaną~ ("to turn, move about, wander"). The sense passed through "to go about seeking" to "to recruit, advertise, woo", parallel to English ~advertise~ from Latin ~advertere~ ("to turn toward"). Cognate with Dutch ~werven~, English ~wharve~, Icelandic ~hverfa~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The root travelled from "going about seeking" to "recruiting"; ~ab-~ names the party the recruit is taken from, one poaches a specialist away from a competitor. The noun ~Abwerbung~ belongs today mostly to the vocabulary of the labour market.
en.abwerfen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

Whatever is thrown off leaves the thrower: the horse its rider, the tree its blossom, the aircraft its load. Figuratively an investment ~wirft~ a return ~ab~; the profit falls off it, much as English speaks of a yield.
en.abwerten:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~werten~:

• ~werten~: Derived from ~Wert~ ("value, worth"), from MHG ~wert~, from OHG ~werd~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("worth, worthy"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"); the connection to value runs through exchange: turning goods over in a transaction. Related to Latin ~versus~ ("turned") and English ~worth~, ~worthy~, ~worship~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys downward motion, often with a sense of dismantling or reduction.

Because ~Wert~ goes back to a root meaning "to turn," ~abwerten~ turns value downward, in currency policy and in social life alike: a currency is devalued, and so, in the very same word, are people.
en.abwiegen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~wiegen~:

• ~wiegen~: Two distinct verbs, both from MHG ~wigen~. Sense 1 ("to weigh"): a northwestern variant of ~wegen~ that generalized the present-singular stem vowel ~i~, from OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, move"); the original ~e~-form survives in the doublet ~wägen~. Sense 2 ("to rock, cradle"): from ~wige~ ("cradle," modern ~Wiege~), from OHG ~wīga~, likely related to Proto-West Germanic *~waggjan~ ("to cause to move"), from the same PIE root. Cognate with English ~weigh~, Dutch ~wegen~, Danish ~veje~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The relevant root is the first of the two ("to weigh," not "to rock a cradle"), and ~ab-~ names the portion taken off a larger quantity. The old ~e~-doublet divides the labour: ~abwiegen~ weighs goods, ~abwägen~ weighs arguments.
en.abwinken:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~winken~:

• ~winken~: From MHG ~winken~, from OHG ~winken~ ("to nod, to blink"), from Proto-West Germanic *~winkōn~ (beside *~winkijan~), from PIE *~weng-~ ("to bend, to curve"), the same root as ~Winkel~ ("angle, corner"). A weak verb, and already weak in OHG; the strong participle ~gewunken~ is a latecomer built on the model of ~sinken~/~gesunken~, not a survival. Cognate with English ~wink~ and ~winch~, Dutch ~wenken~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The hand motion that waves a thing away has long since become the standard formula for declining: ~er winkte ab~ means someone would not even hear it out. At a race the field is ~abgewinkt~, and with that the race is over.
en.abwägen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~wägen~:

• ~wägen~: From MHG ~wegen~ ("to set in motion, to weigh, to be worth"), from OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, to move"). A class V strong verb, ~wägen~, ~wog~, ~gewogen~ (rarely weak ~wägte~, ~gewägt~). It is the doublet of ~wiegen~, which generalized the ~i~ of the old present singular and took over the literal business of weighing, leaving ~wägen~ the figurative one, chiefly in ~abwägen~ and ~erwägen~. The same PIE root gave ~Weg~, ~Wagen~, and English ~way~, ~weigh~, ~wain~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

Since ~wägen~ had long ceded literal weighing to ~wiegen~, the compound is almost never about scales: to ~abwägen~ is to weigh reasons against one another until a judgement settles, and the noun ~Abwägung~ is a term of art in German law.
en.abwählen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~wählen~:

• ~wählen~: From MHG ~weln~, ~welen~, ~wellen~, from OHG ~wellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~walljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waljaną~, from PIE *~welh₁-~ ("to wish, choose"). The umlaut ~ä~ comes from the MHG second- and third-person singular; ~wählen~ and ~wollen~ share the same root. Cognate with English ~well~ (archaic "to wish well"), Dutch ~willen~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

The removal is performed by the very act that installs: a parliament ~wählt~ its chairman and ~wählt~ him ~ab~ again, and a German pupil ~wählt~ a school subject ~ab~ to drop it.
en.abzahlen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

Here ~ab-~ is the sense of carrying through to the end: a debt is paid off in instalments until nothing is outstanding. ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings, but their compounds parted ways; ~abzahlen~ clears a debt, ~abzählen~ counts a set through.
en.abzeichnen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~zeichnen~:

• ~zeichnen~: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, symbol"), from MHG ~zeichen~, from OHG ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~, *~taiknaz~ ("sign"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point"); to ~zeichnen~ is etymologically to make a sign. Cognate with English ~token~, Dutch ~teken~, Danish ~tegn~, Swedish ~tecken~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys copying from a model: reproducing something by taking it off an original.

In the base sense one takes the sign off a model: a map is copied, or a document is initialled and thereby approved. Reflexively the verb has broken away from that; ~es zeichnet sich ab~ says that something is showing in outline before it has arrived.
en.abziehen:
From MHG ~abeziehen~, from OHG ~abaziohan~, from Proto-Germanic *~abateuhaną~. Cognate with Gothic ~aftiuhan~. Compound of ~ab-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). Cognate with English ~tug~, Latin ~dūcere~ ("to lead").
• ~ab-~: From PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). This separable prefix conveys removal, withdrawal, or subtraction.

~Abziehen~ means "to pull off, to withdraw, to subtract, to depart", always with the core image of pulling something away. Its semantic range is astonishing: "to skin" an animal (~einem Hasen das Fell abziehen~), "to subtract" in arithmetic (~drei von fünf abziehen~), "to withdraw" troops (~Truppen abziehen~), and colloquially "to leave, to take off." The Gothic cognate ~aftiuhan~ confirms that this compound existed already in the earliest recorded Germanic, making it one of the oldest ~ab-~ compounds in the language family.
en.abzielen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~zielen~:

• ~zielen~: From ~Ziel~ ("target, goal") + ~-en~; ~Ziel~ descends from MHG ~zil~, from OHG ~zil~, from Proto-West Germanic *~til~, from Proto-Germanic *~tilą~ ("aim, goal, fixed point"). To aim is to direct oneself toward a fixed point. Cognate with Old English ~til~ ("suitable, fitting"), whence English ~till~ ("up to a fixed point").
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys derivation: leading something away from, or tracing it back to, a source.

The prefix traces the path away from the marksman: from the starting point out toward the ~Ziel~. In present-day use hardly any person aims; a measure, a law, or a strategy does, almost always with ~auf~.
en.abzwingen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~zwingen~:

• ~zwingen~: From MHG ~twingen~, from OHG ~dwingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þwinganą~, *~þwinhaną~; the apparent triple shift ~þ~ → ~d~ → ~t~ → ~z~ is regular for words with OHG ~dw-~ and ~tw-~, compare ~Zwerg~ ("dwarf"). A class III strong verb (~zwingen~, ~zwang~, ~gezwungen~). Cognate with Dutch ~dwingen~, Swedish ~tvinga~, Icelandic ~þvinga~, English ~twinge~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys separation or removal: taking something off or away.

To ~abzwingen~ something is to take it from someone against their will; ~ab-~ names the person it is wrung from, and that person stands in the dative. A confession can be forced out of a witness, an answer out of an opponent.
en.abzählen:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~zählen~:

• ~zählen~: From MHG ~zel(e)n~, ~zellen~, from OHG ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~ ("to enumerate, count; to recount, tell"). German split this dual sense: ~zählen~ kept "to count," ~erzählen~ took "to narrate." Cognate with Dutch ~tellen~, English ~tell~ and ~tale~, Danish ~tælle~, Gothic ~talzjan~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix marks completion or termination: carrying an action through to its end, or letting it expire.

The counting runs to the end of the set: one counts off the children, or counts out the change. Its sibling ~abzahlen~ took over the paying of debts, though both verbs descend from the same root meaning "to count, to tell."
en.abändern:
A separable compound of ~ab-~ + ~ändern~:

• ~ändern~: From MHG ~endern~, a denominative verb from ~ander~ ("other, different"), from MHG ~ander~, OHG ~andar~, Proto-West Germanic *~anþar~, Proto-Germanic *~anþeraz~, from PIE *~h₂énteros~ ("other"), a comparative formation from *~h₂ent-~ ("front, forefront"). Cognate with English ~other~, Dutch ~ander~, Old Norse ~annarr~, Danish ~anden~.
• ~ab-~: From MHG ~ab(e)-~, from OHG ~ab(a)-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ab~, from Proto-Germanic *~ab~ ("off, away"), from PIE *~h₂epó~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~of~ and ~off~ (one Old English word that split in two), as well as Latin ~ab~ ("from") and Greek ~apó~. The prefix conveys derivation: leading something away from, or tracing it back to, a source.

~Abändern~ differs from plain ~ändern~ in presupposing an original: what is amended is measured against the version it departed from, which is why legal German reaches for it when a statute is amended rather than merely changed.
en.achten: From Middle High German ~ahten~ ("to consider, heed, esteem"), from Old High German ~ahtōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ahtōn~, a denominative verb derived from *~ahtu~ ("consideration, attention"). The noun *~ahtu~ is of uncertain pre-Germanic origin; it may be related to Proto-Germanic *~ahjaną~ ("to think"), which has been compared to PIE *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see") (cognate with the Gothic verb ~ahjan~ ("to think")), though this connection remains debated among scholars. The verb's core sense of "weighing, attending to" is reflected in its modern meanings: to respect (~achten~), to heed (~darauf achten~), and, with the negative prefix, to disregard (~missachten~). Cognate with Dutch ~achten~, Low German ~achten~, English ~aught~ (from the related noun).
en.achtgeben:
A separable compound of the noun ~acht~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~acht~: The noun ~Acht~ ("attention, heed"), from OHG ~ahta~, from Proto-Germanic *~ahtō~ ("consideration"), the same stem as the verb ~achten~. It survives only bound: in ~achtgeben~ and ~achthaben~, and in the phrases ~in Acht nehmen~ and ~außer Acht lassen~. It is not the homograph ~Acht~ ("outlawry"), which shows a long vowel in OHG ~āhta~ ("persecution"), from Proto-West Germanic *~āhtō~, and which gives the verb ~ächten~. Here: attention, heed, incorporated as the object of the verb.

~Achtgeben~ is the active half of the pair: attention is newly turned toward something, usually with ~auf~. The spelling reform admitted both ~achtgeben~ and ~acht geben~, leaving the compound visibly poised between a word and a phrase.
en.achthaben:
A separable compound of the noun ~acht~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~acht~: The noun ~Acht~ ("attention, heed"), from OHG ~ahta~, from Proto-Germanic *~ahtō~ ("consideration"), the same stem as the verb ~achten~. It survives only bound: in ~achtgeben~ and ~achthaben~, and in the phrases ~in Acht nehmen~ and ~außer Acht lassen~. It is not the homograph ~Acht~ ("outlawry"), which shows a long vowel in OHG ~āhta~ ("persecution"), from Proto-West Germanic *~āhtō~, and which gives the verb ~ächten~. Here: attention, heed, incorporated as the object of the verb.

~Achthaben~ is the stative half of the pair: to ~achtgeben~ is to direct attention, to ~achthaben~ is to hold it. The verb is literary today, met mostly in Luther, whose preterite ~achthatte~ shows how thoroughly noun and verb have grown together.
en.agieren:
From Latin ~agere~ ("to do, to drive, to act"), with the German suffix ~-ieren~. The Latin verb descends from Proto-Italic *~agō~, from PIE *~h₂eǵ-~ ("to drive"), one of the most prolific roots in all of Indo-European. Cognate with Greek ~agō~ ("I lead"), Sanskrit ~ajati~ ("to drive, propel"), and Old Norse ~aka~ ("to drive").

The PIE root *~h₂eǵ-~ has produced an extraordinary family of English words through Latin: ~act~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~agenda~ ("things to be done"), ~navigate~ ("to drive a ship"), ~ambiguous~ ("driven both ways"), ~prodigal~ ("driving forth"), ~examine~ (from ~exigere~, "to drive out, to weigh"), and ~essay~ (from ~exagium~, "a weighing"). Through Greek it gives ~pedagogue~ ("child-driver"), ~demagogue~ ("people-driver"), and ~synagogue~ ("led together"). German ~agieren~ entered the language in the 16th century as part of the massive influx of Latin vocabulary during the Renaissance and Reformation. Unlike native German verbs, ~agieren~ always takes the regular weak ~-ieren~ conjugation pattern, a reliable marker of its foreign origin. In modern usage, it often has a theatrical connotation ("to perform on stage") alongside its general meaning of "to act."
en.ahnen:
From Middle High German ~anen~, from Old High German *~anōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~anōn~, derived from the preposition *~ana~ ("on"), from Proto-Germanic *~an~ ("on"). Cognate with Middle Low German ~ānen~, dialectal Dutch ~anen~ ("to conjecture"), and Saterland Frisian ~oanje~ ("to suspect, guess").

The semantic development from a preposition meaning "on" to a verb meaning "to suspect, to have a presentiment" likely passed through an intermediate sense of "to be on the track of" or "to be onto something." Despite the phonetic similarity, ~ahnen~ ("to suspect") and ~Ahn~ ("ancestor," from Proto-Germanic *~anô~, from PIE *~h₂en-~ "ancestor") are etymologically unrelated, their resemblance is a coincidence that has nonetheless influenced German speakers' perception of both words. The noun ~Ahnung~ ("inkling, presentiment") is derived from ~ahnen~ and appears in the common expression ~keine Ahnung~ ("no idea"), one of the first phrases many German learners acquire.
en.aktivieren:
From ~aktiv~ + ~-ieren~. ~Aktiv~ is borrowed from Latin ~āctīvus~ ("active, practical"), derived from the verb ~agō~ ("to act, to do, to drive"), from PIE *~h₂eǵ-~ ("to drive, to lead"), the same root that gives Greek ~ágō~ ("I lead"), Sanskrit ~ájati~ ("drives"), and English ~act~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~agenda~, and ~essay~ (via French ~essai~ from Latin ~exigere~). The suffix ~-ieren~ marks the standard German pattern for creating verbs from adjectives of Latin or French origin.

~Aktivieren~ means "to activate, to enable, to put into operation," covering a wide range from the physical (activating a machine) to the chemical (converting a substance into a reactive form) to the digital (enabling a software feature). The prefix-free simplicity of ~aktivieren~ masks a complex semantic history: PIE *~h₂eǵ-~ originally meant "to drive cattle", from this pastoral root grew the entire vocabulary of human agency and action. The antonym ~deaktivieren~ ("to deactivate") and the noun ~Aktivierung~ ("activation") follow standard German derivation patterns.
en.aktualisieren:
Formed from ~aktuell~ + ~-isieren~ (the German adaptation of the productive suffix ~-ize~). The adjective ~aktuell~ was borrowed from French ~actuel~ ("current, present"), which in turn comes from Late Latin ~actuālis~ ("active, practical"), from Latin ~āctus~ ("a doing"), from PIE *~h₂eǵ-~ ("to drive, to do").

A notable false friend: German ~aktuell~ means "current, up-to-date," not "actual" (which is German ~tatsächlich~). Accordingly, ~aktualisieren~ means "to update" or "to refresh," not "to actualize." This semantic divergence between German and English is a common source of confusion for learners. The ~-isieren~ suffix is the standard German mechanism for creating verbs from adjectives of Latin or French origin, parallel to English ~-ize~ and French ~-iser~.
en.akzeptieren:
Adapted from Latin ~acceptāre~, the frequentative form of ~accipiō~ ("to receive, accept, take"). ~Accipiō~ is itself a compound of ~ad-~ ("towards") + ~capiō~ ("to take"), from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"), the same root that gives English ~capture~, ~capable~, ~heave~, and German ~heben~ ("to lift").

A frequentative verb in Latin was formed by adding ~-tāre~ to a past participle stem, expressing repeated or habitual action: ~acceptāre~ thus originally meant "to take repeatedly" or "to receive willingly." The German adaptation ~akzeptieren~ adds the standard ~-ieren~ suffix. The Latin past participle ~acceptus~ ("accepted, welcome") also survives directly in the German adjective ~akzeptabel~ and the noun ~Akzeptanz~. The spelling with ~kz~ (rather than ~cc~ as in Latin) reflects a German phonological convention: Latin double ~cc~ before a front vowel, pronounced [kt͡s], is rendered ~kz~.
en.allemachen:
A separable compound of predicative ~alle~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~alle~: The colloquial predicative use of ~alle~ ("all"), in the sense "used up, all gone": ~die Milch ist alle~. The quantifier goes back to MHG ~al~, OHG ~al~, Proto-Germanic *~allaz~, cognate with English ~all~, Dutch ~al~, Gothic ~alls~. Note the register: this predicative ~alle~ is informal and chiefly northern and central German, and it does not decline. The sense of ~alle~ here is the resultative frame: to finish something off, polish it off (~alle machen~).

Colloquial and chiefly northern to central German: what is ~alle gemacht~ has been used up entirely, and from a thing used up it is a short step to a creature killed, the same step English took with ~to finish someone off~.
en.altmachen:
A separable compound of the adjective ~alt~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~alt~: From the adjective ~alt~, MHG and OHG ~alt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ald~, from Proto-Germanic *~aldaz~, originally a past participle, "grown up," to the verb *~alaną~ ("to grow, nourish"), from PIE *~h₂el-~ ("to grow, nourish"). The same PIE root gave Latin ~alere~ ("to nourish"), whose participle ~adultus~ is English ~adult~: German ~alt~ and English ~adult~ both mean, at bottom, "having been made to grow." Cognate with English ~old~ and ~eld~, Dutch ~oud~, Old Saxon ~ald~. The sense of ~alt~ here is the resultative frame: to become or make old (~altwerden~).

Resultative: what is meant is not ageing itself but being made to look old, a dress, a haircut, or a worry can ~altmachen~ someone. Its counterpart ~altwerden~ describes the same state with nobody causing it.
en.analysieren: Borrowed from French ~analyser~ with the addition of the German verbal suffix ~-ieren~. French ~analyser~ derives from the noun ~analyse~, from Medieval Latin ~analysis~, from Ancient Greek ~analusis~ ("a dissolving, a breaking up"), from ~analuein~ ("to unloose, undo"), composed of ~ana-~ ("up, back, throughout") + ~luein~ ("to loosen, untie"), from PIE *~lew-~ ("to cut, loosen, divide"). The suffix ~-ieren~ is the standard German mechanism for absorbing foreign verbs, borrowed itself from Old French ~-ier~ (from Latin ~-āre~ verb endings filtered through French phonology). The etymological image behind ~analysieren~ is thus one of untying or loosening: taking something complex apart into its component threads, the opposite of synthesis (~sunthesis~, "a putting together"). Greek ~luein~ also gave English ~lysis~, ~catalysis~, ~dialysis~, and ~paralysis~, all words about loosening, dissolving, or undoing. German could have coined a native equivalent (perhaps *~zergliedern~, which does exist as a near-synonym meaning "to dissect"), but the Greek-Latin internationalism won out, as it did in nearly every European language.
en.anbauen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~būwen~, from OHG ~būan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~būan~, from Proto-Germanic *~būaną~ ("to dwell, reside"), from PIE *~bʰuH-~ ("to be, become, grow"); one builds where one lives. Cognate with English ~be~, ~bower~ ("dwelling"), ~neighbor~ ("near-dweller"), Dutch ~bouwen~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

Both modern senses lie ready in a root that meant "to dwell" and "to till" at once: one builds a wing onto a house, and one grows grain. In the first the new thing is fastened to what stands; in the second the seed is put into the ground where one lives.
en.anbefehlen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~befehlen~, itself ~be-~ + the now-bound stem ~-fehlen~:

• ~-fehlen~: From MHG ~bevelhen~, from OHG ~bifelahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~felhaną~ ("to hide, entrust, hand over"). The sense passed from "entrust" to "command": whoever hands a thing over to another disposes of it. The stem is no longer a free word and survives only in ~befehlen~ and ~empfehlen~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. The prefix makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

~Anbefehlen~ is the intensified form of ~befehlen~, elevated to archaic today, and it kept the older sense "to entrust" longest: a child or a soul was ~anbefohlen~ to someone's care.
en.anbehalten:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~be-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. The prefix adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.

The ~an-~ carries over from ~anziehen~ ("to put on"): what has been put on is kept on rather than taken off. Without the prefix, ~behalten~ means only "to retain"; ~an-~ is what puts the garment back on the body.
en.anbeißen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~beißen~:

• ~beißen~: From MHG ~bīzen~, from OHG ~bīzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bītaną~, from PIE *~bʰeyd-~ ("to split"). A class I strong verb (~beißen~, ~biss~, ~gebissen~). Cognate with English ~bite~, Dutch ~bijten~, Swedish ~bita~; ~bitter~ is this verb's old participial adjective, literally "biting."
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

The bitten apple is only partly eaten, hence the fish that ~anbeißt~: it takes the bait into its mouth before committing to it. Figuratively, whoever takes an offer up has taken the bait.
en.anbellen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~bellen~:

• ~bellen~: From MHG ~bellen~, from OHG ~bellan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bellaną~ ("to resound, roar"), probably from PIE *~bʰelH-~ ("to sound, howl"), though that reconstruction is not secure. Originally a class III strong verb (~bellen~, ~bal~, ~gebollen~), now weak throughout. Cognate with Old English ~bellan~, English ~bellow~ and ~bell~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

~An-~ turns intransitive ~bellen~ into a transitive verb with an addressee: the dog does not merely bark, it barks at someone. Transferred to people, it names the brusque tone in which someone is snapped at.
en.anbeten:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~beten~:

• ~beten~: From MHG ~beten~, from OHG ~beton~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bedon~, from Proto-Germanic *~bedan~ ("to pray, to ask"), close to *~bidjan~ ("to ask"), from PIE *~gwhedh-~ ("to ask for, beseech"). The narrowing from "ask" to "pray" is a Christianization phenomenon. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bidden~, Danish ~bede~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The root had already narrowed from "to ask" to "to pray"; ~an-~ points the prayer at a recipient and carries it on to worship. From there the step to secular use is short: ~der Angebetete~ is not a god but the object of somebody's infatuation.
en.anbetreffen:
A double compound: separable ~an-~ on inseparable ~betreffen~, itself ~be-~ + ~treffen~:

• ~treffen~: From MHG ~treffen~, from OHG ~treffan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drepan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drepaną~ ("to strike, push, beat"), from PIE *~dʰrebʰ-~, *~dʰreb-~ ("to crack, crush, strike, kill"). The High German consonant shift from *~dr-~ to ~tr-~ obscures the cognate relationship with Old English ~drepan~ ("to strike"). Cognate with Old Norse ~drepa~ ("to kill, strike").
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

The verb survives almost only in the fixed formula ~was … anbetrifft~ ("as far as … is concerned"), where two layers of prefix say what ~betreffen~ already said. The Proto-Germanic sense of striking a blow has worn down to bare relevance: what a matter ~anbetrifft~ no longer strikes it, it merely pertains to it.
en.anbieten:
From Middle High German ~anebieten~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~bieten~:

• ~bieten~: From MHG ~bieten~, from OHG ~biotan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beudan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beudaną~, from PIE *~bʰewdʰ-~ ("to be awake, aware"). A class II strong verb whose PIE root conveys notions of awareness and offering.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an-~, from OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana-~, from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). This separable prefix adds a sense of direction toward or presentation to.

The directional ~an-~ prefix focuses ~bieten~ ("to offer, bid") toward a specific recipient: ~anbieten~ means to offer something directly to someone. The verb's PIE ancestry in "awareness" is semantically apt; to offer is to make another aware of what is available. Cognate with Dutch ~aanbieden~.
en.anbinden:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~binden~:

• ~binden~: From MHG ~binden~, from OHG ~bintan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bindan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bindaną~, from PIE *~bʰendʰ-~ ("to bind, tie"). A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~i~–~a~–~u~ ablaut (~binden~, ~band~, ~gebunden~). Cognate with English ~bind~, Dutch ~binden~, Gothic ~bindan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The literal sense is intact (a horse tied to a post), and the idiom ~kurz angebunden~ ("curt, brusque") keeps the same picture: an animal tethered on a short rope has little room to move.
en.anblasen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~blasen~:

• ~blasen~: From MHG ~blāsen~, from OHG ~blāsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blāsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~blēsaną~, from PIE *~bʰleh₁-~ ("to blow, swell"). A class VII strong verb, its reduplicated preterite worn down to ~blies~ (~blasen~, ~blies~, ~geblasen~). Cognate with English ~blast~, Gothic ~ufblēsan~, Old Norse ~blása~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

What the prefix marks is the kindling, not the blowing: one blows at the embers until the fire takes, and the same ~an-~ opens a hunt when the horn is ~angeblasen~.
en.anblicken:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~blank~, Dutch ~blik~, Old English ~blice~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The root's older meaning makes the compound vivid: if a ~Blick~ was once a flash of light, then to ~anblicken~ someone is to aim that flash at them, a gaze thrown the way a lantern is turned.
en.anbraten:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~braten~:

• ~braten~: From MHG ~brāten~, from OHG ~brātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brēdaną~ ("to roast"), from PIE *~bʰreh₁-~ ("to heat, boil, burn"), the root behind ~brennen~ and English ~brew~. A class VII strong verb (~braten~, ~briet~, ~gebraten~). Cognate with English ~brawn~ (borrowed via Old French), Dutch ~braden~, Old English ~brǣdan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

The partial sense is culinary precision: to ~anbraten~ meat is to brown the outside and leave the middle raw, the deliberate opposite of ~durchbraten~ ("to cook through").
en.anbrechen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

German and English both let a day break, but German marks the onset with a prefix. The same ~an-~ gives the verb its other sense, broaching something intact: an ~angebrochene Flasche~ is a bottle whose seal has been broken, and no more than that.
en.anbrennen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~brennen~:

• ~brennen~: From MHG ~brennen~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: transitive ~brennan~ ("to set on fire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~brannijan~, and intransitive ~brinnan~, from *~brinnan~, of which *~brannijan~ was the causative. The intransitive is from PIE *~bʰrewh₁-~ ("to boil, brew"), making ~brennen~ a cousin of English ~brew~. A Rückumlaut verb: ~ich brenne~ but ~brannte~, ~gebrannt~. Cognate with English ~burn~, Dutch ~branden~, Icelandic ~brenna~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

The root's two Old High German twins settle the argument structure: ~anbrennen~ continues the intransitive ~brinnan~, so it is the food that starts to burn, not the cook who burns it, and ~nichts anbrennen lassen~ ("to let nothing burn") became an idiom for letting no opportunity slip.
en.anbringen:
From ~an-~ + ~bringen~. Compound of:
