• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenḱ-~, likely from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁neḱ-~ ("to bring, reach"). Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~, from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys attachment, arrival, or application.

~Anbringen~ means "to attach, install, mount" (a shelf, a sign), "to apply" (paint, criticism), and "to manage to place" (a joke, a remark into a conversation). All senses flow from the core image of bringing something ~onto~ a surface or into a context. The idiomatic sense of slipping a remark into conversation (~einen Witz anbringen~) reveals a playful metaphorical extension: one ~attaches~ a quip to the flow of talk. The past participle ~angebracht~ has developed an independent adjectival life meaning "appropriate, fitting" (~das ist nicht angebracht~ = "that's not appropriate"), what has been properly placed is deemed suitable.
en.andauern:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~dauern~:

• ~dauern~: Two separate verbs under one spelling. "To last, endure": from MHG ~dūren~, borrowed from Middle Low German ~dūren~, from Latin ~dūrō~, a denominative of ~dūrus~ ("hard, lasting"), from Proto-Italic *~dūros~, from PIE *~dweh₂-~ ("long, far"); cognate with Dutch ~duren~, English ~dure~. "To cause pity" (~er dauert mich~): from MHG ~tūren~, an ablaut variant of ~tiure~ ("dear, costly"), ancestor of ~teuer~, thus a doublet of ~teuer~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout").

The root here is the ~dūrus~ twin, "to last, endure", not the ~teuer~ twin that means "to cause pity"; the reading's meaning settles which of the two homographs the compound continues. The ~an-~ is durative rather than inchoative: it keeps the action going, much as English keeps the same particle in "carry on".
en.andenken:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~teng-~ ("to think, feel"). A mixed-conjugation verb of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~dachte~ pairs the vowel change ~e~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix and ~k~ > ~ch~. Cognate with English ~think~, Dutch ~denken~, Icelandic ~þekkja~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

Modern German uses the verb almost only as a participle of official register: something ~angedacht~ has been thought at but not thought through, which is exactly the partial sense the prefix contributes.
en.andeuten:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~deuten~:

• ~deuten~: From MHG ~diuten~, from OHG ~diuten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þiudijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þiudijaną~ ("to interpret; to point out"), from *~þeudō~ ("people"), from PIE *~tewtéh₂~ ("people"), originally "to make intelligible to the people," the same word that gives ~deutsch~. Cognate with Dutch ~duiden~, Icelandic ~þýða~, Swedish ~tyda~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

The root once meant making a thing intelligible to the people (the same word that gives ~deutsch~), and the prefix stops it halfway: to ~andeuten~ is to make something just intelligible enough to be caught, and no more.
en.andienen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~dienen~:

• ~dienen~: From MHG ~dienen~, from OHG ~dionōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þewanōną~ ("to serve"), a denominative of *~þewaz~ ("servant, slave"), of uncertain further origin, perhaps PIE *~tekʷ-~ ("to run"), the servant as "one who runs errands." Cognate with English ~thane~ (via the noun), Dutch ~dienen~, Danish ~tjene~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The compound keeps the servant's posture of the root: to ~andienen~ is to present something to someone as a service, and in commercial and insurance German the noun ~Andienung~ is the formal tender of goods. Colloquially the offering has soured into pressing something on a person who did not ask for it.
en.andrehen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). Cognate with English ~throw~ (a true cognate: Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist," a sense that "throw a pot" still keeps) plus English ~thread~, Dutch ~draaien~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

The literal gesture is a knob turned until the current flows. The idiom ~jemandem etwas andrehen~ ("to palm something off on someone") draws on a different ~an-~, the one aimed at a person, and the turning becomes a swindle.
en.androhen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~drohen~:

• ~drohen~: From MHG ~drōn~, ~drōwen~, from OHG ~drouwen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrauwijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þraujaną~ ("to threaten"). The archaic variant ~dräuen~, with umlaut from the ~j~, preserves the older vowel pattern. Cognate with Old English ~þrēagan~ ("to rebuke, threaten"), Old Saxon ~thrōian~, Middle Dutch ~drouwen~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

Plain ~drohen~ can hang in the air; ~androhen~ has to be aimed, and it takes a dative for the person threatened. That is why the compound belongs to legal register: a court ~droht~ a penalty ~an~ before it imposes one.
en.andrücken:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The prefix supplies the surface the pressing is against: to ~andrücken~ is to press until the thing holds, where ~eindrücken~ presses until it dents and ~zerdrücken~ until it gives way.
en.aneignen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~eignen~:

• ~eignen~: From MHG ~eigenen~, from OHG ~eiganen~, from Proto-Germanic *~aiginōną~, a denominative from *~aiganaz~ ("owned, one's own"), the past participle of *~aiganą~ ("to possess"), from PIE *~h₂eh₂óyḱe~, from *~h₂eyḱ-~ ("ability, possession"). Originally "to make one's own." Cognate with English ~own~, Dutch ~eigen~, Swedish ~ägna~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The verb is always reflexive (~sich etwas aneignen~) and the reflexive is where the prefix lands: the thing is fastened onto oneself. Since the root already means "to make one's own", from the same Germanic word as English ~own~, the compound intensifies rather than adds.
en.aneinanderhalten:
A separable compound of ~aneinander-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~aneinander-~: Transparently ~an~ ("at, on, against") + ~einander~ ("one another"), the reciprocal pronoun from MHG ~ein ander~. The compound is reciprocal rather than deictic: it says that the participants act on each other, as in ~aneinandergeraten~ ("to come to blows") or ~aneinanderreihen~ ("to string together"). See the entries for ~an~ and for the parallel formation ~durcheinander~. Here ~aneinander-~ one against or onto another: reciprocal contact.

The reciprocal element does work no single prefix could: two things are held up against each other, and the point is the comparison rather than the holding.
en.aneinanderschlagen:
A separable compound of ~aneinander-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~aneinander-~: Transparently ~an~ ("at, on, against") + ~einander~ ("one another"), the reciprocal pronoun from MHG ~ein ander~. The compound is reciprocal rather than deictic: it says that the participants act on each other, as in ~aneinandergeraten~ ("to come to blows") or ~aneinanderreihen~ ("to string together"). See the entries for ~an~ and for the parallel formation ~durcheinander~. Here ~aneinander-~ one against or onto another: reciprocal contact.

Because ~aneinander~ is reciprocal, both objects are struck and neither is the target: glasses are knocked ~aneinander~ in a toast, and the onomatopoeic ancestor *~slak-~ is still audible in the result.
en.anerkennen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~erkennen~ (itself ~er-~ + ~kennen~):

• ~kennen~: From MHG ~kennen~, from OHG ~kennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kannijan~ ("to know"), from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~, a causative form of *~kunnaną~ ("to be able, to know"), formed with the suffix *~-janą~. From PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know").
• ~an-~: From PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). This prefix adds the sense of directing recognition toward something, affirming or acknowledging it.
• ~er-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). This inseparable prefix conveys achievement or completion of the base action.

~Erkennen~ (from OHG ~irkennen~, Proto-West Germanic *~uʀkannijan~) means "to recognize, to perceive," and ~anerkennen~ builds on this: "to acknowledge, to recognize officially, to appreciate." The double-prefix structure (~an-~ + ~er-~ + ~kennen~) is comparatively rare in German and reflects layered derivation: first, ~er-~ transforms ~kennen~ ("to know") into ~erkennen~ ("to come to know, to recognize"), then ~an-~ directs that recognition outward as a formal act of acknowledgment. The PIE root *~ǵneh₃-~ is spectacularly productive across the Indo-European family: it yields English ~know~, ~can~, and ~ken~ (Scottish "to know"), Latin ~cognōscere~ (whence English ~cognition~ and ~recognize~), Greek ~γνῶσις~ (~gnosis~), and Sanskrit ~jānāti~ ("to know"). Cognate with Bavarian ~kennan~, Dutch ~erkennen~.
en.anerziehen:
A double compound: separable ~an-~ on inseparable ~erziehen~, itself ~er-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. Here ~er-~ preserves the prefix's older spatial sense of upward or outward motion.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

~Erziehen~ is a morpheme-for-morpheme twin of Latin ~ēdūcere~: ~er-~ from *~uz-~ ("out, up") over a root from PIE *~dewk-~, precisely ~ex~ + ~dūcere~, whose root is that same *~dewk-~. The outer ~an-~ then fastens the result onto a person, so what is ~anerzogen~ has been drawn up in someone until it sticks, a trait taught rather than inborn.
en.anfahren:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

One compound carries three journeys: a train ~fährt an~ when it starts moving, a carriage ~fährt~ at the gate ~an~ when it arrives, and a person who ~fährt~ another ~an~ snaps at them, the hostile ~an-~ of ~anfallen~ borrowed into a verb of travel.
en.anfallen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

The hostile sense is the old one (a beast or a fit ~fällt~ someone ~an~), but modern bureaucratic German has quietly domesticated it: ~anfallende Kosten~ are costs that accrue, expenses that fall upon you without attacking.
en.anfangen:
From Middle High German ~anevāhen~, from Old High German ~anafāhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~anafą̄han~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~fangen~:

• ~fangen~: From MHG ~vāhen~, from OHG ~fāhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~fanhaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to secure, attach, fasten"). A Class VII strong verb. The modern present stem ~fang-~ was borrowed from the past forms in Middle Low German ~vangen~ and then spread into Central German in the early modern period, a process also seen in ~hängen~. The archaic English ~fang~ ("fang of a tooth; to seize") descends from the same root.
• ~an-~: From Proto-Indo-European *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). This separable prefix expresses direction toward or attachment.

The semantic shift from "to catch, seize" to "to begin" (preserved in ~anfangen~) is striking. The underlying image is one of grasping a thing and setting it in motion, a sense also alive in the noun ~Anfang~ ("beginning, start"). Cognate with Dutch ~aanvangen~, Low German ~anfangen~.
en.anfassen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~fassen~:

• ~fassen~: From MHG ~vazzen~, from OHG ~fazzōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fatōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fatōną~ ("to hold, seize"), a weak class 2 verb, from PIE *~pod-néh₂-ti~, from *~pod-~ ("to fetch"). German kept the sense of grasping and holding, English that of going to retrieve. Cognate with English ~fetch~; the noun ~Fass~ ("barrel") shares the root.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

German kept the root's grasping sense where English took the fetching one, so ~anfassen~ is contact made with the hand and nothing more, and ~mit anfassen~ ("to lend a hand") is that same grip turned into help.
en.anfechten:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~fechten~:

• ~fechten~: From MHG ~vëhten~ ("to fight"), from OHG ~fëhtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fehtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fehtaną~, perhaps from PIE *~peḱ-~ ("to pluck, comb"), though not securely. A class III strong verb (~fechten~, ~focht~, ~gefochten~); the ~o~ of the Präteritum comes from the old plural stem (OHG ~fuhtum~). Cognate with English ~fight~, Dutch ~vechten~, Danish ~fægte~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

The compound began as literal assault and ended up in the courtroom: to ~anfechten~ a judgment is to challenge it. Luther's ~Anfechtung~, the trial that assails a soul, preserves the older sense, and the root is English ~fight~.
en.anfertigen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~fertigen~:

• ~fertigen~: Derived from the adjective ~fertig~ ("finished, ready"), from MHG ~fertec~, from OHG ~fartīg~, originally meaning "ready for a journey," from the noun ~fart~ ("journey"). Cognate with Dutch ~vaardig~ ("ready, swift") and Old English ~fierd~ ("expedition, campaign").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~an~ ("on, at"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). In this compound, the prefix adds a sense of directed production or purposeful creation.

The semantic journey of ~fertig~ is remarkable: it began as "ready for travel" (from ~Fahrt~, "journey"), then broadened to "prepared" in general, and finally settled on "finished, completed", essentially reversing its temporal orientation from looking forward to a journey to looking back at a completed task. The compound ~anfertigen~ thus literally meant something like "to bring to a state of readiness" and now means "to produce, to manufacture." English ~ready~ shows a parallel development from Old English ~rǣde~ ("prepared for riding").
en.anfordern:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~fordern~:

• ~fordern~: From MHG ~vodern~, ~vordern~, from OHG ~fordarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ(a)rōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþą~, from PIE *~pŕ̥-to-~, from *~per-~ ("forward, through"); "to push forward" became "to advance a claim." Not to be confused with umlauted ~fördern~ from the same root. Cognate with English ~forth~, ~forward~ and ~further~, Dutch ~vorderen~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The root already meant advancing a claim; ~an-~ addresses that claim to someone, which is why the compound is the word of requisition forms and dispatch rooms. Note that ~fordern~ ("demand") and ~fördern~ ("promote") come from one root, separated only by an umlaut.
en.anfragen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~fragen~:

• ~fragen~: From MHG ~vrāgen~, from OHG ~frāgēn~, ~frahēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frāgēn~ (a denominative from *~frāgu~, "question"), from Proto-Germanic *~frēgō~ ("question"), from PIE *~preḱ-~ ("to ask"), which also gave Latin ~precor~ and Sanskrit ~pṛcchāti~. Cognate with English ~frain~ (archaic), Dutch ~vragen~, Swedish ~fråga~, Icelandic ~fregna~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The compound is addressed asking: one ~fragt~ a question but ~fragt~ at a person or an office ~an~. In modern German the deverbal noun ~Anfrage~ is far commoner than the verb it comes from.
en.anfügen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~fügen~:

• ~fügen~: From MHG ~füegen~, ~fuogen~, from OHG ~fuogen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōgijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōgijaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to join, attach, fasten"). Reflexive ~sich fügen~ means "to submit": to join oneself to the arrangement of fate. Cognate with Dutch ~voegen~ and archaic English ~fay~ ("to fit closely," from Old English ~fēgan~).
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The root is the joinery word (~fügen~ fits pieces together), and the prefix says where: ~anfügen~ attaches at the end, where ~einfügen~ inserts within and ~zusammenfügen~ makes a whole out of parts.
en.anfühlen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~fühlen~:

• ~fühlen~: From northern MHG ~vüelen~, from OHG ~fuolen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōlijan~ ("to feel"); the further origin is uncertain, presumably related to Old Norse ~falma~ ("to grope"), and possibly a secondary causative of a strong *~falaną~, from PIE *~pelh₁-~ ("to stroke"). Cognate with English ~feel~, Dutch ~voelen~, Danish ~føle~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

Modern ~anfühlen~ is almost always reflexive, and the reflexive reverses the direction of view: ~es fühlt sich rau an~ reports not what the toucher does but what the surface gives back to the hand.
en.anführen:
From Middle High German ~anevüeren~, from Old High German ~anafuoren~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, the causative of ~fahren~ ("to travel"), from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~ ("to cause to go"), from *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ ("going, passage"). Cognate with English ~fare~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~an~ ("on, at"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix here conveys direction and guidance.

The causative relationship between ~fahren~ ("to go") and ~führen~ ("to lead, cause to go") is a textbook example of the Proto-Germanic causative formation with *~-janą~: ~fahren~ means "to travel oneself," while ~führen~ means "to make someone travel", hence "to lead." The compound ~anführen~ has developed two strikingly different meanings: "to lead, to head" (neutral) and "to dupe, to deceive" (pejorative). The second sense likely arose from the image of leading someone astray, a semantic path also visible in English ~to lead someone on~.
en.anfüllen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~füllen~:

• ~füllen~: From MHG ~vüllen~, from OHG ~fullen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fullijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullijaną~ ("to make full"), the causative of *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pl̥h₁nós~ ("full"). English ~fill~ and ~füllen~ are exact cognates, each the causative of its native word for "full." Cognate with English ~fill~, Dutch ~vullen~, Danish ~fylde~, Swedish ~fylla~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

~Anfüllen~ says nothing ~füllen~ could not, except degree: the compound fills a space up to its limit. It survives chiefly in literary registers, most often as the participle ~angefüllt~ describing a room or a vessel already full to the brim.
en.anfüttern:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~füttern~:

• ~füttern~: From MHG ~vuotern~, from OHG ~fuotiren~, derived from the noun ~fuotar~ ("fodder"), from Proto-Germanic *~fōdrą~, from PIE *~peh2-~ ("to guard, graze, feed"). A second, homonymous ~füttern~ ("to line a garment") belongs instead to the other OHG ~fuotar~ ("sheath, wrapping"). Cognate with English dialectal ~to fodder~, Dutch ~voeren~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The verb belongs first to angling and animal keeping (feeding a spot or a creature until it comes of its own accord), and the figurative sense of winning someone over with gifts keeps that same pattern. The homonymous ~füttern~ ("to line a garment") plays no part here.
en.angeben: From Middle High German ~anegeben~, equivalent to prefix ~an-~ (from PIE *~h₂en~, "on, onto") and ~geben~, from MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Victor Klemperer notes in his ~Lingua Tertii Imperii~ (1947) that the sense "to brag, to boast" (the meaning a learner encounters when someone is called an ~Angeber~) entered German from Yiddish. This is a striking example of semantic drift: a humble "give" verb acquiring social arrogance through a specific community's usage.
en.angehen:
From Middle High German ~angēn~, ~angān~, from Old High German ~anagān~. Equivalent to ~an-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gēn~, ~gān~, from OHG ~gēn~, ~gān~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to go").
• ~an-~: From PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix adds the sense of approaching, beginning, or concerning.

~Angehen~ is one of German's most versatile prefix verbs, with meanings that span "to approach" (~jemanden angehen~), "to concern" (~das geht mich nichts an~, "that doesn't concern me"), "to begin" (~die Arbeit geht an~), and "to tackle" (~ein Problem angehen~). The "concerning" sense is particularly idiomatic: it derives from the physical image of something walking up to you: what approaches you is what concerns you. The past participle ~angegangen~ and the separable prefix behavior (~es geht mich an~) mark this as a separable-prefix compound. Cognate with Dutch ~aangaan~.
en.angehören:
From Middle High German ~anegehœren~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~gehören~:

• ~gehören~: From MHG ~gehœren~ ("to listen to, obey"), from OHG ~gihōrian~ ("to hearken to"), from Proto-West Germanic *~gahauʀijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~gahauzijaną~. The prefix ~ge-~ here is the old perfective/collective prefix.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~an~ ("on, at"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix adds a sense of attachment or belonging-to.

The semantic evolution of ~gehören~ is fascinating: it began as "to listen to, to obey" (related to ~hören~, "to hear") and shifted to "to belong to." The logic is that what one hearkens to is what one is beholden to, and by extension, what one belongs to. Old English ~ġehīeran~ and Gothic ~gahausjan~ are cognates that retained the original hearing sense. The further compound ~angehören~ ("to be a member of") intensifies the belonging sense with ~an-~ ("to, at"), emphasizing attachment to a group. English ~hear~ is the root cognate, from PIE *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"), literally "to be sharp-eared."
en.angeloben:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~ge-~ + ~loben~:

• ~loben~: From MHG ~loben~, from OHG ~lobēn~/~lobōn~ ("to praise, approve"), from Proto-West Germanic *~lubōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lubō~, from PIE *~lewbʰ-~ ("to love, desire, praise"), the same root as ~lieb~ and ~Liebe~. Cognate with Old English ~lofian~ ("to praise"), Dutch ~loven~, Swedish ~lova~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

Of the two prefixes only ~an-~ still does visible work: ~geloben~ had already drifted from "praise" to "pledge" before ~an-~ was added to name the authority the pledge is made to. The compound survives chiefly in Austrian official usage, where an ~Angelobung~ is the swearing-in of soldiers and ministers.
en.angießen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~gießen~:

• ~gießen~: From MHG ~giezen~, from OHG ~giozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geutan~ ("to pour"), from Proto-Germanic *~geutaną~, from PIE *~gʰewd-~ ("to pour"). The sense of casting metal and glass is attested since Old High German (participle ~gigozzan~). Cognate with English ~gush~, Dutch ~gieten~, Old English ~geotan~, Gothic ~giutan~, Swedish ~gjuta~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The compound runs in two directions from one image: in the kitchen and the garden one pours liquid onto something, while in the foundry one pours metal around a form, the source of the idiom ~wie angegossen~ ("as if cast on"), said of clothing that fits perfectly.
en.angleichen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~gleichen~:

• ~gleichen~: From MHG ~gelīchen~, from OHG ~gilīhhon~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkōną~ ("to make alike, resemble"), from *~galīkaz~ ("alike, similar"), from *~ga-~ + *~līkam~ ("body, form"), from PIE *~leyg-~ ("image, likeness"). A strong verb (~glich~, ~geglichen~), one of the few built on a deadjectival base. Cognate with English ~like~, Dutch ~gelijken~, Old Norse ~glíkr~, Danish ~ligne~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

Because ~gleichen~ sits on the adjective ~gleich~, ~angleichen~ names a movement rather than a state: two things are brought toward sameness without becoming identical. That is why it is also the linguists' term for the assimilation of one sound to its neighbor.
en.angreifen:
From Middle High German ~anegrīfen~ ("to grab, seize upon, assault, attack"), from Old High German ~anagrīfan~ ("to touch, grab, seize, attack"), from Proto-West Germanic *~anagrīpan~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~greifen~:

• ~greifen~: From MHG ~grīfen~, from OHG ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~ ("to grab, grasp"), from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). Cognate with English ~grip~, ~gripe~, Lithuanian ~griebti~ ("to seize").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). As a verbal prefix, ~an-~ conveys contact, approach, or the beginning of an action.

The semantic development from "to seize upon" to "to attack" is straightforward: an attack is an aggressive grasping at the enemy. In Austrian German, ~angreifen~ retains the older, gentler meaning "to touch, to handle," synonymous with ~anfassen~ or ~berühren~. The related noun ~Angriff~ ("attack") and the sibling compound ~begreifen~ ("to comprehend," literally "to grasp at") both preserve different metaphorical extensions of the same root. Cognate with Dutch ~aangrijpen~ ("to seize, to grip"), Low German ~angriepen~.
en.angucken:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~gucken~:

• ~gucken~: From MHG ~gücken~, ~guggen~ ("to look inquisitively, to peek"), of uncertain origin, perhaps from MHG ~gücken~, OHG ~guckōn~ ("to cuckoo"), via the image of peeping out from cover. The variant ~kucken~ is attributed to influence from Low German ~kieken~. Colloquial and northern/central German; the south prefers ~schauen~. Cognate with Dutch ~kijken~, Luxembourgish ~kucken~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

~Angucken~ is the everyday northern and central German word where the south says ~anschauen~ and the written language says ~ansehen~; the Bundestag protocols are full of it precisely because it belongs to speech.
en.anhaben:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

Two idioms share the form. With a garment as object, ~anhaben~ means to have it on the body, the ~an-~ of contact. With a person in the dative and a negation it means to be unable to harm them: ~er kann mir nichts anhaben~, where the same ~an-~ marks a grip that never takes hold.
en.anhaften:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~haften~:

• ~haften~: From ~Haft~ + ~-en~. ~Haft~ descends through MHG ~haft~, ~hafte~ ("captivity") and OHG ~haft~ to PIE *~kh₂p-tó-~, from *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize"). Hence both senses: "to stick, adhere" (to be held fast) and "to be liable." Cognate with English ~captive~, Latin ~captus~, Old English ~hæft~, Old Irish ~cacht~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

Because the base is the noun ~Haft~, ~anhaften~ inherits the image of being held fast: a stain adheres to cloth and a suspicion adheres to a person by the same verb. Legal ~haften~ ("to be liable") is that same being-held-fast, seen from the debtor's side.
en.anhalten:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, onto"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). As a separable prefix, it adds a sense of continuation or initiation.

~Anhalten~ has two principal senses: "to stop" (transitive and intransitive) and "to persist, to continue" (~die Hitze hält an~, "the heat persists"). These seem contradictory: how can one word mean both "to stop" and "to continue"? The answer lies in the prefix: ~an-~ adds "on, onto," so ~anhalten~ is literally "to hold on." Holding on can mean braking to a standstill (holding on to stop forward motion) or enduring (holding on through time). The derived noun ~Anhalter~ means "hitchhiker", someone who ~hält Autos an~ ("stops cars"). ~Per Anhalter fahren~ ("to travel by hitchhiking") is the phrase rendered in the German title of Douglas Adams's famous novel: ~Per Anhalter durch die Galaxis~ (~The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy~).
en.anhauen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~hauen~:

• ~hauen~: From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). Originally a class VII strong verb (~hauen~, ~hieb~, ~gehauen~), partially weakened colloquially, where ~haute~ competes with ~hieb~. Cognate with English ~hew~, Latin ~cūdere~ ("to strike, forge").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

Colloquially the blow can be a verbal one: ~jemanden um Geld anhauen~ is to accost someone for money, the same metaphor English arrives at, from the same kind of verb, in "to hit someone up."
en.anheben:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb: the past ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ continue the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

Two senses live in the compound. The older is inchoative (~hob an zu singen~, "began to sing"), now archaic and elevated, and it is the sense of the Nietzsche passage quoted. The current one is to raise something part of the way, from which officialese forms the ~Anhebung~ ("increase") of wages and taxes.
en.anheimfallen:
Compound of the frozen adverb ~anheim~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~anheim-~: A frozen adverbial phrase, ~an~ + ~heim~, in which ~heim~ is the old directional accusative "homeward" rather than the locative ~heime~ ("at home"). Early New High German added ~an-~ to make the directional sense explicit once accusative and dative had fallen together in form. The phrase no longer exists as a free adverb and survives only in ~anheimfallen~ ("to pass into someone's possession") and ~anheimstellen~ ("to leave to someone's discretion"), both of elevated register; ~heim~ is cognate with English ~home~. ~anheim-~ marks something as passing into another's possession or keeping.

The compound is legal and elevated: an estate without heirs ~fällt dem Staat anheim~, and a person may fall prey to oblivion or ruin. The subject never acts: it falls, and someone else receives.
en.anheimgeben:
Compound of the frozen adverb ~anheim~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~anheim-~: A frozen adverbial phrase, ~an~ + ~heim~, in which ~heim~ is the old directional accusative "homeward" rather than the locative ~heime~ ("at home"). Early New High German added ~an-~ to make the directional sense explicit once accusative and dative had fallen together in form. The phrase no longer exists as a free adverb and survives only in ~anheimfallen~ ("to pass into someone's possession") and ~anheimstellen~ ("to leave to someone's discretion"), both of elevated register; ~heim~ is cognate with English ~home~. ~anheim-~ hands a matter over to someone else's judgment.

~Anheimgeben~ is the obsolescent twin of ~anheimstellen~: both hand a decision over to someone else's judgment, but only the compound with ~stellen~ is still alive in present-day official prose.
en.anheimstellen:
Compound of the frozen adverb ~anheim~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~anheim-~: A frozen adverbial phrase, ~an~ + ~heim~, in which ~heim~ is the old directional accusative "homeward" rather than the locative ~heime~ ("at home"). Early New High German added ~an-~ to make the directional sense explicit once accusative and dative had fallen together in form. The phrase no longer exists as a free adverb and survives only in ~anheimfallen~ ("to pass into someone's possession") and ~anheimstellen~ ("to leave to someone's discretion"), both of elevated register; ~heim~ is cognate with English ~home~. ~anheim-~ hands a matter over to someone else's judgment.

Of the three ~anheim~ verbs this is the liveliest: ~ich stelle es Ihnen anheim~ is the polite formula by which an office surrenders a decision without offering a recommendation, and one of the very few places the adverb ~anheim~ still appears at all.
en.anhängen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~hängen~:

• ~hängen~: The merger of three OHG verbs: ~hāhan~ (strong, transitive; past ~hieng~, participle ~gehangan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~hą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~hanhaną~; ~hangēn~ (weak, intransitive); and the causative ~hengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hangijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hangijaną~. The distinction is upheld chiefly in the past tense: intransitive ~hing~/~gehangen~ versus transitive ~hängte~/~gehängt~. Cognate with Dutch ~hangen~, English ~hang~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The base verb's threefold merger splits the compound too: transitive and weak ~hängte an~, ~angehängt~ ("to attach something"), intransitive and strong ~hing an~, ~angehangen~ ("to be devoted to someone"). The strong intransitive series carries the elevated sense of attachment that Luther means.
en.anhören:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauʀijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~ ("to hear"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), a compound of *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear") + *~-yéti~ (denominative suffix). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~an~ ("on, at"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix adds a sense of directed, attentive listening.

The PIE etymology of "to hear" is delightfully literal: *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ means "to be sharp-eared," combining the root for "sharp" (also the source of Latin ~acer~ and English ~acrid~) with the root for "ear" (source of Latin ~auris~ and English ~ear~). While ~hören~ means simply "to hear," ~anhören~ implies deliberate, sustained listening, "to listen to" rather than merely "to hear." The reflexive ~sich etwas anhören~ adds the further nuance of enduring something one must listen to, as in ~sich eine Predigt anhören~ ("to sit through a sermon").
en.ankaufen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, a denominative verb from *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"), a loanword from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper"). Cognate with English ~cheap~, Dutch ~kopen~, Danish ~købe~, Icelandic ~kaupa~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

Where ~kaufen~ is any purchase, ~ankaufen~ is acquisition into a holding: museums, dealers, and states ~kaufen an~, and the noun ~Ankauf~ names the transaction from the acquirer's side of the ledger.
en.anklagen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~klagen~:

• ~klagen~: From MHG ~klagen~, from OHG ~klagōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klagōn~ ("to lament, complain"), a denominative verb from *~klagu~ ("lamentation, complaint"). The ultimate origin is uncertain: often compared to Proto-Indo-Iranian *~garjʰ-~, but phonologically difficult; some favor an onomatopoeic origin. It keeps both an emotional and a legal sense.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The base verb keeps an emotional and a legal sense side by side, and the prefix does not choose between them: in the Grundgesetz the Bundestag ~klagt~ the federal president ~an~, while in the fairy tale a grieving man accuses God. Both are the one verb, aiming the complaint at someone.
en.ankleben:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~kleben~:

• ~kleben~: From MHG ~kleben~, from OHG ~klebēn~ ("to stick"), from Proto-West Germanic *~klibēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klibēną~, from PIE *~gleyb-~ ("to stick, adhere"), a durative formation from the strong root *~kleibēną~ ("to adhere, to climb"). Cognate with English ~cleave~ and ~climb~, Old Norse ~klīfa~ ("to climb").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The compound works in both directions: transitively one sticks a notice up, intransitively something sticks to one. Luther uses the second figuratively (sin clings like tar) and that use is still the commonest.
en.anklicken:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~klicken~:

• ~klicken~: Attested from the 16th century, from MHG *~klicken~, preserved in ~zerklicken~ ("to break an eggshell"); ultimately imitative. Either cognate with or formed in parallel to Dutch ~klikken~, English ~click~, French ~cliquer~. The computing sense is a 20th-century semantic loan from English. Regular and weak.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

~Anklicken~ is by far the youngest compound in this family: German built it in the 1980s on English "to click on," turning the English preposition into a separable particle with the object between the two halves; ~klicken Sie den Link an~.
en.anklingen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~klingen~:

• ~klingen~: From MHG ~klingen~, from OHG ~klingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~klinganą~, almost certainly of onomatopoeic origin. A class III strong verb (~klingt~, ~klang~, ~geklungen~), the same pattern as ~singen~. Cognate with English ~clink~ and ~clang~, Middle Dutch ~klinken~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

The verb is almost always figurative: a motif, a reproach, or a memory ~klingt an~, meaning it becomes just barely audible without being stated. The phrase ~etwas anklingen lassen~ turns that into a device for hinting.
en.anknüpfen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~knüpfen~:

• ~knüpfen~: From MHG ~knüpfen~, from OHG ~knupfen~, ~chnuphan~, related to ~Knopf~ ("button, knob"), from MHG ~knopf~, OHG ~knopf~, Proto-Germanic *~knuppaz~ ("lump, clod, knob"). The word belongs to the Germanic ~kn-~ cluster for lumps and knots: ~Knoten~, ~Knochen~, ~Knauf~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

From the knot the verb moves into the figurative: one ~knüpft~ contacts and relationships ~an~, and ~an etwas anknüpfen~ is to take up a thread already laid, an image English draws independently from the same craft in "to pick up the thread."
en.ankommen:
From Middle High German ~anekomen~, from Old High German ~anaqueman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~anakweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~anakwemaną~ ("to come to, come at, arrive"). Compound of ~an-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, from OHG ~queman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~ ("to step"). Cognate with English ~come~, Latin ~venīre~.
• ~an-~: From Proto-Indo-European *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). This separable prefix indicates arrival at a destination.

Gothic preserves the direct ancestor of the compound in ~anaqiman~, showing how old the formation is. The modern idiom ~es kommt drauf an~ ("it depends") (literally "it arrives on it") retains the spatial logic of the prefix. Cognate with Dutch ~aankomen~.
en.ankämpfen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~kämpfen~:

• ~kämpfen~: From MHG ~kempfen~, from OHG *~kempfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kampijan~, a denominal verb from *~kamp~ ("field, battlefield"), borrowed from Latin ~campus~ ("field, open plain"); the sense shifted early from the place of battle to the act of fighting. Latin ~campus~ also gives English ~camp~ and ~champion~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

~Ankämpfen~ almost always takes ~gegen~, and the pairing carries an implication the simple verb lacks: one fights against a current, a rumor, or a fatigue that pushes back. The compound describes sustained resistance, not a battle won.
en.ankündigen:
~An-~ + ~kündigen~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~kündigen~:

• ~kündigen~: From MHG ~kündigen~ ("to make known"), derived from the adjective ~kündic~ (modern ~kundig~, "knowledgeable, informed"). ~Kundig~ descends from OHG ~kundīg~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kunþīg~, from Proto-Germanic *~kunþīgaz~, from *~kunþaz~ ("known"), originally the past participle of *~kunnaną~ ("to know, to be able"), from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know").
• ~an-~: From PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The separable prefix adds a sense of direction toward an audience.

~Ankündigen~ means "to announce, to herald, to give advance notice of." The prefix ~an-~ directs the announcement ~toward~ an audience: to ~ankündigen~ is to make something known ~at~ or ~to~ someone. The PIE root *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know") is one of the most productive in all Indo-European languages: it gave Latin ~gnōscō~ / ~nōscō~ ("to get to know") (whence English ~cognition~, ~recognize~, ~noble~ (via ~nōbilis~, "well-known"), ~note~, and ~notion~), as well as Greek ~gignṓskō~ ("to perceive"), whence ~gnosis~, ~diagnosis~, and ~prognosis~. German ~können~ ("to be able") descends from the same root, reflecting the ancient idea that knowing and being able are the same thing. English ~know~ likewise descends from *~ǵneh₃-~ through the Germanic branch, via Old English ~cnāwan~. Interestingly, ~kündigen~ alone means "to terminate, to give notice" (as in quitting a job), while ~ankündigen~ means simply "to announce"; the prefix reshapes the word entirely. Cognate with Dutch ~aankondigen~.
en.anlachen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~lachen~:

• ~lachen~: From MHG ~lachen~, from OHG ~lahhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~, from PIE *~kleg-~ ("to cry out, sound"). The initial ~hl-~ cluster was simplified to ~l-~ in Old High German. Cognate with English ~laugh~, Dutch ~lachen~, Gothic ~hlahjan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

Unlike ~auslachen~ ("to laugh at, to mock"), ~anlachen~ is friendly: it aims the laughter at someone without making them its butt. Kafka plays on exactly that expectation by having K. laugh at a door. Colloquially, ~sich jemanden anlachen~ also means to win someone over.
en.anlagern:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~lagern~:

• ~lagern~: Derived from the noun ~Lager~ ("camp, store, warehouse"), from MHG ~lëger~, from OHG ~lëgar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~legr~, from Proto-Germanic *~legrą~. The modern form with ~-a-~ is of East Central German origin, influenced by ~Lage~ ("position"). Cognate with English ~lair~, Dutch ~leger~, Danish ~lejr~, Swedish ~läger~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The compound is now almost purely technical and usually reflexive: in chemistry a molecule ~lagert sich an~ another, and in geology material accretes onto a slope. Of ~Lager~ as a place only the settling-down remains, now onto a surface.
en.anlaufen:
~Anlaufen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

The inchoative reading dominates today (an engine ~läuft an~ when it starts up), but the older concrete sense of running up against something survives in ~einen Hafen anlaufen~, to put in at a harbor.
en.anlauten:
~Anlauten~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~lauten~:

• ~lauten~: From MHG ~lūten~ ("to sound, ring"), from OHG ~hlūtēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlūdēn~; ~Laut~ ("sound") plus the suffix ~-en~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlūdaz~ ("loud"). ~lauten~ means "to read as, to run"; ~läuten~ ("to ring") is the factitive of the same root. Cognate with English ~loud~, Dutch ~luid~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

The verb is a term of art in linguistics: a word ~lautet~ with whatever sound it begins with ~an~, and the noun ~Anlaut~ names that initial sound. Here the ~an-~ marks the beginning of a word rather than the beginning of an action.
en.anlegen: Formed from prefix ~an-~ (from PIE *~h₂en~, "on, onto") and ~legen~, from MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The compound traces to Proto-Germanic *~analagjaną~. The causative root *~lagjaną~ ("to lay, to cause to lie") is itself from PIE *~logʰéyeti~, the causative of *~legh-~ ("to lie"). English ~lay~ is a direct cognate. ~Anlegen~ is semantically rich: to lay something on (dock a boat), to put on (a garment), to invest (money), or to create (a garden). The single prefix transforms one root into a dozen contextual meanings.
en.anlehnen:
~Anlehnen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~lehnen~:

• ~lehnen~: A merger of two verbs: MHG ~linen~/~lenen~ (intransitive), from OHG ~hlinēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlinēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlināną~, from PIE *~k̂ley-~ ("to lean, incline"); and MHG ~leinen~ (causative), from OHG ~hleinen~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlainijaną~. A second, archaic ~lehnen~ ("to lend, borrow"), from OHG ~lēhanōn~, survives only in ~entlehnen~ and ~Lehnwort~. Cognate with English ~lean~, Latin ~clīnō~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The compound is usually reflexive (~sich an etwas anlehnen~) and figuratively ~sich an ein Vorbild anlehnen~ means to model oneself on something. The homophonous ~lehnen~ ("to lend") plays no part here; that branch survives only in ~entlehnen~.
en.anleiten:
~Anleiten~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~: the causative *~laidijaną~ of the strong verb *~līþaną~ ("to pass, go") with the suffix *~-janą~ ("to cause to go"), from PIE *~leyt-~ ("to go, depart, die"). ~leiten~ and ~leiden~ are a base-and-causative pair. Cognate with English ~lead~ (OE ~lǣdan~).
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The root's causative force ("to cause to go"), is still legible: to ~anleiten~ someone is to set them going in a task, not merely to tell them about it.
en.anlernen:
~Anlernen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~lernen~:

• ~lernen~: From MHG ~lernen~, from OHG ~lernēn~, ~lirnēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~liʀnēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lizaną~, from PIE *~leys-~ ("track, furrow, trail"): to learn is to follow the trail laid down before. ~lehren~ ("to teach") shares the stem in causative function. Cognate with Old English ~leornian~ (English ~learn~), Dutch ~lernen~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

German distinguishes ~anlernen~ sharply from ~lehren~: an ~angelernter Arbeiter~ was shown one operation on the job rather than schooled in a trade, and the participle keeps a residue of incompleteness.
en.anlesen:
~Anlesen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

The partial reading is what makes the verb useful: ~ein Buch anlesen~ is to read into it far enough to decide whether to go on, and the root's old sense "to gather" suits that, a few letters gathered up rather than the whole harvest.
en.anliegen:
~Anliegen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The compound stays close to the root's literal posture: cloth ~liegt an~ when it rests against the body. The older use with a dative person, "to press someone with a request", has largely given way to the noun ~Anliegen~, a concern or request.
en.anlocken:
~Anlocken~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~locken~:

• ~locken~: From MHG ~locken~, from OHG ~lockōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lokkōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lukkōną~ ("to entice, to lure"). A second, homonymous ~locken~ ("to curl"), from OHG ~lochōn~ and the noun ~Locke~, is etymologically distinct. Related to ~lügen~, Latin ~laciō~ ("I entice"); English has no direct cognate and uses ~lure~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

The bait does the work: ~anlocken~ names the enticement and leaves the destination the prey arrives at unsaid. The root's kinship with ~lügen~ suits it: both come out of the vocabulary of deception.
en.anlächeln:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~lächeln~:

• ~lächeln~: From MHG ~lecheln~, from ~lachen~ ("to laugh") plus the diminutive suffix ~-eln~, literally "to laugh a little," the suffix triggering the umlaut ~a~ → ~ä~. ~lachen~ itself is from MHG ~lachen~, OHG ~lahhen~, Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~. Cognate with English ~laugh~, Old Norse ~hlæja~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The base verb is intransitive; only the prefix gives it an accusative object, and that is the whole force of the compound. Thomas Mann sets the difference side by side in one line: Tadzio ~lächelte~, then ~anlächelte~ him, and only the second reaches a person.
en.anlügen:
~Anlügen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~lügen~:

• ~lügen~: From MHG ~liegen~, from OHG ~liogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~leugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~leuganą~, from PIE *~lewgʰ-~ ("to lie, swear falsely"). A class II strong verb (~lügen~, ~log~, ~gelogen~); the ~ü~ is late, taken from the noun ~Lüge~ to keep the verb from colliding with ~liegen~. Cognate with English ~lie~, Gothic ~liugan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

Where ~belügen~ takes the deceived person as the object of a completed deception, ~anlügen~ aims the lie straight at them; the ~an-~ makes the person addressed the target of the lie.
en.anmachen:
~Anmachen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

The modern range is wide (one ~macht~ a light, a fire, or a salad ~an~), and colloquially ~jemanden anmachen~ is to hit on or to needle someone, the ~an-~ having slid from starting a thing to aiming an action at a person.
en.anmalen:
~Anmalen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~malen~:

• ~malen~: From MHG ~mālen~, from OHG ~mālōn~, ~mālēn~, a denominative of the noun ~māl~ ("spot, mark"), from Proto-West Germanic *~mālijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~mēlijaną~, from *~mēlą~, from PIE *~melh₂-~ ("dark color"). Not to be confused with ~mahlen~ ("to grind"), of separate origin. Cognate with Dutch ~maal~, Greek ~melas~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The root's descent from ~māl~ ("spot, mark") shows in the compound: ~anmalen~ puts color onto a surface rather than bringing a picture into being, which is ~malen~ on its own. It has nothing to do with ~mahlen~ ("to grind").
en.anmelden: Formed from prefix ~an-~ (from PIE *~h₂en~, "on, onto") and ~melden~, from MHG ~mëlden~, from OHG ~mëldōn~, ~mëldēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~melþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~melþōną~, from PIE *~meldʰ-~ ("to ask, pray, speak"). The compound means "to register, to log in, to announce one's arrival." The prefix ~an-~ contributes a sense of directed address: one reports oneself ~an~ (to) an authority or a system. In the digital age, ~anmelden~ has become the standard German verb for "to log in," while ~abmelden~ serves as its antonym "to log out", a mirror-image pair that modern users encounter constantly.
en.anmerken:
~Anmerken~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~merken~:

• ~merken~: From MHG ~merken~, from OHG ~merchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~markijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~markijaną~ ("to mark, notice"), a denominal verb from *~marką~ ("mark, sign"). To notice something is etymologically to leave a mental mark on it. Cognate with English ~mark~ (and ~remark~), Icelandic ~merkja~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

Both readings live in the one compound: you ~merkst etwas an~ by adding a remark, and you ~merkst jemandem etwas an~ by seeing it in them, the root's mental mark, become visible on a face.
en.anmischen:
~Anmischen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~mischen~:

• ~mischen~: From MHG ~mischen~, from OHG ~misken~, from Proto-Germanic *~miskijaną~ ("to mix"), from PIE *~meyḱ-~ ("to mix, knead"), via the inchoative present *~miḱ-sḱé-~. Cognate with English ~mix~, Latin ~misceō~, Greek ~mísgo~, Sanskrit ~miśrá~ ("mixed").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The compound names the making of a mixture rather than the stirring itself: paint, mortar, or a solution is ~angemischt~ and thereby comes into being.
en.annehmen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb.
• ~an-~: From OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana-~, from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). As a separable prefix, ~an-~ adds a sense of acceptance, approach, or adoption: "taking something onto oneself."

The compound has developed a rich semantic range: "to accept" (an offer), "to adopt" (a child), "to assume" (a hypothesis), and "to pass" (a law). The reflexive ~sich annehmen~ ("to take care of, attend to") adds yet another shade. The PIE root *~nem-~ is the same root underlying Greek ~νέμω~ (~nemō~, "to distribute, manage") and German ~Nomade~ (via Latin ~nomas~, "one who wanders in search of pasture"), at bottom, ~annehmen~ means taking what is due to you. Cognate with Dutch ~aannemen~.
en.annähern:
~Annähern~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~nähern~:

• ~nähern~: From the comparative ~näher~ ("nearer") with the verbal suffix ~-n~ ("to make nearer") from the adjective ~nah~, from MHG ~nāch~, OHG ~nāh~, Proto-West Germanic *~nāh~, Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~ ("near"), from PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). Almost always reflexive: ~sich nähern~. Cognate with English ~nigh~ (OE ~nēah~), Dutch ~na~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

The verb is almost always reflexive, and the ~an-~ doubles a comparative that is already inside the root: ~sich annähern~ is to bring oneself nearer to something. The adverb ~annähernd~ ("approximately") froze out of the participle.
en.anordnen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~ordnen~:

• ~ordnen~: From MHG ~ordenen~, from OHG ~ordinōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ordinōn~ ("to order, put in order"), borrowed from Latin ~ōrdināre~ ("to arrange, set in order"), from ~ōrdō~ ("row, rank, order"). A doublet of ~ordinieren~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, onto"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys "on, at, to" or initiation of an action.

~Anordnen~ means "to order, to arrange, to decree." The Latin source ~ōrdō~ originally meant "a row of threads in a loom" before generalizing to any ordered arrangement. German borrowed the verb early (in the OHG period) but gave it a native prefix: ~an-~ adds the sense of directing an order toward someone. The doublet is instructive: ~ordinieren~ entered later via ecclesiastical Latin (meaning "to ordain a priest"), while ~ordnen~ and ~anordnen~ came earlier and stayed secular. English ~order~ and ~ordain~ mirror this split.
en.anpassen:
Equivalent to ~an-~ + ~passen~:

• ~passen~: From MHG ~pazzen~, borrowed from Italian ~passare~ or French ~passer~, from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, from Latin ~passus~ ("step, pace").
• ~an-~: From PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix adds the sense of fitting something onto or adjusting to something.

~Anpassen~ means "to adapt, to adjust, to fit"; one ~passt~ clothing ~an~ (adjusts the fit), ~passt sich an~ a new environment (adapts oneself), or ~passt~ a plan ~an~ new circumstances (adjusts it). The reflexive ~sich anpassen~ ("to adapt oneself") has become central in biological (~Anpassung an die Umwelt~, "adaptation to the environment") and social (~sich der Gesellschaft anpassen~, "to conform to society") discourse. The derived noun ~Anpassung~ ("adaptation") is the standard German translation of Darwin's concept of adaptation: a Latin-rooted verb with an Arabic-influenced French intermediary, now wearing a Germanic prefix and suffix to discuss evolutionary biology. Cognate with Dutch ~aanpassen~.
en.anpfeifen:
~Anpfeifen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~pfeifen~:

• ~pfeifen~: From MHG ~pfīfen~, from OHG ~pfīfōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pīpōn~ ("to play a pipe, to whistle"), an early borrowing from Vulgar Latin *~pīpāre~ ("to chirp, peep"), a word of imitative origin. Originally weak, now a class I strong verb (~pfeifen~, ~pfiff~, ~gepfiffen~). Cognate with English ~pipe~ and ~peep~, French ~piper~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

The referee's whistle gives the modern sense (~ein Spiel anpfeifen~ opens the match), but German kept an older use too: ~jemanden anpfeifen~ is to bawl someone out, the whistle aimed at a person instead of at a beginning.
en.anpreisen:
~Anpreisen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~preisen~:

• ~preisen~: From MHG ~prīsen~ ("to praise"), from MHG ~prīs~ ("price, worth, glory"), borrowed from Old French ~prisier~ ("to appraise, value"), from Late Latin ~pretiāre~, from ~pretium~ ("price, value"). The loanword was later reanalyzed as a class I strong verb (~preisen~, ~pries~, ~gepriesen~) despite having no Germanic ancestry. The same ~pretium~ gives English ~price~, ~prize~, and ~praise~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The commercial history of the root is still audible: ~preisen~ comes from ~prīs~, a price, so to ~anpreisen~ a good is to hold its worth up to a buyer, praise and price tag were never far apart.
en.anprüfen:
~Anprüfen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~prüfen~:

• ~prüfen~: From MHG ~prüeven~, ultimately from Latin ~probāre~ ("to test, approve, prove"), a denominative of ~probus~ ("good, honest, upright"), from Proto-Italic *~proβwos~, from PIE *~pro-bʰuH-wó-s~ ("being foremost"), from *~pro-~ + *~bʰuH-~ ("to be"). It came via Middle Dutch or Middle Low German, which explains the umlaut. Cognate with English ~prove~, ~probe~, French ~prouver~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

A rare formation beside the everyday ~prüfen~: the ~an-~ demotes a full examination to a first look.
en.anraten:
~Anraten~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~raten~:

• ~raten~: From MHG ~rāten~, from OHG ~rātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rēdaną~ ("to decide, advise, interpret"), from PIE *~Hreh₁dh-~ ("to think, arrange"). Both senses, "to advise" and "to guess," descend from that sense of deliberation. Cognate with English ~read~ (originally "to counsel, interpret"), archaic ~rede~, Dutch ~raden~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The root's older sense of deliberation is what the compound preserves: ~anraten~ is counsel offered to someone, and the participle ~angeraten~ has hardened into the predicate "advisable".
en.anrauchen:
~Anrauchen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~rauchen~:

• ~rauchen~: From MHG ~rouchen~, ~röuchen~, from OHG ~rouhhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raukijan~, derived from the noun *~rauki-~ ("smoke"), from Proto-Germanic *~raukiz~, from *~reukaną~ ("to smoke"), possibly from PIE *~h₁rewg-~ ("to belch, emit"). The noun survives as ~Rauch~. Cognate with English ~reek~, Dutch ~rook~, Swedish ~rök~, Danish ~røg~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

The compound is inchoative, not partitive: an ~angerauchte~ cigarette has been lit and begun, and the noun ~Rauch~ sits visibly inside the root.
en.anrechnen:
~Anrechnen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~rechnen~:

• ~rechnen~: From MHG ~rechenen~, from OHG ~rehhanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rekanōn~ ("to count, explain"), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to make straight or right"), the same root as German ~recht~ and Latin ~rectus~. Cognate with English ~reckon~, Dutch ~rekenen~, Low German ~rekenen~, Danish ~regne~.
