• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The bookkeeping metaphor is still live: something is ~angerechnet~ to a person's account, whether as credit against a bill or, in ~hoch anrechnen~, as credit to their character.
en.anreden:
~Anreden~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

For the act of address itself German uses this compound, and the noun ~Anrede~ names the form of address chosen; the ~an-~ marks that the speech has a target.
en.anregen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~regen~:

• ~regen~: From MHG ~regen~ ("to make protrude, to erect, to excite, to move"), from Proto-Germanic *~hragjaną~ ("to make stand, to wake up, to incite"), a causative formation from *~hreganą~ ("to jut out"), from PIE *~krek-~ ("to project, to protrude").
• ~an-~: From OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana-~, from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix adds a sense of initiating or stimulating action.

The verb ~anregen~ means "to stimulate, to inspire, to suggest," carrying a sense of setting something into motion intellectually or physically. The causative origin is visible: Proto-Germanic *~hragjaną~ meant "to cause to stand up or project," and this evolved through Middle High German into the more abstract sense of stirring someone to action or thought. The noun ~Anregung~ ("suggestion, stimulus, inspiration") is widely used in both casual and academic German. The related verb ~sich regen~ ("to stir, to move") preserves the older physical sense. In modern German, ~anregend~ ("stimulating") can describe a conversation, a cup of coffee, or an idea equally well, while the homograph ~Regen~ ("rain") is an entirely unrelated word from a different Proto-Germanic root (*~regną~).
en.anreihen:
~Anreihen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~reihen~:

• ~reihen~: From MHG ~rīhen~, from OHG ~rīhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rīhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rīhaną~ ("to string together, line up"), possibly from PIE *~h₁reyḱ-~ ("to scratch, tear"), though that connection is uncertain. In the sewing senses it appears to have merged with a separate *~wrīhaną~ ("to cover"). Once strong, now weak (~reihte~, ~gereiht~) and felt as a derivative of ~Reihe~. Cognate with Dutch ~rijgen~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The root's old strong inflection is gone, but the image of threading things onto a string survives in the compound: ~sich anreihen~ is to take one's place at the end of a row, one more bead on the thread.
en.anreisen:
~Anreisen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

The root's military prehistory suits the compound: ~anreisen~ is the journey toward a destination and ~abreisen~ the departure, a pair the modern language needs for conferences rather than campaigns.
en.anreißen:
~Anreißen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

The partial reading gives the everyday senses: a package is ~angerissen~ when it is torn just far enough to open, and a topic is ~angerissen~ when it is broached rather than treated. The root's kinship with English ~write~ (both from scratching) makes the technical ~anreißen~, marking out a line, the oldest of the three.
en.anrennen:
~Anrennen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~rennen~:

• ~rennen~: From a merger of two Old High German verbs: the causative ~rennan~ ("to make something run or flow"), from Proto-Germanic *~rannijaną~, and the intransitive ~rinnan~ ("to run, to flow"), from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~, from PIE *~h₃reyH-~ ("to undulate, churn"). A member of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~ich renne~, ~rannte~, ~gerannt~; no umlaut in the preterite. Cognate with English ~run~, Dutch ~rennen~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action against a resistance, usually alongside a ~gegen~ complement.

The compound keeps a military flavor: one runs at what pushes back (a wall, a line of shields, an argument), and the ~gegen~ that so often accompanies it makes the resistance explicit.
en.anrichten:
~Anrichten~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~ ("to straighten, set right, direct"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rihtijaną~, a denominative from the adjective *~rehtaz~ ("straight, right"), from PIE *~h₃reǵtós~ ("right, straightened"), from *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to stretch out, straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~richten~, Gothic ~raihtjan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks bringing something into being by mixing or preparing it; the base action produces the thing itself.

The two living senses look like opposites (~das Essen anrichten~ sets a meal out, ~Schaden anrichten~ wreaks damage), but both are the root's "to arrange, set in order" with the prefix marking the arranging into existence. Only the object decides whether what is brought into being is welcome.
en.anrufen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~ (also ~hruofan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~hropan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hropanan~. The Proto-Germanic origin is unclear; it may be distantly related to *~hrothiz~ ("glory, fame"), but the exact connection is debated. Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~, English dialectal ~roop~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). This prefix adds a directional quality, turning a general shout into a call directed at someone.

The most common modern use of ~anrufen~ is "to telephone," a meaning that emerged only in the 20th century with the spread of telephone technology. Before that, ~anrufen~ meant simply "to call out to someone" or "to invoke" (as in a legal or religious context: ~das Gericht anrufen~, "to appeal to the court"). The initial ~h-~ in OHG ~hruofan~ (reflecting Proto-Germanic *~hr-~) was lost during the transition to Middle High German, as happened with many words beginning with ~hr-~, ~hl-~, ~hn-~. Interestingly, ~rufen~ historically wavered between strong and weak conjugation; weak forms persisted until the 19th century, and the lack of umlaut in the present tense (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~) is a relic of this weak-verb past.
en.anräumen:
~Anräumen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~räumen~:

• ~räumen~: From Early New High German ~reumen~, a Central German umlaut variant of ~raumen~, from MHG ~rūmen~, from OHG ~rūmen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rūmijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rūmijaną~, a factitive verb from the adjective *~rūmaz~ ("roomy, spacious"), from PIE *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open"). Etymologically, "to make room." Cognate with English ~room~, the noun ~Raum~, Bavarian ~rama~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The compound inverts its familiar sibling: where ~aufräumen~ clears a space, ~anräumen~ fills one, the root's literal "to make room", turned toward putting things into that room.
en.anrücken:
~Anrücken~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~rücken~:

• ~rücken~: From MHG ~rücken~, from OHG ~rucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rukkijan~. The verb means "to move, to shift" and is the base of ~verrückt~ ("crazy," literally "shifted, displaced"); the noun ~Rücken~ ("back") is etymologically a separate word. Cognate with English ~rock~, Old Norse ~rykkja~, Old English ~roccian~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

Where plain ~rücken~ is a shove in any direction, ~anrücken~ fixes the direction as toward the speaker's position, and it is said above all of troops: an army ~rückt an~ before it arrives.
en.anrühren:
~Anrühren~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~rühren~:

• ~rühren~: From MHG ~rüeren~, from OHG ~ruoren~, ~hruoren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōzijaną~; the initial ~hr-~ cluster was gradually simplified in German. The semantic range has stayed stable across a millennium: "to stir," both literally and figuratively. Cognate with Dutch ~roeren~ and the now-rare English ~rear~ ("to move, stir"), surviving in "to rear up."
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The compound splits along its object: ~einen Teig anrühren~ is to stir a batter into being, while ~etwas nicht anrühren~ (the reading given here), is to lay no finger on it at all. The second is the older and more literal contact sense, and it is the one the negative idiom preserves.
en.ansagen:
From Middle High German ~anesagen~, from Old High German ~anasagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~anasaggjan~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ ("to say"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~an~ ("on, at"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix conveys direction: saying something ~to~ someone, making an announcement.

The PIE root *~sekʷ-~ also produced Latin ~inquit~ ("says") and Old Irish ~insce~ ("speech"). In modern German, ~ansagen~ has found new life beyond its traditional meaning of "to announce": it is widely used in the colloquial expression ~angesagt sein~ ("to be trendy, in vogue"), a usage that emerged in the late 20th century. The word ~Ansager~ ("announcer") was the standard term for a television presenter before the English loanword ~Moderator~ largely replaced it.
en.ansammeln:
~Ansammeln~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~sammeln~:

• ~sammeln~: From MHG ~samelen~, ~samlen~, by dissimilation from ~samenen~, from Proto-Germanic *~samnōną~ ("to bring together, gather"), derived from *~samanai~ ("together") with the verbal suffix *~-ōną~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, same, together"), the root behind English ~same~ and Latin ~similis~. Cognate with Dutch ~verzamelen~, Swedish ~samla~, Gothic ~samjan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks accumulation or acquisition: building up a holding until it is full or obtained.

The root already means "to bring together"; the prefix adds the running total, which is why the verb is at home with reflexive subjects: dust, capital, and experience all ~sammeln sich an~ without anyone gathering them.
en.ansaufen:
~Ansaufen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~saufen~:

• ~saufen~: From MHG ~sūfen~ ("to sip, drink"), from OHG ~sūfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sūpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sūpaną~, from PIE *~sewp-~, a labial extension of *~sew-~ ("to take liquid, slurp"). A class II strong verb (~saufen~, ~soff~, ~gesoffen~). The drift from "to sip" to today's "to booze" dates only to the sixteenth century. Cognate with English ~sup~, Dutch ~zuipen~, Old Norse ~súpa~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks accumulation or acquisition: building up a holding until it is full or obtained.

Almost always reflexive (~sich einen ansaufen~), the compound treats drunkenness as something acquired by the glassful, a holding built up until it is full. The root's own drift from "to sip" to "to booze" has left it too coarse for anything else.
en.anschaffen:
~Anschaffen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~schaffen~:

• ~schaffen~: Two historically distinct verbs have merged under a single infinitive, distinguished only by their conjugation. The strong ~schaffen~ (~schuf~, ~geschaffen~, "to create") descends from MHG ~schaffen~, OHG ~scaffan~, a byform of ~skephen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skappjan~; the ~-f-~ was chiefly back-formed from the participle ~giscaffan~. The weak ~schaffen~ (~schaffte~, ~geschafft~, "to manage, accomplish") descends from OHG ~skaffōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skapōn~, from the same root. Cognate with Dutch ~scheppen~, English ~shape~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks accumulation or acquisition: building up a holding until it is full or obtained.

The reading is weak (~schaffte an~, ~angeschafft~), which places it on the ~skaffōn~ branch of the merged root, the one that means "to manage, provide," not the strong ~schuf~ branch that means "to create." One procures a thing rather than making it, and the prefix supplies the acquisition.
en.anschalten:
~Anschalten~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~schalten~:

• ~schalten~: From MHG ~schalten~, from OHG ~scaltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaldan~ ("to push, shove"); the further etymology is debated, Pokorny deriving it from PIE *~(s)kelH-~ ("to split, separate"), which would relate it to English ~shell~. The physical sense of shoving a lever became the modern "to switch, shift gears, manage." Cognate with Old Saxon ~skaldan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

The root's oldest sense (shoving a pole or a lever), is startlingly literal here: to switch a machine on was once to push its lever over, and the modern verb has kept the gesture while losing the pole.
en.anschauen: Formed from prefix ~an-~ (from PIE *~h₂en~, "on, onto") and ~schauen~, from MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, feel, take note of"). The prefix transforms "to look" into "to look at" with directed, attentive focus: to gaze upon something. A near-synonym ~ansehen~ (~sehen~ from MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice")) can be interchangeable, but ~anschauen~ tends to carry a slightly more contemplative or visual-aesthetic sense; one ~schaut~ a painting or a landscape ~an~. Note the German idiom ~Schau an!~ ("Well, look at that!"), a trace of the older sense of directed, surprised gaze.
en.anscheinen:
~Anscheinen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~scheinen~:

• ~scheinen~: From MHG ~schīnen~, from OHG ~skīnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skīnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skīnaną~, from PIE *~(s)ḱeh₁y-~ ("to shine, shimmer"). A class I strong verb. It covers both "to shine" and "to seem," a duality reflecting the ancient metaphor of appearances as light. Cognate with English ~shine~, Dutch ~schijnen~, Danish ~skinne~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

Literally "to shine upon": the light is directed at a target the way a glance is in ~ansehen~. The verb has become rare because its present participle broke away and lexicalized as the adverb ~anscheinend~ ("apparently"), the appearance-side of the root's shine/seem duality, frozen into a single word.
en.anscheißen:
~Anscheißen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~scheißen~:

• ~scheißen~: From MHG ~schīzen~, from OHG *~skīzan~ (attested only in the compound ~biskīzan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~skītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skītaną~, from PIE *~skeyd-~ ("to split, separate"); the root's basic sense is separation, not filth. A class I strong verb (~scheißen~, ~schiss~, ~geschissen~). Cognate with English ~shit~, Dutch ~schijten~, Old Norse ~skíta~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The root's Indo-European sense is separation rather than filth, but that abstraction is long gone; what the prefix adds is an addressee, turning the coarse verb into a dressing-down aimed squarely at someone.
en.anschicken:
~Anschicken~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~schicken~:

• ~schicken~: From MHG ~schicken~ ("to outfit oneself, fit in, arrange appropriately"), from OHG *~skihhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skikkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skikkijaną~ ("to order, send"), the causative of the verb underlying MHG ~geschehen~ ("to happen, rush"). The sense "to send" grew from "to make ready to go." Related to English ~chic~ (via French), ~geschickt~, and ~Schicksal~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

The compound is reflexive (~sich anschicken~, to be on the point of doing something), and it preserves the root's medieval sense of arranging and readying oneself, which plain ~schicken~ lost when it narrowed to "send." The prefix supplies the threshold: the action is begun but not yet under way.
en.anschießen:
~Anschießen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb (~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~). Cognate with English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Old Norse ~skjóta~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

The prefix is what distinguishes wounding from killing: an ~angeschossenes~ animal has been shot but not shot dead, the action carried out only part of the way. The same partial reading gives the participle its figurative use for someone politically damaged but still standing.
en.anschlagen:
~Anschlagen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

Contact unifies a wide range: one strikes a limb against a doorframe, strikes up a gait or a note, and nails a notice to a board, and it is that last, physical act of fastening paper to wood that gave German ~Anschlag~ in the sense of a posted proclamation.
en.anschleichen:
~Anschleichen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~schleichen~:

• ~schleichen~: From MHG ~slīchen~, from OHG ~slīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slīkaną~ ("to glide, creep"), from PIE *~sleyg-~ ("to be smooth, slide"). A class I strong verb (~schleichen~, ~schlich~, ~geschlichen~). Cognate with English ~slick~ and ~sleek~, Dutch ~slijken~, Old Norse ~slíkr~ ("smooth").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

The root supplies the manner and the prefix the direction: a gliding, smooth approach aimed at a target that must not notice it. Usually reflexive (~sich an jemanden anschleichen~) and the smoothness is literal, since the same Indo-European root gave English ~slick~.
en.anschließen:
From Middle High German ~aneslieȥen~, equivalent to ~an-~ + ~schließen~:

• ~schließen~: From MHG ~slieȥen~, from OHG ~slioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sleutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sleutaną~, from PIE *~klew-~ ("to close, shut").
• ~an-~: From PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix adds the sense of attachment or connection.

The semantic range of ~anschließen~ runs from the physical ("to connect, to plug in", ~den Computer anschließen~) to the social ("to join", ~sich einer Gruppe anschließen~, "to join a group") to the temporal ("to follow", ~anschließend~, "subsequently"). All these meanings share the image of closing something onto something else: locking one thing to another. The reflexive ~sich anschließen~ is particularly productive: one can attach oneself to a group, an opinion, or a movement. The derived adjective ~anschließend~ ("subsequent, following") has become one of German's most common temporal connectors, its etymological sense of "locking on after" faded to a mere "and then." Cognate with Dutch ~aansluiten~.
en.anschmeißen:
~Anschmeißen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~schmeißen~:

• ~schmeißen~: From MHG ~smīȥen~, from OHG ~smīȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~smītaną~, from PIE *~smeyd-~. A class I strong verb (~schmeißen~, ~schmiss~, ~geschmissen~). Cognate with English ~smite~, Dutch ~smijten~, Danish ~smide~, Gothic ~bismeitan~ ("to smear, to anoint").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

A colloquial twin of ~anwerfen~ and ~anmachen~: the root's violence (it is the cognate of English ~smite~) has bleached away entirely, leaving only the starting of a machine. Nothing gets thrown when you ~schmeiß~ the grill ~an~.
en.anschreiben:
~Anschreiben~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The addressee can be a person written to, but it can equally be a ledger: ~anschreiben lassen~ is to have a purchase put on one's tab, and Luther's book of the living is the same idea at a theological scale, a name entered against an account.
en.anschwellen:
~Anschwellen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~schwellen~:

• ~schwellen~: From MHG ~swëllen~, from OHG ~swëllan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swellaną~ ("to swell"), perhaps from PIE *~swelH-~, though the root is not securely established. A class III strong verb (~schwellen~, ~schwoll~, ~geschwollen~), beside a weak causative ~schwellen~ ("to make swell") from Proto-Germanic *~swallijaną~. Cognate with English ~swell~, Dutch ~zwellen~, Old Norse ~svella~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks accumulation or acquisition: building up a holding until it is full or obtained.

The reading is strong (~schwoll an~, ~angeschwollen~) and therefore intransitive: a river, a sound, or an ankle swells of its own accord. The weak causative twin belongs to whoever does the swelling to something else.
en.ansehen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with Dutch ~zien~, English ~see~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an-~, from OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana-~, from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). This separable prefix directs the base verb's action toward a goal or surface.

The ~an-~ prefix gives ~sehen~ a focused, directed quality: where ~sehen~ is "to see" in general, ~ansehen~ is "to look at" something specifically. The reflexive ~sich ansehen~ ("to watch, to look at for oneself") extends this to viewing as an activity: watching a film, inspecting a site. The noun ~Ansehen~ ("reputation, standing") developed from the sense of "how one is looked upon", social regard crystallized from the directed gaze. Cognate with Dutch ~aanzien~ ("to regard; reputation"), which preserves exactly the same semantic range.
en.ansenken:
~Ansenken~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~senken~:

• ~senken~: From OHG ~senken~, from Proto-Germanic *~sankwijaną~, a causative of *~sinkwaną~ ("to sink"), from PIE *~sengʷ-~ ("to sink, to fall"). ~senken~ is thus the causative partner of ~sinken~: "to cause to sink." The vowel alternation reflects the causative *~-jan-~ suffix, which triggered umlaut. Cognate with Gothic ~sagqjan~, Old Norse ~søkkva~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

A machinist's term. The root is already the causative of ~sinken~, so the verb makes a drill descend; the prefix stops it partway, widening the mouth of a hole rather than boring a new one.
en.ansetzen:
From Middle High German ~anesetzen~, from Old High German ~anasezzen~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place"), a causative of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, from the root *~sed-~ ("to sit"). Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~זעצן~.
• ~an-~: From OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana-~ ("on, onto"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). This prefix adds a sense of attachment, initiation, or application.

The relationship between ~setzen~ and ~sitzen~ mirrors English ~set~ and ~sit~ exactly: both pairs reflect the Proto-Germanic causative pattern where *~-jan-~ turns "to sit" into "to make sit, to place." ~Ansetzen~ is remarkably polysemous in modern German: it can mean "to put on" (a pot), "to schedule" (a meeting), "to begin" (an approach), "to form" (rust), or "to prepare" (a mixture). Cognate with English ~onset~, which shares the same etymological structure (~on~ + ~set~) and originally meant "an attack" before broadening to "beginning." The PIE root *~sed-~ is one of the most well-attested roots in historical linguistics, producing Latin ~sedēre~ ("to sit"), English ~sit~, ~seat~, ~saddle~, and ~sedan~.
en.ansiedeln:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~siedeln~:

• ~siedeln~: From MHG ~sidelen~, from OHG ~sidalen~, derived from ~sidila~ ("seat"), cognate with Old English ~setl~ ("seat, settle"). Related to ~sitzen~ ("to sit") and hence ultimately to English ~settle~, though not a direct cognate of it.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~an~ ("on, at"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix adds a sense of establishing or fixing in place.

The connection between sitting and settling is ancient and deeply embedded across the Indo-European family: to settle somewhere is, at its most basic, to sit down and stay. OHG ~sidila~ ("seat") developed into ~Siedlung~ ("settlement"), and the verb ~siedeln~ preserves this link between physical rest and permanent habitation. English ~settle~ followed a parallel path from Old English ~setl~ ("seat, place to sit") to the verb ~setlan~ ("to place, establish"). The compound ~ansiedeln~ emphasizes the purposeful act of establishing a settlement, often used reflexively (~sich ansiedeln~, "to settle down").
en.ansinnen:
~Ansinnen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~sinnen~:

• ~sinnen~: From MHG ~sinnen~, from OHG ~sinnan~ ("to travel; to strive for; to think"), from Proto-West Germanic *~sinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sinnaną~, from PIE *~sent-~ ("to head for, go; to feel"). A class III strong verb (~sinnen~, ~sann~, ~gesonnen~). The same root gave Latin ~sentīre~, so ~Sinn~ and English ~sense~ are relatives. Cognate with Old English ~sinnan~ ("to meditate on"), Dutch ~zinnen~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

One ~sinnt~ something ~an~ a person in the dative: to expect or demand of them what they would rather not do. The noun ~Ansinnen~ (an unreasonable request), has outlived the verb, which now survives mostly in legal and bureaucratic register.
en.anspielen:
~Anspielen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The target is reached obliquely: to ~auf etwas anspielen~ is to aim a remark at a subject without naming it, and in sport the same directedness passes a ball to a particular teammate. The root's older breadth (dance and entertainment as much as play) makes the metaphor an easy one.
en.ansprechen:
~An-~ + ~sprechen~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~sprechen~:

• ~sprechen~: From MHG ~sprëchen~, from OHG ~sprëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sprekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sprekaną~, probably from PIE *~spregʰ-~ ("to crackle, make noise").
• ~an-~: From PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix adds the sense of direction toward someone or something, initiating contact.

~Ansprechen~ means "to address, to speak to; to appeal to; to respond to (treatment)." The prefix ~an-~ directs the act of speaking toward a target: one ~spricht jemanden an~ by approaching and initiating speech. The secondary sense "to appeal to" (~das spricht mich an~, "that appeals to me") developed from the idea of speech landing on and engaging a listener. The medical sense (~auf ein Medikament ansprechen~ ("to respond to a medication")) is a 20th-century extension of the same logic: the body "responds" when the treatment "speaks to" it. The PIE root *~spregʰ-~ is onomatopoeic (crackling into speech) making ~ansprechen~ ultimately an echo of the very sound of language itself. Cognate with Dutch ~aanspreken~.
en.anspringen:
~Anspringen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~springen~:

• ~springen~: From OHG ~springan~, from Proto-Germanic *~springaną~, from PIE *~sprenǵʰ-~, a nasalized form of *~sperǵʰ-~ ("to move energetically, to hasten, to spring"). A class III strong verb (~springen~, ~sprang~, ~gesprungen~). Cognate with English ~spring~, Dutch ~springen~, Danish ~springe~, Greek ~spérkhō~ ("to hasten").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

The literal reading is a leap directed at a target, a dog ~springt~ its owner ~an~. Everyday modern German uses the verb far more often of engines, where the leap has become the sudden onset of running, and the subject is the machine rather than whatever jumped.
en.anstecken:
~Anstecken~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~stecken~:

• ~stecken~: Modern ~stecken~ merges two verbs: the transitive weak one ("to put, stick something in") from MHG ~stecken~, OHG ~steckōn~, a geminate derivative of ~stëhhan~ (the ancestor of ~stechen~), and the strong intransitive one (archaic ~stak~/~gestocken~, "to be stuck"); the two fused in Early Modern German. Both trace to Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stikaną~, from PIE *~(s)teyg-~ ("to be sharp, stab, goad"). Cognate with English ~stick~ and ~steak~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The reading is weak, so it descends from the transitive ~steckōn~ twin, not the strong intransitive one that means "to be stuck." All three modern senses are contact: a brooch is pinned on, a fire is set by holding a flame to fuel, and a disease is passed by touch, which is why German uses the same verb for a candle and a contagion.
en.anstehen:
~Anstehen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks an action or state continuing over a stretch of time.

Everything the verb means is a standing that lasts: a task ~steht an~ while it waits to be done, a decision is ~angestanden~ while it is deferred, and a queue is people holding position. Goethe's older use (something that ~ansteht~ suits or sits well with a person) is the same image seen from the other side.
en.ansteigen:
~Ansteigen~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks accumulation or acquisition: building up a holding until it is full or obtained.

The root already carries climbing; the prefix converts a physical ascent into a measurable one, which is why the verb belongs to statistics and terrain alike. A road and an unemployment figure ~steigen~ equally well ~an~.
en.anstellen:
From MHG ~anestellen~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put, stand").
• ~an-~: From PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). This separable prefix adds the sense of placing at, turning on, or setting to work.

~Anstellen~ is one of German's most versatile verbs: "to employ" (~jemanden anstellen~), "to turn on" (~das Wasser anstellen~), "to queue up" (~sich anstellen~), and "to behave, to make a fuss" (~sich anstellen~ in its colloquial sense: ~Stell dich nicht so an!~, "Don't make such a fuss!"). The employment sense is the source of ~Angestellte(r)~ ("employee"), one of the most common nouns in German labor law. The PIE root *~stel-~ is enormously productive: it gave Latin ~stāre~ ("to stand"), whence English ~state~, ~station~, ~statue~, and ~install~.
en.ansteuern:
~Ansteuern~ is a separable compound of ~an-~ + ~steuern~:

• ~steuern~: From MHG ~stiuren~, from OHG ~stiuren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stiurijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stiurijaną~. The root noun ~Steuer~ carries two meanings sharing one ancestor: ~das Steuer~ ("rudder, helm") and ~die Steuer~ ("tax," via "supporting post" and "support"). ~Steuern~ thus means both "to steer, navigate, control" and, in archaic or Swiss usage, "to pay a tax." Cognate with English ~steer~, Dutch ~stuur~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

The root is nautical before it is anything else (~das Steuer~ is a rudder), so the compound literally steers toward a destination, and the figurative use for aiming at a goal or a deadline still carries the helm with it.
en.anstimmen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~stimmen~:

• ~stimmen~: From MHG ~stimmen~, from OHG *~stimmen~, a denominative of ~Stimme~ ("voice, vote": OHG ~stimma~, Proto-West Germanic *~stebnu~, Proto-Germanic *~stebnō~, from PIE *~stomen-~ "mouth, muzzle"). Hence the senses "to tune" (an instrument), "to be correct," and "to vote." Cognate with archaic English ~steven~ ("voice"), Dutch ~stem~, Gothic ~stibna~, Ancient Greek ~stóma~ ("mouth").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix is inchoative: it marks the beginning of an action rather than its whole course.

To ~anstimmen~ a song is not to sing it through but to set its first note; the verb names the entry that the others then join. Its link to ~Stimme~ ("voice") is still on the surface.
en.anstoßen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). Cognate with dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce, ricochet"), Dutch ~stoten~, Old Norse ~stauta~ and ~steyta~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The verb keeps its wholly physical sense: the push lands on something. From there come both clinking glasses together and setting a debate in motion.
en.anstreben:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~streben~:

• ~streben~: From MHG ~strëben~, from OHG ~strëbēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stribēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~stribāną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)ter(h₁)-~ ("to be stiff, to exert"), the same root that produced Proto-Germanic *~staraz~ ("stiff"). Cognate with Dutch ~streven~ ("to strive"), English ~strive~ (via Old French ~estriver~, itself borrowed from a Germanic source).
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~an~ ("on, at"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix directs the striving toward a specific goal.

English ~strive~ took a scenic route back to its Germanic origins: it entered English from Old French ~estriver~ ("to quarrel, contend"), which had been borrowed from a Frankish Germanic source related to OHG ~strëbēn~. So ~anstreben~ and ~strive~ are cousins who went on very different journeys before ending up with similar meanings. The PIE root *~(s)ter-~ ("to be stiff, rigid") also produced English ~stare~, ~stark~, ~stern~, and ~stereo~ (via Greek ~stereós~, "solid"), all sharing the core notion of rigidity or firmness.
en.anstreichen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~streichen~:

• ~streichen~: From MHG ~strīchen~, from OHG ~strīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~strīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~strīkaną~ ("to stroke, to rub"), from PIE *~streyg-~ ("to stroke, rub, press"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with English ~strike~, Dutch ~strijken~ ("to iron, to stroke").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The base verb names the movement of the hand, the prefix what that movement lands on: the paint goes onto the surface and stays there. Marking a date in red on a calendar is the same act, one step into metaphor.
en.ansuchen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~suchen~:

• ~suchen~: From MHG ~suochen~, ~süechen~, from OHG ~suohhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sōkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sōkijaną~, from PIE *~seh₂g-~ ("to seek out"). The modern umlautless form reflects the Upper German dialect, which resisted umlaut of long rounded vowels before velars. Cognate with English ~seek~, Dutch ~zoeken~, Danish ~søge~, Gothic ~sōkjan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

~Ansuchen~ survives mainly in Austrian officialese: one does not seek a thing but turns to an authority and asks for something. Elsewhere ~beantragen~ has taken its place.
en.antanzen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~tanzen~:

• ~tanzen~: From MHG ~tanzen~, borrowed via Central German dialects from Old French ~dancier~; the onset ~t-~ shows the route through Middle Low German or Middle Dutch ~dansen~ rather than directly from French. The ultimate origin is disputed, possibly Frankish *~dansōn~ ("to draw along, to pull"). English ~dance~ comes from the same source.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys approach and arrival: motion directed toward a destination.

The auxiliary ~sein~ gives the point away: the change of place, not the dancing, is what matters. Colloquially the verb is often used mockingly of someone who turns up uninvited.
en.antauchen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~tauchen~:

• ~tauchen~: From MHG ~tūchen~, ~touchen~, from OHG *~tūhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dūkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dūkaną~ ("to duck, to dive under"), whose further etymology is uncertain. A class II strong verb that became weak in the early modern period: when it was reintroduced from Central and Low German, the strong conjugation was regularized to weak. Cognate with Dutch ~duiken~, Swedish ~dyka~; a Low German consonant variant of the same root is ~ducken~, cognate with English ~duck~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The verb is Austrian colloquial: ~antauchen~ is to give a shove and, said of oneself, to put one's back into something. How the base verb "to dive" arrived at that sense is not transparent.
en.antippen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~tippen~:

• ~tippen~: From Low German, where the standard High German equivalent would have been ~tüpfen~ ("to dab, dot"). The word has two branches: in the sense "to type, to tap" it derives from the onomatopoeic imitation of light touching, while in the sense "to bet, to guess" (~Lotto tippen~) it comes from the noun ~Tipp~, borrowed from English ~tip~ ("a piece of advice, a hint").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

The base verb's onomatopoeic root is still audible: ~antippen~ is the briefest touch imaginable, which is exactly why it became the standard word for operating a touchscreen.
en.antragen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb whose semantic range broadened from "to drag, pull" to "to carry, bear, wear." Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

To ~antragen~ something to someone is literally to carry it over to them; the image of carrying still stands behind the modern sense "to offer." The related noun ~Antrag~ has drifted away to mean a formal application or motion.
en.antreffen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~treffen~:

• ~treffen~: From MHG ~treffen~, from OHG ~treffan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drepan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drepaną~ ("to strike, push, beat"), from PIE *~dʰrebʰ-~, *~dʰreb-~ ("to crack, crush, strike, kill"). The High German consonant shift from *~dr-~ to ~tr-~ obscures the cognate relationship with Old English ~drepan~ ("to strike"). Cognate with Old Norse ~drepa~ ("to kill, strike").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

~Antreffen~ is encountering on arrival: you find someone where they already are. Since the root originally meant "to strike," today's polite word rests on a decidedly physical image.
en.antreiben:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

One form covers two registers: you ~antreiben~ a herd or a person, and you ~antreiben~ a machine. In the first someone is urging, in the second something supplies the force, the image of driving cattle stands behind both.
en.antreten:
~An-~ + ~treten~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~ ("to tread, to step on"). Cognate with English ~tread~.
• ~an-~: From PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix adds the sense of stepping toward, stepping up to, or stepping into position.

~Antreten~ covers a wide semantic range unified by the image of stepping forward. In its military sense, it means "to fall in, to line up for muster"; the sergeant's bark ~antreten!~ commands soldiers into formation. In sports and politics, it means "to compete, to run" (~gegen einen Gegner antreten~, "to compete against an opponent"; ~zur Wahl antreten~, "to run for election"). With a direct object, it means "to begin" a duty or journey (~eine Reise antreten~, "to set out on a journey"; ~ein Amt antreten~, "to take office"; ~ein Erbe antreten~, "to accept an inheritance"). And in its most physical sense, it means "to kick-start" a motorcycle by stepping on the starter. The derived noun ~Antritt~ ("commencement, start") appears in formal compounds: ~Antrittsrede~ ("inaugural address"), ~Antrittsbesuch~ ("introductory visit"). The metaphor of stepping forward to begin something, to face a challenge, or to take one's place runs through every usage.
en.antrinken:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~trinken~:

• ~trinken~: From MHG ~trinken~, from OHG ~trinkan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drinkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drinkaną~; no non-Germanic cognate has been securely identified, so the word may be a Germanic innovation. Cognate with English ~drink~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Old Norse ~drekka~ and Gothic ~𐌳𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌺𐌰𐌽~ (drigkan).
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks accumulation or acquisition: building up a holding until it is full or obtained.

In ~sich einen Rausch antrinken~ the prefix names what the drinking builds up: the intoxication is accumulated like a stock. An ~angetrunkenes~ glass, by contrast, shows the same prefix's other, partitive reading.
en.antworten: From Middle High German ~antwürten~, from Old High German ~antwurten~, from Proto-Germanic *~andawurdijaną~, a denominative of *~andawurdiją~ ("answer"), itself from *~anda-~ ("against, in return") + *~wurdiją~ ("speech"), a derivative of *~wurdą~ ("word"). The archaic prefix *~anda-~ ("against, in return") is the same element that appears in Gothic ~anda-~ and Old English ~and-~. By surface analysis, the modern verb looks like a denominative of ~Antwort~ ("answer") + ~-en~, which is how most contemporary speakers parse it. The fascinating parallel with English ~answer~ is not accidental: English ~answer~ comes from Old English ~andswaru~ ("a sworn statement against [a charge]"), from ~and-~ ("against") + ~swaru~ ("affirmation, swearing"). Both ~antworten~ and ~answer~ contain the same ancient prefix meaning "against, in return," and both refer to speech made in response to speech, though German built on *~wurdą~ ("word") while English built on *~swarōną~ ("to swear"). The Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ is cognate with Greek ~ἀντί~ (~antí~, "against, opposite"), which gives English ~anti-~. All three descend from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, front, opposite"), whose comparative form *~h₂énteros~ ("the one facing, the other of two") produced Proto-Germanic *~anþeraz~, the ancestor of both German ~ander~ ("other") and English ~other~. In English, the nasal was lost before the fricative by the Ingvaeonic nasal spirant law (*~anþeraz~ → *~āþeraz~ → OE ~ōþer~ → ~other~), while German preserved it (~ander~). So ~antworten~, Greek ~anti-~, German ~ander~, and English ~other~ are all siblings from the same PIE root, the one about facing, fronting, and opposing. Cognate with Dutch ~antwoorden~, Afrikaans ~antwoord~.
en.anvertrauen:
Doubly prefixed: ~an-~ is added to ~vertrauen~, which already carries ~ver-~. A compound of ~an-~ + ~ver-~ + ~trauen~:

• ~trauen~: From MHG ~trūwen~, from OHG ~trūwēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~trūwēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~trūwāną~ ("to trust, believe"), from PIE *~deru-~ ("to be firm, hard, solid"). The same root gave ~treu~ ("faithful"), ~Trost~ ("comfort"), and ~Trauung~ ("wedding ceremony"), as well as English ~trust~, ~true~, and ~tree~. Cognate with Old Norse ~traust~ ("confidence").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

Only the outer ~an-~ separates; the inner ~ver-~ stays fixed, which is why the participle is ~anvertraut~ and not *~angevertraut~. Semantically ~an-~ supplies the recipient: one does not merely trust, one entrusts something to someone.
en.anwachsen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from PIE *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Cognate with English ~wax~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks accumulation or acquisition: building up a holding until it is full or obtained.

The prefix leads two lives in this verb: in ~die Schulden wachsen an~ ("the debts mount up") what counts is accumulation, while in ~die Hand ist angewachsen~ ("the hand has grown back on") it is growing fast to a surface. The auxiliary is ~sein~ either way, because a change of state is at issue.
en.anwarten:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~warten~:

• ~warten~: From MHG ~warten~, from OHG ~wartēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wardēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wardāną~ ("to guard, watch over"), from *~warduz~ ("a guard"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, watch, guard"): one who keeps watch also waits. The older sense persists in ~ein Auto warten~ ("to service a car"). Cognate with English ~ward~, Swedish ~vårda~, Dutch ~bewaren~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks an action or state continuing over a stretch of time.

~Anwarten~ is all but extinct today and survives chiefly in the noun ~Anwartschaft~ ("entitlement, expectancy"). The root's older sense (keeping watch) is easier to feel here than in plain ~warten~.
en.anweisen:
From Middle High German ~anewīsen~. Compound of ~an-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~ (weak verb until the seventeenth or eighteenth century), a West and North Germanic derivation from the adjective ~weise~ ("wise"), from Proto-Germanic *~wīsaz~, from PIE *~weyd-~ ("to see, to know"). Cognate with English ~wise~, Dutch ~wijs~, and related to English ~wit~, ~wisdom~, Latin ~vidēre~ ("to see"), and Sanskrit ~veda~ ("knowledge").
• ~an-~: From OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana-~, from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). The prefix adds a directional or purposive sense.

The verb ~anweisen~ means "to instruct, to direct, to assign, to transfer (money)." The semantic chain runs from "seeing" (PIE) through "knowing" (Germanic) to "showing the way" (~weisen~) to "directing someone toward a task" (~anweisen~). The noun ~Anweisung~ ("instruction, directive") is ubiquitous in bureaucratic and technical German. The PIE root *~weyd-~ is the source of an astonishing range of descendants: Latin ~vidēre~ ("to see") gave English ~video~, ~vision~, and ~evidence~; Sanskrit ~Veda~ ("sacred knowledge") named the oldest Hindu scriptures; and Germanic *~wīsaz~ produced ~wise~, ~wisdom~, and the German ~-weise~ suffix meaning "in the manner of." The financial sense of ~anweisen~ ("to transfer money") derives from directing funds toward a recipient.
en.anwenden: Formed from prefix ~an-~ (from PIE *~h₂en~, "on, onto") and ~wenden~, from MHG ~wenden~, from OHG ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). Cognate with Middle Low German ~anwenden~. The prefix adds the sense of directing or turning something toward a purpose: to ~wenden~ (turn) something ~an~ (onto) a task. The English verb ~apply~ (from Latin ~applicare~, "to fold toward") performs exactly the same semantic work by different means.
en.anwerben:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~werben~:

• ~werben~: From MHG ~werben~, from OHG ~werban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hwerban~, from Proto-Germanic *~hwerbaną~ ("to turn, move about, wander"). The sense passed through "to go about seeking" to "to recruit, advertise, woo", parallel to English ~advertise~ from Latin ~advertere~ ("to turn toward"). Cognate with Dutch ~werven~, English ~wharve~, Icelandic ~hverfa~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks accumulation or acquisition: building up a holding until it is full or obtained.

The root meant "to move about, go around": one who recruits goes around and gathers people in. The same root yields modern ~werben~ in its advertising sense, in both cases the point is winning someone over.
en.anwerfen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix conveys contact or attachment: fastening one thing onto another.

Beside the literal "throw something at something" stands the technical sense: you ~anwerfen~ an engine because it was once set going with a crank or a thrown belt.
en.anzahlen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix marks a partial action: doing something a little, not all the way.

To ~anzahlen~ is to pay part and owe the rest; the prefix marks exactly that beginning of a sum. That ~zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings shows nicely here: a deposit is a counted-out portion.
en.anzeigen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~zeigen~:

• ~zeigen~: From MHG ~zeigen~, from OHG ~zeigōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taigōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikōną~, from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to point out, show"). Cognate with Dutch ~tonen~, Latin ~dīcō~ ("to say, show"), Greek ~deiknúō~ ("to show").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an-~, from OHG ~ana-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana-~, from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). This separable prefix directs the base verb's action toward a recipient or surface.

The ~an-~ prefix sharpens the sense of ~zeigen~ from "to show" into "to indicate, point at, display." In legal German, ~anzeigen~ specifically means "to report to authorities" (to point someone out to the state), giving the word a charged legal register absent from the neutral ~zeigen~. The noun ~Anzeige~ covers both "advertisement" (a directed display) and "police report" (a directed accusation), a semantic duality that reflects the verb's core gesture of pointing something out to a recipient.
en.anziehen:
Compound of ~an-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhanan~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, to lead"). Cognate with English ~tow~, ~tug~, and ~duke~ (the last via Latin ~dux~, "leader," from the same root). Also related to obsolete English ~tee~ ("to draw, lead").
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). This prefix adds the sense of pulling something onto oneself.

The semantic range of ~anziehen~ is remarkably broad: "to put on (clothing)," "to attract," "to tighten (a screw)," and even "to accelerate." All these meanings flow logically from the core image of "pulling onto": you pull clothes onto your body, a magnet pulls iron toward itself, you pull a screw tighter. The Dutch expression ~zich iets aantrekken van~ ("to take something to heart") mirrors the western German idiom ~sich etwas anziehen von~, suggesting a shared metaphorical tradition. English ~attract~ is a Latin calque of the same concept (~ad-~ + ~trahere~ = "to pull toward").
en.anzählen:
A separable compound of ~an-~ + ~zählen~:

• ~zählen~: From MHG ~zel(e)n~, ~zellen~, from OHG ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~ ("to enumerate, count; to recount, tell"). German split this dual sense: ~zählen~ kept "to count," ~erzählen~ took "to narrate." Cognate with Dutch ~tellen~, English ~tell~ and ~tale~, Danish ~tælle~, Gothic ~talzjan~.
• ~an-~: From MHG ~an(e)-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~ ("on, at"), from PIE *~h₂en~ ("on, onto"). Cognate with English ~on~, Dutch ~aan~, Gothic ~ana~, and Greek ~aná~ ("up, throughout"). The prefix directs the action at an addressee: speaking, presenting, or announcing to someone.

The word belongs in the boxing ring: the referee counts over a fighter who is down. Only the umlaut separates it from ~anzahlen~: both go back to one root, the one by way of reckoning, the other by way of paying.
en.arbeiten: From Old High German ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"). The semantic evolution from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" (the lot of the fatherless) to "work" reflects a shift from social condition to the labor it entailed. Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Old Saxon ~arvedian~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same PIE root, English ~orphan~ and Greek ~orphanos~.
en.armmachen:
A separable compound of the adjective ~arm~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~arm~: From the adjective ~arm~ ("poor"), MHG and OHG ~arm~, from Proto-West Germanic *~arm~, from Proto-Germanic *~armaz~ ("poor, wretched"). Beyond Germanic the origin is uncertain; a connection to the root behind ~Arbeit~ ("toil") and Latin ~orbus~ ("bereft") is often proposed but not secure. It is not related to the homonym ~Arm~ ("arm, limb"), which is Proto-Germanic *~armaz~ from PIE *~h₂er-~ ("to join"); the two words merged in sound only. Cognate with Dutch ~arm~, Gothic ~arms~, Swedish ~arm~. The sense of ~arm~ here is the resultative frame: to reduce someone to poverty.

Like ~totschlagen~ ("to beat to death"), the compound names action and result at once: the doing goes on until the person is poor. Written apart (~arm machen~) it is merely a predicative; only joining the words makes a verb of it.
en.atmen:
From Middle High German ~ātemen~, from Old High German ~ātamōn~, derived from Proto-Germanic *~ēþmaz~ ("breath"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁eh₁tmén-~ ("breath"). Equivalent to ~Atem~ ("breath") + ~-en~. Cognate with Dutch ~ademen~ ("to breathe").

The PIE root *~h₁eh₁t-~ connects German breathing to one of the most profound concepts in Indo-European thought: Sanskrit ~ātmán~ ("soul, self, breath") descends from the same source, and in Hindu philosophy, the ~Ātman~ is the true self or soul, the innermost essence that animates all living beings. The semantic chain from "breath" to "soul" is nearly universal across ancient cultures: breath is the visible sign of life, so the word for breath becomes the word for the life force itself. Latin ~anima~ ("breath, soul") and Greek ~psychē~ ("breath, soul") show the same pattern. The archaic German doublet ~Odem~ ("breath"), now largely poetic, also descends from *~ēþmaz~ via a different phonological path.
en.aufarbeiten:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The same verb runs two ways: a piece of furniture is ~aufgearbeitet~, that is restored, and a stack of files or a national past is ~aufgearbeitet~, that is worked through to the end. The root is a reminder in passing that ~Arbeit~ once meant "hardship."
en.aufatmen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~atmen~:

• ~atmen~: From MHG ~ātemen~, from OHG ~ātamōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~ēþmaz~ ("breath"), from PIE *~h₁eh₁tmén-~ ("breath"). Equivalent to ~Atem~ ("breath") + ~-en~. Cognate with Dutch ~ademen~; the archaic doublet ~Odem~ ("breath") descends from *~ēþmaz~ by a different path.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

The verb almost never names ordinary breathing but the single deep breath in which relief becomes visible; the language lets the feeling surface in the body.
en.aufbacken:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~backen~:

• ~backen~: From MHG ~backen~, from OHG ~backan~, an originally weak geminated variant of an older strong verb (MHG ~bachen~, OHG ~bahhan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~bakan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bakaną~, from PIE *~bʰeh₃g-~ ("to roast, bake"). The two blended early, so strong ~buk~ survives beside weak ~backte~. Cognate with English ~bake~, Dutch ~bakken~, Swedish ~baka~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

~Aufbacken~ is not baking but re-baking: a finished roll is briefly heated so that it is fresh again. That puts it with ~aufwärmen~ and ~auffrischen~, where ~auf-~ each time means "restore to good condition."
en.aufbauen:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~būwen~, from OHG ~būan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~būan~, from Proto-Germanic *~būaną~ ("to dwell, reside"), from PIE *~bʰuH-~ ("to be, become, grow"). The same PIE root yields English ~be~, Latin ~fuī~ ("I was"), and Greek ~phúō~ ("to grow").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-Germanic *~up-~, from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). This separable prefix adds an upward or constructive directionality to the base verb.

The ~auf-~ prefix transforms ~bauen~'s basic sense of "to build" into "to build up, construct from the ground up, assemble." The compound is the standard word for constructing something systematically: a building, a business, an argument (~ein Argument aufbauen~). The figurative extensions are productive: ~aufgebaut sein aus~ ("to be composed of"), ~auf etwas aufbauen~ ("to build on something"). Cognate with Dutch ~opbouwen~, Low German ~upbuuen~.
en.aufbehalten:
Doubly prefixed: ~auf-~ is added to ~behalten~, which already carries ~be-~. A compound of ~auf-~ + ~be-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

Only the outer ~auf-~ separates (~er behält den Hut auf~, "he keeps his hat on"), while ~be-~ stays fixed. The basic sense is leaving in place what is up: the hat on the head, the eyes open. In Luther the older reading "to reserve for something" stands alongside it.
en.aufbekommen:
Doubly prefixed: ~auf-~ is added to ~bekommen~, which already carries ~be-~. A compound of ~auf-~ + ~be-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

Literally "to get something open": the verb stresses not the opening but the succeeding; ~ich bekomme das Glas nicht auf~ says the effort is failing. Beside it stands the schoolroom sense "to be set as homework."
en.aufbellen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~bellen~:

• ~bellen~: From MHG ~bellen~, from OHG ~bellan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bellaną~ ("to resound, roar"), probably from PIE *~bʰelH-~ ("to sound, howl"), though that reconstruction is not secure. Originally a class III strong verb (~bellen~, ~bal~, ~gebollen~), now weak throughout. Cognate with Old English ~bellan~, English ~bellow~ and ~bell~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

The prefix turns continuous barking into a single burst: the dog gives one sharp bark. It is used figuratively of people who suddenly snap out an interruption.
en.aufbereiten:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~be-~ + ~reiten~, whose middle member is the ~bereiten~ of "to prepare" rather than the verb "to ride":

• ~reiten~: From MHG ~rīten~, from OHG ~rītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rīdaną~, from PIE *~Hreydʰ-~ ("to set in motion, ride"), likely a suffixed form of *~h₃reyH-~ ("to move, churn"). German ~reiten~ narrowed to horseback riding, while English ~ride~ broadened to vehicles. Cognate with Dutch ~rijden~, Danish ~ride~, Swedish ~rida~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ derives a verb from a noun or adjective, meaning to furnish with or make into that.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.
