The ~be-~ verb here is built not on ~reiten~ "to ride" but on MHG ~bereit~ "ready, equipped", a word that belongs to the riding root all the same, since to be ~bereit~ was originally to be fit to ride out. ~Aufbereiten~ is accordingly technical rather than bodily: ore, water, and data are all ~aufbereitet~, worked up into usable shape.
en.aufbewahren:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~bewahren~:

• ~bewahren~: From MHG ~bewarn~, from OHG ~biwarōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~biwarōną~, compound of *~bi-~ ("about, around") + *~warōną~ ("to guard, protect"), from Proto-Indo-European *~wer-~ ("to become aware of, to heed"). Cognate with English ~beware~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from Proto-Indo-European *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix here conveys preservation and safekeeping, with an underlying spatial metaphor of storing something upward or away.

The PIE root *~wer-~ ("to heed, perceive") is the ancestor of an impressive family: German ~wahren~ ("to preserve"), ~wahrnehmen~ ("to perceive"), ~Wahrheit~ ("truth"), English ~wary~, ~aware~, ~beware~, ~guard~ (via French ~garder~, from Frankish *~wardōn~), and ~ward~/~warden~. The double-prefixed ~aufbewahren~ piles up two layers of protective meaning: ~be-~ wraps the guarding around the object, and ~auf-~ stacks the safekeeping upward. The result means "to store, to keep safe, to preserve", a word that sounds bureaucratic but carries millennia of watchful vigilance in its roots.
en.aufbiegen:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~biegen~:

• ~biegen~: From MHG ~biegen~, from OHG ~biogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beuganą~, from PIE *~bʰewgʰ-~ ("to bend"). A class II strong verb (~biegen~, ~bog~, ~gebogen~). Cognate with English ~bow~ and ~elbow~ ("arm-bend"), Dutch ~buigen~, Sanskrit ~bhujáti~ ("to bend, curve").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

Upward and open coincide here: a hook that is bent up is thereby bent open, and German uses ~aufbiegen~ for undoing a bend as readily as for making one.
en.aufbieten:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~bieten~:

• ~bieten~: From MHG ~bieten~, from OHG ~biotan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beudan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beudaną~, from PIE *~bʰewdʰ-~ ("to be awake, aware"). A class II strong verb whose root conveys awareness and offering. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bieden~, Danish ~byde~, Swedish ~bjuda~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The military sense is the oldest: an ~Aufgebot~ was a public summons, and calling men up uses the same upward metaphor as English "to raise an army." The modern idiom ~alle Kräfte aufbieten~ "to muster all one's strength" keeps it.
en.aufbinden:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~binden~:

• ~binden~: From MHG ~binden~, from OHG ~bintan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bindan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bindaną~, from PIE *~bʰendʰ-~ ("to bind, tie"). A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~i~–~a~–~u~ ablaut (~binden~, ~band~, ~gebunden~). Cognate with English ~bind~, Dutch ~binden~, Gothic ~bindan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

~Aufbinden~ normally undoes a binding rather than making one; in older usage, though, ~auf-~ could equally mean "onto," so the same verb once meant to bind a headdress on.
en.aufblasen:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~blasen~:

• ~blasen~: From MHG ~blāsen~, from OHG ~blāsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blāsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~blēsaną~, from PIE *~bʰleh₁-~ ("to blow, swell"). A class VII strong verb, its reduplicated preterite worn down to ~blies~ (~blasen~, ~blies~, ~geblasen~). Cognate with English ~blast~, Gothic ~ufblēsan~, Old Norse ~blása~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

Whether the breath goes into a bladder or onto a fire, ~aufblasen~ is blowing that makes something grow; the figurative ~aufgeblasen~ "puffed up, conceited" follows the same swelling.
en.aufbleiben:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The ~auf~ is the one in ~aufsein~: to be up is not to have gone to bed, so ~aufbleiben~ is staying awake rather than staying put, of a door, the same verb means staying open.
en.aufblicken:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~blank~, Dutch ~blik~, Old English ~blice~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

Since ~blicken~ began as a flash of light, ~aufblicken~ is literally a gleam sent upward; the figurative "to look up to someone" leads the same double life in German as in English.
en.aufbrauchen:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~brauchen~:

• ~brauchen~: From MHG ~brūchen~, from OHG ~brūhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brūkan~ ("to use, employ, consume"), from Proto-Germanic *~brūkaną~, from PIE *~bʰruHg-~ ("to make use of"). The shift from "use" (still in the noun ~Brauch~) to "need" is modern. Cognate with English ~brook~ ("to tolerate"), Dutch ~bruiken~, Latin ~fruor~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys using something up or consuming it entirely.

Here ~auf-~ empties rather than fills: what is ~aufgebraucht~ is gone, and the compound preserves ~brauchen~'s older meaning "to use," which the modern "to need" has otherwise displaced.
en.aufbrechen:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The intransitive sense (setting out on a journey) is the same image seen from inside: a company that ~aufbricht~ breaks camp open and departs.
en.aufbringen:
From Middle High German ~ūfbringen~. Compound of ~auf-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, from a Pre-Germanic compound *~bʰrenḱ-~, blending Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") with *~h₁neḱ-~ ("to bring, reach"). Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Afrikaans ~bring~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from Proto-Indo-European *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix adds an upward, outward, or provocative force.

The etymology of ~bringen~ is unique among Germanic verbs: it is the only verb in Proto-Germanic with a mixed weak-strong past tense (German ~brachte~ shows both the dental suffix of weak verbs and the ablaut vowel change of strong verbs). This hybrid conjugation suggests that *~bringaną~ was already anomalous in Proto-Germanic. The compound ~aufbringen~ has developed several distinct meanings: "to raise, to muster" (funds or courage), "to infuriate" (someone), and in nautical usage "to seize" (a ship). Cognates include Dutch ~opbrengen~ ("to yield, produce") and the archaic English ~upbring~ ("to bring up, to raise").
en.aufdecken:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~decken~:

• ~decken~: From MHG ~decken~, from OHG ~decchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þakkjan~ ("to cover"), from Proto-Germanic *~þakjaną~, a causative formation from *~þaką~ ("roof, thatch"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to cover"); the verb is etymologically "to roof." Cognate with English ~thatch~, Dutch ~dekken~, Swedish ~täcka~; from the same root Latin ~tegere~, whence English ~protect~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

Since ~decken~ is etymologically "to roof," ~aufdecken~ unroofs; modern German uses it for exposing a scandal exactly as English uses "uncover."
en.aufdrehen:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). Cognate with English ~throw~ (a true cognate: Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist," a sense that "throw a pot" still keeps) plus English ~thread~, Dutch ~draaien~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

A tap, a bottle cap, and a radio are all ~aufgedreht~ by the same turn of the hand; colloquially a person can be ~aufgedreht~ too, wound up rather than opened.
en.aufdringen:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~dringen~:

• ~dringen~: From MHG ~dringen~, from OHG ~dringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þringwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrinhwaną~, from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). A class III strong verb (~dringen~, ~drang~, ~gedrungen~); its causative ~drängen~ carries the expected umlaut. Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~ ("to press") and English ~throng~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

~Aufdringen~ is the strong twin of the weak ~aufdrängen~ and has largely yielded to it; its most visible survivor is the adjective ~aufdringlich~ "pushy, obtrusive."
en.aufdrängen:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~drängen~:

• ~drängen~: From a merger of two Middle High German verbs: ~drengen~, from OHG ~drengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangwijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrangwijaną~ (a causative); and the now-obsolete ~drangen~, from OHG ~drangōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangōn~ (a denominative). Both from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). ~drängen~ took the transitive senses, the strong ~dringen~ the intransitive. Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~, English ~throng~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

~Drängen~ supplies the pressure and ~auf-~ the target: what is ~aufgedrängt~ is pressed onto someone who did not ask for it, and the dative marks that someone.
en.aufeinanderfolgen:
A transparent compound of ~aufeinander-~ + ~folgen~:

• ~folgen~: From MHG ~volgen~, from OHG ~folgēn~ ("to follow, serve faithfully, pursue," attested from the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *~folgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fulgāną~; the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. Cognate with English ~follow~, Dutch ~volgen~, Danish ~følge~, Swedish ~följa~.
• ~aufeinander-~: Transparently ~auf~ ("on, onto") + ~einander~ ("one another," itself ~ein~ plus the reciprocal ~ander~, "other"). It means "onto one another," and in verbal compounds it marks either physical stacking or reciprocal or successive action: ~aufeinanderlegen~ ("to lay one on top of the other"), ~aufeinanderfolgen~ ("to follow one another"). See ~auf-~ for the particle's own history. The sense of ~aufeinander-~ here is: in succession, one after another.

Written as one word it is a verb, written apart an adverb plus a verb, and which to choose is among the more litigated points of German spelling reform; the participle ~aufeinanderfolgend~ "consecutive" is the form most often met.
en.aufeinanderlegen:
A transparent compound of ~aufeinander-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~aufeinander-~: Transparently ~auf~ ("on, onto") + ~einander~ ("one another," itself ~ein~ plus the reciprocal ~ander~, "other"). It means "onto one another," and in verbal compounds it marks either physical stacking or reciprocal or successive action: ~aufeinanderlegen~ ("to lay one on top of the other"), ~aufeinanderfolgen~ ("to follow one another"). See ~auf-~ for the particle's own history. The sense of ~aufeinander-~ here is: one on top of another, stacked.

The reciprocal ~einander~ does the work a second object would otherwise have to do: no further accusative is needed to say what goes on top of what.
en.aufeinanderliegen:
A transparent compound of ~aufeinander-~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~aufeinander-~: Transparently ~auf~ ("on, onto") + ~einander~ ("one another," itself ~ein~ plus the reciprocal ~ander~, "other"). It means "onto one another," and in verbal compounds it marks either physical stacking or reciprocal or successive action: ~aufeinanderlegen~ ("to lay one on top of the other"), ~aufeinanderfolgen~ ("to follow one another"). See ~auf-~ for the particle's own history. The sense of ~aufeinander-~ here is: one on top of another, stacked.

It is the stative partner of ~aufeinanderlegen~ exactly as ~liegen~ is of ~legen~, the causative pair carried whole into the compound.
en.aufeinanderstoßen:
A transparent compound of ~aufeinander-~ + ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). Cognate with dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce, ricochet"), Dutch ~stoten~, Old Norse ~stauta~ and ~steyta~.
• ~aufeinander-~: Transparently ~auf~ ("on, onto") + ~einander~ ("one another," itself ~ein~ plus the reciprocal ~ander~, "other"). It means "onto one another," and in verbal compounds it marks either physical stacking or reciprocal or successive action: ~aufeinanderlegen~ ("to lay one on top of the other"), ~aufeinanderfolgen~ ("to follow one another"). See ~auf-~ for the particle's own history. The sense of ~aufeinander-~ here is: reciprocally, upon each other.

Because ~stoßen~ names a single blow and ~aufeinander~ makes it mutual, the compound needs no reflexive pronoun: two things ~stoßen aufeinander~, and both are struck.
en.auferlegen:
A compound of ~auf-~ + ~er-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

The image of a burden is intact: an obligation is laid on someone, in the dative, as a weight is laid on a surface, and ~auferlegen~ matches English "impose," Latin ~in~ + ~ponere~, morpheme for morpheme.
en.auferstehen:
A compound of ~auf-~ + ~er-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ preserves its own older spatial sense of upward or outward motion.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The doubled upward marking is not redundancy but translation history: ~erstehen~ alone once sufficed, and ~auf-~ was added to render Latin ~resurgere~, whose own ~re-~ + ~surgere~ (from ~sub~ + ~regere~, "to direct from below") is itself a compound of rising.
en.auferwecken:
A compound of ~auf-~ + ~er-~ + ~wecken~:

• ~wecken~: From MHG ~wecken~, from OHG ~wecchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wakkjan~ ("to wake up"), from Proto-Germanic *~wakjaną~, a causative of *~wakaną~ ("to be awake"), from PIE *~weǵ-~ ("to be lively, to wake"), precisely the distinction between ~wachen~ and ~wecken~. Cognate with Dutch ~wekken~, English ~watch~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the onset of a state rather than the state itself.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

~Wecken~ is already the causative of ~wachen~, so ~auferwecken~ stacks two layers of causation on one root: to make someone be awake, and to do it from the dead.
en.auferziehen:
A compound of ~auf-~ + ~er-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ preserves its own older spatial sense of upward or outward motion.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The metaphor is horticultural before it is pedagogical (a child is drawn up like a plant), and Latin ~ēducāre~ "to lead out, to rear" is the same figure with ~dūcere~ standing in for ~ziehen~. Modern German has largely retired ~auferziehen~ in favour of plain ~erziehen~ and ~aufziehen~.
en.auffahren:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

One verb covers a car striking the one ahead, a temper flaring, and Christ ascending; ~fahren~'s old sense "to go" is broad enough that only the direction supplied by ~auf-~ tells them apart.
en.auffallen:
From Middle High German ~ūfvallen~, ~ūffallen~. Compound of ~auf-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~, from PIE *~peh₃l-~ ("to fall").
• ~auf-~: From PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The separable prefix adds a sense of upward motion or sudden appearance.

~Auffallen~ means "to stand out, to be noticeable, to attract attention." The literal image is striking: something that ~falls upward~ (that rises against the expected direction) naturally catches the eye. The cognate Low German form ~upvallen~ confirms the compound's age. In modern usage, the verb is impersonal: ~es fällt mir auf~ ("it strikes me, I notice it"), and the derived adjective ~auffällig~ ("conspicuous, striking") is ubiquitous. The verb captures a deep insight about perception: we notice not what falls as expected, but what ~falls up~, what violates our expectations. Cognate with Dutch ~opvallen~ ("to stand out"), which follows the same metaphor exactly.
en.auffangen:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~fangen~:

• ~fangen~: From MHG ~vāhen~, from OHG ~fāhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~fanhaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to secure, fasten"). A strong verb, originally ~fāhan~ / ~fieng~ / ~gefangan~; the modern present stem ~fang-~ was taken analogically from the past forms. Cognate with English ~fang~, Dutch ~vangen~, West Frisian ~fange~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

What is ~aufgefangen~ is caught before it lands: the verb implies interception in mid-fall, which is why economic writing uses it for cushioning a shock.
en.auffassen:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~fassen~:

• ~fassen~: From MHG ~vazzen~, from OHG ~fazzōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fatōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fatōną~ ("to hold, seize"), a weak class 2 verb, from PIE *~pod-néh₂-ti~, from *~pod-~ ("to fetch"). German kept the sense of grasping and holding, English that of going to retrieve. Cognate with English ~fetch~; the noun ~Fass~ ("barrel") shares the root.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The grasping is mental, as it is in English "grasp" and "take it that way," and the noun ~Auffassung~ "view, interpretation" is now commoner than the verb it comes from.
en.auffinden:
A transparent compound of ~auf-~ + ~finden~:

• ~finden~: From MHG ~vinden~, from OHG ~findan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~finþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to go, pass; path, bridge"). The development from "to go, pass" to "to find" parallels shifts in Slavic. Cognate with English ~find~, Dutch ~vinden~, Low German ~finden~, Danish ~finde~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

~Auffinden~ is ~finden~ with the searching made explicit: one stumbles on a thing with ~finden~, but ~auffinden~ presupposes looking for it, which is why officialese prefers it for missing persons and mislaid objects.
en.auffliegen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~fliegen~:

• ~fliegen~: From MHG ~vliegen~, from OHG ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"), an extension of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim") that also gave ~fließen~. The vowel path *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of class II strong verbs. Cognate with English ~fly~, Dutch ~vliegen~, Danish ~flyve~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The compound stays vivid in both directions: birds fly up, and figuratively what flies up is whatever was meant to stay hidden: a plan, a fraud, a double life. Either way something that was lying still is suddenly airborne.
en.auffordern:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~fordern~:

• ~fordern~: From MHG ~vodern~, ~vordern~, from OHG ~fordarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ(a)rōn~ ("to move forward, to bring to the front"), from *~forþar~ ("further"), ultimately from PIE *~per-~ ("to go forth"). Cognate with English ~further~ (from the same Proto-West Germanic stem). Related to German ~fördern~ ("to promote, support"), which is the same word with umlaut.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-Germanic *~upp~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). As a prefix, it adds urgency or directedness.

The literal sense is "to demand upward": to call upon someone to do something. ~Auffordern~ means "to request, to call upon, to challenge" and carries more urgency than ~bitten~ ("to ask") but less than ~befehlen~ ("to command"). The noun ~Aufforderung~ ("request, summons, prompt") is common in bureaucratic and legal German. The relationship between ~fordern~ ("to demand") and ~fördern~ ("to promote") (distinguished only by umlaut) illustrates how a single root meaning "to bring forward" could split into "to demand something be brought forth" and "to push something forward."
en.aufführen:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, originally the causative of OHG ~faran~ ("to proceed, travel"). From PIE *~per-~ ("to carry, lead forward"). Cognate with English ~fare~ (the base verb) and, more distantly, ~ferry~ (which shares the same causative formation).
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~, from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below").

The MHG compound ~ūfvüeren~ originally meant "to lead up, bring forward." Its theatrical sense "to perform (a play)" developed from the idea of bringing a work forward onto the stage. The reflexive ~sich aufführen~ ("to behave, conduct oneself") adds yet another dimension, sometimes used disapprovingly: ~Führ dich nicht so auf!~ ("Don't carry on like that!").
en.auffüllen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~füllen~:

• ~füllen~: From MHG ~vüllen~, from OHG ~fullen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fullijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullijaną~ ("to make full"), the causative of *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pl̥h₁nós~ ("full"). English ~fill~ and ~füllen~ are exact cognates, each the causative of its native word for "full." Cognate with English ~fill~, Dutch ~vullen~, Danish ~fylde~, Swedish ~fylla~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

~Füllen~ on its own says only that something becomes full; ~auffüllen~ names the level to be reached as well: up to the brim, or back to where it stood before. That is why stocks, gas reserves, and glasses are ~aufgefüllt~ while a hole is merely ~zugefüllt~.
en.aufgeben:
From Middle High German ~ūfgeben~. Compound of ~auf-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-Germanic *~up-~, from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix adds a sense of upward transfer or relinquishment.

The compound's meaning of "to give up, to surrender" derives from the image of giving something upward, releasing it from one's grasp to the sky, as it were. But ~aufgeben~ also means "to post (a letter)" (giving it up to the postal system), "to assign (homework)" (giving a task upward to students from teacher), and historically "to serve food" (giving it up onto the table). These senses all preserve the core gesture of handing something over and away from oneself. The derived noun ~Aufgabe~ ("task, assignment, mission") reframes the act of giving up as a duty received, what is given up by one party becomes the task of another. The phrase ~sich aufgeben~ ("to give up on oneself") is among the most psychologically loaded expressions in German. Cognate with English ~upgive~ (archaic), Dutch ~opgeven~.
en.aufgehen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The verb reaches from a sun that rises to a seam that comes undone to a sum that comes out even. In each case something closed gives way or something hidden emerges, and when a light ~geht~ someone ~auf~, both happen at once.
en.aufglänzen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~glänzen~:

• ~glänzen~: From MHG ~glenzen~, from OHG ~glanzen~, from Proto-Germanic *~glantaz~ ("shining, bright"), from PIE *~gʰlond-o-~, from the root *~gʰlend-~ ("to shine, gleam"). The verb belongs to the Germanic "gl-" phonestheme of light words: ~gleißen~, ~glimmen~, ~Glut~, ~Glas~. Cognate with English ~gleam~, ~glitter~, ~glow~, ~glint~ and ~glisten~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

~Glänzen~ names a state; ~aufglänzen~ names an event: the brief flare that is over in the next moment. The prefix turns a standing light into an instant of one.
en.aufgreifen:
From Middle High German ~ūfgrīfen~. Compound of ~auf-~ + ~greifen~:

• ~greifen~: From MHG ~grīfen~, from OHG ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). Cognate with English ~gripe~ and ~grip~, Dutch ~grijpen~, Swedish ~gripa~. Also related to Lithuanian ~griẽbti~ ("to seize").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from Proto-Indo-European *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix adds the sense of picking up or seizing upon.

The PIE root *~gʰreyb-~ has produced a cluster of English words all revolving around grasping: ~grip~, ~gripe~, ~grope~, and ~grab~ (the last via a secondary formation). The compound ~aufgreifen~ means both "to pick up" in a physical sense and "to take up" in an abstract one, as in taking up an idea or a suggestion. In legal and police contexts, ~aufgreifen~ means "to apprehend, to pick up" a suspect, preserving the original forceful sense of seizing. The Gothic cognate ~greipan~ appears in Wulfila's Bible translation, showing that this verb was already well established across the Germanic world by the 4th century.
en.aufhaben:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The verb inherits two different ~auf-~ prefixes: the one from ~aufsetzen~ when someone has a hat on, and the one from ~aufmachen~ when a shop is open. Only context decides whether something is being worn or standing open.
en.aufhalten:
From Middle High German ~ūfhalten~. Compound of ~auf-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~ ("to hold, keep"). The PIE origin is uncertain; one proposal connects it to *~ḱel-~ ("to hide, conceal"), while others suggest *~kelH-~ ("to rise") or *~kel-~ ("to drive"). Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Swedish ~hålla~, Icelandic ~halda~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~, from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below").

Cognate with Dutch ~ophouden~ ("to stop, to cease") and English ~uphold~ ("to maintain, support"), though the three languages have sent the same compound in different semantic directions. German ~aufhalten~ primarily means "to halt, to stop (someone)" and reflexively "to stay, to sojourn" (~sich aufhalten~). The reflexive use with ~mit~ in the negative, ~sich nicht mit etwas aufhalten~ ("not to bother with something"), adds the nuance of refusing to be delayed by trivial matters.
en.aufheben:
~Auf-~ + ~heben~. Compound of ~auf-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-Germanic *~hafjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, to seize").
• ~auf-~: From PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The separable prefix adds a sense of upward motion or removal.

~Aufheben~ is one of German's most philosophically famous verbs, carrying three seemingly contradictory meanings: "to pick up," "to preserve, to keep," and "to cancel, to abolish." Hegel seized upon this triple meaning to create his concept of ~Aufhebung~ ("sublation"): the dialectical process in which a thesis and antithesis are simultaneously ~negated~, ~preserved~, and ~elevated~ into a synthesis. It is rare for a single word to contain its own opposite (such words are called ~auto-antonyms~ or ~contronyms~), and rarer still for a philosopher to build an entire system on the ambiguity. The three senses are etymologically unified: to lift something ~up~ (~aufheben~) removes it from where it was (cancellation), takes it into one's hands (preservation), and raises it to a higher position (elevation). The colloquial phrase ~gut aufgehoben sein~ ("to be in good hands") uses the preservation sense. Cognate with Dutch ~opheffen~ ("to abolish, to lift up").
en.aufhelfen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~helfen~:

• ~helfen~: From MHG ~hëlfen~, from OHG ~hëlfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helpaną~, from PIE *~ḱelb-~, *~ḱelp-~. A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~e~-~a~-~o~ ablaut pattern (~helfen~, ~half~, ~geholfen~). Cognate with English ~help~, Dutch ~helpen~, Danish ~hjælpe~, Norwegian ~hjelpe~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

~Helfen~ governs the dative, and ~aufhelfen~ keeps it: one helps ~to~ someone up, not ~someone~ up. The upward motion is still wholly literal here: whoever has fallen is set back on their feet.
en.aufholen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~holen~:

• ~holen~: From MHG ~holen~, ~holn~, from OHG ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, possibly from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, summon") via "to summon" → "to go and fetch"; the connection is uncertain. Cognate with Dutch ~halen~, Low German ~halen~, English ~haul~ (via French).
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The origin is nautical: a rope is ~aufgeholt~, hauled up. In modern use the direction has turned from upward to forward: what one makes up is lost ground, lost time, lost growth.
en.aufhängen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~hängen~:

• ~hängen~: The merger of three OHG verbs: ~hāhan~ (strong, transitive; past ~hieng~, participle ~gehangan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~hą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~hanhaną~; ~hangēn~ (weak, intransitive); and the causative ~hengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hangijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hangijaną~. The distinction is upheld chiefly in the past tense: intransitive ~hing~/~gehangen~ versus transitive ~hängte~/~gehängt~. Cognate with Dutch ~hangen~, English ~hang~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

Of the three verbs that fell together in ~hängen~, ~aufhängen~ takes the causative one: it is transitive and weak, ~hängte auf~ and ~aufgehängt~, while the intransitive ~hing~ is left to the picture that hangs on the wall.
en.aufhören:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hōrian~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~ ("to hear, to listen"), from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), a compound of *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear") + *~-yéti~ (denominative suffix). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-Germanic *~upp~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys upward motion, opening, or cessation.

The compound means "to stop, to cease, to quit"; ~Hör auf!~ ("Stop it!"). The connection between "listening" and "stopping" is not immediately obvious, but it likely arose from the idea of heeding a command: when you "listen up" (~aufhören~), you stop what you are doing and pay attention. The PIE etymology of ~hören~ is itself remarkable: *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ literally means "to have sharp ears," a compound that reveals the Proto-Indo-European speakers understood hearing as a sharpening of the ear's attention. The PIE root *~h₂ows-~ ("ear") survives in Latin ~auris~ ("ear"), whence English ~aural~ and ~auricular~. The expression ~Da hört sich alles auf!~ ("That's the limit!" literally "Everything stops hearing itself there!") is a characteristically German way of expressing indignation at something beyond the pale.
en.aufklappen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~klappen~:

• ~klappen~: From Middle Low German ~klappen~, from Old Saxon *~klappōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klappōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klappōną~. The verb is onomatopoeic. Cognate with English ~clap~, Dutch ~klappen~, Old High German ~klapfō~ ("a clapping sound"); also related to ~klaffen~ ("to gape").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The onomatopoeic stem supplies the sound: whatever ~aufklappt~ does so audibly. That is why the verb fits lids, books, and folding knives, but not a door that swings open in silence.
en.aufkleben:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~kleben~:

• ~kleben~: From MHG ~kleben~, from OHG ~klebēn~ ("to stick"), from Proto-West Germanic *~klibēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klibēną~, from PIE *~gleyb-~ ("to stick, adhere"), a durative formation from the strong root *~kleibēną~ ("to adhere, to climb"). Cognate with English ~cleave~ and ~climb~, Old Norse ~klīfa~ ("to climb").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

~Kleben~ is stative at root: something adheres somewhere. The prefix turns it into an act with a target: the stamp goes onto the envelope and stays there.
en.aufklingen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~klingen~:

• ~klingen~: From MHG ~klingen~, from OHG ~klingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~klinganą~, almost certainly of onomatopoeic origin. A class III strong verb (~klingt~, ~klang~, ~geklungen~), the same pattern as ~singen~. Cognate with English ~clink~ and ~clang~, Middle Dutch ~klinken~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

~Klingen~ describes a sound that lasts; ~aufklingen~ describes its onset: the moment the tone steps out of silence. The prefix here points not upward but at the beginning.
en.aufklären:
From ~auf-~ + ~klären~, a calque of Middle Low German ~upklāren~. Compound of a Germanic prefix and a Latin-derived verb:

• ~klären~: From MHG ~klæren~, from the adjective ~klar~, which entered German from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch ~claer~, reinforced by Old French ~cler~, all ultimately from Latin ~clārus~ ("bright, clear, famous").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from Proto-Indo-European *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix conveys clearing up, illumination, or resolution.

The word ~aufklären~ is historically inseparable from the ~Aufklärung~, the German Enlightenment of the 18th century. Immanuel Kant's famous 1784 essay "Was ist Aufklärung?" defined it as humanity's emergence from self-imposed immaturity. The word itself mirrors this intellectual program: ~auf-~ ("up") + ~klären~ ("to clear") = "to clear up, to enlighten." Cognate with Dutch ~opklaren~ ("to clear up," especially of weather). The meteorological sense of clearing up likely preceded the philosophical one, and ~aufklären~ still retains both: the weather clears up (~Das Wetter klärt auf~) and a detective clears up a crime (~einen Fall aufklären~). Latin ~clārus~ also gave English ~clear~, ~clarify~, and ~declare~.
en.aufknüpfen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~knüpfen~:

• ~knüpfen~: From MHG ~knüpfen~, from OHG ~knupfen~, ~chnuphan~, related to ~Knopf~ ("button, knob"), from MHG ~knopf~, OHG ~knopf~, Proto-Germanic *~knuppaz~ ("lump, clod, knob"). The word belongs to the Germanic ~kn-~ cluster for lumps and knots: ~Knoten~, ~Knochen~, ~Knauf~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The same prefix carries two opposite readings here: a knot is ~aufgeknüpft~ when it is undone, a person when they are strung up from a beam. The knot at the root of the word stays visible either way.
en.aufkochen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~kochen~:

• ~kochen~: From MHG ~kochen~, from OHG ~kohhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kokōn~, borrowed from Late Latin ~cocō~, from Latin ~coquō~ ("I cook, I boil"), from PIE *~pekʷ-~ ("to cook, to ripen"). A loan early enough to have undergone the High German shift of ~k~ to ~ch~. Cognate with English ~cook~, Dutch ~koken~, Danish ~koge~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The verb names no lasting state but a single rise: the liquid comes to the boil and is taken off the heat again at once. That a loanword this early from Latin should take on German separability is itself worth noting.
en.aufkommen:
From Middle High German ~ūfkomen~, from Old High German ~ūfqueman~. Compound of ~auf-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~komen~/~quëmen~, from OHG ~quëman~ (rarer ~cuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from the aorist subjunctive of Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ ("to step, to arrive"). Cognate with English ~come~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from Proto-Indo-European *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix conveys emergence or arising.

The OHG form ~quëman~ preserves the ancient ~kw-~ cluster (written ~qu-~) that was later simplified to ~k-~ in most German dialects, a sound change called labiovelar simplification. Gothic ~qiman~ and Old English ~cuman~ show the same root. The compound ~aufkommen~ has branched into several meanings: "to arise, to emerge" (of trends or ideas), "to bear the cost" (~für etwas aufkommen~, "to pay for something"), and "to recover" (from an illness). The PIE root *~gʷem-~ ("to step") also produced Latin ~venīre~ ("to come"), Greek ~baínein~ ("to go"), and Sanskrit ~gámati~ ("goes"), making ~kommen~ a cousin of English ~advent~, ~venue~, and ~acrobat~.
en.aufkündigen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~kündigen~:

• ~kündigen~: From MHG ~kündigen~ ("to make known, to announce"), from the adjective ~kündic~ (modern ~kundig~), from OHG ~kundig~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kunþīg~, from Proto-Germanic *~kunþaz~ ("known"), the past participle of *~kunnaną~ ("to know, be able"), from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"). The sense "to give notice" became standard only in the 19th century, clipped from ~aufkündigen~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The root's history holds a reversal here: ~aufkündigen~ was not built from ~kündigen~; rather the simple ~kündigen~ was clipped out of it in the 19th century. The longer verb kept the weightier cases: alliances, treaties, a political consensus.
en.auflachen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~lachen~:

• ~lachen~: From MHG ~lachen~, from OHG ~lahhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~, from PIE *~kleg-~ ("to cry out, sound"). The initial ~hl-~ cluster was simplified to ~l-~ in Old High German. Cognate with English ~laugh~, Dutch ~lachen~, Gothic ~hlahjan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

~Lachen~ can go on for a while; ~auflachen~ cannot. It names the single burst: the short, often involuntary laugh that breaks out of silence and stops again immediately.
en.aufladen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two historically distinct verbs under one infinitive. ~laden~ (strong, "to load"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"); cognate with English ~lade~ and ~laden~, Lithuanian ~klṓti~. ~laden~ (weak, "to invite, summon"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root found only in Germanic and Anatolian (Hittite ~halzai~).
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

Of the two ~laden~ verbs sharing one infinitive, this one belongs to the strong "to load," not the weak "to invite"; hence ~lud auf~ and ~aufgeladen~. That batteries are now ~aufgeladen~ too is the same image: the load goes onto its carrier.
en.auflaufen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

Literally a ship ~läuft auf~: runs onto ground, onto a sandbank. From the image of matter piling up against an obstacle comes the figurative use: debts, interest, and overtime ~laufen auf~ as well.
en.auflegen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

~Legen~ is the causative of ~liegen~, and the prefix names what a thing is laid on. Out of that grows the figurative sense "to impose": a burden, a tax, a penalty comes to rest on someone.
en.auflehnen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~lehnen~:

• ~lehnen~: A merger of two verbs: MHG ~linen~/~lenen~ (intransitive), from OHG ~hlinēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlinēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlināną~, from PIE *~k̂ley-~ ("to lean, incline"); and MHG ~leinen~ (causative), from OHG ~hleinen~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlainijaną~. A second, archaic ~lehnen~ ("to lend, borrow"), from OHG ~lēhanōn~, survives only in ~entlehnen~ and ~Lehnwort~. Cognate with English ~lean~, Latin ~clīnō~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The path from leaning to rebelling runs through posture: whoever ~sich auflehnt~ raises themselves out of a resting position. Reflexive and construed with ~gegen~ or ~wider~, the verb has surrendered nearly all of its literal sense to the figurative one.
en.auflesen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

Here the stem's older meaning survives intact: ~auflesen~ means to gather, never to read. Whoever gleans ears of grain is doing exactly what ~lesen~ first meant, and what the ~Weinlese~, the grape harvest, still carries in its name.
en.aufleuchten:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~leuchten~:

• ~leuchten~: From OHG ~liuhten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~liuhtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~liuhtijaną~, a factitive verb from *~leuhtą~ ("light") or *~leuhtaz~ ("bright"), from PIE *~lewk-~ ("bright, to shine, to see"). Cognate with MHG ~liuhten~ and English ~light~; from the same root, Latin ~lūx~ and Greek ~leukos~ ("white").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

~Leuchten~ is a factitive formation (to make light) and describes a state. The prefix cuts a single moment out of it: the sudden flash, which happens in eyes as readily as on warning lamps.
en.auflösen:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~lösen~. Cognate with Dutch ~oplossen~:

• ~lösen~: From MHG ~lœsen~, from OHG ~lōsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lausijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausijaną~ ("to make loose, release, set free"), a factitive derivation from *~lausaz~ ("loose, free"), from PIE *~lewh₁-~ ("to loosen, cut apart"). Cognate with English ~loose~ (via Old Norse ~lauss~), obsolete English ~leese~ (from Old English ~līesan~), Danish ~løse~, Swedish ~lösa~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~, from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below").

The Dutch cognate ~oplossen~ has specialized further than its German cousin: it is the standard word for "to solve" (a problem), "to dissolve" (a substance), and even "to resolve" (a conflict). German ~auflösen~ covers similar ground but tends more toward "to dissolve, to disband, to break up." The expression ~sich in Luft auflösen~ ("to dissolve into thin air") captures the most dramatic end of this semantic spectrum.
en.aufmachen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The stem is as general as a verb can be, so the whole meaning rides on the prefix. Reflexively it shifts once more: ~sich aufmachen~ does not mean to open oneself but to set out.
en.aufmerken:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~merken~:

• ~merken~: From MHG ~merken~, from OHG ~merchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~markijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~markijaną~ ("to mark, notice"), a denominal verb from *~marką~ ("mark, sign"). To notice something is etymologically to leave a mental mark on it. Cognate with English ~mark~ (and ~remark~), Icelandic ~merkja~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

Literally it is to set one's mark upon something. In present-day German the verb has lost ground to ~aufpassen~ and ~bemerken~ and sounds biblical and elevated; what stayed alive is the adjective ~aufmerksam~ and the noun ~Aufmerksamkeit~.
en.aufmischen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~mischen~:

• ~mischen~: From MHG ~mischen~, from OHG ~misken~, from Proto-Germanic *~miskijaną~ ("to mix"), from PIE *~meyḱ-~ ("to mix, knead"), via the inchoative present *~miḱ-sḱé-~. Cognate with English ~mix~, Latin ~misceō~, Greek ~mísgo~, Sanskrit ~miśrá~ ("mixed").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

Mixing brings up whatever was lying at the bottom, hence the prefix. In colloquial use the image has sharpened: to ~aufmischen~ a place is to bring it not merely disorder but a fight.
en.aufnehmen:
From Middle High German ~ūfnemen~, from Old High German *~ūfneman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uppneman~. Compound of ~auf-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-Germanic *~upp-~, from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). This separable prefix adds a sense of upward motion, opening, or reception.

The compound's range of meanings ("to pick up," "to record," "to admit (a member)," "to photograph," "to receive (a signal)," "to absorb (a shock)") illustrates how the directional ~auf-~ prefix transforms the basic act of taking into a rich array of receptive and upward-oriented actions. Dutch ~opnemen~ and Old English ~upniman~ are parallel formations. Cognate with Dutch ~opnemen~.
en.aufnähen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~nähen~:

• ~nähen~: From MHG ~nāian~, ~næjen~, from OHG ~nājen~, ~nāian~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēaną~ ("to sew"), from PIE *~(s)neh₁-~ ("to spin, to sew"), a root with an optional initial ~s-~ (~s-mobile~). The instrument noun *~neh₁-dleh₂~ gave, via *~nēþlō~, both ~Nadel~ and English ~needle~. Cognate with Dutch ~naaien~, Latin ~nēre~ ("to spin").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

The prefix names the surface sewn onto, and separates the verb from ~annähen~, which joins one piece to another. An ~Aufnäher~, a patch, sits visibly on top; a button that is ~angenäht~ sits in the seam.
en.aufpassen:
From ~auf-~ + ~passen~, a calque of Dutch ~oppassen~. Compound of a Germanic prefix and a Romance-derived verb:

• ~passen~: Borrowed from French ~passer~ ("to pass"), ultimately from Latin ~passus~ ("step, pace"). Most closely related to German ~passieren~ ("to happen, to pass").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from Proto-Indo-European *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix adds a sense of alertness and upward attention.

The sense of "to be attentive, to pay attention" in ~aufpassen~ is not inherited from the French source but is a native Germanic semantic development within Dutch, from which it was calqued into German. French ~passer~ means simply "to pass," but Dutch ~oppassen~ and its German calque ~aufpassen~ developed the meaning "to watch out, to be careful", perhaps from the idea of stepping up to alertness. The phrase ~pass auf!~ ("watch out!") is one of German's most common warnings. Curiously, ~passen~ in German also means "to fit" (as in clothing), a sense that developed independently from the idea of a step or measure being correct.
en.aufprägen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~prägen~:

• ~prägen~: From MHG ~bræchen~ / ~præchen~ ("to press in, to depict"), from OHG ~giprāhhan~ / ~prāhhan~ ("to press in or scratch by breaking the surface"), formed from the first- and third-person plural preterite of ~prēchan~ / ~prāchun~ ("to break"), making ~prägen~ likely a relative of ~brechen~. The noun ~Prägung~ ("imprint, stamp") shares the root.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

The root's kinship with ~brechen~ stays legible in the act: a die does not lay an image on a coin so much as break it into the surface. Modern ~aufprägen~ has widened into the figurative (an era imprints its character on a generation), but the pressure of the original is intact.
en.aufrauchen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~rauchen~:

• ~rauchen~: From MHG ~rouchen~, ~röuchen~, from OHG ~rouhhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raukijan~, derived from the noun *~rauki-~ ("smoke"), from Proto-Germanic *~raukiz~, from *~reukaną~ ("to smoke"), possibly from PIE *~h₁rewg-~ ("to belch, emit"). The noun survives as ~Rauch~. Cognate with English ~reek~, Dutch ~rook~, Swedish ~rök~, Danish ~røg~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

This is the rarer of two verbs spelled alike: here smoke rises and shows itself, whereas the everyday ~aufrauchen~ (with ~auf-~ in its using-up sense) means to finish a cigarette. The root is the same either way, and the noun ~Rauch~ sits inside both.
en.aufrechnen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~rechnen~:

• ~rechnen~: From MHG ~rechenen~, from OHG ~rehhanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rekanōn~ ("to count, explain"), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to make straight or right"), the same root as German ~recht~ and Latin ~rectus~. Cognate with English ~reckon~, Dutch ~rekenen~, Low German ~rekenen~, Danish ~regne~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

The root's tie to ~recht~ and Latin ~rectus~ makes the reckoning sense feel less like arithmetic than like setting something straight. ~Aufrechnen~ runs in both directions: a sum is charged onto someone's account, or two claims are set against each other until they cancel.
en.aufregen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~regen~:

• ~regen~: From MHG ~regen~ ("to make protrude, to erect, to excite, to move"), from Proto-Germanic *~hragjaną~ ("to make stand, wake up, incite"); synchronically the causative of MHG ~ragen~ ("to project, to tower"). The verb means "to stir, move, rouse", unrelated to the noun ~Regen~ ("rain"), and is most often reflexive (~sich regen~).
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

Because ~regen~ already means "to stir," ~aufregen~ adds not the motion but its direction: what had settled is churned up again. The reflexive ~sich aufregen~ is now by far the commoner form, and the participle ~aufgeregt~ has drifted into a plain adjective.
en.aufreiben:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~reiben~:

• ~reiben~: From MHG ~rīben~, from OHG ~rīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrībaną~ ("to rub"); beyond Germanic uncertain, a PIE *~wreyp-~, labial extension of *~wer-~ ("to turn"), being proposed but not secure. A class I strong verb (~reiben~, ~rieb~, ~gerieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~wrijven~, Old Saxon ~wrīvan~; German dropped the initial ~w-~ before ~r~, as in ~ringen~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The literal reading is a march's blisters: skin rubbed until it opens. From there the verb moved to whole armies (~aufgerieben~ troops are ground down to nothing), and then to people, where ~aufreibend~ describes work that wears its doer away.
en.aufreihen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~reihen~:

• ~reihen~: From MHG ~rīhen~, from OHG ~rīhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rīhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rīhaną~ ("to string together, line up"), possibly from PIE *~h₁reyḱ-~ ("to scratch, tear"), though that connection is uncertain. In the sewing senses it appears to have merged with a separate *~wrīhaną~ ("to cover"). Once strong, now weak (~reihte~, ~gereiht~) and felt as a derivative of ~Reihe~. Cognate with Dutch ~rijgen~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

Speakers now hear ~aufreihen~ as built on the noun ~Reihe~, and for modern German that is not wrong, even though it inverts the history; the verb is the older word. What ~auf-~ contributes is the thread: beads are strung onto something, and only then do they make a row.
en.aufreiten:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~reiten~:

• ~reiten~: From MHG ~rīten~, from OHG ~rītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rīdaną~, from PIE *~Hreydʰ-~ ("to set in motion, ride"), likely a suffixed form of *~h₃reyH-~ ("to move, churn"). German ~reiten~ narrowed to horseback riding, while English ~ride~ broadened to vehicles. Cognate with Dutch ~rijden~, Danish ~ride~, Swedish ~rida~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The verb is a technical survivor of cavalry drill, where riders close up into rank rather than merely ride upward; its ~sein~ auxiliary marks it as a verb of motion. German ~reiten~ having narrowed to horseback, ~aufreiten~ could not follow English ~ride up~ into vehicles.
en.aufreißen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The root's other descendant is English ~write~, which began as scratching a surface, so ~aufreißen~ and writing are one gesture pushed to opposite extremes, the first tearing the surface apart, the second marking it just deeply enough to be read.
en.aufrichten:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~ ("to straighten, set right, direct"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rihtijaną~, a denominative from the adjective *~rehtaz~ ("straight, right"), from PIE *~h₃reǵtós~ ("right, straightened"), from *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to stretch out, straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~richten~, Gothic ~raihtjan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

"Straight" already sits in the root of ~richten~ (the same ~*rehtaz~ that gave English ~right~), so ~aufrichten~ is straightening with a direction added: upward. The moral reading follows the physical one, and someone ~aufgerichtet~ after grief has literally been set back on their feet.
en.aufrollen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~rollen~:

• ~rollen~: From MHG ~rollen~, borrowed from Old French ~roeler~, from Medieval Latin ~rotulāre~ ("to roll"), from Latin ~rotula~ ("small wheel"), diminutive of ~rota~ ("wheel"), from PIE *~ret-~ ("to run, to roll"). Cognate with English ~roll~ (also borrowed from Old French), Dutch ~rollen~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

~Rollen~ is a Romance import that never lost its wheel: Latin ~rota~ still turns inside every ~Rolle~. ~Aufrollen~ accordingly does two opposite things (a cable is wound onto its drum, a flag is unrolled, an old case is reopened), because ~auf-~ can mean "onto" or "open," and the verb never chose.
en.aufrufen:
