~Auf-~ + ~rufen~. Compound of ~auf-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~, ~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~ ("to cry out, call, shout"). The Proto-Germanic etymology is uncertain; a traditional connection to *~hrōþiz~ ("glory, fame") is phonetically problematic. Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~auf-~: From PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix adds the sense of calling upward or outward, summoning to action.

~Aufrufen~ means "to call (someone's name), to call upon, to summon, to invoke." In modern German it has gained a strong technical sense: ~eine Webseite aufrufen~ ("to call up a webpage"), ~eine Funktion aufrufen~ ("to invoke a function"). The older sense of publicly summoning someone by name persists in legal and administrative contexts (~die Zeugen aufrufen~, "to call the witnesses"). A curious linguistic footnote: ~rufen~ originally had both strong and weak conjugation forms coexisting, with the weak pattern attestable into the 19th century. The modern umlautless present-tense conjugations (~du rufst~, ~er ruft~, not the obsolete ~du rüfst~, ~er rüft~) are a relic of this weak-verb influence, as lack of umlaut on rounded diphthongs before labials is regular in Upper German but has only become standard in ~rufen~, not in ~laufen~ or ~saufen~.
en.aufrunden:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~runden~:

• ~runden~: From ~rund~ + ~-en~. ~Rund~ descends from MHG ~runt~, borrowed from Old French ~ront~, from Latin ~rotundus~ ("round"), from ~rota~ ("wheel, disk"), from PIE *~Hróth₂o~ (from *~ret-~ "to run, to roll"), one of the few everyday German adjectives that arrived via Latin and French rather than directly from Proto-Germanic. English ~round~ took the same detour.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The pair ~aufrunden~ and ~abrunden~ splits the direction cleanly, up and down, on a base word that reached German by way of Rome and Paris rather than from Proto-Germanic. Charity appeals exploit the asymmetry: only rounding up is ever offered.
en.aufräumen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~räumen~:

• ~räumen~: From Early New High German ~reumen~, a Central German umlaut variant of ~raumen~, from MHG ~rūmen~, from OHG ~rūmen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rūmijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rūmijaną~, a factitive verb from the adjective *~rūmaz~ ("roomy, spacious"), from PIE *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open"). Etymologically, "to make room." Cognate with English ~room~, the noun ~Raum~, Bavarian ~rama~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix marks reconditioning or working-up: bringing something into fresh or usable condition.

Since ~räumen~ is literally "to make room," ~aufräumen~ names the condition the room is restored to rather than the clearing itself. The older, harder reading survives in ~mit etwas aufräumen~, "to do away with something", Luther's translators used it of armies wiped out.
en.aufrücken:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~rücken~:

• ~rücken~: From MHG ~rücken~, from OHG ~rucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rukkijan~. The verb means "to move, to shift" and is the base of ~verrückt~ ("crazy," literally "shifted, displaced"); the noun ~Rücken~ ("back") is etymologically a separate word. Cognate with English ~rock~, Old Norse ~rykkja~, Old English ~roccian~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The same verb yields ~verrückt~, literally "shifted out of place", a mind can be moved as a chair can. ~Aufrücken~ moves in the good direction: it closes the gap ahead, and by extension means rising a rank. The noun ~Rücken~ "back" only looks related.
en.aufsagen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix marks summoning or proclaiming publicly: calling something out or calling someone forth.

Reciting and renouncing look unrelated until one hears ~auf-~ as "out loud, in public": a poem is declaimed, and a post, a friendship, or a lease is publicly declared over. Grimm uses the second reading: Frau Holle ~sagte ihr den Dienst auf~, gave her notice.
en.aufsammeln:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~sammeln~:

• ~sammeln~: From MHG ~samelen~, ~samlen~, by dissimilation from ~samenen~, from Proto-Germanic *~samnōną~ ("to bring together, gather"), derived from *~samanai~ ("together") with the verbal suffix *~-ōną~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, same, together"), the root behind English ~same~ and Latin ~similis~. Cognate with Dutch ~verzamelen~, Swedish ~samla~, Gothic ~samjan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

~Sammeln~ says only that things end up together; ~auf-~ supplies the stooping and the lifting, so ~aufsammeln~ means gathering from the ground in particular. Its root ~*sem-~ "one, together" also underlies English ~same~: to collect is to make many into one.
en.aufsaugen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~saugen~:

• ~saugen~: From MHG ~sūgen~, from OHG ~sūgan~ ("to suck"), from Proto-West Germanic *~sūgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sūganą~, from PIE *~sewk-~ ("to suck"). Historically a class II strong verb (~saugen~, ~sog~, ~gesogen~), it now inflects weak (~saugte~, ~gesaugt~) just as readily. Cognate with English ~suck~, Dutch ~zuigen~, Danish ~suge~, Old English ~sūcan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys using something up or consuming it entirely.

~Saugen~ is one of the verbs currently changing class, and the compound wobbles with it: both ~saugte auf~ and ~sog auf~ are current. Figuratively it is the completive force that carries: a child who ~saugt~ a language ~auf~ takes in all of it and leaves nothing behind.
en.aufschauen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix directs attention onto something: noticing, minding, or listening out.

The root's English cousin is ~show~, the same act seen from the other side, one language kept "look," the other "make visible." ~Aufschauen~ carries that doubling in miniature: raising the eyes, and looking up ~to~ someone. It is the southern and Austrian word where the north says ~aufsehen~.
en.aufscheinen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~scheinen~:

• ~scheinen~: From MHG ~schīnen~, from OHG ~skīnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skīnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skīnaną~, from PIE *~(s)ḱeh₁y-~ ("to shine, shimmer"). A class I strong verb. It covers both "to shine" and "to seem," a duality reflecting the ancient metaphor of appearances as light. Cognate with English ~shine~, Dutch ~schijnen~, Danish ~skinne~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

The root already hesitates between shining and seeming, and ~aufscheinen~ inherits the hesitation: something flashes into view, or merely turns out to be the case. Austrian officialese took the second road: a name that ~scheint auf~ in a register is simply listed there, light reduced to a database entry.
en.aufschieben:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~schieben~:

• ~schieben~: From MHG ~schieben~, from OHG ~skioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeubaną~, from PIE *~skewbʰ-~ ("to push, to shove, to thrust"). A class II strong verb (~schieben~, ~schob~, ~geschoben~). Cognate with English ~shove~, Dutch ~schuiven~, Danish ~skubbe~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The physical reading (a door or a bolt shoved open) has largely yielded to the temporal one, where what gets pushed is not a door but a deadline. German is unusually literal about procrastination: ~aufschieben~ shoves the thing further along rather than putting it off.
en.aufschießen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb (~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~). Cognate with English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Old Norse ~skjóta~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The Proto-Germanic root meant shoving as much as shooting, which is why the commoner modern ~aufschießen~ is a plant shooting up rather than a lock shot open. Both readings live off the same idea of sudden release.
en.aufschlagen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

Few German verbs fan out so far: a tent is pitched, a book is opened, a price goes up, a ball is served, and a body strikes the ground. The base is a single blow, and ~auf-~ decides each time whether the blow builds something up or lands against something.
en.aufschließen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~schließen~:

• ~schließen~: From MHG ~slieȥen~, from OHG ~sliozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sleutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slūtaną~, *~sleutaną~ ("to lock, shut"); the PIE root is not definitively established. A class II strong verb (~schließen~, ~schloss~, ~geschlossen~). Cognate with Old Saxon ~slūtan~, Dutch ~sluiten~, archaic English ~slot~ ("a bolt").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The verb keeps the lock visible in a way English ~unlock~ does not: ~schließen~ shuts, ~auf-~ reverses it, and archaic English ~slot~ "a bolt" belongs to the same root. A second ~aufschließen~, from the drill ground, means to close ranks, the opposite motion, out of the opposite sense of the prefix.
en.aufschmelzen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~schmelzen~:

• ~schmelzen~: From MHG ~smelzen~, from OHG ~smelzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smeltan~, from Proto-Germanic *~smeltaną~ ("to melt"), from PIE *~(s)meld-~ ("to melt, to soften"). Intransitively a class III strong verb (~schmelzen~, ~schmolz~, ~geschmolzen~), beside a weak causative ~schmelzen~ ("to melt something down"). Cognate with English ~smelt~ and ~melt~ (the same root with and without the mobile ~s-~), and Dutch ~smelten~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix marks reconditioning or working-up: bringing something into fresh or usable condition.

English preserved both halves of this root (~melt~ without the mobile ~s-~ and ~smelt~ with it), and German preserved both halves of the verb, a strong intransitive beside a weak causative. ~Aufschmelzen~ inherits the split: the metal melts, and the smith melts it.
en.aufschneiden:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~schneiden~:

• ~schneiden~: From MHG ~snīden~, from OHG ~snīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~snīþan~ ("to cut"); no secure PIE root has been established, and the word may be a Germanic innovation. A class I strong verb (~schneiden~, ~schnitt~, ~geschnitten~). Cognate with archaic English ~snithe~ ("to cut"), Dutch ~snijden~, Icelandic ~sníða~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

Beside the surgical reading sits a figurative one: an ~Aufschneider~ is a braggart, after the butcher who cuts an extravagantly large slice for show. The root itself has no secure ancestry outside Germanic and may have been coined there.
en.aufschreiben:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

That a Latin loanword ended up conjugating ~schreiben, schrieb, geschrieben~ shows how early it arrived: verbs borrowed later join the weak class without exception. ~Auf-~ names the surface, which is why the wax tablet, the ledger, and the note on a phone are all things one writes ~auf~.
en.aufschwellen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~schwellen~:

• ~schwellen~: From MHG ~swëllen~, from OHG ~swëllan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swellaną~ ("to swell"), perhaps from PIE *~swelH-~, though the root is not securely established. A class III strong verb (~schwellen~, ~schwoll~, ~geschwollen~), beside a weak causative ~schwellen~ ("to make swell") from Proto-Germanic *~swallijaną~. Cognate with English ~swell~, Dutch ~zwellen~, Old Norse ~svella~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The compound keeps the strong conjugation of its root (~schwillt auf~, ~schwoll auf~, ~aufgeschwollen~), and ~auf-~ adds nothing the root does not already imply: it merely makes the direction of the swelling explicit.
en.aufschütteln:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~schütteln~:

• ~schütteln~: From MHG ~schütelen~, from OHG ~scutilōn~, an iterative formation from ~schütten~ ("to pour, to shake") marking repeated back-and-forth motion. ~schütten~ derives from OHG ~scuttēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skudjaną~, perhaps from PIE *~(s)kewt-~ ("to shake, jolt"). Cognate with Dutch ~schudden~ ("to shake").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix marks reconditioning or working-up: bringing something into fresh or usable condition.

The compound is domestic rather than violent: shaking a featherbed does not disturb it but restores its loft, which is why ~aufschütteln~ takes bedding and pillows as its objects and never, say, a bottle.
en.aufsehen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix directs attention onto something: noticing, minding, or listening out.

The literal upward glance survives in the noun ~das Aufsehen~ ("a stir, a sensation"), the thing a crowd looks up at.
en.aufsetzen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

Because the object ends up resting on a surface, one verb covers a hat on a head, a pot on a stove, and a text on paper; ~einen Brief aufsetzen~ is to draft a letter, the writing conceived as ink set onto the page.
en.aufspeichern:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~speichern~:

• ~speichern~: A denominal verb from ~Speicher~ ("storehouse, granary"), from MHG ~spīcher~, OHG ~spīhhāri~, Proto-West Germanic *~spīkārī~, borrowed from Late Latin ~spīcārium~ ("granary"), from ~spīca~ ("ear of grain, spike"). The same Latin word also gives English ~spike~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The compound stays transparent where the root no longer is: ~speichern~ has become the ordinary word for saving a computer file, while ~aufspeichern~ keeps the older image of a granary filling up.
en.aufsperren:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~sperren~:

• ~sperren~: From MHG ~sperren~, from OHG ~sperran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sparrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sparrijaną~ ("to bar, to block"), a denominative verb from *~sparrô~ ("wooden beam, log"), originally to bar a passage with a beam. Cognate with English ~spar~ ("to bolt, bar"; the noun for a wooden beam), Dutch ~sperren~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

Southern German and Austrian usage prefers ~aufsperren~ where the north says ~aufschließen~, and the verb reaches past locks: a mouth or a pair of eyes can be ~aufgesperrt~ too, opened as wide as the beam once barred the passage shut.
en.aufspielen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix marks summoning or proclaiming publicly: calling something out or calling someone forth.

Two readings sit side by side: a band ~spielt auf~, striking up in public, and the reflexive ~sich aufspielen~ turns that same performance into a reproach: to posture, to pass oneself off as something one is not.
en.aufsprechen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~sprechen~:

• ~sprechen~: From MHG ~sprëchen~, from OHG ~sprëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sprekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sprekaną~, probably from PIE *~spregʰ-~ ("to crackle"). The sense developed from an onomatopoeic root meaning "to crackle, make noise" to "to speak." Cognate with Dutch ~spreken~, English ~speak~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

The compound is regional and thinly attested; where it lives it means to start speaking or to speak up, the particle marking the onset rather than the content.
en.aufspringen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~springen~:

• ~springen~: From OHG ~springan~, from Proto-Germanic *~springaną~, from PIE *~sprenǵʰ-~, a nasalized form of *~sperǵʰ-~ ("to move energetically, to hasten, to spring"). A class III strong verb (~springen~, ~sprang~, ~gesprungen~). Cognate with English ~spring~, Dutch ~springen~, Danish ~springe~, Greek ~spérkhō~ ("to hasten").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix marks impact onto a surface: motion that ends against something solid.

One compound covers three things at once: springing up from a seat, springing open (a door, or a crack in dry skin), and springing onto a moving tram, which is the reading glossed here.
en.aufspüren:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~spüren~:

• ~spüren~: From MHG ~spüren~, from OHG ~spurien~, ~spurren~, from Proto-Germanic *~spurjaną~ ("to feel, touch; to search, examine"), a derivative of *~spurą~ ("track, trace"), ultimately from PIE *~sperH-~ ("to kick, step"). Cognate with dialectal English ~speer~ ("to ask, inquire"), Swedish ~spörja~, Dutch ~speuren~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix marks locating, bringing something to light by searching for it.

Root and particle say the same thing twice: ~spüren~ already meant to follow a ~Spur~ ("track"), and ~auf-~ supplies the successful end of the search, the quarry brought to light.
en.aufstehen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The compound keeps its root's suppletive preterite (~stand auf~) and carries a second, political sense: a people that ~steht auf~ rises in revolt, which is where the noun ~der Aufstand~ ("uprising") comes from.
en.aufsteigen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The particle is nearly redundant on a root that already means "to climb," and German spends the surplus on figurative ascent: a team ~steigt auf~ into the next league, an official into the next rank.
en.aufstellen:
Equivalent to ~auf-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stallijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stallijaną~, from PIE *~stelh₂-~ ("to put, to stand").
• ~auf-~: From PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix adds the sense of placing something upright or establishing something.

~Aufstellen~ means "to set up, to erect, to establish"; covering everything from physical placement (~ein Zelt aufstellen~, "to pitch a tent") to abstract establishment (~eine Theorie aufstellen~, "to put forward a theory," ~einen Rekord aufstellen~, "to set a record") to military formation (~Truppen aufstellen~, "to deploy troops"). The prefix ~auf-~ lifts the act of placing into an upright, visible, public position. The derived noun ~Aufstellung~ means "lineup, formation, arrangement", the starting eleven in a football match is the ~Aufstellung~. Cognate with Dutch ~opstellen~.
en.aufstoßen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). Cognate with dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce, ricochet"), Dutch ~stoten~, Old Norse ~stauta~ and ~steyta~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The shove is what distinguishes it: a door is ~aufgestoßen~ with a shoulder or a foot, never with a key, and a third, bodily sense survives in ~mir stößt es auf~, to belch.
en.aufstreben:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~streben~:

• ~streben~: From MHG ~strëben~, from OHG ~strëbēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stribēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~stribāną~ ("to strive, resist"). Cognate with Dutch ~streven~ ("to strive") and English ~strive~ (via Old French ~estriver~, itself borrowed from a Germanic source).
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

Where ~streben~ names effort in any direction, ~aufstreben~ fixes it upward, and the participle ~aufstrebend~ has become the ordinary word for a rising city, career, or economy.
en.aufstören:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~stören~:

• ~stören~: From MHG ~stören~, from OHG ~stōren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~staurijan~; related to Proto-Germanic *~steuran~, whose root meant "to move, to agitate." Cognate with English ~stir~, Old English ~styrian~ ("to stir, move, agitate"), Dutch ~storen~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

~Stören~ has narrowed to "to disturb" while its English cognate ~stir~ kept the physical motion; ~aufstören~ preserves the older, concrete act: game driven out of cover, a sleeper startled out of rest.
en.aufsuchen:
From ~auf-~ + ~suchen~:

• ~suchen~: From MHG ~suochen~, from OHG ~suohhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sōkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sōkijaną~ ("to seek"), from Proto-Indo-European *~seh₂g-~ ("to seek out"). Cognate with English ~seek~, Gothic ~sōkjan~, Old Saxon ~sōkian~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from Proto-Indo-European *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix adds purposefulness to the seeking.

The PIE root *~seh₂g-~ also produced Latin ~sāgīre~ ("to perceive keenly") and Old Irish ~saigim~ ("to seek, pursue"), suggesting that the original sense was more about keen perception than mere searching. The compound ~aufsuchen~ means "to seek out, to visit, to call on"; it implies a deliberate, purposeful visit rather than a casual encounter. Compare English ~upseek~, an archaic cognate. The related noun ~Suche~ ("search") and compound ~Versuch~ ("attempt, experiment") both stem from the same root, showing how "seeking" branches into "trying" and "testing."
en.auftauchen:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~tauchen~:

• ~tauchen~: From MHG ~tūchen~, from OHG ~-tūhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dūkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dūkaną~ ("to duck, dive under"). The ultimate PIE origin is unclear; one theory connects it to *~dʰugʰnéh₂-~, from a root meaning "to fall," which might also be related to *~duganą~ ("to be fit"). Cognate with Dutch ~duiken~, Swedish ~dyka~. A derivative with Low German consonantism is ~ducken~, cognate with and synonymous with English ~duck~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~, from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below").

The word ~tauchen~ had become obsolete in Upper German dialects but was reintroduced from Central German ~dūchen~/~tūchen~ and Middle Low German ~dūken~. In this process, the originally strong verb became weak. The compound ~auftauchen~ literally means "to dive up," describing a submarine, a whale, or a diver surfacing. Its figurative use ("to turn up, to appear") captures the sudden, often unexpected quality of something emerging from hidden depths.
en.aufteilen:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~teilen~:

• ~teilen~: From MHG ~teilen~, from OHG ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~ ("to divide, part, deal"), from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, from PIE *~dʰoyl-~ ("part, watershed"). Cognate with English ~deal~ and Dutch ~delen~.
• ~auf-~: From PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). As a separable prefix, it means "up, open, on."

~Aufteilen~ means "to divide up, to partition, to distribute", literally "to part open," splitting something into portions. The ~auf-~ prefix adds a sense of opening or distributing that plain ~teilen~ ("to share, to divide") lacks: ~teilen~ can mean sharing (without separating), but ~aufteilen~ always implies breaking something into distinct portions. The PIE root produced English ~deal~ (exact cognate), ~dole~ (a distributed share), and ~ordeal~ (originally "a judgment," from the act of distributing or meting out justice).
en.auftragen:
From Middle High German ~ūftragen~. Compound of ~auf-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw"). Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~ ("to carry"), Portuguese ~trazer~ ("to bring").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from Proto-Indo-European *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface or assigning a task upward.

The semantic shift from "to pull, drag" to "to carry, bear" happened within Germanic: what was originally dragged along the ground came to be carried. The compound ~auftragen~ has developed several distinct meanings that seem unrelated on the surface: "to apply" (paint, cream), "to assign, commission" (a task), and "to serve" (food). The connecting thread is the idea of placing something onto or upon: paint onto a canvas, a duty onto a person, food onto a table. English ~draw~ and ~drag~ are doublets from the same Proto-Germanic root, split by dialect: ~drag~ entered English from Old Norse ~draga~, while ~draw~ continued the native Old English ~dragan~.
en.auftreffen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~treffen~:

• ~treffen~: From MHG ~treffen~, from OHG ~treffan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drepan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drepaną~ ("to strike, push, beat"), from PIE *~dʰrebʰ-~, *~dʰreb-~ ("to crack, crush, strike, kill"). The High German consonant shift from *~dr-~ to ~tr-~ obscures the cognate relationship with Old English ~drepan~ ("to strike"). Cognate with Old Norse ~drepa~ ("to kill, strike").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix marks impact onto a surface: motion that ends against something solid.

The root's oldest sense was "to strike," so in technical registers the compound restores what everyday ~treffen~ ("to meet") has lost: a projectile ~trifft auf~ its target, and nobody meets anybody.
en.auftreiben:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The compound runs two ways: cattle driven up to pasture bloat, which yields the reading glossed here, while the commoner modern one is "to scare up, to procure", driving something out of hiding until it is found.
en.auftrennen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~trennen~:

• ~trennen~: From MHG ~trennen~, from OHG ~trennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~trannijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trannijaną~. The deeper etymology is uncertain: the Proto-Germanic root is not securely connected to any PIE root. Cognate with Low German ~trennen~ and Dutch ~tornen~, which has narrowed to "to unpick stitches."
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The compound is the tailor's word: ~trennen~ separates anything at all, but ~auftrennen~ undoes a seam stitch by stitch, exactly the narrowing Dutch performed on the cognate ~tornen~.
en.auftreten:
From Middle High German ~ūftreten~. Compound of ~auf-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~. A class V strong verb cognate with English ~tread~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-Germanic *~up-~, from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). As a separable prefix, ~auf-~ adds upward directionality or the sense of opening, beginning, or public emergence.

The compound's primary senses ("to appear (on stage)," "to occur," "to kick") all derive from the image of stepping upward into visibility. An actor who ~auftritt~ steps forward onto the boards; a problem that ~auftritt~ steps up into one's awareness; an aggressor who ~auftritt~ puts a foot forward in force. The ~Auftritt~ ("appearance, scene, entrance") and the theatrical term ~Auftreten~ ("manner of conducting oneself") preserve the original footstep metaphor. Notably, the ~treten~-based family accounts for nearly every German word for social or institutional entry: ~eintreten~ ("to enter, to join"), ~betreten~ ("to step on"), ~vertreten~ ("to represent"), and ~auftreten~ itself, German social life, from stage to parliament, is expressed through the vocabulary of footsteps. Cognate with Dutch ~optreden~, English ~tread~.
en.aufwachsen:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~ ("to grow"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). Cognate with English ~wax~ (as in "to wax and wane"), Dutch ~wassen~ ("to grow"), Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from Proto-Indo-European *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The prefix emphasizes the upward trajectory of growth.

The PIE root *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase") also produced Latin ~auxilium~ ("help," originally "increase, reinforcement"), Lithuanian ~áukštas~ ("high"), and Greek ~auxánein~ ("to increase"), the source of the modern biological term ~auxin~ (a plant growth hormone). English ~wax~ in the sense of "to grow" (as the moon waxes) preserves the old meaning, though it has been largely displaced by ~grow~ in everyday speech. The compound ~aufwachsen~ means specifically "to grow up" in the sense of childhood and maturation, reinforcing the upward metaphor with ~auf-~. The unrelated homophone ~wachsen~ meaning "to wax, to polish" (from ~Wachs~, "wax") is an entirely different word with a different Proto-Germanic root.
en.aufwarten:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~warten~:

• ~warten~: From MHG ~warten~, from OHG ~wartēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wardēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wardāną~ ("to guard, watch over"), from *~warduz~ ("a guard"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, watch, guard"): one who keeps watch also waits. The older sense persists in ~ein Auto warten~ ("to service a car"). Cognate with English ~ward~, Swedish ~vårda~, Dutch ~bewaren~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix directs attention onto something: noticing, minding, or listening out.

The root's guarding sense is still visible: to ~aufwarten~ is to attend on someone, watchful for what they need, and the modern idiom ~mit etwas aufwarten~ ("to come up with something") keeps the servant's gesture of presenting a dish.
en.aufwaschen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~waschen~:

• ~waschen~: From MHG ~waschen~, from OHG ~wascan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~waskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waskaną~, from an earlier *~watskaną~, a ~ske~-present formation from PIE *~wed-~ ("wet, water"), hence "to make wet (repeatedly)." Cognate with English ~wash~, ~water~, ~wet~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vaske~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix marks reconditioning or working-up: bringing something into fresh or usable condition.

Northern German says ~aufwaschen~ where the south says ~abwaschen~ or ~spülen~; the particle marks the dishes' return to usable condition rather than the removal of the dirt.
en.aufwecken:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~wecken~:

• ~wecken~: From MHG ~wecken~, from OHG ~wecchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wakkjan~ ("to wake up"), from Proto-Germanic *~wakjaną~, a causative of *~wakaną~ ("to be awake"), from PIE *~weǵ-~ ("to be lively, to wake"), precisely the distinction between ~wachen~ and ~wecken~. Cognate with Dutch ~wekken~, English ~watch~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys emergence: arising, appearing, or beginning suddenly.

The root is already a causative (~wachen~ is to be awake, ~wecken~ to make someone so), and ~auf-~ marks the moment the sleep breaks, so ~aufwecken~ stacks a particle on a causative on a stative.
en.aufweichen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~weichen~:

• ~weichen~: From MHG ~wīchen~, from OHG ~wīchan~ ("to yield, give way"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wīkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīkwaną~, from PIE *~h₃weyg-~ ("to start moving, to distance oneself, to bend, wind"). A class I strong verb, "to yield, give way, retreat"; not to be confused with the weak ~weichen~ ("to soften, to soak"), which derives from ~weich~ ("soft"). Cognate with Old English ~wīcan~, Old Norse ~vīkja~, Swedish ~vika~ ("to give way, fold").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix means "open": undoing a closure.

The reading here is the weak ~weichen~ derived from the adjective ~weich~ ("soft"), not the strong ~weichen~ ("to yield") (the conjugation settles it, ~weichte auf~ and not ~wich auf~), and modern politics has taken the verb figuratively: a standard, like a soaked crust, loses its firmness.
en.aufweisen:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, from PIE *~weyd-~ ("to see, to know").
• ~auf-~: From PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). This separable prefix adds a sense of displaying, presenting, or bringing upward to view.

~Aufweisen~ means "to show, to exhibit, to feature", literally to point something upward so it can be seen. It is used in formal or academic registers: ~Das Gebäude weist Schäden auf~ ("The building exhibits damage"). The PIE root *~weyd-~ ("to see, to know") connects ~weisen~ to a vast family of cognates: English ~wise~, ~wit~, and ~vision~ (via Latin ~vidēre~), Sanskrit ~véda~ ("knowledge," as in the Rigveda), and Greek ~εἶδος~ ("form, appearance," whence English ~idea~). The journey from "seeing" to "knowing" to "showing" is preserved in ~aufweisen~: what you point out is what you have seen, and what you have seen is what you know.
en.aufwenden:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~wenden~:

• ~wenden~: From MHG ~wenden~, from OHG ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), the causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). It belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort (preterite ~wandte~, participle ~gewandt~) and has a doubled preterite: ~wandte~ for turning the self or one's attention, the regularized ~wendete~ for physical turning. Cognate with English ~wend~, Armenian ~gind~ ("ring").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys using something up or consuming it entirely.

The compound belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort along with its root and admits both preterites, ~wandte auf~ and ~wendete auf~; the noun ~der Aufwand~ preserves the older vowel and now means expenditure of every kind: effort, money, or ceremony.
en.aufwerfen:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

Throwing earth upward is what built dikes and ramparts (~einen Damm aufwerfen~), and the figurative extension is the one in daily use now: ~eine Frage aufwerfen~, to throw a question up where everyone can see it.
en.aufwerten:
A separable compound of ~auf-~ and ~werten~:

• ~werten~: Derived from ~Wert~ ("value, worth"), from MHG ~wert~, from OHG ~werd~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("worth, worthy"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"); the connection to value runs through exchange: turning goods over in a transaction. Related to Latin ~versus~ ("turned") and English ~worth~, ~worthy~, ~worship~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

The verb is young (coined for currency revaluation and generalized since) yet its root reaches back to a PIE "turn," so upgrading a thing is etymologically turning it over for a better price.
en.aufwiegen:
A separable compound of ~auf~ + ~wiegen~:

• ~wiegen~: Two distinct verbs, both from MHG ~wigen~. Sense 1 ("to weigh"): a northwestern variant of ~wegen~ that generalized the present-singular stem vowel ~i~, from OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, move"); the original ~e~-form survives in the doublet ~wägen~. Sense 2 ("to rock, cradle"): from ~wige~ ("cradle," modern ~Wiege~), from OHG ~wīga~, likely related to Proto-West Germanic *~waggjan~ ("to cause to move"), from the same PIE root. Cognate with English ~weigh~, Dutch ~wegen~, Danish ~veje~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

Of the two ~wiegen~ verbs it is the strong "to weigh" that underlies this one, not the weak "to rock": to ~aufwiegen~ is to put enough into one pan of the balance that the other rises, whence the figurative sense "to offset, to make good."
en.aufzahlen:
A separable compound of ~auf~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

~Aufzahlen~ is paying on top: a sum added over and above a price already agreed. Its near-twin ~aufzählen~ shows how close paying and counting sit: the same root, one umlaut apart.
en.aufzeichnen:
A separable compound of ~auf~ + ~zeichnen~:

• ~zeichnen~: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, symbol"), from MHG ~zeichen~, from OHG ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~, *~taiknaz~ ("sign"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point"); to ~zeichnen~ is etymologically to make a sign. Cognate with English ~token~, Dutch ~teken~, Danish ~tegn~, Swedish ~tecken~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

To ~aufzeichnen~ is to put a mark onto a surface: a sheet, a chart, a register. From the drawn line the word spread to recording of any kind, right through to sound recording, which involves no drawing at all.
en.aufzeigen:
Compound of ~auf-~ + ~zeigen~:

• ~zeigen~: From MHG ~zeigen~, from OHG ~zeigōn~, an intensive form of ~zīhan~ (whence modern ~zeihen~ "to blame, accuse"), ultimately from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point"). Cognate with English ~teach~, Latin ~dīcere~ ("to say"), Greek ~deiknunai~ ("to show").
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf-~, from OHG ~ūf-~, from Proto-Germanic *~upp-~, from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). As a prefix, it conveys "up, upward, open."

The PIE root *~deyḱ-~ produced a remarkable family: Latin ~dīcere~ ("to say"), ~digitus~ ("finger", the pointer), ~index~ ("indicator"), and ~iūdex~ ("judge", one who shows the law). In Germanic, the root went in a different direction: English ~teach~ (originally "to show") and German ~zeigen~ ("to show"). Also related is ~Zeichen~ ("sign, mark"). In Modern German, ~zeigen~ absorbed the synonymous but entirely unrelated MHG ~zöugen~ (cognate with Gothic ~ataugjan~), which is why variant spellings like ~zäugen~ once appeared. The prefix ~auf-~ adds the sense of raising something to visibility: to point out, demonstrate, highlight. In Austria and far-western Germany, ~aufzeigen~ also means "to raise one's hand" in school, literally showing upward.
en.aufziehen:
A separable compound of ~auf~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys upward motion: rising, lifting, or building up.

To ~aufziehen~ a clock is literally to draw its weight back up; the same upward pull sits in ~aufziehen~ "to raise a child" and in a storm ~aufziehen~ over the horizon.
en.aufzwingen:
A separable compound of ~auf~ + ~zwingen~:

• ~zwingen~: From MHG ~twingen~, from OHG ~dwingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þwinganą~, *~þwinhaną~; the apparent triple shift ~þ~ → ~d~ → ~t~ → ~z~ is regular for words with OHG ~dw-~ and ~tw-~, compare ~Zwerg~ ("dwarf"). A class III strong verb (~zwingen~, ~zwang~, ~gezwungen~). Cognate with Dutch ~dwingen~, Swedish ~tvinga~, Icelandic ~þvinga~, English ~twinge~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix conveys applying something onto a surface.

~Aufzwingen~ carries the idea of laying something onto a surface into the social sphere: one lays on another person what that person does not want, and the dative object (~jemandem etwas aufzwingen~) preserves the spatial picture of putting something on top.
en.aufzählen:
A separable compound of ~auf~ + ~zählen~:

• ~zählen~: From MHG ~zel(e)n~, ~zellen~, from OHG ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~ ("to enumerate, count; to recount, tell"). German split this dual sense: ~zählen~ kept "to count," ~erzählen~ took "to narrate." Cognate with Dutch ~tellen~, English ~tell~ and ~tale~, Danish ~tælle~, Gothic ~talzjan~.
• ~auf-~: From MHG ~ūf~, from OHG ~ūf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~up~, from Proto-Germanic *~up~ ("up"), from PIE *~upó~ ("up, from below"). The same preposition, viewed from the other end, gave Latin ~sub~ and Greek ~hypó~ ("under"): motion from below reads as "up" or "under" depending on where the speaker stands. Cognate with English ~up~, Dutch ~op~. The prefix marks summoning or proclaiming publicly: calling something out or calling someone forth.

To ~aufzählen~ is literally to count items off aloud, one after another; an enumeration is a calling-out, not mere arithmetic.
en.ausarbeiten:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

To ~ausarbeiten~ is to work a draft until nothing rough is left: from the sculptor bringing a figure out of the block to the memorandum worked up into finished prose.
en.ausatmen:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~atmen~:

• ~atmen~: From MHG ~ātemen~, from OHG ~ātamōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~ēþmaz~ ("breath"), from PIE *~h₁eh₁tmén-~ ("breath"). Equivalent to ~Atem~ ("breath") + ~-en~. Cognate with Dutch ~ademen~; the archaic doublet ~Odem~ ("breath") descends from *~ēþmaz~ by a different path.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

~Ausatmen~ and ~einatmen~ form the most transparent pair in the German particle-verb system: one action, with only the direction switched. Latin needed distinct stems for the same contrast (~exspirare~, ~inspirare~).
en.ausbauen:
~Aus-~ + ~bauen~. Compound of ~aus-~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~būwen~, from OHG ~būan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~būan~, from Proto-Germanic *~būaną~ ("to dwell, reside"), from PIE *~bʰuH-~ ("to be, become, grow").
• ~aus-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix adds the sense of expansion or development outward.

~Ausbauen~ means "to expand, to develop, to extend", literally "to build outward." Where ~bauen~ alone means "to build, to construct," the prefix ~aus-~ directs the building process outward from an existing structure: one ~baut~ a road network ~aus~ (expands it), ~baut~ a lead ~aus~ (extends it in competition), or ~baut~ an attic ~aus~ (finishes it for habitation). The verb thus straddles the literal and figurative: from physically enlarging a building to abstractly developing a strategy, a relationship, or a competitive advantage. The derived noun ~Ausbau~ ("expansion, development, extension") appears frequently in planning and policy contexts. Cognate with Dutch ~uitbouwen~.
en.ausbedingen:
A compound of ~aus~ + ~be-~ + ~dingen~; the ~aus-~ is separable, the ~be-~ is not:

• ~dingen~: From MHG ~dingen~ ("to negotiate, hire"), from OHG ~dingōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þingōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þingōną~, a verb built on the noun *~þingą~ ("appointed time; assembly"), probably from PIE *~tenk-~ ("to be fitting"). Originally weak; the strong forms ~dang~/~gedungen~ are secondary, so modern German admits both. Cognate with English ~thing~, Dutch ~dingen~, Old Norse ~þing~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

To ~sich etwas ausbedingen~ is to get a condition out of a negotiation and hold the other party to it, the old judicial assembly, the ~Ding~, still standing at the word's root.
en.ausbeten:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~beten~:

• ~beten~: From MHG ~beten~, from OHG ~beton~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bedon~, from Proto-Germanic *~bedan~ ("to pray, to ask"), close to *~bidjan~ ("to ask"), from PIE *~gwhedh-~ ("to ask for, beseech"). The narrowing from "ask" to "pray" is a Christianization phenomenon. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bidden~, Danish ~bede~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

~Ausbeten~ belongs with ~ausreden~ and ~ausharren~: the action is not broken off but carried to its end. That ~beten~ and ~bitten~ share a root makes a prayer, etymologically, a request one prays out to the finish.
en.ausbilden:
Compound of ~aus-~ + ~bilden~:

• ~bilden~: From MHG ~bilden~, ~bileden~, a merger of OHG ~biliden~ (from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþijan~) and OHG ~bilidōn~ (from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþōn~), both derived from *~biliþī~ ("image, likeness"), whence modern ~Bild~ ("picture, image"). The deeper origin is Proto-West Germanic *~bil~ ("equal, alike").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix adds a sense of full development or completion.

The literal sense is "to form out": to shape someone or something into full development. ~Ausbilden~ means "to train, to educate" (especially in vocational or professional contexts), and the noun ~Ausbildung~ ("training, education") is a cornerstone of the German dual-education system, in which apprentices alternate between workplace training and classroom instruction. The MHG predecessor ~ūzbilden~ is already attested. The semantic journey from "image" (~Bild~) to "to form" (~bilden~) to "to train" (~ausbilden~) follows a coherent metaphorical chain: to train someone is to shape them according to an ideal image. Cognate with Dutch ~afbeelden~ ("to depict") and Swedish ~bilda~ ("to form, educate").
en.ausbitten:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~bitten~:

• ~bitten~: From MHG ~bitten~, from OHG ~bitten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~biddjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bidjaną~, from PIE *~gʷʰedʰ-~ ("to ask for, beseech"). A class V strong verb; the noun ~Bitte~ and the particle ~bitte~ come from the same root. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bidden~ ("to pray"), Danish ~bede~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

To ~sich etwas ausbitten~ is to ask a favor out of someone; in the reflexive the tone shifts from asking to demanding: ~das möchte ich mir ausgebeten haben~ is no longer a request at all.
en.ausbleiben:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

~Ausbleiben~ is staying with the sign reversed: whoever ~ausbleibt~ stays outside, and because a failure to appear is more conspicuous than mere absence, it is said of anything expected that does not arrive.
en.ausbleichen:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~bleichen~:

• ~bleichen~: A merger of two verbs: the strong intransitive MHG ~blīchen~ ("to shine, gleam, grow pale"), from OHG ~blīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~blīkaną~; and its weak causative MHG ~bleichen~ ("to make pale"), from OHG ~bleihhen~, from Proto-Germanic *~blaikijaną~. Both from PIE *~bʰleyg-~ ("to shine"). Modern German conjugates it weak, the strong participle ~geblichen~ surviving only marginally. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~bleak~, Dutch ~bleken~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.

Of the two verbs merged in ~bleichen~ it is the weak causative "to make pale" that supplies the sense here, as the weak inflection shows; the ~aus-~ drives it to its end point, the color going until none is left.
en.ausblicken:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~blank~, Dutch ~blik~, Old English ~blice~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

~Ausblicken~ sends the gaze outward, and since a ~Blick~ was originally a flash of light, the image is of a probing beam sweeping the surroundings. The noun ~Ausblick~ has long outstripped the verb in currency.
en.ausbrechen:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

~Ausbrechen~ presupposes that something was shut in: the prisoner, the volcano, the war, the laughter. English ~break out~ is the same picture from the same pieces, minus the High German consonant shift.
en.ausbrennen:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~brennen~:

• ~brennen~: From MHG ~brennen~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: transitive ~brennan~ ("to set on fire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~brannijan~, and intransitive ~brinnan~, from *~brinnan~, of which *~brannijan~ was the causative. The intransitive is from PIE *~bʰrewh₁-~ ("to boil, brew"), making ~brennen~ a cousin of English ~brew~. A Rückumlaut verb: ~ich brenne~ but ~brannte~, ~gebrannt~. Cognate with English ~burn~, Dutch ~branden~, Icelandic ~brenna~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.

~Ausbrennen~ inherits both halves of its base verb: transitively one burns out a city or a wound, intransitively a house burns out until there is nothing left to burn. The modern ~ausgebrannt~ of an exhausted person is a calque of English ~burned out~, and yet lands squarely on the old image.
en.ausbringen:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys distributing or handing out: spreading something outward among recipients.

Its commonest use is ~einen Trinkspruch ausbringen~, to propose a toast: the toast is sent out to the company like the wine that is poured. The verb also survives in farming, where seed or fertilizer is ~ausgebracht~.
en.ausdauern:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~dauern~:

• ~dauern~: Two separate verbs under one spelling. "To last, endure": from MHG ~dūren~, borrowed from Middle Low German ~dūren~, from Latin ~dūrō~, a denominative of ~dūrus~ ("hard, lasting"), from Proto-Italic *~dūros~, from PIE *~dweh₂-~ ("long, far"); cognate with Dutch ~duren~, English ~dure~. "To cause pity" (~er dauert mich~): from MHG ~tūren~, an ablaut variant of ~tiure~ ("dear, costly"), ancestor of ~teuer~, thus a doublet of ~teuer~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The base is the borrowed ~dauern~ "to last," from Latin ~dūrō~, not the MHG ~tūren~ "to move to pity." To ~ausdauern~ is therefore to hold out through the hard thing to its end; ~Ausdauer~, endurance, being the virtue made of it.
en.ausdenken:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~teng-~ ("to think, feel"). A mixed-conjugation verb of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~dachte~ pairs the vowel change ~e~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix and ~k~ > ~ch~. Cognate with English ~think~, Dutch ~denken~, Icelandic ~þekkja~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

To ~sich etwas ausdenken~ is to think a thought all the way through until it stands there as a plan or an invention; the reflexive pronoun makes the thinker the beneficiary of his own idea.
en.ausdeuten:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~deuten~:

• ~deuten~: From MHG ~diuten~, from OHG ~diuten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þiudijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þiudijaną~ ("to interpret; to point out"), from *~þeudō~ ("people"), from PIE *~tewtéh₂~ ("people"), originally "to make intelligible to the people," the same word that gives ~deutsch~. Cognate with Dutch ~duiden~, Icelandic ~þýða~, Swedish ~tyda~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

If ~deuten~ etymologically means making something intelligible to the people, then ~ausdeuten~ means not stopping halfway: the text is expounded until nothing obscure is left in it.
en.ausdienen:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~dienen~:

• ~dienen~: From MHG ~dienen~, from OHG ~dionōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þewanōną~ ("to serve"), a denominative of *~þewaz~ ("servant, slave"), of uncertain further origin, perhaps PIE *~tekʷ-~ ("to run"), the servant as "one who runs errands." Cognate with English ~thane~ (via the noun), Dutch ~dienen~, Danish ~tjene~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

To ~ausdienen~ is to serve out one's term to the last day. Liveliest today is the participle: an ~ausgedientes~ appliance has served its time, like the soldier the image came from.
en.ausdrucken:
A separable compound of ~aus~ + ~drucken~:

• ~drucken~: From MHG ~drucken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~ ("to press"). A doublet of ~drücken~ ("to press, push"), which keeps the expected umlaut; ~drucken~ lacks it because Upper German blocked umlaut before a velar geminate, and the form used by the first, southern printers became the technical term. Polish ~drukować~ was borrowed from it.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

~Ausdrucken~ belongs to printing, not to pressing: the sheet comes out of the machine. Only the umlaut separates it from the near-homophone ~ausdrücken~ "to express, squeeze out", an umlaut the first southern printers never brought with them.
en.ausdrücken:
From Middle High German ~ūzdrücken~. In the sense "to express," a calque of Latin ~exprimere~ ("to press out"). Compound of ~aus-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~ ("to press on, crowd"), from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). Cognate with Welsh ~trychu~ ("to cut"), Lithuanian ~trū́kti~ ("to tear into pieces"). Doublet of ~drucken~ ("to print"), which was originally a southern German variant that later specialized in meaning.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz-~, from OHG ~ūz-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt-~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out").

The physical meaning "to squeeze out" (juice from a lemon, a cigarette stub) and the abstract meaning "to express" (a thought, an emotion) coexist in the same verb, the metaphor of pressing inner content outward into the world. Cognate with Dutch ~uitdrukken~, which underwent the same semantic split. The Latin model ~exprimere~ (literally "to press out") that inspired the abstract sense also gave English ~express~, making ~ausdrücken~ and ~express~ etymological mirror images, one Germanic, one Romance, both built on the same metaphor. The split between ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") is a rare case of a single verb differentiating into two standard forms, each with its own semantic domain.
en.auseinanderbauen:
A separable compound of ~auseinander~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~būwen~, from OHG ~būan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~būan~, from Proto-Germanic *~būaną~ ("to dwell, reside"), from PIE *~bʰuH-~ ("to be, become, grow"); one builds where one lives. Cognate with English ~be~, ~bower~ ("dwelling"), ~neighbor~ ("near-dweller"), Dutch ~bouwen~.
• ~auseinander-~: A transparent compound of ~aus~ ("out") and ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ ("one") + ~ander~ ("other"), literally "out of one another," hence "apart, asunder."
