English builds the same idea from the same pieces in ~one another~ and ~asunder~. ~auseinander-~ marks separation: the parts end up away from each other (~auseinandernehmen~, ~auseinandergehen~).

~Auseinanderbauen~ is a contradiction German takes in stride: one builds something so that it is no longer built. Where ~bauen~ rests on a root meaning "dwell, grow," the particle turns it into undoing.
en.auseinanderbrechen:
A separable compound of ~auseinander~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~auseinander-~: A transparent compound of ~aus~ ("out") and ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ ("one") + ~ander~ ("other"), literally "out of one another," hence "apart, asunder." English builds the same idea from the same pieces in ~one another~ and ~asunder~. ~auseinander-~ marks separation: the parts end up away from each other (~auseinandernehmen~, ~auseinandergehen~).

Unlike ~ausbrechen~, where something escapes an enclosure, in ~auseinanderbrechen~ the whole itself comes apart: from the ship on the reef to the empire that falls to pieces.
en.auseinanderfallen:
A separable compound of ~auseinander~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~auseinander-~: A transparent compound of ~aus~ ("out") and ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ ("one") + ~ander~ ("other"), literally "out of one another," hence "apart, asunder." English builds the same idea from the same pieces in ~one another~ and ~asunder~. ~auseinander-~ marks separation: the parts end up away from each other (~auseinandernehmen~, ~auseinandergehen~).

~Auseinanderfallen~ needs no force from outside: what falls apart has merely stopped holding together. That is why it serves equally for a cupboard and for an argument.
en.auseinandergehen:
A separable compound of ~auseinander-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~auseinander-~: A transparent compound of ~aus~ ("out") and ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ ("one") + ~ander~ ("other"), literally "out of one another," hence "apart, asunder." English builds the same idea from the same pieces in ~one another~ and ~asunder~. ~auseinander-~ marks separation: the parts end up away from each other (~auseinandernehmen~, ~auseinandergehen~).

The image moves from the room into the argument: first people part, then opinions do, and in both the sense of separating stays the same. As a verb of motion it forms its compound conjugations with ~sein~.
en.auseinanderhalten:
A separable compound of ~auseinander-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~auseinander-~: A transparent compound of ~aus~ ("out") and ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ ("one") + ~ander~ ("other"), literally "out of one another," hence "apart, asunder." English builds the same idea from the same pieces in ~one another~ and ~asunder~. ~auseinander-~ marks separation: the parts end up away from each other (~auseinandernehmen~, ~auseinandergehen~).

The separation here is mental: what gets held apart is not objects but notions that would otherwise blur together. English reaches for the same spatial picture in ~tell apart~ and ~keep apart~.
en.auseinandernehmen:
A separable compound of ~auseinander-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~auseinander-~: A transparent compound of ~aus~ ("out") and ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ ("one") + ~ander~ ("other"), literally "out of one another," hence "apart, asunder." English builds the same idea from the same pieces in ~one another~ and ~asunder~. ~auseinander-~ marks separation: the parts end up away from each other (~auseinandernehmen~, ~auseinandergehen~).

Literally "to take apart": the verb describes reducing a machine to its parts, and figuratively pulling an argument apart just as thoroughly.
en.auseinanderreißen:
A separable compound of ~auseinander-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~auseinander-~: A transparent compound of ~aus~ ("out") and ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ ("one") + ~ander~ ("other"), literally "out of one another," hence "apart, asunder." English builds the same idea from the same pieces in ~one another~ and ~asunder~. ~auseinander-~ marks separation: the parts end up away from each other (~auseinandernehmen~, ~auseinandergehen~).

Unlike ~auseinandernehmen~, ~auseinanderreißen~ presupposes force: what is separated was holding together and yields only to the pull. It is often said of families torn apart by war.
en.auseinandersetzen:
From ~auseinander-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~, from PIE *~sodéyeti~, the causative of *~sed-~ ("to sit"). Thus ~setzen~ is literally "to cause to sit," i.e., "to set, to place." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~auseinander-~: From ~aus~ ("out") + ~einander~ ("one another"), from PIE *~úd~ ("out") + *~h₁én~ ("in") + *~h₂enteros~ ("other"). The adverb means "apart, asunder."

The reflexive ~sich auseinandersetzen mit~ ("to engage with, to come to grips with, to examine critically") is the most common modern usage, literally meaning "to set oneself apart with" a topic, implying thorough, often difficult engagement. The non-reflexive ~auseinandersetzen~ means "to explain in detail" or "to take apart." This is one of German's celebrated long compound verbs, combining four etymological layers into a single separable verb. The causative relationship between ~sitzen~ ("to sit") and ~setzen~ ("to set, place") mirrors exactly the English pair ~sit~/~set~, both pairs descend from the same PIE causative formation *~sodéyeti~ ("to cause to sit"), making this a grammatical pattern that has survived intact for over five millennia. English ~asunder~ is a cognate of ~auseinander~, sharing the same Germanic root for "apart."
en.auseinanderstreben:
A separable compound of ~auseinander-~ + ~streben~:

• ~streben~: From MHG ~strëben~, from OHG ~strëbēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stribēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~stribāną~ ("to strive, resist"). Cognate with Dutch ~streven~ ("to strive") and English ~strive~ (via Old French ~estriver~, itself borrowed from a Germanic source).
• ~auseinander-~: A transparent compound of ~aus~ ("out") and ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ ("one") + ~ander~ ("other"), literally "out of one another," hence "apart, asunder." English builds the same idea from the same pieces in ~one another~ and ~asunder~. ~auseinander-~ marks separation: the parts end up away from each other (~auseinandernehmen~, ~auseinandergehen~).

The striving is in the parts themselves: nobody separates them, they press away from one another of their own accord, from a vault thrusting sideways to a coalition coming apart.
en.auserlesen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~er-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ conveys obtaining or acquiring something by means of the base action.

The older sense of ~lesen~ as "to gather" is plain here: choosing is done by gathering out of a larger set. The participle has gone its own way and is now an adjective meaning "choice, exquisite," said of wine as readily as of company.
en.ausfahren:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Because ~fahren~ once meant travel of any kind, ~ausfahren~ covers more than a drive: miners ride down into the shaft and back out again, and landing gear is ~ausgefahren~ by being brought outward.
en.ausfallen:
From Middle High German ~ūzvallen~. Compound of ~aus-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~, from PIE *~pōl-~, possibly a compound of *~h₂epo~ ("off, away") + *~h₃elh₁-~ ("to fall"). Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz-~, from OHG ~ūz-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). As a verbal prefix, it often conveys motion outward or cessation.

The compound ~ausfallen~ has developed a remarkable range of meanings: "to fall out" (hair, teeth), "to be cancelled" (a class, an event), "to fail" (a machine), and "to turn out" (a result). The cancellation sense (where something ~falls out~ of the schedule) is perhaps the most distinctive, since English uses the unrelated "cancel" (from Latin ~cancellāre~). The PIE etymology of ~fallen~ is debated: the compound-root theory connecting it to Latin ~aboleō~ ("to destroy") and Lithuanian ~pùlti~ ("to fall") is attractive but uncertain. Cognate with Dutch ~uitvallen~.
en.ausfassen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~fassen~:

• ~fassen~: From MHG ~vazzen~, from OHG ~fazzōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fatōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fatōną~ ("to hold, seize"), a weak class 2 verb, from PIE *~pod-néh₂-ti~, from *~pod-~ ("to fetch"). German kept the sense of grasping and holding, English that of going to retrieve. Cognate with English ~fetch~; the noun ~Fass~ ("barrel") shares the root.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys distributing or handing out: spreading something outward among recipients.

Austrian, and originally at home in soldiers' slang: to ~ausfassen~ rations is to take receipt of what has been allotted to you. Travelling onward ironically, one also ~fasst~ a prison sentence ~aus~, as though the verdict were a ration.
en.ausfechten:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~fechten~:

• ~fechten~: From MHG ~vëhten~ ("to fight"), from OHG ~fëhtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fehtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fehtaną~, perhaps from PIE *~peḱ-~ ("to pluck, comb"), though not securely. A class III strong verb (~fechten~, ~focht~, ~gefochten~); the ~o~ of the Präteritum comes from the old plural stem (OHG ~fuhtum~). Cognate with English ~fight~, Dutch ~vechten~, Danish ~fægte~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The fight is not begun but finished: a quarrel one ~ausficht~ is settled afterward. The picture comes from the duel and now survives almost only in figurative use.
en.ausfertigen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~fertigen~:

• ~fertigen~: From MHG ~vertigen~ ("to prepare, make ready"), equivalent to ~fertig~ + ~-en~. The adjective ~fertig~ (MHG ~fertec~, OHG ~fartīg~) belongs to ~fart~ ("journey"), from Proto-Germanic *~farą~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross"); ~fertig~ originally meant "ready for a journey." Cognate with Dutch ~vaardig~, Low German ~fardig~, Old English ~fierd~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The verb has migrated into officialese: to ~ausfertigen~ now chiefly means producing a document or a statute in its final, signed form. The ~fertig~ of the stem still holds the old ~fart~, "journey," so that what has been ~ausgefertigt~ is, in a manner of speaking, ready to travel.
en.ausfliegen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~fliegen~:

• ~fliegen~: From MHG ~vliegen~, from OHG ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"), an extension of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim") that also gave ~fließen~. The vowel path *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of class II strong verbs. Cognate with English ~fly~, Dutch ~vliegen~, Danish ~flyve~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Literally birds leaving the nest; figuratively it is said of children leaving home, and of anyone no longer to be found. As a verb of motion it forms its compound conjugations with ~sein~.
en.ausfließen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~fließen~:

• ~fließen~: From MHG ~vlieȥen~, from OHG ~flioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleutaną~ ("to float, stream, flow"), from PIE *~plewd-~ ("to flow, run, swim"). A class II strong verb (~fließen~, ~floss~, ~geflossen~); the zero grade *~flut-~ gave ~Flut~. Cognate with English ~fleet~, ~float~ and ~flood~, Dutch ~vlieten~, Swedish ~flyta~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The verb stays concrete: liquid leaves its vessel. That ~fließen~ and ~fliegen~ go back to the same Indo-European root makes the pair ~ausfließen~/~ausfliegen~ closer kin than their meanings suggest. Like other verbs of motion it takes ~sein~.
en.ausfolgen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~folgen~:

• ~folgen~: From MHG ~volgen~, from OHG ~folgēn~ ("to follow, serve faithfully, pursue," attested from the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *~folgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fulgāną~; the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. Cognate with English ~follow~, Dutch ~volgen~, Danish ~følge~, Swedish ~följa~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys distributing or handing out: spreading something outward among recipients.

In Austrian officialese ~ausfolgen~ means "to hand over, release": an authority ~folgt~ a thing ~aus~ to the party entitled to it. The sense comes not from walking behind but from the older meaning "to comply, accede," since one follows a claim by giving it what it asks.
en.ausfragen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~fragen~:

• ~fragen~: From MHG ~vrāgen~, from OHG ~frāgēn~, ~frahēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frāgēn~ (a denominative from *~frāgu~, "question"), from Proto-Germanic *~frēgō~ ("question"), from PIE *~preḱ-~ ("to ask"), which also gave Latin ~precor~ and Sanskrit ~pṛcchāti~. Cognate with English ~frain~ (archaic), Dutch ~vragen~, Swedish ~fråga~, Icelandic ~fregna~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The asking is not a single question but a going on until nothing is left held back: ~ausfragen~ targets the person rather than the question, and so usually carries a note of intrusiveness that plain ~fragen~ lacks.
en.ausfällen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~fällen~:

• ~fällen~: From MHG ~vellen~, from OHG ~fellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallijaną~ ("to make fall"), a causative of *~fallaną~ ("to fall"), possibly from PIE *~h₃elh₁-~ ("to fall, perish"). The umlaut a to ä is the footprint of the ~jan~-causative, as in ~sitzen~/~setzen~. Cognate with English ~fell~, Dutch ~vellen~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Chemistry took the causative literally: a dissolved substance is made to fall and settles out of solution as a solid. It can be told apart from the identical-looking strong verb ~ausfallen~ ("to be cancelled, to turn out a certain way") only outside the present, since ~es fällt aus~ belongs to both; only ~fällte aus~ against ~fiel aus~ separates them.
en.ausführen: From Middle High German ~ūzvüeren~, Old High German ~ūzfuoren~. By surface analysis, ~aus-~ (from PIE *~úd~, "upwards, out") and ~führen~, from MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). Cognate with Dutch ~uitvoeren~. The range of meanings is characteristic of Germanic prefix-verb productivity: to carry out (execute a plan), to lead out (escort someone), to export (carry goods out), or to elaborate (develop an argument out to its conclusion). Dutch ~uitvoeren~ covers the same semantic territory, showing how deeply the compound is shared across West Germanic.
en.ausfüllen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~füllen~:

• ~füllen~: From MHG ~vüllen~, from OHG ~fullen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fullijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullijaną~ ("to make full"), the causative of *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pl̥h₁nós~ ("full"). English ~fill~ and ~füllen~ are exact cognates, each the causative of its native word for "full." Cognate with English ~fill~, Dutch ~vullen~, Danish ~fylde~, Swedish ~fylla~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

Two uses run side by side: spatially, something fills a space right to its edges; figuratively, an occupation fills a life. The form one ~ausfüllt~ belongs to the first picture, its blank fields occupied down to the last.
en.ausgeben:
From ~aus-~ + ~geben~. Compound of ~aus-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give").
• ~aus-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix adds the sense of giving outward, distributing, or expending.

~Ausgeben~ means "to spend (money)" (~Geld ausgeben~), but also "to dispense" (medication), "to issue" (banknotes, stamps, orders), "to output" (data, in computing), and, colloquially, "to buy someone a drink" (~eine Runde ausgeben~, "to buy a round"). The reflexive ~sich als etwas ausgeben~ ("to pose as, to impersonate") is a fascinating extension: one "gives oneself out" as something one is not, distributing a false identity to the world. The derived adjective ~ausgiebig~ ("extensive, thorough, generous") preserves the sense of giving freely and fully, an ~ausgiebiges Frühstück~ is a lavish breakfast where nothing is held back. The pair ~ausgeben~ (to give out, to spend) and ~eingeben~ (to input, to enter) form a natural antonym in computing terminology. Cognate with English ~outgive~ (archaic "to give out, to distribute"), Dutch ~uitgeven~ ("to spend, to publish", the Dutch sense of "to publish" shows another direction of "giving out": releasing a book into the world).
en.ausgehen: From Middle High German ~ūzgēn~, ~ūzgān~, itself from Old High German ~ūzgangan~, ~ūzgān~, ~ūzgēn~. Equivalent to prefix ~aus-~ (from PIE *~úd~, "upwards, out") and ~gehen~, from MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). Cognate with Dutch ~uitgaan~, Low German ~utgahn~, English ~outgo~, and Swedish and Danish ~utgå~. The compound captures a nuance that German preserves through prefix: motion that takes one out of a bounded space. The same PIE root that gives "go" in English gives ~gehen~ in German, and the ~aus-~ prefix turns an abstract motion into a departure from enclosure: going out to socialize, going out (of a flame), or running out (of stock).
en.ausgießen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~gießen~:

• ~gießen~: From MHG ~giezen~, from OHG ~giozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geutan~ ("to pour"), from Proto-Germanic *~geutaną~, from PIE *~gʰewd-~ ("to pour"). The sense of casting metal and glass is attested since Old High German (participle ~gigozzan~). Cognate with English ~gush~, Dutch ~gieten~, Old English ~geotan~, Gothic ~giutan~, Swedish ~gjuta~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

From the workshop to scripture: ~gießen~ already covered the casting of metal in Old High German, but ~ausgießen~ stayed with liquids and became, in Luther, the image for a spirit poured out over people.
en.ausgleichen:
Compound of ~aus-~ + ~gleichen~:

• ~gleichen~: From MHG ~gelīchen~, from OHG ~gilīhhon~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkōną~ ("to make alike, to compare"). The adjective ~gleich~ ("equal, same") descends from OHG ~gilīh~, a compound of ~ga-~ ("together," from PIE *~ḱóm~) + ~līk-~ ("body, form"), related to ~Leiche~ ("corpse," originally "body").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz-~, from OHG ~ūz-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). This prefix adds a sense of completion, balancing out, or evening.

The original meaning of ~gleich~ was "having the same body/form," a compound that literally said two things looked alike because they shared the same shape. The element ~-līk-~ also produced the English suffix ~-ly~ (originally "having the body/form of") and the word ~like~ (same root). English ~like~, German ~gleich~, and the suffix ~-lich~/~-ly~ are all siblings from the same Germanic root. The compound ~ausgleichen~ means "to equalize, compensate, balance out," carrying the sense of bringing two unequal things into the same form. The sports term ~Ausgleich~ ("equalizer") captures this precisely: the goal that makes the score equal again. The noun ~Gleichgewicht~ ("balance, equilibrium") and the adjective ~gleichgültig~ ("indifferent," literally "equally valid") are further compounds showing the productivity of this root. The morbid origin in ~Leiche~ ("corpse") is long forgotten, but it reminds us that the concept of likeness began with the physical human body.
en.ausgleiten:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~gleiten~:

• ~gleiten~: From MHG ~glīten~, from OHG ~glītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~glīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~glīdaną~, from PIE *~ǵʰleydʰ-~ ("to glide, slide"). A class I strong verb (~gleiten~, ~glitt~, ~geglitten~), though a weak ~gleitete~ turns up in technical prose. Cognate with English ~glide~, Dutch ~glijden~, Low German ~glieden~, Swedish ~glida~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The prefix says where the foot ends up: it glides out from under the body. Alongside the strong ~glitt aus~, technical prose keeps a weak ~gleitete aus~; the compound conjugations take ~sein~.
en.ausgraben:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~graben~:

• ~graben~: From MHG ~graben~, from OHG ~graban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from PIE *~gʰrebʰ-~ ("to dig, scratch, bury"). A class VI strong verb (~graben~, ~grub~, ~gegraben~). Cognate with English ~grave~ as a verb (now only in ~engrave~ and ~graven image~), Gothic ~graban~, Dutch ~graven~, Old Norse ~grafa~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

What is ~ausgegraben~ was already there, lying hidden: the spade brings up potatoes, the dead, or whole cities. Archaeology takes its German term from here, ~Ausgrabung~, "excavation."
en.ausgreifen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~greifen~:

• ~greifen~: From MHG ~grîfen~, from OHG ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). A class I strong verb (~greift~, ~griff~, ~gegriffen~), like ~reiten~ and ~schneiden~. Cognate with English ~gripe~, Dutch ~grijpen~, Low German ~griepen~, Old Norse ~gripa~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys expansion or full development outward.

The grasping here is not the hand's: a horse or a walker ~greift aus~ by throwing the stride far forward. Figuratively an account ~greift weit aus~ when it takes in its subject generously.
en.aushalten:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

It is not the holding that counts but the duration: to ~aushalten~ something is to hold out under it to the end. Beside that stands the older, now disparaging sense "to keep someone financially", likewise a holding across the whole distance.
en.aushandeln:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~handeln~:

• ~handeln~: From MHG ~handeln~, from OHG ~hantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handulōn~, a denominative verb from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~ ("hand") with the frequentative suffix *~-lōną~; the sense broadened from "to handle" to "to act, deal, trade." Cognate with English ~handle~, Dutch ~handelen~, Danish ~handle~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The stem is a reminder that ~handeln~ began as working with the hand and reached bargaining by way of trade. A treaty is ~ausgehandelt~ only once no point is left open.
en.aushauen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~hauen~:

• ~hauen~: From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). Originally a class VII strong verb (~hauen~, ~hieb~, ~gehauen~), partially weakened colloquially, where ~haute~ competes with ~hieb~. Cognate with English ~hew~, Latin ~cūdere~ ("to strike, forge").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The chisel takes away whatever does not belong to the shape: a cistern is ~ausgehauen~ from rock, a figure from a block. The verb still wavers between strong ~hieb~ and weak ~haute~.
en.ausheben:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb: the past ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ continue the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

What gets lifted is the material removed, not the hole: one ~hebt Erde aus~ and is left with the pit. The same picture carries the old military use, in which a ruler ~hob~ troops ~aus~, lifting them out of the populace.
en.aushelfen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~helfen~:

• ~helfen~: From MHG ~hëlfen~, from OHG ~hëlfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helpaną~, from PIE *~ḱelb-~, *~ḱelp-~. A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~e~-~a~-~o~ ablaut pattern (~helfen~, ~half~, ~geholfen~). Cognate with English ~help~, Dutch ~helpen~, Danish ~hjælpe~, Norwegian ~hjelpe~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The helping is a helping out of something: out of need, out of a tight spot. That is why the person stands in the dative, and the thing one is helped out of often goes unmentioned, being understood.
en.ausholen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~holen~:

• ~holen~: From MHG ~holen~, ~holn~, from OHG ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, possibly from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, summon") via "to summon" → "to go and fetch"; the connection is uncertain. Cognate with Dutch ~halen~, Low German ~halen~, English ~haul~ (via French).
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The compound names the preparatory movement itself: the arm goes out before the blow or the stroke follows, which is why ~weit ausholen~ also means to begin an account from far back.
en.auskaufen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, a denominative verb from *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"), a loanword from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper"). Cognate with English ~cheap~, Dutch ~kopen~, Danish ~købe~, Icelandic ~kaupa~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.

What gets bought out is the stock, not the goods: a seller is ~ausgekauft~ only once there is nothing left to be had.
en.auskehren:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~kehren~:

• ~kehren~: A homograph concealing two distinct verbs. ~Kehren~ (1) "to turn": from MHG ~kēren~, from OHG ~kēran~, ~chēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kairijaną~ or *~kausijaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly connected to *~gers-~ ("to twist, bend, turn"). ~Kehren~ (2) "to sweep": from MHG ~kern~, ~keren~, from OHG ~kerian~, ~cherian~, from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~ ("to scrape, scratch"), from PIE *~ger-~ ("to scrape"). Etymologically unrelated, merged through phonological convergence.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The root here is ~kehren~ "to sweep," not ~kehren~ "to turn": what is swept out is the dirt leaving the room. Both verbs are weak, so it is the sense rather than the conjugation that settles which twin this is.
en.auskennen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~kennen~:

• ~kennen~: From MHG ~kennen~, from OHG ~kennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kannijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~ ("to know"), a causative of *~kunnaną~, from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"). A member of the Rückumlaut cohort: the present shows umlaut (~ich kenne~), the preterite does not (~kannte~, ~gekannt~). Cognate with Dutch ~kennen~, Scots and English ~ken~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The compound survives only reflexively: to ~sich auskennen~ is to have covered a territory so thoroughly that nothing in it can surprise you.
en.ausklingen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~klingen~:

• ~klingen~: From MHG ~klingen~, from OHG ~klingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~klinganą~, almost certainly of onomatopoeic origin. A class III strong verb (~klingt~, ~klang~, ~geklungen~), the same pattern as ~singen~. Cognate with English ~clink~ and ~clang~, Middle Dutch ~klinken~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.

The sense has passed from sound to time: an evening ~klingt aus~ like a note fading until nothing more can be heard.
en.auskommen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The modern sense is figurative: to ~auskommen~ on little is to come out of a tight spot. The older, literal "to come out" still shows in Luther’s ~ein Feuer kommt aus~, "a fire breaks out."
en.auskosten:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~kosten~:

• ~kosten~: Two unrelated verbs in one spelling. ~kosten~ "to cost": from MHG ~kosten~, borrowed from Old French ~coster~, from Latin ~cōnstō~ ("to stand firm, be fixed, cost"), from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"); English ~cost~ traveled the same route. ~kosten~ "to taste, to try": from OHG ~kostōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kustōną~ ("to try, taste"), from PIE *~ǵews-~ ("to taste, try"), which also underlies Latin ~gustus~ and English ~gusto~ and ~disgust~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

Of the two verbs merged in ~kosten~, this is the older "to taste, to try," not the French-borrowed "to cost": what is ~ausgekostet~ is a pleasure savoured to the last drop.
en.auskämpfen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~kämpfen~:

• ~kämpfen~: From MHG ~kempfen~, from OHG *~kempfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kampijan~, a denominal verb from *~kamp~ ("field, battlefield"), borrowed from Latin ~campus~ ("field, open plain"); the sense shifted early from the place of battle to the act of fighting. Latin ~campus~ also gives English ~camp~ and ~champion~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The compound names not the fighting but its end: a struggle is ~ausgekämpft~ only when nothing is left to decide.
en.auslachen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~lachen~:

• ~lachen~: From MHG ~lachen~, from OHG ~lahhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~, from PIE *~kleg-~ ("to cry out, sound"). The initial ~hl-~ cluster was simplified to ~l-~ in Old High German. Cognate with English ~laugh~, Dutch ~lachen~, Gothic ~hlahjan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Unlike most ~aus-~ formations, the movement here is aimed at a person: the laughter goes outward and lands on its target, which is why the compound takes a direct object that plain ~lachen~ never has.
en.ausladen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two historically distinct verbs under one infinitive. ~laden~ (strong, "to load"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"); cognate with English ~lade~ and ~laden~, Lithuanian ~klṓti~. ~laden~ (weak, "to invite, summon"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root found only in Germanic and Anatolian (Hittite ~halzai~).
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Of the two ~laden~ verbs this is the strong one, "to load," as the principal parts ~lud aus~, ~ausgeladen~ show. The weak ~laden~ "to invite" yields an identically spelled ~ausladen~ that withdraws an invitation, the same convergence that merged the two base verbs.
en.auslagern:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~lagern~:

• ~lagern~: Derived from the noun ~Lager~ ("camp, store, warehouse"), from MHG ~lëger~, from OHG ~lëgar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~legr~, from Proto-Germanic *~legrą~. The modern form with ~-a-~ is of East Central German origin, influenced by ~Lage~ ("position"). Cognate with English ~lair~, Dutch ~leger~, Danish ~lejr~, Swedish ~läger~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The verb is built on the noun rather than on a verbal stem: what is ~ausgelagert~ leaves the store, in current use a division of a company or the contents of memory alike.
en.auslaufen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.

From liquid running out the sense reaches a deadline running out: a contract ~läuft aus~ the way a vessel empties.
en.auslauten:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~lauten~:

• ~lauten~: From MHG ~lūten~ ("to sound, ring"), from OHG ~hlūtēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlūdēn~; ~Laut~ ("sound") plus the suffix ~-en~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlūdaz~ ("loud"). ~lauten~ means "to read as, to run"; ~läuten~ ("to ring") is the factitive of the same root. Cognate with English ~loud~, Dutch ~luid~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The verb is a term of art in linguistics, formed to the noun ~Auslaut~ ("final sound"): a word ~lautet aus~ in whatever sound stands at its outer edge.
en.ausleben:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The compound turns the verb transitive: it is not a person who lives but a desire or an inclination that gets lived, and lived all the way out.
en.auslegen:
From Middle High German ~ūʒlegen~ ("to display, set out; interpret; lend money"). Compound of ~aus-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~ ("to lay, place"), the causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie"), from PIE *~logʰéyeti~, causative of *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). Cognate with English ~lay~, Dutch ~leggen~, Danish ~laegge~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūʒ~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out").

The MHG verb already had a remarkably wide semantic range: display, interpret, and lend money. All three senses survive in modern German. ~Auslegen~ means "to lay out, display" (goods in a shop), "to interpret, construe" (a text, a law, a remark), and "to advance money" (paying on someone's behalf). Cognate with Dutch ~uitleggen~ ("to explain") and Yiddish ~אויסלייגן~ ("to spell out; interpret; lend money"), both preserving a similar range.
en.ausleihen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~leihen~:

• ~leihen~: From MHG ~līhen~, from OHG ~līhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~līhwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~līhwaną~, from PIE *~leykʷ-~ ("to leave behind"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with English ~loan~ (via Old Norse ~lán~, from *~laihną~ of the same root), Dutch ~lenen~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys distributing or handing out: spreading something outward among recipients.

The base verb hands over and the compound hands out: ~ausleihen~ is first of all "to lend out," and only the reflexive ~sich etwas ausleihen~ reverses the direction into "to borrow."
en.ausleiten:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~: the causative *~laidijaną~ of the strong verb *~līþaną~ ("to pass, go") with the suffix *~-janą~ ("to cause to go"), from PIE *~leyt-~ ("to go, depart, die"). ~leiten~ and ~leiden~ are a base-and-causative pair. Cognate with English ~lead~ (OE ~lǣdan~).
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Since ~leiten~ is itself a causative ("to cause to go"), ~ausleiten~ means precisely to make something go out: water from a basin, heat from a circuit.
en.auslernen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~lernen~:

• ~lernen~: From MHG ~lernen~, from OHG ~lernēn~, ~lirnēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~liʀnēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lizaną~, from PIE *~leys-~ ("track, furrow, trail"): to learn is to follow the trail laid down before. ~lehren~ ("to teach") shares the stem in causative function. Cognate with Old English ~leornian~ (English ~learn~), Dutch ~lernen~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

One who has ~ausgelernt~ follows the trail no further: the compound names the end of an apprenticeship rather than its success.
en.auslesen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The older sense "to gather" survives here: what is ~ausgelesen~ is not a book but the individual items picked out of a mass, hence the vintner’s ~Auslese~.
en.ausleuchten:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~leuchten~:

• ~leuchten~: From OHG ~liuhten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~liuhtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~liuhtijaną~, a factitive verb from *~leuhtą~ ("light") or *~leuhtaz~ ("bright"), from PIE *~lewk-~ ("bright, to shine, to see"). Cognate with MHG ~liuhten~ and English ~light~; from the same root, Latin ~lūx~ and Greek ~leukos~ ("white").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The compound wants a surface as its object: a lamp does not shine, a room is made bright into its corners, and, figuratively, a matter is examined down to its details.
en.ausliefern:
Compound of ~aus-~ + ~liefern~:

• ~liefern~: From MHG ~lieveren~ (attested before 1350), probably borrowed via Middle Dutch and Middle Low German ~lēveren~ from Old French ~livrer~ ("to deliver"), from Latin ~līberāre~ ("to set free, hand over"), from ~līber~ ("free"). The vocalism ~-ie-~ (instead of the expected ~-ē-~) is attributed to hypercorrection. Low German definitely contributed to the spread of the word, which was part of the technical vocabulary of the Hanseatic League. Cognate with Dutch ~leveren~, Swedish ~leverera~, and French ~livrer~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys movement outward, completion, or distribution.

The compound ~ausliefern~ means "to deliver, hand over, extradite", to send something ~aus~ ("out") by ~liefern~ ("delivering") it. The root ~liefern~ is one of the few German verbs with a Romance etymology that entered the language not through courtly culture but through trade: the Hanseatic League's commercial network spread the word from Low German ports across the German-speaking world. The Latin ancestor ~līberāre~ ("to set free") (which also gives English ~liberate~ and ~liberty~) underwent a remarkable semantic narrowing in its passage through Old French into Germanic: from "freeing" to "handing over goods." English ~deliver~ traveled the same Old French path but kept a wider semantic range.
en.ausloben:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~loben~:

• ~loben~: From MHG ~loben~, from OHG ~lobēn~/~lobōn~ ("to praise, approve"), from Proto-West Germanic *~lubōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lubō~, from PIE *~lewbʰ-~ ("to love, desire, praise"), the same root as ~lieb~ and ~Liebe~. Cognate with Old English ~lofian~ ("to praise"), Dutch ~loven~, Swedish ~lova~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys distributing or handing out: spreading something outward among recipients.

The verb preserves the old sense of ~loben~, "to pledge, to promise," which otherwise survives only in ~geloben~: what is ~ausgelobt~ is a reward promised publicly and thereby held out to all comers.
en.auslöschen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~löschen~:

• ~löschen~: Two distinct verbs merged under one spelling. "To extinguish": from MHG ~leschen~, OHG ~lescan~, Proto-West Germanic *~leskan~, Proto-Germanic *~leskaną~ ("to go out"), originally intransitive, the causative sense developing later; cognate with Dutch ~lessen~. "To delete, unload (cargo)": borrowed from Low German ~lössen~, ~lossen~, from the ancestor of ~los~ ("free, rid of").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.

Of the two ~löschen~ verbs this is the older "to go out," not the Low German "to unload cargo." The prefix reinforces a meaning the base already carries and adds finality to it.
en.auslösen:
~Aus-~ + ~lösen~. Compound of ~aus-~ + ~lösen~:

• ~lösen~: From MHG ~lœsen~, ~lōsen~, from OHG ~lōsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lausijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausijaną~, a factitive verb derived from *~lausaz~ ("loose, free"), from PIE *~lewh₁-~ ("to loosen, cut apart").
• ~aus-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix adds a sense of releasing outward, completing a process of liberation.

~Auslösen~ means "to trigger, to initiate, to cause; to ransom", two senses united by the image of releasing something from constraint. The triggering sense (~eine Reaktion auslösen~, "to trigger a reaction"; ~den nächsten Börsencrash auslösen~, "to trigger the next stock-market crash") envisions a mechanism held in check that is suddenly set free. The ransoming sense (~einen Gefangenen auslösen~, "to ransom a prisoner") is the older meaning: to pay the price that frees someone from captivity. The derived noun ~Auslöser~ means both "trigger" (on a camera or a gun) and, figuratively, "the thing that set events in motion." The English cognate ~loose~ descends from Old Norse ~lauss~ (from the same Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~), while ~lose~ comes from a different path through Old English ~losian~. German ~lösen~ and English ~loose~ are thus cousins, not siblings, arriving at similar sounds from slightly different routes through the same Proto-Germanic family.
en.ausmachen:
From ~aus-~ + ~machen~. Compound of:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~makōn~, from *~mak~ ("fit, suitable") + *~-ōn~, ultimately from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with English ~make~, Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz-~, from OHG ~ūz-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). As a verbal prefix, it can convey completion, extinction, or determination.

~Ausmachen~ is a lexical chameleon with at least five major senses: "to turn off" (a light), "to make up, constitute" (a sum), "to matter" (~es macht nichts aus~ = "it doesn't matter"), "to agree upon, arrange" (a meeting), and "to make out, discern" (something in the distance). This polysemy makes it one of the trickier German verbs for learners. The "turn off" sense (extinguishing something ~out~) parallels English "put out" (a fire), while the "constitute" sense reflects the idea of ~making out~ a total. The "to matter" sense is perhaps the most idiomatic: ~macht dir das etwas aus?~ ("does that bother you?") literally asks whether something "makes something out" of the situation for you. The PIE root *~mag-~ ("to knead") points to the most physical origin of all: shaping dough with one's hands.
en.ausmalen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~malen~:

• ~malen~: From MHG ~mālen~, from OHG ~mālōn~, ~mālēn~, a denominative of the noun ~māl~ ("spot, mark"), from Proto-West Germanic *~mālijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~mēlijaną~, from *~mēlą~, from PIE *~melh₂-~ ("dark color"). Not to be confused with ~mahlen~ ("to grind"), of separate origin. Cognate with Dutch ~maal~, Greek ~melas~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

Literally a surface is filled to its edges; reflexively the same image moves inward: to ~sich etwas ausmalen~ is to finish a picture in the mind.
en.ausnehmen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The taking-out can be physical (a fish is ~ausgenommen~, gutted), or logical, when a case is taken out of a rule; the frozen participle ~ausgenommen~ has meanwhile hardened into a preposition, "except."
en.ausnutzen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~nutzen~:

• ~nutzen~: From MHG ~nutzen~, ~nützen~, from OHG ~nuzzōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~nutōną~, from *~nutō~ ("use"), from *~nutiz~ ("useful"), from *~neutaną~ ("to enjoy, use"), from PIE *~newd-~ ("to acquire, make use of"). ~nützen~ is now a chiefly southern conjugation, ~nutzen~ the standard one.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The compound carries a judgment: an opportunity is ~ausgenutzt~, but so is a person, and then it sounds a reproach that plain ~nutzen~ does not.
en.auspacken:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~packen~:

• ~packen~: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~packen~, from Old Saxon *~pakko~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pakkō~, from Proto-Germanic *~pakkô~ ("bundle, pack"), of debated ultimate origin. The absence of the High German consonant shift confirms it entered via Low German trade routes. Cognate with English ~pack~, Dutch ~pakken~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The compound reverses ~packen~; colloquially, though, someone who tells all they know also ~packt aus~, as if knowledge were a bundle.
en.auspfeifen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~pfeifen~:

• ~pfeifen~: From MHG ~pfīfen~, from OHG ~pfīfōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pīpōn~ ("to play a pipe, to whistle"), an early borrowing from Vulgar Latin *~pīpāre~ ("to chirp, peep"), a word of imitative origin. Originally weak, now a class I strong verb (~pfeifen~, ~pfiff~, ~gepfiffen~). Cognate with English ~pipe~ and ~peep~, French ~piper~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

~Auspfeifen~ comes from the theatre: the audience whistles a performer off the stage. The cultural reversal is worth noting: in German-speaking countries whistling signals disapproval, while in English-speaking ones it is often a form of applause.
en.ausprobieren:
From ~aus-~ + ~probieren~. ~Probieren~ derives from Latin ~probāre~ ("to test, to inspect, to approve, to prove"), a denominal verb from ~probus~ ("good, fit, virtuous"), from PIE *~pro-bʰuH-s~ ("being in front"), from *~pro-~ ("forward") + *~bʰuH-~ ("to be"). ~Probieren~ is a doublet of both ~proben~ ("to rehearse") and ~prüfen~ ("to examine, to test"), all from the same Latin root but via different routes.

• ~probieren~: Directly from Latin ~probāre~. The sense in German is "to try, to taste, to sample", not "to probe" in the clinical English sense. This is a subtle false friend: English ~probe~ (also from ~probāre~) has narrowed to mean investigation or intrusion, while German ~probieren~ kept the lighter sense of tasting or trying.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūȥ~, OHG ~ūȥ~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~. The prefix here adds the sense of thoroughness or completion, testing something all the way through.
en.ausprägen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~prägen~:

• ~prägen~: From MHG ~bræchen~ / ~præchen~ ("to press in, to depict"), from OHG ~giprāhhan~ / ~prāhhan~ ("to press in or scratch by breaking the surface"), formed from the first- and third-person plural preterite of ~prēchan~ / ~prāchun~ ("to break"), making ~prägen~ likely a relative of ~brechen~. The noun ~Prägung~ ("imprint, stamp") shares the root.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys expansion or full development outward.

The metaphor comes from minting: a design is struck fully out of the blank. Today the verb appears mostly in its participle ~ausgeprägt~, which functions as an adjective meaning "pronounced, markedly developed."
en.ausrauchen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~rauchen~:

• ~rauchen~: From MHG ~rouchen~, ~röuchen~, from OHG ~rouhhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raukijan~, derived from the noun *~rauki-~ ("smoke"), from Proto-Germanic *~raukiz~, from *~reukaną~ ("to smoke"), possibly from PIE *~h₁rewg-~ ("to belch, emit"). The noun survives as ~Rauch~. Cognate with English ~reek~, Dutch ~rook~, Swedish ~rök~, Danish ~røg~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The compound covers both driving something out of hiding with smoke and smoking a pipe down to the end. The root names smoke before it names the act: the verb derives from the noun ~Rauch~.
en.ausrechnen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~rechnen~:

• ~rechnen~: From MHG ~rechenen~, from OHG ~rehhanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rekanōn~ ("to count, explain"), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to make straight or right"), the same root as German ~recht~ and Latin ~rectus~. Cognate with English ~reckon~, Dutch ~rekenen~, Low German ~rekenen~, Danish ~regne~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

~Ausrechnen~ carries reckoning through to a finished result; someone who ~sich etwas ausrechnen~ can see it coming. The same participle yields the adverb ~ausgerechnet~ ("of all things"), which has cut loose from the verb's meaning entirely.
en.ausreden:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The verb carries two readings: intransitively, ~jemanden ausreden lassen~ is "to let someone finish speaking"; transitively, ~jemandem etwas ausreden~ is "to talk someone out of something," where the prefix marks removal rather than completion. The noun ~Ausrede~ ("excuse") belongs with the second.
en.ausreichen:
Compound of ~aus-~ + ~reichen~:

• ~reichen~: From MHG ~reichen~, from OHG ~reihhen~, ~reichen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raikijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~raikijaną~ ("to reach, stretch out, extend"). Cognate with English ~reach~ and Dutch ~reiken~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys sufficiency or completion.

The compound literally means "to reach out sufficiently" and has come to mean simply "to suffice, to be enough": ~Das Geld reicht aus~ ("The money is enough"). The adjective ~ausreichend~ ("sufficient, adequate") is also used as a school grade in Germany, equivalent to a D, the lowest passing mark, which tells students their performance ~reicht gerade aus~ ("just barely suffices"). The root verb ~reichen~ preserves both the physical sense ("to hand, to pass") and an older sense of sufficiency (~Das reicht!~ "That's enough!"). English ~reach~ underwent the opposite semantic narrowing, losing the sufficiency meaning and retaining only the physical extension. The PIE ancestor *~raikijaną~ meant "to stretch out the hand," an image that survives whenever a German speaker says ~Reichen Sie mir bitte das Salz~ ("Please pass me the salt").
en.ausreisen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Today ~ausreisen~ is a word of officialdom: leaving a national territory, the counterpart of ~einreisen~. That is a long way from a root that first meant setting out on a campaign. Like other verbs of change of place, it forms its perfect with ~sein~.
en.ausreiten:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~reiten~:

• ~reiten~: From MHG ~rīten~, from OHG ~rītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rīdaną~, from PIE *~Hreydʰ-~ ("to set in motion, ride"), likely a suffixed form of *~h₃reyH-~ ("to move, churn"). German ~reiten~ narrowed to horseback riding, while English ~ride~ broadened to vehicles. Cognate with Dutch ~rijden~, Danish ~ride~, Swedish ~rida~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Because ~reiten~ narrowed to horseback in German, ~ausreiten~ can only mean riding out on a horse; English "to ride out" leaves the conveyance open.
en.ausreißen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Beside the literal tearing out, ~ausreißen~ developed an intransitive sense "to run away, bolt," whence ~Ausreißer~, which names both a runaway and a statistical outlier.
en.ausrichten:
From Middle High German ~ūzrihten~. Compound of ~aus-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~ ("to right, to direct").
• ~aus-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The separable prefix adds a sense of outward direction or completion.

~Ausrichten~ carries a remarkable range of meanings: "to align, to orient, to deliver (a message), to organize (an event), to accomplish." The root ~richten~ means "to straighten, to direct, to judge" (cognate with English ~right~), and the prefix ~aus-~ pushes this straightening outward, toward completion. When you ~eine Nachricht ausrichten~ ("deliver a message"), you are directing words outward to their recipient. When you ~ein Fest ausrichten~ ("host a festival"), you bring an event into proper arrangement. The MHG compound ~ūzrihten~ already carried the sense of equipping or furnishing, showing that the "arranging outward" metaphor is centuries old. Cognate with Dutch ~uitrichten~.
en.ausrinnen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~rinnen~:

• ~rinnen~: From MHG ~rinnen~, from OHG ~rinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~ ("to run, flow"); the PIE source is debated, most often given as *~h₃reyH-~ ("to churn, set in motion"). A class III strong verb (~rinnen~, ~rann~, ~geronnen~). German ~rennen~ is its causative, from *~rannijaną~. Cognate with English ~run~, Gothic ~rinnan~, Swedish ~rinna~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

~Ausrinnen~ is liveliest in southern German and Austrian usage, where the north prefers ~auslaufen~. As a verb of change of state it takes ~sein~ in the perfect (~ist ausgeronnen~).
en.ausrollen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~rollen~:

• ~rollen~: From MHG ~rollen~, borrowed from Old French ~roeler~, from Medieval Latin ~rotulāre~ ("to roll"), from Latin ~rotula~ ("small wheel"), diminutive of ~rota~ ("wheel"), from PIE *~ret-~ ("to run, to roll"). Cognate with English ~roll~ (also borrowed from Old French), Dutch ~rollen~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys expansion or full development outward.

The newest use (~ausrollen~ a piece of software or a programme) is a calque of English "to roll out," which closes a circle: the word returns from a language that had borrowed it, as German did, from Old French.
en.ausrufen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. A parallel weak form in Middle High German explains why the modern present lacks the expected umlaut (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Beside the individual's outcry stands public proclamation: one ~ruft~ a republic or a state of emergency ~aus~. German accordingly calls the mark ~!~ an ~Ausrufezeichen~, an "exclamation sign."
en.ausruhen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~ruhen~:

• ~ruhen~: From MHG ~ruo(we)n~, from OHG ~ruowēn~ ("to rest"), derived from the noun ~ruowa~ ("rest, peace, quiet"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rōu~, from Proto-Germanic *~rōwō~, from PIE *~h₁reh₁-~ ("to rest"), a root of remarkably narrow and stable meaning. Cognate with ~Ruhe~, Dutch ~rusten~ (a different formation on the same base), Gothic ~rimis~ ("rest").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

~Ausruhen~ is nearly always reflexive: ~sich ausruhen~, to rest until fully recovered. The idiom ~sich auf seinen Lorbeeren ausruhen~, "to rest on one's laurels," turns the image reproachful.
en.ausrutschen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~rutschen~:

• ~rutschen~: From MHG ~rutzen~, ~rützen~, an onomatopoeic formation imitating the sound of sliding, with a later shift from ~-tz-~ to ~-tsch-~ (as in ~fletschen~); perhaps related to OHG ~rūtezzen~. The noun ~Rutsche~ ("slide, chute") derives from the verb. English ~rutch~ and ~rutsch~ are borrowed from German or its Low German cognates.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The verb takes ~sein~ in the perfect (~ist ausgerutscht~). An ~Ausrutscher~ has long meant a verbal or social lapse as much as a fall on the ice, the same transfer English makes with "slip."
en.ausräumen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~räumen~:

• ~räumen~: From Early New High German ~reumen~, a Central German umlaut variant of ~raumen~, from MHG ~rūmen~, from OHG ~rūmen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rūmijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rūmijaną~, a factitive verb from the adjective *~rūmaz~ ("roomy, spacious"), from PIE *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open"). Etymologically, "to make room." Cognate with English ~room~, the noun ~Raum~, Bavarian ~rama~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Since ~räumen~ already means "to make room," ~ausräumen~ nearly doubles the idea: making room by moving the contents outward. Figuratively, one clears away doubts or objections.
en.ausrücken:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~rücken~:

• ~rücken~: From MHG ~rücken~, from OHG ~rucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rukkijan~. The verb means "to move, to shift" and is the base of ~verrückt~ ("crazy," literally "shifted, displaced"); the noun ~Rücken~ ("back") is etymologically a separate word. Cognate with English ~rock~, Old Norse ~rykkja~, Old English ~roccian~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

~Ausrücken~ belongs to military and fire-brigade vocabulary: a unit or a fire crew ~rückt aus~, the counterpart being ~einrücken~. The same root sits inside ~verrückt~, literally "shifted out of place."
en.aussagen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

In modern German ~aussagen~ belongs above all to the language of the courts: a witness ~sagt aus~, testifies. The noun ~Aussage~ reaches further, naming in logic the proposition that can be true or false.
en.aussaugen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~saugen~:

• ~saugen~: From MHG ~sūgen~, from OHG ~sūgan~ ("to suck"), from Proto-West Germanic *~sūgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sūganą~, from PIE *~sewk-~ ("to suck"). Historically a class II strong verb (~saugen~, ~sog~, ~gesogen~), it now inflects weak (~saugte~, ~gesaugt~) just as readily. Cognate with English ~suck~, Dutch ~zuigen~, Danish ~suge~, Old English ~sūcan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.

The compound runs from literally sucking something out to draining a victim: whoever ~aussaugt~ a country leaves it nothing. Like the base verb it wavers between strong and weak inflection (~sog aus~ alongside ~saugte aus~).
en.ausschalten:
From Middle High German ~ūzschalten~, equivalent to ~aus-~ + ~schalten~:

• ~schalten~: From MHG ~schalten~, from OHG ~scaltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaldan~ ("to push, shove"). Further etymology is obscure; according to Pokorny, possibly from PIE *~(s)kelH-~ ("to split, separate"), in which case related to English ~shell~. Cognate with Old Saxon ~skaldan~ ("to push").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix conveys removal or deactivation.

The literal sense is "to switch out": to push something out of its active state. ~Ausschalten~ means "to switch off, to turn off, to disable; to eliminate, neutralize." The second, figurative sense ("to eliminate a rival, to neutralize an opponent") reveals a darker dimension: one "switches off" a person as though they were a machine. The root ~schalten~ originally meant "to push" or "to shove" in Old High German, and its modern meaning "to switch" preserves the physical gesture of pushing a lever or mechanism. The compound ~Schalter~ ("switch; counter, window at a service desk") unites both the electrical and bureaucratic senses through the same image of a mechanism that controls access. Dutch ~uitschakelen~ is the exact cognate.
en.ausschauen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
