• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

~Ausschauen~ is the southern German and Austrian counterpart of ~aussehen~, and it keeps alongside it the literal sense of keeping a lookout. That the same root yields English "show" measures how close looking and making-visible once were.
en.ausscheiden:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~scheiden~:

• ~scheiden~: From MHG ~scheiden~, from OHG ~sceidan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaiþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaiþaną~, from PIE *~skeyt-~ ("to cut, separate"). Cognate with English ~shed~ (originally "to separate"), Dutch ~scheiden~, West Frisian ~skiede~, and Greek ~skhizein~ ("to split," source of ~schism~).
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

A verb with three homes: in physiology the body secretes, in sport a team is knocked out, in office one retires from service. All three continue the root's basic sense of separating, the sense that also carries ~Scheidung~ ("divorce").
en.ausscheißen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~scheißen~:

• ~scheißen~: From MHG ~schīzen~, from OHG *~skīzan~ (attested only in the compound ~biskīzan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~skītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skītaną~, from PIE *~skeyd-~ ("to split, separate"); the root's basic sense is separation, not filth. A class I strong verb (~scheißen~, ~schiss~, ~geschissen~). Cognate with English ~shit~, Dutch ~schijten~, Old Norse ~skíta~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Because the root originally meant "to split, separate," the prefix here is very nearly pleonastic: it spells out what the base verb already carried. The word belongs throughout to coarse colloquial speech.
en.ausschenken:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schenken~:

• ~schenken~: From MHG ~schenken~, from OHG ~scenken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skankijan~ ("to pour, serve"). The sense "to give as a gift" grew out of pouring a drink for a guest, the paradigmatic act of generosity; the pouring sense retreated into ~Wein einschenken~ and ~Schenke~ ("tavern"). Cognate with Dutch ~schenken~ ("to pour; to give"), English ~skink~ (archaic) and ~shank~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys distributing or handing out: spreading something outward among recipients.

~Ausschenken~ preserves the base verb's older meaning: while plain ~schenken~ now means "to give as a gift," the compound still means pouring, and, in a tavern, serving drinks across the bar, as ~Ausschank~ and ~Schankwirtschaft~ attest.
en.ausscheren:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~scheren~:

• ~scheren~: Two verbs share this spelling. The strong ~scheren~ ("to shear, cut") comes from MHG ~schërn~, OHG ~skeran~, Proto-West Germanic *~skeran~, Proto-Germanic *~skeraną~, from PIE *~(s)ker-~ ("to cut"); a class IV strong verb (~scheren~, ~schor~, ~geschoren~), cognate with English ~shear~, Dutch ~scheren~, Old Norse ~skera~. The weak ~scheren~ ("to bother oneself about"; also "to clear off") is a separate and later word, first attested in the fifteenth century as Late MHG ~schern~ ("to hurry, escape"), of uncertain origin, and inflects weak throughout (~scherte~, ~geschert~).
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Of the two ~scheren~ verbs, ~ausscheren~ belongs to the weak one: it inflects weak (~scherte aus~, ~ist ausgeschert~) and takes ~sein~ in the perfect, as a verb of change of place should. It means pulling out of a lane or a formation, and figuratively breaking with a common line, not cutting wool.
en.ausschicken:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schicken~:

• ~schicken~: From MHG ~schicken~ ("to outfit oneself, fit in, arrange appropriately"), from OHG *~skihhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skikkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skikkijaną~ ("to order, send"), the causative of the verb underlying MHG ~geschehen~ ("to happen, rush"). The sense "to send" grew from "to make ready to go." Related to English ~chic~ (via French), ~geschickt~, and ~Schicksal~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Because ~schicken~ first meant "to make ready," ~ausschicken~ is literally "to get someone ready to set out." It now sounds archaic; present-day German reaches instead for ~losschicken~ or ~aussenden~.
en.ausschildern:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schildern~:

• ~schildern~: Borrowed in the 16th century from Middle Low German or Dutch ~schilderen~ ("to paint"), from the noun ~schilder~ ("painter"), from ~schild~ ("shield"), the painter of heraldic designs on shields. ~schild~ is from Middle Dutch ~schilt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeldu~, from Proto-Germanic *~skelduz~, from PIE *~(s)keyt-~ ("shield, cover"). Cognate with English ~shield~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

Here the word returns to its starting point: ~schildern~ had drifted away from the shield to mean "to describe," but ~ausschildern~ reattaches it to the literal signs with which a route is marked from end to end.
en.ausschlafen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schlafen~:

• ~schlafen~: From MHG ~slāfen~, from OHG ~slāfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slāpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slēpaną~, of uncertain further origin, possibly related to *~slapaz~ ("weak, lax, limp"), ancestor of ~schlaff~. A class VII strong verb of the reduplicating class (~schlafen~, ~schlief~, ~geschlafen~). Cognate with English ~sleep~, Dutch ~slapen~, Gothic ~𐍃𐌻𐌴𐍀𐌰𐌽~ (slēpan).
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

~Ausschlafen~ means sleeping one's fill, usually reflexively (~sich ausschlafen~); transitively one ~schläft~ a hangover ~aus~, sleeping until nothing of it is left.
en.ausschlagen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The compound covers a wide field: a horse's kick, a tooth struck loose, and, in the older idiom, the way an affair "turns out" well or badly. Add to that refusal, since to decline an offer is to strike it away from oneself.
en.ausschleichen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schleichen~:

• ~schleichen~: From MHG ~slīchen~, from OHG ~slīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slīkaną~ ("to glide, creep"), from PIE *~sleyg-~ ("to be smooth, slide"). A class I strong verb (~schleichen~, ~schlich~, ~geschlichen~). Cognate with English ~slick~ and ~sleek~, Dutch ~slijken~, Old Norse ~slíkr~ ("smooth").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The root says how one moves, the prefix says from where: ~ausschleichen~ is to leave a room in such a way that nobody notices.
en.ausschließen: Formed from prefix ~aus-~ (from PIE *~úd~, "upwards, out") and ~schließen~, from MHG ~slieȥen~, from OHG ~sliozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sleutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slūtaną~, *~sleutaną~ ("to lock, shut"). The root ~schließen~ descends from Middle High German ~slieȥen~, Old High German ~sliozan~, Proto-West Germanic *~sleutan~, and Proto-Germanic *~slūtaną~ / *~sleutaną~, meaning "to lock, shut." Cognate with Dutch ~sluiten~, and, strikingly, English ~slot~. To "slot out" is a false friend here: English ~slot~ kept the narrow physical sense (a groove or opening), while German ~schließen~ and ~ausschließen~ developed the abstract sense of closing off and excluding.
en.ausschneiden:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schneiden~:

• ~schneiden~: From MHG ~snīden~, from OHG ~snīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~snīþan~ ("to cut"); no secure PIE root has been established, and the word may be a Germanic innovation. A class I strong verb (~schneiden~, ~schnitt~, ~geschnitten~). Cognate with archaic English ~snithe~ ("to cut"), Dutch ~snijden~, Icelandic ~sníða~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The compound names both the cut and what the cut leaves behind, hence ~Ausschnitt~ for a clipping from a newspaper and for the neckline of a dress alike.
en.ausschreiben:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Two modern meanings run side by side: to ~ausschreiben~ an abbreviation is to write it out in full, while to ~ausschreiben~ a post or a contract is to announce it publicly. Only the second produced the noun ~Ausschreibung~ ("tender, call for bids").
en.ausschreiten:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schreiten~:

• ~schreiten~: From MHG ~schrīten~, from OHG ~skrītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīþan~ ("to step, stride"), from Proto-Germanic *~skrīþaną~ ("to walk, glide, crawl"), from PIE *~(s)kreyt-~ ("to stride"), an extension of *~(s)krey-~ ("to go about"). Cognate with Lithuanian ~skrìsti~ ("to rush, run"), Latvian ~skrìet~ ("to run, fly"). Related to ~Schritt~ ("step").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys expansion or full development outward.

The step is carried out to its full reach: ~ausschreiten~ is to walk vigorously and with long strides, not merely to walk out. Goethe still has alongside it a sense now extinct, "to decry someone as something."
en.ausschweigen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schweigen~:

• ~schweigen~: From MHG ~swīgen~, from OHG ~swīgēn~ ("to be silent"), from Proto-West Germanic *~swīgēn~. Originally weak, it developed strong forms in early Middle High German and now inflects strong (~schwieg~, ~geschwiegen~), unusual, since most German verbs moved the other way. Cognate with Old English ~swīgian~, Old Saxon ~swīgōn~ (weak), Old Norse ~svigna~ ("to bend, give way").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

Almost always used reflexively: ~sich über etwas ausschweigen~ is to keep one's silence consistently all the way through, which is rather more than merely saying nothing.
en.ausschwimmen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schwimmen~:

• ~schwimmen~: From MHG ~swimmen~, from OHG ~swimman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~swimman~, from Proto-Germanic *~swimmaną~ ("to swim, float"), from PIE *~swem-~ ("to be in motion, to swim"). A class III strong verb (~schwimmen~, ~schwamm~, ~geschwommen~). Cognate with English ~swim~, Dutch ~zwemmen~, Danish ~svømme~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

To reach open water by swimming: the prefix carries the direction the root lacks on its own, since ~schwimmen~ says only how the motion happens.
en.ausschütteln:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~schütteln~:

• ~schütteln~: From MHG ~schütelen~, from OHG ~scutilōn~, an iterative formation from ~schütten~ ("to pour, to shake") marking repeated back-and-forth motion. ~schütten~ derives from OHG ~scuttēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skudjaną~, perhaps from PIE *~(s)kewt-~ ("to shake, jolt"). Cognate with Dutch ~schudden~ ("to shake").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The iterative root supplies the back and forth, the prefix supplies the goal: the shaking continues until the vessel or the cloth is empty.
en.aussehen:
From Middle High German ~ūzsehen~. Compound of ~aus-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with Dutch ~zien~, English ~see~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz-~, from OHG ~ūz-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ut-~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). This separable prefix adds an outward or emergent sense to the base verb.

The compound's literal sense is "to look out" (as through a window) and from this developed the dominant modern meaning "to appear, to look (a certain way)": the impression projected outward toward the viewer. The parallel Yiddish ~אויסזען~ (~oyszen~) and Dutch ~uitzien~ preserve identical structure and meaning, while Scandinavian equivalents (~se ut~ in Swedish and Norwegian, ~se ud~ in Danish) express the same idea with postverbal ~ut/ud~. A false friend for English speakers: "he looks good" is ~er sieht gut aus~, not *~er schaut gut~.
en.aussenden:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~senden~:

• ~senden~: From MHG ~senden~, from OHG ~senten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sandijaną~, from PIE *~sont-eye-~, a causative of *~sent-~ ("to walk, travel"), originally "to cause to go." It has a double Präteritum: ~sendete~ for broadcasting, ~sandte~ (a Rückumlaut form) for sending a letter. Cognate with English ~send~, Dutch ~zenden~, Gothic ~sandjan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

In the compound the meaning decides the Präteritum: a transmitter ~sendete~ signals ~aus~, but a master ~sandte~ his messengers ~aus~. The causative "to make go" is still transparent in both.
en.aussetzen:
Compound of ~aus-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~, a causative of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit"), from PIE *~sed-~ ("to sit").
• ~aus-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix adds the sense of outward placement, exposure, or cessation.

~Aussetzen~ unfolds into a striking range of meanings, all derived from "setting something out": to expose (someone to danger, setting them out in the open), to abandon (a child or animal, setting them out and leaving), to release (a captive animal back into the wild, setting it out to freedom), to suspend (an activity, setting it outside the flow of events), to stop (of a machine or heartbeat, ceasing to operate), and to miss a turn (in a game, being set outside the round). The abandonment sense is perhaps the most emotionally charged: ~ein Kind aussetzen~ evokes the ancient practice of infant exposure, known in German legal history as ~Kindesaussetzung~. The word ~ausgesetzt~ ("exposed") functions as both past participle and adjective, describing vulnerability itself. Cognate with Dutch ~uitzetten~, Luxembourgish ~aussetzen~.
en.aussinnen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~sinnen~:

• ~sinnen~: From MHG ~sinnen~, from OHG ~sinnan~ ("to travel; to strive for; to think"), from Proto-West Germanic *~sinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sinnaną~, from PIE *~sent-~ ("to head for, go; to feel"). A class III strong verb (~sinnen~, ~sann~, ~gesonnen~). The same root gave Latin ~sentīre~, so ~Sinn~ and English ~sense~ are relatives. Cognate with Old English ~sinnan~ ("to meditate on"), Dutch ~zinnen~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The thinking here runs all the way to a finished plan, which is why the compound usually takes something cunning or malicious as its object. The strong participle ~gesonnen~ survives mainly as an adjective now, meaning "minded, inclined."
en.aussparen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~sparen~:

• ~sparen~: From MHG ~sparn~, from OHG ~sparēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sparēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~sparaz~ ("sparing, frugal"), from PIE *~speh₁-~ ("to thrive, prosper; to leave untouched"). The same root produced Latin ~prosperus~, whence English ~prosper~. Cognate with English ~spare~, Dutch ~sparen~, Icelandic ~spara~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

From sparing to omitting: what is ~ausgespart~ is deliberately left blank, in painting the unpainted area, in a text the question left untouched. The prefix here excludes from a whole rather than leading out of a container.
en.ausspeichern:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~speichern~:

• ~speichern~: A denominal verb from ~Speicher~ ("storehouse, granary"), from MHG ~spīcher~, OHG ~spīhhāri~, Proto-West Germanic *~spīkārī~, borrowed from Late Latin ~spīcārium~ ("granary"), from ~spīca~ ("ear of grain, spike"). The same Latin word also gives English ~spike~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The Late Latin granary has become computer storage, and the compound is now almost purely technical: data are ~ausgespeichert~ from memory, as grain was once fetched from the ~Speicher~.
en.aussperren:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~sperren~:

• ~sperren~: From MHG ~sperren~, from OHG ~sperran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sparrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sparrijaną~ ("to bar, to block"), a denominative verb from *~sparrô~ ("wooden beam, log"), originally to bar a passage with a beam. Cognate with English ~spar~ ("to bolt, bar"; the noun for a wooden beam), Dutch ~sperren~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The beam that once barred a passage now keeps people outside. The noun ~Aussperrung~ is labor law's countermove to the ~Streik~: the employers lock the workforce out.
en.aussprechen:
From Middle High German ~ūzsprëchen~, from Old High German ~ūzsprehhan~. Compound of ~aus-~ + ~sprechen~:

• ~sprechen~: From MHG ~sprëchen~, from OHG ~sprëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sprekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sprekaną~ ("to speak"), probably from PIE *~spregʰ-~ ("to crackle"). Cognate with English ~speak~, Dutch ~spreken~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz-~, from OHG ~ūz-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt-~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). As a prefix, it conveys the sense of "out, outward, completely."

The connection between "cracking/crackling" and "speaking" in the PIE root *~spregʰ-~ suggests that the earliest Germanic conception of speech was of sounds bursting forth, noises that crack the silence. The ~aus-~ prefix in ~aussprechen~ reinforces this outward motion: to "speak out" a word is to pronounce it fully, to articulate it. The verb also carries the sense of "to utter" something otherwise kept silent, and reflexively (~sich aussprechen~) means "to pour one's heart out" or "to declare oneself in favour of something." In its intransitive use (~Lass ihn aussprechen!~), it means "to finish speaking", to let someone speak completely out to the end.
en.ausstatten: Formed from prefix ~aus-~ (from PIE *~úd~, "upwards, out") and the now-obsolete verb ~statten~. The core verb ~statten~, from Middle High German ~staten~ ("to help do something; to add"), appears to be a denominal formation from Proto-Germanic *~stadiz~ ("place, location"), from Proto-Indo-European *~stéh₂tis~ ("standing, position"). The related noun ~Statt~ (now chiefly surviving in compounds like ~Statthalter~ and the preposition ~statt~ "instead of") is a doublet of ~Stadt~ ("city") and cognate with English ~stead~, as in ~homestead~ and ~instead~. To "outfit" someone is thus, at root, to "place out" a full complement of equipment or furnishings.
en.ausstechen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~stechen~:

• ~stechen~: From MHG ~stëchen~, from OHG ~stëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stekaną~ ("to stab, prick"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to stick, poke"). Cognate with Dutch ~steken~ ("to stab, sting"), Old Norse ~stinga~, English ~stick~ (originally "to stab, pierce").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

From an eye to a cookie to a rival: the same formation covers gouging out an eye, cutting shapes out of dough, and, figuratively, ~jemanden ausstechen~; to outdo someone and displace him from his position.
en.ausstehen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

Two meanings from one formation: to ~ausstehen~ something is to endure it to the end, while something that ~aussteht~ is still outstanding and unsettled. The suppletive Präteritum ~stand aus~ belongs to both.
en.aussteigen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Climbing out of a carriage is the base meaning, but present-day German also gets out of treaties, out of nuclear power, and out of one's own life, hence ~Aussteiger~ for someone who takes leave of the bourgeois order.
en.ausstellen:
Compound of ~aus-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, to position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, to put, to post, to stand"). Cognate with English ~stall~ and ~still~.
• ~aus-~: From OHG ~ūz-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt-~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). This prefix conveys the sense of putting forth or outward.

The verb ~ausstellen~ has two principal meanings that developed from the same image of "placing outward": first, "to exhibit, to display" (as in a museum exhibition, ~Ausstellung~), and second, "to issue" (a document, certificate, or receipt). In both cases, something is being put out into the world for others to see or use. The PIE root *~stel-~ is remarkably productive, giving rise to German ~Stelle~ ("place, position, job"), ~Gestalt~ ("form, figure"), English ~install~, ~stall~, and Greek ~stēlē~ ("upright stone slab"). The noun ~Ausstellung~ ("exhibition") is one of the most common German cultural terms, used for everything from art shows to trade fairs. The double meaning of ~ausstellen~ occasionally creates ambiguity: ~einen Pass ausstellen~ means "to issue a passport," not "to exhibit" one.
en.aussterben:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~sterben~:

• ~sterben~: From MHG ~stërben~, from OHG ~stërban~, from Proto-Germanic *~sterbaną~, from PIE *~(s)terp-~ ("to lose force, become numb") or *~sterbʰ-~ ("to become stiff"), both traceable to *~ster-~ ("stiff, rigid"). A class III strong verb (~stirbt~, ~starb~, ~gestorben~). Cognate with English ~starve~, Dutch ~sterven~, West Frisian ~stjerre~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.

The root already meant becoming stiff; the prefix carries that to the last member of a line. So a family, a species, or a word ~stirbt aus~, and a deserted square is said to be ~wie ausgestorben~.
en.aussteuern:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~steuern~:

• ~steuern~: From MHG ~stiuren~, from OHG ~stiuren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stiurijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stiurijaną~. The root noun ~Steuer~ carries two meanings sharing one ancestor: ~das Steuer~ ("rudder, helm") and ~die Steuer~ ("tax," via "supporting post" and "support"). ~Steuern~ thus means both "to steer, navigate, control" and, in archaic or Swiss usage, "to pay a tax." Cognate with English ~steer~, Dutch ~stuur~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys distributing or handing out: spreading something outward among recipients.

Of the root noun's two branches, this compound belongs to the branch of support rather than the rudder: the ~Aussteuer~ is the dowry with which a daughter was provided. Engineering later pulled the word back toward the rudder branch, in the sense of driving an amplifier to full level.
en.ausstoßen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). Cognate with dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce, ricochet"), Dutch ~stoten~, Old Norse ~stauta~ and ~steyta~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The same prefix carries two directions of "out": to ~ausstoßen~ a sigh or a gas is to produce it, while to ~ausstoßen~ a person is to banish him from the community, hence ~der Ausgestoßene~, the outcast.
en.ausstrahlen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~strahlen~:

• ~strahlen~: A 16th-century denominative verb from the noun ~Strahl~ ("ray, beam") with the verbal suffix ~-en~. ~Strahl~ traces to MHG ~strāle~, from OHG ~strāla~ ("arrow"), from Proto-West Germanic *~strālu~ ("arrow"); the sense "ray of light" arose in the 17th century as a metaphor from the arrow's straight flight. Cognate with Dutch ~straal~ and the rare English ~streal~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The compound pushes the arrow-flight metaphor further: heat, light, and finally broadcast programming are ~ausgestrahlt~. Said of a person it yields ~Ausstrahlung~, the charisma that radiates from them.
en.aussuchen:
Compound of ~aus-~ + ~suchen~:

• ~suchen~: From MHG ~suochen~, from OHG ~suohhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sōkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sōkijaną~, from PIE *~seh₂g-~ ("to seek out"). Originally an Upper German form without umlaut on the long rounded vowel before a velar consonant, reinforced against the umlauted Central German form (compare Luxembourgish ~sichen~) by the umlautless past forms. Cognate with English ~seek~, Dutch ~zoeken~, Low German ~söken~, Danish ~søge~, and Gothic ~sokjan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys selection or extraction from a group.

The compound literally means "to seek out," i.e., to pick or choose from available options. While ~suchen~ means simply "to search," ~aussuchen~ implies a completed selection: ~Such dir etwas aus!~ ("Pick something out for yourself!"). The reflexive ~sich etwas aussuchen~ is the everyday German equivalent of English "to choose." The English cognate ~seek~ shares the same PIE root *~seh₂g-~, which also produced Latin ~sagīre~ ("to perceive keenly"), the ancestor of English ~sagacious~ and ~presage~. A seeker, in the Indo-European mind, was someone with keen perception.
en.austauschen:
~Aus-~ + ~tauschen~. Compound of ~aus-~ + ~tauschen~:

• ~tauschen~: From MHG ~tiuschen~, derived from ~tūschen~, related to ~täuschen~ ("to deceive"). The semantic shift ran from "to deceive" to "to trick someone into buying one's goods" to "to trade, to exchange", a revealing commentary on medieval market ethics. The further origin of ~tūschen~ is uncertain.
• ~aus-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix adds the sense of completeness or thoroughness, a full exchange, in and out.

~Austauschen~ means "to exchange, to replace, to substitute", a verb of symmetric transfer: what goes out is matched by what comes in. One ~tauscht~ ideas ~aus~ (exchanges them in conversation), ~tauscht~ a defective part ~aus~ (replaces it), or ~tauscht~ prisoners ~aus~ (swaps them between sides). The derived noun ~Austausch~ ("exchange") appears in contexts from student exchanges (~Schüleraustausch~) to information sharing (~Informationsaustausch~). The kinship between ~tauschen~ ("to swap") and ~täuschen~ ("to deceive") (both from the same Middle High German root) is one of German etymology's most entertaining revelations: to trade and to trick were once, at some level, the same act.
en.austeilen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~teilen~:

• ~teilen~: From MHG ~teilen~ and OHG ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~ ("to divide, part, deal"), from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, a denominative of *~dailiz~ ("part, share"), from PIE *~dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo-~, tentatively from *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, set, place"), though the precise PIE derivation is uncertain. Cognate with English ~deal~, Dutch ~delen~, Danish ~dele~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys distributing or handing out: spreading something outward among recipients.

The root already carried the dividing; the prefix adds the direction toward the recipients. The English cognate ~deal~ shows the same doubling, dealing out cards as readily as measuring a share.
en.austragen:
From Middle High German ~ūztragen~, from Old High German ~ūztragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūtdragan~. Compound of ~aus-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). Cognate with Dutch ~dragen~, English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Danish ~drage~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix conveys outward movement or completion.

The compound means "to carry out, to deliver (mail); to bear (a child to term); to settle (a dispute); to hold (a competition)." Each sense extends the image of carrying something to its destination or conclusion. The mail carrier (~Briefträger~) ~trägt die Post aus~ ("carries out the mail"), while a pregnant woman ~trägt ein Kind aus~ ("carries a child to term"). The connection between German ~tragen~ ("to carry") and English ~draw~ / ~drag~ is not immediately obvious but perfectly regular: the semantic shift from "to drag" to "to carry" happened within Germanic, while English preserved the older "pulling" sense. Portuguese ~trazer~ ("to bring") is also cognate, having inherited the same root through Latin.
en.austreiben:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

From cattle driven out to pasture to the demon a priest ~austreibt~, and on into child-rearing, since ~jemandem etwas austreiben~ is to break someone of a habit for good.
en.austreten:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Stepping out of a room was transferred early: one ~tritt~ out of a party or the church. In the passive the literal tread stays visible, in the ~ausgetretene~ steps of an old staircase.
en.austrinken:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~trinken~:

• ~trinken~: From MHG ~trinken~, from OHG ~trinkan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drinkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drinkaną~; no non-Germanic cognate has been securely identified, so the word may be a Germanic innovation. Cognate with English ~drink~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Old Norse ~drekka~ and Gothic ~𐌳𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌺𐌰𐌽~ (drigkan).
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.

The prefix names not the drinking but the emptied vessel: ~austrinken~ is to drink to the last drop, which is why the verb wants an object where plain ~trinken~ does without one.
en.austrocknen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~trocknen~:

• ~trocknen~: A deadjectival verb from the adjective ~trocken~ ("dry") with the verbal suffix ~-en~. ~Trocken~ traces to MHG ~trucken~, from OHG ~truckan~, ~trokkan~ ("dried out"), from Proto-West Germanic *~drukn~, from Proto-Germanic *~druknaz~ ("dry"), from PIE *~dʰerǵʰ-~ ("to become hard or solid"), an extension of *~dʰer-~ ("to hold, hold fast"). Cognate with Old Saxon ~drokno~ and Old English ~gedrycnan~ ("to dry up").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.

The compound works in both directions: a riverbed dries out by itself, and a drought dries it out, with one form covering both; either way the moisture is gone to the last drop.
en.austräumen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~träumen~:

• ~träumen~: From MHG ~troumen~ and OHG ~troumen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~draumijan~, a denominative verb from the noun *~draum~ (whence ~Traum~), from Proto-Germanic *~draumaz~, from PIE *~dʰrewgʰ-~ ("to deceive, to harm"); the ancient Indo-Europeans thus viewed dreams as fundamentally deceptive experiences. Cognate with English ~dream~, Dutch ~dromen~, Swedish ~drömma~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

A dream that is ~ausgeträumt~ has been dreamt to the end, and in figurative use is definitively over. The old root of deception still sounds through it: the dream one has finished dreaming is usually one that proved an illusion.
en.ausverkaufen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~ver-~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, a denominative verb from *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"), a loanword from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper"). Cognate with English ~cheap~, Dutch ~kopen~, Danish ~købe~, Icelandic ~kaupa~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys using something up, or extinguishing it, until nothing is left.

Two prefixes stack on one stem here: ~verkaufen~ is already a finished verb, and ~aus-~ supplies the limit past which nothing is left. The two behave differently: the inner ~ver-~ stays welded to the stem while the outer ~aus-~ detaches, which is why German says „er verkauft aus“.
en.auswachsen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from PIE *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Cognate with English ~wax~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The main modern use is reflexive and figurative: „das wächst sich aus“ says that a difficulty is not cured but finishes its own growth and disappears in the process, time rather than intervention.
en.auswandern:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~wandern~:

• ~wandern~: From MHG ~wandern~, from OHG *~wantarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandarōn~, formed from *~wandōn~ ("to turn") with the frequentative suffix *~-rōn~ (not a single journey but repeated, meandering motion), from Proto-Germanic *~wandōną~, from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, to wind"). Cognate with English ~wander~, Danish ~vandre~, Swedish ~vandra~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The stem carries a frequentative suffix and properly means repeated back-and-forth motion; the prefix aims that motion once, and one way. To emigrate is precisely not to wander.
en.auswaschen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~waschen~:

• ~waschen~: From MHG ~waschen~, from OHG ~wascan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~waskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waskaną~, from an earlier *~watskaną~, a ~ske~-present formation from PIE *~wed-~ ("wet, water"), hence "to make wet (repeatedly)." Cognate with English ~wash~, ~water~, ~wet~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vaske~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The verb admits either role as its object: one washes out the stain that leaves, and equally the wound or the cloth it leaves. What the prefix fixes is the direction, not which of the two is meant.
en.auswechseln:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~wechseln~:

• ~wechseln~: From MHG ~wëhseln~, from OHG *~wehsalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wihslōną~, from PIE *~weyk-~, *~weyḱ-~ ("to change, bend, yield"). Cognate with Dutch ~wisselen~, Luxembourgish ~wiesselen~, English ~week~, German ~Woche~, and Latin ~vicis~ ("change, turn, alternation").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The stem means exchange as alternation, a taking of turns that continues, the same root sits inside ~Woche~ ("week"). The prefix makes the process one-way: what is swapped out does not come round again.
en.ausweichen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~weichen~:

• ~weichen~: From MHG ~wīchen~, from OHG ~wīchan~ ("to yield, give way"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wīkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīkwaną~, from PIE *~h₃weyg-~ ("to start moving, to distance oneself, to bend, wind"). A class I strong verb, "to yield, give way, retreat"; not to be confused with the weak ~weichen~ ("to soften, to soak"), which derives from ~weich~ ("soft"). Cognate with Old English ~wīcan~, Old Norse ~vīkja~, Swedish ~vika~ ("to give way, fold").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

The compound belongs to the strong ~weichen~ "to yield, give way," not to the identically spelled weak ~weichen~ "to soak"; the class I strong ablaut (~wich~, ~gewichen~) settles the question. To dodge is to step aside, not to soften anything.
en.ausweinen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~weinen~:

• ~weinen~: From MHG ~weinen~, from OHG ~weinōn~ ("to cry, lament"), from Proto-Germanic *~wainōną~ ("to wail, weep"), from PIE *~wáy~ ("woe!"), originally an exclamation of grief. Related to ~Weh~ ("woe, pain"), from Proto-Germanic *~waiwô~, from the same exclamatory root. Cognate with Gothic ~wainon~, Old Norse ~veina~, Old English ~wānian~, Dutch ~wenen~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The verb is used reflexively: it is not the tears that are wept out but the grief that is wept to its end. The stem goes back to a bare cry of pain, and the prefix gives that cry a stopping point.
en.ausweisen:
From Middle High German ~ūzweizen~, from Old High German ~ūzwīsen~. Compound of ~aus-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~ ("to show, direct"), a causative derived from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from PIE *~weyd-~ ("to see, to know"). The adjective ~weise~ ("wise") is cognate with English ~wise~, Dutch ~wijs~, and Latin ~vidēre~ ("to see"), all from the same root, which links knowledge to vision.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix conveys outward direction or proof.

The compound means "to expel, to deport; to identify, prove" and reflexively ~sich ausweisen~ means "to identify oneself." The semantic bridge between "showing the way out" (expulsion) and "showing who one is" (identification) lies in the root ~weisen~ ("to show, to point"). The ~Ausweis~ ("identity card") is literally "that which shows outward", an external proof of who one is. The connection between seeing, knowing, and wisdom runs deep in Indo-European languages: Latin ~vidēre~ ("to see") shares the same PIE root *~weyd-~ as German ~wissen~ ("to know") and ~weise~ ("wise"). To the Indo-Europeans, knowledge was something seen.
en.auswerfen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

Net, anchor, ash, lava, and today a spent cartridge or a disc: what the compound's uses share is not the force of the throw but the fact that the object leaves whatever was holding it.
en.auswerten:
Compound of ~aus-~ + ~werten~:

• ~werten~: A verbal derivation from the adjective ~wert~ ("worth, valuable"), from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("worthy, valuable"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"). Compare English ~worth~.
• ~aus-~: From OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Here the prefix means "out" in the sense of extracting or deriving results.

~Auswerten~ means "to evaluate, to analyze, to interpret (data)", literally "to value out," extracting meaning or value from raw material. It is the standard German verb for data analysis: ~Daten auswerten~, ~Ergebnisse auswerten~, ~Statistiken auswerten~. The PIE root *~wert-~ ("to turn") connects value to turning: the original sense was "to turn toward," hence "to regard, to esteem," hence "worth." The same root produced Latin ~vertere~ ("to turn," whence English ~convert~, ~reverse~, ~versus~). The noun ~Auswertung~ ("evaluation, analysis") is indispensable in scientific and statistical German.
en.auswiegen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~wiegen~:

• ~wiegen~: Two distinct verbs, both from MHG ~wigen~. Sense 1 ("to weigh"): a northwestern variant of ~wegen~ that generalized the present-singular stem vowel ~i~, from OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, move"); the original ~e~-form survives in the doublet ~wägen~. Sense 2 ("to rock, cradle"): from ~wige~ ("cradle," modern ~Wiege~), from OHG ~wīga~, likely related to Proto-West Germanic *~waggjan~ ("to cause to move"), from the same PIE root. Cognate with English ~weigh~, Dutch ~wegen~, Danish ~veje~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

Of the two identically spelled verbs, the one underneath here is the strong ~wiegen~ "to determine the weight," not the weak ~wiegen~ "to rock" that belongs to the ~Wiege~ ("cradle"); the strong forms ~wog~, ~gewogen~ mark the choice. The prefix requires the weighing to be carried through, until the beam comes to rest.
en.auswirken:
From Middle High German ~uzwurken~. Compound of ~aus-~ + ~wirken~:

• ~wirken~: From MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijanan~, a denominative verb from *~werkan~ ("work"), from PIE *~werg-~ ("to do, to work"). Cognate with English ~work~, Dutch ~werken~, and Greek ~ergon~ ("work," as in ~energy~).
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~uz-~, from OHG ~uz-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ut-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ut~ ("out"), from PIE *~ud~ ("upwards, away, out"). This prefix adds a sense of "out" or "thoroughly" to the base verb.

In MHG there were actually two competing forms: ~wirken~ (with ~i~, prevailing in ~Central German~) and ~wurken~ (with ~u~, prevailing in ~Upper German~). The ~i~-form won out in the written standard by the 18th century. Today ~sich auswirken~ is almost always used reflexively, meaning "to have an effect," while the base verb ~wirken~ retains meanings like "to work, to have an effect, to knit." The English cognate ~work~ preserves the broader semantic scope that ~wirken~ has gradually narrowed.
en.auswringen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~wringen~:

• ~wringen~: Borrowed into standard German from Low German ~wringen~, from Middle Low German ~wringen~, from Old Saxon ~wringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wringaną~, from PIE *~wrengʰ-~ ("to turn, to twist"), a nasalized extension of *~wer-~. A class III strong verb (~wringen~, ~wrang~, ~gewrungen~); the inherited High German reflex of the very same verb is ~ringen~. Cognate with English ~wring~, Old English ~wringan~, Dutch ~wringen~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

German kept both reflexes of the same root and divided the labour between them: the borrowed ~wringen~ stayed with wet laundry, while the inherited ~ringen~ moved into the figurative and now wrestles with decisions rather than with cloth.
en.auswählen: Formed from prefix ~aus-~ (from PIE *~úd~, "upwards, out") and ~wählen~, from MHG ~weln~, from ~welen~, ~wellen~, from OHG ~wellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~walljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waljaną~, from PIE *~welh₁-~ ("to wish, choose"). The semantic logic is identical to English ~pick out~: to single out from among alternatives. The prefix ~aus-~ here has a selective, extractive sense (lifting one item out of a set) rather than the directional or exhaustive sense it carries in other compounds.
en.auszahlen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys distributing or handing out: spreading something outward among recipients.

Reflexively the direction reverses: „es zahlt sich aus“ says the sum comes back to whoever advanced it. That the stem originally meant counting out is still legible in that reckoning.
en.auszeichnen:
Equivalent to ~aus-~ + ~zeichnen~:

• ~zeichnen~: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, symbol"), from MHG ~zeichen~, from OHG ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~, from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point").
• ~aus-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix adds the sense of singling out or distinguishing.

~Auszeichnen~ means "to distinguish, to honor, to award" and also "to mark, to price" (in retail: ~Waren auszeichnen~, "to price goods"). The reflexive ~sich auszeichnen~ means "to distinguish oneself, to excel." The derived noun ~Auszeichnung~ covers both senses: an award or honor, and a price tag. The semantic link is illuminating: to ~auszeichnen~ is to "mark out", whether marking a person for distinction or marking a product with its price, the underlying gesture is the same: making something visible by putting a sign (~Zeichen~) on it. The PIE root *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point") that underlies ~Zeichen~ also gives Latin ~dīcere~ ("to say") and ~index~ ("pointer"), making ~auszeichnen~ and ~indicate~ distant PIE cousins. Cognate with Dutch ~uitblinken~ (a different compound for the distinction sense).
en.ausziehen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys motion outward, out of an enclosure or container.

One verb, three common readings, all sharing a single image: one pulls off a coat, one moves out of a flat, and an army sets out for war. The reading glossed here is the second: leaving a dwelling.
en.auszählen:
A separable compound of ~aus-~ + ~zählen~:

• ~zählen~: From MHG ~zel(e)n~, ~zellen~, from OHG ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~ ("to enumerate, count; to recount, tell"). German split this dual sense: ~zählen~ kept "to count," ~erzählen~ took "to narrate." Cognate with Dutch ~tellen~, English ~tell~ and ~tale~, Danish ~tælle~, Gothic ~talzjan~.
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz~, from OHG ~ūz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~ ("out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Cognate with English ~out~, Dutch ~uit~, Old Norse ~út~, Gothic ~ūt~. The prefix conveys thoroughness or completion: carrying an action all the way through.

The prefix requires the counting to be exhaustive: an election result is counted out when no ballot remains, and a boxer when the full ten seconds have elapsed.
en.ausüben:
Compound of ~aus-~ + ~üben~:

• ~üben~: From MHG ~üeben~, ~uoben~, from OHG ~uoben~, from Proto-Germanic *~ōbijaną~ ("to do, practice"), the causative-iterative formation to a lost strong verb *~afaną~, from PIE *~h₃ep-~ ("to labor, work").
• ~aus-~: From MHG ~ūz-~, from OHG ~ūz-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt-~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). Here the prefix conveys thoroughness or the outward-directed performance of an action.

The base verb ~üben~ means "to practice, drill": to perform something repeatedly for improvement. The prefix ~aus-~ transforms this into "to exercise, exert, practice" in the sense of carrying out an activity in the real world: ~einen Beruf ausüben~ ("to practice a profession"), ~Druck ausüben~ ("to exert pressure"), ~Macht ausüben~ ("to wield power"). The shift from repetitive practice to active performance is the key semantic contribution of ~aus-~. The PIE root *~h₃ep-~ ("to labor, work") also gave Latin ~opus~ ("work") and ~opera~, making ~üben~ and ~opera~ distant cousins, both tracing back to the fundamental human concept of purposeful labor.
en.autostoppen:
A separable compound of ~auto~ + ~stoppen~:

• ~stoppen~: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~stoppen~, from Old Saxon *~stoppōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stoppōn~; the ultimate origin is debated: possibly from Proto-Germanic *~stuppōną~, from PIE *~(s)tewp-~ ("to push, stick"), or possibly from Latin ~stuppō~ ("to stop up, plug"). Only the figurative sense "to halt" entered standard High German; the doublet ~stopfen~ preserves the original concrete "to plug, stop up."
• ~auto~: An incorporated noun: ~Auto~, clipped from ~Automobil~, borrowed around 1900 from French ~automobile~. That word is a hybrid coinage of the 1870s, Greek ~autós~ ("self") welded to Latin ~mobilis~ ("movable"), "self-moving", and its mixed parentage annoyed purists in both France and Germany at the time. German clipped the Greek half and French the Latin half, which is why a German drives an ~Auto~ while a Frenchman drives an ~automobile~ and, colloquially, a ~mobile~. The sense of ~auto~ here is the noun ~Auto~ incorporated as an adverbial of means: by car.

Strictly the word is not a freshly built compound but a verb formed on the noun ~Autostopp~, itself modelled on French ~auto-stop~. The two languages name different halves of the scene: German the vehicle that is halted, English the waiting traveller's thumb in ~hitchhike~.
en.backen:
From Middle High German ~backen~, from Old High German ~backan~, an originally weak verb and geminated variant of an older strong verb: MHG ~bachen~, from OHG ~bahhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bakan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bakaną~, from PIE *~bʰeh₃g-~ ("to roast, bake"). The two verbs (strong ~bachen~ and weak ~backen~) blended early, each developing both weak and strong forms. The strong form ~bachen~ was originally predominant in Upper German dialects, but ~backen~ prevailed in the modern standard because it was common in Central German and aligned with Middle Low German ~backen~.

Cognate with English ~bake~, Dutch ~bakken~, Danish ~bage~, Swedish ~baka~, and also distantly with Greek ~phōgō~ ("to roast"). The verb retains optional strong conjugation in modern German: alongside the regular weak past tense ~backte~, the strong form ~buk~ (and even ~büke~ in the subjunctive) survives, particularly in literary and regional usage. This dual conjugation pattern is a living fossil of the historical merger of the two verbs. The English cognate ~bake~ has lost all trace of its strong-verb heritage and conjugates entirely regularly. The PIE root *~bʰeh₃g-~ points to a deep antiquity for this culinary technology: the Indo-Europeans were already baking over five thousand years ago, and the word for it has survived relatively intact across millennia.
en.bankrottgehen:
A separable compound of ~bankrott~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~bankrott~: From the adjective and noun ~bankrott~, borrowed around 1500 from Italian ~banca rotta~ ("broken bench"), the ~rotta~ continuing Latin ~rupta~ ("broken"). The ~banca~ was the money-changer's trestle table at the market, the same word that gave English ~bank~; a dealer who could not pay was said to have a broken one. The picturesque claim that creditors literally smashed the table is a later embellishment, but the borrowing itself is well attested. Early German spelled it ~Panckarotta~, then ~Banquerott~ under French influence. The sense of ~bankrott~ here is the resultative frame: to go bankrupt (~bankrottgehen~).

~Gehen~ contributes no motion here but the passage into a state, as in ~verloren gehen~ ("to get lost") or ~kaputtgehen~ ("to break"). To ~bankrottgehen~ is to suffer the condition; to ~bankrottmachen~ is to bring it about.
en.basieren:
Borrowed from French ~baser~ ("to base, to have as a foundation"), from ~base~ ("base, foundation"), from Old French ~base~, from Latin ~basis~, from Greek ~básis~ ("step, pedestal, base"), from PIE *~gʷm̥-ti-~ ("a stepping"), from *~gʷem-~ ("to come, to go, to step"). The same PIE root gives English ~come~, German ~kommen~, Latin ~veniō~ ("I come"), and Greek ~baínō~ ("I walk, I step").

~Basieren~ is used both transitively ("to base something on") and intransitively ("to be based on"): ~der Film basiert auf wahren Begebenheiten~ ("the film is based on true events"). The word entered German through the prestige of French intellectual and scientific discourse in the 17th and 18th centuries, when French was the language of European courts and academies. The ~-ieren~ suffix marks it as a Romance adaptation. The underlying metaphor (a building resting on its base) runs from Greek architecture through Latin engineering to modern German argumentation: one's argument, like one's building, must ~auf etwas basieren~.
en.basteln:
An Upper German verb, from earlier ~besteln~, an iterative (frequentative) of MHG ~besten~ ("to tie, to bind, to lace"), from Proto-West Germanic *~bastijan~ ("to plait, to sew, to weave"). The vowel ~-a-~ may reflect dialectal influence or readaptation to the underlying noun ~Bast~ ("bast, inner bark"), from MHG and OHG ~bast~ ("inner bark of trees").

~Basteln~ means "to do handicrafts, to tinker, to do DIY", to make things by hand in an amateur, creative fashion. In medieval usage, the word carried a slightly pejorative connotation: it referred to the work of craftsmen without guild membership, unsanctioned handwork. The modern sense has shed this stigma entirely; ~basteln~ now evokes cheerful creativity, especially children's arts and crafts (~Bastelnachmittag~, "crafting afternoon") or hobby electronics (~an einem Radio basteln~, "to tinker with a radio"). The noun ~Bastler~ ("hobbyist, tinkerer, DIY enthusiast") is affectionate. The connection to ~Bast~ ("bast fiber") is fitting: bast was one of the earliest materials humans worked with their hands: binding, weaving, and plaiting the fibrous inner bark of linden and willow trees into rope, mats, and baskets.
en.bauen: From Middle High German ~būwen~, from Old High German ~būan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~būan~, from Proto-Germanic *~būaną~ ("to dwell, reside"), from PIE *~bʰuH-~ ("to be, become, grow"). The semantic journey from "to be, exist" to "to dwell" to "to build" reflects how habitation and construction are inseparable: one builds where one lives. The same PIE root *~bʰuH-~ is extraordinarily productive across Indo-European, yielding English ~be~ (via PGmc *~beuną~), Latin ~fuī~ ("I was"), Greek ~phúō~ ("to grow, bring forth"), and Sanskrit ~bhavati~ ("to be, become"). In the Germanic branch, the original sense of "dwelling" survives in ~Bauer~ ("farmer," literally "one who dwells on the land"), ~Nachbar~ ("neighbor," literally "one who dwells nearby"), and ~Bau~ ("structure, building"). Cognate with Dutch ~bouwen~, English ~bower~ ("dwelling"), ~neighbor~ (from Old English ~nēahgebūr~, "near-dweller"), Danish ~bygge~.
en.beachten:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~achten~:

• ~achten~: From MHG ~ahten~, from OHG ~ahtōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ahtōn~, a denominative verb from *~ahtu~ ("consideration, attention"), of uncertain pre-Germanic origin.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix typically transforms an intransitive verb into a transitive one, here applying attention directly to an object.

The ~be-~ prefix shifts ~achten~ ("to consider, heed generally") into the specifically transitive ~beachten~ ("to pay attention to, to observe, to comply with"). The distinction is visible in legal and instructional registers: ~beachten Sie~, not *~achten Sie~, is the standard formula in German instruction manuals and official notices. The negative ~unbeachtet~ ("unheeded, unnoticed") collapses back toward ~achten~'s older sense of ignoring. Cognate with Dutch ~beachten~ (archaic), Dutch ~in acht nemen~ (the functional equivalent).
en.beantragen:
From ~be-~ + ~Antrag~ + ~-en~, equivalent to ~be-~ + ~antragen~, which is ~an-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~Antrag~: From MHG ~antrac~, a verbal noun derived from ~antragen~ ("to carry toward, to propose"), itself composed of ~an-~ (from PIE *~h₂en~, "on, onto") + ~tragen~ (from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~, from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~, "to pull, draw").
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The prefix makes the verb transitive: to direct a formal request at someone.

~Beantragen~ means "to apply for, to formally request, to propose", exclusively in bureaucratic and legal contexts. It is the verb of official paperwork: one ~beantragt~ a visa, a building permit, a divorce. The word perfectly encodes the German administrative concept that formal proposals must be ~carried toward~ (~antragen~) an authority and ~directed at~ (~be-~) the relevant office. The derived noun ~Antrag~ itself has drifted from its literal meaning of "carrying toward" to "application, motion, proposal", and in dated usage, even "marriage proposal" (~einen Antrag machen~). Cognate formations exist in Dutch (~aanvragen~, using a different root but the same structure).
en.beantworten: ~Beantworten~ is not simply ~be-~ + ~antworten~ in the usual prefixation sense but a denominal verb formed directly from ~Antwort~ ("answer") with ~be-~ and the infinitive suffix ~-en~. ~Antwort~ comes from Middle High German ~antwürte~, from Old High German ~antwurti~, from Proto-Germanic *~andawurdiją~, itself from *~anda-~ ("against") and *~wurdiją~ ("speech, conversation"), a derivative of *~wurdą~ ("word, speech"). The noun's gender shifted from neuter to feminine through semantic association with ~Frage~ ("question"). A grammatically significant contrast: ~antworten~ ("to answer") governs the dative (~jemandem antworten~ ("to answer someone")), while ~beantworten~ governs the accusative: ~eine Frage beantworten~ ("to answer a question"). The prefix ~be-~ here adds transitivity, shifting the object from the person answered to the thing answered. Cognates include Dutch ~antwoord~ and Afrikaans ~antwoord~.
en.bearbeiten: From ~be-~ + ~arbeiten~ ("to work"). The prefix ~be-~ (from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~, "on, at, near") makes the base verb transitive. ~Arbeiten~ derives from Old High German ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"), semantic evolution from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" (the lot of the fatherless) to "work." ~Bearbeiten~ intensifies and directs that labor: to process, to work on, to treat a material or topic. The prefix strips away intransitivity and focuses the action on an object; ~er arbeitet~ ("he works") becomes ~er bearbeitet den Text~ ("he processes the text"). Cognate with Dutch ~bewerken~.
en.beatmen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~atmen~:

• ~atmen~: From MHG ~ātemen~, from OHG ~ātamōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~ēþmaz~ ("breath"), from PIE *~h₁eh₁tmén-~ ("breath"). Equivalent to ~Atem~ ("breath") + ~-en~. Cognate with Dutch ~ademen~; the archaic doublet ~Odem~ ("breath") descends from *~ēþmaz~ by a different path.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

The difference is between doing and undergoing: ~atmen~ is something one does oneself, ~beatmen~ something done to a person who no longer can. The prefix supplies the object the stem has no room for.
en.beauftragen:
Derived from ~be-~ + ~Auftrag~ + ~-en~. Notably, this verb is not derived from the strong verb ~auftragen~ ("to apply, to serve food") but directly from the noun ~Auftrag~ ("commission, assignment, order"):

• ~Auftrag~: A deverbal noun from ~auftragen~ ("to carry upon, to apply"), from MHG ~ūftragen~, composed of ~auf-~ ("up, upon," from PIE *~upó~, "up from below") + ~tragen~ ("to carry," from MHG ~tragen~, OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~, "to draw, drag"). Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~.
• ~be-~: From Proto-Germanic *~bi~ ("by, near"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). Turns the noun into a transitive verb.

The derivation from the noun rather than the verb explains why ~beauftragen~ conjugates weakly (~beauftragte~, ~beauftragt~) rather than with the strong ablaut pattern of ~tragen~ (~trug~, ~getragen~). This is a common German pattern: when a verb is derived from a noun (even if that noun itself came from a strong verb), the result is always a weak verb. The semantic chain runs from "to carry up" (~auftragen~) to "the thing carried up / laid upon someone" (~Auftrag~, a task or commission) to "to give someone a commission" (~beauftragen~). English ~draw~ is the cognate of ~tragen~, both from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~, with the semantic split happening early: the Germanic branch kept "to carry," while the English branch specialized toward "to drag, to draw."
en.bebauen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~būwen~, from OHG ~būan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~būan~, from Proto-Germanic *~būaną~ ("to dwell, reside"), from PIE *~bʰuH-~ ("to be, become, grow"); one builds where one lives. Cognate with English ~be~, ~bower~ ("dwelling"), ~neighbor~ ("near-dweller"), Dutch ~bouwen~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ conveys applying something over a surface or covering it.

The verb covers both things one can do to ground: to ~bebauen~ it is to put buildings on it or to till it. The stem's older sense, "to dwell," holds the two together: one builds where one lives.
en.bedanken:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~danken~. Apparently not attested before Modern German (thus after 1400):

• ~danken~: From MHG ~danken~, from OHG ~dankōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankōną~ ("to thank"), a denominative from *~þankaz~ ("thought, gratitude").
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). This inseparable prefix makes the verb reflexive-transitive: while ~danken~ takes a dative ("to thank someone"), ~sich bedanken~ emphasizes the act from the thanker's perspective.

~Sich bedanken~ means "to express one's thanks, to say thank you" and is slightly more emphatic or formal than simple ~danken~. The ~be-~ prefix transforms the dative construction (~jemandem danken~) into an accusative-reflexive one (~sich bei jemandem bedanken~), shifting the grammatical focus to the grateful person's active expression. The root noun *~þankaz~ ("thought") reveals that Germanic gratitude is literally "thinking of" someone, a semantic parallel to English ~thank~ (from ~think~). The connection between thought and gratitude is preserved in the German phrase ~Ich denke an dich~ ("I think of you"), where ~denken~ and ~danken~ share the same Proto-Germanic ancestor. Cognate with Dutch ~bedanken~, English ~thank~, Danish ~takke~.
en.bedauern:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~dauern~:

• ~dauern~: Two separate verbs under one spelling. "To last, endure": from MHG ~dūren~, borrowed from Middle Low German ~dūren~, from Latin ~dūrō~, a denominative of ~dūrus~ ("hard, lasting"), from Proto-Italic *~dūros~, from PIE *~dweh₂-~ ("long, far"); cognate with Dutch ~duren~, English ~dure~. "To cause pity" (~er dauert mich~): from MHG ~tūren~, an ablaut variant of ~tiure~ ("dear, costly"), ancestor of ~teuer~, thus a doublet of ~teuer~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

Of the two verbs spelled ~dauern~, the one underneath is the second ("to move to pity," a relative of ~teuer~ ("dear, costly")), not the Latin-derived "to last." The older ~mich dauert es~ makes the thing the subject; the compound inverts that and puts the verb in the person's hands.
en.bedecken:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~decken~:

• ~decken~: From MHG ~decken~, from OHG ~decchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þakkjan~ ("to cover"), from Proto-Germanic *~þakjaną~, a causative formation from *~þaką~ ("roof, thatch"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to cover"); the verb is etymologically "to roof." Cognate with English ~thatch~, Dutch ~dekken~, Swedish ~täcka~; from the same root Latin ~tegere~, whence English ~protect~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ conveys applying something over a surface or covering it.

Because the stem etymologically means "to roof," the compound in a sense doubles the covering: the roof is already inside the verb, and the prefix spreads it across the whole surface.
en.bedenken:
From Middle High German ~bedenken~, from Old High German ~bidenken~, ~pidenken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~biþankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~biþankijaną~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, ~thenken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~tong-éye-ti~, causative of *~teng-~ ("to think, feel, perceive, know").
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The prefix makes the verb transitive.

~Bedenken~ means "to consider, to reflect upon, to have reservations about." The prefix ~be-~ takes the intransitive act of thinking and gives it a direct object: one does not merely ~denken~ (think) but ~bedenkt~ (thinks over, considers) something specific. As a noun, ~Bedenken~ means "misgivings, reservations", one's considered doubts. Cognate with English ~bethink~ (archaic, "to think about, to consider"), Dutch ~bedenken~ ("to think up, to consider"), and more distantly with Latin ~tongeō~ ("to know"). The English cognate ~think~ underwent a curious phonetic shift: Proto-Germanic *~þ~ became English ~th~ but German ~d~ (via the High German consonant shift), making ~denken~ and ~think~ less obviously related than they truly are.
en.bedeuten:
From Middle High German ~bediuten~, ~betiuten~, from Old High German ~bidiuten~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~deuten~:

• ~deuten~: From MHG ~diuten~, from OHG ~diuten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þiudijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þiudijaną~, derived from Proto-Germanic *~þeudō~ ("people, nation"), the same root as Old English ~þēod~ ("people").
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix typically transforms an intransitive verb into a transitive one.

The original sense of ~deuten~ was "to explain to the people", to interpret, make intelligible. The surprising etymological kinship between ~bedeuten~ ("to mean") and ~Deutsch~ ("German") reflects their shared root: both trace to the Proto-Germanic word for "people," *~þeudō~.

As discussed in ~A History of the German Verb System~, the PIE root *~tewtéh₂~ (from *~tew-~, "to swell, be strong"), which became Proto-Germanic *~þeudō~, is a candidate for the Yamnaya endonym, what they called themselves before history named them. If true, the verb ~bedeuten~ carries a 5,000-year-old echo: "to explain to the people" may refer to ~that~ people, the steppe-riding speakers of Proto-Indo-European whose migrations gave rise to nearly half the world's languages today.

Cognate with Dutch ~beduiden~, Icelandic ~þýða~ ("to translate"), Swedish ~tyda~, Danish ~tyde~.
en.bedienen: From ~be-~ + ~dienen~ ("to serve").
