Cognate with English ~by~ and, in its unstressed form, with the English prefix ~be-~ (~become~, ~beset~): the two are one word split by stress, exactly as German split separable ~bei-~ from inseparable ~be-~. The prefix conveys placing something alongside something else, adding it to what is there.

The verb belongs chiefly to Swiss and Austrian official and legal usage: what is ~beigezogen~ is an expert, a lawyer, or, as in the inquiry report quoted here, another authority's files. The sense is always a drawing-in for reinforcement, never a drawing-away.
en.beißen: From MHG ~bīzen~, from OHG ~bīzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bītaną~, from PIE *~bʰeyd-~ ("to split"). A class I strong verb (~beißen~, ~biss~, ~gebissen~). Cognate with English ~bite~, Dutch ~bijten~, Low German ~bieten~, Danish ~bide~, Swedish ~bita~. German ~bitter~ and English ~bitter~ are both the old participial adjective of this verb, literally "biting," said of what bites the tongue.
en.bejagen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~jagen~:

• ~jagen~: From MHG ~jagen~ ("to hurry, drive, pursue, hunt"), from OHG ~jagōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~jagōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~jakkōną~, a ~nā~-iterative formation, likely rebuilt from PIE *~h₁eyǵʰ-~ ("to strive, chase"). Attested since the eighth century; further pre-Germanic etymology is obscure.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

The difference from ~jagen~ lies in the object: one hunts an individual animal but ~bejagt~ a population or a territory, the prefix turns pursuit into something managed across an area, which is why the word lives chiefly in hunting and conservation usage.
en.bekanntgeben:
A separable compound of ~bekannt~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~bekannt~: The past participle of ~bekennen~ (~be-~ + ~kennen~, "to know"), long since an ordinary adjective meaning "known, familiar". ~Kennen~ goes back to OHG ~kennen~, from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~, a causative of *~kunnaną~, from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"), so the causative sense "to make known" that ~kennen~ itself lost is exactly what ~bekanntgeben~ and ~bekanntmachen~ preserve. Cognate with Dutch ~bekend~ and archaic English ~beknown~. The sense of ~bekannt~ here is: brought into public knowledge, made generally known.

The compound is separable, as the quoted sentence from the Basic Law shows: ~gibt ... bekannt~. A date, a result, a decision is ~bekanntgegeben~, and ~Bekanntgabe~ remains the administrative term for the act.
en.bekanntmachen:
A separable compound of ~bekannt~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~bekannt~: The past participle of ~bekennen~ (~be-~ + ~kennen~, "to know"), long since an ordinary adjective meaning "known, familiar". ~Kennen~ goes back to OHG ~kennen~, from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~, a causative of *~kunnaną~, from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"), so the causative sense "to make known" that ~kennen~ itself lost is exactly what ~bekanntgeben~ and ~bekanntmachen~ preserve. Cognate with Dutch ~bekend~ and archaic English ~beknown~. The sense of ~bekannt~ here is: brought into public knowledge, made generally known.

The same pattern with a different verb, and with a second meaning that ~bekanntgeben~ lacks: one can make not only a piece of news known but also two people known to each other, and then it means to introduce them.
en.bekehren:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~kehren~:

• ~kehren~: A homograph concealing two distinct verbs. ~Kehren~ (1) "to turn": from MHG ~kēren~, from OHG ~kēran~, ~chēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kairijaną~ or *~kausijaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly connected to *~gers-~ ("to twist, bend, turn"). ~Kehren~ (2) "to sweep": from MHG ~kern~, ~keren~, from OHG ~kerian~, ~cherian~, from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~ ("to scrape, scratch"), from PIE *~ger-~ ("to scrape"). Etymologically unrelated, merged through phonological convergence.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

Of the two ~kehren~ it is the first, "to turn," that is present here: a person is converted by being turned around, not by being swept out. English ~convert~ carries the same image, from Latin ~convertere~ ("to turn around"), and Greek ~metánoia~ makes a change of mind a change of direction.
en.bekennen:
~Be-~ + ~kennen~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~kennen~:

• ~kennen~: From MHG ~kennen~, from OHG ~kennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kannjan~, a causative of *~kunnan~ ("to know"), from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~ ("to make known"), from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know").
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The prefix here makes the verb transitive and intensifies the action, from mere knowing to active declaration.

~Bekennen~ means "to confess, to profess, to avow", to make one's knowledge or belief public. The prefix ~be-~ transforms interior knowing (~kennen~) into outward declaration. The compound appears already in Old High German as ~bikennen~ ("to recognize, acknowledge"). The derived noun ~Bekenntnis~ ("confession, creed") carries deep religious weight in German: the ~Augsburger Bekenntnis~ (Augsburg Confession, 1530) was the foundational document of Lutheranism. The reflexive ~sich bekennen zu~ ("to profess, to declare allegiance to") remains one of the most forceful verbs of commitment in German. Cognate with Dutch ~bekennen~ ("to confess").
en.beklagen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~klagen~:

• ~klagen~: From MHG ~klagen~, from OHG ~klagōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klagōn~ ("to lament, complain"), a denominative verb from *~klagu~ ("lamentation, complaint"). The ultimate origin is uncertain: often compared to Proto-Indo-Iranian *~garjʰ-~, but phonologically difficult; some favor an onomatopoeic origin. It keeps both an emotional and a legal sense.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

Of the two senses ~klagen~ preserves, the legal one yields ~der Beklagte~, the defendant in court, and the emotional one yields a ~beklagenswert~ fate. Used reflexively the word shifts once more: ~sich über etwas beklagen~ is to lodge a complaint.
en.bekochen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~kochen~:

• ~kochen~: From MHG ~kochen~, from OHG ~kohhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kokōn~, borrowed from Late Latin ~cocō~, from Latin ~coquō~ ("I cook, I boil"), from PIE *~pekʷ-~ ("to cook, to ripen"). A loan early enough to have undergone the High German shift of ~k~ to ~ch~. Cognate with English ~cook~, Dutch ~koken~, Danish ~koge~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

The shift of object is the whole point of the word: a soup is cooked, but a guest is ~bekocht~, the person being fed becomes the direct object, and the food that was actually cooked drops out of the sentence.
en.bekommen:
From Middle High German ~bekomen~, from Old High German ~biqueman~, ~bikweman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bikweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~bikwemaną~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from the aorist subjunctive of PIE *~gʷemt~ ("to take a step, arrive"), from *~gʷem-~ ("to step").
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix typically transforms an intransitive verb into a transitive one.

Despite the compound's formal resemblance to English ~become~, the two have diverged sharply in meaning: German ~bekommen~ means "to receive, get," while English ~become~ means "to come to be." This false-friend pair is a famous pitfall for learners in both directions. Cognate with Dutch ~bekomen~.
en.bekriegen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~kriegen~:

• ~kriegen~: From MHG ~kriegen~ ("to war, to strive for"), a verbalization of ~Krieg~ ("war"), from OHG ~krig~, from Proto-West Germanic *~krīg~, whose origin is debated. The "obtaining" sense overshadowed the military one; colloquial modern German ~kriegen~ simply means "to get." Cognate with Dutch ~krijgen~ ("to get"), Bavarian ~kriagn~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

The word is a reservation for its older meaning: while plain ~kriegen~ colloquially means only "to get," ~bekriegen~ preserves the ~Krieg~ it was built from, and that ~be-~ + ~kriegen~ should not add up to "obtain" is one of the neater traps in the German lexicon.
en.bekämpfen:
From Middle High German ~bekempfen~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~kampfen~:

• ~kampfen~: From MHG ~kempfen~, from OHG *~kempfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kampijan~, a denominative verb from *~kamp~ ("field, battlefield"), itself borrowed from Latin ~campus~ ("field"). The semantic journey from "open field" to "battlefield" to "fight" reflects how combat in the ancient world took place on open terrain. Cognate with English ~camp~ (which retained the spatial sense) and ~champion~ (via Old French from Latin ~campio~, "fighter on the field").
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). This prefix makes the verb transitive, turning the intransitive "to fight" into "to fight against something."

The word ~Kampf~ is one of several Latin military loans that entered Germanic languages during the centuries of Roman-Germanic contact along the ~limes~, the empire's northern frontier. Dutch ~kampen~ ("to fight, to struggle") is a close cognate, while English ~combat~ arrived later from French, covering similar semantic ground through an entirely different route.
en.bekümmern:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~kümmern~:

• ~kümmern~: From MHG ~kumbern~, from the noun ~kumber~ ("rubble, obstruction, distress"), probably borrowed from Old French *~combre~, from Medieval Latin ~combrus~ ("barricade"), from Latin ~cumulus~ ("heap") or Gaulish *~komberū~; alternatively from Proto-West Germanic *~kumbr~, Proto-Germanic *~kumbraz~ ("burden, sorrow"). Cognate with Dutch ~kommer~ ("distress").
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

The word hangs on the noun ~Kummer~ ("grief") and splits into two uses: transitively, a piece of news ~bekümmert~ whoever hears it; reflexively, one ~bekümmert sich um~ something, and there the grief has turned into concern in the sense of taking care, the sense the quoted sentence attests.
en.belachen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~lachen~:

• ~lachen~: From MHG ~lachen~, from OHG ~lahhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~, from PIE *~kleg-~ ("to cry out, sound"). The initial ~hl-~ cluster was simplified to ~l-~ in Old High German. Cognate with English ~laugh~, Dutch ~lachen~, Gothic ~hlahjan~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

Unlike ~auslachen~ ("to mock"), ~belachen~ need not be derisive: what is ~belacht~ is what has been met with laughter. The verb is now rare and literary, and turns up mostly in the passive.
en.beladen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two historically distinct verbs under one infinitive. ~laden~ (strong, "to load"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"); cognate with English ~lade~ and ~laden~, Lithuanian ~klṓti~. ~laden~ (weak, "to invite, summon"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root found only in Germanic and Anatolian (Hittite ~halzai~).
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ conveys applying something over a surface or covering it.

The strong conjugation (~belud~, ~beladen~) shows which of the two twins is at work here: the strong ~laden~ "to load," not the weak ~laden~ "to invite." The cargo moves into a ~mit~-phrase, and the vehicle or animal carrying it becomes the direct object.
en.belagern:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~lagern~:

• ~lagern~: Derived from the noun ~Lager~ ("camp, store, warehouse"), from MHG ~lëger~, from OHG ~lëgar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~legr~, from Proto-Germanic *~legrą~. The modern form with ~-a-~ is of East Central German origin, influenced by ~Lage~ ("position"). Cognate with English ~lair~, Dutch ~leger~, Danish ~lejr~, Swedish ~läger~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

The image is literal: an army pitches its ~Lager~ ("camp") around a town, and intransitive camping becomes a besieging of the town itself. Figuratively, reporters can now ~belagern~ a house.
en.belasten:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~Last~ + ~-en~:

• ~Last~: From MHG ~last~, from OHG ~last~, ~hlast~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlasti~ ("load, burden"), from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"). The initial ~hl-~ cluster, still visible in OHG, was simplified to ~l-~ in later German. Cognate with English ~last~ (in the sense of a unit of weight/cargo) and ~laden~ ("to load"); English ~ballast~ is a compound containing the same root.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near").

The semantic range of ~belasten~ maps neatly onto different kinds of burden: physical ("to load, to stress"), psychological ("to burden, to weigh on"), legal ("to incriminate"), and financial ("to debit, to charge an account"). The related ~belästigen~ ("to harass, to bother") looks similar but derives from the adjective ~lästig~ ("annoying") and carries a distinctly different meaning, an annoyance rather than a load.
en.belaufen:
From Middle High German ~beloufen~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~laufen~. Cognate with Dutch ~belopen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~ ("to jump forward, to leap"), from PIE *~klewb-~ ("to spring, to hop"). Cognate with Dutch ~lopen~, English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix typically transforms an intransitive verb into a transitive one.

The reflexive ~sich belaufen auf~ means "to amount to, to total", an oddly physical metaphor for a numerical concept, as though a sum "runs itself" to a certain point. The root verb ~laufen~ underwent a dramatic semantic shift: Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~ meant "to leap, to jump," and this sense is preserved in English ~leap~, while German ~laufen~ gradually broadened from "leaping" to "running" to simply "going on foot." The initial ~hl-~ cluster, still visible in Old High German ~hloufan~, was simplified to ~l-~ during the Middle High German period, a common fate for initial clusters throughout Germanic. Lithuanian ~klùpti~ ("to stumble") is a distant Baltic cousin from the same PIE root.
en.beleben:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

The verb covers both senses: restoring life to the dead or exhausted, and filling a place with bustle. The participle ~belebt~ has broken away from the verb into an ordinary adjective: a ~belebte~ street is a busy one, not a resuscitated one.
en.belegen: ~Belegen~ combines the prefix ~be-~ (from PIE *~h₁epi~, "on, at, near," making the verb transitive) with ~legen~ ("to lay, place"), from Middle High German ~legen~, from Old High German ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~, a causative form of the root *~legh-~ ("to lie, lay down"). The prefix ~be-~ shifts the meaning from the intransitive placement to covering or occupying a space entirely. Cognates of ~legen~ include English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~, and the English prefix verb ~belay~, the nautical term for securing a rope, which is the direct English cognate of ~belegen~. A delightful false friend: ~belegen~ can mean "to book" (a seat, table, or room) as well as "to document" or "to coat", contexts where laying something upon a surface shifts into reservation or proof.
en.belehnen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~lehnen~:

• ~lehnen~: A merger of two verbs: MHG ~linen~/~lenen~ (intransitive), from OHG ~hlinēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlinēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlināną~, from PIE *~k̂ley-~ ("to lean, incline"); and MHG ~leinen~ (causative), from OHG ~hleinen~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlainijaną~. A second, archaic ~lehnen~ ("to lend, borrow"), from OHG ~lēhanōn~, survives only in ~entlehnen~ and ~Lehnwort~. Cognate with English ~lean~, Latin ~clīnō~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

This is where the second, archaic branch survives: not the ~lehnen~ of leaning, but the one of lending, otherwise left only in ~entlehnen~ and ~Lehnwort~. A lord ~belehnt~ his vassal, the recipient becomes the direct object, while the fief itself moves into a ~mit~-phrase.
en.belehren:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~lehren~:

• ~lehren~: From MHG ~lēren~, from OHG ~lēren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laiʀijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~laizijaną~ ("to teach"), a causative of *~lizaną~ ("to learn"), from PIE *~leys-~ ("track, furrow, trail"): to teach is "to cause someone to follow a track." Cognate with Dutch ~leren~, Danish ~lære~, archaic English ~lear~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.

Where ~lehren~ is neutral, ~belehren~ has picked up a condescending note in modern use: to ~belehren~ someone is to know better than they do. It stays neutral only in set official phrases such as ~eines Besseren belehrt werden~ ("to be set straight").
en.beleihen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~leihen~:

• ~leihen~: From MHG ~līhen~, from OHG ~līhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~līhwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~līhwaną~, from PIE *~leykʷ-~ ("to leave behind"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with English ~loan~ (via Old Norse ~lán~, from *~laihną~ of the same root), Dutch ~lenen~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

The money one lends ~against~ a house becomes a house one ~beleiht~: the pledge itself moves into the object slot. The class I strong conjugation (~belieh~, ~beliehen~) is inherited unchanged.
en.beleuchten:
From Middle High German ~beliuhten~, from Old High German ~biliuhten~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~leuchten~:

• ~leuchten~: From OHG ~liuhten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~liuhtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~liuhtijaną~, a denominative or factitive verb from *~leuhtą~ ("light") or *~leuhtaz~ ("light, bright"), ultimately from PIE *~lewk-~ ("to shine"). Cognate with English ~light~, Dutch ~lichten~, and Latin ~lux~ ("light").
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("at, by, near"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). This prefix makes the verb transitive, turning "to shine" into "to illuminate (something)."

The PIE root *~lewk-~ is one of the most productive roots in Indo-European languages, giving rise not only to ~leuchten~ and ~light~ but also to Latin ~lūcēre~ ("to shine"), whence ~lucid~ and ~Lucifer~ (literally "light-bearer"). The ~be-~ prefix transforms intransitive ~leuchten~ ("to shine, glow") into transitive ~beleuchten~ ("to illuminate, to shed light on"), a pattern found across dozens of German ~be-~ verbs. In figurative usage, ~beleuchten~ also means "to examine" or "to shed light on a topic," mirroring English "to illuminate a subject."
en.belieben:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~lieben~:

• ~lieben~: From MHG ~lieben~, an alteration of the rarer MHG ~liuben~ ("to make dear"), from OHG ~liuben~; denominative of the adjective ~lieb~, from MHG ~liep~, OHG ~liob~, Proto-West Germanic *~leub~, Proto-Germanic *~leubaz~ ("dear, beloved"), from PIE *~lewbʰ-~ ("to desire, love"). English ~love~ is from the related but distinct root *~lubō~. Cognate with English ~lief~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ derives a verb from a noun or adjective, meaning to furnish with or make into that.

Middle High German built from this a verb meaning "to become dear, to please," and that is where the modern verb's peculiar construction comes from: the person does not love the thing, the thing pleases the person; ~wie es Ihnen beliebt~ ("as you please"). The participle ~beliebt~ "popular" is by now far commoner than the verb it came from.
en.beliefern:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~liefern~:

• ~liefern~: From MHG ~lieveren~ (attested before 1350), probably borrowed via Middle Dutch and Middle Low German ~lēveren~, from Old French ~livrer~, from Latin ~līberō~ ("I free, release, deliver"), from ~līber~ ("free"). The word belonged to the Hanseatic League's trade vocabulary. Cognate with Dutch ~leveren~, English ~deliver~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

One delivers goods ~to~ a customer, but one ~beliefert~ the customer: the recipient becomes the object and the goods move into a ~mit~-phrase. The word still belongs almost entirely to the commercial register its root came from.
en.bellen: From MHG ~bellen~, from OHG ~bellan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bellaną~ ("to resound, roar"), probably from a PIE root *~bʰelH-~ ("to sound, howl"), though that reconstruction is not secure. Originally a class III strong verb (MHG ~bellen~, ~bal~, ~gebollen~); modern German conjugates it weak throughout. Cognate with Old English ~bellan~ ("to bellow, roar") and English ~bellow~. English ~bell~ belongs to the same root: the instrument is named for the noise it makes.
en.belohnen:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~Lohn~ + ~-en~:

• ~Lohn~: From MHG ~lôn~, from OHG ~lōn~ ("reward, wages"), from Proto-West Germanic *~laun~, from Proto-Germanic *~launą~, from PIE *~leh₂w-~ ("to capture, enjoy, profit"). Cognate with Old English ~lēan~ ("reward"), Gothic ~laun~, and (surprisingly) Latin ~lucrum~ ("profit," whence English ~lucre~ and ~lucrative~) and Greek ~leía~ ("booty, spoils").
• ~be-~: Inseparable prefix from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). Here it functions as a transitivizer, turning the noun ~Lohn~ into a transitive verb meaning "to give a reward to."

~Belohnen~ means "to reward." The deep etymology reveals that ~Lohn~ ("wages, reward") and ~lucre~ ("monetary gain") share a common ancestor in the PIE root *~leh₂w-~, whose original sense was "to seize, to enjoy the fruits of seizure." The semantic path from "captured spoils" to "earned wages" to "reward" reflects the evolution from raiding economies to settled labor. The related Old English word ~lēan~ ("reward") died out in English, replaced by the French borrowing ~reward~ (from Old Norman French ~rewarder~, "to regard, to repay"). German preserved the native Germanic term, making ~belohnen~ a linguistic survivor.
en.belächeln:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~lächeln~:

• ~lächeln~: From MHG ~lecheln~, from ~lachen~ ("to laugh") plus the diminutive suffix ~-eln~, literally "to laugh a little," the suffix triggering the umlaut ~a~ → ~ä~. ~lachen~ itself is from MHG ~lachen~, OHG ~lahhen~, Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~. Cognate with English ~laugh~, Old Norse ~hlæja~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

Same root, two prefixes, two attitudes: to ~anlächeln~ someone is friendly, to ~belächeln~ them is to look down on them. The diminutive inside the word ("to laugh a little") suits the patronizing sense better than an outright ~belachen~ would.
en.belügen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~lügen~:

• ~lügen~: From MHG ~liegen~, from OHG ~liogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~leugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~leuganą~, from PIE *~lewgʰ-~ ("to lie, swear falsely"). A class II strong verb (~lügen~, ~log~, ~gelogen~); the ~ü~ is late, taken from the noun ~Lüge~ to keep the verb from colliding with ~liegen~. Cognate with English ~lie~, Gothic ~liugan~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

~Lügen~ takes no object: one simply lies. ~Belügen~ supplies one, and it is always a person: you ~belügen~ somebody, never a lie. The class II strong conjugation (~belog~, ~belogen~) survives intact, late ~ü~ and all.
en.bemalen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~malen~:

• ~malen~: From MHG ~mālen~, from OHG ~mālōn~, ~mālēn~, a denominative of the noun ~māl~ ("spot, mark"), from Proto-West Germanic *~mālijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~mēlijaną~, from *~mēlą~, from PIE *~melh₂-~ ("dark color"). Not to be confused with ~mahlen~ ("to grind"), of separate origin. Cognate with Dutch ~maal~, Greek ~melas~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ conveys applying something over a surface or covering it.

The difference lies in what becomes the object: ~malen~ takes the picture, ~bemalen~ takes the surface it goes onto, while the paint moves into a ~mit~-phrase. That the root goes back to a word for "spot, mark" suits a verb about covering a surface.
en.bemeistern:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~meistern~:

• ~meistern~: From MHG ~meisteren~, from OHG ~meistarōn~ ("to master, direct"), from the noun ~Meister~, from OHG ~meistar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~maistar~, borrowed from Latin ~magister~ ("master, teacher"), from PIE *~meg-~ ("great") via the superlative suffix *~-is-tero-~. ~Meister~ is a doublet of ~Magister~ and ~Maestro~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.

The word now sounds archaic; ~beherrschen~ and plain ~meistern~ have all but displaced it. In older literature it likes the reflexive (~sich bemeistern~ is to keep one's composure), and there it sometimes governs the genitive.
en.bemerken:
From Middle High German ~bemerken~, equivalent to ~be-~ + ~merken~:

• ~merken~: From MHG ~merken~, from OHG ~merken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~markōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~markōną~ ("to mark, to note"), from *~markō~ ("boundary, sign"), from PIE *~merǵ-~ ("boundary, edge").
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The prefix makes the verb transitive, directing the act of noting onto a specific object.

~Bemerken~ means "to notice, to remark, to observe", one ~bemerkt~ something that catches one's attention. The derived noun ~Bemerkung~ ("remark, comment, observation") straddles the boundary between perception and speech: a ~Bemerkung~ can be something you merely notice or something you say aloud. The PIE root *~merǵ-~ ("boundary, edge") connects ~bemerken~ to an unexpectedly concrete origin: to notice something is to mark its boundary, to distinguish it from its surroundings. The same root gives English ~mark~, ~margin~, ~marquee~, and ~march~ (as in "the Welsh Marches", border regions). Cognate with Dutch ~bemerken~, ~opmerken~.
en.bemitleiden:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~mitleiden~:

• ~mitleiden~: From ~mit-~ ("with") plus ~leiden~ ("to suffer"); wholly inseparable, and a calque of Latin ~compatī~, itself a calque of Ancient Greek ~συμπαθεῖν~ (sympatheîn), the same chain that gives English ~compassion~ and ~sympathy~. The noun ~Mitleid~ is far commoner than the verb, which is chiefly literary. For the root, see ~leiden~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

A doubly built word: ~be-~ is added to the already compound ~mitleiden~ and turns the person one suffers ~with~ into a direct object. That is what made the verb usable, where bare ~mitleiden~ stayed literary.
en.bemühen:
From ~be-~ + ~Mühe~ + ~-en~. Compound of ~be-~ + the denominal verb derived from ~Mühe~:

• ~Mühe~: From MHG ~müeje~, ~müe~, from OHG ~muohī~, from the verb ~mühen~ ("to toil"), from Proto-West Germanic *~mōjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~mōjaną~ ("to tire"), from PIE *~meh₃-~ ("to cause toil, be a burden"). Cognate with Latin ~mōlēs~ ("burden, mass"), Greek ~mōlos~ ("turmoil"), and Slavic *~majati~ ("to detain, tire"). Cognate with Dutch ~bemoeien~ ("to interfere, to meddle").
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The prefix makes the verb transitive and reflexive: to direct effort at something or someone.

~Bemühen~ means "to make an effort, to take trouble" (reflexive ~sich bemühen~) and, less commonly, "to trouble, to bother" (transitive: ~darf ich Sie bemühen?~, "may I trouble you?"). The polite imperative ~bemühen Sie sich nicht!~ ("don't trouble yourself!") is a standard courtesy formula. The derived noun ~Bemühung~ ("effort, endeavor") appears frequently in formal correspondence. Dutch ~bemoeien~ is a cognate but has shifted toward negative meddling ("to interfere"), while German ~bemühen~ retains the more neutral sense of earnest effort, the two words illustrate how the same compound can drift in opposite evaluative directions across closely related languages.
en.benehmen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ forms a verb used only reflexively: the action turns back on the one performing it and never reaches an outside object.

The older, non-reflexive ~benehmen~ "to take away, deprive" has died out except in legal formulas; what remains is ~sich benehmen~. How that became "to conduct oneself" is visible in ~sich nehmen~ in the sense "to carry oneself", the same inward turn that also underlies the noun ~das Benehmen~ ("manners").
en.benennen:
From Middle High German ~benennen~, from Old High German *~binemnen~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~nennen~:

• ~nennen~: From MHG ~nennen~, ~nemmen~, ~nemnen~, from OHG ~nemnen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~namnijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~namnijaną~ ("to name"), a denominative from *~namô~ ("name"), from PIE *~h₁nómn̥~ ("name").
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The prefix makes the verb transitive with the sense of bestowing a name upon.

~Benennen~ means "to name, to designate, to label", to bestow a name ~upon~ something or someone. Where ~nennen~ simply means "to call" or "to name," the prefix ~be-~ adds the sense of formal designation or bestowal. The PIE root *~h₁nómn̥~ ("name") is one of the most stable words in all Indo-European languages, barely changing across thousands of years: Latin ~nōmen~, Greek ~ónoma~ (with metathesis), Sanskrit ~nā́man~, Old Irish ~ainm~, and English ~name~ all descend from it. The Old Saxon cognate ~binemnian~ and Old English ~benemnan~ show the same ~be-~ + ~name~ compound across the West Germanic languages. The archaic English ~bename~ ("to name, to designate") is a direct cognate, though it fell out of use centuries ago. Cognate with Dutch ~benoemen~, Swedish ~benämna~, Old English ~benemnan~.
en.benutzen:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~nutzen~:

• ~nutzen~: From MHG ~nutzen~, from OHG ~nuzzōn~, a denominative verb from the noun ~Nutz~ ("use, benefit"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nuti~, from PGmc *~nutją~, from PIE *~h₂ewd-~ ("to enjoy, benefit"). The double spelling ~nutzen~/~nützen~ in modern German reflects a North-South dialect split, with ~nutzen~ (without umlaut) prevailing in the North and ~nützen~ in the South.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix typically transforms an intransitive verb into a transitive one.

The ~be-~ prefix adds a transitive, directed quality: while ~nutzen~ can be used intransitively ("es nutzt nichts", "it is of no use"), ~benutzen~ is always transitive and implies actively putting something to use. Cognate with English ~need~ (via the same PGmc root), Dutch ~benutten~.
en.benötigen:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~nötigen~:

• ~nötigen~: From MHG ~nōtigen~, from OHG ~nōtigōn~, a denominative verb ("to compel, necessitate") derived from the adjective ~nötig~ ("necessary"), itself from the noun ~Not~ ("distress, need, compulsion"), from OHG ~nōt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~naudi~, from Proto-Germanic *~naudiz~, from PIE *~neh₂w-tí-s~, a *~ti-~-stem related to the root of *~nawiz~ ("corpse"). The connection between "need" and "corpse" reflects a grim ancient logic: the PIE root evokes the state of the dead (inertness, absence of vital force) and the Germanic word shifted this toward the desperate need or compulsion that threatens to reduce the living to that state.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix typically transforms an intransitive or adjective-derived verb into a transitive one.

The ~be-~ prefix shifts ~nötigen~ (intransitive "to compel") toward the transitive "to need, require." The semantic distinction in German is subtle: ~brauchen~ and ~benötigen~ both mean "to need," but ~benötigen~ carries a more formal register. Cognate with Dutch ~benodigden~, English ~need~ (from the same PIE root via *~naudiz~).
en.beobachten:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~Obacht~ + ~-en~:

• ~Obacht~ (root): From MHG ~ob-~ + ~Acht~. The element ~ob-~ is a preposition meaning "over, upon, above" (cognate with Latin ~ob-~). ~Acht~ here is from the noun of "attention, heed" (OHG ~ahta~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ahtu~), not from ~acht~ ("eight"). The compound ~Obacht~ thus means "watching over, heedful attention from above", a watchful, supervisory gaze. The related survival ~Obacht geben~ ("to pay attention") still appears in Southern German and Austrian speech.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix typically transforms an intransitive verb into a transitive one.

The layering is vivid: ~beobachten~ = be- + ob- + Acht + -en = "to apply upward-directed attention to something," a verb built from three ancient strata of meaning. The English near-parallel is ~observe~ (Latin ~ob-~ + ~servāre~, "to watch over"), which uses the same Latin prefix ~ob-~ in the same spatial sense of oversight. Cognate with Dutch ~observeren~ (a later Latin borrowing for the same concept).
en.bepflanzen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~pflanzen~:

• ~pflanzen~: From MHG ~pflanzen~, from OHG ~pflanzōn~, a denominative verb from ~pflanza~ ("plant"), borrowed from Latin ~planta~ ("a shoot, cutting"), itself of uncertain origin. The change from Latin ~pl-~ to ~pfl-~ belongs to the High German consonant shift. Cognate with English ~plant~ (which shows no shift), Luxembourgish ~Planz~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ conveys applying something over a surface or covering it.

The object changes sides: one plants rampion, but one ~bepflanzt~ the bed, the ground becomes the object and the plants move into a ~mit~-phrase. The initial ~pfl-~ betrays how old the borrowing is: only a word already in German before the High German consonant shift could still undergo it.
en.beraten: ~Beraten~ combines the prefix ~be-~ (from PIE *~h₁epi~, "on, at, near," making the verb transitive) with ~raten~ ("to advise, counsel; to guess"), from Middle High German ~rāten~, from Old High German ~rātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rēdaną~, from PIE *~Hreh₁dʰ-~ ("to think, arrange"). The same Germanic root produced Old English ~rǣdan~, which became modern English ~read~, a remarkable semantic journey from "to interpret, counsel" to "to interpret written text." The cognate English ~rede~ (archaic: "counsel, advice") preserves the older meaning. Beraten appears in Old High German as ~birātan~ and in Middle High German as ~berāten~, with the obsolete English ~berede~ and ~beread~ as direct cognates. The noun ~Rat~ ("council, advice") and the city-council chamber ~Rathaus~ descend from the same root. ~Beraten~ adds the transitive force of ~be-~: one ~berät~ a person (gives them counsel), but also ~berät eine Frage~ (deliberates on a question).
en.berechnen:
Equivalent to ~be-~ + ~rechnen~:

• ~rechnen~: From MHG ~rechenen~, from OHG ~rehhanōn~, related to Proto-Germanic *~rekōną~ ("to count, to explain, to reckon").
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The prefix makes the verb transitive and adds the sense of applying calculation to something.

~Berechnen~ means "to calculate, to compute, to charge", the ~be-~ prefix transforms ~rechnen~ ("to do arithmetic") into a transitive verb that applies calculation to a specific object: one ~berechnet~ a cost, a trajectory, a probability, or a fee. The additional sense "to charge" (~Wir berechnen Ihnen 50 Euro~, "We'll charge you 50 euros") shows the natural extension from counting to billing: what you calculate, you charge. The derived adjective ~berechnend~ ("calculating, scheming") carries a pejorative sense: a ~berechnender Mensch~ is someone who computes every social interaction for personal advantage. English ~reckon~ is a direct cognate of ~rechnen~, and both the German and English words retain the dual sense of mathematical computation and informal estimation (~I reckon~ ≈ ~ich rechne damit~). Cognate with Dutch ~berekenen~.
en.berechtigen:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~recht~ + ~-igen~, a denominal derivation from the noun ~Recht~ ("right, law"):

• ~Recht~: From MHG ~rëht~, from OHG ~rëht~, from Proto-West Germanic *~reht~ ("right, straight"), from Proto-Germanic *~rehtaz~, from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, to direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~recht~, Danish ~ret~, Icelandic ~réttur~, Latin ~rēctus~ ("straight"), and Sanskrit ~ṛjú~ ("upright").
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix makes the verb transitive: to confer a right upon someone.

The verb means "to entitle, to authorize", literally "to make right for someone." The ~be-~ prefix provides the crucial transitive frame: ~recht~ alone is an adjective ("right, correct"), but ~berechtigen~ acts upon a person, conferring ~Recht~ upon them. The PIE root *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, to make right") produced an astonishingly wide family: Latin ~rēx~ ("king," originally "the one who directs"), ~rēgula~ ("rule"), and ~regiō~ ("direction, region"); Sanskrit ~rājan~ ("king"); Irish ~rí~ ("king"); and Germanic ~recht~/~right~. The Indo-European concept of justice was thus inseparable from straightness: what is ~recht~ is what is straight, not crooked.
en.bereden:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

Two readings share the word, depending on what becomes the object. ~Etwas bereden~ is "to talk something over" and stays close to the base verb; ~jemanden bereden~, by contrast, means "to talk someone round", the older sense, and much the commoner one in literature.
en.beregen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~regen~:

• ~regen~: From MHG ~regen~ ("to make protrude, to erect, to excite, to move"), from Proto-Germanic *~hragjaną~ ("to make stand, wake up, incite"); synchronically the causative of MHG ~ragen~ ("to project, to tower"). The verb means "to stir, move, rouse", unrelated to the noun ~Regen~ ("rain"), and is most often reflexive (~sich regen~).
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

A largely extinct verb. Where the base word usually stays reflexive (~sich regen~, "to stir"), ~beregen~ directs the motion at an outside object. In older chancery German this developed into "to mention, to raise," a sense that survived in the participle ~beregt~ "aforesaid."
en.beregnen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~regnen~:

• ~regnen~: From MHG ~regenen~, from OHG ~reganōn~, a denominative from the noun ~regan~ ("rain"), from Proto-West Germanic *~regn~, from Proto-Germanic *~regną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, possibly *~Hreǵʰ-~ ("to flow water"). The verb is impersonal (~es regnet~), a construction inherited from Proto-Germanic. Cognate with English ~rain~, Dutch ~regenen~, Swedish ~regna~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ conveys applying something over a surface or covering it.

The base verb has no real subject and certainly no object: ~es regnet~ ("it is raining"). ~Beregnen~ supplies one: the surface the rain falls on. In modern use the word belongs to agriculture: a ~Beregnungsanlage~ ("sprinkler system") waters the field when the sky declines to.
en.bereichern:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~reicher~ + ~-n~, a deadjectival derivation from ~reich~ ("rich"):

• ~reich~: From MHG ~rīch~, ~rīche~, from OHG ~rīhhi~ ("noble, mighty, of high birth"), a ~ja~-stem adjective from Proto-Germanic *~rīkijaz~, derived from the noun *~rīk-~ ("ruler, prince"). This noun is widely regarded as an early Celtic loanword into Germanic, cognate with Latin ~rēx~ ("king"), both from PIE *~h₃rēǵs~ ("king, ruler"). Cognate with Dutch ~rijk~, English ~rich~, Old Norse ~ríkr~, and Old English ~rīce~ (whence the ~-ric(k)~ in names like ~Fredrick~ and ~bishopric~).
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix creates a transitive verb meaning "to make rich."

The verb means "to enrich", literally "to make rich upon." The reflexive ~sich bereichern~ ("to enrich oneself") often carries a negative connotation of illicit gain. The adjective ~reich~ preserves a remarkable layer of Celtic-Germanic contact: the Germanic peoples borrowed the word *~rīk-~ from their Celtic neighbors, probably during the La Tene period (roughly 5th to 1st centuries BC). The original meaning was "ruler, chief," not "wealthy," and the semantic shift from "powerful" to "rich" happened gradually within Germanic. The same Celtic root gave English ~rich~ via Old French ~riche~, which itself was a Frankish (Germanic) re-borrowing, making ~rich~ a word that bounced from Celtic to Germanic to Romance and back to Germanic again.
en.bereinigen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~reinigen~:

• ~reinigen~: From MHG ~reinegen~, ~reinigen~, a denominative from the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean"), which descends from MHG ~reine~, OHG ~reini~, Proto-West Germanic *~hrainī~, Proto-Germanic *~hrainiz~, from PIE *~krey-~ ("to divide, sift, separate"), purity being what remains once impurities are sifted away. Cognate with Dutch ~reinigen~, Swedish ~ren~, Icelandic ~hreinn~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.

Unlike ~reinigen~, ~bereinigen~ is almost never meant literally: what gets ~bereinigt~ are disputes, lists, and statistics. Administrative German has hardened it into the phrase ~bereinigt um~, used to strip a distorting effect out of a figure, the sifting already present in the root, applied to bookkeeping.
en.bereisen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

One travels ~to~ Italy, but one ~bereist~ Italy: the destination becomes the object, and with it the perspective shifts, a country you have ~bereist~ is one you have crossed and come to know, not merely one you set out for.
en.bereiten:
From Middle High German ~bereiten~, from Old High German ~bireitan~. By surface analysis, ~bereit~ + ~-en~; historically a denominal verb from the Proto-Germanic adjective *~raidaz~ ("ready, arranged"), with the prefix ~bi-~ (ancestral form of modern ~be-~). The adjective *~raidaz~ derives from PIE *~rēy-~ ("to arrange, prepare"). The derived verb *~raidijaną~ meant "to make ready, to equip."

The word ~bereiten~ is not to be confused with ~reiten~ ("to ride"), despite the similar appearance. While ~reiten~ descends from PGmc *~rīdaną~ (PIE *~reydʰ-~, "to ride"), ~bereiten~ descends from PGmc *~raidaz~ (PIE *~rēy-~, "to arrange"). The two roots are entirely unrelated. Modern German preserves ~bereiten~ primarily in elevated or fixed expressions (~Freude bereiten~ ("to give joy"), ~Schwierigkeiten bereiten~ ("to cause difficulties")), while the simplex ~reiten~ in the readying sense has vanished, surviving only in the adjective ~bereit~ ("ready") and the compound ~vorbereiten~ ("to prepare"). English ~ready~ is a direct cognate of ~bereit~, both descending from PGmc *~raidaz~: to be ready is etymologically to be "arranged." Cognate with Dutch ~bereiden~, English ~ready~.
en.bereiterklären:
A separable compound of ~bereit~ + ~er-~ + ~klären~:

• ~klären~: From MHG ~klæren~, denominal from ~klar~ ("clear, bright"), borrowed from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch ~klār~, from Old French ~cler~, from Latin ~clārus~ ("bright, renowned"). English ~clear~ arrived by the same route: cousins by borrowing rather than inheritance.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ derives a verb from an adjective, meaning to bring into that state.
• ~bereit~: From MHG ~bereite~, from OHG ~bireiti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raidī~, from Proto-Germanic *~raidaz~ ("ready, arranged, prepared"), from PIE *~h₂rey-~ ("to count, order"). Cognate with English ~ready~, Dutch ~bereid~, Gothic ~garaiþs~ ("ordered"). As a verbal particle it is resultative: the verb puts something into a state of readiness, as in ~bereitstellen~, ~bereithalten~. The sense of ~bereit~ here is: into a state of readiness.

The word is a phrase set hard: ~sich bereit erklären~, to declare oneself willing. It is used only reflexively, and the particle separates as a matter of course; ~er erklärt sich bereit~.
en.bereithalten:
A separable compound of ~bereit~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~bereit~: From MHG ~bereite~, from OHG ~bireiti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raidī~, from Proto-Germanic *~raidaz~ ("ready, arranged, prepared"), from PIE *~h₂rey-~ ("to count, order"). Cognate with English ~ready~, Dutch ~bereid~, Gothic ~garaiþs~ ("ordered"). As a verbal particle it is resultative: the verb puts something into a state of readiness, as in ~bereitstellen~, ~bereithalten~. The sense of ~bereit~ here is: held available, kept on hand.

The verb describes not an action but a provision: what is ~bereitgehalten~ sits unused, waiting against the moment it is needed. Being separable, it strands the particle at the end of a main clause; ~er hält Ersatzteile bereit~.
en.bereitlegen:
A separable compound of ~bereit~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~bereit~: From MHG ~bereite~, from OHG ~bireiti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raidī~, from Proto-Germanic *~raidaz~ ("ready, arranged, prepared"), from PIE *~h₂rey-~ ("to count, order"). Cognate with English ~ready~, Dutch ~bereid~, Gothic ~garaiþs~ ("ordered"). As a verbal particle it is resultative: the verb puts something into a state of readiness, as in ~bereitstellen~, ~bereithalten~. The sense of ~bereit~ here is: prepared in advance for use.

The difference from ~bereithalten~ is the difference between a state and a gesture: laying something out is done once, in advance, so that nothing has to be hunted for later. Since ~legen~ is the causative of ~liegen~, the compound literally means "to cause something to lie ready."
en.bereitstehen:
A separable compound of ~bereit~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~bereit~: From MHG ~bereite~, from OHG ~bireiti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raidī~, from Proto-Germanic *~raidaz~ ("ready, arranged, prepared"), from PIE *~h₂rey-~ ("to count, order"). Cognate with English ~ready~, Dutch ~bereid~, Gothic ~garaiþs~ ("ordered"). As a verbal particle it is resultative: the verb puts something into a state of readiness, as in ~bereitstellen~, ~bereithalten~. The sense of ~bereit~ here is: held available, kept on hand.

The counterpart of ~bereithalten~ seen from the thing's own side: what somebody keeps ready ~steht bereit~. The subject is therefore usually inanimate (a car, a funding program, a database) and said of a person it means standing by for others.
en.bereitstellen:
Compound of ~bereit~ ("ready") + ~stellen~ ("to put, place"):

• ~bereit~: From MHG ~bereite~, from OHG ~bireiti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raidī~, from Proto-Germanic *~raidaz~ ("ready, arranged, prepared"), from PIE *~h₂roy-dʰh₁-~ ("arranged"), from *~h₂rey-~ ("to count, order"). Cognate with English ~ready~.
• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put, stand").

The compound literally means "to place in a state of readiness", that is, "to provide, supply, make available." It is a separable-prefix verb (~er stellt bereit~) where the first element is not a traditional prefix but the adjective ~bereit~. The kinship between German ~bereit~ and English ~ready~ is not immediately obvious because the English word lost the ~be-~ prefix through phonological erosion, while German preserved it. Both ultimately trace back to a PIE root meaning "to put in order", readiness as the state of being arranged. In modern usage, ~bereitstellen~ is especially common in technical and administrative contexts: ~Mittel bereitstellen~ ("to provide funds"), ~Daten bereitstellen~ ("to make data available").
en.bergen:
From Middle High German ~bërgen~, from Old High German ~bergan~ ("to hide, protect, salvage"), from Proto-West Germanic *~bergan~, from Proto-Germanic *~berganą~ ("to hide, protect"), from PIE *~bʰergʰ-~ ("to take care of, protect, preserve"). A class III strong verb. Cognate with English ~bury~ (originally "to shelter, protect"; the modern sense of interring the dead is a semantic narrowing), Dutch ~bergen~, Old Norse ~bjarga~ ("to save, help"), Gothic ~bairgan~ ("to hide"), and Old Irish ~commairge~ ("protection").

The semantic range of ~bergen~ is remarkable: it means "to rescue" (from a shipwreck or avalanche), "to salvage" (a sunken ship), "to recover" (a body), and "to contain, hold" (~in sich bergen~, "to hold within itself"). The reflexive ~sich verbergen~ ("to hide oneself") preserves the original "hide" sense more transparently. The connection between ~bergen~ and English ~bury~ is a striking example of semantic divergence from a shared root: German kept the "rescue/protect" sense while English narrowed to "put underground." The PIE root *~bʰergʰ-~ also produced the Proto-Slavic *~borgъ~ that became Russian ~berech'~ ("to guard, protect"), showing remarkable semantic stability across the Indo-European family. The place name ~Salzburg~ ("salt fortress") uses the related noun ~Burg~ ("castle, fortress"), a fortified place where one is protected.
en.berichten:
From Middle High German ~berihten~ ("to put in order; to instruct, to lecture"), from Old High German ~birihten~ ("to make correct"), from Proto-West Germanic *~birinhtijan~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~ ("to straighten, set straight"), from Proto-Germanic *~rihtijaną~, from *~rehtaz~ ("straight"), from PIE *~h₃reǵtós~ ("right, straightened"), from *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to stretch out, straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~richten~, Latin ~regō~ ("I rule, direct").
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix typically transforms an intransitive verb into a transitive one.

The prefix ~be-~ shifted the sense of "to straighten" toward "to set right, put in order, instruct", and from there, "to report" (as in giving a straight account of events). The sense of "to execute" (as in a judicial sentence, still heard in ~hinrichten~) also derives from "to put right according to the law." Cognate with Dutch ~berichten~, English ~beright~ (archaic).
en.beringen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~ringen~:

• ~ringen~: From MHG ~ringen~, from OHG ~ringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wringaną~ ("to twist, wring"), from a nasalized form of PIE *~wergʰ-~ ("to turn, twist"). A class III strong verb (~ringen~, ~rang~, ~gerungen~). Despite appearances it has nothing to do with ~Ring~. Cognate with English ~wring~, ~wrong~ (originally "twisted"), Dutch ~wringen~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ derives a verb from a noun or adjective, meaning to furnish with or make into that.

The decomposition is formal rather than historical: ~beringen~ is built on the noun ~Ring~, and the strong verb ~ringen~ merely resembles it, as the root entry's own warning about ~Ring~ makes plain.
en.bersten: From MHG ~bresten~, from OHG ~brestan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brestan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brestaną~ ("to burst, break"); the deeper PIE ancestry is uncertain. A class IV strong verb (~bersten~, ~barst~, ~geborsten~). The modern ~-er-~ is not original: Middle Low German metathesized the ~-r-~ of ~brestan~, and the metathesized form displaced the inherited one. English did the same thing independently (Old English ~berstan~ beside earlier ~brestan~), so ~bersten~ and ~burst~ line up today by way of two separate accidents. Cognate with Dutch ~barsten~, Old Norse ~bresta~, Swedish ~brista~.
en.berufen:
From Middle High German ~beruofen~, from Old High German ~biruofan~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~, ~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~. The origin is uncertain; it may be related to *~hrōþiz~ ("glory, fame"), with the ~-p-~ arising from analogical association with the similar-sounding *~wōpijaną~ ("to cry out"). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~be-~: From OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi~ ("by, near"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). Makes the verb transitive and adds a sense of direction toward.

The ~be-~ prefix transforms "to call" into "to call upon, to appoint, to summon to an office." In modern German, ~berufen~ carries the sense of formal appointment or vocation: ~jemanden auf einen Lehrstuhl berufen~ ("to appoint someone to a professorial chair"). The related noun ~Beruf~ ("profession, vocation") is literally a "calling," a calque of Latin ~vocātiō~, Martin Luther coined this usage to argue that every honest trade, not just the priesthood, constituted a divine calling. The adjective ~berufen~ can also mean "qualified" or "authorized," but superstitiously, ~Ich will es nicht berufen~ means "I don't want to jinx it", the idea being that calling attention to good fortune might summon bad luck. This superstitious sense preserves an ancient belief in the magical power of spoken words. The modern present tense notably lacks umlaut (~du berufst~, not *~du berüfst~), because the historical umlaut on the rounded diphthong ~uo~ never established itself here, unlike in most other strong verbs.
en.beruhen:
~Be-~ + ~ruhen~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~ruhen~:

• ~ruhen~: From MHG ~ruo(we)n~, from OHG ~ruowēn~, derived from the noun ~ruowa~ ("rest, peace"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rōu~, from Proto-Germanic *~rōō~ ("calm, rest"), from PIE *~h₁reh₁-~ ("quiet, calm"). Cognate with the Sanskrit ~rātrī~ ("night").
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). This prefix typically transforms an intransitive verb into a transitive one, but here it shifts ~ruhen~ ("to rest") toward a more abstract, relational sense: "to rest upon" becomes "to be based on."

~Beruhen~ means "to be based on, to rest upon, to depend on", exclusively in the figurative sense. One says ~die Anklage beruht auf Indizien~ ("the charge rests on circumstantial evidence") or uses the fixed phrase ~etwas auf sich beruhen lassen~ ("to let something rest, to leave a matter be"). Unlike ~ruhen~ itself, which retains strong physical connotations of sleeping, resting, and lying buried, ~beruhen~ exists entirely in the abstract domain. The ~be-~ prefix has lifted the verb off the bed, so to speak, and onto the plane of logic and causation.
en.beruhigen:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~ruhig~ + ~-en~:

• ~ruhig~: From MHG ~ruowec~ ("quiet"), from ~Ruhe~ ("rest, quiet, peace"). ~Ruhe~ descends from OHG ~ruowa~ ("peace, quiet, rest"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rōu~ ("calm, rest"), from Proto-Germanic *~rōō~, from PIE *~h₁reh₁-~ ("quiet, calm"). Cognate with Sanskrit ~rātri~ ("night"), whence Hindi ~rāt~ ("night").
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). This inseparable prefix makes the verb transitive, directing the calming action at a specific person or situation.

~Beruhigen~ means "to calm, to reassure, to soothe", the ~be-~ prefix transforms the adjective ~ruhig~ ("calm, quiet") into a transitive verb. ~Beruhige dich!~ ("Calm down!") is one of the most frequently heard imperatives in German. The reflexive ~sich beruhigen~ ("to calm down") and the noun ~Beruhigung~ ("reassurance, calming") complete the word family. A ~Beruhigungsmittel~ ("sedative," literally "calming-agent") is the pharmaceutical extension. The connection between PIE *~h₁reh₁-~ ("quiet") and Sanskrit ~rātri~ ("night") is poetic: night as the time of quiet, of rest.
en.berücken:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~rücken~:

• ~rücken~: From MHG ~rücken~, from OHG ~rucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rukkijan~. The verb means "to move, to shift" and is the base of ~verrückt~ ("crazy," literally "shifted, displaced"); the noun ~Rücken~ ("back") is etymologically a separate word. Cognate with English ~rock~, Old Norse ~rykkja~, Old English ~roccian~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

The modern sense is metaphorical: to ~berücken~ someone is to move them without their noticing, and the older, concrete image is of a net drawn over prey.
en.berücksichtigen:
A triple derivation chain: ~Rück-~ ("back") + ~Sicht~ ("sight, view") → ~Rücksicht~ ("consideration, regard") → be- + ~rücksichtigen~:

• ~rücksichtigen~ (intermediate verb): A now-rare denominative verb "to have consideration for," formed from ~Rücksicht~ + the verbalizing suffix ~-igen~. In modern use it survives almost exclusively in the prefixed form ~berücksichtigen~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix transforms the denominative verb ~rücksichtigen~ into a fully transitive form meaning "to take into account, to consider."
• ~Rücksicht~ (root noun): An 18th-century calque of Latin ~respectus~ ("a looking back; regard, consideration"), from ~re-~ ("back") + ~spectus~ (from ~specere~, "to look"). German translates each Latin element precisely: ~Rück-~ ("back, return") for ~re-~, and ~Sicht~ ("sight, view") for ~spectus~. ~Sicht~ derives from MHG ~siht~, from OHG ~siht~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sihti~, formed from the root of ~sehen~ ("to see"), from PGmc *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~sight~.

The full semantic chain runs: PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see") → Germanic "sight" → German "a looking back" → "regard, respect" → "to take into regard." The derivation mirrors Latin ~respectus~ precisely: ~Rücksicht nehmen~ corresponds to ~respectum habere~, and ~berücksichtigen~ provides a single-verb equivalent of the Latin compound.
en.berühren:
~Be-~ + ~rühren~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~rühren~:

• ~rühren~: From MHG ~rüeren~, from OHG ~ruoren~, ~hruoren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōzijaną~ ("to stir"), a causative formation from *~hrōzaz~ ("active, stirring, moving"), possibly from PIE *~kroHs-~ (a root connected to stirring and shock). Cognate with Dutch ~roeren~ ("to stir"), and the now-rare English ~rear~ ("to move, to stir").
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The prefix directs the action of stirring or touching toward a specific object, making the verb transitive: to touch something.

~Berühren~ means "to touch" in both the physical and emotional sense: ~berühr das nicht!~ ("don't touch that!") and ~ihre Geschichte hat mich tief berührt~ ("her story deeply touched me"). In geometry, ~berühren~ means "to be tangent to"; a circle ~berührt~ a line at exactly one point. The derived noun ~Berührung~ ("touch, contact") appears in the elegant compound ~Berührungsangst~ ("fear of contact, inhibition about engaging with something"), a word that captures reluctance to engage with unfamiliar ideas, people, or technologies. The underlying verb ~rühren~ itself means "to stir" (as in cooking: ~die Soße rühren~) and "to move emotionally" (~zu Tränen gerührt~, "moved to tears"), preserving both the physical and affective senses from which ~berühren~ drew its dual nature. The military command ~rührt euch!~ ("at ease!," literally "stir yourselves!") uses ~rühren~ in yet another sense, permission to move after standing at attention.
en.besagen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

Unlike ~sagen~, ~besagen~ takes an inanimate subject: people ~sagen~ things, while a clause, a statistic, or a rule ~besagt~ them.
en.besaufen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~saufen~:

• ~saufen~: From MHG ~sūfen~ ("to sip, drink"), from OHG ~sūfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sūpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sūpaną~, from PIE *~sewp-~, a labial extension of *~sew-~ ("to take liquid, slurp"). A class II strong verb (~saufen~, ~soff~, ~gesoffen~). The drift from "to sip" to today's "to booze" dates only to the sixteenth century. Cognate with English ~sup~, Dutch ~zuipen~, Old Norse ~súpa~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ forms a verb used only reflexively: the action turns back on the one performing it and never reaches an outside object.

The compound exists only as ~sich besaufen~, and it completes the base verb's drift: where ~saufen~ once meant to sip, ~sich besaufen~ names drinking carried through to its effect on the drinker himself.
en.beschaffen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~schaffen~:

• ~schaffen~: Two historically distinct verbs have merged under a single infinitive, distinguished only by their conjugation. The strong ~schaffen~ (~schuf~, ~geschaffen~, "to create") descends from MHG ~schaffen~, OHG ~scaffan~, a byform of ~skephen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skappjan~; the ~-f-~ was chiefly back-formed from the participle ~giscaffan~. The weak ~schaffen~ (~schaffte~, ~geschafft~, "to manage, accomplish") descends from OHG ~skaffōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skapōn~, from the same root. Cognate with Dutch ~scheppen~, English ~shape~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

Its weak inflection (~beschaffte~, ~beschafft~) puts the compound on the ~skaffōn~ side of the split: ~beschaffen~ obtains something that already exists rather than bringing it into being, so the strong "to create" twin is not its ancestor.
en.beschallen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~schallen~:

• ~schallen~: From MHG ~schallen~, a denominal formation on ~Schall~ ("sound"); the Grimms took it instead as a reshaping of the older strong MHG ~schellen~ ("to resound"), from Proto-West Germanic *~skellan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skellaną~, from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, shout") with s-mobile. Normally weak today (~schallte~, ~geschallt~), it keeps the strong Präteritum ~scholl~ as an elevated variant. Cognate with Old Norse ~skjalla~, Old English ~sciellan~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

The compound is modern and largely technical: what is ~beschallt~ is the body or the room the sound is directed into, whether by an ultrasound probe or by a public-address system.
en.beschauen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.

Where ~schauen~ is a glance, ~beschauen~ is a deliberate looking-over, which is why officialdom kept it: the meat inspector's ~Fleischbeschau~ and the ~Beschauer~ of a painting both come from this compound.
en.bescheiden:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~scheiden~:

• ~scheiden~: From MHG ~scheiden~, from OHG ~sceidan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaiþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaiþaną~, from PIE *~skeyt-~ ("to cut, separate"). Cognate with English ~shed~ (originally "to separate"), Dutch ~scheiden~, West Frisian ~skiede~, and Greek ~skhizein~ ("to split," source of ~schism~).
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

The adjective ~bescheiden~ "modest" is this verb's own participle grown independent: someone who has been allotted his share, and knows it, keeps to it, which is why the sense of formal apportionment survives most visibly in ~es war ihm beschieden~ "it was his lot."
en.bescheinen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~scheinen~:

• ~scheinen~: From MHG ~schīnen~, from OHG ~skīnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skīnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skīnaną~, from PIE *~(s)ḱeh₁y-~ ("to shine, shimmer"). A class I strong verb. It covers both "to shine" and "to seem," a duality reflecting the ancient metaphor of appearances as light. Cognate with English ~shine~, Dutch ~schijnen~, Danish ~skinne~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

Of the base verb's two senses only the light passes into the compound: ~bescheinen~ never means "to seem," and its object is always the surface the light falls on.
en.bescheißen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~scheißen~:

• ~scheißen~: From MHG ~schīzen~, from OHG *~skīzan~ (attested only in the compound ~biskīzan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~skītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skītaną~, from PIE *~skeyd-~ ("to split, separate"); the root's basic sense is separation, not filth. A class I strong verb (~scheißen~, ~schiss~, ~geschissen~). Cognate with English ~shit~, Dutch ~schijten~, Old Norse ~skíta~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ conveys applying something over a surface or covering it.

The compound is older in the record than its own base: OHG ~biskīzan~ is attested where the simplex is not, and the everyday modern sense is no longer literal at all but "to cheat."
en.beschenken:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~schenken~:

• ~schenken~: From MHG ~schenken~, from OHG ~scenken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skankijan~ ("to pour, serve"). The sense "to give as a gift" grew out of pouring a drink for a guest, the paradigmatic act of generosity; the pouring sense retreated into ~Wein einschenken~ and ~Schenke~ ("tavern"). Cognate with Dutch ~schenken~ ("to pour; to give"), English ~skink~ (archaic) and ~shank~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

The two verbs differ in what they take as object: you ~schenken~ a gift, but you ~beschenken~ a person, the recipient, who in the root's older picture was the guest whose cup was filled.
en.bescheren:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~scheren~:

• ~scheren~: Two verbs share this spelling. The strong ~scheren~ ("to shear, cut") comes from MHG ~schërn~, OHG ~skeran~, Proto-West Germanic *~skeran~, Proto-Germanic *~skeraną~, from PIE *~(s)ker-~ ("to cut"); a class IV strong verb (~scheren~, ~schor~, ~geschoren~), cognate with English ~shear~, Dutch ~scheren~, Old Norse ~skera~. The weak ~scheren~ ("to bother oneself about"; also "to clear off") is a separate and later word, first attested in the fifteenth century as Late MHG ~schern~ ("to hurry, escape"), of uncertain origin, and inflects weak throughout (~scherte~, ~geschert~).
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

Neither of the root's two verbs is a comfortable fit: ~bescheren~ inflects weak, like the "bother oneself about" verb, but its sense descends from the strong ~scheren~ "to cut" by way of cutting off a share, an allotted portion. The gift sense narrowed later, and today the noun ~Bescherung~ names the Christmas Eve distribution of presents.
en.beschicken:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~schicken~:

• ~schicken~: From MHG ~schicken~ ("to outfit oneself, fit in, arrange appropriately"), from OHG *~skihhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skikkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skikkijaną~ ("to order, send"), the causative of the verb underlying MHG ~geschehen~ ("to happen, rush"). The sense "to send" grew from "to make ready to go." Related to English ~chic~ (via French), ~geschickt~, and ~Schicksal~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

The compound's object is not the person sent but the place or thing supplied: one ~beschickt~ a trade fair with exhibits or a blast furnace with ore, and Luther's older usage extends this to putting a household in order.
en.beschießen:
