The regular sound change from Proto-Germanic ~-þ-~ to German ~-t-~ in the uninflected form was then generalized across the paradigm; the older ~-d-~ is preserved in related words ~Würde~ ("dignity") and ~würdig~ ("worthy"). A cognate of particular interest: English ~worth~ and German ~Wert~ are doublets, and the sentence "What is it worth?" maps exactly onto "Was ist es wert?" , same structure, same root.
en.bewirken:
From Middle High German ~bewirken~, ~bewürken~, from Old High German ~biwurken~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~wirken~:

• ~wirken~: From MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~ ("to make, produce, effect"), from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~werǵ-~ ("to work"). Cognate with English ~work~, Dutch ~werken~, Greek ~érgon~ ("work"), and the organ name in ~Chirurg~ (from Greek ~kheirourgós~, "hand-worker"). An Upper German variant *~wurkijaną~ (OHG ~wurken~, MHG ~würken~) coexisted for centuries; the Central German ~i~-form prevailed in the written language by the 18th century.
• ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The prefix directs the working toward a result, making the verb mean "to work upon" in the sense of causing.

~Bewirken~ means "to bring about, to cause, to effect", a formal verb of causation. Where ~wirken~ alone means "to work, to have an effect, to seem," ~bewirken~ focuses on the result: ~die Medizin hat eine Verbesserung bewirkt~ ("the medicine brought about an improvement"). It occupies a register above ~verursachen~ ("to cause") and well above ~machen~ ("to make, to do"). The PIE root *~werǵ-~ is one of the most productive in the Indo-European family: it gives Greek ~érgon~ ("work," whence ~energy~, ~allergy~, ~liturgy~), Latin ~urgēre~ ("to press"), and Old English ~weorc~ (modern ~work~). The connection between German ~wirken~/~bewirken~ and English ~work~ is therefore genuine cognacy, not mere resemblance.
en.bewohnen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~wohnen~:

• ~wohnen~: From MHG ~wonen~, from OHG ~wonēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wunēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wunāną~, from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to wish, love, strive for"); to inhabit a place is to love it enough to remain. The same root underlies ~Wonne~ ("bliss"), ~wünschen~, and ~gewinnen~. Cognate with English ~wont~ ("accustomed"), Dutch ~wonen~, Gothic ~wunan~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

~Wohnen~ wants a preposition, ~bewohnen~ an object: one lives in a house, or one ~bewohnt~ it. The participle is the everyday form (houses are ~bewohnt~ or ~unbewohnt~) and ~Bewohner~ ("inhabitant") comes of the same formation.
en.bewundern:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~wundern~, from ~Wunder~ ("wonder, miracle"):

• ~Wunder~: From MHG ~wunder~, from OHG ~wuntar~, from Proto-Germanic *~wundrą~, from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to wish, desire, strive for, love"). Cognate with English ~wonder~, Dutch ~wonder~, Danish ~under~.
• ~be-~: Inseparable prefix from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). Here it functions as a transitivizer, making the reflexive ~sich wundern~ ("to wonder at") into the transitive ~bewundern~ ("to admire").

~Bewundern~ means "to admire," while the simpler ~sich wundern~ means "to be surprised, to wonder." The prefix ~be-~ transforms passive astonishment into active admiration. The PIE root *~wenh₁-~ ("to desire, strive for") reveals that ~wonder~ was originally an expression of longing or desire: one wondered at what one wished for. The same root produced Latin ~Venus~ (goddess of desire), ~venārī~ ("to hunt," originally "to pursue with desire," whence English ~venison~), and Old English ~wynn~ ("joy, delight"). The German compound ~Wunderkind~ ("child prodigy," literally "wonder child") entered English unchanged.
en.bewähren:
Compound of ~be-~ + ~währen~, a deadjectival derivation from ~wahr~ ("true"):

• ~wahr~: From MHG ~wār~, ~wǣre~, from OHG ~wār~, ~wāri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wār~, from Proto-Germanic *~wēraz~ ("true, reliable"), from PIE *~weh₁ros~ ("true"), from *~weh₁-~ ("to be true"). Cognate with English archaic ~ware~ ("aware"), Dutch ~waar~ ("true"), Latin ~vērus~ ("true"), and Irish ~fíor~ ("true").
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix adds transitivity and intensification.

The reflexive ~sich bewähren~ means "to prove oneself, to stand the test", literally "to make oneself true." The adjective ~wahr~ descends from a PIE root *~weh₁-~ whose reflexes encode the concept of truth across the Indo-European world: Latin ~vērus~ ("true") gave English ~very~, ~verify~, and ~verdict~ ("a true saying"); Old Irish ~fíor~ means "true"; and Proto-Slavic *~věra~ means "faith, belief" (whence Russian ~вера~). The related German verb ~wahren~ means "to preserve, to maintain," while ~wahrnehmen~ means "to perceive", suggesting that truth, preservation, and perception were linked in the Germanic mind. English ~aware~ is a distant relative through the same Proto-Germanic adjective.
en.bewältigen:
From Middle High German ~bewältigen~, derived from ~be-~ + ~waltig~ + ~-en~, in which ~waltig~ is an obsolete variant of ~gewaltig~ ("powerful, mighty"). Compound of ~be-~ + the obsolete adjective ~waltig~:

• ~waltig~: From MHG ~waltic~, related to ~walten~ ("to rule, govern"), from OHG ~waltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~waldan~ ("to reign"), from Proto-Germanic *~waldaną~, from PIE *~h₂welh₁-~ ("to rule, be strong"). The noun ~Gewalt~ ("power, force") shares this root, from OHG ~giwalt~, Proto-Germanic *~gawaldą~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). This prefix makes the verb transitive: "to overpower" something.

The semantic development from "to exercise power over" to "to master, cope with, overcome" reflects the journey from raw physical dominance to intellectual and emotional mastery. Cognate with English ~wield~, which underwent a similar semantic broadening from ruling to skillful handling. The root also appears in Icelandic ~valda~ ("to cause"), Polish ~wladac~ ("to rule"), and Russian ~vladet'~ ("to own, command"), revealing a pan-Indo-European concept of power. The related noun ~Bewältigung~ plays a prominent role in modern German discourse, notably in the compound ~Vergangenheitsbewältigung~ ("coming to terms with the past"), a word so culturally specific that it is often borrowed untranslated into English.
en.bezahlen:
From Middle High German ~bezaln~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from PGmc *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~ (in the counting sense: "all told" means "all counted"), Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~ ("to speak"), Danish ~tal~ ("number").
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix adds a transitive, directed quality, while ~zahlen~ can be used intransitively ("ich zahle", "I pay"), ~bezahlen~ more explicitly takes a direct object (the thing or person paid).

The conceptual bridge from "counting" to "paying" runs through the ancient practice of counting out coins aloud when settling a debt. English preserves the counting sense in ~teller~ (one who tells/counts, as in a bank teller). German ~Zahl~ ("number") and ~zahlen~ ("to pay") descend from the same root, making every act of paying in German etymologically an act of counting. Cognate with Dutch ~betalen~, Danish ~betale~.
en.bezaubern:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~zaubern~:

• ~zaubern~: From MHG ~zoubern~, from OHG ~zouberōn~, ~zoubarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taubrōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taubrōną~, derived from *~taubrą~ ("magic, sorcery"), which is of uncertain further origin, perhaps linked to *~tawjaną~ ("to make, prepare"). Cognate with English ~tiver~, Dutch ~toveren~, Old Norse ~taufr~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.

The compound was originally literal (to lay magic on someone), and only the weakening from bewitching to delighting turns ~bezaubernd~ into a compliment.
en.bezeichnen:
From Middle High German ~bezeichenen~, from Old High German ~bizeihhanen~, ~bizeihnen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bitaiknijan~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~zeichnen~:

• ~zeichnen~: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, mark"), from MHG ~zeichen~, from OHG ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~ ("sign"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to point out, show"). A denominative verb: "to make a sign, to mark."
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix typically transforms an intransitive verb into a transitive one.

The PIE root *~deyḱ-~ is remarkably productive across languages: it yields ~Zeichen~ ("sign"), ~zeigen~ ("to show"), ~zeihen~ ("to accuse"), Latin ~dīcō~ ("I say, point out"), Greek ~deiknumi~ ("I show"), and English ~teach~ (from OE ~tǣcan~, from the same root). The ~be-~ prefix shifts the basic meaning of "to make a mark" toward "to designate, label, characterize." Cognate with Dutch ~betekenen~ ("to mean, signify"), English ~betoken~.
en.bezeigen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~zeigen~:

• ~zeigen~: From MHG ~zeigen~, from OHG ~zeigōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taigōn~, possibly from Proto-Germanic *~taikōną~ (iterative), an intensive derivative of OHG ~zīhan~ ("to accuse"), ultimately from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to point out, show"), whence also ~Zeichen~ ("sign") and English ~teach~. In Modern German it absorbed the unrelated MHG ~zöugen~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.

~Bezeigen~ survives today mainly in elevated and reflexive turns of phrase, where one ~bezeigt~ oneself grateful or obliged; elsewhere plain ~zeigen~ has crowded it out. Despite the resemblance it shares nothing with ~bezeugen~: that verb belongs to PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull"), this one to *~deyḱ-~ ("to point out").
en.bezeugen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~zeugen~:

• ~zeugen~: From MHG ~ziugen~, from OHG ~giziugon~, from ~ziug~ ("equipment, gear"), from Proto-West Germanic *~teug~, Proto-Germanic *~teugą~, related to *~teuhaną~ ("to pull"), from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). Originally "to bring forth using tools"; hence "to beget" and "to testify." Cognate with English ~tug~, Dutch ~tuig~, Old Norse ~tygi~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.

The base verb reaches its object through ~von~ (one ~zeugt von~ something), and the prefixed verb takes that object directly: to ~bezeugen~ a thing. That the root meant pulling, or bringing forth with tools, suits a witness, who brings evidence forth.
en.beziehen:
From Middle High German ~beziehen~, from Old High German ~biziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~biteuhan~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from PGmc *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). Class II strong verb. Cognate with Latin ~dūcere~ ("to lead") (the source of English ~duke~ and ~duct~) and with English ~tow~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"). This prefix typically transforms an intransitive verb into a transitive one.

~Beziehen~ has accumulated a striking range of meanings, all traceable to the root idea of "pulling toward or over": to move into (a flat, you "draw" yourself into it), to subscribe to (a journal, you "draw" it to yourself), to source (from a supplier, you "draw" goods from them), to cover (a bed or cushion, you "draw" fabric over it), and to refer (to something, you "draw" a connection). The reflexive ~sich beziehen auf~ ("to refer to") was probably influenced by Latin ~referre~ ("to carry back, refer"). The derived noun ~Beziehung~ ("relationship, connection") shows the same root abstraction, a relationship is a mutual drawing-toward. Cognate with Dutch ~betrekken~.
en.bezwingen:
An inseparable compound of ~be-~ + ~zwingen~:

• ~zwingen~: From MHG ~twingen~, from OHG ~dwingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þwinganą~, *~þwinhaną~; the apparent triple shift ~þ~ → ~d~ → ~t~ → ~z~ is regular for words with OHG ~dw-~ and ~tw-~, compare ~Zwerg~ ("dwarf"). A class III strong verb (~zwingen~, ~zwang~, ~gezwungen~). Cognate with Dutch ~dwingen~, Swedish ~tvinga~, Icelandic ~þvinga~, English ~twinge~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.

~Zwingen~ compels someone to do something; ~bezwingen~ carries the compulsion through, so that the opponent, the mountain, or one's own impulse actually gives way.
en.biegen:
From Middle High German ~biegen~, from Old High German ~biogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beuganą~, from PIE *~bʰewgʰ-~ ("to bend"). Cognate with Sanskrit ~bhujáti~ ("to bend, curve").

~Biegen~ is a class II strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~biegen~, ~bog~, ~gebogen~. It means "to bend, to curve, to turn (a corner)." The idiom ~auf Biegen und Brechen~ ("by hook or by crook," literally "by bending and breaking") pairs the verb with its semantic opposite, suggesting that one will either bend something into shape or break it trying. The PIE root *~bʰewgʰ-~ specialized in Germanic for physical bending, while in English the cognate ~bow~ (as in bowing one's head) preserved a more social and gestural sense. The English noun ~bow~ (of a ship) and the word ~elbow~ (literally "arm-bend," from OE ~elnboga~) are also related. Dutch ~buigen~, Danish ~bøje~, and Swedish ~böja~ are immediate Germanic siblings.
en.bieten: From Middle High German ~bieten~, from Old High German ~biotan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beudan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beudaną~, from PIE *~bʰewdʰ-~ ("to be awake, aware"). A class II strong verb whose PIE root conveys notions of awareness and offering. Cognate with Low German ~bieden~, Dutch ~bieden~, English ~bid~, Danish ~byde~, Swedish ~bjuda~.
en.bilden: From Middle High German ~bilden~, ~bileden~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: ~biliden~ ("to form into an image"), from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþijan~, and ~bilidōn~ ("to copy, represent"), from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþōn~. Both derive from the Proto-West Germanic noun *~biliþī~ (whence German ~Bild~, "image, picture"). ~Bild~ itself traces from OHG ~bilidi~, ~biladi~, attested since the 8th century, first in the sense "model, exemplar" and later "likeness, copy"; its further pre-Germanic origin is obscure; German Wiktionary notes only a Germanic stem *~bil-~ meaning "form," with no secure PIE etymology established. The semantic history of ~bilden~ (from "to give something an image or form" through "to educate, cultivate") reflects the deep German cultural connection between ~Bild~ ("image") and ~Bildung~ ("education, formation of character"), the latter concept central to German Idealist philosophy. ~Bildung~ is not merely instruction but the shaping of the whole person as if forming a work of art. Cognate with Dutch ~beelden~, Swedish ~bilda~.
en.binden:
From Middle High German ~binden~, from Old High German ~bintan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bindan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bindaną~, from PIE *~bʰendʰ-~ ("to bind, tie"). A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~i~–~a~–~u~ ablaut pattern (~binden~, ~band~, ~gebunden~). Cognate with Low German ~binden~, Dutch ~binden~, English ~bind~, Danish ~binde~, Gothic ~bindan~.

The PIE root *~bʰendʰ-~ has left an extraordinarily wide trail across the Indo-European family. Sanskrit ~bandhati~ ("to bind, to tie") is a direct cognate, and the English loanword ~bandana~ descends from a Hindi derivative of the same Sanskrit root, meaning "a tied thing." The Germanic noun ~Band~ ("ribbon, bond, volume"), English ~band~ and ~bond~, and even ~bundle~ all spring from this same ancient root. To bind a book (~ein Buch binden~) is thus one of the oldest metaphors still alive in everyday German, the same PIE root that described tying physical bonds in the Bronze Age steppe now describes the spine of a paperback.
en.bitten:
From Middle High German ~bitten~, from Old High German ~bitten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~biddjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bidjaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷʰedʰ-~ ("to ask for, beseech"). A class V strong verb. Cognate with Low German ~bidden~, Dutch ~bidden~ ("to pray"), English ~bid~ (in the sense "to ask, invite"), Danish ~bede~.

The PIE root *~gʷʰedʰ-~ carries the sense of earnest supplication, the same root that underlies Old Norse ~biðja~, Gothic ~bidjan~, and Sanskrit ~bādh-~ (to press, urge). English ~bid~ is a direct cognate in one of its etymological strands; the modern English word has been complicated by conflation with a second, unrelated Old English verb, ~bēodan~ ("to offer, announce"), from PIE *~bʰewdʰ-~, which contributed the commercial sense "to bid at auction." German ~bitten~ remained uncontaminated by that conflation and preserves the pure sense of asking or requesting. The related noun ~Bitte~ ("request, please") and the polite particle ~bitte~ (the most pervasive politeness word in the German language) descend directly from the same root. Dutch ~bidden~ drifted toward specifically religious supplication, a semantic narrowing that German ~bitten~ avoided.
en.blankziehen:
A separable compound of ~blank~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~blank~: From the adjective ~blank~ ("shining, bare"), MHG ~blanc~ ("shining, white"), OHG ~blanc~, from Proto-Germanic *~blankaz~, from PIE *~bʰleg-~ ("to shine, burn"), the same root behind Latin ~flagrāre~ and, by the other half of its sense, English ~black~ ("burnt") and ~bleach~. The Germanic word was borrowed into Romance as French ~blanc~ and Italian ~bianco~, and English then took ~blank~ back from French, so German ~blank~ and English ~blank~ are one word that made a round trip. Cognate with Dutch ~blank~, Swedish ~blank~. The sense of ~blank~ here is the resultative frame: to rub or draw something to that state (~blankputzen~, ~blankziehen~).

The reference is to drawing a weapon from its sheath: the blade is ~blank~, bare and gleaming, only once it is out. Today the expression is usually figurative, for a quarrel carried on in the open.
en.blasen: From MHG ~blāsen~, from OHG ~blāsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blāsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~blēsaną~, from PIE *~bʰleh₁-~ ("to blow, swell"). A class VII strong verb, with the reduplicated preterite of that class long since worn down to the modern ~blies~ (~blasen~, ~blies~, ~geblasen~). Cognate with Gothic ~ufblēsan~ ("to puff up"), Old Norse ~blása~, Swedish ~blåsa~, English ~blast~. The same PIE root produced Latin ~flāre~ ("to blow"), which makes ~blasen~ a distant relative of English ~inflate~ and ~flatulence~.
en.blaumachen:
A separable compound of ~blau~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~blau~: From the adjective ~blau~, MHG ~blā~, OHG ~blāo~, from Proto-Germanic *~blēwaz~, from PIE *~bʰleh₁-wos~, cognate with Latin ~flāvus~ ("golden yellow"), one of the sharper color shifts in the family. English ~blue~ is the same Germanic word re-imported, borrowed from Old French ~bleu~, itself from Frankish. The particle's sense in ~blaumachen~ ("to skip work") is of disputed origin: it is usually traced to ~blauer Montag~, the Monday before Ash Wednesday named for the liturgical blue of Lent and later the artisans' unworked Monday, while the popular dyers' explanation (woad-dyed cloth oxidizing in the air while the dyer idled) is rejected by most linguists, and a derivation from Rotwelsch ~lau~ ("for nothing") has also been proposed. The sense of ~blau~ here is: to skip work or school, of disputed origin (~blaumachen~).

What is unusual here is that the adjective names no property of anything: nothing turns blue. That opacity is exactly why the expression's origin is still disputed.
en.bleiben: From Middle High German ~blīben~, ~belīben~ ("to remain in the same position, pause"), from Old High German ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~ ("to remain"), a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"). The semantic development from "to stick" to "to remain" reflects how physical adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
en.bleichen: A merger of two verbs: the strong intransitive MHG ~blīchen~ ("to shine, gleam, grow pale"), from OHG ~blīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~blīkaną~; and its weak causative MHG ~bleichen~ ("to make pale"), from OHG ~bleihhen~, from Proto-Germanic *~blaikijaną~. Both go back to PIE *~bʰleyg-~ ("to shine"). Modern German conjugates ~bleichen~ weak, the old strong participle ~geblichen~ surviving only marginally. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~bleak~, Dutch ~bleken~ and ~blijken~ ("to turn out, be evident," still holding the older sense of coming to light), Danish ~blege~; the adjective ~bleich~ and the noun ~Blech~ ("sheet metal," the shiny stuff) are from the same root.
en.blicken:
From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine").

The root noun ~Blick~ ("glance, look") is cognate with Dutch ~blik~ ("look, glance; tin"), Danish ~blik~ ("look, glance; tin"), Icelandic ~blik~ ("gleam, shine"), and Old English ~blice~ ("an exposure, manifestation"). The PIE root *~bʰleyǵ-~ also underlies ~bleichen~ ("to bleach"), English ~bleach~, and ~blank~, all carrying the idea of a bright, shining surface. A ~Blick~ is thus a flash of light turned into a directed gaze, and ~blicken~ retains that original sense of a sudden, luminous perception. In modern colloquial German, ~blicken~ has also developed the meaning "to get it, to understand" (~Du blickst es einfach nicht~ ("You just don't get it")), a semantic extension from visual to mental comprehension.
en.blockieren:
Borrowed in the 17th century from French ~bloquer~ ("to enclose, to block"), from Old French ~bloquer~, derived from ~bloc~ ("block, log"), from Middle Dutch ~blok~ ("tree trunk"), from Proto-West Germanic *~blokk~, from Proto-Germanic *~blukką~ ("beam, log"), from PIE *~bʰelǵ-~ ("thick plank, beam, prop").

~Blockieren~ is a Germanic word that traveled to France and came back. Proto-Germanic *~blukką~ ("beam, log") was borrowed into Old French as ~bloc~, which developed the verb ~bloquer~ ("to obstruct with a log"), which German then re-borrowed as ~blockieren~ in the 17th century. This round trip (Germanic to French to Germanic) is a common pattern for words that gained new semantic layers during their French sojourn. The original concrete image of blocking a road with a log has generalized to any form of obstruction: ~eine Straße blockieren~ ("to block a road"), ~Verhandlungen blockieren~ ("to block negotiations"), ~das Rad blockiert~ ("the wheel locks up").
en.bloßlegen:
A separable compound of ~bloß~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~bloß~: From the adjective ~bloß~ ("bare, naked"), from MHG ~blōȥ~, from OHG ~blōz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blaut~, from Proto-Germanic *~blautaz~ ("soft, weak, bare"); the deeper origin is uncertain, possibly PIE *~bʰlew-~ ("weak"). Cognate with Dutch ~bloot~ ("bare"), Old Norse ~blautr~ ("soft, wet"), Swedish ~blott~ ("merely"), Danish ~blød~ ("soft"); English ~bloat~ is usually traced to the Old Norse relative. In verbs the adjective is resultative: ~bloßlegen~ is to lay something bare, ~bloßstellen~ to expose a person. The sense of ~bloß~ here is: to expose to view, to lay open.

~Legen~ is the causative of ~liegen~, so ~bloßlegen~ literally means bringing something into an uncovered state: used of excavations, of pipes and nerves, and equally of connections one uncovers.
en.bloßstellen:
A separable compound of ~bloß~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~bloß~: From the adjective ~bloß~ ("bare, naked"), from MHG ~blōȥ~, from OHG ~blōz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blaut~, from Proto-Germanic *~blautaz~ ("soft, weak, bare"); the deeper origin is uncertain, possibly PIE *~bʰlew-~ ("weak"). Cognate with Dutch ~bloot~ ("bare"), Old Norse ~blautr~ ("soft, wet"), Swedish ~blott~ ("merely"), Danish ~blød~ ("soft"); English ~bloat~ is usually traced to the Old Norse relative. In verbs the adjective is resultative: ~bloßlegen~ is to lay something bare, ~bloßstellen~ to expose a person. The sense of ~bloß~ here is: to expose a person, to show them up.

~Stellen~ stands to ~stehen~ as ~legen~ does to ~liegen~; but what is laid bare here is a person, and the exposure is social rather than physical. That separates ~bloßstellen~ cleanly from ~bloßlegen~, which uncovers things.
en.brachliegen:
A separable compound of ~brach~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~brach~: From ~Brache~ / ~brach~ ("fallow"), OHG ~brāhha~ ("the breaking up, the first plowing of a field"), an ablaut noun to Proto-Germanic *~brekan~, the verb that is modern ~brechen~. Fallow land is thus literally broken land. The verb ~brachliegen~ grew out of the MHG phrase ~in brāche ligen~, lost its preposition in the sixteenth century and fused into one word in the nineteenth. The same noun named June: ~Brachmonat~, the month the fallow was plowed. The sense of ~brach~ here is: unused, lying idle, of talent or capital as well as of land (~brachliegen~).

The agricultural sense receded along with the three-field system; today it is mainly talents, capital, and factory floors that lie fallow.
en.braten: From MHG ~brāten~, from OHG ~brātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brēdaną~ ("to roast"), from PIE *~bʰreh₁-~ ("to heat, boil, burn"), the root behind ~brennen~ and ~brühen~ as well as English ~brew~ and ~broth~. A class VII strong verb (~braten~, ~briet~, ~gebraten~). Cognate with Dutch ~braden~, Old English ~brǣdan~ ("to roast"), Old Norse ~bráðr~. English ~brawn~ ("muscle") is the same Germanic word borrowed the long way round: Frankish *~brādō~ ("roast meat, the fleshy part of the leg") entered Old French as ~braon~ and passed from there into English.
en.brauchen: From Middle High German ~brūchen~, from Old High German ~brūhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brūkan~ ("to use, employ, consume"), from Proto-Germanic *~brūkaną~, from PIE *~bʰruHg-~ ("to make use of"). The semantic shift from "to use" (still preserved in the noun ~Brauch~, "custom, usage") to "to need" is a modern development; the older sense persists in formal and legal registers. Cognate with Dutch ~bruiken~, English ~brook~ ("to tolerate, bear"), Latin ~fruor~ ("to enjoy").
en.brechen: ~Brechen~ comes from Middle High German ~brëchen~, from Old High German ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"). This is the same word as English ~break~: the two are direct cognates, separated only by the High German consonant shift (Proto-Germanic *b remained *b in English but the vowel and consonant system diverged thereafter). The same PIE root underlies Latin ~frangere~ ("to break"), whose past participle ~fractus~ gives English ~fracture~, ~fragment~, and ~fraction~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Old Saxon ~brekan~, and Danish ~brække~. ~Brechen~ covers a remarkable semantic range in modern German: to break physically, to vomit (~brechen~ colloquially), to violate a promise (~ein Versprechen brechen~), and to refract light (~Licht brechen~), all held together by the PIE root's core sense of sudden separation.
en.breittreten:
A separable compound of ~breit~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~breit~: From the adjective ~breit~, MHG and OHG ~breit~, from Proto-West Germanic *~braid~, from Proto-Germanic *~braidaz~ ("broad"). Beyond Germanic it has no secure etymology, and the standard handbooks leave it unexplained. It is the same word as English ~broad~, which preserves the old noun in ~breadth~. Cognate with Dutch ~breed~, Gothic ~braiþs~, Swedish ~bred~. The sense of ~breit~ here is: broad, wide.

Literally one treads a thing broad until it lies flat; figuratively one flattens a topic by going over it again and again. The image stays the same; only the ground is a conversation.
en.brennen:
From Middle High German ~brennen~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: ~brennan~ ("to set on fire," transitive) from Proto-West Germanic *~brannijan~, and ~brinnan~ ("to be on fire," intransitive) from Proto-West Germanic *~brinnan~. The transitive form *~brannijan~ was the causative of *~brinnan~, formed with Proto-Germanic *~-janą~. The intransitive *~brinnaną~ derives from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰrewh₁-~ ("to boil, brew"), making ~brennen~ an unexpected cousin of English ~brew~ and ~broth~. Cognate with English ~burn~, Dutch ~branden~, Swedish ~brinna~, Icelandic ~brenna~.

The merger of two originally distinct verbs into a single paradigm is relatively rare in German. In modern usage, ~brennen~ handles both the transitive sense ("to burn something") and the intransitive ("to be on fire"), a job that required two separate verbs in Old High German. The noun ~Brand~ ("fire, blaze") preserves the ancient strong-verb ablaut grade.

~Brennen~ is also the clearest exemplar of the so-called Rückumlaut verbs: a small group of weak verbs whose present forms carry umlaut (~ich brenne~, with umlaut e from earlier a), but whose preterite forms do not (~brannte~, ~gebrannt~). Phonologically, the *~i~- of the *~-jan-~ suffix that triggered umlaut in the present was syncopated early from the preterite suffix, so umlaut never spread there. Jacob Grimm coined the term ~Rückumlaut~ ("reversed umlaut") for this pattern, though phonologically it represents non-occurring rather than reversed umlaut. Other members of the cohort include ~kennen~/~kannte~, ~nennen~/~nannte~, ~rennen~/~rannte~, ~senden~/~sandte~, ~wenden~/~wandte~, and, with an additional consonant change in the past, ~denken~/~dachte~ and ~bringen~/~brachte~.
en.bringen: From Middle High German ~bringen~, from Old High German ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from a pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring") or *~h₂nek-~ ("to reach, attain"). This verb exhibits a mixed conjugation in Germanic: its past tense ~brachte~ combines a strong-verb vowel change (~i~ > ~a~, from the o-grade *~bʰronk-~) with a weak-verb dental suffix (~-te~). Like ~denken~ (~dachte~), ~bringen~ also shows a consonant change in the preterite (the ~g~ before the dental suffix became ~ch~ by an early Germanic process). Both verbs are traditionally counted in the Rückumlaut cohort, weak verbs whose preterite carries no umlaut because the umlaut-triggering *~i~- was syncopated early from the preterite suffix (other members: ~brennen~/~brannte~, ~kennen~/~kannte~, ~nennen~/~nannte~, ~rennen~/~rannte~, ~senden~/~sandte~, ~wenden~/~wandte~; see ~brennen~ for the underlying mechanism). Some linguists, however, distinguish ~bringen~'s vowel change (i > a, from the o-grade *~bʰronk-~) as a true ablaut grade shift rather than the umlaut removal seen in ~denken~. Cognate with Low German ~brengen~, Dutch ~brengen~, Afrikaans ~bring~, English ~bring~, West Frisian ~bringe~, Gothic ~briggan~.
en.brinnen: Not an independent verb of modern German. ~Brinnen~ was the intransitive strong verb "to be on fire": MHG ~brinnen~, OHG ~brinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brinnaną~, from PIE *~bʰrewh₁-~ ("to boil, brew"), which makes it an unexpected cousin of English ~brew~ and ~broth~. A class III strong verb (~brinnen~, ~brann~, ~gebrunnen~), it survives in German only inside ~verbrennen~; elsewhere it was absorbed by ~brennen~, which began as its transitive causative *~brannijan~ ("to set on fire"). The old intransitive is still a living verb in Swedish ~brinna~ and Icelandic ~brenna~, and English ~burn~ continues both halves of the pair in one word.
en.buchen: ~Buchen~ ("to book, reserve") in its commercial sense is a denominal verb from ~Buch~ ("book"), modelled after English ~to book~. ~Buch~ itself descends from Middle High German ~buoch~, Old High German ~buoh~, Proto-West Germanic *~bōk~, and Proto-Germanic *~bōks~, cognate with English ~book~ and, more surprisingly, English ~beech~, from the same root *~bōks~. Early Germanic writing was scratched onto beech-wood tablets, and the tree name became the word for a written document. There is also a separate, older German verb ~buchen~ meaning "of or relating to the beech tree" (an adjective), from ~Buche~ ("beech"). The commercial sense (booking a hotel, a flight) is thus a modern reborrowing of a concept that traveled from Germanic beech forests to Old English ~bōc~ to modern English ~to book~ and back into German. ~Buchen~ joins English and German in a circular etymological journey spanning fifteen centuries.
en.dabeibleiben:
A separable compound of ~dabei~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~dabei~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~bei~ ("by, at"), meaning "thereby, alongside it, present at it." It is transparently compositional; see the entries for ~da(r)-~ and ~bei~. In verbs such as ~dabeisein~ and ~dabeibleiben~ it locates the subject at an event rather than moving anything. ~dabei-~ marks continued attendance rather than motion.

Unlike the spatial verbs in this group, this one is not about a place but about persistence: one sticks with an activity, a statement, or a decision.
en.dabeihaben:
A separable compound of ~dabei~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~dabei~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~bei~ ("by, at"), meaning "thereby, alongside it, present at it." It is transparently compositional; see the entries for ~da(r)-~ and ~bei~. In verbs such as ~dabeisein~ and ~dabeibleiben~ it locates the subject at an event rather than moving anything. ~dabei-~ places the subject at the scene, present and participating.

~Haben~ originally meant to grasp; in ~dabeihaben~ only the carrying is left: one has a thing along, not in hand.
en.dabeistehen:
A separable compound of ~dabei~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~dabei~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~bei~ ("by, at"), meaning "thereby, alongside it, present at it." It is transparently compositional; see the entries for ~da(r)-~ and ~bei~. In verbs such as ~dabeisein~ and ~dabeibleiben~ it locates the subject at an event rather than moving anything. ~dabei-~ places the subject at the scene, present and participating.

The verb carries an overtone of inaction: whoever ~dabeisteht~ is precisely not intervening, the same reserve that sits inside English ~bystander~.
en.dableiben:
A separable compound of ~da~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~da~: The deictic adverb ~da~ ("there, then"), from MHG ~dā~, from OHG ~dār~, from Proto-Germanic *~þar~, from the PIE demonstrative stem *~to-~, the same stem behind English ~there~, ~that~, and ~the~. In verbal compounds it points at a place or situation already established in the discourse: ~dableiben~ ("to stay put"), ~dastehen~ ("to stand there"). It is the base of the large family of ~da(r)-~ compounds (~dazu~, ~davon~, ~dahin~). The sense of ~da-~ here is: remaining in place rather than departing.

The combination is nearly tautological, since ~bleiben~ already means to stay; the particle supplies the place. The pleasing part is that ~bleiben~ itself contains a fused *~bi-~, the same prefix that is still productive as ~be-~.
en.dafürhalten:
A separable compound of ~dafür~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~dafür~: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~für~ ("for"): a pronominal adverb standing in for "for it, for that", since German avoids a preposition plus personal pronoun when the referent is not a person. ~Da~ is from OHG ~dār~, from the demonstrative stem that also gives ~der~ and ~das~, ultimately PIE *~tó-~. As a verbal particle it carries the sense of advocacy or substitution: ~dafürhalten~ is to be of the opinion, and the nominalized ~das Dafürhalten~ is "one's view". The sense of ~dafür-~ here is: for it, for that, the pronominal referent.

The verb survives mainly in the elevated formula ~ich halte dafür, dass …~, which Luther's translation made familiar. English ~to hold that~ uses the same verb in the same sense.
en.dafürstehen:
A separable compound of ~dafür~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~dafür~: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~für~ ("for"): a pronominal adverb standing in for "for it, for that", since German avoids a preposition plus personal pronoun when the referent is not a person. ~Da~ is from OHG ~dār~, from the demonstrative stem that also gives ~der~ and ~das~, ultimately PIE *~tó-~. As a verbal particle it carries the sense of advocacy or substitution: ~dafürhalten~ is to be of the opinion, and the nominalized ~das Dafürhalten~ is "one's view". The sense of ~dafür-~ here is: in favor of, in support of something.

Strictly the verb means to answer for something, to guarantee that it holds. In present-day usage, especially political usage, it shifts toward standing up for a cause.
en.dagegenhalten:
A separable compound of ~dagegen~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~dagegen~: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~gegen~ ("against"), a pronominal adverb for "against it, against that". ~Gegen~ is from MHG ~gegen~, OHG ~gegin~, ~gagan~ ("toward, opposite"), from Proto-Germanic *~gagin~. As a particle it is either oppositional (~dagegenhalten~, to counter; ~dagegenstimmen~, to vote against) or plainly locational (~dagegenlehnen~, to lean against it). The sense of ~dagegen-~ here is: against it, in opposition to it.

Two readings run alongside each other: the literal holding of one thing against another, for comparison, and the figurative countering of an argument.
en.dagegenwirken:
A separable compound of ~dagegen~ + ~wirken~:

• ~wirken~: From MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~, from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~wérǵom~, from *~werǵ-~ ("to make, work"). Early on it merged with the dialectal ~würken~ (from OHG ~wurken~), which left the written language in the 18th century. Cognate with English ~work~ and ~wrought~, Dutch ~werken~.
• ~dagegen~: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~gegen~ ("against"), a pronominal adverb for "against it, against that". ~Gegen~ is from MHG ~gegen~, OHG ~gegin~, ~gagan~ ("toward, opposite"), from Proto-Germanic *~gagin~. As a particle it is either oppositional (~dagegenhalten~, to counter; ~dagegenstimmen~, to vote against) or plainly locational (~dagegenlehnen~, to lean against it). The sense of ~dagegen-~ here is: against it, in opposition to it.

~Wirken~ means not to act but to take effect; ~dagegenwirken~ is therefore less an attack than a counterforce set against a development.
en.dahaben:
A separable compound of ~da~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~da~: The deictic adverb ~da~ ("there, then"), from MHG ~dā~, from OHG ~dār~, from Proto-Germanic *~þar~, from the PIE demonstrative stem *~to-~, the same stem behind English ~there~, ~that~, and ~the~. In verbal compounds it points at a place or situation already established in the discourse: ~dableiben~ ("to stay put"), ~dastehen~ ("to stand there"). It is the base of the large family of ~da(r)-~ compounds (~dazu~, ~davon~, ~dahin~). The sense of ~da-~ here is: present, on the spot.

Colloquial, and used almost only with an object: whoever ~dahat~ something has it in stock or on hand.
en.daherkommen:
A separable compound of ~daher~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~daher~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~her~ ("toward the speaker"), literally "from there, hither." The deictic contrast that governs this whole group is that ~her-~ points toward the speaker and ~hin-~ away from the speaker. Alongside the spatial sense it carries a causal one, "hence, therefore"; in verbs such as ~daherkommen~ and ~daherreden~ the spatial reading dominates, often with a dismissive tinge. The sense of ~daher-~ here is: motion from there toward the speaker.

Alongside the spatial reading of approaching, a judging one has developed colloquially: whatever ~daherkommt~ as harmless merely looks that way.
en.daherreden:
A separable compound of ~daher~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~daher~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~her~ ("toward the speaker"), literally "from there, hither." The deictic contrast that governs this whole group is that ~her-~ points toward the speaker and ~hin-~ away from the speaker. Alongside the spatial sense it carries a causal one, "hence, therefore"; in verbs such as ~daherkommen~ and ~daherreden~ the spatial reading dominates, often with a dismissive tinge. ~daher-~ often adds a dismissive or aimless tone to the action.

Here the particle contributes nothing spatial any more, only the dismissive tone: ~daherreden~ is talking without thinking.
en.daherschwimmen:
A separable compound of ~daher-~ + ~schwimmen~:

• ~schwimmen~: From MHG ~swimmen~, from OHG ~swimman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~swimman~, from Proto-Germanic *~swimmaną~ ("to swim, float"), from PIE *~swem-~ ("to be in motion, to swim"). A class III strong verb (~schwimmen~, ~schwamm~, ~geschwommen~). Cognate with English ~swim~, Dutch ~zwemmen~, Danish ~svømme~.
• ~daher-~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~her~ ("toward the speaker"), literally "from there, hither." The deictic contrast that governs this whole group is that ~her-~ points toward the speaker and ~hin-~ away from the speaker. Alongside the spatial sense it carries a causal one, "hence, therefore"; in verbs such as ~daherkommen~ and ~daherreden~ the spatial reading dominates, often with a dismissive tinge. The sense of ~daher-~ here is: motion from there toward the speaker.

The compound describes less the swimming itself than the appearing: what ~daherschwimmt~ drifts up until the onlooker can see it. Like the other verbs of motion in this group it forms its perfect with ~sein~.
en.dahinfahren:
A separable compound of ~dahin-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~dahin-~: A transparent compound of the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") and ~hin~ ("thither, away from the speaker"), so "to that place, thither." From the spatial sense German developed a temporal one: what has gone thither is gone for good, which is why ~dahin sein~ means "to be finished, lost, done for." ~dahin-~ marks motion toward a place already named, "there, to that point."

Beside the spatial reading "to travel there" stands an elevated one, already dominant in Luther: "to pass away, to depart this life." The direction away from the speaker becomes the direction out of life, and ~fahren~'s old broad sense "to go, travel" carries it easily.
en.dahinleben:
A separable compound of ~dahin-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~dahin-~: A transparent compound of the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") and ~hin~ ("thither, away from the speaker"), so "to that place, thither." From the spatial sense German developed a temporal one: what has gone thither is gone for good, which is why ~dahin sein~ means "to be finished, lost, done for." Of a slow wasting or drifting, with no goal in view (~dahinsiechen~, ~dahinleben~).

The difference between ~leben~ and ~dahinleben~ is not one of activity but of judgment: to ~dahinleben~ is to live without aim or claim, the time simply passing along with the person.
en.dahinschmelzen:
A separable compound of ~dahin-~ + ~schmelzen~:

• ~schmelzen~: From MHG ~smelzen~, from OHG ~smelzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smeltan~, from Proto-Germanic *~smeltaną~ ("to melt"), from PIE *~(s)meld-~ ("to melt, to soften"). Intransitively a class III strong verb (~schmelzen~, ~schmolz~, ~geschmolzen~), beside a weak causative ~schmelzen~ ("to melt something down"). Cognate with English ~smelt~ and ~melt~ (the same root with and without the mobile ~s-~), and Dutch ~smelten~.
• ~dahin-~: A transparent compound of the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") and ~hin~ ("thither, away from the speaker"), so "to that place, thither." From the spatial sense German developed a temporal one: what has gone thither is gone for good, which is why ~dahin sein~ means "to be finished, lost, done for." Of a slow wasting or drifting, with no goal in view (~dahinsiechen~, ~dahinleben~).

The compound takes up the strong intransitive branch of ~schmelzen~, not the weak causative: what melts away does so of its own accord: snow, a fortune, a lead. The figurative use is the commoner one: a majority melts away.
en.dahinschwinden:
A separable compound of ~dahin-~ + ~schwinden~:

• ~schwinden~: From MHG ~swinden~, from OHG ~swintan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swindaną~. A class III strong verb. The simplex still exists in literary German meaning "to dwindle, wane, fade." Cognate with Dutch ~zwinden~ ("to disappear"), Danish ~svinde~, Swedish ~svinna~.
• ~dahin-~: A transparent compound of the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") and ~hin~ ("thither, away from the speaker"), so "to that place, thither." From the spatial sense German developed a temporal one: what has gone thither is gone for good, which is why ~dahin sein~ means "to be finished, lost, done for." Temporally, of time passing and being gone (~dahingehen~, ~dahinschwinden~).

The simplex ~schwinden~ already says "to dwindle, to fade"; the particle adds no new meaning but duration, not that something dwindles, but that it is in the course of vanishing over time.
en.dahinsterben:
A separable compound of ~dahin-~ + ~sterben~:

• ~sterben~: From MHG ~stërben~, from OHG ~stërban~, from Proto-Germanic *~sterbaną~, from PIE *~(s)terp-~ ("to lose force, become numb") or *~sterbʰ-~ ("to become stiff"), both traceable to *~ster-~ ("stiff, rigid"). A class III strong verb (~stirbt~, ~starb~, ~gestorben~). Cognate with English ~starve~, Dutch ~sterven~, West Frisian ~stjerre~.
• ~dahin-~: A transparent compound of the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") and ~hin~ ("thither, away from the speaker"), so "to that place, thither." From the spatial sense German developed a temporal one: what has gone thither is gone for good, which is why ~dahin sein~ means "to be finished, lost, done for." Of a slow wasting or drifting, with no goal in view (~dahinsiechen~, ~dahinleben~).

Unlike plain ~sterben~, the compound rarely names a single death: it is the dying off of many over time, which is why it attaches to peoples, generations, and whole populations.
en.dahinterhalten:
A separable compound of ~dahinter-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~dahinter-~: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~hinter~ ("behind"), a pronominal adverb meaning "behind it, behind that". ~Hinter~ is from OHG ~hintar~, from Proto-Germanic *~hinder~, a comparative of the stem that also gives English ~hind~ and ~behind~. The particle is often figurative rather than spatial: ~dahinterkommen~ is to get to the bottom of something, ~dahinterstehen~ to back it. The sense of ~dahinter-~ here is: behind it, at the back of it.

Here the particle is purely spatial: something is held behind something else. That is worth noting, because in the commoner verbs ~dahinter-~ has gone figurative: ~dahinterkommen~ and ~dahinterstehen~ have not named a place for a long time.
en.dahinterkommen:
A separable compound of ~dahinter-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~dahinter-~: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~hinter~ ("behind"), a pronominal adverb meaning "behind it, behind that". ~Hinter~ is from OHG ~hintar~, from Proto-Germanic *~hinder~, a comparative of the stem that also gives English ~hind~ and ~behind~. The particle is often figurative rather than spatial: ~dahinterkommen~ is to get to the bottom of something, ~dahinterstehen~ to back it. The sense of ~dahinter-~ here is figuratively: at the bottom of the matter, behind the appearance.

The metaphor is spatial but sits differently from the English one: where English gets to the bottom of a matter, German gets behind it, the appearance stands in front, the truth behind.
en.daliegen:
A separable compound of ~da-~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~da-~: The deictic adverb ~da~ ("there, then"), from MHG ~dā~, from OHG ~dār~, from Proto-Germanic *~þar~, from the PIE demonstrative stem *~to-~, the same stem behind English ~there~, ~that~, and ~the~. In verbal compounds it points at a place or situation already established in the discourse: ~dableiben~ ("to stay put"), ~dastehen~ ("to stand there"). It is the base of the large family of ~da(r)-~ compounds (~dazu~, ~davon~, ~dahin~). The sense of ~da-~ here is: there, at the place or situation already in view.

With ~dastehen~ and ~dableiben~ it forms a small group of posture verbs in which ~da-~ does nothing but fix the place. The overtone is often helplessness: whoever lies there lies and does nothing else.
en.danebenhalten:
A separable compound of ~daneben-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~daneben-~: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~neben~ ("next to"), a pronominal adverb meaning "beside it, next to that". ~Neben~ is itself a reduction of MHG ~in eben~ ("on a level with"), from OHG ~in ebani~, the same ~eben~ as English ~even~. Beside the plain spatial sense, the particle carries a productive sense of missing the mark: ~danebengehen~ and ~danebenschießen~ are to go wide, to miss. The sense of ~daneben-~ here is: beside it, next to that.

The plain spatial sense holds here: two things are held side by side in order to compare them. The productive sense of missing the mark that ~daneben-~ otherwise carries does not reach this verb.
en.danebenschießen:
A separable compound of ~daneben-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb (~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~). Cognate with English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Old Norse ~skjóta~.
• ~daneben-~: Transparently ~da~ ("there, it") + ~neben~ ("next to"), a pronominal adverb meaning "beside it, next to that". ~Neben~ is itself a reduction of MHG ~in eben~ ("on a level with"), from OHG ~in ebani~, the same ~eben~ as English ~even~. Beside the plain spatial sense, the particle carries a productive sense of missing the mark: ~danebengehen~ and ~danebenschießen~ are to go wide, to miss. The sense of ~daneben-~ here is: wide of the mark, to miss, to go wrong.

The verb has come loose from actual shooting: to ~danebenschießen~ can equally be to guess wrong or to say the wrong thing. The same extension shows in ~danebengehen~ and colloquial ~danebenliegen~.
en.danken:
From Middle High German ~danken~, from Old High German ~dankōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankōną~, a denominative verb derived from *~þankaz~ ("thought, gratitude"), from Proto-Indo-European *~teng-~ ("to perceive, think, feel"). Cognate with Dutch ~danken~, English ~thank~, Danish ~takke~.

The PIE root *~teng-~ is the common ancestor of both German ~danken~ ("to thank") and ~denken~ ("to think"), and likewise of English ~thank~ and ~think~. These are not coincidentally similar words: they descend from the same ancient root. To thank someone originally meant to hold them in thought, to bear them in mind. The Proto-Germanic noun *~þankaz~ carried both meanings: "thought, remembrance" and "gratitude." English ~thank~ and ~think~ (from Old English ~þanc~ and ~þencan~) are doublets from this same source. The phrase ~vielen Dank~ ("many thanks") thus preserves, in every syllable, a word that once meant simply "a thought."
en.danksagen:
A separable compound of ~dank~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~dank~: An incorporated noun: ~Dank~ ("thanks"), MHG ~danc~, OHG ~danc~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankaz~ ("thought, gratitude"), from PIE *~teng-~ ("to perceive, think"). The noun is thus the same word as ~Gedanke~ ("thought"), and the pair matches English ~thank~/~think~ exactly: to thank someone was to hold them in mind. In ~danksagen~ the noun stands as the incorporated object of the verb. The sense of ~dank~ here is the noun ~Dank~ incorporated as object: to render thanks.

The compound stands beside the free phrase ~Dank sagen~ out of which it fused, and it has kept that phrase's elevated, largely liturgical tone; the noun ~Danksagung~ ("thanksgiving") is now commoner than the verb.
en.daranhalten:
A separable compound of ~daran-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~daran-~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~an~ ("on, at"), meaning "on it, at it, to it." Transparently compositional; see the entries for ~da(r)-~ and ~an~. It commonly reduces to ~dran~ in speech, and in verbs such as ~daransetzen~ and ~daranmachen~ it marks the thing to which effort is applied. ~daran-~ marks the object to which effort or attention is applied.

The use here is entirely literal: one thing is held against another, usually to see whether it fits. The same verb survives reflexively and in colloquial contraction with a quite different sense: ~sich ranhalten~ means to get a move on.
en.daranmachen:
A separable compound of ~daran-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~daran-~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~an~ ("on, at"), meaning "on it, at it, to it." Transparently compositional; see the entries for ~da(r)-~ and ~an~. It commonly reduces to ~dran~ in speech, and in verbs such as ~daransetzen~ and ~daranmachen~ it marks the thing to which effort is applied. ~daran-~ marks the setting-about of a task.

In its usual meaning the verb is reflexive: ~sich daranmachen~, to set about a task, colloquially contracted to ~sich ranmachen~. Beside it stands the older literal use, to fasten something onto something, which the Bible translation still shows.
en.daransetzen:
A separable compound of ~daran-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~daran-~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~an~ ("on, at"), meaning "on it, at it, to it." Transparently compositional; see the entries for ~da(r)-~ and ~an~. It commonly reduces to ~dran~ in speech, and in verbs such as ~daransetzen~ and ~daranmachen~ it marks the thing to which effort is applied. ~daran-~ marks the object to which effort or attention is applied.

The ~setzen~ here is the gambler's: one stakes something on a wager, and what is staked can be lost. The fixed phrase ~alles daransetzen~ ("to stake everything on it") preserves exactly that image.
en.daraufhalten:
A separable compound of ~darauf-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~darauf-~: A transparent pronominal adverb: the deictic ~da~ + ~auf~, with the ~-r-~ inserted to keep the two vowels apart. It stands for "on it, on that" where English would use a preposition with a pronoun, and it also carries a temporal sense, "thereupon, next." The colloquial contraction is ~drauf~. See the entries for ~da(r)-~ and ~auf~. The sense of ~darauf-~ here is: on it, onto that.

Literally, something is held onto something else. Beside that, ~halten~ with ~auf~ heads a whole field of figurative phrases (~große Stücke auf jemanden halten~ ("to think highly of someone"), ~auf sich halten~ ("to keep up appearances")), in which nothing of an upward motion survives.
en.darbieten:
A separable compound of ~dar-~ + ~bieten~:

• ~bieten~: From MHG ~bieten~, from OHG ~biotan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beudan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beudaną~, from PIE *~bʰewdʰ-~ ("to be awake, aware"). A class II strong verb whose root conveys awareness and offering. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bieden~, Danish ~byde~, Swedish ~bjuda~.
• ~dar-~: From OHG ~dara~ ("thither, to that place"), an extended form of OHG ~thār~/~dār~ ("there"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þār~. The directional -~r-~ marked motion toward a place, distinguishing ~dar~ ("thither") from static ~da~ ("there"). In Modern German ~dar-~ is largely fossilized, surviving as the bound form of ~da-~ before a vowel and in verbs such as ~darstellen~, ~darlegen~, ~darbieten~, and ~darbringen~, where it conveys setting something forth before an audience. English preserves the exact parallel in ~there-~ compounds such as ~therefore~ and ~thereby~. ~dar-~ presents or sets something forth before an audience.

The related noun ~Darbietung~ ("performance") shows where the verb settled: not offering a good for sale but presenting something before an audience. Used reflexively it needs no presenter at all: a view that ~sich darbietet~ does so of its own accord.
en.darbringen:
A separable compound of ~dar-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~dar-~: From OHG ~dara~ ("thither, to that place"), an extended form of OHG ~thār~/~dār~ ("there"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þār~. The directional -~r-~ marked motion toward a place, distinguishing ~dar~ ("thither") from static ~da~ ("there"). In Modern German ~dar-~ is largely fossilized, surviving as the bound form of ~da-~ before a vowel and in verbs such as ~darstellen~, ~darlegen~, ~darbieten~, and ~darbringen~, where it conveys setting something forth before an audience. English preserves the exact parallel in ~there-~ compounds such as ~therefore~ and ~thereby~. ~dar-~ offers or hands something over.

Of the ~dar-~ verbs this one has narrowed the most: it survives almost only in the sacral register, where an offering is ~dargebracht~. It carries ~bringen~'s mixed conjugation over unchanged; ~brachte dar~, ~dargebracht~.
en.darlegen:
Compound of ~dar-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, the causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie"), from PIE *~logʰéyeti~, the causative form of *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). Cognate with English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~dar-~: From OHG ~dār~ ("there, thither"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þār~, from Proto-Germanic *~þar~ ("there"). Related to ~da~ ("there") and the English prefix ~there-~ (as in ~therefore~). The prefix conveys presenting something for inspection, placing it "there" before the audience.

The compound means "to set forth, to explain, to present", to "lay there" an argument or facts for examination. The prefix ~dar-~ is an archaic adverbial form of ~da~ ("there") that survives almost exclusively in a few fixed compounds: ~darlegen~, ~darstellen~ ("to present, to portray"), ~darbieten~ ("to offer"). The root ~legen~ stands in a classic causative relationship with ~liegen~ ("to lie"): ~legen~ means "to cause to lie, to lay," and the pair descends from a PIE construction where adding *~-éye-~ to a verb created its causative. English preserves the same pair: ~lay~ (causative) versus ~lie~ (base).
en.darniederliegen:
A separable compound of ~darnieder-~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~darnieder-~: A compound adverb: the deictic ~da(r)-~ + ~nieder~ ("down"), MHG ~dânidere~ ("down there, at that lower place"). The ~dar-~ variant spread from the fifteenth century under Middle Low German influence beside the older ~danieder~, and both spellings survive. ~Nieder~ itself is Proto-Germanic *~niþar~, from PIE *~ni-~ ("down"), the same element as English ~nether~ and ~beneath~. The word is now archaic and elevated, holding on chiefly in ~darniederliegen~. The sense of ~darnieder-~ here is: prostrate, laid low by illness or ruin (~darniederliegen~).

The verb is the adverb's last living home, and it has come loose from the body: not only the sick lie prostrate but trade, the economy, and morale as well. The elevated, nearly biblical tone clings to it throughout.
en.darstellen:
From ~dar-~ + ~stellen~. Compound of:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb meaning "to place, set", the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand").
• ~dar-~: From Old High German ~dara~ ("thither, to that place"), itself from an extended form of OHG ~thār~/~dār~ ("there"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þār~. The directional -~r-~ suffix marked motion toward a place, distinguishing ~dar~ ("thither") from the static ~da~ ("there"). In Modern German, ~dar-~ is largely fossilized, surviving chiefly in compound verbs like ~darstellen~, ~darlegen~, and ~darbringen~; as a productive prefix before vowels it persists as a variant of ~da-~.

The compound ~darstellen~ (literally "to set forth, place there") shifted from its concrete spatial meaning to the abstract senses of "to represent, depict, portray," much as English ~present~ shifted from "to place before" to "to introduce, perform." Cognate with Dutch ~voorstellen~ (same semantic development, different prefix).
en.darunterhalten:
A separable compound of ~darunter-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~darunter-~: The pronominal adverb ~darunter~, from ~da~ ("there") with the linking ~-r-~ that appears before a vowel-initial second element, plus the particle ~unter~ ("under, beneath"). Like the whole ~da(r)-~ family it refers back to something already mentioned rather than pointing at a place, so it is "under it, among them" rather than "under there." See the entries for ~da-~ and ~unter~. The sense of ~darunter-~ here is: under or beneath the thing referred to.

It is the exact counterpart of ~darüberhalten~, and both are purely spatial: the hand under the tap, the vessel under the spout. Nothing remains in the verb of the figurative "among a group already mentioned" that ~darunter~ otherwise carries.
en.darwägen:
A separable compound of ~dar-~ + ~wägen~:

• ~wägen~: From MHG ~wegen~ ("to set in motion, to weigh, to be worth"), from OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, to move"). A class V strong verb, ~wägen~, ~wog~, ~gewogen~ (rarely weak ~wägte~, ~gewägt~). It is the doublet of ~wiegen~, which generalized the ~i~ of the old present singular and took over the literal business of weighing, leaving ~wägen~ the figurative one, chiefly in ~abwägen~ and ~erwägen~. The same PIE root gave ~Weg~, ~Wagen~, and English ~way~, ~weigh~, ~wain~.
• ~dar-~: From OHG ~dara~ ("thither, to that place"), an extended form of OHG ~thār~/~dār~ ("there"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þār~. The directional -~r-~ marked motion toward a place, distinguishing ~dar~ ("thither") from static ~da~ ("there"). In Modern German ~dar-~ is largely fossilized, surviving as the bound form of ~da-~ before a vowel and in verbs such as ~darstellen~, ~darlegen~, ~darbieten~, and ~darbringen~, where it conveys setting something forth before an audience. English preserves the exact parallel in ~there-~ compounds such as ~therefore~ and ~thereby~. ~dar-~ offers or hands something over.

The verb has died out and survives almost only in the Luther Bible, where silver is weighed out and handed over. The choice of ~wägen~ is telling: in Luther's day ~wiegen~ had not yet taken over the literal business of weighing, and what happens here happens on a balance, not in the mind.
en.darüberhalten:
A separable compound of ~darüber-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~darüber-~: Transparently ~dar-~ + ~über~ ("over, above"), a pronominal adverb meaning "over it, about that". The ~-r-~ is not inserted: ~dar~ is the older full form, OHG ~dara~, ~dār~, and it survives precisely before vowel-initial elements (~darauf~, ~darin~, ~darum~), while bare ~da~ stands before consonants (~damit~, ~davon~). As a particle it is spatial (~darüberlegen~, to lay over) or, following ~über~'s own metaphor, topical ("about it"). The sense of ~darüber-~ here is: over it, above it.

The particle is to be read spatially here, not topically: the point is holding something over something, usually to shield or cover it. The commoner topical reading of ~darüber~ (to be annoyed about it, to speak about it) stays out of this verb.
en.darüberliegen:
A separable compound of ~darüber-~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~darüber-~: Transparently ~dar-~ + ~über~ ("over, above"), a pronominal adverb meaning "over it, about that". The ~-r-~ is not inserted: ~dar~ is the older full form, OHG ~dara~, ~dār~, and it survives precisely before vowel-initial elements (~darauf~, ~darin~, ~darum~), while bare ~da~ stands before consonants (~damit~, ~davon~). As a particle it is spatial (~darüberlegen~, to lay over) or, following ~über~'s own metaphor, topical ("about it"). The sense of ~darüber-~ here is: over it, above it.

Beside the spatial arrangement the verb has found a soberly modern use: figures, costs, and readings lie above a mark. The metaphor matches the English one, only without motion: the value lies above the threshold, it does not rise over it.
en.dastehen:
A separable compound of ~da-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~da-~: The deictic adverb ~da~ ("there, then"), from MHG ~dā~, from OHG ~dār~, from Proto-Germanic *~þar~, from the PIE demonstrative stem *~to-~, the same stem behind English ~there~, ~that~, and ~the~. In verbal compounds it points at a place or situation already established in the discourse: ~dableiben~ ("to stay put"), ~dastehen~ ("to stand there"). It is the base of the large family of ~da(r)-~ compounds (~dazu~, ~davon~, ~dahin~). The sense of ~da-~ here is: there, at the place or situation already in view.

Beside literally standing in a place, the verb has a figurative use that is now the commoner one: to ~gut~ or ~schlecht dastehen~ is to be in a good or bad position. Often the overtone is of being left standing alone and at a loss.
en.dauern:
~Dauern~ carries two entirely separate senses with distinct etymological origins that have been grafted together under one spelling.

~Dauern~ "to last, endure": From Middle High German ~dūren~, borrowed from Middle Low German ~dūren~, itself from Latin ~dūrō~ ("to last, endure, harden"), a denominative verb from ~dūrus~ ("hard, lasting"). Latin ~dūrus~ derives from Proto-Italic *~dūros~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dweh₂-~ ("long, far"), the same root underlying Sanskrit ~dūra-~ ("far, distant") and Ancient Greek ~dērós~ ("long"). The path into German ran through Low German contact in the 12th century, gradually displacing the older native form ~weren~ (a forerunner of modern ~währen~). Cognate with Dutch ~duren~, English ~dure~.

~Dauern~ "to cause pity, to feel sorry for" (as in ~er dauert mich~, "I feel sorry for him"): From Middle High German ~tūren~, itself an ablaut variant of ~tiure~ ("dear, precious, costly"), the Middle High German ancestor of modern ~teuer~. The original sense was "to be dear, to be costly (to someone)", hence "to be felt as a loss, to arouse pity." The initial ~d-~ in the modern form results from Low German influence on the High German form. This sense is thus a doublet of ~teuer~ by a different phonological route.
en.davonfahren:
A separable compound of ~davon-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~davon-~: The compound adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~von~ ("from, of"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: "from that." See the ~da~ and ~von~ entries for their separate histories. In verbs ~davon-~ almost always means "away, off": movement away from a place.

In modern German the verb presupposes a vehicle; in older texts it does not. Luther's ~Renner~ are chariot horses, and ~fahren~'s old broad sense makes the compound simply "to depart" there. Like ~davonlaufen~ and ~davonkommen~ it forms its perfect with ~sein~.
en.davongehen:
A separable compound of ~davon~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~davon~: The compound adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~von~ ("from, of"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: "from that." See the ~da~ and ~von~ entries for their separate histories. In verbs ~davon-~ almost always means "away, off": movement away from a place.

The root already carried the sense "to leave" on its own, so ~davon~ restates in the modern compound what the bare verb once did by itself.
en.davonkommen:
A separable compound of ~davon~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~davon~: The compound adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~von~ ("from, of"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: "from that." See the ~da~ and ~von~ entries for their separate histories. With verbs of motion it usually implies escape or flight, as in running off.

In practice ~davonkommen~ rarely describes a change of place; it describes surviving an ordeal lightly, which is why the fixed phrase ~mit einem blauen Auge davonkommen~ ("to get off with a black eye") is its most familiar shape.
en.davonlaufen:
