A separable compound of ~davon~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~davon~: The compound adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~von~ ("from, of"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: "from that." See the ~da~ and ~von~ entries for their separate histories. With verbs of motion it usually implies escape or flight, as in running off.

Alongside literal flight the figurative use is common: prices, time, and thoughts can all run away from a person without anyone taking a step.
en.davonmachen:
A separable compound of ~davon~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~davon~: The compound adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~von~ ("from, of"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: "from that." See the ~da~ and ~von~ entries for their separate histories. With verbs of motion it usually implies escape or flight, as in running off.

The verb exists only reflexively: ~sich davonmachen~ is "to make oneself scarce," and the ~sich~ names no real object but belongs to the idiom.
en.davonreisen:
A separable compound of ~davon~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~davon~: The compound adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~von~ ("from, of"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: "from that." See the ~da~ and ~von~ entries for their separate histories. In verbs ~davon-~ almost always means "away, off": movement away from a place.

Since ~reisen~ originally meant "to set out," ~davonreisen~ is very nearly a doubling: the setting-out and the away-from-here packed into one word.
en.davonrennen:
A separable compound of ~davon~ + ~rennen~:

• ~rennen~: From a merger of two Old High German verbs: the causative ~rennan~ ("to make something run or flow"), from Proto-Germanic *~rannijaną~, and the intransitive ~rinnan~ ("to run, to flow"), from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~, from PIE *~h₃reyH-~ ("to undulate, churn"). A member of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~ich renne~, ~rannte~, ~gerannt~; no umlaut in the preterite. Cognate with English ~run~, Dutch ~rennen~.
• ~davon~: The compound adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~von~ ("from, of"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: "from that." See the ~da~ and ~von~ entries for their separate histories. With verbs of motion it usually implies escape or flight, as in running off.

~Davonrennen~ is the hastier sibling of ~davonlaufen~, and the base verb's Rückumlaut pattern survives in the compound: ~rannte davon~, ~davongerannt~.
en.davonstehlen:
A separable compound of ~davon~ + ~stehlen~:

• ~stehlen~: From MHG ~stëln~, from OHG ~stelan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stelan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stelaną~ ("to steal"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to rob, steal"). A common Germanic verb with remarkably consistent meaning. Cognate with English ~steal~, Gothic ~stilan~, Old Norse ~stela~, Dutch ~stelen~.
• ~davon~: The compound adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~von~ ("from, of"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: "from that." See the ~da~ and ~von~ entries for their separate histories. With verbs of motion it usually implies escape or flight, as in running off.

This verb too is reflexive, and what is stolen is not someone else's property but one's own person: you remove yourself unnoticed, the way a thief removes an object. English draws exactly the same picture with ~to steal away~.
en.davontragen:
A separable compound of ~davon~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb whose semantic range broadened from "to drag, pull" to "to carry, bear, wear." Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~davon~: The compound adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~von~ ("from, of"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: "from that." See the ~da~ and ~von~ entries for their separate histories. In verbs ~davon-~ almost always means "away, off": movement away from a place.

Beside the literal carrying-off stands a figurative use for whatever someone takes away from an event: the victory, the prize, an injury.
en.davorhalten:
A separable compound of ~davor~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~davor~: The pronominal adverb ~davor~, from ~da~ ("there") plus the particle ~vor~ ("before, in front of"). It is both spatial ("in front of it") and temporal ("before that, beforehand"), and like all the ~da(r)-~ adverbs it refers back to something already mentioned. See the entries for ~da-~ and ~vor~. The sense of ~davor-~ here is: in front of the thing referred to.

Spatial and transparent: whatever is ~davorgehalten~ stands between a viewer and the thing concealed, and the ~da~ always points back at something already mentioned.
en.dazufügen:
A separable compound of ~dazu~ + ~fügen~:

• ~fügen~: From MHG ~füegen~, ~fuogen~, from OHG ~fuogen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōgijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōgijaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to join, attach, fasten"). Reflexive ~sich fügen~ means "to submit": to join oneself to the arrangement of fate. Cognate with Dutch ~voegen~ and archaic English ~fay~ ("to fit closely," from Old English ~fēgan~).
• ~dazu~: Transparently ~da~ ("there") + ~zu~ ("to"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: ~dazu~ is "to it, to that." In verbal compounds it means "in addition, on top of that": ~dazugeben~ ("to add"), ~dazulernen~ ("to learn something further"), ~dazugehören~ ("to belong to it"). See ~da~ and ~zu-~. The sense of ~dazu-~ here is: in addition, as a further increment.

Literally "to join to it", the root already means "to join," and the adverb supplies only the target. In present-day usage ~hinzufügen~ is the ordinary form, and ~dazufügen~ sounds old-fashioned beside it.
en.dazugeben:
A separable compound of ~dazu~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~dazu~: Transparently ~da~ ("there") + ~zu~ ("to"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: ~dazu~ is "to it, to that." In verbal compounds it means "in addition, on top of that": ~dazugeben~ ("to add"), ~dazulernen~ ("to learn something further"), ~dazugehören~ ("to belong to it"). See ~da~ and ~zu-~. The sense of ~dazu-~ here is: in addition, as a further increment.

A transparent compound: what is given is given to what is already there, the measure of flour that goes into the dough afterward, or the amount that rounds a sum up.
en.dazugehören:
A separable compound of ~dazu~ + ~ge-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~dazu~: Transparently ~da~ ("there") + ~zu~ ("to"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: ~dazu~ is "to it, to that." In verbal compounds it means "in addition, on top of that": ~dazugeben~ ("to add"), ~dazulernen~ ("to learn something further"), ~dazugehören~ ("to belong to it"). See ~da~ and ~zu-~. The sense of ~dazu-~ here is: belonging with what is already there.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.

The separability is mixed: ~dazu~ detaches, ~ge-~ never does; ~das gehört dazu~. The path from hearing to belonging runs through listening in the sense of obeying: the household you obeyed was the household you counted yourself part of. The modern verb no longer has anything to do with hearing as perception.
en.dazukommen:
A separable compound of ~dazu~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~dazu~: Transparently ~da~ ("there") + ~zu~ ("to"), one of the ~da(r)-~ pronominal adverbs that stand in for a preposition plus a pronoun: ~dazu~ is "to it, to that." In verbal compounds it means "in addition, on top of that": ~dazugeben~ ("to add"), ~dazulernen~ ("to learn something further"), ~dazugehören~ ("to belong to it"). See ~da~ and ~zu-~. The sense of ~dazu-~ here is: in addition, as a further increment.

The verb covers both: the person who joins a group already gathered, and the item that gets added to a list already made.
en.dazwischengehen:
A separable compound of ~dazwischen~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~dazwischen~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~zwischen~ ("between"), meaning "in between, in the middle of it." ~zwischen~ goes back to OHG ~in zwiskēn~ ("between the two"), built on the numeral ~zwei~ ("two"), so the sense of twoness is still inside the word. In verbs such as ~dazwischenkommen~ and ~dazwischenreden~ it marks an intrusion into an ongoing course of events. ~dazwischen-~ intrudes into something already under way.

The spatial reading (to step between two things) is the older one; the figurative reading now dominates, in which whoever ~dazwischengeht~ breaks up a quarrel or cuts off a speech.
en.dazwischenkommen:
A separable compound of ~dazwischen~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~dazwischen~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~zwischen~ ("between"), meaning "in between, in the middle of it." ~zwischen~ goes back to OHG ~in zwiskēn~ ("between the two"), built on the numeral ~zwei~ ("two"), so the sense of twoness is still inside the word. In verbs such as ~dazwischenkommen~ and ~dazwischenreden~ it marks an intrusion into an ongoing course of events. ~dazwischen-~ intrudes into something already under way.

The verb lives chiefly in the impersonal phrase ~wenn nichts dazwischenkommt~ ("if nothing comes up"), where the subject is an unnamed obstacle that cuts across a plan.
en.dazwischenwerfen:
A separable compound of ~dazwischen~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~dazwischen~: The pronominal adverb ~da~ ("there") + ~zwischen~ ("between"), meaning "in between, in the middle of it." ~zwischen~ goes back to OHG ~in zwiskēn~ ("between the two"), built on the numeral ~zwei~ ("two"), so the sense of twoness is still inside the word. In verbs such as ~dazwischenkommen~ and ~dazwischenreden~ it marks an intrusion into an ongoing course of events. ~dazwischen-~ positions something in the space between two others.

What gets thrown is usually not an object but a word: to ~dazwischenwerfen~ a remark is to hurl it into a speech already under way.
en.deaktivieren:
Compound of ~de-~ + ~aktivieren~:

• ~aktivieren~: From ~aktiv~ + ~-ieren~. ~Aktiv~ is borrowed from Latin ~āctīvus~ ("active, practical"), from ~āctus~, past participle of ~agere~ ("to do, to drive"), from PIE *~h₂eǵ-~ ("to drive"). The suffix ~-ieren~ is the standard German adaptation of Latin/French ~-āre~/~-er~ for creating verbs from borrowed adjectives.
• ~de-~: A Latin-derived prefix meaning "un-, de-," borrowed into German from Latin ~dē~ ("from, down, away"), from PIE *~de-~ ("from"). It reverses the action of the base verb.

The verb means "to deactivate, to disable." It is a fully Latinate creation on German soil; every morpheme traces back to Latin: ~dē~ ("away") + ~āctīvus~ ("active") + ~-āre~ (verbal suffix). The PIE root *~h₂eǵ-~ ("to drive") produced an enormous family across Indo-European: Latin ~agere~ ("to do") yielded English ~act~, ~agent~, ~agenda~, ~agitate~; Greek ~ágein~ ("to lead") yielded ~pedagogue~ and ~demagogue~; and Sanskrit ~ájati~ ("to drive") continued the original sense. German borrowed ~aktivieren~ relatively late, as part of the 18th-century wave of Latinate technical vocabulary. Its antonym ~deaktivieren~ followed naturally.
en.decken: From Middle High German ~decken~, from Old High German ~decchen~, ~thecken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þakkjan~ ("to cover"), from Proto-Germanic *~þakjaną~ ("to cover, to roof"), a causative formation from *~þaką~ ("roof, thatch"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to cover"). The verb is thus etymologically "to roof": to place a covering over something, as one covers a house with thatch. The PIE root *~(s)teg-~ is extraordinarily productive: it gave Latin ~tegere~ ("to cover"), whence English ~protect~, ~detect~, ~integument~; Latin ~toga~ (a garment that covers); Latin ~tēgula~ ("roof tile"), whence English ~tile~ and German ~Ziegel~; and Greek ~stegos~ ("roof"), whence ~stegosaurus~ (the "roofed lizard," named for its bony back plates). Within Germanic, the same root produced English ~thatch~, Dutch ~dekken~, Swedish ~täcka~, and Danish ~tække~. The semantic range of modern ~decken~ extends far beyond roofing: one ~deckt~ a table (sets it, literally "covers" it with cloth and dishes), ~deckt~ expenses (covers them financially), ~deckt~ an opponent in sports (covers or marks them), and ~deckt~ a mare (covers her, the equestrian breeding term). The noun ~Decke~ ("blanket, ceiling, cover") and ~Dach~ ("roof") are siblings from the same root.
en.definieren: ~Definieren~ ("to define") is borrowed directly from Latin ~dēfīnīre~ ("to set a boundary, mark out limits, define"), from ~dē-~ (an intensifying prefix, here meaning "completely, fully") + ~fīnīre~ ("to limit, bound, end"), from ~fīnis~ ("boundary, end, goal"). The etymology of Latin ~fīnis~ itself is disputed: it may derive from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeygʷ-~ ("to stick, fix"), which also produced Latin ~fīgere~ ("to fasten"), a boundary marker being literally something stuck in the ground. Alternatively it may trace to *~bʰeyd-~ ("to split"), a boundary being a place of division. English ~fine~ (as in "fine arts," meaning "finished, complete"), ~final~, ~finish~, ~finance~, and ~confine~ all share this Latin ancestor. When one ~definiert~ a concept, one is etymologically "drawing its boundaries completely", marking where it ends and something else begins.
en.demonstrieren:
From Latin ~dēmōnstrāre~ ("to point out, show, demonstrate"), a compound of ~dē-~ ("from, down") + ~mōnstrāre~ ("to show"), itself from ~mōnstrum~ ("divine omen, portent"), from ~monēre~ ("to warn, advise"), from PIE *~mon-eye-~ (causative of *~men-~ "to think"). Borrowed into German in the early sixteenth century with the meaning "to show, to prove." The protest sense ("to take part in a demonstration") developed after 1850 under influence from the derived noun ~Demonstration~.

The Latin etymon ~mōnstrum~ originally meant a divine omen or warning sign, something shown by the gods as a portent. It is the same word that gave English ~monster~ (a prodigious or unnatural creature seen as an omen). So ~demonstrieren~ and ~Monster~ are, etymologically, siblings: both descend from the act of divine showing. The PIE root *~men-~ ("to think") is extraordinarily productive: it yielded Latin ~mens~ ("mind"), Greek ~menos~ ("spirit"), Sanskrit ~manas~ ("mind"), English ~mind~, ~mental~, ~monitor~, ~monument~, and ~money~ (from ~Monēta~, an epithet of Juno, in whose temple coins were minted).
en.denken: From Middle High German ~denken~, from Old High German ~denken~, ~thenken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~teng-~ ("to think, feel"). A mixed-conjugation verb: its past tense ~dachte~ combines a vowel change (~e~ > ~a~, from the removal of the nasal-conditioned umlaut) with a weak dental suffix (~-te~). ~Denken~ belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort, weak verbs whose preterite does not carry umlaut because the umlaut-triggering *~i~- was syncopated early from the preterite suffix. Other members: ~brennen~/~brannte~, ~kennen~/~kannte~, ~nennen~/~nannte~, ~rennen~/~rannte~, ~senden~/~sandte~, ~wenden~/~wandte~. ~Denken~ also shares with ~bringen~ (~brachte~) an additional consonant change in the past (the ~k~ before the dental suffix became ~ch~ by an early Germanic process); some linguists therefore interpret ~bringen~'s vowel change as a true ablaut grade shift rather than the umlaut removal seen in ~denken~ (see ~brennen~ for the underlying Rückumlaut mechanism). The same PIE root yields ~Dank~ ("thanks") and ~Gedanke~ ("thought"), reflecting the deep semantic connection between thinking and thanking in the Germanic languages. Cognate with Bavarian ~denkn~, Dutch ~denken~, Low German ~denken~, West Frisian ~tinke~, English ~think~, Icelandic ~þekkja~.
en.deuten:
From Middle High German ~diuten~, from Old High German ~diuten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þiudijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þiudijaną~ ("to associate with; to interpret; to point out"), derived from Proto-Germanic *~þeudō~ ("people"), from PIE *~tewtéh₂~ ("people"). Cognate with Dutch ~duiden~ ("to indicate, to interpret"), Icelandic ~þýða~ ("to translate"), Swedish ~tyda~ ("to interpret, to decipher"), Danish ~tyde~ ("to interpret").

The semantic path from "people" to "interpret" is one of the most fascinating in Germanic etymology. The original meaning was "to make intelligible to the people", to translate from learned or sacred language into the common tongue. This is precisely the same word that gives German ~deutsch~ ("German"), literally "of the people," via Proto-Germanic *~þiudiskaz~ ("pertaining to the people"), which distinguished the vernacular Germanic languages from Latin. To ~deuten~ was, in a sense, to speak ~deutsch~, to render comprehensible in the people's language. The modern meanings ("to interpret" (dreams, omens, texts: ~Träume deuten~) and "to point" (~auf etwas deuten~, "to point at something")) both descend from this original act of making meaning accessible. The derived noun ~Bedeutung~ ("meaning, significance") and the adjective ~deutlich~ ("clear, distinct") preserve the interpretive core. That ~deutsch~ and ~deuten~ share a root is not mere folk etymology but genuine linguistic kinship: both spring from the Proto-Germanic concept of "the people" and their language.
en.dichthalten:
A separable compound of ~dicht~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~dicht~: From the adjective ~dicht~ ("dense, tight, watertight"), from MHG ~dīchte~, OHG ~dīhti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þīhtī~, from Proto-Germanic *~þinhtaz~. The modern vowel comes from Middle Low German ~dicht~ rather than the native High German development, which surfaces as early modern ~deicht~. Cognate with Dutch ~dicht~ and English ~tight~. In verbs it is resultative or adverbial: ~dichtmachen~ is to shut something tight, ~dichthalten~ to keep a secret. The sense of ~dicht~ here is: tight, sealed, the resultative state.

Literally a vessel or a seam holds tight; colloquially a person holds tight by not giving a secret away, the mouth imagined as a joint that lets nothing through.
en.dichtmachen:
A separable compound of ~dicht~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~dicht~: From the adjective ~dicht~ ("dense, tight, watertight"), from MHG ~dīchte~, OHG ~dīhti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þīhtī~, from Proto-Germanic *~þinhtaz~. The modern vowel comes from Middle Low German ~dicht~ rather than the native High German development, which surfaces as early modern ~deicht~. Cognate with Dutch ~dicht~ and English ~tight~. In verbs it is resultative or adverbial: ~dichtmachen~ is to shut something tight, ~dichthalten~ to keep a secret. The sense of ~dicht~ here is: shut, closed up for good.

The adjective names the state the object is put into. Colloquially the object is usually a business shutting for good: ~einen Laden dichtmachen~, to close a shop down.
en.dienen: From Middle High German ~dienen~, from Old High German ~dionōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þewanōną~ ("to serve"), a denominative verb derived from *~þewaz~ ("servant, slave"). The etymology of *~þewaz~ is uncertain; one hypothesis derives it from PIE *~tekʷ-~ ("to run"), with "servant" as "one who runs (errands)"; another connects it to *~tew(h₂)-~ ("to swell, grow"), though neither etymology is secure. The same Proto-Germanic root *~þewaz~ underlies Old English ~þegn~ ("thane, servant"), which by a remarkable social elevation came to mean "warrior, nobleman" and eventually became the Scottish title ~thane~, immortalized in Shakespeare's ~Macbeth~. Cognate with Dutch ~dienen~, English ~thane~ (via the related noun), Danish ~tjene~.
en.dingen: From MHG ~dingen~ ("to negotiate, hire"), from OHG ~dingōn~ ("to hold court, negotiate"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þingōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þingōną~, a verb built on the noun *~þingą~ ("appointed time; assembly"), probably from PIE *~tenk-~ ("to be fitting, suitable"). Originally a weak verb: the strong forms ~dang~ and ~gedungen~ are a secondary acquisition that appears to have begun in Middle Low German, so modern German admits both ~dingte~/~gedingt~ and ~dang~/~gedungen~. Cognate with Dutch ~dingen~ ("to haggle, bid"), Danish ~tinge~, and, through the parent noun, English ~thing~ and Old Norse ~þing~. That noun is ~Ding~, which travelled from "assembly" to "the matter debated there" to "any object whatever," the same drift that left English with ~thing~ while Iceland kept its ~Alþingi~.
en.diskutieren: Borrowed into German from French ~discuter~, from Latin ~discutiō~ ("to shake apart, scatter, examine, discuss"), a compound of ~dis-~ ("apart") + ~quatiō~ ("to shake"). Latin ~quatiō~ derives from Proto-Italic *~kʷatjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kwot-i-~ ("to shake"). The original sense of ~discutiō~ was entirely physical ("to smash to pieces, disperse") and only later shifted to the figurative sense of "to examine thoroughly, to sift through arguments." This semantic journey from "shaking apart" to intellectual analysis is a vivid metaphor: a discussion, etymologically, is a shaking-apart of ideas. German received ~diskutieren~ via French contact, using the standard ~-ieren~ suffix that marks French and Latin loanverbs and always produces weak verbs. Cognate with French ~discuter~, English ~discuss~, Spanish ~discutir~, Italian ~discutere~.
en.dokumentieren: A denominative verb derived from the noun ~Dokument~ ("document"), with the productive ~-ieren~ suffix. ~Dokument~ was borrowed from Latin ~documentum~ ("lesson, proof, example"), from the verb ~doceō~ ("to teach, to show"), from PIE *~doḱ-éye-ti~, the causative of *~deḱ-~ ("to accept, to receive, to perceive"). The semantic shift from "a lesson" to "a written proof" happened in Medieval Latin, where ~documentum~ came to mean a charter or official record, something that ~teaches~ you the truth by ~showing~ evidence. The same PIE root *~deḱ-~ produced Latin ~decēns~ ("fitting, proper"), whence English ~decent~, and ~doctor~ (originally "a teacher"), as well as Greek ~dóksa~ ("opinion, glory"), whence English ~doxology~ and ~orthodox~. German ~dokumentieren~ thus etymologically means "to teach through evidence." Cognate with Dutch ~documenteren~, English ~document~, French ~documenter~.
en.dominieren:
Borrowed in the 14th century from Latin ~dominārī~ ("to rule, to dominate"), from ~dominus~ ("lord, master"), from ~domus~ ("house, household"), from PIE *~dóm-~ ("house"), from the root *~dem-~ ("to build, to put together"). Cognate with English ~dominate~, French ~dominer~, Italian ~dominare~.

~Dominieren~ means "to dominate, to prevail, to be predominant." As a Latin borrowing, it stands alongside native Germanic synonyms like ~beherrschen~ ("to rule over") and ~vorherrschen~ ("to predominate"), but ~dominieren~ carries a specifically forceful connotation: asserting supremacy rather than merely holding authority. The PIE root *~dem-~ ("to build") reveals a domestic origin for the concept of dominion: the ~dominus~ was literally the master of the ~domus~, the household. This root produced an extraordinary range of descendants: Latin ~domesticus~ (whence English ~domestic~), ~domicilium~ (whence ~domicile~), Greek ~démos~ ("the people," originally "district", whence ~democracy~), Russian ~dom~ ("house"), and English ~timber~ (from Proto-Germanic *~timrą~, "building material"). The journey from "house" to "lord" to "to dominate" traces the expansion of authority from a single household to an empire.
en.drangehen:
A separable compound of ~dran~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~dran~: The colloquial contraction of ~daran~ (~da~ + ~an~, "at it, on it"), parallel to ~drauf~ for ~darauf~ and ~drin~ for ~darin~. It is not the same reduction as ~ran~, which contracts ~heran~ and keeps that word's deictic pull toward the speaker. In verbs it belongs to the spoken register: ~drankommen~ is to have one's turn, ~dranbleiben~ to stick with something. The sense of ~dran-~ here is: at it, on it, colloquial for ~daran~.

Colloquially it is above all the telephone verb: ~drangehen~ is to pick up, shortened from ~an das Telefon gehen~. Beside that stands the sense of setting about a task.
en.drankommen:
A separable compound of ~dran~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~dran~: The colloquial contraction of ~daran~ (~da~ + ~an~, "at it, on it"), parallel to ~drauf~ for ~darauf~ and ~drin~ for ~darin~. It is not the same reduction as ~ran~, which contracts ~heran~ and keeps that word's deictic pull toward the speaker. In verbs it belongs to the spoken register: ~drankommen~ is to have one's turn, ~dranbleiben~ to stick with something. The sense of ~dran-~ here is: at it, on it, colloquial for ~daran~.

The reading glossed here is inadvertent contact. Far more often, though, ~drankommen~ means to have one's turn: in a classroom it is what happens when the teacher calls on you.
en.draufdrücken:
A separable compound of ~drauf~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~drauf~: A colloquial contraction of ~darauf~, which is the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") plus ~auf~ ("on"), joined by the linking ~-r-~ that German inserts whenever ~da~ precedes a vowel-initial preposition (~darin~, ~darüber~, ~daran~). It is a pronominal adverb, standing in for "on it, on that" rather than naming a direction. ~drauf-~ means "on it, onto it," pointing back at something already mentioned.

Transparent: the pressure comes from above onto a surface, a button, a lid. That ~drücken~ and ~drucken~ share one root is explained by the craft itself: printing was pressing the set type down onto the paper.
en.draufgeben:
A separable compound of ~drauf~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~drauf~: A colloquial contraction of ~darauf~, which is the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") plus ~auf~ ("on"), joined by the linking ~-r-~ that German inserts whenever ~da~ precedes a vowel-initial preposition (~darin~, ~darüber~, ~daran~). It is a pronominal adverb, standing in for "on it, on that" rather than naming a direction. ~drauf-~ means "on it, onto it," pointing back at something already mentioned.

Whatever is ~draufgegeben~ comes on top of a measure already full: the surcharge, the encore, the fifth part added beyond the assessed value.
en.draufgehen:
A separable compound of ~drauf~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~drauf~: A colloquial contraction of ~darauf~, which is the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") plus ~auf~ ("on"), joined by the linking ~-r-~ that German inserts whenever ~da~ precedes a vowel-initial preposition (~darin~, ~darüber~, ~daran~). It is a pronominal adverb, standing in for "on it, on that" rather than naming a direction. Spoken and informal in register; the written form is ~darauf-~.

Idiomatic and no longer recoverable from its parts: whatever ~draufgeht~ is used up or destroyed, the money, the time, and in coarse usage the person.
en.draufhaben:
A separable compound of ~drauf~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~drauf~: A colloquial contraction of ~darauf~, which is the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") plus ~auf~ ("on"), joined by the linking ~-r-~ that German inserts whenever ~da~ precedes a vowel-initial preposition (~darin~, ~darüber~, ~daran~). It is a pronominal adverb, standing in for "on it, on that" rather than naming a direction. Spoken and informal in register; the written form is ~darauf-~.

Idiomatic as well: to ~draufhaben~ something is to have mastered it. The phrase pictures a skill as something laid on and ready to be called up at any moment.
en.draufhalten:
A separable compound of ~drauf-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~drauf-~: A colloquial contraction of ~darauf~, which is the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") plus ~auf~ ("on"), joined by the linking ~-r-~ that German inserts whenever ~da~ precedes a vowel-initial preposition (~darin~, ~darüber~, ~daran~). It is a pronominal adverb, standing in for "on it, on that" rather than naming a direction. ~drauf-~ means "on it, onto it," pointing back at something already mentioned.

The sense is literal: one thing is held on top of another. Colloquially it has also become a verb of aiming: to point a camera or a gun at something is simply to ~draufhalten~.
en.draufkommen:
A separable compound of ~drauf-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~drauf-~: A colloquial contraction of ~darauf~, which is the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") plus ~auf~ ("on"), joined by the linking ~-r-~ that German inserts whenever ~da~ precedes a vowel-initial preposition (~darin~, ~darüber~, ~daran~). It is a pronominal adverb, standing in for "on it, on that" rather than naming a direction. ~drauf-~ means "on it, onto it," pointing back at something already mentioned.

The movement is figurative: what one arrives on is a thought, not a place. English builds the same image with "to hit on it," and in German the idea remains something one has to get onto first.
en.drauflosarbeiten:
A separable compound of ~drauflos-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~drauflos-~: A stacked contraction: ~darauf~ reduced to ~drauf~ ("thereupon"), plus ~los~ ("loose, off"), the inceptive particle of ~loslegen~ and ~loslaufen~. The whole marks a beginning that is heedless of consequence; ~drauflosreden~ is to start talking and keep going without thinking. It is colloquial and appears only in verbs of this heedless-onset type. ~drauflos-~ marks a heedless, unplanned beginning of the action.

The compound names no kind of work, only the way it starts: at once, without a plan and without hesitation.
en.drauflosfahren:
A separable compound of ~drauflos-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~drauflos-~: A stacked contraction: ~darauf~ reduced to ~drauf~ ("thereupon"), plus ~los~ ("loose, off"), the inceptive particle of ~loslegen~ and ~loslaufen~. The whole marks a beginning that is heedless of consequence; ~drauflosreden~ is to start talking and keep going without thinking. It is colloquial and appears only in verbs of this heedless-onset type. ~drauflos-~ marks a heedless, unplanned beginning of the action.

What is striking is that the destination is precisely what is missing: ~fahren~ normally wants a direction, and ~drauflos-~ replaces it with the absence of one. You simply set off, and where you are going is decided on the way.
en.drauflosreden:
A separable compound of ~drauflos-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~drauflos-~: A stacked contraction: ~darauf~ reduced to ~drauf~ ("thereupon"), plus ~los~ ("loose, off"), the inceptive particle of ~loslegen~ and ~loslaufen~. The whole marks a beginning that is heedless of consequence; ~drauflosreden~ is to start talking and keep going without thinking. It is colloquial and appears only in verbs of this heedless-onset type. ~drauflos-~ implies carrying on without thought or aim.

~Reden~ on its own is neutral; the whole colouring of the compound sits in the particle. It turns speaking into speaking without a stop and without a thought, from which the listener gets nothing but the flow itself.
en.draufstehen:
A separable compound of ~drauf-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~drauf-~: A colloquial contraction of ~darauf~, which is the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") plus ~auf~ ("on"), joined by the linking ~-r-~ that German inserts whenever ~da~ precedes a vowel-initial preposition (~darin~, ~darüber~, ~daran~). It is a pronominal adverb, standing in for "on it, on that" rather than naming a direction. ~drauf-~ means "on it, onto it," pointing back at something already mentioned.

Alongside the literal standing on something, the verb has taken on the sense of what is printed: whatever ~draufsteht~ on a sign or a package is written there, the same transfer visible in English "it says on the label."
en.draufzahlen:
A separable compound of ~drauf-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~drauf-~: A colloquial contraction of ~darauf~, which is the demonstrative ~da~ ("there") plus ~auf~ ("on"), joined by the linking ~-r-~ that German inserts whenever ~da~ precedes a vowel-initial preposition (~darin~, ~darüber~, ~daran~). It is a pronominal adverb, standing in for "on it, on that" rather than naming a direction. ~drauf-~ means "on it, onto it," pointing back at something already mentioned.

The paying is done on top, over and above what was agreed. From this comes the commoner figurative reading: whoever ~draufzahlt~ on a deal comes out of it worse off than they went in.
en.drehen:
From Middle High German ~dræjen~, ~dræhen~, from Old High German ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from Proto-Indo-European *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, twist, turn"). Cognate with Bavarian ~drahn~, Dutch ~draaien~, English ~throw~.

The cognate with English ~throw~ is not a false friend but a true one; it is simply that ~throw~ has shifted its meaning dramatically since the Old English period. Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist, turn," not "to hurl," and the act of hurling was expressed by the now-archaic ~weorpan~ (cognate with German ~werfen~). At some point in the Middle English period, ~throw~ displaced ~weorp-~ as the word for tossing and was itself displaced by ~warp~ as the word for twisting, a near-complete swap of semantic roles. The shared ancestry with ~drehen~ is visible in Dutch ~draaien~, Low German ~draien~. The PIE root *~terh₁-~ also underlies Latin ~terere~ ("to rub, wear away"), English ~thread~ (something twisted), and English ~throw~ (in the potters' sense: "to throw a pot" still means "to shape clay on a turning wheel").
en.dreinreden:
A separable compound of ~drein-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~drein-~: A colloquial contraction of ~darein~ (~da~ + ~ein~, "into it"). In the verbs that keep it (~dreinschauen~, ~dreinreden~) the literal "into" sense is largely bleached: ~dreinreden~ is to talk into someone else's business, ~dreinschauen~ simply to look a certain way. See the entries for ~da-~ and ~ein~. The sense of ~drein-~ here is: interfering in something already under way.

The spatial sense has bleached away entirely: what is talked into is not a space but somebody else’s business. The compound has thereby become a verb of interference, closer to "to butt in" than to any literal speaking-into.
en.dreschen: From MHG ~dreschen~, from OHG ~dreskan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þreskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þreskaną~, probably from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, turn"). A class III strong verb (~dreschen~, ~drosch~, ~gedroschen~). Cognate with English ~thresh~ and its doublet ~thrash~, Dutch ~dorsen~, Low German ~dörschen~, Danish ~tærske~, Swedish ~tröska~. Germanic threshing was done by treading the grain underfoot, and Romance borrowed the word in that sense: Italian ~trescare~ ("to caper, to dance") still stamps.
en.dringen:
From Middle High German ~dringen~, from Old High German ~dringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þringwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrinhwaną~, from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). Akin to ~drängen~ ("to push, urge") and ~Drang~ ("urge, drive"). Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~ ("to press, to crowd") and, more distantly, with English ~throng~.

~Dringen~ is a class III strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~dringen~, ~drang~, ~gedrungen~. It means "to press through, to penetrate, to insist urgently." The related causative ~drängen~ ("to urge, to push") has the expected umlaut marking of Germanic causative formation: the base vowel ~a~ from the past tense grade becomes ~ä~ in the derived verb. The noun ~Drang~ ("drive, urge, impulse") is famous from the literary movement ~Sturm und Drang~ ("Storm and Drive"), the late 18th-century revolt against rationalist constraints that launched German Romanticism. English ~throng~ (a pressing crowd) preserves the original sense of people pressing together. The initial Proto-Germanic *~þr-~ cluster regularly became ~dr-~ in Old High German through the consonant shift.
en.drohen:
From Middle High German ~drōn~, ~drōwen~, from Old High German ~drouwen~, ~drōwen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrauwijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þraujaną~ ("to threaten"). The archaic variant ~dräuen~ preserves the older vowel pattern more faithfully. Cognate with Old English ~þrēagan~ ("to rebuke, threaten"), Old Saxon ~thrōian~, Middle Dutch ~drouwen~.

The shift from ~drouwen~ to ~drohen~ involved a simplification of the diphthong ~ou~ to long ~ō~ and loss of the ~w~, a common phonological development in Middle High German. The older form ~dräuen~ (with umlaut from the ~j~ in *~þrauwijan~) survives in literary German and Luther's Bible translation but is otherwise archaic. The derived noun ~Drohung~ ("threat") and the compound ~bedrohen~ ("to threaten someone directly") are far more common in modern usage than the simplex ~drohen~ in isolation. English lost its cognate ~threaten~ (from ~þrēat~, a different formation) but the related Old English ~þrēagan~ ("to rebuke") died out, leaving no direct modern English reflex of this particular Germanic root.
en.drucken:
From Middle High German ~drucken~, from Old High German ~drucchen~/~drukken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~ ("to press"). This is a doublet of ~drücken~ ("to press, push"), which preserves the expected umlaut. The lack of umlaut in ~drucken~ reflects Upper German dialect phonology, where umlaut before a velar geminate was blocked. Since the first German printers (Gutenberg and his successors) were based in the south, this southern dialectal form became the established technical term for printing in the seventeenth century.

The semantic split is clean: ~drucken~ means "to print" (text, books, newspapers), while ~drücken~ means "to press, push" (a button, a hand). Both descend from the same Proto-Germanic root, but the printing revolution cemented two distinct verbs. The derived noun ~Druck~ can mean both "print" and "pressure," preserving the original unity. Polish ~drukować~ ("to print") was borrowed from German ~drucken~.
en.drunterhalten:
A separable compound of ~drunter-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~drunter-~: A colloquial contraction of ~darunter~ (~da~ + ~unter~, "under it"). It survives mostly in speech and in the set phrase ~drunter und drüber gehen~ ("to go every which way, to be chaos"), where the paired reduced adverbs do the work. See the entries for ~da-~ and ~unter~. The sense of ~drunter-~ here is: under the thing referred to.

~Drunterhalten~ is the exact counterpart of ~drüberhalten~, and the two reduced forms live most happily as a pair anyway: the set phrase ~drunter und drüber~ keeps them together.
en.drängen:
From a merger of two Middle High German verbs: (1) MHG ~drengen~, from OHG ~drengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangwijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrangwijaną~; and (2) the now-obsolete ~drangen~, from MHG ~drangen~, from OHG ~drangōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangōn~. Both derive ultimately from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~ ("to press, push") and, more distantly, with English ~throng~ (a pressing crowd).

The fact that two separate verbs merged into a single modern form is an unusual etymological event. The causative *~þrangwijaną~ ("to cause to press") and the denominative *~þrangōn~ ("to act like a press/crowd") converged because their meanings overlapped so thoroughly. The related strong verb ~dringen~ ("to penetrate, press through") preserves the intransitive sense, while ~drängen~ took over the transitive and causative meanings ("to push, urge, press someone"). The noun ~Drang~ ("urge, drive, pressure"), as in ~Sturm und Drang~ ("Storm and Stress"), the famous 18th-century literary movement, derives from the same root. The English word ~throng~ entered the language from Old Norse ~þrǫng~ ("crowd"), itself from the same Proto-Germanic family, making it a Scandinavian cousin of this purely West Germanic verb.
en.drüberhalten:
A separable compound of ~drüber-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~drüber-~: A colloquial contraction of ~darüber~ (~da~ + ~über~, "over it, about it"). It is the reduced form of speech and of fixed phrases, standing to ~darüber~ as ~rüber~ stands to ~herüber~. See the entries for ~da-~ and ~über~. The sense of ~drüber-~ here is: over or above the thing referred to.

Here the holding becomes covering: what is held over a thing shields it, a hand over a candle, a cloth over a basket.
en.drücken: From Middle High German ~drücken~, from Old High German ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Low German ~drücken~, Old English ~þryċċan~ (surviving in dialectal English ~thrutch~). A striking consequence of the same root is the doublet within German itself: ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") descend from the same Old High German verb, with the printing sense arising from Gutenberg-era specialization of the pressing gesture. Welsh ~trychu~ ("to cut") and Lithuanian ~trū́kti~ ("to tear, burst") are cognates outside Germanic, illuminating the original sense of forceful rupture.
en.durcharbeiten:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.

The compound has two readings, both from the thoroughness sense: to keep working without a break (to ~durcharbeiten~ the night), and to work one’s way through material piece by piece, a book for instance. Reflexive ~sich durcharbeiten~ returns to the spatial sense and means to force a way through.
en.durchatmen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~atmen~:

• ~atmen~: From MHG ~ātemen~, from OHG ~ātamōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~ēþmaz~ ("breath"), from PIE *~h₁eh₁tmén-~ ("breath"). Equivalent to ~Atem~ ("breath") + ~-en~. Cognate with Dutch ~ademen~; the archaic doublet ~Odem~ ("breath") descends from *~ēþmaz~ by a different path.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.

The breath is meant to run right through the body, not merely the throat; hence "tief durchatmen" for the deliberate intake of air that in German, as in English, has become an image of pausing.
en.durchbeißen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~beißen~:

• ~beißen~: From MHG ~bīzen~, from OHG ~bīzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bītaną~, from PIE *~bʰeyd-~ ("to split"). A class I strong verb (~beißen~, ~biss~, ~gebissen~). Cognate with English ~bite~, Dutch ~bijten~, Swedish ~bita~; ~bitter~ is this verb's old participial adjective, literally "biting."
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

Literally the tooth goes from one side to the other. Reflexively it becomes endurance: ~sich durchbeißen~ is to see a hard thing through with one’s teeth clenched.
en.durchblicken:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~blank~, Dutch ~blik~, Old English ~blice~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

Beyond looking through a window or a telescope, the verb has two common figurative uses: ~etwas durchblicken lassen~ is to hint at something, and colloquially ~durchblicken~ is to finally see through a tangled matter.
en.durchbrechen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys severing: dividing something into two parts.

This verb is the model case of the separability doublet: stressed, separable ~dúrchbrechen~ is to break in two (~er brach den Stock durch~), while unstressed, inseparable ~durchbréchen~ is to breach a barrier (~er durchbrach die Linie~). The same letters, two verbs, and only the stress tells them apart. The separable verb then divides once more by auxiliary: with ~sein~, a board gives way or troops break through (~die Panzer sind durchgebrochen~), so one spelling holds three readings.
en.durchbrennen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~brennen~:

• ~brennen~: From MHG ~brennen~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: transitive ~brennan~ ("to set on fire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~brannijan~, and intransitive ~brinnan~, from *~brinnan~, of which *~brannijan~ was the causative. The intransitive is from PIE *~bʰrewh₁-~ ("to boil, brew"), making ~brennen~ a cousin of English ~brew~. A Rückumlaut verb: ~ich brenne~ but ~brannte~, ~gebrannt~. Cognate with English ~burn~, Dutch ~branden~, Icelandic ~brenna~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.

The burning is carried through to the end, until the filament is gone; a fuse or a bulb ~brennt durch~. From that sudden parting comes the colloquial sense of bolting: to ~mit jemandem durchbrennen~ is to run off with someone just as abruptly.
en.durchbringen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

What is brought through gets from one side to the other: a motion through parliament, a patient through an illness, a family through the winter. Ironically it inverts: ~sein Geld durchbringen~ is to run it through until none is left.
en.durchdrehen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). Cognate with English ~throw~ (a true cognate: Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist," a sense that "throw a pot" still keeps) plus English ~thread~, Dutch ~draaien~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

Literally something is turned through a device, meat through a grinder. From there the path runs by way of the spinning wheel that keeps turning without grip to the present main sense: whoever ~durchdreht~ is racing free and losing control.
en.durchdringen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~dringen~:

• ~dringen~: From MHG ~dringen~, from OHG ~dringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þringwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrinhwaną~, from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). A class III strong verb (~dringen~, ~drang~, ~gedrungen~); its causative ~drängen~ carries the expected umlaut. Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~ ("to press") and English ~throng~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

Here too separability carries two meanings: separable ~dúrchdringen~ is intransitive and means to get through, to prevail in the end, while inseparable ~durchdríngen~ is transitive and fills a whole (~der Ton durchdrang den Saal~). The causative ~drängen~ shows how much pressure the root holds.
en.durcheinanderbringen:
A separable compound of ~durcheinander-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~durcheinander-~: Transparently ~durch~ ("through") + ~einander~ ("one another"): through one another, hence jumbled, in confusion. ~Durch~ is from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~, cognate with English ~through~. The particle is resultative (~durcheinanderbringen~ is to muddle something, ~durcheinanderreden~ to talk over one another), and the nominalized ~das Durcheinander~ ("the mess") is the same word. The sense of ~durcheinander-~ here is: through one another, jumbled, in disorder.

The verb is resultative: it names not the manner of acting but the state that results. What has been ~durcheinandergebracht~ is a ~Durcheinander~, the very same word, merely nominalized.
en.durcheinanderkommen:
A separable compound of ~durcheinander-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~durcheinander-~: Transparently ~durch~ ("through") + ~einander~ ("one another"): through one another, hence jumbled, in confusion. ~Durch~ is from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~, cognate with English ~through~. The particle is resultative (~durcheinanderbringen~ is to muddle something, ~durcheinanderreden~ to talk over one another), and the nominalized ~das Durcheinander~ ("the mess") is the same word. The sense of ~durcheinander-~ here is: into confusion, muddled up.

~Durcheinanderkommen~ is the intransitive counterpart of ~durcheinanderbringen~: there someone throws a thing into disorder, here it falls into disorder by itself, and usually it is thoughts, names or dates that get muddled.
en.durchfallen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

The falling passes through an opening. Figuratively one falls through an examination (the exam does not hold the candidate) and a play that ~durchfällt~ with its audience finds no purchase either.
en.durchfließen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~fließen~:

• ~fließen~: From MHG ~vlieȥen~, from OHG ~flioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleutaną~ ("to float, stream, flow"), from PIE *~plewd-~ ("to flow, run, swim"). A class II strong verb (~fließen~, ~floss~, ~geflossen~); the zero grade *~flut-~ gave ~Flut~. Cognate with English ~fleet~, ~float~ and ~flood~, Dutch ~vlieten~, Swedish ~flyta~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

Separability here parcels out the syntax: separable ~dúrchfließen~ is intransitive (~das Wasser fließt durch~), inseparable ~durchflíeßen~ transitive (~der Fluss durchfließt das Tal~). The same root also produced ~Flut~, the identical movement made a noun.
en.durchfragen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~fragen~:

• ~fragen~: From MHG ~vrāgen~, from OHG ~frāgēn~, ~frahēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frāgēn~ (a denominative from *~frāgu~, "question"), from Proto-Germanic *~frēgō~ ("question"), from PIE *~preḱ-~ ("to ask"), which also gave Latin ~precor~ and Sanskrit ~pṛcchāti~. Cognate with English ~frain~ (archaic), Dutch ~vragen~, Swedish ~fråga~, Icelandic ~fregna~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

Almost always reflexive: ~sich durchfragen~ is to not know the way and to assemble it question by question until you arrive. The crossing here is done not with one’s feet but with the directions of strangers.
en.durchführen:
Compound of ~durch-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~, from PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross, pass through") combined with *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), a compound root suggesting "to see across, to look through." Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~, West Frisian ~troch~, Yiddish ~durkh~.

The compound means "to carry out, to execute, to implement", literally to lead something all the way through to completion. The spatial metaphor is transparent: a plan or project is guided through the full extent of its path from start to finish. The English expression ~carry through~ shares the same spatial-completive logic. Cognate with Dutch ~doorvoeren~.
en.durchfüttern:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~füttern~:

• ~füttern~: From MHG ~vuotern~, from OHG ~fuotiren~, derived from the noun ~fuotar~ ("fodder"), from Proto-Germanic *~fōdrą~, from PIE *~peh2-~ ("to guard, graze, feed"). A second, homonymous ~füttern~ ("to line a garment") belongs instead to the other OHG ~fuotar~ ("sheath, wrapping"). Cognate with English dialectal ~to fodder~, Dutch ~voeren~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

The passage here is temporal rather than spatial: someone who is ~durchgefüttert~ is kept fed over a long stretch at another's expense, a grudging overtone the word has never lost.
en.durchgeben:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

Alongside literally handing something through an opening stands the commoner modern use, which is figurative: news, readings, and announcements are ~durchgegeben~, passed along from one station to the next.
en.durchgehen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

~Durchgehen~ takes ~sein~ as its auxiliary, as verbs of motion do. Several idioms have grown out of the literal walking-through: a horse that ~durchgeht~ bolts, and to let someone ~etwas durchgehen~ is to let it pass unchallenged.
en.durchgraben:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~graben~:

• ~graben~: From MHG ~graben~, from OHG ~graban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from PIE *~gʰrebʰ-~ ("to dig, scratch, bury"). A class VI strong verb (~graben~, ~grub~, ~gegraben~). Cognate with English ~grave~ as a verb (now only in ~engrave~ and ~graven image~), Gothic ~graban~, Dutch ~graven~, Old Norse ~grafa~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). • ~greifen~: From MHG ~grîfen~, from OHG ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). • ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. en.durchhalten:

• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. en.durchhängen:

The spatial figure is slightly askew here: a sagging rope does not pass through anything but gives way in the middle. Figuratively, ~durchhängen~ names a stretch of flagging energy.
en.durchklingen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~klingen~:

• ~klingen~: From MHG ~klingen~, from OHG ~klingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~klinganą~, almost certainly of onomatopoeic origin. A class III strong verb (~klingt~, ~klang~, ~geklungen~), the same pattern as ~singen~. Cognate with English ~clink~ and ~clang~, Middle Dutch ~klinken~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The verb is now almost purely figurative: a reservation ~klingt durch~ in a speech, carrying through the wording without ever being said outright.
en.durchkommen:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. ~Durchkommen~ takes ~sein~ and covers a wide range, from physically getting through a space to passing an examination, or a bill.
en.durchkriechen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~kriechen~:

• ~kriechen~: From MHG ~kriechen~, from OHG ~kriohhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kreukan~, from Proto-Germanic *~kreukaną~; Kroonen traces the root to PIE *~ger-~ ("to turn, bend, twist"), but the deeper etymology is not secure. A class II strong verb (~kriechen~, ~kroch~, ~gekrochen~).
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

The compound is literal and transparent: the way leads on all fours from one side to the other.
en.durchlaufen:
Compound of ~durch-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~ ("to jump forward, to leap"), from PIE *~klewb-~ ("to spring, to hop"). Cognate with Dutch ~lopen~, English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~, from PIE *~terkʷ-~ ("to cross, pass through"). Cognate with English ~through~. The prefix conveys traversal from beginning to end.

As an inseparable compound (~durchláufen~, stressed on ~-lau-~), it means "to pass through, to go through (a process, a stage)": ~ein Programm durchlaufen~ ("to go through a program"). As a separable compound (~dúrchlaufen~, stressed on ~durch-~), it means "to run through without stopping" or "to wear through (shoes) by running." The stress distinction changes both meaning and grammar: inseparable ~durchlaufen~ takes no ~ge-~ in the past participle (~hat durchlaufen~), while separable ~durchlaufen~ does (~ist durchgelaufen~). This stress-based split between separable and inseparable verbs is a distinctive feature of German that has no direct parallel in English. The PIE root *~terkʷ-~ ("to cross through") is also the ancestor of English ~through~ and ~thorough~, originally the same word.
en.durchleiten:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~: the causative *~laidijaną~ of the strong verb *~līþaną~ ("to pass, go") with the suffix *~-janą~ ("to cause to go"), from PIE *~leyt-~ ("to go, depart, die"). ~leiten~ and ~leiden~ are a base-and-causative pair. Cognate with English ~lead~ (OE ~lǣdan~).
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

Since ~leiten~ is itself already a causative ("to make go"), ~durchleiten~ means, strictly, "to make something go through," which suits pipes, cables, and power grids well.
en.durchlesen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.

The prefix aims at completeness rather than at a path: to ~durchlesen~ something is to get through the text to its last word, in the root's old image, to gather up every letter.
en.durchliegen:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb.
