• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

What is meant is wear caused by lying alone: a mattress is ~durchgelegen~ until the sleeper's weight has pressed right through it at one spot.
en.durchmachen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Again the passage is temporal: one ~macht~ an illness, a crisis, or a sleepless night ~durch~ and comes out the other side.
en.durchmischen:

• ~mischen~: From MHG ~mischen~, from OHG ~misken~, from Proto-Germanic *~miskijaną~ ("to mix"), from PIE *~meyḱ-~ ("to mix, knead"), via the inchoative present *~miḱ-sḱé-~. Cognate with English ~mix~, Latin ~misceō~, Greek ~mísgo~, Sanskrit ~miśrá~ ("mixed").
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The prefix marks thoroughness: to ~durchmischen~ is to mix into the last corner of the mass, hence also the sociological talk of a well ~durchmischt~ neighbourhood.
en.durchnehmen:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The expression belongs to the classroom: to ~durchnehmen~ a topic is to work through it point by point to the end.
en.durchringen:

• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.

The verb occurs only reflexively: to ~sich durchringen~ to a decision is to have wrestled with oneself until the resistance gave way. The old image of twisting and wringing still underlies it, and, despite appearances, ~Ring~ has nothing to do with it.
en.durchrinnen:

• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). ~Durchrinnen~ takes ~sein~ and preserves the root's older sense "to run, flow," heard more plainly still in its cognate English ~run~.
en.durchsagen:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

The path here is a channel: a message is ~durchgesagt~ over loudspeakers or radio, and the noun ~die Durchsage~ has become commoner than the verb it comes from.
en.durchschauen:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

The verb is itself a separability doublet: separable ~dúrchschauen~ ("to look through something"), inseparable ~durchscháuen~ ("to see someone or something for what it is"). The gaze that passes through the surface is the same in both.
en.durchscheinen:

• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). The root covers both "to shine" and "to seem," and ~durchscheinen~ draws on both: light shines through a fabric, and an attitude shines through a text.
en.durchschlafen:

• ~schlafen~: From MHG ~slāfen~, from OHG ~slāfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slāpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slēpaną~, of uncertain further origin, possibly related to *~slapaz~ ("weak, lax, limp"), ancestor of ~schlaff~. • ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

The passage is temporal: one ~schläft~ the night ~durch~ without waking, for new parents, the decisive vocabulary item of a baby's first year.
en.durchschlagen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

Literally a projectile strikes through a wall; figuratively a cause ~schlägt durch~ to its effect. Reflexively, by contrast, ~sich durchschlagen~ means to scrape a living.
en.durchschneiden:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~schneiden~:

• ~schneiden~: From MHG ~snīden~, from OHG ~snīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~snīþan~ ("to cut"); no secure PIE root has been established, and the word may be a Germanic innovation. A class I strong verb (~schneiden~, ~schnitt~, ~geschnitten~). Cognate with archaic English ~snithe~ ("to cut"), Dutch ~snijden~, Icelandic ~sníða~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys severing: dividing something into two parts.

Here too a doublet stands: separable ~dúrchschneiden~ ("to cut in two") and inseparable ~durchschnéiden~ ("to traverse"), as a road ~durchschneidet~ a landscape. The reading described is the separable one.
en.durchschwimmen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~schwimmen~:

• ~schwimmen~: From MHG ~swimmen~, from OHG ~swimman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~swimman~, from Proto-Germanic *~swimmaną~ ("to swim, float"), from PIE *~swem-~ ("to be in motion, to swim"). A class III strong verb (~schwimmen~, ~schwamm~, ~geschwommen~). Cognate with English ~swim~, Dutch ~zwemmen~, Danish ~svømme~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

The separable ~dúrchschwimmen~ is intransitive and takes ~sein~ (one swims across and arrives on the far bank), while the inseparable ~durchschwímmen~ makes the water itself a direct object.
en.durchschütteln:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~schütteln~:

• ~schütteln~: From MHG ~schütelen~, from OHG ~scutilōn~, an iterative formation from ~schütten~ ("to pour, to shake") marking repeated back-and-forth motion. ~schütten~ derives from OHG ~scuttēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skudjaną~, perhaps from PIE *~(s)kewt-~ ("to shake, jolt"). Cognate with Dutch ~schudden~ ("to shake").
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.

Since ~schütteln~ is already an iterative, ~durch-~ intensifies an inherently repeated motion: the shaking goes on until the mass is mixed through and through.
en.durchsehen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.

The compound covers two images: a gaze passing through something transparent, and going over a stack of paper from the first page to the last. The second is the everyday sense today.
en.durchsetzen:
~Durch-~ + ~setzen~. Compound of ~durch-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, place"), the causative of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit"), from PIE *~sed-~ ("to sit").
• ~durch-~: From PIE *~terkʷ-~ ("to cross, pass through"). The prefix adds the sense of pushing through or carrying through to completion.

~Durchsetzen~ is one of those German verbs whose meaning shifts dramatically depending on whether it is separable or inseparable. As an inseparable verb (~durchsetzen~, stress on ~-setz-~), it means "to intersperse, to permeate"; a crowd ~durchsetzt~ with undercover agents, a text ~durchsetzt~ with errors. As a separable verb (~durchsetzen~, stress on ~durch-~), it means "to push through, to enforce, to prevail"; one ~setzt~ a plan ~durch~ or ~setzt sich durch~ ("prevails"). The reflexive ~sich durchsetzen~ is among the most common uses: to assert oneself, to succeed against resistance. The underlying image in both cases is "setting something through" an obstacle, but whether the obstacle is permeated passively or overcome actively depends on stress placement alone. Cognate with Dutch ~doorzetten~ ("to persevere, to push through").
en.durchspielen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.

What gets played through is something with a beginning and an end: a piece of music, a match, or figuratively a scenario whose consequences one wants to follow to the finish.
en.durchstarten:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~starten~:

• ~starten~: Borrowed from English ~start~ with the German verbal suffix ~-en~. English ~start~ traces from Middle English ~sterten~ ("to leap up suddenly"), Old English ~styrtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sturtijan~ ("to startle, set in motion"), from PIE *~(s)ter-~ ("to be stiff"). German ~stürzen~ descends from the same root; the sense "to begin" developed first in English.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.

In aviation ~durchstarten~ is to abort a landing, open the throttle, and climb away again; colloquially it means a forceful fresh start. The mixture is worth noting: an English loan verb takes an old Germanic particle as though it had always been German.
en.durchstechen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~stechen~:

• ~stechen~: From MHG ~stëchen~, from OHG ~stëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stekaną~ ("to stab, prick"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to stick, poke"). Cognate with Dutch ~steken~ ("to stab, sting"), Old Norse ~stinga~, English ~stick~ (originally "to stab, pierce").
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

What is meant is a thrust whose point emerges on the far side, hence the noun ~Durchstich~ for a cut driven through a dyke or an isthmus. The inseparable ~durchstéchen~ is the stress-distinguished twin.
en.durchstehen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.

Nothing is literally stood here: ~durchstehen~ means bearing a strain from its beginning to its end. The image of standing fast rather than giving way is the one English keeps in ~to stand it~.
en.durchsteigen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

The separable ~dúrchsteigen~ is intransitive, takes ~sein~ in the perfect, and describes climbing through an opening: a window, a gap in a fence. It differs from mountaineering's inseparable ~durchstéigen~ ("to climb a face") in both stress and object.
en.durchstellen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

The word belongs to the switchboard: a call is put through from one line to another. The particle preserves the image of the old patch panel, where the connection really was pushed through.
en.durchstreichen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~streichen~:

• ~streichen~: From MHG ~strīchen~, from OHG ~strīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~strīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~strīkaną~ ("to stroke, to rub"), from PIE *~streyg-~ ("to stroke, rub, press"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with English ~strike~, Dutch ~strijken~ ("to iron, to stroke").
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

The stroke runs from one side of the word to the other and thereby cancels it. It must be kept apart from the identically spelled inseparable ~durchstréichen~, which means "to roam or range through."
en.durchtrennen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~trennen~:

• ~trennen~: From MHG ~trennen~, from OHG ~trennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~trannijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trannijaną~. The deeper etymology is uncertain: the Proto-Germanic root is not securely connected to any PIE root. Cognate with Low German ~trennen~ and Dutch ~tornen~, which has narrowed to "to unpick stitches."
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys severing: dividing something into two parts.

Unlike most ~durch-~ verbs, the particle here names not the motion but the result: the two halves come apart. Fittingly, the base verb's own origin is unusually dark; ~trennen~ is one of the few Germanic verbs with no secure Indo-European connection.
en.durchwachsen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from PIE *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Cognate with English ~wax~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

Roots grow through a crack in a wall; fat grows through a cut of meat. The second image yields the frozen participle ~durchwachsen~ for streaky bacon, and, extended wryly, "ein durchwachsener Tag" for a day with good streaks and bad.
en.durchziehen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys passage from one side to the other.

One spelling holds three readings here, and ~durchziehen~ is the first verb in Konjugieren to need three. The separable ~dúrchziehen~ splits by auxiliary. With ~haben~, someone pulls or threads something through (~er hat den Faden durchgezogen~). With ~sein~, troops, a herd, or a rain shower pass through a place (~das Rudel ist durchgezogen~). The inseparable ~durchzíehen~ takes ~haben~ and drops the ~ge-~, and it is figurative: a motif or a scent runs through something and fills it (~das Motiv hat den Roman durchzogen~). Colloquially, the separable verb with ~haben~ has also come to mean "to see something through against resistance".
en.durchzählen:
A separable compound of ~durch-~ + ~zählen~:

• ~zählen~: From MHG ~zel(e)n~, ~zellen~, from OHG ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~ ("to enumerate, count; to recount, tell"). German split this dual sense: ~zählen~ kept "to count," ~erzählen~ took "to narrate." Cognate with Dutch ~tellen~, English ~tell~ and ~tale~, Danish ~tælle~, Gothic ~talzjan~.
• ~durch-~: From MHG ~durch~, from OHG ~duruh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurhw~. The deeper origin is disputed: a compound of PIE *~terh₂-~ ("to cross") with either *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), hence "to see across," or the enclitic *~-kʷe~ ("and"). Like ~um-~, ~durch-~ is a separability doublet: separable and stressed for literal traversal (~dúrchbrechen~, "to break in two"), inseparable for figurative penetration (~durchbréchen~, "to breach"). The senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with English ~through~ and ~thorough~, Dutch ~door~. As a separable prefix, it conveys carrying an action through to completion, thoroughly.

A group is counted from its first member to its last, with none skipped; in ranks, each person calls out their own number. The particle guarantees completeness, not direction.
en.dürfen: From Middle High German ~durfen~, ~dürfen~, from Old High German ~durfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þurban~, from Proto-Germanic *~þurbaną~, from PIE *~terp-~ ("to satiate, enjoy"). A preterite-present verb: its present-tense conjugations descend from what was originally a past-tense (perfect) formation, giving it the irregular present paradigm typical of this class (~darf~, ~darfst~, ~darf~ rather than the expected weak endings). The original sense of "to need" (still preserved in ~bedürfen~) shifted in Modern German to "to be allowed to." Cognate with Ancient Greek ~terpo~ ("I delight, please"), English ~tharf~ (archaic, "to need").
en.ehren:
From Middle High German ~ēren~, from Old High German ~ēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~aizāną~, from PIE *~h₂eys-~ ("to respect, to be in awe of"). Derived from the noun ~Ehre~ ("honor"), which descends from OHG ~ēra~ ("honor, fame, sense of honor"), from Proto-West Germanic *~aiʀu~, from Proto-Germanic *~aizō~. Cognate with Old Norse ~eir~ ("pardon, gentleness"), Old Saxon ~ēra~ ("honor, protection, pardon"), Old English ~ār~ ("honor, help, pardon"), and Dutch ~eer~ ("honor").

The verb ~ehren~ means "to honor, to respect, to pay tribute to." The connection to Latin ~aestimāre~ ("to value, to acknowledge"), whence English ~esteem~ and ~estimate~, has been proposed via the PIE root, suggesting that the Indo-European speakers linked the concept of honor with the act of valuation. The proverb ~Ehrlich währt am längsten~ ("Honesty lasts the longest") uses the derived adjective ~ehrlich~ ("honest," literally "honor-like"). The compound ~Ehrenamt~ ("honorary office, volunteer position") reflects the German cultural concept of unpaid civic duty performed for honor rather than payment, a cornerstone of German community life that has no single-word English equivalent. The expression ~jemandem die letzte Ehre erweisen~ ("to pay someone the last honor") refers to attending a funeral, connecting ~Ehre~ to rites of passage.
en.eignen:
From Middle High German ~eigenen~, from Old High German ~eiganen~, from Proto-Germanic *~aiginōną~, a denominative verb derived from *~aiganaz~ ("owned, one's own"), the past participle of *~aiganą~ ("to possess, own"), from PIE *~h₂eh₂óyḱe~, from *~h₂eyḱ-~ ("ability, possession"). The verb ~eignen~ thus originally meant "to make one's own, to appropriate", a sense still visible in the reflexive ~sich etwas aneignen~ ("to acquire, appropriate something for oneself"). The modern reflexive ~sich eignen~ ("to be suited, to be fit for") developed from the idea of being the proper or fitting owner of some quality or role.

The adjective ~eigen~ ("own, characteristic") shares the same PGmc root and is cognate with English ~own~ and Dutch ~eigen~. The PIE root *~h₂eyḱ-~ ("ability, possession") also underlies Gothic ~aigan~ ("to have") and Old English ~āgan~ ("to own"), the latter giving English ~owe~ (its present tense) and ~ought~ (its past tense). Cognate with Swedish ~ägna~, English ~own~.
en.einarbeiten:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

Two readings share the form: to work something into a text is to make it part of an existing whole, while ~sich einarbeiten~ is to work oneself into a new job until one belongs to it. In both, the thing worked into is the larger structure.
en.einatmen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~atmen~:

• ~atmen~: From MHG ~ātemen~, from OHG ~ātamōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~ēþmaz~ ("breath"), from PIE *~h₁eh₁tmén-~ ("breath"). Equivalent to ~Atem~ ("breath") + ~-en~. Cognate with Dutch ~ademen~; the archaic doublet ~Odem~ ("breath") descends from *~ēþmaz~ by a different path.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The counterpart is ~ausatmen~, and because the base verb goes transparently back to the noun ~Atem~ ("breath"), ~einatmen~ means literally "to take breath in."
en.einbauen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~būwen~, from OHG ~būan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~būan~, from Proto-Germanic *~būaną~, from PIE *~bʰuH-~ ("to grow, to become, to dwell").
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). This separable prefix adds the sense of inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure.

~Einbauen~ means "to install, to build in, to incorporate", a concept central to modern engineering and construction. You ~baust eine Küche ein~ ("install a kitchen"), ~baust ein Feature ein~ ("incorporate a feature"), or ~baust einen Motor ein~ ("install an engine"). The PIE root *~bʰuH-~ ("to grow, to become") is astonishingly productive: it yields English ~be~, ~build~, ~booth~, and ~bower~, as well as Greek ~φύω~ ("to grow," whence ~physics~ and ~physiology~) and Latin ~fuī~ ("I was"). The semantic chain from "growing" to "dwelling" to "building" to "building in" shows language faithfully tracking human cultural evolution from nomadic life to settled construction.
en.einbegreifen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~be-~ + ~greifen~:

• ~greifen~: From MHG ~grîfen~, from OHG ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). A class I strong verb (~greift~, ~griff~, ~gegriffen~), like ~reiten~ and ~schneiden~. Cognate with English ~gripe~, Dutch ~grijpen~, Low German ~griepen~, Old Norse ~gripa~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ promotes what the base verb governs with a preposition or in the dative to a direct object.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

The doubly prefixed verb has grown rare in finite use and survives mainly in its participle: "Bedienung einbegriffen" ("service included"). What is grasped here is not understood but enclosed; the older, spatial meaning of ~greifen~ shows through.
en.einbehalten:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~be-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys enclosing or containing: shutting something in.

The use today is almost entirely fiscal and legal: an authority withholds a share instead of paying it out. The particle marks that the money stays inside, not that anything moves inward.
en.einbekennen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~be-~ + ~kennen~:

• ~kennen~: From MHG ~kennen~, from OHG ~kennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kannijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~ ("to know"), a causative of *~kunnaną~, from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"). • ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

The verb is chiefly Austrian and administrative; income is declared to the authorities. The particle points to entry in a register: the admission is put on the record, not merely spoken.
en.einberufen:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. • ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). • ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). Two uses run side by side: a body is convened, and a conscript is called up. Both call someone in to a place appointed for them.
en.einbestellen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~be-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). • ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Today's use is diplomatic: a ministry summons an ambassador in to receive a protest. Because ~bestellen~ is barely felt as ~be-~ + ~stellen~ any more, the compound is semantically flat: the particle carries the whole of the "in" meaning.
en.einbeziehen:
A modern compound of ~ein-~ + ~beziehen~:

• ~beziehen~: From MHG ~beziehen~, from OHG ~biziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~biteuhan~. Compound of ~be-~ + ~ziehen~:
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). As a separable prefix, it means "in, into."
  - ~be-~: From PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"), makes the verb transitive.
  - ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). Cognate with English ~tow~ (via Old English ~tēon~), Latin ~dūcō~ ("I lead"), and English ~duke~ (via Latin).

The sense "to refer to" in ~beziehen~ is probably a calque of Latin ~referre~ ("to carry back, to refer"). The compound ~einbeziehen~ ("to include, to involve") thus literally means "to pull into," a vivid spatial metaphor for inclusion. The PIE root *~dewk-~ has produced a remarkable constellation of words across the Indo-European languages: Latin ~dūcō~ gave us ~duke~, ~educate~, ~deduce~, ~conduct~, and ~produce~, while the Germanic branch gave us ~ziehen~, ~tow~, and ~tie~. All go back to the fundamental human action of pulling or leading. Cognate with Dutch ~betrekken~ ("to involve"), which uses a different root verb but the same ~be-~ prefix pattern.
en.einbiegen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~biegen~:

• ~biegen~: From MHG ~biegen~, from OHG ~biogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beuganą~, from PIE *~bʰewgʰ-~ ("to bend"). A class II strong verb (~biegen~, ~bog~, ~gebogen~). Cognate with English ~bow~ and ~elbow~ ("arm-bend"), Dutch ~buigen~, Sanskrit ~bhujáti~ ("to bend, curve").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The verb is intransitive and forms its perfect with ~sein~. The image is of the path itself bending inward and leading into a side street.
en.einbilden:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~bilden~:

• ~bilden~: From MHG ~bilden~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: ~biliden~ ("to form into an image"), from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþijan~, and ~bilidōn~ ("to copy, represent"), from *~biliþōn~; both from the noun *~biliþī~ (whence ~Bild~), whose pre-Germanic origin is obscure, with no secure PIE etymology. Cognate with Dutch ~beelden~, Swedish ~bilda~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The verb is used reflexively with a dative: ~sich etwas einbilden~ is to build an image into one's own head, and the base verb keeps that descent from ~Bild~ visible. The participle ~eingebildet~ has broken free and hardened into an adjective meaning "conceited."
en.einbinden:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~binden~:

• ~binden~: From MHG ~binden~, from OHG ~bintan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bindan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bindaną~ ("to bind, tie"), from PIE *~bʰendʰ-~ ("to tie, bind"). Cognate with English ~bind~, Dutch ~binden~, Danish ~binde~, Sanskrit ~bandhati~ ("binds").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁en~ ("in"). As a verbal prefix, ~ein-~ conveys inward motion or incorporation.

The original concrete sense was "to bind something in," particularly book-binding: ~ein Buch einbinden~ means "to bind a book" in a protective cover. The modern figurative meanings ("to integrate" and "to involve") developed naturally from this: to bind something or someone into a larger whole. ~Jemanden in die Entscheidung einbinden~ ("to involve someone in the decision") treats participation as a kind of binding-in. The noun ~Einbindung~ ("integration, involvement") reflects this abstract usage.
en.einblasen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~blasen~:

• ~blasen~: From MHG ~blāsen~, from OHG ~blāsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blāsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~blēsaną~, from PIE *~bʰleh₁-~ ("to blow, swell"). A class VII strong verb, its reduplicated preterite worn down to ~blies~ (~blasen~, ~blies~, ~geblasen~). Cognate with English ~blast~, Gothic ~ufblēsan~, Old Norse ~blása~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Literally, air is blown into something; figuratively, one blows someone their lines, which is exactly what a prompter in the theatre does. Both times something passes inward through a narrow opening.
en.einbrechen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The same prefix carries three readings here: a thief breaks his way inward, ice gives way underfoot, and night falls, in German, breaks in. The third is the most surprising: the onset of a state is imagined as a sudden breaking inward, much as English imagines it as falling in ~nightfall~.
en.einbrennen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~brennen~:

• ~brennen~: From MHG ~brennen~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: transitive ~brennan~ ("to set on fire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~brannijan~, and intransitive ~brinnan~, from *~brinnan~, of which *~brannijan~ was the causative. The intransitive is from PIE *~bʰrewh₁-~ ("to boil, brew"), making ~brennen~ a cousin of English ~brew~. A Rückumlaut verb: ~ich brenne~ but ~brannte~, ~gebrannt~. Cognate with English ~burn~, Dutch ~branden~, Icelandic ~brenna~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

What is burned in is a mark that will not come off: a brand in hide, a pattern in wood or clay. Figuratively an image burns itself into memory, and that figurative reading is now the commoner one.
en.einbringen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from PIE *~bʰrenk-~, a blend of *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring, to reach").
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix conveys the sense of bringing something inward, into a system or enclosure.

~Einbringen~ means "to bring in": covering the harvest (~die Ernte einbringen~, "to bring in the harvest"), financial yield (~Gewinn einbringen~, "to yield profit"), legislative proposals (~einen Gesetzentwurf einbringen~, "to introduce a bill"), and personal contribution (~sich einbringen~, "to contribute, to get involved"). The agricultural sense is likely the oldest: gathering the crop and bringing it inside the barn. The parliamentary sense (introducing a bill into the legislative body) mirrors English ~introduce~ (Latin "to lead inward") and French ~introduire~, all sharing the metaphor of bringing something across a threshold into an enclosed deliberative space. The reflexive ~sich einbringen~ has become a popular buzzword in modern German corporate and civic discourse, meaning to invest oneself actively in a group or project. Cognate with Dutch ~inbrengen~.
en.eindecken:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~decken~:

• ~decken~: From MHG ~decken~, from OHG ~decchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þakkjan~ ("to cover"), from Proto-Germanic *~þakjaną~, a causative formation from *~þaką~ ("roof, thatch"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to cover"); the verb is etymologically "to roof." Cognate with English ~thatch~, Dutch ~dekken~, Swedish ~täcka~; from the same root Latin ~tegere~, whence English ~protect~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys enclosing or containing: shutting something in.

Because ~decken~ is etymologically "to roof," ~eindecken~ in the building trade is close to a tautology: roofing a roof. The reflexive has drifted: ~sich mit Vorräten eindecken~ is to stock up, to get one's supplies under a roof.
en.eindenken:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~teng-~ ("to think, feel"). A mixed-conjugation verb of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~dachte~ pairs the vowel change ~e~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix and ~k~ > ~ch~. Cognate with English ~think~, Dutch ~denken~, Icelandic ~þekkja~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Eindenken~ is all but always reflexive and takes ~in~: ~sich in eine fremde Lage eindenken~ turns reflection into travel, a walking into someone else's point of view.
en.eindrehen:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). • ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Eindrehen~ covers both the screw going into the wood and the hair going onto curlers. In each, the going-in is produced by the turning rather than merely accompanied by it.
en.eindringen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~dringen~:

• ~dringen~: From MHG ~dringen~, from OHG ~dringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þringwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrinhwaną~, from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). A class III strong verb (~dringen~, ~drang~, ~gedrungen~); its causative ~drängen~ carries the expected umlaut. Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~ ("to press") and English ~throng~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Eindringen~ takes ~sein~ and keeps the root's force: never mere entry, always entry against resistance: hence ~Eindringling~ ("intruder") and the sense of penetrating a subject.
en.eindrucken:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~drucken~:

• ~drucken~: From MHG ~drucken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~ ("to press"). A doublet of ~drücken~ ("to press, push"), which keeps the expected umlaut; ~drucken~ lacks it because Upper German blocked umlaut before a velar geminate, and the form used by the first, southern printers became the technical term. Polish ~drukować~ was borrowed from it.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

~Eindrucken~ and ~eindrücken~ divide neatly what Old High German held as one verb: the first sets a text into an existing page, the second physically presses an object in.
en.eindrücken:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix marks destructive collapse inward: something is stove in or falls in on itself.

~Eindrücken~ is the physical half of the doublet, and what it leaves is a dent. That dent was the original ~Eindruck~ before the word turned mental, the same road Latin ~imprimere~ ("to press in") travelled to English ~impression~.
en.einernten:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~ernten~:

• ~ernten~: From MHG ~ernen~, from OHG ~arnon~, from Proto-Germanic *~azanōną~, a denominative from the noun *~azaniz~ ("harvest"), from PIE *~seh1-~ ("to sow"). The modern ~-t-~ (first in MHG ~ernde~) arose from a merger with OHG ~arnōt~. Cognate with English ~earn~, which generalized the same Proto-Germanic source to "to gain by labor."
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Literally ~einernten~ brings the harvest in; today it is mostly figurative, reaping scorn or ingratitude, the same drift from fieldwork to desert that English ~earn~ completed outright.
en.einfahren:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einfahren~ holds several trades together: the miner descends the shaft, the train pulls into the station, and a new car is ~eingefahren~ until it runs smoothly.
en.einfallen:
From MHG ~invallen~, from OHG ~infallan~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~, possibly from PIE *~h₃elh₁-~ ("to fall") with a prefix *~h₂epo-~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). This separable prefix conveys inward motion, falling into something.

~Einfallen~ means "to occur to (someone), to come to mind" and also "to collapse, to cave in" and "to invade." The cognitive sense (~es fällt mir ein~ ("it occurs to me," literally "it falls into me")) provides a vivid metaphor: thoughts drop into the mind unbidden, like objects falling into a container. The military sense (~in ein Land einfallen~, "to invade a country") is older and more literal: troops falling into enemy territory. The impersonal construction ~mir fällt etwas ein~ ("something occurs to me") is one of the most useful everyday expressions in German, with its opposite ~mir fällt nichts ein~ ("nothing comes to mind") being the student's eternal lament during exams.
en.einfangen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~fangen~:

• ~fangen~: From MHG ~vāhen~, from OHG ~fāhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~fanhaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to secure, fasten"). A strong verb, originally ~fāhan~ / ~fieng~ / ~gefangan~; the modern present stem ~fang-~ was taken analogically from the past forms. Cognate with English ~fang~, Dutch ~vangen~, West Frisian ~fange~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys enclosing or containing: shutting something in.

~Einfangen~ ends not at the seizing but at the keeping, which is why one can also capture a light or a mood, held without ever being grasped.
en.einfassen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~fassen~:

• ~fassen~: From MHG ~vazzen~, from OHG ~fazzōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fatōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fatōną~ ("to hold, seize"), a weak class 2 verb, from PIE *~pod-néh₂-ti~, from *~pod-~ ("to fetch"). German kept the sense of grasping and holding, English that of going to retrieve. Cognate with English ~fetch~; the noun ~Fass~ ("barrel") shares the root.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys enclosing or containing: shutting something in.

~Einfassen~ names the border, not the contents: a stone is set in gold, a flower bed edged with stones; the noun ~Einfassung~ is precisely that rim.
en.einfinden:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~finden~:

• ~finden~: From MHG ~vinden~, from OHG ~findan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~finþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to go, pass; path, bridge"). The development from "to go, pass" to "to find" parallels shifts in Slavic. Cognate with English ~find~, Dutch ~vinden~, Low German ~finden~, Danish ~finde~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einfinden~ is always reflexive and formal in register: to ~sich einfinden~ is to present oneself at an appointed place, the ~finden~ here is not searching but the root's older "going."
en.einflechten:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~flechten~:

• ~flechten~: From MHG ~vlëhten~, from OHG ~flëhtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~flehtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~flehtaną~, from PIE *~pleḱ-~ ("to plait, weave"). A class III strong verb (~flechten~, ~flocht~, ~geflochten~), its Präteritum ~o~ generalized from the old plural stem. Cognate with English ~flax~, Dutch ~vlechten~, Old Norse ~flétta~, Swedish ~fläta~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

From braid to speech: ~einflechten~ first leads a strand into a plait, then slips a remark into a conversation without breaking its thread.
en.einfließen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~fließen~:

• ~fließen~: From MHG ~vlieȥen~, from OHG ~flioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleutaną~ ("to float, stream, flow"), from PIE *~plewd-~ ("to flow, run, swim"). A class II strong verb (~fließen~, ~floss~, ~geflossen~); the zero grade *~flut-~ gave ~Flut~. Cognate with English ~fleet~, ~float~ and ~flood~, Dutch ~vlieten~, Swedish ~flyta~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einfließen~ is now nearly always figurative: figures feed into a calculation, and to ~eine Bemerkung einfließen lassen~ is to drop a remark as though it had arrived on its own.
en.einfrieren:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~frieren~:

• ~frieren~: From MHG ~vriesen~ (beside ~vrieren~), from OHG ~friosan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~freusan~, from Proto-Germanic *~freusaną~, from PIE *~prews-~ ("to freeze, frost"). A class II strong verb (~frieren~, ~fror~, ~gefroren~); the ~r~ arose by grammatischer Wechsel in the past forms and spread to the infinitive, as in ~verlieren~. Cognate with English ~freeze~ and ~frost~, Dutch ~vriezen~, Danish ~fryse~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix marks the onset of a state, the moment of entering into it.

Intransitive ~einfrieren~ takes ~sein~ and names the moment frost sets in; transitively and figuratively one freezes wages, funds, or negotiations; they stop moving without going away.
en.einfügen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~fügen~. Cognate with Dutch ~invoegen~.

• ~fügen~: From MHG ~füegen~, ~fuogen~, from OHG ~fuogen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōgijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōgijaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to join, attach"). Cognate with Dutch ~voegen~ and the dated English ~fay~ ("to join, fit together").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn-~, from OHG ~in-~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). This prefix adds the sense of inserting or placing into.

The PIE root *~peh₂ḱ-~ connects ~einfügen~ to a remarkable family of words about joining and agreement. Through Latin ~pacisci~ ("to agree, make a covenant"), it produced English ~peace~, ~pact~, ~pacify~, and ~pay~ (originally "to appease"). English ~fair~ is also a distant relative, via the Germanic branch of the root. The reflexive ~sich einfügen~ means "to fit in, to adapt," capturing the social dimension of joining a group. The noun ~Fuge~ ("joint, seam") and the musical term ~Fuge~ ("fugue," a composition where voices are joined in imitation) both descend from the same root. The compound is transparent: to place (~fügen~) something in (~ein~), making it one of those German verbs that is easier to understand etymologically than its Latin-derived English equivalent ~insert~ (from Latin ~inserere~, "to plant in").
en.einfühlen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~fühlen~:

• ~fühlen~: From northern MHG ~vüelen~, from OHG ~fuolen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōlijan~ ("to feel"); the further origin is uncertain, presumably related to Old Norse ~falma~ ("to grope"), and possibly a secondary causative of a strong *~falaną~, from PIE *~pelh₁-~ ("to stroke"). Cognate with English ~feel~, Dutch ~voelen~, Danish ~føle~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

This verb gave the noun ~Einfühlung~, the guiding term of nineteenth-century aesthetics, which Edward Titchener carried into English in 1909 as ~empathy~, coined on Greek ~empatheia~. The English word is thus a loan translation of this German compound.
en.einführen:
From Middle High German ~īnvüeren~, equivalent to ~ein-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, a causative of Proto-Germanic *~faraną~ ("to travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross, to go through").
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix adds the sense of bringing something inward or initiating.

~Einführen~ means both "to introduce" (a concept, a person, a reform) and "to import" (goods into a country), the prefix ~ein-~ captures the act of leading something inward, whether into awareness or across a border. The derived noun ~Einführung~ ("introduction") is the standard German word for an introductory text, course, or presentation. The import sense gives ~Einfuhr~ ("import"), a nominalization that pairs neatly with ~Ausfuhr~ ("export," from ~ausführen~), the in-leading and out-leading of goods. Cognate with Dutch ~invoeren~.
en.einfüllen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~füllen~:

• ~füllen~: From MHG ~vüllen~, from OHG ~fullen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fullijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullijaną~ ("to make full"), the causative of *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pl̥h₁nós~ ("full"). English ~fill~ and ~füllen~ are exact cognates, each the causative of its native word for "full." Cognate with English ~fill~, Dutch ~vullen~, Danish ~fylde~, Swedish ~fylla~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einfüllen~ puts something into a vessel; the vessel itself is not ~eingefüllt~ but ~gefüllt~. A form, likewise, is not filled in but ~ausgefüllt~; German assigns the directions differently from English.
en.eingeben:
From Middle High German ~īngeben~, from Old High German ~ingeban~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~geban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (which replaced the native Old English ~giefan~ only in form, keeping the meaning), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). As a separable verbal prefix, it means "in, into."

The literal meaning is "to give in(to)," yielding two principal modern senses: "to enter, to input" (data into a computer or system) and "to inspire, to suggest" (an idea into someone's mind). The computing sense is a natural modern extension of the older meaning: feeding information into a machine is metaphorically giving something into it. The older sense of divine or creative inspiration (~Eingebung~, "inspiration, intuition") preserves the idea that ideas are "given into" the mind from an external source. Cognate with Scots ~ingive~. The PIE root *~gʰebʰ-~ shows an intriguing semantic ambiguity between "to give" and "to take" across different branches: while Germanic languages settled on "to give," Slavic languages like Russian developed "to seize, to take" from the same root, suggesting the original sense may have been the neutral physical act of transferring, with the direction depending on perspective.
en.eingehen:
~Ein-~ + ~gehen~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from OHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave").
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix adds the sense of going into, entering.

~Eingehen~ is one of German's most semantically branched verbs. As a separable verb it means: "to enter (into an agreement), to go into (a topic), to shrink (of fabric), to wither and die (of plants), to arrive (of mail)." The image in each case is something moving inward: into a contract, into a subject, into smaller dimensions, into death, into a mailbox. The phrase ~auf etwas eingehen~ ("to address, respond to, engage with something") is ubiquitous in academic and professional discourse: one ~geht ein auf~ a question by entering into it. The sense "to wither" (~die Pflanze geht ein~, "the plant is dying") uses the same inward-collapse metaphor: the plant goes into itself, contracts, and ceases. The PIE root *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave") produces the paradox that "going" originally meant "leaving", a reminder that direction is always relative to a starting point. Cognate with Dutch ~ingaan~.
en.eingestehen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~ge-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The ~ein-~ here is not the spatial one but the conceding one, as in ~einräumen~ and ~einwilligen~: something is let stand against oneself. ~Gestehen~ alone already means "to confess"; ~eingestehen~ adds that the confessing is reluctant.
en.eingießen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~gießen~:

• ~gießen~: From MHG ~giezen~, from OHG ~giozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geutan~ ("to pour"), from Proto-Germanic *~geutaną~, from PIE *~gʰewd-~ ("to pour"). The sense of casting metal and glass is attested since Old High German (participle ~gigozzan~). Cognate with English ~gush~, Dutch ~gieten~, Old English ~geotan~, Gothic ~giutan~, Swedish ~gjuta~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Eingießen~ is the everyday filling of a vessel; the technical sense of casting metal and glass stays with plain ~gießen~ and the noun ~Guss~.
en.eingraben:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~graben~:

• ~graben~: From MHG ~graben~, from OHG ~graban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from PIE *~gʰrebʰ-~ ("to dig, scratch, bury"). A class VI strong verb (~graben~, ~grub~, ~gegraben~). Cognate with English ~grave~ as a verb (now only in ~engrave~ and ~graven image~), Gothic ~graban~, Dutch ~graven~, Old Norse ~grafa~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Eingraben~ runs from burying in soil, through soldiers digging themselves in, to cutting an inscription into stone; reflexively and figuratively an image ~gräbt sich ins Gedächtnis ein~. English says ~engrave~ for that, by way of French, but from the same Germanic root.
en.eingreifen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~greifen~:

• ~greifen~: From MHG ~grîfen~, from OHG ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). A class I strong verb (~greift~, ~griff~, ~gegriffen~), like ~reiten~ and ~schneiden~. Cognate with English ~gripe~, Dutch ~grijpen~, Low German ~griepen~, Old Norse ~gripa~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Quite literally, gearwheels ~greifen ineinander ein~; from that came intervening in a course of events, and the noun ~Eingriff~ is today both a measure of state and a surgical operation.
en.einhalten:
From ~ein-~ + ~halten~, an alteration of the older ~innehalten~, which originally shared the same meanings but has since narrowed to "to pause, to wait":

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~, from PIE *~kel-~ ("to drive, to herd").
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix conveys the sense of holding something inward, keeping it contained, or maintaining an internal commitment.

~Einhalten~ primarily means "to keep, to stick to, to comply with": rules (~Regeln einhalten~), deadlines (~Fristen einhalten~), promises (~Versprechen einhalten~), and appointments (~Termine einhalten~). The underlying image is of holding something inside, keeping it intact rather than letting it slip. The older and now rare sense of "to hold back, to contain" survives in literary usage: ~Er konnte die nervösen Pferde nicht mehr einhalten~ ("He could no longer hold back the nervous horses"). A colloquial sense unique to German is "to hold one's pee" (~Kannst du noch einhalten?~ ("Can you hold it in?")) holding something in quite literally. The dated literary usage ~Haltet ein!~ ("Desist!") preserves the imperative sense of stopping, halting an action by holding it in check. The derived noun ~Einhaltung~ ("compliance, observance") is a staple of legal and regulatory German. Related to ~Einhalt~ ("halt, cessation"), as in ~Einhalt gebieten~ ("to put a stop to"). Cognate with Dutch ~inhouden~ ("to contain, to hold back").
en.einhandeln:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~handeln~:

• ~handeln~: From MHG ~handeln~, from OHG ~hantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handulōn~, a denominative verb from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~ ("hand") with the frequentative suffix *~-lōną~; the sense broadened from "to handle" to "to act, deal, trade." Cognate with English ~handle~, Dutch ~handelen~, Danish ~handle~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Originally one acquired something by barter; today the verb is nearly always reflexive and reserved for the unwelcome: ~sich Ärger einhandeln~, to land oneself in trouble.
en.einheben:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb: the past ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ continue the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einheben~ is Austrian officialese: taxes and fees are ~eingehoben~ there, where German administration ~erhebt~ them: the same root under a different prefix.
en.einherfahren:
A separable compound of ~einher-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~einher-~: The adverb ~ein~ (the older directional "in," as in ~einsteigen~) + ~her~ ("toward the speaker"), yielding "along, forth." It is transparently compositional and no longer used freely. In ~einhergehen~ it once described walking along in a particular manner, and the modern idiom ~einhergehen mit~ ("to go hand in hand with") extends that from gait to abstract accompaniment. The sense of ~einher-~ here is: motion along or forth, often describing manner of gait.

~Einherfahren~ is archaic today, surviving mainly in biblical language where God ~fährt einher~ upon the clouds. The image carries there only because ~fahren~ still holds its broad old sense of travelling: a chariot is meant, not a car.
en.einhergehen:
A separable compound of ~einher-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave").
