The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~einher-~: The adverb ~ein~ (the older directional "in," as in ~einsteigen~) + ~her~ ("toward the speaker"), yielding "along, forth." It is transparently compositional and no longer used freely. In ~einhergehen~ it once described walking along in a particular manner, and the modern idiom ~einhergehen mit~ ("to go hand in hand with") extends that from gait to abstract accompaniment. The sense of ~einher-~ here is in modern use, accompaniment: one thing going together with another.

Of the few ~einher-~ verbs, ~einhergehen~ alone stayed in everyday use, and it gave up its motion to do so: what ~einhergeht~ with something now merely occurs alongside it. The walking itself (proud or wretched) survives in biblical and poetic register.
en.einherschreiten:
A separable compound of ~einher-~ + ~schreiten~:

• ~schreiten~: From MHG ~schrīten~, from OHG ~skrītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīþan~ ("to step, stride"), from Proto-Germanic *~skrīþaną~ ("to walk, glide, crawl"), from PIE *~(s)kreyt-~ ("to stride"), an extension of *~(s)krey-~ ("to go about"). Cognate with Lithuanian ~skrìsti~ ("to rush, run"), Latvian ~skrìet~ ("to run, fly"). Related to ~Schritt~ ("step").
• ~einher-~: The adverb ~ein~ (the older directional "in," as in ~einsteigen~) + ~her~ ("toward the speaker"), yielding "along, forth." It is transparently compositional and no longer used freely. In ~einhergehen~ it once described walking along in a particular manner, and the modern idiom ~einhergehen mit~ ("to go hand in hand with") extends that from gait to abstract accompaniment. The sense of ~einher-~ here is: motion along or forth, often describing manner of gait.

~Einherschreiten~ belongs wholly to the elevated register: ~schreiten~ is already more ceremonious than ~gehen~, and ~einher-~ heightens it further, one strides forth in order to be seen.
en.einholen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~holen~:

• ~holen~: From MHG ~holen~, ~holn~, from OHG ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get, draw"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~halōną~, *~hulōną~ ("to call, fetch, summon"), from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, cry, summon"). Related to English ~haul~ (borrowed into English from Old French ~haler~, which was itself borrowed from a Germanic source).
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). As a separable prefix, it means "in, into."

~Einholen~ has two distinct meanings: "to catch up with" (~einen Vorsprung einholen~ = "to close a lead") and "to fetch, to obtain" (~Erkundigungen einholen~ = "to make inquiries," ~Genehmigungen einholen~ = "to obtain approvals"). The connection between ~holen~ and English ~haul~ reveals a circular borrowing: Proto-Germanic *~halōną~ was borrowed into Old French as ~haler~, which was then borrowed into Middle English as ~haul~. So English ~haul~ is a Germanic word that took a detour through French before returning to the Germanic family.
en.einigen:
From Middle High German ~einegen~, ~einigen~, from Old High German ~gieinīgen~. Compound of ~ein~ + ~-igen~:

• ~ein~: From MHG ~ein~, from OHG ~ein~ ("one"), from Proto-West Germanic *~ain~, from Proto-Germanic *~ainaz~, from PIE *~h₁óynos~ ("one, single"). Cognate with English ~one~, Dutch ~een~, Danish ~en~.
• ~-igen~: A denominal/deadjectival suffix forming verbs from adjectives or nouns.

The verb means "to unite, to agree" and reflexively ~sich einigen~ means "to come to an agreement." The derivation from ~ein~ ("one") is transparent: to ~einigen~ is to make ~einig~ ("united, in agreement"), which is to make parties into "one." The OHG form ~gieinīgen~ shows the ~gi-~ prefix (modern ~ge-~) that was common in Old High German for creating perfective or resultative verbs. The word is inseparable from German political history: ~die (Wieder)vereinigung~ ("the (Re)unification") of 1990 uses the same root, and the motto ~Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit~ ("Unity and Justice and Freedom") opens the German national anthem. The PIE root *~h₁óynos~ also gave Latin ~ūnus~ ("one"), whence English ~union~, ~unite~, and ~unanimous~.
en.einjagen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~jagen~:

• ~jagen~: From MHG ~jagen~ ("to hurry, drive, pursue, hunt"), from OHG ~jagōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~jagōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~jakkōną~, a ~nā~-iterative formation, likely rebuilt from PIE *~h₁eyǵʰ-~ ("to strive, chase"). Attested since the eighth century; further pre-Germanic etymology is obscure.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The compound survives today almost only in fixed phrases such as ~jemandem Angst einjagen~ ("to strike fear into someone"): the fear is driven into the person the way game is driven into a net.
en.einkaufen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, borrowed from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, petty tradesman, huckster"). Cognate with English ~cheap~ (originally "trade, bargain," from Old English ~cēap~ "bargain, cattle"), Dutch ~kopen~, Swedish ~köpa~, and Danish ~købe~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~in~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys movement inward or acquisition.

The compound literally means "to buy in", to bring purchased goods into the household. ~Einkaufen~ is the standard German word for grocery shopping and general retail purchasing: ~einkaufen gehen~ ("to go shopping"). The etymology of ~kaufen~ is remarkable: it is one of the oldest Latin loanwords in Germanic, borrowed during the Roman trading period along the Rhine frontier. Latin ~caupō~ meant a petty trader or tavern keeper, and the Germanic peoples adopted it to describe the act of commercial exchange itself. English ~cheap~ underwent an even more dramatic shift: from "trade" to "bargain" to "inexpensive." The related German noun ~Kaufmann~ ("merchant") literally means "trade-man" and preserves the original commercial sense. The expression ~Einkaufswagen~ ("shopping cart") and ~Einkaufszentrum~ ("shopping center") are compound-of-a-compound formations typical of German's love of agglutination.
en.einkehren:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~kehren~:

• ~kehren~: A homograph concealing two distinct verbs. ~Kehren~ (1) "to turn": from MHG ~kēren~, from OHG ~kēran~, ~chēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kairijaną~ or *~kausijaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly connected to *~gers-~ ("to twist, bend, turn"). ~Kehren~ (2) "to sweep": from MHG ~kern~, ~keren~, from OHG ~kerian~, ~cherian~, from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~ ("to scrape, scratch"), from PIE *~ger-~ ("to scrape"). Etymologically unrelated, merged through phonological convergence.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Of the two verbs the homograph conceals, ~einkehren~ belongs to ~kehren~ (1) "to turn": one turns in at an inn rather than sweeping it out. Figuratively, quiet or peace can ~einkehren~ as well, a state that arrives and stays like a lodger.
en.einkochen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~kochen~:

• ~kochen~: From MHG ~kochen~, from OHG ~kohhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kokōn~, borrowed from Late Latin ~cocō~, from Latin ~coquō~ ("I cook, I boil"), from PIE *~pekʷ-~ ("to cook, to ripen"). A loan early enough to have undergone the High German shift of ~k~ to ~ch~. Cognate with English ~cook~, Dutch ~koken~, Danish ~koge~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys enclosing or containing: shutting something in.

The verb leads two lives: a sauce ~kocht ein~ by losing volume, while fruit ~wird eingekocht~ by being sealed boiling-hot into jars. Only the second reading accounts for the prefix; the first is an extension of it.
en.einkommen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The finite verb is now rare and officialese (~um etwas einkommen~, "to petition for something"); the word's ordinary modern life is the nominalized infinitive ~das Einkommen~, "income", literally that which comes in.
en.einkriegen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~kriegen~:

• ~kriegen~: From MHG ~kriegen~ ("to war, to strive for"), a verbalization of ~Krieg~ ("war"), from OHG ~krig~, from Proto-West Germanic *~krīg~, whose origin is debated. The "obtaining" sense overshadowed the military one; colloquial modern German ~kriegen~ simply means "to get." Cognate with Dutch ~krijgen~ ("to get"), Bavarian ~kriagn~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

A purely colloquial compound that keeps ~kriegen~ in its older sense of obtaining: to ~einkriegen~ someone is to catch up with them. Reflexively, ~sich einkriegen~ means instead "to get hold of oneself, to calm down."
en.einladen:
~Ein-~ + ~laden~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two distinct verbs converged on this infinitive in Modern German. The weak verb "to invite" (the one active in ~einladen~) derives from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root shared with Hittite ~halzai~ ("to invoke, call out"). The strong verb "to load" derives from OHG ~hladan~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~.
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix adds the sense of direction inward or bringing into.

The semantic journey of ~einladen~ from "to load in" to "to invite" is one of German's most charming etymological surprises. The literal sense (loading guests into one's home or vehicle) crystallized as the dominant figurative meaning, completely eclipsing any loading sense in the compound. Today ~einladen~ means exclusively "to invite," while the loading sense requires the strong-conjugation ~laden~ on its own. The Hittite cognate ~halzai~ makes this verb a rare bridge to Anatolian (one of the oldest branches of Indo-European) giving ~einladen~ an etymology that reaches back roughly 4,000 years to the earliest attested Indo-European languages. The noun ~Einladung~ ("invitation") is the result: a word built on "loading" that now means only "an invitation to come in." Cognate with Dutch ~uitnodigen~.
en.einlagern:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~lagern~:

• ~lagern~: Derived from the noun ~Lager~ ("camp, store, warehouse"), from MHG ~lëger~, from OHG ~lëgar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~legr~, from Proto-Germanic *~legrą~. The modern form with ~-a-~ is of East Central German origin, influenced by ~Lage~ ("position"). Cognate with English ~lair~, Dutch ~leger~, Danish ~lejr~, Swedish ~läger~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Because the root is itself derived from the noun ~Lager~, the compound says the same thing twice: goods are put into the store. In geology ~einlagern~ additionally describes one substance becoming embedded within a layer.
en.einlassen:
From Middle High German ~īnlāzen~, from Old High German ~inlāzan~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~lassen~:

• ~lassen~: From MHG ~lāzen~, ~lān~, from OHG ~lāȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lātan~ ("to let, allow"), from Proto-Germanic *~lētaną~ ("to leave behind, allow"), from PIE *~leh₁d-~ ("to let, to leave behind"). Cognate with Dutch ~laten~, English ~let~.
• ~ein-~: Related to ~in~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix conveys inward movement.

The compound means "to let in, to admit" and reflexively ~sich einlassen auf~ means "to get involved in, to engage with." The reflexive sense carries a connotation of risk; ~sich auf etwas einlassen~ implies committing to something uncertain, letting oneself ~in~ to a situation that may prove difficult. The root ~lassen~ belongs to the seventh class of strong verbs and retains the archaic reduplicating pattern in its past tense (~ließ~, from the old reduplicated form). The PIE root *~leh₁d-~ also produced Latin ~lassus~ ("tired, weary"): to let go is to become exhausted. English ~let~ is the direct cognate, while ~late~ (originally "slow, tardy") may also be related through the sense of "leaving behind, remaining."
en.einlaufen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

From the ship that ~einläuft~ into harbor the verb runs off in two quite different directions: a shirt ~läuft ein~ when it shrinks in the wash, and shoes are ~eingelaufen~ until they fit.
en.einleben:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix marks becoming familiar through practice: repetition makes something fluent, or someone at home in it.

The verb is reflexive: one ~lebt sich ein~, and it takes a while. What changes is not the place but one's relation to it, a familiarity that only elapsed time can produce.
en.einlegen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~ ("to lay"), the causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie"). Cognate with English ~lay~, Dutch ~leggen~, Danish ~laegge~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). As a separable prefix, it conveys the sense of placing something into a container or medium.

~Einlegen~ means "to insert, to put in, to pickle", literally to lay something in. Its range of meanings is remarkably broad: ~Gurken einlegen~ ("to pickle cucumbers," i.e., to lay them into brine), ~eine Pause einlegen~ ("to take a break," i.e., to insert a pause), ~ein gutes Wort einlegen~ ("to put in a good word"), and ~eine CD einlegen~ ("to insert a CD"). The pickling sense gave rise to the noun ~Einlage~ ("insert, deposit, filling"), used in contexts from banking (a deposit) to soup (the noodles or dumplings added as filling). The PIE root *~legʰ-~ ("to lie, to lay") is one of the most productive in Indo-European, yielding English ~lay~, ~lie~, ~law~, ~ledger~, Latin ~lectus~ ("bed"), and Greek ~lekhos~ ("bed, lair").
en.einleiten:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~laidijaną~ ("to lead, guide, conduct"), a causative of *~līþaną~ ("to go, travel"). Cognate with English ~lead~, Old Saxon ~lēdian~, Old Norse ~leiða~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~in~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys movement inward or initiation.

The compound means "to introduce, to initiate, to begin"; one ~leitet ein Verfahren ein~ ("initiates a proceeding"), ~leitet eine Rede ein~ ("opens a speech"), or ~leitet Maßnahmen ein~ ("introduces measures"). The image is of leading something inward, into existence or action. The noun ~Einleitung~ ("introduction") is the standard term for the opening section of a book, essay, or piece of music. The root verb ~leiten~ is the causative partner of an older verb meaning "to go" (still preserved in ~Leitfaden~ "guideline," literally "guiding thread"): to ~leiten~ is to "cause to go," i.e., to lead. English ~lead~ descends from the same Proto-Germanic causative. The coincidence that English ~lead~ (the verb) and ~lead~ (the metal) are spelled identically is purely accidental, the metal comes from a completely different root.
en.einlenken:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~lenken~:

• ~lenken~: From MHG ~lenken~, from OHG ~lanca~ ("hip, flank"), related to ~Gelenk~ ("joint"), from Proto-Germanic *~gahlankiją~, from *~hlankaz~ ("flexible, lank, slender"). The path from "joint" to "to steer, guide" ran through bending and turning at a joint. Cognate with English ~lank~ (and ~link~); OHG ~hlanka~ also gave French ~flanc~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Literally one ~lenkt~ into a road; in an argument, the person who ~lenkt ein~ is the one who turns off their own course toward the other. The metaphor has taken over so completely that the steering is barely audible any more.
en.einlesen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Two uses run alongside each other: a machine ~liest~ data ~ein~, and a person ~liest sich~ into a subject. In the first the text moves inward; in the second the reader does.
en.einliefern:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~liefern~:

• ~liefern~: From MHG ~lieveren~ (attested before 1350), probably borrowed via Middle Dutch and Middle Low German ~lēveren~, from Old French ~livrer~, from Latin ~līberō~ ("I free, release, deliver"), from ~līber~ ("free"). The word belonged to the Hanseatic League's trade vocabulary. Cognate with Dutch ~leveren~, English ~deliver~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The Hanseatic trade word now delivers chiefly people: one is ~eingeliefert~ to a hospital or a prison. The road from ~līber~ "free" to a committal that ends freedom is one of the sharper semantic reversals in the German lexicon.
en.einlösen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~lösen~:

• ~lösen~: From MHG ~lœsen~, ~lōsen~, from OHG ~lōsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lausijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausijaną~, a causative of *~leusaną~ ("to lose, let loose"), denominative via *~lausaz~ ("loose, free"), from PIE *~lewh₁-~ ("to cut, sever, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ (via Old Norse ~lauss~), Dutch ~lozen~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Originally one ~löste~ a pledge ~ein~ by paying money in for it; the voucher lives on from that, and so, figuratively, does the promise that gets ~eingelöst~. The prefix is by now so fused that it can hardly be translated on its own.
en.einmachen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys enclosing or containing: shutting something in.

The verb belongs in the pantry: fruit and vegetables are ~eingemacht~, sealed boiling into jars. The nominalized participle ~das Eingemachte~ ("the preserves") gave German the idiom ~ans Eingemachte gehen~: to break into the reserves one meant to spare.
en.einmelden:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~melden~:

• ~melden~: From MHG ~mëlden~, from OHG ~mëldōn~, ~mëldēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~melþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~melþōną~, from PIE *~meldʰ-~ ("to ask, pray, speak"). The original sense was supplicatory speech; ~melden~ keeps only the communicative side: "to report, register." Cognate with Dutch ~melden~, English ~meld~ (partial).
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

A young administrative and military coinage: to ~einmelden~ is to enter oneself into an existing structure rather than merely to report something. The supplicatory speech buried in ~melden~ has here become a form to fill out.
en.einmischen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~mischen~:

• ~mischen~: From MHG ~mischen~, from OHG ~misken~, from Proto-Germanic *~miskijaną~ ("to mix"), from PIE *~meyḱ-~ ("to mix, knead"), via the inchoative present *~miḱ-sḱé-~. Cognate with English ~mix~, Latin ~misceō~, Greek ~mísgo~, Sanskrit ~miśrá~ ("mixed").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

Almost always reflexive: one ~mischt sich~ into an affair, on the metaphor of a substance getting into a mass where it does not belong. The noun ~Einmischung~ ("interference") is now chiefly a word of diplomacy.
en.einnehmen:
From Middle High German ~īnnemen~, from Old High German ~inneman~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due").
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix adds the sense of taking inward, receiving, or absorbing.

~Einnehmen~ covers a remarkable semantic range, all unified by the notion of taking something in: to take (a meal, medicine), to take up (a position or place), to capture (a fortress), and to win over (a person's affections). The military sense (~eine Stadt einnehmen~ ("to capture a city")) preserves the oldest and most concrete meaning: taking something inward, under one's control. The derived noun ~Einnahme~ means "income, revenue" (money taken in) as well as "capture" (a stronghold taken in). The gentler sense of ~einnehmend~ ("charming, winning") shows how the metaphor of conquest softened: a person with an ~einnehmendes Wesen~ ("engaging manner") captures your sympathy rather than your city. Cognate with Dutch ~innemen~.
en.einordnen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~ordnen~:

• ~ordnen~: From MHG ~ordenen~, from OHG ~ordinōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ordinōn~ ("to put in order"), borrowed from Latin ~ōrdināre~ ("to arrange"), from ~ōrdō~ ("row, rank, order"), from Proto-Italic *~ordō~, probably from PIE *~h₂er-~ ("to fit together"). Doublet of ~ordinieren~. Cognate with English ~order~, Italian ~ordinare~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

From shelf to category: one ~ordnet~ a book ~ein~, a finding into a context, and in traffic one ~ordnet sich~ into a lane. In every case the order already exists and takes the new thing in.
en.einpacken:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~packen~:

• ~packen~: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~packen~, from Old Saxon *~pakko~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pakkō~, from Proto-Germanic *~pakkô~ ("bundle, pack"), of debated ultimate origin. The absence of the High German consonant shift confirms it entered via Low German trade routes. Cognate with English ~pack~, Dutch ~pakken~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys enclosing or containing: shutting something in.

Literally the object is shut in by its wrapping. From that, colloquial German developed ~dann kannst du einpacken~, "then you might as well pack up," meaning give up, because there is nothing left to be had.
en.einpflanzen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~pflanzen~:

• ~pflanzen~: From MHG ~pflanzen~, from OHG ~pflanzōn~, a denominative verb from ~pflanza~ ("plant"), borrowed from Latin ~planta~ ("a shoot, cutting"), itself of uncertain origin. The change from Latin ~pl-~ to ~pfl-~ belongs to the High German consonant shift. Cognate with English ~plant~ (which shows no shift), Luxembourgish ~Planz~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The cutting goes into the soil, and the metaphor goes with it: surgeons ~pflanzen~ a pacemaker ~ein~, and teachers ~pflanzen~ values ~ein~ in a child. Latin ~planta~ has travelled a long way from its garden bed.
en.einpflegen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~pflegen~:

• ~pflegen~: From MHG ~phlëgen~, from OHG ~plëgan~ ("to take care of, be responsible for"), from Proto-West Germanic *~plehan~, a strong class-5 verb; its past-tense forms survive in the archaic literary ~pflog~. Cognate with Dutch ~plegen~, Old English ~plēon~, Old Norse ~plega~; via Medieval Latin *~pleviō~, also with English ~pledge~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

An office coinage of the computer age: data are ~eingepflegt~ into a system. OHG ~plëgan~ "to take care of, be responsible for" has thus ended up in database maintenance: the diligence survives, its object does not.
en.einplanen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~planen~:

• ~planen~: Denominal verb from the noun ~Plan~, borrowed from French ~plan~ ("plan, ground plan"), from either ~planter~ ("to plant") or, more widely accepted, Latin ~planus~ ("flat, level"), from PIE *~pleh₂-~ ("flat, broad"). Cognate with English ~plan~, Dutch ~plannen~, Swedish ~planera~, French ~planifier~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

Not the planning itself but the taking of an item into a plan that already exists: an appointment, a sum, a person is given a slot in what is already there. The verb therefore always presupposes a plan.
en.einpreisen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~preisen~:

• ~preisen~: From MHG ~prīsen~ ("to praise"), from MHG ~prīs~ ("price, worth, glory"), borrowed from Old French ~prisier~ ("to appraise, value"), from Late Latin ~pretiāre~, from ~pretium~ ("price, value"). The loanword was later reanalyzed as a class I strong verb (~preisen~, ~pries~, ~gepriesen~) despite having no Germanic ancestry. The same ~pretium~ gives English ~price~, ~prize~, and ~praise~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

The youngest verb in this set, a calque of English ~to price in~ from the language of finance: a risk is reckoned into the price. That the root goes back via ~pretium~ to the same source as English ~price~ makes the borrowing something of a homecoming.
en.einprägen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~prägen~:

• ~prägen~: From MHG ~bræchen~ / ~præchen~ ("to press in, to depict"), from OHG ~giprāhhan~ / ~prāhhan~ ("to press in or scratch by breaking the surface"), formed from the first- and third-person plural preterite of ~prēchan~ / ~prāchun~ ("to break"), making ~prägen~ likely a relative of ~brechen~. The noun ~Prägung~ ("imprint, stamp") shares the root.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The coiner's die is the image beneath the verb: something is pressed into a surface and stays there. Reflexively, ~sich etwas einprägen~ means to commit something to memory, and ethology calls ~Prägung~ ("imprinting") exactly the impression that can no longer be erased.
en.einrechnen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~rechnen~:

• ~rechnen~: From MHG ~rechenen~, from OHG ~rehhanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rekanōn~ ("to count, explain"), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to make straight or right"), the same root as German ~recht~ and Latin ~rectus~. Cognate with English ~reckon~, Dutch ~rekenen~, Low German ~rekenen~, Danish ~regne~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

The item is not merely counted but taken into a reckoning that already exists. The participle ~eingerechnet~ has broken loose from that and now works almost as a preposition: ~die Gebildeten eingerechnet~, "the educated included."
en.einreden:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Two constructions, two meanings: ~jemandem etwas einreden~ is to talk someone into believing something, while ~auf jemanden einreden~ is to talk at them without letting up. In both, the speech is aimed inward, at the hearer rather than at the matter.
en.einreiben:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~reiben~:

• ~reiben~: From MHG ~rīben~, from OHG ~rīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrībaną~ ("to rub"); beyond Germanic uncertain, a PIE *~wreyp-~, labial extension of *~wer-~ ("to turn"), being proposed but not secure. A class I strong verb (~reiben~, ~rieb~, ~gerieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~wrijven~, Old Saxon ~wrīvan~; German dropped the initial ~w-~ before ~r~, as in ~ringen~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The prefix carries the whole claim here: ointment is not spread onto the skin but rubbed into it. Without ~ein-~ the substance would stay on the surface.
en.einreichen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~reichen~:

• ~reichen~: From MHG ~reichen~, from OHG ~reihhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raikijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~raikijaną~ ("to stretch out, reach"), a causative o-grade derivation from PIE *~Hreyǵ-~ ("to stretch out, reach"). Cognate with English ~reach~, Dutch ~reiken~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in").

The literal sense is "to reach something in": to extend or hand something into an authority's domain. Modern usage has fully specialized to mean "to submit, to hand in" (a document, an application, a complaint). The underlying spatial metaphor of reaching inward persists: one ~reicht ein~ a ~Klage~ (lawsuit), a ~Bewerbung~ (application), or a ~Petition~ (petition), each time stretching the document across a threshold toward someone who will receive it.
en.einreisen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

In modern usage the meaning has narrowed to the legal-administrative: ~einreisen~ is to cross a national border, and the verb takes the auxiliary ~sein~.
en.einreißen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix marks destructive collapse inward: something is stove in or falls in on itself.

Beside the concrete demolition of buildings, a figurative sense survives: a bad habit or abuse ~reißt ein~, spreading unchecked.
en.einrichten:
~Ein-~ + ~richten~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rihtijaną~, a denominative of *~rehtaz~ ("straight"), from PIE *~h₃reǵtós~, from *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to stretch out, straighten, direct").
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix adds the sense of directing something inward, setting it up inside a space.

~Einrichten~ means "to set up, furnish, arrange, or establish", the image of straightening things inward, into a space, until they are ordered correctly. ~Eine Wohnung einrichten~ ("to furnish an apartment") captures the core sense: making a space right by placing things within it. The related noun ~Einrichtung~ means both "furnishings" and "institution, facility", a semantic duality that mirrors the two applications of the verb. The same PIE root *~h₃reǵ-~ underlies Latin ~regō~ ("to rule, direct") and English ~right~, ~reign~, and ~regiment~. To set something right is, in the oldest layer of the language, to straighten it. Cognate with Dutch ~inrichten~.
en.einrollen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~rollen~:

• ~rollen~: From MHG ~rollen~, borrowed from Old French ~roeler~, from Medieval Latin ~rotulāre~ ("to roll"), from Latin ~rotula~ ("small wheel"), diminutive of ~rota~ ("wheel"), from PIE *~ret-~ ("to run, to roll"). Cognate with English ~roll~ (also borrowed from Old French), Dutch ~rollen~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The verb covers both rolling an object inward and curling up into a spiral: a hedgehog ~rollt sich ein~.
en.einräumen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~räumen~:

• ~räumen~: From MHG ~rūmen~, from OHG ~rūman~, ~rūmman~, derived from the noun ~Raum~ ("room, space"). ~Raum~ from MHG ~rūm~, from OHG ~rūm~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rūm~, from Proto-Germanic *~rūmą~ ("room, space"), from PIE *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open, to make space"). Cognate with English ~room~, Dutch ~ruimte~, Old Norse ~rúm~.
• ~ein-~: Related to ~in~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix conveys inward placement.

The compound means "to put away (into a cupboard or room); to concede, to admit (a point); to grant (rights or authority)." The semantic leap from "putting things into a space" to "conceding a point" is bridged by the metaphor of making space for someone else's position; to ~einräumen~ an objection is to clear room for it in one's own argument. The root ~Raum~ is cognate with English ~room~: both descend from Proto-Germanic *~rūmą~, and the PIE root *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open") reveals the original, physical sense of creating space by clearing or breaking open ground. The adjective ~geräumig~ ("spacious") preserves the direct connection, while the verb ~aufräumen~ ("to tidy up") uses a different prefix to mean "to clear space upward."
en.einrücken:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~rücken~:

• ~rücken~: From MHG ~rücken~, from OHG ~rucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rukkijan~. The verb means "to move, to shift" and is the base of ~verrückt~ ("crazy," literally "shifted, displaced"); the noun ~Rücken~ ("back") is etymologically a separate word. Cognate with English ~rock~, Old Norse ~rykkja~, Old English ~roccian~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The verb splits into two uses: the military "to march in" and the typographic-legal "to insert a passage of text", both from the same underlying inward motion.
en.einrühren:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~rühren~:

• ~rühren~: From MHG ~rüeren~, from OHG ~ruoren~, ~hruoren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōzijaną~; the initial ~hr-~ cluster was gradually simplified in German. The semantic range has stayed stable across a millennium: "to stir," both literally and figuratively. Cognate with Dutch ~roeren~ and the now-rare English ~rear~ ("to move, stir"), surviving in "to rear up."
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The prefix fixes the goal of the motion: an ingredient is not merely stirred but stirred into a mass and dispersed through it.
en.einsagen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The verb belongs to school and theater: the prompter ~sagt~ the actor's lines ~ein~, feeding them to him under his breath.
en.einsammeln:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~sammeln~:

• ~sammeln~: From MHG ~samelen~, ~samlen~, by dissimilation from ~samenen~, from Proto-Germanic *~samnōną~ ("to bring together, gather"), derived from *~samanai~ ("together") with the verbal suffix *~-ōną~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, same, together"), the root behind English ~same~ and Latin ~similis~. Cognate with Dutch ~verzamelen~, Swedish ~samla~, Gothic ~samjan~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Against plain ~sammeln~, the prefix stresses bringing the scattered together into one place: fruit from the field, tests from the pupils.
en.einsaugen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~saugen~:

• ~saugen~: From MHG ~sūgen~, from OHG ~sūgan~ ("to suck"), from Proto-West Germanic *~sūgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sūganą~, from PIE *~sewk-~ ("to suck"). Historically a class II strong verb (~saugen~, ~sog~, ~gesogen~), it now inflects weak (~saugte~, ~gesaugt~) just as readily. Cognate with English ~suck~, Dutch ~zuigen~, Danish ~suge~, Old English ~sūcan~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The verb works both concretely (a sponge ~saugt~ water ~ein~), and figuratively, for the eager absorption of impressions.
en.einschalten:
From ~ein-~ + ~schalten~, perhaps modeled after its antonym ~ausschalten~:

• ~schalten~: From MHG ~schalten~, from OHG ~scaltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaldan~ ("to push, to shove"). The further etymology is obscure; according to Pokorny, it may derive from PIE *~(s)kelH-~ ("to split, to separate"), in which case it is related to English ~shell~. Cognate with Old Saxon ~skaldan~ ("to push").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~in-~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁en~ ("in"). Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~.

The original meaning of ~schalten~ was physical: "to push, to shove, to propel." From this developed the sense of operating a mechanism by pushing a lever or switch, which led to the modern meanings "to switch, to shift (gears), to control." The compound ~einschalten~ thus literally means "to push in" or "to switch in," hence "to turn on, to activate." It is also used reflexively (~sich einschalten~) to mean "to intervene, to get involved," as if inserting oneself into a process. The suggestion that ~einschalten~ may have been modeled after ~ausschalten~ is an interesting case of a word being back-formed from its antonym, though both are now completely established in their own right.
en.einschauen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

In southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage ~einschauen~ ordinarily means "to look in briefly, to drop by."
en.einschenken:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schenken~:

• ~schenken~: From MHG ~schenken~, from OHG ~scenken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skankijan~ ("to pour, serve"). The sense "to give as a gift" grew out of pouring a drink for a guest, the paradigmatic act of generosity; the pouring sense retreated into ~Wein einschenken~ and ~Schenke~ ("tavern"). Cognate with Dutch ~schenken~ ("to pour; to give"), English ~skink~ (archaic) and ~shank~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The idiom ~jemandem reinen Wein einschenken~ ("to pour someone pure wine"), meaning to tell someone the unvarnished truth, keeps the literal sense of pouring alive.
en.einschieben:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schieben~:

• ~schieben~: From MHG ~schieben~, from OHG ~skioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeubaną~, from PIE *~skewbʰ-~ ("to push, to shove, to thrust"). A class II strong verb (~schieben~, ~schob~, ~geschoben~). Cognate with English ~shove~, Dutch ~schuiven~, Danish ~skubbe~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The verb ranges from the concrete (sliding a tray into the oven), to the temporal insertion of an extra appointment or, as here, an intercalary day.
en.einschießen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb (~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~). Cognate with English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Old Norse ~skjóta~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix marks destructive collapse inward: something is stove in or falls in on itself.

The glossed sense "to break by shooting" is one of several: the verb also covers sighting in a weapon (test-firing to adjust it) and injecting money.
en.einschlafen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schlafen~:

• ~schlafen~: From MHG ~slāfen~, from OHG ~slāfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slāpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slēpaną~, of uncertain further origin, possibly related to *~slapaz~ ("weak, lax, limp"), ancestor of ~schlaff~. A class VII strong verb of the reduplicating class (~schlafen~, ~schlief~, ~geschlafen~). Cognate with English ~sleep~, Dutch ~slapen~, Gothic ~𐍃𐌻𐌴𐍀𐌰𐌽~ (slēpan).
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix marks the onset of a state, the moment of entering into it.

The prefix turns the state ~schlafen~ into the entry into it, which is why the verb takes the auxiliary ~sein~. Figuratively a foot ~schläft ein~, and so does a friendship.
en.einschlagen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix marks destructive collapse inward: something is stove in or falls in on itself.

The verb is remarkably polysemous: "to smash," to ~einen Weg einschlagen~ ("choose a direction"), the strike of lightning, and the handshake that seals a deal. The quoted passage shows the "choose a path" sense.
en.einschleichen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schleichen~:

• ~schleichen~: From MHG ~slīchen~, from OHG ~slīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slīkaną~ ("to glide, creep"), from PIE *~sleyg-~ ("to be smooth, slide"). A class I strong verb (~schleichen~, ~schlich~, ~geschlichen~). Cognate with English ~slick~ and ~sleek~, Dutch ~slijken~, Old Norse ~slíkr~ ("smooth").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The reflexive ~sich einschleichen~ is the norm: one sneaks into a house, a gathering, or, as in Kafka, into someone's thoughts. The unnoticed intrusion usually carries a negative overtone.
en.einschließen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schließen~:

• ~schließen~: From MHG ~slieȥen~, from OHG ~sliozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sleutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slūtaną~, *~sleutaną~ ("to lock, shut"); the PIE root is not definitively established. A class II strong verb (~schließen~, ~schloss~, ~geschlossen~). Cognate with Old Saxon ~slūtan~, Dutch ~sluiten~, archaic English ~slot~ ("a bolt").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys enclosing or containing: shutting something in.

The verb spans from locking a person away to logical inclusion, "all costs included" (~alle Kosten eingeschlossen~).
en.einschneiden:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schneiden~:

• ~schneiden~: From MHG ~snīden~, from OHG ~snīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~snīþan~ ("to cut"); no secure PIE root has been established, and the word may be a Germanic innovation. A class I strong verb (~schneiden~, ~schnitt~, ~geschnitten~). Cognate with archaic English ~snithe~ ("to cut"), Dutch ~snijden~, Icelandic ~sníða~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Beside the concrete notching, the verb lives on in the adjective ~einschneidend~: an ~einschneidende Maßnahme~ is a measure that cuts deep, a drastic one.
en.einschreiben:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Reflexively ~sich einschreiben~ means "to enroll, to register oneself"; as the noun ~Einschreiben~ it is also the term for registered mail.
en.einschreiten:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schreiten~:

• ~schreiten~: From MHG ~schrīten~, from OHG ~skrītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīþan~ ("to step, stride"), from Proto-Germanic *~skrīþaną~ ("to walk, glide, crawl"), from PIE *~(s)kreyt-~ ("to stride"), an extension of *~(s)krey-~ ("to go about"). Cognate with Lithuanian ~skrìsti~ ("to rush, run"), Latvian ~skrìet~ ("to run, fly"). Related to ~Schritt~ ("step").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The verb is now almost exclusively figurative: an authority ~schreitet ein~, stepping in against some development. The literal "to stride in" has grown rare.
en.einschränken:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~schränken~:

• ~schränken~: From MHG ~schrenken~ ("to place crosswise"), from OHG ~screnken~ ("to spread out, throw down"), from Proto-Germanic *~skrankijaną~ ("to cause to shrink; to limit, restrict"). Related to ~Schrank~ ("cabinet, cupboard"), from OHG ~scranc~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrank~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrankaz~ ("grid, barrier"), probably from PIE *~(s)ker-~ ("to bend, turn").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁en~ ("in"). As a verbal prefix, ~ein-~ conveys inward motion or confinement.

The compound literally conveys the idea of placing something within barriers or limits. The related noun ~Schranke~ ("barrier, gate") preserves the concrete sense of a physical limitation, while ~einschränken~ has moved fully into the abstract domain of constraining, limiting, or restricting. The reflexive ~sich einschränken~ means "to economize" or "to tighten one's belt."
en.einschulen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schulen~:

• ~schulen~: Derived from the noun ~Schule~ with the verbal suffix ~-en~. From MHG ~schuole~, from OHG ~scuola~, borrowed from Latin ~schola~ ("leisure for learning, school"), from Ancient Greek ~scholē~ (~σχολή~, "leisure, rest"), from PIE *~seǵʰ-~ ("to hold"). English ~school~ is borrowed from the same Latin source.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix marks becoming familiar through practice: repetition makes something fluent, or someone at home in it.

The verb has two uses: a child is ~eingeschult~ when admitted to school, and an employee (or, in Nietzsche, a conscience), is ~eingeschult~, drilled into a particular response.
en.einschwören:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~schwören~:

• ~schwören~: From MHG ~swern~, from OHG ~swerien~, from Proto-West Germanic *~swarjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swarjaną~, from PIE *~swer-~ ("to speak, to talk"). A class VI strong verb (~schwören~, ~schwor~, ~geschworen~); the older Präteritum ~schwur~ is now archaic. Cognate with English ~swear~, Dutch ~zweren~, Danish ~sværge~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

Built with ~auf~: a team is ~auf den Sieg eingeschworen~ (rallied to victory), troops to a goal; the prefix binds many into one shared resolve.
en.einschätzen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~schätzen~:

• ~schätzen~: From MHG ~schetzen~, a verbal formation from ~Schatz~ ("treasure"). ~Schatz~ descends from MHG ~schaz~, from OHG ~skaz~, ~scaz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skatt~ ("cattle, treasure"), from Proto-Germanic *~skattaz~. Cognate with Old Norse ~skattr~ (whence Danish ~skat~, Swedish ~skatt~, all meaning "tax, treasure"), Gothic ~skatts~ ("money"), Dutch ~schat~, English ~scat~ (dialectal: "tax, tribute").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). As a separable prefix here, it adds the sense of placing something into a category or framework.

~Einschätzen~ means "to assess, to estimate, to evaluate", literally to place a value (~Schatz~) on something. The semantic path from ~Schatz~ ("treasure") to ~schätzen~ ("to estimate, to value") is transparent: to appraise is to determine how much treasure something is worth. The Proto-Germanic *~skattaz~ originally meant "cattle" (the oldest form of wealth in pastoral Indo-European society) before shifting to "money, treasure." This cattle-to-currency shift is paralleled by Latin ~pecūnia~ ("money") from ~pecus~ ("cattle") and English ~fee~ from Proto-Germanic *~fehu~ ("cattle, property").
en.einsehen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys "in, into."

~Einsehen~ means "to look into" literally (a document, a file) and "to realize, to understand" figuratively. The metaphorical leap from "looking into" to "understanding" appears in many languages: English ~insight~ (literally "seeing in"), Latin ~inspicere~ ("to look into," whence ~inspect~), and Greek ~ennoeō~ ("to perceive," from ~en-~ "in" + ~noeō~ "to think"). The derived noun ~Einsicht~ ("insight, realization") perfectly mirrors its English cognate.
en.einsenden:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~senden~:

• ~senden~: From MHG ~senden~, from OHG ~senten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sandijaną~, from PIE *~sont-eye-~, a causative of *~sent-~ ("to walk, travel"), originally "to cause to go." It has a double Präteritum: ~sendete~ for broadcasting, ~sandte~ (a Rückumlaut form) for sending a letter. Cognate with English ~send~, Dutch ~zenden~, Gothic ~sandjan~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The prefix aims the sending at a receiving point: one ~sendet~ a contribution, a solution, or a form ~ein~, to an editorial office or an authority.
en.einsetzen:
From Middle High German ~īnsetzen~, ~insetzen~, from Old High German ~insezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~insattjan~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~. A causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit"): literally "to cause to sit," hence "to set, place."
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~in-~, from OHG ~in-~, from Proto-Germanic *~in-~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). As a verbal prefix, ~ein-~ adds the sense of "into" or "in place."

The compound's range of meanings ("to insert," "to deploy (troops)," "to stake (money)," "to begin (music)") all derive from the core sense of placing something into position or into action. Cognate with Dutch ~inzetten~ and English ~inset~, a partial cognate.
en.einsparen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~sparen~:

• ~sparen~: From MHG ~sparn~, from OHG ~sparēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sparēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~sparaz~ ("sparing, frugal"), from PIE *~speh₁-~ ("to thrive, prosper; to leave untouched"). The same root produced Latin ~prosperus~, whence English ~prosper~. Cognate with English ~spare~, Dutch ~sparen~, Icelandic ~spara~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Unlike the other ~ein-~ formations, ~einsparen~ denotes no inward motion but the reduction of spending or consumption; here the prefix is intensifying, in the sense of "to save entirely."
en.einspeisen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~speisen~:

• ~speisen~: From MHG ~spīsen~ ("to feed"), a denominative verb from MHG ~spīse~ ("food"), from Medieval Latin ~spēsa~, from Latin ~expēnsa~ ("money paid out"), from ~expendere~ ("to weigh out, pay out"). A weak verb throughout its history. Cognate with Dutch ~spijzen~; the same Latin source gave English ~expense~ and ~spend~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

The verb is a modern technical term: electricity is fed into the grid, data into a system, a proposal into a process.
en.einsperren:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~sperren~:

• ~sperren~: From MHG ~sperren~, from OHG ~sperran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sparrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sparrijaną~ ("to bar, to block"), a denominative verb from *~sparrô~ ("wooden beam, log"), originally to bar a passage with a beam. Cognate with English ~spar~ ("to bolt, bar"; the noun for a wooden beam), Dutch ~sperren~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys enclosing or containing: shutting something in.

The prefix turns "barring a passage" into "shutting a person or animal in"; the bolt now faces inward.
en.einspielen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

Modern ~einspielen~ ranges from "to record" (music) through "to bring in" (box-office takings) to "to load, to apply" (a backup or an update), in each, something plays into a system or medium.
en.einspringen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~springen~:

• ~springen~: From OHG ~springan~, from Proto-Germanic *~springaną~, from PIE *~sprenǵʰ-~, a nasalized form of *~sperǵʰ-~ ("to move energetically, to hasten, to spring"). A class III strong verb (~springen~, ~sprang~, ~gesprungen~). Cognate with English ~spring~, Dutch ~springen~, Danish ~springe~, Greek ~spérkhō~ ("to hasten").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einspringen~ carries the image of jumping in over to standing in at short notice for someone who has dropped out; one leaps into the gap that has opened.
en.einstechen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~stechen~:

• ~stechen~: From MHG ~stëchen~, from OHG ~stëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stekaną~ ("to stab, prick"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to stick, poke"). Cognate with Dutch ~steken~ ("to stab, sting"), Old Norse ~stinga~, English ~stick~ (originally "to stab, pierce").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

In ~einstechen~ the point penetrates a surface; the emphasis falls on breaking through the surface, not merely on the stab.
en.einstecken:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~stecken~:

• ~stecken~: Modern ~stecken~ merges two verbs: the transitive weak one ("to put, stick something in") from MHG ~stecken~, OHG ~steckōn~, a geminate derivative of ~stëhhan~ (the ancestor of ~stechen~), and the strong intransitive one (archaic ~stak~/~gestocken~, "to be stuck"); the two fused in Early Modern German. Both trace to Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stikaną~, from PIE *~(s)teyg-~ ("to be sharp, stab, goad"). Cognate with English ~stick~ and ~steak~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einstecken~ draws on the transitive weak ~stecken~: something is put into a pocket or a sheath.
en.einstehen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

From spatial "standing in" (stepping into a place) came the figurative "to vouch for": to take on liability or responsibility for someone or something.
en.einsteigen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stīgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~ ("to climb, ascend"), from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to stride, to step, to go"). Cognate with obsolete English ~sty~ ("to ascend"), Dutch ~stijgen~ ("to rise"), Danish ~stige~, and Swedish ~stiga~.
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). As a separable prefix, it means "in, into."

~Einsteigen~ means "to board, to get in, to enter (a vehicle)", literally "to climb in." One ~steigt ein~ in a bus, a train, a car, or an airplane. Figuratively, it also means "to get involved in, to enter (a business or discussion)": ~in ein Geschäft einsteigen~ ("to enter into a business"). The PIE root *~steygʰ-~ is the ancestor of English ~stair~ (from Proto-Germanic *~staigrī~, "that which one climbs"). The modern German opposite ~aussteigen~ ("to get out, to exit") has developed the colloquial extended meaning of "to drop out" (~aus der Gesellschaft aussteigen~ = "to drop out of society").
en.einstellen:
From Middle High German ~īnstellen~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~in-~, from OHG ~in-~, from Proto-Germanic *~in-~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). This separable prefix expresses motion inward or placement into a defined space.

~Einstellen~ is one of the most semantically productive compound verbs in German, carrying several meanings that look quite unrelated until the spatial metaphor underlying them is understood. To hire someone (~jemanden einstellen~) is literally to place them into the workforce. To adjust a dial (~die Temperatur einstellen~) is to set it into the correct position. To stop an activity (~die Produktion einstellen~) is to put it into a state of rest. To insert a line of text is to place it into a document. All derive from the core image of ~stellen~ with the directional force of ~ein-~: placing something into its proper slot. The reflexive ~sich einstellen~ ("to arrive, to occur" (as when a feeling sets in)), adds yet another dimension: the thing places itself in. Cognate with Dutch ~instellen~.
en.einstimmen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~stimmen~:

• ~stimmen~: From MHG ~stimmen~, from OHG *~stimmen~, a denominative of ~Stimme~ ("voice, vote": OHG ~stimma~, Proto-West Germanic *~stebnu~, Proto-Germanic *~stebnō~, from PIE *~stomen-~ "mouth, muzzle"). Hence the senses "to tune" (an instrument), "to be correct," and "to vote." Cognate with archaic English ~steven~ ("voice"), Dutch ~stem~, Gothic ~stibna~, Ancient Greek ~stóma~ ("mouth").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

In ~einstimmen~ one's own voice joins a song already sounding; one joins in a song or in applause.
en.einstoßen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). Cognate with dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce, ricochet"), Dutch ~stoten~, Old Norse ~stauta~ and ~steyta~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix marks destructive collapse inward: something is stove in or falls in on itself.

~Einstoßen~ means a destructive pushing inward: a door, a window, or, as in the Grimms, a nest is stove in.
en.einstufen:
Compound of ~ein-~ + ~Stufe~ + ~-n~:

• ~Stufe~: From MHG ~stuofe~, from OHG ~stuofa~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stōpā~, related to the verb *~stappjan~ ("to tread, to step"). Cognate with Old Saxon ~stōpo~, Dutch ~stoep~ ("stoop, front steps"), and English ~stoop~ (the porch steps of a house, a word borrowed into American English from Dutch).
• ~ein-~: Related to ~in~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~, from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix conveys placement into a category.

The verb means "to classify, to rank, to categorize", to place something or someone into a ~Stufe~ ("step, level, grade"). The noun ~Stufe~ originally meant a physical step or stair and gradually extended to abstract levels and grades.
