The compound ~Einstufung~ ("classification") is standard in bureaucratic and academic German: ~Einstufungstest~ ("placement test") determines which ~Stufe~ a student enters. The English word ~stoop~ (the raised platform at a house entrance) traveled from Dutch ~stoep~ to New Amsterdam (later New York) in the 17th century, preserving the same Proto-West Germanic root in an unexpected American context. The South African English ~stoep~ ("veranda") is a parallel borrowing from Afrikaans.
en.einstürzen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~stürzen~:

• ~stürzen~: From MHG ~stürzen~, from OHG ~sturzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sturtijan~ ("to fall down, tumble"), of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly from PIE *~ster-~ ("to be stiff") via a dental extension *~sterd-~, though the derivation is debated. Cognate with English ~start~, a doublet from the same Proto-West Germanic source, from which the meanings have diverged radically.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix marks destructive collapse inward: something is stove in or falls in on itself.

~Einstürzen~ is the intransitive counterpart: the structure gives way and falls in on itself, rather than being pushed in by someone.
en.eintauchen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~tauchen~:

• ~tauchen~: From MHG ~tūchen~, ~touchen~, from OHG *~tūhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dūkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dūkaną~ ("to duck, to dive under"), whose further etymology is uncertain. A class II strong verb that became weak in the early modern period: when it was reintroduced from Central and Low German, the strong conjugation was regularized to weak. Cognate with Dutch ~duiken~, Swedish ~dyka~; a Low German consonant variant of the same root is ~ducken~, cognate with English ~duck~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Eintauchen~ continues the image of ducking under: something is dipped into a liquid, literally as well as figuratively (to immerse oneself in a subject).
en.eintauschen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~tauschen~:

• ~tauschen~: From MHG ~tiuschen~, derived from ~tūschen~, related to ~täuschen~ ("to deceive"), both of uncertain further origin. The sense ran from "to deceive" to "to trick someone into buying one's goods" to "to trade, exchange, barter"; ~tauschen~ lost the negative connotation along the way while ~täuschen~ retained it.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

In ~eintauschen~ one takes something in through a trade, giving up one thing and receiving another in its place.
en.einteilen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~teilen~:

• ~teilen~: From MHG ~teilen~ and OHG ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~ ("to divide, part, deal"), from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, a denominative of *~dailiz~ ("part, share"), from PIE *~dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo-~, tentatively from *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, set, place"), though the precise PIE derivation is uncertain. Cognate with English ~deal~, Dutch ~delen~, Danish ~dele~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

~Einteilen~ organizes a whole into sections or categories: hours, tasks, or, as here, fields of action are sorted into groups.
en.eintippen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~tippen~:

• ~tippen~: From Low German, where the standard High German equivalent would have been ~tüpfen~ ("to dab, dot"). The word has two branches: in the sense "to type, to tap" it derives from the onomatopoeic imitation of light touching, while in the sense "to bet, to guess" (~Lotto tippen~) it comes from the noun ~Tipp~, borrowed from English ~tip~ ("a piece of advice, a hint").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Eintippen~ is young and technical: characters are entered into a field or device by way of the keyboard.
en.eintragen:
~Ein-~ + ~tragen~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, carry, bear"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to draw, drag").
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix adds the sense of carrying into or inscribing into.

~Eintragen~ means "to enter, to register, to record", to carry information into a book, a list, or a database. The underlying metaphor is physical: one ~trägt~ (carries, bears) data ~ein~ (into) a written record. The reflexive ~sich eintragen~ ("to sign in, to register oneself") and the noun ~Eintrag~ ("entry, record") are central to German bureaucratic life, from hotel guest books to commercial registers (~Handelsregister~). The verb can also mean "to yield, to bring in" (profit): ~das Geschäft trägt viel ein~ ("the business yields a lot"), where the image shifts from inscription to income flowing inward. Cognate with Dutch ~indragen~ ("to bring in, contribute"). The PIE root *~dʰregʰ-~ connects ~tragen~ to English ~draw~ and ~drag~, the physical labor of hauling something from one place to another, now abstracted to moving a pen across paper.
en.eintreffen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~treffen~:

• ~treffen~: From MHG ~treffen~, from OHG ~treffan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drepan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drepaną~ ("to strike, push, beat"), from PIE *~dʰrebʰ-~, *~dʰreb-~ ("to crack, crush, strike, kill"). The High German consonant shift from *~dr-~ to ~tr-~ obscures the cognate relationship with Old English ~drepan~ ("to strike"). Cognate with Old Norse ~drepa~ ("to kill, strike").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Eintreffen~ has two branches: the spatial "to arrive" (to reach a place) and the figurative "to come true" (a prediction comes to pass).
en.eintreiben:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Eintreiben~ means driving cattle into the pen; from it grew the figurative "to collect debts or taxes."
en.eintreten:
~Ein-~ + ~treten~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~ ("to tread, to step on"). The West Germanic descendants regularized the verb's ablaut by replacing the original ~u~ vowel with ~e~ in the present tense, but the original vocalism may have survived longer in some High German dialects; the Medieval Latin loanword ~trottō~ ("to trot") likely reflects this older pronunciation. Cognate with English ~tread~.
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The prefix adds the sense of entering, moving inward.

~Eintreten~ is a remarkably versatile compound. Its core meaning is "to enter, to step in" (~bitte treten Sie ein!~, "please come in!"), but it extends to "to occur, to happen" (~ein unerwartetes Ereignis ist eingetreten~, "an unexpected event has occurred"), "to join" an organization (~in eine Partei eintreten~, "to join a party"), and "to advocate for" (~für die Menschenrechte eintreten~, "to stand up for human rights"). With a direct object and ~haben~, it means "to kick in" (~die Tür eintreten~, "to kick the door in") or "to tread down" (soil). This wide semantic spread (entering, occurring, joining, advocating, kicking) all stems from the physical act of stepping into a space, with each meaning extending the metaphor of crossing a threshold.
en.einvernehmen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~ver-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einvernehmen~ is a legal term, chiefly Austrian: to ~einvernehmen~ someone is to take down their statement formally, the perceptive ~vernehmen~ ("to perceive, to interrogate") with an added ~ein-~.
en.einwandern:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~wandern~:

• ~wandern~: From MHG ~wandern~, from OHG *~wantarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandarōn~, formed from *~wandōn~ ("to turn") with the frequentative suffix *~-rōn~ (not a single journey but repeated, meandering motion), from Proto-Germanic *~wandōną~, from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, to wind"). Cognate with English ~wander~, Danish ~vandre~, Swedish ~vandra~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einwandern~ is migration into a country; its counterpart is ~auswandern~ ("to emigrate").
en.einwechseln:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~wechseln~:

• ~wechseln~: From MHG ~wëhseln~, from OHG *~wehsalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wihslōną~, from PIE *~weyk-~, *~weyḱ-~ ("to change, bend, yield"). Cognate with Dutch ~wisselen~, Luxembourgish ~wiesselen~, English ~week~, German ~Woche~, and Latin ~vicis~ ("change, turn, alternation").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

~Einwechseln~ brings someone or something in to replace another: a player into the game, or money into a different currency.
en.einwecken:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~wecken~:

• ~wecken~: From MHG ~wecken~, from OHG ~wecchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wakkjan~ ("to wake up"), from Proto-Germanic *~wakjaną~, a causative of *~wakaną~ ("to be awake"), from PIE *~weǵ-~ ("to be lively, to wake"), precisely the distinction between ~wachen~ and ~wecken~. Cognate with Dutch ~wekken~, English ~watch~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys enclosing or containing: shutting something in.

The decomposition ~ein-~ + ~wecken~ is formal only: ~einwecken~ "to preserve, to can" has nothing to do with ~wecken~ "to wake," but is denominal from ~Weck~, the brand of preserving jars sold by Johann Weck, whose name became the generic term for home canning.
en.einweichen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~weichen~:

• ~weichen~: From MHG ~wīchen~, from OHG ~wīchan~ ("to yield, give way"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wīkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīkwaną~, from PIE *~h₃weyg-~ ("to start moving, to distance oneself, to bend, wind"). A class I strong verb, "to yield, give way, retreat"; not to be confused with the weak ~weichen~ ("to soften, to soak"), which derives from ~weich~ ("soft"). Cognate with Old English ~wīcan~, Old Norse ~vīkja~, Swedish ~vika~ ("to give way, fold").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einweichen~ "to soak" belongs to the weak ~weichen~ (from ~weich~ "soft"), not to the strong ~weichen~ "to yield" that heads the bullet: laundry or dried legumes are placed in water to soften.
en.einweisen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative verb from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from PIE *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know"). A class I strong verb; its senses "to show, point" and "to direct, expel" both direct knowledge or attention. Cognate with English ~wise~, ~wit~, ~wizard~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

~Einweisen~ inducts someone into a task, an office, or, in the medical sense, into a clinic; ~weisen~ "to show, direct" supplies the underlying sense of directing someone in.
en.einwenden:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~wenden~:

• ~wenden~: From MHG ~wenden~, from OHG ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), the causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). It belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort (preterite ~wandte~, participle ~gewandt~) and has a doubled preterite: ~wandte~ for turning the self or one's attention, the regularized ~wendete~ for physical turning. Cognate with English ~wend~, Armenian ~gind~ ("ring").
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inserting or incorporating something into a larger structure or category.

~Einwenden~ means bringing an objection into the discussion: one interposes something against a claim.
en.einwerfen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einwerfen~ ranges from the literal throwing-in (a coin, a letter) to the figurative interjecting of a remark into a conversation.
en.einwirken:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~wirken~:

• ~wirken~: From MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~, from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~wérǵom~, from *~werǵ-~ ("to make, work"). Early on it merged with the dialectal ~würken~ (from OHG ~wurken~), which left the written language in the 18th century. Cognate with English ~work~ and ~wrought~, Dutch ~werken~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

In ~einwirken~ a force or an influence acts upon something and changes it; one acts on someone or something.
en.einwählen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~wählen~:

• ~wählen~: From MHG ~weln~, ~welen~, ~wellen~, from OHG ~wellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~walljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waljaną~, from PIE *~welh₁-~ ("to wish, choose"). The umlaut ~ä~ comes from the MHG second- and third-person singular; ~wählen~ and ~wollen~ share the same root. Cognate with English ~well~ (archaic "to wish well"), Dutch ~willen~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einwählen~ is a telecommunications term: one dials into a network or system, thereby establishing a connection.
en.einzahlen:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix conveys inward motion: going or putting into something.

~Einzahlen~ narrows the inward motion to money: the sum moves ~into~ an account or fund, the opposite of paying out with ~auszahlen~.
en.einziehen:
From MHG ~inziehen~. Compound of ~ein-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Dutch ~tien~ (obsolete), Old Norse ~toga~, and English ~tug~.
• ~ein-~: From PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). This separable prefix adds the sense of movement inward.

~Einziehen~ means "to move in" (to a new home), "to draft" (into military service), "to collect" (debts, taxes), "to retract" (claws), and "to absorb" (moisture). The semantic thread is always drawing or pulling inward. The housing sense (~in eine Wohnung einziehen~) is the most common in everyday speech and pairs neatly with ~ausziehen~ ("to move out"). The PIE root *~dewk-~ also produced Latin ~dūcere~ ("to lead"), whence English ~duke~, ~educate~, ~conduct~, and ~produce~.
en.einüben:
A separable compound of ~ein-~ + ~üben~:

• ~üben~: From MHG ~üeben~, ~uoben~, from OHG ~uoben~, from Proto-Germanic *~ōbijaną~ ("to do, practice"), the causative-iterative formation of a lost strong verb *~afaną~, from PIE *~h₃ep-~ ("to labor, work, toil"), which also gives Latin ~opus~ and ~opera~. Cognate with Dutch ~oefenen~, Old Saxon ~ōbian~, Old Norse *~œfa~ (Icelandic ~æfa~).
• ~ein-~: From MHG ~īn~, from OHG ~in~, from Proto-West Germanic *~in~, from Proto-Germanic *~in~ ("in, into"), from PIE *~h₁én~ ("in"). The particle is the stressed adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, not the numeral ~ein~ ("one"), with which it coincides only in spelling. Cognate with English ~in~, Latin ~in~, Greek ~en~. The prefix marks becoming familiar through practice: repetition makes something fluent, or someone at home in it.

~Einüben~ stresses the result of practice: through repetition a routine is mastered until it sits securely.
en.eislaufen:
A separable compound of ~eis~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~eis~: The noun ~Eis~ ("ice"), from MHG ~īs~, from OHG ~īs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~īs~, from Proto-Germanic *~īsą~, from PIE *~h₁eyH-~ ("ice, frost"). It is incorporated as an adverbial of place: ~eislaufen~ is "to run on ice," that is, to skate. Cognate with English ~ice~, Dutch ~ijs~, Old Norse ~íss~, Swedish ~is~. The sense of ~eis~ here is: in ~eislaufen~, moving on ice, skating.

~Eislaufen~ belongs to the small group of verbs with an incorporated noun and takes the auxiliary ~sein~, since it denotes a change of place.
en.empfangen:
From Middle High German ~enphāhen~, from Old High German ~intvāhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~andfanhaną~. Compound of ~emp-~ (variant of ~ent-~) + ~fangen~:

• ~fangen~: From MHG ~vāhen~, from OHG ~fāhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~fanhaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to secure, to attach, to fasten").
• ~emp-~: A variant of ~ent-~, from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Before labials (~f~, ~pf~), ~ent-~ becomes ~emp-~ for phonological reasons. The prefix here conveys the sense of receiving or taking in, facing something and accepting it.

~Empfangen~ means "to receive, to welcome, to conceive (a child)", senses that span from the formal (~einen Gast empfangen~, "to receive a guest") to the biological. The Old High German form ~intvāhan~ shows the original prefix ~int-~ (= ~ent-~) still intact; the shift to ~emp-~ before ~f~ is the same sound change seen in ~empfinden~ and ~empfehlen~. Cognate with Dutch ~ontvangen~, Old Saxon ~antfāhan~. The PIE root *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to secure, to fasten") makes the etymological image one of catching and holding: reception as a deliberate act of grasping what comes toward you, which also explains why English ~fang~ (the tooth that seizes prey) shares the same ancestor.
en.empfehlen:
From Middle High German ~enpfelhen~, ~enphelhen~, ~entfelhen~, ~intfelhen~, from Old High German ~intfelhan~, ~intfelahan~. Compound of ~emp-~ + the archaic root ~felhan~:

• ~felhan~: From Proto-Germanic *~felhaną~, of uncertain PIE origin. Two competing theories: if the primary sense was "to go, enter," it may be related to *~fulgāną~ ("to follow"); if "to conceal" was primary, it may connect to a PIE root *~pel-~ ("to cover, wrap"). The Old High German verb ~felhan~ meant "to preserve, entrust, confide in, surrender."
• ~emp-~: A variant of ~ent-~, from MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~, from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). The form ~emp-~ (rather than ~ent-~) arose through assimilation before the labial consonants ~f-~ and ~pf-~, the same process that gives ~empfinden~ rather than *~entfinden~.

A critical false friend lurks here: ~empfehlen~ ("to recommend") is etymologically related to ~befehlen~ ("to command, order"), both descending from OHG ~felhan~, but is ~not~ related to ~fehlen~ ("to be missing, to lack"), which has a different and separately borrowed history (from Old French ~faillir~). The prefix ~emp-~ shifts the archaic sense of "entrusting" into the modern sense of putting someone or something forward as worthy of confidence. Cognate with Dutch ~bevelen~ (via ~befehlen~).
en.empfinden:
From Middle High German ~enpfinden~, ~entfinden~, from Old High German ~intfindan~, equivalent to ~emp-~ (variant of ~ent-~) + ~finden~:

• ~finden~: From MHG ~vinden~, from OHG ~findan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to tread, walk, find the way").
• ~emp-~: A variant of ~ent-~, from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Before labial consonants (~f~, ~pf~), the prefix ~ent-~ assimilates to ~emp-~: compare ~empfangen~ (from ~ent-~ + ~fangen~), ~empfehlen~ (from ~ent-~ + ~fehlen/befehlen~).

~Empfinden~ means "to feel, to sense, to perceive through the sense organs", a class IIIa strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~empfinden~, ~empfand~, ~empfunden~. The semantic logic of the compound is beautiful: ~ent-~ / ~emp-~ in its original sense of "facing, encountering" + ~finden~ ("to find") yields "to find oneself facing something, to encounter a sensation." The word occupies a specific register between physical sensation (~er empfand die Kälte am ganzen Körper~, "he felt the cold all over his body") and emotional perception (~Mitleid empfinden~, "to feel compassion"). The derived noun ~Empfindung~ ("sensation, feeling") and the adjective ~empfindlich~ ("sensitive, touchy") extend this perceptual focus. The adjective ~empfindsam~ ("sentimental") was coined by G. E. Lessing in 1768 as a calque of English ~sentimental~, itself newly minted by Laurence Sterne.
en.emporblicken:
A separable compound of ~empor-~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~blank~, Dutch ~blik~, Old English ~blice~.
• ~empor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~enbor~, ~embor~, from ~in bor~ ("into the height"), with OHG ~bor~ ("height, upper space"), a noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *~beraną~ ("to bear, carry, lift"). The ~-nb-~ assimilated to ~-mp-~, as in ~Wimper~, and the phrase hardened into a single adverb. The height, in other words, is what has been lifted up: the same root as English ~bear~ and ~birth~. ~empor-~ means upward motion, "aloft, up on high."

~Emporblicken~ joins the upward direction to the gaze and often carries the overtone of reverence: to ~emporblicken~ toward someone is to look up to them.
en.emporfahren:
A separable compound of ~empor-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~empor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~enbor~, ~embor~, from ~in bor~ ("into the height"), with OHG ~bor~ ("height, upper space"), a noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *~beraną~ ("to bear, carry, lift"). The ~-nb-~ assimilated to ~-mp-~, as in ~Wimper~, and the phrase hardened into a single adverb. The height, in other words, is what has been lifted up: the same root as English ~bear~ and ~birth~. ~empor-~ means upward motion, "aloft, up on high."

~Emporfahren~ takes the abruptness from ~fahren~: it denotes less a gradual rise than a sudden starting up, as from sleep.
en.emporhalten:
A separable compound of ~empor-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~empor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~enbor~, ~embor~, from ~in bor~ ("into the height"), with OHG ~bor~ ("height, upper space"), a noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *~beraną~ ("to bear, carry, lift"). The ~-nb-~ assimilated to ~-mp-~, as in ~Wimper~, and the phrase hardened into a single adverb. The height, in other words, is what has been lifted up: the same root as English ~bear~ and ~birth~. ~empor-~ means upward motion, "aloft, up on high."

~Emporhalten~ names the literal holding of an object aloft; for the figurative „uphold“ modern German more often uses ~aufrechterhalten~.
en.emporheben:
A separable compound of ~empor-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb: the past ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ continue the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~.
• ~empor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~enbor~, ~embor~, from ~in bor~ ("into the height"), with OHG ~bor~ ("height, upper space"), a noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *~beraną~ ("to bear, carry, lift"). The ~-nb-~ assimilated to ~-mp-~, as in ~Wimper~, and the phrase hardened into a single adverb. The height, in other words, is what has been lifted up: the same root as English ~bear~ and ~birth~. ~empor-~ means upward motion, "aloft, up on high."

~Emporheben~ in a sense doubles the direction, since ~heben~ already contains the upward lift; the prefix makes the height explicit and lifts the register.
en.emporhelfen:
A separable compound of ~empor-~ + ~helfen~:

• ~helfen~: From MHG ~hëlfen~, from OHG ~hëlfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helpaną~, from PIE *~ḱelb-~, *~ḱelp-~. A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~e~-~a~-~o~ ablaut pattern (~helfen~, ~half~, ~geholfen~). Cognate with English ~help~, Dutch ~helpen~, Danish ~hjælpe~, Norwegian ~hjelpe~.
• ~empor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~enbor~, ~embor~, from ~in bor~ ("into the height"), with OHG ~bor~ ("height, upper space"), a noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *~beraną~ ("to bear, carry, lift"). The ~-nb-~ assimilated to ~-mp-~, as in ~Wimper~, and the phrase hardened into a single adverb. The height, in other words, is what has been lifted up: the same root as English ~bear~ and ~birth~. ~empor-~ means upward motion, "aloft, up on high."

~Emporhelfen~ governs the dative (~jemandem emporhelfen~) and usually means the figurative advancing of someone to rank or success rather than merely helping them to their feet.
en.emporkommen:
A separable compound of ~empor-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~empor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~enbor~, ~embor~, from ~in bor~ ("into the height"), with OHG ~bor~ ("height, upper space"), a noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *~beraną~ ("to bear, carry, lift"). The ~-nb-~ assimilated to ~-mp-~, as in ~Wimper~, and the phrase hardened into a single adverb. The height, in other words, is what has been lifted up: the same root as English ~bear~ and ~birth~. ~empor-~ means upward motion, "aloft, up on high."

~Emporkommen~ is almost always figurative: it denotes social rise, which is why an ~Emporkömmling~ is a parvenu or upstart.
en.emporsteigen:
A separable compound of ~empor-~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~empor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~enbor~, ~embor~, from ~in bor~ ("into the height"), with OHG ~bor~ ("height, upper space"), a noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *~beraną~ ("to bear, carry, lift"). The ~-nb-~ assimilated to ~-mp-~, as in ~Wimper~, and the phrase hardened into a single adverb. The height, in other words, is what has been lifted up: the same root as English ~bear~ and ~birth~. ~empor-~ means upward motion, "aloft, up on high."

~Emporsteigen~ underlines the height attained on a verb already pointing upward; it often serves the elevated image of smoke, sun, or stars that rise up.
en.emporstreben:
A separable compound of ~empor-~ + ~streben~:

• ~streben~: From MHG ~strëben~, from OHG ~strëbēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stribēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~stribāną~ ("to strive, resist"). Cognate with Dutch ~streven~ ("to strive") and English ~strive~ (via Old French ~estriver~, itself borrowed from a Germanic source).
• ~empor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~enbor~, ~embor~, from ~in bor~ ("into the height"), with OHG ~bor~ ("height, upper space"), a noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *~beraną~ ("to bear, carry, lift"). The ~-nb-~ assimilated to ~-mp-~, as in ~Wimper~, and the phrase hardened into a single adverb. The height, in other words, is what has been lifted up: the same root as English ~bear~ and ~birth~. ~empor-~ means upward motion, "aloft, up on high."

~Emporstreben~ joins direction to volition: towers and trees strive upward, but so does the ambitious person reaching for something higher.
en.emportragen:
A separable compound of ~empor-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb whose semantic range broadened from "to drag, pull" to "to carry, bear, wear." Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~empor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~enbor~, ~embor~, from ~in bor~ ("into the height"), with OHG ~bor~ ("height, upper space"), a noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *~beraną~ ("to bear, carry, lift"). The ~-nb-~ assimilated to ~-mp-~, as in ~Wimper~, and the phrase hardened into a single adverb. The height, in other words, is what has been lifted up: the same root as English ~bear~ and ~birth~. ~empor-~ means upward motion, "aloft, up on high."

~Emportragen~ names the carrying of a load upward; the prefix's elevated color sets it nearer ~emporheben~ than the everyday ~hinauftragen~.
en.emporwachsen:
A separable compound of ~empor-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from PIE *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Cognate with English ~wax~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~empor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~enbor~, ~embor~, from ~in bor~ ("into the height"), with OHG ~bor~ ("height, upper space"), a noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *~beraną~ ("to bear, carry, lift"). The ~-nb-~ assimilated to ~-mp-~, as in ~Wimper~, and the phrase hardened into a single adverb. The height, in other words, is what has been lifted up: the same root as English ~bear~ and ~birth~. ~empor-~ means upward motion, "aloft, up on high."

~Emporwachsen~ names the upward growth of plants, buildings, or, figuratively, of people and ideas that develop toward a height.
en.enden:
From Middle High German ~enden~, from Old High German ~entōn~ ("to end, to complete, to die"), attested since the 8th century. A denominative verb derived from the noun ~Ende~:

~Ende~ traces to OHG ~enti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andī~, from Proto-Germanic *~andijaz~, from PIE *~h₂entíos~ ("front, forehead"), itself from *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front").

The semantic journey from "forehead" to "end" is one of the more surprising in Germanic etymology. The PIE root *~h₂ent-~ referred to the front of the head, the face turned outward, the foremost surface of a thing. In Proto-Germanic, this gave *~andijaz~, which came to mean the farthest extent of something, the outermost point, the frontier, the edge. As the word entered OHG it had already shifted from "front" to "extremity," and from "extremity" to "terminus": the end is the point at which a thing faces outward no further. German ~Ende~ and English ~end~ are exact cognates, both descending from this root. The same PIE root *~h₂ent-~ also appears in the German prefix ~ent-~ and in Latin ~ante~ ("before"), a reminder that "front" and "before" are closely allied concepts. The verb ~enden~ is a simple denominative: to end is to bring something to its ~Ende~. Its OHG antecedent ~entōn~ already carried the sense of dying (reaching the ultimate end), a usage preserved in literary German to this day.
en.engagieren: Borrowed from French ~engager~ ("to pledge, to commit, to hire"), with the verb ending replaced by the German ~-ieren~ suffix. French ~engager~ derives from Old French ~engagier~ ("to pawn, to pledge"), from ~en-~ ("in") + ~gage~ ("pledge"), from Frankish *~wadja~ ("pledge"), from Proto-Germanic *~wadjō~ / *~wadją~ ("pledge, guarantee"), from PIE *~wedʰ-~ ("to guarantee, to pledge"). The etymology is thus circular: a Germanic word (*~wadja~) traveled into Old French via the Frankish conquerors of Gaul, evolved through centuries of French phonology into ~gage~ and then ~engager~, and was reborrowed back into German as ~engagieren~ in the 17th century, unrecognizable to German speakers as their own ancestor. The Proto-Germanic root also gives Gothic ~wadi~ ("pledge"), Old English ~wedd~ ("pledge, vow"; whence English ~wed~, originally "to pledge"), and Old High German ~wetti~ ("collateral, security agreement"; whence modern ~Wette~, "bet"). So ~engagieren~ and ~Wette~ are distant cousins reunited after a thousand-year detour through France. In modern German, ~engagieren~ means "to hire (an artist)" and, reflexively, ~sich engagieren~ means "to get involved, to commit oneself (to a cause)": ~sich politisch engagieren~ ("to be politically active"). The derived noun ~Engagement~ retains its French pronunciation. Cognate with English ~engage~, Portuguese ~engajar~, Romanian ~angaja~.
en.entbieten:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~bieten~:

• ~bieten~: From MHG ~bieten~, from OHG ~biotan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beudan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beudaną~, from PIE *~bʰewdʰ-~ ("to be awake, aware"). A class II strong verb whose root conveys awareness and offering. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bieden~, Danish ~byde~, Swedish ~bjuda~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ preserves the prefix's older sense of facing or moving toward.

~Entbieten~ keeps the old directional sense of ~ent-~: to ~einen Gruß entbieten~ is to hold a greeting out toward someone; the verb now survives only in elevated, formulaic use.
en.entbinden:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~binden~:

• ~binden~: From MHG ~binden~, from OHG ~bintan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bindan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bindaną~, from PIE *~bʰendʰ-~ ("to bind, tie"). A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~i~–~a~–~u~ ablaut (~binden~, ~band~, ~gebunden~). Cognate with English ~bind~, Dutch ~binden~, Gothic ~bindan~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

~Entbinden~ is the undoing of a binding: to release someone from a duty. From the same image (the child is loosed) came the medical sense „to deliver a child.“
en.entbrennen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~brennen~:

• ~brennen~: From MHG ~brennen~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: transitive ~brennan~ ("to set on fire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~brannijan~, and intransitive ~brinnan~, from *~brinnan~, of which *~brannijan~ was the causative. The intransitive is from PIE *~bʰrewh₁-~ ("to boil, brew"), making ~brennen~ a cousin of English ~brew~. A Rückumlaut verb: ~ich brenne~ but ~brannte~, ~gebrannt~. Cognate with English ~burn~, Dutch ~branden~, Icelandic ~brenna~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ marks the beginning or emergence of something.

~Entbrennen~ is inchoative: not the burning itself but its onset, a quarrel or a passion flares up. As already with ~brennen~, the intransitive image governs.
en.entdecken:
From Middle High German ~endecken~, from Old High German ~intthecken~, ~inthecken~. Compound of ~ent-~ + ~decken~:

• ~decken~: From MHG ~decken~, from OHG ~decchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þakkjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þakjaną~, from Proto-Germanic *~þaką~ ("roof, cover"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to cover"). Cognate with West Frisian ~dekke~, Dutch ~dekken~, English ~thatch~, Swedish ~täcka~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~, from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). This prefix often adds a sense of away, un-, or de-.

The literal meaning of ~entdecken~ is "to un-cover, to remove a covering", the ~ent-~ prefix reverses the action of ~decken~ ("to cover"). From this concrete sense, the verb generalized to "to discover," the same metaphor underlying English ~uncover~ ("to discover") and French ~découvrir~ ("to discover," from ~couvrir~, "to cover"). English ~discover~ itself follows the same pattern via Latin ~discooperiō~. The shared PIE root *~(s)teg-~ ("to cover") also shows up in English ~stegosaurus~ (the "roofed lizard") and Latin ~tēctum~ ("roof"). Cognate with Dutch ~ontdekken~, Danish ~opdage~ (different prefix, same root verb).
en.entehren:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~ehren~:

• ~ehren~: From MHG ~ēren~, from OHG ~ēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~aizāną~, from PIE *~h₂eys-~ ("to respect, to be in awe of"), derived from the noun ~Ehre~ ("honor"), from OHG ~ēra~, from Proto-West Germanic *~aiʀu~, from Proto-Germanic *~aizō~. Cognate with Dutch ~eer~, Old English ~ār~ ("honor, help, pardon"), Old Norse ~eir~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

~Entehren~ takes away again the ~Ehre~ that lies in the verb ~ehren~: it is the privative counterpart of honoring.
en.enteignen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~eignen~:

• ~eignen~: From MHG ~eigenen~, from OHG ~eiganen~, from Proto-Germanic *~aiginōną~, a denominative from *~aiganaz~ ("owned, one's own"), the past participle of *~aiganą~ ("to possess"), from PIE *~h₂eh₂óyḱe~, from *~h₂eyḱ-~ ("ability, possession"). Originally "to make one's own." Cognate with English ~own~, Dutch ~eigen~, Swedish ~ägna~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

~Enteignen~ reverses ~eignen~: what is someone's own is taken from them, usually by the state.
en.entfahren:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

~Entfahren~ now means almost only an involuntary slipping out: a word or a sigh ~entfährt~ someone before they can hold it back; the auxiliary is ~sein~.
en.entfallen:
Compound of ~ent-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~ ("to fall"), from PIE *~pōl-~ (possibly from a compound of *~h₂epo~ "off, away" + *~h₃elh₁-~ "to fall"). Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). As a prefix, ~ent-~ typically conveys removal, reversal, or separation.

The three modern meanings elegantly reflect the prefix's separative force applied to falling: "to drop away" (something falls from one's hands), "to lapse or be cancelled" (something falls away from the schedule), and "to slip one's memory" (something falls away from one's mind). The last sense offers a vivid metaphor: a forgotten thing has literally "fallen away from" the speaker.
en.entfalten:
Compound of ~ent-~ + ~falten~:

• ~falten~: From MHG ~valden~, ~valten~, from OHG ~faldan~, ~faltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~falþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~falþaną~, from pre-Germanic *~polt-~, from PIE *~pel-~ ("to fold"). The irregular forms with ~-t-~ arose through early levelling of ~Grammatischer Wechsel~ (Verner's law alternation) but remained rare in both Old and Middle High German. They likely established themselves by analogy with the several German verbs in ~-alten~ (~halten~, ~schalten~, ~spalten~, ~walten~), as no verbs in ~-alden~ survived. Cognate with English ~fold~, Dutch ~vouwen~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-Germanic *~andi-~ ("away, against"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Here the prefix reverses the base action: unfolding what was folded.

The literal sense is "to un-fold," and the semantic extension to "to develop, to unfurl, to deploy" is natural and vivid. One can ~ein Tuch entfalten~ ("unfold a cloth"), ~Aktivitäten entfalten~ ("develop activities"), or ~seine Persönlichkeit entfalten~ ("unfold one's personality"). The PIE root *~pel-~ also gives Latin ~-plex~ (as in ~duplex~, ~complex~), Greek ~-plasios~ ("-fold"), and English ~-ply~ (as in ~multiply~), making ~entfalten~ a distant relative of ~complicated~ (literally "folded together") and ~simple~ (literally "one-fold"). The English cognate ~fold~ descends from the same Proto-Germanic root but via Old English ~fealdan~, which preserved the original ~-d-~ that German analogically replaced with ~-t-~.
en.entfernen:
From Middle High German ~entverren~, analyzable as ~ent-~ + ~fern~ + ~-en~ (deadjectival verb suffix). Compound of ~ent-~ + ~fern~:

• ~fern~: From MHG ~verren~, from OHG ~ferrana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ferrai~ ("far, distant"), from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (locative form *~per-nóy~, "to cross, pass"). The same PIE root *~per-~ also underlies English ~far~, and more distantly Latin ~per-~ and Greek ~peri-~. Cognate with English ~far~, Dutch ~ver~, Danish ~fjern~, Icelandic ~fjær~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~, from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). This prefix often adds a sense of away, un-, or de-.

The verb literally means "to make distant, to remove into the distance", the ~ent-~ prefix conveys the movement away, while ~fern~ supplies the notion of distance. The reflexive ~sich entfernen~ ("to move away, leave") is extremely common in modern German, but the transitive form ("to remove something") is equally current. The spatial metaphor (distance as something actively created) is preserved in every use of the word. Cognate with Dutch ~verwijderen~ (the functional equivalent).
en.entflechten:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~flechten~:

• ~flechten~: From MHG ~vlëhten~, from OHG ~flëhtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~flehtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~flehtaną~, from PIE *~pleḱ-~ ("to plait, weave"). A class III strong verb (~flechten~, ~flocht~, ~geflochten~), its Präteritum ~o~ generalized from the old plural stem. Cognate with English ~flax~, Dutch ~vlechten~, Old Norse ~flétta~, Swedish ~fläta~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

~Entflechten~ is the undoing of a braid; in modern use it names the unbundling of interlocked corporations or responsibilities.
en.entfliehen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~fliehen~:

• ~fliehen~: From MHG ~vliehen~, from OHG ~fliohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuhaną~ ("to flee"), probably from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to fly, flee"), an enlargement of *~plew-~. A class II strong verb, and thus the etymological sibling of ~fliegen~. Cognate with English ~flee~, Dutch ~vlieden~, and Gothic ~þliuhan~ (with secondary ~þ-~).
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

~Entfliehen~ intensifies the away-motion already in ~fliehen~ with the sense of getting free; it governs the dative of what one flees and takes ~sein~.
en.entfließen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~fließen~:

• ~fließen~: From MHG ~vlieȥen~, from OHG ~flioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleutaną~ ("to float, stream, flow"), from PIE *~plewd-~ ("to flow, run, swim"). A class II strong verb (~fließen~, ~floss~, ~geflossen~); the zero grade *~flut-~ gave ~Flut~. Cognate with English ~fleet~, ~float~ and ~flood~, Dutch ~vlieten~, Swedish ~flyta~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

~Entfließen~ names the streaming forth from a source (a brook ~entfließt~ the rock); it governs the dative of the origin and takes the auxiliary ~sein~.
en.entfolgen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~folgen~:

• ~folgen~: From MHG ~volgen~, from OHG ~folgēn~ ("to follow, serve faithfully, pursue," attested from the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *~folgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fulgāną~; the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. Cognate with English ~follow~, Dutch ~volgen~, Danish ~følge~, Swedish ~följa~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

~Entfolgen~ is a recent coinage of social media: the ~ent-~ undoes the following, exactly as English ~unfollow~ does.
en.entführen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

~Entführen~ is leading-away in the literal sense: since ~führen~ is the causative „to make go,“ ~entführen~ means „to make someone go away from here“, against their will.
en.entgegenarbeiten:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. It also carries an adversarial sense: acting counter to something, opposing or contradicting it.

~Entgegenarbeiten~ governs the dative (~jemandem~ or ~einer Sache entgegenarbeiten~) and denotes deliberate working against something, not mere resistance.
en.entgegenbringen:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. With verbs of giving it means "holding out toward" the person who is coming.

In practice the compound is almost always figurative: what one "brings toward" another is an attitude (trust, sympathy, respect), far more often than a physical thing.
en.entgegengehen:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. ~entgegen-~ marks motion toward something that is itself approaching: going out to meet it.

Beyond the literal "go to meet someone," the verb readily turns figurative: one goes toward a fate or an age (~der Ewigkeit entgegengehen~), heading into what is itself approaching.
en.entgegenhalten:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. With verbs of giving it means "holding out toward" the person who is coming.

Literally one holds an object out toward someone; the everyday sense is figurative, "to counter with," objecting to a claim by holding an argument up against it.
en.entgegenkommen:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. ~entgegen-~ marks motion toward something that is itself approaching: going out to meet it.

The literal "come to meet" has worn into the everyday figurative sense "to accommodate, oblige" (to move partway toward another's wishes), which is the reading attested here.
en.entgegennehmen:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. ~entgegen-~ marks motion toward something that is itself approaching: going out to meet it.

Against plain ~nehmen~ "take," the compound is the receiver's formal counterpart to a giver's gesture: one "takes toward oneself" what is being handed over: an award, an application, an oath.
en.entgegenrufen:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. A parallel weak form in Middle High German explains why the modern present lacks the expected umlaut (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. ~entgegen-~ marks motion toward something that is itself approaching: going out to meet it.

The calling is aimed back at someone approaching or across a gap, a shout sent toward the one who is coming, as in the answering voices Aschenbach hears.
en.entgegenschlagen:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. It also carries an adversarial sense: acting counter to something, opposing or contradicting it.

With a personal subject the verb is the assault its gloss names; with an abstract one (heat, a smell, a wave of feeling) the direction reverses, and something strikes toward the perceiver, which is the sense the quoted sentence attests.
en.entgegensehen:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. ~entgegen-~ marks motion toward something that is itself approaching: going out to meet it.

Concrete "look toward" shades quickly into the fixed figurative ~einer Sache entgegensehen~ "to await, look forward to": to face what is coming.
en.entgegensetzen:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. It also carries an adversarial sense: acting counter to something, opposing or contradicting it.

One sets one thing against another; the past participle ~entgegengesetzt~ has hardened into an ordinary adjective meaning simply "opposite," which is why it no longer always reads as a live verb.
en.entgegenstehen:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. It also carries an adversarial sense: acting counter to something, opposing or contradicting it.

Beyond a body barring the way, the verb is the standard bureaucratic idiom ~einer Sache entgegenstehen~ "to be an obstacle to," governing the dative, as the legal texts here use it of rules and hindrances.
en.entgegenstellen:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. It also carries an adversarial sense: acting counter to something, opposing or contradicting it.

It is the transitive, causative counterpart to ~entgegenstehen~: where that verb has something stand in the way, this one puts it there, and reflexively ~sich entgegenstellen~ is to actively resist.
en.entgegenstreben:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~streben~:

• ~streben~: From MHG ~strëben~, from OHG ~strëbēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stribēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~stribāną~ ("to strive, resist"). Cognate with Dutch ~streven~ ("to strive") and English ~strive~ (via Old French ~estriver~, itself borrowed from a Germanic source).
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. ~entgegen-~ marks motion toward something that is itself approaching: going out to meet it.

The gloss takes the "striving toward a goal" reading; note that the same verb also serves the opposite, "to strive against, resist," so context alone tells which direction the striving runs.
en.entgegenwirken:
A separable compound of ~entgegen-~ + ~wirken~:

• ~wirken~: From MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~, from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~wérǵom~, from *~werǵ-~ ("to make, work"). Early on it merged with the dialectal ~würken~ (from OHG ~wurken~), which left the written language in the 18th century. Cognate with English ~work~ and ~wrought~, Dutch ~werken~.
• ~entgegen-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: from MHG ~engegen~, from OHG ~ingagan~, ~ingegin~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andagagin~, literally "in against," built on the element that also yields ~gegen~ ("against, toward"). Old English ~onġēan~ is the very same formation, and it is the direct ancestor of English ~again~ and ~against~. It also carries an adversarial sense: acting counter to something, opposing or contradicting it.

The everyday administrative verb for "counteract," governing a dative object, one works against a trend, a problem, a risk, as the official prose here does.
en.entgehen:
Compound of ~ent-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from OHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Swedish ~gå~.
• ~ent-~: From PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). As a prefix, it means "away, un-, de-."

~Entgehen~ means "to escape, to avoid, to elude", literally "to go away from." The dative construction ~jemandem entgehen~ ("to escape someone's notice") is particularly common: ~Diese Tatsache ist mir entgangen~ ("This fact escaped my notice"). The spelling with ~-h-~ in modern German ~gehen~ is a purely orthographic addition modeled on ~sehen~ ("to see"), where the ~h~ was originally etymological. In Old High German, the verb was simply ~gān~; no ~h~ at all.
en.entgelten:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~gelten~:

• ~gelten~: From MHG ~gelten~, from OHG ~geltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~geldaną~, possibly from PIE *~gʰeldʰ-~. The range narrowed over time: OHG ~geltan~ meant "to pay, repay, be worth," while the modern verb centers on "to be valid, to count." Cognate with English ~yield~ (from the same root), Dutch ~gelden~, Icelandic ~gjalda~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ preserves the prefix's older sense of facing or moving toward.

The prefix's reciprocal force gives the verb its sense of requital (to pay or atone in return) and it survives in the noun ~Entgelt~ "remuneration" and beside ~vergelten~ "to repay."
en.entgleiten:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~gleiten~:

• ~gleiten~: From MHG ~glīten~, from OHG ~glītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~glīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~glīdaną~, from PIE *~ǵʰleydʰ-~ ("to glide, slide"). A class I strong verb (~gleiten~, ~glitt~, ~geglitten~), though a weak ~gleitete~ turns up in technical prose. Cognate with English ~glide~, Dutch ~glijden~, Low German ~glieden~, Swedish ~glida~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

Literally something slips out of one's grasp; figuratively a situation or a mood slips beyond one's control, and Mann lets even a gaze slip free into the haze of the sea.
en.enthaften:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~haften~:

• ~haften~: From ~Haft~ + ~-en~. ~Haft~ descends through MHG ~haft~, ~hafte~ ("captivity") and OHG ~haft~ to PIE *~kh₂p-tó-~, from *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize"). Hence both senses: "to stick, adhere" (to be held fast) and "to be liable." Cognate with English ~captive~, Latin ~captus~, Old English ~hæft~, Old Irish ~cacht~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

Built on ~haften~ in its "be held in custody" branch (the root's ~Haft~ "captivity"), the verb releases someone from arrest, the prefix undoing the holding-fast.
en.enthalten:
From Middle High German ~enthalten~. Compound of ~ent-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~, from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). This prefix often adds a sense of away, un-, or de-.

The compound was influenced by ~innehalten~ and ~einhalten~ (literally "to hold inside"), which shaped both its "to contain" sense (compare ~Inhalt~, "contents," from the same root complex) and its reflexive "to abstain" sense (~sich enthalten~, "to refrain"). Cognate with Dutch ~onthouden~ ("to remember, withhold") and ~inhouden~ ("to contain"), Middle Low German ~enthōlden~.
en.entheben:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb: the past ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ continue the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

The compound survives chiefly in the fixed idiom ~jemanden seines Amtes entheben~ "to remove someone from office," governing a genitive, the exact construction the Basic Law uses of judges here.
en.entkommen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

The thing escaped stands in the dative (~den Taliban entkommen~, ~der Gefahr entkommen~), the prefix carrying the getting-free that the plain verb of coming would not express alone.
en.entladen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two historically distinct verbs under one infinitive. ~laden~ (strong, "to load"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"); cognate with English ~lade~ and ~laden~, Lithuanian ~klṓti~. ~laden~ (weak, "to invite, summon"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root found only in Germanic and Anatolian (Hittite ~halzai~).
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

Here ~laden~ is the strong verb "to load" (family s), not the weak ~laden~ "to invite," so ~entladen~ is the clean reversal "unload", and by extension the discharge of a battery or a storm.
en.entlangfahren:
A separable compound of ~entlang-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~entlang-~: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~entlanc~ ("along"), whose first element is the old preposition ~ant-~, ~ent-~ ("facing, opposite") that also stands in ~entgegen~, plus ~lang~ ("long"). English ~along~ is the same formation on native soil, from Old English ~andlang~, the very same two morphemes. As a particle it is directional: ~entlanggehen~ is to walk along something, ~entlangfahren~ to drive along it. The sense of ~entlang-~ here is: alongside a line, edge, or path.

The path travelled stands in the accusative (~die Küste entlangfahren~) the particle fixing the route as a line followed along its length.
en.entlanggehen:
A separable compound of ~entlang-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~entlang-~: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~entlanc~ ("along"), whose first element is the old preposition ~ant-~, ~ent-~ ("facing, opposite") that also stands in ~entgegen~, plus ~lang~ ("long"). English ~along~ is the same formation on native soil, from Old English ~andlang~, the very same two morphemes. As a particle it is directional: ~entlanggehen~ is to walk along something, ~entlangfahren~ to drive along it. The sense of ~entlang-~ here is: alongside a line, edge, or path.

A verb of motion taking ~sein~, with the route in the accusative (~die Mauer entlanggehen~), walking a line to its end.
en.entlassen:
Compound of ~ent-~ + ~lassen~:

• ~lassen~: From MHG ~lāzen~, ~lān~, from OHG ~lāȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lātan~ ("to let, allow"), from Proto-Germanic *~lētaną~ ("to leave behind, allow"), from PIE *~leh₁d-~ ("to let, to leave behind"). Cognate with Dutch ~laten~, English ~let~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~ ("against, facing"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). As a prefix, it conveys reversal, removal, or release.

The compound means "to release, to discharge, to dismiss, to lay off." The ~ent-~ prefix adds the sense of releasing from an obligation or bond: a doctor ~entlässt~ a patient from the hospital, an employer ~entlässt~ an employee from their position. The noun ~Entlassung~ covers both the neutral sense of "discharge" and the harsher sense of "dismissal" or "layoff." The word carries considerable weight in German labor law, where ~Entlassung~ triggers formal legal protections (~Kündigungsschutz~, "protection against dismissal") that are among the strongest in Europe. The combination of ~ent-~ ("away from") and ~lassen~ ("to let") creates a precise image: to let someone go away from where they have been held.
en.entlasten:
Compound of ~ent-~ + ~lasten~, a denominal derivation from ~Last~ ("load, burden"):

• ~Last~: From MHG ~last~, from OHG ~last~, ~hlast~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlasti~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, to lay out"). The initial OHG ~hl-~ cluster was simplified to ~l-~ during the Middle High German period. Cognate with English ~last~ (in the sense of a unit of weight or cargo) and ~ballast~ (which preserves the noun in a compound). Related to English ~laden~ ("loaded").
