• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~ ("against, facing"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). As a prefix, it conveys removal or reversal.

The verb means "to relieve, to unburden, to exonerate", to remove a ~Last~ ("burden") from someone. In legal contexts, ~entlasten~ means "to exonerate" (to remove the burden of guilt), and ~Entlastung~ is the legal term for "exoneration" or "acquittal." In accounting, ~Entlastung~ refers to the formal approval and discharge of a board's management ("ratification"). The ~ent-~ prefix performs its characteristic reversal: where ~belasten~ means "to burden" (using ~be-~ to place a load upon), ~entlasten~ removes the load. This elegant ~be-~/~ent-~ mirror pair (burdening and unburdening) is a productive pattern in German.
en.entlaufen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

The emphasis falls on the flight itself, and the source escaped stands in the dative: proverbially of animals that run off from their owners, and here of servants fleeing their master.
en.entlehnen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~lehnen~:

• ~lehnen~: A merger of two verbs: MHG ~linen~/~lenen~ (intransitive), from OHG ~hlinēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlinēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlināną~, from PIE *~k̂ley-~ ("to lean, incline"); and MHG ~leinen~ (causative), from OHG ~hleinen~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlainijaną~. A second, archaic ~lehnen~ ("to lend, borrow"), from OHG ~lēhanōn~, survives only in ~entlehnen~ and ~Lehnwort~. Cognate with English ~lean~, Latin ~clīnō~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

The root here is not ~lehnen~ "to lean" but the archaic ~lehnen~ "to lend, borrow" (family w) that otherwise survives only in ~Lehnwort~; ~entlehnen~ is to take on loan, today chiefly of words a language borrows.
en.entleihen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~leihen~:

• ~leihen~: From MHG ~līhen~, from OHG ~līhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~līhwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~līhwaną~, from PIE *~leykʷ-~ ("to leave behind"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with English ~loan~ (via Old Norse ~lán~, from *~laihną~ of the same root), Dutch ~lenen~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

Since ~leihen~ already covers both lending and borrowing, the prefix pins the direction to taking-from: ~entleihen~ is to borrow from a source, a book from a library.
en.entlieben:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~lieben~:

• ~lieben~: From MHG ~lieben~, an alteration of the rarer MHG ~liuben~ ("to make dear"), from OHG ~liuben~; denominative of the adjective ~lieb~, from MHG ~liep~, OHG ~liob~, Proto-West Germanic *~leub~, Proto-Germanic *~leubaz~ ("dear, beloved"), from PIE *~lewbʰ-~ ("to desire, love"). English ~love~ is from the related but distinct root *~lubō~. Cognate with English ~lief~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

A modern, mostly reflexive coinage (~sich entlieben~) that simply reverses ~lieben~: to fall out of love, undoing the state the base verb names.
en.entlohnen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~lohnen~:

• ~lohnen~: From MHG ~lōnen~, from OHG ~lōnōn~, a denominal verb from ~lōn~ ("reward, wage"), from Proto-West Germanic *~laun~, from Proto-Germanic *~launą~, from PIE *~leh₂w-~ ("gain, prize, booty"), payment as something won. Cognate with Old English ~lēan~; the English cognate ~lean~ is now obsolete.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

The compound denotes paying out a wage; here ~ent-~ carries the sense of rendering forth, so that ~entlohnen~ names the full remuneration of work performed more emphatically than plain ~lohnen~.
en.entmieten:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~mieten~:

• ~mieten~: From MHG ~mieten~, from OHG ~mietan~, a denominative of the noun ~Miete~ ("rent, reward"), which via MHG ~miete~ and OHG ~mieta~ goes back to Proto-West Germanic *~miʀdu~, Proto-Germanic *~mizdō~, and PIE *~misdʰéh₂~ ("reward, compensation"). Cognate with Gothic ~mizdo~, English ~meed~ (archaic), Greek ~misthos~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

A recent term of real-estate jargon: a landlord ~entmietet~ a building by clearing it of its tenants, usually in order to renovate it or re-let it at a higher rent.
en.entmischen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~mischen~:

• ~mischen~: From MHG ~mischen~, from OHG ~misken~, from Proto-Germanic *~miskijaną~ ("to mix"), from PIE *~meyḱ-~ ("to mix, knead"), via the inchoative present *~miḱ-sḱé-~. Cognate with English ~mix~, Latin ~misceō~, Greek ~mísgo~, Sanskrit ~miśrá~ ("mixed").
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

~Entmischen~ undoes a blending: a mixture is separated back into its components, as oil from water or isotopes in a centrifuge.
en.entnehmen:
From Middle High German ~entnëmen~, from Old High German ~intneman~. Compound of ~ent-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due").
• ~ent-~: From PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). As a prefix, ~ent-~ conveys separation, removal, or extraction, taking something away from where it was.

~Entnehmen~ means "to take out, to remove, to extract" in formal registers; ~Bitte Karte entnehmen~ ("Please remove card") is the phrase every German ATM user knows by heart. Beyond the physical sense, ~entnehmen~ also means "to learn, to conclude, to gather" from a source; ~Ihrem Brief entnehme ich, dass...~ ("From your letter I gather that..."). This abstract extension treats information as something physically extracted from a container (the letter, the document, the silence). The derived noun ~Entnahme~ means "removal, withdrawal, extraction"; ~Blutentnahme~ ("blood draw") and ~Probeentnahme~ ("sample extraction") are standard medical and scientific terms. The ~ent-~ prefix's separative force makes ~entnehmen~ more formal and precise than simple ~herausnehmen~ ("to take out"), lending it a clinical or bureaucratic register. Cognate with Dutch ~ontnemen~ ("to deprive of, to take away").
en.entnerven:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~nerven~:

• ~nerven~: A modern denominative from the noun ~Nerv~ ("nerve"), via the colloquial ~auf die Nerven gehen~. ~Nerv~ was borrowed from Latin ~nervus~ ("sinew, tendon"), partly through French ~nerf~, from Proto-Italic *~(s)nēuros~, from PIE *~snḗh₁wr̥~ ("sinew"). The sense "to annoy" is a twentieth-century colloquial development unique to German. Cognate with Greek ~neuron~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

Literally "to rob of nerve": ~entnerven~ means to strip someone of composure and strength until they are worn down.
en.entpacken:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~packen~:

• ~packen~: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~packen~, from Old Saxon *~pakko~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pakkō~, from Proto-Germanic *~pakkô~ ("bundle, pack"), of debated ultimate origin. The absence of the High German consonant shift confirms it entered via Low German trade routes. Cognate with English ~pack~, Dutch ~pakken~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

A computing term: ~entpacken~ reverses compression and restores a file from its archive, the exact inverse of ~packen~.
en.entraten:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~raten~:

• ~raten~: From MHG ~rāten~, from OHG ~rātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rēdaną~ ("to decide, advise, interpret"), from PIE *~Hreh₁dh-~ ("to think, arrange"). Both senses, "to advise" and "to guess," descend from that sense of deliberation. Cognate with English ~read~ (originally "to counsel, interpret"), archaic ~rede~, Dutch ~raden~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

A now almost extinct strong verb governing the genitive: ~einer Sache entraten~ means to be able to do without it, to forgo it.
en.entreißen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

~Entreißen~ joins the tearing force of the simplex to the separating ~ent-~: to snatch something from someone's hand or grip with a jerk, also figuratively, as in snatching from oblivion.
en.entrichten:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~ ("to straighten, set right, direct"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rihtijaną~, a denominative from the adjective *~rehtaz~ ("straight, right"), from PIE *~h₃reǵtós~ ("right, straightened"), from *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to stretch out, straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~richten~, Gothic ~raihtjan~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

Like ~entlohnen~, ~entrichten~ belongs to the verbs of payment: a debt, tax, or fee is "set right," that is, settled; the ~ent-~ stresses the full discharge.
en.entrinnen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~rinnen~:

• ~rinnen~: From MHG ~rinnen~, from OHG ~rinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~ ("to run, flow"); the PIE source is debated, most often given as *~h₃reyH-~ ("to churn, set in motion"). A class III strong verb (~rinnen~, ~rann~, ~geronnen~). German ~rennen~ is its causative, from *~rannijaną~. Cognate with English ~run~, Gothic ~rinnan~, Swedish ~rinna~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

~Entrinnen~ is the elevated word for flight: as water runs out of a vessel, one escapes a danger or one's fate, the movement of flight is already latent in the flowing simplex.
en.entrücken:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~rücken~:

• ~rücken~: From MHG ~rücken~, from OHG ~rucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rukkijan~. The verb means "to move, to shift" and is the base of ~verrückt~ ("crazy," literally "shifted, displaced"); the noun ~Rücken~ ("back") is etymologically a separate word. Cognate with English ~rock~, Old Norse ~rykkja~, Old English ~roccian~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

~Entrücken~ shifts (~rücken~) something or someone entirely out of the ordinary world: into rapture, into the beyond, or, in the participle ~entrückt~, into a dreamy absence.
en.entsagen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

~Entsagen~ is a speech act of disavowal: one renounces something (an office, a claim, the world), and is thereby freed of it; the verb governs the dative.
en.entscheiden:
From Middle High German ~entscheiden~, from Old High German ~intskeiden~. Compound of ~ent-~ + ~scheiden~:

• ~scheiden~: From MHG ~scheiden~, from OHG ~sceidan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaiþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaiþaną~, from PIE *~skey-~ ("to split, dissect"). Cognate with Dutch ~scheiden~, West Frisian ~skiede~, English ~shed~, Irish ~scian~ ("knife"), Ancient Greek ~skhízō~ ("to split"), and Sanskrit ~cyati~ ("he cuts off").
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~, from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). This prefix often adds a sense of away, un-, or de-.

The semantic development of ~entscheiden~ (from "to cut apart, separate" to "to decide") parallels Latin ~dēcīdere~ (literally "to cut off," from ~caedere~, "to cut"), which also yielded the English word ~decide~. Two languages, one metaphor: a decision is a cut that divides options apart. Cognate with Dutch ~ontscheiden~, Low German ~entscheden~.
en.entschlafen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~schlafen~:

• ~schlafen~: From MHG ~slāfen~, from OHG ~slāfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slāpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slēpaną~, of uncertain further origin, possibly related to *~slapaz~ ("weak, lax, limp"), ancestor of ~schlaff~. A class VII strong verb of the reduplicating class (~schlafen~, ~schlief~, ~geschlafen~). Cognate with English ~sleep~, Dutch ~slapen~, Gothic ~𐍃𐌻𐌴𐍀𐌰𐌽~ (slēpan).
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ marks the beginning or emergence of something.

The inceptive ~ent-~ marks the entry into sleep; as a euphemism ~entschlafen~ became the gentle word for dying, a peaceful "falling asleep."
en.entschlagen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

Now almost only reflexive and with the genitive: ~sich einer Sache entschlagen~ means to shake it off oneself, a worry, a thought, an obligation.
en.entschließen:
Compound of ~ent-~ + ~schließen~:

• ~schließen~: From MHG ~slieȝen~, from OHG ~sliozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sleutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sleutaną~, *~slūtaną~ ("to lock, shut"). The PIE origin is uncertain; traditionally connected to *~(s)klewd-~ ("to lock"), from *~(s)kleh₂w-~ ("nail, hook, pin, key"), from *~(s)kel-~ ("to crook, bend"). Cognate with Old Saxon ~slūtan~, Dutch ~sluiten~, English ~slot~.
• ~ent-~: From PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). This prefix carries a sense of reversal, undoing, or decisive separation.

The literal sense is "to un-lock": to open a decision that was previously closed. The reflexive ~sich entschließen~ means "to decide, to resolve, to make up one's mind," and the noun ~Entschluss~ ("decision, resolution") is the standard word for a firm resolve. The metaphor is striking: a decision is imagined as a lock being opened, releasing a course of action. The base verb ~schließen~ appears in an extraordinary range of compounds: ~beschließen~ ("to decide, to resolve"), ~abschließen~ ("to lock, to conclude"), ~einschließen~ ("to lock in, to include"), ~ausschließen~ ("to lock out, to exclude"). The English cognate ~slot~ (a narrow opening) preserves the physical sense of the lock mechanism. Latin ~clāvis~ ("key"), whence English ~clavicle~ and ~conclave~, may be a distant cousin if the traditional PIE etymology is correct.
en.entschuldigen:
From Middle High German ~entschuldigen~ ("to absolve, to exonerate"). Surface analysis: ~ent-~ + ~schuldig~ ("guilty") + ~-en~, literally "to de-guilt":

• ~schuldig~: From ~Schuld~ ("guilt, debt, fault"). ~Schuld~ from MHG ~schult~, from OHG ~sculd~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skuldi~, from Proto-Germanic *~skuldō~, from PIE *~skel-~ ("to owe, to be obliged"). Cognate with obsolete English ~shild~ ("debt, fault, guilt"), Dutch ~schuld~, and English ~shall~ (which originally expressed obligation: "I shall" = "I owe it").
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~ ("against, facing"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). The prefix conveys removal or reversal.

The verb means "to excuse, to apologize", literally "to un-guilt." The reflexive ~sich entschuldigen~ ("to excuse oneself, to apologize") is one of the most common polite expressions in German: ~Entschuldigung!~ ("Excuse me!"). The MHG meaning was stronger: "to absolve, to exonerate," a legal and religious term for removing guilt. Over the centuries, the meaning softened from juridical absolution to social courtesy. The connection between ~Schuld~ ("guilt") and ~Schuld~ ("debt") is not coincidental: they are the same word, reflecting the ancient equation of moral guilt with financial obligation. English ~shall~ descends from the same root, preserving the original sense of obligation, and Gothic ~skulan~ ("to owe, to be obligated") confirms the shared Germanic ancestry.
en.entschwinden:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~schwinden~:

• ~schwinden~: From MHG ~swinden~, from OHG ~swintan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swindaną~. A class III strong verb. The simplex still exists in literary German meaning "to dwindle, wane, fade." Cognate with Dutch ~zwinden~ ("to disappear"), Danish ~svinde~, Swedish ~svinna~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

~Entschwinden~ is the poetic intensification of ~schwinden~: not merely to wane but to slip away entirely from sight and reach.
en.entsenden:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~senden~:

• ~senden~: From MHG ~senden~, from OHG ~senten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sandijaną~, from PIE *~sont-eye-~, a causative of *~sent-~ ("to walk, travel"), originally "to cause to go." It has a double Präteritum: ~sendete~ for broadcasting, ~sandte~ (a Rückumlaut form) for sending a letter. Cognate with English ~send~, Dutch ~zenden~, Gothic ~sandjan~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

~Entsenden~ is the formal word for sending forth: one ~entsendet~ delegates, envoys, or troops, the ~ent-~ directs the sending away from oneself into the distance.
en.entsetzen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

Literally "to set out of composure": one who is ~entsetzt~ has been jolted out of mental balance. The same verb once also meant "to depose from office" and "to relieve a besieged town."
en.entsichern:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~sichern~:

• ~sichern~: A denominative verb from the adjective ~sicher~ ("safe, secure"): OHG ~sihhurōn~ ("to justify, to vouch for"), whence MHG ~sichern~. ~sicher~ is itself a loanword: from OHG ~sihur~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sikur~, from Latin ~sēcūrus~ ("carefree"), from ~sē-~ ("without") + ~cūra~ ("care"); ~sē-~ from PIE *~sue-~ ("self, one's own"). English ~secure~ and ~sure~ descend from the same Latin root.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

~Entsichern~ reverses the ~sichern~ of a weapon: the safety catch is released so that it can fire.
en.entsinnen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~sinnen~:

• ~sinnen~: From MHG ~sinnen~, from OHG ~sinnan~ ("to travel; to strive for; to think"), from Proto-West Germanic *~sinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sinnaną~, from PIE *~sent-~ ("to head for, go; to feel"). A class III strong verb (~sinnen~, ~sann~, ~gesonnen~). The same root gave Latin ~sentīre~, so ~Sinn~ and English ~sense~ are relatives. Cognate with Old English ~sinnan~ ("to meditate on"), Dutch ~zinnen~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ marks the beginning or emergence of something.

~Sich einer Sache entsinnen~ means to bring it back out of memory; the ~ent-~ lets the recollection surface again.
en.entsorgen:
Compound of ~ent-~ + ~sorgen~, a denominal derivation via the noun ~Sorge~ ("care, worry"):

• ~sorgen~: From MHG ~sorgen~, from OHG ~sorgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~surgāną~, from PIE *~swergʰ-~ ("to watch over, to worry; to be ill, to suffer"). The noun ~Sorge~ ("care, worry, sorrow") is cognate with English ~sorrow~, Dutch ~zorg~, Danish ~sorg~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~ ("against, facing"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). The prefix conveys removal.

The verb means "to dispose of (waste)", literally "to de-worry," to remove the object of concern. The word is strikingly modern: although its MHG ancestor ~entsorgen~ originally meant "to free from worry," the old meaning fell out of use, and the modern waste-disposal sense emerged only in the 1980s, during the environmental movement. Some commentators have claimed ~entsorgen~ originated as Nazi-era bureaucratic euphemism, but the evidence points instead to its independent reinvention in postwar environmental discourse. The irony is rich: a word that once meant "to relieve anxiety" now refers to the very activity (waste management), that causes considerable anxiety in environmentally conscious Germany, a country that takes its ~Mülltrennung~ ("waste sorting") with legendary seriousness.
en.entspannen:
Compound of ~ent-~ + ~spannen~:

• ~spannen~: From MHG ~spannen~, from OHG ~spannan~, from Proto-Germanic *~spannaną~, originally a strong verb of the seventh class. The long ~-nn-~ comes from an earlier form *~spanwaną-~. Perhaps ultimately an ablaut form related to *~spinnaną~ ("to spin"), or alternatively from PIE *~spend-~ ("to stretch"), comparing Lithuanian ~spęsti~ ("to snare") and Latvian ~spanda~ ("strap"). Cognate with English ~span~ and ~spin~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-Germanic *~andi-~ ("away, against"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Here the prefix acts as a reversal: undoing the tension.

The literal sense is "to un-tension," i.e., to release from a stretched or strained state, yielding "to relax, to ease." The word works both transitively (~einen Bogen entspannen~, "to unstring a bow") and reflexively (~sich entspannen~, "to relax"). The physical metaphor of releasing a taut bowstring or spring extends naturally to psychological relaxation. English ~span~ (a unit of measurement based on the stretched hand) is the closest cognate, preserving the root sense of stretching. The compound ~Entspannung~ ("relaxation, detente") gained particular political currency during the Cold War as the German equivalent of ~detente~, and indeed, French ~detente~ is itself a structural parallel, from ~des-~ ("un-") + ~tendre~ ("to stretch"), from Latin ~tendere~, making it a twin of ~entspannen~ built from completely different etymological material.
en.entsperren:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~sperren~:

• ~sperren~: From MHG ~sperren~, from OHG ~sperran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sparrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sparrijaną~ ("to bar, to block"), a denominative verb from *~sparrô~ ("wooden beam, log"), originally to bar a passage with a beam. Cognate with English ~spar~ ("to bolt, bar"; the noun for a wooden beam), Dutch ~sperren~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

~Entsperren~ lifts a block: to free an account, a phone, or an access again, the reverse of ~sperren~.
en.entspiegeln:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~spiegeln~:

• ~spiegeln~: From MHG ~spiegeln~, a denominative verb from the noun ~Spiegel~ ("mirror"), from MHG ~spiegel~, OHG ~spiegal~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spēgl~, an early borrowing from Latin ~speculum~ ("mirror"), from ~specere~ ("to look at"), from PIE *~speḱ-~ ("to see, to observe"). The same root gave English ~spectacle~ and ~spy~, and German ~spähen~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

An optics term: a lens or pair of spectacles is ~entspiegelt~ by suppressing its reflection with a coating; the ~ent-~ takes the mirroring away from the glass.
en.entsprechen:
From Middle High German ~entsprechen~ (implied), from Old High German ~intsprehhōn~. Compound of ~ent-~ + ~sprechen~:

• ~sprechen~: From MHG ~sprëchen~, from OHG ~sprëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sprekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sprekaną~, probably from PIE *~spregʰ-~ ("to crackle"). The semantic development from "to crackle, make noise" to "to speak" parallels the evolution seen in many languages where words for speech derive from words for sound. Cognate with Dutch ~spreken~, English ~speak~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~, from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). This prefix often adds a sense of away, un-, or de-.

The compound's semantic development (from "to speak in response to" to "to correspond to, match, comply with") reflects a characteristic use of ~ent-~ to convey a reciprocal or countering relationship. ~Einer Sache entsprechen~ ("to comply with something") and ~dem Bild entsprechen~ ("to match the image") both capture this sense of meeting or answering to something. Cognate with Dutch ~overeenkomen~ (the functional equivalent, though formed differently).
en.entsprießen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~sprießen~:

• ~sprießen~: From MHG ~sprieʒen~, from OHG ~spriozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spreutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~spreutaną~ ("to sprout"), from PIE *~sper-~ ("to strew, scatter"). A class II strong verb (~sprießen~, ~spross~, ~gesprossen~). Cognate with English ~sprout~, Dutch ~spruiten~, Scots ~sproot~; Ancient Greek ~σπείρω~ (speírō, "I sow") goes back to the same root.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ marks the beginning or emergence of something.

~Entsprießen~ pictures growth issuing from an origin: a plant (but in elevated use also a lineage or a thought) ~entsprießt~ a soil or a source.
en.entspringen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~springen~:

• ~springen~: From OHG ~springan~, from Proto-Germanic *~springaną~, from PIE *~sprenǵʰ-~, a nasalized form of *~sperǵʰ-~ ("to move energetically, to hasten, to spring"). A class III strong verb (~springen~, ~sprang~, ~gesprungen~). Cognate with English ~spring~, Dutch ~springen~, Danish ~springe~, Greek ~spérkhō~ ("to hasten").
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ marks the beginning or emergence of something.

~Entspringen~ names both the source of a river and the origin of an idea: each "springs forth" from its beginning. Alongside this survives the older, literal sense of running off or breaking loose.
en.entstammen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~stammen~:

• ~stammen~: A denominative verb from ~Stamm~ ("trunk, stem, tribe, stock") with the suffix ~-en~. ~Stamm~ derives from MHG ~stam~, OHG ~stam~, Proto-Germanic *~stamnaz~, *~stamniz~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand, stay"). Cognate with English ~stem~, Dutch ~stam~, Danish ~stamme~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ marks the beginning or emergence of something.

~Entstammen~ denotes origin: one ~entstammt~ a family, an era, or a source, the ~ent-~ points back to the origin from which something arises.
en.entstehen:
From Middle High German ~entstēn~, ~entstān~, from Old High German ~intstantan~, ~intstantēn~. Compound of ~ent-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand").
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~, from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). This prefix often adds a sense of away, un-, or de-.

The compound's semantic development from "to stand away/forth" to "to come into being, arise" reflects how the ~ent-~ prefix here conveys emergence or inception rather than its more common sense of removal.
en.entsteigen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ marks the beginning or emergence of something.

~Entsteigen~ joins climbing to the emergent ~ent-~: an elevated word for rising out of something: a carriage, a bed, the sea from which a figure emerges like a god.
en.entstellen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

~Entstellen~ sets (~stellen~) something out of its proper shape: a face is disfigured, a report or a picture falsified; always the true form is knocked out of place.
en.entstören:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~stören~:

• ~stören~: From MHG ~stören~, from OHG ~stōren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~staurijan~; related to Proto-Germanic *~steuran~, whose root meant "to move, to agitate." Cognate with English ~stir~, Old English ~styrian~ ("to stir, move, agitate"), Dutch ~storen~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

~Entstören~ is a term of art in engineering: to rid a device of the interference signals that disturb its operation.
en.enttäuschen:
Compound of ~ent-~ + ~täuschen~ ("to deceive"). Coined in the 19th century as a German replacement for the French loanwords ~desabusiren~ (from French ~désabuser~) and ~detrompiren~ (from French ~détromper~):

• ~täuschen~: From MHG ~tiuschen~, derived from ~tūschen~ ("to exchange surreptitiously"), related to ~tauschen~ ("to trade, to exchange"). The semantic development was "to swap" > "to trick someone into a trade" > "to deceive" (DWDS).
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~ ("against, facing"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). The prefix conveys reversal.

The verb means "to disappoint", but its literal, etymological meaning is "to un-deceive," to tear away a deception and reveal the truth. This is the opposite of what "disappoint" feels like: one would expect "un-deceiving" to be positive (and in fact, the original 19th-century sense was neutral, simply "to free from an illusion"). Over time, however, the word shifted from describing the removal of delusion to describing the emotional pain that follows when reality falls short of expectation. The underlying ~täuschen~ ("to deceive") derives from ~tauschen~ ("to exchange"), with the semantic pathway "to exchange" > "to palm off, to trick into a swap" > "to deceive generally." This connection between trading and trickery is ancient and cross-linguistic: English ~trick~ may derive from Old French ~trichier~ ("to cheat"), and Latin ~dolus~ means both "cunning" and "fraud."
en.entwachsen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from PIE *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Cognate with English ~wax~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ marks the beginning or emergence of something.

Governing the dative, ~entwachsen~ joins the literal sense of growing forth out of something to the figurative "to outgrow": growing beyond a thing and leaving it behind.
en.entwarnen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~warnen~:

• ~warnen~: From MHG ~warnen~ ("to watch over, to protect"), from OHG ~warnōn~ ("to deny, to refuse"), from Proto-West Germanic *~warnōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~warnōną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, to perceive, to watch out for"): from refusing danger for oneself to cautioning others. Cognate with English ~warn~, Old English ~wyrnan~, Old Norse ~varna~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

~Entwarnen~ is the counterpart of ~warnen~: not to warn of a danger but to announce that the danger has passed.
en.entweichen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~weichen~:

• ~weichen~: From MHG ~wīchen~, from OHG ~wīchan~ ("to yield, give way"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wīkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīkwaną~, from PIE *~h₃weyg-~ ("to start moving, to distance oneself, to bend, wind"). A class I strong verb, "to yield, give way, retreat"; not to be confused with the weak ~weichen~ ("to soften, to soak"), which derives from ~weich~ ("soft"). Cognate with Old English ~wīcan~, Old Norse ~vīkja~, Swedish ~vika~ ("to give way, fold").
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys release, escape, or getting free.

The root is the strong ~weichen~ ("to yield, give way"), not the weak ~weichen~ ("to soak"); ~entweichen~ is the silent slipping-away of gas, smoke, or a fugitive.
en.entwenden:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~wenden~:

• ~wenden~: From MHG ~wenden~, from OHG ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), the causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). It belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort (preterite ~wandte~, participle ~gewandt~) and has a doubled preterite: ~wandte~ for turning the self or one's attention, the regularized ~wendete~ for physical turning. Cognate with English ~wend~, Armenian ~gind~ ("ring").
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

From ~wenden~ "to turn, turn away," ~entwenden~ became the elevated word for stealing: to turn a thing away from its owner and make off with it.
en.entwerfen:
From Middle High German ~entwerfen~. Compound of ~ent-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). The ~-p-~ in the Germanic form likely arose after resonants in words beginning with labial consonants. Cognate with English ~warp~ (originally "to throw"), Dutch ~werpen~, and via Greek ~rhembō~ ("to turn in circles"), the source of English ~rhombus~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-Germanic *~andi-~ ("away, against"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). This inseparable prefix adds a sense of reversal, removal, or inception to the base verb.

The literal sense is "to throw out" or "to cast forth," and the semantic development to "to design, to draft, to sketch" reflects the idea of casting forth an idea into physical form. Cognate with Dutch ~ontwerpen~ ("to design"), which preserves the same prefix-root combination. The relationship between ~werfen~ ("to throw") and English ~warp~ illustrates a dramatic semantic divergence from a shared ancestor: German kept the concrete "throw" meaning, while English ~warp~ shifted from "to throw" to "to twist, to distort" (with the weaving sense of "warp threads" reflecting the PIE meaning "to bend"). The noun ~Entwurf~ ("design, draft, blueprint") is the corresponding deverbal noun, parallel to how English ~draft~ originally meant "something drawn or pulled."
en.entwerten:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~werten~:

• ~werten~: Derived from ~Wert~ ("value, worth"), from MHG ~wert~, from OHG ~werd~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("worth, worthy"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"); the connection to value runs through exchange: turning goods over in a transaction. Related to Latin ~versus~ ("turned") and English ~worth~, ~worthy~, ~worship~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

~Entwerten~ strips a thing of its ~Wert~ ("value"), whether figuratively (money, arguments) or physically, as a ticket is ~entwertet~ by being punched.
en.entwickeln:
Compound of ~ent-~ + ~wickeln~. Calque of French ~développer~.

• ~wickeln~: From MHG ~wickeln~ ("to wind, wrap around"), a denominative of ~wickel~, from OHG ~wickili~ ("fibres wound around the distaff"), from Proto-Germanic *~wikaną~ ("to bend"), from PIE *~weg-~ ("to weave"). Related to ~Wickel~ ("anything wrapped, especially a cloth around a poultice"). The OHG noun is a diminutive of ~wiohha~ ("bundle of fibres, wick"), cognate with Dutch ~wiek~, English ~wick~, and Latin ~velum~ ("cloth, veil").
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-Germanic *~and-~, from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). This prefix often adds a sense of away, un-, or de-.

The semantic development from "to unwrap" to "to develop" parallels French ~développer~ (from ~des-~ + Old French ~voloper~, "to wrap"), which ~entwickeln~ was coined to translate. Both languages arrived at "develop" via the metaphor of unfolding something hidden.
en.entwinden:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~winden~:

• ~winden~: From MHG ~winden~, from OHG ~wintan~, from Proto-Germanic *~windaną~ ("to wind, to wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). Cognate with English ~wind~ (the verb, "to coil"), Dutch ~winden~, Danish ~vinde~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

~Entwinden~ is the forcible twisting of something out of a grasp: to wrest a thing from someone, or reflexively to work oneself free.
en.entwürdigen:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~würdigen~:

• ~würdigen~: From ~würdig~ ("worthy") + ~-en~; ~würdig~ from ~Würde~ ("dignity, worth") + ~-ig~, and ~Würde~ from MHG ~wirde~, from OHG ~wirdī~, related to Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("valuable, worthy"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"). Cognate with English ~worth~ and ~worthy~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

~Entwürdigen~ strips a person of ~Würde~ ("dignity"), the exact opposite of the related ~würdigen~, which bestows it.
en.entzaubern:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~zaubern~:

• ~zaubern~: From MHG ~zoubern~, from OHG ~zouberōn~, ~zoubarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taubrōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taubrōną~, derived from *~taubrą~ ("magic, sorcery"), which is of uncertain further origin, perhaps linked to *~tawjaną~ ("to make, prepare"). Cognate with English ~tiver~, Dutch ~toveren~, Old Norse ~taufr~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.

~Entzaubern~ undoes the spell; Max Weber's "~Entzauberung~ of the world" made the word a byword for modernity's loss of the magical.
en.entziehen:
Compound of ~ent-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). Cognate with Low German ~tehn~, Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~teon~, and Old Norse ~toga~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~andi-~, from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). This prefix conveys separation, removal, or reversal.

The compound literally means "to pull away from," yielding the modern senses of "to withdraw, deprive, extract." The reflexive form ~sich entziehen~ means "to evade, to escape from," adding a layer of agency to the withdrawal. The PIE root *~dewk-~ is remarkably productive: it yielded Latin ~ducere~ ("to lead"), giving English ~duke~, ~conduct~, ~produce~, ~reduce~, ~educate~, and ~deduce~. English ~tie~ is also from the same root, via the idea of pulling tight. English ~tug~ and ~tow~ are further relatives. The German noun ~Entzug~ ("withdrawal") is widely known in the compound ~Entzugserscheinungen~ ("withdrawal symptoms"), one of those long German compound nouns that compresses into a single word what English needs a phrase to express. The obsolete English verb ~tee~ ("to draw, lead") was a direct cognate of ~ziehen~ that did not survive.
en.entzweibrechen:
A separable compound of ~entzwei-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~entzwei-~: From MHG ~enzwei~, from the phrase ~in zwei~ ("in two"). The first element is the reduced preposition ~in~, not the prefix ~ent-~, though it was later respelled under that prefix's influence, a case of folk reanalysis frozen into the orthography. It is a resultative: ~entzweibrechen~ is to break something so that it ends up in two pieces. ~zwei~ is cognate with English ~two~. The sense of ~entzwei-~ here is resultative: leaves the object broken in two, in pieces.

~Entzweibrechen~ works both ways, like bare ~brechen~. Something can break in two by itself, with ~sein~ (~der Ast ist entzweigebrochen~), or one can break an object in two, with ~haben~. Its sister verb ~entzweigehen~ knows only the first, the mere falling-apart.
en.entzweigehen:
A separable compound of ~entzwei-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~entzwei-~: From MHG ~enzwei~, from the phrase ~in zwei~ ("in two"). The first element is the reduced preposition ~in~, not the prefix ~ent-~, though it was later respelled under that prefix's influence, a case of folk reanalysis frozen into the orthography. It is a resultative: ~entzweibrechen~ is to break something so that it ends up in two pieces. ~zwei~ is cognate with English ~two~. The sense of ~entzwei-~ here is resultative: leaves the object broken in two, in pieces.

Here ~gehen~ carries not its sense of motion but that of passing into a state: ~entzweigehen~ simply means to break, to fall to pieces.
en.entzweireißen:
A separable compound of ~entzwei-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~entzwei-~: From MHG ~enzwei~, from the phrase ~in zwei~ ("in two"). The first element is the reduced preposition ~in~, not the prefix ~ent-~, though it was later respelled under that prefix's influence, a case of folk reanalysis frozen into the orthography. It is a resultative: ~entzweibrechen~ is to break something so that it ends up in two pieces. ~zwei~ is cognate with English ~two~. The sense of ~entzwei-~ here is resultative: leaves the object broken in two, in pieces.

~Reißen~ contributes the violent tearing; in the Luther verse it stands intransitively (the cord ~reißt entzwei~ of its own accord) beside the ordinary transitive use.
en.entäußern:
An inseparable compound of ~ent-~ + ~äußern~:

• ~äußern~: From MHG ~ūzeren~ ("to bring out, express"), deadjectival from ~äußer~ ("outer"), the comparative of ~aus~ / ~außen~, from MHG ~ūȥ~, OHG ~ūȥ~, Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, Proto-Germanic *~ūt~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"), bringing the inner outward. A doublet of English ~out~; related to English ~utter~, Dutch ~uit~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ conveys removal, taking away, or separation.

~Entäußern~ is reflexive and governs the genitive (~sich einer Sache entäußern~): one gives away from oneself what ~äußern~ brings outward, here to the point of complete relinquishment.
en.erachten:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~achten~:

• ~achten~: From MHG ~ahten~ ("to consider, heed"), from OHG ~ahtōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ahtōn~, a denominative of *~ahtu~ ("consideration, attention"), of uncertain pre-Germanic origin, possibly to Proto-Germanic *~ahjaną~ ("to think"), compared to PIE *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), though debated. Cognate with Dutch ~achten~, English ~aught~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

~Erachten~ narrows ~achten~ "to heed, weigh" to the settled judgment: to ~erachten~ something right or necessary is to hold it so after deliberation.
en.erahnen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~ahnen~:

• ~ahnen~: From MHG ~anen~, from OHG *~anōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~anōn~, from the preposition *~ana~ ("on"), from Proto-Germanic *~an~ ("on"). Cognate with Middle Low German ~ānen~, dialectal Dutch ~anen~ ("to conjecture"), Saterland Frisian ~oanje~ ("to suspect").
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

~Erahnen~ raises ~ahnen~ to half-knowledge: not merely to sense dimly but to make out something hidden in outline.
en.erarbeiten:
~Er-~ + ~arbeiten~. Compound of ~er-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From MHG ~arbeiten~, from OHG ~arabeitōn~, ~arbeitōn~, from OHG ~arabeit~ ("labor, hardship"), from Proto-West Germanic *~arbaiþi~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidiz~ ("work, hardship"), possibly from PIE *~h₃erbʰ-~ ("to change status, to orphan").
• ~er-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix adds the sense of achievement through effort or completion of a process.

~Erarbeiten~ means "to achieve through work, to develop through effort, to work out." The ~er-~ prefix transforms the simple act of working into the completed result of that work: one does not merely ~arbeitet~, one ~erarbeitet~ a result, a plan, a competence. The underlying etymological image is almost poignant: if ~arbeiten~ indeed descends from a root meaning "orphan, hardship" (as suggested by the connection to PIE *~h₃erbʰ-~ and Gothic ~arbaiþs~, "toil, distress"), then ~erarbeiten~ captures the full arc of labor as suffering that yields an outcome. The reflexive ~sich etwas erarbeiten~ ("to earn something through hard work") emphasizes the personal investment required. There is no shortcut implied; unlike ~verdienen~ ("to earn," which can be passive), ~erarbeiten~ insists on active, sustained effort.
en.erbauen:
From Middle High German ~erbouwen~. Compound of ~er-~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~buwen~, from OHG ~buan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~buwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~buwaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~bhuH-~ ("to be, become, grow, dwell"). The semantic journey from "to dwell" to "to build" reflects the Germanic settlers' deepening attachment to fixed homesteads. Cognate with English ~build~ (via a different branch), Dutch ~bouwen~, and English ~be~, ~been~ (via the same PIE root).
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uz-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"), from Proto-Indo-European *~ud~ ("upwards, away, out"). This prefix often adds a sense of achievement or completion to the base verb. Doublet of ~ur-~.

The ~er-~ prefix intensifies the base verb, lending ~erbauen~ the elevated sense of "to construct, to edify." In modern German, the reflexive ~sich erbauen~ means "to be edified" in a spiritual or emotional sense, a meaning that grew from the literal act of building churches and monuments.
en.erbeten:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~beten~:

• ~beten~: From MHG ~beten~, from OHG ~beton~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bedon~, from Proto-Germanic *~bedan~ ("to pray, to ask"), close to *~bidjan~ ("to ask"), from PIE *~gwhedh-~ ("to ask for, beseech"). The narrowing from "ask" to "pray" is a Christianization phenomenon. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bidden~, Danish ~bede~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ conveys obtaining or acquiring something by means of the base action.

~Erbeten~ "to obtain by praying" is the weak counterpart of the strong ~erbitten~; both go back ultimately to the same root as ~bitten~ and ~beten~.
en.erbieten:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~bieten~:

• ~bieten~: From MHG ~bieten~, from OHG ~biotan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beudan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beudaną~, from PIE *~bʰewdʰ-~ ("to be awake, aware"). A class II strong verb whose root conveys awareness and offering. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bieden~, Danish ~byde~, Swedish ~bjuda~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ preserves its own older spatial sense of upward or outward motion.

Usually reflexive: to ~erbieten~ oneself is to offer to perform something, holding the offer forth as it were.
en.erbitten:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~bitten~:

• ~bitten~: From MHG ~bitten~, from OHG ~bitten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~biddjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bidjaną~, from PIE *~gʷʰedʰ-~ ("to ask for, beseech"). A class V strong verb; the noun ~Bitte~ and the particle ~bitte~ come from the same root. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bidden~ ("to pray"), Danish ~bede~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ conveys obtaining or acquiring something by means of the base action.

Unlike plain ~bitten~, ~erbitten~ aims at the outcome: not merely to ask but to obtain the thing asked for through asking.
en.erbleichen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~bleichen~:

• ~bleichen~: A merger of two verbs: the strong intransitive MHG ~blīchen~ ("to shine, gleam, grow pale"), from OHG ~blīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~blīkaną~; and its weak causative MHG ~bleichen~ ("to make pale"), from OHG ~bleihhen~, from Proto-Germanic *~blaikijaną~. Both from PIE *~bʰleyg-~ ("to shine"). Modern German conjugates it weak, the strong participle ~geblichen~ surviving only marginally. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~bleak~, Dutch ~bleken~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the onset of a state rather than the state itself.

~Erbleichen~ names the onset of pallor: turning white with fright; poetically it also serves as a veiled word for dying.
en.erblicken:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~blank~, Dutch ~blik~, Old English ~blice~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

~Erblicken~ turns the ongoing ~blicken~ "to look" into the momentary instant of noticing, to catch sight of something all at once.
en.erbrechen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ preserves its own older spatial sense of upward or outward motion.

~Erbrechen~ has two faces: to break forcibly open (a seal, a letter) and, usually reflexively, to break the stomach's contents upward and out; sich ~erbrechen~ means to vomit.
en.erbringen:
Compound of ~er-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~ ("to bring"), probably from a Pre-Germanic compound *~bʰrenk̂-~, combining PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") and *~h₁nek̂-~ ("to bring, reach"). Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"). This prefix often adds a sense of achievement or completion to the base verb. Doublet of ~ur-~.

The ~er-~ prefix transforms "to bring" into "to bring about, to produce, to yield", conveying the successful result of bringing. It appears most often in formal or bureaucratic contexts: ~einen Beweis erbringen~ ("to furnish proof"), ~eine Leistung erbringen~ ("to render a service"), ~ein Opfer erbringen~ ("to make a sacrifice"). The verb ~bringen~ itself is unusual among Germanic verbs in having a mixed weak-and-strong past tense (~brachte~, ~gebracht~), a pattern unique in Proto-Germanic.
en.erdenken:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~teng-~ ("to think, feel"). A mixed-conjugation verb of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~dachte~ pairs the vowel change ~e~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix and ~k~ > ~ch~. Cognate with English ~think~, Dutch ~denken~, Icelandic ~þekkja~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ conveys obtaining or acquiring something by means of the base action.

~Erdenken~ brings forth something new by ~denken~: not to think about something but to devise it, to invent it.
en.erdrücken:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ carries the base action to a fatal end.

Literally to press to death; in the Luther verse a mother smothers her child in her sleep. Figuratively an ~erdrückende~ majority or burden overwhelms.
en.ereignen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~eignen~:

• ~eignen~: From MHG ~eigenen~, from OHG ~eiganen~, from Proto-Germanic *~aiginōną~, a denominative from *~aiganaz~ ("owned, one's own"), the past participle of *~aiganą~ ("to possess"), from PIE *~h₂eh₂óyḱe~, from *~h₂eyḱ-~ ("ability, possession"). Originally "to make one's own." Cognate with English ~own~, Dutch ~eigen~, Swedish ~ägna~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the onset of a state rather than the state itself.

The transparent split into ~er-~ + ~eignen~ "to make one's own" is folk-etymological: ~ereignen~ descends from MHG ~eröugen~, ~eräugnen~ "to set before the eyes, cause to appear" (from ~Auge~ "eye"), and was only later reshaped toward ~eigen~. The root bullet is therefore formal only.
en.erfahren:
From Middle High German ~ervarn~, from Old High German ~irfaran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀfaran~. Compound of ~er-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, ~varen~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"). This prefix often adds a sense of completion or result to the base verb. Doublet of ~ur-~.

The completive ~er-~ prefix transforms the base sense of "to travel" into "to find out, learn through experience"; one discovers by traveling through, by undergoing a journey. This semantic link between physical travel and the acquisition of knowledge is beautifully preserved in the noun ~Erfahrung~ ("experience"), literally "a traveling through." Cognate with Old English ~āfaran~ (whence obsolete English ~afare~, "to depart, set out").
en.erfangen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~fangen~:

• ~fangen~: From MHG ~vāhen~, from OHG ~fāhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~fanhaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to secure, fasten"). A strong verb, originally ~fāhan~ / ~fieng~ / ~gefangan~; the modern present stem ~fang-~ was taken analogically from the past forms. Cognate with English ~fang~, Dutch ~vangen~, West Frisian ~fange~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

~Erfangen~ "to catch, seize" is archaic today; the ~er-~ stresses the successful seizing of game or foe.
en.erfassen:
From ~er-~ + ~fassen~:

• ~fassen~: From MHG ~vazzen~, from OHG ~fazzōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fatōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fatōną~ ("to fetch, hold"), ultimately cognate with English ~fetch~. The connection is one of the more surprising Germanic pairs: both descend from a root meaning "to get, obtain."
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"). This completive prefix transforms the act of grasping into a fully achieved comprehension or registration. Doublet of ~ur-~.

The compound means "to grasp, to seize, to comprehend, to record (data)", the ~er-~ prefix driving the simple act of grabbing through to completion: one doesn't merely touch but fully takes hold, in the physical sense (~einen Dieb erfassen~, "to apprehend a thief") and the cognitive sense (~eine Idee erfassen~, "to grasp an idea"). In modern administrative and statistical language, ~erfassen~ has become the standard term for recording and registering data, "to capture" in the technical sense, as in ~Daten erfassen~. The related ~Fassung~ ("composure; version") and ~unfassbar~ ("incomprehensible," literally "ungraspable") show the root's wide idiomatic reach. Cognate with Dutch ~vatten~.
en.erfinden:
From Middle High German ~ervinden~, from Old High German ~irfindan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀfinþan~. Compound of ~er-~ + ~finden~:

• ~finden~: From MHG ~vinden~, from OHG ~findan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~finþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to go, pass; path, bridge"). Cognate with English ~find~, Dutch ~vinden~, Danish ~finde~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). This prefix adds a sense of achievement or completion to the base verb.

The semantic journey from "to find completely" to "to invent" is a remarkable one: ~erfinden~ moved from the idea of thorough discovery to the creation of something entirely new. The PIE root *~pent-~ originally meant "to tread a path," so ~finden~ traces back to the notion of coming upon something while walking, and ~erfinden~ extends that to arriving at something that did not exist before. The noun ~Erfindung~ ("invention") and ~Erfinder~ ("inventor") are among the most productive derivatives in modern German.
en.erfließen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~fließen~:

• ~fließen~: From MHG ~vlieȥen~, from OHG ~flioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleutaną~ ("to float, stream, flow"), from PIE *~plewd-~ ("to flow, run, swim"). A class II strong verb (~fließen~, ~floss~, ~geflossen~); the zero grade *~flut-~ gave ~Flut~. Cognate with English ~fleet~, ~float~ and ~flood~, Dutch ~vlieten~, Swedish ~flyta~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ preserves its own older spatial sense of upward or outward motion.

~Erfließen~ carries the image of flowing forth into the abstract: in legal and chancery language a consequence ~erfließt~ from a premise, as water from a spring.
en.erfolgen:
From Middle High German ~erfolgen~, from Old High German ~irfolgēn~. Compound of ~er-~ + ~folgen~:

• ~folgen~: From MHG ~volgen~, from OHG ~folgēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~folgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fulgāną~. Cognate with Dutch ~volgen~, Low German ~folgen~, English ~follow~, Danish ~følge~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"). This prefix often adds a sense of completion or result to the base verb. Doublet of ~ur-~.

The compound's primary modern sense ("to occur, to result, to ensue") reflects the completive force of ~er-~: an outcome that follows through to its conclusion. The cognate relationship between ~folgen~ and English ~follow~ is not immediately obvious in Modern German spelling, but the OHG form ~folgēn~ makes the shared Proto-Germanic origin transparent. Cognate with Dutch ~evolgen~ (archaic).
en.erfordern:
From Middle High German ~ervordern~, from Old High German ~irfordarōn~. Equivalent to ~er-~ + ~fordern~:

• ~fordern~: From MHG ~vordern~, from OHG ~fordarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~furþrōną~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþrōną~, from *~furþraz~ ("further, forward"), from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross, go through").
• ~er-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The completive prefix emphasizes the full extent of what is demanded.

The distinction between ~fordern~ ("to demand") and ~erfordern~ ("to require") is subtle but important: ~fordern~ implies an agent making a demand (~der Chef fordert Pünktlichkeit~, "the boss demands punctuality"), while ~erfordern~ implies an impersonal, situational necessity (~die Situation erfordert Geduld~, "the situation requires patience"). The ~er-~ prefix strips away the personal element, transforming a demand into a requirement, from something one person asks of another to something a situation asks of everyone. Cognate with Dutch ~vereisen~ (a different compound with the same meaning).
en.erforschen:
Compound of ~er-~ + ~forschen~:

• ~forschen~: From MHG ~vorschen~, from OHG ~forscōn~ ("to ask, to inquire, to investigate"), from Proto-West Germanic *~fraskōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fraskōną~, likely related to *~frehnaną~ ("to ask"), from PIE *~preḱ-~ ("to ask, to request"). Cognate with Latin ~poscō~ ("I demand"), ~precor~ ("I pray"), Sanskrit ~pr̥ccháti~ ("he asks"), and English ~pray~ (via Old French ~preier~, from Latin ~precārī~).
• ~er-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). This prefix adds the sense of thorough completion, researching something to the end.

~Erforschen~ means "to explore, to investigate, to research thoroughly"; ~den Weltraum erforschen~ ("to explore outer space"), ~die Ursachen erforschen~ ("to investigate the causes"). The noun ~Forscher~ ("researcher, explorer") and ~Forschung~ ("research") are central to German academic and scientific vocabulary. The PIE root *~preḱ-~ ("to ask") connects scientific inquiry with prayer and supplication in a profound etymological circle: to research and to pray both begin with asking. The semantic shift from "to ask questions" to "to conduct systematic investigation" occurred within German itself during the medieval period, as ~forschen~ moved from casual inquiry to the structured questioning that defines the scientific method.
en.erfragen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~fragen~:

• ~fragen~: From MHG ~vrāgen~, from OHG ~frāgēn~, ~frahēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frāgēn~ (a denominative from *~frāgu~, "question"), from Proto-Germanic *~frēgō~ ("question"), from PIE *~preḱ-~ ("to ask"), which also gave Latin ~precor~ and Sanskrit ~pṛcchāti~. Cognate with English ~frain~ (archaic), Dutch ~vragen~, Swedish ~fråga~, Icelandic ~fregna~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ conveys obtaining or acquiring something by means of the base action.

The compound narrows ~fragen~ „to ask“ to its result: not the questioning itself but the information secured by it, so ~etwas erfragen~ is „to find something out by asking“.
en.erfreuen:
From Middle High German ~ervröuwen~, ~ervröwen~, from Old High German ~irfrewen~. Compound of ~er-~ + ~freuen~:

• ~freuen~: From MHG ~vröuwen~, ~vreuwen~, from OHG ~frewen~, ~frouwen~, derived from OHG ~frō~, ~frao~ ("glad"). The adjective ~froh~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~frawaz~ ("quick, glad"). Equivalent to ~froh~ + ~-en~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). This prefix often adds a sense of achievement or completion to the base verb.

The ~er-~ prefix intensifies ~freuen~ ("to please, to be glad") into a sense of causing or experiencing full delight. While ~sich freuen~ means "to be happy," ~erfreuen~ means "to delight" someone else, or in its reflexive form ~sich erfreuen~ with the genitive, "to enjoy" something. English ~frolic~ is a distant cousin, borrowed from Dutch ~vrolijk~ ("merry"), which shares the same Proto-Germanic root *~frawaz~. The Old High German vowel ~ö~/~öu~ in ~vröuwen~ reflects the Germanic umlaut triggered by the ~-j-~ in the verb derivation, a phonological process that left its fingerprints all over German's vowel system.
en.erfrieren:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~frieren~:

• ~frieren~: From MHG ~vriesen~ (beside ~vrieren~), from OHG ~friosan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~freusan~, from Proto-Germanic *~freusaną~, from PIE *~prews-~ ("to freeze, frost"). A class II strong verb (~frieren~, ~fror~, ~gefroren~); the ~r~ arose by grammatischer Wechsel in the past forms and spread to the infinitive, as in ~verlieren~. Cognate with English ~freeze~ and ~frost~, Dutch ~vriezen~, Danish ~fryse~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ carries the base action to a fatal end.

With ~er-~ supplying the fatal outcome, ~erfrieren~ is not merely to feel cold but to die of it; it forms its perfect with ~sein~, as change-of-state verbs do.
en.erfühlen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~fühlen~:

• ~fühlen~: From northern MHG ~vüelen~, from OHG ~fuolen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōlijan~ ("to feel"); the further origin is uncertain, presumably related to Old Norse ~falma~ ("to grope"), and possibly a secondary causative of a strong *~falaną~, from PIE *~pelh₁-~ ("to stroke"). Cognate with English ~feel~, Dutch ~voelen~, Danish ~føle~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ conveys obtaining or acquiring something by means of the base action.

~Erfühlen~ frames touch as a means of discovery: what plain ~fühlen~ merely does, ~erfühlen~ carries to knowledge gained through the fingertips.
en.erfüllen:
From Middle High German ~ervüllen~, from Old High German ~irfullen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀfullijan~. Compound of ~er-~ + ~füllen~:

• ~füllen~: From MHG ~vüllen~, from OHG ~fullen~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullijaną~, a denominative of *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pleh₁-~ ("to fill"). Cognate with Dutch ~vullen~, English ~fill~, Danish ~fylde~, Swedish ~fylla~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"). This prefix often adds a sense of completion or achievement. Doublet of ~ur-~.

The ~er-~ prefix gives ~erfüllen~ its characteristic sense of complete, achieving fulfillment, not merely filling, but filling to completion, satisfying entirely. A wish, a promise, a quota: all ~erfüllt~ when fully accomplished. The PIE root *~pleh₁-~ is also the ancestor of English ~full~, Latin ~plēnus~ ("full"), and Greek ~plḗrēs~ ("full"). Cognate with Dutch ~vervullen~.
en.ergeben:
From Middle High German ~ergeben~, from Old High German ~irgeban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀgeban~, from Proto-Germanic *~uzgebaną~. Compound of ~er-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with Dutch ~geven~, English ~give~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"). This prefix often adds a sense of completion or result to the base verb. Doublet of ~ur-~.

The semantic range of ~ergeben~ is notably wide: "to yield" (literally, to give out completely), "to result in" (the calculation yields a result), and, as the reflexive ~sich ergeben~, "to surrender" or "to turn out to be." The sense of ~ergeben~ as an adjective ("devoted, submissive") derives from the same completive force: one who has wholly given themselves over. Cognate with obsolete English ~agive~, Dutch ~overgeven~.
en.ergehen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~gehen~:
