Cognate with English ~ordeal~, which descends from the same Proto-Germanic root *~uzdailiją~ ("judicial decision").
en.ertragen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb whose semantic range broadened from "to drag, pull" to "to carry, bear, wear." Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

The path from ~tragen~ „to carry“ to ~ertragen~ „to endure“ runs through the idea of carrying a burden through to the end, what one bears up under, rather than sets down.
en.ertrinken:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~trinken~:

• ~trinken~: From MHG ~trinken~, from OHG ~trinkan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drinkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drinkaną~; no non-Germanic cognate has been securely identified, so the word may be a Germanic innovation. Cognate with English ~drink~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Old Norse ~drekka~ and Gothic ~𐌳𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌺𐌰𐌽~ (drigkan).
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ carries the base action to a fatal end.

~Ertrinken~ is the intransitive counterpart to drowning someone: the subject perishes in water, ~er-~ carrying the ordinary ~trinken~ „to drink“ to its grim, involuntary extreme.
en.erträumen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~träumen~:

• ~träumen~: From MHG ~troumen~ and OHG ~troumen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~draumijan~, a denominative verb from the noun *~draum~ (whence ~Traum~), from Proto-Germanic *~draumaz~, from PIE *~dʰrewgʰ-~ ("to deceive, to harm"); the ancient Indo-Europeans thus viewed dreams as fundamentally deceptive experiences. Cognate with English ~dream~, Dutch ~dromen~, Swedish ~drömma~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ conveys obtaining or acquiring something by means of the base action.

What one ~erträumt~ is brought into being only in the imagination (a dreamed-of future, a longed-for life) real as a wish and no further.
en.ertöten:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~töten~:

• ~töten~: From MHG ~tœten~, from OHG *~tōten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~daudijan~ ("to make dead, to kill"), from Proto-Germanic *~daudijaną~, a factitive of *~daudaz~ ("dead") + *~-janą~ ("to make X"), transparently ~tot~ + ~-en~. Compare English ~deaden~. Cognate with Dutch ~doden~, Old Norse ~deyða~, Gothic ~dauþjan~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

Because ~töten~ already means „to kill“, ~er-~ adds not a fatal outcome but thoroughness: ~ertöten~ is figurative (to deaden or mortify a feeling, an urge, the flesh), snuffing it out completely.
en.erwachsen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from PIE *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Cognate with English ~wax~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

~Erwachsen~ splits by subject: of a person it is „to grow up“, and the past participle ~erwachsen~ „grown-up, adult“ froze into an adjective; of a thing it is „to arise, accrue“, an advantage or a disadvantage that ~erwächst~ from a circumstance.
en.erwarten:
Compound of ~er-~ + ~warten~:

• ~warten~: From MHG ~warten~, from OHG ~wartēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wardēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wardāną~ ("to guard, protect, watch over"), from Proto-Germanic *~warduz~ ("guard"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, watch"). Cognate with Old Saxon ~wardōn~, Swedish ~vårda~, English ~ward~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"). This prefix often adds a sense of completion or result to the base verb. Doublet of ~ur-~.

The ~er-~ prefix shifts ~warten~ (to wait, to watch) from a state of watchful waiting into a forward-oriented expectation: ~erwarten~ is not merely to wait but to await with anticipation, to count on an outcome. The same PIE root *~wer-~ ("to heed") underlies English ~ward~, ~warden~, and ~aware~; and, borrowed via Old French from Frankish, English ~guard~ traces to the same ancestral root. Cognate with Dutch ~verwachten~ (a parallel compound with ~ver-~ in place of ~er-~).
en.erwecken:
From Middle High German ~erwecken~, from Old High German ~irwekken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uzwakkjan~. Compound of ~er-~ + ~wecken~:

• ~wecken~: From MHG ~wecken~, from OHG ~wecchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wakkjan~ ("to wake up, to awaken"), the causative form of *~wakēn~ ("to be awake"), from Proto-Indo-European *~weg-~ ("to be lively, active"). Cognate with English ~wake~, Dutch ~wekken~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uz-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"), from Proto-Indo-European *~ud~ ("upwards, away, out"). This prefix adds completeness or thoroughness.

The compound intensifies the causative meaning: while ~wecken~ is simply "to wake (someone) up," ~erwecken~ means "to awaken, to arouse, to rouse", often in a figurative or spiritual sense. One wakes a sleeping child with ~wecken~, but one ~erweckt~ feelings, memories, or even the dead. The biblical ~Auferweckung~ ("resurrection") is built on this same verb. The PIE root *~weg-~ ("to be lively, active") also produced Latin ~vigil~ ("watchful"), giving English ~vigil~, ~vigilant~, and ~vigor~.
en.erwehren:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~wehren~:

• ~wehren~: From MHG ~weren~, from OHG ~werien~, from Proto-West Germanic *~warjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~warjaną~ ("to defend, to ward off, to protect"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to close, to cover, to protect"). Most commonly used reflexively: ~sich wehren~ ("to defend oneself"). Cognate with English ~weir~, ~ward~, ~guard~, Dutch ~weren~, Old Norse ~verja~, Gothic ~warjan~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

~Erwehren~ is used only reflexively and with the genitive: ~sich jemandes erwehren~ is to carry the warding-off through to success.
en.erweichen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~weichen~:

• ~weichen~: From MHG ~wīchen~, from OHG ~wīchan~ ("to yield, give way"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wīkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīkwaną~, from PIE *~h₃weyg-~ ("to start moving, to distance oneself, to bend, wind"). A class I strong verb, "to yield, give way, retreat"; not to be confused with the weak ~weichen~ ("to soften, to soak"), which derives from ~weich~ ("soft"). Cognate with Old English ~wīcan~, Old Norse ~vīkja~, Swedish ~vika~ ("to give way, fold").
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ derives a verb from an adjective, meaning to bring into that state.

This is the weak ~weichen~ from ~weich~ ("soft"), not the strong ~weichen~ ("to yield"): ~erweichen~ is to make soft, often figuratively, to soften someone's heart.
en.erweisen:
~Er-~ + ~weisen~. Compound of ~er-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~ ("to show, point out"), from PIE *~weyd-~ ("to see").
• ~er-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix adds the sense of achievement, completion, or emergence into evidence.

~Erweisen~ means "to prove, to show, to render (a service)." The reflexive ~sich erweisen als~ ("to prove to be, to turn out as") is particularly common: ~er erwies sich als zuverlässig~ ("he proved to be reliable"). The non-reflexive can mean "to render" in formal contexts: ~jemandem einen Dienst erweisen~ ("to render someone a service"), ~jemandem Ehre erweisen~ ("to pay someone honor"). The PIE root *~weyd-~ ("to see") connects seeing, knowing, and showing in a single etymological thread: to ~er-weisen~ is to make something visibly evident, to bring knowledge out into the open. The same root gave Latin ~vidēre~ ("to see"), Greek ~eidos~ ("form"), and Sanskrit ~veda~ ("knowledge"), making ~erweisen~ a distant cousin of English ~wisdom~, ~witness~, and ~video~. Cognate with Dutch ~erwijzen~ (archaic).
en.erweitern:
From ~er-~ + ~weitern~, where ~weitern~ is an obsolete verb derived from the comparative of ~weit~ ("wide, broad, far"):

• ~weit~: From MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~. Cognate with Dutch ~wijd~, English ~wide~, Low German ~wied~, Danish ~vid~, Swedish ~vid~.
• ~er-~: From Proto-Indo-European *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The completive prefix transforms "to make wider" into "to expand, to extend fully."

The derivation runs: ~weit~ → comparative ~weiter~ ("wider") → denominative *~weitern~ ("to make wider") → prefixed ~erweitern~ ("to expand, enlarge, broaden"). The intermediate verb ~weitern~ fell out of use, surviving only in this compound and a few dialects. The noun ~Erweiterung~ ("expansion, extension, widening") is used in mathematics (~Erweiterung eines Bruchs~, "extension of a fraction") and in everyday speech (~EU-Erweiterung~, "EU enlargement").
en.erwerben:
From Middle High German ~erwerben~, from Old High German ~irwerban~. Equivalent to ~er-~ + ~werben~. Cognate with Dutch ~verwerven~.

• ~werben~: From MHG ~wërben~, from OHG ~wërban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hwerban~, from Proto-Germanic *~hwerbaną~ ("to turn, move around"). A class III strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~werven~ ("to recruit"), Icelandic ~hverfa~ ("to turn, disappear"), Faroese ~hvørva~ ("to disappear"), and (more distantly) English ~whirl~ via a parallel PIE root.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"). This completive prefix transforms the turning motion of ~werben~ into a fully achieved acquisition. Doublet of ~ur-~.

The semantic journey of ~werben~ is one of German's most striking: from "to turn around" (Proto-Germanic) to "to move about on business" (Old High German), then to "to court, recruit, advertise" (Modern German), and in the compound ~erwerben~ to "to acquire, earn." The connecting thread is the turning motion of commerce: hawking wares, making rounds, drumming up custom. That the same verb underlies both ~Werbung~ ("advertising") and ~erwerben~ ("to acquire") reveals an ancient truth: advertising is the turning that produces getting. The English near-cognate ~whirl~ preserved the literal spinning sense, while the Germanic mercantile senses developed along their own path. A surviving compound that keeps the older sense is ~bewerben~ ("to apply for a job," literally "to turn toward something"). Cognate with Dutch ~verwerven~, Icelandic ~hverfa~.
en.erwirken:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~wirken~:

• ~wirken~: From MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~, from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~wérǵom~, from *~werǵ-~ ("to make, work"). Early on it merged with the dialectal ~würken~ (from OHG ~wurken~), which left the written language in the 18th century. Cognate with English ~work~ and ~wrought~, Dutch ~werken~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ conveys obtaining or acquiring something by means of the base action.

~Erwirken~ is to obtain something by acting or petitioning, in law, to secure a ruling or acquittal.
en.erwischen:
Compound of ~er-~ + ~wischen~:

• ~wischen~: From MHG ~wischen~, from OHG ~wisken~ ("to wipe, to move quickly"), from Proto-Germanic *~wiskijaną~ ("to wipe, to move swiftly"). The original sense was a quick, darting motion: wiping or whisking.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out of, from"), from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). As an inseparable prefix, it conveys achievement, attainment, or sudden completion.

The verb ~erwischen~ means "to catch, to nab, to get hold of"; ~einen Dieb erwischen~ ("to catch a thief"), ~den letzten Zug erwischen~ ("to catch the last train"), ~jemanden beim Schummeln erwischen~ ("to catch someone cheating"). The semantic development from "quick wiping motion" to "catching" passed through the idea of a swift grabbing movement: you ~erwischen~ someone the way you might ~wischen~ (swipe) at a fly. The ~er-~ prefix adds the sense of successful completion, not just swiping but actually catching. Colloquially, ~es hat ihn erwischt~ ("it got him") can mean anything from catching a cold to falling in love to dying, depending on context, a remarkable range of fates all described by the same image of being suddenly seized. The related English ~whisk~ (from Old Norse ~viska~, a Germanic cousin of ~wischen~) preserves the sense of rapid sweeping motion.
en.erwägen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~wägen~:

• ~wägen~: From MHG ~wegen~ ("to set in motion, to weigh, to be worth"), from OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, to move"). A class V strong verb, ~wägen~, ~wog~, ~gewogen~ (rarely weak ~wägte~, ~gewägt~). It is the doublet of ~wiegen~, which generalized the ~i~ of the old present singular and took over the literal business of weighing, leaving ~wägen~ the figurative one, chiefly in ~abwägen~ and ~erwägen~. The same PIE root gave ~Weg~, ~Wagen~, and English ~way~, ~weigh~, ~wain~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

Where ~abwägen~ weighs two things against each other, ~erwägen~ carries the deliberation of a single matter through to a conclusion.
en.erwählen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~wählen~:

• ~wählen~: From MHG ~weln~, ~welen~, ~wellen~, from OHG ~wellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~walljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waljaną~, from PIE *~welh₁-~ ("to wish, choose"). The umlaut ~ä~ comes from the MHG second- and third-person singular; ~wählen~ and ~wollen~ share the same root. Cognate with English ~well~ (archaic "to wish well"), Dutch ~willen~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

~Erwählen~ is the solemn, definitive picking-out, the completed choice, where plain ~wählen~ names only the act.
en.erwähnen:
A 16th-century alteration of the earlier form ~gewähnen~, from Middle High German ~gewähenen~, ~gewahen~, from Old High German ~giwahanen~, ~giwahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gawahwan~ ("to say, mention"), from Proto-Germanic *~gawahwaną~, from *~ga-~ + *~wahwaną~, from PIE *~wekʷ-~ ("to speak").

The 16th-century reshaping swapped the prefix ~ge-~ for ~er-~, bringing the verb into line with other achievement verbs (the ~er-~ prefix conveys completion: "to bring to mention"). This substitution can create the impression that ~erwähnen~ is related to ~wähnen~ ("to suppose, imagine"), which descends from a different root entirely, Proto-West Germanic *~wānijan~, from a stem *~wōni-~ related to PIE *~wen-~ ("to desire, strive for"). The resemblance is a coincidence of form: the two verbs are not cognate. The true root of ~erwähnen~, PIE *~wekʷ-~, is the same root underlying Latin ~vōx~ ("voice"), ~vocāre~ ("to call"), and English ~voice~ and ~vocal~, all ultimately from the same "speaking" root. Cognate with Dutch ~gewagen~ ("to mention, refer to").
en.erwünschen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~wünschen~:

• ~wünschen~: From MHG ~wünschen~, from OHG ~wunsken~ ("to choose, wish, desire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wunskijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wunskijaną~, from *~wunskaz~ ("wish, desire"), from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to wish, love"), which also underlies ~Wonne~ ("bliss") and English ~win~. Cognate with English ~wish~, Dutch ~wensen~, Danish ~ønske~, Sanskrit ~vāṃchati~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ conveys obtaining or acquiring something by means of the base action.

Today the verb survives almost only in the participle ~erwünscht~ ("desired, welcome"); the finite ~erwünschen~ has become rare.
en.erzeigen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~zeigen~:

• ~zeigen~: From MHG ~zeigen~, from OHG ~zeigōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taigōn~, possibly from Proto-Germanic *~taikōną~ (iterative), an intensive derivative of OHG ~zīhan~ ("to accuse"), ultimately from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to point out, show"), whence also ~Zeichen~ ("sign") and English ~teach~. In Modern German it absorbed the unrelated MHG ~zöugen~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

~Erzeigen~ is to render or show something (to show mercy or honour), but it is now archaic, largely displaced by ~erweisen~.
en.erzeugen:
From ~er-~ + ~zeugen~:

• ~zeugen~: From MHG ~ziugen~, ~geziugen~, from OHG ~giziugon~, a denominative verb from ~Zeug~ ("stuff, gear, equipment, tools"). ~Zeug~ itself derives from MHG ~ziuc~, from OHG ~giziug~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teug~, ultimately a nominal derivative of *~teuhaną~ ("to pull, lead"), which also underlies ~ziehen~ ("to pull, draw"), from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead").
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"). The completive prefix turns the act of producing or witnessing into the fully achieved result: something brought into being. Doublet of ~ur-~.

The root ~zeugen~ has two seemingly unrelated modern senses ("to beget, procreate" and "to testify, bear witness"), but both trace to the same image: producing or bringing forward. A witness produces testimony; a parent produces offspring. ~Zeuge~ ("witness") shares this root, as does the archaic noun ~Gezeugs~ ("tools, implements," i.e., things produced). The deeper PIE root *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead") ties ~zeugen~ to Latin ~dūcere~ ("to lead"), the source of English ~duke~, ~duct~, and ~produce~. This makes ~erzeugen~ a distant relative of English ~produce~, both meaning "to bring something forward" from a common ancestor who simply pulled. ~Überzeugen~ ("to convince"), another compound on the same root, is the rhetorical version of the same act: to pull someone over to one's position through testimony. Cognate with Dutch ~getuigen~ (witness sense), English ~tow~ (via the same PIE *~dewk-~ root shared with ~ziehen~).
en.erziehen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.

The image is of drawing up or out: from the ~ziehen~ (drawing) of a child comes its ~erziehen~ (raising) to maturity, much as Latin ~educare~ meant "to lead out."
en.erzielen:
From ~er-~ + ~zielen~, where ~zielen~ is a denominative verb from ~Ziel~ ("goal, target, aim"):

• ~zielen~: From ~Ziel~ + verbal ~-en~. ~Ziel~: from MHG ~zil~, from OHG ~zil~, from Proto-West Germanic *~til~, from Proto-Germanic *~tilą~ ("goal, mark"). Cognate with Old English ~til~ ("goal"), which survives in the preposition ~till~ (originally "up to the mark").
• ~er-~: From Proto-Indo-European *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The completive prefix turns the act of aiming (~zielen~) into the achievement of hitting or obtaining a result.

The word ~Ziel~ itself covers both the physical sense (a target on an archery range) and the abstract sense (a goal in life or sport). ~Erzielen~ specializes in the achievement of quantifiable results: one ~erzielt~ a goal in football (~ein Tor erzielen~), a profit (~einen Gewinn erzielen~), or a record price. The completive ~er-~ is semantically precise: aiming (~zielen~) becomes scoring (~erzielen~). The Old English cognate ~til~ links to the modern preposition ~till/until~, whose core sense was "reaching the mark."
en.erzwingen:
An inseparable compound of ~er-~ + ~zwingen~:

• ~zwingen~: From MHG ~twingen~, from OHG ~dwingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þwinganą~, *~þwinhaną~; the apparent triple shift ~þ~ → ~d~ → ~t~ → ~z~ is regular for words with OHG ~dw-~ and ~tw-~, compare ~Zwerg~ ("dwarf"). A class III strong verb (~zwingen~, ~zwang~, ~gezwungen~). Cognate with Dutch ~dwingen~, Swedish ~tvinga~, Icelandic ~þvinga~, English ~twinge~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ conveys obtaining or acquiring something by means of the base action.

Where ~zwingen~ compels a person, ~erzwingen~ takes the forced-out result as its object: to force an acquittal or a confession.
en.erzählen:
From Middle High German ~erzellen~, from Old High German ~irzellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀtalljan~. Equivalent to ~er-~ + ~zählen~. Compound of two elements:

• ~zählen~: From MHG ~zel(e)n~, from OHG ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~, which carried both "to count" and "to recount, tell" from its earliest attestation.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("up, out"). This prefix often adds a sense of completion or result to the base verb. Doublet of ~ur-~.

The semantic shift from "counting" to "narrating" (powered by the completive ~er-~ prefix) is one of German's most striking lexical developments. The underlying Proto-Germanic root *~taljaną~ already held both meanings, but ~erzählen~ specialized entirely in the narrative sense: to give a full, complete account. The parallel with English is striking: ~tell~ (from the same root) underwent the same journey from counting to narrating, while ~teller~ at a bank and ~telling beads~ preserve the counting sense. The English word ~recount~ (to narrate) makes the metaphor explicit: to re-count events is to tell them. Cognate with Dutch ~vertellen~ ("to narrate," with a different prefix but the same root).
en.eröffnen:
From Middle High German ~eroffenen~, from Old High German ~iroffanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀupanōjan~. Equivalent to ~er-~ + ~öffnen~:

• ~öffnen~: From MHG ~öffenen~, ~offenen~, from OHG ~offanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~upanōn~, a denominative from Proto-Germanic *~upanaz~ ("open"), from PIE *~upo~ ("up, up from under"). Cognate with English ~open~, Dutch ~openen~, Danish ~åbne~.
• ~er-~: From Proto-Indo-European *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix lends a sense of initiation or ceremonial beginning: "opening up" to completion.

While ~öffnen~ is the everyday word for opening a door or window, ~eröffnen~ carries a more formal or initiatory sense: one ~eröffnet~ a conference, a bank account, a trial, or a new shop. The completive ~er-~ transforms a simple action into an event. The related noun ~Eröffnung~ appears in legal, musical, and commercial contexts, a ~Eröffnungsfest~ is a grand opening, and a symphony's ~Eröffnungssatz~ is its opening movement.
en.essen:
From Middle High German ~ëȥȥen~, from Old High German ~ëȥȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~etan~, from Proto-Germanic *~etaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ed-~ ("to eat"). A class V strong verb. Cognate with Low German ~eten~, Dutch ~eten~, English ~eat~, Danish ~æde~, Norwegian ~ete~, Swedish ~äta~, Yiddish ~עסן~ (esn), Gothic ~itan~. Non-Germanic cognates include Latin ~edō~, Ancient Greek ~édō~, Sanskrit ~ádmi~, Russian ~yestʹ~, and Scottish Gaelic ~ith~.

Few PIE roots are as conservative as *~h₁ed-~. Across five thousand years and dozens of languages, the word for "to eat" has scarcely changed: Latin ~edō~, Greek ~édō~, Sanskrit ~ádmi~, German ~essen~, and English ~eat~ all reflect the same ancient root, differing only by the regular sound changes of each branch. The PIE root also yields Latin ~edō~, the source of English ~edible~, ~obese~ (from ~ob-esus~, "eaten up"), and ~comestible~, making ~essen~ a distant relative of all of those. The geminate ~ss~ in the German infinitive reflects a Proto-West Germanic pattern of consonant strengthening. Notably, ~essen~ in Modern German is conventionally reserved for human eating; one says ~fressen~ when animals eat (and, rudely, when humans eat greedily), a distinction without an exact parallel in English.
en.etablieren:
Borrowed in the 17th century from French ~établir~ ("to establish"), from Old French ~establir~, from Latin ~stabilīre~ ("to make firm, to confirm, to establish"), from ~stabilis~ ("firm, steady"), from ~stāre~ ("to stand"), from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The German suffix ~-ieren~ marks the standard adaptation pattern for Romance verbs entering German.

The semantic journey from "to make firm" to "to establish" is straightforward, but the word's social history in German is more interesting. In the 18th and 19th centuries, ~etablieren~ carried a strong commercial sense: a merchant ~etablierte~ a business, and the reflexive ~sich etablieren~ ("to establish oneself") implied achieving financial and social respectability. The derived French loanword ~Etablissement~ took on a seedier coloring in German, often euphemistically referring to a nightclub or house of ill repute, a sense the French original does not share. Modern German has largely rehabilitated ~etablieren~ into neutral usage: political parties ~etablieren sich~ in parliament, scientific theories ~etablieren sich~ in textbooks. The related adjective ~etabliert~ ("established, well-established") carries no negative connotation. Cognate roots appear across the Indo-European spectrum: Latin ~stabilis~ gives English ~stable~, ~establish~, and ~state~; the same PIE *~steh₂-~ yields German ~stehen~, ~Stand~, ~Staat~, and ~stabil~, making ~etablieren~ a long-distance cousin, returned via French, of words that never left German.
en.existieren: ~Existieren~ ("to exist") is borrowed from Latin ~exsistere~ / ~existere~ ("to step forth, emerge, come into being, exist"), from ~ex-~ ("out, forth") + ~sistere~ ("to cause to stand, to place, to halt"), from Proto-Italic *~sistō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). That PIE root is one of the most productive in Indo-European: it produced Latin ~stāre~ ("to stand"), English ~stand~, ~state~, ~station~, ~statute~, ~stable~, and ~substance~, as well as Ancient Greek ~ἵστημι~ (~hístēmi~, "I cause to stand") and Sanskrit ~तिष्ठति~ (~tíṣṭhati~, "he stands"). The Latin compound ~exsistere~ thus literally means "to stand out", to emerge from non-being into being. English ~exist~ traveled the same route via Old French ~exister~. A philosophically interesting cognate: ~Bestand~ ("existence, stock, inventory") and ~bestehen~ ("to exist, persist, pass a test") share the same PIE root, showing that German preserved the standing metaphor natively while also borrowing the Latin learned form.
en.fahren: From Middle High German ~varn~, ~varen~, from Old High German ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose broad original sense of "to go, travel" narrowed in Modern German to emphasize vehicular travel, while the older general sense of "going" survives in derivatives like ~Erfahrung~ ("experience," literally "a traveling through") and ~Gefahr~ ("danger," literally "a lying in wait on the journey"). The related causative ~führen~ ("to lead, to conduct") derives from the same root: the weak formation *~fōrijaną~ ("to cause to go"), built with the Proto-Germanic causative suffix *~-janą~, supplies the transitive counterpart to strong intransitive ~fahren~, the same pattern as ~sitzen~/~setzen~, ~liegen~/~legen~, and ~fallen~/~fällen~. Cognate with Dutch ~varen~, English ~fare~, Danish ~fare~.
en.fallen: From Middle High German ~vallen~, from Old High German ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~. The ultimate PIE origin is uncertain; one proposed reconstruction connects it to a compound *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"), related to Ancient Greek ~apóllūmi~ ("to destroy, kill") and Lithuanian ~pùlti~ ("to fall, rush"). A class VII strong verb with a reduplicated past tense in Proto-Germanic. The semantic range of ~fallen~ has remained remarkably stable across two millennia; the word for a leaf falling in Old High German is the same word used today for falling in love (~sich verlieben~) or for a soldier falling in battle (~fallen im Krieg~). The related weak causative ~fällen~ ("to fell, to cause to fall") derives from the same root via the Proto-Germanic suffix *~-janą~ (*~fallijaną~); the umlaut a → ä is the trace of that formation, the same pattern as ~sitzen~/~setzen~ and ~liegen~/~legen~. Cognate with Low German ~fallen~, Dutch ~vallen~, English ~fall~, Danish ~falde~, Icelandic ~falla~, Swedish ~falla~.
en.falschliegen:
A separable compound of ~falsch~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~falsch~: From the adjective ~falsch~ ("false, wrong"), MHG ~valsch~, OHG ~falsc~, an early borrowing directly from Latin ~falsus~ ("deceived, false"), the past participle of ~fallere~ ("to deceive"), later reinforced by Old French ~fals~. English ~false~ goes back to the same Latin word, taken up separately, one of the few adjectives the two languages borrowed from Latin independently. In verbs it is adverbial: ~falschspielen~ is to cheat at cards or to play out of tune, ~falschliegen~ to be mistaken. The sense of ~falsch~ here is: wrongly, incorrectly, adverbial.

~Falschliegen~ is the recent colloquial formation and separates freely; ~da liegst du falsch~ ("there you're wrong").
en.falschspielen:
A separable compound of ~falsch~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~falsch~: From the adjective ~falsch~ ("false, wrong"), MHG ~valsch~, OHG ~falsc~, an early borrowing directly from Latin ~falsus~ ("deceived, false"), the past participle of ~fallere~ ("to deceive"), later reinforced by Old French ~fals~. English ~false~ goes back to the same Latin word, taken up separately, one of the few adjectives the two languages borrowed from Latin independently. In verbs it is adverbial: ~falschspielen~ is to cheat at cards or to play out of tune, ~falschliegen~ to be mistaken. The sense of ~falsch~ here is: deceitfully, by cheating.

Here the compound means cheating at play, not the musical "out of tune" sense that ~falsch spielen~ can also carry.
en.fangen: ~Fangen~ comes from Middle High German ~vāhen~, from Old High German ~fāhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~fanhaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to secure, attach, fasten"). The original strong verb had the vowel pattern ~fāhan~ / ~fieng~ / ~gefangan~; the modern present stem ~fang-~ was borrowed from the past forms under the influence of Middle Low German ~vangen~, spreading through Central German dialects in the early modern period. The same analogical leveling shaped ~hängen~, though ~hängen~ completed the shift more quickly because it already had two variant verbs reinforcing each other. Cognate with English ~fang~ (originally "that which seizes"), Dutch ~vangen~, West Frisian ~fange~, and, more distantly, Albanian ~peng~ ("to hinder, hold captive"). The PIE root *~peh₂ḱ-~ also produced Latin ~pangere~ ("to fix, fasten") and ~pax~ ("peace, compact"), making ~fangen~ a distant relative of English ~peace~.
en.fassen:
From MHG ~vazzen~, from OHG ~fazzōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fatōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fatōną~ ("to hold, seize"), from PIE *~pod-néh₂-ti~, from *~pod-~ ("to fetch"). Cognate with English ~fetch~.

The connection between ~fassen~ and English ~fetch~ is one of the more startling cognate pairs in the Germanic family: both descend from the same PIE root, yet they diverged dramatically, German keeping the sense of grasping and holding, English developing the sense of going to retrieve. The Proto-Germanic verb *~fatōną~ was a weak class 2 verb meaning "to hold, seize," and its descendants in German spread across an exceptionally rich idiomatic range: ~sich fassen~ ("to compose oneself, pull oneself together"), ~Fassung~ ("composure; version of a text"), ~unfassbar~ ("incomprehensible, literally ungraspable"), ~fassungslos~ ("speechless, stunned"), and the compound ~umfassen~ ("to encompass"). The cognitive metaphor of understanding as physical grasping runs deep: in German one ~fasst~ an idea, in English one ~grasps~ it, and in Latin one ~comprehendit~ it, all three verbs from different roots sharing the same bodily image. The noun ~Fass~ ("barrel, cask") shares the same root, a container that holds things. Note that ~fassen~ is not related to the English verb "to fast" (dietary abstinence), which derives from Proto-Germanic *~fastōną~ ("to hold firm, abstain"), a different root that produced a false-friend surface resemblance.
en.fechten: From MHG ~vëhten~ ("to fight"), from OHG ~fëhtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fehtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fehtaną~, perhaps from PIE *~peḱ-~ ("to pluck, comb"), though that last step is not secure. A class III strong verb (~fechten~, ~focht~, ~gefochten~); the ~o~ of the Präteritum was generalized from the old plural stem (OHG ~fuhtum~). Cognate with English ~fight~, Dutch ~vechten~, Low German ~fechten~, Danish ~fægte~. German narrowed the word to fencing while English kept the broad sense; the older breadth survives in the noun ~Gefecht~ ("engagement, combat").
en.fehlbesetzen:
A separable compound of ~fehl-~ + ~be-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~fehl-~: Not the modern noun ~Fehler~ ("error") but an older adverbial ~fehl~ ("amiss, wrongly"), from the obsolete noun ~Fehl~ ("fault"), beside the verb ~fehlen~, which MHG ~vēlen~ borrowed from Old French ~faillir~, from Vulgar Latin *~fallīre~, from Latin ~fallere~ ("to deceive, disappoint"). As a free word it survives only in the fixed phrase ~fehl am Platz~; everywhere else it is bound to verbs: ~fehlschlagen~ ("to fail"), ~fehlgehen~ ("to go astray"). English ~fail~, ~fault~, ~false~, and ~fallacy~ all descend from the same Latin verb. The sense of ~fehl-~ here is: in error, missing the intended target.

Built on ~besetzen~ ("to fill or cast a role"): ~fehlbesetzen~ is to fill it with the wrong choice; to miscast a role or misappoint to a post.
en.fehlen: From Middle High German ~vælen~, ~velen~, ~valen~, borrowed from Old French ~faillir~ ("to fail, be lacking"), from Latin ~fallō~ ("to deceive, cause to stumble"), from PIE *~(s)gʷʰh₂el-~ ("to stumble"), with a semantic development from "to stumble" through "to deceive." This makes ~fehlen~ one of the relatively few common German verbs that entered the language via Old French rather than through Germanic inheritance, a legacy of medieval courtly and trade contact. The semantic shift from "to deceive" through "to fall short" to "to be missing, to be lacking" follows the trajectory of French ~faillir~: what fails is what is not there when needed. The same Latin root gives English ~fail~, ~false~, and ~fallible~. Cognate with English ~fail~, French ~faillir~, Italian ~fallire~.
en.fehlgehen:
A separable compound of ~fehl-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~fehl-~: Not the modern noun ~Fehler~ ("error") but an older adverbial ~fehl~ ("amiss, wrongly"), from the obsolete noun ~Fehl~ ("fault"), beside the verb ~fehlen~, which MHG ~vēlen~ borrowed from Old French ~faillir~, from Vulgar Latin *~fallīre~, from Latin ~fallere~ ("to deceive, disappoint"). As a free word it survives only in the fixed phrase ~fehl am Platz~; everywhere else it is bound to verbs: ~fehlschlagen~ ("to fail"), ~fehlgehen~ ("to go astray"). English ~fail~, ~fault~, ~false~, and ~fallacy~ all descend from the same Latin verb. The sense of ~fehl-~ here is: wrongly, amiss, off the mark.

~Fehlgehen~ literally means to take the wrong road and figuratively to err; both readings are old.
en.fehlleiten:
A separable compound of ~fehl-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~: the causative *~laidijaną~ of the strong verb *~līþaną~ ("to pass, go") with the suffix *~-janą~ ("to cause to go"), from PIE *~leyt-~ ("to go, depart, die"). ~leiten~ and ~leiden~ are a base-and-causative pair. Cognate with English ~lead~ (OE ~lǣdan~).
• ~fehl-~: Not the modern noun ~Fehler~ ("error") but an older adverbial ~fehl~ ("amiss, wrongly"), from the obsolete noun ~Fehl~ ("fault"), beside the verb ~fehlen~, which MHG ~vēlen~ borrowed from Old French ~faillir~, from Vulgar Latin *~fallīre~, from Latin ~fallere~ ("to deceive, disappoint"). As a free word it survives only in the fixed phrase ~fehl am Platz~; everywhere else it is bound to verbs: ~fehlschlagen~ ("to fail"), ~fehlgehen~ ("to go astray"). English ~fail~, ~fault~, ~false~, and ~fallacy~ all descend from the same Latin verb. The sense of ~fehl-~ here is: wrongly, amiss, off the mark.

~Fehlleiten~ is to lead in the wrong direction: to misroute a letter or lead a person astray.
en.fehlschlagen:
A separable compound of ~fehl-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~fehl-~: Not the modern noun ~Fehler~ ("error") but an older adverbial ~fehl~ ("amiss, wrongly"), from the obsolete noun ~Fehl~ ("fault"), beside the verb ~fehlen~, which MHG ~vēlen~ borrowed from Old French ~faillir~, from Vulgar Latin *~fallīre~, from Latin ~fallere~ ("to deceive, disappoint"). As a free word it survives only in the fixed phrase ~fehl am Platz~; everywhere else it is bound to verbs: ~fehlschlagen~ ("to fail"), ~fehlgehen~ ("to go astray"). English ~fail~, ~fault~, ~false~, and ~fallacy~ all descend from the same Latin verb. The sense of ~fehl-~ here is: unsuccessfully, coming to nothing.

The image is of a blow that misses its mark; from it comes the abstract ~fehlschlagen~ ("to miscarry, fail").
en.feiern:
From Middle High German ~vīren~, from Old High German ~fīrōn~, a denominative verb derived from Old High German ~fīra~ (whence modern ~Feier~), itself borrowed from Latin ~fēriae~ ("religious holidays, festivals"). Cognate with Dutch ~vieren~.

Latin ~fēriae~ is from Proto-Italic *~fēsiās~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰéh₁s-yo-s~, derived from *~dʰéh₁s~ ("god, godhead, deity"). The same PIE root underlies Latin ~fēstus~ ("festive") (whence English ~feast~ and ~festival~) and Ancient Greek ~theîos~ ("divine"). ~Feiern~ is thus one of the rare German verbs whose etymology leads directly into Latin and ultimately into the divine: a holiday (~Feiertag~) was originally a day set aside for the gods. The route from Latin into German passed through the early Christian church, which adopted the Roman calendar vocabulary for its own feast days. The modern sense of ~feiern~ (throwing a birthday party, celebrating New Year's) is secular, but the word retains its sacred pedigree. Cognate (distantly) with English ~feast~ and ~festival~ via the Latin root.
en.feilbieten:
A separable compound of ~feil-~ + ~bieten~:

• ~bieten~: From MHG ~bieten~, from OHG ~biotan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beudan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beudaną~, from PIE *~bʰewdʰ-~ ("to be awake, aware"). A class II strong verb whose root conveys awareness and offering. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bieden~, Danish ~byde~, Swedish ~bjuda~.
• ~feil-~: The archaic adjective ~feil~ ("for sale, to be had for money"), from MHG ~veile~, from OHG ~feili~, from Proto-West Germanic *~failī~. Cognate with Dutch ~veil~ and Old Norse ~falr~, and connected to Ancient Greek ~πωλέω~ (~pōléō~, "to sell"), the verb that also gives English ~monopoly~ its second half. The adjective has died out as a free word and survives only in ~feilbieten~ and ~feilhalten~, both meaning to offer goods for sale, often figuratively and disparagingly. ~feil-~ offers the object publicly for sale.

~Feilbieten~ stresses the active offering, ~feilhalten~ the keeping-in-stock; often figurative, as in hawking one's convictions.
en.feilhaben:
A separable compound of ~feil-~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~feil-~: The archaic adjective ~feil~ ("for sale, to be had for money"), from MHG ~veile~, from OHG ~feili~, from Proto-West Germanic *~failī~. Cognate with Dutch ~veil~ and Old Norse ~falr~, and connected to Ancient Greek ~πωλέω~ (~pōléō~, "to sell"), the verb that also gives English ~monopoly~ its second half. The adjective has died out as a free word and survives only in ~feilbieten~ and ~feilhalten~, both meaning to offer goods for sale, often figuratively and disparagingly. ~feil-~ offers the object publicly for sale.

Beside the literal "to have for sale," ~feilhaben~ survives in the idiom ~Maulaffen feilhaben~ ("to stand about gaping").
en.feilhalten:
A separable compound of ~feil-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~feil-~: The archaic adjective ~feil~ ("for sale, to be had for money"), from MHG ~veile~, from OHG ~feili~, from Proto-West Germanic *~failī~. Cognate with Dutch ~veil~ and Old Norse ~falr~, and connected to Ancient Greek ~πωλέω~ (~pōléō~, "to sell"), the verb that also gives English ~monopoly~ its second half. The adjective has died out as a free word and survives only in ~feilbieten~ and ~feilhalten~, both meaning to offer goods for sale, often figuratively and disparagingly. ~feil-~ offers the object publicly for sale.

~Feilhalten~ is to keep goods ready for sale, like the disguised queen at market in Grimm.
en.fernbleiben:
A separable compound of ~fern~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~fern~: From MHG ~verre~, ~verren~, from OHG ~ferro~, ~ferrana~ ("far off, from afar"), from an old Proto-Germanic locative adverb *~ferrai~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross, to pass through"). Cognate with English ~far~, Dutch ~ver~, Danish ~fjern~, Gothic ~fairra~. The same root, in its "through, beyond" sense, gave Latin ~per~ and Greek ~peri-~, so ~fern~ and ~perimeter~ are distant relatives, appropriately enough. Resultative in the other direction: keeping something far off, at arm's length (~fernhalten~, ~fernbleiben~).

~Fernbleiben~ takes the dative and forms its perfect with ~sein~: to stay away from a meeting or from school.
en.ferngucken:
A separable compound of ~fern~ + ~gucken~:

• ~gucken~: From MHG ~gücken~, ~guggen~ ("to look inquisitively, to peek"), of uncertain origin, perhaps from MHG ~gücken~, OHG ~guckōn~ ("to cuckoo"), via the image of peeping out from cover. The variant ~kucken~ is attributed to influence from Low German ~kieken~. Colloquial and northern/central German; the south prefers ~schauen~. Cognate with Dutch ~kijken~, Luxembourgish ~kucken~.
• ~fern~: From MHG ~verre~, ~verren~, from OHG ~ferro~, ~ferrana~ ("far off, from afar"), from an old Proto-Germanic locative adverb *~ferrai~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross, to pass through"). Cognate with English ~far~, Dutch ~ver~, Danish ~fjern~, Gothic ~fairra~. The same root, in its "through, beyond" sense, gave Latin ~per~ and Greek ~peri-~, so ~fern~ and ~perimeter~ are distant relatives, appropriately enough. The adjective means "far, distant"; the compound verb acts at or across a distance (~fernsehen~, ~fernsteuern~).

~Ferngucken~ is the colloquial northern- and central-German counterpart to ~fernsehen~.
en.fernhalten:
A separable compound of ~fern~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~fern~: From MHG ~verre~, ~verren~, from OHG ~ferro~, ~ferrana~ ("far off, from afar"), from an old Proto-Germanic locative adverb *~ferrai~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross, to pass through"). Cognate with English ~far~, Dutch ~ver~, Danish ~fjern~, Gothic ~fairra~. The same root, in its "through, beyond" sense, gave Latin ~per~ and Greek ~peri-~, so ~fern~ and ~perimeter~ are distant relatives, appropriately enough. Resultative in the other direction: keeping something far off, at arm's length (~fernhalten~, ~fernbleiben~).

~Fernhalten~ is transitive or reflexive: to keep someone from something, or to keep oneself away from it.
en.fernliegen:
A separable compound of ~fern~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~fern~: From MHG ~verre~, ~verren~, from OHG ~ferro~, ~ferrana~ ("far off, from afar"), from an old Proto-Germanic locative adverb *~ferrai~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross, to pass through"). Cognate with English ~far~, Dutch ~ver~, Danish ~fjern~, Gothic ~fairra~. The same root, in its "through, beyond" sense, gave Latin ~per~ and Greek ~peri-~, so ~fern~ and ~perimeter~ are distant relatives, appropriately enough. The adjective means "far, distant"; the compound verb acts at or across a distance (~fernsehen~, ~fernsteuern~).

~Fernliegen~ is stative: ~es liegt mir fern~ means that something is wholly alien to one, or far from one's intention.
en.fernschauen:
A separable compound of ~fern~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~fern~: From MHG ~verre~, ~verren~, from OHG ~ferro~, ~ferrana~ ("far off, from afar"), from an old Proto-Germanic locative adverb *~ferrai~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross, to pass through"). Cognate with English ~far~, Dutch ~ver~, Danish ~fjern~, Gothic ~fairra~. The same root, in its "through, beyond" sense, gave Latin ~per~ and Greek ~peri-~, so ~fern~ and ~perimeter~ are distant relatives, appropriately enough. The adjective means "far, distant"; the compound verb acts at or across a distance (~fernsehen~, ~fernsteuern~).

~Fernschauen~ names either watching television, after the southern-German and Austrian ~schauen~, or literally gazing into the distance.
en.fernsehen:
A separable compound of ~fern~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~fern~: From MHG ~verre~, ~verren~, from OHG ~ferro~, ~ferrana~ ("far off, from afar"), from an old Proto-Germanic locative adverb *~ferrai~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross, to pass through"). Cognate with English ~far~, Dutch ~ver~, Danish ~fjern~, Gothic ~fairra~. The same root, in its "through, beyond" sense, gave Latin ~per~ and Greek ~peri-~, so ~fern~ and ~perimeter~ are distant relatives, appropriately enough. The adjective means "far, distant"; the compound verb acts at or across a distance (~fernsehen~, ~fernsteuern~).

~Fernsehen~ is the standard word; the nominalized ~das Fernsehen~ names the medium itself.
en.fernsteuern:
A separable compound of ~fern~ + ~steuern~:

• ~steuern~: From MHG ~stiuren~, from OHG ~stiuren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stiurijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stiurijaną~. The root noun ~Steuer~ carries two meanings sharing one ancestor: ~das Steuer~ ("rudder, helm") and ~die Steuer~ ("tax," via "supporting post" and "support"). ~Steuern~ thus means both "to steer, navigate, control" and, in archaic or Swiss usage, "to pay a tax." Cognate with English ~steer~, Dutch ~stuur~.
• ~fern~: From MHG ~verre~, ~verren~, from OHG ~ferro~, ~ferrana~ ("far off, from afar"), from an old Proto-Germanic locative adverb *~ferrai~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross, to pass through"). Cognate with English ~far~, Dutch ~ver~, Danish ~fjern~, Gothic ~fairra~. • ~stecken~: Modern ~stecken~ merges two verbs: the transitive weak one ("to put, stick something in") from MHG ~stecken~, OHG ~steckōn~, a geminate derivative of ~stëhhan~ (the ancestor of ~stechen~), and the strong intransitive one (archaic ~stak~/~gestocken~, "to be stuck"); the two fused in Early Modern German. Both trace to Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stikaną~, from PIE *~(s)teyg-~ ("to be sharp, stab, goad"). Cognate with English ~stick~ and ~steak~.
• ~fest~: From the adjective ~fest~ ("firm, fixed, solid"), from MHG ~vest~, from OHG ~festi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fastī~, from Proto-Germanic *~fastuz~, probably from PIE *~pastV-~ ("solid, stable"). Cognate with Dutch ~vast~, Swedish ~fast~, Gothic ~fastan~ ("to hold fast"), and with English ~fast~ in its older sense "firmly fixed," preserved in "hold fast" and "steadfast." English ~fast~ "quick" is that same word: to run fast was first to run hard and unwaveringly, and only later to run quickly. It can also mean "secured, held in place," as when something is fastened down or someone is detained.

Intransitive "to be stuck, unable to move on", the sense glossed here, distinct from transitive ~feststecken~, "to pin (hair, a hem) in place."
en.feststehen:
A separable compound of ~fest~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~fest~: From the adjective ~fest~ ("firm, fixed, solid"), from MHG ~vest~, from OHG ~festi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fastī~, from Proto-Germanic *~fastuz~, probably from PIE *~pastV-~ ("solid, stable"). Cognate with Dutch ~vast~, Swedish ~fast~, Gothic ~fastan~ ("to hold fast"), and with English ~fast~ in its older sense "firmly fixed," preserved in "hold fast" and "steadfast." English ~fast~ "quick" is that same word: to run fast was first to run hard and unwaveringly, and only later to run quickly. The particle adds a sense of firmness, fixedness, or permanence.

Literally to stand firm and immovable, but in modern usage chiefly abstract; ~es steht fest~, "it is certain, settled."
en.feststellen:
Compound of ~fest-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~.
• ~fest-~: From MHG ~vest~, ~veste~, from OHG ~festi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fastī~, from PIE *~pastV-~ ("solid, stable"). Cognate with English ~fast~ (in the archaic sense of "firmly fixed," as in "hold fast"), Dutch ~vast~, Swedish ~fast~.

The literal meaning of ~feststellen~ is "to place firmly", to put something down in such a way that it stays put. From this spatial metaphor come both of the verb's principal modern senses: "to establish a fact" (to fix it as true, to put it on the record so that it cannot be moved) and "to determine, to ascertain" (to arrive at a settled conclusion). The compound is a relatively modern coinage; MHG and OHG had no single equivalent word, relying instead on circumlocutions. Its closest English functional parallel is "to establish" or "to determine," though neither captures the Germanic concreteness of ~feststellen~'s spatial metaphor as precisely. The same ~fest-~ element appears in ~festhalten~ ("to hold fast"), ~festlegen~ ("to fix, to lay down"), and ~festigen~ ("to consolidate"), a family of verbs all built on the image of gripping or placing something so securely that it cannot shift. Cognate with Dutch ~vaststellen~.
en.festtreten:
A separable compound of ~fest~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~fest~: From the adjective ~fest~ ("firm, fixed, solid"), from MHG ~vest~, from OHG ~festi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fastī~, from Proto-Germanic *~fastuz~, probably from PIE *~pastV-~ ("solid, stable"). Cognate with Dutch ~vast~, Swedish ~fast~, Gothic ~fastan~ ("to hold fast"), and with English ~fast~ in its older sense "firmly fixed," preserved in "hold fast" and "steadfast." English ~fast~ "quick" is that same word: to run fast was first to run hard and unwaveringly, and only later to run quickly. In a resultative compound the adjective names the end state: the action is carried on until the object is firmly fixed.

To tread earth or snow down until it is packed firm.
en.festziehen:
A separable compound of ~fest~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~fest~: From the adjective ~fest~ ("firm, fixed, solid"), from MHG ~vest~, from OHG ~festi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fastī~, from Proto-Germanic *~fastuz~, probably from PIE *~pastV-~ ("solid, stable"). Cognate with Dutch ~vast~, Swedish ~fast~, Gothic ~fastan~ ("to hold fast"), and with English ~fast~ in its older sense "firmly fixed," preserved in "hold fast" and "steadfast." English ~fast~ "quick" is that same word: to run fast was first to run hard and unwaveringly, and only later to run quickly. In a resultative compound the adjective names the end state: the action is carried on until the object is firmly fixed.

To pull a knot, strap, or screw tight until it holds.
en.filmen:
A denominative verb from ~Film~ + ~-en~. The noun ~Film~ was borrowed from English ~film~, which descends from Old English ~filmen~ ("membrane, thin skin"), from Proto-West Germanic *~filmin-~, from Proto-Germanic *~filmin-~ ("thin skin, membrane"), from Proto-Indo-European *~pel-mo-~ ("membrane"), from the root *~pel-~ ("to cover, skin").

In a charming etymological boomerang, the word traveled from Germanic to English, where it underwent a remarkable semantic shift (from "membrane" to "thin coating" (1577) to "photographic coating" (1845) to "motion picture" (1895)) before being borrowed back into German in the early twentieth century. Old English ~filmen~ meant "foreskin" or "caul," and no Anglo-Saxon could have imagined that this humble anatomical term would one day name an art form.
en.finanzieren: From ~Finanz~ + ~-ieren~. ~Finanz~ derives from French ~finance(s)~, from Middle French ~finer~ ("to pay a ransom, to settle a debt"), from ~fin~ ("end"), from Latin ~fīnis~ ("end, boundary, limit"). The semantic chain is elegant: a debt is "ended" by payment, so ~finance~ originally meant "an ending", specifically, the ending of an obligation through payment. The sense shifted from "ransom payment" (mid-fifteenth century) to "taxation" (late fifteenth century) to "management of money" (eighteenth century). German naturalized the verb with the standard ~-ieren~ suffix, making ~finanzieren~ ("to finance, to fund") feel thoroughly German despite its Romance pedigree. The Latin root ~fīnis~ also gives German ~Finale~, ~Definition~, and ~Infinitiv~, the last being a grammatical term meaning "the form without an ending," a fitting irony for a verb-conjugation app. Cognate with English ~finance~, French ~financer~, Italian ~finanziare~.
en.finden: From Middle High German ~vinden~, from Old High German ~findan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~finþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to go, pass; path, bridge"). The semantic development from "to go, pass" to "to find" parallels similar shifts in Slavic languages. Cognate with Bavarian ~findn~, Low German ~finden~, Dutch ~vinden~, English ~find~, Danish ~finde~.
en.fixieren:
Borrowed from Latin ~fixum~ ("that which is fixed, a fixed sum"), the neuter past participle of ~figere~ ("to fasten, to fix"), possibly influenced by Medieval Latin ~fixāre~ ("to make fast"). The ~-ieren~ suffix is the standard German adaptation of French/Latin ~-ier~/~-āre~ verb endings.

The Latin verb ~figere~ derives from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeygʷ-~ ("to stick, to fix"). The meanings of ~fixieren~ branched in the sixteenth century when alchemists adopted ~fix~ to mean "stable, non-volatile" (a substance that would not evaporate). From this came the sense of "to make permanent" and then "to stare at fixedly." In modern German, ~fixieren~ can mean "to fix in place," "to stare at intently," or "to define precisely", all descendants of the alchemists' quest to make the volatile stable.
en.flachlegen:
A separable compound of ~flach~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~flach~: From the adjective ~flach~ ("flat, level, shallow"), from MHG ~vlach~, from OHG ~flah~, from Proto-Germanic *~flakaz~, from PIE *~pleh₂k-~ ("flat, broad"), the root behind Greek ~πλάξ~ (~plax~, "flat plate") and, through it, English ~plaque~ and ~placenta~. In a resultative compound it names the end state: the action leaves its object flat. Cognate with Dutch ~vlak~, Old Norse ~flakna~ ("to flake off"), English ~flake~. The sense of ~flach~ here is: leaving the object lying flat.

To lay something down flat; reflexively and colloquially, to lie down for a rest.
en.flechten: From MHG ~vlëhten~, from OHG ~flëhtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~flehtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~flehtaną~, from PIE *~pleḱ-~ ("to plait, weave"). A class III strong verb (~flechten~, ~flocht~, ~geflochten~), its Präteritum ~o~ generalized from the old plural stem. Cognate with Dutch ~vlechten~, Old Norse ~flétta~, Swedish ~fläta~, and probably English ~flax~ (the plant one plaits). The same PIE root reached English by the Latin road as well, through ~plectere~ and ~plicāre~: ~plait~, ~complex~, and ~ply~ are all cousins of ~Flechte~.
en.fliegen: ~Fliegen~ comes from Middle High German ~vliegen~, from Old High German ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from Proto-Indo-European *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"). The PIE root *~plewk-~ is an extended form of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim"), which also produced ~fließen~ ("to flow"), Latin ~pluere~ ("to rain"), and Greek ~plein~ ("to sail"). Motion through a fluid medium (whether water or air) was once a single conceptual domain. The High German consonant shift turned Proto-Germanic *fl- into German fl- unchanged (labial fricatives were unaffected), but the vowel shift from Proto-Germanic *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of German Class II strong verbs. Cognate with Dutch ~vliegen~, English ~fly~, Danish ~flyve~, and Low German ~flegen~. Compare also Bavarian ~fliagn~, which preserves an older vowel.
en.fliehen:
From Middle High German ~vliehen~, from Old High German ~fliohan~ ("to flee"), from Proto-West Germanic *~fleuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuhaną~ ("to flee"), probably from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to fly, flee"), an enlargement of *~plew-~ ("to flow, run"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with English ~flee~ (from OE ~flēon~), Dutch ~vlieden~, and Gothic ~þliuhan~ (with secondary ~þ-~).

The PIE root *~plewk-~ is also the source of ~fliegen~ ("to fly") and ~Flucht~ ("flight, escape"), making ~fliehen~ and ~fliegen~ etymological siblings, the original root encompassed rapid motion through any medium. The English cognates ~flee~ and ~fly~ mirror this German pair perfectly. Gothic ~þliuhan~ is puzzling: it shows an unexpected ~þ-~ (th-sound) where all other Germanic languages have ~f-~. Linguists debate whether the Gothic form preserves an archaic consonant or reflects a secondary change unique to Gothic. The noun ~Flüchtling~ ("refugee"), derived from ~Flucht~, entered international discourse during the European migration crisis of 2015, a word with five-thousand-year-old roots describing an experience as old as humanity itself.
en.fließen: From Middle High German ~vlieȥen~, from Old High German ~flioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleutaną~ ("to float, to stream, to flow"), from PIE *~plewd-~ ("to flow, to run, to swim"). A class II strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~fließen~, ~floss~, ~geflossen~. The PIE root *~plewd-~ produced an extensive water-vocabulary across Indo-European: Latin ~pluvia~ ("rain"), whence English ~pluvial~; Latvian ~plūdi~ ("flood"); Lithuanian ~pláuti~ ("to wash"); and Greek ~pleō~ ("I sail"). Within Germanic, the root gave English ~fleet~ (originally "a place where water flows," then the ships gathered there), ~float~, ~flood~, Dutch ~vlieten~ ("to flow," archaic/literary), Swedish ~flyta~ ("to float"), and Icelandic ~fljóta~. The zero-grade form *~flut-~ produced German ~Flut~ ("flood, high tide"), English ~flood~, and Dutch ~vloed~. The derived noun ~Fluss~ ("river") is literally "a flowing", Germanic languages conceptualize rivers as the action of flowing made permanent, whereas Latin ~flūmen~ (from ~fluere~, "to flow," a different PIE root) took the same metaphorical path independently. The compound ~Einfluss~ ("influence") calques Latin ~influentia~, a flowing-in of one thing upon another.
en.folgen: From Middle High German ~volgen~, from Old High German ~folgēn~ (attested from the 8th century, meaning "to follow, serve faithfully, pursue"), from Proto-West Germanic *~folgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fulgāną~. The ultimate pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. The Old High German forms reveal an early semantic range that blended physical following, loyal service, and pursuit, reflecting the social structures of early Germanic society in which following a lord was the fundamental act of the ~comitatus~ (the warrior band). German ~folgen~ and English ~follow~ are doublets: both descend from the same Proto-Germanic root, but ~follow~ entered Middle English via Old Norse ~fylgja~ through Old English ~folgian~. Cognate with Dutch ~volgen~, English ~follow~, Danish ~følge~, Swedish ~följa~.
en.fordern:
From Middle High German ~vodern~, ~vordern~, from Old High German ~fordarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ(a)rōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþą~, from PIE *~pŕ̥-to-~, from *~per-~ ("forward, through"). The semantic development from "to push forward" to "to demand, claim" reflects the notion of asserting or advancing a claim. The PIE root *~per-~ is shared with the separable prefix ~vor-~ and with English ~forth~, ~forward~, and ~further~, all sharing the spatial sense of moving ahead.

German learners must take care to distinguish ~fordern~ ("to demand") from the near-homophone ~fördern~ ("to promote, advance, support"). Despite their near-identical sound, they descend from the same Proto-Germanic root and once overlapped in meaning; the umlaut in ~fördern~ (from MHG ~vürdern~, OHG ~furdiren~, from PWGmc *~furþrijan~) marks its more specifically "forward-moving" sense, while ~fordern~ settled on the sense of making a forward claim or assertion. Cognate with English ~further~ (via the same PIE root), Dutch ~vorderen~.
en.formen: From Middle High German ~formen~, a denominative verb derived from the noun ~Form~, from Middle High German ~form~, borrowed from Latin ~forma~ ("shape, figure, appearance"). The ultimate origin of Latin ~forma~ is uncertain, but it may derive from Etruscan *~morma~, itself from Ancient Greek ~morphe~ ("shape, fashion, outward form"), with dissimilation of *~m-m~ to *~f-m~, as also seen in Latin ~formica~ ("ant") and ~formido~ ("scarecrow, ghost"). This Latin-to-Greek connection means that ~formen~ and English ~morph~ are distant cousins, both tracing back to the Greek concept of visible shape. The German ~-ieren~ suffix was not used here, unlike with many other Latin-derived verbs; instead German created a straightforward denominative from the noun, giving ~formen~ its clean, native-sounding conjugation. English ~form~ (both noun and verb) is a sibling borrowing from the same Latin source, arriving via Old French ~fourme~.
en.formulieren: Borrowed from French ~formuler~, itself from Latin ~fōrmula~ ("a small pattern or mold, form, rule, principle, method"), the diminutive of ~forma~ ("form, shape, figure"). The Latin ~forma~ is of uncertain origin; some scholars connect it to Greek ~morphḗ~ ("form, shape") via metathesis, while others derive it from an Etruscan source. German ~formulieren~ follows the standard ~-ieren~ suffix pattern for verbs borrowed from Romance languages, a productive pattern since the Middle High German period, when courtly culture imported hundreds of French verbs. The diminutive origin is telling: a ~formula~ was not just any form but a ~small~ form, a precise template, and ~formulieren~ preserves this sense of careful, deliberate shaping of language. The related noun ~Form~ entered German directly from French ~forme~, while ~Formel~ ("formula") came through Latin. English ~formulate~ traveled a parallel path, from the same Latin diminutive via French. Cognate with Dutch ~formuleren~, Italian ~formulare~, Spanish ~formular~.
en.fortbestehen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~be-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys continuation: carrying on with what was already under way.

In ~fortbestehen~, ~bestehen~ appears in its intransitive reading "to endure, go on existing"; the same ~be-~ formation used transitively means "to withstand, get through," while here the particle stresses persistence over time.
en.fortbilden:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~bilden~:

• ~bilden~: From MHG ~bilden~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: ~biliden~ ("to form into an image"), from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþijan~, and ~bilidōn~ ("to copy, represent"), from *~biliþōn~; both from the noun *~biliþī~ (whence ~Bild~), whose pre-Germanic origin is obscure, with no secure PIE etymology. Cognate with Dutch ~beelden~, Swedish ~bilda~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys continuation: carrying on with what was already under way.

~Fortbilden~ means carrying education onward: one keeps training someone, or oneself, beyond what has already been learned.
en.fortbleiben:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

~Fortbleiben~ is absence as a state: one who stays away does not return but remains gone.
en.fortdauern:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~dauern~:

• ~dauern~: Two separate verbs under one spelling. "To last, endure": from MHG ~dūren~, borrowed from Middle Low German ~dūren~, from Latin ~dūrō~, a denominative of ~dūrus~ ("hard, lasting"), from Proto-Italic *~dūros~, from PIE *~dweh₂-~ ("long, far"); cognate with Dutch ~duren~, English ~dure~. "To cause pity" (~er dauert mich~): from MHG ~tūren~, an ablaut variant of ~tiure~ ("dear, costly"), ancestor of ~teuer~, thus a doublet of ~teuer~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys continuation: carrying on with what was already under way.

This is the first ~dauern~, the one from Latin ~dūrō~ ("to last"), not its homograph ~dauern~ ("to arouse pity"): to ~fortdauern~ is to keep on lasting without interruption.
en.fortfahren:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

Alongside the literal "to drive off," ~fortfahren~ early developed the figurative "to continue, carry on", the reading that appears in the attested sentence.
en.fortführen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys continuation: carrying on with what was already under way.

~Fortführen~ carries two readings: the spatial "to lead away, abduct" and the figurative "to continue, carry on"; the attested sentence shows the latter.
en.fortgeben:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

~Fortgeben~ means to give something out of one's hand and out of one's own possession; the particle marks the away-from-oneself.
en.fortgehen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

~Fortgehen~ is moving away from a place; in the attested sentence it is the girls who have left the dance.
en.fortjagen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~jagen~:

• ~jagen~: From MHG ~jagen~ ("to hurry, drive, pursue, hunt"), from OHG ~jagōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~jagōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~jakkōną~, a ~nā~-iterative formation, likely rebuilt from PIE *~h₁eyǵʰ-~ ("to strive, chase"). Attested since the eighth century; further pre-Germanic etymology is obscure.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

~Fortjagen~ joins the driving sense of ~jagen~ to the particle: not the hunting of game, but the driving-off of something unwanted.
en.fortkommen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

~Fortkommen~ first means "to get away, escape"; colloquially it yields "make yourself scarce", exactly the turn of phrase in the attested sentence.
en.fortleben:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys continuation: carrying on with what was already under way.
