~Fortleben~ means to live on, to persist past some break; in Luther it is the stubborn persistence in greed.
en.fortlegen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

~Fortlegen~ is a putting-aside: one lays an object away from oneself in another spot.
en.fortlocken:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~locken~:

• ~locken~: From MHG ~locken~, from OHG ~lockōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lokkōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lukkōną~ ("to entice, to lure"). A second, homonymous ~locken~ ("to curl"), from OHG ~lochōn~ and the noun ~Locke~, is etymologically distinct. Related to ~lügen~, Latin ~laciō~ ("I entice"); English has no direct cognate and uses ~lure~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

This is the first ~locken~ ("to entice, lure"), not its homograph ~locken~ ("to curl"): to ~fortlocken~ is to draw someone away from a place by enticement.
en.fortnehmen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

~Fortnehmen~ is a taking-away in the literal sense: to take something and carry it off, as the elves do the changeling.
en.fortpflanzen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~pflanzen~:

• ~pflanzen~: From MHG ~pflanzen~, from OHG ~pflanzōn~, a denominative verb from ~pflanza~ ("plant"), borrowed from Latin ~planta~ ("a shoot, cutting"), itself of uncertain origin. The change from Latin ~pl-~ to ~pfl-~ belongs to the High German consonant shift. Cognate with English ~plant~ (which shows no shift), Luxembourgish ~Planz~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys continuation: carrying on with what was already under way.

~Fortpflanzen~ transfers the image of setting a plant into the ground onto the passing-on of life from one generation to the next.
en.fortreisen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

~Fortreisen~ is departure by travel: one sets out and moves away from a place.
en.forträumen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~räumen~:

• ~räumen~: From Early New High German ~reumen~, a Central German umlaut variant of ~raumen~, from MHG ~rūmen~, from OHG ~rūmen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rūmijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rūmijaną~, a factitive verb from the adjective *~rūmaz~ ("roomy, spacious"), from PIE *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open"). Etymologically, "to make room." Cognate with English ~room~, the noun ~Raum~, Bavarian ~rama~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

~Forträumen~ means to clear something away and free up the space, the underlying "make room" of ~räumen~, directed away from the spot.
en.fortschaffen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~schaffen~:

• ~schaffen~: Two historically distinct verbs have merged under a single infinitive, distinguished only by their conjugation. The strong ~schaffen~ (~schuf~, ~geschaffen~, "to create") descends from MHG ~schaffen~, OHG ~scaffan~, a byform of ~skephen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skappjan~; the ~-f-~ was chiefly back-formed from the participle ~giscaffan~. The weak ~schaffen~ (~schaffte~, ~geschafft~, "to manage, accomplish") descends from OHG ~skaffōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skapōn~, from the same root. Cognate with Dutch ~scheppen~, English ~shape~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

This is the weak ~schaffen~ ("to manage, convey," ~schaffte~, ~geschafft~), not the strong ~schaffen~ ("to create"): to ~fortschaffen~ is to carry something off, to remove it.
en.fortschleifen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~schleifen~:

• ~schleifen~: Two verbs share this spelling. The strong ~schleifen~ ("to grind, whet, polish") is from MHG ~slīfen~, OHG ~slīfan~, Proto-West Germanic *~slīpan~, Proto-Germanic *~slīpaną~ ("to slide, to whet"): class I, ~schleifen~, ~schliff~, ~geschliffen~, cognate with English ~slip~, Dutch ~slijpen~. The weak ~schleifen~ ("to drag; to raze a fortress") is from MHG ~sleifen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slaipijan~ ("to cause to slide"), the causative of the first, and inflects ~schleifte~, ~geschleift~; a doublet of ~schleppen~, cognate with Dutch ~slepen~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

This is the weak ~schleifen~ ("to drag," ~schleifte~, ~geschleift~), not the strong ~schleifen~ ("to whet, polish"): to ~fortschleifen~ is to drag something away over the ground.
en.fortschreiben:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys continuation: carrying on with what was already under way.

In administrative German, ~fortschreiben~ is updating by continuing to write: a plan or figure is not composed anew but brought up to date.
en.fortschreiten:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~schreiten~:

• ~schreiten~: From MHG ~schrīten~, from OHG ~skrītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīþan~ ("to step, stride"), from Proto-Germanic *~skrīþaną~ ("to walk, glide, crawl"), from PIE *~(s)kreyt-~ ("to stride"), an extension of *~(s)krey-~ ("to go about"). Cognate with Lithuanian ~skrìsti~ ("to rush, run"), Latvian ~skrìet~ ("to run, fly"). Related to ~Schritt~ ("step").
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys onward progress.

~Fortschreiten~ turns the stride of ~schreiten~ into an image of progress; the attested sentence measures "how far" a process has advanced.
en.fortsetzen:
Compound of ~fort-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place"), a causative of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit"), from PIE *~sed-~ ("to sit"). Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~fort~ ("forth, onward"), from Proto-West Germanic *~furþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþ~ ("forth, forward"), from PIE *~per~ ("to cross; across, before"). As a verbal prefix, ~fort-~ conveys continuation or onward motion. Cognate with English ~forth~.

The compound literally means "to set forth" or "to place onward," yielding the modern sense "to continue." The derived noun ~Fortsetzung~ ("continuation, sequel") is familiar to anyone who has seen the words ~Fortsetzung folgt~ ("to be continued") at the end of a serialized story.
en.fortwerfen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

~Fortwerfen~ is a throwing-away: the attested sentence shows the decisive gesture of hurling "everything else" from oneself.
en.fortwähren:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~währen~:

• ~währen~: From MHG ~wëren~, ~wërn~, from OHG ~wërēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~weʀēn~, related to OHG ~wesen~ ("to be, exist"); the deeper connection runs through Proto-Germanic *~wēraz~ ("true"), from PIE *~weh₁ros~, from *~weh₁-~ ("true, trustworthy"); what is true is what stands firm and persists. Cognate with Latin ~vērus~, Irish ~fíor~, Slavic *~vě̀ra~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys continuation: carrying on with what was already under way.

~Fortwähren~ means to endure, to persist without break; the finite verb is now rare, while the participial adjective ~fortwährend~ ("constant") stayed common.
en.fortzahlen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys continuation: carrying on with what was already under way.

~Fortzahlen~ means to keep paying: the payments continue without interruption, as wages do during illness.
en.fortziehen:
A separable compound of ~fort-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~fort-~: From MHG ~vort~, from OHG ~forth~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþa~, from PIE *~per-~ ("forward, across"), the same root that gave ~vor-~. Cognate with English ~forth~, Dutch ~voort~. The particle conveys going away, off from a place.

~Fortziehen~ works both transitively (to pull something away), and intransitively: to move away, to relocate.
en.fotografieren: Derived from the noun ~Fotografie~, which comes ultimately from Ancient Greek ~phos~ (genitive ~photos~, "light") + ~grapho~ ("I write"), literally "light-writing." The verb was formed by adding the German ~-ieren~ suffix (from French ~-er~ via Latin ~-are~) to the stem ~fotograf-~. The word ~Fotografie~ itself may have been influenced by English ~photography~, which was coined around 1839, likely by Sir John Herschel, though the Franco-Brazilian inventor Hercules Florence also used the term independently. German originally spelled the word with ~Ph-~ as ~Photographieren~, faithfully reflecting the Greek ~phi~; the reformed spelling with ~F-~ was officially adopted in 1996 as part of the German orthographic reform. The shift from ~Ph~ to ~F~ remains one of the most visible and sometimes contested changes of that reform. English ~photograph~ and French ~photographier~ are direct cognates, all children of the same Greek compound.
en.fragen: From Middle High German ~vrāgen~, from Old High German ~frāgēn~, ~frahēn~/~frāhēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frāgēn~ (a denominative derived from *~frāgu~, "question"), from Proto-Germanic *~frēgō~ ("question"), from PIE *~preḱ-~ ("to ask"). The PIE root *~preḱ-~ is widespread and productive: it yields Latin ~precor~ ("I pray, beseech"), Sanskrit ~pṛcchāti~ ("asks"), and Persian ~porsīdan~ ("to ask"). The -~h~- spellings in Old High German (~frahēn~) reflect a retention of the Proto-Germanic laryngeal trace; the ~-g-~ forms ultimately prevailed. Cognate with Saterland Frisian ~fräigje~, Dutch ~vragen~, Low German ~fragen~, English ~frain~ (archaic, "to ask, inquire"), Swedish ~fråga~, Icelandic ~fregna~.
en.freigeben:
Compound of ~frei~ + ~geben~:

• ~frei~: From MHG ~vri~, from OHG ~fri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fri~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from Proto-Indo-European *~prey-~ ("to love, to free"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~.
• ~geben~: From MHG ~geben~, from OHG ~geban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~ ("to give"), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (via Norse), Dutch ~geven~.

The compound literally means "to give free" or "to release." Its modern uses range from "to release, to approve" (freeing a product or document for distribution) to "to take time off" (~einen Tag freigeben~). The PIE root *~prey-~ originally meant "to love", in the ancient Germanic world, a "free" person was one among the beloved kin group, as opposed to slaves and outsiders. Freedom was, at its root, belonging.
en.freihaben:
A separable compound of ~frei~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~frei~: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves, and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~. In a resultative compound ~frei-~ names the end state: the action continues until the object is free or clear.

To ~freihaben~ is to have time off: a stretch that belongs to oneself rather than to work.
en.freihalten:
A separable compound of ~frei~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~frei~: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves, and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~. In a resultative compound ~frei-~ names the end state: the action continues until the object is free or clear.

~Freihalten~ is to keep a place or area clear of occupation; figuratively, ~jemandem den Rücken freihalten~ is to keep someone's back clear so they can work undisturbed.
en.freikaufen:
A separable compound of ~frei~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, a denominative verb from *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"), a loanword from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper"). Cognate with English ~cheap~, Dutch ~kopen~, Danish ~købe~, Icelandic ~kaupa~.
• ~frei~: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves, and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~. It can also mean releasing someone or something, setting it at liberty.

To ~freikaufen~ is to buy someone or something loose by payment: money in place of the chain.
en.freilegen:
A separable compound of ~frei~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~frei~: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves, and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~. Hence senses of clearing, exposing, or uncovering something that had been blocked.

To ~freilegen~ is to lay bare what was covered: a wall, a root, a hidden connection.
en.freimachen:
A separable compound of ~frei~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~frei~: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves, and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~. In a resultative compound ~frei-~ names the end state: the action continues until the object is free or clear.

~Freimachen~ ranges from clearing a path, through ~sich freimachen~ (to undress), to the postal sense of franking a letter, putting a stamp on it.
en.freinehmen:
A separable compound of ~frei~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~frei~: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves, and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~. In a resultative compound ~frei-~ names the end state: the action continues until the object is free or clear.

Used reflexively (~sich freinehmen~) it means to take time off work.
en.freischalten:
A separable compound of ~frei~ + ~schalten~:

• ~schalten~: From MHG ~schalten~, from OHG ~scaltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaldan~ ("to push, shove"); the further etymology is debated, Pokorny deriving it from PIE *~(s)kelH-~ ("to split, separate"), which would relate it to English ~shell~. The physical sense of shoving a lever became the modern "to switch, shift gears, manage." Cognate with Old Saxon ~skaldan~.
• ~frei~: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves, and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~. Hence senses of clearing, exposing, or uncovering something that had been blocked.

~Freischalten~ is today chiefly technical: to make a connection, an account, or a feature available.
en.freisetzen:
A separable compound of ~frei~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~frei~: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves, and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~. It can also mean releasing someone or something, setting it at liberty.

~Freisetzen~ spans the physical (releasing energy or gases) and the corporate euphemism for laying workers off.
en.freisprechen:
A separable compound of ~frei~ + ~sprechen~:

• ~sprechen~: From MHG ~sprëchen~, from OHG ~sprëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sprekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sprekaną~, probably from PIE *~spregʰ-~ ("to crackle"). The sense developed from an onomatopoeic root meaning "to crackle, make noise" to "to speak." Cognate with Dutch ~spreken~, English ~speak~.
• ~frei~: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves, and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~. It can also mean releasing someone or something, setting it at liberty.

~Freisprechen~ is the legal acquittal, but it belongs to the trades too: the ~Freisprechung~ releases an apprentice from indenture into journeyman status.
en.freistellen:
A separable compound of ~frei~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~frei~: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves, and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~. It can also mean releasing someone or something, setting it at liberty.

~Freistellen~ unites three senses: to exempt someone from an obligation, to grant an employee leave, and to leave something to one's discretion (~es ist Ihnen freigestellt~).
en.freitesten:
A separable compound of ~frei~ + ~testen~:

• ~testen~: Borrowed from English ~test~ with the German verbal suffix ~-en~, entering German in the twentieth century as a scientific and technical borrowing. English ~test~ comes from Middle English ~test~, ~teste~, from Old French ~test~ ("an earthen vessel in which metals were tried"), from Latin ~testum~ ("earthen pot"), related to Latin ~testa~ ("clay pot, potsherd") and ~terra~ ("earth, land").
• ~frei~: From the adjective ~frei~ ("free"), from MHG ~vrī~, from OHG ~frī~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frī~, from Proto-Germanic *~frijaz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, to be dear"). Cognate with English ~free~, Dutch ~vrij~, Danish ~fri~. The semantic bridge is a household one: the free members of a household were the beloved ones, the kin, as opposed to the slaves, and the same root gives ~Freund~ and English ~friend~. Hence senses of clearing, exposing, or uncovering something that had been blocked.

~Freitesten~ is a recent coinage of the pandemic years: a negative test frees one from a quarantine or restriction.
en.fremdgehen:
A separable compound of ~fremd~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~fremd~: From the adjective ~fremd~ ("foreign, strange, not one's own"), from MHG ~vremde~, from OHG ~fremidi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~framiþī~, from Proto-Germanic *~framaþiz~, a derivative of *~fram~ ("forth, away from"). What is ~fremd~ is literally what is away, and that very adverb is the direct ancestor of English ~from~. Cognate with Dutch ~vreemd~, Swedish ~främmande~, West Frisian ~frjemd~, Gothic ~framaþeis~. The sense of ~fremd~ here is: outside the household, the family, or the couple.

To ~fremdgehen~ is to go outside the relationship: to be unfaithful.
en.fressen: From Middle High German ~vrezzen~, from Old High German ~frezzan~ (also ~firezzan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~fraetan~. This is a compound of the prefix ~fr-~ (an unstressed form of ~ver-~) + ~essen~ ("to eat"). The base verb ~essen~ traces from MHG ~ezzen~, OHG ~ezzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~etan~, from Proto-Germanic *~etaną~, from PIE *~h₁ed-~ ("to eat"). Cognate with Dutch ~vreten~, English ~fret~ (in its archaic sense "to eat away, corrode"), Gothic ~fraitan~, and Swedish ~fräta~ ("to corrode"). The prefix ~ver-~/~fr-~ adds a sense of consuming completely or destructively, giving ~fressen~ the connotation of devouring or eating voraciously. In modern German, ~fressen~ is used exclusively for animals eating (or, pejoratively, for humans eating in a rude or greedy manner), while ~essen~ is reserved for polite human eating. This human/animal distinction is a uniquely German innovation not found in other Germanic languages. English ~fret~, though now meaning "to worry," preserves the original sense of gnawing or eating away; a fretted surface is one that has been corroded, and fretwork in architecture involves cutting or eating into wood.
en.freuen: From Middle High German ~vro(u)wen~, ~vre(u)wen~, from Old High German ~frewen~, ~frouwen~, a denominative derivation of Old High German ~fro~, ~frao~ ("glad"). The underlying adjective ~froh~ descends from MHG ~vro~, OHG ~fro~, from Proto-Germanic *~frawaz~ ("quick, glad"). Cognate with Dutch ~vrolijk~, whence also English ~frolic~.
en.frieren: From MHG ~vriesen~ (beside ~vrieren~), from OHG ~friosan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~freusan~, from Proto-Germanic *~freusaną~, from PIE *~prews-~ ("to freeze, frost"). A class II strong verb (~frieren~, ~fror~, ~gefroren~). The ~r~ is not original: it arose by grammatischer Wechsel in the past forms and was then carried back into the infinitive, exactly as in ~verlieren~; MHG still had ~vriesen~ beside ~vror~. Cognate with English ~freeze~ and ~frost~, Dutch ~vriezen~, Danish ~fryse~, and Latin ~pruīna~ ("hoarfrost").
en.fungieren:
From Latin ~fungor~ ("to perform, discharge, execute") + the German verb-forming suffix ~-ieren~. The Latin ~fungor~ descends from Proto-Italic *~fungor~, from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰewg-~ ("to enjoy, to be of use"), formed with a nasal infix (*~bʰu-ne-g-ti~).

The PIE root *~bʰewg-~ also produced Sanskrit ~bhunakti~ ("he enjoys") and possibly Latin ~fructus~ ("enjoyment, fruit, profit"), though the latter connection is debated. The semantic path from "to enjoy" to "to perform a function" passed through the intermediate sense of "to be occupied with": one first enjoys a role, then simply occupies it. In modern German, ~fungieren~ is a formal word meaning "to serve as, to act as," typically describing an official role or capacity.

German ~funktionieren~ is a sibling cognate: both verbs trace back to the same Latin ~fungor~, but by different routes; ~fungieren~ borrows the verb directly, while ~funktionieren~ starts from the derived noun ~fūnctiō~ (built on the supine stem ~funct-~) and only later becomes a verb again in German. Not strict doublets, but close relatives with complementary senses: ~fungieren~ preserves the Latin verb's human, role-based meaning ("to serve as"), while ~funktionieren~ inherits the abstracted, mechanistic sense of the noun ("to work properly").
en.funktionieren:
Attested ca. 1800, from ~Funktion~ + the verbal suffix ~-ieren~, modeled on French ~fonctionner~. ~Funktion~ is a borrowing from Latin ~fūnctiō~ ("performance, execution"), itself from ~fungor~ ("to perform, execute, discharge"), from Proto-Italic *~fungōr~, from PIE *~bʰewg-~ ("to enjoy, be of use"). The ~-ieren~ suffix is the standard naturalizer for Latin and French loanverbs in German, entering via Old French contact in the 12th–13th century; it always produces weak verbs. This contrasts sharply with earlier Latin borrowings like ~schreiben~ (from Latin ~scrībō~), which arrived during the Roman period and were fully assimilated into the strong-verb system. Cognate with French ~fonctionner~, English ~function~, Dutch ~functioneren~. The deep PIE root *~bʰewg-~ also underlies English ~brook~ ("to tolerate, make use of").

German ~fungieren~ is a sibling cognate: both verbs ultimately descend from the same Latin ~fungor~, but by different paths; ~fungieren~ borrows the verb directly, while ~funktionieren~ takes the detour through the derived noun ~fūnctiō~. They are therefore not strict doublets but close relatives. The meanings split accordingly: ~fungieren~ describes people in roles ("he serves as chairman"), while ~funktionieren~ describes things that work properly ("the machine works").
en.fällen:
From Middle High German ~vellen~, from Old High German ~fellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallijaną~ ("to make fall"), a causative of *~fallaną~ ("to fall"), possibly from PIE *~h₃elh₁-~ ("to fall, to perish"), with a prefix *~h₂epo~ ("off, away"). Cognate with English ~fell~ (as in "to fell a tree"), Dutch ~vellen~.

The causative relationship between ~fallen~ ("to fall") and ~fällen~ ("to cause to fall, to fell") is a textbook example of the Proto-Germanic ~jan~-causative, exactly parallel to ~sitzen~/~setzen~ ("sit"/"set") and ~liegen~/~legen~ ("lie"/"lay"). The umlaut in ~fällen~ (a to ä) is the footprint of this ancient causative suffix, which contained a front vowel that pulled the root vowel forward. In modern German, ~fällen~ means both "to fell" (a tree) and "to render, to pass" (a judgment: ~ein Urteil fällen~). The judicial sense developed from the image of a decisive, downward stroke, just as a tree is brought down with finality, so too is a verdict delivered. The PIE root *~h₃elh₁-~ may connect to Greek ~apollȳmi~ ("to destroy, to kill") and Latin ~aboleō~ ("to destroy"), though this etymology remains debated among specialists.
en.fördern: From Middle High German ~vürdern~, from Old High German ~furdiren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~furþrijan~ ("to move forward, to bring to the front"). A denominative of the archaic comparative adverb ~fürder~ ("further, forward"), itself from Proto-West Germanic *~forþar~, from PIE *~per-~ ("before, in front, first") with a comparative suffix. The modern spelling with ~ö~ (rather than the expected ~ü~) arose through conflation with the related word ~vorder~ (whence modern ~fordern~, "to demand"), probably reinforced by Middle Low German ~vȫrder~ / ~vȫrderen~. The near-homophone pair ~fördern~ ("to promote, support") and ~fordern~ ("to demand") is a persistent pitfall even for native speakers and a nearly untranslatable distinction for learners. Cognate with English ~further~ (both as adverb and as verb "to further a cause"), Dutch ~vorderen~.
en.fügen: From Middle High German ~füegen~, ~fuogen~, from Old High German ~fuogen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōgijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōgijaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to join, to attach, to fasten"). ~Fügen~ means "to join, to fit together" and, reflexively, "to submit, to comply" (~sich fügen~); the person who ~sich fügt~ joins themselves to the arrangement of fate or authority. The noun ~Fügung~ means "decree of fate, providence", events that have been joined together by a higher hand. ~Sich in sein Schicksal fügen~ ("to accept one's fate") is one of the great stoic phrases of the German language. The PIE root *~peh₂ḱ-~ connects ~fügen~ to a surprisingly wide family: Latin ~pāx~ ("peace", literally a state of being joined, fastened together) yields English ~peace~, ~pact~, and ~pacify~; Latin ~pangō~ ("to fasten, to fix") gives ~compact~ and ~page~ (a sheet fastened in a book). The archaic English verb ~fay~ ("to fit closely, to join") is a direct Germanic cognate of ~fügen~, from Old English ~fēgan~, though it survives today only in specialized carpentry usage. Dutch ~voegen~ ("to join, to add") is the living cognate. The distance from PIE "to fasten" to German "to accept one's fate" traces a philosophical journey: what is fastened together by destiny cannot be unfastened by human will.
en.fühlen: From northern Middle High German ~vüelen~ (generally spelled ~vulen~), from Old High German ~fuolen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōlijan~ ("to feel"). The ultimate etymology is uncertain; the root is presumably related to Old Norse ~falma~ ("to grope, feel; to be astonished"), and possibly a secondary causative of a strong verb *~falaną~, from PIE *~pelh₁-~ ("to stroke"). Possible cognates include Latin ~palpō~ ("to stroke, soothe") and Ancient Greek ~psēlaphāō~ ("to feel, grope"). Upper German dialects of Middle High German used ~enphinden~ instead; Modern German ~empfinden~ ("to sense, perceive") has been chiefly confined to higher register as a result, while ~fühlen~ dominates everyday speech. Cognate with Dutch ~voelen~, English ~feel~, Danish ~føle~.
en.führen: From Middle High German ~vüeren~, from Old High German ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). The causative formation ("to make go," hence "to lead") follows a productive Germanic pattern in which a long-vowel derivative of a strong verb creates a new weak verb with transitive meaning. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
en.füllen: ~Füllen~ ("to fill") descends from Middle High German ~vüllen~, Old High German ~fullen~, and Proto-West Germanic *~fullijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullijaną~ ("to make full"). This is the causative formation of *~fullaz~ ("full"), from Proto-Indo-European *~pl̥h₁nós~ ("full"). Cognates include Dutch ~vullen~, Danish ~fylde~, Swedish ~fylla~, and English ~fill~, all from the identical Proto-Germanic causative. English ~fill~ and German ~füllen~ are thus perfect cognates: each is the causative of its native word for "full" (*~full~ / ~voll~), with the characteristic Proto-Germanic causative suffix *~-ijaną~. Latin ~plenus~ ("full") descends from the same PIE root, giving English ~plenty~, ~complete~, and ~replenish~. The simple parallel ("to full" meaning "to make full") survived intact in both West Germanic branches.
en.fürchten:
From Middle High German ~vürhten~, from Old High German ~furihtan~, a denominative verb derived from the noun ~Furcht~ ("fear"). The noun ~Furcht~ descends from MHG ~vorht~, ~vorhte~, from OHG ~forhta~, from Proto-Germanic *~furhtō~ ("fear"), from PIE *~pr̥k-~ ("to fear"). The modern vowel ~-ü-~ reflects mutual influence between the verb (which had umlauted forms) and the noun (which originally had ~-o-~). Cognate with obsolete Dutch ~vrucht~ (still preserved in ~godsvrucht~, "fear of God"), Middle Low German ~vruchte~, and more distantly with English ~fright~, though that word derives from a different nominal stem (Proto-Germanic *~furhtį̄~). The Old English adjective ~forht~ ("afraid") is the closest English relative of ~Furcht~ itself.

The PIE root *~pr̥k-~ connects fear to a physical response. In Luther's Bible, ~fürchten~ famously appears in the phrase ~Fürchte dich nicht~ ("Fear not"), one of the most frequently repeated commands in Scripture. The reflexive construction ~sich fürchten~ ("to be afraid") is the standard colloquial form, while the transitive ~fürchten~ ("to fear something") is somewhat more literary. This split between transitive and reflexive mirrors a common pattern in German emotion verbs: the transitive form treats the emotion as directed outward, while the reflexive form internalizes it.
en.füttern:
From Middle High German ~vuotern~, from Old High German ~fuotiren~, derived from the noun ~fuotar~ ("fodder"), from Proto-Germanic *~fōdrą~ ("fodder"), from Proto-Indo-European *~peh2-~ ("to guard, graze, feed"). Equivalent to ~Futter~ + ~-n~. Cognate with English dialectal ~to fodder~, Dutch ~voeren~ ("to feed").

There is a second, homonymous ~füttern~ meaning "to line (a garment)," also from MHG ~vuotern~, but derived from a different (though probably distantly related) noun OHG ~fuotar~ ("sheath, wrapping, lining"). The PIE root *~peh2-~ ("to feed, to guard") is remarkably productive: it also gave rise to English ~food~, ~feed~, ~foster~, ~pasture~, and Latin ~pābulum~ ("food, fodder") and ~pāstor~ ("shepherd"), the shepherd being, at root, the feeder.
en.garantieren:
From French ~garantir~, from Old French ~guarantir~ ("to protect"), from Old French ~guarant~ (whence modern French ~garant~, "guarantor"), from the present participle of an early Romance verb ~garir~ / ~guarir~, from Frankish *~warjan~ ("to protect, to warrant").

The Frankish root *~warjan~ is also the ancestor of English ~warrant~, ~warranty~, and ~ware~ (as in ~beware~), all carrying the sense of protective vigilance. Old French ~guarantir~ also gave English ~guarantee~ (via Anglo-Norman). So German ~garantieren~ and English ~guarantee~ and ~warrant~ are all cousins, their shared Frankish ancestor having entered both languages via Norman French.
en.geben: From Middle High German ~gëben~, from Old High German ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with Dutch ~geven~, English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
en.gebieten:
From Middle High German ~gebieten~, from Old High German ~gibiotan~. Compound of ~ge-~ + ~bieten~:

• ~bieten~: From MHG ~bieten~, from OHG ~biotan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beudan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beudaną~, from PIE *~bʰewdʰ-~ ("to be awake, aware"). Cognate with English ~bid~ (in the sense "to offer, to command"), Dutch ~bieden~, Swedish ~bjuda~.
• ~ge-~: From OHG ~gi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). In this verb it adds a sense of collective authority or completive force.

Cognate with Old English ~ġebēodan~ and Old Saxon ~gibiodan~. The semantic journey from PIE "to be aware" through Proto-Germanic "to offer, to announce" to modern German "to command" reveals a fascinating power dynamic: awareness became announcement, and announcement became command. English ~bid~ preserves both the "offer" sense ("to bid at auction") and the "command" sense ("to bid someone do something"), having merged two originally separate Old English verbs (~biddan~ "to ask" and ~bēodan~ "to offer"). The related noun ~Gebot~ ("commandment") appears in the Ten Commandments (~die Zehn Gebote~), making this one of the most culturally resonant words in German.
en.gebrauchen:
From Old High German ~gibruhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gabrukan~. Compound of ~ge-~ + ~brauchen~:

• ~brauchen~: From MHG ~bruchen~, from OHG ~bruhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brukan~ ("to use, employ, consume"), from Proto-Germanic *~brukaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰruHg-~ ("to make use of, to enjoy"). Cognate with English ~brook~ (in the archaic sense "to tolerate, to make use of"), Dutch ~gebruiken~.
• ~ge-~: From OHG ~gi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from Proto-Indo-European *~kom~ ("beside, near, by, with"). This prefix here adds a sense of collective completion or thoroughness.

The ~ge-~ prefix intensifies the sense of using something to its full purpose. Dutch ~gebruiken~ is a precise cognate, showing the same prefix pattern. English ~brook~, now archaic outside the phrase "will not brook," once meant "to use, to enjoy", the same meaning that German ~brauchen~ has retained for centuries. The shift in English from "to use" to "to tolerate" represents a narrowing from active enjoyment to mere endurance.
en.gebären: From Middle High German ~gebërn~, from Old High German ~gibëran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gaberan~, from Proto-Germanic *~gaberaną~, a compound of *~ga-~ + *~beraną~ ("to carry, bear"), the latter from PIE *~bʰéreti~, from *~bʰer-~ ("to carry, bear"). The prefix *~ga-~ (the ancestor of modern ~ge-~, from PIE *~ḱóm~, "beside, near, by, with") here marks completion or resultant state. The simplex *~bären~ ("to give birth") is extinct in standard Modern German; ~gebären~ is effectively the only survivor of the family in the birthing sense. English ~bear~ (to give birth) and Latin ~ferō~ ("I carry") are cognates through *~bʰer-~, making ~gebären~, English ~bear~, Latin ~ferō~, and Greek ~pherō~ all distant relatives. One of the oldest and most archaic verbs in the language: its strong ablaut class (class IV) and the now-defunct simplex root attest to enormous age. Cognate with English ~bear~, Dutch ~baren~, Gothic ~bairan~.
en.gedeihen:
An inseparable compound of ~ge-~ + ~deihen~:

• ~deihen~: Not an independent verb of modern German; it survives only inside ~gedeihen~ ("to thrive"). From MHG ~dīhen~, from OHG ~thīhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þīhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þinhaną~ ("to thrive"), from PIE *~tenk-~ ("to become firm, thicken"). Historically a class III strong verb; modern ~gedeihen~ follows class I (~gedeihen~, ~gedieh~, ~gediehen~). Cognate with Old English ~þēon~, Gothic ~gaþeihan~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ marks completion or arrival at a result, the prefix's old perfective force.

The related noun survives in the phrase ~auf Gedeih und Verderb~, literally “for thriving or ruin,” that is, for better or worse, at another's mercy.
en.gedenken:
An inseparable compound of ~ge-~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~teng-~ ("to think, feel"). A mixed-conjugation verb of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~dachte~ pairs the vowel change ~e~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix and ~k~ > ~ch~. Cognate with English ~think~, Dutch ~denken~, Icelandic ~þekkja~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ adds thoroughness to the base action.

~Gedenken~ governs the genitive (~der Toten gedenken~, to commemorate the dead), and means deliberate, honoring remembrance, not mere ~denken~.
en.gefallen:
From Middle High German ~gevallen~, from Old High German ~gifallan~. Compound of ~ge-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~, from PIE *~pōl-~ ("to fall"). A class VII strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~vallen~, English ~fall~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~, from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). Here the prefix marks completion or arrival at a state, the terminative aspect.

The semantic leap is striking: the root means "to fall" and the prefix marks completion or arrival, yet the compound means "to please." The likely bridge is the idiom of falling into favor, something that "falls" pleasingly to one's taste. Medieval German ~gevallen~ already carried this sense of "coming to please, meeting with approval." The dative construction ~mir gefällt~ ("it pleases me," literally "it falls to me") preserves this spatial metaphor of something landing agreeably within one's sphere. Cognate with Dutch ~gevallen~ ("to please, to fall").
en.gefrieren:
An inseparable compound of ~ge-~ + ~frieren~:

• ~frieren~: From MHG ~vriesen~ (beside ~vrieren~), from OHG ~friosan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~freusan~, from Proto-Germanic *~freusaną~, from PIE *~prews-~ ("to freeze, frost"). A class II strong verb (~frieren~, ~fror~, ~gefroren~); the ~r~ arose by grammatischer Wechsel in the past forms and spread to the infinitive, as in ~verlieren~. Cognate with English ~freeze~ and ~frost~, Dutch ~vriezen~, Danish ~fryse~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ conveys collectivity: doing something together or with others.

~Gefrieren~ names the passage of a liquid into the solid state; unlike ~frieren~, which often just means to feel cold, it denotes freezing solid.
en.gefährden:
From late Middle High German ~gevērden~, derived from the noun ~Gefahr~ ("danger"). The noun ~Gefahr~ descends from MHG ~gevāre~, ~gevære~, from OHG ~fāra~, from Proto-Germanic *~fērō~ ("danger, ambush"). The ~ge-~ prefix (from PIE *~ḱóm~, "beside, near, by, with") here serves as a collective intensifier on the noun, and the verb is formed by adding the ~-en~ suffix to the noun. An alternative derivation treats ~gefährden~ as a prefixed form of the now-obsolete verb ~fährden~ with the prefix ~ge-~.

Cognate with English ~fear~ and Dutch ~gevaar~ ("danger"). The connection between German ~Gefahr~ ("danger") and English ~fear~ is a striking example of semantic parallel: both derive from the same Proto-Germanic root *~fērō~, and both revolve around the concept of threat and peril. The Proto-Germanic word originally meant something like "ambush" or "hostile approach," which naturally split into the danger itself (~Gefahr~) and the emotion it provokes (~fear~). Old English ~fǣr~ meant "sudden danger, calamity" before shifting to the emotional response. The verb ~gefährden~ ("to endanger, to jeopardize") is thus etymologically something like "to put into a state of ambush."
en.gegenlesen:
A separable compound of ~gegen-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~gegen-~: The preposition ~gegen~ ("against, toward"), from MHG ~gegen~, from OHG ~gagan~, from Proto-Germanic *~gagin~. Cognate with Old Norse ~gegn~, Dutch ~tegen~, and English ~again~ and ~against~; ~again~ originally meant "back toward, in the opposite direction," and its modern sense "once more" is a later development. As a verbal particle it supplies opposition or facing, as in ~gegenüberstehen~ and ~gegenhalten~. The sense of ~gegen-~ here is: a counter-move answering a prior one.

To ~gegenlesen~ is to read a text over a second time to check it: against the original or against error.
en.gegenwirken:
A separable compound of ~gegen-~ + ~wirken~:

• ~wirken~: From MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~, from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~wérǵom~, from *~werǵ-~ ("to make, work"). Early on it merged with the dialectal ~würken~ (from OHG ~wurken~), which left the written language in the 18th century. Cognate with English ~work~ and ~wrought~, Dutch ~werken~.
• ~gegen-~: The preposition ~gegen~ ("against, toward"), from MHG ~gegen~, from OHG ~gagan~, from Proto-Germanic *~gagin~. Cognate with Old Norse ~gegn~, Dutch ~tegen~, and English ~again~ and ~against~; ~again~ originally meant "back toward, in the opposite direction," and its modern sense "once more" is a later development. As a verbal particle it supplies opposition or facing, as in ~gegenüberstehen~ and ~gegenhalten~. The sense of ~gegen-~ here is opposition: acting against something or someone.

To ~gegenwirken~ is to set a counter-force against an effect; today ~entgegenwirken~ is the more usual word.
en.gegenzeichnen:
A separable compound of ~gegen-~ + ~zeichnen~:

• ~zeichnen~: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, symbol"), from MHG ~zeichen~, from OHG ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~, *~taiknaz~ ("sign"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point"); to ~zeichnen~ is etymologically to make a sign. Cognate with English ~token~, Dutch ~teken~, Danish ~tegn~, Swedish ~tecken~.
• ~gegen-~: The preposition ~gegen~ ("against, toward"), from MHG ~gegen~, from OHG ~gagan~, from Proto-Germanic *~gagin~. Cognate with Old Norse ~gegn~, Dutch ~tegen~, and English ~again~ and ~against~; ~again~ originally meant "back toward, in the opposite direction," and its modern sense "once more" is a later development. As a verbal particle it supplies opposition or facing, as in ~gegenüberstehen~ and ~gegenhalten~. The sense of ~gegen-~ here is: a counter-move answering a prior one.

To ~gegenzeichnen~ is to confirm an existing signature with a second one: the minister countersigns what the president has signed.
en.gegenüberstehen:
A separable compound of ~gegenüber-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~gegenüber-~: Transparently ~gegen~ ("toward, against") + ~über~ ("over"), over against, that is, facing, opposite. ~Gegen~ is from OHG ~gegin~, ~gagan~, from Proto-Germanic *~gagin~; ~über~ is from OHG ~ubar~, from PIE *~upér~, cognate with English ~over~. English once had the exact counterpart ~over against~ ("opposite"), now archaic. As a particle it is positional: ~gegenüberstehen~ is to stand facing, ~gegenüberstellen~ to confront or to juxtapose. The sense of ~gegenüber-~ here is: facing, opposite, positioned across from.

It stands most often in a figurative use: one stands ~gegenüber~ a task, a problem, or an opponent, confronted by it, though not necessarily in enmity.
en.gegenüberstellen:
A separable compound of ~gegenüber-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~gegenüber-~: Transparently ~gegen~ ("toward, against") + ~über~ ("over"), over against, that is, facing, opposite. ~Gegen~ is from OHG ~gegin~, ~gagan~, from Proto-Germanic *~gagin~; ~über~ is from OHG ~ubar~, from PIE *~upér~, cognate with English ~over~. English once had the exact counterpart ~over against~ ("opposite"), now archaic. As a particle it is positional: ~gegenüberstehen~ is to stand facing, ~gegenüberstellen~ to confront or to juxtapose. The sense of ~gegenüber-~ here is: set side by side for comparison.

The noun ~Gegenüberstellung~ lives in two fields: the forensic (a police lineup put before a witness) and the analytical, in which figures or arguments are set side by side for comparison.
en.gehaben:
An inseparable compound of ~ge-~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.

Now archaic and reflexive: ~sich gehaben~ meant “to fare, to conduct oneself,” and survives in the noun ~das Gehaben~ (demeanor) and the farewell ~Gehab dich wohl!~ (“fare thee well”).
en.gehen: From Middle High German ~gan~, ~gen~, from Old High German ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The conjugation ~gen~ instead of ~gan~ is of Bavarian origin. The ~-h-~ was introduced into the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~, in which it had become mute but was retained in spelling. Cognate with Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gaan~, ~gahn~, English ~go~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
en.gehören:
From Middle High German ~gehœren~ ("to listen to, obey"), from Old High German ~gihōrian~ ("to hearken to"), from Proto-West Germanic *~gahauʀijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~gahauzijaną~. Compound of ~ge-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with Dutch ~horen~, English ~hear~, Danish ~høre~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~, from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). This prefix often adds a collective or completive sense.

The semantic shift from "to listen to, obey" to "to belong to" reflects the medieval feudal sense of owing obedience: what one "hearkens to" is what one is subject to, and hence belongs to.
en.gelangen: From Middle High German ~gelangen~, from Old High German ~gilangōn~, synchronically analyzed in Modern German as an ablaut formation from ~gelingen~ ("to succeed"), though the historical relationship is with ~langen~ ("to reach"). ~Langen~ derives from Middle High German ~langen~, from Old High German ~langēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~langōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~langōną~, a denominative of *~langaz~ ("long"), from PIE *~dlongʰos~ ("long"). The prefix ~ge-~ (from PIE *~ḱóm~, "beside, near, by, with") marks completion or arrival: "to reach all the way to a destination." The semantic path is vivid: to "long" (reach, extend) is to span the distance between oneself and an endpoint, and ~gelangen~ captures that arrival. Cognate with Dutch ~geraken~ (parallel compound), English ~long~ (via *~langaz~).
en.geleiten:
From MHG ~geleiten~, from OHG ~gileitan~, ~gileiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~galaidijaną~. Compound of ~ge-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~laidijaną~, a causative of *~līþaną~ ("to pass, to go by"), from PIE *~leyt-~ ("to go, depart, die"). Cognate with Old English ~lǣdan~ (whence English ~lead~), Old Saxon ~lēdian~, Old Norse ~leiða~.
• ~ge-~: From PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). This inseparable prefix adds a sense of collective completion, accompanying thoroughly.

~Geleiten~ means "to escort, to accompany, to conduct", to lead someone with care through or toward something. The ~ge-~ prefix intensifies the companionship aspect: not just leading, but accompanying throughout. The word carries a formal, even ceremonial tone: one ~geleitet~ a dignitary to their seat or the deceased to their grave (~das letzte Geleit~, "the last escort"). The derived noun ~Geleit~ ("escort, safe conduct") was a legal term in medieval Germany, a ~Geleitbrief~ guaranteed safe passage through a lord's territory.
en.gelingen:
From Middle High German ~gelingen~, from Old High German ~gilingan~, a prefixed form of ~lingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lingwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lingwaną~, from PIE *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ ("lightweight; swift"). Compound of ~ge-~ + the archaic simplex ~lingen~:

• ~lingen~: From OHG ~lingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lingwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lingwaną~, from PIE *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ ("lightweight; swift"). The simplex ~lingen~ (meaning "to make progress, proceed, succeed") survived into Middle Low German but is no longer a standalone verb in Modern German.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~, from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). This prefix often adds a collective or completive sense.

The semantic development from "swift, lightweight" to "to proceed, succeed" reflects a conceptual link between ease of movement and successful outcome; what moves swiftly meets no resistance and therefore succeeds. ~Gelingen~ is an impersonal verb in Modern German: one says ~es gelingt mir~ ("it succeeds for me") rather than constructing a personal subject, a grammatical relic of the verb's impersonal origins. Cognate with Middle Low German ~lingen~, Yiddish ~געלינגען~ (~gelingen~).
en.geloben:
An inseparable compound of ~ge-~ + ~loben~:

• ~loben~: From MHG ~loben~, from OHG ~lobēn~/~lobōn~ ("to praise, approve"), from Proto-West Germanic *~lubōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lubō~, from PIE *~lewbʰ-~ ("to love, desire, praise"), the same root as ~lieb~ and ~Liebe~. Cognate with Old English ~lofian~ ("to praise"), Dutch ~loven~, Swedish ~lova~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.

~Geloben~ is the solemn promise; the military ~Gelöbnis~ (oath) and the ~Gelobte Land~ (Promised Land) carry it on; the old closeness to ~loben~ (“to praise”) has faded.
en.gelten: From Middle High German ~gelten~, from Old High German ~geltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~geldaną~, possibly from PIE *~gʰeldʰ-~. The semantic range has narrowed over time: in Old High German, ~geltan~ meant "to pay, repay, be worth," while Modern German ~gelten~ centers on "to be valid, to count, to apply." Cognate with Dutch ~gelden~, English ~yield~ (from the same root, with a semantic shift from "paying" to "giving way"), Icelandic ~gjalda~.
en.genehmigen:
From ~genehm~ ("acceptable, agreeable") + ~-igen~ (verb-forming suffix). The adjective ~genehm~ descends from Middle High German ~genaeme~, ultimately from the root of ~nehmen~ ("to take"):

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nemen~, from OHG ~neman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). Cognate with English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Dutch ~nemen~.

The semantic thread is elegant: something ~genehm~ is literally "takeable" or "acceptable", that which one is willing to take. To ~genehmigen~ is therefore "to make acceptable," hence "to approve, to authorize." The PIE root *~nem-~ had the intriguing double meaning of both giving and taking what is owed, which survives in Greek ~nemein~ ("to distribute, to manage") and ~nomos~ ("law, custom"), the source of English ~economy~, ~nomad~, and ~astronomy~. To approve something is, at its deepest root, to declare it lawfully distributed.
en.generieren: From Latin ~generāre~ ("to beget, to produce, to generate"), with the German ~-ieren~ suffix replacing the Latin infinitive ending. Latin ~generāre~ derives from ~genus~ ("birth, descent, origin, kind"), from PIE *~ǵenh₁-~ ("to beget, to produce, to give birth"). This PIE root is extraordinarily productive across Indo-European languages, yielding Latin ~genus~, ~gens~ ("clan"), and ~gignere~ ("to beget"), Greek ~genesis~ ("origin"), and English ~kin~, ~kind~, ~king~ (literally "son of the clan"), and ~gentle~ (via Old French from Latin ~gentilis~). German borrowed ~generieren~ as a learned term, and it has seen explosive growth in the age of computing: ~generierte Inhalte~ ("generated content") is now commonplace. Related German borrowings from the same Latin root include ~Generation~, ~Generator~, ~generativ~, and ~Genre~ (the last via French). The word ~genieren~ ("to embarrass"), despite its similar appearance, comes from a completely different French source and is a false friend.
en.genesen:
An inseparable compound of ~ge-~ + ~nesen~:

• ~nesen~: ~nesen~ is no longer an independent German verb: it survives only inside ~genesen~ ("to recover") and its noun ~Genesung~. From OHG ~nesan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~nesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~nesaną~ ("to survive, recover"), from PIE *~nes-~ ("to return home safely"). Cognate with Gothic ~ganisan~, Old English ~nesan~; the causative *~nazjaną~ gives ~nähren~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ marks completion or arrival at a result, the prefix's old perfective force.

The old perfective force of ~ge-~ shifted ~nesen~ "to survive" to arriving at health; the verb takes ~sein~ because it names a change of state.
en.genießen:
From Middle High German ~geniezen~, from Old High German ~giniozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ganeutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~neutaną~, from PIE *~newd-~ ("to seize, grasp, use"). Compound of ~ge-~ + the archaic simplex ~nießen~ ("to use, enjoy"):

• ~nießen~: From MHG ~nieȥen~, from OHG ~nioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~neutaną~, from PIE *~newd-~ ("to seize, grasp, use").
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~, from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). This prefix often adds a collective or completive sense.

The simplex ~nießen~ has largely vanished from Modern German, surviving only in derivatives: ~genießen~ ("to enjoy"), ~Nutznießer~ ("beneficiary"), and the legal term ~Nießbrauch~ ("usufruct," literally "use-enjoyment"). The PIE root *~newd-~ is the same one that underlies ~nutzen~, both verbs trace to the same ancient idea of taking what is useful. German thus has two descendants of the same root: the everyday ~nutzen~ ("to use") and the more exalted ~genießen~ ("to enjoy"), the latter having acquired a sense of pleasurable fullness through the completive ~ge-~ prefix. Cognate with Dutch ~genieten~, Yiddish ~genisn~.
en.genügen: From Middle High German ~genüegen~, from Old High German ~ginuogen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ganōgijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ganōgijaną~, from the adjective *~ganōgaz~ ("enough, sufficient"), ultimately from PIE *~h₂eh₂nóḱe~ ("he has reached, he has attained"), the perfective of *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, to attain"). The semantic evolution is elegant: what is "enough" is what has been ~reached~, the point of sufficiency. The collective prefix *~ga-~ (modern ~ge-~) intensifies the sense: not merely reached but ~fully~ reached. The related adjective ~genug~ ("enough") descends from the same Proto-Germanic adjective *~ganōgaz~. English ~enough~ is a direct cognate (from Old English ~genōg~, from the same source), as are Dutch ~genoeg~, Icelandic ~nog~, and Norwegian ~nok~. The verb ~genügen~ is formally a ~-jan-~ causative: it meant "to cause to be enough, to satisfy," though in modern German it is simply intransitive ("to suffice, to be enough"). The related adjective ~genügsam~ ("frugal, easily satisfied") preserves the older sense beautifully: someone who is ~genügsam~ is someone for whom the point of ~enough~ is easily reached. Cognate with Dutch ~genoegen~ ("to satisfy").
en.geradebiegen:
A separable compound of ~gerade~ + ~biegen~:

• ~biegen~: From MHG ~biegen~, from OHG ~biogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beuganą~, from PIE *~bʰewgʰ-~ ("to bend"). A class II strong verb (~biegen~, ~bog~, ~gebogen~). Cognate with English ~bow~ and ~elbow~ ("arm-bend"), Dutch ~buigen~, Sanskrit ~bhujáti~ ("to bend, curve").
• ~gerade~: From the adjective ~gerade~ ("straight"), whose history is genuinely tangled. MHG ~gerat~, ~gerade~ answers to OHG ~gihradi~, pointing to Proto-Germanic *~hradaz~ ("quick"), but a homophonous MHG ~gerat~ ("even", of numbers), built on ~ge-~ plus the stem of ~Rad~ ("wheel"), has clearly influenced it; etymologists differ over how much of the modern word comes from which. Both lines are still visible in the senses "straight" and "even-numbered". In verbs the "straight" sense is the live one: ~geradebiegen~ is to straighten out, ~geradestehen~ to answer for something. The sense of ~gerade~ here is: to put right, to set straight again.

From the literal bending of a bent wire back into line to the figurative sense of salvaging a botched situation; the latter now dominates.
en.geradestehen:
A separable compound of ~gerade~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~gerade~: From the adjective ~gerade~ ("straight"), whose history is genuinely tangled. MHG ~gerat~, ~gerade~ answers to OHG ~gihradi~, pointing to Proto-Germanic *~hradaz~ ("quick"), but a homophonous MHG ~gerat~ ("even", of numbers), built on ~ge-~ plus the stem of ~Rad~ ("wheel"), has clearly influenced it; etymologists differ over how much of the modern word comes from which. Both lines are still visible in the senses "straight" and "even-numbered". In verbs the "straight" sense is the live one: ~geradebiegen~ is to straighten out, ~geradestehen~ to answer for something. The sense of ~gerade~ here is: upright, erect.

The image is upright posture: to ~geradestehen~ for something is to face responsibility for it rather than duck away.
en.geraten:
From Middle High German ~gerāten~, from Old High German ~girātan~ ("to counsel, decide, turn towards, take care of"), from Proto-West Germanic *~garādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~garēdaną~ ("to have a plan for, to take forethought of, to purpose, to intend"), equivalent to ~ge-~ + ~raten~:

• ~raten~: From MHG ~rāten~, from OHG ~rātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rēdaną~ ("to decide, to advise"), from PIE *~Hreh₁dʰ-~ ("to think, arrange").
• ~ge-~: From PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). As a historical inseparable prefix, ~ge-~ originally conveyed collectivity or completion.

~Geraten~ means "to turn out, to succeed; to thrive; to get into (a state)", senses that have drifted far from the root verb ~raten~ ("to advise, to guess"). The semantic path runs from "to counsel, decide" through "to arrange oneself, to find one's way" to "to turn out (well or badly)." The construction ~in etwas geraten~ ("to get into something") (~in Schwierigkeiten geraten~ ("to get into trouble"), ~in Vergessenheit geraten~ ("to fall into oblivion"), ~außer Kontrolle geraten~ ("to get out of control")) is among the most productive in modern German. Cognate with Middle Low German ~gerâden~, Dutch ~geraden~ ("to form an assumption, guess"), and Gothic ~garēdan~ ("to provide for, intend"). English ~read~ is a distant cousin: it descends from the same PIE root *~Hreh₁dʰ-~, having shifted from "to advise, interpret" to "to interpret written symbols", a semantic leap that German ~raten~ never made.
en.geringhalten:
A separable compound of ~gering~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~gering~: From the adjective ~gering~ ("slight, small"), from MHG ~geringe~, from OHG ~giringi~, ~ringi~ ("low, plain, simple, light, easy"), from Proto-Germanic *~ringwaz~ ("small, light, quick"), of uncertain origin, though possibly from PIE *~wrengʷʰ-~ ("to squeeze, wring"). Cognate with Yiddish ~גרינג~ (~gring~, "light, easy"). In verbs it supplies the low end of an evaluative scale: ~geringschätzen~ is to hold in low regard. The sense of ~gering~ here is: slight, small, the low end of a scale.

~Gering~ supplies the measure here: effort, cost, or number is deliberately kept small and low.
en.geringschätzen:
A separable compound of ~gering~ + ~schätzen~:

• ~schätzen~: A denominal verb from ~Schatz~ ("treasure"), from MHG ~schaz~, OHG ~scaz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skatt~ ("cattle, treasure"), an early Germanic word in which cattle served as a measure of wealth. Cognate with Old Norse ~skattr~ (whence Danish ~skat~ and Swedish ~skatt~, both "tax"), Gothic ~skatts~, Old English ~sċeatt~.
• ~gering~: From the adjective ~gering~ ("slight, small"), from MHG ~geringe~, from OHG ~giringi~, ~ringi~ ("low, plain, simple, light, easy"), from Proto-Germanic *~ringwaz~ ("small, light, quick"), of uncertain origin, though possibly from PIE *~wrengʷʰ-~ ("to squeeze, wring"). Cognate with Yiddish ~גרינג~ (~gring~, "light, easy"). In verbs it supplies the low end of an evaluative scale: ~geringschätzen~ is to hold in low regard. The sense of ~gering~ here is: held in low regard, disparaged.

Since ~schätzen~ comes from ~Schatz~ ("treasure") and means "to value," ~geringschätzen~ is literally to rate something as of little worth, hence "to disdain."
en.gerinnen:
An inseparable compound of ~ge-~ + ~rinnen~:

• ~rinnen~: From MHG ~rinnen~, from OHG ~rinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~ ("to run, flow"); the PIE source is debated, most often given as *~h₃reyH-~ ("to churn, set in motion"). A class III strong verb (~rinnen~, ~rann~, ~geronnen~). German ~rennen~ is its causative, from *~rannijaną~. Cognate with English ~run~, Gothic ~rinnan~, Swedish ~rinna~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ conveys collectivity: doing something together or with others.

The collective ~ge-~ gathers the flowing into a running-together: the dispersed particles of a liquid run together and set.
en.gernhaben:
A separable compound of ~gern-~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~gern-~: From the adverb ~gern~ ("gladly, willingly"), MHG ~gerne~, OHG ~gerno~, the adverb to the lost adjective OHG ~gern~ ("eager, desirous"), from Proto-Germanic *~gernaz~, from PIE *~ǵʰer-~ ("to want, desire"). The English cognate is ~yearn~ (Old English ~giernan~), so ~gernhaben~ is at root to have something yearningly. Also cognate with Gothic ~gairns~ and with German ~begehren~ ("to covet"). The sense of ~gern-~ here is: expressing fondness or liking.

Unlike the synonymous ~mögen~, ~gernhaben~ splits apart in the sentence ("ich habe dich gern") and shares the irregular conjugations of ~haben~.
en.geruhen:
An inseparable compound of ~ge-~ + ~ruhen~:

• ~ruhen~: From MHG ~ruo(we)n~, from OHG ~ruowēn~ ("to rest"), derived from the noun ~ruowa~ ("rest, peace, quiet"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rōu~, from Proto-Germanic *~rōwō~, from PIE *~h₁reh₁-~ ("to rest"), a root of remarkably narrow and stable meaning. Cognate with ~Ruhe~, Dutch ~rusten~ (a different formation on the same base), Gothic ~rimis~ ("rest").
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.

The path from "to rest" to "to deign" runs through "finding pleasure in something"; the word survives today only as a formal, faintly ironic courtesy.
en.geschehen:
From Middle High German ~geschehen~, ~geschēn~, ~geschegen~, from Old High German ~giskehan~, ~scehan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skehan~ ("to spring, come up, emerge, happen"). In contrast to most German ~ge-~ verbs, the ~ge-~ in ~geschehen~ is not a separable or inseparable prefix added to an existing simplex; it fused into the root at the Proto-Germanic level, and no simplex *~schehen~ exists or has ever existed in German. The whole word is the root.

The Proto-West Germanic form derives from a root meaning "to spring, shoot, come quickly into being", a vivid physical image for the sudden occurrence of events. The same root appears in Old High German ~scehan~ ("to happen"), which co-existed with the prefixed form before the ~ge-~ variant won out entirely. Cognate with Dutch ~geschieden~ ("to happen, to occur; to divorce", the two senses having diverged from the same root). The related noun ~Geschehnis~ ("occurrence, event") and the participial use of ~das Geschehene~ ("what has happened, the done deed") preserve the verb's core sense of things irrevocably coming to pass.
en.gestalten:
Denominal verb from the noun ~Gestalt~ ("form, shape, figure") with the verbal suffix ~-en~. ~Gestalt~ itself descends from the 14th century as a participial substantive of ~stellen~ (literally "the placed, arranged thing"), from Middle High German ~gestalt~ (past participle used as a noun), from ~ge-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~, from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put").
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~, from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). This prefix often adds a collective or completive sense.

German Wiktionary notes that while ~gestalten~ is structurally a conversion from the noun ~Gestalt~, an archaic simplex ~stalten~ once existed independently before vanishing. The noun ~Gestalt~ achieved global fame through Gestalt psychology (~Gestaltpsychologie~), founded in the early 20th century, which took the word's core sense (a whole that is more than the sum of its arranged parts) as its central insight. The verb ~gestalten~ thus means not merely "to form" but "to actively shape into a coherent whole." Cognate with Dutch ~gestalte~ (noun).
en.gestatten:
From Middle High German ~gestaten~, from Old High German ~gistatōn~, related to ~Statt~ ("place, stead"), from MHG ~stat~, from OHG ~stat~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stadi~, from Proto-Germanic *~stadiz~, from PIE *~stéh₂tis~ ("standing, place"). Cognate with English ~stead~.

~Gestatten~ means "to permit, to allow", a formal, even courtly alternative to ~erlauben~. The semantic path from "place" to "permission" runs through the idea of granting someone a place or a standing: to ~gestatten~ is, etymologically, to give someone a stead, a place where they may act. The prefix ~ge-~ here functions as a perfective marker (as in OHG ~gistatōn~), completing the act of granting. The polite formula ~Gestatten Sie?~ ("May I?" or "Do you permit?") is still common in formal German, spoken when entering a room or introducing oneself. English ~instead~ preserves the same root: "in (the) stead" means "in (the) place (of)."
en.gestehen:
An inseparable compound of ~ge-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.

Behind "to confess" lies the idea of standing by a statement: to ~gestehen~ is to stand behind the truth rather than deny it.
en.gesundbeten:
