A separable compound of ~gesund~ + ~beten~:

• ~beten~: From MHG ~beten~, from OHG ~beton~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bedon~, from Proto-Germanic *~bedan~ ("to pray, to ask"), close to *~bidjan~ ("to ask"), from PIE *~gwhedh-~ ("to ask for, beseech"). The narrowing from "ask" to "pray" is a Christianization phenomenon. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bidden~, Danish ~bede~.
• ~gesund~: From the adjective ~gesund~ ("healthy"), from MHG ~gesunt~, from OHG ~gisunt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gasund~, from Proto-Germanic *~sundaz~ ("healthy, unharmed") with the prefix *~ga-~. Cognate with Dutch ~gezond~ and English ~sound~, the same word with the prefix worn away, Old English ~gesund~, surviving in the fixed phrase ~safe and sound~. In verbs the adjective is resultative: ~gesundschreiben~ is to certify someone fit, ~gesundbeten~ to heal by prayer. The sense of ~gesund~ here is: back to soundness, cured.

Originally to heal by prayer; now usually mocking, for talking a bad situation into looking well.
en.gesundmelden:
A separable compound of ~gesund~ + ~melden~:

• ~melden~: From MHG ~mëlden~, from OHG ~mëldōn~, ~mëldēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~melþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~melþōną~, from PIE *~meldʰ-~ ("to ask, pray, speak"). The original sense was supplicatory speech; ~melden~ keeps only the communicative side: "to report, register." Cognate with Dutch ~melden~, English ~meld~ (partial).
• ~gesund~: From the adjective ~gesund~ ("healthy"), from MHG ~gesunt~, from OHG ~gisunt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gasund~, from Proto-Germanic *~sundaz~ ("healthy, unharmed") with the prefix *~ga-~. Cognate with Dutch ~gezond~ and English ~sound~, the same word with the prefix worn away, Old English ~gesund~, surviving in the fixed phrase ~safe and sound~. In verbs the adjective is resultative: ~gesundschreiben~ is to certify someone fit, ~gesundbeten~ to heal by prayer. The sense of ~gesund~ here is: declared fit or well.

The counterpart of ~sich krankmelden~ ("to call in sick"): one reports back, declared well and fit to work again.
en.getrauen:
An inseparable compound of ~ge-~ + ~trauen~:

• ~trauen~: From MHG ~trūwen~, from OHG ~trūwēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~trūwēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~trūwāną~ ("to trust, believe"), from PIE *~deru-~ ("to be firm, hard, solid"). The same root gave ~treu~ ("faithful"), ~Trost~ ("comfort"), and ~Trauung~ ("wedding ceremony"), as well as English ~trust~, ~true~, and ~tree~. Cognate with Old Norse ~traust~ ("confidence").
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.

~Sich getrauen~ is to trust oneself with something; the base verb's trust becomes the nerve to venture the step.
en.gewarten:
An inseparable compound of ~ge-~ + ~warten~:

• ~warten~: From MHG ~warten~, from OHG ~wartēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wardēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wardāną~ ("to guard, watch over"), from *~warduz~ ("a guard"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, watch, guard"): one who keeps watch also waits. The older sense persists in ~ein Auto warten~ ("to service a car"). Cognate with English ~ward~, Swedish ~vårda~, Dutch ~bewaren~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.

The now-archaic ~gewarten~ governs the genitive ("einer Sache gewarten") and preserves ~warten~ in its older sense of awaiting and attending upon.
en.gewinnen: From Middle High German ~gewinnen~, ~winnen~, from Old High German ~winnan~, ~giwinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~winnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~winnaną~, from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to strive, wish, desire, love"). The PIE root *~wenh₁-~ conveys striving and desire, and its descendants branched widely: Latin ~venus~ ("love, desire") and the goddess ~Venus~ descend from the same root, as does English ~win~. The semantic shift from "to strive, toil" to "to win, gain" reflects how effort became identified with its reward, the same trajectory seen in archaic OHG ~winnan~ ("to struggle, suffer") moving toward Modern German ~gewinnen~ ("to win, to obtain"). The ~ge-~ prefix adds a collective or completive sense. Cognate with Dutch ~winnen~, Low German ~winnen~, Old English ~ġewinnan~ (English ~win~), Norwegian ~vinne~, and Swedish ~vinna~. Also related to English ~Venus~ and Latin ~venus~ via PIE *~wenh₁-~.
en.gewähren:
From Middle High German ~gewern~, from Old High German ~giwerēn~, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *~warjan~ ("to defend, ward off"), from Proto-Germanic *~warjaną~, from an ~o~-grade ablaut of PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, watch, guard"). The ~ge-~ prefix (from PIE *~ḱóm~, "beside, near, by, with") adds a completive or collective sense. Cognate with English ~guarantee~ and ~warrant~, both of which entered English via Old French but trace back to the same Frankish Germanic root.

The semantic evolution from "to defend" to "to grant" is a fascinating case of perspective shift: what was originally an act of protection (warding off threats) came to be understood from the beneficiary's perspective as an act of granting safety or permission. English ~ware~ ("cautious"), ~wary~, ~ward~, and ~guard~ (via French, from Frankish *~wardōn~) all descend from the same PIE root *~wer-~. Even ~garage~ is a distant relative, from French ~garer~ ("to shelter"), from Frankish *~warōn~. The modern German phrase ~Gewähr leisten~ ("to guarantee") preserves the original protective sense, while ~jemandem etwas gewähren~ ("to grant someone something") reflects the completed semantic shift from protection to permission.
en.gewährleisten: A compound of ~Gewähr~ ("guarantee, warranty") + ~leisten~ ("to accomplish, perform"). Not a prefixed verb but a verbal noun compound. ~Gewähr~ derives from Old High German (a related form to ~wahren~, "to safeguard"), ultimately connected to Proto-West Germanic *~warōn~ from Proto-Germanic *~warō~ ("care, attention"), possibly from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, watch, guard"). ~Leisten~ derives from Middle High German ~leisten~, from Old High German ~leisten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laistijan~, originally "to follow a track" (see *~laistaz~, "footprint"), evolving to "to accomplish, fulfill." The compound literally means "to perform a guarantee": to carry out the act of warranting something. The noun ~Gewähr~ shares its root with ~wahr~ ("true") and ~wahren~ ("to safeguard"), a cluster of words about truthfulness, reliability, and protection. Cognate with Dutch ~garanderen~ (parallel meaning via different roots), English ~warranty~ (from a parallel Germanic source through Old French).
en.gewöhnen:
From Middle High German ~gewenen~, a byform of ~gewennen~, from Old High German ~giwennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gawannjan~, a prefixed form of *~wannjan~. The base verb traces to Proto-Germanic *~wanjaną~ ("to accustom"), from *~wanaz~ ("accustomed"), from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to love, to desire, to strive for"). Cognate with English ~wean~ (originally "to accustom," later narrowed to "to accustom a child away from the breast"), Dutch ~wennen~ or ~gewennen~. The prefix ~ge-~ (from PIE *~ḱóm~, "beside, near, by, with") adds a perfective or collective nuance.

The modern spelling with ~ö~ is a historical curiosity: it results from sporadic rounding of MHG /e/ near labial consonants, reinforced by association with related words that had original /o/, such as ~Gewohnheit~ ("habit"), ~gewohnt~ ("accustomed"), and ~gewöhnlich~ ("usual, ordinary"). Speakers reinterpreted ~gewöhnlich~ as a derivative of ~gewöhnen~, but historically it descends independently from MHG ~gewonlich~. The PIE root *~wenh₁-~ ("to love, to desire") connects ~gewöhnen~ to Latin ~Venus~ (goddess of love) and ~venia~ ("favor"), revealing that at the deepest level, becoming accustomed to something was once understood as growing to love it.
en.gießen:
From Middle High German ~giezen~, from Old High German ~giozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geutan~ ("to pour"), from Proto-Germanic *~geutaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰewd-~ ("to pour").

Cognate with Dutch ~gieten~, Old Saxon ~giotan~, Old English ~geotan~, Old Norse ~gjota~ (whence Danish ~gyde~, Swedish ~gjuta~), Gothic ~giutan~. Further Indo-European cognates include Latin ~fundō~ ("to pour, to smelt"), Greek ~cheo~ ("to pour"), and Sanskrit ~juhoti~ ("he sacrifices", by pouring libations). English ~gush~ is a related form.

The sense of "pouring" metals and glass is attested since Old High German times through the participle ~gigozzan~ ("poured, cast"). This makes ~gießen~ one of the oldest technical terms still in daily use: a ~Gießkanne~ ("watering can") and a ~Gießerei~ ("foundry") both preserve the ancient act of controlled pouring. The connection to Latin ~fundō~ (whence English ~found~, as in founding metals, ~foundry~, and ~fusion~) shows that pouring and casting were among the earliest specialized activities to receive their own vocabulary across the Indo-European world.
en.glattstellen:
A separable compound of ~glatt~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~glatt~: From the adjective ~glatt~ ("smooth, slippery"), from MHG ~glat~, from OHG ~glat~ ("shining, bright, clear"), from Proto-West Germanic *~glad~, from Proto-Germanic *~gladaz~, from PIE *~ǵʰlādʰ-~, an extension of *~ǵʰel-~ ("to shine, gleam"). Cognate with Dutch ~glad~, Old Norse ~glaðr~ ("glad, bright"), Latin ~glaber~ ("smooth, hairless"), and English ~glad~, which is the same word: Old English ~glæd~ meant "bright, shining" before it meant "cheerful", while German kept the tactile sense instead. In verbs it is resultative or adverbial: ~glattstreichen~ is to smooth out, ~glattgehen~ to come off without a hitch. The sense of ~glatt~ here is: smooth, even, the resultative state.

A trading term: an open position is made "flat", that is, balanced out and closed.
en.glattziehen:
A separable compound of ~glatt~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~glatt~: From the adjective ~glatt~ ("smooth, slippery"), from MHG ~glat~, from OHG ~glat~ ("shining, bright, clear"), from Proto-West Germanic *~glad~, from Proto-Germanic *~gladaz~, from PIE *~ǵʰlādʰ-~, an extension of *~ǵʰel-~ ("to shine, gleam"). Cognate with Dutch ~glad~, Old Norse ~glaðr~ ("glad, bright"), Latin ~glaber~ ("smooth, hairless"), and English ~glad~, which is the same word: Old English ~glæd~ meant "bright, shining" before it meant "cheerful", while German kept the tactile sense instead. In verbs it is resultative or adverbial: ~glattstreichen~ is to smooth out, ~glattgehen~ to come off without a hitch. The sense of ~glatt~ here is: smooth, even, the resultative state.

Literally pulling fabric or creases smooth; figuratively ironing out the rough spots in a process.
en.glauben:
From Middle High German ~gelouben~, ~gelöuben~, from Old High German ~gilouben~, from Proto-West Germanic *~galaubijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~galaubijaną~, a compound of *~ga-~ + *~laubijaną~. The root *~laubijaną~ derives from *~laubō~ ("permission, leave"), from PIE *~lewbʰ-~ ("to like, desire, love"). The semantic trajectory runs from "to hold dear, to love" through "to grant leave, to permit" to "to believe, trust", a striking path from affection to credence. The Upper German form with ~-au-~ (rather than the Central German umlauted variant) was reinforced by the related noun ~Glaube~ ("belief, faith"), while the umlaut survives in derived forms like ~gläubig~ ("devout, credulous") and ~abergläubisch~ ("superstitious"). The connection to love is preserved cross-linguistically: English ~believe~ descends from the same PIE root, and English ~love~ is a direct cognate of the *~lewbʰ-~ family. Cognate with Bavarian ~glaubn~, Dutch ~geloven~, Low German ~glöven~, Gothic ~galaubjan~, and English ~believe~.

The pairing of ~glauben~ and ~believe~ conceals a puzzle: both words share the same Proto-Germanic root *~laubijaną~, yet they wear different prefixes. German chose *~ga-~ (which became ~ge-~, then eroded to the ~g-~ in ~glauben~), while English chose *~bi-~ (which became ~be-~). Both prefixes were available in both languages, Old English had ~gelīefan~ (with ~ge-~) alongside ~belȳfan~ (with ~be-~), and it was ~belȳfan~ that won out. Old High German settled on ~gilouben~ (with ~gi-~, later ~ge-~), and that form prevailed, the prefix gradually wearing down: ~gilouben~ → ~gelouben~ → ~glouben~ → ~glauben~. The two prefixes were not even doing very different work: in early Germanic, both *~bi-~ and *~ga-~ could serve as perfective or intensifying markers on verbs, nudging the meaning from "to hold dear" toward the completed state of "to have come to trust." It is one of those cases where two sister dialects made an arbitrary lexical choice and then each committed to it for a millennium. The result is that German learners of English, and English learners of German, routinely fail to recognize ~glauben~ and ~believe~ as cognates, when in fact they are the same word dressed in different prefixes. Dutch ~geloven~ sided with German (keeping ~ge-~), Gothic ~galaubjan~ likewise, while the Scandinavian languages abandoned both forms in favor of unrelated words (~tro~ in Swedish, Danish, and Norwegian, from Old Norse ~trúa~, cognate with English ~true~ and ~trust~). So the modern Germanic languages offer three different solutions to the same semantic need: German and Dutch built "believe" from "love" with ~ge-~, English built it from "love" with ~be-~, and Scandinavian started over entirely with "trust." The erosion of *~ga-~ to ~g-~ in ~glauben~ is not an isolated accident; the same prefix met the same fate across the Germanic family, and English took the process one step further. English ~enough~ and German ~genug~ are cognates from Proto-Germanic *~ganōgaz~ (*~ga-~ + *~nōgaz~, from *~nahaną~, "to suffice"). In Old English the word was still ~genōg~, transparently prefixed; by Middle English it had weakened to ~inough~ and ~ynough~; modern ~enough~ retains only a silent-looking ~e-~ as the last ghost of the prefix. So where German wore *~ga-~ down to ~g-~ (~glauben~, ~genug~), English wore it all the way to nothing, or nearly nothing. (A tempting parallel is ~yesterday~/~gestern~, but that is a false friend: the ~ge-~ in ~gestern~ is not the prefix at all but part of the root, from PIE *~ǵʰdyes-~ + the comparative suffix *~-tero-~, cognate with Latin ~herī~ and Greek ~khthés~.)
en.gleichbehandeln:
A separable compound of ~gleich~ + ~be-~ + ~handeln~:

• ~handeln~: From MHG ~handeln~, from OHG ~hantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handulōn~, a denominative verb from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~ ("hand") with the frequentative suffix *~-lōną~; the sense broadened from "to handle" to "to act, deal, trade." Cognate with English ~handle~, Dutch ~handelen~, Danish ~handle~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~gleich~: From MHG ~gelīch~, from OHG ~gilīh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~galīk~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkaz~, literally "having the same body or form": the collective prefix *~ga-~ plus the noun *~līką~ ("body, shape"). Cognate with English ~like~ and ~alike~, Dutch ~gelijk~, Old Norse ~líkr~; the English adverb suffix ~-ly~ is the same element worn down. That buried noun *~līką~ still stands on its own as German ~Leiche~ ("corpse") and in English ~lychgate~, the churchyard gate where the body was set down. The adjective means "equal, alike, the same"; the compound verb makes one thing equal to another (~gleichsetzen~, ~gleichstellen~).

The three layers build on one another: ~handeln~ "to act," with ~be-~ to the transitive ~behandeln~ "to treat someone," and with ~gleich~ to the demand of treating everyone the same way.
en.gleichen:
From MHG ~gelīchen~, from OHG ~gilīhhon~, ~gilihhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkōną~ ("to make alike, to resemble"), derived from *~galīkaz~ ("alike, similar"), a compound of *~ga-~ (collective prefix) + *~līkam~ ("body, form"), from PIE *~leyg-~ ("image, likeness, similarity"). Cognate with Dutch ~gelijken~, English ~like~ (both the adjective and the verb), Old English ~gelīcian~ ("to please") and ~gelīc~ ("alike"), Old Norse ~glíkr~, Danish ~ligne~.

~Gleichen~ means "to resemble, to be equal to" and is a strong verb (glich, geglichen), one of the few strong verbs derived from a denominal/deadjectival base. The adjective ~gleich~ ("equal, same, alike") lost its prefix ~ge-~ through phonetic erosion in Early New High German, but the verb preserved it as the initial ~gl-~. The underlying metaphor is illuminating: PIE *~leyg-~ meant "body, form", to be alike was originally to share the same bodily form. This root produced English ~like~, ~alike~, ~likeness~, ~lich~ (a corpse, literally "a body"), the suffix ~-ly~ (originally "having the body/form of"), and ~ilk~ ("same kind"). The word ~like~ in English descends from the same Proto-Germanic *~galīkaz~, meaning that ~gleichen~ and ~like~ are doublets, siblings that traveled different phonetic paths from the same ancestor.
en.gleichkommen:
A separable compound of ~gleich~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~gleich~: From MHG ~gelīch~, from OHG ~gilīh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~galīk~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkaz~, literally "having the same body or form": the collective prefix *~ga-~ plus the noun *~līką~ ("body, shape"). Cognate with English ~like~ and ~alike~, Dutch ~gelijk~, Old Norse ~líkr~; the English adverb suffix ~-ly~ is the same element worn down. That buried noun *~līką~ still stands on its own as German ~Leiche~ ("corpse") and in English ~lychgate~, the churchyard gate where the body was set down. Of matching or measuring up to something (~gleichkommen~).

Built with the dative: something ~kommt~ another thing ~gleich~ when it matches it exactly in worth or effect.
en.gleichmachen:
A separable compound of ~gleich~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~gleich~: From MHG ~gelīch~, from OHG ~gilīh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~galīk~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkaz~, literally "having the same body or form": the collective prefix *~ga-~ plus the noun *~līką~ ("body, shape"). Cognate with English ~like~ and ~alike~, Dutch ~gelijk~, Old Norse ~líkr~; the English adverb suffix ~-ly~ is the same element worn down. That buried noun *~līką~ still stands on its own as German ~Leiche~ ("corpse") and in English ~lychgate~, the churchyard gate where the body was set down. Also "level, even," of surfaces and of accounts brought into balance (~ausgleichen~, ~gleichmachen~).

~Gleichmachen~ aims at leveling differences: reaching as far as the familiar "dem Erdboden gleichmachen," to raze to the ground.
en.gleichschalten:
A separable compound of ~gleich~ + ~schalten~:

• ~schalten~: From MHG ~schalten~, from OHG ~scaltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaldan~ ("to push, shove"); the further etymology is debated, Pokorny deriving it from PIE *~(s)kelH-~ ("to split, separate"), which would relate it to English ~shell~. The physical sense of shoving a lever became the modern "to switch, shift gears, manage." Cognate with Old Saxon ~skaldan~.
• ~gleich~: From MHG ~gelīch~, from OHG ~gilīh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~galīk~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkaz~, literally "having the same body or form": the collective prefix *~ga-~ plus the noun *~līką~ ("body, shape"). Cognate with English ~like~ and ~alike~, Dutch ~gelijk~, Old Norse ~líkr~; the English adverb suffix ~-ly~ is the same element worn down. That buried noun *~līką~ still stands on its own as German ~Leiche~ ("corpse") and in English ~lychgate~, the churchyard gate where the body was set down. Also "level, even," of surfaces and of accounts brought into balance (~ausgleichen~, ~gleichmachen~).

Borrowed from electrical engineering (bringing several devices to the same switch setting), the word became, in 1933, the byword ~Gleichschaltung~ for the forced alignment of every institution to the Nazi line.
en.gleichsehen:
A separable compound of ~gleich~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~gleich~: From MHG ~gelīch~, from OHG ~gilīh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~galīk~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkaz~, literally "having the same body or form": the collective prefix *~ga-~ plus the noun *~līką~ ("body, shape"). Cognate with English ~like~ and ~alike~, Dutch ~gelijk~, Old Norse ~líkr~; the English adverb suffix ~-ly~ is the same element worn down. That buried noun *~līką~ still stands on its own as German ~Leiche~ ("corpse") and in English ~lychgate~, the churchyard gate where the body was set down. Of matching or measuring up to something (~gleichkommen~).

With the dative, "jemandem gleichsehen" means to resemble; the idiom "das sieht dir gleich" shifts it ironically to "that's just like you."
en.gleichsetzen:
A separable compound of ~gleich~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~gleich~: From MHG ~gelīch~, from OHG ~gilīh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~galīk~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkaz~, literally "having the same body or form": the collective prefix *~ga-~ plus the noun *~līką~ ("body, shape"). Cognate with English ~like~ and ~alike~, Dutch ~gelijk~, Old Norse ~líkr~; the English adverb suffix ~-ly~ is the same element worn down. That buried noun *~līką~ still stands on its own as German ~Leiche~ ("corpse") and in English ~lychgate~, the churchyard gate where the body was set down. The adjective means "equal, alike, the same"; the compound verb makes one thing equal to another (~gleichsetzen~, ~gleichstellen~).

~Gleichsetzen~ asserts the full equality of two things, often critically, when two unlike things are improperly put on one level.
en.gleichstellen:
A separable compound of ~gleich~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~gleich~: From MHG ~gelīch~, from OHG ~gilīh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~galīk~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkaz~, literally "having the same body or form": the collective prefix *~ga-~ plus the noun *~līką~ ("body, shape"). Cognate with English ~like~ and ~alike~, Dutch ~gelijk~, Old Norse ~líkr~; the English adverb suffix ~-ly~ is the same element worn down. That buried noun *~līką~ still stands on its own as German ~Leiche~ ("corpse") and in English ~lychgate~, the churchyard gate where the body was set down. The adjective means "equal, alike, the same"; the compound verb makes one thing equal to another (~gleichsetzen~, ~gleichstellen~).

Unlike the conceptual ~gleichsetzen~, ~gleichstellen~ means equality in law: granting two groups the same standing.
en.gleichziehen:
A separable compound of ~gleich~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~gleich~: From MHG ~gelīch~, from OHG ~gilīh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~galīk~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkaz~, literally "having the same body or form": the collective prefix *~ga-~ plus the noun *~līką~ ("body, shape"). Cognate with English ~like~ and ~alike~, Dutch ~gelijk~, Old Norse ~líkr~; the English adverb suffix ~-ly~ is the same element worn down. That buried noun *~līką~ still stands on its own as German ~Leiche~ ("corpse") and in English ~lychgate~, the churchyard gate where the body was set down. Of matching or measuring up to something (~gleichkommen~).

From competition: to ~gleichziehen~ is to close a lead and end up level.
en.gleiten: From MHG ~glīten~, from OHG ~glītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~glīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~glīdaną~, from PIE *~ǵʰleydʰ-~ ("to glide, slide"). A class I strong verb (~gleiten~, ~glitt~, ~geglitten~), though a weak ~gleitete~ turns up in technical prose. Cognate with English ~glide~, Dutch ~glijden~, Low German ~glieden~, Swedish ~glida~.
en.glimmen: From MHG ~glimmen~ ("to glow, gleam"), from Proto-Germanic *~glimmaną~, from PIE *~ǵʰley-~ ("to shine, shimmer"). Modern German inflects it both ways: the strong ~glomm~, ~geglommen~ has held on in written and elevated register, while weak ~glimmte~, ~geglimmt~ has dominated ordinary usage since the eighteenth century. Cognate with English ~gleam~, ~glimmer~, and ~glimpse~, Dutch ~glimmen~, Norwegian ~glime~. Its root belongs to the unusually large and unusually consistent Germanic ~gl-~ family of light words (~Glanz~, ~glühen~, ~Glas~, English ~glow~ and ~glitter~), all extensions of PIE *~ǵʰel-~.
en.glänzen:
From Middle High German ~glenzen~, from Old High German ~glanzen~, from Proto-Germanic *~glantaz~ ("shining, bright"), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰlond-o-~, from the root *~gʰlend-~ ("to shine, to gleam").

This verb belongs to a rich cluster of Germanic "gl-" words denoting light and vision: ~gleißen~ ("to glitter"), ~glimmen~ ("to glow"), ~glitzern~ ("to sparkle"), ~Glut~ ("embers"), and ~Glas~ ("glass," originally meaning "amber" or "something shiny"). English preserves the same pattern in ~gleam~, ~glitter~, ~glow~, ~gloss~, ~glint~, and ~glisten~. This "gl-" phonestheme (where an initial consonant cluster carries consistent semantic associations without being a true morpheme) is one of the most striking sound-meaning patterns in the Germanic languages.
en.graben: From MHG ~graben~, from OHG ~graban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from PIE *~gʰrebʰ-~ ("to dig, scratch, bury"). A class VI strong verb (~graben~, ~grub~, ~gegraben~). Cognate with Gothic ~graban~, Dutch ~graven~, Old Norse ~grafa~, and English ~grave~ as a verb ("to dig, to engrave"), which has otherwise died out and survives only in ~engrave~ and the phrase ~graven image~. Where English kept just the noun, German kept the whole family alive (~Grab~, ~Graben~, ~Grube~), and Polish ~grzebać~ ("to bury") shows the root reaching well beyond Germanic.
en.gratulieren:
Borrowed from Latin ~grātulārī~ ("to wish joy, to congratulate"), from ~grātus~ ("pleasing, thankful"), from PIE *~gʷerH-~ ("to praise, to welcome"). Cognate with Latin ~grātia~ ("grace, favor"), whence English ~grace~, ~grateful~, ~gratitude~, and ~congratulate~.

~Gratulieren~ is used with the dative case: ~jemandem gratulieren~ ("to congratulate someone"), most commonly ~zum Geburtstag gratulieren~ ("to wish a happy birthday"). The PIE root *~gʷerH-~ ("to praise") is the source of an enormous family of "positivity" words: Latin ~grātia~ produced English ~grace~, ~gracious~, ~grateful~, ~gratis~ (originally "out of kindness"), and ~ingrate~; the same root likely produced Sanskrit ~gūrtí-~ ("praise, welcome").
en.greifen:
From Middle High German ~grîfen~, from Old High German ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~grijpen~, Low German ~griepen~, English ~gripe~, and Old Norse ~gripa~.

The PIE root *~gʰreyb-~ is attested in Baltic cognates as well: Lithuanian ~griẽbti~ ("to seize") and ~graibýti~ share the same ancestry, as does Latvian ~gribêt~ ("to wish, desire"), a striking semantic divergence in which the Baltic branch preserved a sense of striving or wanting from what was originally a physical act of grasping. German has developed ~greifen~ into a rich family of compounds: ~begreifen~ ("to comprehend," literally "to grasp around"), ~eingreifen~ ("to intervene," literally "to grasp in"), ~angreifen~ ("to attack, to corrode"), and ~ergreifen~ ("to seize, to move emotionally"). The idea that understanding is a form of grasping (~begreifen~) is one of the most striking conceptual metaphors in the language, and it is ancient. The ablaut series ~greift~/~griff~/~gegriffen~ follows the class I pattern, the same as ~reiten~ and ~schneiden~.
en.großschreiben:
A separable compound of ~groß~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~groß~: From MHG ~grōȥ~, from OHG ~grōȥ~ ("big, thick, coarse"), from Proto-Germanic *~grautaz~, from PIE *~gʰrewd-~ ("to grind, crush"), from *~gʰer-~ ("to rub, grind"). Cognate with Old Saxon ~grōt~, Dutch ~groot~, English ~great~. The root's older sense of coarse grinding survives in English ~groats~ and ~grits~ and in German ~Grütze~: what is "great" was first what was coarse-grained. The sense of ~groß~ here is: literally "large", as of writing a letter as a capital.

In modern use ~großschreiben~ carries a figurative sense alongside the literal one: to write a letter as a capital, but also to prize something highly, as in ~Pünktlichkeit wird hier großgeschrieben~ ("punctuality counts for a great deal here").
en.großziehen:
A separable compound of ~groß~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~groß~: From MHG ~grōȥ~, from OHG ~grōȥ~ ("big, thick, coarse"), from Proto-Germanic *~grautaz~, from PIE *~gʰrewd-~ ("to grind, crush"), from *~gʰer-~ ("to rub, grind"). Cognate with Old Saxon ~grōt~, Dutch ~groot~, English ~great~. The root's older sense of coarse grinding survives in English ~groats~ and ~grits~ and in German ~Grütze~: what is "great" was first what was coarse-grained. The sense of ~groß~ here is: as a resultative adjective, "to full size", of rearing a child or animal.

~Großziehen~ names the whole arc of rearing (bringing a child or young animal all the way to full size), and stands close to everyday ~aufziehen~ as a near-synonym.
en.gründen:
Inherited from Middle High German ~gründen~, from Old High German ~grunten~ ("to fathom, to investigate"). A denominative verb formed from ~Grund~ ("ground, bottom, foundation") with derivational umlaut (u → ü):

~Grund~ traces to OHG ~grunt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grundu~, from Proto-Germanic *~grunduz~, from PIE *~gʰr̥mtu-~. Cognate with West Frisian ~grûn~, Dutch ~grond~, and English ~ground~.

The OHG verb ~grunten~ meant "to fathom", to sound the depth of water, to investigate the bottom of a matter. This sense still echoes in ~ergründen~ ("to fathom, to get to the bottom of something"). ~Gründen~, by contrast, shifted from probing the ground to creating it: "to found, to establish", to put something on a secure foundation. The same metaphor appears in English ~ground~ (as in "to ground one's argument"). The umlaut (~Grund~ → ~gründen~) is a hallmark of denominative weak verbs in German: it signals that the verb was derived from the noun rather than inherited directly. The noun ~Grund~ itself remains semantically rich: it serves simultaneously as "ground" (the earth underfoot), "bottom" (the floor of a lake), "reason" (the ground of an argument), and "foundation" (the basis of a building), all the more remarkable because these senses converge in a single word that goes back to a PIE root simply meaning "earth, soil." Cognate with Dutch ~gronden~.
en.grüßen:
From Middle High German ~grüezen~, from Old High German ~gruozzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grōtijan~. The noun ~Gruß~ ("greeting") is a deverbal form from Middle High German ~gruoȥ~. Cognate with Dutch ~groeten~, West Frisian ~groetsje~, and English ~greet~ (from the same Proto-West Germanic root, without any prefix).

The semantic range of ~grüßen~ is narrower than its English cognate ~greet~: where English ~greet~ can mean both "to welcome" and "to react with emotion" (as in "the news was greeted with dismay"), German ~grüßen~ remains anchored in the act of salutation, a wave, a nod, a spoken hello. The compound ~begrüßen~ adds the ~be-~ prefix to make the greeting act outwardly directed and transitive: one ~grüßt~ in general, but one ~begrüßt~ a specific person or proposal. The Proto-West Germanic root *~grōtijan~ likely carried the original sense of physical approach or hailing, a greeting as an act of reaching toward someone.
en.gucken:
From Middle High German ~gücken~, ~guggen~ ("to look inquisitively, to peek, to peer"), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a specialized use of MHG ~gücken~, ~gucken~ ("to cuckoo, to call or cry like a cuckoo"), from Old High German ~guckōn~, ~gukkōn~ ("to cuckoo"), the semantic link being the cuckoo's habit of poking its head out from cover, or the notion of peeping out curiously. The common pronunciation with initial ~k-~ (also spelled ~kucken~) is often attributed to influence from Low German ~kieken~ (from Middle Low German ~kīken~), though this pronunciation extends surprisingly far southward (compare Luxembourgish ~kucken~ and Dutch ~kijken~).

~Gucken~ is the everyday, colloquial word for "to look" in northern and central Germany, while southern German and Austrian varieties prefer ~schauen~. It rarely appears in formal writing, where ~sehen~, ~blicken~, or ~schauen~ take its place. Despite its informal register, ~gucken~ is enormously productive: ~angucken~ ("to look at"), ~zugucken~ ("to watch"), ~weggucken~ ("to look away"), ~durchgucken~ ("to look through"), ~Guckloch~ ("peephole"). The compound ~Kuckuck~ ("cuckoo") (if the etymological connection holds) would make ~gucken~ one of the few verbs potentially derived from a bird's call. The spelling debate between ~gucken~ (standard) and ~kucken~ (reflecting actual pronunciation) has generated more heat among German orthography enthusiasts than one might expect for a monosyllabic verb.
en.gutheißen:
A separable compound of ~gut~ + ~heißen~:

• ~heißen~: From MHG ~heiȥen~, from OHG ~heiȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haitan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haitaną~, tentatively from PIE *~ḱeyd-~ ("to call"). The original sense was "to command"; "to be called" developed from the passive use. Cognate with Dutch ~heten~, Gothic ~haitan~, English ~behest~ and archaic ~hight~.
• ~gut~: The adjective ~gut~ ("good"), from MHG ~guot~, from OHG ~guot~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gōd~, from Proto-Germanic *~gōdaz~, cognate with English ~good~ and Dutch ~goed~. In these compounds it is resultative or evaluative: ~gutmachen~ is to make something good again, ~gutheißen~ to judge it good, ~gutschreiben~ to enter it on the favorable side of an account. The sense of ~gut~ here is evaluative: judges or declares something good.

~Gutheißen~ takes a plain accusative object and is the standard verb for formally endorsing something; its opposite is ~missbilligen~.
en.gutmachen:
A separable compound of ~gut~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~gut~: The adjective ~gut~ ("good"), from MHG ~guot~, from OHG ~guot~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gōd~, from Proto-Germanic *~gōdaz~, cognate with English ~good~ and Dutch ~goed~. In these compounds it is resultative or evaluative: ~gutmachen~ is to make something good again, ~gutheißen~ to judge it good, ~gutschreiben~ to enter it on the favorable side of an account. The sense of ~gut~ here is resultative: brings the object into a good state, makes amends.

The strengthened form ~wiedergutmachen~ is now the more common one, and its noun ~Wiedergutmachung~ became the postwar word for reparations, making good a wrong on a national scale.
en.gutschreiben:
A separable compound of ~gut~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~gut~: The adjective ~gut~ ("good"), from MHG ~guot~, from OHG ~guot~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gōd~, from Proto-Germanic *~gōdaz~, cognate with English ~good~ and Dutch ~goed~. In these compounds it is resultative or evaluative: ~gutmachen~ is to make something good again, ~gutheißen~ to judge it good, ~gutschreiben~ to enter it on the favorable side of an account. The sense of ~gut~ here is: in commercial use, credits to the favorable side of an account.

Its noun ~Gutschrift~ is the credit entry itself, and the mirror-image operation on the other side of the ledger is ~belasten~, to debit.
en.gären: From MHG ~jesen~, from OHG ~jesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~jesaną~, from PIE *~yes-~ ("to boil, foam, ferment"). Two changes produced the modern shape: the initial ~j-~ hardened to ~g-~ before front vowels from Middle High German on, and the ~r~ was carried in from the past forms ~gor~, ~gegoren~ (as in ~verlieren~), reinforced by association with the unrelated adjective ~gar~ ("done, fully cooked"). Historically a class V strong verb; the modern ~gor~/~gegoren~ vocalism is analogical, and today the strong forms are usual for literal fermenting while the weak ~gärte~, ~gegärt~ is preferred figuratively (~es gärte im Volk~). Cognate with English ~yeast~, German ~Gischt~ ("spray, foam"), and Ancient Greek ~ζέω~ (zéō, "to boil").
en.gönnen:
From MHG ~gunnen~, from OHG ~giunnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gaunnan~ ("to grant"), from the prefix *~ga-~ + *~unnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~unnaną~ ("to grant"), from PIE *~h₃neh₂-~ ("to enjoy"). Cognate with Dutch ~gunnen~, Yiddish ~ginen~. The PIE root also appears in Greek ~oninēmi~ ("to be of use, to help") and ~aponēto~ ("to have joy of something").

~Gönnen~ is one of those German words that English simply cannot translate with a single term. It means "to not begrudge someone something": to be genuinely happy that another person has or enjoys something. ~Ich gönne dir den Erfolg~ means "I'm happy for your success" with no trace of envy. The negation ~missgönnen~ ("to begrudge, to envy") and the noun ~Missgunst~ ("envy, resentment") expose the default expectation: ~Gunst~ ("favor, goodwill") is the positive baseline. The reflexive ~sich etwas gönnen~ means "to treat oneself, to allow oneself a pleasure", again, granting oneself permission to enjoy. The PIE root *~h₃neh₂-~ ("to enjoy") has been remarkably faithful to its original meaning across five millennia, even as the social dimension (the emphasis on non-envious generosity) is a distinctly Germanic innovation.
en.haben:
From Middle High German ~haben~, from Old High German ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Cognate with Dutch ~hebben~, English ~have~, Danish ~have~, Old Norse ~hafa~, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (~haban~).

~Haben~ and Latin ~habēō~ ("to have") are one of the most celebrated false-cognate pairs in Indo-European linguistics. Despite near-identical spelling, identical meaning, and centuries of scholarly confusion, the two words descend from entirely different PIE roots: ~haben~ from *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize") and ~habēō~ from *~gʰeh₁bʰ-~ ("to grab, take"). The resemblance is pure coincidence: the kind of accident that makes historical linguistics treacherous. ~Haben~'s actual Latin cousin is ~capiō~ ("I take, I seize"), the ancestor of English ~captive~, ~capture~, ~capable~, ~captain~, and ~accept~ (from ~ad-~ + ~capiō~). German ~akzeptieren~ thus descends from the same PIE root as ~haben~, via Latin rather than Germanic inheritance. The same root also gives German ~heben~ ("to lift"): to have and to heave are, at bottom, the same word: to grasp something is both to possess it and to lift it.

Perhaps the deepest irony is that Germanic and Romance languages independently chose their respective "have" verbs (etymologically unrelated), to build compound past tenses: German ~ich habe gesungen~ and French ~j'ai chanté~ are structurally identical constructions ("I have sung"), yet ~haben~ and ~avoir~ (from ~habēō~) share no common ancestor. This parallel development is a hallmark of the Western European ~Sprachbund~, a linguistic area in which neighboring but unrelated languages converge on shared grammatical structures through centuries of contact. The ~Sprachbund~ also produced the definite article, the relative clause with a relative pronoun, and the distinction between ~sein~ and ~haben~ as perfect auxiliaries (compare French ~je suis allé~ / ~j'ai mangé~ with German ~ich bin gegangen~ / ~ich habe gegessen~), all features that feel natural to European speakers but are typologically unusual worldwide. That two unrelated "have" verbs independently became the scaffolding for compound tenses across the Roman ~limes~ is a reminder that grammar can be borrowed just as readily as vocabulary.
en.haften:
From ~Haft~ + ~-en~. ~Haft~ descends from MHG ~haft~, ~hafte~ ("captivity"), from OHG ~haft~, ~hafta~, immediately cognate with Middle Dutch ~hachte~, Middle Low German ~hafte~, Old English ~hæft~ ("captive"), and further with Latin ~captus~ ("seized") and Old Irish ~cacht~ ("captive"). The Latin and Germanic forms both derive from PIE *~kh₂p-tó-~ (from *~keh₂p-~ "to seize, grasp"), making ~haften~ and English ~captive~ cognates from the same root.

~Haften~ means "to stick, adhere, cling" and "to be liable, to be responsible", two senses united by the "captivity" root. The "adhesion" sense developed from the idea of being held fast, clinging to a surface. The legal meaning is especially productive: ~haftbar~ ("liable"), ~Haftpflicht~ ("liability"), ~Haftpflichtversicherung~ ("liability insurance"), and ~Haft~ itself now primarily means "custody, imprisonment." That Latin ~captus~ and Germanic ~haft~ are cognates is beautifully confirmed by the same semantic range: both moved from "seized" to "held" to "bound."
en.halten: From Middle High German ~halten~, from Old High German ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with Bavarian ~hoidn~, Low German ~holden~, Dutch ~houden~, English ~hold~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
en.haltmachen:
A separable compound of ~halt~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~halt~: From the noun and military interjection ~Halt!~ ("stop!"), a deverbal of ~halten~ ("to hold, to stop"), from MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. ~Haltmachen~ is literally "to make a halt," the noun taken as the object of ~machen~. English ~halt~ in the military sense is the same word, borrowed by way of French ~halte~, which French had itself taken from German. The sense of ~halt~ here is: in ~haltmachen~, making a halt.

The verb lives on most vividly in the idiom ~vor nichts haltmachen~, "to stop at nothing," where not even the gravest obstacle brings the subject to a halt.
en.handeln: From Middle High German ~handeln~, from Old High German ~hantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handulōn~, a denominative verb derived from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~ ("hand") with the frequentative suffix *~-lōną~. The underlying noun ~Hand~ traces from MHG ~hant~, from OHG ~hant~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handu~, from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~. The semantic development from "to handle (with the hand)" to "to act, deal, trade" reflects a concrete-to-abstract broadening typical of denominative verbs. Cognate with Dutch ~handelen~, English ~handle~, Danish ~handle~, Swedish ~handla~.
en.hassen:
From Middle High German ~hazzen~, from Old High German ~hazzon~, from Proto-Germanic *~hatāną~, a stative-fientive verb derived from *~hataz~ ("hate, hostility"), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh2d-~ ("grief, hatred").

Cognate with English ~hate~, Dutch ~haten~, Old Norse ~hata~, Gothic ~hatan~. The PIE root *~keh2d-~ also produced Greek ~kēdos~ ("care, grief, mourning") and Welsh ~cas~ ("hatred"). The Proto-Germanic noun *~hataz~ survives in Old English ~hete~ and is the source of English ~hate~. Interestingly, the Greek descendant ~kēdos~ developed in the opposite emotional direction, coming to mean "care, concern" and eventually "funeral rites", suggesting that the PIE root may have originally denoted intense emotional engagement rather than a specific negative emotion.
en.hauen:
From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). Cognate with English ~hew~.

~Hauen~ means "to hit, to strike, to chop, to hew" and is one of German's oldest action verbs. Originally a class VII strong verb (~hauen~, ~hieb~, ~gehauen~), it has partially weakened in colloquial speech, where ~haute~ competes with ~hieb~ as the past tense. In everyday German, ~hauen~ is the child's word for hitting: ~Er hat mich gehauen!~ ("He hit me!") is the universal playground complaint. But the verb also has a vigorous literary and technical life: ~in Stein hauen~ ("to carve in stone"), ~Holz hauen~ ("to chop wood"), ~hau ab!~ ("beat it!, get lost!"). The English cognate ~hew~ has retained the more dignified "chop, carve" meaning. The PIE root *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, forge") also connects to Latin ~cūdere~ ("to strike, to forge").
en.haushalten:
A separable compound of ~haus~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~haus~: The noun ~Haus~ ("house"), from MHG ~hūs~, from OHG ~hūs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hūs~, from Proto-Germanic *~hūsą~, of uncertain further origin, possibly from PIE *~(s)kew-~ ("to cover, conceal"), though this is not secure. It is incorporated as the object of the verb: ~haushalten~ is "to hold house," to keep house and, by extension, to economize. Cognate with English ~house~, Dutch ~huis~, Old Norse ~hús~, Swedish ~hus~. The sense of ~haus~ here is: in ~haushalten~, keeping house and managing resources.

The noun ~Haushalt~ spans both senses at once (a household and a fiscal budget), and ~mit etwas haushalten~ has narrowed to "to use something sparingly," as in ~mit seinen Kräften haushalten~, to husband one's strength.
en.heben:
From Middle High German ~heben~, ~heven~, from Old High German ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb; the past tense ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ descend from the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~, Swedish ~häva~.

The curious shift from "to seize" (PIE) to "to lift" (Germanic) reflects the same conceptual move as in English ~heave~: the act of taking hold of something is inseparable from lifting it. The same PIE root *~keh₂p-~ also produced Latin ~capiō~ ("I take, I seize"), giving English ~capture~, ~capable~, ~captain~, and, via the frequentative ~acceptāre~, German ~akzeptieren~. So ~heben~ and ~akzeptieren~, despite looking nothing alike, are distant PIE cousins: both descend from the same ancient root meaning "to grasp." The derived noun ~Hebel~ ("lever") preserves the physical mechanics of the verb: a lever is the tool that lifts. Cognate with Dutch ~heffen~, English ~heave~.
en.heilen:
From Middle High German ~heilen~, from Old High German ~heilen~ (causative, "to make whole") and ~heilēn~ (inchoative, "to become whole"), from Proto-West Germanic *~hailijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hailijaną~ ("to heal, make whole, save"), derived from *~hailaz~ ("whole, healthy, uninjured"), from PIE *~kéh₂ilos~ ("healthy, whole"). Cognate with English ~heal~ (from OE ~hǣlan~), Dutch ~helen~, Old Norse ~heila~.

The adjective ~heil~ ("whole, sound") is the source of both ~heilen~ and English ~whole~ (from OE ~hāl~, with the same meaning). The ~w-~ in ~whole~ is a late English spelling addition; historically ~hale~ and ~whole~ are the same word. English ~hale~ ("robust, healthy") preserves the original form. The connection between wholeness and health runs deep: to ~heilen~ is to restore something to its ~heile~ ("whole") state. The word ~heilig~ ("holy") is also from ~heil~; to be holy is, etymologically, to be whole and inviolate.
en.heiligsprechen:
A separable compound of ~heilig~ + ~sprechen~:

• ~sprechen~: From MHG ~sprëchen~, from OHG ~sprëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sprekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sprekaną~, probably from PIE *~spregʰ-~ ("to crackle"). The sense developed from an onomatopoeic root meaning "to crackle, make noise" to "to speak." Cognate with Dutch ~spreken~, English ~speak~.
• ~heilig~: From the adjective ~heilig~ ("holy, sacred"), MHG ~heilec~, OHG ~heilag~, from Proto-Germanic *~hailagaz~, a derivative of *~hailaz~ ("whole, sound, uninjured"), modern German ~heil~. The same stem gives English ~whole~, ~hale~, ~heal~, and ~holy~: in Germanic, holiness and wholeness are one idea, and what is sacred is what is intact. In a resultative compound it names the state conferred, as in ~heiligsprechen~ ("to canonize," literally "to speak holy"). The sense of ~heilig~ here is: resulting in sanctified status.

In Church usage ~heiligsprechen~ is the final step, canonization; the preceding and lesser act is ~seligsprechen~, beatification; one is declared ~selig~ ("blessed") before ever being declared ~heilig~.
en.heimbringen:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. ~heim-~ means "home, homeward": the verb's action is directed back to the home.

~Heimbringen~ is transitive: one brings a person or thing home, so the verb requires an object that does not make the journey under its own power.
en.heimfahren:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. It is a bare directional adverb, not a preposition, which is why it takes no article and governs no case.

~Heimfahren~ is intransitive motion homeward by vehicle and forms its perfect with ~sein~, marking a change of place rather than an action performed on an object.
en.heimfinden:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~finden~:

• ~finden~: From MHG ~vinden~, from OHG ~findan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~finþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to go, pass; path, bridge"). The development from "to go, pass" to "to find" parallels shifts in Slavic. Cognate with English ~find~, Dutch ~vinden~, Low German ~finden~, Danish ~finde~.
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. ~heim-~ means "home, homeward": the verb's action is directed back to the home.

~Heimfinden~ turns ~finden~ inward on the traveler: not to find an object but to find one's own way back home, often against confusion or dark.
en.heimführen:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. By extension it can mean returning to one's own country or place of origin.

Beyond its plain sense of leading someone home, ~heimführen~ carries the old marriage idiom ~eine Braut heimführen~, to take a bride into one's house, that is, to wed her.
en.heimgehen:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. ~heim-~ means "home, homeward": the verb's action is directed back to the home.

Alongside its literal "to go home," ~heimgehen~ serves as a gentle euphemism for dying (to go home in the final sense), much as English speaks of being called home.
en.heimholen:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~holen~:

• ~holen~: From MHG ~holen~, ~holn~, from OHG ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, possibly from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, summon") via "to summon" → "to go and fetch"; the connection is uncertain. Cognate with Dutch ~halen~, Low German ~halen~, English ~haul~ (via French).
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. By extension it can mean returning to one's own country or place of origin.

~Heimholen~ adds the errand to the homecoming: to go, fetch, and bring back: and in older usage, to bring a bride into the house, that is, to marry.
en.heimkehren:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~kehren~:

• ~kehren~: A homograph concealing two distinct verbs. ~Kehren~ (1) "to turn": from MHG ~kēren~, from OHG ~kēran~, ~chēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kairijaną~ or *~kausijaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly connected to *~gers-~ ("to twist, bend, turn"). ~Kehren~ (2) "to sweep": from MHG ~kern~, ~keren~, from OHG ~kerian~, ~cherian~, from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~ ("to scrape, scratch"), from PIE *~ger-~ ("to scrape"). Etymologically unrelated, merged through phonological convergence.
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. By extension it can mean returning to one's own country or place of origin.

~Heimkehren~ is the literary word for returning home, and its noun ~Heimkehr~ names the homecoming as a theme, the soldier's, the wanderer's, the exile's return.
en.heimkommen:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. ~heim-~ means "home, homeward": the verb's action is directed back to the home.

~Heimkommen~ is the plain intransitive arrival home, built with ~sein~, the endpoint of any homecoming, reached without another's doing.
en.heimleuchten:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~leuchten~:

• ~leuchten~: From OHG ~liuhten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~liuhtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~liuhtijaną~, a factitive verb from *~leuhtą~ ("light") or *~leuhtaz~ ("bright"), from PIE *~lewk-~ ("bright, to shine, to see"). Cognate with MHG ~liuhten~ and English ~light~; from the same root, Latin ~lūx~ and Greek ~leukos~ ("white").
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. ~heim-~ means "home, homeward": the verb's action is directed back to the home.

Literally to light someone's way home with a lamp, ~heimleuchten~ turned ironic: ~jemandem heimleuchten~ now means to give someone a sharp piece of one's mind, to send them packing.
en.heimreisen:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. It is a bare directional adverb, not a preposition, which is why it takes no article and governs no case.

~Heimreisen~ is to make the journey home, ~reisen~ carrying its full sense of a proper trip rather than a short outing; like other verbs of motion it takes ~sein~.
en.heimschicken:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~schicken~:

• ~schicken~: From MHG ~schicken~ ("to outfit oneself, fit in, arrange appropriately"), from OHG *~skihhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skikkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skikkijaną~ ("to order, send"), the causative of the verb underlying MHG ~geschehen~ ("to happen, rush"). The sense "to send" grew from "to make ready to go." Related to English ~chic~ (via French), ~geschickt~, and ~Schicksal~.
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. It is a bare directional adverb, not a preposition, which is why it takes no article and governs no case.

~Heimschicken~ sends another person or thing home rather than going oneself: dismissal or return effected at a distance, from the sender's standpoint.
en.heimsuchen:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~suchen~:

• ~suchen~: From MHG ~suochen~, ~süechen~, from OHG ~suohhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sōkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sōkijaną~, from PIE *~seh₂g-~ ("to seek out"). The modern umlautless form reflects the Upper German dialect, which resisted umlaut of long rounded vowels before velars. Cognate with English ~seek~, Dutch ~zoeken~, Danish ~søge~, Gothic ~sōkjan~.
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. ~heim-~ means "home, homeward": the verb's action is directed back to the home.

~Heimsuchen~ began as "to seek someone out at home," a neutral visit, and darkened over time to "to afflict, to scourge": its noun ~Heimsuchung~ means a visitation of calamity, even as ~Mariä Heimsuchung~ keeps the older, benign sense of the Visitation.
en.heimtrauen:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~trauen~:

• ~trauen~: From MHG ~trūwen~, from OHG ~trūwēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~trūwēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~trūwāną~ ("to trust, believe"), from PIE *~deru-~ ("to be firm, hard, solid"). The same root gave ~treu~ ("faithful"), ~Trost~ ("comfort"), and ~Trauung~ ("wedding ceremony"), as well as English ~trust~, ~true~, and ~tree~. Cognate with Old Norse ~traust~ ("confidence").
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. ~heim-~ means "home, homeward": the verb's action is directed back to the home.

~Heimtrauen~ is used reflexively: ~sich heimtrauen~ is to have the nerve to go home: the homeward movement, held back by fear or shame.
en.heimzahlen:
A separable compound of ~heim~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~heim~: From the noun ~Heim~ ("home"), used in verbs as the old adverbial accusative of direction, "homeward." From MHG ~heim~, from OHG ~heim~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haim~, from Proto-Germanic *~haimaz~ ("home, village"), from PIE *~ḱóymos~ ("settlement, home"). Cognate with English ~home~, Dutch ~heem~, Swedish ~hem~; the same root surfaces in Latin ~cīvis~ ("citizen"), one who belongs to a settlement. ~heim-~ means "home, homeward": the verb's action is directed back to the home.

~Heimzahlen~ has left literal payment behind: ~es jemandem heimzahlen~ means to pay someone back in the sense of revenge, to repay a wrong in kind.
en.heiraten:
From Middle High German ~hīrāten~, derived from MHG ~hīrāt~ ("marriage"), whence modern German ~Heirat~. The noun comes from Old High German ~hīrāt~ ("wedding, marriage"), from Proto-West Germanic *~hīwarād~. The compound literally meant something like "household counsel" or "household arrangement," from *~hīwa-~ ("household, family") + *~rād~ ("counsel, plan"). Cognate with Old English ~hīred~ ("family, household"), whence the English word ~hird~ (a Scandinavian royal retinue, re-borrowed through Old Norse ~hirð~ from Old English).

The etymology reveals that marriage in Germanic society was fundamentally a household arrangement, not a matter of romantic love but of establishing a domestic partnership. The ~-rāt~ element is the same word that appears in ~Rat~ ("counsel, advice") and in the ~-rad~ that underlies names like ~Konrad~ ("bold counsel"). English ~hird~, a king's household guard, preserves the same Proto-West Germanic compound but specialized toward the military-household meaning. Modern English has no direct cognate for ~heiraten~; instead it uses ~marry~, borrowed from French ~marier~, itself from Latin ~marītāre~. The German word thus preserves a distinctly Germanic conception of marriage as domestic establishment, while English adopted the Roman view.
en.heißen: From Middle High German ~heiȥen~, from Old High German ~heiȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haitan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haitaną~, tentatively from PIE *~ḱeyd-~ ("to call"). The original sense was "to command, order" (still preserved in the construction ~jemanden etwas heißen~), with the meaning "to be called, be named" developing from the passive use: "to be called (something)" became the dominant sense. Cognate with Bavarian ~haßn~, ~hoaßn~, Yiddish ~heysn~, Dutch ~heten~, Low German ~heten~, ~heiten~, Old Norse ~heita~, Gothic ~haitan~. The most direct English cognate is the archaic verb ~hight~ ("called, named"), from Old English ~hātan~, which survives in Spenser and other early-modern poets (~a goodly knight, hight George~). Like ~heißen~, it froze in the passive sense "to be called." Also cognate with English ~hest~, ~behest~, which preserve the original "command" meaning.
en.heißmachen:
A separable compound of ~heiß~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~heiß~: From the adjective ~heiß~ ("hot"), MHG ~heiȥ~, OHG ~heiȥ~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hait~, from Proto-Germanic *~haitaz~. As a resultative it names the end state: ~heißlaufen~ is to run until hot, to overheat. Cognate with English ~hot~ and ~heat~, Dutch ~heet~, Old Norse ~heitr~, Swedish ~het~. Despite the near-identity of the modern forms, this adjective is generally held to be unrelated to the verb ~heißen~ ("to be called"), which goes back to Proto-Germanic *~haitaną~. The sense of ~heiß~ here is: resulting in the object becoming hot.

Beyond the literal "to make hot," ~jemandem heißmachen~ works figuratively: to fire someone up, to make them keen or anxious about something.
en.helfen: From Middle High German ~hëlfen~, from Old High German ~hëlfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helpaną~, from PIE *~ḱelb-~, *~ḱelp-~. A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~e~-~a~-~o~ ablaut pattern (~helfen~, ~half~, ~geholfen~). Cognate with Low German ~helpen~, Dutch ~helpen~, English ~help~, Danish ~hjælpe~, Norwegian ~hjelpe~.
en.hellsehen:
A separable compound of ~hell~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~hell~: From the adjective ~hell~ ("bright, light"), from MHG ~hel~, which meant "resounding, loud" before it meant "shining"; the word began as a term of hearing and crossed over to sight. It belongs to OHG ~hellan~ ("to resound"), the source of modern ~hallen~ ("to echo") and ~Hall~ ("reverberation"), from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, shout"), the root also behind Latin ~calāre~ and Greek ~καλέω~ (~kaléō~, "I call"). German still keeps both channels: a ~helle Stimme~ is a high clear voice and a ~helles Zimmer~ a well-lit room. The sense of ~hell~ here is: clear and undimmed, of sound or of perception.

~Hellsehen~ applies ~hell~, "clear, bright," to perception rather than light: to see clearly what is hidden or yet to come, whence ~Hellseher~, a clairvoyant, the very word ~clairvoyant~ being French for "clear-seeing."
en.herabblicken:
A separable compound of ~herab-~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~blank~, Dutch ~blik~, Old English ~blice~.
• ~herab-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ab~ ("off, down"), so "downward and toward the speaker", the motion seen from below. Its mirror image is ~hinab~, the same descent away from the speaker. ~herab-~ marks downward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point below.

„herabblicken“ is directed seeing from above downward; figuratively (to look down on someone), it takes on the disdain that clings elsewhere to ~herab-~.
en.herabfliegen:
A separable compound of ~herab-~ + ~fliegen~:

• ~fliegen~: From MHG ~vliegen~, from OHG ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"), an extension of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim") that also gave ~fließen~. The vowel path *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of class II strong verbs. Cognate with English ~fly~, Dutch ~vliegen~, Danish ~flyve~.
• ~herab-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ab~ ("off, down"), so "downward and toward the speaker", the motion seen from below. Its mirror image is ~hinab~, the same descent away from the speaker. ~herab-~ marks downward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point below.

~Herabfliegen~ is the downward flight of a winged creature: a bird, an angel, or, in a fairy tale, helpful doves.
en.herabsetzen:
A separable compound of ~herab-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~herab-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ab~ ("off, down"), so "downward and toward the speaker", the motion seen from below. Its mirror image is ~hinab~, the same descent away from the speaker. Figuratively, of condescension or disparagement, looking down on someone (~herabsehen~, ~herabsetzen~).

~Herabsetzen~ parts early from the spatial picture: one lowers a price, an age, or a penalty: or, with no number at all, a person's worth.
en.herabsteigen:
A separable compound of ~herab-~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~herab-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ab~ ("off, down"), so "downward and toward the speaker", the motion seen from below. Its mirror image is ~hinab~, the same descent away from the speaker. ~herab-~ marks downward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point below.

~Herabsteigen~ is a controlled, step-by-step descent (not a fall) often from a height such as a mountain, tree, or altar down toward the onlooker.
en.herabstürzen:
A separable compound of ~herab-~ + ~stürzen~:

• ~stürzen~: From MHG ~stürzen~, from OHG ~sturzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sturtijan~ ("to fall down, tumble"), of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly from PIE *~ster-~ ("to be stiff") via a dental extension *~sterd-~, though the derivation is debated. Cognate with English ~start~, a doublet from the same Proto-West Germanic source, from which the meanings have diverged radically.
• ~herab-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ab~ ("off, down"), so "downward and toward the speaker", the motion seen from below. Its mirror image is ~hinab~, the same descent away from the speaker. ~herab-~ marks downward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point below.

Where ~herabsteigen~ is a measured descent, ~herabstürzen~ is the sudden, uncontrolled fall: from water cascading down to a plunging body.
en.herabwürdigen:
A separable compound of ~herab-~ + ~würdigen~:

• ~würdigen~: From ~würdig~ ("worthy") + ~-en~; ~würdig~ from ~Würde~ ("dignity, worth") + ~-ig~, and ~Würde~ from MHG ~wirde~, from OHG ~wirdī~, related to Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("valuable, worthy"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"). Cognate with English ~worth~ and ~worthy~.
• ~herab-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ab~ ("off, down"), so "downward and toward the speaker", the motion seen from below. Its mirror image is ~hinab~, the same descent away from the speaker. Figuratively, of condescension or disparagement, looking down on someone (~herabsehen~, ~herabsetzen~).

~Herabwürdigen~ lowers ~Würde~ itself: it denies someone the worth that ~würdigen~ grants, the same root, turned the opposite way.
en.heranbilden:
A separable compound of ~heran-~ + ~bilden~:

• ~bilden~: From MHG ~bilden~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: ~biliden~ ("to form into an image"), from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþijan~, and ~bilidōn~ ("to copy, represent"), from *~biliþōn~; both from the noun *~biliþī~ (whence ~Bild~), whose pre-Germanic origin is obscure, with no secure PIE etymology. Cognate with Dutch ~beelden~, Swedish ~bilda~.
• ~heran-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at, up to"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~ran~. Figuratively it marks taking on a task, or growing up toward a standard.

~Heranbilden~ means deliberately raising and training up successors: skilled workers, pupils, a new generation are brought up to a competence.
en.heranbrechen:
A separable compound of ~heran-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~heran-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at, up to"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~ran~. ~heran-~ means approaching: coming up to the speaker or to a point of reference.

~Heranbrechen~ joins the approach of ~heran-~ to the sudden force of ~brechen~: a day, a storm, or a wave breaks on, drawing unstoppably nearer.
en.heranführen:
A separable compound of ~heran-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
