• ~heran-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at, up to"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~ran~. With transitive verbs it means bringing something nearer.

~Heranführen~ is the transitive counterpart of approaching: one leads someone or something nearer: literally to a place, figuratively to a subject.
en.herangehen:
A separable compound of ~heran-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~heran-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at, up to"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~ran~. Figuratively it marks taking on a task, or growing up toward a standard.

~Herangehen~ has shifted almost wholly into the figurative: one approaches a task, a problem, a matter: the image of stepping up survives only as an attitude.
en.heranhalten:
A separable compound of ~heran-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~heran-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at, up to"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~ran~. With transitive verbs it means bringing something nearer.

~Heranhalten~ brings something up close to a reference point and keeps it there; one holds a sample, a tape measure, an ear up to the object.
en.herankommen:
A separable compound of ~heran-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~heran-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at, up to"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~ran~. ~heran-~ means approaching: coming up to the speaker or to a point of reference.

~Herankommen~ is simply drawing nearer under one's own power; beside it stands the idiom „an etwas nicht herankommen,“ for what stays out of reach.
en.heranmachen:
A separable compound of ~heran-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~heran-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at, up to"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~ran~. Figuratively it marks taking on a task, or growing up toward a standard.

~Sich heranmachen~ is always reflexive and often carries a whiff of intent: one sets about a task, or, as in Kafka, sidles up to a person.
en.heranreichen:
A separable compound of ~heran-~ + ~reichen~:

• ~reichen~: From MHG ~reichen~, from OHG ~reihhen~, ~reichen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raikijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~raikijaną~, from PIE *~Hroyǵ-éye-ti~, a causative o-grade of *~Hreyǵ-~ ("to stretch out, reach"). The causative "to cause to stretch" broadened to "to reach," "to hand to," and "to suffice." Cognate with English ~reach~, Dutch ~reiken~, Danish ~række~.
• ~heran-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at, up to"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~ran~. ~heran-~ means approaching: coming up to the speaker or to a point of reference.

~Heranreichen~ means extending as far as a reference point; figuratively, in „an jemanden nicht heranreichen,“ it becomes failing to measure up to a standard.
en.herantreten:
A separable compound of ~heran-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~heran-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at, up to"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~ran~. ~heran-~ means approaching: coming up to the speaker or to a point of reference.

~Herantreten~ is the more formal drawing near: one steps up to a window, but also approaches an authority or comes to someone with a request.
en.heranwachsen:
A separable compound of ~heran-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from PIE *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Cognate with English ~wax~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~heran-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at, up to"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~ran~. Figuratively it marks taking on a task, or growing up toward a standard.

~Heranwachsen~ is growing toward a measure, usually adulthood, a child, but figuratively also a movement or a danger, grows up.
en.heranziehen:
Compound of ~heran-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ ("to pull, to lead"). Cognate with Old English ~teon~ ("to pull, to draw"), Latin ~ducere~ ("to lead"), and English ~tow~, ~tug~, and ~duke~ (via Latin).
• ~heran-~: From ~her~ ("hither, toward the speaker") + ~an~ ("on, at"). The element ~her~ descends from OHG ~hera~, from Proto-Germanic *~hiz~ ("this"), from Proto-Indo-European *~kis~ ("this, here"). The combined prefix conveys movement approaching the speaker.

The compound means "to draw near, to pull closer," and by extension "to consult, to cite" (drawing a source toward oneself) or "to train, to raise" (drawing a person upward toward competence). The PIE root *~dewk-~ has an astonishingly wide range of descendants: Latin ~ducere~ yielded ~duke~, ~duchess~, ~conduct~, ~produce~, ~educate~, and ~deduce~. To ~heranziehen~ a source in an argument is, etymologically, to lead it toward you.
en.heraufbeschwören:
A separable compound of ~herauf-~ + ~be-~ + ~schwören~:

• ~schwören~: From MHG ~swern~, from OHG ~swerien~, from Proto-West Germanic *~swarjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swarjaną~, from PIE *~swer-~ ("to speak, to talk"). A class VI strong verb (~schwören~, ~schwor~, ~geschworen~); the older Präteritum ~schwur~ is now archaic. Cognate with English ~swear~, Dutch ~zweren~, Danish ~sværge~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~herauf-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and toward the speaker." Its mirror image is ~hinauf~, the same motion away from the speaker. Also of time and weather moving in on one (~heraufziehen~, of a storm).

From the spatial „to call up from below,“ a fixed sense „to bring about, to unleash“ has grown: one conjures up a danger, a war, a calamity, usually something dire.
en.heraufbringen:
A separable compound of ~herauf-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~herauf-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and toward the speaker." Its mirror image is ~hinauf~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herauf-~ marks upward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point.

~Heraufbringen~ is carrying or conducting something from below up toward the speaker; in Luther, even bringing a dead man up from the underworld.
en.herauffahren:
A separable compound of ~herauf-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~herauf-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and toward the speaker." Its mirror image is ~hinauf~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herauf-~ marks upward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point.

The older sense of ~fahren~, „to move, to travel,“ lives on in ~herauffahren~: in Luther an east wind or a breaker comes up, long before the word was tied to vehicles.
en.heraufgeben:
A separable compound of ~herauf-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~herauf-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and toward the speaker." Its mirror image is ~hinauf~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herauf-~ marks upward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point.

~Heraufgeben~ is handing an object from below up to someone above, the everyday inverse of handing down.
en.heraufhalten:
A separable compound of ~herauf-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~herauf-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and toward the speaker." Its mirror image is ~hinauf~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herauf-~ marks upward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point.

~Heraufhalten~ means holding something up toward the speaker so that it can be taken or seen.
en.heraufkommen:
A separable compound of ~herauf-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~herauf-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and toward the speaker." Its mirror image is ~hinauf~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herauf-~ marks upward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point.

~Heraufkommen~ is coming up under one's own power toward the speaker; people up the stairs, but figuratively also a storm or a new age.
en.heraufschicken:
A separable compound of ~herauf-~ + ~schicken~:

• ~schicken~: From MHG ~schicken~ ("to outfit oneself, fit in, arrange appropriately"), from OHG *~skihhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skikkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skikkijaną~ ("to order, send"), the causative of the verb underlying MHG ~geschehen~ ("to happen, rush"). The sense "to send" grew from "to make ready to go." Related to English ~chic~ (via French), ~geschickt~, and ~Schicksal~.
• ~herauf-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and toward the speaker." Its mirror image is ~hinauf~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herauf-~ marks upward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point.

~Heraufschicken~ is causing someone or something to come up; one sends it upward without carrying it oneself.
en.heraufsetzen:
A separable compound of ~herauf-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~herauf-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and toward the speaker." Its mirror image is ~hinauf~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herauf-~ marks upward motion oriented toward the speaker or the vantage point.

~Heraufsetzen~ is the exact counterpart of ~herabsetzen~: one raises a price, a fee, an age rather than lowering it.
en.herausbekommen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~be-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys bringing something out into the open: publishing, discovering, or making public.

~Herausbekommen~ means bringing a solution or answer to light; alongside it stands the concrete „einen Fleck herausbekommen,“ getting a stain out with effort.
en.herausbrechen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

As a strong intransitive taking ~sein~, ~herausbrechen~ describes something forcing its way out under pressure: an abscess, a confession, a hidden thing that suddenly erupts into the open.
en.herausbringen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys bringing something out into the open: publishing, discovering, or making public.

In modern use ~herausbringen~ has narrowed toward publishing or releasing (a book, a record, a product brought before the public), whereas Luther still uses it literally, for fetching a thing out.
en.herausdringen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~dringen~:

• ~dringen~: From MHG ~dringen~, from OHG ~dringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þringwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrinhwaną~, from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). A class III strong verb (~dringen~, ~drang~, ~gedrungen~); its causative ~drängen~ carries the expected umlaut. Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~ ("to press") and English ~throng~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

~Herausdringen~ (strong, with ~sein~) is said of sound, light, or liquid that penetrates outward from an enclosed space: a cry heard through a wall, smoke leaking from a fire.
en.herausfinden:
~Heraus-~ + ~finden~, where ~heraus-~ is itself a compound of ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") + ~aus-~ ("out"). Compound of ~her-~ + ~aus-~ + ~finden~:

• ~finden~: From MHG ~vinden~, from OHG ~findan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to tread, to go, to find the way").
• ~her-~: From PIE *~ḱís~ ("this, here"). The prefix indicates direction toward the speaker.
• ~aus-~: From PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). The prefix adds a sense of outward extraction.

~Herausfinden~ means "to find out, to discover, to figure out." The double prefix creates a vivid spatial metaphor: to find something ~out~ and bring it ~here~: to extract hidden knowledge and draw it toward oneself. Cognate with English ~find out~, which Wiktionary notes as a semantic parallel. The PIE root *~pent-~ ("to tread, to go") reveals an ancient connection between finding and walking: you ~find~ things by treading the ground, by going along a ~path~ (English ~path~ is from the same root). Latin ~pōns~ ("bridge," originally "path over water") is a cognate, as is Greek ~póntos~ ("sea", the thing you cross). The double-prefix pattern (~heraus-~, ~herein-~, ~herüber-~) is characteristically German: it specifies both the origin point and the direction of motion in a single verb, achieving a spatial precision that English typically requires a phrasal verb to match.
en.herausfordern:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~fordern~:

• ~fordern~: From MHG ~vodern~, ~vordern~, from OHG ~fordarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ(a)rōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþą~, from PIE *~pŕ̥-to-~, from *~per-~ ("forward, through"); "to push forward" became "to advance a claim." Not to be confused with umlauted ~fördern~ from the same root. Cognate with English ~forth~, ~forward~ and ~further~, Dutch ~vorderen~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

~Herausfordern~ literally means "to call someone out" (to summon an opponent forth, as to a duel), and from that comes its modern sense of challenging or provoking; the base ~fordern~ "to demand" supplies the summons, ~heraus-~ the calling into the open.
en.herausgeben:
Compound of ~heraus-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~geben~, from OHG ~geban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~ ("to give"), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (via Norse), Dutch ~geven~.
• ~heraus-~: From ~her~ ("hither, toward the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"). The element ~her~ descends from OHG ~hera~, from Proto-Germanic *~hiz~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kis~ ("this, here"). The element ~aus~ descends from OHG ~uz~, from Proto-Germanic *~ut~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ud~ ("upwards, away, out"). Together they mean "out toward the speaker."

The compound literally means "to give out (toward the speaker)," yielding the modern senses of "to publish" (giving a book out to the world), "to return, hand over" (giving change back), and "to edit" (in the sense of preparing for publication). A ~Herausgeber~ is an editor or publisher. Dutch ~uitgeven~ ("to publish, to spend") shows the same semantic development with its own prefix ~uit-~ ("out"), confirming that the metaphor of publication as "giving out" runs deep in the Germanic languages.
en.herausgehen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

Beyond the literal stepping outdoors, the idiom ~aus sich herausgehen~ "to come out of one's shell" shows the compound's reach into the figurative.
en.herausgreifen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~greifen~:

• ~greifen~: From MHG ~grîfen~, from OHG ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). A class I strong verb (~greift~, ~griff~, ~gegriffen~), like ~reiten~ and ~schneiden~. Cognate with English ~gripe~, Dutch ~grijpen~, Low German ~griepen~, Old Norse ~gripa~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

From physically reaching in and grasping comes the abstract ~herausgreifen~: to single out one point or example from a larger set for attention.
en.heraushalten:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

Most often reflexive (~sich aus etwas heraushalten~, to keep out of a matter, to stay uninvolved), though it also serves literally, holding an object out of a window.
en.herausheben:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb: the past ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ continue the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

Literally to lift out; figuratively to single out for emphasis, to make one thing stand out against its background, the sense in which a report highlights a finding.
en.herausholen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~holen~:

• ~holen~: From MHG ~holen~, ~holn~, from OHG ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, possibly from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, summon") via "to summon" → "to go and fetch"; the connection is uncertain. Cognate with Dutch ~halen~, Low German ~halen~, English ~haul~ (via French).
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

Beyond fetching an object out, ~herausholen~ commonly means to extract the most from something: ~das Beste herausholen~, to get the best out of a situation.
en.herauskommen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

The everyday ~herauskommen~ extends to results and outcomes (~dabei kommt nichts heraus~, "nothing comes of it") the sense of a conclusion emerging from a process.
en.herauskriegen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~kriegen~:

• ~kriegen~: From MHG ~kriegen~ ("to war, to strive for"), a verbalization of ~Krieg~ ("war"), from OHG ~krig~, from Proto-West Germanic *~krīg~, whose origin is debated. The "obtaining" sense overshadowed the military one; colloquial modern German ~kriegen~ simply means "to get." Cognate with Dutch ~krijgen~ ("to get"), Bavarian ~kriagn~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys bringing something out into the open: publishing, discovering, or making public.

Colloquial ~kriegen~ "to get" gives ~herauskriegen~ the sense of "to work out, to ascertain": to get an answer out of a puzzle or a person.
en.herauslösen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~lösen~:

• ~lösen~: From MHG ~lœsen~, ~lōsen~, from OHG ~lōsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lausijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausijaną~, a causative of *~leusaną~ ("to lose, let loose"), denominative via *~lausaz~ ("loose, free"), from PIE *~lewh₁-~ ("to cut, sever, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ (via Old Norse ~lauss~), Dutch ~lozen~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

~Herauslösen~ is to detach or isolate a part from a whole: a substance dissolved out of a mixture, a passage lifted from its context.
en.herausnehmen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

Beyond literally taking something out, the reflexive ~sich etwas herausnehmen~ means to take a liberty, to presume, as in Nietzsche's exclamation ~Was nahmt ihr euch heraus!~
en.herausreden:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

Reflexive ~sich herausreden~ means to talk one's way out, to make excuses: to escape a charge or obligation by talking rather than acting.
en.herausreißen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

Literally to tear out; figuratively, ~jemanden herausreißen~ is to rescue someone from danger or difficulty, the sense Luther's psalm gives it.
en.herausschaffen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~schaffen~:

• ~schaffen~: Two historically distinct verbs have merged under a single infinitive, distinguished only by their conjugation. The strong ~schaffen~ (~schuf~, ~geschaffen~, "to create") descends from MHG ~schaffen~, OHG ~scaffan~, a byform of ~skephen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skappjan~; the ~-f-~ was chiefly back-formed from the participle ~giscaffan~. The weak ~schaffen~ (~schaffte~, ~geschafft~, "to manage, accomplish") descends from OHG ~skaffōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skapōn~, from the same root. Cognate with Dutch ~scheppen~, English ~shape~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

Built on weak ~schaffen~ "to manage, accomplish" (family ~w~, not strong ~schaffen~ "to create"), ~herausschaffen~ means to succeed in getting something or someone out: to convey out of a difficult place.
en.herausschauen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

Southern ~schauen~ "to look" gives ~herausschauen~ "to look out": to peer out from an opening, and colloquially ~dabei schaut nichts heraus~, "nothing comes of it."
en.herausschmecken:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~schmecken~:

• ~schmecken~: From MHG ~smecken~, from OHG ~smecchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smakkijan~ ("to taste"), from *~smakku~ ("a taste"). In southern and Austrian German ~schmecken~ also means "to smell." Cognate with English ~smack~ (as in "it smacks of"), Dutch ~smaken~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys bringing something out into the open: publishing, discovering, or making public.

~Herausschmecken~ is to detect a particular flavor within a dish: to taste out one ingredient from the whole, a perceptual discovering.
en.herausschmeißen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~schmeißen~:

• ~schmeißen~: From MHG ~smīȥen~, from OHG ~smīȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~smītaną~, from PIE *~smeyd-~. A class I strong verb (~schmeißen~, ~schmiss~, ~geschmissen~). Cognate with English ~smite~, Dutch ~smijten~, Danish ~smide~, Gothic ~bismeitan~ ("to smear, to anoint").
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

Colloquial and blunt, ~herausschmeißen~ is to throw someone out: to eject forcibly from a place or a position.
en.herausschneiden:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~schneiden~:

• ~schneiden~: From MHG ~snīden~, from OHG ~snīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~snīþan~ ("to cut"); no secure PIE root has been established, and the word may be a Germanic innovation. A class I strong verb (~schneiden~, ~schnitt~, ~geschnitten~). Cognate with archaic English ~snithe~ ("to cut"), Dutch ~snijden~, Icelandic ~sníða~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

~Herausschneiden~ is to cut something out: a shape from cloth or paper, a scene from a film, a tumor from tissue.
en.herausschreiben:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

~Herausschreiben~ is to copy or extract in writing: to write out selected words or figures from a source, as Kafka's K. copies rare vocabulary from the dictionary.
en.herausstechen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~stechen~:

• ~stechen~: From MHG ~stëchen~, from OHG ~stëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stekaną~ ("to stab, prick"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to stick, poke"). Cognate with Dutch ~steken~ ("to stab, sting"), Old Norse ~stinga~, English ~stick~ (originally "to stab, pierce").
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

From literally pricking or piercing outward, ~herausstechen~ means to stand out, to be conspicuous, a color or a talent that catches the eye against its surroundings.
en.herausstellen:
Compound of ~heraus-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from Proto-Indo-European *~stel-~ ("to place, put, stand"). Cognate with English ~stall~ and ~still~, Dutch ~stellen~.
• ~heraus-~: From ~her~ ("hither, toward the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"). The element ~her~ descends from OHG ~hera~, from Proto-Germanic *~hiz~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kis~ ("this, here"). The element ~aus~ descends from OHG ~uz~, from Proto-Germanic *~ut~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ud~ ("upwards, away, out"). Together they mean "out toward the speaker."

The compound literally means "to place out (toward the speaker)," hence "to expose, to highlight, to emphasize." The reflexive ~sich herausstellen~ means "to turn out, to become apparent", something places itself out into the open. This metaphor of truth as spatial emergence is ancient: what is hidden is inside, what is revealed comes out. The PIE root *~stel-~ also produced Greek ~stellein~ ("to set, to send") and Latin ~locus~ (from an older *~stlocus~), making ~herausstellen~ a distant cousin of English ~locate~.
en.herausstreichen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~streichen~:

• ~streichen~: From MHG ~strīchen~, from OHG ~strīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~strīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~strīkaną~ ("to stroke, to rub"), from PIE *~streyg-~ ("to stroke, rub, press"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with English ~strike~, Dutch ~strijken~ ("to iron, to stroke").
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys bringing something out into the open: publishing, discovering, or making public.

Despite the base ~streichen~ "to strike out," ~herausstreichen~ means to extol or emphasize: to make a merit prominent and press it on the listener.
en.heraussuchen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~suchen~:

• ~suchen~: From MHG ~suochen~, ~süechen~, from OHG ~suohhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sōkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sōkijaną~, from PIE *~seh₂g-~ ("to seek out"). The modern umlautless form reflects the Upper German dialect, which resisted umlaut of long rounded vowels before velars. Cognate with English ~seek~, Dutch ~zoeken~, Danish ~søge~, Gothic ~sōkjan~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

~Heraussuchen~ is to search out and pick: to select particular items from a larger stock, sorting the wanted from the rest.
en.heraustreten:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

~Heraustreten~ is to step forth into view: a person emerging from a doorway or a crowd, and figuratively a pattern or truth that becomes apparent.
en.herauswerfen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

So ~herauswerfen~ is the literal „throwing outward,“ which readily extends to throwing a person out.
en.herausziehen:
A separable compound of ~heraus-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~heraus-~: Transparently ~her-~ ("hither, toward the speaker") plus ~aus~ ("out"), hence "out toward the speaker": the mirror of ~hinaus~, "out away from the speaker." This her/hin opposition is the single most useful fact about the whole deictic group. Colloquial German contracts ~heraus~ to ~raus~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~aus-~. The particle conveys outward motion toward the speaker.

~Herausziehen~ is extraction in the literal sense: drawing something out of an enclosure into view, here figuratively with a fishing hook.
en.herbeiführen:
A separable compound of ~herbei-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~herbei-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~bei~ ("by, near"), so "hither, to this spot", motion that ends up close to the speaker. Unlike the other ~her-~ compounds it names no axis, only arrival at the near point. Often of summoning or fetching something so that it is at hand (~herbeirufen~, ~herbeischaffen~).

Unlike its spatial siblings, ~herbeiführen~ has shifted wholly into the abstract: it no longer „leads“ an object over but a state or an event: „to bring about, to cause.“
en.herbeikommen:
A separable compound of ~herbei-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~herbei-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~bei~ ("by, near"), so "hither, to this spot", motion that ends up close to the speaker. Unlike the other ~her-~ compounds it names no axis, only arrival at the near point. ~herbei-~ marks motion up to the speaker, "over here, near."

As in „your time has come near,“ the spatial drawing-close can transfer to time: an approaching moment.
en.herbeilocken:
A separable compound of ~herbei-~ + ~locken~:

• ~locken~: From MHG ~locken~, from OHG ~lockōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lokkōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lukkōną~ ("to entice, to lure"). A second, homonymous ~locken~ ("to curl"), from OHG ~lochōn~ and the noun ~Locke~, is etymologically distinct. Related to ~lügen~, Latin ~laciō~ ("I entice"); English has no direct cognate and uses ~lure~.
• ~herbei-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~bei~ ("by, near"), so "hither, to this spot", motion that ends up close to the speaker. Unlike the other ~her-~ compounds it names no axis, only arrival at the near point. Often of summoning or fetching something so that it is at hand (~herbeirufen~, ~herbeischaffen~).

~Herbeilocken~ joins enticement to direction: to set something in motion toward the speaker by allurement.
en.herbeirufen:
A separable compound of ~herbei-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. A parallel weak form in Middle High German explains why the modern present lacks the expected umlaut (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~herbei-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~bei~ ("by, near"), so "hither, to this spot", motion that ends up close to the speaker. Unlike the other ~her-~ compounds it names no axis, only arrival at the near point. Often of summoning or fetching something so that it is at hand (~herbeirufen~, ~herbeischaffen~).

~Herbeirufen~ is calling with an effect: the call is meant to bring the summoned to the speaker's side.
en.herbeischaffen:
A separable compound of ~herbei-~ + ~schaffen~:

• ~schaffen~: Two historically distinct verbs have merged under a single infinitive, distinguished only by their conjugation. The strong ~schaffen~ (~schuf~, ~geschaffen~, "to create") descends from MHG ~schaffen~, OHG ~scaffan~, a byform of ~skephen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skappjan~; the ~-f-~ was chiefly back-formed from the participle ~giscaffan~. The weak ~schaffen~ (~schaffte~, ~geschafft~, "to manage, accomplish") descends from OHG ~skaffōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skapōn~, from the same root. Cognate with Dutch ~scheppen~, English ~shape~.
• ~herbei-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~bei~ ("by, near"), so "hither, to this spot", motion that ends up close to the speaker. Unlike the other ~her-~ compounds it names no axis, only arrival at the near point. Often of summoning or fetching something so that it is at hand (~herbeirufen~, ~herbeischaffen~).

Here the weak ~schaffen~ „to procure, obtain“ lives on (family w): ~herbeischaffen~ means to bring something so that it is on hand.
en.herbeiziehen:
A separable compound of ~herbei-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~herbei-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~bei~ ("by, near"), so "hither, to this spot", motion that ends up close to the speaker. Unlike the other ~her-~ compounds it names no axis, only arrival at the near point. Often of summoning or fetching something so that it is at hand (~herbeirufen~, ~herbeischaffen~).

~Herbeiziehen~ draws something over to one's own position, literally or figuratively, as in adducing a piece of evidence.
en.herbringen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

~Herbringen~ is the counterpart of ~hinbringen~: to carry something to the speaker's place.
en.hereinfallen:
A separable compound of ~herein-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~herein-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ein~ ("in, into"), so "inward and toward the speaker", the movement of someone entering the room one is standing in. Its mirror image is ~hinein~, the same motion away from the speaker. Figuratively, of drawing someone into a situation, often an unwelcome one (~hereinlegen~, "to take in, to dupe").

Literally „to fall in,“ as into a pit; figuratively „auf jemanden hereinfallen“: to be taken in, deceived.
en.hereinfinden:
A separable compound of ~herein-~ + ~finden~:

• ~finden~: From MHG ~vinden~, from OHG ~findan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~finþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to go, pass; path, bridge"). The development from "to go, pass" to "to find" parallels shifts in Slavic. Cognate with English ~find~, Dutch ~vinden~, Low German ~finden~, Danish ~finde~.
• ~herein-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ein~ ("in, into"), so "inward and toward the speaker", the movement of someone entering the room one is standing in. Its mirror image is ~hinein~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herein-~ marks inward motion oriented toward the speaker.

Reflexive „sich hereinfinden“ shifts the inward motion into the figurative: to settle into something, to find one's way in.
en.hereingeben:
A separable compound of ~herein-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~herein-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ein~ ("in, into"), so "inward and toward the speaker", the movement of someone entering the room one is standing in. Its mirror image is ~hinein~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herein-~ marks inward motion oriented toward the speaker.

~Hereingeben~ is handing something from outside to inside, toward the speaker.
en.hereingehen:
A separable compound of ~herein-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~herein-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ein~ ("in, into"), so "inward and toward the speaker", the movement of someone entering the room one is standing in. Its mirror image is ~hinein~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herein-~ marks inward motion oriented toward the speaker.

~Hereingehen~ describes entering from the vantage of someone already inside.
en.hereinkommen:
A separable compound of ~herein-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~herein-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ein~ ("in, into"), so "inward and toward the speaker", the movement of someone entering the room one is standing in. Its mirror image is ~hinein~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herein-~ marks inward motion oriented toward the speaker.

~Hereinkommen~ takes the same path as ~hereingehen~ but stresses arrival at the speaker rather than the walking.
en.hereinlegen:
A separable compound of ~herein-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~herein-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ein~ ("in, into"), so "inward and toward the speaker", the movement of someone entering the room one is standing in. Its mirror image is ~hinein~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herein-~ marks inward motion oriented toward the speaker.

The same formation also carries the well-known figurative „jemanden hereinlegen,“ „to dupe“; the reading glossed here, however, is the literal one of laying something in.
en.hereinrufen:
A separable compound of ~herein-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. A parallel weak form in Middle High German explains why the modern present lacks the expected umlaut (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~herein-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ein~ ("in, into"), so "inward and toward the speaker", the movement of someone entering the room one is standing in. Its mirror image is ~hinein~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herein-~ marks inward motion oriented toward the speaker.

~Hereinrufen~ is calling so that the one called enters the speaker's room.
en.hereinstecken:
A separable compound of ~herein-~ + ~stecken~:

• ~stecken~: Modern ~stecken~ merges two verbs: the transitive weak one ("to put, stick something in") from MHG ~stecken~, OHG ~steckōn~, a geminate derivative of ~stëhhan~ (the ancestor of ~stechen~), and the strong intransitive one (archaic ~stak~/~gestocken~, "to be stuck"); the two fused in Early Modern German. Both trace to Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stikaną~, from PIE *~(s)teyg-~ ("to be sharp, stab, goad"). Cognate with English ~stick~ and ~steak~.
• ~herein-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~ein~ ("in, into"), so "inward and toward the speaker", the movement of someone entering the room one is standing in. Its mirror image is ~hinein~, the same motion away from the speaker. ~herein-~ marks inward motion oriented toward the speaker.

~Hereinstecken~ joins putting or sticking with motion inward and toward the speaker.
en.herfallen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

In „über jemanden ~herfallen~“ the fall becomes assault: to pounce on someone suddenly and violently.
en.herführen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

~Herführen~ is the transitive counterpart of ~herkommen~: to conduct someone or something to the speaker's place.
en.hergeben:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

~Hergeben~ means to hand something over toward the speaker, often with a connotation of surrendering reluctantly („sein Leben hergeben,“ to give up one's life).
en.hergehen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

Beside the spatial „vor jemandem ~hergehen~“ stands the impersonal „es geht … her“ for how an event unfolds („hart,“ „lustig hergehen“).
en.herhalten:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

To „have to ~herhalten~“ means to serve as a substitute or a target: holding oneself out for something.
en.herholen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~holen~:

• ~holen~: From MHG ~holen~, ~holn~, from OHG ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, possibly from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, summon") via "to summon" → "to go and fetch"; the connection is uncertain. Cognate with Dutch ~halen~, Low German ~halen~, English ~haul~ (via French).
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

~Herholen~ nearly doubles the base sense of ~holen~, which already means „to go and bring back“; ~her-~ makes the direction toward the speaker explicit.
en.herhören:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

~Herhören~ directs the listening toward the speaker: „hör mal her“ demands attention his way.
en.herkommen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

Beside „komm her,“ ~herkommen~ carries the figurative sense of origin: „wo etwas herkommt“ is where it comes from.
en.herlaufen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

In practice ~herlaufen~ appears most often as ~vor jemandem herlaufen~: to run on ahead while still moving in the onlooker's direction.
en.herleiten:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~: the causative *~laidijaną~ of the strong verb *~līþaną~ ("to pass, go") with the suffix *~-janą~ ("to cause to go"), from PIE *~leyt-~ ("to go, depart, die"). ~leiten~ and ~leiden~ are a base-and-causative pair. Cognate with English ~lead~ (OE ~lǣdan~).
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. The sense of ~her-~ here is: It can also point backward in time, meaning "from then until now."

From the spatial "to lead hither" came the abstract sense "to derive, deduce": tracing a thought or claim back to its origin.
en.hermachen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

The prefix is largely bleached here: reflexive ~sich hermachen~ means "to set to, approach," while the modern ~viel hermachen~ means "to make an impression."
en.herreisen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

~Herreisen~ denotes traveling toward the speaker's location ("to come here" by way of a journey), and, as a verb of motion, takes the auxiliary ~sein~.
en.herreißen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

~Herreißen~ is tearing in the speaker's direction: to snatch something toward oneself, to grab it up.
en.herrichten:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~ ("to straighten, set right, direct"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rihtijaną~, a denominative from the adjective *~rehtaz~ ("straight, right"), from PIE *~h₃reǵtós~ ("right, straightened"), from *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to stretch out, straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~richten~, Gothic ~raihtjan~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

The prefix is bleached here; ~herrichten~ now simply means "to put in order, get ready," no longer marking any direction.
en.herrschen:
From MHG ~hērschen~, ~hērsen~, from OHG ~hērrisōn~, ~hērisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hairisōn~ ("to be strong, to dominate"). The surface form was remodeled after ~Herr~ already during the MHG period.

~Herr~ itself descends from MHG ~hērre~, OHG ~hēriro~ / ~hērro~, originally the comparative of ~hēr~ ("grey-haired, noble, venerable"), from Proto-Germanic *~hairaz~ ("grey"). Cognates: Dutch ~heer~, Old English ~hār~, English ~hoar~ and ~hoary~, Old Norse ~hárr~. The same root also gives modern German ~hehr~ ("sublime, noble"), so ~Herr~, ~herrschen~, ~herrlich~, and ~Herrschaft~ all descend from an ancestral word meaning "grey-haired," the authority of an elder embedded in each.
en.herrühren:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~rühren~:

• ~rühren~: From MHG ~rüeren~, from OHG ~ruoren~, ~hruoren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōzijaną~; the initial ~hr-~ cluster was gradually simplified in German. The semantic range has stayed stable across a millennium: "to stir," both literally and figuratively. Cognate with Dutch ~roeren~ and the now-rare English ~rear~ ("to move, stir"), surviving in "to rear up."
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. The sense of ~her-~ here is: It can also point backward in time, meaning "from then until now."

From the spatial "to stir from somewhere" came the fixed idiom ~von etwas herrühren~, "to have one's origin in something", origin in time and cause, not motion.
en.hersagen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

~Hersagen~ is saying "out, toward the listener": to recite something from memory, often to reel it off mechanically.
en.herstellen:
Compound of ~her-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, from Proto-Germanic *~hiri~ ("here, hither"), from PIE *~ḱís~ ("this, here"). This separable prefix conveys motion toward the speaker ("hither") as opposed to ~hin-~, which conveys motion away.

~Herstellen~ had a long first life as a purely spatial verb: in the 16th century it meant only "to place here, to set down toward the speaker", the directional counterpart of ~hinstellen~ ("to place over there"). Its modern sense of "to manufacture, to produce" is surprisingly recent, developing only around 1900 as a shortening of ~wiederherstellen~ ("to restore, to reconstruct"). The original ~wiederherstellen~ meant to bring something back to its former state: to restore it to where it had been. When speakers began dropping the ~wieder-~ prefix and using ~herstellen~ alone, the sense broadened from "restore" to "make" in general. This makes ~herstellen~ one of the few common German verbs whose dominant modern meaning is the product of a late semantic compression rather than centuries of gradual development. The noun ~Hersteller~ ("manufacturer, producer") followed the verb into this new sense and is now indispensable in business and product labeling. Cognate with Dutch ~herstellen~ (in the narrower sense of "restore").
en.herumdrehen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). Cognate with English ~throw~ (a true cognate: Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist," a sense that "throw a pot" still keeps) plus English ~thread~, Dutch ~draaien~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. It can also mean simply "the other way around," of turning or reversing something.

Alongside the concrete turning (to ~herumdrehen~ something) stands the phrase ~an etwas herumdrehen~, "to tinker with, to manipulate something."
en.herumfahren:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.

~Herumfahren~ is undirected driving through a space: this way and that, with no fixed destination.
en.herumfliegen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~fliegen~:

• ~fliegen~: From MHG ~vliegen~, from OHG ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"), an extension of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim") that also gave ~fließen~. The vowel path *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of class II strong verbs. Cognate with English ~fly~, Dutch ~vliegen~, Danish ~flyve~.
