• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.

~Herumfliegen~ carries the circling, aimless ~herum-~ over to flying, and, as in Goethe, to whirling in a dance.
en.herumfragen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~fragen~:

• ~fragen~: From MHG ~vrāgen~, from OHG ~frāgēn~, ~frahēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frāgēn~ (a denominative from *~frāgu~, "question"), from Proto-Germanic *~frēgō~ ("question"), from PIE *~preḱ-~ ("to ask"), which also gave Latin ~precor~ and Sanskrit ~pṛcchāti~. Cognate with English ~frain~ (archaic), Dutch ~vragen~, Swedish ~fråga~, Icelandic ~fregna~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.

~Herumfragen~ means to question many people in turn; the ~herum-~ spreads the action across a whole circle of people asked.
en.herumführen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.

~Herumführen~ means to guide someone about a place while showing it; the ~herum-~ turns leading into a tour.
en.herumgehen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.

~Herumgehen~ is walking around something or wandering about aimlessly; as a verb of motion it takes ~sein~.
en.herumhängen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~hängen~:

• ~hängen~: The merger of three OHG verbs: ~hāhan~ (strong, transitive; past ~hieng~, participle ~gehangan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~hą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~hanhaną~; ~hangēn~ (weak, intransitive); and the causative ~hengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hangijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hangijaną~. The distinction is upheld chiefly in the past tense: intransitive ~hing~/~gehangen~ versus transitive ~hängte~/~gehängt~. Cognate with Dutch ~hangen~, English ~hang~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. With verbs of activity it often adds an aimless, idle sense: fiddling about rather than getting anywhere.

~Herumhängen~ carries the idle ~herum-~ over to hanging: to loaf around somewhere with no real purpose.
en.herumkommen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.

~Herumkommen~ means literally "to get around something," figuratively "to see much of the world"; as a verb of motion it takes ~sein~.
en.herumkriegen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~kriegen~:

• ~kriegen~: From MHG ~kriegen~ ("to war, to strive for"), a verbalization of ~Krieg~ ("war"), from OHG ~krig~, from Proto-West Germanic *~krīg~, whose origin is debated. The "obtaining" sense overshadowed the military one; colloquial modern German ~kriegen~ simply means "to get." Cognate with Dutch ~krijgen~ ("to get"), Bavarian ~kriagn~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. It can also mean simply "the other way around," of turning or reversing something.

From the spatial "to turn around" came the figurative sense: to ~herumkriegen~ someone is to bring them around to one's own view.
en.herumlaufen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.

~Herumlaufen~ is running about with no destination; as a verb of motion it takes ~sein~.
en.herumreisen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.

~Herumreisen~ means to travel from place to place without a fixed route; as a verb of motion it takes ~sein~.
en.herumschlagen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. With verbs of activity it often adds an aimless, idle sense: fiddling about rather than getting anywhere.

Reflexive ~sich mit etwas herumschlagen~ means "to struggle wearily and continually with something"; the ~herum-~ turns striking into a grinding, endless wrestle.
en.herumspinnen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~spinnen~:

• ~spinnen~: From MHG ~spinnen~, from OHG ~spinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~spinnaną~, from PIE *~(s)penh₁-~ ("to draw, stretch, spin"). A class III strong verb (~spinnen~, ~spann~, ~gesponnen~). Cognate with English ~spin~, Dutch ~spinnen~, Swedish ~spinna~, Danish ~spinde~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. With verbs of activity it often adds an aimless, idle sense: fiddling about rather than getting anywhere.

Literally "to spin in circles"; colloquially, however, ~herumspinnen~ means "to fool around, to act crazy", the idle ~herum-~ has shifted the sense entirely into the figurative.
en.herumsprechen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~sprechen~:

• ~sprechen~: From MHG ~sprëchen~, from OHG ~sprëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sprekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sprekaną~, probably from PIE *~spregʰ-~ ("to crackle"). The sense developed from an onomatopoeic root meaning "to crackle, make noise" to "to speak." Cognate with Dutch ~spreken~, English ~speak~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.

Reflexive ~sich herumsprechen~ means "to get around," of news spreading from mouth to mouth.
en.herumspringen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~springen~:

• ~springen~: From OHG ~springan~, from Proto-Germanic *~springaną~, from PIE *~sprenǵʰ-~, a nasalized form of *~sperǵʰ-~ ("to move energetically, to hasten, to spring"). A class III strong verb (~springen~, ~sprang~, ~gesprungen~). Cognate with English ~spring~, Dutch ~springen~, Danish ~springe~, Greek ~spérkhō~ ("to hasten").
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.

~Herumspringen~ is boisterous jumping this way and that; as a verb of motion it takes ~sein~.
en.herumstehen:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. ~herum-~ conveys motion around or about something, whether encircling it or milling about within it.

~Herumstehen~ is standing idly about the various spots of a space: standing there doing nothing.
en.herumtreiben:
A separable compound of ~herum-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~herum-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~um~ ("around"); see those entries for their separate histories. In everyday speech it contracts to ~rum~. With verbs of activity it often adds an aimless, idle sense: fiddling about rather than getting anywhere.

The verb is usually reflexive (~sich herumtreiben~) and carries a disreputable tint: to loiter or gad about in bad company rather than merely to move.
en.herunterbrechen:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. ~herunter-~ means downward motion toward the speaker: down from up there to here.

The compound names a thing breaking loose above and falling; the ~herunter-~ supplies the downward path that bare ~brechen~ does not carry on its own.
en.herunterdrücken:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. ~herunter-~ means downward motion toward the speaker: down from up there to here.

Here the motion is literal: forcing something physically downward (a lever, a key, a lid) rather than lowering a figure or a price.
en.herunterfahren:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. ~herunter-~ means downward motion toward the speaker: down from up there to here.

The reading glossed here is the literal one, driving downhill; but the same verb has become the ordinary word for shutting a computer or a plant down.
en.herunterfallen:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. ~herunter-~ means downward motion toward the speaker: down from up there to here.

An intransitive change of place: the thing itself comes down, and the perfect takes ~sein~ (~ist heruntergefallen~), not ~haben~.
en.herunterhalten:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. ~herunter-~ means downward motion toward the speaker: down from up there to here.

Unlike its siblings of motion, this one names a maintained position: keeping a thing held low, resisting its rise rather than bringing it down.
en.herunterhandeln:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~handeln~:

• ~handeln~: From MHG ~handeln~, from OHG ~hantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handulōn~, a denominative verb from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~ ("hand") with the frequentative suffix *~-lōną~; the sense broadened from "to handle" to "to act, deal, trade." Cognate with English ~handle~, Dutch ~handelen~, Danish ~handle~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. By extension it means reducing something: bringing a price, a volume, or a fever down.

What is brought down here is a price: to bargain a seller into a lower figure through persistent haggling.
en.herunterkommen:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. ~herunter-~ means downward motion toward the speaker: down from up there to here.

The literal descent is transparent, but the participle ~heruntergekommen~ has hardened into an adjective for a person or place gone to seed, a figurative fall the bare verb never took.
en.herunterladen:
A calque of English ~download~. Compound of ~herunter-~ ("down") + ~laden~ ("to load"):

• ~laden~: From MHG ~laden~ (strong verb), from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~ ("to load"), from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"). Cognate with English ~laden~ and ~lade~. Related to Lithuanian ~klóti~ ("to lay, spread, pave"), Russian ~klad~ ("treasure", something laid away).
• ~herunter-~: From ~her~ ("hither, toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"), ultimately from PIE *~ḱís~ ("this, here") + *~n̥dʰér~ ("under").

~Herunterladen~ is a modern German calque (loan-translation) of English ~download~, mapping ~down-~ to ~herunter-~ and ~-load~ to ~-laden~. The strong conjugation of ~laden~ (~lädt~, ~lud~, ~geladen~) carries over, producing forms like ~er lädt herunter~, ~er lud herunter~, ~er hat heruntergeladen~. The competing anglicism ~downloaden~ also exists in colloquial German but is considered less standard. The informal contraction ~runterladen~ is common in everyday speech. The antonym ~hochladen~ ("to upload") follows the same calque pattern. These digital-age compounds demonstrate German's productive capacity for translating English technical vocabulary through native morphology rather than simply borrowing, a tradition stretching back to seventeenth-century language purists like Philipp von Zesen.
en.heruntermachen:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. By extension it means reducing something: bringing a price, a volume, or a fever down.

Here the downward figure has turned social: to ~jemanden heruntermachen~ is to run a person down, to belittle, a use that stretches the reducing sense to a person's standing.
en.herunterrutschen:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~rutschen~:

• ~rutschen~: From MHG ~rutzen~, ~rützen~, an onomatopoeic formation imitating the sound of sliding, with a later shift from ~-tz-~ to ~-tsch-~ (as in ~fletschen~); perhaps related to OHG ~rūtezzen~. The noun ~Rutsche~ ("slide, chute") derives from the verb. English ~rutch~ and ~rutsch~ are borrowed from German or its Low German cognates.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. ~herunter-~ means downward motion toward the speaker: down from up there to here.

A gliding descent rather than a fall: the thing keeps contact with a surface as it goes down, and like other verbs of motion it takes ~sein~ in the perfect.
en.heruntersetzen:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. By extension it means reducing something: bringing a price, a volume, or a fever down.

The thing set lower here is typically a price or a rank: to mark a good down, or to demote, the transitive counterpart to a figure that has come down on its own.
en.herunterspielen:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. By extension it means reducing something: bringing a price, a volume, or a fever down.

The figurative object here is significance: to play a matter down, to make it seem smaller than it is, reducing not a quantity but the weight given to something.
en.herunterstoßen:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). Cognate with dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce, ricochet"), Dutch ~stoten~, Old Norse ~stauta~ and ~steyta~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. ~herunter-~ means downward motion toward the speaker: down from up there to here.

A violent, transitive descent: the subject drives something down by force, rather than merely letting it drop.
en.herunterziehen:
A separable compound of ~herunter-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~herunter-~: The compound adverb ~her~ ("toward the speaker") + ~unter~ ("under"); see those entries for their separate histories. Colloquially it contracts to ~runter~. ~herunter-~ means downward motion toward the speaker: down from up there to here.

The subject draws something down toward itself (a blind, a hat brim, a corner of the mouth) the pulling counterpart to shoving or dropping.
en.hervorbrechen:
A separable compound of ~hervor-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~hervor-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~ "forward, in front"), together "forth and toward the speaker", out from behind or beneath something, into view. ~hervor-~ marks emergence into view, "forth, out from."

The verb keeps the suddenness of ~brechen~: what emerges does so with force (light from cloud, water from rock, an army from cover), bursting into view rather than easing into it.
en.hervorbringen:
A separable compound of ~hervor-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~hervor-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~ "forward, in front"), together "forth and toward the speaker", out from behind or beneath something, into view. ~hervor-~ marks emergence into view, "forth, out from."

Causative where its siblings are intransitive: the subject brings something forth (a sound, a fruit, a work), making it emerge rather than emerging itself.
en.hervorgehen:
A separable compound of ~hervor-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~hervor-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~ "forward, in front"), together "forth and toward the speaker", out from behind or beneath something, into view. ~hervor-~ marks emergence into view, "forth, out from."

Here the emergence has gone wholly abstract: one fact ~geht aus~ another ~hervor~ (proceeds, results, follows from it) the spatial "coming forth" turned into logical consequence.
en.hervorheben:
Compound of ~hervor-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~ (rarer ~heffen~), from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~ ("to lift, to heave"), from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, to grasp"). Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~haeve~.
• ~hervor-~: A compound prefix from ~her-~ (from PIE *~ḱís~, "this (here)," conveying motion toward the speaker) + ~vor-~ (from PIE *~preh₂~, "before, in front"), together meaning "forth, out from."

~Hervorheben~ means "to emphasize, to highlight, to bring forth", literally to lift something out into view. The noun ~Hervorhebung~ ("emphasis, highlighting") is used in typography, rhetoric, and everyday speech. The PIE root *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, to grasp") connects lifting with grasping across the Indo-European branches: Latin ~capiō~ ("I seize") gave English ~capture~, ~capable~, ~accept~, and ~anticipate~. The related noun ~Hefe~ ("yeast") preserves the original fricative: yeast is literally "that which lifts" the dough.
en.hervorrufen:
Compound of ~hervor-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~, ~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hropan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hropaną~ ("to call, to cry out"). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~ ("to call"), English dialectal ~roop~.
• ~hervor-~: From ~her~ ("hither, toward the speaker") + ~vor~ ("before, forward"). The element ~her~ descends from OHG ~hera~, from Proto-Germanic *~hiz~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kis~ ("this, here"). The element ~vor~ descends from OHG ~fora~, from Proto-Germanic *~fura~, from Proto-Indo-European *~per~ ("before, in front"). Together they convey "forward out toward the speaker."

The compound literally means "to call forth (toward the speaker)," hence "to cause, to evoke, to provoke." One ~ruft~ Gefühle ~hervor~ ("calls forth feelings") or ~ruft~ eine Reaktion ~hervor~ ("provokes a reaction"). The OHG form ~hruofan~ preserves an initial ~h-~ that was later lost, a common Germanic development (compare ~hring~ becoming ~Ring~). The metaphor of causation as summoning (calling something out of hiding into existence) is shared with English ~evoke~ (from Latin ~evocare~, "to call out") and ~provoke~ (from Latin ~provocare~, "to call forth").
en.hervorsehen:
A separable compound of ~hervor-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~hervor-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~ "forward, in front"), together "forth and toward the speaker", out from behind or beneath something, into view. ~hervor-~ marks emergence into view, "forth, out from."

The verb is intransitive and quiet: a thing merely lets itself be seen, peeping out from behind or beneath something into view.
en.hervorstechen:
A separable compound of ~hervor-~ + ~stechen~:

• ~stechen~: From MHG ~stëchen~, from OHG ~stëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stekaną~ ("to stab, prick"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to stick, poke"). Cognate with Dutch ~steken~ ("to stab, sting"), Old Norse ~stinga~, English ~stick~ (originally "to stab, pierce").
• ~hervor-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~ "forward, in front"), together "forth and toward the speaker", out from behind or beneath something, into view. Figuratively, of something standing out or being brought to notice (~hervorheben~, ~hervorragen~).

The literal ~stechen~ (to prick) survives here only as a metaphor: a thing so prominent it seems to jab the eye, standing out sharply from its surroundings.
en.hervortauchen:
A separable compound of ~hervor-~ + ~tauchen~:

• ~tauchen~: From MHG ~tūchen~, ~touchen~, from OHG *~tūhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dūkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dūkaną~ ("to duck, to dive under"), whose further etymology is uncertain. A class II strong verb that became weak in the early modern period: when it was reintroduced from Central and Low German, the strong conjugation was regularized to weak. Cognate with Dutch ~duiken~, Swedish ~dyka~; a Low German consonant variant of the same root is ~ducken~, cognate with English ~duck~.
• ~hervor-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~ "forward, in front"), together "forth and toward the speaker", out from behind or beneath something, into view. ~hervor-~ marks emergence into view, "forth, out from."

The image is of surfacing: a thing rises into view as a diver breaks the water, the ~tauchen~ lending the emergence a sense of coming up from below or behind.
en.hervortreten:
A separable compound of ~hervor-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~hervor-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~ "forward, in front"), together "forth and toward the speaker", out from behind or beneath something, into view. ~hervor-~ marks emergence into view, "forth, out from."

The most literal of the group: someone or something physically steps forth into view, whence the figurative use of a feature that becomes prominent.
en.hervorziehen:
A separable compound of ~hervor-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~hervor-~: A transparent compound of ~her-~ ("hither," marking motion toward the speaker, from OHG ~hera~, from the Proto-Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~, from PIE *~ḱi-~ "this") and ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~ "forward, in front"), together "forth and toward the speaker", out from behind or beneath something, into view. ~hervor-~ marks emergence into view, "forth, out from."

The pulling counterpart of the group: the subject draws something out from concealment (a wallet, a weapon, a hidden thing) into the open.
en.herzeigen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~zeigen~:

• ~zeigen~: From MHG ~zeigen~, from OHG ~zeigōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taigōn~, possibly from Proto-Germanic *~taikōną~ (iterative), an intensive derivative of OHG ~zīhan~ ("to accuse"), ultimately from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to point out, show"), whence also ~Zeichen~ ("sign") and English ~teach~. In Modern German it absorbed the unrelated MHG ~zöugen~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

The ~her-~ turns the showing toward the speaker: to hold a thing out for the onlooker to see, a slightly regional, homely variant of plain ~zeigen~.
en.herziehen:
A separable compound of ~her-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~her-~: From MHG ~her~, from OHG ~hera~, belonging to the Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ ("this, here"), from PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"), the same stem that yields ~hier~ and ~heute~ ("this day"). Cognate with English ~here~ and, through the same demonstrative, English ~he~. ~her-~ marks motion toward the speaker ("hither") and is the exact counterpart of ~hin-~, which marks motion away from the speaker. This opposition is the organizing fact of the whole deictic group.

In the glossed sense the ~her-~ names relocation toward the speaker: to move one's home here; the mined sentence instead attests the older ~hinter jemandem herziehen~, trailing along behind someone.
en.herüberkommen:
A separable compound of ~herüber-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~herüber-~: The deictic adverb ~her-~ plus the particle ~über~ ("over, across"): motion across and toward the speaker. ~Her-~ points toward the speaker and ~hin-~ away from the speaker (the single fact that unlocks this whole family) so ~herüber~ is "over to this side" and ~hinüber~ "over to that one." Colloquially contracted to ~rüber~. See the entries for ~her-~ and ~über~. The sense of ~herüber-~ here is: across, toward the speaker.

As an intransitive verb of motion, ~herüberkommen~ takes the auxiliary ~sein~; it always presupposes a speaker, on whose side the motion ends.
en.hierbleiben:
A separable compound of ~hier-~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~hier-~: The adverb ~hier~ ("here"), from MHG ~hier~, from OHG ~hier~, from Proto-Germanic *~hēr~, formed to the demonstrative stem *~hi-~ ("this"), from PIE *~ḱe-~ ("this, here"). As a particle it simply fixes the action at the speaker's location, as in ~hierbleiben~ ("to stay here"). Cognate with English ~here~, Dutch ~hier~, Old Norse ~hér~, Gothic ~hēr~; the same demonstrative stem sits inside English ~he~ and German ~heute~, originally "on this day." The sense of ~hier-~ here is: staying or remaining put.

Both parts remain ordinary free words, so the compound is wholly transparent; like ~bleiben~ it forms its perfect with ~sein~: ~ist hiergeblieben~.
en.hierhergehören:
A separable compound of ~hierher-~ + ~ge-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.
• ~hierher-~: The adverb ~hier~ ("here") compounded with the deictic ~her~ ("hither"): literally "here-hither". Like the rest of the ~her-~ / ~hin-~ family it is transparently compositional (~her-~ points motion toward the speaker, ~hin-~ away from the speaker), and its etymology is that of its two parts. The sense of ~hierher-~ here is: directional, "to this place, over here".

In ~gehören~ the base has drifted far from ~hören~ "to hear" and means "to belong"; ~hierher-~ adds the location, so the whole means to belong in this place, and, said of a remark, to be relevant here.
en.hierherkommen:
A separable compound of ~hierher-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~hierher-~: The adverb ~hier~ ("here") compounded with the deictic ~her~ ("hither"): literally "here-hither". Like the rest of the ~her-~ / ~hin-~ family it is transparently compositional (~her-~ points motion toward the speaker, ~hin-~ away from the speaker), and its etymology is that of its two parts. The sense of ~hierher-~ here is: directional, "to this place, over here".

With ~kommen~ the compound is fully transparent (to come to this place) and, like other motion verbs, forms its perfect with ~sein~.
en.hinabklettern:
A separable compound of ~hinab-~ + ~klettern~:

• ~klettern~: An iterative verb formed in Early New High German from ~kletten~, from PIE *~gleyt-~ ("to cling to, cleave, stick"), from the root *~gley-~ ("to stick, smear"). The iterative ~-ern~ suffix emphasizes repeated action. Related to ~Klette~ ("burr") and to ~Kleid~ ("garment"), originally something that clings to the body.
• ~hinab-~: The deictic adverb ~hin~ ("thither, away from the speaker") compounded with ~ab~ ("off, down"): motion downward and away. Transparently compositional; the etymology belongs to the two component entries, and the deictic contrast is with ~herab~ ("down toward the speaker"). The sense of ~hinab-~ here is: directional, "down, downward".

~Klettern~ contributes the manner (a scrambling, hand-and-foot descent rather than a plain walk down), and the iterative ~-ern~ keeps the sense of repeated clutching even on the way down.
en.hinabsteigen:
A separable compound of ~hinab-~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~hinab-~: The deictic adverb ~hin~ ("thither, away from the speaker") compounded with ~ab~ ("off, down"): motion downward and away. Transparently compositional; the etymology belongs to the two component entries, and the deictic contrast is with ~herab~ ("down toward the speaker"). The sense of ~hinab-~ here is: directional, "down, downward".

~Steigen~ by itself says only "move on a gradient" (it serves ~hinauf-~ as readily as ~hinab-~), so here the particle alone fixes the direction as downward and away from the speaker.
en.hinarbeiten:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle conveys motion toward a destination, paired against ~her-~ for motion toward the speaker.

Here the motion is figurative: one travels nowhere but directs sustained effort toward a goal, ~auf etwas hinarbeiten~, the particle pointing at the aim rather than a place.
en.hinaufgeben:
A separable compound of ~hinauf-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~hinauf-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and away from the speaker", the climb seen from the bottom. Its mirror image is ~herauf~, the same ascent toward the speaker. ~hinauf-~ marks upward motion oriented away from the speaker.

~Geben~ contributes the transfer and ~hinauf-~ the direction: to hand or pass something up to a higher place.
en.hinaufgehen:
A separable compound of ~hinauf-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~hinauf-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and away from the speaker", the climb seen from the bottom. Its mirror image is ~herauf~, the same ascent toward the speaker. ~hinauf-~ marks upward motion oriented away from the speaker.

With ~gehen~ the compound is the plain intransitive to go up (on foot, away from the speaker) and, like other motion verbs, forms its perfect with ~sein~.
en.hinaufhalten:
A separable compound of ~hinauf-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~hinauf-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and away from the speaker", the climb seen from the bottom. Its mirror image is ~herauf~, the same ascent toward the speaker. ~hinauf-~ marks upward motion oriented away from the speaker.

~Halten~ "to hold" with the upward particle gives "to hold something up": raising an object into a higher position rather than moving oneself.
en.hinaufschauen:
A separable compound of ~hinauf-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~hinauf-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and away from the speaker", the climb seen from the bottom. Its mirror image is ~herauf~, the same ascent toward the speaker. ~hinauf-~ marks upward motion oriented away from the speaker.

With ~schauen~ (the southern, Austrian and Swiss verb for looking) the gaze itself travels upward and away, to look up at something above; ~heraufschauen~ would turn the same look toward the speaker.
en.hinaufsteigen:
A separable compound of ~hinauf-~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~hinauf-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~auf~ ("up, onto"), so "upward and away from the speaker", the climb seen from the bottom. Its mirror image is ~herauf~, the same ascent toward the speaker. ~hinauf-~ marks upward motion oriented away from the speaker.

Again the neutral ~steigen~ carries only the vertical motion; the particle alone fixes the direction: here as an ascent, away from the speaker and toward a height, the exact opposite of a descent.
en.hinausbringen:
A separable compound of ~hinaus-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~hinaus-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. Colloquially it contracts to ~raus~, a contraction it shares with ~heraus~. Its counterpart ~heraus-~ traces the same outward path toward the speaker: the one inside goes ~hinaus~, and the one already outside watches him come ~heraus~.

~Bringen~ carries an object along, so ~hinausbringen~ is to convey something out (to carry or see it outside), while the counterpart ~herausbringen~ moves the same load toward the speaker.
en.hinausgeben:
A separable compound of ~hinaus-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~hinaus-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. Colloquially it contracts to ~raus~, a contraction it shares with ~heraus~. Its counterpart ~heraus-~ traces the same outward path toward the speaker: the one inside goes ~hinaus~, and the one already outside watches him come ~heraus~.

~Geben~ supplies the transfer and ~hinaus-~ the outward, speaker-distal path, so the compound is to hand or give something out, of a house or window, or, in older usage, to marry a daughter out of the family.
en.hinausgehen:
A separable compound of ~hinaus-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~hinaus-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. Colloquially it contracts to ~raus~, a contraction it shares with ~heraus~. ~hinaus-~ means motion out of something, directed away from the speaker.

With ~gehen~ the compound is the everyday to go out: out of a room or building and away from the speaker; figuratively ~über etwas hinausgehen~ is to exceed or go beyond it.
en.hinaushalten:
A separable compound of ~hinaus-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~hinaus-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. Colloquially it contracts to ~raus~, a contraction it shares with ~heraus~. With expressions of time or measure it means "beyond," going past a limit.

Here the particle is temporal, not spatial: ~hinaushalten~ is to hold out, to stretch something out beyond the point where it should have ended.
en.hinauskommen:
A separable compound of ~hinaus-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~hinaus-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. Colloquially it contracts to ~raus~, a contraction it shares with ~heraus~. Its counterpart ~heraus-~ traces the same outward path toward the speaker: the one inside goes ~hinaus~, and the one already outside watches him come ~heraus~.

With ~kommen~ the compound is the intransitive to come out, reaching the outside from within; figuratively ~über etwas nicht hinauskommen~ is to fail to get past a stage.
en.hinauslaufen:
A separable compound of ~hinaus-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~hinaus-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. Colloquially it contracts to ~raus~, a contraction it shares with ~heraus~. ~hinaus-~ means motion out of something, directed away from the speaker.

With ~laufen~ the literal sense is to run out; but the compound is better known figuratively (~auf etwas hinauslaufen~, "to amount to, to come down to"), where the running-out becomes a metaphor for where a matter finally ends up.
en.hinauslehnen:
A separable compound of ~hinaus-~ + ~lehnen~:

• ~lehnen~: A merger of two verbs: MHG ~linen~/~lenen~ (intransitive), from OHG ~hlinēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlinēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlināną~, from PIE *~k̂ley-~ ("to lean, incline"); and MHG ~leinen~ (causative), from OHG ~hleinen~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlainijaną~. A second, archaic ~lehnen~ ("to lend, borrow"), from OHG ~lēhanōn~, survives only in ~entlehnen~ and ~Lehnwort~. Cognate with English ~lean~, Latin ~clīnō~.
• ~hinaus-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. Colloquially it contracts to ~raus~, a contraction it shares with ~heraus~. Its counterpart ~heraus-~ traces the same outward path toward the speaker: the one inside goes ~hinaus~, and the one already outside watches him come ~heraus~.

~Lehnen~ here is the intransitive "lean" branch (see the two-verb merger in the bullet), used reflexively: ~sich hinauslehnen~, to lean oneself out and away from the speaker: from a window or over a railing.
en.hinausschieben:
A separable compound of ~hinaus-~ + ~schieben~:

• ~schieben~: From MHG ~schieben~, from OHG ~skioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeubaną~, from PIE *~skewbʰ-~ ("to push, to shove, to thrust"). A class II strong verb (~schieben~, ~schob~, ~geschoben~). Cognate with English ~shove~, Dutch ~schuiven~, Danish ~skubbe~.
• ~hinaus-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. Colloquially it contracts to ~raus~, a contraction it shares with ~heraus~. With expressions of time or measure it means "beyond," going past a limit.

~Schieben~ "to push" with the particle's temporal sense yields to postpone: to push a matter out beyond its appointed time rather than through space.
en.hinauswerfen:
A separable compound of ~hinaus-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~hinaus-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~aus~ ("out"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. Colloquially it contracts to ~raus~, a contraction it shares with ~heraus~. ~hinaus-~ means motion out of something, directed away from the speaker.

~Werfen~ "to throw" gives the forceful member of the set: ~hinauswerfen~ is to throw or fling something out, and idiomatically to eject or fire a person.
en.hinbekommen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~be-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle conveys setting something down in a particular place.

Both prefixes are bleached here: ~bekommen~ has long meant "to get" rather than "to come to," and ~hin-~ adds not a real direction but the sense of getting something into shape, so the colloquial compound means to manage or pull something off.
en.hindern: From Middle High German ~hindern~, from Old High German ~hintaren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hindrōną~ ("to hinder"), derived from the adverb *~hinder~ ("back, behind"). The adverb itself likely comes from PIE *~ḱem-tér-~ ("down, back, through"), from *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near"), though an alternative theory derives it from *~ḱís~ ("this"). The semantic path from "behind" to "to obstruct" is intuitive: what is behind you blocks the way forward. Cognate with English ~hinder~, Dutch ~hinderen~. The related Latin ~contrā~ ("against") descends from the same PIE root, making ~hindern~ a distant cousin of English ~counter~ and ~contrary~.
en.hindeuten:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~deuten~:

• ~deuten~: From MHG ~diuten~, from OHG ~diuten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þiudijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þiudijaną~ ("to interpret; to point out"), from *~þeudō~ ("people"), from PIE *~tewtéh₂~ ("people"), originally "to make intelligible to the people," the same word that gives ~deutsch~. Cognate with Dutch ~duiden~, Icelandic ~þýða~, Swedish ~tyda~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle conveys motion toward a destination, paired against ~her-~ for motion toward the speaker.

Here the motion is figurative and gestural: ~auf etwas hindeuten~ is to point at a thing, the particle directing attention toward it; extended, facts or signs "point to" a conclusion.
en.hindurchgehen:
A separable compound of ~hindurch-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~hindurch-~: The deictic adverb ~hin-~ plus the particle ~durch~ ("through"): motion through something and away from the speaker. ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; ~hindurch~ therefore traces a path all the way out the far side, and it is used of stretches of time endured from end to end as readily as of space. See the entries for ~hin-~ and ~durch~. The sense of ~hindurch-~ here is: away from the speaker, passing through something.

With ~gehen~ the compound stays literal and spatial (to pass through and out the far side, as through a parted sea) leaving the temporal "throughout" reading to contexts of duration.
en.hineinblicken:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~blank~, Dutch ~blik~, Old English ~blice~.
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. ~hinein-~ means motion into something, directed away from the speaker.

~Blicken~ makes it the gaze, not the body, that travels inward: ~hineinblicken~ is to look into something, directed away from the speaker: into a room, a container, or, figuratively, into oneself.
en.hineinbringen:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. ~hinein-~ means motion into something, directed away from the speaker.

~Bringen~ conveys an object, so ~hineinbringen~ is to take or carry something in, into an enclosed space and away from the speaker; ~hereinbringen~ would move the same thing inward toward the speaker.
en.hineingeben:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. ~hinein-~ means motion into something, directed away from the speaker.

~Geben~ supplies the transfer and ~hinein-~ the inward, speaker-distal path: to put or add something into something: in southern usage especially of adding an ingredient to a dish.
en.hineingehen:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. ~hinein-~ means motion into something, directed away from the speaker.

The literal sense of stepping from outside to inside extends figuratively to entering into a situation.
en.hineinkommen:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. ~hinein-~ means motion into something, directed away from the speaker.

It often denotes getting in through a narrow opening, as in the image of the foot that will not go into the shoe.
en.hineinmischen:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~mischen~:

• ~mischen~: From MHG ~mischen~, from OHG ~misken~, from Proto-Germanic *~miskijaną~ ("to mix"), from PIE *~meyḱ-~ ("to mix, knead"), via the inchoative present *~miḱ-sḱé-~. Cognate with English ~mix~, Latin ~misceō~, Greek ~mísgo~, Sanskrit ~miśrá~ ("mixed").
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. Figuratively it marks throwing oneself into an activity or a situation.

Used reflexively (~sich hineinmischen~) it denotes meddling uninvited in others' affairs; in Nietzsche the older, more concrete notion of mixing something into things is at work.
en.hineinpassen:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~passen~:

• ~passen~: Borrowed from French ~passer~, with Dutch ~passen~ as intermediary, from Old French ~passer~, from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, a denominative of Latin ~passus~ ("step, pace"), from ~pandō~ ("to spread"), from PIE *~pet-~ ("to spread, extend"). A false friend: ~passen~ most often means "to fit, to suit," not "to pass by." Cognate with English ~pass~ and ~pace~.
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. ~hinein-~ means motion into something, directed away from the speaker.

It denotes that an object or person fits exactly into a given space or frame.
en.hineinrufen:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. A parallel weak form in Middle High German explains why the modern present lacks the expected umlaut (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. ~hinein-~ means motion into something, directed away from the speaker.

Here it is the voice, not the speaker, that performs the inward motion; one calls from outside into a space.
en.hineinspielen:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. Figuratively it marks throwing oneself into an activity or a situation.

Figuratively ~hineinspielen~ means to enter into a matter as a contributing factor, a circumstance that plays a part in something.
en.hineinstecken:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~stecken~:

• ~stecken~: Modern ~stecken~ merges two verbs: the transitive weak one ("to put, stick something in") from MHG ~stecken~, OHG ~steckōn~, a geminate derivative of ~stëhhan~ (the ancestor of ~stechen~), and the strong intransitive one (archaic ~stak~/~gestocken~, "to be stuck"); the two fused in Early Modern German. Both trace to Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stikaną~, from PIE *~(s)teyg-~ ("to be sharp, stab, goad"). Cognate with English ~stick~ and ~steak~.
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. ~hinein-~ means motion into something, directed away from the speaker.

Concretely it means pushing an object in, like a key into a lock; figuratively one puts money or effort into something.
en.hineinversetzen:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~ver-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. Figuratively it marks throwing oneself into an activity or a situation.

Reflexively (~sich in jemanden hineinversetzen~), it denotes mentally transposing oneself into another's position; ~ver-~ supplies the displacement, ~hinein-~ the goal.
en.hineinziehen:
A separable compound of ~hinein-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~hinein-~: The compound adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~ein~ ("in"); see the ~her~ entry for the deictic pair. ~Hin~ comes from MHG ~hin~, from OHG ~hina~, from the same Germanic deictic stem *~hi-~ that gives ~her~ and ~hier~. Colloquially it contracts to ~rein~, a contraction it shares with ~herein~. ~hinein-~ means motion into something, directed away from the speaker.

Concretely it pulls a body inward, as the hand in Luther's verse; figuratively one draws someone into a quarrel or affair.
en.hinfahren:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

Transitively ~hinfahren~ means to drive someone to a place; in Goethe the older, generalized sense of coasting along in the rut of habit is at work.
en.hinfallen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

Built with the auxiliary ~sein~, it denotes falling to the ground; ~hin-~ gives the motion its goal, the ground.
en.hingeben:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

Literally giving away from one's hand; reflexively (~sich hingeben~) it denotes devoting oneself wholly to a cause or person.
en.hingehen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

Beside the spatial sense stands the figurative use for the passing of time (~die Tage gehen hin~).
en.hingehören:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~ge-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

The compound denotes that something belongs in a particular place; ~hin-~ names the spot into which it fits.
en.hingucken:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~gucken~:

• ~gucken~: From MHG ~gücken~, ~guggen~ ("to look inquisitively, to peek"), of uncertain origin, perhaps from MHG ~gücken~, OHG ~guckōn~ ("to cuckoo"), via the image of peeping out from cover. The variant ~kucken~ is attributed to influence from Low German ~kieken~. Colloquial and northern/central German; the south prefers ~schauen~. Cognate with Dutch ~kijken~, Luxembourgish ~kucken~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

A colloquial, northern and central German counterpart to ~hinsehen~; ~hin-~ directs the gaze to a point.
en.hinhalten:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

Concretely one holds something out to someone, like the old man's hat in Mann; figuratively ~hinhalten~ means to put someone off with empty promises.
en.hinhören:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

~Hin-~ directs the hearing toward a source; the verb means attentive, focused listening, not mere hearing.
en.hinkommen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

Unlike ~hingehen~, ~hinkommen~ stresses arrival at the goal; colloquially also "to suffice" or "to be about right" (~das kommt hin~).
en.hinkriegen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~kriegen~:

• ~kriegen~: From MHG ~kriegen~ ("to war, to strive for"), a verbalization of ~Krieg~ ("war"), from OHG ~krig~, from Proto-West Germanic *~krīg~, whose origin is debated. The "obtaining" sense overshadowed the military one; colloquial modern German ~kriegen~ simply means "to get." Cognate with Dutch ~krijgen~ ("to get"), Bavarian ~kriagn~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

Colloquially ~hinkriegen~ means to bring something off or get it into order, an idiomatic turn on ~kriegen~ "to get" that has left the spatial sense of ~hin-~ behind.
en.hinlegen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~.
