Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle conveys setting something down in a particular place.

The transitive counterpart to ~hinfallen~: one lays something down at a place; colloquially "to pull off a great performance."
en.hinnehmen:
From Middle High German ~hinnemen~, from Old High German ~hinaneman~. Compound of ~hin-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due").
• ~hin-~: From Old High German ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from PIE *~ḱís~ ("this, here"). This directional prefix indicates motion away from the speaker.

The literal sense is "to take away," but the modern meaning has shifted to "to accept, to put up with", often with a connotation of reluctant resignation. The PIE root *~nem-~ is the ancestor of Greek ~nemein~ ("to distribute"), which gave rise to ~Nemesis~, the goddess who distributed what was due. English ~nimble~ is a cognate through the same Germanic root. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, Danish ~nemme~ ("to learn, grasp").
en.hinreisen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

~Hin-~ names the destination of the journey; the verb stresses traveling there rather than arriving.
en.hinreißen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

Concretely a tearing away; figuratively, and so most often used, enthusiasm or passion carries a person off, as Goethe's narrator is swept away into lively sympathy.
en.hinrichten:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~ ("to straighten, set right, direct"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rihtijaną~, a denominative from the adjective *~rehtaz~ ("straight, right"), from PIE *~h₃reǵtós~ ("right, straightened"), from *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to stretch out, straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~richten~, Gothic ~raihtjan~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

The modern sense "to execute" grew together from ~richten~ "to set in order, to deal with someone" and ~hin-~ "away, to naught"; to ~hinrichten~ someone originally meant to dispatch him to his end.
en.hinrücken:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~rücken~:

• ~rücken~: From MHG ~rücken~, from OHG ~rucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rukkijan~. The verb means "to move, to shift" and is the base of ~verrückt~ ("crazy," literally "shifted, displaced"); the noun ~Rücken~ ("back") is etymologically a separate word. Cognate with English ~rock~, Old Norse ~rykkja~, Old English ~roccian~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

~Rücken~ means shifting with a jerk; ~hin-~ gives the direction: in Luther, being caught up into the clouds.
en.hinschauen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

Like ~hingucken~, but stylistically more neutral; ~schauen~ is moreover the ordinary word for "to see" in southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage.
en.hinschreiben:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle conveys setting something down in a particular place.

~Hinschreiben~ applies that placing to writing: the words are set down onto the page, often quickly and in passing.
en.hinsehen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

In ~hinsehen~ it is the gaze rather than the body that travels toward the point in view.
en.hinsetzen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle conveys setting something down in a particular place.

Used reflexively (~sich hinsetzen~) the subject sets themselves down into the place where they then sit.
en.hinstellen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle conveys setting something down in a particular place.

Like its base ~stellen~, ~hinstellen~ sets the object down upright, not laid flat.
en.hinsterben:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~sterben~:

• ~sterben~: From MHG ~stërben~, from OHG ~stërban~, from Proto-Germanic *~sterbaną~, from PIE *~(s)terp-~ ("to lose force, become numb") or *~sterbʰ-~ ("to become stiff"), both traceable to *~ster-~ ("stiff, rigid"). A class III strong verb (~stirbt~, ~starb~, ~gestorben~). Cognate with English ~starve~, Dutch ~sterven~, West Frisian ~stjerre~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

Here the spatial motion fades into a perfective „away“ sense: to ~hinsterben~ is to die off, to pass slowly away.
en.hinstürzen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~stürzen~:

• ~stürzen~: From MHG ~stürzen~, from OHG ~sturzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sturtijan~ ("to fall down, tumble"), of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly from PIE *~ster-~ ("to be stiff") via a dental extension *~sterd-~, though the derivation is debated. Cognate with English ~start~, a doublet from the same Proto-West Germanic source, from which the meanings have diverged radically.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

~Hinstürzen~ joins the directional goal to the violence of ~stürzen~: a hurried, often headlong rush toward a place.
en.hintanhalten:
A separable compound of ~hintan-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~hintan-~: A fossilized adverb, no longer used on its own. It arose in MHG by univerbation of ~hin~ + ~dan~ (an older local form of ~dann~), and was afterwards reanalyzed as ~hint~ (a variant of today's ~hinten~, "at the back") plus ~an~, a folk etymology that stuck. It means "to the rear, out of the way," and survives only in a small set of elevated, faintly bureaucratic verbs: ~hintanstellen~ and ~hintansetzen~ ("to set aside, subordinate"), ~hintanhalten~ ("to hold off"). The sense of ~hintan-~ here is: held off, kept at a distance.

Applied to ~halten~, this is to keep something (a danger, a disadvantage) at a distance and from coming to pass.
en.hintanlegen:
A separable compound of ~hintan-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~hintan-~: A fossilized adverb, no longer used on its own. It arose in MHG by univerbation of ~hin~ + ~dan~ (an older local form of ~dann~), and was afterwards reanalyzed as ~hint~ (a variant of today's ~hinten~, "at the back") plus ~an~, a folk etymology that stuck. It means "to the rear, out of the way," and survives only in a small set of elevated, faintly bureaucratic verbs: ~hintanstellen~ and ~hintansetzen~ ("to set aside, subordinate"), ~hintanhalten~ ("to hold off"). The sense of ~hintan-~ here is: to the rear, set behind other things.

~Hintanlegen~ sets something toward the back, behind what matters more, a rare, elevated formation met almost only in bureaucratic register today.
en.hintansetzen:
A separable compound of ~hintan-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~hintan-~: A fossilized adverb, no longer used on its own. It arose in MHG by univerbation of ~hin~ + ~dan~ (an older local form of ~dann~), and was afterwards reanalyzed as ~hint~ (a variant of today's ~hinten~, "at the back") plus ~an~, a folk etymology that stuck. It means "to the rear, out of the way," and survives only in a small set of elevated, faintly bureaucratic verbs: ~hintanstellen~ and ~hintansetzen~ ("to set aside, subordinate"), ~hintanhalten~ ("to hold off"). The sense of ~hintan-~ here is: subordinated, given lower priority.

With ~setzen~ it means to rate something lower and place it behind other concerns.
en.hintanstellen:
A separable compound of ~hintan-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~hintan-~: A fossilized adverb, no longer used on its own. It arose in MHG by univerbation of ~hin~ + ~dan~ (an older local form of ~dann~), and was afterwards reanalyzed as ~hint~ (a variant of today's ~hinten~, "at the back") plus ~an~, a folk etymology that stuck. It means "to the rear, out of the way," and survives only in a small set of elevated, faintly bureaucratic verbs: ~hintanstellen~ and ~hintansetzen~ ("to set aside, subordinate"), ~hintanhalten~ ("to hold off"). The sense of ~hintan-~ here is: to the rear, set behind other things.

~Hintanstellen~ is the commonest of these formations and lives mostly in its figurative sense: to set something back, to deny it priority.
en.hinterfragen:
A modern compound of ~hinter-~ + ~fragen~:

• ~fragen~: From MHG ~vrāgen~, from OHG ~frāgēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frāgēn~. Cognate with Dutch ~vragen~, Swedish ~fråga~, English dialectal ~frain~ ("to inquire").
• ~hinter-~: From Old High German ~hintar~ ("behind"), from Proto-Germanic *~hinder~, ultimately from PIE *~ḱís~ ("this, here") via a comparative formation. As an inseparable verbal prefix, ~hinter-~ adds a sense of going behind or beneath the surface.

The verb ~hinterfragen~ means "to question critically, to scrutinize", literally to ask behind something, probing beyond the surface. It is a relatively recent coinage, entering standard German in the twentieth century as part of intellectual and journalistic discourse. Unlike the simple ~fragen~ ("to ask"), ~hinterfragen~ implies skepticism and analytical depth.
en.hintergehen:
An inseparable compound of ~hinter-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~hinter-~: From MHG ~hinter~, from OHG ~hintar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hindar~, from Proto-Germanic *~hinder~ ("behind"), a comparative formation on PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). The same deictic root gives German ~hier~ and ~heute~ and English ~here~ and ~hence~. ~hinter-~ conveys getting behind the surface of something, hence scrutiny or deception.

The inseparable stress (~hinterGEHen~) separates the sense „to deceive“ from separable ~HINtergehen~ „to walk behind“: one figuratively gets behind the deceived person's back.
en.hinterherpfeifen:
A separable compound of ~hinterher-~ + ~pfeifen~:

• ~pfeifen~: From MHG ~pfīfen~, from OHG ~pfīfōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pīpōn~ ("to play a pipe, to whistle"), an early borrowing from Vulgar Latin *~pīpāre~ ("to chirp, peep"), a word of imitative origin. Originally weak, now a class I strong verb (~pfeifen~, ~pfiff~, ~gepfiffen~). Cognate with English ~pipe~ and ~peep~, French ~piper~.
• ~hinterher-~: Transparently ~hinter~ ("behind") + ~her~, the deictic adverb of motion toward the speaker or reference point. It means "behind, after" in space and "afterwards" in time: ~hinterherlaufen~ ("to run after"), ~hinterherfahren~ ("to drive along behind"). The deictic contrast that organizes this whole family is ~her-~ toward the speaker versus ~hin-~ away from the speaker. See ~hinter-~ and ~her-~. The sense of ~hinterher-~ here is: in pursuit of, trailing someone or something.

~Hinterherpfeifen~ sends the whistle after someone walking away: the leering whistle at a passer-by's back.
en.hinterherreisen:
A separable compound of ~hinterher-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~hinterher-~: Transparently ~hinter~ ("behind") + ~her~, the deictic adverb of motion toward the speaker or reference point. It means "behind, after" in space and "afterwards" in time: ~hinterherlaufen~ ("to run after"), ~hinterherfahren~ ("to drive along behind"). The deictic contrast that organizes this whole family is ~her-~ toward the speaker versus ~hin-~ away from the speaker. See ~hinter-~ and ~her-~. The sense of ~hinterher-~ here is: behind, following after in space.

~Hinterherreisen~ is to journey after someone, following them to the place they reached first.
en.hinterherräumen:
A separable compound of ~hinterher-~ + ~räumen~:

• ~räumen~: From Early New High German ~reumen~, a Central German umlaut variant of ~raumen~, from MHG ~rūmen~, from OHG ~rūmen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rūmijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rūmijaną~, a factitive verb from the adjective *~rūmaz~ ("roomy, spacious"), from PIE *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open"). Etymologically, "to make room." Cognate with English ~room~, the noun ~Raum~, Bavarian ~rama~.
• ~hinterher-~: Transparently ~hinter~ ("behind") + ~her~, the deictic adverb of motion toward the speaker or reference point. It means "behind, after" in space and "afterwards" in time: ~hinterherlaufen~ ("to run after"), ~hinterherfahren~ ("to drive along behind"). The deictic contrast that organizes this whole family is ~her-~ toward the speaker versus ~hin-~ away from the speaker. See ~hinter-~ and ~her-~. The sense of ~hinterher-~ here is: afterwards, subsequently in time.

~Hinterherräumen~ is to tidy up what someone else leaves behind; the action follows the mess in time.
en.hinterherwerfen:
A separable compound of ~hinterher-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~hinterher-~: Transparently ~hinter~ ("behind") + ~her~, the deictic adverb of motion toward the speaker or reference point. It means "behind, after" in space and "afterwards" in time: ~hinterherlaufen~ ("to run after"), ~hinterherfahren~ ("to drive along behind"). The deictic contrast that organizes this whole family is ~her-~ toward the speaker versus ~hin-~ away from the speaker. See ~hinter-~ and ~her-~. The sense of ~hinterher-~ here is: in pursuit of, trailing someone or something.

Literally one throws something after a departing person; figuratively, as in the citation, to throw money after someone is to lavish it wastefully.
en.hinterlassen:
Compound of ~hinter-~ + ~lassen~:

• ~lassen~: From MHG ~lāzen~, ~lān~, from OHG ~lāȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lātan~ ("to let, to allow"), from Proto-Germanic *~lētaną~ ("to leave behind, to allow"), from PIE *~leh₁d-~ ("to let, to leave behind").
• ~hinter-~: Meaning "behind," from Proto-Germanic *~hinder~ ("behind"), from PIE *~ḱom-tero-~ ("on this side"), a comparative formation from *~ḱom~ ("beside, near"). As an inseparable prefix, ~hinter-~ conveys leaving something in one's wake or behind one.

~Hinterlassen~ means "to leave behind, to bequeath"; ~ein Erbe hinterlassen~ ("to leave an inheritance"), ~Spuren hinterlassen~ ("to leave traces"), ~eine Nachricht hinterlassen~ ("to leave a message"). The inseparable prefix ~hinter-~ distinguishes this from the separable ~hinter etwas lassen~ (which would mean "to leave behind something" in a more literal, spatial sense). The PIE root *~leh₁d-~ ("to leave behind") makes ~hinterlassen~ doubly emphatic about departure: both the prefix and the root verb encode the concept of leaving. Cognate with English ~let~ (from the same Germanic root) and Dutch ~nalaten~ ("to bequeath," using a different prefix but the same root verb). The noun ~Hinterlassenschaft~ ("estate, legacy") preserves the formal, testamentary register of the verb.
en.hinterlegen:
An inseparable compound of ~hinter-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~hinter-~: From MHG ~hinter~, from OHG ~hintar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hindar~, from Proto-Germanic *~hinder~ ("behind"), a comparative formation on PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). The same deictic root gives German ~hier~ and ~heute~ and English ~here~ and ~hence~. ~hinter-~ conveys position or motion behind something.

~Hinterlegen~ is to place something into safekeeping: a deposit, a pledge, in the citation the capital held as security.
en.hintertreiben:
An inseparable compound of ~hinter-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~hinter-~: From MHG ~hinter~, from OHG ~hintar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hindar~, from Proto-Germanic *~hinder~ ("behind"), a comparative formation on PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). The same deictic root gives German ~hier~ and ~heute~ and English ~here~ and ~hence~. ~hinter-~ conveys getting behind the surface of something, hence scrutiny or deception.

~Hintertreiben~ is to foil a plan secretly and from behind; the emphasis falls on the covert working.
en.hinterziehen:
An inseparable compound of ~hinter-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~hinter-~: From MHG ~hinter~, from OHG ~hintar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hindar~, from Proto-Germanic *~hinder~ ("behind"), a comparative formation on PIE *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). The same deictic root gives German ~hier~ and ~heute~ and English ~here~ and ~hence~. ~hinter-~ conveys getting behind the surface of something, hence scrutiny or deception.

In ~Steuern hinterziehen~ („to evade taxes“) the sense narrowed to secretly withholding what is owed, spiriting it away behind the tax office's back.
en.hinunterdrücken:
A separable compound of ~hinunter-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~hinunter-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~unter~ ("under, below"), so "downward and away from the speaker", the descent seen from above. Its mirror image is ~herunter~, the same descent toward the speaker; colloquial ~runter~ replaces both. ~hinunter-~ marks downward motion oriented away from the speaker.

~Hinunterdrücken~ joins the downward orientation to the force of ~drücken~: to press something down and away from the speaker.
en.hinunterhalten:
A separable compound of ~hinunter-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~hinunter-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~unter~ ("under, below"), so "downward and away from the speaker", the descent seen from above. Its mirror image is ~herunter~, the same descent toward the speaker; colloquial ~runter~ replaces both. ~hinunter-~ marks downward motion oriented away from the speaker.

~Hinunterhalten~ is to hold an object downward, out over an edge or down into a depth.
en.hinunterklettern:
A separable compound of ~hinunter-~ + ~klettern~:

• ~klettern~: An iterative verb formed in Early New High German from ~kletten~, from PIE *~gleyt-~ ("to cling to, cleave, stick"), from the root *~gley-~ ("to stick, smear"). The iterative ~-ern~ suffix emphasizes repeated action. Related to ~Klette~ ("burr") and to ~Kleid~ ("garment"), originally something that clings to the body.
• ~hinunter-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~unter~ ("under, below"), so "downward and away from the speaker", the descent seen from above. Its mirror image is ~herunter~, the same descent toward the speaker; colloquial ~runter~ replaces both. ~hinunter-~ marks downward motion oriented away from the speaker.

~Hinunterklettern~ is the climbing descent, downward and away from the speaker: hand and foot, as ~klettern~ demands.
en.hinunterrutschen:
A separable compound of ~hinunter-~ + ~rutschen~:

• ~rutschen~: From MHG ~rutzen~, ~rützen~, an onomatopoeic formation imitating the sound of sliding, with a later shift from ~-tz-~ to ~-tsch-~ (as in ~fletschen~); perhaps related to OHG ~rūtezzen~. The noun ~Rutsche~ ("slide, chute") derives from the verb. English ~rutch~ and ~rutsch~ are borrowed from German or its Low German cognates.
• ~hinunter-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~unter~ ("under, below"), so "downward and away from the speaker", the descent seen from above. Its mirror image is ~herunter~, the same descent toward the speaker; colloquial ~runter~ replaces both. ~hinunter-~ marks downward motion oriented away from the speaker.

~Hinunterrutschen~ is the gliding slide downward, its onomatopoeic base verb already carrying the sound of it.
en.hinunterschauen:
A separable compound of ~hinunter-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~hinunter-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~unter~ ("under, below"), so "downward and away from the speaker", the descent seen from above. Its mirror image is ~herunter~, the same descent toward the speaker; colloquial ~runter~ replaces both. ~hinunter-~ marks downward motion oriented away from the speaker.

As with ~hinsehen~, it is the gaze that moves, not the body: ~hinunterschauen~ turns the Upper-German ~schauen~ downward.
en.hinunterziehen:
A separable compound of ~hinunter-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~hinunter-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~unter~ ("under, below"), so "downward and away from the speaker", the descent seen from above. Its mirror image is ~herunter~, the same descent toward the speaker; colloquial ~runter~ replaces both. ~hinunter-~ marks downward motion oriented away from the speaker.

~Hinunterziehen~ joins the pulling force of ~ziehen~ to the downward direction: drawing something down and away from the speaker.
en.hinweggehen:
A separable compound of ~hinweg-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~hinweg-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~weg~ ("away"), the two elements reinforcing each other: motion off and away, with no return implied. The stress distinguishes the particle ~hinwég-~ from the noun-derived adverb ~Hínweg~ ("the way there"). Figuratively, of overriding or brushing aside an obstacle or an objection (~sich hinwegsetzen~, ~hinwegtäuschen~).

Figuratively, ~über etwas hinweggehen~ is to pass over an objection or a question rather than dwell on it, as in the Kafka citation.
en.hinwegkommen:
A separable compound of ~hinweg-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~hinweg-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~weg~ ("away"), the two elements reinforcing each other: motion off and away, with no return implied. The stress distinguishes the particle ~hinwég-~ from the noun-derived adverb ~Hínweg~ ("the way there"). Figuratively, of overriding or brushing aside an obstacle or an objection (~sich hinwegsetzen~, ~hinwegtäuschen~).

"Über etwas hinwegkommen" means to leave a disappointment or a loss behind: the motion off and past turned wholly inward.
en.hinwegschauen:
A separable compound of ~hinweg-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~hinweg-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~weg~ ("away"), the two elements reinforcing each other: motion off and away, with no return implied. The stress distinguishes the particle ~hinwég-~ from the noun-derived adverb ~Hínweg~ ("the way there"). Figuratively, of overriding or brushing aside an obstacle or an objection (~sich hinwegsetzen~, ~hinwegtäuschen~).

~Hinwegschauen~ is a variant of ~hinwegsehen~: to let one's gaze pass over something and so pass it by.
en.hinwegsehen:
A separable compound of ~hinweg-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~hinweg-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~weg~ ("away"), the two elements reinforcing each other: motion off and away, with no return implied. The stress distinguishes the particle ~hinwég-~ from the noun-derived adverb ~Hínweg~ ("the way there"). Figuratively, of overriding or brushing aside an obstacle or an objection (~sich hinwegsetzen~, ~hinwegtäuschen~).

Literally one looks out over someone or something; figuratively it means to deliberately overlook a shortcoming.
en.hinwegsetzen:
A separable compound of ~hinweg-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~hinweg-~: A transparent compound of ~hin-~ ("thither," marking motion away from the speaker) and ~weg~ ("away"), the two elements reinforcing each other: motion off and away, with no return implied. The stress distinguishes the particle ~hinwég-~ from the noun-derived adverb ~Hínweg~ ("the way there"). ~hinweg-~ marks motion away and off, over and past something.

Concretely a rider or horse leaps over an obstacle; in the reflexive ~sich hinwegsetzen~ this has become the disregarding of an objection.
en.hinweisen:
~Hin-~ + ~weisen~. Compound of ~hin-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative of *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from PIE *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know").
• ~hin-~: From PIE *~ḱís~ ("this, here"), with a directional shift away from the speaker. ~Hin-~ indicates movement or pointing away from the speaker's position, toward some other place or thing.

~Hinweisen~ means "to point out, to indicate, to draw attention to." The prefix ~hin-~ directs the act of showing away from the speaker toward the referent: one ~weist hin auf~ something by directing another's knowledge or gaze toward it. The noun ~Hinweis~ ("hint, pointer, reference, note") is ubiquitous in German signage, footnotes, and official communication. The underlying PIE root *~weyd-~ ("to see, know") is the same root that gives Latin ~videō~ ("I see"), Sanskrit ~veda~ ("I know"), and English ~wise~, ~wit~, and ~wizard~. To point out is, at the deepest etymological layer, to cause someone to see, a remarkably literal metaphor. Cognate with Dutch ~aanwijzen~.
en.hinwerfen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle conveys setting something down in a particular place.

~Hinwerfen~ is to throw something down carelessly or to cast it away; colloquially one also throws it all in when giving something up.
en.hinwirken:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~wirken~:

• ~wirken~: From MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~, from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~wérǵom~, from *~werǵ-~ ("to make, work"). Early on it merged with the dialectal ~würken~ (from OHG ~wurken~), which left the written language in the 18th century. Cognate with English ~work~ and ~wrought~, Dutch ~werken~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle conveys motion toward a destination, paired against ~her-~ for motion toward the speaker.

In ~auf etwas hinwirken~ the motion is wholly figurative: one directs one's effort steadily toward a goal without moving oneself at all.
en.hinziehen:
A separable compound of ~hin-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~hin-~: From OHG ~hina~, from Proto-Germanic *~hina~ ("away from here, thither"), from the PIE demonstrative stem *~ḱi-~ ("this, here"). ~Hin-~ points away from the speaker and ~her-~ toward the speaker; English once drew the same line with ~thither~ and ~hither~. Cognate with English ~hence~ and ~here~. The particle indicates motion away from the speaker, toward some other place.

Intransitively ~hinziehen~ means "to move off, to betake oneself to a place"; Luther's ~ziehe hin~ is the biblical "go your way."
en.hinzubekommen:
A separable compound of ~hinzu-~ + ~be-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~hinzu-~: The deictic adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~zu~ ("to, toward"), yielding "to it in addition." The orientation contrast is the key fact for this whole group: ~hin-~ points away from the speaker, ~her-~ toward the speaker. In ~hinzufügen~ and ~hinzukommen~ the sense is additive rather than spatial: something joins what is already there. The sense of ~hinzu-~ here is additive: joins something to what is already present.

~Bekommen~ has long been a fixed word for "to receive"; ~hinzu-~ adds the sense "in addition," so that one receives something on top.
en.hinzufügen:
~Hin-~ + ~zu-~ + ~fügen~. A double-prefix compound:

• ~fügen~: From MHG ~füegen~, ~fuogen~, from OHG ~fuogen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōgijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōgijaną~ ("to join, fit together"), from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to join, attach, fasten").
• ~hin-~: From PIE *~ḱís~ ("this, here"). The prefix indicates motion away from the speaker.
• ~zu-~: From PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"). The prefix adds directionality toward a goal or target.

~Hinzufügen~ means "to add", literally "to join (something) toward (a destination) away from here." The double prefix ~hinzu-~ creates a vivid spatial image: something is fitted (~fügen~) in the direction of (~zu-~) a destination that is away from the speaker (~hin-~). The root verb ~fügen~ itself is related to English ~fay~ (an archaic word meaning "to fit closely") and Dutch ~voegen~ ("to join, grout"). The PIE root *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to fasten") also gave Latin ~pāx~ ("peace", originally "a binding agreement") and ~pangere~ ("to fasten, fix"), making ~hinzufügen~ a distant relative of English ~peace~ and ~pact~. In computing, ~hinzufügen~ has become the standard German equivalent of "add", the button you click to add items to a cart or entries to a list.
en.hinzukommen:
A separable compound of ~hinzu-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~hinzu-~: The deictic adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~zu~ ("to, toward"), yielding "to it in addition." The orientation contrast is the key fact for this whole group: ~hin-~ points away from the speaker, ~her-~ toward the speaker. In ~hinzufügen~ and ~hinzukommen~ the sense is additive rather than spatial: something joins what is already there. The sense of ~hinzu-~ here is additive: joins something to what is already present.

In the fixed phrase "es kommt hinzu, dass …," ~hinzukommen~ has faded entirely into a connective meaning "moreover", exactly the use the chosen sentence shows.
en.hinzutreten:
A separable compound of ~hinzu-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~hinzu-~: The deictic adverb ~hin~ ("away from the speaker") + ~zu~ ("to, toward"), yielding "to it in addition." The orientation contrast is the key fact for this whole group: ~hin-~ points away from the speaker, ~her-~ toward the speaker. In ~hinzufügen~ and ~hinzukommen~ the sense is additive rather than spatial: something joins what is already there. The sense of ~hinzu-~ here is: motion toward a goal away from the speaker.

Concretely one steps up to a place or a person; from this comes the figurative sense "to be added, to join."
en.hocharbeiten:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

Used reflexively (~sich hocharbeiten~) the verb describes a laborious rise through one's own work, from the bottom up.
en.hochdienen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~dienen~:

• ~dienen~: From MHG ~dienen~, from OHG ~dionōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þewanōną~ ("to serve"), a denominative of *~þewaz~ ("servant, slave"), of uncertain further origin, perhaps PIE *~tekʷ-~ ("to run"), the servant as "one who runs errands." Cognate with English ~thane~ (via the noun), Dutch ~dienen~, Danish ~tjene~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

~Sich hochdienen~ maps the ascent onto a career: one climbs rank by rank in service, usually in the military or officialdom.
en.hochdrehen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). Cognate with English ~throw~ (a true cognate: Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist," a sense that "throw a pot" still keeps) plus English ~thread~, Dutch ~draaien~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys raising something to a higher position.

~Hochdrehen~ is to bring a dial or engine to a higher setting by turning it: the volume, the revs.
en.hochfahren:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

Beside the literal driving upward stands the technical sense "to bring into operation": a power plant or a computer is booted up.
en.hochfliegen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~fliegen~:

• ~fliegen~: From MHG ~vliegen~, from OHG ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"), an extension of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim") that also gave ~fließen~. The vowel path *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of class II strong verbs. Cognate with English ~fly~, Dutch ~vliegen~, Danish ~flyve~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

~Hochfliegen~ means to fly up into the air; figuratively one speaks of "high-flying plans."
en.hochgehen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

Literally something goes up; in everyday politics interest rates and prices "go up," and figuratively a charge "goes up" too; it explodes.
en.hochhalten:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys raising something to a higher position.

Concretely one holds something up, as Kafka's uncle holds the candle; figuratively one holds an ideal or a tradition high.
en.hochheben:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb: the past ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ continue the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys raising something to a higher position.

~Hochheben~ is the plain raising of an object; the strong ~heben~ (~hob~, ~gehoben~) carries the upward motion.
en.hochklappen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~klappen~:

• ~klappen~: From Middle Low German ~klappen~, from Old Saxon *~klappōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klappōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klappōną~. The verb is onomatopoeic. Cognate with English ~clap~, Dutch ~klappen~, Old High German ~klapfō~ ("a clapping sound"); also related to ~klaffen~ ("to gape").
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys raising something to a higher position.

~Hochklappen~ describes folding a hinged part upward: a seat, a collar, a lid.
en.hochkochen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~kochen~:

• ~kochen~: From MHG ~kochen~, from OHG ~kohhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kokōn~, borrowed from Late Latin ~cocō~, from Latin ~coquō~ ("I cook, I boil"), from PIE *~pekʷ-~ ("to cook, to ripen"). A loan early enough to have undergone the High German shift of ~k~ to ~ch~. Cognate with English ~cook~, Dutch ~koken~, Danish ~koge~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

Literally liquid boils up; figuratively outrage or an old quarrel boils up again.
en.hochkommen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

~Hochkommen~ means to make one's way up; it often stands for a rise to standing or power.
en.hochkriechen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~kriechen~:

• ~kriechen~: From MHG ~kriechen~, from OHG ~kriohhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kreukan~, from Proto-Germanic *~kreukaną~; Kroonen traces the root to PIE *~ger-~ ("to turn, bend, twist"), but the deeper etymology is not secure. A class II strong verb (~kriechen~, ~kroch~, ~gekrochen~).
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

~Hochkriechen~ joins creeping motion to an upward direction: a vine or an insect creeping up a wall.
en.hochladen:
A modern compound of ~hoch~ + ~laden~, and a calque of English ~upload~:

• ~hoch~: From Middle High German ~hōch~, from Old High German ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to bend; crooked"). The semantic shift from "bent, arched" to "high" may reflect the image of an arching peak.
• ~laden~: From MHG ~laden~ (strong verb), from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~. Cognate with English ~laden~ and ~load~.

This is a textbook example of a loan translation: German speakers needed a word for the digital concept of uploading and calqued it directly from English ~upload~ by substituting ~hoch~ ("up") + ~laden~ ("to load"). Its counterpart ~herunterladen~ ("to download") is calqued the same way. The computing sense dates to the 1990s, but ~laden~ itself has been loading cargo since the early medieval period.
en.hochnehmen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys raising something to a higher position.

Literally one takes something up; colloquially ~jemanden hochnehmen~ also means to tease or pull someone's leg.
en.hochrechnen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~rechnen~:

• ~rechnen~: From MHG ~rechenen~, from OHG ~rehhanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rekanōn~ ("to count, explain"), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to make straight or right"), the same root as German ~recht~ and Latin ~rectus~. Cognate with English ~reckon~, Dutch ~rekenen~, Low German ~rekenen~, Danish ~regne~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

~Hochrechnen~ is a term of statistics: from a sample one extrapolates up to the whole: at elections, the famous first projection.
en.hochschauen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

~Schauen~ is the southern German and Austrian counterpart to northern ~sehen~, so ~hochschauen~ carries that regional colouring.
en.hochschlafen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~schlafen~:

• ~schlafen~: From MHG ~slāfen~, from OHG ~slāfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slāpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slēpaną~, of uncertain further origin, possibly related to *~slapaz~ ("weak, lax, limp"), ancestor of ~schlaff~. A class VII strong verb of the reduplicating class (~schlafen~, ~schlief~, ~geschlafen~). Cognate with English ~sleep~, Dutch ~slapen~, Gothic ~𐍃𐌻𐌴𐍀𐌰𐌽~ (slēpan).
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

A literal "sleep upward" scarcely exists; ~hochschlafen~ is thoroughly figurative and pejorative: to advance oneself through sexual relationships.
en.hochschätzen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~schätzen~:

• ~schätzen~: A denominal verb from ~Schatz~ ("treasure"), from MHG ~schaz~, OHG ~scaz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skatt~ ("cattle, treasure"), an early Germanic word in which cattle served as a measure of wealth. Cognate with Old Norse ~skattr~ (whence Danish ~skat~ and Swedish ~skatt~, both "tax"), Gothic ~skatts~, Old English ~sċeatt~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys raising something to a higher position.

In ~hochschätzen~ the ~hoch~ names not place but worth: one values someone or something greatly, holding them in high regard.
en.hochspielen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys raising something to a higher position.

~Hochspielen~ is usually figurative: to ~hochspielen~ an issue is to inflate its importance rather than to raise any physical object.
en.hochstecken:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~stecken~:

• ~stecken~: Modern ~stecken~ merges two verbs: the transitive weak one ("to put, stick something in") from MHG ~stecken~, OHG ~steckōn~, a geminate derivative of ~stëhhan~ (the ancestor of ~stechen~), and the strong intransitive one (archaic ~stak~/~gestocken~, "to be stuck"); the two fused in Early Modern German. Both trace to Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stikaną~, from PIE *~(s)teyg-~ ("to be sharp, stab, goad"). Cognate with English ~stick~ and ~steak~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys raising something to a higher position.

This is the transitive weak ~stecken~ ("to pin, fasten"), not the strong intransitive one; one pins one's hair up.
en.hochsteigen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

~Steigen~ already carries the upward motion, which ~hoch-~ intensifies; taking ~sein~ as its auxiliary, ~hochsteigen~ describes smoke, mist, or feelings rising up.
en.hochstellen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys raising something to a higher position.

~Hochstellen~ ranges from turning up a collar to setting a dial higher.
en.hochtragen:
A separable compound of ~hoch~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb whose semantic range broadened from "to drag, pull" to "to carry, bear, wear." Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~hoch~: Not a prefix but the adjective ~hoch~ ("high") used adverbially, from MHG ~hōch~, from OHG ~hōh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauh~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauhaz~, from PIE *~kewk-~ ("to elevate"). Cognate with English ~high~, Dutch ~hoog~, Swedish ~hög~, Gothic ~hauhs~. The adverb conveys upward motion: the base verb performed in an upward direction.

~Hochtragen~ is to carry a load upward, for instance up the stairs.
en.hoffen:
From Middle High German ~hoffen~ (first attested 12th century), from northern Old High German *~hoffōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hopōn~. The ultimate pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. The word's early attestation is exclusively in northern and central German dialects; it was absent from Upper German, where it only became established in later Middle High German, gradually displacing the now-obsolete ~gedingen~ ("to have hope, trust"). Some scholars have proposed that all continental Germanic forms derive from Old English ~hopian~, introduced to the continent by Anglo-Saxon missionaries, which would make ~hoffen~ a remarkably late addition to the German vocabulary, arriving through religious rather than inherited channels.

Whether missionary loan or parallel inheritance, the word displaced a native competitor (~gedingen~, related to ~Ding~, "thing, assembly") and established itself as the sole common word for hope in German. Its exact PIE ancestry remains debated, with no secure cognate outside Germanic. Cognate with Dutch ~hopen~, English ~hope~, Danish ~håbe~, Swedish ~hoppas~, Yiddish ~האָפֿן~ (~hofn~).
en.holen: From Middle High German ~holen~, ~holn~, from Old High German ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get, draw"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, possibly from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, cry, summon"). The semantic development would be from "to summon, call (someone to come)" → "to go and fetch, retrieve." The connection to PIE *~kelh₁-~ is uncertain but paralleled by similar "call → fetch" developments in other languages. Wiktionary directs readers to English ~haul~ for related forms. The cognate English word ~haul~ (from Old French ~haler~, of Germanic origin) shares the sense of pulling something toward oneself, pointing to an underlying idea of directed movement. Cognate with Low German ~halen~, Dutch ~halen~ ("to fetch, get"), English ~haul~ (via French).
en.hängen:
Modern German ~hängen~ is the result of the gradual merger of three historically distinct Old High German verbs, all related in meaning and ancestry:

1. OHG ~hāhan~ (strong, chiefly transitive), past ~hieng~, participle ~gehangan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~hanhaną~, the original strong verb meaning "to be suspended."
2. OHG ~hangēn~ (weak, intransitive), a related form also meaning "to hang."
3. OHG ~hengen~ (weak, transitive/causative), from Proto-West Germanic *~hangijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hangijaną~, a causative formation meaning "to hang something, to cause to hang."

Verbs 1 and 2 merged first, combining the present stem ~hang-~ from ~hangēn~ with the strong past forms (~hing~, ~gehangen~) of ~hāhan~. This merger is first attested in the north and spread southward through Middle Low German and into Central German during the 14th century. The causative verb 3 (ancestor of modern transitive ~hängen~) was kept formally separate into the 20th century, at least by prescriptive grammarians, but colloquial usage steadily conflated all three. Today the distinction is upheld primarily in the past tense: intransitive ~hing~/~gehangen~ ("the coat was hanging") versus transitive ~hängte~/~gehängt~ ("she hung the coat"). This mirrors the English ~lie~/~lay~ distinction, which likewise collapses in casual speech. Cognate with Dutch ~hangen~, English ~hang~.
en.hören: From Middle High German ~hœren~, from Old High German ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). The PIE root is a compound construction meaning literally "to have sharp ears", a vivid image of acute hearing built into the very fabric of the word. Cognate with Dutch ~horen~, English ~hear~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
en.identifizieren: Borrowed from French ~identifier~, from Medieval Latin ~identificāre~, a compound of Latin ~identicus~ ("identical") + ~faciō~ ("to make, to do"). ~Identicus~ derives from Late Latin ~identitās~ ("sameness"), from Latin ~idem~ ("the same"), from the demonstrative pronoun ~is~ ("he, it") + ~-dem~ (an emphatic particle), ultimately from PIE *~ey-~ ("he, that"). The ~-fizieren~ ending reflects the standard German adaptation of Latin ~-ficāre~ (from ~faciō~, from PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ "to put, to place, to make"). To ~identifizieren~ is thus, etymologically, "to make the same": to establish that two things are one. The verb entered German during the Enlightenment period, when scientific taxonomy demanded precise language for classification. The reflexive form ~sich identifizieren mit~ ("to identify with") extends the etymology beautifully: to declare oneself ~the same as~ another. Cognate with Dutch ~identificeren~, English ~identify~, Spanish ~identificar~.
en.ignorieren:
From Latin ~ignōrō~ ("I do not know, I disregard"), with the German suffix ~-ieren~. The Latin verb ultimately derives from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know, to recognize"), with the Latin privative prefix ~in-~ (becoming ~ig-~ before ~n~) negating the root. The derivation within Latin is disputed: it may be a denominative from ~ignārus~ ("ignorant"), or it may have shifted from the ~-ā-~ to ~-ō-~ stem under the influence of ~ignōtus~ ("unknown").

The PIE root *~ǵneh₃-~ is one of the most productive in all of Indo-European, giving Latin ~nōscō~ and ~cognōscō~ ("I learn, I know"), Greek ~gignōskō~ (whence English ~diagnosis~ and ~prognosis~), and the Germanic family including English ~know~, ~can~ (originally "to know how"), ~ken~ (Scottish "to know"), ~cunning~ (originally "knowing"), and German ~kennen~ ("to know a person") and ~können~ ("to be able"). The irony is that ~ignorieren~ (a word about not knowing) is built from one of the richest "knowing" roots in human language. German borrowed this verb from Latin in the 16th century, and it coexists with the native German synonym ~missachten~ ("to disregard"). In modern usage, ~ignorieren~ specifically implies deliberately choosing not to acknowledge something, whereas ~nicht wissen~ is simply not knowing, a crucial distinction that the Latin original also made.
en.informieren:
Borrowed from French ~informer~, from Latin ~īnfōrmō~ ("to shape, form, train, instruct"), a compound of Latin ~in-~ ("into") + ~fōrma~ ("form, shape"). The Latin ~fōrma~ has an uncertain etymology, possibly borrowed from Etruscan, itself perhaps from Greek ~morphē~ ("shape, form"), with a dissimilation *~m~-~m~ > *~f~-~m~.

The original Latin sense of ~īnfōrmō~ was literal and physical: "to shape, give form to." The semantic shift from "to give form to" to "to instruct, inform" reflects the metaphor of education as shaping the mind, the same metaphor underlying English ~inform~ and ~formation~. German received the verb through French during the period when -~ieren~ borrowings were flooding the language (roughly 12th–17th centuries via Old French and later French contact), giving it the characteristic weak -~ieren~ conjugation that marks Latin-French loanwords in German. Like ~funktionieren~, ~präsentieren~, and ~konjugieren~, it entered the language as a fully formed loanword rather than being built from native roots. Cognate with English ~inform~, French ~informer~, Spanish ~informar~, Italian ~informare~.
en.innehaben:
A separable compound of ~inne-~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~inne-~: An old adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, meaning "within, inside," from OHG ~inne~/~inna~, cognate with Old Saxon ~inna~ and Old Norse ~inni~. It is no longer a free word and survives bound in ~innehalten~ ("to pause"), ~innewerden~ ("to become aware"), ~innehaben~ ("to hold an office"), and ~innewohnen~ ("to be inherent in"). English shows the same adverb nominalized in ~inn~, originally simply the place one is in. The sense of ~inne-~ here is: inward or internal location rather than motion.

~Innehaben~ means holding an office, position, or rank: possessing something as one's own.
en.innehalten:
A separable compound of ~inne-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~inne-~: An old adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, meaning "within, inside," from OHG ~inne~/~inna~, cognate with Old Saxon ~inna~ and Old Norse ~inni~. It is no longer a free word and survives bound in ~innehalten~ ("to pause"), ~innewerden~ ("to become aware"), ~innehaben~ ("to hold an office"), and ~innewohnen~ ("to be inherent in"). English shows the same adverb nominalized in ~inn~, originally simply the place one is in. The sense of ~inne-~ here is: with ~halten~, a holding-in that reads as pausing.

The leap from spatial "holding within" to temporal pausing is the interesting part: one pauses in motion as in speech.
en.innewohnen:
A separable compound of ~inne-~ + ~wohnen~:

• ~wohnen~: From MHG ~wonen~, from OHG ~wonēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wunēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wunāną~, from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to wish, love, strive for"); to inhabit a place is to love it enough to remain. The same root underlies ~Wonne~ ("bliss"), ~wünschen~, and ~gewinnen~. Cognate with English ~wont~ ("accustomed"), Dutch ~wonen~, Gothic ~wunan~.
• ~inne-~: An old adverbial form of the preposition ~in~, meaning "within, inside," from OHG ~inne~/~inna~, cognate with Old Saxon ~inna~ and Old Norse ~inni~. It is no longer a free word and survives bound in ~innehalten~ ("to pause"), ~innewerden~ ("to become aware"), ~innehaben~ ("to hold an office"), and ~innewohnen~ ("to be inherent in"). English shows the same adverb nominalized in ~inn~, originally simply the place one is in. ~inne-~ marks something as held or contained within.

~Innewohnen~ is purely figurative: a quality or force is inherent in a thing rather than added to it from outside.
en.inspirieren:
Borrowed in the sixteenth century from Latin ~īnspīrāre~ ("to breathe into, to blow upon"), from ~in-~ ("into") + ~spīrāre~ ("to breathe"). The Latin verb's earliest sense was literally "to breathe into," used of divine breath animating creation. Related to Latin ~spīritus~ ("breath, spirit"), whence German ~Spiritus~ and English ~spirit~. Also related to German ~konspirieren~ ("to conspire," literally "to breathe together") and ~transpirieren~ ("to transpire").

The theological sense (God breathing life or creative power into a person) was the primary meaning when the word entered German. The secular sense "to give someone a creative idea" developed later, preserving the metaphor of something being breathed into the mind from outside. English ~inspire~ arrived via Old French from the same Latin source.
en.installieren: ~Installieren~ is a borrowing from Medieval Latin ~installāre~ ("to place in a stall, to install in an office, especially to seat a canon in his choir stall"), composed of Latin ~in-~ ("in, into") and ~stallāre~, derived from ~stallus~ ("stall, seat, choir stall"). ~Stallus~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~stallaz~ ("standing place"), from Proto-Indo-European *~stel-~ ("to place, put, stand still"). That PIE root is the ancestor of English ~stall~, ~stale~, and ~install~ itself (via the same Latin path), and of German ~Stall~ ("stable, livestock pen"). The original ecclesiastical meaning ("to seat a newly appointed canon in his stall in the choir") survives in English "to install someone in office." The jump to technology ("to install software") is a 20th-century extension of the same idea: placing something in its proper location so it can function.
en.integrieren: ~Integrieren~ is borrowed from Latin ~integrāre~ ("to make whole, renew, restore"), from ~integer~ ("untouched, whole, sound, honest"), from Proto-Italic *~əntagros~, built from *~n̥-~ (the PIE negative prefix) + *~teh₂g-~ ("to touch"). That touching root also produced Latin ~tangere~ ("to touch"), ~tactus~ ("touch"), and English ~tangent~, ~tact~, ~contact~, and ~contagion~. So ~integer~ literally means "not-touched", hence "whole, intact, uncorrupted." The noun ~Integrität~ and the mathematical term ~Integral~ share this ancestry: an integer is a number left whole, not cut into fractions. English ~entire~ comes from the same root via Old French. A cultural note: in German, ~integrieren~ carries a strong second meaning of social integration (incorporating people into a community), making its etymology ("making whole") feel especially apt.
en.interessieren: Borrowed in the 17th century from French ~intéresser~ ("to interest, to concern"), from Latin ~interesse~ ("to be between, to be present, to matter"), a compound of ~inter-~ ("between, among") + ~esse~ ("to be"), from PIE *~h₁es-~ ("to be"). The semantic leap from "to be between" to "to matter, to concern" reflects the Roman legal and financial use of ~interest~ (third-person singular present of ~interesse~) as a formula meaning "it makes a difference", and from there, the noun ~interest~ in the financial sense of a stake or share in something. The abstract ~inter-esse~, "being-between," captures the idea of having a stake in something, of standing between pure detachment and full possession. Cognate with English ~interest~, French ~intéresser~, Spanish ~interesar~, Dutch ~interesseren~.
en.interpretieren: From French ~interpréter~, from Old French ~enterpreter~, from Latin ~interpretārī~ ("to explain, expound, interpret"), a deponent verb derived from the noun ~interpres~ ("agent, intermediary, interpreter"). Latin ~interpres~ is composed of ~inter~ ("between") and a derivation from PIE *~per-~ ("to sell, to traffic in; forward, through"), yielding an original sense of "one who goes between", a broker, a middleman, a go-between. The proposed reconstruction traces through *~enter-poro-~ ("going between") to *~enterpress~ via regular sound changes. German adopted the verb through French with the ~-ieren~ suffix, the standard pathway for Romance and Latin verbs into German. Cognate with English ~interpret~, French ~interpréter~, Italian ~interpretare~. The word ~Dolmetscher~ ("interpreter" in the oral-translation sense) is a fascinating contrast: it entered German from Turkic ~dilmaç~ via Hungarian, showing that German has two words for "interpreter" from opposite ends of the ancient world. ~Interpretieren~ is used for textual, musical, and legal interpretation, while ~dolmetschen~ is reserved for oral translation between languages.
en.investieren: ~Investieren~ is borrowed from Latin ~investīre~ ("to clothe, to surround, to envelop"), from ~in-~ ("in, into") + ~vestīre~ ("to clothe"), from ~vestis~ ("garment, clothing"), from Proto-Italic *~westis~, from Proto-Indo-European *~wes-~ ("to be dressed, wear clothes"). That PIE root is the source of English ~wear~, Gothic ~wasti~ ("garment"), and Old Armenian ~զgest~. The financial sense of ~investieren~ (to put capital to work), arose in 17th-century Italian banking: ~investire~ was used to describe "dressing" money in productive assets, cloaking capital in ventures that would return profit. The metaphor traveled from Italian into French ~investir~ and then into English ~invest~ and German ~investieren~. The original Latin ~investīre~ also gave English ~investiture~ (the ceremony of cloaking someone in the robes of an office) and ~investigate~, literally "to trace footprints," via a different Latin compound.
en.irreführen:
A separable compound of ~irre-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~irre-~: The adjective and adverb ~irre~ ("astray, confused"), from MHG ~irre~, from OHG ~irri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~irrī~, from Proto-Germanic *~irzijaz~ ("bewildered, lost"), from PIE *~h₁ers-~ ("to wander").
