Cognate with English ~lame~, Dutch ~lam~, Old Norse ~lami~, Swedish ~lam~. In resultative compounds it names the endpoint: to lay something lame is to bring it to a standstill. The sense of ~lahm~ here is: figuratively, brought to a standstill or rendered inoperative.

Today ~lahmlegen~ is almost always figurative: a strike lays traffic lame, an attack a whole network, not a limb is paralyzed but an entire operation brought to a halt.
en.landen: Denominal from ~Land~ ("land, country"), via Middle Low German ~landen~. The noun ~Land~ descends from Proto-West Germanic *~land~, from Proto-Germanic *~landą~, from Proto-Indo-European *~lendʰ-~ ("land, heath"). An earlier native German verb ~länden~ was displaced by the borrowed Low German form. Both the German noun ~Land~ and the English noun and verb ~land~ share the same Proto-Germanic ancestor *~landą~, making ~landen~ and English ~to land~ direct cognates, two sister-languages coining the same verb from the same noun independently.
en.langgehen:
A separable compound of ~lang~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~lang~: From MHG ~lanc~, from OHG ~lang~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lang~, from Proto-Germanic *~langaz~, from PIE *~dlongʰos~ ("long"). Cognate with English ~long~, Dutch ~lang~, Latin ~longus~. As a separable element it is an ordinary adjective in a resultative or extent-denoting frame. The sense of ~lang~ here is: with verbs of motion, "along".

~Langgehen~ belongs to the colloquial register and denotes walking along a stretch; here ~lang~ construes the route as an extent to be traversed.
en.langmachen:
A separable compound of ~lang~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~lang~: From MHG ~lanc~, from OHG ~lang~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lang~, from Proto-Germanic *~langaz~, from PIE *~dlongʰos~ ("long"). Cognate with English ~long~, Dutch ~lang~, Latin ~longus~. As a separable element it is an ordinary adjective in a resultative or extent-denoting frame. The sense of ~lang~ here is: of duration, "for a long time".

In the compound ~lang~ points at time: to ~langmachen~ something is to draw it out, to make it last longer than necessary.
en.lassen: From Middle High German ~lāzen~, ~lān~, from Old High German ~lāȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lātan~ ("to let, allow"), from Proto-Germanic *~lētaną~ ("to leave behind, allow"), from PIE *~leh₁d-~ ("to let, leave behind"). Cognate with Bavarian ~lassn~, Dutch ~laten~, English ~let~.
en.laufen: From Middle High German ~loufen~, from Old High German ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with Dutch ~lopen~, English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Danish ~løbe~.
en.lauten: ~Lauten~ ("to read, run, be worded; to sound") descends from Middle High German ~lūten~ ("to sound, ring"), Old High German ~hlūtēn~, and Proto-West Germanic *~hlūdēn~. It is equivalent to ~Laut~ ("sound") plus the verbal suffix ~-en~. ~Laut~ itself comes from the Proto-Germanic adjective *~hlūdaz~ ("loud"), the same root that gives English ~loud~, Dutch ~luid~, and Old Norse ~hljóð~. A subtle distinction in modern German: ~lauten~ means "to read as, to run" (as in ~das Urteil lautet~, "the verdict reads"), while ~läuten~ ("to ring bells") is historically the factitive (causative) form of the same root, "to make sound." Over time, ~läuten~ absorbed the general sense of sounding, while ~lauten~ narrowed to the meaning of textual or verbal content. They share an ancestor but now describe entirely different acts.
en.leben: From Middle High German ~lëben~, from Old High German ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The semantic development from "to cling, stick" to "to remain alive" parallels the related ~bleiben~ ("to remain"), which shares the same PIE root. Cognate with Old Saxon ~libbian~ (Middle Low German ~leven~), Dutch ~leven~, English ~live~, West Frisian ~libje~, Old Norse ~lifa~ (Swedish ~leva~), Gothic ~liban~.
en.leerlaufen:
A separable compound of ~leer~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~leer~: From MHG ~lǣre~, ~lēr~, from OHG ~lāri~ ("empty, bare"), from Proto-West Germanic *~lāʀi~, from Proto-Germanic *~lēziz~. Cognate with Dutch ~laar~ and Bavarian ~lar~; there is no surviving English relative, and the origin beyond Germanic is uncertain. DWDS derives it from the preterite-plural stem of ~lesen~ ("to gather, glean"), which would make the original sense "gleaned over" (a harvested field left open to the poor) and only later "containing nothing". The sense of ~leer~ here is: of a machine or engine, "without load, idling".

~Leerlaufen~ spans two images: a container draining itself, and an engine turning without load: the idling in which the gears spin while moving nothing.
en.leerrauchen:
A separable compound of ~leer~ + ~rauchen~:

• ~rauchen~: From MHG ~rouchen~, ~röuchen~, from OHG ~rouhhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raukijan~, derived from the noun *~rauki-~ ("smoke"), from Proto-Germanic *~raukiz~, from *~reukaną~ ("to smoke"), possibly from PIE *~h₁rewg-~ ("to belch, emit"). The noun survives as ~Rauch~. Cognate with English ~reek~, Dutch ~rook~, Swedish ~rök~, Danish ~røg~.
• ~leer~: From MHG ~lǣre~, ~lēr~, from OHG ~lāri~ ("empty, bare"), from Proto-West Germanic *~lāʀi~, from Proto-Germanic *~lēziz~. Cognate with Dutch ~laar~ and Bavarian ~lar~; there is no surviving English relative, and the origin beyond Germanic is uncertain. DWDS derives it from the preterite-plural stem of ~lesen~ ("to gather, glean"), which would make the original sense "gleaned over" (a harvested field left open to the poor) and only later "containing nothing". The sense of ~leer~ here is as a resultative adjective, "empty": the verb acts until nothing is left.

~Leerrauchen~ follows the pattern ~leer~ forms with any verb of consumption: one acts until the supply (here the pack) is used up.
en.legen: From Middle High German ~legen~, from Old High German ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative derivation of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The causative formation ("to cause to lie," hence "to lay") mirrors exactly the relationship between ~liegen~ ("to lie") and ~legen~ ("to lay"), and between English ~lie~ and ~lay~. The same causative pattern appears in German ~setzen~ (from ~sitzen~, "to sit") and ~stellen~ (from ~stehen~, "to stand"): in each pair, a strong intransitive verb of posture spawns a weak transitive causative. This systematic grammatical pairing descends from Proto-Indo-European. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~, Swedish ~lägga~.
en.lehnen:
From a merger of two interrelated Old High German verbs:

1. MHG ~linen~/~lenen~ (intransitive "to lean"), from OHG ~hlinēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlinēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlināną~ ("to lean"), from PIE *~k̂ley-~ ("to lean, incline"). Cognate with Latin ~clīnō~ ("to slope, incline") and Greek ~klinō~ ("to bend, lean").
2. MHG ~leinen~ (transitive/causative "to lean something"), from OHG ~hleinen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlainijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlainijaną~, the causative form of the above.

The merger occurred in Central and Low German dialects, where the vowels converged to ~ē~. Some Upper German dialects still distinguish the transitive and intransitive forms. Cognate with Dutch ~leunen~ and English ~lean~.

A second, archaic ~lehnen~ ("to lend, borrow"), from OHG ~lēhanōn~, survives only in the derivative ~entlehnen~ ("to borrow a word or concept") and in compounds like ~Lehnwort~ ("loanword") and ~Lehnübersetzung~ ("calque, loan translation").
en.lehren:
From Middle High German ~lēren~, from Old High German ~lēren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laiʀijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~laizijaną~ ("to teach"), a causative derived from *~lizaną~ ("to learn"), from PIE *~leys-~ ("track, furrow, trace, trail"). The underlying metaphor is that teaching means "to cause someone to follow a track." Cognate with Low German ~lehren~, Dutch ~leren~, Afrikaans ~leer~, Danish ~lære~, Norwegian ~lære~, Swedish ~lära~, and archaic English ~lear~ ("to learn, to teach").

Closely related to German ~lernen~ ("to learn"), which descends from the same Proto-Germanic root *~lizaną~ through a different derivational path. English ~lore~ ("accumulated knowledge") is another sibling, from Proto-Germanic *~laizō~ ("teaching, lore"). The PIE root *~leys-~ ("track, furrow") reveals an agricultural metaphor at the heart of education: to learn was to follow a furrow, and to teach was to cause someone to follow one. In some Middle English dialects, ~learn~ could itself mean "to teach" (a usage that survives dialectally in "I'll learn you!"), preserving the original ambiguity between the causative and stative senses that German resolved by splitting into two separate verbs.
en.leichtfallen:
A separable compound of ~leicht~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~leicht~: From MHG ~līht(e)~, from OHG ~līht~, from Proto-West Germanic *~līht~, from Proto-Germanic *~linhtaz~, from PIE *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ ("light, not heavy"). Cognate with English ~light~ (not heavy), Dutch ~licht~, Danish ~let~, Latin ~levis~. The same root names the lungs (German ~Lunge~, English ~lung~) the organ that floats when the rest of the carcass sinks. The sense of ~leicht~ here is: the adjective ~leicht~ ("light, easy") as the resulting state.

~Leichtfallen~ is almost always impersonal with a dative: something comes easily to me. Its counterpart ~schwerfallen~ is built as an exact mirror.
en.leiden: ~Leiden~ comes from Middle High German ~līden~, from Old High German ~līdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~līþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~līþaną~ ("to go, travel"). The original sense was purely spatial: to go, to travel, to pass through. Over time the meaning narrowed to "to endure" and then "to suffer", a trajectory from journeying to hardship that mirrors the lived experience of passage. The semantic shift was reinforced by convergence with Middle High German ~leiden~ ("to be sorry, suffer, be hated"), itself from Old High German ~leidēn~, and by the noun ~Leid~ ("sorrow"), preserved today in the ubiquitous expression ~das tut mir leid~ ("I'm sorry," literally "that does me sorrow"). The surface similarity made the merger feel natural. This second strand, from Proto-Germanic *~laiþaz~ ("hateful, hostile"), is cognate with English ~loathe~ ("to detest") and ~loath~ ("reluctant"). The first strand, from *~līþaną~ ("to go"), yields a classic false friend: ~leiden~ is NOT cognate with English ~lead~; it is instead cognate with English ~lithe~ ("flexible, supple"), Dutch ~lijden~, and Low German ~lieden~. The spatial ancestor survives in the causative ~leiten~ ("to lead, guide", literally "to cause to go," built from the same root with the causative suffix *~-janą~), in compounds like ~begleiten~ ("to accompany") and ~einleiten~ ("to introduce"), and in place names such as ~Leiden~ (the Dutch city: "the watery passage").
en.leihen: From MHG ~līhen~, from OHG ~līhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~līhwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~līhwaną~, from PIE *~leykʷ-~ ("to leave behind"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with English ~loan~ (via Old Norse ~lán~, from Proto-Germanic *~laihną~, derived from the same PIE root), Dutch ~lenen~.
en.leisten: From Middle High German ~leisten~, from Old High German ~leisten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laistijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~laistijaną~, a denominative of *~laistaz~ ("track, trace, footprint"), from Proto-Indo-European *~leys-~ ("to track, pursue; track, furrow, trace, trail"). The verb originally meant "to track, follow" (to follow in someone's footsteps) and evolved into "to perform, carry out, accomplish." This semantic journey from literal path-following to figurative achievement is a remarkably concrete-to-abstract shift: to fulfill an obligation is to follow the track it has laid out. English ~last~ (in "lasting shoe") is a direct cognate (OE ~lǣstan~, "to follow, perform"), and the shoemaker's ~last~ (the foot-shaped form used to make shoes) is the noun *~laistaz~ itself, a "footprint" in wood. Cognate with English ~last~ (OE ~lǣstan~), Old Frisian ~lēsta~, Old Saxon ~lēstian~, Dutch ~leisten~ (archaic).
en.leiten: ~Leiten~ ("to lead, guide, conduct") descends from Middle High German ~leiten~, Old High German ~leiten~, and Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~. It is the causative of the older strong verb *~līþaną~ ("to pass, go, travel"), built with the Proto-Germanic causative suffix *~-janą~: "to cause to go, to make travel." The PIE root is *~leyt-~ ("to go, depart, die"), which also produced Latin ~lītus~ ("shore", the place where the sea "goes"), Avestan ~iriθiieiti~ ("to die, pass away"), and Tocharian A ~litā-~ ("to pass on"). The English cognate ~lead~ (to guide) is its exact parallel, Old English ~lǣdan~ from the same Proto-Germanic causative. Despite their divergent modern meanings, ~leiten~ and ~leiden~ are not false friends but a base-and-causative pair from the same root: *~līþaną~ ("to go") gave ~leiden~ (which narrowed from "to travel" through "to endure" to "to suffer"), and its causative *~laidijaną~ ("to cause to go") gave ~leiten~ ("to lead"). The verb genuinely unrelated to ~leiten~ is ~lassen~ ("to let, permit, allow"), from the separate Proto-Germanic root *~lētaną~, the same root that gave English ~let~.
en.lenken: From Middle High German ~lenken~, from Old High German ~lanca~ ("hip, flank"), related to ~Gelenk~ ("joint"). The noun ~Gelenk~ descends from MHG ~gelenke~ ("joint, bend, waist"), from OHG ~gilenki~, from Proto-Germanic *~gahlankiją~, from *~hlankaz~ ("flexible, lank, slender"). Cognate with English ~lank~ (related to ~link~) and Hunsrik ~lenke~. The semantic journey from "hip/joint" to "to steer, guide, direct" traveled through the idea of bending and turning at a joint. A joint is a point of articulation that allows redirection of movement, so ~lenken~ came to mean directing or steering something along a new path. The compound ~Lenkrad~ ("steering wheel," literally "steering-wheel") is the everyday reminder of this etymology, as is ~Ablenkung~ ("distraction, deflection"). The relationship between ~lenken~ and ~Gelenk~ mirrors the English connection between ~joint~ and ~articulate~ (from Latin ~articulus~, "small joint"). English ~lank~ preserves the physical sense of the root: something long, thin, and flexible. The related OHG ~hlanka~ ("side, flank, hip") also produced the French loanword ~flanc~ (whence English ~flank~), showing a Germanic word that traveled into Romance.
en.lernen: From Middle High German ~lernen~, from Old High German ~lernēn~, ~lirnēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~liʀnēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lizaną~, from PIE *~leys-~ ("track, furrow, trace, trail"). The PIE root conveys the image of following a track or tracing a path, and from this physical metaphor, Germanic developed the meaning of acquiring knowledge: to learn is to follow the trail laid down by those who came before. This same root underlies ~lore~ and ~lear~ (archaic English for "learning, knowledge"). The historically close verb ~lehren~ ("to teach") shares the same Germanic stem in its causative function: "to cause to learn." ~Lernen~ is attested in German since the 8th century. Cognate with Old English ~leornian~ (Modern English ~learn~), Old Frisian ~lernia~, Middle Low German ~lernen~, and Dutch ~lernen~.
en.lesen: From Middle High German ~lësen~, from Old High German ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The semantic shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), reflects how reading was originally conceived as gathering letters or words. Cognate with Low German ~lesen~, Dutch ~lezen~, Afrikaans ~lees~, English ~lease~ (archaic, "to gather").
en.leuchten:
From OHG ~liuhten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~liuhtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~liuhtijaną~, a factitive/denominative verb derived from *~leuhtą~ ("light") or *~leuhtaz~ ("light, bright"), both from PIE *~lewk-~ ("bright, to shine, to see"). Cognate with MHG ~liuhten~. The verb is attested since the 8th century.

The PIE root *~lewk-~ is one of the great etymological treasures of the Indo-European family. It produced Latin ~lūx~ ("light"), whence English ~lucid~, ~translucent~, ~elucidate~, and the name ~Lucifer~ ("light-bearer"); Greek ~leukos~ ("white"), whence ~leukemia~ (a disease of "white" blood cells); Sanskrit ~roká-~ ("light"); and Lithuanian ~laũkas~ ("pale"). The Germanic branch developed *~lewk-~ into the noun *~leuhtą~ ("light") and the adjective *~leuhtaz~ ("bright"), whence both the German verb ~leuchten~ ("to shine, to glow") and the noun ~Licht~ ("light"). English ~light~ is a cognate. The modern German word ~Leuchtturm~ ("lighthouse," literally "shining tower") and ~Leuchtstoff~ ("fluorescent material") build directly on this ancient root.
en.lieben:
Formally from Middle High German ~lieben~, an alteration (modeled on the adjective ~liep~) of the rarer MHG ~liuben~ ("to make dear, treat in a friendly way"), from Old High German ~liuben~. Denominative of the adjective ~lieb~ ("dear, beloved"), from MHG ~liep~, from OHG ~liob~, from Proto-West Germanic *~leub~, from Proto-Germanic *~leubaz~ ("dear, beloved"), from PIE *~lewbʰ-~ ("to desire, love").

The Modern German verb ~lieben~ has a complicated history: the Old High German simplex ~liobōn~ ("to love") apparently left no direct continuation, and the modern sense was derived in late Middle High German from the noun ~Liebe~ ("love") on the model of ~minnen~ ("to love"), from ~Minne~ (the courtly word for love), which had acquired a sexual overtone by that period. As a result, ~lieben~ is absent from most traditional German dialects, which prefer constructions like ~lieb haben~ or ~gern haben~ instead. English ~love~ derives from a related but distinct Proto-Germanic root *~lubō~ (noun), while the adjective ~lief~ (archaic English, "beloved, dear") is a direct cognate of German ~lieb~. Cognate with Dutch ~lieven~, English ~lief~, archaic English ~love~ (the verb, via *~lubōną~).
en.liefern:
From Middle High German ~lieveren~ (attested before 1350), probably borrowed via Middle Dutch and Middle Low German ~lēveren~ (the ~ie~ vocalism in German being due to hypercorrection), ultimately from Old French ~livrer~, from Latin ~līberō~ ("I free, release, deliver"), from ~līber~ ("free"). The word was part of the technical vocabulary of the Hanseatic League, the powerful trading network of northern European merchants, which spread it from Low German into standard High German, a linguistic footprint of medieval commercial power.

The route from Latin "to free" to German "to deliver" is semantically transparent: to hand over goods is to release them to another party. The same Latin root ~līberō~ gives English ~liberate~, ~deliver~ (via Old French ~delivrer~), and the name ~Liberia~. Note that German ~liefern~ ("to deliver") is therefore a distant cousin of ~liberally~ and ~liberty~; trading and freedom share a root. Cognate with Dutch ~leveren~, Swedish ~leverera~, French ~livrer~.
en.liegen: From Middle High German ~ligen~, from Old High German ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~, with the stem generalized from the second- and third-person singular), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The related weak causative ~legen~ ("to lay, to cause to lie") derives from the same root via the Proto-Germanic suffix *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~), the same pattern as English ~lie~/~lay~ and as ~sitzen~/~setzen~ and ~fallen~/~fällen~. Cognate with Low German ~liggen~, Dutch ~liggen~, English ~lie~, Danish ~ligge~, Gothic ~ligan~.
en.loben:
From Middle High German ~loben~, from Old High German ~lobēn~/~lobōn~ ("to praise, approve, hold dear"), from Proto-West Germanic *~lubōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lubō~, from PIE *~lewbʰ-~ ("to love, desire, praise"). Cognate with Old English ~lofian~ ("to praise"), Old Norse ~lofa~ ("to praise, promise"), Dutch ~loven~ ("to praise"), Swedish ~lova~ ("to promise, praise").

~Loben~ is related to the noun ~Lob~ ("praise") and to ~lieb~ ("dear, beloved") and ~Liebe~ ("love"), all from PIE *~lewbʰ-~. The root reveals an ancient equation between praising and loving: to praise someone was to declare one's affection. English ~love~ comes from the same PIE root via a different branch (OE ~lufu~). Old English ~lofian~ ("to praise") survives fossilized in the word ~loft~ (originally a raised gallery in a church from which hymns of praise were sung) and in ~aloft~. The compound ~Lobgesang~ ("hymn, song of praise") echoes the medieval world where ~loben~ was the language of devotion.
en.locken:
From Middle High German ~locken~, from Old High German ~lockōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lokkōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lukkōną~ ("to entice, to lure"). Related to ~lügen~ ("to lie"), Latin ~laciō~ ("I entice, I lure"), and Slovak ~lákať~ ("to allure"). There is a second, homonymous verb ~locken~ ("to curl") from OHG ~lochōn~, derived from the noun ~Locke~ ("curl"), but the two verbs are etymologically distinct.

The connection between ~locken~ ("to lure") and ~lügen~ ("to lie") hints at a deep Germanic association between enticement and deception: to lure someone is, at root, a form of lying. The Latin cognate ~laciō~ likewise means "to entice" and is the ancestor of English ~lace~ (originally a snare or noose) and ~delicious~ (through ~dēliciae~, "enticements, delights"), though these Latin connections are disputed. English has no direct Germanic cognate of ~locken~ in common use; it instead uses ~lure~, borrowed from Old French. German ~Lockvogel~ ("decoy bird," literally "lure-bird") preserves the original concrete sense of baiting traps, while the modern figurative use (~ein Angebot, das Kunden lockt~ ("an offer that attracts customers")) shows how trapping became marketing.
en.lockermachen:
A separable compound of ~locker~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~locker~: First recorded in Early New High German as ~loger~ in the fifteenth century, a Central German form beside MHG ~lücke~, ~lugge~ ("loose"), which survives dialectally as Upper German ~luck~ and Swiss ~lugg~; the ~-er~ is the suffix of ~bitter~, ~lauter~, ~munter~. Probably related to ~Lücke~ ("gap") and ~Loch~ ("hole"), but secure cognates outside German are lacking. The verb ~lockern~ was formed from the adjective only in the eighteenth century. The sense of ~locker~ here is: the adjective ~locker~ ("loose, slack") as the resulting state.

Beside the synthetic ~lockern~, the analytic ~lockermachen~ carries a vivid colloquial sense: Geld lockermachen, to make someone part with their money.
en.lohnen: From Middle High German ~lōnen~, from Old High German ~lōnōn~, a denominal verb from ~lōn~ ("reward, wage"), from Proto-West Germanic *~laun~, from Proto-Germanic *~launą~, from Proto-Indo-European *~leh₂w-~ ("gain, prize, booty"). Cognate with Old English ~lēan~ ("reward, recompense"). The English cognate ~lean~ in this sense is now obsolete, but it survived long enough to be recorded in Old English poetry. The PIE root also underlies the idea of payment as something captured or won, an early conceptual link between labor and the spoils of contest.
en.losbrechen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. It can mark separation from a fixed point, of a vehicle or a rope being let go.

Beside the literal breaking-away of a piece from its hold, ~losbrechen~ lives above all in the image of sudden eruption: a storm, a thunderstorm, a burst of cheering breaks loose.
en.losfahren:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. It can mark separation from a fixed point, of a vehicle or a rope being let go.

~Losfahren~ captures the instant of departure: the vehicle breaks from rest and sets itself in motion.
en.losgeben:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. It also keeps its literal adjectival sense of releasing, loosening, or detaching something.

In Luther's Bible ~losgeben~ means the releasing of a servant or captive; the bond is loosened and the person let go into freedom.
en.losgehen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. As a particle ~los-~ most often marks inception: ~loslaufen~ is not "to run loose" but "to start running."

~Losgehen~ sheds the literal walking: it marks the start ("here we go"), and in the phrase auf jemanden losgehen the resolute advance upon a target.
en.loskaufen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, a denominative verb from *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"), a loanword from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper"). Cognate with English ~cheap~, Dutch ~kopen~, Danish ~købe~, Icelandic ~kaupa~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. It also keeps its literal adjectival sense of releasing, loosening, or detaching something.

~Loskaufen~ turns freedom into a commodity: a captive is redeemed by payment. The commercial stem ~kaufen~, ultimately from Latin ~caupō~, frames the release as a purchase.
en.loslachen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~lachen~:

• ~lachen~: From MHG ~lachen~, from OHG ~lahhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~, from PIE *~kleg-~ ("to cry out, sound"). The initial ~hl-~ cluster was simplified to ~l-~ in Old High German. Cognate with English ~laugh~, Dutch ~lachen~, Gothic ~hlahjan~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. As a particle ~los-~ most often marks inception: ~loslaufen~ is not "to run loose" but "to start running."

~Loslachen~ captures the sudden burst: not a laughter that lasts, but the moment it breaks out.
en.loslaufen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. As a particle ~los-~ most often marks inception: ~loslaufen~ is not "to run loose" but "to start running."

Fittingly for the sudden dash, ~laufen~ keeps in its cognates ~leap~ and ~lope~ the old sense of springing: ~loslaufen~ is a leap into motion.
en.loslegen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. As a bare imperative, ~los!~ survives on its own: "go, get on with it."

In ~loslegen~ the literal laying has faded: what remains is the drive of ~los!~, to begin with full force, with nothing actually laid.
en.loslösen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~lösen~:

• ~lösen~: From MHG ~lœsen~, ~lōsen~, from OHG ~lōsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lausijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausijaną~, a causative of *~leusaną~ ("to lose, let loose"), denominative via *~lausaz~ ("loose, free"), from PIE *~lewh₁-~ ("to cut, sever, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ (via Old Norse ~lauss~), Dutch ~lozen~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. It also keeps its literal adjectival sense of releasing, loosening, or detaching something.

~Loslösen~ doubles its meaning: ~lösen~ itself goes back to Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~ ("loose, free"), the very root of ~los-~. The compound stacks two reflexes of the same word.
en.losmachen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. It also keeps its literal adjectival sense of releasing, loosening, or detaching something.

~Losmachen~ is the concrete undoing of a fastening: a knot, a rope, a boat is cast off; reflexively, sich losmachen means to free oneself from a tie.
en.losreißen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. It can mark separation from a fixed point, of a vehicle or a rope being let go.

~Losreißen~ is strongest reflexively: sich losreißen names the violent tearing of oneself away, often from a person or place the heart clings to.
en.lossagen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. It also keeps its literal adjectival sense of releasing, loosening, or detaching something.

~Lossagen~ is a speech act: to renounce something (sich von etwas lossagen) is to declare oneself free of a tie (a belief, a group, a person), severing it by the word.
en.losschießen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb (~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~). Cognate with English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Old Norse ~skjóta~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. As a particle ~los-~ most often marks inception: ~loslaufen~ is not "to run loose" but "to start running."

~Losschießen~ means to open fire; figuratively it lives in the call schieß los! , out with it, start talking.
en.losschlagen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. It also keeps its literal adjectival sense of releasing, loosening, or detaching something.

~Losschlagen~ spreads wide: to knock something loose, auf jemanden losschlagen to lay into someone, and commercially Waren losschlagen to offload goods cheaply.
en.lostreten:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. As a particle ~los-~ most often marks inception: ~loslaufen~ is not "to run loose" but "to start running."

~Lostreten~ is today mostly figurative: an avalanche, a debate, a chain reaction is set off: the kick that dislodges a stone and starts the slope sliding.
en.losziehen:
A separable compound of ~los-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~los-~: From the adjective ~los~ ("loose, free, unattached"), from MHG ~lōs~, from OHG ~lōs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laus~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausaz~, probably from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, loosen"). Cognate with English ~loose~ and Dutch ~los~. The German suffix ~-los~ and the English suffix ~-less~ are this same adjective, worn down into a bound ending. As a bare imperative, ~los!~ survives on its own: "go, get on with it."

~Losziehen~ has two faces: setting out together on a march or adventure, and, with ~über~, railing against someone: running them down behind their back.
en.lächeln:
From Middle High German ~lecheln~, formed from ~lachen~ ("to laugh") + the diminutive suffix ~-eln~:

• ~lachen~: From MHG ~lachen~, from OHG ~lahhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~ ("to laugh"). Cognate with English ~laugh~, Dutch ~lachen~, and Old Norse ~hlæja~.
• ~-eln~: A diminutive verbal suffix indicating a lesser, gentler, or more tentative version of the base action.

~Lächeln~ is a diminutive of ~lachen~, literally "to laugh a little." The vowel change from ~a~ to ~ä~ (umlaut) is triggered by the diminutive suffix, just as ~Haus~ becomes ~Häuschen~. This is one of the rare cases where German's diminutive system extends to verbs rather than nouns. The distinction between ~lachen~ (open, audible laughter) and ~lächeln~ (a quiet, gentle smile) exactly parallels the diminutive's function: softening and miniaturizing. English ~laugh~ and German ~lachen~ are exact cognates, but English has no equivalent diminutive verb; ~smile~ comes from an entirely different root (Proto-Germanic *~smīlāną~). The Mona Lisa's enigmatic expression is a ~Lächeln~, never a ~Lachen~.
en.löschen: Two etymologically distinct verbs have merged under this spelling. The first, meaning "to extinguish," descends from Middle High German ~leschen~, Old High German ~lescan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~leskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~leskaną~ ("to go out, be extinguished"). Cognate with Dutch ~lessen~. The original Proto-Germanic verb meant the fire goes out on its own; the transitive causative meaning (to put out a fire) developed later. The second, meaning "to delete, unload (cargo)," was borrowed from Low German ~lössen~, ~lossen~, from Middle Low German ~lössen~, derived from the ancestor of ~los~ ("free, rid of"). The spelling ~löschen~ for this second verb arose from later association with the first: unloaded cargo was figuratively "extinguished" from the ship's manifest. Today the digital-age meaning "to delete a file" continues exactly this metaphor.
en.lösen: From Middle High German ~lœsen~, ~lōsen~, from Old High German ~lōsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lausijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lausijaną~, a causative of *~leusaną~ ("to lose, let loose"), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewh₁-~ ("to cut, sever, separate, loosen, lose"). The verb is denominative via the adjective *~lausaz~ ("loose, free"), literally "to make loose." The same PIE root underlies English ~lose~ and ~loose~, Latin ~luere~ ("to release, atone"), Ancient Greek ~lúō~ ("to loosen, liberate"), and Sanskrit ~lūna~ ("cut, severed"). The semantic range of ~lösen~ (from untying a knot to solving a problem to buying a ticket) all trace back to the original idea of releasing something that was bound. Cognate with Dutch ~lozen~, English ~loose~ (via Old Norse ~lauss~), obsolete English ~leese~ (from Old English ~līesan~), Danish ~løse~, Faroese ~loysa~, Icelandic ~leysa~, Norwegian ~løse~, Swedish ~lösa~.
en.lügen: From MHG ~liegen~, from OHG ~liogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~leugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~leuganą~, from PIE *~lewgʰ-~ ("to lie, swear falsely"). A class II strong verb (~lügen~, ~log~, ~gelogen~). The ~ü~ is irregular and late: the expected Early New High German form is ~liegen~, and the vowel was taken over from the noun ~Lüge~ to keep the verb from colliding with ~liegen~ ("to lie down"), German rebuilding a verb's stem to avoid a pun. Cognate with Dutch ~liegen~, Gothic ~liugan~, Danish ~lyve~, Swedish ~ljuga~ and English ~lie~, which also hides inside ~warlock~, Old English ~wǣrloga~ ("oath-breaker").
en.machen: From Middle High German ~machen~, from Old High German ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
en.madigmachen:
A separable compound of ~madig~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~madig~: From the noun ~Made~ ("maggot") plus the adjective suffix ~-ig~, hence "full of maggots, maggot-eaten." ~Made~ goes back to MHG ~made~, OHG ~mado~, from Proto-West Germanic *~maþō~, from Proto-Germanic *~maþô~. Cognate with Old English ~maþa~, Dutch ~made~, Gothic ~maþa~; English ~maggot~ and ~mawkish~ (originally "maggoty") belong to the same family through Old Norse ~maðkr~. The resultative is vivid: to make a thing maggoty in someone's eyes is to spoil it for them. The sense of ~madig~ here is: figuratively, of spoiling something for someone by running it down.

The verb takes a dative of the person and an accusative of the thing (to ~madigmachen~ something to someone), and today is used almost only figuratively.
en.malen:
From Middle High German ~mālen~, from Old High German ~mālōn~, ~mālēn~, a denominative verb from the noun ~māl~ ("spot, stain, mark"), from Proto-West Germanic *~mālijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~mēlijaną~, itself derived from *~mēlą~ ("mark, spot"). The ultimate PIE root is *~melh₂-~ ("dark color"), which also gives Lithuanian ~mėlas~ ("black") and Greek ~melas~ ("dark-colored, black"), the source of English ~melancholy~ (literally "black bile") and ~melanin~.

The semantic path from "mark, stain" to "to paint" is intuitive: the earliest painting was essentially making marks. Cognate with Dutch ~maal~ ("mark") and the German noun ~Mal~ ("mark, time, occasion") and ~Mahl~ ("meal", originally a "marked time" for eating). Be careful not to confuse ~malen~ ("to paint") with ~mahlen~ ("to grind"), which despite their similar sound have completely different origins: ~mahlen~ comes from Proto-Germanic *~malaną~ ("to grind"), from PIE *~melh₂-~ ("to grind"). Ironically, the "to paint" and "to grind" roots may ultimately be related at the deepest PIE level, both involving the notion of rubbing or crushing, since dark pigments were made by grinding minerals, but at the Proto-Germanic stage they were already distinct words.
en.malnehmen:
A separable compound of ~mal~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~mal~: From the noun ~Mal~ ("time, instance"), from MHG ~māl~ ("point in time, mark"), from OHG ~māl~, from Proto-Germanic *~mēlą~, from PIE *~meh₁-~ ("to measure"). Cognate with Gothic ~mēl~ ("time"), Dutch ~maal~, and English ~meal~, which began as "an appointed time" and only later meant the food eaten at one; the older sense survives in ~piecemeal~. The noun is incorporated adverbially from arithmetic's ~drei mal vier~: to take a number a given number of times. The sense of ~mal~ here is: in arithmetic, "times", hence to multiply.

~Malnehmen~ is the everyday counterpart to the learned ~multiplizieren~ and keeps the strong inflection of ~nehmen~ (~nahm mal~, ~malgenommen~).
en.markieren:
Borrowed from French ~marquer~ ("to mark, to indicate"), from Frankish *~markōn~ ("to mark, to note"), from Proto-Germanic *~markō~ ("boundary, border, sign"), from PIE *~merǵ-~ ("edge, boundary"). The German verb was formed with the standard ~-ieren~ suffix for naturalized Romance verbs.

The word's journey is circular: a Frankish Germanic root traveled into Old French, was reshaped by Romance phonology, and then returned to German with a French suffix. The native German noun ~Marke~ ("brand, mark, stamp") was separately borrowed from French ~marque~, which has the same Frankish origin. English ~mark~ is a direct cognate of the original Germanic root, having never taken the detour through French. In modern internet-era German, ~markieren~ has acquired the additional meaning "to tag" someone on social media.
en.mattsetzen:
A separable compound of ~matt~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~matt~: Two borrowings that fell together. The sense "weak, exhausted, dull" is MHG ~mat~ (thirteenth century), most likely from Old French ~mat~ ("defeated, downcast"). The chess sense arrived around 1200 in the phrase ~schāch unde mat~, from Old French ~mat~, from Arabic ~māt~ ("he is dead"), the second word of Persian ~šāh māt~, the king is helpless. English ~checkmate~ is the same phrase, and the verbal use preserves that sharper sense: to leave an opponent no move. The sense of ~matt~ here is: in chess, "checkmated", hence to outmaneuver an opponent completely.

Figuratively, to ~mattsetzen~ someone is to render them powerless: to leave them no move, as on the chessboard.
en.mausrutschen:
A separable compound of ~maus-~ + ~rutschen~:

• ~rutschen~: From MHG ~rutzen~, ~rützen~, an onomatopoeic formation imitating the sound of sliding, with a later shift from ~-tz-~ to ~-tsch-~ (as in ~fletschen~); perhaps related to OHG ~rūtezzen~. The noun ~Rutsche~ ("slide, chute") derives from the verb. English ~rutch~ and ~rutsch~ are borrowed from German or its Low German cognates.
• ~maus-~: An intensifier of disputed origin, familiar from ~mausetot~ ("stone dead"). It looks like ~Maus~ ("mouse"), and speakers have long read it that way, but the older Low German form is ~mūsdōd~ beside ~mursdōd~, ~morsdōd~ ("quite dead"), which points to a Low German intensifying element perhaps connected with ~morsch~ ("rotten") rather than to the animal. The mouse reading is probably a folk etymology, encouraged by the equally intensifying ~mäuschenstill~. Either way, its work in a compound is purely emphatic. The sense of ~maus-~ here is: outwardly the noun ~Maus~ ("mouse"), though that identification is likely secondary.

In ~mausrutschen~, though, the ~Maus~ is literally the computer's pointing device (itself named after the animal), so this recent coinage, "to slip with the mouse, to misclick," has nothing to do with the intensifying ~maus-~ of ~mausetot~.
en.maßhalten:
A separable compound of ~maß~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~maß~: The noun ~Maß~ ("measure, moderation"), from MHG ~māȥe~, from OHG ~māȥa~, a derivative of ~messen~ ("to measure"), from Proto-Germanic *~metaną~, from PIE *~med-~ ("to measure, to take appropriate measures"). It is incorporated as the verb's object: ~maßhalten~ is literally "to hold measure", while ~maßregeln~ is denominal from ~Maßregel~ ("regulation"). The same root gives English ~mete~ and, through Latin, ~moderate~ and ~modest~, words that keep ~Maß~'s second sense of restraint. The sense of ~maß~ here is: in the extended sense "moderation, restraint".

The verb is intransitive and usually appears as an admonition: to show restraint in eating, in judgment, in spending.
en.maßnehmen:
A separable compound of ~maß~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~maß~: The noun ~Maß~ ("measure, moderation"), from MHG ~māȥe~, from OHG ~māȥa~, a derivative of ~messen~ ("to measure"), from Proto-Germanic *~metaną~, from PIE *~med-~ ("to measure, to take appropriate measures"). It is incorporated as the verb's object: ~maßhalten~ is literally "to hold measure", while ~maßregeln~ is denominal from ~Maßregel~ ("regulation"). The same root gives English ~mete~ and, through Latin, ~moderate~ and ~modest~, words that keep ~Maß~'s second sense of restraint. The sense of ~maß~ here is: the incorporated noun "measure", standing as the verb's object.

~Maßnehmen~ is the tailor's term: to take someone's measure is to record their measurements for a garment.
en.meiden: From MHG ~mīden~, from OHG ~mīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~mīþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~mīþaną~, from PIE *~meyth₂-~ ("to change, switch"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~mijden~, Old English ~mīþan~ ("to avoid, conceal"), Old Saxon ~mīthan~.
en.meinen: From Middle High German ~meinen~, from Old High German ~meinen~, from Proto-Germanic *~mainijaną~ ("to mean, think; lament"), from PIE *~moyn-éye-ti~ ("to intend, give an opinion"), a causative formation from the root *~meyn-~. The semantic range of the PIE root covered intending, opining, and expressing, a cluster that persists across its descendants. The Germanic cognates include both the intellectual sense ("to mean, think") and an emotional one: ~meinen~ is also related to English ~moan~, where the root's sense of "lamenting, expressing" took a sorrowful turn. The Irish cognate ~mían~ ("wish, desire") preserves yet another facet of the original meaning. Cognate with Dutch ~menen~, West Frisian ~miene~, English ~mean~ and ~moan~, and Old Irish ~mían~.
en.meistern:
From Middle High German ~meisteren~, from Old High German ~meistarōn~ ("to master, to direct"), derived from the noun ~Meister~ ("master"), from OHG ~meistar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~maistar~, borrowed from Latin ~magister~ ("master, teacher, chief"), from PIE *~meg-~ ("great") via the superlative suffix *~-is-tero-~. The noun ~Meister~ is thus a doublet of ~Magister~ and ~Maestro~, all from the same Latin source.

The verb means "to master, to overcome, to manage successfully"; ~eine Herausforderung meistern~ ("to master a challenge"), ~eine schwierige Situation meistern~ ("to handle a difficult situation"). The Latin source ~magister~ literally meant "the greater one" (from ~magnus~ "great"), a formation parallel to ~minister~ ("the lesser one," from ~minus~ "less"); the master commands while the minister serves. This pair reveals Roman social hierarchy frozen in morphology. In the German trades, ~Meister~ carries enormous prestige: the ~Meisterbrief~ ("master craftsman's certificate") is the highest qualification in the vocational system, and many trades legally require it to open a business. The compound ~Meisterstück~ ("masterpiece") originally referred to the work a journeyman had to produce to earn the ~Meister~ title, a tradition dating to the medieval guild system that is still practiced in some crafts today.
en.melden: From Middle High German ~mëlden~, from Old High German ~mëldōn~, ~mëldēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~melþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~melþōną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~meldʰ-~ ("to ask, pray, speak"). The same PIE root underlies Lithuanian ~maldýti~ ("to implore"), Proto-Slavic *~modlìti~ ("to ask, pray"), Hittite ~māldi~ ("to recite, make a vow"), and Old Armenian ~małtʻ~ ("prayer, supplication"). The original sense was religious or supplicatory speech; ~melden~ retains the communicative dimension while shedding the devotional one, now meaning simply "to report, announce, register." A curious parallel: the PIE *~meldʰ-~ root appears across Indo-European in prayer and invocation contexts, but in German it survives only in the bureaucratic sense of filing a report. Cognate with Dutch ~melden~, Low German ~mellen~, English ~meld~ (a partial cognate, via Dutch ~melden~, used in card games to mean "to declare").
en.melken: From MHG ~melken~, from OHG ~melchan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~melkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~melkaną~, from PIE *~h₂melǵ-~ ("to milk"). A class III strong verb (~melken~, ~molk~, ~gemolken~), though weak forms (~melkte~, ~gemelkt~) are now common. Cognate with English ~milk~, Dutch ~melken~, Danish ~malke~, and, from the same PIE root, Latin ~mulgēre~ and Ancient Greek ~ἀμέλγειν~ (amélgein). The noun ~Milch~ looks unrelated only because OHG ~miluh~ carried a short vowel after the ~l~.
en.merken: From Middle High German ~merken~, from Old High German ~merchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~markijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~markijaną~ ("to mark, notice"), a denominal verb from *~marką~ ("mark, sign"). Cognate with Dutch ~merken~, Icelandic ~merkja~, Old English ~marc~, and modern English ~mark~ (including ~remark~, which entered English via French but traces to the same Germanic root). The core semantic movement is from physical inscription (leaving a mark on a surface) to cognitive attention: to notice something is, in an older idiom, to leave a mental mark on it. German ~Marke~ ("brand, token, stamp") and ~merken~ share this common ancestor, making the act of noticing etymologically an act of marking.
en.messen:
From Middle High German ~mezzen~, from Old High German ~mezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~metan~, from Proto-Germanic *~metaną~, from PIE *~med-~ ("to measure, to take appropriate measures"). A class V strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~meten~, English ~mete~ (as in "to mete out"), Old English ~metan~.

The PIE root *~med-~ is spectacularly productive across the Indo-European family: it gives Latin ~medeor~ ("I heal", originally "I take the right measure"), whence English ~medicine~, ~remedy~, and ~moderate~; Greek ~μέδω~ ("I rule over, I measure") and ~μέτρον~ (~metron~, "measure"), whence ~meter~, ~metric~, ~geometry~, and ~symmetry~; and Latin ~meditārī~ ("to reflect upon"), whence ~meditate~. The semantic thread connecting all these descendants is "taking the right measure", whether of a physical quantity (~messen~), of a punishment (~mete out~), of a disease (~medicine~), or of one's thoughts (~meditate~). German ~Maß~ ("measure") and ~Meter~ (borrowed back from Greek via French) both descend from the same ancient root, one through native inheritance and one through learned borrowing.
en.mieten: From Middle High German ~mieten~, from Old High German ~mietan~, a denominative verb formed from the noun ~Miete~ ("rent, reward"). The noun ~Miete~ descends from MHG ~miete~, from OHG ~mieta~, from Proto-West Germanic *~miʀdu~ ("reward"), from Proto-Germanic *~mizdō~, from PIE *~misdʰéh₂~ ("reward, compensation"). The PIE root reveals a deep connection between rental payment and the ancient concept of reciprocal reward. Cognate with Gothic ~mizdo~ ("reward"), Old English ~meord~ ("reward"), Greek ~misthos~ ("wages, pay"), and Sanskrit ~midha~ ("reward, prize"). The semantic development from "reward" to "rent" reflects the narrowing of a general concept of compensation into a specific financial transaction. English ~meed~ ("a deserved share, reward"), now archaic and poetic, is the direct English cognate, sharing the same Proto-Germanic ancestor. The modern German word ~Miete~ has also taken on the secondary meaning of an earthen clamp for storing root vegetables, though that ~Miete~ is a separate word entirely, borrowed from Low German and ultimately from Latin ~mēta~ ("cone").
en.minimieren: Derived from ~Minimum~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-ieren~. ~Minimum~ is borrowed from Latin ~minimum~, the neuter superlative of ~minimus~ ("smallest, least"), from ~minor~ ("smaller"), ultimately from PIE *~mey-~ ("small"), the same root that gave English ~minus~, ~minor~, ~minute~, ~diminish~, and ~minister~ (originally "a lesser servant"). The suffix ~-ieren~ is the standard German mechanism for creating verbs from Latin and French borrowings, corresponding to French ~-er~ and English ~-ize~. The antonym ~maximieren~ is built on the same pattern from Latin ~maximum~.
en.mischen:
From Middle High German ~mischen~ ("to mix"), from Old High German ~misken~ ("to mix"), from Proto-Germanic *~miskijaną~ ("to mix"), from PIE *~meyḱ-~ ("to mix, knead"), via the inchoative present *~miḱ-sḱé-~. Cognate with English ~mix~, Latin ~misceō~ ("to mix"), Greek ~mísgo~ ("to mix"), Old Church Slavonic ~měšati~ ("to mix"), Lithuanian ~maišyti~ ("to mix"), Sanskrit ~miśrá~ ("mixed"), Welsh ~mysgu~ ("to mix").

The PIE root *~meyḱ-~ has an astonishingly wide reach across the Indo-European family, appearing in nearly every branch with the same core meaning. The Latin descendant ~misceō~ gave English ~miscellaneous~ and ~promiscuous~ (literally "thoroughly mixed"). The Germanic path through *~miskijaną~ produced both German ~mischen~ and (via Old English *~mixian~) English ~mix~. French ~mélange~ ("mixture") is also probably of Germanic origin, borrowed from Frankish *~misken~ with a fossilized Germanic suffix. The German verb covers both the general sense "to mix" and the specialized card-game sense "to shuffle."
en.mitarbeiten:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys participation: taking part in something others are doing.

One works ~on~ something or ~in~ a body; the prefix turns solitary labor into shared effort.
en.mitbekommen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~be-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

~Bekommen~ has become a purely idiomatic "to receive"; with ~mit-~ added, ~mitbekommen~ means partly "to be given something to take along," partly, figuratively, "to catch, to grasp."
en.mitbestimmen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~be-~ + ~stimmen~:

• ~stimmen~: From MHG ~stimmen~, from OHG *~stimmen~, a denominative of ~Stimme~ ("voice, vote": OHG ~stimma~, Proto-West Germanic *~stebnu~, Proto-Germanic *~stebnō~, from PIE *~stomen-~ "mouth, muzzle"). Hence the senses "to tune" (an instrument), "to be correct," and "to vote." Cognate with archaic English ~steven~ ("voice"), Dutch ~stem~, Gothic ~stibna~, Ancient Greek ~stóma~ ("mouth").
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys participation: taking part in something others are doing.

The related noun ~die Mitbestimmung~ is a cornerstone of German labor law: the workforce's right to share in company decisions.
en.mitbringen:
From ~mit-~ + ~bringen~. Compound of:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, from a pre-Germanic compound root *~bʰrenḱ-~, likely from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁neḱ-~ ("to bring, reach"). Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit-~, from OHG ~mit-~, ~miti-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~, from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys accompaniment, doing something along with someone or bringing something along.

~Bringen~ is one of the most unusual verbs in Germanic: it has a mixed past tense combining both strong (ablaut: ~brachte~) and weak (dental suffix: ~-te~) features, the only known case of this mixture in Proto-Germanic. This anomaly arises from its compound PIE origin. ~Mitbringen~ ("to bring along") is among the most common separable-prefix verbs in everyday German; one ~bringt~ a gift ~mit~ to a party, or ~bringt~ experience ~mit~ to a job. The question ~Was soll ich mitbringen?~ ("What should I bring?") is a fixture of German social life. Cognate with Hunsrik ~mitbringe~.
en.mitdenken:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~teng-~ ("to think, feel"). A mixed-conjugation verb of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~dachte~ pairs the vowel change ~e~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix and ~k~ > ~ch~. Cognate with English ~think~, Dutch ~denken~, Icelandic ~þekkja~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys inclusion: doing something too, in addition to the rest.

Like ~denken~, it follows the Rückumlaut mixed class (~dachte mit~, ~mitgedacht~); to ~mitdenken~ something is to factor it into one's reasoning from the outset.
en.miterleben:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~er-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ conveys obtaining or acquiring something by means of the base action.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys inclusion: doing something too, in addition to the rest.

~Miterleben~ is transitive (one lives an event through alongside others), and denotes sharing in a moment that others live through as well.
en.mitfahren:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

~Mitfahren~ is the passenger's verb; from it comes ~Mitfahrgelegenheit~, the chance of a lift in someone's car.
en.mitfolgen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~folgen~:

• ~folgen~: From MHG ~volgen~, from OHG ~folgēn~ ("to follow, serve faithfully, pursue," attested from the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *~folgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fulgāną~; the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. Cognate with English ~follow~, Dutch ~volgen~, Danish ~følge~, Swedish ~följa~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

~Mitfolgen~ ("to go along, to accompany") is now archaic and survives almost only in older, biblical texts.
en.mitfühlen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~fühlen~:

• ~fühlen~: From northern MHG ~vüelen~, from OHG ~fuolen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōlijan~ ("to feel"); the further origin is uncertain, presumably related to Old Norse ~falma~ ("to grope"), and possibly a secondary causative of a strong *~falaną~, from PIE *~pelh₁-~ ("to stroke"). Cognate with English ~feel~, Dutch ~voelen~, Danish ~føle~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

The noun ~Mitgefühl~ mirrors Latin ~compassio~ morpheme for morpheme, "feeling-with," the same image as English ~compassion~.
en.mitgeben:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

Beside the literal "to give someone something to take along" stands the figurative ~jemandem etwas auf den Weg mitgeben~: to send someone off with a piece of advice or a blessing.
en.mitgehen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

Colloquially, ~etwas mitgehen lassen~ (to "let something go along") means to pilfer it.
en.mithalten:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys participation: taking part in something others are doing.

~Mithalten~ is intransitive and governs ~mit~ + dative: to keep pace with someone or something, to hold one's own in comparison.
en.mithelfen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~helfen~:

• ~helfen~: From MHG ~hëlfen~, from OHG ~hëlfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helpaną~, from PIE *~ḱelb-~, *~ḱelp-~. A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~e~-~a~-~o~ ablaut pattern (~helfen~, ~half~, ~geholfen~). Cognate with English ~help~, Dutch ~helpen~, Danish ~hjælpe~, Norwegian ~hjelpe~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys participation: taking part in something others are doing.

Like ~helfen~, it governs the dative; the prefix ranks the doer among the others lending a hand.
en.mithören:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys inclusion: doing something too, in addition to the rest.

~Mithören~ ranges from innocently "hearing along" to tapping a conversation: secretly listening in on what is meant for others.
en.mitklingen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~klingen~:

• ~klingen~: From MHG ~klingen~, from OHG ~klingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~klinganą~, almost certainly of onomatopoeic origin. A class III strong verb (~klingt~, ~klang~, ~geklungen~), the same pattern as ~singen~. Cognate with English ~clink~ and ~clang~, Middle Dutch ~klinken~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

Figuratively, an undertone or a shade of meaning is said to ~klingen mit~, to be present unspoken; a strong verb like ~klingen~ (~klang mit~, ~mitgeklungen~).
en.mitkommen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

Beside the literal "to come along" stands the figurative ~nicht mitkommen~: being unable to keep up with the pace or the argument.
en.mitkriegen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~kriegen~:

• ~kriegen~: From MHG ~kriegen~ ("to war, to strive for"), a verbalization of ~Krieg~ ("war"), from OHG ~krig~, from Proto-West Germanic *~krīg~, whose origin is debated. The "obtaining" sense overshadowed the military one; colloquial modern German ~kriegen~ simply means "to get." Cognate with Dutch ~krijgen~ ("to get"), Bavarian ~kriagn~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

~Mitkriegen~ is the colloquial variant of ~mitbekommen~, using ~kriegen~ rather than ~bekommen~ for "to get", both "to be given something to take along" and "to notice."
en.mitleiden:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~leiden~:

• ~leiden~: From MHG ~līden~, from OHG ~līdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~līþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~līþaną~ ("to go, travel"); the sense narrowed through "to endure" to "to suffer," reinforced by convergence with MHG ~leiden~ ("to be sorry"), from Proto-Germanic *~laiþaz~ ("hateful"). Not cognate with English ~lead~, but with ~lithe~, ~loathe~, Dutch ~lijden~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

From the verb comes the noun ~das Mitleid~ ("pity"), image for image the Greek ~sympátheia~, "suffering-with," which lives on in English ~sympathy~.
en.mitmachen:
Compound of ~mit-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with English ~make~, Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit(i)~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (as in ~amid~, ~midway~), Greek ~meta~ ("with, after").

The literal sense is "to make along with, to do along," meaning "to participate, to join in."
