The verb is remarkably versatile in colloquial German: ~eine Reise mitmachen~ ("to go along on a trip"), ~eine Mode mitmachen~ ("to follow a fashion"), ~viel mitmachen müssen~ ("to have had to endure a lot"), and ~da mache ich nicht mit~ ("I'm not going along with that"). The English cognate ~make~ and German ~machen~ have tracked closely in meaning for over a millennium, both expanding from a concrete PIE sense of kneading or mixing into the most general-purpose "doing" verb in their respective languages. Cognate also with Hunsrik ~mitmache~, carried to Brazil by German settlers in the 19th century.
en.mitmischen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~mischen~:

• ~mischen~: From MHG ~mischen~, from OHG ~misken~, from Proto-Germanic *~miskijaną~ ("to mix"), from PIE *~meyḱ-~ ("to mix, knead"), via the inchoative present *~miḱ-sḱé-~. Cognate with English ~mix~, Latin ~misceō~, Greek ~mísgo~, Sanskrit ~miśrá~ ("mixed").
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys participation: taking part in something others are doing.

~Mitmischen~ takes the literal "mixing in" into the figurative: to get actively involved in something, often where one is not welcome.
en.mitnehmen:
Compound of ~mit-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due").
• ~mit-~: From PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). This separable prefix adds the sense of accompaniment or inclusion, taking something along.

~Mitnehmen~ means "to take along, to take with"; ~Nimm einen Regenschirm mit!~ ("Take an umbrella along!"). But it has a vivid colloquial extension: ~mitgenommen~ (past participle) means "worn out, battered, exhausted": someone who has been "taken along" by life's hardships looks ~mitgenommen~. The fast-food phrase ~zum Mitnehmen~ ("to go, takeaway") has become ubiquitous. The PIE root *~nem-~ is fascinating because it meant both "to give" and "to take" one's allotted portion: the ambiguity reflects a world where distribution and receipt were two sides of the same act. Greek ~νέμω~ ("to distribute, to allot") and ~Nemesis~ (the goddess of rightful distribution turned retribution) descend from the same root. Cognate with Dutch ~meenemen~, Low German ~mitnehmen~, Danish ~nemme~ ("to learn, to grasp", from the "take in" sense).
en.mitreden:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys participation: taking part in something others are doing.

Beyond merely talking along, ~mitreden~ often means to have a say in a matter.
en.mitreisen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

The compound keeps ~reisen~'s modern "travel" sense: the companion shares the journey.
en.mitreißen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

Figuratively, ~mitreißen~ means to sweep others along: a speech or an enthusiasm that carries an audience away.
en.mitschneiden:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~schneiden~:

• ~schneiden~: From MHG ~snīden~, from OHG ~snīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~snīþan~ ("to cut"); no secure PIE root has been established, and the word may be a Germanic innovation. A class I strong verb (~schneiden~, ~schnitt~, ~geschnitten~). Cognate with archaic English ~snithe~ ("to cut"), Dutch ~snijden~, Icelandic ~sníða~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

~Mitschneiden~ comes from tape editing: a broadcast or conversation is recorded as it plays.
en.mitschwingen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~schwingen~:

• ~schwingen~: From MHG ~swingen~, from OHG ~swingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swinganą~ ("to swing, to fling"), with no securely reconstructed PIE source. A class III strong verb (~schwingen~, ~schwang~, ~geschwungen~). Cognate with English ~swing~, Old English ~swingan~ ("to beat, to flog"), Low German ~swingen~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

Figuratively, a worry or undertone ~schwingt mit~, present without being spoken.
en.mitsingen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~singen~:

• ~singen~: From MHG ~singen~, from OHG ~singan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~singwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~singwaną~, from PIE *~sengʷʰ-~ ("to recite, intone, chant"), connected to Ancient Greek ~ὀμφή~ (omphḗ, "divine voice, oracle"). A class III strong verb (~singen~, ~sang~, ~gesungen~). Cognate with English ~sing~, Gothic ~𐍃𐌹𐌲𐌲𐍅𐌰𐌽~ (siggwan), Dutch ~zingen~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys participation: taking part in something others are doing.

~Mitsingen~ means to join in the singing of others.
en.mitspielen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys participation: taking part in something others are doing.

~Mitspielen~ ranges from joining a game, to going along with a pretense, to the figurative sense of a circumstance "playing a part."
en.mitteilen:
From Middle High German ~miteteilen~, equivalent to ~mit-~ + ~teilen~:

• ~teilen~: From MHG ~teilen~, from OHG ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, from PIE *~deh₂y-~ ("to divide, to share").
• ~mit-~: From PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). The prefix adds the sense of sharing or participating.

~Mitteilen~ literally means "to share a part with", to divide something (information, news) and give a portion to someone else. The derived noun ~Mitteilung~ ("communication, notification, message") is standard in formal and administrative German. The compound is transparent in its structure: ~mit~ ("with") + ~teilen~ ("to divide") = to divide with someone, i.e., to share information. The related noun ~Mitleid~ ("compassion," literally "suffering-with") shows the same prefix in its empathic sense. Cognate with Dutch ~meedelen~.
en.mittragen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb whose semantic range broadened from "to drag, pull" to "to carry, bear, wear." Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

From literally carrying a load together, ~mittragen~ extends to the figurative: to share responsibility for a decision and back it.
en.mitunterzeichnen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~unter-~ + ~zeichnen~:

• ~zeichnen~: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, symbol"), from MHG ~zeichen~, from OHG ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~, *~taiknaz~ ("sign"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point"); to ~zeichnen~ is etymologically to make a sign. Cognate with English ~token~, Dutch ~teken~, Danish ~tegn~, Swedish ~tecken~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys inclusion: doing something too, in addition to the rest.

To ~unterzeichnen~, placing one's name beneath, ~mit-~ adds the further signatory: one sets one's name alongside the others.
en.mitwirken:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~wirken~:

• ~wirken~: From MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~, from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~wérǵom~, from *~werǵ-~ ("to make, work"). Early on it merged with the dialectal ~würken~ (from OHG ~wurken~), which left the written language in the 18th century. Cognate with English ~work~ and ~wrought~, Dutch ~werken~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys participation: taking part in something others are doing.

~Mitwirken~ is to have a hand in a work and contribute to its coming about.
en.mitzeichnen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~zeichnen~:

• ~zeichnen~: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, symbol"), from MHG ~zeichen~, from OHG ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~, *~taiknaz~ ("sign"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point"); to ~zeichnen~ is etymologically to make a sign. Cognate with English ~token~, Dutch ~teken~, Danish ~tegn~, Swedish ~tecken~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys participation: taking part in something others are doing.

Beyond literally drawing together, in officialese ~mitzeichnen~ means to co-approve a document by adding one's initials.
en.mitziehen:
A separable compound of ~mit-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~mit-~: From MHG ~mit(e)~, from OHG ~mit~, ~miti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~midi~, from Proto-Germanic *~midi~ ("with, among"), from PIE *~me~ ("in the middle of, near"). Cognate with English ~mid~ (still visible in ~amid~ and in ~midwife~, literally "with-woman," one who is with the mother) and with Greek ~metá~ ("with, after"). The prefix conveys accompaniment: going along with someone or bringing something along.

From literally moving along with a group, ~mitziehen~ extends to keeping pace: going along with a plan and matching its stride.
en.mobilmachen:
A separable compound of ~mobil~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~mobil~: Borrowed from French ~mobile~, from Latin ~mōbilis~ ("movable," from *~movibilis~, to ~movēre~ "to move"). The German military use dates from about 1800 and keeps the literal sense: to put troops on a war footing is to make them movable. Its doublet is ~Möbel~ (French ~meuble~, from Latin ~mōbilia~ ("movable goods")) so furniture is etymologically the property one could carry away. Cognate with English ~mobile~, ~mobilize~. The sense of ~mobil~ here is specifically military: to mobilize, to put on a war footing.

In military use ~mobilmachen~ is to put troops on a war footing; colloquially it now often means to get forces moving.
en.montieren: Borrowed from French ~monter~ with the addition of the German verbal suffix ~-ieren~. The French source traces from Middle French ~monter~, from Old French ~monter~, from Vulgar Latin *~montāre~, from Latin ~mons~ (~montem~, "mountain"). The original French sense was "to go up, to climb," from the idea of ascending a mountain. The semantic shift to "to mount, to assemble" arose from the notion of placing something up or putting components together, as one might mount a horse or mount a piece of equipment into position. The ~-ieren~ suffix is German's standard mechanism for adapting French and Latin verbs, paralleling patterns like ~reparieren~, ~organisieren~, and ~installieren~. English ~mount~ is a direct cognate from the same French source, and the technical sense of ~montieren~ in German closely mirrors English ~to mount~ in mechanical and engineering contexts. In film, ~Montage~ (borrowed from French) preserves the assembly metaphor, referring to the cutting and joining of shots into a unified sequence.
en.motivieren: Borrowed from French ~motiver~, itself derived from ~motif~ ("motive") + the verbal suffix ~-er~. French ~motif~ descends from Medieval Latin ~motivus~ ("moving, impelling"), from Latin ~motus~, the past participle of ~movere~ ("to move"), from PIE *~mewh₁-~ ("to push away, move"). The German verb adds the standard ~-ieren~ suffix used for French and Latin loanwords. The word entered German during the 18th century as part of the broader wave of French intellectual vocabulary that shaped the language of Enlightenment discourse. English ~motivate~ arrived via the same Latin root but took a slightly different path through the adjective ~motive~. The PIE root *~mewh₁-~ is extraordinarily productive: it also yielded Latin ~momentum~ (a "movement," giving English ~moment~ and ~momentum~), ~mobile~ ("movable"), ~emotion~ (literally "a moving out"), and ~motor~. German ~Motiv~ serves double duty as both "motive" (reason for action) and "motif" (recurring artistic theme), preserving a unity that English splits between two borrowed words.
en.mögen: From Middle High German ~mugen~, from Old High German ~mugan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~magan~, from Proto-Germanic *~maganą~, from PIE *~megʰ-~ ("to be able, have power"). A preterite-present verb: its present-tense conjugations descend from original past-tense forms, which accounts for the absence of personal endings in the first- and third-person singular (~mag~, not *~magt~). Cognate with Dutch ~mogen~, English ~may~, Icelandic ~mega~, Gothic ~magan~.
en.müssen: From Middle High German ~müeȥen~, from Old High German ~muoȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~mōtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~mōtaną~. A preterite-present verb derived from a secondary perfect of PIE *~mēd-~ ("to measure, ensure compliance, take care of"). Alternatively connected to the same root as Proto-Germanic *~mōtą~ ("meeting"). The preservation of the original diphthong can still be seen in Bavarian ~muass~. Cognate with Dutch ~moeten~, English ~must~, Old Norse ~mega~.
en.nacharbeiten:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys checking or verifying by going back over something.

~Nacharbeiten~ is to go back over finished work to improve it, or to make up what was missed.
en.nachbacken:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~backen~:

• ~backen~: From MHG ~backen~, from OHG ~backan~, an originally weak geminated variant of an older strong verb (MHG ~bachen~, OHG ~bahhan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~bakan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bakaną~, from PIE *~bʰeh₃g-~ ("to roast, bake"). The two blended early, so strong ~buk~ survives beside weak ~backte~. Cognate with English ~bake~, Dutch ~bakken~, Swedish ~baka~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys repetition or imitation: doing again what someone else did.

~Nachbacken~ is to make a baked good again by following an original recipe.
en.nachbauen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~būwen~, from OHG ~būan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~būan~, from Proto-Germanic *~būaną~ ("to dwell, reside"), from PIE *~bʰuH-~ ("to be, become, grow"); one builds where one lives. Cognate with English ~be~, ~bower~ ("dwelling"), ~neighbor~ ("near-dweller"), Dutch ~bouwen~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys repetition or imitation: doing again what someone else did.

~Nachbauen~ is to build something anew faithfully after a model: to make a replica.
en.nachbehandeln:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~be-~ + ~handeln~:

• ~handeln~: From MHG ~handeln~, from OHG ~hantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handulōn~, a denominative verb from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~ ("hand") with the frequentative suffix *~-lōną~; the sense broadened from "to handle" to "to act, deal, trade." Cognate with English ~handle~, Dutch ~handelen~, Danish ~handle~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

~Behandeln~ directs one's dealing at an object; ~nach-~ places it afterward: the follow-up treatment comes after the main procedure.
en.nachbestellen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~be-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

~Nachbestellen~ is to place a further order afterward for more of the same.
en.nachbeten:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~beten~:

• ~beten~: From MHG ~beten~, from OHG ~beton~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bedon~, from Proto-Germanic *~bedan~ ("to pray, to ask"), close to *~bidjan~ ("to ask"), from PIE *~gwhedh-~ ("to ask for, beseech"). The narrowing from "ask" to "pray" is a Christianization phenomenon. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bidden~, Danish ~bede~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys repetition or imitation: doing again what someone else did.

From repeating a prayer after the one who leads it, ~nachbeten~ turns pejorative: to parrot an opinion unthinkingly.
en.nachbilden:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~bilden~:

• ~bilden~: From MHG ~bilden~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: ~biliden~ ("to form into an image"), from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþijan~, and ~bilidōn~ ("to copy, represent"), from *~biliþōn~; both from the noun *~biliþī~ (whence ~Bild~), whose pre-Germanic origin is obscure, with no secure PIE etymology. Cognate with Dutch ~beelden~, Swedish ~bilda~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys repetition or imitation: doing again what someone else did.

~Nachbilden~ is to form something after a model: to make a reproduction.
en.nachbleiben:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys following after, pursuing something that has gone ahead.

~Nachbleiben~ is rare today; it means to stay behind or be left undone, as in the Luther passage, the work that would go unfinished.
en.nachblicken:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~blank~, Dutch ~blik~, Old English ~blice~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys following after, pursuing something that has gone ahead.

~Nachblicken~ is to follow a departing person or thing with one's gaze.
en.nachdenken:
~Nach-~ + ~denken~. Compound of ~nach-~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, ~thenken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~tong-éye-ti~, causative of *~teng-~ ("to think, feel, perceive, know").
• ~nach-~: From PIE *~h₂neḱ~ ("to reach, to attain"). The separable prefix adds a sense of following after, pursuing.

~Nachdenken~ means "to reflect, to ponder, to think carefully about." Where ~denken~ is simply "to think," ~nachdenken~ is to think ~after~: to follow a thought to its conclusion, to trace its implications. The prefix ~nach-~ here conveys pursuit: the thinker chases after an idea, turning it over repeatedly. The construction ~über etwas nachdenken~ ("to reflect on something") is one of the most common intellectual verbs in German. As a neuter noun, ~das Nachdenken~ ("reflection, contemplation") is used without an article in the elegant phrase ~nach reiflichem Nachdenken~ ("after mature reflection"). Cognate with Hunsrik ~nohdenke~, Dutch ~nadenken~ ("to think over, to ponder").
en.nachdrucken:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~drucken~:

• ~drucken~: From MHG ~drucken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~ ("to press"). A doublet of ~drücken~ ("to press, push"), which keeps the expected umlaut; ~drucken~ lacks it because Upper German blocked umlaut before a velar geminate, and the form used by the first, southern printers became the technical term. Polish ~drukować~ was borrowed from it.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys repetition or imitation: doing again what someone else did.

~Nachdrucken~ is to print again what has already been printed, historically often the unauthorized reprint that printing privileges guarded against.
en.nachempfinden:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~emp-~ + ~finden~:

• ~finden~: From MHG ~vinden~, from OHG ~findan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~finþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to go, pass; path, bridge"). The development from "to go, pass" to "to find" parallels shifts in Slavic. Cognate with English ~find~, Dutch ~vinden~, Low German ~finden~, Danish ~finde~.
• ~emp-~: A variant of ~ent-~, from MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). The form ~emp-~ arose by assimilation before the labials ~f~ and ~pf~, and survives in only three verbs: ~empfangen~, ~empfehlen~ and ~empfinden~. ~emp-~ is the phonologically conditioned form of ~ent-~ before ~f~ and ~pf~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys repetition or imitation: doing again what someone else did.

~Empfinden~ is to perceive a feeling; ~nach-~ turns it into empathy: to re-experience in oneself what another felt.
en.nacherzählen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~er-~ + ~zählen~:

• ~zählen~: From MHG ~zel(e)n~, ~zellen~, from OHG ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~ ("to enumerate, count; to recount, tell"). German split this dual sense: ~zählen~ kept "to count," ~erzählen~ took "to narrate." Cognate with Dutch ~tellen~, English ~tell~ and ~tale~, Danish ~tælle~, Gothic ~talzjan~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys repetition or imitation: doing again what someone else did.

The compound names the retelling of a story one has heard or read, in one's own words, the ~nach-~ here marks recounting again what another has told.
en.nachfahren:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys following after, pursuing something that has gone ahead.

~Nachfahren~ denotes following behind someone who has driven on ahead, governing the dative; figuratively something intangible can ~nachfahren~ a person too.
en.nachfolgen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~folgen~:

• ~folgen~: From MHG ~volgen~, from OHG ~folgēn~ ("to follow, serve faithfully, pursue," attested from the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *~folgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fulgāną~; the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. Cognate with English ~follow~, Dutch ~volgen~, Danish ~følge~, Swedish ~följa~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys following after, pursuing something that has gone ahead.

Beyond spatial following, ~nachfolgen~ also carries the sense of succession: the successor takes the predecessor's place.
en.nachfragen:
A compound of ~nach-~ + ~fragen~:

• ~fragen~: From MHG ~vrāgen~, from OHG ~frāgēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frāgēn~. Cognate with Dutch ~vragen~, Swedish ~fråga~.
• ~nach-~: From Old High German ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, from PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). As a verbal prefix, ~nach-~ adds a sense of "after" or "following up."

The verb means "to inquire further, to follow up with a question", asking after something that has already been stated or left unclear. The PIE root *~h₂neḱ-~ also gave rise to Latin ~nancīscor~ ("I obtain") and Sanskrit ~naśati~ ("to reach"), all sharing the idea of reaching or arriving at something. Cognate with Dutch ~navragen~.
en.nachfühlen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~fühlen~:

• ~fühlen~: From northern MHG ~vüelen~, from OHG ~fuolen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōlijan~ ("to feel"); the further origin is uncertain, presumably related to Old Norse ~falma~ ("to grope"), and possibly a secondary causative of a strong *~falaną~, from PIE *~pelh₁-~ ("to stroke"). Cognate with English ~feel~, Dutch ~voelen~, Danish ~føle~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys repetition or imitation: doing again what someone else did.

~Nachfühlen~ means to inwardly reconstruct another's feeling, to feel it, as it were, a second time.
en.nachführen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

~Nachführen~ means to bring something up to the latest state, updating it after the fact; technically also the continual readjustment of, say, a piece of equipment.
en.nachfüllen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~füllen~:

• ~füllen~: From MHG ~vüllen~, from OHG ~fullen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fullijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullijaną~ ("to make full"), the causative of *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pl̥h₁nós~ ("full"). English ~fill~ and ~füllen~ are exact cognates, each the causative of its native word for "full." Cognate with English ~fill~, Dutch ~vullen~, Danish ~fylde~, Swedish ~fylla~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

~Nachfüllen~ denotes filling up again a supply that has been emptied or reduced.
en.nachgeben:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys yielding or slackening, giving way rather than holding firm.

~Nachgeben~ ranges from physical yielding (a material gives way under pressure), to a person relenting and abandoning resistance.
en.nachgehen:
From Middle High German ~nāchgān~, from Old High German ~nāhgān~, from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhwagān~. Compound of ~nach-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from OHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave, go").
• ~nach-~: From OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, from PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). As a prefix, it conveys "after, following."

The literal meaning is "to go after," which branches into several figurative senses: "to pursue," "to investigate" (as in ~einer Sache nachgehen~), and "to be slow" (of a clock). The spelling with ~-h-~ in ~gehen~ was introduced by analogy with ~sehen~, where the ~h~ had become silent but was retained in writing. Cognate with Dutch ~nagaan~.
en.nachgeraten:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~ge-~ + ~raten~:

• ~raten~: From MHG ~rāten~, from OHG ~rātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rēdaną~ ("to decide, advise, interpret"), from PIE *~Hreh₁dh-~ ("to think, arrange"). Both senses, "to advise" and "to guess," descend from that sense of deliberation. Cognate with English ~read~ (originally "to counsel, interpret"), archaic ~rede~, Dutch ~raden~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ marks completion or arrival at a result, the prefix's old perfective force.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys repetition or imitation: doing again what someone else did.

The verb describes someone turning out to resemble a forebear in nature or appearance: one turns out after the model of a predecessor.
en.nachgießen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~gießen~:

• ~gießen~: From MHG ~giezen~, from OHG ~giozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geutan~ ("to pour"), from Proto-Germanic *~geutaną~, from PIE *~gʰewd-~ ("to pour"). The sense of casting metal and glass is attested since Old High German (participle ~gigozzan~). Cognate with English ~gush~, Dutch ~gieten~, Old English ~geotan~, Gothic ~giutan~, Swedish ~gjuta~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

~Nachgießen~ means to pour in more liquid to top up a partly emptied vessel.
en.nachhalten:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys checking or verifying by going back over something.

~Nachhalten~ in modern usage denotes the monitoring follow-up of whether what was agreed has actually been carried out.
en.nachholen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~holen~:

• ~holen~: From MHG ~holen~, ~holn~, from OHG ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, possibly from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, summon") via "to summon" → "to go and fetch"; the connection is uncertain. Cognate with Dutch ~halen~, Low German ~halen~, English ~haul~ (via French).
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

~Nachholen~ denotes doing later what was left undone at its proper time, making up for what was missed.
en.nachhängen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~hängen~:

• ~hängen~: The merger of three OHG verbs: ~hāhan~ (strong, transitive; past ~hieng~, participle ~gehangan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~hą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~hanhaną~; ~hangēn~ (weak, intransitive); and the causative ~hengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hangijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hangijaną~. The distinction is upheld chiefly in the past tense: intransitive ~hing~/~gehangen~ versus transitive ~hängte~/~gehängt~. Cognate with Dutch ~hangen~, English ~hang~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys following after, pursuing something that has gone ahead.

~Nachhängen~ carries the spatial "following after" inward: one lingers on a thought or memory that will not let go.
en.nachjagen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~jagen~:

• ~jagen~: From MHG ~jagen~ ("to hurry, drive, pursue, hunt"), from OHG ~jagōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~jagōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~jakkōną~, a ~nā~-iterative formation, likely rebuilt from PIE *~h₁eyǵʰ-~ ("to strive, chase"). Attested since the eighth century; further pre-Germanic etymology is obscure.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys following after, pursuing something that has gone ahead.

~Nachjagen~ means headlong pursuit: of someone fleeing, and figuratively of a goal or of fame.
en.nachkaufen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, a denominative verb from *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"), a loanword from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper"). Cognate with English ~cheap~, Dutch ~kopen~, Danish ~købe~, Icelandic ~kaupa~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

~Nachkaufen~ denotes the later purchase of further units of what one already owns.
en.nachklingen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~klingen~:

• ~klingen~: From MHG ~klingen~, from OHG ~klingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~klinganą~, almost certainly of onomatopoeic origin. A class III strong verb (~klingt~, ~klang~, ~geklungen~), the same pattern as ~singen~. Cognate with English ~clink~ and ~clang~, Middle Dutch ~klinken~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

~Nachklingen~ means that a tone or impression goes on resonating after its source has fallen silent.
en.nachkommen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys following after, pursuing something that has gone ahead.

Beyond arriving after others, ~nachkommen~ also carries the sense of fulfilment: to ~nachkommen~ a duty or a request is to satisfy it.
en.nachladen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two historically distinct verbs under one infinitive. ~laden~ (strong, "to load"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"); cognate with English ~lade~ and ~laden~, Lithuanian ~klṓti~. ~laden~ (weak, "to invite, summon"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root found only in Germanic and Anatolian (Hittite ~halzai~).
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). ~Nachsteigen~ literally means to climb after; colloquially ~jemandem nachsteigen~ means to court or doggedly pursue someone.
en.nachstellen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys repetition or imitation: doing again what someone else did.

The gloss names the imitative sense of "reenacting" a scene; the citations instead show the older ~jemandem nachstellen~ "to pursue, to lie in wait for."
en.nachtragen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb whose semantic range broadened from "to drag, pull" to "to carry, bear, wear." Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

Beyond the literal "carrying after" of the citation, ~nachtragen~ means adding to a text later, and, figuratively, ~jemandem etwas nachtragen~, to hold a grudge.
en.nachtreten:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

~Nachtreten~ is the kick delivered after the fight is already decided; figuratively it denotes spitefully piling on someone already beaten.
en.nachverfolgen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~ver-~ + ~folgen~:

• ~folgen~: From MHG ~volgen~, from OHG ~folgēn~ ("to follow, serve faithfully, pursue," attested from the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *~folgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fulgāną~; the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. Cognate with English ~follow~, Dutch ~volgen~, Danish ~følge~, Swedish ~följa~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys following after, pursuing something that has gone ahead.

~Verfolgen~ is already intensified following; ~nach-~ adds the notion of tracking something continuously over time; hence tracing a process or a parcel.
en.nachverhandeln:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~ver-~ + ~handeln~:

• ~handeln~: From MHG ~handeln~, from OHG ~hantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handulōn~, a denominative verb from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~ ("hand") with the frequentative suffix *~-lōną~; the sense broadened from "to handle" to "to act, deal, trade." Cognate with English ~handle~, Dutch ~handelen~, Danish ~handle~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

~Verhandeln~ carries dealing through to an agreement; ~nach-~ starts afresh once that agreement already stands; one renegotiates a settled deal after the fact.
en.nachvollziehen:
Compound of ~nach-~ + ~vollziehen~:

• ~vollziehen~: Itself a compound of ~voll~ ("full") + ~ziehen~ ("to pull, draw"), from MHG ~volleziehen~, from OHG ~follaziohan~. ~Voll~ descends from OHG ~foll~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullaz~, from PIE *~pl̥h₁nós~ ("full"). ~Ziehen~ from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). Cognate with Dutch ~voltrekken~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhw~ ("near, close"), from PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). As a prefix, it means "after, following, re-."

The literal sense is "to carry out after": to retrace and reconstruct in one's mind what someone else has done or thought. ~Nachvollziehen~ means "to comprehend, to understand by mentally retracing" and fills a gap that English struggles to express in a single word. It is not mere understanding but empathetic reconstruction: following the same mental path another person walked. The word is a mid-20th-century coinage, surprisingly young for such a deeply embedded concept. The base verb ~vollziehen~ means "to carry out, to execute" (a law, a sentence), itself a calque of Latin ~exsequī~ ("to follow out"). The PIE root *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead") also yielded Latin ~dūcere~ ("to lead"), whence English ~duke~, ~conduct~, and ~education~.
en.nachwachsen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from PIE *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Cognate with English ~wax~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

~Nachwachsen~ means the regrowth of what was lost or the growing-up of the next generation; what is missing is replaced after the fact.
en.nachwandeln:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~wandeln~:

• ~wandeln~: From MHG ~wandeln~, from OHG ~wantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandōną~, from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). It means both "to walk, stroll" and "to change, transform" (~sich wandeln~), both from the root idea of turning. Cognate with English ~wend~ and ~wind~, Dutch ~wandelen~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys following after, pursuing something that has gone ahead.

Here the base sense of ~wandeln~ as "to walk, to stride" is alive: ~nachwandeln~ means to walk after someone, biblically often in the sense of following after foreign gods.
en.nachweinen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~weinen~:

• ~weinen~: From MHG ~weinen~, from OHG ~weinōn~ ("to cry, lament"), from Proto-Germanic *~wainōną~ ("to wail, weep"), from PIE *~wáy~ ("woe!"), originally an exclamation of grief. Related to ~Weh~ ("woe, pain"), from Proto-Germanic *~waiwô~, from the same exclamatory root. Cognate with Gothic ~wainon~, Old Norse ~veina~, Old English ~wānian~, Dutch ~wenen~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys following after, pursuing something that has gone ahead.

~Nachweinen~ means to weep after a lost person or thing: mourning what is gone.
en.nachweisen:
~Nach-~ + ~weisen~. Compound of ~nach-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~ ("to show, to point out"), from PIE *~weyd-~ ("to see").
• ~nach-~: From PIE *~h₂neḱ~ ("to reach, attain"). The prefix adds the sense of following after, tracing back, or verification through pursuit.

~Nachweisen~ means "to prove, to demonstrate, to detect, to verify", literally "to show after" or "to point out by following the trail." The prefix ~nach-~ contributes a forensic quality: one does not merely show something (~weisen~), one traces it, follows the evidence, and then shows it to be true. The derived noun ~Nachweis~ ("proof, evidence, certificate, verification") is ubiquitous in German bureaucracy, science, and law: one needs a ~Nachweis~ for everything from vaccination status (~Impfnachweis~) to proof of income (~Einkommensnachweis~) to scientific detection (~DNA-Nachweis~). The verb can take a dative object: ~jemandem etwas nachweisen~ ("to prove something against someone"), often in a legal or investigative context, "to catch someone out." The PIE root *~weyd-~ ("to see") thus achieves its most rigorous expression here: ~nachweisen~ is seeing that has been verified through systematic pursuit. Cognate with Dutch ~nawijzen~ (rare).
en.nachzahlen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys doing something afterwards, later than the main event.

The compound names the settling of a still-outstanding amount after the fact, a back payment.
en.nachzählen:
A separable compound of ~nach-~ + ~zählen~:

• ~zählen~: From MHG ~zel(e)n~, ~zellen~, from OHG ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~ ("to enumerate, count; to recount, tell"). German split this dual sense: ~zählen~ kept "to count," ~erzählen~ took "to narrate." Cognate with Dutch ~tellen~, English ~tell~ and ~tale~, Danish ~tælle~, Gothic ~talzjan~.
• ~nach-~: From MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~ ("near, close"), from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~, generally connected to PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). The particle is the same word as the adjective ~nah~ ("near"). Cognate with English ~nigh~, whose old comparative and superlative survive as ~near~ and ~next~. The prefix conveys checking or verifying by going back over something.

The compound is counting something a second time in order to check and confirm the total.
en.nahekommen:
A separable compound of ~nahe~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~nahe~: From MHG ~nāhe~, ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~ ("near"), of uncertain further origin. Cognate with English ~nigh~, Dutch ~na~, Gothic ~nēƕ~. English preserves the whole old paradigm as three separate words: ~nigh~ is the positive, ~near~ the old comparative, and ~next~ the old superlative. In verbal compounds ~nahe-~ marks approach: ~nahebringen~, ~nahelegen~ ("to suggest," literally "to lay near"). The sense of ~nahe~ here is: approaching, drawing close to someone or something.

The compound describes drawing near to someone or something, often figuratively, coming close to a goal or an ideal.
en.nahelegen:
A separable compound of ~nahe~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~nahe~: From MHG ~nāhe~, ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~ ("near"), of uncertain further origin. Cognate with English ~nigh~, Dutch ~na~, Gothic ~nēƕ~. English preserves the whole old paradigm as three separate words: ~nigh~ is the positive, ~near~ the old comparative, and ~next~ the old superlative. In verbal compounds ~nahe-~ marks approach: ~nahebringen~, ~nahelegen~ ("to suggest," literally "to lay near"). The sense of ~nahe~ here is: figuratively, made accessible or intimate.

Literally to lay something near someone, the compound has turned figurative: to suggest, to strongly imply.
en.naheliegen:
A separable compound of ~nahe~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~nahe~: From MHG ~nāhe~, ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~ ("near"), of uncertain further origin. Cognate with English ~nigh~, Dutch ~na~, Gothic ~nēƕ~. English preserves the whole old paradigm as three separate words: ~nigh~ is the positive, ~near~ the old comparative, and ~next~ the old superlative. In verbal compounds ~nahe-~ marks approach: ~nahebringen~, ~nahelegen~ ("to suggest," literally "to lay near"). The sense of ~nahe~ here is: figuratively, made accessible or intimate.

What lies near at hand is easy to reach, so the compound means to be obvious, to suggest itself.
en.nahestehen:
A separable compound of ~nahe~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~nahe~: From MHG ~nāhe~, ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~nāhw~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~ ("near"), of uncertain further origin. Cognate with English ~nigh~, Dutch ~na~, Gothic ~nēƕ~. English preserves the whole old paradigm as three separate words: ~nigh~ is the positive, ~near~ the old comparative, and ~next~ the old superlative. In verbal compounds ~nahe-~ marks approach: ~nahebringen~, ~nahelegen~ ("to suggest," literally "to lay near"). The sense of ~nahe~ here is: approaching, drawing close to someone or something.

The compound is stative: to stand near someone is to be closely connected to them, an intimacy or allegiance rather than a movement.
en.nebeneinanderhalten:
A separable compound of ~nebeneinander-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~nebeneinander-~: Transparently ~neben~ ("beside") + ~einander~ ("one another"), hence "side by side." ~Neben~ is itself a fossil: OHG ~in eban~ ("on the same level") contracted through MHG ~eneben~ into a preposition, so it still contains ~eben~ ("level, even"). As a particle it says only that the action puts things alongside each other. The sense of ~nebeneinander-~ here is: of arranging or setting things in parallel.

The compound is to hold two things side by side, typically in order to compare them.
en.nehmen: From Middle High German ~nëmen~, from Old High German ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Low German ~nehmen~, Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~ ("to learn, grasp"), Swedish ~förnimma~ ("to perceive").
en.neigen:
From a merger of MHG ~nīgen~ (intransitive, strong) and ~neigen~ (transitive, weak), from OHG ~nīgan~ and ~neigen~ respectively, from Proto-Germanic *~hnīganą~ (strong, intransitive: "to bow, to bend") and its causative *~hnaigijaną~ (weak, transitive: "to make bow, to incline"). The strong verb *~hnīganą~ descends from PIE *~kneygʷʰ-~ ("to bend, droop"). Cognate with Dutch ~nijgen~ and ~neigen~, Old English ~hnīgan~ ("to bow") and ~hnǣgan~ ("to cause to bow"), Old Norse ~hnīga~ and ~hneiga~.

The strong forms (~neigen~, ~nieg~, ~geniegen~) vanished from the standard language by the 16th century, though they survive in dialects, making ~neigen~ an example of a once-strong verb that went entirely weak. The modern verb means "to incline, to lean, to tend", both physically (to tilt) and metaphorically (~dazu neigen~, "to tend to, to be inclined to"). The noun ~Neigung~ ("inclination, tendency") carries both senses. The PIE root *~kneygʷʰ-~ also produced Latin ~conīveō~ ("I blink, I overlook", literally "I bend together [the eyelids]") and ~nītor~ ("I lean on"), showing how the concept of bending diverged into remarkably different physical actions across the Indo-European branches.
en.nennen: From Middle High German ~nennen~, ~nemmen~, ~nemnen~, from Old High German ~nemnen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~namnijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~namnijaną~, a denominative verb derived from Proto-Germanic *~namô~ ("name"), from PIE *~h₁nómn̥~ ("name"). The verb literally means "to name" (that is, "to perform the act of giving a name") and has not meaningfully drifted from its PIE origin across more than five millennia. ~Nennen~ exhibits the same mixed conjugation as ~bringen~ and ~denken~: it forms its past tense ~nannte~ with a vowel change plus a weak dental suffix, rather than following either a purely strong or purely weak paradigm. Like ~kennen~ (its close relative via the same PIE root *~ǵneh₃-~ "to know"), ~nennen~ belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort, whose members do not show umlaut in the preterite: ~brennen~/~brannte~, ~kennen~/~kannte~, ~rennen~/~rannte~, ~senden~/~sandte~, ~wenden~/~wandte~, ~denken~/~dachte~, and ~bringen~/~brachte~ (see ~brennen~ for the phonological explanation). Cognate with Old English ~nemnan~, Middle English ~nemnen~, Swedish ~nämna~, and Hunsrik ~nenne~.
en.nerven: A modern denominative verb formed from the noun ~Nerv~ ("nerve"), via the colloquial expression ~auf die Nerven gehen~ ("to get on someone's nerves"). ~Nerv~ was borrowed from Latin ~nervus~ ("sinew, tendon"), partly through French ~nerf~. Latin ~nervus~ comes from earlier *~neuros~ (by metathesis), from Proto-Italic *~(s)nēuros~, from PIE *~snḗh₁wr̥~ ("sinew, tendon"). Cognate with Greek ~neuron~ (whence English ~neuron~ and ~neurotic~) and Old English ~sinu~ ("sinew"). The meaning shift from "sinew" to "nerve" occurred in medical Latin; the further shift to "to annoy" is a twentieth-century colloquial development unique to German, where the anatomical term became a metaphor for irritation.
en.neustarten:
A separable compound of ~neu~ + ~starten~:

• ~starten~: Borrowed from English ~start~ with the German verbal suffix ~-en~. English ~start~ traces from Middle English ~sterten~ ("to leap up suddenly"), Old English ~styrtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sturtijan~ ("to startle, set in motion"), from PIE *~(s)ter-~ ("to be stiff"). German ~stürzen~ descends from the same root; the sense "to begin" developed first in English.
• ~neu~: From MHG ~niuwe~, from OHG ~niuwi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niwi~, from Proto-Germanic *~niwjaz~, from PIE *~néwos~ ("new"). Cognate with English ~new~, Dutch ~nieuw~, Danish ~ny~, Latin ~novus~, Greek ~neos~, Sanskrit ~navas~. The sense of ~neu~ here is: of doing something over again, afresh.

A modern coinage on the borrowed ~starten~: to start again, most often a device or a program.
en.niederblicken:
A separable compound of ~nieder-~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~blank~, Dutch ~blik~, Old English ~blice~.
• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). Cognate with English ~nether~, which survives chiefly in ~netherworld~ and in the name of the ~Netherlands~: the low countries, ~die Niederlande~, the same compound word in both languages. The particle conveys downward motion: lowering or setting down.

The compound directs the gaze downward, the literal act of looking down, as opposed to the figurative "looking down on" someone that ~herabblicken~ carries.
en.niederbrechen:
A separable compound of ~nieder-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). Cognate with English ~nether~, which survives chiefly in ~netherworld~ and in the name of the ~Netherlands~: the low countries, ~die Niederlande~, the same compound word in both languages. The particle conveys forcing something down: striking, suppressing, or defeating it.

The compound is to break something down until it collapses (a wall, a structure), the particle marking the fall to the ground.
en.niederbrennen:
A separable compound of ~nieder-~ + ~brennen~:

• ~brennen~: From MHG ~brennen~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: transitive ~brennan~ ("to set on fire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~brannijan~, and intransitive ~brinnan~, from *~brinnan~, of which *~brannijan~ was the causative. • ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederfallen:

• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederführen:

• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederhalten:

• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederhauen:

• ~hauen~: From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). • ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederkommen:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederlegen:
A separable compound of ~nieder-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. • ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niedermachen:

• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederreden:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). • ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederreißen:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. • ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederringen:
A separable compound of ~nieder-~ + ~ringen~:

• ~ringen~: From MHG ~ringen~, from OHG ~ringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wringaną~ ("to twist, wring"), from a nasalized form of PIE *~wergʰ-~ ("to turn, twist"). • ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). ~Niederringen~ carries wrestling into the image of subjugation: forcing an opponent to the ground and so defeating them.
en.niederrinnen:

• ~rinnen~: From MHG ~rinnen~, from OHG ~rinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~ ("to run, flow"); the PIE source is debated, most often given as *~h₃reyH-~ ("to churn, set in motion"). • ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederschauen:
A separable compound of ~nieder-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). • ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). Cognate with English ~nether~, which survives chiefly in ~netherworld~ and in the name of the ~Netherlands~: the low countries, ~die Niederlande~, the same compound word in both languages. en.niederschießen:
A separable compound of ~nieder-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue").
