• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederschlagen:

• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). ~Niederschlagen~ ranges from striking a blow to quelling a revolt; literally it also means the lowering of the eyes, as in the example.
en.niederschreiben:

• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niedersetzen:

• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). Cognate with English ~nether~, which survives chiefly in ~netherworld~ and in the name of the ~Netherlands~: the low countries, ~die Niederlande~, the same compound word in both languages. The particle conveys downward motion: lowering or setting down.

en.niederstechen:

• ~stechen~: From MHG ~stëchen~, from OHG ~stëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stekaną~ ("to stab, prick"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to stick, poke"). Cognate with Dutch ~steken~ ("to stab, sting"), Old Norse ~stinga~, English ~stick~ (originally "to stab, pierce").
• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). Cognate with English ~nether~, which survives chiefly in ~netherworld~ and in the name of the ~Netherlands~: the low countries, ~die Niederlande~, the same compound word in both languages. The particle conveys forcing something down: striking, suppressing, or defeating it.

~Niederstechen~ is the fatal stabbing; the ~nieder-~ turns a mere thrust into the felling of the one struck.
en.niederstoßen:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). • ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). ~Niederstoßen~ is transitively to thrust something to the ground; intransitively, though, the swooping descent of a bird of prey, as in the example.
en.niederstürzen:

• ~stürzen~: From MHG ~stürzen~, from OHG ~sturzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sturtijan~ ("to fall down, tumble"), of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly from PIE *~ster-~ ("to be stiff") via a dental extension *~sterd-~, though the derivation is debated. • ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). en.niederwerfen:

• ~nieder-~: Not a prefix but the adverb and adjective ~nieder~ ("low, down"), from MHG ~nider~, from OHG ~nidar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~niþer~, from Proto-Germanic *~niþer~, a comparative formation on PIE *~ni-~ ("down"). ~Niederwerfen~ reaches from physically throwing someone down to crushing a revolt; reflexively it is prostration in worship.
en.notieren: From Middle High German ~notieren~, borrowed from Latin ~notō~ ("I mark, note, observe"), from ~nota~ ("a mark, sign, note"). ~Nota~ is likely related to ~nōscō~ ("I come to know"), from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"), the same root behind English ~know~, ~notice~, Greek ~gnōsis~, and Sanskrit ~jñā~. The verb entered German through medieval scholarly Latin, reflecting the transmission of literate culture from Roman to Germanic lands. In modern German, ~notieren~ means "to jot down, to note," and also has a specialized financial sense: "to be quoted at" (a price), paralleling English ~note~ in stock-exchange usage. Cognate with French ~noter~, Italian ~notare~, English ~note~.
en.nutzen: From Middle High German ~nutzen~, ~nützen~, from Old High German ~nuzzōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~nutōną~, from *~nutō~ ("use"), from *~nutiz~ ("useful"), from *~neutaną~ ("to enjoy, use, catch"), from PIE *~newd-~ ("to acquire, make use of"). The verb was originally restricted to Upper German and East Central German dialects, the former preferring the conjugation ~nutzen~, the latter preferring ~nützen~. By way of hypercorrection, ~nützen~ has now become a chiefly southern conjugation; Low German and West Central German originally used other verbs (namely ~brauchen~ for the transitive function) and prefer ~nutzen~ in modern standard German. Cognate with modern ~Nutzen~ (noun, "benefit, use").
en.nähen:
From MHG ~nāian~, ~næjen~, from OHG ~nājen~, ~nāian~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēaną~ ("to sew"). Cognate with German ~Nadel~ ("needle") and English ~needle~ (both from the instrument noun formed on the same root), Dutch ~naaien~, Gothic ~nēþla~ ("needle").

The PIE root *~(s)neh₁-~ ("to spin, to sew") is notable for its optional initial ~s-~, the so-called ~s-mobile~, a mysterious phonological feature of Proto-Indo-European where certain roots could appear with or without an initial ~s-~ with no change in meaning. The ~s-~less variant produced Latin ~nēre~ ("to spin") and Greek ~nêma~ ("thread"), whence English ~nematic~ (describing thread-like liquid-crystal arrangements). The instrument noun *~neh₁-dleh₂~ ("that which sews") traveled through Proto-Germanic *~nēþlō~ to produce both German ~Nadel~ and English ~needle~, one of the clearest cases where a common tool name reveals a shared craft tradition stretching back to the prehistoric Indo-European homeland.
en.näherbringen:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~näher~: The comparative of ~nahe~ ("near"), from MHG ~næher~, from OHG ~nāhōr~. As a particle it means "closer, nearer," and the compounds it forms denote mostly figurative approach: ~näherbringen~ ("to bring closer, make accessible"), ~sich nähern~. English ~near~ is the same comparative, frozen: Old English ~nēar~ was the comparative of ~nēah~ ("nigh"), so English lost the positive and kept the comparative where German kept both. The sense of ~näher~ here is: figuratively, making something more accessible or better understood.

The compound is mostly figurative: to bring a subject or idea closer to someone, making it accessible.
en.näherkommen:
A separable compound of ~näher~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~näher~: The comparative of ~nahe~ ("near"), from MHG ~næher~, from OHG ~nāhōr~. As a particle it means "closer, nearer," and the compounds it forms denote mostly figurative approach: ~näherbringen~ ("to bring closer, make accessible"), ~sich nähern~. English ~near~ is the same comparative, frozen: Old English ~nēar~ was the comparative of ~nēah~ ("nigh"), so English lost the positive and kept the comparative where German kept both. The sense of ~näher~ here is: approaching, drawing near to someone or something.

The compound describes closing a distance, literal or figurative, step by step.
en.nähern:
From the comparative form ~näher~ ("nearer") with the verbal suffix ~-n~, itself from the adjective ~nah~ ("near"), from MHG ~nāch~, from OHG ~nāh~, from Proto-West Germanic *~nāh~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēhwaz~ ("near"), from PIE *~h₂neḱ-~ ("to reach, attain"). Cognate with English ~nigh~ (from OE ~nēah~), Dutch ~na~.

~Nähern~ is almost always reflexive: ~sich nähern~ ("to approach, to draw near"). The word is a denominal verb built from a comparative: "to make nearer." The PIE root *~h₂neḱ-~ also produced Sanskrit ~naśati~ ("to reach, attain") and Latin ~nancīscī~ ("to obtain"). German ~nach~ ("after, toward") is a doublet of ~nah~, both descend from the same root, but ~nach~ specialized as a preposition while ~nah~ remained an adjective. The English cognate ~nigh~ survives mainly in poetry and the fixed phrase "nigh impossible."
en.näherrücken:
A separable compound of ~näher~ + ~rücken~:

• ~rücken~: From MHG ~rücken~, from OHG ~rucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rukkijan~. The verb means "to move, to shift" and is the base of ~verrückt~ ("crazy," literally "shifted, displaced"); the noun ~Rücken~ ("back") is etymologically a separate word. Cognate with English ~rock~, Old Norse ~rykkja~, Old English ~roccian~.
• ~näher~: The comparative of ~nahe~ ("near"), from MHG ~næher~, from OHG ~nāhōr~. As a particle it means "closer, nearer," and the compounds it forms denote mostly figurative approach: ~näherbringen~ ("to bring closer, make accessible"), ~sich nähern~. English ~near~ is the same comparative, frozen: Old English ~nēar~ was the comparative of ~nēah~ ("nigh"), so English lost the positive and kept the comparative where German kept both. The sense of ~näher~ here is: closer, nearer, into greater proximity.

Since ~rücken~ is to shift by small increments, the compound suggests approach in stages rather than a single move.
en.näherstehen:
A separable compound of ~näher~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~näher~: The comparative of ~nahe~ ("near"), from MHG ~næher~, from OHG ~nāhōr~. As a particle it means "closer, nearer," and the compounds it forms denote mostly figurative approach: ~näherbringen~ ("to bring closer, make accessible"), ~sich nähern~. English ~near~ is the same comparative, frozen: Old English ~nēar~ was the comparative of ~nēah~ ("nigh"), so English lost the positive and kept the comparative where German kept both. The sense of ~näher~ here is: closer, nearer, into greater proximity.

Where the other ~näher-~ compounds express movement, this one holds still: to ~näherstehen~ is to be closer, most often in the figurative sense of personal closeness.
en.nähertreten:
A separable compound of ~näher~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~näher~: The comparative of ~nahe~ ("near"), from MHG ~næher~, from OHG ~nāhōr~. As a particle it means "closer, nearer," and the compounds it forms denote mostly figurative approach: ~näherbringen~ ("to bring closer, make accessible"), ~sich nähern~. English ~near~ is the same comparative, frozen: Old English ~nēar~ was the comparative of ~nēah~ ("nigh"), so English lost the positive and kept the comparative where German kept both. The sense of ~näher~ here is: approaching, drawing near to someone or something.

The compound is a step made toward someone or something: physical approach, or in older usage the taking up of a matter.
en.nützen: From Middle High German ~nützen~, a variant of ~nutzen~, from Old High German ~nuzzōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~nutōną~, *~nutjōną~, derived from *~nutō~ ("use, enjoyment"), from *~nutiz~ ("useful"), from *~neutaną~ ("to enjoy, use"), from PIE *~newd-~ ("to acquire, make use of"). The ~ü~ form arose in East Central German dialects through umlaut, while Upper German dialects preferred ~nutzen~ without umlaut. By hypercorrection, ~nützen~ became the standard southern form, while northern Germany adopted ~nutzen~. Both forms coexist in modern standard German with identical meaning. Cognate with Lithuanian ~nauda~ ("benefit"), Russian ~nuzhda~ ("need"). English ~enjoy~ is unrelated, but the archaic English ~nait~ ("to use") descends from the same Proto-Germanic verb *~neutaną~.
en.offenbaren:
From ~offenbar~ ("manifest, obvious") + ~-en~. ~Offenbar~ is composed of ~offen~ ("open") + ~-bar~ ("-able, carrying"):

• ~offen~: From MHG ~offen~, from OHG ~offan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~opan~, from Proto-Germanic *~upanaz~, originally a past participle meaning "lying on top" and hence "uncovered, open," derived from *~upp~ ("up"), from PIE *~upo~ ("up, over"). Cognate with English ~open~, Dutch ~open~, Swedish ~öppen~.
• ~-bar~: From OHG ~-bāri~, from Proto-Germanic *~-bērijaz~ ("carrying, bearing"), from *~beraną~ ("to bear"), from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry, bear").

The literal sense of ~offenbar~ is thus "carrying openness", something that bears itself openly, that is evident. ~Offenbaren~ means "to reveal, to disclose," and in religious usage, "to reveal" in the divine sense, as in die ~Offenbarung~ des Johannes (the Book of Revelation). The past participle may appear as either ~offenbart~ (the prescribed form) or ~geoffenbart~ (with the ~ge-~ prefix that is normally suppressed in inseparable-prefix verbs).
en.offenbleiben:
A separable compound of ~offen~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~offen~: From MHG ~offen~, from OHG ~offan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~opan~, from Proto-Germanic *~upanaz~, originally a past participle meaning "lifted up" and hence "uncovered, open," derived from *~upp~ ("up"), from PIE *~upo~ ("up, over"). Cognate with English ~open~, Dutch ~open~, Swedish ~öppen~. As a verbal particle it is resultative: ~offenlegen~ ("to disclose," literally "to lay open"), ~offenstehen~, ~offenbleiben~. The sense of ~offen~ here is: left unsettled, not yet closed or decided.

~Offenbleiben~ means figuratively that a question stays unresolved; not the door but the decision remains open.
en.offenhalten:
A separable compound of ~offen~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~offen~: From MHG ~offen~, from OHG ~offan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~opan~, from Proto-Germanic *~upanaz~, originally a past participle meaning "lifted up" and hence "uncovered, open," derived from *~upp~ ("up"), from PIE *~upo~ ("up, over"). Cognate with English ~open~, Dutch ~open~, Swedish ~öppen~. As a verbal particle it is resultative: ~offenlegen~ ("to disclose," literally "to lay open"), ~offenstehen~, ~offenbleiben~. The sense of ~offen~ here is: into an open or uncovered state.

~Offenhalten~ actively keeps something in an open state; the example shows the literal reading, a door held open with a foot.
en.offenlegen:
A separable compound of ~offen~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~offen~: From MHG ~offen~, from OHG ~offan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~opan~, from Proto-Germanic *~upanaz~, originally a past participle meaning "lifted up" and hence "uncovered, open," derived from *~upp~ ("up"), from PIE *~upo~ ("up, over"). Cognate with English ~open~, Dutch ~open~, Swedish ~öppen~. As a verbal particle it is resultative: ~offenlegen~ ("to disclose," literally "to lay open"), ~offenstehen~, ~offenbleiben~. The sense of ~offen~ here is: disclosed, laid bare, made public.

~Offenlegen~ means laying bare and disclosing what was hidden: making data, intentions, or connections visible.
en.offenstehen:
A separable compound of ~offen~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~offen~: From MHG ~offen~, from OHG ~offan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~opan~, from Proto-Germanic *~upanaz~, originally a past participle meaning "lifted up" and hence "uncovered, open," derived from *~upp~ ("up"), from PIE *~upo~ ("up, over"). Cognate with English ~open~, Dutch ~open~, Swedish ~öppen~. As a verbal particle it is resultative: ~offenlegen~ ("to disclose," literally "to lay open"), ~offenstehen~, ~offenbleiben~. The sense of ~offen~ here is: into an open or uncovered state.

~Offenstehen~ is literally to stand open, like Kafka's gate to the Law, and figuratively to be available to someone, as when a legal recourse "stands open."
en.optimieren: A denominative verb formed from the noun ~Optimum~ ("optimum, the best state"), with the productive ~-ieren~ suffix. ~Optimum~ was borrowed from Latin ~optimum~, the neuter of ~optimus~ ("best"), the superlative of ~bonus~ ("good"). ~Optimus~ derives from an earlier Latin *~opitumus~, from ~ops~ ("power, resources, wealth"), from PIE *~h₃ep-~ ("to work, to produce"). The same root gave Latin ~opus~ ("work"), ~opera~ ("effort, work"), ~opulentus~ ("wealthy"), and ~officium~ ("duty, office"), whence English ~operate~, ~opulent~, and ~office~. German ~optimieren~ thus etymologically means "to make the most powerful, to bring to peak performance." The word entered German in the 20th century as a technical term from mathematics and engineering, then spread to everyday language. The related adjective ~optimal~ and noun ~Optimierung~ ("optimization") are ubiquitous in modern German business and technology discourse. A nice irony: the PIE root *~h₃ep-~ ("to work") also produced Latin ~opus~, so ~optimieren~ is, at its deepest root, about ~working~ something into its best state. Cognate with Dutch ~optimaliseren~, English ~optimize~, French ~optimiser~.
en.ordnen:
From Middle High German ~ordenen~, from Old High German ~ordinōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ordinōn~ ("to order, put in order"), borrowed from Latin ~ōrdināre~ ("to arrange, set in order"), from ~ōrdō~ ("row, rank, order"), from Proto-Italic *~ordō~, probably from PIE *~h₂er-~ ("to fit together"). Doublet of ~ordinieren~ ("to ordain"). Cognate with English ~order~ (via Old French, from the same Latin source), Dutch ~ordenen~, and Italian ~ordinare~.

The journey from PIE *~h₂er-~ ("to fit together") to modern ~ordnen~ traces a remarkable semantic stability: the idea of fitting things into their proper arrangement has survived over five millennia. Latin ~ōrdō~ originally described a row of threads in a loom (a warp that held everything in place) before generalizing to any row, rank, or sequence. The derivative ~Ordnung~ ("order, tidiness") is practically a national concept: ~Ordnung muss sein~ ("there must be order") is the quintessential German maxim.
en.organisieren: Borrowed from French ~organiser~ (attested from the 17th century), from Medieval Latin ~organizāre~, from Latin ~organum~ ("instrument, tool, organ"), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ~órganon~ ("tool, instrument"), from PIE *~werǵ-~ ("to work"). The Greek ~órganon~ is the same word that gave the world the philosophical term "organon" (as in Aristotle's logical works, his tool for reasoning), the musical ~organ~, and the biological ~organ~. The semantic path from "tool" to "organization" runs through the idea of coordinating instruments or parts into a working whole, as individual pipes are organized into a functioning organ. German received ~organisieren~ through French in the same period as many other learned ~-ieren~ borrowings flooded the language. The ~-ieren~ suffix, entering via Old French contact from the 12th century onward, marks it as a loanverb and guarantees weak conjugation. Cognate with English ~organize~, French ~organiser~, Spanish ~organizar~, Italian ~organizzare~.
en.orientieren: Borrowed from French ~orienter~, itself from ~orient~ ("east, the direction of the rising sun"), from Old French ~oriant~, from Latin ~oriens~ ("rising"), the present active participle of ~orior~ ("to rise, to be born"), from Italic *~orjōr~, from PIE *~h₃er-~ ("to stir, to rise"). The underlying image is vivid: medieval European maps placed east at the top (toward the ~Orient~, where the sun rises), so ~orienter~ originally meant "to align a map with east at the top", that is, to find one's bearings by the sunrise. The reflexive ~sich orientieren~ ("to orient oneself, to get one's bearings") preserves this navigational metaphor. German added the standard ~-ieren~ suffix for French-derived verbs, and the Hunsrik cognate ~orïenteere~ shows the same borrowing pattern among German emigrants in Brazil. Cognate with English ~orient~, Italian ~orientare~, Spanish ~orientar~. The Latin root *~h₃er-~ also gives us Greek ~ὄρνῡμι~ ("to stir up") and Sanskrit ~ṛṇóti~ ("to move").
en.packen: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~packen~, from Old Saxon *~pakko~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pakkō~, from Proto-Germanic *~pakkô~ ("bundle, pack"). The ultimate origin is debated: the word may derive from an early contact with Vulgar Latin *~paccō~ or Celtic languages, or it may be a native Germanic formation; the absence of the expected High German consonant shift (~p~ should have become ~pf~ or ~f~ in OHG) confirms it entered High German from the north via Low German trade routes rather than descending through the native High German line. ~Packen~ means "to pack" but also "to grab, to seize": the two senses unite in the physical act of grasping and bundling: you ~packst~ things into a suitcase, but you also ~packst~ someone by the arm. The colloquial ~Das packen wir!~ ("We can handle it!") extends the grabbing sense to mastery over a situation. The imperative ~Pack dich!~ ("Beat it!") adds another layer: to pack yourself away, to bundle yourself off. Cognate with English ~pack~, Dutch ~pakken~, Swedish ~packa~, Danish ~pakke~. The noun ~Pack~ in German also means "rabble, riffraff", a pejorative use where people are treated as a mere bundle, a mass without individuality.
en.passen: Borrowed from French ~passer~, with Dutch ~passen~ as an intermediary and reinforcing influence; compare the German noun ~Pass~. French ~passer~ derives from Middle French ~passer~, from Old French ~passer~, from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, a denominative verb from Latin ~passus~ ("step, pace"), from ~pandō~ ("to spread, stretch out"), from PIE *~pet-~ ("to spread, extend"). The Latin word ~passus~ measured the Roman double-step (roughly 1.5 meters) and gave English ~pace~ and the unit ~passus~ in Roman surveying. German ~passen~ entered primarily through Dutch trade contact and retains the Dutch sense of "to fit, to suit" alongside the French-influenced sense of "to pass." A notable false friend lurks nearby: English ~pass~ and German ~passen~ overlap in sports contexts (passing a ball), but ~passen~ most commonly means "to fit" or "to suit," not "to pass by." The noun ~Pass~ (mountain pass, passport) is a separate borrowing from the same Latin root. Cognate with French ~passer~, Dutch ~passen~, Italian ~passare~, English ~pass~, ~pace~.
en.passieren:
Borrowed from French ~passer~, from Old French ~passer~, from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, derived from Latin ~passus~ ("step"), the past participle of ~pandere~ ("to spread out, stretch"), from Proto-Italic *~patnō~, from PIE *~peth₂-~ ("to spread out"). A "step" (Latin ~passus~) was thus literally "a spreading", of the legs in walking.

German ~passieren~ carries two distinct meanings that developed along different semantic lines: "to pass (a place, a border, an obstacle)" and "to happen, occur." The second sense ("Was ist passiert?" , "What happened?") is a calque of the French intransitive use of ~passer~ in the same sense, particularly in the construction ~il se passe quelque chose~ ("something is happening"). English ~pass~ is a direct cognate from the same Old French source. The Latin unit of measurement the ~passus~ (roughly 1.48 meters, a double step) gave the world the ~mille passuum~ ("a thousand paces") from which English ~mile~ derives. Cognate with English ~pass~, Dutch ~passeren~, Spanish ~pasar~, Italian ~passare~.
en.pfeifen: From MHG ~pfīfen~, from OHG ~pfīfōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pīpōn~ ("to play a pipe, to whistle"), an early borrowing from Vulgar Latin *~pīpāre~ ("to chirp, peep"), a word of imitative origin. The ~pf-~ proves the loan was already in the language before the High German consonant shift, old enough to be carried through it. Originally weak, it was later pulled into class I by rhyming strong verbs such as ~greifen~ and ~schleifen~, and is now strong (~pfeifen~, ~pfiff~, ~gepfiffen~). Cognate with the noun ~Pfeife~ and, from the same Latin source, English ~pipe~ and ~peep~, Dutch ~pijpen~, and French ~piper~.
en.pflanzen: From Middle High German ~pflanzen~, from Old High German ~pflanzōn~, a denominative verb from ~pflanza~ ("plant"), which was borrowed from Latin ~planta~ ("a shoot, cutting, plant"). The phonological change from Latin ~pl-~ to German ~pfl-~ is part of the High German consonant shift and is one of the most distinctive markers of Old High German. The same shift turned Latin ~piper~ into German ~Pfeffer~ and Latin ~platea~ into ~Platz~. Latin ~planta~ itself is of uncertain origin but may be related to ~planus~ ("flat"), a plant being something pressed flat into the soil. English ~plant~ was also borrowed from Latin but shows no consonant shift, having come via Old English from the same Latin source. Cognate with Luxembourgish ~Planz~.
en.pflegen: From Middle High German ~phlëgen~, from Old High German ~plëgan~ ("to take care of, be responsible for, stand up for"), from Proto-West Germanic *~plehan~. The Proto-West Germanic verb is a strong class-5 verb meaning "to stand up for, be responsible for," and its past tense forms survive in the archaic German literary past tense ~pflog~ (rarely used today but occasionally found in elevated or ironic registers). Cognate with Dutch ~plegen~, Old English ~plēon~, Old Norse ~plega~, and Old Saxon ~plegan~. The descendants of *~plehan~ in the reconstruction include a borrowing path into Medieval Latin as *~pleviō~ ("to pledge"), which fed into Old French ~plege~ and ultimately into English ~pledge~, making ~pflegen~ and English ~pledge~ distant relatives, the one meaning "to tend, nurture, maintain" and the other "a solemn promise," both rooted in the ancient idea of taking responsibility for something.
en.planen:
Denominal verb derived from the noun ~Plan~, which was borrowed from French ~plan~ ("plan, ground plan"). French ~plan~ derives either from the verb ~planter~ ("to plant, set firmly") or from Latin ~planus~ ("flat, level"), the latter being the more widely accepted source. Latin ~planus~ traces from PIE *~pleh₂-~ ("flat, broad"). The architectural sense (a flat drawing representing a structure) then generalized to the modern sense of any scheme or design.

Interestingly, English ~plan~ entered the language via the same French source as German ~Plan~, meaning both languages acquired the word independently through the same medieval and early-modern channel of French architectural and technical vocabulary. The related Latin ~planus~ also gives German ~Plan~ its second meaning of "plain, flat terrain" (as in ~Hochebene~), though the planning sense has long since become dominant. Cognate with Dutch ~plannen~, English ~plan~, Swedish ~planera~, French ~planifier~.
en.plattmachen:
A separable compound of ~platt~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~platt~: Borrowed in the seventeenth century from Low German and Dutch ~plat~, itself from Old French ~plat~ ("flat"), from Vulgar Latin *~plattus~, from Greek ~platýs~ ("broad, flat"). English ~plate~ and ~platter~ come from the same French word, and ~place~ from the related Greek ~plateîa~ ("broad street"). The adjective also names a language: ~Plattdeutsch~ was the plain, level speech of the north as against elevated High German. The sense of ~platt~ here is: the adjective ~platt~ ("flat, flattened") as the resulting state.

~Plattmachen~ means to make something ~platt~, that is flat, to level it to the ground.
en.platzieren: From French ~placer~ ("to place") with the German suffix ~-ieren~, a verb-forming ending used to adapt foreign (especially French and Latin) words into German conjugation patterns. A later spelling reform reanalyzed the word as ~Platz~ + ~-ieren~, aligning it visually with its semantic root. The noun ~Platz~ descends from MHG ~plaz~, borrowed from Old French ~place~, from Latin ~platēa~ ("broad street"), from Greek ~plateia hodos~ ("broad way"), from PIE *~pleth₂-~ ("broad, flat"). This makes ~platzieren~ a case of round-trip borrowing: a Latin word traveled into French, was borrowed into German as a noun (~Platz~), and then the French verb derived from the same Latin root was borrowed separately with ~-ieren~, only for German speakers to later reinterpret the verb as derived from their own noun. Cognate with English ~place~ (via Norman French), Dutch ~plaatsen~, Italian ~piazzare~. The PIE root *~pleth₂-~ also gives English ~flat~, ~plaza~, and ~platypus~ ("flat-footed"), making this humble rental-office verb a distant cousin of the duck-billed platypus.
en.positionieren: Derived from ~Position~ ("position") with the verb-forming suffix ~-ieren~. ~Position~ was borrowed from Latin ~positiō~ ("a placing, position"), from ~positus~ ("placed"), the past participle of ~pōnō~ ("I place, put"), from an older form *~posinō~, a compound of *~po-~ (from PIE *~h₂epo~ "off, away") + *~sinō~ ("I let, place"). The PIE root *~tḱey-~ ("to settle, dwell") has been proposed as the ultimate source. German ~positionieren~ means "to position" and has gained currency in both physical and abstract senses (as in ~sich positionieren~, "to take a stance"). The suffix ~-ieren~ marks it as a learned borrowing, distinguishing it from native Germanic compounds like ~hinstellen~.
en.posten:
Borrowed from English ~post~ (in the internet sense "to post a message"), itself from English ~post~ ("mail, dispatch"), from French ~poste~, from Italian ~posta~ ("station, mail"), from Vulgar Latin *~posta~, from Latin ~posita~ (feminine past participle of ~pōnere~ "to place"), originally referring to a relay station where horses were ~placed~ for messengers.

~Posten~ is one of the youngest verbs in the German language, entering common usage in the 1990s with the rise of internet forums and then social media. It means "to post" a message, photo, or update online. The irony of its etymology is rich: a word that began with Roman relay riders placing fresh horses at stations along imperial roads now describes placing digital content on servers. The German language already had an older ~posten~ (from the noun ~Posten~, "post, position, guard duty"), but the internet sense is unmistakably an English borrowing. The ~Duden~ dictionary officially recognized the internet sense in the early 2000s. Unlike many English borrowings that German speakers resist (the infamous ~Denglisch~ debate), ~posten~ has been widely accepted, perhaps because the German alternatives (~veröffentlichen~ ("to publish"), ~einstellen~ ("to place in")), feel too formal for the casual act of sharing a photo of one's lunch.
en.preisen: From MHG ~prīsen~ ("to praise"), a derivative of MHG ~prīs~ ("price, worth, glory", modern ~Preis~), borrowed from Old French ~prisier~ ("to appraise, value"), from Late Latin ~pretiāre~, from ~pretium~ ("price, value"). Like ~pfeifen~, this loanword was later reanalyzed as a class I strong verb (~preisen~, ~pries~, ~gepriesen~) despite having no Germanic ancestry at all. The same Latin ~pretium~ gives English the triplet ~price~, ~prize~, and ~praise~, three words that German keeps under the single roof of ~Preis~.
en.preisgeben:
A separable compound of ~preis~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~preis~: The noun in an older sense, not the modern ~Preis~ ("price"). ~Preisgeben~ appears about 1600 meaning "to give up as booty, to abandon to seizure," and its ~preis~ is generally traced to Old French ~prise~ ("a taking, capture, prize"), the source of German ~Prise~ and of English ~prize~ in the naval sense of a captured ship. It was early conflated with the homophonous ~Preis~ ("praise, worth, price"), from MHG ~prīs~, from Old French ~pris~, from Latin ~pretium~ ("value, payment"), distinct words, and the verb preserves the first. Dutch ~prijsgeven~ is the same formation. The sense of ~preis~ here is: the older noun "booty, that which is surrendered": to give up, abandon.

Today ~preisgeben~ is almost wholly figurative: to surrender a secret, a principle, or a defenceless person to seizure; the concrete "booty" of its origin has faded.
en.probieren:
From Latin ~probō~ ("to approve, test, examine"), from ~probus~ ("good, fit"), from PIE *~pro-bʰuH-s~ ("being in front"), composed of *~pro-~ ("forward") + *~bʰuH-~ ("to be"). A doublet of ~proben~ ("to rehearse") and ~prüfen~ ("to test, examine"), all three descending from the same Latin source by different routes and at different periods.

The meaning "to try, to taste, to sample" represents the examining/testing sense of Latin ~probō~ rather than the approving sense. The German proverb ~Probieren geht über Studieren~ ("Trying beats studying") captures the empirical spirit the word carries. The ~-ieren~ suffix marks it as a learned Latin borrowing, distinguishing it from the more natively adapted ~prüfen~ (which entered earlier and underwent more thorough sound changes, passing through Old French ~prover~ and Middle High German ~prüeven~). The same Latin root gives English ~prove~, ~probe~, ~probable~, ~probation~, and ~approbation~. The Italian ~provare~, Spanish ~probar~, and French ~prouver~ are all sisters of ~probieren~.
en.produzieren: Borrowed from Latin ~prōdūcō~ ("to lead forth, bring out, extend, produce"), a compound of ~prō-~ ("forward, forth") + ~dūcō~ ("to lead, draw"), from Proto-Italic *~doukō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ ("to draw, pull"). English ~tow~ (as in to tow a boat) is a cognate via the Germanic branch of the same PIE root. The Latin verb's core meaning was spatial ("to bring something forward" or "to extend"), which extends naturally to agricultural and theatrical production: ~prōdūcere~ was used of bringing a crop to fruition or of staging a performance. German borrowed ~produzieren~ with the productive ~-ieren~ suffix, which always creates weak verbs from Latin and French loanwords. Cognate with English ~produce~, French ~produire~, Spanish ~producir~, Italian ~produrre~. The related Latin ~dux~ ("leader," from the same ~dūcō~) gave Italian ~duce~ and English ~duke~: a "leader" is, etymologically, someone who draws others forward.
en.profitieren: Borrowed from French ~profiter~ ("to benefit, profit"), from Old French ~profit~ (modern French ~profit~), from Latin ~prōfectus~ ("advance, progress, growth, increase, profit"), the past participle of ~prōficiō~ ("to go forward, advance, make progress, be useful"), a compound of ~prō-~ ("forward") + ~faciō~ ("to make, do"). The Latin root sense is fundamentally one of forward motion: profit is progress. English ~profit~ arrived via the same Old French channel. German ~profitieren~ was formed with the standard ~-ieren~ suffix, marking it as a French loanverb with weak conjugation. Cognate with English ~profit~, French ~profiter~, Spanish ~profitar~, Italian ~profittare~.
en.prägen: ~Prägen~ ("to mint, coin; to shape, leave an impression") derives from Middle High German ~bræchen~ / ~præchen~ ("to press in, to depict"), from Old High German ~giprāhhan~ / ~prāhhan~ ("to press in or scratch by breaking the surface"). These forms arose from the first and third person plural preterite forms of ~prēchan~ / ~prāchun~ ("to break"), making ~prägen~ a verb that is likely related to ~brechen~ ("to break"). The noun ~Prägung~ ("imprint, coinage, stamp") shares the root. The semantic development moves from physically breaking or incising a surface (the action of a die striking metal to mint a coin), to the broader sense of leaving a lasting impression: ~ein Erlebnis prägt einen~ ("an experience shapes you"). The abstract sense dominates in modern usage, but the metalworking origin remains visible in ~Münzprägung~ ("coin minting").
en.präsentieren: Inherited from Middle High German ~prēsentieren~, borrowed from Old French ~présenter~ (modern French ~présenter~). The French verb derives from Latin ~praesentō~ ("to place before, present"), a denominative of ~praesens~ ("present, at hand"), itself the present active participle of ~praesum~ ("to be before, preside over"), from ~prae-~ ("before") + ~sum~ ("to be"), from PIE *~h₁es-~ ("to be"). The ~-ieren~ suffix (German's productive borrowing suffix for foreign verbs) arrived through Old French contact beginning in the 12th–13th centuries and became the standard treatment for learned Latin and French borrowings, distinguishing them from native Germanic strong verbs (compare ~schreiben~, borrowed from Latin ~scrībō~ directly in the Roman period and fully assimilated into the strong-verb system). A word that has traveled from PIE "to be" through Latin "to be before" through French "to place before" to modern German boardrooms and PowerPoint slides. Cognate with French ~présenter~, English ~present~ (verb), Spanish ~presentar~, Italian ~presentare~.
en.prüfen: From Middle High German ~prüeven~ (first attested in the 13th century), ultimately from Latin ~probāre~ ("to test, approve, prove"), a denominative of ~probus~ ("good, honest, upright"), from Proto-Italic *~proβwos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~pro-bʰuH-wó-s~ ("being foremost, excellent"), from *~pro-~ ("forward") + *~bʰuH-~ ("to be"). Unlike the ~-ieren~ borrowings, ~prüfen~ entered German very early (before the ~-ieren~ suffix pattern was productive) and was fully assimilated into the native weak-verb system. The route was almost certainly through Middle Dutch or Middle Low German, which would explain the umlaut (~ü~ rather than ~o~): the form *~prōfijan~ underwent High German umlaut to produce ~prüeven~. English ~prove~ arrived from the same Latin source via Old French, as did ~probe~ (a more direct Latin borrowing). That ~prüfen~, ~prove~, and ~probe~ are all triplets from the same Latin root (with ~prüfen~ the oldest German survivor) illustrates how a single Latin verb can splinter into phonologically distinct words across centuries of borrowing. Cognate with English ~prove~, ~probe~, Dutch ~proeven~, French ~prouver~.
en.publikmachen:
A separable compound of ~publik~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~publik~: Borrowed from Latin ~pūblicus~ ("of the people, public"), formed to ~populus~ ("people") under the influence of ~pūbēs~ ("adult population"), and reinforced by French ~public~. In German it survives chiefly in particle constructions: to make, or to become, public knowledge. Cognate with English ~public~, ~publish~, ~republic~. The sense of ~publik~ here is: "public, publicly known" as the resulting state.

~Publikmachen~ means to make something generally known; the adjective ~publik~ now stands almost only in this pairing with ~machen~ or ~werden~.
en.punkten:
From the noun ~Punkt~ ("point, dot"), from Middle High German ~punct~, borrowed from Late Latin ~pūnctus~ ("point, dot"), from Latin ~pungō~ ("to prick, puncture"), from PIE *~pewǵ-~ ("to prick, punch").

~Punkten~ is a relatively modern back-formation meaning "to score, to gain points." While ~Punkt~ has been in German since the medieval period, the verb ~punkten~ only became common in the 20th century, initially in sports journalism. The PIE root *~pewǵ-~ ("to prick") also produced Latin ~pugnus~ ("fist") and Greek ~pugmḗ~ ("fist, boxing"), whence English ~pugilist~. The semantic journey from "prick" to "point" to "score" is delightful: a tiny puncture mark became a dot, a dot became a unit of scoring, and the noun became a verb. German ~Punkt~ is also a false friend for English speakers: ~Punkt drei Uhr~ means "at three o'clock sharp."
en.qualifizieren:
From Medieval Latin ~qualificāre~ ("to characterize, to designate"), a compound of Latin ~quālis~ ("of what kind") + ~-ficāre~ (from ~facere~ "to make"), from PIE *~kʷo-~ ("who, what," the interrogative stem) + *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, to make"). Borrowed into German in the early modern period.

~Qualifizieren~ means "to qualify", both transitively ("to make suitable, to describe") and reflexively (~sich qualifizieren~, "to become qualified"). The PIE interrogative stem *~kʷo-~ is one of the most productive roots in the family: it generated Latin ~quis~ ("who"), ~quod~ ("what"), ~quandō~ ("when"), English ~who~, ~what~, ~when~, ~where~, ~which~, ~how~, German ~wer~, ~was~, ~wann~, ~wo~, ~welch~, and ~wie~. Every question word in both languages traces back to this single interrogative particle.
en.querdenken:
A separable compound of ~quer-~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~teng-~ ("to think, feel"). A mixed-conjugation verb of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~dachte~ pairs the vowel change ~e~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix and ~k~ > ~ch~. Cognate with English ~think~, Dutch ~denken~, Icelandic ~þekkja~.
• ~quer-~: From MHG ~twer~, ~dwer~ (also ~quer~), from OHG ~twerh~ ("oblique, transverse"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þwerh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þwerhaz~ ("crooked, athwart"); the initial ~tw-~ became ~qu-~ in Early New High German. Cognate with English ~thwart~ (which English took from Old Norse ~þvert~) and, probably, with ~queer~, borrowed from Low German, so ~quer~ and ~queer~ are doublets, both starting from "crosswise, off-kilter." In verbal compounds it means "across, athwart": ~querschießen~, ~sich querstellen~ ("to obstruct"). The sense of ~quer-~ here is: crosswise, transversely, at an angle to the expected direction.

~Querdenken~ means to think deliberately against the accustomed direction: unconventionally, against the grain.
en.querlesen:
A separable compound of ~quer-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~quer-~: From MHG ~twer~, ~dwer~ (also ~quer~), from OHG ~twerh~ ("oblique, transverse"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þwerh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þwerhaz~ ("crooked, athwart"); the initial ~tw-~ became ~qu-~ in Early New High German. Cognate with English ~thwart~ (which English took from Old Norse ~þvert~) and, probably, with ~queer~, borrowed from Low German, so ~quer~ and ~queer~ are doublets, both starting from "crosswise, off-kilter." In verbal compounds it means "across, athwart": ~querschießen~, ~sich querstellen~ ("to obstruct"). The sense of ~quer-~ here is: crosswise, transversely, at an angle to the expected direction.

~Querlesen~ is quick reading that runs crosswise over the text: skimming a text rather than following it line by line.
en.querschießen:
A separable compound of ~quer-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb (~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~). Cognate with English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Old Norse ~skjóta~.
• ~quer-~: From MHG ~twer~, ~dwer~ (also ~quer~), from OHG ~twerh~ ("oblique, transverse"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þwerh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þwerhaz~ ("crooked, athwart"); the initial ~tw-~ became ~qu-~ in Early New High German. Cognate with English ~thwart~ (which English took from Old Norse ~þvert~) and, probably, with ~queer~, borrowed from Low German, so ~quer~ and ~queer~ are doublets, both starting from "crosswise, off-kilter." In verbal compounds it means "across, athwart": ~querschießen~, ~sich querstellen~ ("to obstruct"). The sense of ~quer-~ here is: obstructively, cutting across someone else's course.

~Querschießen~ figuratively means to thwart a plan: to shoot across the course of something and so obstruct it.
en.querschlagen:
A separable compound of ~quer-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~quer-~: From MHG ~twer~, ~dwer~ (also ~quer~), from OHG ~twerh~ ("oblique, transverse"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þwerh~, from Proto-Germanic *~þwerhaz~ ("crooked, athwart"); the initial ~tw-~ became ~qu-~ in Early New High German. Cognate with English ~thwart~ (which English took from Old Norse ~þvert~) and, probably, with ~queer~, borrowed from Low German, so ~quer~ and ~queer~ are doublets, both starting from "crosswise, off-kilter." In verbal compounds it means "across, athwart": ~querschießen~, ~sich querstellen~ ("to obstruct"). The sense of ~quer-~ here is: crosswise, transversely, at an angle to the expected direction.

~Querschlagen~ here means a projectile's deflection at an angle: the ricochet that departs from its path.
en.ranhalten:
A separable compound of ~ran-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~ran-~: A colloquial contraction of ~heran~ (~her-~ "toward the speaker" + ~an~ "at, on"), of the same everyday register as ~rauf~, ~raus~, ~rein~, ~rüber~. The deictic contrast is the useful fact: ~her-~ orients motion toward the speaker, ~hin-~ away from the speaker. As a particle it brings something up close. The sense of ~ran-~ here is: colloquial for ~heran~; often exhortative, of getting down to a task.

~Sich ranhalten~ colloquially means "to get a move on, to keep at it": the image of drawing close to a task becomes the drive to get it done briskly.
en.raten:
From Middle High German ~rāten~, from Old High German ~rātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rēdaną~ ("to decide, advise, interpret"), from PIE *~Hreh₁dh-~ ("to think, arrange"). Cognate with Dutch ~raden~, English ~read~ (originally "to counsel, interpret"), Danish ~råde~.

The dual meanings "to advise" and "to guess" both descend from the original Germanic sense of deliberation and interpretation. English ~read~ underwent an even more dramatic semantic shift: from "to interpret, counsel" (as in Old English ~rǣdan~) to the modern sense of deciphering written text. The German noun ~Rat~ ("counsel, advice") and ~Rathaus~ ("town hall," literally "counsel house") preserve the older advisory meaning. The archaic English word ~rede~ ("counsel") is a direct cognate.
en.rauchen: From Middle High German ~rouchen~, ~röuchen~, from Old High German ~rouhhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raukijan~, derived from the noun *~rauki-~ ("smoke"), from Proto-Germanic *~raukiz~, from *~reukaną~ ("to smoke"), possibly from PIE *~h₁rewg-~ ("to belch, emit"). The noun survives as modern ~Rauch~ ("smoke"). Cognate with English ~reek~, Dutch ~rook~ ("smoke"), Swedish ~rök~, Danish ~røg~. In Old English, ~rēocan~ meant simply "to smoke" or "to steam," but its descendant ~reek~ has taken on a strongly negative connotation ("to stink"). The specific sense "to smoke tobacco" entered German in the late seventeenth century as a calque of French ~fumer~, itself a semantic extension from "to emit smoke" to "to inhale smoke." The related verb ~räuchern~ ("to smoke food, to fumigate") preserves the umlauted form that was once a variant of ~rauchen~ itself.
en.raufgehen:
A separable compound of ~rauf-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~rauf-~: The colloquial contraction of ~herauf~ ("up, up toward the speaker"), itself ~her-~ + ~auf~. It belongs with ~raus~, ~rein~, ~runter~, ~rüber~ and ~ran~, all reduced from ~her-~ compounds. In speech the reduced form has largely displaced ~hinauf~ as well, so it no longer reliably carries ~her-~'s toward-the-speaker orientation. The sense of ~rauf-~ here is: directional, "up, upward".

~Raufgehen~ covers both literal upward movement (going up the stairs) and the rising of prices or figures.
en.raufhalten:
A separable compound of ~rauf-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~rauf-~: The colloquial contraction of ~herauf~ ("up, up toward the speaker"), itself ~her-~ + ~auf~. It belongs with ~raus~, ~rein~, ~runter~, ~rüber~ and ~ran~, all reduced from ~her-~ compounds. In speech the reduced form has largely displaced ~hinauf~ as well, so it no longer reliably carries ~her-~'s toward-the-speaker orientation. The sense of ~rauf-~ here is: colloquially for either ~herauf~ or ~hinauf~, the deictic contrast neutralized.

~Raufhalten~ means to hold something up or aloft; the colloquial short form here stands equally for ~herauf~ and ~hinauf~.
en.rausbringen:
A separable compound of ~raus-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~raus-~: A colloquial contraction of ~heraus~ ("out hither, out toward the speaker"), and in everyday speech of ~hinaus~ ("out thither") as well: the reduced form has lost the deictic contrast that the two full forms carry. Written standard German uses the unreduced ~heraus-~ or ~hinaus-~. Deictically neutral, unlike the full forms it replaces: it serves for motion both toward and away from the speaker.

~Rausbringen~ ranges from literally carrying something outside to the figurative "to release, put on the market" or "to throw someone off".
en.rausdrehen:
A separable compound of ~raus-~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). Cognate with English ~throw~ (a true cognate: Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist," a sense that "throw a pot" still keeps) plus English ~thread~, Dutch ~draaien~.
• ~raus-~: A colloquial contraction of ~heraus~ ("out hither, out toward the speaker"), and in everyday speech of ~hinaus~ ("out thither") as well: the reduced form has lost the deictic contrast that the two full forms carry. Written standard German uses the unreduced ~heraus-~ or ~hinaus-~. Spoken and informal in register.

~Rausdrehen~ denotes turning out a screw or a bulb: the unscrewing and removing in a single motion.
en.rausfliegen:
A separable compound of ~raus-~ + ~fliegen~:

• ~fliegen~: From MHG ~vliegen~, from OHG ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"), an extension of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim") that also gave ~fließen~. The vowel path *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of class II strong verbs. Cognate with English ~fly~, Dutch ~vliegen~, Danish ~flyve~.
• ~raus-~: A colloquial contraction of ~heraus~ ("out hither, out toward the speaker"), and in everyday speech of ~hinaus~ ("out thither") as well: the reduced form has lost the deictic contrast that the two full forms carry. Written standard German uses the unreduced ~heraus-~ or ~hinaus-~. ~raus-~ marks outward motion, "out."

~Rausfliegen~ is usually figurative: to "fly out" of a job, a club, or a competition: that is, to be thrown out or eliminated.
en.rausgehen:
A separable compound of ~raus-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~raus-~: A colloquial contraction of ~heraus~ ("out hither, out toward the speaker"), and in everyday speech of ~hinaus~ ("out thither") as well: the reduced form has lost the deictic contrast that the two full forms carry. Written standard German uses the unreduced ~heraus-~ or ~hinaus-~. ~raus-~ marks outward motion, "out."

~Rausgehen~ simply means "to go outside"; colloquially also "to come out of oneself," to become more animated.
en.raushalten:
A separable compound of ~raus-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~raus-~: A colloquial contraction of ~heraus~ ("out hither, out toward the speaker"), and in everyday speech of ~hinaus~ ("out thither") as well: the reduced form has lost the deictic contrast that the two full forms carry. Written standard German uses the unreduced ~heraus-~ or ~hinaus-~. Spoken and informal in register.

~Sich raushalten~ means to keep out of a matter: to stay uninvolved; the outward motion here has turned wholly figurative.
en.rauskommen:
A separable compound of ~raus-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~raus-~: A colloquial contraction of ~heraus~ ("out hither, out toward the speaker"), and in everyday speech of ~hinaus~ ("out thither") as well: the reduced form has lost the deictic contrast that the two full forms carry. Written standard German uses the unreduced ~heraus-~ or ~hinaus-~. ~raus-~ marks outward motion, "out."

~Rauskommen~ ranges from stepping out of a room to the sense of an outcome: "something comes of it," a result becoming visible.
en.rauskriegen:
A separable compound of ~raus-~ + ~kriegen~:

• ~kriegen~: From MHG ~kriegen~ ("to war, to strive for"), a verbalization of ~Krieg~ ("war"), from OHG ~krig~, from Proto-West Germanic *~krīg~, whose origin is debated. The "obtaining" sense overshadowed the military one; colloquial modern German ~kriegen~ simply means "to get." Cognate with Dutch ~krijgen~ ("to get"), Bavarian ~kriagn~.
• ~raus-~: A colloquial contraction of ~heraus~ ("out hither, out toward the speaker"), and in everyday speech of ~hinaus~ ("out thither") as well: the reduced form has lost the deictic contrast that the two full forms carry. Written standard German uses the unreduced ~heraus-~ or ~hinaus-~. Spoken and informal in register.

~Rauskriegen~ colloquially means both "to get something out, to remove it" and "to figure out", the latter as if extracting the answer.
en.rauslassen:
A separable compound of ~raus-~ + ~lassen~:

• ~lassen~: From MHG ~lāzen~, ~lān~, from OHG ~lāȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lātan~ ("to let, allow"), from Proto-Germanic *~lētaną~ ("to leave behind, allow"), from PIE *~leh₁d-~ ("to let, leave behind"). Cognate with English ~let~, Dutch ~laten~, Bavarian ~lassn~.
• ~raus-~: A colloquial contraction of ~heraus~ ("out hither, out toward the speaker"), and in everyday speech of ~hinaus~ ("out thither") as well: the reduced form has lost the deictic contrast that the two full forms carry. Written standard German uses the unreduced ~heraus-~ or ~hinaus-~. Deictically neutral, unlike the full forms it replaces: it serves for motion both toward and away from the speaker.

~Rauslassen~ means to let someone or something out: dropping off a passenger, letting out the dog, or venting pent-up anger.
en.rausschmeißen:
A separable compound of ~raus-~ + ~schmeißen~:

• ~schmeißen~: From MHG ~smīȥen~, from OHG ~smīȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~smītaną~, from PIE *~smeyd-~. A class I strong verb (~schmeißen~, ~schmiss~, ~geschmissen~). Cognate with English ~smite~, Dutch ~smijten~, Danish ~smide~, Gothic ~bismeitan~ ("to smear, to anoint").
• ~raus-~: A colloquial contraction of ~heraus~ ("out hither, out toward the speaker"), and in everyday speech of ~hinaus~ ("out thither") as well: the reduced form has lost the deictic contrast that the two full forms carry. Written standard German uses the unreduced ~heraus-~ or ~hinaus-~. Deictically neutral, unlike the full forms it replaces: it serves for motion both toward and away from the speaker.

~Rausschmeißen~ is the blunt counterpart of ~hinauswerfen~: to throw someone out unceremoniously, often from a post, a bar, or an apartment.
en.reagieren: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ~reagō~ ("to act back, react"), a compound of ~re-~ ("back, again") + ~agō~ ("to drive, act"), from Proto-Italic *~agō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ ("to drive"). Latin ~agō~ is one of the most productive roots in the Latin lexicon: it underlies ~agent~, ~agenda~, ~action~, ~exact~, and ~navigate~ (via ~navis~ + ~agere~, "to drive a ship"). The Medieval Latin ~reagō~ is itself a scholarly coinage of the early modern period, formed in chemistry and natural philosophy to describe the behavior of substances upon one another. German borrowed ~reagieren~ directly from this Neo-Latin scientific vocabulary in the 17th–18th century, using the standard ~-ieren~ suffix that naturalizes Latin verbs into the German weak-verb system. Cognate with English ~react~, French ~réagir~, Dutch ~reageren~, Spanish ~reaccionar~.
en.realisieren:
Borrowed from French ~réaliser~, from Middle French ~real~ ("actual") + ~-iser~, from Old French ~reel~, from Latin ~reālis~ ("of or relating to things"), from ~rēs~ ("thing, event, deed, fact").

The French verb ~réaliser~ entered German carrying the sense "to make real, to implement", its core meaning. The sense "to become aware of" (~to realize~ in the English cognitive sense) is a semantic loan from English ~realize~ and is colloquially common but considered an anglicism, sometimes frowned upon by purists. So ~realisieren~ in formal German means "to bring something into existence," not merely to notice it, an important distinction for learners translating English sentences. The Latin ~rēs~ is one of the most ancient and productive roots in the language: it also underlies ~real~, ~republic~ (~rēs pūblica~, "public matter"), and ~reify~.
en.recherchieren: Borrowed from French ~rechercher~ ("to search again, investigate"), from Old French ~recerchier~, a compound of ~re-~ ("again") + ~cerchier~ ("to look for, search"), from Latin ~circāre~ ("to go around"), from ~circus~ ("circle"), from Greek ~kirkos~, from PIE *~(s)ker-~ ("to turn, bend"). The word thus carries the literal sense of "searching again": going back over ground already covered. English ~research~ comes from the same French source. Interestingly, ~recherchieren~ in German specifically means investigative research (as a journalist or detective would do), while academic research is typically ~forschen~. French ~recherché~ ("sought after, exquisite") comes from the same root and has been borrowed directly into English as a term for something elaborately refined.
en.rechnen:
From Middle High German ~rechenen~, from Old High German ~rehhanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rekanōn~ ("to count, explain"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to make straight or right"). Cognate with Low German ~rekenen~, Dutch ~rekenen~, English ~reckon~, Danish ~regne~.

The PIE root *~h₃reǵ-~ is also the ancestor of Latin ~rectus~ ("straight, right") and its English descendants: ~correct~, ~direct~, ~erect~. German ~recht~ ("right, correct") is a sibling from the same root. The semantic link is not accidental: to reckon is to make things come out right, to straighten the accounts. English ~reckon~ (from Old English ~recenian~) shares this ancestry directly; it was first attested meaning "to explain, set in order" before narrowing to calculation and then to the colloquial sense "to suppose, figure." The connection between rightness and reckoning runs deep: justice was long conceived as a kind of arithmetic, and ~Gericht~ ("court of law") shares the same ~recht~ root. Cognate with Dutch ~rekenen~, English ~reckon~, Latin ~rectus~.
en.rechtdrehen:
A separable compound of ~recht-~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). Cognate with English ~throw~ (a true cognate: Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist," a sense that "throw a pot" still keeps) plus English ~thread~, Dutch ~draaien~.
• ~recht-~: From MHG ~rëht~, from OHG ~rëht~, from Proto-West Germanic *~reht~ ("right, straight"), from Proto-Germanic *~rehtaz~, from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~recht~, Latin ~rēctus~. The same root, through Latin ~regere~ and ~rēx~, gives English ~correct~, ~direct~ and ~regent~, and, natively, German ~Reich~. The sense of ~recht-~ here is: adverbially, "properly, as it should be".

Here ~recht-~ carries not the sense "correct" but the spatial "to the right, clockwise"; ~rechtdrehen~ describes a wind veering clockwise. Both meanings trace to one root: the right hand was the "correct," straight one.
en.rechtfertigen:
From Middle High German ~rëhtvertegen~/~rëhtvertigen~, derived from MHG ~rëhtvertec~/~rëhtvertic~ ("just, proper, righteous"). The compound consists of ~recht~ + ~fertigen~:

• ~recht~: From MHG ~rëht~, from OHG ~rëht~, from Proto-West Germanic *~reht~ ("right, straight"), from Proto-Germanic *~rehtaz~, from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~recht~, Latin ~rēctus~.
• ~fertigen~: From MHG ~vertigen~/~vertegen~ ("to prepare, make ready"), from the adjective ~fertig~, from OHG ~fartīg~, derived from ~fart~ ("journey"). The original sense was "to make ready for a journey."

The compound literally meant "to make right" or "to prepare righteousness," evolving into the modern legal and moral sense of "to justify, to defend one's actions." The derived noun ~Rechtfertigung~ is the standard German equivalent of English ~justification~. In theology, ~Rechtfertigung~ is the key term for the Protestant doctrine of justification by faith (~sola fide~), central to Luther's Reformation. English ~justify~ comes from Latin ~iustificāre~, a calque of the same concept: ~iustus~ ("just") + ~facere~ ("to make").
en.rechtschreiben:
A separable compound of ~recht-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~recht-~: From MHG ~rëht~, from OHG ~rëht~, from Proto-West Germanic *~reht~ ("right, straight"), from Proto-Germanic *~rehtaz~, from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~recht~, Latin ~rēctus~. The same root, through Latin ~regere~ and ~rēx~, gives English ~correct~, ~direct~ and ~regent~, and, natively, German ~Reich~. The sense of ~recht-~ here is: adverbially, "properly, as it should be".

~Rechtschreiben~ survives today almost only as the noun ~Rechtschreibung~ ("orthography"), the "correct writing" that follows the spelling norm.
en.reden: From Middle High German ~reden~, from Old High German ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion, view, mind"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ ("account, reason, proof"), a striking parallel: the Latin noun that gives us English ~ratio~, ~rational~, and ~reason~ is a cognate of the German word for everyday talk. The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech, speaking with clarity and purpose. English ~rede~ ("counsel, advice") is also a cognate, surviving in archaic or dialectal use, and the same root underlies German ~Rat~ ("counsel, advice"). To speak (~reden~), in this etymology, is to render an account.
en.reduzieren: Borrowed from Latin ~redūcō~ ("to lead back, bring back, restore, reduce"), a compound of ~re-~ ("back") + ~dūcō~ ("to lead, draw"), from Proto-Italic *~doukō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ ("to draw, pull"), the same root underlying ~produzieren~ and, via the Germanic branch, English ~tow~. The original Latin sense of ~redūcō~ was entirely spatial and military: "to lead troops back, to withdraw." The mathematical sense (reducing a fraction, reducing an equation) is a metaphorical extension of the idea of "bringing back" to a simpler or more fundamental state. German borrowed ~reduzieren~ through French ~réduire~ or directly from the Latin learned vocabulary, applying the standard ~-ieren~ suffix. Cognate with English ~reduce~, French ~réduire~, Spanish ~reducir~, Italian ~ridurre~. The Latin ~dux~ ("leader," from the same ~dūcō~) underlies English ~duke~, making ~reduzieren~ and ~Herzog~ surprising distant relatives by way of the PIE root *~dewk-~.
en.reflektieren:
Borrowed from Latin ~reflectere~ ("to bend back, to turn back"), composed of ~re-~ ("back, again") + ~flectere~ ("to bend"). Entered German in the early seventeenth century with the optical meaning "to reflect (light)," then developed the intellectual meaning "to reflect (upon), to contemplate" in the second half of that century, and by the mid-eighteenth century acquired the further sense "to aspire to, to have designs on" (~auf etwas reflektieren~).

~Reflektieren~ is a remarkable case of semantic layering across centuries: the physical meaning (a mirror ~reflektiert~ light), the intellectual meaning (~über etwas reflektieren~, "to reflect on something"), and the aspirational meaning (~auf eine Stelle reflektieren~, "to have one's eye on a position") coexist in modern German. The Latin root ~flectere~ ("to bend") also produced English ~flexible~, ~deflect~, ~inflect~, and ~genuflect~. The aspirational third sense is uniquely German: neither English ~reflect~ nor French ~refléchir~ developed this usage, making it a false friend in that particular register.
en.regeln: ~Regeln~ is a denominal verb formed directly from the noun ~Regel~ ("rule, regulation") with the infinitive suffix ~-n~. ~Regel~ entered German in Old High German as ~regula~, borrowed from Latin ~rēgula~ ("straight stick, ruler, rule"), a diminutive of Latin ~regere~ ("to rule, direct, keep straight"), from Proto-Italic *~regō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, make right"). That PIE root is extraordinarily productive: it yielded Latin ~rēx~ ("king"), Sanskrit ~rājati~ ("to rule"), and, via French, English ~rule~, ~royal~, ~rector~, and ~correct~. The cognate English ~rail~ (as in a fence rail) also descends from ~rēgula~ via Old French. So when one ~regelt~ a Situation, one is etymologically "putting it on a straight stick."
en.regen:
From MHG ~regen~ ("to make protrude, to erect, to excite, to move"), from Proto-Germanic *~hragjaną~ ("to make stand, wake up, incite"). By synchronic analysis, the causative of MHG ~ragen~ ("to project, to tower").

~Regen~ (the verb, not to be confused with ~Regen~ the noun meaning "rain," which has a completely different etymology) means "to stir, to move, to rouse." It is most commonly encountered in the reflexive ~sich regen~ ("to stir, to move, to show signs of life"): ~Kein Blatt regt sich~ ("Not a leaf stirs"), ~der Widerstand regt sich~ ("resistance is stirring"). The proverb ~Sich regen bringt Segen~ ("To stir brings blessing," i.e., hard work pays off) is one of Germany's most beloved rhyming proverbs. The derived adjective ~rege~ ("lively, active, brisk") preserves the positive-energy sense. The compound ~an-regen~ ("to stimulate, to inspire") and its noun ~Anregung~ ("stimulus, suggestion") are among the verb's most productive descendants.
en.registrieren:
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ~registrāre~ ("to record, enter in a register"), from ~registrum~ ("register, list"), a singular form of Late Latin ~regesta~ ("items recorded"), neuter plural of ~regestus~, past participle of Latin ~regerere~ ("to carry back, to record"), from ~re-~ ("back") + ~gerere~ ("to carry, bear"). The ~-ieren~ suffix is the standard German adaptation of French/Latin ~-er~ / ~-āre~ verb endings, used productively for learned and technical borrowings since the Middle High German period.

The word entered German during the late medieval expansion of administrative and legal Latin. Cognate in formation with French ~registrer~, Italian ~registrare~, English ~register~. Some scholars note that the meaning of ~registrum~ was influenced by association with unrelated Latin ~regere~ ("to rule"), giving it an added connotation of official authority. The verb remains firmly technical and administrative in register: one ~registriert~ births, trademarks, and domain names. The reflexive ~sich registrieren~ ("to register oneself") has gained new life in the digital age as the standard verb for creating online accounts.
en.regnen: From Middle High German ~regenen~, from Old High German ~reganōn~, a denominative verb derived from the noun ~regan~ ("rain"), from Proto-West Germanic *~regn~, from Proto-Germanic *~regną~. The PIE origin is uncertain but possibly *~Hreǵʰ-~ ("to flow water"), which may also be the source of Latin ~rigō~ ("I irrigate, moisten") and Albanian ~rrjedh~ ("to flow"). The verb is impersonal in German (~es regnet~, "it rains"), a construction inherited from Proto-Germanic, where weather verbs lacked a real subject. Cognate with English ~rain~, Dutch ~regenen~, Danish ~regne~, Swedish ~regna~. The English expression "it's raining cats and dogs" has no German equivalent; instead, German says ~es gießt wie aus Eimern~ ("it pours as if from buckets").
en.reiben: From MHG ~rīben~, from OHG ~rīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrībaną~ ("to rub"). Beyond Germanic the origin is uncertain: a PIE *~wreyp-~, a labial extension of *~wer-~ ("to turn"), is proposed but not secure. A class I strong verb (~reiben~, ~rieb~, ~gerieben~), cognate with Dutch ~wrijven~ and Old Saxon ~wrīvan~; German dropped the initial ~w-~ before ~r~, exactly as it did in ~ringen~. The verb also passed into Old French as ~riper~, and English ~ribald~ traces back through French to this same Germanic root.
en.reichen:
From Middle High German ~reichen~, from Old High German ~reihhen~, ~reichen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raikijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~raikijaną~, from PIE *~Hroyǵ-éye-ti~, a causative o-grade of *~Hreyǵ-~ ("to stretch out, reach"). Cognate with Lithuanian ~ráižytis~ ("to keep stretching"), Old Irish ~rigid~ ("to stretch").

The PIE causative formation ("to cause to stretch"), evolved into the broad semantic range of Modern German ~reichen~: "to reach, extend," "to hand (something) to someone," "to suffice, be enough." The sense of "sufficiency" (as in ~das reicht~, "that's enough") developed from the physical image of something extending far enough to arrive at its goal. English ~reach~ (from the same root) covers the first two senses but not the third; no single English word captures all three meanings. The ~er-~ prefixed form ~erreichen~ ("to achieve, attain") strips away the sense of sufficiency and focuses on completion: the goal is not just approached but fully reached. Cognate with Dutch ~reiken~, English ~reach~, Danish ~række~.
en.reihen: From MHG ~rīhen~, from OHG ~rīhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rīhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rīhaną~ ("to string together, line up"), possibly from PIE *~h₁reyḱ-~ ("to scratch, tear"), though that connection is uncertain. In the sewing senses ("to tack, to baste") it appears to have merged with a separate *~wrīhaną~ ("to cover"). Once strong, it is weak in modern German (~reihte~, ~gereiht~) and is now felt as a derivative of the noun ~Reihe~ ("row, series"). Cognate with Dutch ~rijgen~ and Middle Low German ~rīhen~.
en.reinfallen:
A separable compound of ~rein-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~rein-~: In these verbs this is not the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean") but the colloquial contraction of ~herein~, and often of ~hinein~ as well; that is, ~her~ or ~hin~ + ~ein~ ("in"). The two words are homographs with unrelated histories, and only the directional one forms these compounds. ~rein-~ means motion into something, the informal counterpart of ~herein-~ and ~hinein-~.

~Reinfallen~ literally means "to fall in," but far more often the figurative "to be taken in, to be duped", to fall for a scam.
en.reinfeiern:
A separable compound of ~rein-~ + ~feiern~:

• ~feiern~: From MHG ~vīren~, from OHG ~fīrōn~, a denominative from OHG ~fīra~ (whence ~Feier~), borrowed from Latin ~fēriae~ ("religious holidays"), from Proto-Italic *~fēsiās~, from PIE *~dʰéh₁s-yo-s~, from *~dʰéh₁s~ ("god, deity"). A ~Feiertag~ was originally a day set aside for the gods. Cognate with Dutch ~vieren~, distantly English ~feast~.
• ~rein-~: In these verbs this is not the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean") but the colloquial contraction of ~herein~, and often of ~hinein~ as well; that is, ~her~ or ~hin~ + ~ein~ ("in"). The two words are homographs with unrelated histories, and only the directional one forms these compounds. ~rein-~ means motion into something, the informal counterpart of ~herein-~ and ~hinein-~.

~Reinfeiern~ means to celebrate right into an approaching day: to party into a birthday or the new year; the "into" motion here is temporal.
en.reingehen:
A separable compound of ~rein-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~rein-~: In these verbs this is not the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean") but the colloquial contraction of ~herein~, and often of ~hinein~ as well; that is, ~her~ or ~hin~ + ~ein~ ("in"). The two words are homographs with unrelated histories, and only the directional one forms these compounds. ~rein-~ means motion into something, the informal counterpart of ~herein-~ and ~hinein-~.

~Reingehen~ means "to go in," and colloquially "to fit in", when something ~reingeht~, fits inside a container.
en.reinhauen:
A separable compound of ~rein-~ + ~hauen~:

• ~hauen~: From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). Originally a class VII strong verb (~hauen~, ~hieb~, ~gehauen~), partially weakened colloquially, where ~haute~ competes with ~hieb~. Cognate with English ~hew~, Latin ~cūdere~ ("to strike, forge").
• ~rein-~: In these verbs this is not the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean") but the colloquial contraction of ~herein~, and often of ~hinein~ as well; that is, ~her~ or ~hin~ + ~ein~ ("in"). The two words are homographs with unrelated histories, and only the directional one forms these compounds. It belongs to spoken and informal register; written standard German prefers the full forms.

~Reinhauen~ covers a broad colloquial range: to strike hard, but also to dig heartily into a meal.
en.reinhängen:
A separable compound of ~rein-~ + ~hängen~:

• ~hängen~: The merger of three OHG verbs: ~hāhan~ (strong, transitive; past ~hieng~, participle ~gehangan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~hą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~hanhaną~; ~hangēn~ (weak, intransitive); and the causative ~hengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hangijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hangijaną~. The distinction is upheld chiefly in the past tense: intransitive ~hing~/~gehangen~ versus transitive ~hängte~/~gehängt~. Cognate with Dutch ~hangen~, English ~hang~.
• ~rein-~: In these verbs this is not the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean") but the colloquial contraction of ~herein~, and often of ~hinein~ as well; that is, ~her~ or ~hin~ + ~ein~ ("in"). The two words are homographs with unrelated histories, and only the directional one forms these compounds. It belongs to spoken and informal register; written standard German prefers the full forms.
