~Sich reinhängen~ colloquially means "to throw oneself into something, to give it everything": one figuratively hangs oneself into the task.
en.reinigen: From Middle High German ~reinegen~, ~reinigen~, a denominative verb derived from the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean"). ~Rein~ descends from MHG ~reine~, from OHG ~reini~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrainī~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrainiz~, from PIE *~krey-~ ("to divide, to sift, to separate"). The semantic path from "sifting" to "clean" is intuitive: purity is what remains after impurities have been sifted away. The same PIE root *~krey-~ produced Greek ~krī́nō~ ("to separate, to decide, to judge") (whence English ~crisis~, ~critic~, and ~criterion~) and Old Irish ~criathar~ ("sieve"). English ~riddle~ (the sieve, not the puzzle) is also a cognate. The Germanic *~hr-~ cluster (from PIE *~kr-~) lost its initial ~h~ in High German but survives in Old Norse ~hreinn~ ("clean, pure"), which via Norse settlers entered Old French as ~raïncer~ ("to cleanse"), giving English ~rinse~. So ~reinigen~ and ~rinse~ are distant cousins, reunited through a chain of borrowings. Cognate with Dutch ~reinigen~, Swedish ~ren~ ("clean"), Icelandic ~hreinn~.
en.reinkommen:
A separable compound of ~rein-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~rein-~: In these verbs this is not the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean") but the colloquial contraction of ~herein~, and often of ~hinein~ as well; that is, ~her~ or ~hin~ + ~ein~ ("in"). The two words are homographs with unrelated histories, and only the directional one forms these compounds. ~rein-~ means motion into something, the informal counterpart of ~herein-~ and ~hinein-~.

~Reinkommen~ means "to come in, to get inside"; of guests as much as of money that comes in.
en.reinmachen:
A separable compound of ~rein-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~rein-~: In these verbs this is not the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean") but the colloquial contraction of ~herein~, and often of ~hinein~ as well; that is, ~her~ or ~hin~ + ~ein~ ("in"). The two words are homographs with unrelated histories, and only the directional one forms these compounds. It belongs to spoken and informal register; written standard German prefers the full forms.

~Reinmachen~ colloquially means "to put in, to add in"; to put something into a container.
en.reinscheißen:
A separable compound of ~rein-~ + ~scheißen~:

• ~scheißen~: From MHG ~schīzen~, from OHG *~skīzan~ (attested only in the compound ~biskīzan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~skītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skītaną~, from PIE *~skeyd-~ ("to split, separate"); the root's basic sense is separation, not filth. A class I strong verb (~scheißen~, ~schiss~, ~geschissen~). Cognate with English ~shit~, Dutch ~schijten~, Old Norse ~skíta~.
• ~rein-~: In these verbs this is not the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean") but the colloquial contraction of ~herein~, and often of ~hinein~ as well; that is, ~her~ or ~hin~ + ~ein~ ("in"). The two words are homographs with unrelated histories, and only the directional one forms these compounds. ~rein-~ means motion into something, the informal counterpart of ~herein-~ and ~hinein-~.

~Reinscheißen~ is the vulgar, literal formation "to defecate into something"; the base meaning is the plain motion inward.
en.reinstecken:
A separable compound of ~rein-~ + ~stecken~:

• ~stecken~: Modern ~stecken~ merges two verbs: the transitive weak one ("to put, stick something in") from MHG ~stecken~, OHG ~steckōn~, a geminate derivative of ~stëhhan~ (the ancestor of ~stechen~), and the strong intransitive one (archaic ~stak~/~gestocken~, "to be stuck"); the two fused in Early Modern German. Both trace to Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stikaną~, from PIE *~(s)teyg-~ ("to be sharp, stab, goad"). Cognate with English ~stick~ and ~steak~.
• ~rein-~: In these verbs this is not the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean") but the colloquial contraction of ~herein~, and often of ~hinein~ as well; that is, ~her~ or ~hin~ + ~ein~ ("in"). The two words are homographs with unrelated histories, and only the directional one forms these compounds. ~rein-~ means motion into something, the informal counterpart of ~herein-~ and ~hinein-~.

~Reinstecken~ means "to stick in, insert": a key into a lock as much as, figuratively, money or effort into a project.
en.reinwaschen:
A separable compound of ~rein~ + ~waschen~:

• ~waschen~: From MHG ~waschen~, from OHG ~wascan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~waskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waskaną~, from an earlier *~watskaną~, a ~ske~-present formation from PIE *~wed-~ ("wet, water"), hence "to make wet (repeatedly)." Cognate with English ~wash~, ~water~, ~wet~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vaske~.
• ~rein~: The adjective ~rein~ ("clean, pure"), from MHG ~reine~, from OHG ~reini~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrainī~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrainiz~ ("clean, pure"). Cognate with Dutch ~rein~, Gothic ~hrains~. In separable compounds the adjective is resultative.

Here ~rein~ is not the directional particle but the adjective ~rein~ ("clean"): resultatively "to wash clean", and figuratively to clear someone of suspicion.
en.reinziehen:
A separable compound of ~rein-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~rein-~: In these verbs this is not the adjective ~rein~ ("pure, clean") but the colloquial contraction of ~herein~, and often of ~hinein~ as well; that is, ~her~ or ~hin~ + ~ein~ ("in"). The two words are homographs with unrelated histories, and only the directional one forms these compounds. It belongs to spoken and informal register; written standard German prefers the full forms.

The compound's directional core (pulling something in) carries both uses: the literal drawing-in and the slangy "sich etwas reinziehen" for eagerly consuming food, drink, or media.
en.reisen: From Middle High German ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from Old High German ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, derived from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"). The Proto-Germanic root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") is the direct ancestor of both Old English ~rīsan~ and thus English ~rise~. German ~reisen~ is a cognate of English ~rise~, with the German verb retaining an older meaning "to fall" alongside the travel sense, both descending from a root about directional movement, setting out, departing. The semantic shift from "rising up, setting out" to "traveling" happened through the military context: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign, a sortie, an armed departure. Only later did the word shed its martial sense and become the everyday word for a journey.
en.reiten: From Middle High German ~rīten~, from Old High German ~rītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rīdaną~, from PIE *~Hreydʰ-~ ("to set in motion, ride"), likely a suffixed form of *~h₃reyH-~ ("to move, churn"). Cognate with English ~ride~, Dutch ~rijden~, Danish ~ride~, Swedish ~rida~, Old Irish ~réidid~ ("to ride, drive"). German ~reiten~ has narrowed to mean riding on horseback (or on an animal), whereas English ~ride~ has broadened to include vehicles. For traveling by car or bus, German uses ~fahren~. In Dutch, ~rijden~ has taken the opposite path from German, primarily meaning "to drive (a vehicle)" rather than horseback riding. The past participle ~geritten~ preserves the old strong conjugation pattern with vowel change (ei to i), a relic of the Indo-European ablaut system.
en.reißen:
From Middle High German ~rīȥen~, from Old High German ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two similar Proto-West Germanic verbs:

• *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline")
• *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~

Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~ ("to rip, tear"), Low German ~rieten~ ("to rip, tear"), Luxembourgish ~räissen~ ("to scratch, tear").

The merger of two distinct verbs into one is a rare etymological event, and it left ~reißen~ with an unusually broad semantic field: "to tear, rip, pull, snatch, sketch." The sketching sense (as in ~Grundriss~ = "floor plan," literally "ground-sketch") preserves the older "scratch, inscribe" meaning from *~wrītaną~. This same root gave English ~write~, which originally meant "to scratch, carve" (runes into wood or stone) before shifting to its modern meaning. Thus German ~reißen~ ("to tear") and English ~write~ are distant cousins, both descending from the act of scratching marks into a surface. The connection is also visible in Swedish ~rita~ ("to draw, sketch") and Icelandic ~ríta~ ("to scratch, write"). Compare also Dutch ~wrijten~ ("to argue, quarrel"), where the "scratching" metaphor extends to verbal conflict.
en.rennen:
From a merger of two Old High German verbs: transitive/causative ~rennan~ ("to make something run or flow"), from Proto-Germanic *~rannijaną~, the causative of *~rinnaną~ ("to run, to flow"); and intransitive ~rinnan~ ("to run, to flow"), from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~, from PIE *~h₃reyH-~ ("to undulate, churn"). A similar merger of transitive and intransitive roots occurred in Dutch ~rennen~ and English ~run~.

The PIE root *~h₃reyH-~ connects running with flowing water, a vivid equation of rapid human motion with the surge of a stream. This root also produced Middle Irish ~rian~ ("river, way"), Proto-Slavic *~rěka~ ("river," whence Russian ~reká~), Latin ~rīvus~ ("stream," whence English ~river~ and ~rival~, originally "one who shares the same stream"), and, most strikingly, the Celtic-Gaulish ~Rēnos~ ("that which flows"), which is the source of the name of the river ~Rhine~. The semantic collapse of two distinct Proto-Germanic verbs (causative *~rannijaną~ and intransitive *~rinnaną~) into a single modern verb is mirrored in English ~run~, where the transitive ("to run a business") and intransitive ("to run fast") coexist in one lemma. The German noun ~Rinne~ ("gutter, channel") preserves the original water-flow sense. ~Rennen~ is a member of the Rückumlaut cohort: present ~ich renne~ (with umlaut e from a), preterite ~rannte~, participle ~gerannt~; the umlaut does not appear in the preterite. Other members: ~brennen~, ~kennen~, ~nennen~, ~senden~, ~wenden~, ~denken~, ~bringen~; see ~brennen~ for the mechanism.
en.reparieren:
Borrowed in the 16th century from Latin ~reparāre~ ("to restore, renew, repair"), from ~re-~ ("back, again") + ~parāre~ ("to prepare, provide, arrange"), from PIE *~perh₃-~ ("to grant, provide"). Compare English ~repair~ (via Old French ~reparer~, from the same Latin source).

The Latin root ~parāre~ ("to prepare") is spectacularly productive in European languages. From it descend English ~prepare~, ~compare~, ~separate~, ~apparatus~, and ~pare~, each prefixed form taking the "arrange, make ready" sense in a different direction. Unlike the native German word ~flicken~ ("to patch, mend"), which evokes homespun repair, ~reparieren~ carries a more professional, technical connotation; one ~flickt~ a torn sock but ~repariert~ a broken machine.
en.repräsentieren: Borrowed from Latin ~repraesentāre~ ("to bring before, make present, represent"), a compound of ~re-~ ("again, back") + ~praesentāre~ ("to present, show"), from ~praesēns~ ("present, at hand"), from ~prae-~ ("before") + the present participle of ~esse~ ("to be"). The Latin verb originally meant "to make something present again": to bring an absent thing vividly before the mind. German ~repräsentieren~ entered the language through learned Latin usage, with the ~ä~ reflecting German phonological adaptation. It carries both the political sense ("to represent a constituency") and the social sense ("to make an impressive appearance"), the latter being particularly prominent in German. The suffix ~-ieren~ marks it as a learned Latinate borrowing, as with ~positionieren~ and ~reservieren~.
en.reservieren: Borrowed from French ~réserver~, from Latin ~reservāre~ ("to keep back, save up"), a compound of ~re-~ ("back, again") + ~servāre~ ("to preserve, keep, guard"). Latin ~servāre~ derives from a denominative to Proto-Italic *~serwā~ or *~serwom~ ("observation, heedance"), ultimately from PIE *~ser-~ ("to guard, watch over"). The same Latin root gives English ~reserve~, ~preserve~, ~conserve~, and ~observe~ (literally "to watch toward"). In German, ~reservieren~ is used primarily for booking tables, seats, and hotel rooms, where English would say "to reserve." The related noun ~Reservierung~ ("reservation") and ~Reserve~ ("reserve, backup") are also thoroughly naturalized in German. Cognate with French ~réserver~, Italian ~riservare~, Spanish ~reservar~.
en.retten: From Middle High German ~retten~, from Old High German ~hretten~ or ~retten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hraddjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hradjaną~ ("to save, rescue"). Cognate with Dutch ~redden~, English ~redd~ (dialectal for "to tidy, clear"), and the partially related English ~rid~, the latter borrowed partly from an Old English form of the same root, ~hreddan~ ("to deliver, rescue"). The English connection is a surprise: when speakers say "to rid oneself of something," they are reaching for a word that shares ancient ancestry with German ~retten~ ("to rescue, save").
en.richten:
From Middle High German ~richten~, from Old High German ~rihten~ ("to straighten, set right, direct"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~ ("to make straight"), from Proto-Germanic *~rihtijaną~, a denominative verb derived from the adjective *~rehtaz~ ("straight, right"), from PIE *~h₃reǵtós~ ("right, straightened"), from *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to stretch out, straighten, direct"). The same PIE root *~h₃reǵ-~ underlies Latin ~regō~ ("I rule, direct"), Sanskrit ~rájati~ ("rules"), and ultimately English ~right~, ~reign~, and ~regiment~. A causative denominative: "to make (something) straight/right."

The modern semantic range of ~richten~ extends in several directions from the original sense of straightening: "to direct" (~den Blick richten~, "to direct one's gaze"), "to judge" (literally "to set right according to law"), "to execute" (~hinrichten~, still in use), and "to set up" (~Richtfest~, the topping-out ceremony when roof beams are set straight). The judicial sense is ancient: Gothic ~garaihtjan~ already carried it. Cognate with Dutch ~richten~, English ~right~, Old English ~rihtian~, Gothic ~raihtjan~.
en.richtigliegen:
A separable compound of ~richtig~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~richtig~: The adjective ~richtig~ ("correct, proper"), from MHG ~rihtec~, formed with the suffix ~-ig~ on ~richten~ ("to set straight, direct, judge"), itself a causative built to ~recht~, from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"). Its root relatives are English ~right~ and, through Latin ~regere~, ~correct~ and ~direct~. In separable compounds the adjective is resultative. The sense of ~richtig~ here is: predicatively, "correctly, rightly", of judging or of being in the right position.

"richtigliegen" carries the image of lying in the right place over to being correct: to be right in one's guess.
en.richtigstellen:
A separable compound of ~richtig~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~richtig~: The adjective ~richtig~ ("correct, proper"), from MHG ~rihtec~, formed with the suffix ~-ig~ on ~richten~ ("to set straight, direct, judge"), itself a causative built to ~recht~, from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"). Its root relatives are English ~right~ and, through Latin ~regere~, ~correct~ and ~direct~. In separable compounds the adjective is resultative. The sense of ~richtig~ here is: as a resultative adjective, "into a correct state", as of setting a statement right.

The resultative ~richtig~ names the end state: a statement is put into a correct state, that is, corrected.
en.riechen:
From MHG ~riechen~, from OHG ~riohhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~reukan~, from Proto-Germanic *~reukaną~, from PIE *~h₁rewg-~ ("to belch, to roar"). Cognate with English ~reek~, Dutch ~rieken~, Danish ~ryge~ ("to smoke"), Swedish ~ryka~ ("to steam, smoke"). Related to German ~Rauch~ ("smoke") and ~Geruch~ ("smell, odor").

The semantic journey from PIE "to belch" to German "to smell" is a wonderfully circuitous one. The original sense involved emitting something: vapor, smoke, belching gas. Proto-Germanic *~reukaną~ shifted toward the emission of smoke or fumes, and the meaning then pivoted from the emitter to the perceiver: from "to give off fumes" to "to detect fumes" to "to smell" in general. English ~reek~ preserves an intermediate stage: it means "to stink", still focused on the emission, but specifically an unpleasant one. German ~riechen~ generalized to cover all smelling, pleasant or foul. The noun ~Geruch~ ("smell, odor") and the related ~Rauch~ ("smoke") both spring from the same root, preserving the ancient link between smoke and sensation. Greek ~erygganō~ ("I belch") is a cousin from the same PIE root, confirming the original oral-emission sense.
en.ringen: From MHG ~ringen~, from OHG ~ringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wringaną~ ("to twist, wring"), from a nasalized form of PIE *~wergʰ-~ ("to turn, twist"). A class III strong verb (~ringen~, ~rang~, ~gerungen~). Cognate with English ~wring~, Dutch ~wringen~, and Low German ~wringen~, which German reborrowed as the doublet ~wringen~ ("to wring out laundry"). Despite appearances it has nothing to do with ~Ring~ (from Proto-Germanic *~hringaz~); its true relatives are ~Ringen~ and ~Ringkampf~ ("wrestling"), and English ~wrong~ belongs here too, having meant "twisted, crooked".
en.rinnen: From MHG ~rinnen~, from OHG ~rinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~ ("to run, flow"); the PIE source is debated, most often given as *~h₃reyH-~ ("to churn, set in motion"). A class III strong verb (~rinnen~, ~rann~, ~geronnen~). Cognate with English ~run~, Gothic ~rinnan~, Swedish ~rinna~, and Dutch ~rennen~. German ~rennen~ ("to run") is its causative, from *~rannijaną~, "to make flow", so the two verbs are one root divided between what water does and what a runner does.
en.rollen:
From Middle High German ~rollen~, borrowed from Old French ~roeler~, from Medieval Latin ~rotulāre~ ("to roll"), from Latin ~rotula~ ("small wheel"), diminutive of ~rota~ ("wheel"). The Latin ~rota~ derives from Proto-Indo-European *~ret-~ ("to run, to roll"). Cognate with Dutch ~rollen~, English ~roll~ (also borrowed from Old French). The related noun ~Rolle~ entered German in the fifteenth century, likewise via Old French ~rolle~ and probably through Middle Dutch ~rolle~.

The semantic extension of ~Rolle~ from "scroll, cylinder" to "theatrical role" was a later semantic loan from French ~role~, originally referring to the rolled-up script an actor read from. English ~role~ followed the same French path.
en.rotsehen:
A separable compound of ~rot~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~rot~: From MHG ~rōt~, from OHG ~rōt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raud~, from Proto-Germanic *~raudaz~, from PIE *~h₁rewdʰ-~ ("red"). Cognate with English ~red~, Dutch ~rood~, Danish ~rød~, Latin ~ruber~, Greek ~erythrós~, Sanskrit ~rudhira-~. It is among the most stable color words in Indo-European, recognizable in nearly every branch. The sense of ~rot~ here is: of blushing, or of marking something in red.

"rotsehen" is figurative: to lose control in sudden rage; the red is the color of anger, not anything actually seen.
en.rufen:
From Middle High German ~ruofen~, from Old High German ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~. A class VII strong verb. The origin of *~hrōpaną~ is uncertain. One theory connects it to *~hrōþiz~ ("glory, fame," the first element of names like ~Hrodulf~/~Rudolf~), though the phonetic relationship is problematic. Another theory proposes a connection to the raven's call (comparing Ancient Greek ~kórax~ ("raven"), Latin ~corvus~ ("raven"), and Lithuanian ~šárka~ ("magpie")) treating the root as an imitation of a carrying cry that was generalized to all calling out. Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.

The historical forms show an initial ~hr-~ cluster (Old High German ~hruofan~) that was reduced to ~r-~ as Germanic languages systematically shed their initial ~h~ before consonants. The same process affected ~hring~ → ~Ring~ and ~hrōþ~ → ~Ruhm~. A parallel weak form of ~rufen~ also existed in Middle High German and persisted into the 19th century; its legacy can be seen in the modern present tense, which lacks the umlaut that would be expected from a purely strong paradigm (~du rufst~, ~er ruft~ rather than the historically expected *~du rüfst~, *~er rüft~).
en.ruhen:
From MHG ~ruo(we)n~, from OHG ~ruowēn~ ("to rest"), derived from the noun ~ruowa~ ("rest, peace, quiet"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rōu~ ("calm, rest"), from Proto-Germanic *~rōwō~, from PIE *~h₁reh₁-~ ("to rest"). Cognate with ~Ruhe~ ("rest, peace, quiet"), Dutch ~rusten~ (from a different formation on the same base), Gothic ~rimis~ ("rest").

~Ruhen~ means "to rest, to lie still, to be at peace", both physically and metaphorically. One can say ~die Arbeit ruht~ ("work has ceased"), ~hier ruht...~ ("here lies..." on a gravestone), or ~auf sich ruhen~ ("to be at ease with oneself"). The PIE root *~h₁reh₁-~ had a remarkably narrow semantic range: it meant simply "to be still, to rest," and this sense has remained stable across millennia and language branches. The phrase ~Ruhe in Frieden~ ("rest in peace") is the German equivalent of Latin ~requiēscat in pāce~, though the German and Latin terms derive from entirely different PIE roots, a case of cultural convergence in funerary language.
en.rumbringen:
A separable compound of ~rum-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~rum-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herum~ ("around, about"), itself ~her-~ + ~um~. The reduction is confined to speech and informal writing; the standard compound is ~herum-~. Spoken and informal in register.

"rumbringen" colloquially means to get the time around: to pass or while it away.
en.rumkommen:
A separable compound of ~rum-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~rum-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herum~ ("around, about"), itself ~her-~ + ~um~. The reduction is confined to speech and informal writing; the standard compound is ~herum-~. ~rum-~ marks circular or aimless motion, "around, about."

"rumkommen" means to get around a good deal: to reach many places.
en.rumlaufen:
A separable compound of ~rum-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~rum-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herum~ ("around, about"), itself ~her-~ + ~um~. The reduction is confined to speech and informal writing; the standard compound is ~herum-~. ~rum-~ marks circular or aimless motion, "around, about."

"rumlaufen" denotes walking or roaming aimlessly about.
en.rummachen:
A separable compound of ~rum-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~rum-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herum~ ("around, about"), itself ~her-~ + ~um~. The reduction is confined to speech and informal writing; the standard compound is ~herum-~. Often carries a dismissive tint of purposelessness (~rumsitzen~, ~rumlaufen~).

"rummachen" is casual for fooling around: messing about with something, or making out.
en.rumschmeißen:
A separable compound of ~rum-~ + ~schmeißen~:

• ~schmeißen~: From MHG ~smīȥen~, from OHG ~smīȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~smītaną~, from PIE *~smeyd-~. A class I strong verb (~schmeißen~, ~schmiss~, ~geschmissen~). Cognate with English ~smite~, Dutch ~smijten~, Danish ~smide~, Gothic ~bismeitan~ ("to smear, to anoint").
• ~rum-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herum~ ("around, about"), itself ~her-~ + ~um~. The reduction is confined to speech and informal writing; the standard compound is ~herum-~. Spoken and informal in register.

"rumschmeißen" means to sling something about, also figuratively to throw money around.
en.rumstehen:
A separable compound of ~rum-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~rum-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herum~ ("around, about"), itself ~her-~ + ~um~. The reduction is confined to speech and informal writing; the standard compound is ~herum-~. Often carries a dismissive tint of purposelessness (~rumsitzen~, ~rumlaufen~).

"rumstehen" denotes standing idly about.
en.runden:
From ~rund~ + ~-en~. ~Rund~ descends from MHG ~runt~, borrowed from Old French ~ront~, from Latin ~rotundus~ ("round"), from ~rota~ ("wheel, disk"), from PIE *~Hróth₂o~ (from *~ret-~ "to run, to roll").

~Runden~ means "to round (off), to make round" and is especially common in mathematical and commercial contexts: ~auf ganze Zahlen runden~ ("to round to whole numbers"), ~abrunden~ and ~aufrunden~ ("to round down" and "to round up"). The etymological journey is striking: a PIE root meaning "to roll" produced Latin ~rota~ ("wheel"), which produced ~rotundus~ ("round"), which was borrowed into Old French as ~ront~, which was borrowed into Middle High German as ~runt~, making this one of the few everyday German adjectives that arrived via Latin and French rather than directly from Proto-Germanic. English ~round~ took the same French detour.
en.rundgehen:
A separable compound of ~rund~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~rund~: Borrowed in MHG as ~runt~ from Old French ~ront~, ~roont~, from Latin ~rotundus~ ("round"), a derivative of ~rota~ ("wheel"). English ~round~ is the same borrowing made independently, and ~rotund~, ~rotate~, and ~roulette~ go back to ~rota~ as well; the inherited German word from that root is ~Rad~ ("wheel"), so the loan and the native word are distant relatives. As a particle it names roundness, or figuratively completeness, as the outcome. The sense of ~rund~ here is: the adjective ~rund~ ("round") as the resulting state.

"rundgehen" means to go around in a circle; "es geht rund" additionally means that things are getting lively.
en.runterdrücken:
A separable compound of ~runter-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~runter-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herunter~ ("down hither"), and in everyday speech of ~hinunter~ ("down thither") as well, so that the reduced form covers both directions the full forms distinguish. Written standard German uses ~herunter-~ or ~hinunter-~. Deictically neutral, unlike the full forms it replaces.

"runterdrücken" means to press something down.
en.runtergehen:
A separable compound of ~runter-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~runter-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herunter~ ("down hither"), and in everyday speech of ~hinunter~ ("down thither") as well, so that the reduced form covers both directions the full forms distinguish. Written standard German uses ~herunter-~ or ~hinunter-~. ~runter-~ marks downward motion, "down."

"runtergehen" ranges from literal descent to the falling of prices or figures.
en.runterhalten:
A separable compound of ~runter-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~runter-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herunter~ ("down hither"), and in everyday speech of ~hinunter~ ("down thither") as well, so that the reduced form covers both directions the full forms distinguish. Written standard German uses ~herunter-~ or ~hinunter-~. Spoken and informal in register.

"runterhalten" means to hold something down, keeping it low.
en.runterkommen:
A separable compound of ~runter-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~runter-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herunter~ ("down hither"), and in everyday speech of ~hinunter~ ("down thither") as well, so that the reduced form covers both directions the full forms distinguish. Written standard German uses ~herunter-~ or ~hinunter-~. ~runter-~ marks downward motion, "down."

"runterkommen" literally means to come down, and colloquially to calm down.
en.runterladen:
A separable compound of ~runter-~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two historically distinct verbs under one infinitive. ~laden~ (strong, "to load"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"); cognate with English ~lade~ and ~laden~, Lithuanian ~klṓti~. ~laden~ (weak, "to invite, summon"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root found only in Germanic and Anatolian (Hittite ~halzai~).
• ~runter-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herunter~ ("down hither"), and in everyday speech of ~hinunter~ ("down thither") as well, so that the reduced form covers both directions the full forms distinguish. Written standard German uses ~herunter-~ or ~hinunter-~. Deictically neutral, unlike the full forms it replaces.

"runterladen" is to download; ~laden~ here is the strong "to load", not its weak "to invite" twin.
en.runterschauen:
A separable compound of ~runter-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~runter-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herunter~ ("down hither"), and in everyday speech of ~hinunter~ ("down thither") as well, so that the reduced form covers both directions the full forms distinguish. Written standard German uses ~herunter-~ or ~hinunter-~. ~runter-~ marks downward motion, "down."

~Runterschauen~ is to turn one's gaze downward: from a height, a window, or the top of a stairway.
en.rutschen: From Middle High German ~rutzen~, ~rützen~, an onomatopoeic formation imitating the sound of sliding, with a later shift from ~-tz-~ to ~-tsch-~ (as also seen in ~fletschen~). Perhaps related to Old High German ~rūtezzen~. English ~rutch~ and ~rutsch~ are borrowed from German or its Low German cognates. The noun ~Rutsche~ ("slide, chute") derives from the verb, and the festive New Year's greeting ~Guten Rutsch!~ ("Happy New Year!," literally "good slide") is a beloved German idiom, though some etymologists have proposed a folk-etymological connection to Yiddish ~Rosh~ (as in ~Rosh Hashanah~, "head of the year").
en.räumen:
From Early New High German ~reumen~, a Central German umlaut variant of the regular form ~raumen~, from MHG ~rūmen~, from OHG ~rūmen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rūmijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rūmijaną~, a factitive verb derived from the adjective *~rūmaz~ ("roomy, spacious"), from PIE *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open"). Cognate with Bavarian ~rama~. The form ~raumen~ (without umlaut) was standard in Upper German regions until the 17th century and survives in dialects.

The verb means "to clear, to vacate, to tidy up", etymologically, "to make room." The adjective ~geräumig~ ("spacious") preserves the original adjectival sense. The noun ~Raum~ ("room, space") is a sibling from the same Proto-Germanic root. English ~room~ is a cognate (from Old English ~rūm~, from the same *~rūmaz~), as is the archaic ~roomy~. The PIE root *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open") (also the source of Latin ~rūs~ ("country," i.e., open land)) reveals the original image: spaciousness as something torn or cleared open. The related ~aufräumen~ ("to tidy up, to clear away") and ~einräumen~ ("to put away, to concede") extend the root with different prefixes.
en.rübermachen:
A separable compound of ~rüber-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~rüber-~: A colloquial contraction of ~herüber~ (~her-~ "toward the speaker" + ~über~ "over, across"), belonging with ~rauf~, ~raus~, ~rein~, ~ran~ in casual speech. It marks motion across to this side, the speaker's side. The sense of ~rüber-~ here is: colloquial for ~herüber~; informal register.

"rübermachen" colloquially means to get oneself across to the other side: often over a border into another country.
en.rückbesinnen:
A separable compound of ~rück-~ + ~be-~ + ~sinnen~:

• ~sinnen~: From MHG ~sinnen~, from OHG ~sinnan~ ("to travel; to strive for; to think"), from Proto-West Germanic *~sinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sinnaną~, from PIE *~sent-~ ("to head for, go; to feel"). A class III strong verb (~sinnen~, ~sann~, ~gesonnen~). The same root gave Latin ~sentīre~, so ~Sinn~ and English ~sense~ are relatives. Cognate with Old English ~sinnan~ ("to meditate on"), Dutch ~zinnen~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ forms a verb used only reflexively: the action turns back on the one performing it and never reaches an outside object.
• ~rück-~: A bound combining form, never a free word. It is the older stem of ~Rücken~ ("back"), from OHG ~(h)ruggi~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), and it reaches verbs by way of ~zurück~, OHG ~zi rugge~, "toward the back." Compounds keep the short form (~rückerstatten~, ~rückfragen~, ~Rückkehr~) where a finite verb would take the full adverb ~zurück~. English ~ridge~ is the same Proto-Germanic word: Old English ~hrycg~ meant both a person's back and the spine of a hill. The sense of ~rück-~ here is: in response, referring back to something already said.

"sich rückbesinnen" means to call something past back to mind; ~rück-~ supplies the backward reference while ~be-~ makes the verb purely reflexive.
en.rückdrehen:
A separable compound of ~rück-~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). Cognate with English ~throw~ (a true cognate: Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist," a sense that "throw a pot" still keeps) plus English ~thread~, Dutch ~draaien~.
• ~rück-~: A bound combining form, never a free word. It is the older stem of ~Rücken~ ("back"), from OHG ~(h)ruggi~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), and it reaches verbs by way of ~zurück~, OHG ~zi rugge~, "toward the back." Compounds keep the short form (~rückerstatten~, ~rückfragen~, ~Rückkehr~) where a finite verb would take the full adverb ~zurück~. English ~ridge~ is the same Proto-Germanic word: Old English ~hrycg~ meant both a person's back and the spine of a hill. The sense of ~rück-~ here is: back, backwards, in the reverse direction.

"rückdrehen" denotes turning back in the opposite, anticlockwise direction.
en.rücken: From Middle High German ~rücken~, from Old High German ~rucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rukkijan~. Cognate with Old Norse ~rykkja~, Old English ~roccian~, and modern English ~rock~ (as in "to rock back and forth"). The verb means "to move, to shift, to push", often with the sense of a short, deliberate motion: ~einen Stuhl rücken~ ("to move a chair"), ~näher rücken~ ("to move closer"), ~in den Mittelpunkt rücken~ ("to move into the spotlight"). The noun ~Rücken~ ("back"), from MHG ~rücke~, from OHG ~rucki~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrugi~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~, is a separate word etymologically (cognate with English ~ridge~) though folk etymology naturally connects the two (one moves by pushing with one's back). The verb ~rücken~ is also the base of ~verrückt~ ("crazy," literally "shifted, displaced"), perhaps the most entertaining derivative, implying that a ~verrückter~ person has been mentally "moved out of place."
en.rückwärtsfahren:
A separable compound of ~rückwärts-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~rückwärts-~: From ~Rücken~ ("back") plus the adverbial suffix ~-wärts~, from OHG ~-wert~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("turned toward"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"), exactly the English ~-ward~ of ~backward~ and ~homeward~. ~Rücken~ itself goes back to OHG ~(h)rukki~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~, whose English descendant is ~ridge~, the back or spine of a hill. As a particle it orients the action backward. The sense of ~rückwärts-~ here is: "backward, in reverse".

"rückwärtsfahren" points the driving backward: to drive in reverse.
en.rückzahlen:
A separable compound of ~rück-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~rück-~: A bound combining form, never a free word. It is the older stem of ~Rücken~ ("back"), from OHG ~(h)ruggi~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), and it reaches verbs by way of ~zurück~, OHG ~zi rugge~, "toward the back." Compounds keep the short form (~rückerstatten~, ~rückfragen~, ~Rückkehr~) where a finite verb would take the full adverb ~zurück~. English ~ridge~ is the same Proto-Germanic word: Old English ~hrycg~ meant both a person's back and the spine of a hill. The sense of ~rück-~ here is: returning something to its origin or to an earlier state.

"rückzahlen" returns a payment to its origin: to repay or refund.
en.rücküberweisen:
A separable compound of ~rück-~ + ~über-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative verb from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from PIE *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know"). A class I strong verb; its senses "to show, point" and "to direct, expel" both direct knowledge or attention. Cognate with English ~wise~, ~wit~, ~wizard~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys transfer or handing over to someone.
• ~rück-~: A bound combining form, never a free word. It is the older stem of ~Rücken~ ("back"), from OHG ~(h)ruggi~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), and it reaches verbs by way of ~zurück~, OHG ~zi rugge~, "toward the back." Compounds keep the short form (~rückerstatten~, ~rückfragen~, ~Rückkehr~) where a finite verb would take the full adverb ~zurück~. English ~ridge~ is the same Proto-Germanic word: Old English ~hrycg~ meant both a person's back and the spine of a hill. The sense of ~rück-~ here is: returning something to its origin or to an earlier state.

"rücküberweisen" joins both contributions: ~über-~ names the transfer, ~rück-~ its return to the sender.
en.rühren: From Middle High German ~rüeren~, from Old High German ~ruoren~, ~hruoren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōzijaną~. The initial ~hr-~ cluster, common in older Germanic, was gradually simplified in German (compare English loss of initial ~wr-~ in ~write~). Cognate with Dutch ~roeren~ and the now-rare English ~rear~ ("to move, stir"), which survives mainly in the phrase "to rear up." The semantic range has stayed remarkably stable across a millennium: ~rühren~ still means "to stir" both literally (a pot) and figuratively (emotions). The compound ~anrühren~ preserves an older nuance of "to touch," while ~berühren~ ("to touch, to affect") shows the emotional dimension at full strength.
en.sagen: From Middle High German ~sagen~, from Old High German ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with Low German ~seggen~, Dutch ~zeggen~, English ~say~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
en.salzen: From MHG ~salzen~, from OHG ~salzan~, from Proto-Germanic *~saltaną~, a derivative of *~saltą~ ("salt"), from PIE *~séh₂ls~. The finite forms are weak today (~salzte~), but the old strong past participle ~gesalzen~ survives beside the regularized ~gesalzt~. Cognate with English ~salt~, Dutch ~zouten~, and Swedish ~salta~; the same PIE noun gives Latin ~sāl~ and Ancient Greek ~ἅλς~ (háls). Through Latin it reaches English as ~salary~, ~salad~, ~sauce~, and ~sausage~, while German keeps the metaphor working in ~gesalzene Preise~, prices that sting.
en.sammeln:
From Middle High German ~samelen~, ~samlen~, regarded as formed by dissimilation from ~samenen~, which ultimately derives from Proto-Germanic *~samnōną~ ("to bring together, gather, collect, assemble"). Alternatively, inherited from Old High German *~samalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~samalōn~. The Proto-Germanic root *~samnōną~ is derived from *~samanai~ ("together") combined with the verbal suffix *~-ōną~, and *~samanai~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~sem-~ ("one, same, together").

The PIE root *~sem-~ is one of the most productive in Indo-European: it underlies Latin ~semel~ ("once"), ~similis~ ("similar"), ~simul~ ("at the same time"), and English ~same~, ~seem~, ~simple~, and ~some~. The idea of oneness and togetherness are the same idea: to make something one is to bring its parts together. German ~zusammen~ ("together") preserves *~sem-~ in its ~sam-~ portion. The same root appears in Greek ~homos~ ("same"), whence ~homogeneous~, ~homologous~, and the prefix ~homo-~. Cognate with Dutch ~verzamelen~, Swedish ~samla~, Danish ~samle~, Gothic ~samjan~.
en.satthaben:
A separable compound of ~satt~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~satt~: From MHG ~sat~, from OHG ~sat~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sad~, from Proto-Germanic *~sadaz~, from PIE *~seh₂-~ ("to satiate"). Cognate with Dutch ~zat~, Danish ~sat~, and English ~sad~, which in Old English meant "sated, weary" long before it meant "sorrowful"; the same root gives Latin ~satis~ ("enough"), whence English ~satisfy~ and ~saturate~. In separable compounds the adjective is resultative: the verb continues until the subject has had its fill. The sense of ~satt~ here is: with ~haben~, "to be fed up with".

~Satthaben~ shifts the image of being full into the figurative: to have a thing ~satt~ is to have had enough of it and to be weary of it.
en.sattsehen:
A separable compound of ~satt~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~satt~: From MHG ~sat~, from OHG ~sat~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sad~, from Proto-Germanic *~sadaz~, from PIE *~seh₂-~ ("to satiate"). Cognate with Dutch ~zat~, Danish ~sat~, and English ~sad~, which in Old English meant "sated, weary" long before it meant "sorrowful"; the same root gives Latin ~satis~ ("enough"), whence English ~satisfy~ and ~saturate~. In separable compounds the adjective is resultative: the verb continues until the subject has had its fill. The sense of ~satt~ here is: reflexively, "until one has had enough" of seeing, hearing or eating something.

~Sattsehen~ is always reflexive: one looks one's fill at something beautiful until the eye is sated, or, as negated here, never is.
en.saubermachen:
A separable compound of ~sauber~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~sauber~: The adjective ~sauber~ ("clean"), from MHG ~sūber~, from OHG ~sūbar~, borrowed from Latin ~sōbrius~ ("sober, temperate, level-headed"), itself from ~sē-~ ("without") + ~ēbrius~ ("drunk"). The sense drifted from "temperate" through "unblemished" to "clean". Cognate with Dutch ~zuiver~ and, by a different route out of the same Latin word, English ~sober~. In a resultative compound the adjective names the end state: to verb something until it is clean. The sense of ~sauber~ here is in ~saubermachen~: to clean up.

~Saubermachen~ is the everyday word for cleaning and tidying up.
en.saufen: From MHG ~sūfen~ ("to sip, drink"), from OHG ~sūfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sūpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sūpaną~, from PIE *~sewp-~, a labial extension of *~sew-~ ("to take liquid, slurp"). A class II strong verb (~saufen~, ~soff~, ~gesoffen~). Cognate with Dutch ~zuipen~, Swedish ~supa~, Old Norse ~súpa~, Old English ~sūpan~ and English ~sup~. The same PIE root with a velar extension instead of a labial gave ~saugen~, and the labial form also underlies English ~soup~ and Sanskrit ~sūpaḥ~ ("broth"); the drift from neutral "to sip" to today's "to booze" dates only to the sixteenth century.
en.saugen: From MHG ~sūgen~, from OHG ~sūgan~ ("to suck"), from Proto-West Germanic *~sūgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sūganą~, from PIE *~sewk-~ ("to suck"). Historically a class II strong verb (~saugen~, ~sog~, ~gesogen~), it now inflects weak (~saugte~, ~gesaugt~) just as readily, and the weak forms dominate in the technical ~staubsaugen~. Cognate with Dutch ~zuigen~, Low German ~sugen~, Danish ~suge~, Old English ~sūcan~ and English ~suck~. Latin ~sūgere~ ("to suck") belongs to the same root and returned to English as ~suction~; the slang sense "to be bad" is a recent loan-translation of English ~suck~.
en.schaden:
From Middle High German ~schaden~, from Old High German ~scadōn~, denominal from the noun ~Schaden~ ("damage, harm"). The noun derives from OHG ~scado~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaþō~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaþô~ ("injury, harm"), whence also the verb *~skaþōną~ ("to injure, harm"). Cognate with English ~scathe~ (via Old Norse), Dutch ~schade~, Swedish ~skada~, Danish ~skade~.

The English cognate ~scathe~ survives mainly in the negative adjective ~unscathed~ ("without harm") and the derived ~scathing~ ("harshly critical"). German ~schaden~ takes the dative case (~das schadet ihm~ ("that harms him")), a pattern typical of verbs expressing disadvantage or harm. The idiomatic expression ~Es kann nicht schaden~ ("It can't hurt") is the German equivalent of the English shrug-and-try-it phrase.
en.schaffen:
Two historically distinct verbs have merged under a single infinitive in Modern German, distinguished only by their conjugation:

The strong verb (~schuf~, ~geschaffen~, "to create") descends from Middle High German ~schaffen~, from Old High German ~scaffan~, a byform of ~skephen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skappjan~. The form with ~-f-~ was chiefly back-formed from the past participle ~giscaffan~ but was also influenced by the weak verb below. The older form ~skephen~ survives in the archaic variant ~schöpfen~ ("to create"). Cognate with Dutch ~scheppen~, English ~shape~.

The weak verb (~schaffte~, ~geschafft~, "to manage, accomplish") descends from Middle High German ~schaffen~, from Old High German ~skaffōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skapōn~, from the same root as the strong verb. The semantic distinction between the two conjugations (strong for divine or artistic creation, weak for practical accomplishment) only established itself clearly in Modern German.
en.schallen: From MHG ~schallen~, a denominal formation on ~Schall~ ("sound"); the Grimms took it instead as a reshaping of the older strong MHG ~schellen~ ("to resound"), from Proto-West Germanic *~skellan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skellaną~, from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, shout") with s-mobile. Normally weak today (~schallte~, ~geschallt~), it keeps the strong Präteritum ~scholl~ as an elevated variant inherited from that older verb. Cognate with Old Norse ~skjalla~ ("to clash, resound"), Icelandic ~skella~, Old English ~sciellan~, and within German with ~Schall~, ~schellen~ and ~Schelle~. The same PIE root gave Latin ~calāre~ ("to call out") and its derivative ~Kalendae~, the day on which the new moon was proclaimed, and so, at length, English ~calendar~.
en.schalten:
From Middle High German ~schalten~, from Old High German ~scaltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaldan~ ("to push, shove"). Further etymology is debated: according to Pokorny, from PIE *~(s)kelH-~ ("to split, separate"), which would make it related to English ~shell~. Cognate with Old Saxon ~skaldan~ ("to push").

The semantic development from "to push, shove" to modern "to switch, shift (gears), to manage" is striking. The original physical sense of shoving a lever or bolt evolved into the technical meaning of operating a switch or gear mechanism. In modern German, ~schalten~ is the standard verb for switching electrical devices, shifting gears in a car (~Schaltgetriebe~ = "manual transmission"), and by extension, for managing or directing (~schalten und walten~ = "to do as one pleases," literally "to switch and govern"). The compound ~Schalter~ means both "switch" and "counter/window" (at a bank or post office), two kinds of interfaces where something gets directed. The idiom ~schalten und walten~ was already proverbial in Middle High German, pairing two near-synonyms for emphasis.
en.schauen: From Middle High German ~schouwen~, from Old High German ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, feel, take note of"). The same PIE root, via Old English ~scēawian~, gives modern English ~show~, a striking semantic reversal: the Germanic descendants of this root divide between the intransitive "to look" (German ~schauen~) and the transitive "to make visible" (English ~show~). The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage, where ~Schau!~ and ~schau mal!~ serve as colloquial equivalents of standard German ~guck mal!~ Cognate with Old English ~scēawian~, English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~ ("to inspect").
en.scheckiglachen:
A separable compound of ~scheckig~ + ~lachen~:

• ~lachen~: From MHG ~lachen~, from OHG ~lahhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~, from PIE *~kleg-~ ("to cry out, sound"). The initial ~hl-~ cluster was simplified to ~l-~ in Old High German. Cognate with English ~laugh~, Dutch ~lachen~, Gothic ~hlahjan~.
• ~scheckig~: The adjective ~scheckig~ ("blotchy, piebald"), from MHG ~scheckeht~, to MHG ~schecke~, borrowed from Old French ~eschec~, plural ~eschès~ ("chess; chessboard"), a pattern named for the board. The noun ~Schecke~ ("piebald horse") was back-formed from the adjective in the 16th century. English ~check~, ~checkered~, ~chess~, and ~exchequer~ all descend from that same Old French word, which goes back through Arabic to Persian ~šāh~ ("king"), so a mottled German horse and the British Exchequer are named from the same chessboard. The sense of ~scheckig~ here is in ~sich scheckig lachen~: to the point of helpless laughter.

In ~sich scheckig lachen~, the image of a mottled coat transfers to a face turning blotchy and red with laughter.
en.scheiden: From Middle High German ~scheiden~, from Old High German ~sceidan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaiþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaiþaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~skeyt-~ ("to cut, separate"). Cognate with Dutch ~scheiden~, West Frisian ~skiede~, and English ~shed~ (as in "to shed" skin or tears, originally "to separate"). The PIE root produced a rich network of cognates across the Indo-European family: Irish ~scian~ ("knife"), Lithuanian ~skiesti~ ("to separate"), Old Church Slavonic ~cěditi~ ("to filter, strain"), Greek ~skhizein~ ("to split," source of English ~schism~ and ~schizophrenia~), and Sanskrit ~chyati~ ("he cuts off"). The German noun ~Entscheidung~ ("decision") literally means "a cutting apart" of alternatives.
en.scheinen: From Middle High German ~schīnen~, from Old High German ~skīnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skīnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skīnaną~, from PIE *~(s)ḱeh₁y-~ ("to shine, shimmer"). A class I strong verb. The modern verb covers two related senses: "to shine" (physical light) and "to seem, appear", a duality that reflects the ancient metaphor of appearances as light cast onto the observer. This ambiguity between shining and seeming is shared by Latin ~lucēre~ ("to shine") and its derivative ~illūsiō~. The German cognate ~Schein~ ("shine; appearance; certificate") preserves the full range, and the pejorative ~zum Schein~ ("for appearances only") shows the "seeming" sense at its most skeptical. Cognate with Dutch ~schijnen~, Low German ~schienen~, English ~shine~, Danish ~skinne~, and the Esperanto borrowing ~ŝajni~ ("to seem").
en.scheitern: A verbal formation from ~Scheiter~, the plural of ~Scheit~ ("log, billet of firewood"), from Middle High German ~schīt~, from Old High German ~scīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skīd~ ("piece of wood"), from Proto-Germanic *~skīdą~, from PIE *~skeyd-~ ("to split, to separate"), an extension of *~skey-~ ("to cut"). In the 16th century, the compounds ~zuscheitern~ and ~zerscheitern~ appeared first, meaning "to break into pieces (logs)", like a ship shattering against rocks into firewood-sized fragments. The shortened form ~scheitern~ likely arose by analogy with phrases like ~zu Scheitern gehen~ ("to go to pieces, to fall apart"). The semantic shift from "to splinter like a log" to "to fail" is vivid and dramatic: a project that ~scheitert~ doesn't merely not succeed; it breaks apart catastrophically, like a vessel dashed on the shoals. The root noun ~Scheit~ is cognate with Old Norse ~skíð~ ("plank, billet, ski"): yes, ~Ski~ is a doublet of ~Scheit~, both meaning "a piece of split wood." One piece you burn for warmth; the other you strap to your feet and slide downhill. Also cognate with English ~shide~ (archaic "a piece of split wood"), Greek ~σχίζα~ ("splinter"), and Lithuanian ~skìedra~ ("chip"). The PIE root *~skey-~ also yields ~scheiden~ ("to separate, to divorce") and English ~shed~, all preserving the ancient concept of cutting apart.
en.scheißen: From MHG ~schīzen~, from OHG *~skīzan~ (attested only in the compound ~biskīzan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~skītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skītaną~, from PIE *~skeyd-~ ("to split, separate"). A class I strong verb (~scheißen~, ~schiss~, ~geschissen~). Cognate with Dutch ~schijten~, Low German ~schieten~, Danish ~skide~, Old Norse ~skíta~ and English ~shit~. The root's basic sense is separation, not filth: Latin ~scindere~ and Ancient Greek ~σχίζειν~ ("to split") descend from the same PIE etymon and gave English ~schism~ and ~schizophrenia~; the Germanic verb began as a decorous word for voiding and hardened into the language's bluntest one.
en.schelten: From MHG ~schëlten~, from OHG ~skeltan~ (8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *~skeldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeldaną~ ("to revile, blame"). A class III strong verb (~schelten~, ~schalt~, ~gescholten~). Cognate with Dutch ~schelden~, Old Frisian ~skelda~, Low German ~schelden~, Old Low Franconian ~skeldan~. The deeper origin is uncertain: it is usually taken as a dental extension of PIE *~skel-~/*~kelh₁-~ ("to shout, resound"), the root behind ~schallen~ and ~schellen~, which would make scolding a species of noise-making. English ~scold~ looks like the obvious cognate but probably is not; it is generally derived from Old Norse ~skáld~ ("poet, lampooner"). The verb survives in the noun ~Schelte~ and, negated, in ~unbescholten~ ("of unblemished reputation").
en.schenken:
From Middle High German ~schenken~, from Old High German ~scenken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skankijan~ ("to pour, serve"). Related to ~Schenke~ ("tavern, inn") and ~Schenkel~ ("thigh, shank"). Cognate with Dutch ~schenken~ ("to pour; to give"), English ~skink~ (archaic, "to pour, to serve drink").

The semantic journey from "to pour" to "to give as a gift" is one of German's most vivid etymological stories. In medieval Germanic culture, the act of pouring a drink for a guest was itself the paradigmatic act of generosity: the host who poured was giving. Over time, the meaning broadened from pouring drink to giving any gift, while the original "pouring" sense retreated to fixed expressions like ~Wein einschenken~ ("to pour wine") and the noun ~Schenke~ ("tavern," originally a place where drinks were poured). Dutch ~schenken~ preserves both senses equally ("to pour" and "to give") making the Dutch usage a living fossil of the semantic transition. English ~shank~ (the leg bone) is a cognate of ~Schenkel~ from the same root, the original connection being the tilting motion of pouring.
en.scheren: Two verbs share this spelling. The strong ~scheren~ ("to shear, cut") comes from MHG ~schërn~, from OHG ~skeran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeran~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeraną~, from PIE *~(s)ker-~ ("to cut"); it is a class IV strong verb (~scheren~, ~schor~, ~geschoren~), cognate with Dutch ~scheren~, Low German ~scheren~, Danish ~skære~, Old Norse ~skera~ and English ~shear~. The weak ~scheren~ ("to bother oneself about"; also "to clear off") is a separate and later word, first attested in the fifteenth century as Late MHG ~schern~ ("to hurry, escape") and of uncertain origin (possibly from OHG ~scerōn~ ("to be exuberant"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kerd-~ ("to leap, swing")), and it inflects weak throughout (~scherte~, ~geschert~). From the cutting root German keeps ~Schere~ ("scissors") and ~Schar~, while English keeps ~short~, ~share~, ~shore~ and the doublet ~shirt~/~skirt~, each of them originally a cut-off piece. The verb conjugated here is the strong ~scheren~ ("to shear, cut": ~schor~, ~geschoren~), not its weak homograph.
en.schicken: From Middle High German ~schicken~ ("to outfit oneself, fit in, arrange appropriately"), from Old High German *~skihhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skikkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skikkijaną~ ("to order, send"), the causative of the verb underlying Middle High German ~geschehen~ ("to happen, rush"). The modern sense "to send" developed from the earlier "to dispatch, make ready to go", to arrange something so that it departs. Related to English ~chic~ (via French, ultimately from the same Germanic source), which preserves the original sense of fitting arrangement. The family of words also includes ~geschickt~ ("skilled, adept"), skill being a matter of fitting arrangement, and ~Schicksal~ ("fate, destiny"), where fate is the dispatch one cannot refuse.
en.schieben: From Middle High German ~schieben~, from Old High German ~skioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeubaną~, from PIE *~skewbʰ-~ ("to push, to shove, to thrust"). The word is attested since the 9th century. As a class II strong verb, ~schieben~ displays the ablaut series ~ie~ > ~o~ > ~o~ (~schieben~, ~schob~, ~geschoben~). ~Schieben~ means "to push, to shove", physically moving something by applying force from behind. But it also means "to slide" (as in sliding a drawer), "to traffic" or "to profiteer" in colloquial usage (~Schwarzmarktgeschäfte schieben~, "to run black-market deals"), and in the expression ~die Schuld auf jemanden schieben~ ("to shift the blame onto someone"), where the pushing is metaphorical. The phrase ~auf die lange Bank schieben~ ("to put off, to procrastinate", literally "to push onto the long bench") may originate from the medieval practice of storing unresolved court documents on a long bench, where they gathered dust. Cognate with English ~shove~ (which underwent the Great Vowel Shift while German kept the diphthong), Dutch ~schuiven~, Low German ~schuven~, Danish ~skubbe~. The PIE root *~skewbʰ-~ may also be related to Lithuanian ~skubėti~ ("to hurry", to push oneself along). The derived noun ~Schub~ ("push, thrust, batch") and ~Schublade~ ("drawer", literally "push-load," something you push and pull) round out the family.
en.schieflachen:
A separable compound of ~schief~ + ~lachen~:

• ~lachen~: From MHG ~lachen~, from OHG ~lahhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~, from PIE *~kleg-~ ("to cry out, sound"). The initial ~hl-~ cluster was simplified to ~l-~ in Old High German. Cognate with English ~laugh~, Dutch ~lachen~, Gothic ~hlahjan~.
• ~schief~: The adjective ~schief~ ("crooked, askew"), from northern MHG ~schief~/~schīf~, taken from Middle Low German ~schēf~, from Old Saxon *~skēf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaib~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaibaz~. Cognate with Dutch ~scheef~, Swedish ~skev~, and Old Norse ~skeifr~; English ~skew~ resembles it but reached English through Old Northern French and is not securely the same word. In verbs it is resultative and figurative; ~schiefgehen~ is for a plan to come out crooked, that is, to go wrong. The sense of ~schief~ here is resultative: leaves the object crooked or at a slant.

~Schieflachen~ takes the adjective literally: one laughs until standing bent and crooked.
en.schieflaufen:
A separable compound of ~schief~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~schief~: The adjective ~schief~ ("crooked, askew"), from northern MHG ~schief~/~schīf~, taken from Middle Low German ~schēf~, from Old Saxon *~skēf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaib~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaibaz~. Cognate with Dutch ~scheef~, Swedish ~skev~, and Old Norse ~skeifr~; English ~skew~ resembles it but reached English through Old Northern French and is not securely the same word. In verbs it is resultative and figurative; ~schiefgehen~ is for a plan to come out crooked, that is, to go wrong. The sense of ~schief~ here is: figuratively, turning out wrong or badly.

~Schieflaufen~ carries the image of a crooked gait over to the course of events: something takes a wrong turn and fails.
en.schiefliegen:
A separable compound of ~schief~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~schief~: The adjective ~schief~ ("crooked, askew"), from northern MHG ~schief~/~schīf~, taken from Middle Low German ~schēf~, from Old Saxon *~skēf~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaib~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaibaz~. Cognate with Dutch ~scheef~, Swedish ~skev~, and Old Norse ~skeifr~; English ~skew~ resembles it but reached English through Old Northern French and is not securely the same word. In verbs it is resultative and figurative; ~schiefgehen~ is for a plan to come out crooked, that is, to go wrong. The sense of ~schief~ here is: figuratively, turning out wrong or badly.

~Schiefliegen~ concerns not position in space but in judgment: to ~schiefliegen~ is to be mistaken.
en.schießen: From Middle High German ~schiezen~, from Old High German ~sciozan~, ~sciozzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~. The Proto-Germanic root yielded an impressive family of cognates: English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Swedish ~skjuta~, Danish ~skyde~, Icelandic ~skjóta~, and Old Norse ~skjóta~. The related noun ~Schuss~ ("shot") entered English directly as a skiing term, a straight, fast downhill run, preserving the original sense of rapid forward motion. The zero-grade form Proto-Germanic *~skutiz~ ("a shooting, a shot") is the ancestor of ~Schuss~. The original meaning of ~schießen~ was broader than firearms: it meant any rapid, propulsive motion, shooting an arrow, of course, but also shooting a bolt (on a door), or a plant shooting up from the ground. This last sense survives in the compound ~aufschießen~ and in the idiom ~ins Kraut schießen~ ("to run to seed," literally "to shoot into the herb"), used figuratively when something proliferates out of control.
en.schildern: Borrowed in the 16th century from Middle Low German or Dutch ~schilderen~ ("to paint, to coat"). The Dutch verb derives from the noun ~schilder~ ("painter"), itself from ~schild~ ("shield"). In medieval times, shields were decorated with coats of arms, and the craftsman who painted these heraldic designs onto shields was called a ~schilder~. This artisan gradually expanded beyond heraldic work to paint other subjects, and the verb broadened accordingly. Dutch ~schild~ descends from Middle Dutch ~schilt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeldu~, from Proto-Germanic *~skelduz~ ("shield"), from PIE *~(s)keyt-~ ("shield, cover"). Cognate with English ~shield~ and Danish ~skjold~. The semantic shift from "to paint a shield" to "to paint" to modern German "to describe, to depict (in words)" is a beautiful case of metaphorical expansion: first painting concrete images on shields, then painting pictures generally, and finally "painting pictures with words." English ~depict~ follows a parallel trajectory from the physical to the verbal.
en.schinden: From MHG ~schinden~, ~schinten~ ("to flay, peel; torment; cheat"), from OHG ~skinten~ (9th century), a denominal verb built on Proto-Germanic *~skinþą~ ("hide, peel, bark"), from PIE *~(s)ken-~ ("to split off"), a nasal extension of *~sek-~ ("to cut"), the skin being what is cut off. Originally weak, it took on strong inflection in Middle High German by analogy with ~binden~ and ~finden~, and now runs as a class III strong verb (~schinden~, ~schund~, ~geschunden~). Cognate with Low German ~schinnen~, Old Norse ~skinn~, Swedish ~skinn~ and English ~skin~, itself a Norse loan into English. The literal flaying survives only in derivatives (~Schinder~, ~Schindmähre~, ~Schindluder treiben~), while the living verb means to work someone, or oneself, to the bone.
en.schlafen: ~Schlafen~ comes from Middle High German ~slāfen~, from Old High German ~slāfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slāpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slēpaną~. Cognate with English ~sleep~, Dutch ~slapen~, Low German ~slapen~, and Gothic ~𐍃𐌻𐌴𐍀𐌰𐌽~ (slēpan), all of identical meaning across the Germanic family. The Proto-Germanic origin is uncertain: it may be related to *~slapaz~ ("weak, lax, limp"), the ancestor of German ~schlaff~ ("slack, limp, flaccid"), connecting sleep to the physical limpness of the sleeping body. This possible German-internal cognate pair (~schlafen~ / ~schlaff~) captures something real: sleep is the state of going slack. An older theory derives the root from PIE *~sleh₁-~, possibly related to ~languor~ and Old English ~slæc~ ("lazy"), but the connection remains debated. The Class VII strong verb ~schlafen~, ~schlief~, ~geschlafen~ belongs to the reduplicating class, whose Präteritum (~schlief~) reflects an ancient pattern of vowel modification rather than a simple ablaut grade.
en.schlagen: From Middle High German ~slahen~, from Old High German ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from a Proto-Indo-European *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently of onomatopoeic origin. The modern ~-g-~ in the infinitive and present tense is a secondary insertion by analogy with the past-tense forms (~schlug~) and the related noun ~Schlag~ ("blow, strike, beat"), a phenomenon known as Grammatischer Wechsel (Verner's Law alternation later regularized by analogy). The same root produced an extraordinary range of modern German compounds: ~vorschlagen~ ("to suggest," literally "to strike forward"), ~nachschlagen~ ("to look up in a reference"), ~beschlagen~ ("to shoe a horse"), ~erschlagen~ ("to strike dead"), ~einschlagen~ ("to hammer in; to take a path"). English ~slay~ and ~slog~ both derive from the same Proto-Germanic root (Old English ~slēan~, "to strike, beat, smite"). Cognate with Low German and Dutch ~slaan~, Old English ~slēan~, Danish ~slå~, Swedish ~slå~, Norwegian ~slå~.
en.schlapplachen:
A separable compound of ~schlapp~ + ~lachen~:

• ~lachen~: From MHG ~lachen~, from OHG ~lahhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~, from PIE *~kleg-~ ("to cry out, sound"). The initial ~hl-~ cluster was simplified to ~l-~ in Old High German. Cognate with English ~laugh~, Dutch ~lachen~, Gothic ~hlahjan~.
• ~schlapp~: A Low German form, from Middle Low German ~slap~ ("limp, flaccid"), a doublet of High German ~schlaff~; both go back to Proto-Germanic *~slap-~ and are usually traced to PIE *~(s)leh₂b-~ ("to be weak, limp"), the root also behind ~schlafen~ and Latin ~labāre~ ("to totter"). Cognate with Dutch ~slap~. The Low German ~p~ against High German ~ff~ is the giveaway that the word travelled north to south rather than passing through the High German consonant shift. The sense of ~schlapp~ here is: as a resultative adjective, "limp, exhausted".

~Schlapplachen~ names laughing to exhaustion: one laughs oneself limp until one's strength gives out.
en.schlappmachen:
A separable compound of ~schlapp~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~schlapp~: A Low German form, from Middle Low German ~slap~ ("limp, flaccid"), a doublet of High German ~schlaff~; both go back to Proto-Germanic *~slap-~ and are usually traced to PIE *~(s)leh₂b-~ ("to be weak, limp"), the root also behind ~schlafen~ and Latin ~labāre~ ("to totter"). Cognate with Dutch ~slap~. The Low German ~p~ against High German ~ff~ is the giveaway that the word travelled north to south rather than passing through the High German consonant shift. The sense of ~schlapp~ here is: of a person giving out, "to the point of collapse from exhaustion".

~Schlappmachen~ is to give out and flag under exertion or heat.
en.schlechtmachen:
A separable compound of ~schlecht~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~schlecht~: From MHG ~slëht~, from OHG ~slëht~ ("straight, level, plain"), from Proto-Germanic *~slihtaz~ ("smooth, level"); the origin beyond Germanic is uncertain. Cognate with English ~slight~, Dutch ~slecht~, Swedish ~slät~, Icelandic ~sléttur~. ~schlecht~ and ~schlicht~ are one word split in two: "plain, simple" stayed with ~schlicht~ while ~schlecht~ slid from "plain" to "inferior" to "bad", much the slide English ~slight~ made from "smooth" to "trifling". The sense of ~schlecht~ here is as a resultative adjective, "badly": the verb makes its object bad or worse.

~Schlechtmachen~ is disparagement in words: one runs a person or thing down by speaking ill of it.
en.schlechtreden:
A separable compound of ~schlecht~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~schlecht~: From MHG ~slëht~, from OHG ~slëht~ ("straight, level, plain"), from Proto-Germanic *~slihtaz~ ("smooth, level"); the origin beyond Germanic is uncertain. Cognate with English ~slight~, Dutch ~slecht~, Swedish ~slät~, Icelandic ~sléttur~. ~schlecht~ and ~schlicht~ are one word split in two: "plain, simple" stayed with ~schlicht~ while ~schlecht~ slid from "plain" to "inferior" to "bad", much the slide English ~slight~ made from "smooth" to "trifling". The sense of ~schlecht~ here is: of speech, "disparagingly", as in running someone down.

~Schlechtreden~ aims at talk about absent third parties or institutions: one talks down an achievement, a place, or a person.
en.schleichen: From MHG ~slīchen~, from OHG ~slīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slīkaną~ ("to glide, creep"), from PIE *~sleyg-~ ("to be smooth, slide, be slimy"). A class I strong verb (~schleichen~, ~schlich~, ~geschlichen~). Cognate with Dutch ~slijken~, Low German ~sliken~, Old Norse ~slíkr~ ("smooth") and English ~slick~ and ~sleek~; English ~slink~ matches in sense but not in form and belongs to a different root. The smoothness in the etymon still shows in what the verb is used for: a ~Schleichweg~ is a back road, and ~Schleichwerbung~ is advertising that slips past you unannounced.
en.schleifen: Two verbs share this spelling, and only the conjugation tells them apart. The strong ~schleifen~ ("to grind, whet, polish") comes from MHG ~slīfen~, from OHG ~slīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slīpaną~ ("to slide, to whet"); it is a class I strong verb (~schleifen~, ~schliff~, ~geschliffen~), cognate with Dutch ~slijpen~, Low German ~slipen~, Swedish ~slipa~ and English ~slip~. The weak ~schleifen~ ("to drag; to raze a fortress") comes from MHG ~sleifen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slaipijan~ ("to cause to slide"), the causative of the first, and inflects ~schleifte~, ~geschleift~; it is a doublet of ~schleppen~, borrowed from Middle Low German ~slêpen~, and is cognate with Dutch ~slepen~. The division of labour is tidy in the dictionary and less so in practice, which is the etymological joke of the pair: a razed fortress (~geschleift~) and a cut diamond (~geschliffen~) are one and the same act of sliding, parted only by whose hand does the sliding. The verb conjugated here is the strong ~schleifen~ ("to grind, whet": ~schliff~, ~geschliffen~), not its weak homograph.
en.schleißen: From MHG ~slīȥen~, from OHG ~slīȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slītaną~ ("to tear apart"), of uncertain further origin; a link to PIE *~sleyd-~ ("to rend, injure") has been proposed but is not secure. A class I strong verb (~schleißen~, ~schliss~, ~geschlissen~). Cognate with English ~slit~, Dutch ~slijten~, Old Norse ~slíta~, Danish ~slide~ ("to wear out"). The simple verb is now rare, living on chiefly in ~verschleißen~ and the noun ~Verschleiß~ ("wear and tear"), and once named the winter-evening chore of stripping feathers for bedding, ~Federschleißen~.
en.schließen: From Middle High German ~slieȥen~, from Old High German ~sliozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sleutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slūtaną~, *~sleutaną~ ("to lock, shut"). The PIE root is not definitively established, but the Germanic root carried the sense of fastening or locking, the sliding of a bolt into place. A class II strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~schließen~, ~schloss~, ~geschlossen~. The modern spelling with ~sch-~ reflects the High German consonant shift from earlier *~sl-~, while Dutch ~sluiten~ preserves the unshifted cluster. One peculiarity of English: the Wiktionary entry lists ~slot~ as a cognate of ~schließen~.
