~Umformen~ is to give material a new shape: from the smith at his metal to the transformation of an equation.
en.umgeben:
Compound of ~um-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~geben~, from OHG ~geban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebanan~, from PIE *~ghebh-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (though the English form was heavily influenced by Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~um(b)(e)-~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂mbhi~ ("around, on either side of"). Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (as in ~ambiguous~, literally "going around both sides") and Greek ~amphi-~ (as in ~amphitheater~).

As an inseparable compound (stressed on ~-ge-~), ~umgeben~ means "to surround," literally "to give around." The metaphor is of encircling something by "giving" or placing oneself all around it. The PIE root *~ghebh-~ has a surprisingly broad semantic range: alongside "to give," it also carried notions of "to grab, to seize" in some branches (compare Latvian ~gabties~, "to snatch," and Old Church Slavonic ~gabati~, "to seize"). The shift between "to give" and "to grab" may reflect different perspectives on the same physical exchange. The participle ~umgeben~ also functions as an adjective meaning "surrounded" (~von Bergen umgeben~, "surrounded by mountains"), one of those German participles that has essentially become a standalone word in its own right.
en.umgehen:
~Um-~ + ~gehen~. Compound of ~um-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from OHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave").
• ~um-~: From PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). The prefix in its separable use adds a sense of going around or circulating; in its inseparable use, a sense of bypassing or circumventing.

~Umgehen~ is one of the classic German separability pairs, where stress placement alone changes meaning. The separable ~umgehen~ (stress on ~um-~) means "to circulate, go around, deal with", as in ~mit jemandem umgehen~ ("to deal with, to treat someone") or a rumor ~geht um~ ("goes around, circulates"). The inseparable ~umgehen~ (stress on ~ge-~) means "to circumvent, bypass, avoid", as in ~ein Gesetz umgehen~ ("to circumvent a law"). Both meanings trace to the same spatial logic of going around something, but the separable form emphasizes circulation while the inseparable emphasizes avoidance. This stress-based distinction (inseparable meaning derived from uninterruptible prefix fusion) is one of the most productive patterns in German morphology. The PIE root *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave") produces the paradox that "going" originally meant "leaving", direction is always relative to a starting point. Cognate with Dutch ~omgaan~.
en.umgraben:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~graben~:

• ~graben~: From MHG ~graben~, from OHG ~graban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from PIE *~gʰrebʰ-~ ("to dig, scratch, bury"). A class VI strong verb (~graben~, ~grub~, ~gegraben~). Cognate with English ~grave~ as a verb (now only in ~engrave~ and ~graven image~), Gothic ~graban~, Dutch ~graven~, Old Norse ~grafa~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys motion around something, circling or circulating.

~Umgraben~ means to dig out a patch of ground and turn the earth as one does, so that the whole surface is worked through and the lower layers are brought to the top.
en.umgucken:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~gucken~:

• ~gucken~: From MHG ~gücken~, ~guggen~ ("to look inquisitively, to peek"), of uncertain origin, perhaps from MHG ~gücken~, OHG ~guckōn~ ("to cuckoo"), via the image of peeping out from cover. The variant ~kucken~ is attributed to influence from Low German ~kieken~. Colloquial and northern/central German; the south prefers ~schauen~. Cognate with Dutch ~kijken~, Luxembourgish ~kucken~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys motion around something, circling or circulating.

~Umgucken~ means to turn and take in one's surroundings; like the base verb ~gucken~ it stays colloquial and northern-to-central German in flavor.
en.umhaben:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys motion around something, circling or circulating.

~Umhaben~ means to wear a garment such as a scarf or coat draped around oneself; the ~um-~ marks its position all around the body.
en.umhauen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~hauen~:

• ~hauen~: From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). Originally a class VII strong verb (~hauen~, ~hieb~, ~gehauen~), partially weakened colloquially, where ~haute~ competes with ~hieb~. Cognate with English ~hew~, Latin ~cūdere~ ("to strike, forge").
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys toppling: falling or knocking over.

~Umhauen~ means to bring a tree or post down with a blow; the colloquial "das haut mich um" ("that bowls me over") carries that felling over to the emotions.
en.umhergehen:
A separable compound of ~umher-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~umher-~: The preposition ~um~ ("around") compounded with the deictic adverb ~her~ ("hither"): motion in a circuit, and by extension in no particular direction at all. Transparently compositional; the etymology belongs to the two component entries. The sense of ~umher-~ here is: directional, "around, about, in all directions".

~Umhergehen~ describes walking with no fixed goal, this way and that through a space; the ~umher-~ spreads the motion out in every direction.
en.umherziehen:
A separable compound of ~umher-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~umher-~: The preposition ~um~ ("around") compounded with the deictic adverb ~her~ ("hither"): motion in a circuit, and by extension in no particular direction at all. Transparently compositional; the etymology belongs to the two component entries. The sense of ~umher-~ here is: with verbs of motion, an aimless or wandering manner.

~Umherziehen~ is moving about with no fixed abode: wandering from place to place, as travelers and nomads do.
en.umkehren:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~kehren~:

• ~kehren~: A homograph concealing two distinct verbs. ~Kehren~ (1) "to turn": from MHG ~kēren~, from OHG ~kēran~, ~chēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kairijaną~ or *~kausijaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly connected to *~gers-~ ("to twist, bend, turn"). ~Kehren~ (2) "to sweep": from MHG ~kern~, ~keren~, from OHG ~kerian~, ~cherian~, from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~ ("to scrape, scratch"), from PIE *~ger-~ ("to scrape"). Etymologically unrelated, merged through phonological convergence.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys motion around something, circling or circulating.

This is ~kehren~ (1) "to turn," not ~kehren~ (2) "to sweep": ~umkehren~ is turning about and going back, and by extension the reversal of a path or resolve already taken.
en.umklappen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~klappen~:

• ~klappen~: From Middle Low German ~klappen~, from Old Saxon *~klappōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klappōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klappōną~. The verb is onomatopoeic. Cognate with English ~clap~, Dutch ~klappen~, Old High German ~klapfō~ ("a clapping sound"); also related to ~klaffen~ ("to gape").
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys toppling: falling or knocking over.

~Umklappen~ means folding something over or down on a hinge or joint (a backrest, a table leg, a collar), so that it comes to lie flat.
en.umkommen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys toppling: falling or knocking over.

~Umkommen~ means to lose one's life, to perish, violently or through hardship; here the ~um-~ carries the fossilized sense "to death" that it shares with ~umbringen~.
en.umkämpfen:
An inseparable compound of ~um-~ + ~kämpfen~:

• ~kämpfen~: From MHG ~kempfen~, from OHG *~kempfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kampijan~, a denominal verb from *~kamp~ ("field, battlefield"), borrowed from Latin ~campus~ ("field, open plain"); the sense shifted early from the place of battle to the act of fighting. Latin ~campus~ also gives English ~camp~ and ~champion~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, ~um(b)-~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on both sides"). Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ and Ancient Greek ~amphí-~, whence English ~ambiguous~ and ~amphitheater~. ~um-~, as an inseparable prefix, conveys surrounding or encircling something.

~Umkämpfen~ means to fight over a place or prize from every side; in its participle ~umkämpft~ it stands for anything hotly contested: a position, a market, an electoral district.
en.umlagern:
An inseparable compound of ~um-~ + ~lagern~:

• ~lagern~: Derived from the noun ~Lager~ ("camp, store, warehouse"), from MHG ~lëger~, from OHG ~lëgar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~legr~, from Proto-Germanic *~legrą~. The modern form with ~-a-~ is of East Central German origin, influenced by ~Lage~ ("position"). Cognate with English ~lair~, Dutch ~leger~, Danish ~lejr~, Swedish ~läger~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, ~um(b)-~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on both sides"). Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ and Ancient Greek ~amphí-~, whence English ~ambiguous~ and ~amphitheater~. ~um-~, as an inseparable prefix, conveys surrounding or encircling something.

As an inseparable verb, ~umlagern~ means to surround or besiege on all sides (as a crowd throngs around a star). The gloss "transfer, relocate" instead names the separable twin ~umlagern~, "to restack goods elsewhere."
en.umlaufen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys motion around something, circling or circulating.

~Umlaufen~ is running around something or circulating in a circuit, hence ~Umlauf~ for the circulation of money or rumors.
en.umlauten:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~lauten~:

• ~lauten~: From MHG ~lūten~ ("to sound, ring"), from OHG ~hlūtēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlūdēn~; ~Laut~ ("sound") plus the suffix ~-en~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlūdaz~ ("loud"). ~lauten~ means "to read as, to run"; ~läuten~ ("to ring") is the factitive of the same root. Cognate with English ~loud~, Dutch ~luid~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys change or conversion: doing something over differently.

~Umlauten~ is the linguistic term for a vowel changing its sound (~a~ to ~ä~, ~u~ to ~ü~), that is, taking the ~Umlaut~; the ~um-~ carries the sense of a change in sound.
en.umlegen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys toppling: falling or knocking over.

~Umlegen~ means to bring something upright down flat: a lever, a collar, a blade; alongside stand the readings "to drape something around the body" and to "spread costs" across many.
en.umleiten:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~: the causative *~laidijaną~ of the strong verb *~līþaną~ ("to pass, go") with the suffix *~-janą~ ("to cause to go"), from PIE *~leyt-~ ("to go, depart, die"). ~leiten~ and ~leiden~ are a base-and-causative pair. Cognate with English ~lead~ (OE ~lǣdan~).
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys motion around something, circling or circulating.

~Umleiten~ means to route traffic, a pipe, or a river around an obstacle; the noun ~Umleitung~ names the detour.
en.umlenken:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~lenken~:

• ~lenken~: From MHG ~lenken~, from OHG ~lanca~ ("hip, flank"), related to ~Gelenk~ ("joint"), from Proto-Germanic *~gahlankiją~, from *~hlankaz~ ("flexible, lank, slender"). The path from "joint" to "to steer, guide" ran through bending and turning at a joint. Cognate with English ~lank~ (and ~link~); OHG ~hlanka~ also gave French ~flanc~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys motion around something, circling or circulating.

~Umlenken~ means to steer a motion, a rope, or one's attention in another direction; an ~Umlenkrolle~ (guide pulley) leads a rope around a corner.
en.umlernen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~lernen~:

• ~lernen~: From MHG ~lernen~, from OHG ~lernēn~, ~lirnēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~liʀnēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lizaną~, from PIE *~leys-~ ("track, furrow, trail"): to learn is to follow the trail laid down before. ~lehren~ ("to teach") shares the stem in causative function. Cognate with Old English ~leornian~ (English ~learn~), Dutch ~lernen~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys change or conversion: doing something over differently.

~Umlernen~ means to replace what one has learned with something new: adjusting to changed circumstances or a new trade; the ~um-~ marks doing it over differently.
en.umlügen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~lügen~:

• ~lügen~: From MHG ~liegen~, from OHG ~liogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~leugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~leuganą~, from PIE *~lewgʰ-~ ("to lie, swear falsely"). A class II strong verb (~lügen~, ~log~, ~gelogen~); the ~ü~ is late, taken from the noun ~Lüge~ to keep the verb from colliding with ~liegen~. Cognate with English ~lie~, Gothic ~liugan~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys change or conversion: doing something over differently.

~Umlügen~ means to turn something into its opposite or another shape by lying: recasting the truth through falsehood; the ~um-~ carries the sense of transforming change.
en.ummelden:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~melden~:

• ~melden~: From MHG ~mëlden~, from OHG ~mëldōn~, ~mëldēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~melþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~melþōną~, from PIE *~meldʰ-~ ("to ask, pray, speak"). • ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. en.umsetzen:

• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. en.umstellen:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put, stand"). Cognate with English ~stall~ and Dutch ~stellen~.
• ~um-~: From OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of").

With stress on ~-stellen~ (inseparable: ~die Polizei umstellt das Gebäude~), it means "to surround, to encircle." Same prefix, same root, but different stress patterns yield different semantics, different syntax, and different past participles (~umgestellt~ vs. ~umstellt~).
en.umstimmen:

• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. As a separable prefix, it conveys change or conversion: doing something over differently.

~Umstimmen~ literally is to tune an instrument differently; far more often "jemanden umstimmen" means to change someone's mind, in both a setting is reset.
en.umstoßen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). Cognate with dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce, ricochet"), Dutch ~stoten~, Old Norse ~stauta~ and ~steyta~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys toppling: falling or knocking over.

~Umstoßen~ topples something from its footing with a shove; figuratively it overturns plans, verdicts, or rulings.
en.umstreiten:
An inseparable compound of ~um-~ + ~streiten~:

• ~streiten~: From MHG ~strīten~, from OHG ~strītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~strīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~strīdaną~, probably from Pre-Germanic *~streydʰh₁-~, a compound of PIE *~strey-~ ("to resist") + *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, place"). Cognate with English ~stride~, Dutch ~strijden~ ("to fight, struggle"), Low German ~striden~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, ~um(b)-~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on both sides"). Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ and Ancient Greek ~amphí-~, whence English ~ambiguous~ and ~amphitheater~. ~um-~, as an inseparable prefix, conveys surrounding or encircling something.

Inseparable, ~umstreiten~ denotes contesting a matter from all sides; in practice almost only the participle ~umstritten~ "contested, disputed" survives.
en.umstürzen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~stürzen~:

• ~stürzen~: From MHG ~stürzen~, from OHG ~sturzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sturtijan~ ("to fall down, tumble"), of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly from PIE *~ster-~ ("to be stiff") via a dental extension *~sterd-~, though the derivation is debated. Cognate with English ~start~, a doublet from the same Proto-West Germanic source, from which the meanings have diverged radically.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys toppling: falling or knocking over.

~Umstürzen~ is a toppling to the ground or a bringing-down; charged politically, the noun ~Umsturz~ is the violent overthrow of an order.
en.umtauschen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~tauschen~:

• ~tauschen~: From MHG ~tiuschen~, derived from ~tūschen~, related to ~täuschen~ ("to deceive"), both of uncertain further origin. The sense ran from "to deceive" to "to trick someone into buying one's goods" to "to trade, exchange, barter"; ~tauschen~ lost the negative connotation along the way while ~täuschen~ retained it.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys change or conversion: doing something over differently.

~Umtauschen~ is to give one item back for another: the prefix stresses that one thing takes the place of the other.
en.umtreiben:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys motion around something, circling or circulating.

~Umtreiben~ is a restless driving to and fro; today it lives on mainly in the figurative: a question that ~umtreibt~ someone gives them no peace.
en.umtreten:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys toppling: falling or knocking over.

~Umtreten~ is a treading-down or a turning-over by a kick; the terse gloss "boot" leaves open whether it is kicking an object over or twisting one's own ankle.
en.umverteilen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~ver-~ + ~teilen~:

• ~teilen~: From MHG ~teilen~ and OHG ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~ ("to divide, part, deal"), from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, a denominative of *~dailiz~ ("part, share"), from PIE *~dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo-~, tentatively from *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, set, place"), though the precise PIE derivation is uncertain. Cognate with English ~deal~, Dutch ~delen~, Danish ~dele~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys repositioning: moving something from one place to another.

~Umverteilen~ distributes anew what is already distributed; the ~um-~ resets the allocation elsewhere; a keyword of tax and welfare debate.
en.umwandeln:
Compound of ~um-~ + ~wandeln~:

• ~wandeln~: From MHG ~wandeln~, from OHG ~wantalōn~ ("to change, to wander"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wandalōn~, a frequentative derived from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn, to change"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, to wind"). Cognate with English ~wend~ (as in "to wend one's way"), ~wander~, ~wind~ (the verb), Dutch ~wandelen~ ("to walk, to stroll").
• ~um-~: From MHG ~um(be)~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~, from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). As a separable prefix here, it conveys the sense of changing something over, transforming.

~Umwandeln~ means "to transform, to convert, to transmute", literally to turn something around, to change it into something else. The noun ~Umwandlung~ ("transformation, conversion") is used in chemistry (~Stoffumwandlung~, "material conversion"), law (~Umwandlung einer Strafe~, "commutation of a sentence"), and biology (~Umwandlung von Energie~, "energy conversion"). The PIE root *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn") is one of the great motion roots of Indo-European, producing English ~wind~ (the verb), ~wander~, ~wend~, and through the Gmc tribal name *~Wandilōz~ ("the wanderers"), the name of the ~Vandals~, the Germanic tribe whose sack of Rome in 455 CE made their name synonymous with destruction.
en.umwenden:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~wenden~:

• ~wenden~: From MHG ~wenden~, from OHG ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), the causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). It belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort (preterite ~wandte~, participle ~gewandt~) and has a doubled preterite: ~wandte~ for turning the self or one's attention, the regularized ~wendete~ for physical turning. Cognate with English ~wend~, Armenian ~gind~ ("ring").
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys motion around something, circling or circulating.

~Umwenden~ is a turning to the other side (a page, a roast), or, reflexively, an about-face of the whole body.
en.umwerben:
An inseparable compound of ~um-~ + ~werben~:

• ~werben~: From MHG ~werben~, from OHG ~werban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hwerban~, from Proto-Germanic *~hwerbaną~ ("to turn, move about, wander"). The sense passed through "to go about seeking" to "to recruit, advertise, woo", parallel to English ~advertise~ from Latin ~advertere~ ("to turn toward"). Cognate with Dutch ~werven~, English ~wharve~, Icelandic ~hverfa~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, ~um(b)-~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on both sides"). Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ and Ancient Greek ~amphí-~, whence English ~ambiguous~ and ~amphitheater~. ~um-~, as an inseparable prefix, conveys surrounding or encircling something.

Inseparable, ~umwerben~ is sustained courting from every side: the one wooed stands at the center of many attentions at once.
en.umwerfen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys toppling: falling or knocking over.

~Umwerfen~ is throwing an object to the ground; colloquially a piece of news can ~umwerfen~ a person too, when it bowls them over.
en.umziehen:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys repositioning: moving something from one place to another.

Separable, ~umziehen~ is changing residence; the inseparable doublet ~umziehen~ instead means "to surround, to encircle." The citation shows the older separable sense "to roam about."
en.umändern:
A separable compound of ~um-~ + ~ändern~:

• ~ändern~: From MHG ~endern~, a denominative verb from ~ander~ ("other, different"), from MHG ~ander~, OHG ~andar~, Proto-West Germanic *~anþar~, Proto-Germanic *~anþeraz~, from PIE *~h₂énteros~ ("other"), a comparative formation from *~h₂ent-~ ("front, forefront"). Cognate with English ~other~, Dutch ~ander~, Old Norse ~annarr~, Danish ~anden~.
• ~um-~: From MHG ~umbe~, from OHG ~umbi~, from Proto-West Germanic *~umbi~, from Proto-Germanic *~umbi~ ("around"), from PIE *~h₂m̥bʰi~ ("around, on either side of"). ~Um-~ is one of German's separability doublets: stressed and separable it is literal and spatial (~úmfahren~, "to run over"), unstressed and inseparable it is figurative (~umfáhren~, "to drive around"); the senses below are the separable ones. Cognate with Latin ~ambi-~ (in ~ambiguous~, literally "driving both ways") and Greek ~amphí-~ (in ~amphitheater~, a theater with seats all around). As a separable prefix, it conveys change or conversion: doing something over differently.

~Umändern~ nearly doubles its base verb: ~ändern~ already means to make different, and ~um-~ merely reinforces the making-over.
en.unterbewerten:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~bewerten~:

• ~bewerten~: A denominal verb from ~Wert~ ("value, worth") with the prefix ~be-~ (from PIE *~h₁epi~, "on, at, near") and ~-en~. ~Wert~ is from MHG ~wert~, from OHG ~werd~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~, from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"), the sense being something turned over in trade. Cognate with English ~worth~ and ~weird~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

~Unterbewerten~ is to rate something below its true worth; here ~unter-~ stands for "too little," a quantitative reading alongside the purely spatial one.
en.unterbezahlen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~bezahlen~:

• ~bezahlen~: From MHG ~bezaln~, a compound of ~be-~ + ~zahlen~. ~zahlen~ is from MHG ~zaln~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"); paying is etymologically counting out coins. The prefix ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("at, near"), adds a transitive, directed quality. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

Here ~unter-~ marks a measure below what is proper: to be underpaid is to receive less wage than one is due.
en.unterbinden:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~binden~:

• ~binden~: From MHG ~binden~, from OHG ~bintan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bindan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bindaną~, from PIE *~bʰendʰ-~ ("to bind, tie"). A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~i~–~a~–~u~ ablaut (~binden~, ~band~, ~gebunden~). Cognate with English ~bind~, Dutch ~binden~, Gothic ~bindan~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys interruption, cutting into an action already under way.

The image is originally surgical (to ~unterbinden~ a vessel is to tie it off) from which the modern sense "to prevent a process, to put a stop to it" generalized.
en.unterbrechen:
From MHG ~underbrëchen~, from OHG ~untarbrehhan~, a calque of Latin ~interrumpere~ ("to break between"):

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"). Cognate with English ~break~, Dutch ~breken~, Old Saxon ~brekan~.
• ~unter-~: From PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). In this compound it carries the sense of "between, in the middle of."

~Unterbrechen~ is a rare example of a documented calque (a word-for-word translation) from Latin into Old High German. Latin ~inter-~ ("between") + ~rumpere~ ("to break") was rendered as OHG ~untar-~ + ~brehhan~, producing a Germanic compound with identical internal structure. The verb means "to interrupt", to break into the middle of something. The noun ~Unterbrechung~ ("interruption") follows naturally. The PIE root *~bʰreg-~ is one of the most broadly preserved roots in the family: it appears in Latin ~frangere~ ("to break," whence English ~fracture~, ~fragment~, and ~fraction~), and it has remained semantically stable (meaning "to break"), in an unbroken line from PIE through Proto-Germanic to modern German and English. Cognate with Dutch ~onderbreken~, another parallel calque.
en.unterbringen:
Compound of ~unter-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, from PIE *~bʰrenk-~ ("to bring"). Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Afrikaans ~bring~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). As a separable prefix, it means "under" or "among," here conveying the idea of placing something into shelter or accommodation.

The literal sense is "to bring under (a roof)," i.e., to accommodate, to house, to place somewhere. From this spatial meaning, ~unterbringen~ has developed figurative uses: ~Waren unterbringen~ ("to store goods"), ~ein Kind unterbringen~ ("to place a child," as in foster care), and ~eine Bemerkung unterbringen~ ("to slip in a remark"). The underlying metaphor of bringing something under shelter or into a contained space applies equally to people, objects, and words. English ~bring~ is the direct cognate of ~bringen~, and the two verbs have maintained remarkably parallel meanings for over a millennium. The PIE root *~bʰrenk-~ is notable for being one of the few Proto-Indo-European roots whose Germanic reflexes show an anomalous nasal infix that has never been fully explained; ~bringen~ is simply an etymological puzzle that linguists continue to debate.
en.unterdrücken:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys subjection or subordination to an authority.

Literally "to press down," the verb developed its modern sense of political and psychological oppression, holding someone or something down by force.
en.unterfangen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~fangen~:

• ~fangen~: From MHG ~vāhen~, from OHG ~fāhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~fanhaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to secure, fasten"). A strong verb, originally ~fāhan~ / ~fieng~ / ~gefangan~; the modern present stem ~fang-~ was taken analogically from the past forms. Cognate with English ~fang~, Dutch ~vangen~, West Frisian ~fange~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys support or sustenance from below.

From the concrete "to support from below, to reach under" (in building, to ~unterfangen~ a foundation is to underpin it) came the reflexive "sich unterfangen," meaning "to presume, to venture something."
en.unterfordern:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~fordern~:

• ~fordern~: From MHG ~vodern~, ~vordern~, from OHG ~fordarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ(a)rōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþą~, from PIE *~pŕ̥-to-~, from *~per-~ ("forward, through"); "to push forward" became "to advance a claim." Not to be confused with umlauted ~fördern~ from the same root. Cognate with English ~forth~, ~forward~ and ~further~, Dutch ~vorderen~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

Here ~unter-~ marks a measure below what is needed: to be underchallenged is to be asked for less than one is capable of.
en.unterführen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

Concretely spatial: a road or path is led beneath another, which is also the source of the noun ~Unterführung~ ("underpass").
en.untergehen:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. Stressed and separable, ~unter-~ is literal and spatial: something goes, is placed, or is written underneath.

From the sun's sinking below the horizon, ~untergehen~ extended to every kind of ruin: a ship, an empire, a world goes under.
en.untergraben:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~graben~:

• ~graben~: From MHG ~graben~, from OHG ~graban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from PIE *~gʰrebʰ-~ ("to dig, scratch, bury"). A class VI strong verb (~graben~, ~grub~, ~gegraben~). Cognate with English ~grave~ as a verb (now only in ~engrave~ and ~graven image~), Gothic ~graban~, Dutch ~graven~, Old Norse ~grafa~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

From the literal digging-under of a wall to bring it down, the verb became an image for the covert erosion of authority or trust.
en.unterhalten:
From Middle High German ~underhalten~. Compound of ~unter-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly from *~ḱel-~ ("to hide, conceal") or *~kelH-~ ("to rise"). Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~, from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). As an inseparable prefix (as in this verb), it carries a sustaining or supporting sense rather than a purely spatial one.

The verb ~unterhalten~ is notable for bearing two quite different meanings: "to entertain, to converse with" (reflexive ~sich unterhalten~) and "to maintain, to support" (e.g. a family or a building). Both senses derive from the underlying image of "holding something up from below", supporting it. The entertainment sense arose from the idea of sustaining someone's attention or spirits. The noun ~Unterhaltung~ similarly means both "entertainment" and "maintenance" (as in ~Straßenunterhaltung~ = "road maintenance"). Cognate with Hunsrik ~unnerhalle~. The inseparable prefix distinguishes ~unterhalten~ from separable ~untergehen~ ("to go under, to perish"), a morphological contrast that encodes whether ~unter-~ modifies the verb's meaning structurally or merely directionally.
en.unterheben:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb: the past ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ continue the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. It also means "among, in the middle of," as of mixing one thing in with others.

A culinary term: to ~unterheben~ something is to fold it gently in among a mixture without letting it collapse, egg white into a batter, for instance.
en.unterkommen:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. With verbs of housing it means bringing someone under a roof, into shelter or accommodation.

With the particle's housing sense: to ~unterkommen~ is to find a roof, a lodging, or a position.
en.unterkriegen:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~kriegen~:

• ~kriegen~: From MHG ~kriegen~ ("to war, to strive for"), a verbalization of ~Krieg~ ("war"), from OHG ~krig~, from Proto-West Germanic *~krīg~, whose origin is debated. The "obtaining" sense overshadowed the military one; colloquial modern German ~kriegen~ simply means "to get." Cognate with Dutch ~krijgen~ ("to get"), Bavarian ~kriagn~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. Stressed and separable, ~unter-~ is literal and spatial: something goes, is placed, or is written underneath.

From the spatial "to get someone under" came the fixed phrase "sich nicht unterkriegen lassen": to refuse to be discouraged or defeated.
en.unterlaufen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

From "running beneath something" came the image of circumvention: a rule is unterlaufen when one slips unnoticed beneath it.
en.unterlegen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

Concretely "to lay something underneath"; figuratively a text is unterlegt with music or a claim with data, underpinned, as it were.
en.unterliegen:
From Middle High German ~unterligen~, from Old High German ~untarliggan~ ("to lie beneath"), equivalent to ~unter-~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down").
• ~unter-~: From PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). As an inseparable prefix here, it conveys the sense of being beneath or being subjected to.

~Unterliegen~ means "to be subject to" (~einer Pflicht unterliegen~, "to be subject to an obligation") or "to be defeated, to succumb" (~dem Gegner unterliegen~, "to lose to the opponent"). The physical image is powerful: the one who lies underneath has been pinned, overcome, forced down. This is the exact semantic equivalent of English ~underlie~ (and the related ~succumb~, from Latin ~sub-~ + ~cumbere~, "to lie under"), confirming that the metaphor of spatial position as power relation is deeply rooted in Indo-European thought. Cognate with Dutch ~onderliggen~, English ~underlie~, Gothic ~𐌻𐌹𐌲𐌰𐌽~.
en.untermalen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~malen~:

• ~malen~: From MHG ~mālen~, from OHG ~mālōn~, ~mālēn~, a denominative of the noun ~māl~ ("spot, mark"), from Proto-West Germanic *~mālijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~mēlijaną~, from *~mēlą~, from PIE *~melh₂-~ ("dark color"). Not to be confused with ~mahlen~ ("to grind"), of separate origin. Cognate with Dutch ~maal~, Greek ~melas~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

From the painter's ~Untermalung~, the priming first layer of color, comes also the figurative "to provide background music", laying a ground over which something else appears.
en.untermischen:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~mischen~:

• ~mischen~: From MHG ~mischen~, from OHG ~misken~, from Proto-Germanic *~miskijaną~ ("to mix"), from PIE *~meyḱ-~ ("to mix, knead"), via the inchoative present *~miḱ-sḱé-~. Cognate with English ~mix~, Latin ~misceō~, Greek ~mísgo~, Sanskrit ~miśrá~ ("mixed").
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. It also means "among, in the middle of," as of mixing one thing in with others.

The particle here means "in among": something is untergemischt into a mass, blended in with it.
en.unternehmen:
From Middle High German ~undernëmen~, from Old High German ~untarnëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~underneman~. Compound of ~unter-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due").
• ~unter-~: From PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). As an inseparable prefix here, ~unter-~ conveys the sense of support or undertaking from below.

The modern meaning of "to undertake, to attempt, to do" was first attested in the 16th century. The derived noun ~Unternehmen~ ("enterprise, company") and ~Unternehmer~ ("entrepreneur") emerged later, turning the verbal concept of "taking something on from underneath" into the institutional foundations of capitalism. English ~undertake~ is a precise calque: ~under-~ + ~take~ mirrors ~unter-~ + ~nehmen~ exactly, and both languages extended the meaning from "to take upon oneself" to more specialized senses (English ~undertaker~ famously narrowing to the funeral business, while German ~Unternehmer~ stayed with commerce). Cognate with Dutch ~ondernemen~ and obsolete English ~undernim~.
en.unterordnen:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~ordnen~:

• ~ordnen~: From MHG ~ordenen~, from OHG ~ordinōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ordinōn~ ("to put in order"), borrowed from Latin ~ōrdināre~ ("to arrange"), from ~ōrdō~ ("row, rank, order"), from Proto-Italic *~ordō~, probably from PIE *~h₂er-~ ("to fit together"). Doublet of ~ordinieren~. Cognate with English ~order~, Italian ~ordinare~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. Stressed and separable, ~unter-~ is literal and spatial: something goes, is placed, or is written underneath.

Literally "to arrange under" (to place at a lower rank), whence the hierarchical "sich unterordnen": to submit to a higher authority.
en.unterreden:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys being between or among, from the merged root meaning "between".

With the "between" sense: to ~unterreden~ with someone (or, as in Nietzsche, with one's own soul) is to exchange words back and forth, which also gives the noun ~Unterredung~ ("conversation").
en.unterrichten:
From Middle High German ~underrihten~, from Old High German compound of ~untar-~ + ~rihten~. Equivalent to ~unter-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~ ("to right, to straighten, to direct"), related to ~recht~ ("right, correct"). Cognate with English ~right~ (both the adjective and the verb).
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~ndher~ ("under, beneath"). As an inseparable prefix, ~unter-~ here conveys a sense of "between" or supportive direction, as in guiding someone.

The literal meaning is something like "to direct (someone) underneath" or "to set right among," which evolved into "to instruct, to teach." The verb ~unterrichten~ is an inseparable compound (stress falls on ~-rich-~, not ~unter-~), distinguishing it from the separable ~unter|richten~ (which does not exist as a standard verb). Cognate with Middle Low German ~underrichten~ and Saterland Frisian ~unnergjuchte~. The semantic connection between "directing" and "teaching" is natural: a teacher directs the understanding of students, setting their knowledge "right." English ~instruct~ follows the same logic, from Latin ~instruere~ ("to build up, to arrange, to inform").
en.untersagen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys subjection or subordination to an authority.

The verb is now purely prohibitive (to ~untersagen~ something is to forbid it) with ~unter-~ carrying the exercise of authority from above rather than any literal subjection.
en.unterscheiden:
From Middle High German ~underscheiden~, equivalent to ~unter-~ + ~scheiden~. Compound of ~unter-~ + ~scheiden~:

• ~scheiden~: From MHG ~scheiden~, from OHG ~sceidan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaiþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaiþaną~, from PIE *~skey-~ ("to split, dissect"). Cognate with Dutch ~scheiden~, English ~shed~, Ancient Greek ~skhízō~ ("to split").
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~, from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). In this compound, ~unter-~ does not mean "beneath" but rather "between", the sense of being positioned in the space separating two things, which is the conceptual basis for distinguishing them.

The semantic logic of ~unterscheiden~ ("to distinguish, differentiate") mirrors that of ~entscheiden~ ("to decide"): both rely on the metaphor of cutting. Where ~entscheiden~ cuts options apart (deciding between them), ~unterscheiden~ cuts between two things to reveal the gap that separates them. Latin ~discernere~ ("to distinguish") uses the same spatial logic: ~dis-~ ("apart") + ~cernere~ ("to sift, separate"). English ~discern~ and ~discriminate~ belong to the same conceptual family. Cognate with Dutch ~onderscheiden~.
en.unterschieben:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~schieben~:

• ~schieben~: From MHG ~schieben~, from OHG ~skioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeubaną~, from PIE *~skewbʰ-~ ("to push, to shove, to thrust"). A class II strong verb (~schieben~, ~schob~, ~geschoben~). Cognate with English ~shove~, Dutch ~schuiven~, Danish ~skubbe~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. Stressed and separable, ~unter-~ is literal and spatial: something goes, is placed, or is written underneath.

From the concrete "to shove something underneath" to the figurative "jemandem etwas unterschieben": to foist something on someone or attribute it to them falsely.
en.unterschlagen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

Literally "to strike under," to conceal; hence the legal ~unterschlagen~: to withhold entrusted money or, as here, documents and keep them for oneself.
en.unterschreiben:
Compound of ~unter-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, cut, incise"). Cognate with English ~scribe~, ~shrive~, Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~, from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). As an inseparable prefix here, it conveys "under, beneath."

~Unterschreiben~ means "to sign" (a document), literally "to write under." The concept is universal: English ~subscribe~ is a calque from Latin ~subscrībere~ ("to write under"), Dutch has ~ondertekenen~ ("to sign under"), and French uses ~souscrire~. All preserve the ancient practice of writing one's name beneath the text of a document to indicate consent. The root verb ~schreiben~ is itself a fascinating cultural borrowing: the Germanic peoples had no native word for writing (their runic inscriptions used ~ritzen~, "to scratch"), so when they encountered Roman literacy, they borrowed the Latin verb wholesale. The original PIE root *~(s)kreybʰ-~ meant "to scratch" or "to cut", a reminder that the earliest writing was carved, not inked.
en.unterschreiten:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~schreiten~:

• ~schreiten~: From MHG ~schrīten~, from OHG ~skrītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīþan~ ("to step, stride"), from Proto-Germanic *~skrīþaną~ ("to walk, glide, crawl"), from PIE *~(s)kreyt-~ ("to stride"), an extension of *~(s)krey-~ ("to go about"). Cognate with Lithuanian ~skrìsti~ ("to rush, run"), Latvian ~skrìet~ ("to run, fly"). Related to ~Schritt~ ("step").
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

Conceived spatially, a value lies beneath a limit: to unterschreiten a minimum wage or threshold is to fall below it.
en.unterschätzen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~schätzen~:

• ~schätzen~: A denominal verb from ~Schatz~ ("treasure"), from MHG ~schaz~, OHG ~scaz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skatt~ ("cattle, treasure"), an early Germanic word in which cattle served as a measure of wealth. Cognate with Old Norse ~skattr~ (whence Danish ~skat~ and Swedish ~skatt~, both "tax"), Gothic ~skatts~, Old English ~sċeatt~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

~Unter-~ marks a measure below the true one: to underestimate something is to reckon its worth too low.
en.untersetzen:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. Stressed and separable, ~unter-~ is literal and spatial: something goes, is placed, or is written underneath.

Concretely "to set something underneath": hence the ~Untersetzer~ ("coaster"); in bureaucratic usage extended to "to underpin with data or measures."
en.untersinken:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~sinken~:

• ~sinken~: From MHG ~sinken~, from OHG ~sinkan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sinkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sinkwaną~, from PIE *~sengʷ-~ ("to sink, to drop"). A class III strong verb (~sinken~, ~sank~, ~gesunken~); the weak causative ~senken~ is its transitive partner. Cognate with English ~sink~, Dutch ~zinken~, Danish ~synke~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. Stressed and separable, ~unter-~ is literal and spatial: something goes, is placed, or is written underneath.

The particle's pure downward motion: what untersinkt goes into the depths, sinks away.
en.unterstehen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys subjection or subordination to an authority.

To be subject to an authority is to stand under it: the agency untersteht the ministry, the school the laws of the Länder.
en.unterstellen:
Compound of ~unter-~ + ~stellen~, with two distinct etymologies and meanings depending on stress:

• ~stellen~: From Middle High German ~stellen~, from Old High German ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from Proto-Indo-European *~stel-~ ("to place, put, stand").
• ~unter-~: From Middle High German ~unter~, from Old High German ~untar~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Indo-European *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). As a separable prefix it means "under" literally; as an inseparable prefix it takes on abstract meanings.

The separable ~UNTERstellen~ means "to put underneath, to shelter" (~das Auto unterstellen~, "to put the car under cover"). The inseparable ~unterSTELLen~ has two meanings: "to assume, to suppose" (calqued from Latin ~suppōnere~, literally "to place under," the same metaphor that gives English ~suppose~) and "to impute, to accuse" (~jemandem etwas unterstellen~, "to accuse someone of something"). Dutch ~veronderstellen~ preserves the same Latin-influenced semantic development.
en.untersteuern:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~steuern~:

• ~steuern~: From MHG ~stiuren~, from OHG ~stiuren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stiurijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stiurijaną~. The root noun ~Steuer~ carries two meanings sharing one ancestor: ~das Steuer~ ("rudder, helm") and ~die Steuer~ ("tax," via "supporting post" and "support"). ~Steuern~ thus means both "to steer, navigate, control" and, in archaic or Swiss usage, "to pay a tax." Cognate with English ~steer~, Dutch ~stuur~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

In vehicle dynamics a car that understeers turns less sharply than the steering input dictates. Here ~unter-~ carries the sense of a shortfall, a falling below a target (as in ~unterschätzen~ ("to underestimate")), distinct from the literal "beneath."
en.unterstreichen:
Compound of ~unter-~ + ~streichen~:

• ~streichen~: From MHG ~strichen~, from OHG ~strihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~strikan~, from Proto-Germanic *~strikanan~, from PIE *~streyg-~ ("to stroke, to rub, to press"). Cognate with English ~strike~ and Dutch ~strijken~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, beneath"), from PIE *~ndher~ ("under, beneath"). As an inseparable prefix here, it conveys the spatial sense of "underneath."

The literal meaning is "to stroke underneath," which is to say, to draw a line under something, to underline. English ~underline~ and ~underscore~ are exact calques of the same concept. The figurative extension to "to emphasize, to stress" follows naturally from the typographic practice of underlining important text. The base verb ~streichen~ itself has a remarkably wide semantic field: "to stroke, to paint, to spread (butter), to cross out, to cancel, to roam."
