All these meanings trace back to the basic motion of moving something across a surface. The cognate English ~strike~ shares the physical-motion core but developed its own distinctive range of meanings ("to hit, to strike a match, to go on strike").
en.unterstützen:
From Middle High German ~understüzzen~, from Old High German ~untarstuzzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~understuttijan~. Compound of ~unter-~ + ~stützen~:

• ~stützen~: Attested as a simplex only since the 17th century, probably after Middle Low German ~stütten~ as a back-formation from the inherited compound ~unterstützen~ itself. Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *~stuttijan~. Related to Proto-Germanic *~stuþs~, whence English ~stud~ ("protrusion; post").
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~, from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). As an inseparable prefix, ~unter-~ adds a sense of support from below.

The simplex ~stützen~ was probably extracted from this compound rather than the reverse: ~unterstützen~ is the historically primary form. Cognate with Dutch ~stutten~ ("to support"), and, by borrowing from Low German, Norwegian ~støtte~, Swedish ~stötta~.
en.untersuchen: First attested in the 15th century as ~undersuochen~. The existence of an unattested Old High German *~untarsuohhen~ is probable; compare Old Saxon ~undarsōkian~ (whence Low German ~ünnersöken~), Old Dutch ~undersuoken~ (whence Dutch ~onderzoeken~), and Old English ~undersecan~ (whence archaic English ~underseek~), all from Proto-West Germanic *~undersōkijan~ ("to search under or between"). Equivalent to ~unter-~ + ~suchen~. ~Unter-~ derives from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). ~Suchen~ derives from Old High German ~suohhen~, from Proto-Germanic *~sōkijaną~, from PIE *~seh₂g-~ ("to seek out"). The spatial metaphor (searching beneath the surface) evolved naturally into the modern sense of "to investigate, examine." Dutch ~onderzoeken~, English ~underseek~ (archaic), and Old Saxon ~undarsōkian~ are direct structural parallels. Cognate with Dutch ~onderzoeken~, Low German ~ünnersöken~.
en.untertauchen:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~tauchen~:

• ~tauchen~: From MHG ~tūchen~, ~touchen~, from OHG *~tūhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dūkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dūkaną~ ("to duck, to dive under"), whose further etymology is uncertain. A class II strong verb that became weak in the early modern period: when it was reintroduced from Central and Low German, the strong conjugation was regularized to weak. Cognate with Dutch ~duiken~, Swedish ~dyka~; a Low German consonant variant of the same root is ~ducken~, cognate with English ~duck~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. Stressed and separable, ~unter-~ is literal and spatial: something goes, is placed, or is written underneath.

Literally the body dives beneath the surface of the water; figuratively ~untertauchen~ also means to vanish into the crowd and go to ground, untraceable by pursuers.
en.unterteilen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~teilen~:

• ~teilen~: From MHG ~teilen~ and OHG ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~ ("to divide, part, deal"), from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, a denominative of *~dailiz~ ("part, share"), from PIE *~dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo-~, tentatively from *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, set, place"), though the precise PIE derivation is uncertain. Cognate with English ~deal~, Dutch ~delen~, Danish ~dele~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

~Unterteilen~ means to break a whole into subordinate sections; here ~unter-~ is the hierarchical extension of "beneath": the resulting parts sit one level below the whole.
en.untertreiben:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys literal position beneath something.

~Untertreiben~ is the counterpart of ~übertreiben~ ("to exaggerate"): to present something as less than it is. Here too ~unter-~ marks a shortfall (a falling short of the true measure) rather than a spatial position.
en.untervermieten:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~ver-~ + ~mieten~:

• ~mieten~: From MHG ~mieten~, from OHG ~mietan~, a denominative of the noun ~Miete~ ("rent, reward"), which via MHG ~miete~ and OHG ~mieta~ goes back to Proto-West Germanic *~miʀdu~, Proto-Germanic *~mizdō~, and PIE *~misdʰéh₂~ ("reward, compensation"). Cognate with Gothic ~mizdo~, English ~meed~ (archaic), Greek ~misthos~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. With verbs of housing it means bringing someone under a roof, into shelter or accommodation.

~Vermieten~ is to let living space to a tenant for payment; the leading ~unter-~ turns this into a second-order handing-on: the subtenant takes the space from the tenant, not from the owner.
en.unterwandern:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~wandern~:

• ~wandern~: From MHG ~wandern~, from OHG *~wantarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandarōn~, formed from *~wandōn~ ("to turn") with the frequentative suffix *~-rōn~ (not a single journey but repeated, meandering motion), from Proto-Germanic *~wandōną~, from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, to wind"). Cognate with English ~wander~, Danish ~vandre~, Swedish ~vandra~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys being between or among, from the merged root meaning "between".

~Unterwandern~ means to work one's way gradually and unobtrusively into a group in order to change it from within: the "wandering" happens covertly, in among the ranks it penetrates.
en.unterweisen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative verb from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from PIE *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know"). A class I strong verb; its senses "to show, point" and "to direct, expel" both direct knowledge or attention. Cognate with English ~wise~, ~wit~, ~wizard~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys support or sustenance from below.

~Unterweisen~ means to instruct, to teach someone in something; here ~unter-~ is lexicalized in the didactic sense it shares with ~unterrichten~, and sorts cleanly under none of its ordinary uses.
en.unterwerfen:
An inseparable compound of ~unter-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under-~, from OHG ~untar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"), with which PIE *~h₁n̥ter~ ("between, among") merged in Germanic. Cognate with English ~under~ and, through the second root, with Latin ~inter~. ~unter-~ conveys subjection or subordination to an authority.

~Unterwerfen~ brings someone under another's dominion, literally cast "under the throw"; reflexively, ~sich unterwerfen~ is to bow to an authority.
en.unterwinden:
A separable compound of ~unter-~ + ~winden~:

• ~winden~: From MHG ~winden~, from OHG ~wintan~, from Proto-Germanic *~windaną~ ("to wind, to wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). Cognate with English ~wind~ (the verb, "to coil"), Dutch ~winden~, Danish ~vinde~.
• ~unter-~: From MHG ~under~, from OHG ~untar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~ ("under, between, among"), from PIE *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Cognate with English ~under~, Dutch ~onder~, Sanskrit ~adhás~ ("below"). Proto-Germanic *~under~ appears to have absorbed a second, distinct etymon meaning "between" (the source of Latin ~inter~), which is why the particle still carries both senses. The unstressed inseparable ~unter-~ is a different creature, taking abstract senses of support, subjection, and interruption.

The reflexive ~sich unterwinden~ ("to take something upon oneself, to presume") is archaic today and survives almost only in Luther's German. Though the compound is filed here as separable, in attestation it behaves inseparably (~unterwinde sich~, ~unterwanden sich~), precisely the unstressed, abstract use the bullet above names.
en.unterzeichnen:
Compound of ~unter-~ + ~zeichnen~:

• ~zeichnen~: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, symbol"), from Middle High German ~zeichen~, from Old High German ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~ ("sign"), from Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ ("to show"). Cognate with English ~token~ and Dutch ~teken~.
• ~unter-~: From Middle High German ~unter~, from Old High German ~untar~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Indo-European *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath"). Here the prefix literally means "under"; one writes one's name under the text of a document.

~Unterzeichnen~ ("to sign") is always inseparable and carries a formal register, used for treaties, contracts, and official documents. The verb literally means "to draw beneath", to place one's mark under the text. Compare English ~undersign~ and the related noun ~Unterzeichner~ ("signatory"). The PIE root *~deyḱ-~ ("to show") also produced Latin ~dīcere~ ("to say," originally "to point out"), Greek ~deiknynai~ ("to show"), and English ~teach~ (originally "to show").
en.unterziehen:
Compound of ~unter-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From Middle High German ~ziehen~, from Old High German ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). Cognate with obsolete English ~tee~ ("to draw, lead"), Gothic ~tiuhan~, and from the same PIE root as Latin ~dūcere~ ("to lead"), which gave English ~duke~, ~conduct~, ~produce~, and ~educate~.
• ~unter-~: From Middle High German ~unter~, from Old High German ~untar~, from Proto-Germanic *~under~, from Proto-Indo-European *~n̥dʰér~ ("under, beneath").

The separable ~UNTERziehen~ means "to put on underneath" (clothing). The inseparable ~unterZIEHen~ means "to subject to" or reflexively ~sich unterziehen~ ("to undergo"), as in ~sich einer Operation unterziehen~ ("to undergo surgery"). The metaphor of being "pulled under" something captures the sense of submitting to a process. The PIE root *~dewk-~ is remarkably productive: through Latin alone it generated ~duct~, ~duke~, ~educate~, ~deduce~, ~introduce~, ~reduce~, and ~seduce~.
en.variieren:
Borrowed from French ~varier~, from Latin ~variāre~ ("to change, to make different, to diversify"), from ~varius~ ("diverse, variegated, changeable"), from PIE *~weh₁-ro-~ ("bent, crooked") or possibly *~weh₂-ro-~. The word entered German in the 16th century.

Latin ~varius~ originally described something spotted or multicolored (a surface with contrasting patches) before generalizing to "diverse, changeable." The same root produced English ~vary~, ~various~, ~variety~, and ~varicose~ (veins that are "bent" or "twisted"). ~Variieren~ in German means "to vary, to modify, to diversify" and is used in both everyday and technical contexts: recipes ~variieren~, opinions ~variieren~, and musical themes ~variieren~ (the ~Variation~ being a fundamental form in classical music). Bach's ~Goldberg-Variationen~, composed in Leipzig, gave the word particular cultural resonance in German-speaking lands. The derived noun ~Variante~ ("variant") and the adjective ~variabel~ ("variable") entered German through the same Latin-French channel.
en.verabschieden:
From ~ver-~ + ~Abschied~ + ~-en~. A denominal verb formed from ~Abschied~ ("farewell, parting"):

• ~Abschied~: From MHG ~abeschit~, equivalent to ~ab-~ ("away, off," from PIE *~h₂epó~) + ~Schied~ ("separation, divorce"), from ~scheiden~ ("to separate"), from OHG ~sceidan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaiþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaiþaną~, from PIE *~skeyd-~ ("to split, to separate"). The same root as ~scheitern~ above.
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds completeness or formality to the act.

~Verabschieden~ is a double-prefix construction (~ver-~ + ~ab-~) built on a noun rather than directly on the verb ~scheiden~. It means "to say goodbye to" (reflexive: ~sich verabschieden~), "to see off, to dismiss," and, in parliamentary usage, "to pass, to adopt (a law)." The parliamentary sense is the most surprising: when the Bundestag ~verabschiedet ein Gesetz~, it "sends the law on its way": the legislative body bids farewell to the bill as it leaves the chamber and enters the world as binding law. The reflexive ~sich aus der Politik verabschieden~ ("to take leave of politics") preserves the original farewell sense in a formal register. The root verb ~scheiden~ is cognate with English ~shed~ (to separate, to cast off), Greek ~σχίζω~ ("to split," whence ~schism~), and Lithuanian ~skíesti~ ("to separate").
en.verachten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~achten~:

• ~achten~: From MHG ~ahten~ ("to consider, heed"), from OHG ~ahtōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ahtōn~, a denominative of *~ahtu~ ("consideration, attention"), of uncertain pre-Germanic origin, possibly to Proto-Germanic *~ahjaną~ ("to think"), compared to PIE *~h₃ekʷ-~ ("to see"), though debated. Cognate with Dutch ~achten~, English ~aught~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ reverses or negates the base action.

~Achten~ is to esteem, to hold in regard; ~verachten~ turns this into its opposite, to regard someone as worthless.
en.verankern:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~ankern~:

• ~ankern~: From Middle High German ~ankern~, a denominative verb from the noun ~Anker~ ("anchor"). ~Anker~ traces to Old High German ~anker~, ~ankero~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ankurō~, from Proto-Germanic *~ankurô~. The Germanic word was borrowed from Latin ~ancora~ (also spelled ~anchora~), itself from Greek ~ankyra~ ("anchor"), related to ~ankos~ ("bend, hook"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂enk-~ ("to bend").
• ~ver-~: From Middle High German ~ver-~, from Old High German ~far-~, ~fir-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Indo-European *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix often adds a sense of completion or intensification.

~Verankern~ means "to anchor firmly" both literally (a ship) and figuratively (a principle in a constitution: ~in der Verfassung verankert~, "enshrined in the constitution"). The ~ver-~ prefix intensifies the anchoring, emphasizing permanence. The PIE root *~h₂enk-~ ("to bend") also produced Latin ~angulus~ ("angle, corner"), English ~angle~ and ~ankle~, and German ~Angelhaken~ ("fishhook"), all reflecting the concept of a bent or hooked shape.
en.veranlassen:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~Anlass~ + ~-en~:

• ~Anlass~: From MHG ~anelāz~, ~anlāz~, a deverbal noun from ~anlassen~ ("to start, set going"), literally "a letting-on." The verb ~lassen~ descends from MHG ~lāzen~, from OHG ~lāȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lātan~ ("to let, allow"), from Proto-Germanic *~lētaną~ ("to leave behind, allow"), from PIE *~leh₁d-~ ("to let, leave behind"). Cognate with English ~let~ and Dutch ~laten~.
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a causative, completive sense, bringing about a cause.

~Veranlassen~ means "to cause, to prompt, to arrange for something to happen", an elegant three-layered word. At its core is ~lassen~ ("to let"), prefixed with ~an-~ to form ~Anlass~ ("occasion, cause", literally "a letting-on"), then further prefixed with ~ver-~ to create a causative verb: "to create the occasion for." The noun ~Veranlassung~ ("instigation, cause") appears frequently in official correspondence: ~auf Veranlassung des Ministers~ ("at the instigation of the minister"). The PIE root *~leh₁d-~ has a satisfying doublet in English: ~let~ (Germanic path) and ~late~ (from the same root via the adjective meaning "slow, tardy", one who has been "left behind").
en.veranschlagen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~anschlagen~:

• ~anschlagen~: A compound of ~an-~ + ~schlagen~. ~schlagen~ is from MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, apparently onomatopoeic; a class VI strong verb (~schlagen~, ~schlug~, ~geschlagen~). The prefix ~an-~, from OHG ~ana~, from Proto-Germanic *~ana~, from PIE *~h₂en-~ ("on, onto"), cognate with English ~on~, adds the sense of striking onto a surface.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Veranschlagen~ is to set an amount in advance and fix it by calculation; ~ver-~ carries the act of assessing through to a settled reckoning.
en.veranstalten:
From ~ver-~ + ~Anstalt~ + ~-en~, attested from the early 18th century. Compound of ~ver-~ + the denominal verb derived from ~Anstalt~:

• ~Anstalt~: From MHG ~anstalt~, a deverbal noun from ~anstellen~ ("to set up, arrange"), itself from ~an-~ + ~stellen~. ~Stellen~: from MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put, stand").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix conveys thoroughness and completion, to bring an arrangement fully into being.

~Veranstalten~ means "to organize, to arrange, to stage", exclusively for events and occasions: concerts, festivals, competitions, demonstrations. One ~veranstaltet~ a wedding reception but not a bookshelf. The word is structurally layered: ~stellen~ ("to place") became ~anstellen~ ("to set up") became ~Anstalt~ ("institution, arrangement") became ~veranstalten~ ("to arrange an event"), each derivation adding a level of organizational complexity. The derived nouns ~Veranstalter~ ("organizer") and ~Veranstaltung~ ("event") are ubiquitous in German cultural life. ~Anstalt~ itself followed a separate semantic path from "arrangement" to "institution," particularly ~Irrenanstalt~ ("insane asylum") and ~Strafanstalt~ ("penal institution"), giving it a darker coloring that ~veranstalten~ has entirely escaped. The colloquial accusation ~was veranstaltest du für einen Lärm?~ ("what kind of racket are you staging?") adds a note of mock-theatrical indignation.
en.verantworten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~antworten~:

• ~antworten~: From MHG ~antwürten~, from OHG ~antwurten~, from Proto-Germanic *~andawurdijaną~, a denominative of *~andawurdiją~ ("answer"), from *~anda-~ ("against, in return") + *~wurdą~ ("word"); *~anda-~ from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, front, opposite"); English ~answer~ is built the same way. Cognate with Dutch ~antwoorden~, Afrikaans ~antwoord~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Antworten~ is the plain reply; ~verantworten~ is to answer for an action, to give account of it, the answer carried through into accountability.
en.verarbeiten:
From ~ver-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"). The semantic arc from "orphan" through "hardship" to "labor" reflects the lot of the fatherless in ancient society, whose work was the defining condition of their existence. Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, English ~orphan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a thoroughgoing, transformative sense, working something all the way through until it is processed into a new state.

The prefix ~ver-~ applied to ~arbeiten~ produces a verb meaning "to process, to work through, to come to terms with." Material is ~verarbeitet~ when it is transformed into a product; grief or trauma is ~verarbeitet~ when one has worked through it emotionally, a usage that would have been familiar to Freud, for whom the German term for psychological processing was literally the verb for industrial transformation. The metaphor of the factory and the metaphor of mourning share the same word. Cognate with Dutch ~verwerken~.
en.verbauen:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~būwen~, from OHG ~būan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~būan~, from Proto-Germanic *~būaną~, from PIE *~bʰuH-~ ("to be, to grow, to dwell"). Cognate with English ~build~ (via a different derivation), Dutch ~bouwen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, *~fur-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). As a verbal prefix, it can mean "away" (consuming), "wrongly" (spoiling), or "completion."

The prefix ~ver-~ gives ~verbauen~ two distinct senses, both involving the "using up" or "spoiling" meanings of the prefix. First, "to use up in building": ~das ganze Geld verbauen~ ("to spend all the money on construction"). Second, and more commonly, "to block or obstruct by building": ~jemandem die Aussicht verbauen~ ("to block someone's view by building"). The figurative extension ~sich die Zukunft verbauen~ ("to ruin one's future," literally "to build over one's future") is especially vivid: the image is of someone erecting walls that block their own path forward. A third sense, "to build incorrectly" (~ein schlecht verbautes Haus~), draws on the ~ver-~ prefix's "wrongly" meaning. This semantic range (consuming, obstructing, and botching) illustrates why ~ver-~ is often called the most versatile and unpredictable of all German prefixes.
en.verbeißen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~beißen~:

• ~beißen~: From MHG ~bīzen~, from OHG ~bīzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bītaną~, from PIE *~bʰeyd-~ ("to split"). A class I strong verb (~beißen~, ~biss~, ~gebissen~). Cognate with English ~bite~, Dutch ~bijten~, Swedish ~bita~; ~bitter~ is this verb's old participial adjective, literally "biting."
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Sich verbeißen~ is to sink one's teeth in with dogged persistence and not let go; alongside it, in "sich das Lachen verbeißen" ("to stifle a laugh"), sits the sense of biting something back, holding it shut.
en.verbergen:
From Middle High German ~verbergen~, from Old High German ~firbergan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frabergan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~bergen~:

• ~bergen~: From MHG ~bërgen~, from OHG ~bergan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bergan~, from Proto-Germanic *~berganą~ ("to take care of, preserve, protect"), from PIE *~bʰergʰ-~ ("to take care of, protect, preserve"). Cognate with Old English ~forbeorgan~ ("to forbear, refrain"), Dutch ~verbergen~ ("to hide").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix intensifies the base verb's sense of concealment.

The base verb ~bergen~ has a fascinating semantic range: "to recover, to salvage, to rescue." It is the word used for recovering bodies from wreckage, salvaging a sunken ship, or rescuing mountaineers. The noun ~Burg~ ("castle, fortress") is a relative, from Proto-Germanic *~burgaz~, a place that shelters and protects. ~Verbergen~ takes the protective sense of ~bergen~ and turns it inward: to shelter something from sight, to conceal. The past participle ~verborgen~ ("hidden, secret") has become a common adjective in its own right.
en.verbessern:
From ~ver-~ + ~bessern~:

• ~bessern~: A denominative from the adjective ~besser~ ("better"), from MHG ~beȥȥer~, from OHG ~beȥȥiro~, from Proto-West Germanic *~batiʀō~, from Proto-Germanic *~batizô~ (the comparative of *~bataz~, "good"), from PIE *~bʰed-~ ("good"). Cognate with English ~better~, Dutch ~beter~, Sanskrit ~bhadrá~ ("blessed, fortunate, good").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a completive sense, improving something all the way, bringing it to a better state.

The chain runs from PIE *~bʰed-~ ("good") through Proto-Germanic's comparative form *~batizô~ ("better"), to OHG ~beȥȥiro~, to ~besser~, to the denominative verb ~bessern~ ("to better, to improve"), and finally to ~verbessern~ with the completive ~ver-~ prefix driving it toward "to improve thoroughly, to correct." In a pedagogical context, ~verbessern~ is the standard word for correcting a student's work; a teacher ~verbessert~ an essay. The Sanskrit cognate ~bhadrá~ ("fortunate, good") is a reminder that the PIE root for goodness spread from the steppes to the subcontinent. Cognate with Dutch ~verbeteren~.
en.verbiegen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~biegen~:

• ~biegen~: From MHG ~biegen~, from OHG ~biogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beuganą~, from PIE *~bʰewgʰ-~ ("to bend"). A class II strong verb (~biegen~, ~bog~, ~gebogen~). Cognate with English ~bow~ and ~elbow~ ("arm-bend"), Dutch ~buigen~, Sanskrit ~bhujáti~ ("to bend, curve").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Biegen~ is plain bending; ~verbiegen~ bends something out of true: it becomes deformed, and figuratively ~sich verbiegen~ is to abandon one's principles to fit in.
en.verbieten:
From Middle High German ~verbieten~, from Old High German ~farbiotan~. Equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~bieten~:

• ~bieten~: From MHG ~bieten~, from OHG ~biotan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beudan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beudaną~, from PIE *~bʰewdʰ-~ ("to be aware, to make aware").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). The prefix here reverses or negates the action of offering; what is offered is now forbidden.

~Verbieten~ means "to forbid, to prohibit, to ban." The semantic relationship between ~bieten~ ("to offer") and ~verbieten~ ("to forbid") is one of German's most elegant prefix transformations: the ~ver-~ prefix negates the offering, turning "I present this to you" into "I withhold this from you." The derived noun ~Verbot~ ("prohibition, ban") is formed with the ~-t~ suffix (compare ~Gebot~, "commandment," from ~gebieten~) and is ubiquitous in German public life: ~Rauchverbot~ ("smoking ban"), ~Fahrverbot~ ("driving ban"), ~Verbotsschild~ ("prohibition sign"). The English cognate ~forbid~ (from Old English ~forbēodan~) is a perfect structural parallel: ~for-~ corresponds to ~ver-~, and ~bid~ to ~bieten~, both from the same PGmc *~beudaną~. So ~verbieten~ and ~forbid~ are not merely similar: they are the same compound, independently preserved in two sister languages. Cognate with Dutch ~verbieden~, English ~forbid~.
en.verbilden:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~bilden~:

• ~bilden~: From MHG ~bilden~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: ~biliden~ ("to form into an image"), from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþijan~, and ~bilidōn~ ("to copy, represent"), from *~biliþōn~; both from the noun *~biliþī~ (whence ~Bild~), whose pre-Germanic origin is obscure, with no secure PIE etymology. Cognate with Dutch ~beelden~, Swedish ~bilda~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Bilden~ forms and educates; ~verbilden~ shapes in the wrong direction: the schooling miscarries and molds amiss.
en.verbinden:
From Middle High German ~verbinden~, from Old High German ~firbintan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frabindan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~binden~:

• ~binden~: From MHG ~binden~, from OHG ~bintan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bindan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bindaną~, from PIE *~bʰendʰ-~ ("to bind, tie"). A class III strong verb with ablaut ~binden~, ~band~, ~gebunden~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a completive or intensive sense, binding something thoroughly or together.

The ~ver-~ prefix amplifies the root sense of binding into "to connect, unite, link" and, in a medical context, "to bandage." The noun ~Verband~ ("association, bandage, compound") derives from the same compound. English ~band~, ~bond~, and ~bind~ all descend from the same PIE *~bʰendʰ-~, as does Sanskrit ~bandhana~ ("binding, bond") and Latin ~offendimentum~ ("chin-strap"). The cognate Old English ~forbindan~ ("to bind up, bandage") followed nearly the same compounding strategy. Cognate with Dutch ~verbinden~, Old English ~forbindan~, Sanskrit ~bandhana~.
en.verbitten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~bitten~:

• ~bitten~: From MHG ~bitten~, from OHG ~bitten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~biddjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bidjaną~, from PIE *~gʷʰedʰ-~ ("to ask for, beseech"). A class V strong verb; the noun ~Bitte~ and the particle ~bitte~ come from the same root. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bidden~ ("to pray"), Danish ~bede~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ reverses or negates the base action.

~Bitten~ is to request; the reflexive ~sich etwas verbitten~ turns the request on its head into a firm refusal: one demands expressly that something not be done.
en.verbleiben:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~ ("to remain, stay"), from OHG ~bilīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~ ("to remain"), from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, to adhere"). Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~ ("to remain"), archaic English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a sense of continuity and formality, remaining in a fixed state.

~Verbleiben~ is the formal, administrative cousin of ~bleiben~. While ~bleiben~ is the everyday word for "to stay," ~verbleiben~ appears in official contexts: ~im Amt verbleiben~ ("to remain in office"), ~Wir verbleiben mit freundlichen Grüßen~ ("We remain with friendly greetings", a formal letter closing). The noun ~Verbleib~ ("whereabouts") is standard in missing-person reports. The PIE root *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere") also produced Greek ~lípos~ ("grease, fat") and English ~life~ (via Proto-Germanic *~lībą~, originally "that which persists, continued existence"). The semantic chain from "to stick" to "to remain" to "to stay alive" is beautifully logical.
en.verbleichen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~bleichen~:

• ~bleichen~: A merger of two verbs: the strong intransitive MHG ~blīchen~ ("to shine, gleam, grow pale"), from OHG ~blīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~blīkaną~; and its weak causative MHG ~bleichen~ ("to make pale"), from OHG ~bleihhen~, from Proto-Germanic *~blaikijaną~. Both from PIE *~bʰleyg-~ ("to shine"). Modern German conjugates it weak, the strong participle ~geblichen~ surviving only marginally. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~bleak~, Dutch ~bleken~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

~Bleichen~ is growing pale; ~verbleichen~ carries it to its end: the color dies away entirely, and in older usage ~verbleichen~ meant outright "to die."
en.verbraten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~braten~:

• ~braten~: From MHG ~brāten~, from OHG ~brātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brēdaną~ ("to roast"), from PIE *~bʰreh₁-~ ("to heat, boil, burn"), the root behind ~brennen~ and English ~brew~. A class VII strong verb (~braten~, ~briet~, ~gebraten~). Cognate with English ~brawn~ (borrowed via Old French), Dutch ~braden~, Old English ~brǣdan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys using up, consuming, or wearing away.

Literally ~verbraten~ is to ruin food by frying it too long; colloquially one ~verbrät~ money or time, either way something is uselessly used up.
en.verbrauchen:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~brauchen~:

• ~brauchen~: From MHG ~brūchen~, from OHG ~brūhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brūkan~ ("to use, employ, consume"), from Proto-Germanic *~brūkaną~, from PIE *~bʰruHg-~ ("to make use of, to enjoy"). Cognate with English ~brook~ ("to tolerate, endure") and Dutch ~bruiken~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, *~fur-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here it carries the sense of "away, through, completely", using something until it is gone.

The compound means "to consume, to use up, to expend"; ~Strom verbrauchen~ ("to consume electricity"), ~Benzin verbrauchen~ ("to use up gasoline"). The ~ver-~ prefix pushes ~brauchen~ ("to need, to use") past mere usage into complete consumption: what is ~verbraucht~ is spent, exhausted, used up. The English cognate ~brook~ (as in "I will not brook any interference") has narrowed dramatically from "to use" to "to tolerate," surviving mainly in literary English. The noun ~Verbraucher~ ("consumer") is the standard German term in economics and law, parallel to ~Verbraucherschutz~ ("consumer protection"). The PIE root *~bʰruHg-~ is distinct from the similar-looking *~bʰewg-~ ("to enjoy, to bend"), though both involve a sense of deriving benefit, a coincidence that has confused more than one etymologist.
en.verbrechen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Brechen~ is to break; ~verbrechen~ is to do wrong by an act: ~das Verbrechen~, "the crime," is the misdeed so committed.
en.verbreiten:
From ~ver-~ + ~breiten~, a deadjectival verb from ~breit~ ("broad, wide"):

• ~breiten~: From the adjective ~breit~, from MHG ~breit~, from OHG ~breit~, from Proto-West Germanic *~braid~, from Proto-Germanic *~braidaz~ ("broad, wide"). Cognate with English ~broad~, Dutch ~breed~, Swedish ~bred~.
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). The prefix here adds the sense of spreading outward or making widely known.

~Verbreiten~ means "to spread, to disseminate, to propagate", etymologically, "to make broad." The reflexive ~sich verbreiten~ ("to spread oneself") is used for diseases, rumors, species, and ideas: anything that extends its range. The derived noun ~Verbreitung~ ("distribution, spread, prevalence") is standard in scientific and media contexts. German ~breit~ and English ~broad~ are direct cognates from PGmc *~braidaz~, though they have diverged phonologically: the German diphthong ~ei~ (from earlier ~ai~) corresponds to English ~oa~ (from earlier ~ā~). The adjective ~verbreitet~ ("widespread, common") functions as a participial adjective; ~weit verbreitet~ ("widely spread") is one of German's most common collocations. Cognate with Dutch ~verbreiden~.
en.verbrennen:
From Middle High German ~verbrennen~, from Old High German ~firbrinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frabrinnan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~brennen~:

• ~brennen~: From MHG ~brennen~, a merger of two OHG verbs: ~brennan~ ("to set on fire," transitive) from Proto-West Germanic *~brannijan~, and ~brinnan~ ("to be on fire," intransitive) from *~brinnan~. The transitive *~brannijan~ was the causative of *~brinnan~, both ultimately from PIE *~bʰrewh₁-~ ("to boil, brew"), making ~brennen~ an unexpected cousin of English ~brew~ and ~broth~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the sense of complete destruction, burning something up entirely.

The archaic English cognate ~forburn~ ("to burn up completely") preserves the same prefix-plus-verb pattern, though it fell out of use centuries ago. Cognate with Dutch ~verbranden~. The completive sense of ~ver-~ in ~verbrennen~ is the same one found in ~verbrauchen~ ("to use up") and ~verschwinden~ ("to vanish"), things that are gone for good.
en.verbringen:
From Middle High German ~verbringen~, equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, from PIE *~bʰrenk-~ ("to bring").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). The prefix here adds the sense of completion or passing through a duration.

~Verbringen~ means almost exclusively "to spend (time)"; ~den Sommer am Meer verbringen~ ("to spend the summer at the sea"). The ~ver-~ prefix transforms the physical act of bringing into a temporal one: time is "brought through" to completion. This is one of the cases where ~ver-~ functions as a perfectivizing prefix, marking the passage of a duration from beginning to end. The word is notably more formal than the colloquial alternative ~Zeit totschlagen~ ("to kill time"), and it carries no negative connotation: one ~verbringt~ time pleasantly or productively. Cognate with Dutch ~doorbrengen~ (a calque using ~door-~ instead of ~ver-~).
en.verbuchen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~buchen~:

• ~buchen~: In its commercial sense ("to book, reserve"), a denominal verb from ~Buch~, modelled on English ~to book~. ~Buch~ is from MHG ~buoch~, OHG ~buoh~, Proto-West Germanic *~bōk~, Proto-Germanic *~bōks~, the same root as English ~beech~, early Germanic writing being scratched onto beech tablets. A separate older ~buchen~ is an adjective, "of the beech tree." Cognate with English ~book~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Buchen~ enters; ~verbuchen~ carries the entry through to completion: an amount is posted finally to an account, and figuratively one ~verbucht~ a success, chalks it up.
en.verdanken:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~danken~:

• ~danken~: From MHG ~danken~, from OHG ~dankōn~ ("to thank"), from Proto-West Germanic *~þankōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankōną~, derived from *~þankaz~ ("thought, gratitude"). Cognate with English ~thank~, Dutch ~danken~, Danish ~takke~, Old English ~þancian~.
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). In this compound, the prefix shifts the direction of gratitude, not thanking someone directly, but owing something to someone.

~Verdanken~ means "to owe, to have to thank for"; ~Das verdanke ich dir~ ("I owe that to you," "I have you to thank for that"). Unlike ~danken~ ("to thank"), which is the active expression of gratitude, ~verdanken~ describes the relationship of indebtedness: it identifies the source to which something is owed. The PIE root *~teng-~ ("to think, to feel") links thinking and thanking in a profound way: to thank someone is literally to think of them, to hold them in mind. This thought-gratitude connection is perfectly preserved in English, where ~think~ and ~thank~ are doublets from the same root. The German noun ~Dank~ ("thanks, gratitude") and ~Gedanke~ ("thought") are likewise siblings, both descending from Proto-Germanic *~þankaz~.
en.verdecken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~decken~:

• ~decken~: From MHG ~decken~, from OHG ~decchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þakkjan~ ("to cover"), from Proto-Germanic *~þakjaną~, a causative formation from *~þaką~ ("roof, thatch"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to cover"); the verb is etymologically "to roof." Cognate with English ~thatch~, Dutch ~dekken~, Swedish ~täcka~; from the same root Latin ~tegere~, whence English ~protect~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys closing or covering: something is shut, blocked, or hidden from view.

~Decken~ lays something over; ~verdecken~ covers so as to keep what lies beneath from view: it conceals, not merely covers.
en.verdenken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~teng-~ ("to think, feel"). A mixed-conjugation verb of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~dachte~ pairs the vowel change ~e~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix and ~k~ > ~ch~. Cognate with English ~think~, Dutch ~denken~, Icelandic ~þekkja~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Denken~ is plain thinking; in the idiom ~jemandem etwas verdenken~ the thinking turns reproachful: one holds it against someone, thinks the worse of them for it.
en.verderben:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~derben~:

• ~derben~: Not an independent verb of modern German; it survives only inside ~verderben~ ("to spoil, ruin"). From MHG ~derben~ ("to perish"), from Proto-West Germanic *~derban~, from Proto-Germanic *~derbaną~ ("to work; to perish"), from PIE *~dʰerHbʰ-~ ("to labor, perish"). A class III strong verb, and the compound keeps the ablaut intact: ~verderben~, ~verdarb~, ~verdorben~. Cognate with Old English ~deorfan~, Lithuanian ~dirbti~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

The root ~derben~ already carried "to perish"; ~ver-~ drives it to completion; something is utterly undone, whether food going bad or a person morally ruined.
en.verdeutlichen:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~deutlich~ + ~-en~:

• ~deutlich~: From MHG ~diuticlīche~ (adverb), from ~diuten~ ("to interpret, explain"), from OHG ~diuten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þiudijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þiudijaną~, derived from *~þeudō~ ("people"). Cognate with Old English ~þēod~ ("people, nation") and English ~Dutch~ (originally meaning simply "of the people").
• ~ver-~: Inseparable prefix from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here it functions as a causative intensifier, meaning "to make (something) so."

~Verdeutlichen~ means "to clarify, to make clear." The deep history of ~deutlich~ is remarkable: its ancestor *~þeudō~ meant "people," and the derived verb *~þiudijaną~ meant "to make popular, to make accessible to the people", hence "to interpret, to explain in plain language." Over centuries, "explained for ordinary folk" became simply "clear, plain." The prefix ~ver-~ intensifies this into "to make clear." English ~Dutch~ and German ~deutsch~ are the same word: both originally meant "of the people, vernacular," as opposed to Latin, the language of the clergy.
en.verdienen:
From MHG ~verdienen~, from OHG ~firdionōn~, ~firthiniōn~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~dienen~, and a calque of Latin ~deservio~:

• ~dienen~: From MHG ~dienen~, from OHG ~dionōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þiunōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~þewaz~ ("servant, bondsman"), from PIE *~tekʷ-~ ("to run, flee"). Cognate with Old English ~þēow~ ("servant"), Gothic ~þius~ ("servant").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix strengthens the root toward completion, serving all the way through, thereby earning.

The fact that ~verdienen~ is a documented calque of Latin ~deservio~ ("to serve fully, to deserve") is linguistically remarkable. Latin ~deservio~ is itself built from ~de-~ ("thoroughly") + ~servio~ ("to serve"), the same structural logic as ~ver-~ + ~dienen~. Both languages independently hit upon the same conceptual move: to earn or deserve something is to have served for it completely. The modern German word carries both senses (~verdienen~ means both "to earn" (money) and "to deserve" (merit)) just as English ~deserve~ preserves only the merit sense while ~earn~ covers the financial one. Cognate with Dutch ~verdienen~.
en.verdrehen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). Cognate with English ~throw~ (a true cognate: Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist," a sense that "throw a pot" still keeps) plus English ~thread~, Dutch ~draaien~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

From the literal twisting of an object grew the figurative sense of distortion: to ~verdrehen~ facts is to turn them out of their true position.
en.verdreschen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~dreschen~:

• ~dreschen~: From MHG ~dreschen~, from OHG ~dreskan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þreskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þreskaną~, probably from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, turn"). A class III strong verb (~dreschen~, ~drosch~, ~gedroschen~). Cognate with English ~thresh~ and its doublet ~thrash~, Dutch ~dorsen~, Swedish ~tröska~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

The base verb ~dreschen~ once separated grain from chaff; in the compound with ~ver-~ it is colloquial for thrashing someone soundly.
en.verdrießen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~drießen~:

• ~drießen~: No longer an independent verb of modern German: ~drießen~ survives only inside ~verdrießen~ ("to annoy, vex") and its noun ~Verdruss~. From MHG ~driezen~, from OHG ~-driozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þreutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þreutaną~ ("to trouble, weary"), from PIE *~trewd-~ ("to push, press"). A class II strong verb, which is why the compound still yields ~verdross~, ~verdrossen~. Cognate with Old English ~þrēotan~, Latin ~trudere~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Since ~drießen~ has died out as a free verb, its sense "to trouble" survives only in this compound, and in the adjective ~verdrossen~ ("disgruntled").
en.verdrucken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~drucken~:

• ~drucken~: From MHG ~drucken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~ ("to press"). A doublet of ~drücken~ ("to press, push"), which keeps the expected umlaut; ~drucken~ lacks it because Upper German blocked umlaut before a velar geminate, and the form used by the first, southern printers became the technical term. Polish ~drukować~ was borrowed from it.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Drucken~ ("to print") and ~drücken~ ("to press") are doublets of the same Old High German verb; ~verdrucken~ belongs to the first, technical branch and means to misprint.
en.verdrängen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~drängen~:

• ~drängen~: From a merger of two Middle High German verbs: ~drengen~, from OHG ~drengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangwijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrangwijaną~ (a causative); and the now-obsolete ~drangen~, from OHG ~drangōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangōn~ (a denominative). Both from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). ~drängen~ took the transitive senses, the strong ~dringen~ the intransitive. Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~, English ~throng~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

The spatial meaning (to push someone or something out of its place) also yielded the psychological term ~Verdrängung~ ("repression"), the pushing of a thought out of consciousness.
en.verdrücken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

Literally "to press away," but current almost only reflexively: ~sich verdrücken~ means to slip off unnoticed.
en.verehren:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~ehren~:

• ~ehren~: From MHG ~ēren~, from OHG ~ēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~aizāną~, from PIE *~h₂eys-~ ("to respect, to be in awe of"), derived from the noun ~Ehre~ ("honor"), from OHG ~ēra~, from Proto-West Germanic *~aiʀu~, from Proto-Germanic *~aizō~. Cognate with Dutch ~eer~, Old English ~ār~ ("honor, help, pardon"), Old Norse ~eir~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Ehren~ is to give due respect; ~ver-~ raises it to veneration, respect mingled with awe or love.
en.vereinbaren:
From Middle High German ~vereinbæren~, analyzable as ~ver-~ + ~ein~ + ~-bar~ + ~-en~:

• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). The prefix here conveys completion or thoroughness, making something fully ~ein~ ("one").
• ~ein~: From MHG ~ein~, from OHG ~ein~, from Proto-Germanic *~ainaz~, from PIE *~h₂óynos~ ("one"). Cognate with English ~one~, Dutch ~een~, Latin ~ūnus~.
• ~-bar~: An adjectival suffix meaning "able to be, capable of" (compare English ~-able~).
• ~-en~: The verbal infinitive suffix.

The morphological logic is exquisite: to ~vereinbaren~ is literally "to make-one-able", to bring multiple parties or positions into unity, to make agreement possible. The word means "to agree upon, to arrange, to reconcile" and is the standard verb for scheduling appointments (~einen Termin vereinbaren~), reaching agreements (~eine Regelung vereinbaren~), and reconciling contradictions (~diese Aussagen lassen sich schwer vereinbaren~, "these statements are hard to reconcile"). The derived noun ~Vereinbarung~ ("agreement, arrangement") is ubiquitous in legal and business German. The related verb ~verlautbaren~ ("to announce, to make public") follows an identical formation pattern: ~ver-~ + ~laut~ + ~-bar~ + ~-en~.
en.vereinen:
~Ver-~ + ~einen~. From ~ver-~ + ~ein~ + ~-en~:

• ~ein~: From MHG ~ein~, from OHG ~ein~ ("one"), from Proto-Germanic *~ainaz~, from PIE *~h₁óynos~ ("one"). Cognate with English ~one~, Dutch ~een~, Latin ~ūnus~ (from the same PIE root via Italic).
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix conveys thoroughness and completion, to make fully one.

~Vereinen~ means "to unite, to join together, to combine." The word achieved its greatest rhetorical weight in the phrase ~die Vereinten Nationen~ ("the United Nations") and in the historic context of German reunification: ~das vereinte Deutschland~ ("united Germany"). The closely related verb ~vereinigen~ (built with the same components but an additional ~-ig-~ suffix) is nearly synonymous but tends toward more abstract or political usage (~Wiedervereinigung~, "reunification"). The derived noun ~Verein~ ("club, association, society") is one of the most characteristically German institutions: from sports clubs to choral societies to rabbit-breeding associations, the ~Verein~ is the organizing principle of German civic life. The wry observation ~die Deutschen gründen einen Verein~ ("Germans found a club") whenever two or more share a hobby captures something real about German associational culture. The PIE root *~h₁óynos~ ("one") ultimately gives both German ~ein~ and Latin ~ūnus~, making ~vereinen~ and English ~unite~ (from Latin ~unīre~) etymological cousins expressing the same idea through entirely different derivational paths.
en.vereinfachen:
A denominative verb formed with ~ver-~ + ~einfach~ + ~-en~:

• ~einfach~: From ~ein-~ ("one") + ~-fach~ ("fold"), literally "onefold", compare English ~onefold~ and ~simple~ (from Latin ~simplex~, also literally "one-fold").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix functions as a verbalizer, turning an adjective into a verb meaning "to make [adjective]."

The ~ver-~ prefix in its verbalizing role appears across dozens of German adjectives: ~vereinfachen~ ("to simplify"), ~vergrößern~ ("to enlarge"), ~verbessern~ ("to improve"). The underlying adjective ~einfach~ entered German in the 16th century, modeled on Latin ~simplex~, and ~vereinfachen~ followed naturally. The English cognate of ~-fach~ survives in ~manifold~, ~twofold~, and ~threefold~.
en.vereinigen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~einigen~:

• ~einigen~: From MHG ~einegen~, ~einigen~, from OHG ~gieinīgen~, formed from ~ein~ + the verb-forming suffix ~-igen~. ~ein~ goes back through Proto-West Germanic *~ain~ and Proto-Germanic *~ainaz~ to PIE *~h₁óynos~ ("one, single"); to ~einigen~ is thus to make parties into "one." Cognate with English ~one~, Dutch ~een~, Danish ~en~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Where ~einigen~ brings parties to agreement, ~vereinigen~ joins them into an actual unit; hence the ~United~ States and the German ~Wiedervereinigung~ ("reunification").
en.verenden:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~enden~:

• ~enden~: From MHG ~enden~, from OHG ~entōn~ ("to end, to complete, to die"), a denominative from ~Ende~ (OHG ~enti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andī~, from Proto-Germanic *~andijaz~, from PIE *~h₂entíos~ "front, forehead," from *~h₂ent-~ "face, front"). Cognate with English ~end~, the prefix ~ent-~ and Latin ~ante~ ("before").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Plain ~enden~ ("to stop") is driven by ~ver-~ to a fatal conclusion: ~verenden~ is said of an animal's death.
en.verfahren:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

From spatial ~fahren~ ("to travel a route") arose the figurative "to proceed, to act"; one ~verfährt~ with a matter as one takes a road.
en.verfallen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

From the image of falling down came that of decline: a building, a right, or a deadline ~verfällt~ by slowly falling out of validity and standing.
en.verfangen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~fangen~:

• ~fangen~: From MHG ~vāhen~, from OHG ~fāhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~fanhaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to secure, fasten"). A strong verb, originally ~fāhan~ / ~fieng~ / ~gefangan~; the modern present stem ~fang-~ was taken analogically from the past forms. Cognate with English ~fang~, Dutch ~vangen~, West Frisian ~fange~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Used almost only reflexively: ~sich verfangen~ is to become so caught in something that one cannot get free, in a net or in one's own contradiction.
en.verfassen:
From Middle High German ~verfazzen~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~fassen~:

• ~fassen~: From MHG ~vazzen~, from OHG ~fazzōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fatōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fatōną~ ("to fetch, hold"), from PIE *~pod-~ ("to fetch"), itself possibly related to *~ped-~ ("to walk, step"). Cognate with English ~fetch~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix can indicate completion, transformation, or the result of an action.

The semantic journey from "to grasp, seize" (~fassen~) to "to compose, write" (~verfassen~) runs through the intermediate sense of "to put into a form", one still visible in ~fassen~ itself, which can mean "to formulate, express." The ~ver-~ prefix adds completive force, so ~verfassen~ is roughly "to fully formulate" and hence "to author, compose, draft." The derivative ~Verfassung~ means both "constitution" (a nation's foundational document) and "state, condition" (one's physical or mental constitution), the same word for a country's governing text and for one's personal well-being.
en.verfechten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~fechten~:

• ~fechten~: From MHG ~vëhten~ ("to fight"), from OHG ~fëhtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fehtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fehtaną~, perhaps from PIE *~peḱ-~ ("to pluck, comb"), though not securely. A class III strong verb (~fechten~, ~focht~, ~gefochten~); the ~o~ of the Präteritum comes from the old plural stem (OHG ~fuhtum~). Cognate with English ~fight~, Dutch ~vechten~, Danish ~fægte~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

From ~fechten~ ("to fight, fence") comes standing up for a cause: to ~verfechten~ a view is to fight for it as with a blade.
en.verfehlen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~fehlen~:

• ~fehlen~: From MHG ~vælen~, ~velen~, ~valen~, borrowed from Old French ~faillir~ ("to fail, be lacking"), from Latin ~fallō~ ("to deceive, cause to stumble"), from PIE *~(s)gʷʰh₂el-~ ("to stumble"). One of the few common German verbs that entered the language via Old French rather than by Germanic inheritance. Cognate with English ~fail~, French ~faillir~, Italian ~fallire~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Fehlen~ is to be lacking; made transitive with ~ver-~ it becomes missing: failing to hit a target, catch a train, or meet a person.
en.verfertigen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~fertigen~:

• ~fertigen~: From MHG ~vertigen~ ("to prepare, make ready"), equivalent to ~fertig~ + ~-en~. The adjective ~fertig~ (MHG ~fertec~, OHG ~fartīg~) belongs to ~fart~ ("journey"), from Proto-Germanic *~farą~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to cross"); ~fertig~ originally meant "ready for a journey." Cognate with Dutch ~vaardig~, Low German ~fardig~, Old English ~fierd~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Fertigen~ ("to make ready, produce") is carried to its conclusion by ~ver-~: to ~verfertigen~ something is to finish making it.
en.verfilmen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~filmen~:

• ~filmen~: A denominative verb from ~Film~ + ~-en~. The noun was borrowed from English ~film~, from Old English ~filmen~ ("membrane, thin skin"), from Proto-West Germanic and Proto-Germanic *~filmin-~, from PIE *~pel-mo-~ ("membrane"), from the root *~pel-~ ("to cover, skin"). A returning loan: "membrane" to "coating" to "motion picture."
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ derives a verb from a noun or adjective, meaning to make something into that.

Unlike plain ~filmen~ ("to record with a camera"), ~verfilmen~ means turning a work (usually a book) into a film.
en.verflechten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~flechten~:

• ~flechten~: From MHG ~vlëhten~, from OHG ~flëhtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~flehtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~flehtaną~, from PIE *~pleḱ-~ ("to plait, weave"). A class III strong verb (~flechten~, ~flocht~, ~geflochten~), its Präteritum ~o~ generalized from the old plural stem. Cognate with English ~flax~, Dutch ~vlechten~, Old Norse ~flétta~, Swedish ~fläta~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

From the craft of ~flechten~ ("to plait") came an image of connection: interwoven interests or economies are as knit together as the strands of a basket.
en.verfliegen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~fliegen~:

• ~fliegen~: From MHG ~vliegen~, from OHG ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"), an extension of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim") that also gave ~fließen~. The vowel path *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of class II strong verbs. Cognate with English ~fly~, Dutch ~vliegen~, Danish ~flyve~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

As a scent or a mood dissolves into the air, so time ~verfliegt~: the process runs out until nothing of it remains.
en.verfolgen:
From ~ver-~ + ~folgen~, a calque of Latin ~persequor~:

• ~folgen~: From MHG ~volgen~, from OHG ~folgēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fulgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fulgāną~. Cognate with English ~follow~, Dutch ~volgen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds persistent, forward direction, following relentlessly onward.

The calque of Latin ~persequor~ (itself ~per-~ ("through, thoroughly") + ~sequor~ ("to follow")) shows the same structural thinking as ~ver-~ + ~folgen~. In English, the Latin-derived descendant is ~persecute~ (via the past-participial stem ~persecutus~), which has narrowed to its most extreme sense; German ~verfolgen~ covers the full range from "to pursue" (a goal) to "to follow" (a story) to "to prosecute" (in law) to "to persecute" (historically). The historical weight of ~verfolgen~ in German is thus considerable: the noun ~Verfolgung~ ("pursuit, persecution") carries the legacy of political and religious persecution across centuries. Cognate with Dutch ~vervolgen~, Swedish ~förfölja~.
en.verformen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~formen~:

• ~formen~: From MHG ~formen~, a denominative from the noun ~Form~ (MHG ~form~), borrowed from Latin ~forma~ ("shape, figure, appearance"), whose origin is uncertain: perhaps from Etruscan *~morma~, from Ancient Greek ~morphe~ ("shape"), with dissimilation of *~m-m~ to *~f-m~. German built a plain denominative here rather than an ~-ieren~ verb. Cognate with English ~form~ and ~morph~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Formen~ gives shape; ~verformen~ takes it out of its proper shape: a workpiece ~verformt~ under load or heat.
en.verfügen:
From Middle High German ~vervüegen~, ~ferfüegen~, from ~ver-~ + ~fügen~:

• ~fügen~: From MHG ~füegen~, ~fuogen~, from OHG ~fuogen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōgijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōgijaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to join, attach"). Cognate with Dutch ~voegen~, and distantly with English ~fair~ (from the same PIE root via a different branch), Latin ~pāx~ ("peace"), and English ~peace~ and ~pact~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix often adds a sense of away, wrongly, or completion.

The compound ~verfügen~ developed two distinct senses from the core meaning of "to join, arrange completely": "to decree, to order" (arranging something officially into place) and, as ~verfügen über~, "to have at one's disposal" (having something joined to one's hand, within reach). The PIE root *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to join") also underlies English ~fay~ (archaic, "to join two surfaces perfectly") and the peace/pact cluster through Latin. Cognate with German Low German ~verfögen~, Dutch ~vervoegen~, Danish ~forføje~, Swedish ~förfoga~.
en.verführen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Führen~ ("to lead") becomes misleading with ~ver-~: to ~verführen~ is to lead another off the right path.
en.vergeben:
From Middle High German ~vergeben~, from Old High German ~fargeban~. Equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). The prefix here adds the sense of giving away completely or giving over.

~Vergeben~ means both "to forgive" (~jemandem vergeben~, "to forgive someone") and "to award, to assign" (~einen Auftrag vergeben~, "to award a contract," ~eine Stelle ist schon vergeben~, "the position is already taken"). The forgiveness sense derives from the idea of giving something away completely: releasing the debt, surrendering the grievance. The awarding sense derives from the idea of giving something out, distributing it. The derived noun ~Vergebung~ ("forgiveness") is elevated and theological, while ~Vergabe~ ("allocation, awarding") is administrative. English ~forgive~ (from Old English ~forġiefan~) is a structural cognate: ~for-~ corresponds to ~ver-~, and ~give~ to ~geben~, both from PGmc *~gebaną~. The parallel is exact: ~vergeben~ and ~forgive~ are the same compound word preserved independently in two branches of West Germanic. Cognate with Dutch ~vergeven~, English ~forgive~.
en.vergehen:
From Middle High German ~vergān~, ~vergāngēn~, from Old High German ~firgān~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fragān~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from OHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here it conveys the sense of passing away, disappearing.

The literal sense is "to go away completely," yielding "to pass (of time), to fade, to expire." The past participle ~vergangen~ is used as an adjective meaning "past" (~die vergangene Woche~, "last week"), and the noun ~Vergangenheit~ means "the past", literally "the state of having gone away." The verb also has a darker reflexive use: ~sich an jemandem vergehen~ means "to commit an offense against someone," where "going away" from proper conduct becomes transgression. English preserves a striking parallel in ~to pass away~ (to die) and ~the past~ (what has gone), showing that both Germanic languages independently developed this metaphor of time as motion. The ~ver-~ prefix here works in its "away, to disappearance" sense, the same one found in ~verschwinden~ ("to vanish"), ~verlieren~ ("to lose"), and ~vergessen~ ("to forget").
en.vergelten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~gelten~:

• ~gelten~: From MHG ~gelten~, from OHG ~geltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~geldaną~, possibly from PIE *~gʰeldʰ-~.
