The range narrowed over time: OHG ~geltan~ meant "to pay, repay, be worth," while the modern verb centers on "to be valid, to count." Cognate with English ~yield~ (from the same root), Dutch ~gelden~, Icelandic ~gjalda~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

The old sense of ~gelten~ ("to pay, repay") is preserved here: to ~vergelten~ is to pay back good with good and ill with ill.
en.vergessen:
From Middle High German ~vergëȥȥen~, from Old High German ~firgëȥȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fragetan~ ("to give up, forget"). Compound of ~ver-~ + the extinct root *~getan~:

• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a sense of losing or going wrong: "seizing wrongly" → "losing one's grip on."
• *~getan~: From Proto-Germanic *~getaną~ ("to find a way, attain, acquire"), from PIE *~gʰe(n)d-~ ("to take, seize"). Cognate with Latin ~prehendō~ ("to snatch, seize"), Ancient Greek ~χανδάνω~ (~khandánō~, "to hold, contain"). The simplex is extinct in modern German; it survives only inside compounds.

The original sense of *~fragetaną~ was "to give up one's grasp on, release." From "releasing grip" → "losing hold" → "forgetting" is a natural semantic slide. What makes ~vergessen~ a superb teaching example is that English ~forget~ follows the identical path: from Old English ~forġietan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fragetan~, the same compound, the same PIE root, the same metaphor. The German prefix ~ver-~ and the English prefix ~for-~ are cognates (both from *~fra-~); the root *~getan~ is the ancestor of the English dialectal ~yet~ and archaic ~get~ in the sense of "to reach, find." Cognate with Dutch ~vergeten~, West Frisian ~fergette~, English ~forget~.
en.vergießen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~gießen~:

• ~gießen~: From MHG ~giezen~, from OHG ~giozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geutan~ ("to pour"), from Proto-Germanic *~geutaną~, from PIE *~gʰewd-~ ("to pour"). The sense of casting metal and glass is attested since Old High German (participle ~gigozzan~). Cognate with English ~gush~, Dutch ~gieten~, Old English ~geotan~, Gothic ~giutan~, Swedish ~gjuta~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

From ~gießen~ ("to pour") comes shedding: blood or tears are poured out, away from the body.
en.vergleichen:
From Middle High German ~verglīchen~, from Old High German ~firgalīhhōn~. Equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~gleichen~:

• ~gleichen~: From MHG ~gelīchen~, from OHG ~gilīhhōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~galīkōną~, a denominative of *~galīkaz~ ("having the same form or body"), from *~ga-~ (collective prefix) + *~-līkaz~ ("body, form"), from PIE *~leyg-~ ("image, likeness, similarity"). Cognate with English ~like~ (verb), Dutch ~lijken~, Swedish ~lika~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds completive and comparative force, bringing a likening all the way through, converting resemblance into systematic analysis.

The PIE root *~leyg-~ ("image, likeness") gave both German ~gleich~ ("same, equal") and English ~like~. Old English ~līcian~ ("to please, resemble") is the same verb as ~gleichen~, but the two diverged over time: English ~like~ shifted toward approval and pleasure while German ~gleichen~ stayed with resemblance. ~Vergleichen~ with its completive ~ver-~ prefix became the word for deliberate comparison, not merely noticing similarity but measuring it. The legal noun ~Vergleich~ ("comparison; out-of-court settlement") reflects this: parties to a dispute are ~verglichen~, brought into formal equivalence and resolved. Cognate with Dutch ~vergelijken~, English ~like~.
en.verglimmen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~glimmen~:

• ~glimmen~: From MHG ~glimmen~ ("to glow, gleam"), from Proto-Germanic *~glimmaną~, from PIE *~ǵʰley-~ ("to shine, shimmer"). Modern German inflects it both ways: strong ~glomm~, ~geglommen~ holds on in elevated register, while weak ~glimmte~, ~geglimmt~ has dominated ordinary usage since the eighteenth century. Cognate with English ~gleam~, ~glimmer~ and ~glimpse~, Dutch ~glimmen~, Norwegian ~glime~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

Where ~glimmen~ names a faint glow, ~ver-~ carries it to its end: the embers ~verglimmen~ until the last spark dies.
en.vergraben:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~graben~:

• ~graben~: From MHG ~graben~, from OHG ~graban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from PIE *~gʰrebʰ-~ ("to dig, scratch, bury"). A class VI strong verb (~graben~, ~grub~, ~gegraben~). Cognate with English ~grave~ as a verb (now only in ~engrave~ and ~graven image~), Gothic ~graban~, Dutch ~graven~, Old Norse ~grafa~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys closing or covering: something is shut, blocked, or hidden from view.

Vergraben lives in both directions: literally one buries treasure in the earth, figuratively one buries one's face in one's hands or oneself in work.
en.vergreifen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~greifen~:

• ~greifen~: From MHG ~grîfen~, from OHG ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). A class I strong verb (~greift~, ~griff~, ~gegriffen~), like ~reiten~ and ~schneiden~. Cognate with English ~gripe~, Dutch ~grijpen~, Low German ~griepen~, Old Norse ~gripa~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

Vergreifen today is almost only reflexive: sich an etwas vergreifen means to lay hold of something unlawfully, whether of another's property or, figuratively, of good taste.
en.vergrößern:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~größer~ (comparative of ~groß~) + ~-n~:

• ~groß~: From MHG ~grōȥ~, from OHG ~grōȥ~ ("big, thick, coarse"), from Proto-Germanic *~grautaz~, from PIE *~gʰrewd-~ ("to grind, crush"), from *~gʰer-~ ("to rub, grind"). Cognate with Old Saxon ~grōt~, Dutch ~groot~, English ~great~.
• ~ver-~: Inseparable prefix from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here it functions as a causative intensifier: "to make (more so)."

~Vergrößern~ means "to enlarge, to magnify, to increase." Like ~nähern~ (from the comparative ~näher~), it is built from a comparative form: ~größer~ ("bigger") becomes a verb meaning "to make bigger." The underlying adjective ~groß~ has a surprising origin in PIE *~gʰrewd-~ ("to grind"): the original sense was "coarse, coarse-grained" (as in ground material), which shifted to "thick, large, great." English ~great~ is the cognate, and its semantic journey parallels the German: from "coarse, thick" to "big" to "important, magnificent." The related German words ~Grieß~ ("semolina"), ~Grütze~ ("groats"), and ~grob~ ("coarse") all preserve the original grinding sense.
en.vergucken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~gucken~:

• ~gucken~: From MHG ~gücken~, ~guggen~ ("to look inquisitively, to peek"), of uncertain origin, perhaps from MHG ~gücken~, OHG ~guckōn~ ("to cuckoo"), via the image of peeping out from cover. The variant ~kucken~ is attributed to influence from Low German ~kieken~. Colloquial and northern/central German; the south prefers ~schauen~. Cognate with Dutch ~kijken~, Luxembourgish ~kucken~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

Sich vergucken is colloquially two-sided: either to see something wrong or to fall for someone.
en.vergären:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~gären~:

• ~gären~: From MHG ~jesen~, from OHG ~jesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~jesaną~, from PIE *~yes-~ ("to boil, foam, ferment"). The initial ~j-~ hardened to ~g-~, and the ~r~ was carried in from the past forms ~gor~, ~gegoren~. Historically a class V strong verb; today the strong forms serve literal fermenting and weak ~gärte~, ~gegärt~ the figurative sense. Cognate with English ~yeast~, German ~Gischt~, Ancient Greek ~ζέω~ (zéō, "to boil").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

The base verb ~gären~ names the ongoing process; ~vergären~ takes it to its end; the must ferments until no sugar is left and the fermentation dies out on its own.
en.vergönnen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~gönnen~:

• ~gönnen~: From MHG ~gunnen~, from OHG ~giunnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gaunnan~ ("to grant"), from the prefix *~ga-~ + *~unnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~unnaną~ ("to grant"), from PIE *~h₃neh₂-~ ("to enjoy"). To ~gönnen~ is to not begrudge someone something. Cognate with Dutch ~gunnen~, Yiddish ~ginen~, Greek ~oninēmi~ ("to be of use").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Gönnen~ is to not begrudge another something; ~vergönnen~ is the elevated form, often used in the passive: "es ist mir vergönnt" means "it is granted to me."
en.verhaften:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~haften~:

• ~haften~: From ~Haft~ + ~-en~. ~Haft~ descends through MHG ~haft~, ~hafte~ ("captivity") and OHG ~haft~ to PIE *~kh₂p-tó-~, from *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize"). Hence both senses: "to stick, adhere" (to be held fast) and "to be liable." Cognate with English ~captive~, Latin ~captus~, Old English ~hæft~, Old Irish ~cacht~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

From the image of making fast came the modern main sense "to arrest": the arrested person is seized and held; alongside it survives "to be verhaftet to something" in the sense of being inwardly bound.
en.verhalten:
From Middle High German ~verhalten~, from Old High German ~firhaltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frahaldan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~, from PIE *~kel-~ ("to drive, to herd").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the sense of holding something in check or directing one's manner of holding.

The reflexive ~sich verhalten~ ("to behave, to conduct oneself") is the dominant modern usage, literally "to hold oneself in a particular way." The impersonal ~es verhält sich so~ ("the matter stands thus, it is the case that") uses ~verhalten~ to describe how facts are configured relative to each other. The noun ~Verhalten~ ("behavior") and adjective ~verhalten~ ("restrained, subdued") both descend from the same source. Martin Heidegger famously used ~sich verhalten zu~ ("to comport oneself toward") as a key term in ~Sein und Zeit~: ~Dasein~ is the being that can ~sich verhalten~ toward its own existence, that is, relate to and take a stance on its own being. The legal jargon sense ~sich zu etwas verhalten~ ("to take a position on, to address") extends the metaphor of holding to judicial deliberation. Cognate with Middle Low German ~vörhōlden~, Dutch ~verhouden~ ("to be in proportion"), English ~forhold~ (archaic).
en.verhandeln:
From ~ver-~ + ~handeln~. Compound of:

• ~handeln~: From OHG ~hantalōn~ ("to grasp, take in hand, handle"), from MHG ~handeln~ ("to do, carry out, conduct"), from ~Hand~ ("hand"), from Proto-West Germanic *~handu~, from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~. The semantic journey from "grasping with the hand" to "dealing, trading" occurred via merchant language in the 16th century.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the sense of thoroughness and completion.

The progression from physical handling to abstract negotiation is mirrored in English ~handle~ (from the same Germanic root). German ~verhandeln~ literally means "to deal through completely", to negotiate until a matter is resolved. The noun ~Verhandlung~ ("negotiation, trial") reveals the word's importance in legal and diplomatic language. Cognate with English ~handle~, Dutch ~verhandelen~.
en.verhassen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~hassen~:

• ~hassen~: From MHG ~hazzen~, from OHG ~hazzon~, from Proto-Germanic *~hatāną~, a stative-fientive verb derived from *~hataz~ ("hate, hostility"), from PIE *~keh2d-~ ("grief, hatred"). Cognate with English ~hate~, Dutch ~haten~, Old Norse ~hata~, Gothic ~hatan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

As a finite verb verhassen is rare; what stays alive is chiefly the participle verhasst "generally hated, detested."
en.verhauen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~hauen~:

• ~hauen~: From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). Originally a class VII strong verb (~hauen~, ~hieb~, ~gehauen~), partially weakened colloquially, where ~haute~ competes with ~hieb~. Cognate with English ~hew~, Latin ~cūdere~ ("to strike, forge").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Verhauen leads two lives: the coarse "to thrash" and the colloquial "to botch thoroughly", to mess up an exam.
en.verheben:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb: the past ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ continue the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

Sich verheben belongs to the reflexive "sich ver-" verbs of mishap: one lifts wrongly and pulls a muscle, much as one sprains an ankle or wrenches a joint.
en.verhehlen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~hehlen~:

• ~hehlen~: From MHG ~heln~, from OHG ~helan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helaną~, from PIE *~ḱel-~ ("to cover, conceal"). Originally a class IV strong verb (~helan~, ~hal~, ~gaholan~), now conjugated weak (~hehlte~, ~gehehlt~); the old strong participle survives in ~verhohlen~ and ~unverhohlen~. Cognate with Old English ~helan~, Latin ~cēlāre~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Since ~hehlen~ already means "to conceal," ver- here only reinforces the base sense; today verhehlen is literary and usually stands negated, "I will not conceal."
en.verheilen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~heilen~:

• ~heilen~: From MHG ~heilen~, from OHG ~heilen~ (causative, "to make whole") and ~heilēn~ (inchoative, "to become whole"), from Proto-West Germanic *~hailijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hailijaną~, from *~hailaz~ ("whole, healthy"), from PIE *~kéh₂ilos~ ("healthy, whole"). Cognate with English ~heal~, Dutch ~helen~, Old Norse ~heila~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Verheilen is the intransitive healing-to-completion of a wound: it closes over until nothing remains open; the auxiliary is "sein."
en.verheiraten:
From ~ver-~ + ~heiraten~. Compound of:

• ~heiraten~: From MHG ~hīrāten~, derived from ~hīrāt~ ("marriage"), from OHG ~hīrāt~ ("wedding, marriage"), from Proto-West Germanic *~hīwarād~. This compound word originally meant something like "household arrangement", from *~hīwą~ ("household, family") + *~rādą~ ("counsel, plan").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the sense of completion, the definitive act of joining in marriage.

The Old English cognate ~hīred~ meant "family, household, retinue," showing the same root but a different semantic path. The reflexive form ~sich verheiraten~ ("to get married") uses ~ver-~ to mark the irrevocable change of state, much as ~sich verlieben~ marks the irreversible plunge into love. The root *~hīwą~ is also the ancestor of English ~hide~ (a unit of land sufficient to support one household).
en.verheißen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~heißen~:

• ~heißen~: From MHG ~heiȥen~, from OHG ~heiȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haitan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haitaną~, tentatively from PIE *~ḱeyd-~ ("to call"). The original sense was "to command"; "to be called" developed from the passive use. Cognate with Dutch ~heten~, Gothic ~haitan~, English ~behest~ and archaic ~hight~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

From ~heißen~ "to command, to say" came the solemn "to pledge": the verheißene land is the promised one. The verb is now elevated and biblically colored.
en.verhelfen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~helfen~:

• ~helfen~: From MHG ~hëlfen~, from OHG ~hëlfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helpaną~, from PIE *~ḱelb-~, *~ḱelp-~. A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~e~-~a~-~o~ ablaut pattern (~helfen~, ~half~, ~geholfen~). Cognate with English ~help~, Dutch ~helpen~, Danish ~hjælpe~, Norwegian ~hjelpe~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Verhelfen always governs "someone to something": one obtains for another what is due or lacking, not merely helping in a general way.
en.verhindern:
From MHG ~verhindern~, from OHG ~firhintaren~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~hindern~:

• ~hindern~: From MHG ~hindern~, from OHG ~hintaren~. Denominative from ~hinter~ ("behind, in back of"). ~Hinter~ is from OHG ~hintar~, from Proto-Germanic *~hinder~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱem-tér-~ ("down, back, along, through"), related to *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). Cognate with Old English ~hinder~ ("in the rear"), Gothic ~hindar~ ("beyond").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a completive or intensifying sense, blocking something all the way, preventing it entirely.

The structural metaphor of ~verhindern~ is vivid: to place something ~hinter~ ("behind") an action, using ~ver-~ to make the hindrance complete, thereby preventing it. The English cognate ~hinder~ (as both verb and adjective) descends directly from the same Proto-Germanic root, and the archaic English adverb ~hinder~ (meaning "in the rear") is the same word. Cognate with English ~hinder~, Dutch ~verhinderen~.
en.verhängen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~hängen~:

• ~hängen~: The merger of three OHG verbs: ~hāhan~ (strong, transitive; past ~hieng~, participle ~gehangan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~hą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~hanhaną~; ~hangēn~ (weak, intransitive); and the causative ~hengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hangijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hangijaną~. The distinction is upheld chiefly in the past tense: intransitive ~hing~/~gehangen~ versus transitive ~hängte~/~gehängt~. Cognate with Dutch ~hangen~, English ~hang~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys closing or covering: something is shut, blocked, or hidden from view.

From the concrete verhängen (draping something with a cloth) came the legal turn "to impose a penalty": the sanction is, as it were, hung over the person concerned.
en.verhören:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Transitively verhören means "to interrogate, to question"; reflexively, by contrast, sich verhören means "to mishear", the same form, two opposite prefix functions.
en.verjagen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~jagen~:

• ~jagen~: From MHG ~jagen~ ("to hurry, drive, pursue, hunt"), from OHG ~jagōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~jagōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~jakkōną~, a ~nā~-iterative formation, likely rebuilt from PIE *~h₁eyǵʰ-~ ("to strive, chase"). Attested since the eighth century; further pre-Germanic etymology is obscure.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

Verjagen adds to mere hunting the goal of removal: what counts is not the pursuit but that the pursued clears the field.
en.verkaufen:
From Middle High German ~verkoufen~, from Old High German ~firkoufen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frakōpōn~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, itself a denominative of *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"), borrowed from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper, petty trader"), likely a pre-Latin Mediterranean loanword. The noun *~kaupô~ also yields modern German ~Kaufmann~ ("merchant") and the place-name element ~-kauf~ in towns like ~Kaufbeuren~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix often adds a sense of completion, disposal, or doing something definitively away.

A remarkable Latin borrowing that spread across all of Germanic: Latin ~caupō~ (the lowly innkeeper who sold food and drink) gave Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, which became ~kaufen~ (to buy), ~verkaufen~ (to sell), Dutch ~kopen~ / ~verkopen~, and, via a different route, English ~cheap~ (originally "a bargain, a market," from the same root, as in the London place name ~Cheapside~). Cognate with Dutch ~verkopen~, Yiddish ~פֿאַרקויפֿן~ (~farkoyfn~).
en.verkehren:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~kehren~:

• ~kehren~: A homograph concealing two distinct verbs. ~Kehren~ (1) "to turn": from MHG ~kēren~, from OHG ~kēran~, ~chēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kairijaną~ or *~kausijaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly connected to *~gers-~ ("to twist, bend, turn"). ~Kehren~ (2) "to sweep": from MHG ~kern~, ~keren~, from OHG ~kerian~, ~cherian~, from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~ ("to scrape, scratch"), from PIE *~ger-~ ("to scrape"). Etymologically unrelated, merged through phonological convergence.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Verkehren goes back to ~kehren~ "to turn," not to the identical-sounding "to sweep": from turning to and fro came "to move about, to keep company", one verkehrt in a circle, just as ships verkehren between two ports.
en.verkennen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~kennen~:

• ~kennen~: From MHG ~kennen~, from OHG ~kennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kannijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~ ("to know"), a causative of *~kunnaną~, from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"). A member of the Rückumlaut cohort: the present shows umlaut (~ich kenne~), the preterite does not (~kannte~, ~gekannt~). Cognate with Dutch ~kennen~, Scots and English ~ken~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ reverses or negates the base action.

Verkennen negates recognizing: one knows, but wrongly; one misjudges a situation, a talent, a person, and precisely thereby gets them wrong.
en.verklagen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~klagen~:

• ~klagen~: From MHG ~klagen~, from OHG ~klagōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klagōn~ ("to lament, complain"), a denominative verb from *~klagu~ ("lamentation, complaint"). The ultimate origin is uncertain: often compared to Proto-Indo-Iranian *~garjʰ-~, but phonologically difficult; some favor an onomatopoeic origin. It keeps both an emotional and a legal sense.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Verklagen takes up the legal side of ~klagen~ and directs it against a person: to klagen is to voice grief or to file suit; to verklagen someone is to take them to court.
en.verklappen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~klappen~:

• ~klappen~: From Middle Low German ~klappen~, from Old Saxon *~klappōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klappōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klappōną~. The verb is onomatopoeic. Cognate with English ~clap~, Dutch ~klappen~, Old High German ~klapfō~ ("a clapping sound"); also related to ~klaffen~ ("to gape").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

Verklappen is nautical: waste is disposed of into the sea by opening a vessel's bottom flaps, hence "ver-klappen," from ~Klappe~ ("flap").
en.verkleben:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~kleben~:

• ~kleben~: From MHG ~kleben~, from OHG ~klebēn~ ("to stick"), from Proto-West Germanic *~klibēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klibēną~, from PIE *~gleyb-~ ("to stick, adhere"), a durative formation from the strong root *~kleibēną~ ("to adhere, to climb"). Cognate with English ~cleave~ and ~climb~, Old Norse ~klīfa~ ("to climb").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys closing or covering: something is shut, blocked, or hidden from view.

Verkleben means gluing shut and sticking together: a joint is sealed, an envelope glued up, and in the passive one's eyes verkleben, stick shut.
en.verklicken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~klicken~:

• ~klicken~: Attested from the 16th century, from MHG *~klicken~, preserved in ~zerklicken~ ("to break an eggshell"); ultimately imitative. Either cognate with or formed in parallel to Dutch ~klikken~, English ~click~, French ~cliquer~. The computing sense is a 20th-century semantic loan from English. Regular and weak.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

Sich verklicken is recent and purely digital: the mouse-click goes astray, formed on the model of sich vertippen ("to mistype") and sich verwählen ("to misdial").
en.verklingen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~klingen~:

• ~klingen~: From MHG ~klingen~, from OHG ~klingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~klinganą~, almost certainly of onomatopoeic origin. A class III strong verb (~klingt~, ~klang~, ~geklungen~), the same pattern as ~singen~. Cognate with English ~clink~ and ~clang~, Middle Dutch ~klinken~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

Verklingen is the sounding-out of a tone: the sound grows fainter and fainter until it has wholly passed away: the prefix carries the gradual dying-out.
en.verklären:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~klären~:

• ~klären~: From MHG ~klæren~, denominal from ~klar~ ("clear, bright"), borrowed from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch ~klār~, from Old French ~cler~, from Latin ~clārus~ ("bright, renowned"). English ~clear~ arrived by the same route: cousins by borrowing rather than inheritance.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

From making clear came making radiant: religiously the Transfiguration of Christ, secularly the glossing-over of the past; one sees it in a transfigured light.
en.verkneifen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~kneifen~:

• ~kneifen~: An adaptation of the older ~kneipen~, from Middle Low German ~knīpen~, from Old Saxon *~knīpan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~knīpan~, from PIE *~gneybʰ-~ ("to pinch"). A class I strong verb (~kneifen~, ~kniff~, ~gekniffen~); the ~-f-~ is an artificial respelling that displaced ~kneipen~ only over the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Cognate with Dutch ~knijpen~, English ~knife~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys closing or covering: something is shut, blocked, or hidden from view.

From pinching came pinching-shut and suppressing: one verkneift oneself a laugh, a remark, the pain, the lips as if pinched closed.
en.verknüpfen:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~knüpfen~:

• ~knüpfen~: From MHG ~knüpfen~, from OHG ~knupfen~, related to ~Knopf~ ("button, knob"), from Proto-Germanic *~knuppaz~ ("lump, clod, knob"), from PIE *~gnewbʰ-~ (an extension of *~gen-~, "to compress, to pinch"). Cognate with Dutch ~knoop~ ("knot, button"), Old Irish ~gnobh~ ("knot"), Lithuanian ~gniáubti~ ("to embrace").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). In this verb, ~ver-~ adds a sense of completion or togetherness to the action.

The basic verb ~knüpfen~ means "to tie, to knot," while ~verknüpfen~ intensifies this to "to link, to connect, to combine." In modern usage, ~verknüpfen~ frequently appears in computing contexts (~Dateien verknüpfen~, "to link files") and abstract reasoning (~Ideen verknüpfen~, "to connect ideas"). The relationship between ~knüpfen~, ~Knopf~ ("button"), and ~Knoten~ ("knot") reveals a whole family of Germanic words built around the tactile notion of pressing and tying. English ~knot~ is a cousin from the same Germanic stock, and the silent ~k~ in English ~knot~, ~knob~, and ~knack~ preserves an ancient consonant cluster that German still pronounces.
en.verkochen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~kochen~:

• ~kochen~: From MHG ~kochen~, from OHG ~kohhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kokōn~, borrowed from Late Latin ~cocō~, from Latin ~coquō~ ("I cook, I boil"), from PIE *~pekʷ-~ ("to cook, to ripen"). A loan early enough to have undergone the High German shift of ~k~ to ~ch~. Cognate with English ~cook~, Dutch ~koken~, Danish ~koge~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

Verkochen is both: intransitively the water boils away until the pot is dry, transitively one boils fruit down to a pulp: in both the cooking runs to its end.
en.verkommen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

Literally "to come down": ~ver-~ turns the coming toward decay, so ~verkommen~ describes a thing going to seed and running down of its own accord.
en.verkosten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~kosten~:

• ~kosten~: Two unrelated verbs in one spelling. ~kosten~ "to cost": from MHG ~kosten~, borrowed from Old French ~coster~, from Latin ~cōnstō~ ("to stand firm, be fixed, cost"), from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"); English ~cost~ traveled the same route. ~kosten~ "to taste, to try": from OHG ~kostōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kustōną~ ("to try, taste"), from PIE *~ǵews-~ ("to taste, try"), which also underlies Latin ~gustus~ and English ~gusto~ and ~disgust~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verkosten~ belongs to the ~kosten~ "to taste, to sample" branch (not "to cost"): ~ver-~ heightens the sampling into a deliberate, thorough tasting-through, as of wine.
en.verkriechen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~kriechen~:

• ~kriechen~: From MHG ~kriechen~, from OHG ~kriohhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kreukan~, from Proto-Germanic *~kreukaną~; Kroonen traces the root to PIE *~ger-~ ("to turn, bend, twist"), but the deeper etymology is not secure. A class II strong verb (~kriechen~, ~kroch~, ~gekrochen~).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys closing or covering: something is shut, blocked, or hidden from view.

Almost always reflexive: ~sich verkriechen~ is to withdraw into a hiding place, so ~ver-~ carries the sense of getting out of sight rather than mere motion away.
en.verkämpfen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~kämpfen~:

• ~kämpfen~: From MHG ~kempfen~, from OHG *~kempfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kampijan~, a denominal verb from *~kamp~ ("field, battlefield"), borrowed from Latin ~campus~ ("field, open plain"); the sense shifted early from the place of battle to the act of fighting. Latin ~campus~ also gives English ~camp~ and ~champion~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

Sich verkämpfen means to get bogged down in a hopeless fight and wear oneself out in it, the prefix casts the fighting as misdirected.
en.verkümmern:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~kümmern~:

• ~kümmern~: From MHG ~kumbern~, from the noun ~kumber~ ("rubble, obstruction, distress"), probably borrowed from Old French *~combre~, from Medieval Latin ~combrus~ ("barricade"), from Latin ~cumulus~ ("heap") or Gaulish *~komberū~; alternatively from Proto-West Germanic *~kumbr~, Proto-Germanic *~kumbraz~ ("burden, sorrow"). Cognate with Dutch ~kommer~ ("distress").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

Turned intransitive, ~verkümmern~ describes something withering under want or neglect, the distress of the base ~kümmern~ running out, under ~ver-~, all the way to atrophy.
en.verkünden:
From Middle High German ~verkunden~, from Old High German ~farkunden~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frakunthijan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~kunden~:

• ~kunden~: From MHG ~kunden~, from OHG ~kunden~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kunthijan~ ("to make known"), from Proto-Germanic *~kunthijanan~, a causative formed from *~kunthaz~ ("known"), which derives from *~kunnanan~ ("to know"), from PIE *~gneh₃-~ ("to know"). Cognate with English ~kithe~ (Scottish dialectal, "to make known"), Dutch ~verkondigen~, and Old English ~forcythan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~far-~, ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth, completely"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix here intensifies the action, giving a sense of making something widely or completely known.

The PIE root *~gneh₃-~ is extraordinarily productive across Indo-European languages: it gives English ~know~, ~can~ (originally "to know how"), ~kenning~, ~cunning~, Latin ~gnoscere~ (whence ~recognize~, ~cognition~), Greek ~gnosis~, and Sanskrit ~jnana~. The semantic core of ~verkunden~ is "to make known completely" or "to announce publicly," used especially in solemn, official, or religious contexts: ~das Evangelium verkunden~ ("to proclaim the Gospel"), ~ein Urteil verkunden~ ("to pronounce a verdict").
en.verkündigen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~kündigen~:

• ~kündigen~: From MHG ~kündigen~ ("to make known, to announce"), from the adjective ~kündic~ (modern ~kundig~), from OHG ~kundig~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kunþīg~, from Proto-Germanic *~kunþaz~ ("known"), the past participle of *~kunnaną~ ("to know, be able"), from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"). The sense "to give notice" became standard only in the 19th century, clipped from ~aufkündigen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Against plain ~kündigen~ "to make known," ~ver-~ lifts the announcing into a solemn, public register: the language of messengers and prophets.
en.verkürzen:
From ~ver-~ + ~kürzen~. Compound of:

• ~kürzen~: A deadjectival verb from ~kurz~ ("short"), from MHG ~kurz~, from OHG ~kurz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kurt~, borrowed from Latin ~curtus~ ("shortened, cut short"). Latin ~curtus~ itself comes from PIE *~(s)ker-~ ("to cut").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix functions as a verbalizer and intensifier, meaning "to make thoroughly [adjective]."

The Latin origin of ~kurz~ makes it one of the earliest Latin loanwords in Germanic, adopted during the Roman military presence along the Rhine and Danube. English ~curt~ (blunt, rudely brief) comes from the same Latin source but has narrowed to a purely figurative sense, while German ~verkürzen~ retains both physical shortening and the abstract sense of "to shorten, abridge." Cognate with Dutch ~verkorten~, English ~curtail~ (from Old French ~courtald~, also from Latin ~curtus~).
en.verlachen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~lachen~:

• ~lachen~: From MHG ~lachen~, from OHG ~lahhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~, from PIE *~kleg-~ ("to cry out, sound"). The initial ~hl-~ cluster was simplified to ~l-~ in Old High German. Cognate with English ~laugh~, Dutch ~lachen~, Gothic ~hlahjan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Ver-~ makes intransitive ~lachen~ transitive and turns it disparagingly on an object: to ~verlachen~ someone is to belittle them by laughing: the same contemptuous turn as in ~verspotten~ and ~verhöhnen~.
en.verladen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two historically distinct verbs under one infinitive. ~laden~ (strong, "to load"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"); cognate with English ~lade~ and ~laden~, Lithuanian ~klṓti~. ~laden~ (weak, "to invite, summon"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root found only in Germanic and Anatolian (Hittite ~halzai~).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

This is the strong ~laden~ "to load" (not the weak ~laden~ "to invite"): ~verladen~ is the loading of goods onto a means of transport, ~ver-~ carrying the loading through to completion.
en.verlagern:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~lagern~:

• ~lagern~: Derived from the noun ~Lager~ ("camp, store, warehouse"), from MHG ~lëger~, from OHG ~lëgar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~legr~, from Proto-Germanic *~legrą~. The modern form with ~-a-~ is of East Central German origin, influenced by ~Lage~ ("position"). Cognate with English ~lair~, Dutch ~leger~, Danish ~lejr~, Swedish ~läger~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

Here ~ver-~ expresses a change of place: ~verlagern~ is to move something out of its former position to another, literally or figuratively (a burden, a debate).
en.verlanden:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~landen~:

• ~landen~: Denominal from ~Land~ ("land, country"), via Middle Low German ~landen~; an earlier native German ~länden~ was displaced by it. ~Land~ descends from Proto-West Germanic *~land~, Proto-Germanic *~landą~, from PIE *~lendʰ-~ ("land, heath"). English ~to land~ is the same noun-to-verb step, taken independently.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ derives a verb from a noun or adjective, meaning to make something into that.

From the noun ~Land~: ~verlanden~ describes a body of water gradually turning into land as it silts up; ~ver-~ forming from ~Land~ the inchoative "to become land."
en.verlangen:
From Middle High German ~verlangen~, equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~langen~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~langen~:

• ~langen~: From MHG ~langen~, from OHG ~langēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~langōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~langōną~, a denominative verb derived from the adjective *~langaz~ ("long"), from PIE *~dlongʰos~ ("long"). The base verb ~langen~ means "to reach (for), to extend", literally "to make long, to stretch out toward."
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds an intensifying or completive force: "longing fully, reaching outward."

The connection to ~lang~ ("long") is preserved transparently in ~verlangen~: to desire something is to "stretch out toward" it, to reach for what is not yet within grasp. The same spatial metaphor of extension underlies English ~long~ (as in "to long for"), which is a cognate from the same PIE *~dlongʰos~. Latin ~longus~ ("long") descends from the same root, making ~verlangen~ and English ~longing~ etymological relatives by a common PIE ancestor. Cognate with Dutch ~verlangen~.
en.verlassen:
From Middle High German ~verlāzen~, from Old High German ~firlāzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fralātan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fralētaną~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~lassen~:

• ~lassen~: From MHG ~lāzen~, ~lān~, from OHG ~lāȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lātan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lētaną~, from PIE *~leh₁d-~ ("to let, leave behind").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix here adds a completive or intensive sense, leaving finally, leaving behind entirely.

The ~ver-~ prefix intensifies ~lassen~'s sense of "letting go" into a more complete, often emotionally weighted act of abandonment. The reflexive construction ~sich auf jemanden verlassen~ ("to rely on someone") developed from the notion of fully entrusting oneself to another (abandoning oneself to their care), which is semantically the mirror image of the active sense "to abandon." This double life (to abandon / to rely on) makes ~verlassen~ one of the most semantically rich reflexive pairs in German. Cognate with Dutch ~verlaten~, archaic English ~forlet~ ("to abandon, forsake"), Middle Low German ~vorlaten~.
en.verlaufen:
From Middle High German ~verloufen~, from Old High German ~farlaufan~, ~farloufan~. Equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~loufan~, ~hloufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~, from PIE *~klewb-~ ("to spring, stumble").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). The prefix here adds the sense of running its course, going astray, or passing through time.

~Verlaufen~ means "to proceed, to run its course" (~Die Verhandlungen verliefen gut~, "The negotiations went well"), "to get lost" (reflexive: ~sich verlaufen~, "to lose one's way"), and "to fade, to dissipate" (~Die Farbe verläuft~, "The color bleeds/fades"). All three meanings derive from the image of running forward and away: events run their course, a person runs off the path, colors run past their boundaries. The derived noun ~Verlauf~ ("course, progress, progression") is standard in medical (~Krankheitsverlauf~, "course of an illness"), temporal (~im Verlauf des Tages~, "over the course of the day"), and narrative contexts. Cognate with Dutch ~verlopen~.
en.verlauten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~lauten~:

• ~lauten~: From MHG ~lūten~ ("to sound, ring"), from OHG ~hlūtēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlūdēn~; ~Laut~ ("sound") plus the suffix ~-en~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlūdaz~ ("loud"). ~lauten~ means "to read as, to run"; ~läuten~ ("to ring") is the factitive of the same root. Cognate with English ~loud~, Dutch ~luid~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Usually in ~verlauten lassen~: to let something get out and be heard. ~Ver-~ raises ~lauten~ "to sound" to becoming known before others.
en.verleben:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys using up, consuming, or wearing away.

With a span of time as object, ~ver-~ construes ~leben~ as the using-up of that span: to ~verleben~ a time is to pass it in living until it is gone.
en.verlegen:
From Middle High German ~verlegen~ ("to misplace, obstruct"), from Old High German ~firleggen~ ("to cover"). Compound of ~ver-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~ ("to lay, place in a resting position"), the causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie"), from PIE *~logʰéyeti~, from the root *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). Cognate with English ~lay~, Danish ~laegge~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the sense of "away, wrongly" (in "misplace") and of completion or transformation (in "publish, lay down").

~Verlegen~ is a master class in German polysemy. A single verb covers: to misplace (~die Brille verlegen~), to lay or install (~ein Kabel verlegen~), to reschedule (~eine Besprechung verlegen~), to transfer (~Arbeitskräfte verlegen~), and to publish (~ein Buch verlegen~). The publishing sense gave rise to ~Verlag~ ("publishing house") and ~Verleger~ ("publisher"). As an adjective, ~verlegen~ means "embarrassed", from an entirely separate etymology tracing back through MHG to OHG ~firlegan~ ("sluggish, adulterous"), from ~firliggen~ ("to lie wrongly"), literally preserving the medieval association between idleness and moral failing.
en.verleiden:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~leiden~:

• ~leiden~: From MHG ~līden~, from OHG ~līdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~līþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~līþaną~ ("to go, travel"); the sense narrowed through "to endure" to "to suffer," reinforced by convergence with MHG ~leiden~ ("to be sorry"), from Proto-Germanic *~laiþaz~ ("hateful"). Not cognate with English ~lead~, but with ~lithe~, ~loathe~, Dutch ~lijden~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ derives a verb from a noun or adjective, meaning to make something into that.

~Verleiden~ goes back to the adjective ~leid~ "loathsome, hateful" (present in the ~leiden~ entry as Proto-Germanic *~laiþaz~ "hateful"): to ~verleiden~ something to someone is to make it hateful and unbearable to them.
en.verleihen:
From Middle High German ~verlīhen~, from Old High German ~firlīhan~. Equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~leihen~:

• ~leihen~: From MHG ~līhen~, from OHG ~līhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~līhwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~līhwaną~, from PIE *~leykʷ-~ ("to leave behind"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with English ~loan~ (via Old Norse ~lán~, from Proto-Germanic *~laihną~, derived from the same PIE root), Dutch ~lenen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a conferring sense, lending or granting something out completely, placing it with another.

The PIE root *~leykʷ-~ ("to leave behind") is the ancestor of both ~leihen~ and English ~loan~. The conceptual link is direct: to lend is to leave something with another temporarily. English ~loan~ entered the language through Old Norse ~lán~, a Norse borrowing that displaced the native Old English cognate ~lǣn~ ("loan, grant"). The semantic range of ~verleihen~ is broader than simple lending: one can ~verleihen~ a prize (to award it), a quality (to lend it to something), or a tool (to loan it out). The bestowing and lending senses both flow from the root idea of leaving something with another. Cognate with Dutch ~verlenen~, English ~loan~.
en.verleiten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~: the causative *~laidijaną~ of the strong verb *~līþaną~ ("to pass, go") with the suffix *~-janą~ ("to cause to go"), from PIE *~leyt-~ ("to go, depart, die"). ~leiten~ and ~leiden~ are a base-and-causative pair. Cognate with English ~lead~ (OE ~lǣdan~).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

To the causative ~leiten~ "to lead": ~ver-~ bends the leading in the wrong direction, so ~verleiten~ means "to lead astray, to induce into something harmful."
en.verlernen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~lernen~:

• ~lernen~: From MHG ~lernen~, from OHG ~lernēn~, ~lirnēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~liʀnēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lizaną~, from PIE *~leys-~ ("track, furrow, trail"): to learn is to follow the trail laid down before. ~lehren~ ("to teach") shares the stem in causative function. Cognate with Old English ~leornian~ (English ~learn~), Dutch ~lernen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ reverses or negates the base action.

~Ver-~ reverses ~lernen~: what was once mastered slips away again. ~Verlernen~ is the exact counter-motion to learning, a skill decaying through disuse.
en.verlesen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Ver-~ marks the ~lesen~ as going wrong: ~sich verlesen~ is to make a mistake in reading. Spelled alike but to be kept apart is transitive ~verlesen~ "to read out aloud, to announce", the sense the corpus attests.
en.verletzen:
From ~ver-~ + ~letzen~, an archaic verb meaning "to harm, to injure":

• ~letzen~: From MHG ~letzen~, from OHG ~lezzen~, from Proto-Germanic *~latjaną~. Related to ~letzt~ ("last") and ~Leid~ ("suffering").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). The prefix here intensifies the harmful action.

~Verletzen~ means "to injure, to hurt, to violate"; one can ~verletzen~ a person (physically or emotionally), a law, a treaty, or someone's rights. The base verb ~letzen~ is archaic in modern German but survives in the adjective ~letzt~ ("last"), the conceptual bridge being "the final blow," the one that finishes. MHG ~letzen~ had the remarkable enantiodromic property of meaning both "to refresh, to comfort" (as in a farewell feast, a ~Letze~) AND "to harm, to injure", opposite meanings in a single word. The refreshment sense survives in the Swiss German expression ~Letzi~ (a farewell party) and in the archaic noun ~Labsal~ / ~Letze~ ("refreshment at parting"). The ~ver-~ prefix resolved this ambiguity by fixing the meaning firmly on the harmful side. The derived noun ~Verletzung~ ("injury, violation") is among the most common words in medical and legal German. Cognate with Dutch ~kwetsen~ (a different root) and English ~last~ (a distant relative via the same PGmc root).
en.verlieben:
From ~ver-~ + ~lieben~. Compound of:

• ~lieben~: From ~Liebe~ ("love"), from MHG ~liebe~ ("joy, affection"), from OHG ~liob~, ~lioba~ ("fortune, joy, pleasantness"), from Proto-West Germanic *~leubu~ ("love"), from Proto-Germanic *~lubō~, from PIE *~lewbʰ-~ ("to love, desire").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the inchoative sense of entering a new state.

The reflexive ~sich verlieben~ ("to fall in love") captures the moment of transformation: the ~ver-~ prefix signals an irrevocable crossing into a new emotional state. English ~love~ descends from the same PIE root *~lewbʰ-~ via a different Germanic branch (Old English ~lufu~). The PIE root also gave Latin ~lubēre~, ~libēre~ ("to please"), source of English ~libido~. Cognate with Dutch ~verliefd~ ("in love").
en.verlieren:
From Middle High German ~verliesen~, from Old High German ~firliosan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fraleusan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fraleusaną~. Compound of ~ver-~ + the archaic root verb ~liesen~ ("to lose"):

• ~liesen~: The archaic simplex survives only in compounds. From Proto-Germanic *~leusaną~, from PIE *~leu-~ ("to detach, divide, cut"). Cognate with Ancient Greek ~λύω~ (~lúō~, "to loosen, untie, dissolve"), Latin ~solvō~ ("to loosen, dissolve"), and ultimately related to English ~lose~, ~loose~, ~loss~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix reinforces and doubles down on the meaning of loss already present in the root, a semantically emphatic pattern sometimes called pleonastic prefixation.

The semantic reinforcement (the prefix ~ver-~ piling "wrongly" or "away" onto a root already meaning "to lose") is a vivid Germanic habit of underlining loss through compounding. The archaic simplex ~liesen~ survives in ~Verlies~ ("dungeon"), originally a place where things (or people) are "lost." A notable cognate is English ~forlorn~, from Old English ~forloren~, the past participle of ~forleosan~ ("to lose entirely"), built from the same Proto-Germanic components. Cognate with Dutch ~verliezen~, English ~forlorn~.
en.verloben:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~loben~:

• ~loben~: From MHG ~loben~, from OHG ~lobēn~/~lobōn~ ("to praise, approve"), from Proto-West Germanic *~lubōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lubō~, from PIE *~lewbʰ-~ ("to love, desire, praise"), the same root as ~lieb~ and ~Liebe~. Cognate with Old English ~lofian~ ("to praise"), Dutch ~loven~, Swedish ~lova~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Despite its nearness to ~loben~ "to praise," ~verloben~ belongs to the older sense "to vow, to pledge solemnly": ~sich verloben~ is to bind oneself to another in marriage by a binding pledge.
en.verlocken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~locken~:

• ~locken~: From MHG ~locken~, from OHG ~lockōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lokkōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~lukkōną~ ("to entice, to lure"). A second, homonymous ~locken~ ("to curl"), from OHG ~lochōn~ and the noun ~Locke~, is etymologically distinct. Related to ~lügen~, Latin ~laciō~ ("I entice"); English has no direct cognate and uses ~lure~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Ver-~ intensifies ~locken~ "to lure, entice" into an insistent tempting: to ~verlocken~ is to entice so strongly that the pull is hard to resist.
en.verlohnen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~lohnen~:

• ~lohnen~: From MHG ~lōnen~, from OHG ~lōnōn~, a denominal verb from ~lōn~ ("reward, wage"), from Proto-West Germanic *~laun~, from Proto-Germanic *~launą~, from PIE *~leh₂w-~ ("gain, prize, booty"), payment as something won. Cognate with Old English ~lēan~; the English cognate ~lean~ is now obsolete.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Usually impersonal and reflexive: ~es verlohnt sich~ means a thing is worth the reward of the effort; ~ver-~ lifting ~lohnen~ "to reward" into a weighing of cost against gain.
en.verlorengehen:
A separable compound of ~verloren~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~verloren~: The past participle of ~verlieren~ ("to lose"), used predicatively: ~verlorengehen~ is literally "to go lost", the German counterpart of English ~get lost~ and ~go missing~. ~Verlieren~ is from MHG ~verliesen~, from OHG ~firliosan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fraleusaną~, from PIE *~lewH-~ ("to cut off, to loosen"); the ~-r-~ of the modern infinitive was levelled in from the participle, so ~verloren~ preserves the older shape of the two. English keeps the very same participle in ~forlorn~ and ~lovelorn~. The sense of ~verloren~ here is in ~verlorengehen~: to get lost, to go missing, to be wasted.

~Verlorengehen~ supplies the intransitive counterpart to ~verlieren~ "to lose": not someone losing something, but something passing of itself into the state of being lost.
en.verlängern:
From ~ver-~ + ~längern~ (to lengthen), a denominative verb from ~länger~ (longer), comparative of ~lang~ (long). Compound of ~ver-~ + the root adjective ~lang~:

• ~lang~: From MHG ~lanc~, from OHG ~lang~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lang~, from Proto-Germanic *~langaz~, from PIE *~dlongʰos~ ("long"). Cognate with English ~long~, Dutch ~lang~, Latin ~longus~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). In this word, the prefix carries an intensive or augmentative force, making something thoroughly longer.

The verb is formed by a common German derivational pattern: adjective comparative + ~-ern~ suffix (as in ~vergrößern~, ~verbessern~). The umlaut in ~längern~ comes from the comparative suffix ~-er~, which triggered i-mutation of the root vowel ~a~ to ~ä~. The PIE root *~dlongʰos~ appears across the Indo-European world with remarkable semantic consistency (Latin ~longus~, Greek ~dólikhos~ ("long"), Sanskrit ~dīrgháḥ~ ("long")) making "long" one of the most stable adjective meanings over five thousand years of linguistic change.
en.verlöschen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~löschen~:

• ~löschen~: Two distinct verbs merged under one spelling. "To extinguish": from MHG ~leschen~, OHG ~lescan~, Proto-West Germanic *~leskan~, Proto-Germanic *~leskaną~ ("to go out"), originally intransitive, the causative sense developing later; cognate with Dutch ~lessen~. "To delete, unload (cargo)": borrowed from Low German ~lössen~, ~lossen~, from the ancestor of ~los~ ("free, rid of").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

This is the ~löschen~ branch "to extinguish" (not "to unload cargo"): originally intransitive, ~verlöschen~ describes a fire or light slowly going out and dying.
en.verlügen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~lügen~:

• ~lügen~: From MHG ~liegen~, from OHG ~liogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~leugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~leuganą~, from PIE *~lewgʰ-~ ("to lie, swear falsely"). A class II strong verb (~lügen~, ~log~, ~gelogen~); the ~ü~ is late, taken from the noun ~Lüge~ to keep the verb from colliding with ~liegen~. Cognate with English ~lie~, Gothic ~liugan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Ver-~ marks the ~lügen~ as falsifying: to ~verlügen~ something is to give a false account of it through lies. The participle ~verlogen~ "thoroughly mendacious" lives on as an adjective.
en.vermachen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

Here ~ver-~ carries the giving-away: to ~vermachen~ something to someone is to make it over to them by testament, property passing to another at death.
en.vermeiden:
From MHG ~vermīden~, from OHG ~firmīdan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~meiden~:

• ~meiden~: From MHG ~mīden~, from OHG ~mīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~mīþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~mīþaną~, from PIE *~meyth₂-~ ("to change, switch"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~mijden~, Old English ~mīþan~ ("to avoid, conceal"), Old Saxon ~mīthan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix intensifies the act of shunning, avoiding something completely, keeping well away.

The PIE root *~meyth₂-~ ("to change, switch") gives the original sense of switching away from something, turning aside, which in Germanic narrowed specifically to avoidance and shunning. The expected Grammatischer Wechsel forms of the past tense (*~mitt~, *~gemitten~) were levelled out in modern German, possibly to avoid confusion with the preposition ~mit~ and the adverb ~mitten~. Cognate with Dutch ~vermijden~, Old English ~mīþan~.
en.vermeinen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~meinen~:

• ~meinen~: From MHG ~meinen~, from OHG ~meinen~, from Proto-Germanic *~mainijaną~ ("to mean, think; lament"), from PIE *~moyn-éye-ti~ ("to intend, give an opinion"), a causative formation from the root *~meyn-~. Cognate with English ~mean~ and ~moan~, Dutch ~menen~, Old Irish ~mían~ ("wish, desire").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Ver-~ tints ~meinen~ "to think, to be of the opinion" toward the presumptuous or mistaken: to ~vermeinen~ is to suppose firmly, often wrongly: the same shading kept in the adjective ~vermeintlich~ "supposed, ostensible."
en.vermelden:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~melden~:

• ~melden~: From MHG ~mëlden~, from OHG ~mëldōn~, ~mëldēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~melþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~melþōną~, from PIE *~meldʰ-~ ("to ask, pray, speak"). The original sense was supplicatory speech; ~melden~ keeps only the communicative side: "to report, register." Cognate with Dutch ~melden~, English ~meld~ (partial).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Ver-~ raises ~melden~ "to report" into the formal and complete: ~vermelden~ is the ceremonious announcing of a message, often with a lofty tinge.
en.vermerken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~merken~:

• ~merken~: From MHG ~merken~, from OHG ~merchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~markijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~markijaną~ ("to mark, notice"), a denominal verb from *~marką~ ("mark, sign"). To notice something is etymologically to leave a mental mark on it. Cognate with English ~mark~ (and ~remark~), Icelandic ~merkja~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Ver-~ construes ~merken~ "to notice" as setting down: to ~vermerken~ is to write the noticed thing down or put it on record: a mark that stays.
en.vermieten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~mieten~:

• ~mieten~: From MHG ~mieten~, from OHG ~mietan~, a denominative of the noun ~Miete~ ("rent, reward"), which via MHG ~miete~ and OHG ~mieta~ goes back to Proto-West Germanic *~miʀdu~, Proto-Germanic *~mizdō~, and PIE *~misdʰéh₂~ ("reward, compensation"). Cognate with Gothic ~mizdo~, English ~meed~ (archaic), Greek ~misthos~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

"To rent out" is the transactional flip side of ~mieten~: the tenant takes a dwelling for money, the landlord hands its use away; the prefix carries the direction of the transfer here.
en.vermischen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~mischen~:

• ~mischen~: From MHG ~mischen~, from OHG ~misken~, from Proto-Germanic *~miskijaną~ ("to mix"), from PIE *~meyḱ-~ ("to mix, knead"), via the inchoative present *~miḱ-sḱé-~. Cognate with English ~mix~, Latin ~misceō~, Greek ~mísgo~, Sanskrit ~miśrá~ ("mixed").
