• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Unlike plain ~mischen~, ~vermischen~ stresses the complete merging of the parts; used reflexively (as in the quoted sentence), it describes formerly separate things running together beyond distinction.
en.vermissen:
From MHG ~vermissen~, from OHG ~firmissen~, equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~missen~:

• ~missen~: From MHG ~missen~, from OHG ~missan~ ("to miss, to lack"), from Proto-Germanic *~missijaną~ ("to miss, to fail"), from *~missō~ ("wrongly, amiss"), from PIE *~mey(t)-~ ("to change, to exchange"). Cognate with English ~miss~, Old English ~missan~, Old Norse ~missa~.
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix intensifies the sense of lacking, of being without.

~Vermissen~ means "to miss (someone or something absent)": to feel the lack of a person, an object, or a quality. This is the emotional missing: ~Ich vermisse dich~ ("I miss you"), ~Wir vermissen ihn sehr~ ("We miss him greatly"). It should not be confused with ~verpassen~ ("to miss" in the sense of failing to catch a train or opportunity). The Proto-Germanic root *~missō~ ("wrongly, amiss") reveals the original sense: to miss is to err, to go wrong, to fail to hit the mark. This same root produced English ~miss~ in all its senses (missing a target, missing a person), ~mistake~ (a miss-taking), and ~amiss~ ("wrongly"). The emotional sense (the ache of absence) is a medieval semantic development, extending the idea of "lacking" from a factual observation to a felt experience.
en.vermitteln:
From MHG ~vermitteln~. By surface analysis, ~ver-~ + ~Mittel~ + ~-n~:

• ~Mittel~: From MHG ~mittel~, from OHG ~mittil~, from Proto-Germanic *~midlą~ ("middle"), a derivative of *~midjaz~ ("middle"), from PIE *~médʰyos~ ("middle"). Cognate with Dutch ~middel~, English ~middle~, Latin ~medius~ ("middle"), Sanskrit ~madhya~ ("middle").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a completive or channeling sense, mediating something all the way through to resolution.

The chain ~médʰyos~ → ~midlą~ → ~mittil~ → ~Mittel~ → ~vermitteln~ traces the concept of "the middle" becoming "the means" (the thing in the middle position between two parties) and then "to mediate" (to act as that middle thing). The PIE root *~médʰyos~ is extraordinarily productive: it yields Latin ~medius~ (→ English ~medium~, ~mediation~, ~mediocre~), Greek ~mésos~ ("middle"), Sanskrit ~madhya~, and, through Proto-Germanic, English ~mid~, ~middle~, and ~midst~. German ~vermitteln~ is thus the verbalized form of this ancient spatial concept, applied to the social act of standing between two parties. Cognate with Dutch ~bemiddelen~, English ~mediate~ (via Latin, as a parallel form).
en.vermuten:
~Ver-~ + ~Mut~/~muten~. From Middle Low German ~vormōden~, composed of ~vor-~ ("for") + ~mōden~ ("to want, ask for"), synchronically analyzable as ~ver-~ + ~muten~, from ~Mut~ + ~-en~:

• ~Mut~: From MHG ~muot~, from OHG ~muot~, from Proto-West Germanic *~mōdd~, from Proto-Germanic *~mōdaz~ ("mind, sense, courage, anger"), from PIE *~mō-tó-s~, a lengthened-grade nominal formation from *~meh₁-~ ("to endeavor; will, temper"), which may be a semantic extension of *~meh₁-~ in its more basic sense "to measure." Cognate with English ~mood~, Dutch ~moed~, and possibly Latin ~mōs~ ("will, humor, custom").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). The prefix here conveys an attempt or approximation, a mental reaching-forward.

~Vermuten~ means "to assume, suppose, suspect", literally something like "to have a presentiment about, to pre-sense." The semantic path from ~Mut~ ("courage, mood, mind") to ~vermuten~ ("to suppose") runs through the older meaning of ~Mut~ as "mind, inner state": to ~ver-muten~ was to cast one's mind forward toward something not yet certain. The English cognate ~mood~ preserves the psychological sense but has shed the intellectual one, while German split the word's inheritance: ~Mut~ narrowed to "courage" in most modern contexts, while ~vermuten~ kept the cognitive dimension alive. A false friend lurks nearby: English ~mood~ shares the same Proto-Germanic ancestor as ~Mut~, but ~vermuten~ has nothing to do with "being moody."
en.vermögen:
From Middle High German ~vermügen~ or ~vermugen~, from Old High German ~firmugan~ or ~firmagan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~framagan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~mögen~:

• ~mögen~: From MHG ~mugen~, from OHG ~mugan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~magan~, from Proto-Germanic *~maganą~, from PIE *~megʰ-~ ("to be able, to have power"). Cognate with English ~may~, Dutch ~mogen~, Icelandic ~mega~, and Gothic ~magan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix intensifies the base verb, adding a sense of thoroughgoing ability.

The PIE root *~megʰ-~ is the source of English ~may~, ~might~, and ~machine~ (via Greek ~mēkhanē~, "contrivance," from ~mekhos~, "means"). In German, ~vermögen~ means "to be capable of" and also functions as a noun meaning "fortune, wealth, assets," reflecting the idea that one's ability is one's true wealth. The OHG forms show both ~a~-grade (~firmagan~) and ~u~-grade (~firmugan~), reflecting the ablaut patterns of this ancient preterite-present verb. English ~may~ and German ~mögen~ are thus siblings, both descending from the same Proto-Germanic modal verb, though English lost the ~ver-~ compound entirely.
en.vernehmen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

From "taking to oneself" grew the modern perceptual sense "to hear, to become aware," which further branched into the legal "to interrogate"; the prefix is largely bleached here.
en.verneigen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~neigen~:

• ~neigen~: A merger of MHG ~nīgen~ (intransitive, strong) and ~neigen~ (transitive, weak), from OHG ~nīgan~ and ~neigen~, from Proto-Germanic *~hnīganą~ ("to bow, bend") and its causative *~hnaigijaną~, from PIE *~kneygʷʰ-~ ("to bend, droop"). The strong forms vanished by the 16th century: a once-strong verb that went entirely weak. Cognate with Old English ~hnīgan~, Old Norse ~hnīga~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Where ~neigen~ means a mere leaning, ~verneigen~ names the completed, formal bow, almost always used reflexively.
en.vernichten:
From MHG ~vernihten~, from ~nihten~, from ~niht~ ("nothing"). Surface analysis: ~ver-~ + ~nicht~ + ~-en~:

• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This inseparable prefix adds a sense of completion and thoroughness, here transforming "nothing" into the act of making nothing.

~Vernichten~ means "to annihilate, to destroy utterly, to exterminate", literally "to make into nothing." It is one of the most absolute verbs in the German language, admitting no degrees: what is ~vernichtet~ is gone completely. The word's etymology mirrors that of English ~annihilate~, which derives from Latin ~ad-~ + ~nihil~ ("nothing"), both languages independently built "destroy" from "nothing," but through their own linguistic materials. The derived adjective ~vernichtend~ ("devastating, crushing") is common in both military and figurative contexts: ~eine vernichtende Niederlage~ ("a crushing defeat"). The noun ~Vernichtung~ ("annihilation, destruction") carries heavy historical weight in German.
en.verordnen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~ordnen~:

• ~ordnen~: From MHG ~ordenen~, from OHG ~ordinōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ordinōn~ ("to put in order"), borrowed from Latin ~ōrdināre~ ("to arrange"), from ~ōrdō~ ("row, rank, order"), from Proto-Italic *~ordō~, probably from PIE *~h₂er-~ ("to fit together"). Doublet of ~ordinieren~. Cognate with English ~order~, Italian ~ordinare~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

From the "putting in order" of ~ordnen~ came the authoritative "to decree, ordain"; the modern medical sense "to prescribe" is a later narrowing.
en.verpacken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~packen~:

• ~packen~: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~packen~, from Old Saxon *~pakko~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pakkō~, from Proto-Germanic *~pakkô~ ("bundle, pack"), of debated ultimate origin. The absence of the High German consonant shift confirms it entered via Low German trade routes. Cognate with English ~pack~, Dutch ~pakken~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys closing or covering: something is shut, blocked, or hidden from view.

~Verpacken~ narrows ~packen~ to wrapping for protection or shipment: what is packed disappears into its casing, as in the quoted image of nested network packets.
en.verpassen:
~Ver-~ + ~passen~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~passen~:

• ~passen~: Borrowed from French ~passer~ ("to pass"), via Dutch ~passen~, ultimately from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, from Latin ~passus~ ("step").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). The prefix adds a sense of missing, passing beyond, or failing.

~Verpassen~ means "to miss (an opportunity, a bus, a deadline)", one of the most common verbs of everyday frustration. The prefix ~ver-~ here carries its sense of "going past, going wrong": to ~verpassen~ a train is to let it ~pass beyond~ you. The root ~passen~ itself has a layered borrowing history, entering German from French via Dutch during the medieval trade networks of the Low Countries. Latin ~passus~ ("step") comes from ~pandō~ ("to spread, extend"), from PIE *~peth₂-~ ("to spread out"). A second, colloquial meaning of ~verpassen~ is "to give someone something unpleasant" (~jemandem eine Ohrfeige verpassen~ ("to give someone a slap")), where the ~ver-~ prefix shifts from "missing" to "inflicting." Cognate with Dutch ~verpassen~.
en.verpfeifen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~pfeifen~:

• ~pfeifen~: From MHG ~pfīfen~, from OHG ~pfīfōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pīpōn~ ("to play a pipe, to whistle"), an early borrowing from Vulgar Latin *~pīpāre~ ("to chirp, peep"), a word of imitative origin. Originally weak, now a class I strong verb (~pfeifen~, ~pfiff~, ~gepfiffen~). Cognate with English ~pipe~ and ~peep~, French ~piper~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

From "whistling" as a signal grew the colloquial sense of giving someone away by informing; the snitch "blows the whistle" and hands the other over to the authorities.
en.verpflegen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~pflegen~:

• ~pflegen~: From MHG ~phlëgen~, from OHG ~plëgan~ ("to take care of, be responsible for"), from Proto-West Germanic *~plehan~, a strong class-5 verb; its past-tense forms survive in the archaic literary ~pflog~. Cognate with Dutch ~plegen~, Old English ~plēon~, Old Norse ~plega~; via Medieval Latin *~pleviō~, also with English ~pledge~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

From the "taking care" of ~pflegen~, ~verpflegen~ narrowed to the systematic provision of food and drink; the noun ~Verpflegung~ denotes the fare itself.
en.verpflichten:
From Middle High German ~verphlichten~. Equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~Pflicht~ + ~-en~:

• ~Pflicht~: From OHG ~pfliht~, from Proto-West Germanic *~plihti~, related to ~pflegen~ ("to care for, tend"), from MHG ~phlëgen~, from OHG ~plëgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~plehan~. The noun ~Pflicht~ ("duty, obligation") is built on the same root as ~pflegen~, duty as the care one owes. Cognate with English ~plight~ (in the sense of a sworn obligation, as in "to plight one's troth"), Dutch ~plicht~, Danish ~pligt~, Yiddish ~פֿליכט~ (~flikht~).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a completive or binding sense, bringing someone fully under an obligation.

English ~plight~ in the phrase "to plight one's troth" (to pledge faithfulness) is the same word as ~Pflicht~: both descend from Proto-West Germanic *~plihti~ ("care, responsibility, duty"). The modern English ~plight~ in the sense of "a bad situation" is a different word (from Old French ~pleit~, "condition"), a false friend within English itself. ~Verpflichten~ binds someone to a duty completely, committing them through the totality of their care. Cognate with Dutch ~verplichten~.
en.verraten:
From Middle High German ~verrāten~, from Old High German ~firrātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frarādan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~raten~:

• ~raten~: From MHG ~rāten~, from OHG ~rātan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rādan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rēdaną~, from PIE *~Hreh₁dʰ-~ ("to arrange, to consider").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries a sense of wrongdoing, misdirection, or reversal, turning counsel into betrayal.

The semantic shift in ~verraten~ is dramatic: ~raten~ means "to advise, to guess," but ~verraten~ means "to betray, to give away (a secret)." The ~ver-~ prefix twists counsel into treachery: advice given to the wrong party becomes betrayal. This negative transformation by ~ver-~ is paralleled in English ~bewray~ (archaic "to betray," from ~be-~ + ~wray~ "to accuse"). Cognate with Dutch ~verraden~. The root verb ~raten~ is cognate with English ~read~ (which originally meant "to advise, to interpret") and Danish ~råde~ ("to advise, to rule"), a remarkable case where "reading" and "advising" share an ancestor in the PIE concept of arranging or making sense of things.
en.verrauchen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~rauchen~:

• ~rauchen~: From MHG ~rouchen~, ~röuchen~, from OHG ~rouhhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raukijan~, derived from the noun *~rauki-~ ("smoke"), from Proto-Germanic *~raukiz~, from *~reukaną~ ("to smoke"), possibly from PIE *~h₁rewg-~ ("to belch, emit"). The noun survives as ~Rauch~. Cognate with English ~reek~, Dutch ~rook~, Swedish ~rök~, Danish ~røg~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

Literally "to vanish as smoke," ~verrauchen~ usually describes, figuratively, how anger or resentment dissolves of its own accord until nothing remains, hence the auxiliary ~sein~.
en.verrechnen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~rechnen~:

• ~rechnen~: From MHG ~rechenen~, from OHG ~rehhanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rekanōn~ ("to count, explain"), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to make straight or right"), the same root as German ~recht~ and Latin ~rectus~. Cognate with English ~reckon~, Dutch ~rekenen~, Low German ~rekenen~, Danish ~regne~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Transitively one offsets amounts against each other, carrying them into a final total; reflexively, though (as in the quoted sentence), ~sich verrechnen~ tips into the opposite, the miscalculation.
en.verreden:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Sich verreden~ means to trip over one's own words: the prefix marks the speech as gone wrong, a slip of the tongue.
en.verreiben:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~reiben~:

• ~reiben~: From MHG ~rīben~, from OHG ~rīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrībaną~ ("to rub"); beyond Germanic uncertain, a PIE *~wreyp-~, labial extension of *~wer-~ ("to turn"), being proposed but not secure. A class I strong verb (~reiben~, ~rieb~, ~gerieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~wrijven~, Old Saxon ~wrīvan~; German dropped the initial ~w-~ before ~r~, as in ~ringen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verreiben~ means to spread a substance completely by rubbing: an ointment, a pigment, a powder is rubbed until it is evenly worked in.
en.verreisen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Verreisen~ takes from ~reisen~ above all the being-away: not the traveling as such but the being-gone-from-home is foregrounded; hence the auxiliary ~sein~.
en.verreißen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

From "tearing to pieces" grew the figurative sense of ripping a work apart in a review; alongside it survives the concrete sense in jerking a steering wheel.
en.verrennen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~rennen~:

• ~rennen~: From a merger of two Old High German verbs: the causative ~rennan~ ("to make something run or flow"), from Proto-Germanic *~rannijaną~, and the intransitive ~rinnan~ ("to run, to flow"), from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~, from PIE *~h₃reyH-~ ("to undulate, churn"). A member of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~ich renne~, ~rannte~, ~gerannt~; no umlaut in the preterite. Cognate with English ~run~, Dutch ~rennen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Sich verrennen~ means to run oneself into a wrong direction or a fixed idea one can no longer escape: the prefix marks the running as gone astray.
en.verrichten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~ ("to straighten, set right, direct"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rihtijaną~, a denominative from the adjective *~rehtaz~ ("straight, right"), from PIE *~h₃reǵtós~ ("right, straightened"), from *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to stretch out, straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~richten~, Gothic ~raihtjan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verrichten~ denotes carrying a task or duty through to its end: one performs a prayer, a job, an office, as in the quoted Grimm sentence.
en.verringern:
From ~ver-~ + archaic ~ringern~ ("to make lighter, soften, weaken"), a verbal formation from ~gering~ ("little, low"):

• ~gering~: From MHG ~geringe~, from OHG ~giringi~, ~ringi~ ("low, plain, simple, light, easy"), from Proto-Germanic *~ringwaz~ ("small, light, quick"), of uncertain origin, though possibly from PIE *~wrengʷʰ-~ ("to squeeze, wring"). Cognate with Yiddish ~גרינג~ (~gring~, "light, easy").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds completive force.

The intermediate verb ~ringern~ ("to lessen, make small") is now archaic, leaving ~verringern~ as the surviving compound. The adjective ~gering~ ("little, insignificant") is still very much alive, but its direct verbal derivative has been supplanted by the prefixed form. The possibly related PIE root *~wrengʷʰ-~ ("to squeeze, wring") would suggest an original image of something being squeezed small, though this connection remains uncertain. The Greek cognate ~ρίμφα~ (~rhímpha~, "fast, quickly") preserves the "quick, light" sense of the Proto-Germanic ancestor rather than the "small" sense that prevailed in German.
en.verrufen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. A parallel weak form in Middle High German explains why the modern present lacks the expected umlaut (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Verrufen~ means to bring someone into ill repute; the prefix turns the ~Rufen~ ("calling") against its object, so that the participle ~verrufen~ today mostly means, adjectivally, "disreputable."
en.verräumen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~räumen~:

• ~räumen~: From Early New High German ~reumen~, a Central German umlaut variant of ~raumen~, from MHG ~rūmen~, from OHG ~rūmen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rūmijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rūmijaną~, a factitive verb from the adjective *~rūmaz~ ("roomy, spacious"), from PIE *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open"). Etymologically, "to make room." Cognate with English ~room~, the noun ~Raum~, Bavarian ~rama~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Räumen~ makes room; ~verräumen~ does so by carrying off: the object is put away in its place and out of the way.
en.verrücken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~rücken~:

• ~rücken~: From MHG ~rücken~, from OHG ~rucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rukkijan~. The verb means "to move, to shift" and is the base of ~verrückt~ ("crazy," literally "shifted, displaced"); the noun ~Rücken~ ("back") is etymologically a separate word. Cognate with English ~rock~, Old Norse ~rykkja~, Old English ~roccian~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Verrücken~ is the shifting out of an established position; from this "having been put out of order" comes the adjective ~verrückt~ ("crazy"), transferring the displacement to the mind.
en.verrühren:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~rühren~:

• ~rühren~: From MHG ~rüeren~, from OHG ~ruoren~, ~hruoren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōzijaną~; the initial ~hr-~ cluster was gradually simplified in German. The semantic range has stayed stable across a millennium: "to stir," both literally and figuratively. Cognate with Dutch ~roeren~ and the now-rare English ~rear~ ("to move, stir"), surviving in "to rear up."
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verrühren~ narrows ~rühren~ to stirring ingredients together completely, until an even mass forms, a kitchen word beside the more general ~vermischen~.
en.versagen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

Originally "to refuse, deny" (to deny someone something), ~versagen~ tipped into the intransitive "to fail, give out", one's strength, nerves, or heart fails, as in Kafka.
en.versalzen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~salzen~:

• ~salzen~: From MHG ~salzen~, from OHG ~salzan~, from Proto-Germanic *~saltaną~, a derivative of *~saltą~ ("salt"), from PIE *~séh₂ls~. The finite forms are weak today (~salzte~), but the old strong past participle ~gesalzen~ survives beside the regularized ~gesalzt~. Cognate with English ~salt~, Dutch ~zouten~, Swedish ~salta~; the same PIE noun gives Latin ~sāl~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Versalzen~ means to spoil a dish with too much salt; the prefix marks the ~salting~ as overdone and gone wrong, figuratively also "jemandem etwas versalzen" = to spoil someone's pleasure.
en.versammeln:
From ~ver-~ + ~sammeln~. Cognate with Dutch ~verzamelen~. Compound of:

• ~sammeln~: From MHG ~sameln~, ~samlen~, probably by dissimilation from ~samenen~, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *~samnōną~ ("to gather, collect"). Alternatively inherited from OHG *~samalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~samalōn~ ("to bring together, assemble").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix intensifies the base verb, giving the sense of gathering completely, assembling as a whole.

The Proto-Germanic root *~samnōną~ is also the source of English ~same~ (things gathered together are alike) and ~some~ (a gathered portion). The ~Ver-sammlung~ ("assembly") has been a key word in German political life since the medieval ~Reichsversammlung~ (imperial assembly). Dutch ~verzamelen~ ("to collect") is an exact cognate, while English ~assemble~ took a parallel path through Old French from Latin ~assimulāre~.
en.versaufen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~saufen~:

• ~saufen~: From MHG ~sūfen~ ("to sip, drink"), from OHG ~sūfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sūpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sūpaną~, from PIE *~sewp-~, a labial extension of *~sew-~ ("to take liquid, slurp"). A class II strong verb (~saufen~, ~soff~, ~gesoffen~). The drift from "to sip" to today's "to booze" dates only to the sixteenth century. Cognate with English ~sup~, Dutch ~zuipen~, Old Norse ~súpa~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys using up, consuming, or wearing away.

~Versaufen~ colloquially means to squander money or property on drink: the prefix carries the using-up, the means consumed entirely in the drinking.
en.verschaffen:
From ~ver-~ + ~schaffen~. Compound of:

• ~schaffen~ (weak verb, "to manage, procure"): From MHG ~schaffen~ (strong verb), from OHG ~scafan~, ~scaffen~, a byform of ~skephen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skappjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skapjaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly related to *~skabaną~ ("to shave, scrape") via a semantic shift from "to scrape, hollow out" to "to form, shape." The strong verb form ~skephen~ survives in the archaic variant ~schöpfen~ ("to create"). Cognate with Dutch ~scheppen~, English ~shape~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a sense of completion or procurement, bringing something about fully.

~Verschaffen~ means "to procure, obtain, provide" (~sich Zugang verschaffen~ = "to gain access," ~jemandem Arbeit verschaffen~ = "to find someone work"). It uses the weak conjugation of ~schaffen~ (~schaffte~, ~geschafft~, meaning "to manage, accomplish") rather than the strong conjugation (~schuf~, ~geschaffen~, meaning "to create"). This strong/weak split in ~schaffen~ is one of the most interesting in German: ~Gott schuf die Welt~ ("God created the world") versus ~Ich habe es geschafft~ ("I managed it"). ~Verschaffen~ always takes the weak form, focusing on the practical act of procurement rather than divine creation. The etymological connection to English ~shape~ (both from Proto-Germanic *~skapjaną~) is obscured by centuries of sound change but the semantic parallel of "forming, making" is still visible.
en.verschallen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schallen~:

• ~schallen~: From MHG ~schallen~, a denominal formation on ~Schall~ ("sound"); the Grimms took it instead as a reshaping of the older strong MHG ~schellen~ ("to resound"), from Proto-West Germanic *~skellan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skellaną~, from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, shout") with s-mobile. Normally weak today (~schallte~, ~geschallt~), it keeps the strong Präteritum ~scholl~ as an elevated variant. Cognate with Old Norse ~skjalla~, Old English ~sciellan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

~Verschallen~ means that a sound gradually dies away until it can no longer be heard; the same ~ver-~ sits in the surviving participle ~verschollen~ ("lost, missing").
en.verschalten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schalten~:

• ~schalten~: From MHG ~schalten~, from OHG ~scaltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaldan~ ("to push, shove"); the further etymology is debated, Pokorny deriving it from PIE *~(s)kelH-~ ("to split, separate"), which would relate it to English ~shell~. The physical sense of shoving a lever became the modern "to switch, shift gears, manage." Cognate with Old Saxon ~skaldan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verschalten~ means the interconnecting of several elements into a network or circuit; the reflexive ~sich verschalten~, by contrast, is the switching mistake.
en.verschauen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

In southern and Austrian usage ~sich verschauen~ (in someone) means to fall in love, literally to "mislook," the fateful slip of the first glance.
en.verscheiden:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~scheiden~:

• ~scheiden~: From MHG ~scheiden~, from OHG ~sceidan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaiþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaiþaną~, from PIE *~skeyt-~ ("to cut, separate"). Cognate with English ~shed~ (originally "to separate"), Dutch ~scheiden~, West Frisian ~skiede~, and Greek ~skhizein~ ("to split," source of ~schism~).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Verscheiden~ is an elevated word for dying, a "departing" from life; it inflects strong, and its participle ~verschieden~ coincides with the adjective ~verschieden~ ("different").
en.verscheißen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~scheißen~:

• ~scheißen~: From MHG ~schīzen~, from OHG *~skīzan~ (attested only in the compound ~biskīzan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~skītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skītaną~, from PIE *~skeyd-~ ("to split, separate"); the root's basic sense is separation, not filth. A class I strong verb (~scheißen~, ~schiss~, ~geschissen~). Cognate with English ~shit~, Dutch ~schijten~, Old Norse ~skíta~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Verscheißen~ is coarse for befouling or spoiling with excrement; the ~ver-~ here marks the ruin the base verb's action brings about.
en.verschenken:
From ~ver-~ + ~schenken~. Compound of:

• ~schenken~: From MHG ~schenken~, from OHG ~scenken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skankijan~ ("to pour, serve"), from Proto-Germanic *~skankijaną~, a causative from *~skankaz~ ("askew, crooked"), from PIE *~(s)keng-~ ("to limp, be crooked").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the sense of giving away completely, parting with something irrevocably.

The semantic journey from "crooked" to "give as a gift" is one of the most entertaining in German etymology: the original meaning was "to pour drink" (tilting the vessel at an angle), then "to serve drink at a tavern," then "to give freely" (because the innkeeper sometimes poured one on the house). German ~Geschenk~ ("gift") and ~einschenken~ ("to pour a drink") preserve both ends of this journey. English ~skink~ (an archaic word for "to pour drink") is a distant cousin through the same Germanic root.
en.verschicken:
From ~ver-~ + ~schicken~. Compound of:

• ~schicken~: From MHG ~schicken~ ("to arrange, order, put in place"), from Proto-West Germanic *~skikkijan~ ("to arrange, put in order"), related to Proto-Germanic *~skikkijaną~. The original meaning was "to arrange, put in order," and the modern sense "to send" developed from the idea of dispatching something to its proper place.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the sense of sending away to a distance.

The semantic shift from "arrange" to "send" happened in the late medieval period, when arranging goods for transport naturally came to mean dispatching them. The related noun ~Schicksal~ ("fate, destiny") preserves the older sense of "arrangement", fate as what has been arranged for you. English ~ship~ (as in "to ship goods") underwent a strikingly similar shift from a vessel to the act of sending. Cognate with Dutch ~beschikken~ ("to arrange, dispose").
en.verschieben:
From Middle High German ~verschieben~, from Old High German ~firskioban~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~schieben~:

• ~schieben~: From MHG ~schieben~, from OHG ~skioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeubaną~, from PIE *~skewbʰ-~ ("to push, to shove").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix conveys completion or transformation of the base action, pushing something into a different position, whether spatially or temporally.

~Verschieben~ means both "to move, to shift (physically)" and "to postpone, to defer", a beautiful case where spatial displacement became temporal displacement. You can ~einen Schrank verschieben~ ("shift a wardrobe") or ~einen Termin verschieben~ ("postpone an appointment"), and the underlying metaphor is identical: pushing something to a different place. Cognate with Dutch ~verschuiven~. The root verb ~schieben~ is cognate with English ~shove~, Low German ~schuven~, and Danish ~skubbe~, all from the same PIE root describing forceful pushing.
en.verschießen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb (~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~). Cognate with English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Old Norse ~skjóta~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys using up, consuming, or wearing away.

~Verschießen~ means to fire off or use up (ammunition), and also to fade (a colour ~verschießt~); in both the ~ver-~ carries the idea of using up.
en.verschlafen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schlafen~:

• ~schlafen~: From MHG ~slāfen~, from OHG ~slāfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slāpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slēpaną~, of uncertain further origin, possibly related to *~slapaz~ ("weak, lax, limp"), ancestor of ~schlaff~. A class VII strong verb of the reduplicating class (~schlafen~, ~schlief~, ~geschlafen~). Cognate with English ~sleep~, Dutch ~slapen~, Gothic ~𐍃𐌻𐌴𐍀𐌰𐌽~ (slēpan).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Verschlafen~ is to miss something by sleeping: an alarm, an appointment, figuratively a whole development; the ~ver-~ turns harmless sleeping into a failure.
en.verschlagen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Verschlagen~ names being driven off course: a storm drives a ship, one is stranded in some far place; distinct from it are the adjective ~verschlagen~ ("cunning") and the idiom ~es verschlägt einem die Sprache~ ("to be left speechless").
en.verschleißen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schleißen~:

• ~schleißen~: From MHG ~slīȥen~, from OHG ~slīȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slītaną~ ("to tear apart"), of uncertain further origin; a link to PIE *~sleyd-~ ("to rend, injure") is proposed but not secure. A class I strong verb (~schleißen~, ~schliss~, ~geschlissen~), now rare outside ~verschleißen~. Cognate with English ~slit~, Dutch ~slijten~, Danish ~slide~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys using up, consuming, or wearing away.

~Verschleißen~ yields the noun ~Verschleiß~ ("wear and tear"), ubiquitous in engineering and economics; the ~ver-~ turns the base verb's tearing into slow, complete using-up.
en.verschließen:
From ~ver-~ + ~schließen~. Compound of:

• ~schließen~: From MHG ~slieȝen~, from OHG ~sliozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sleutan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slūtaną~, *~sleutaną~ ("to lock, shut"). The original sense was specifically "to lock with a bolt or bar."
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the sense of completeness, locking something up tight.

The Proto-Germanic root gave Dutch ~sluiten~ ("to close"), while English ~slot~ (originally "a bar to lock a door") preserves the same source with a narrowed meaning. German ~Schlüssel~ ("key") is a derivative, literally "the thing that locks." The ~ver-~ prefix in ~verschließen~ adds the nuance of sealing away, locking up completely; one cannot simply ~schließen~ a secret, but one can ~verschließen~ it. The past participle ~verschlossen~ has also come to describe a person's character: reserved, closed-off.
en.verschlingen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schlingen~:

• ~schlingen~: From MHG ~slingen~, from OHG ~slingan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slingwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slingwaną~ ("to wind, to twist"), probably related to *~slinkaną~ ("to creep, to slink"). A class III strong verb (~schlingen~, ~schlang~, ~geschlungen~). A Central German change of ~-nd-~ to ~-ng-~ pulled in MHG ~slinden~ ("to devour"), whence the sense "to gulp down." Cognate with English ~sling~ and ~slink~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys using up, consuming, or wearing away.

~Verschlingen~ means to gulp down greedily and, figuratively, to devour a book; alongside it runs the sense "to interweave, entwine," from the base verb's twisting.
en.verschmelzen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schmelzen~:

• ~schmelzen~: From MHG ~smelzen~, from OHG ~smelzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smeltan~, from Proto-Germanic *~smeltaną~ ("to melt"), from PIE *~(s)meld-~ ("to melt, to soften"). Intransitively a class III strong verb (~schmelzen~, ~schmolz~, ~geschmolzen~), beside a weak causative ~schmelzen~ ("to melt something down"). Cognate with English ~smelt~ and ~melt~ (the same root with and without the mobile ~s-~), and Dutch ~smelten~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verschmelzen~ names two things flowing together into one: intransitive strong, transitive-causative weak; the ~ver-~ here carries less the completion than the "togetherness" of the two parts.
en.verschneiden:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schneiden~:

• ~schneiden~: From MHG ~snīden~, from OHG ~snīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~snīþan~ ("to cut"); no secure PIE root has been established, and the word may be a Germanic innovation. A class I strong verb (~schneiden~, ~schnitt~, ~geschnitten~). Cognate with archaic English ~snithe~ ("to cut"), Dutch ~snijden~, Icelandic ~sníða~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verschneiden~ means to cut into shape, to trim; also to blend (wines) and, archaically, to castrate (a ~Verschnittener~ is a eunuch), the senses fan out widely.
en.verschonen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schonen~:

• ~schonen~: From MHG ~schōnen~, derived from the adjective ~schön~ ("beautiful"), from OHG ~scōni~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skaunī~, from Proto-Germanic *~skauniz~, whose original sense was likely "to look at, behold" and hence "worth beholding." The shift to "to spare" reflects treating beautiful things gently. Cognate with English ~sheen~ (originally "beautiful, bright").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verschonen~ means to spare someone something: ~jemanden mit etwas verschonen~; the ~ver-~ intensifies the protecting already present in ~schonen~.
en.verschreiben:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Verschreiben~ means to assign by writing: a doctor prescribes a medicine; reflexively ~sich einer Sache verschreiben~ is to devote oneself to it, while ~sich verschreiben~ can also simply mean to make a slip of the pen.
en.verschreien:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schreien~:

• ~schreien~: From MHG ~schrīen~, from OHG ~scrīan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrīaną~ ("to cry, scream"). A class I strong verb (~schreien~, ~schrie~, ~geschrien~). Related to English ~scream~ (via Middle Dutch ~scremen~), cognate with Dutch ~schreien~ ("to weep"), Old Norse ~skræma~ ("to terrify").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Verschreien~ means to decry, to bring into bad repute; more common than the verb today is the participle in ~verschrien sein~ ("to be notorious").
en.verschweigen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schweigen~:

• ~schweigen~: From MHG ~swīgen~, from OHG ~swīgēn~ ("to be silent"), from Proto-West Germanic *~swīgēn~. Originally weak, it developed strong forms in early Middle High German and now inflects strong (~schwieg~, ~geschwiegen~), unusual, since most German verbs moved the other way. Cognate with Old English ~swīgian~, Old Saxon ~swīgōn~ (weak), Old Norse ~svigna~ ("to bend, give way").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys closing or covering: something is shut, blocked, or hidden from view.

~Verschweigen~ means to keep something deliberately unsaid, to hush it up; the ~ver-~ turns mere silence into active concealment, as the noun ~Verschwiegenheit~ ("discretion") attests.
en.verschwimmen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schwimmen~:

• ~schwimmen~: From MHG ~swimmen~, from OHG ~swimman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~swimman~, from Proto-Germanic *~swimmaną~ ("to swim, float"), from PIE *~swem-~ ("to be in motion, to swim"). A class III strong verb (~schwimmen~, ~schwamm~, ~geschwommen~). Cognate with English ~swim~, Dutch ~zwemmen~, Danish ~svømme~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

~Verschwimmen~ means to grow blurred, indistinct: outlines, boundaries, memories blur; the ~ver-~ lets the clear image dissolve until nothing sharp remains.
en.verschwinden:
From Middle High German ~verswinden~, from Old High German ~firswintan~, ~farswindan~. Equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~schwinden~:

• ~schwinden~: From MHG ~swinden~, from OHG ~swintan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swindaną~. A class III strong verb. The simplex ~schwinden~ still exists in literary German with the meaning "to dwindle, wane, fade." Cognate with Dutch ~zwinden~ ("to disappear"), Danish ~svinde~, Swedish ~svinna~, Norwegian ~svinne~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds completive and directional force, dwindling away entirely, disappearing to completion.

The most surprising cognate is English ~swindle~. The English verb is a back-formation from ~swindler~, which was borrowed directly from German ~Schwindler~, a person who causes things (including money) to vanish, from ~schwindeln~ ("to be dizzy, to swindle"). So English ~swindle~ traces back through German to the same Proto-Germanic root *~swindaną~ that underlies ~verschwinden~. To make something disappear and to defraud someone have always been close neighbors. Cognate with Dutch ~verzwinden~, English ~swindle~ (via German ~Schwindler~).
en.verschwören:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schwören~:

• ~schwören~: From MHG ~swern~, from OHG ~swerien~, from Proto-West Germanic *~swarjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swarjaną~, from PIE *~swer-~ ("to speak, to talk"). A class VI strong verb (~schwören~, ~schwor~, ~geschworen~); the older Präteritum ~schwur~ is now archaic. Cognate with English ~swear~, Dutch ~zweren~, Danish ~sværge~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Sich verschwören~ is to bind oneself by oath, with others, and hence to conspire, to plot; the conspiratorial sense grows out of the mutual swearing.
en.verschätzen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~schätzen~:

• ~schätzen~: A denominal verb from ~Schatz~ ("treasure"), from MHG ~schaz~, OHG ~scaz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skatt~ ("cattle, treasure"), an early Germanic word in which cattle served as a measure of wealth. Cognate with Old Norse ~skattr~ (whence Danish ~skat~ and Swedish ~skatt~, both "tax"), Gothic ~skatts~, Old English ~sċeatt~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

Reflexive ~sich verschätzen~ means to be off in one's estimate; the ~ver-~ turns neutral appraising into appraising gone wrong.
en.versehen:
From Middle High German ~versehen~, from Old High German ~firsehan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frasehwan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sehen~, from OHG ~sehan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, to perceive").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries multiple semantic loads depending on the construction: completion (to provide fully), misdirection (to see wrongly), and anticipation (to foresee).

~Versehen~ splits into fascinatingly divergent meanings all rooted in altered seeing. As a transitive verb, ~mit etwas versehen~ means "to provide with, to equip with", to see to it that something is furnished. As a reflexive ~sich versehen~, it means "to make a mistake", to see wrongly, to misjudge. The archaic reflexive ~sich eines Besseren versehen~ meant "to expect better", to foresee. The noun ~Versehen~ ("oversight, mistake") crystallizes the negative sense: a failure of seeing. Cognate with Old English ~forsēon~ ("to overlook, to despise") and Dutch ~verzien~, both sharing the "wrongly seen" semantics. The Old English cognate's meaning of "to despise" (literally "to look past someone") shows how the ~ver-~ prefix could push "seeing" toward contemptuous disregard.
en.versenden:
From MHG ~versenden~, from OHG ~firsenten~, equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~senden~:

• ~senden~: From MHG ~senden~, from OHG ~senten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sandijaną~, a causative of *~sinþaną~ ("to go, to travel"), from PIE *~sent-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~send~, Dutch ~zenden~, Danish ~sende~, Gothic ~sandjan~.
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix adds a sense of sending away, dispatching completely.

The literal sense is "to send away": to dispatch, to ship. ~Versenden~ means "to send out, to ship, to dispatch" and is the standard verb for mailing packages, shipping goods, or distributing mailings. It is more formal and comprehensive than simple ~senden~ ("to send"), implying distribution to multiple recipients or dispatch through a logistics system. The noun ~Versand~ ("dispatch, shipping") is ubiquitous in e-commerce. The PIE root *~sent-~ ("to go") underwent a causative transformation in Proto-Germanic: *~sandijaną~ means literally "to cause to go", a beautifully transparent etymology for the act of sending. The same root appears in Old Irish ~sét~ ("path, way"), Armenian ~əntʿanac~ ("way"), and Latin ~sentīre~ ("to feel", originally perhaps "to go mentally toward"), whence English ~sense~, ~sentence~, and ~sentiment~. Cognate with Dutch ~verzenden~ ("to send, to ship").
en.versenken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~senken~:

• ~senken~: From OHG ~senken~, from Proto-Germanic *~sankwijaną~, a causative of *~sinkwaną~ ("to sink"), from PIE *~sengʷ-~ ("to sink, to fall"). ~senken~ is thus the causative partner of ~sinken~: "to cause to sink." The vowel alternation reflects the causative *~-jan-~ suffix, which triggered umlaut. Cognate with Gothic ~sagqjan~, Old Norse ~søkkva~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Versenken~ means to send to the depths, to submerge: a ship, a treasure; reflexively ~sich in etwas versenken~ is to immerse oneself in thought.
en.versetzen:
From Middle High German ~versetzen~, from Old High German ~firsezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~frasattjan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, a causative derived from Proto-Germanic *~sitjaną~ ("to sit"). Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the sense of displacement, setting something elsewhere.

Cognate with Dutch ~verzetten~ ("to move, shift") and archaic English ~forset~. Like ~verlegen~, ~versetzen~ is richly polysemous: to move or displace (~einen Baum versetzen~), to transfer (~nach Karlsruhe versetzt werden~), to promote to the next school grade (~er wird versetzt~), to put into a state (~in Angst versetzen~, "to frighten"), to pawn (~das Silberbesteck versetzen~), to deal a blow (~einen Klaps versetzen~), and colloquially to stand someone up (~er hat mich versetzt~). The common thread is displacement: setting something or someone into a different position, state, or situation. In literary German, ~versetzte er~ was once a standard speech tag meaning "he replied, retorted," now largely archaic. The proverbial ~der Glaube kann Berge versetzen~ ("faith can move mountains") preserves the physical-displacement sense at its most dramatic.
en.versichern:
From Middle High German ~versichern~, equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~sichern~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~sichern~:

• ~sichern~: From ~sicher~ + ~-n~, where ~sicher~ descends from MHG ~siher~, from OHG ~sihur~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sikur~ ("secure, sure"), borrowed from Latin ~sēcūrus~ ("without care, carefree"), from ~sē-~ ("without") + ~cūra~ ("care, concern").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix adds a sense of completion or thoroughness.

The insurance sense of ~versichern~, which emerged in the 17th century, is a calque (loan translation) of Italian ~assicurare~ ("to insure"), itself built from ~a-~ + ~sicuro~ ("secure"). This means German and Italian independently constructed the same metaphor from the same Latin root: "to make secure." English ~assure~ and ~insure~ followed the same pattern through French. The dual meaning of ~versichern~ elegantly mirrors this history: "to assure" (to make someone feel secure in a belief) and "to insure" (to make someone financially secure against loss). The noun ~Versicherung~ ("insurance") is one of the most common German words in daily life. The ultimate Latin root ~cūra~ ("care") also produced English ~cure~, ~curious~, ~accurate~, and ~secure~, all revolving around the concept of care and its absence.
en.versiegen: Despite the identical spelling, ~versiegen~ ("to dry up, run dry") does not belong to ~siegen~ ("to win a victory"). It continues MHG ~versīgen~, from ~sīgen~ ("to sink, trickle, drip down"; OHG ~sīgan~); the ~ver-~ marks the gradual running-out until nothing flows. The coincidence with ~siegen~ is purely phonetic.
en.versinken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~sinken~:

• ~sinken~: From MHG ~sinken~, from OHG ~sinkan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sinkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sinkwaną~, from PIE *~sengʷ-~ ("to sink, to drop"). A class III strong verb (~sinken~, ~sank~, ~gesunken~); the weak causative ~senken~ is its transitive partner. Cognate with English ~sink~, Dutch ~zinken~, Danish ~synke~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Versinken~ means to sink down, to go under: a ship, the sun, and figuratively to sink into sleep or thought; the ~ver-~ carries the sinking through to disappearance.
en.versorgen:
From ~ver-~ + ~sorgen~:

• ~sorgen~: From MHG ~sorgen~, from OHG ~sorgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~surgāną~, from *~surgō~ ("worry, sorrow, care"), from PIE *~swergʰ-~ ("to watch over, worry; be ill, suffer"). The semantic duality of watchful care and anxious suffering is present in the root itself. Cognate with Dutch ~zorgen~, English ~sorrow~, Danish ~sørge~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a thoroughgoing, providing sense, caring for something completely, ensuring that needs are fully met.

~Versorgen~ takes the dual root of ~sorgen~ (care and concern), and resolves it firmly toward the positive pole: to provide for, to supply, to look after. While ~sorgen~ can still tip toward worry (~sich sorgen um~, "to worry about"), ~versorgen~ almost exclusively denotes active provision. A hospital ~versorgt~ patients; a government ~versorgt~ the population with electricity; parents ~versorgen~ their children. The ~ver-~ prefix converts the act of caring into the act of ensuring that care is carried through to its object. Cognate with Dutch ~verzorgen~.
en.verspeisen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~speisen~:

• ~speisen~: From MHG ~spīsen~ ("to feed"), a denominative verb from MHG ~spīse~ ("food"), from Medieval Latin ~spēsa~, from Latin ~expēnsa~ ("money paid out"), from ~expendere~ ("to weigh out, pay out"). A weak verb throughout its history. Cognate with Dutch ~spijzen~; the same Latin source gave English ~expense~ and ~spend~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys using up, consuming, or wearing away.

~Verspeisen~ means to eat up entirely and sounds more genteel than plain ~essen~; the ~ver-~ carries the idea of consuming the food to the last.
en.versperren:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~sperren~:

• ~sperren~: From MHG ~sperren~, from OHG ~sperran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sparrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sparrijaną~ ("to bar, to block"), a denominative verb from *~sparrô~ ("wooden beam, log"), originally to bar a passage with a beam. Cognate with English ~spar~ ("to bolt, bar"; the noun for a wooden beam), Dutch ~sperren~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys closing or covering: something is shut, blocked, or hidden from view.

~Versperren~ means to make impassable, to obstruct: a path, a view, a door; the ~ver-~ and the base verb's original "barring with a beam" combine into a thorough shutting-off.
en.verspielen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys using up, consuming, or wearing away.

~Verspielen~ means to gamble away, to forfeit through folly: money, a chance, one's credibility; distinct from it is the adjective ~verspielt~ ("playful, whimsical").
en.versprechen:
From Middle High German ~versprechen~ ("to guarantee"), from Old High German ~firsprehhan~ ("to defend verbally, to warrant"), from Proto-West Germanic *~frasprekan~. Analyzable as ~ver-~ + ~sprechen~:

• ~sprechen~: From MHG ~sprëchen~, from OHG ~sprëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sprekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sprekaną~, probably from PIE *~spregʰ-~ ("to crackle, make noise"). Cognate with Dutch ~spreken~, English ~speak~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix originally gave a completive or forward-directed sense, speaking forth, speaking on behalf of.

~Versprechen~ carries two opposite meanings held in grammatical tension. When transitive (~ich verspreche dir~, "I promise you"), it means to commit: to speak something forth and bind yourself to it. When reflexive (~ich verspreche mich~, "I misspeak"), it means to err in speaking: a later transparent derivation exploiting the prefix's sense of deviation. The verb thus embodies the double nature of ~ver-~: forward completion (a promise) and errant deviation (a slip of the tongue) are both housed in a single form. The sense "to promise" is attested from Old High German; the reflexive "to misspeak" is a later development. Cognate with Low German ~vorspreken~.
en.verspüren:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~spüren~:

• ~spüren~: From MHG ~spüren~, from OHG ~spurien~, ~spurren~, from Proto-Germanic *~spurjaną~ ("to feel, touch; to search, examine"), a derivative of *~spurą~ ("track, trace"), ultimately from PIE *~sperH-~ ("to kick, step"). Cognate with dialectal English ~speer~ ("to ask, inquire"), Swedish ~spörja~, Dutch ~speuren~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verspüren~ means to feel, to sense: an urge, a pain, an effect; the ~ver-~ intensifies the inner perceiving already in ~spüren~.
en.verstecken:
From Middle High German ~verstecken~, from Old High German ~firstekken~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~stecken~:

• ~stecken~: From MHG ~stecken~, from OHG ~steckōn~, a geminated (consonant-doubled) derivative of OHG ~stehhan~ (whence modern ~stechen~, "to sting, prick, stab"). The semantic development from "to pierce, stick" to "to be fixed in place, to put into" runs through the idea of a pointed object driven into a surface and remaining there.
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix intensifies and completes the action: to stick something away so thoroughly that it cannot be found.

~Verstecken~ means "to hide, to conceal." The reflexive ~sich verstecken~ ("to hide oneself") is the verb every German child knows from the game ~Verstecken~ ("hide and seek"). The related noun ~Versteck~ ("hiding place") drops the verbal suffix. Cognate with Dutch ~versteken~ ("to hide"). The underlying verb ~stecken~ preserves a fascinating grammatical fossil: transitively it has always been weak (~steckte~), but intransitively it once had strong past-tense forms (~stak~, Konjunktiv II ~stäke~). These strong forms, though still technically attested, have become archaic and unintelligible to many native speakers, a rare case of a strong-verb pattern dying within recorded history.
en.verstehen:
From Middle High German ~verstān~, ~virstēn~, ~vorstēn~, ~ferstān~, from Old High German ~firstān~, ~firstēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~frastāną~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix often adds a sense of away, wrongly, or completion.

The semantic development from "to stand before, against" to "to understand" parallels English ~understand~ (literally "to stand among") and Latin ~comprehendere~ ("to grasp"). The notion is of positioning oneself in relation to something in order to grasp it, a spatial metaphor for cognition shared across the Germanic languages. Cognate with Bavarian ~versteh~, Dutch ~verstaan~, Middle Low German ~vorstān~. Compare also archaic English ~forstand~ ("to understand").
en.verstehlen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~stehlen~:

• ~stehlen~: From MHG ~stëln~, from OHG ~stelan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stelan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stelaną~ ("to steal"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to rob, steal"). A common Germanic verb with remarkably consistent meaning. Cognate with English ~steal~, Gothic ~stilan~, Old Norse ~stela~, Dutch ~stelen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Sich verstehlen~ means to steal away, to slip off in secret; the verb itself is now rare, but its participle ~verstohlen~ ("furtive, stealthy") lives on as an adjective.
en.versteigern:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~steigern~:

• ~steigern~: The causative of ~steigen~ ("to climb, rise"), formed with the ~-ern~ suffix: "to make something climb, to increase." ~Steigen~ descends from MHG ~stîgen~, OHG ~stīgan~, Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb, stride"). Cognate with English ~stair~ and the obsolete ~sty~ ("to climb"), Ancient Greek ~στείχω~ (~steíkhō~, "I go").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Versteigern~ joins ~steigern~ to the prefix's disposal sense: the goods are sold off while the bids are driven upward (gesteigert) until the item falls to the highest bidder.
en.verstellen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Verstellen~ carries the prefix's amiss sense both spatially (something is shifted out of its correct position), and figuratively: ~sich verstellen~ means to put on a false front.
en.versterben:
From MHG ~versterben~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~sterben~:

• ~sterben~: From MHG ~stërben~, from OHG ~stërban~, from Proto-Germanic *~sterbaną~, from PIE *~sterbʰ-~ ("to be stiff, become stiff"). Cognate with Dutch ~sterven~, Low German ~starven~, Frisian ~stjerre~, and English ~starve~.
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This inseparable prefix adds a sense of completion and finality, dying to the end, dying completely.

~Versterben~ is the formal, euphemistic, and respectful way to say "to die" in German, roughly equivalent to English "to pass away." Where ~sterben~ is neutral and direct, ~versterben~ adds a veil of formality appropriate for obituaries, official announcements, and solemn contexts. The past participle ~verstorben~ functions as an adjective meaning "deceased" (~der verstorbene Professor~, "the late professor").
