The English cognate ~starve~ underwent a dramatic semantic narrowing: while German ~sterben~ retained the general meaning "to die," English ~starve~ specialized to mean "to die of hunger", a shift that occurred in Middle English. The PIE root *~sterbʰ-~ ("to be stiff, become stiff") connects death to rigor mortis, a grimly literal etymology.
en.versteuern:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~steuern~:

• ~steuern~: From MHG ~stiuren~, from OHG ~stiuren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stiurijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stiurijaną~. The root noun ~Steuer~ carries two meanings sharing one ancestor: ~das Steuer~ ("rudder, helm") and ~die Steuer~ ("tax," via "supporting post" and "support"). ~Steuern~ thus means both "to steer, navigate, control" and, in archaic or Swiss usage, "to pay a tax." Cognate with English ~steer~, Dutch ~stuur~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Versteuern~ draws on the now-buried tax branch of ~steuern~ (~die Steuer~, "tax"): income is versteuert once the tax due on it has been fully paid.
en.verstimmen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~stimmen~:

• ~stimmen~: From MHG ~stimmen~, from OHG *~stimmen~, a denominative of ~Stimme~ ("voice, vote": OHG ~stimma~, Proto-West Germanic *~stebnu~, Proto-Germanic *~stebnō~, from PIE *~stomen-~ "mouth, muzzle"). Hence the senses "to tune" (an instrument), "to be correct," and "to vote." Cognate with archaic English ~steven~ ("voice"), Dutch ~stem~, Gothic ~stibna~, Ancient Greek ~stóma~ ("mouth").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Verstimmen~ literally means to throw an instrument out of tune, and figuratively to put someone in a bad mood, in both, a tuning gone wrong.
en.verstinken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~stinken~:

• ~stinken~: From MHG ~stinken~, from OHG ~stinkan~, ~stincan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stinkwaną~, from PIE *~stengʷ-~ ("to push, thrust"); West Germanic specialized the verb to emitting a smell. A class III strong verb (~stinken~, ~stank~, ~gestunken~). Cognate with English ~stink~ and ~stench~, Dutch ~stinken~, Old English ~stincan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

~Verstinken~ applies the prefix's dying-away sense to ~stinken~: the stench disperses of its own accord over time until none of it is left.
en.verstoßen:
From MHG ~verstōzen~, from OHG ~firstōzan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~(s)tewd-~ ("to push, hit"). Cognate with Gothic ~stautan~, Old Norse ~stauta~, Dutch ~stoten~ ("to push, bump"), and dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce"). Non-Germanic cognates include Latin ~tundō~ ("I beat") and Sanskrit ~tudáti~ ("to strike, goad").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This inseparable prefix adds a sense of completion, excess, or wrongful action, here intensifying the thrust into an act of expulsion.

~Verstoßen~ means "to expel, to cast out, to violate (a law or rule)", the ~ver-~ prefix transforms a physical push into an act of permanent exclusion. ~Ein verstoßenes Kind~ ("a cast-out child") carries immense emotional weight. The legal sense ~gegen ein Gesetz verstoßen~ ("to violate a law") shifts the metaphor: one pushes through or against a boundary that should hold firm. The PIE root *~(s)tewd-~ connects ~stoßen~ to Latin ~tundō~ ("I beat, I pound"), whence English ~contusion~, a bruise being literally a place where flesh has been struck.
en.verstrahlen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~strahlen~:

• ~strahlen~: A 16th-century denominative verb from the noun ~Strahl~ ("ray, beam") with the verbal suffix ~-en~. ~Strahl~ traces to MHG ~strāle~, from OHG ~strāla~ ("arrow"), from Proto-West Germanic *~strālu~ ("arrow"); the sense "ray of light" arose in the 17th century as a metaphor from the arrow's straight flight. Cognate with Dutch ~straal~ and the rare English ~streal~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Verstrahlen~ is a coinage of the atomic age: ~strahlen~ turned transitive and pejorative: a place or a body is contaminated by radioactive radiation.
en.verstreben:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~streben~:

• ~streben~: From MHG ~strëben~, from OHG ~strëbēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stribēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~stribāną~ ("to strive, resist"). Cognate with Dutch ~streven~ ("to strive") and English ~strive~ (via Old French ~estriver~, itself borrowed from a Germanic source).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys binding or fusing several things into one.

The root entry gives ~streben~ "to strive"; ~verstreben~, however, belongs to the noun ~die Strebe~ ("strut, brace," from the same stem) and means, in construction, to tie members together into a rigid frame with struts.
en.verstreichen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~streichen~:

• ~streichen~: From MHG ~strīchen~, from OHG ~strīhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~strīkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~strīkaną~ ("to stroke, to rub"), from PIE *~streyg-~ ("to stroke, rub, press"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with English ~strike~, Dutch ~strijken~ ("to iron, to stroke").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

From ~streichen~ (a gliding stroke across) ~verstreichen~ takes the running-out of time: a deadline or an opportunity verstreicht when it slips away unused.
en.verstärken:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~stärken~:

• ~stärken~: From MHG ~sterken~, from OHG ~sterken~, a denominative verb from ~stark~ ("strong"), from Proto-West Germanic *~stark~, from Proto-Germanic *~starkuz~, from PIE *~ster-~ / *~sterg-~ ("stiff, rigid, strong").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix intensifies the base verb, carrying the sense of thorough or complete transformation.

~Verstärken~ means "to reinforce, to amplify, to strengthen", the ~ver-~ prefix pushes ~stärken~ ("to strengthen") toward completion or intensification. You ~verstärkst~ a wall (reinforce it), a signal (amplify it), a team (bolster it), or a tendency (intensify it). The derived noun ~Verstärker~ ("amplifier") is the standard term in electronics and music; a guitar ~Verstärker~ is an amp. ~Verstärkung~ means "reinforcement" in both military and general senses. The root adjective ~stark~ is cognate with English ~stark~ (which shifted from "strong" to "utter, bare, harsh", a ~stark~ contrast originally meant a ~strong~ contrast) and Dutch ~sterk~ ("strong"). The PIE root *~ster-~ / *~sterg-~ ("stiff, rigid") also connects to English ~stare~ (with rigid eyes) and ~stork~ (the stiff-legged bird), Latin ~re-stringere~ ("to restrict", whence ~strict~), and Greek ~στερεός~ ("solid, firm", whence ~stereo~).
en.verstören:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~stören~:

• ~stören~: From MHG ~stören~, from OHG ~stōren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~staurijan~; related to Proto-Germanic *~steuran~, whose root meant "to move, to agitate." Cognate with English ~stir~, Old English ~styrian~ ("to stir, move, agitate"), Dutch ~storen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verstören~ deepens ~stören~ into a profound, often psychological derangement; the older sense "to lay waste, to devastate" (as in Luther), survives now only figuratively.
en.versuchen:
From ~ver-~ + ~suchen~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~suchen~:

• ~suchen~: From MHG ~suochen~, ~süechen~, from OHG ~suohhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sōkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sōkijaną~, from PIE *~seh₂g-~ ("to seek out"). Cognate with Dutch ~zoeken~, Low German ~söken~, Danish ~søge~, English ~seek~, Gothic ~sōkjan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix often adds a sense of away, wrongly, or completion.

The ~ver-~ prefix gives ~versuchen~ the sense of seeking something out to its conclusion, hence "to try, attempt." The word is famously polysemous: in religious contexts it means "to tempt" (as in the Lord's Prayer: ~führe uns nicht in Versuchung~, "lead us not into temptation"), while in everyday speech it simply means "to try." The two senses share the underlying idea of putting something, or someone, to the test by seeking its limits. Cognate with archaic English ~forseek~. Cognate with Dutch ~verzoeken~.
en.vertauschen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~tauschen~:

• ~tauschen~: From MHG ~tiuschen~, derived from ~tūschen~, related to ~täuschen~ ("to deceive"), both of uncertain further origin. The sense ran from "to deceive" to "to trick someone into buying one's goods" to "to trade, exchange, barter"; ~tauschen~ lost the negative connotation along the way while ~täuschen~ retained it.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Vertauschen~ puts one thing in the place of another: unlike plain ~tauschen~ (a mutual trade), it aims at substitution, often unnoticed or by mistake.
en.verteidigen:
From Middle High German ~verteidingen~, from ~vertagedingen~, itself derived from ~teidinc~, ~tagedinc~, originally meaning "court day with negotiations," from ~tac~ ("day") + ~ding~ ("negotiation, thing"). The semantic development ran: "court day" > "to defend in court" > "to defend" generally. Cognate with Dutch ~verdedigen~.

• ~Ding~: From MHG ~ding~, from OHG ~ding~, from Proto-Germanic *~þingą~ ("thing, assembly, matter").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first").
• ~Tag~: From MHG ~tac~, from OHG ~tag~, from Proto-Germanic *~dagaz~, from PIE *~dʰegʷʰ-~ ("to burn").

The etymology of ~verteidigen~ is one of the most colorful in German. It has nothing to do with a root meaning "defend"; it grew out of the medieval Germanic legal assembly (~Ding~, ~Thing~), the same institution that gave English its word ~thing~ (originally "assembly, matter brought before an assembly"). A ~Tagedinc~ was a day appointed for legal proceedings; to ~vertagedingen~ was to conduct business at such a proceeding, specifically to argue one's case. The word was then phonologically compressed through ~verteidingen~ to modern ~verteidigen~, losing all visible trace of ~Tag~ and ~Ding~ along the way. The obsolete synonym ~defendieren~, borrowed directly from Latin ~dēfendere~, never displaced the native formation.
en.verteilen:
From Middle High German ~verteilen~, from Old High German ~farteilen~, ~firteilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fradailijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fradailijaną~. Equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~teilen~:

• ~teilen~: From MHG ~teilen~, from OHG ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, from *~dailiz~ ("part, share"), tentatively from PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, set, place"). Cognate with English ~deal~ (in the card-dealing sense), Dutch ~delen~, Swedish ~dela~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a distributive sense, dividing something out completely among recipients.

The distinction between ~teilen~ and ~verteilen~ is the difference between dividing and distributing: ~teilen~ splits something into parts; ~verteilen~ sends those parts out among recipients. A teacher ~teilt die Klasse~ ("divides the class") but ~verteilt die Aufgaben~ ("distributes the tasks"). The connection to English ~deal~ is worth noting: to deal cards, to deal goods, to make a deal all involve distributing portions, the same semantic core. Dutch ~verdelen~ is a direct cognate. Cognate with Dutch ~verdelen~.
en.vertiefen:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~tief~ + ~-en~:

• ~tief~: From MHG ~tief~, ~tiuf~, from OHG ~tiuf~, ~tiof~, from Proto-West Germanic *~deup~, from Proto-Germanic *~deupaz~, from PIE *~dʰewbʰ-~ ("deep"). Cognate with English ~deep~, Dutch ~diep~, Danish ~dyb~, Old Norse ~djúpr~.
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries a sense of intensification, making something more deeply so.

~Vertiefen~ means "to deepen" both literally (a channel, a groove) and figuratively (~sich in ein Thema vertiefen~ = "to immerse oneself in a topic," ~Kenntnisse vertiefen~ = "to deepen one's knowledge"). The reflexive ~sich vertiefen~ beautifully captures the image of sinking deeper into something: a book, a problem, a thought. English ~deep~ and German ~tief~ are exact cognates, differing only in the regular consonant shift. The modern German idiom ~in Gedanken vertieft~ ("lost in thought," literally "deepened in thoughts") captures the metaphor of intellectual depth.
en.vertippen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~tippen~:

• ~tippen~: From Low German, where the standard High German equivalent would have been ~tüpfen~ ("to dab, dot"). The word has two branches: in the sense "to type, to tap" it derives from the onomatopoeic imitation of light touching, while in the sense "to bet, to guess" (~Lotto tippen~) it comes from the noun ~Tipp~, borrowed from English ~tip~ ("a piece of advice, a hint").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Sich vertippen~ means to hit the wrong key while typing: a coinage of the typewriter and keyboard age, belonging to ver-'s reflexive slip family (cf. ~sich verschreiben~, ~sich verlesen~).
en.vertragen:
From Middle High German ~vertragen~, from Old High German ~firtragan~, ~fartragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fradraganą~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag, carry"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to drag, pull").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the sense of endurance and bearing through.

The meaning "to bear, endure, tolerate" comes from the literal sense of carrying a burden through to the end. The reflexive ~sich vertragen~ ("to get along") extends the metaphor: two people who can bear each other's weight. The noun ~Vertrag~ ("contract, treaty") captures the idea of mutual obligation borne by both parties. English ~draw~ and ~drag~ descend from the same Proto-Germanic root, as does Dutch ~verdragen~ ("to tolerate"). Cognate with Low German ~verdragen~.
en.vertrauen:
From Middle High German ~vertrūwen~, ~vertriuwen~, from Old High German ~firtrūwēn~, ~firtrūēn~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~trauen~:

• ~trauen~: From MHG ~trūwen~, from OHG ~trūwēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~trūwēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~trūwāną~, derived from *~triwwiz~ ("faithful, loyal"), from PIE *~drewh₂-~ ("steady, firm, solid"). Cognate with English ~true~, ~trust~, ~truce~, Dutch ~vertrouwen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix intensifies the base verb: to trust ~thoroughly~ or ~completely~.

The PIE root *~drewh₂-~ ("steady, firm") is also the source of *~dóru~ ("tree, wood"), the connection being that a tree is the archetypal firm, solid thing. Thus ~vertrauen~ ("to trust"), English ~true~, and English ~tree~ all share a common ancestor, linked by the concept of steadfastness. The noun ~Vertrauen~ ("trust, confidence") is among the most important words in German public discourse; ~Vertrauensfrage~ ("vote of confidence") can bring down a government, and ~Vertrauensvorschuss~ ("advance trust") describes the credit of goodwill extended to someone not yet proven. Cognate with Dutch ~vertrouwen~, Low German ~vertruggen~.
en.vertreiben:
From Middle High German ~vertrīben~, from Old High German ~firtrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fradrīban~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~, from PIE *~dʰreybʰ-~ ("to drive, push"). Cognate with English ~drive~, Dutch ~drijven~, Swedish ~driva~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here it adds a sense of driving away completely.

Cognate with Old English ~fordrīfan~ ("to drive away") and Dutch ~verdrijven~. The relationship between German ~treiben~ and English ~drive~ is one of the most elegant demonstrations of Grimm's Law in action: the PIE *~dʰ-~ became Germanic *~d-~ became Old High German ~t-~ (via the High German consonant shift), while English preserved the Germanic ~d-~. The semantic range of ~vertreiben~ is striking: it means both "to drive out, to expel" (~die Bewohner vertreiben~, "to expel the residents") and "to sell, to market" (~Waren vertreiben~, "to sell goods") and even "to pass time" (~sich die Zeit vertreiben~, "to while away the time"). The commercial sense developed from the idea of "driving goods to market," while the temporal sense treats boredom as something to be driven away.
en.vertreten:
From MHG ~vertrëten~, from OHG ~firtretan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fratredan~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~. A class V strong verb. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix shifts the spatial sense of stepping into the abstract registers of representation and advocacy, stepping in on behalf of another.

The semantic range of ~vertreten~ is impressively wide and rests entirely on spatial metaphor: to step in front of someone (blocking them, ~jemandem den Weg vertreten~), to step in place of someone (representing them, ~jemanden vertreten~), and reflexively, to accidentally step wrong (~sich den Fuß vertreten~, "to sprain one's ankle"). The political and legal senses (an attorney who ~vertritt~ a client, a parliamentarian who ~vertritt~ constituents) flow naturally from "stepping into the position of another." Cognate with Dutch ~vertreden~, English ~tread~ (underlying root).
en.vertrinken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~trinken~:

• ~trinken~: From MHG ~trinken~, from OHG ~trinkan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drinkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drinkaną~; no non-Germanic cognate has been securely identified, so the word may be a Germanic innovation. Cognate with English ~drink~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Old Norse ~drekka~ and Gothic ~𐌳𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌺𐌰𐌽~ (drigkan).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys using up, consuming, or wearing away.

~Vertrinken~ turns money or an inheritance into drink and uses it up in the process: the object is squandered, as with ~verspielen~ ("to gamble away") or ~verprassen~ ("to fritter away").
en.vertrocknen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~trocknen~:

• ~trocknen~: A deadjectival verb from the adjective ~trocken~ ("dry") with the verbal suffix ~-en~. ~Trocken~ traces to MHG ~trucken~, from OHG ~truckan~, ~trokkan~ ("dried out"), from Proto-West Germanic *~drukn~, from Proto-Germanic *~druknaz~ ("dry"), from PIE *~dʰerǵʰ-~ ("to become hard or solid"), an extension of *~dʰer-~ ("to hold, hold fast"). Cognate with Old Saxon ~drokno~ and Old English ~gedrycnan~ ("to dry up").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks a gradual dying away: the process runs itself out until nothing of it remains.

~Vertrocknen~ applies the prefix's running-out sense to moisture: a plant, a brook, or a body of water dries out entirely until no water is left.
en.verursachen:
From ~ver-~ + ~Ursache~ + ~-en~:

• ~Ursache~: From MHG ~ursache~, equivalent to ~ur-~ + ~Sache~. ~Ur-~: From MHG ~ur-~, from OHG ~ur-~, ~ir-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, from within"); doublet of ~er-~. ~Sache~: From MHG ~sache~, from OHG ~sahha~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saku~, from Proto-Germanic *~sakō~. Cognate with English ~sake~ (as in "for your sake"), Dutch ~zaak~, Swedish ~sak~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix has a causative or instrumental sense, making something the originating cause of an effect.

~Ursache~ literally means "the original thing" or "the primal matter", the ~ur-~ prefix (cognate with the prefix in ~ursprünglich~, "original") marking something as first or primordial, and ~Sache~ meaning "thing, matter, affair." English ~sake~ is a cognate of ~Sache~: "for your sake" originally meant "for your matter, your cause", the same legal and causal sense that ~Ursache~ carries in German. ~Verursachen~ ("to cause") is the verb built on this compound noun. Cognate with Dutch ~veroorzaken~, English ~sake~ (cognate of ~Sache~).
en.verurteilen:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~urteilen~:

• ~urteilen~: From MHG ~urteilen~, a denominative verb from ~Urteil~ ("judgment, verdict"), which displaced the synonymous MHG ~erteilen~. ~Urteil~ derives from MHG ~urteil~, from OHG ~urteil~, ~urteili~, from Proto-Germanic *~uzdailiją~ ("judicial decision, verdict"), literally "a dealing out," a compound of *~uz-~ ("out") + *~dailiz~ ("part, portion"), from PIE *~úd~ ("out") + *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, do"). Cognate with Dutch ~oordeel~ and English ~ordeal~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix intensifies the base verb toward a decisive, final judgment.

The connection between ~Urteil~ ("judgment") and English ~ordeal~ is striking: both descend from the Germanic concept of "dealing out" justice, but their meanings diverged radically. English ~ordeal~ originally referred to a trial by divine judgment (walking on hot coals, being thrown into water), while German ~Urteil~ stayed close to the core juridical sense. The ~ver-~ prefix in ~verurteilen~ pushes the meaning from neutral "to judge" toward "to condemn, convict, sentence", judgment with a negative outcome.
en.verwachsen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from PIE *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Cognate with English ~wax~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys closing or covering: something is shut, blocked, or hidden from view.

~Verwachsen~ means to vanish under growth: a path or a ruin becomes overgrown until plants cover it; said of bones and wounds it instead means to knit together, growing into a single whole.
en.verwalten:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~walten~:

• ~walten~: From MHG ~walten~, from OHG ~waltan~ ("to rule, hold sway"), from Proto-West Germanic *~waldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waldaną~ ("to rule"), from PIE *~h₂welh₁-~ ("to rule, be strong"). Cognate with English ~wield~, Icelandic ~valda~, Polish ~władać~ ("to wield, rule"), Russian ~владеть~ ("to possess, own").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). As a prefix, ~ver-~ can indicate completion, transformation, or intensification.

The simple verb ~walten~ is now archaic and largely restricted to fixed expressions like ~schalten und walten~ ("to do as one pleases") and ~seines Amtes walten~ ("to perform one's duties"). The prefix ~ver-~ transformed the elevated, sovereign meaning of "to rule" into the more bureaucratic "to manage, administer." The related nouns ~Gewalt~ ("power, force, violence") and ~Verwaltung~ ("administration") both descend from the same root, showing the full range from raw power to orderly governance.
en.verwandeln:
From Middle High German ~verwandelen~, ~ferwandelen~, from Old High German ~firwantalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~frawandlōną~. Compound of ~ver-~ + ~wandeln~:

• ~wandeln~: From MHG ~wandeln~, from OHG ~wantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandalōn~, a frequentative of *~wandijan~ ("to turn"), from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~, causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, to turn"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, to wind, to braid").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). The prefix adds a sense of thoroughgoing transformation.

~Verwandeln~ means "to transform, to metamorphose, to convert." The prefix ~ver-~ intensifies ~wandeln~ ("to change, to walk") into a complete, irreversible transformation. The PIE root *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn") connects ~verwandeln~ to a vast family of turning words: English ~wind~ (the verb), ~wander~, ~wend~; German ~winden~ ("to wind"), ~Wand~ ("wall", originally a woven wattle partition), and ~wandern~ ("to wander, to hike"). The related noun ~Verwandlung~ ("transformation, metamorphosis") is the German title of Kafka's famous novella, published in 1915, about Gregor Samsa's transformation into an insect. The word ~verwandt~ ("related, akin") is the past participle of an older sense of ~verwenden~ ("to turn toward"), reflecting the idea that relatives are people "turned toward" each other. Cognate with Dutch ~verwandelen~ (archaic), Low German ~verwanneln~.
en.verwarnen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~warnen~:

• ~warnen~: From MHG ~warnen~ ("to watch over, to protect"), from OHG ~warnōn~ ("to deny, to refuse"), from Proto-West Germanic *~warnōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~warnōną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, to perceive, to watch out for"): from refusing danger for oneself to cautioning others. Cognate with English ~warn~, Old English ~wyrnan~, Old Norse ~varna~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verwarnen~ is the official counterpart of ~warnen~: an authority, a referee, or a police officer verwarnt with a formal reprimand, whereas ~warnen~ merely alerts to a danger.
en.verwaschen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~waschen~:

• ~waschen~: From MHG ~waschen~, from OHG ~wascan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~waskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waskaną~, from an earlier *~watskaną~, a ~ske~-present formation from PIE *~wed-~ ("wet, water"), hence "to make wet (repeatedly)." Cognate with English ~wash~, ~water~, ~wet~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vaske~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys using up, consuming, or wearing away.

~Verwaschen~ means to wear colors or outlines down to a blur by washing; it most often appears as the adjective ~verwaschen~ "faded, indistinct," including figuratively of woolly, vague wording.
en.verweben:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~weben~:

• ~weben~: From MHG ~weben~, from OHG ~weban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~weban~, from Proto-Germanic *~webaną~, from PIE *~webʰ-~ ("to weave, braid"). Originally a class V strong verb (OHG ~weban~, ~wab~, ~giweban~); modern German conjugates it weak (~webte~, ~gewebt~) for the literal craft, while the strong ~wob~, ~gewoben~ (an analogical remodelling on the pattern of ~heben~, ~hob~, ~gehoben~) belongs to elevated and figurative use. Cognate with English ~weave~ and ~web~, Dutch ~weven~, Danish ~væve~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys binding or fusing several things into one.

~Verweben~ weaves several threads or motifs into a single fabric; often figurative (voices, themes, lives interwoven), with elevated usage taking the strong forms ~verwob~, ~verwoben~.
en.verwechseln:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~wechseln~:

• ~wechseln~: From MHG ~wëhseln~, from OHG *~wehsalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wihslōną~, from PIE *~weyk-~, *~weyḱ-~ ("to change, bend, yield"). Cognate with Dutch ~wisselen~, Luxembourgish ~wiesselen~, English ~week~, German ~Woche~, and Latin ~vicis~ ("change, turn, alternation").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Verwechseln~ means to take one thing for another in one's mind; from ~wechseln~ ("to change, exchange"), the ~ver-~ makes it the error of mistaking one for the other.
en.verwehren:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~wehren~:

• ~wehren~: From MHG ~weren~, from OHG ~werien~, from Proto-West Germanic *~warjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~warjaną~ ("to defend, to ward off, to protect"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to close, to cover, to protect"). Most commonly used reflexively: ~sich wehren~ ("to defend oneself"). Cognate with English ~weir~, ~ward~, ~guard~, Dutch ~weren~, Old Norse ~verja~, Gothic ~warjan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys closing or covering: something is shut, blocked, or hidden from view.

~Verwehren~ means to bar someone's access to something: the view, entry, a right; from ~wehren~ ("to ward off"), the ~ver-~ makes it a denial that shuts the thing off.
en.verweigern:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~weigern~:

• ~weigern~: From MHG ~weigeren~, from OHG ~weigarōn~ ("to refuse, to be stubborn"), from Proto-West Germanic *~waigrōn~ ("to be stubborn"), derived from OHG ~weigar~ ("stubborn, reluctant"). The adjective likely traces to Proto-Germanic *~waigraz~ ("resistant").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, *~fur-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here it intensifies the refusal expressed by the base verb.

The verb ~verweigern~ means "to refuse, to deny, to withhold"; ~den Gehorsam verweigern~ ("to refuse obedience"), ~die Aussage verweigern~ ("to refuse to testify"), ~den Zutritt verweigern~ ("to deny entry"). The ~ver-~ prefix intensifies the refusal: while ~sich weigern~ means "to refuse" (reflexively), ~verweigern~ is transitive and more formal, focusing on what is being withheld. The related noun ~Verweigerung~ appears in the compound ~Kriegsdienstverweigerung~ ("conscientious objection to military service"), a word of 28 letters that is entirely unremarkable in German legal discourse. The concept of ~Wehrdienstverweigerung~ ("refusal of military service") became especially significant in postwar Germany, where the right to refuse military service was enshrined in the ~Grundgesetz~ (Basic Law) as Article 4, paragraph 3, a direct response to the moral catastrophe of citizens who did not refuse.
en.verweisen:
From Middle High German ~verwīsen~, from Old High German ~firwīsan~. Equivalent to ~ver-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~ ("to show, direct"), from PIE *~weyd-~ ("to see, know").
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). The prefix here adds the sense of directing away or directing toward.

~Verweisen~ carries two seemingly opposed meanings that are actually two sides of the same coin: "to refer" (~auf etwas verweisen~, "to point to something") and "to expel" (~jemanden des Landes verweisen~, "to banish someone from the country"). Both senses derive from the act of directing: one directs attention toward a reference, or one directs a person away from a place. The derived noun ~Verweis~ means both "reference" and "reprimand", a formal finger-pointing that can be informational or punitive. The academic use (~auf eine Quelle verweisen~, "to cite a source") and the disciplinary use (~einen Verweis erteilen~, "to issue a reprimand") coexist peacefully, unified by the underlying gesture of pointing. Cognate with Dutch ~verwijzen~.
en.verwenden:
From Middle High German ~verwenden~, ~ferwenden~, from Old High German ~firwenten~ ("to turn away, avert, dissuade, hold back"). Compound of ~ver-~ + ~wenden~:

• ~wenden~: From MHG ~wenden~, from OHG ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~, a causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix often adds a sense of away, wrongly, or completion.

The semantic development from "to turn away" to "to use, employ" reflects the completive force of the ~ver-~ prefix applied to the notion of turning: what is fully turned toward a purpose is thereby used up or applied. Cognate with Middle Low German ~vorwenden~, Low German ~verwenden~.
en.verwerfen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Verwerfen~ throws something aside: a plan, a hypothesis, an appeal is verworfen and so cast away; alongside stand technical senses, such as the faulting of rock strata or the warping of wood.
en.verwerten:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~werten~:

• ~werten~: Derived from ~Wert~ ("value, worth"), from MHG ~wert~, from OHG ~werd~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("worth, worthy"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"); the connection to value runs through exchange: turning goods over in a transaction. Related to Latin ~versus~ ("turned") and English ~worth~, ~worthy~, ~worship~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verwerten~ means to turn something to use or profit: to utilize waste, exploit rights, monetize data; from ~werten~ ("to assess value"), the ~ver-~ marks the actual realizing of the value, not merely its appraisal.
en.verwiegen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~wiegen~:

• ~wiegen~: Two distinct verbs, both from MHG ~wigen~. Sense 1 ("to weigh"): a northwestern variant of ~wegen~ that generalized the present-singular stem vowel ~i~, from OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, move"); the original ~e~-form survives in the doublet ~wägen~. Sense 2 ("to rock, cradle"): from ~wige~ ("cradle," modern ~Wiege~), from OHG ~wīga~, likely related to Proto-West Germanic *~waggjan~ ("to cause to move"), from the same PIE root. Cognate with English ~weigh~, Dutch ~wegen~, Danish ~veje~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verwiegen~ belongs to the weighing branch of ~wiegen~ ("to determine the weight"), not to the identically spelled ~wiegen~ ("to rock, cradle"); the strong conjugation (~verwog~, ~verwogen~) confirms it. It is a trade and seafaring term for weighing out goods.
en.verwinden:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~winden~:

• ~winden~: From MHG ~winden~, from OHG ~wintan~, from Proto-Germanic *~windaną~ ("to wind, to wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). Cognate with English ~wind~ (the verb, "to coil"), Dutch ~winden~, Danish ~vinde~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verwinden~ means to wind one's way out of a hardship and get over it: to get over a loss, an insult; the ~ver-~ carries the winding through the difficulty to its end. In technical usage ~verwinden~ also means the twisting of a structural part.
en.verwirken:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~wirken~:

• ~wirken~: From MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~, from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~wérǵom~, from *~werǵ-~ ("to make, work"). Early on it merged with the dialectal ~würken~ (from OHG ~wurken~), which left the written language in the 18th century. Cognate with English ~work~ and ~wrought~, Dutch ~werken~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

In modern use ~verwirken~ means to forfeit a right or claim through one's own conduct: the deed rebounds on the doer, who loses what was his.
en.verwirklichen:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~wirklich~ + ~-en~:

• ~wirklich~: From ~wirken~ ("to work, to have effect") + ~-lich~ ("having the quality of"). ~Wirken~ descends from MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~ ("to work, to effect"), from PIE *~werǵ-~ ("to work, to do"). Cognate with English ~work~, Greek ~érgon~ ("work," whence ~energy~, ~ergonomic~), ~organ~.
• ~ver-~: From PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix adds the sense of bringing something to completion, making it fully real.

~Verwirklichen~ means "to realize, to make real, to actualize"; ~einen Traum verwirklichen~ ("to realize a dream"), ~sich selbst verwirklichen~ ("to fulfill oneself, to achieve self-actualization"). The reflexive ~Selbstverwirklichung~ ("self-actualization") became a key concept in postwar German psychology and philosophy. The word's structure is deeply layered: ~wirken~ ("to work, to effect") becomes ~wirklich~ ("real, actual", literally "having the quality of working, of being effective"), which becomes ~verwirklichen~ ("to make real", to bring into the realm of the effective and actual). The PIE root *~werǵ-~ connects working and reality across the Indo-European world: Greek ~érgon~ ("work") gave English ~energy~ ("in-work"), ~liturgy~ ("people's work"), ~metallurgy~ ("metal-working"), and ~surgeon~ (via Greek ~kheirourgós~, "hand-worker").
en.verwundern:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~wundern~:

• ~wundern~: From MHG ~wundern~, from OHG ~wuntarōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wundrōną~, from the noun *~wundrą~ ("wonder, miracle"), whence ~Wunder~; that noun may derive from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to desire, wish for, love") via *~wn̥h₁-tro-m~, hence something "wished for." English ~wonder~ is a sibling via Old English ~wundrian~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

Today ~verwundern~ survives chiefly in the reflexive ~sich verwundern~ and the participle ~verwundert~, the plain ~sich wundern~ having taken over most everyday use.
en.verwählen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~wählen~:

• ~wählen~: From MHG ~weln~, ~welen~, ~wellen~, from OHG ~wellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~walljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waljaną~, from PIE *~welh₁-~ ("to wish, choose"). The umlaut ~ä~ comes from the MHG second- and third-person singular; ~wählen~ and ~wollen~ share the same root. Cognate with English ~well~ (archaic "to wish well"), Dutch ~willen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Sich verwählen~ means to dial the wrong number on the telephone: a young coinage from the era of the rotary dial, in which ~wählen~ means to dial a number.
en.verwöhnen:
From Middle High German ~verwenen~, ~vorwenen~, ~ferwenen~, equivalent to ~ver-~ + the now-extinct verb ~wöhnen~. Cognate with Low German ~verwennen~, Dutch ~verwennen~. Compound of:

• ~wöhnen~: An extinct verb related to ~gewöhnen~ ("to accustom"), from MHG ~wenen~, ~wennen~, from OHG ~wennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wannjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wanjaną~ ("to accustom"), from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to wish, love, strive for").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix carries the sense of doing something to excess or in a wrong direction.

The umlaut ~ö~ (instead of expected ~e~) arose through sporadic rounding in Middle High German, likely reinforced by related words with original /o/ like ~Gewohnheit~ ("habit") and ~gewohnt~ ("accustomed"). English ~wean~ descends from the same Proto-West Germanic root *~wannjan~, originally meaning "to accustom (a child to food other than milk)." The semantic path of ~verwöhnen~ runs from "to accustom wrongly" to "to pamper, spoil", the ~ver-~ prefix marking that the accustoming has gone too far.
en.verwünschen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~wünschen~:

• ~wünschen~: From MHG ~wünschen~, from OHG ~wunsken~ ("to choose, wish, desire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wunskijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wunskijaną~, from *~wunskaz~ ("wish, desire"), from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to wish, love"), which also underlies ~Wonne~ ("bliss") and English ~win~. Cognate with English ~wish~, Dutch ~wensen~, Danish ~ønske~, Sanskrit ~vāṃchati~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

The compound turns a wish malign: to ~verwünschen~ someone is to wish them ill or lay a curse on them, and in the fairy tale a ~verwünschtes~ castle is one bound under such a spell.
en.verzaubern:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~zaubern~:

• ~zaubern~: From MHG ~zoubern~, from OHG ~zouberōn~, ~zoubarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taubrōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taubrōną~, derived from *~taubrą~ ("magic, sorcery"), which is of uncertain further origin, perhaps linked to *~tawjaną~ ("to make, prepare"). Cognate with English ~tiver~, Dutch ~toveren~, Old Norse ~taufr~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

The compound carries the conjuring through to its full effect on an object: to ~verzaubern~ someone is to put them wholly under a spell, whether to bewitch or to charm.
en.verzeichnen:
Compound of ~ver-~ + ~zeichnen~:

• ~zeichnen~: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, mark, token"), from MHG ~zeichen~, from OHG ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~ ("sign, token, indicator"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, indicate, point out"). Cognate with English ~token~, Dutch ~teken~, Swedish ~tecken~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a sense of thorough completion.

The base verb ~zeichnen~ means "to draw, to sketch": to make signs on paper. ~Verzeichnen~ shifts the meaning to "to record, to list, to register": creating an authoritative written record. The reflexive ~sich verzeichnen~ means "to misdraw," where the ~ver-~ prefix takes its other common sense of "wrongly, astray." The noun ~Verzeichnis~ ("directory, index, catalogue") is one of the most common derivatives.
en.verzeigen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~zeigen~:

• ~zeigen~: From MHG ~zeigen~, from OHG ~zeigōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taigōn~, possibly from Proto-Germanic *~taikōną~ (iterative), an intensive derivative of OHG ~zīhan~ ("to accuse"), ultimately from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to point out, show"), whence also ~Zeichen~ ("sign") and English ~teach~. In Modern German it absorbed the unrelated MHG ~zöugen~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

Chiefly Swiss and legal, ~verzeigen~ means to report or denounce someone to the authorities, the showing turned against its object.
en.verzeihen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~zeihen~:

• ~zeihen~: From OHG ~zīhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~tīhaną~ ("to show, point out; to blame, accuse"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show"). Cognate with Latin ~dīcō~ ("to speak, say"), Ancient Greek ~δείκνυμι~ (~deíknumi~, "to show"), and English ~token~ (from the related *~taikną~, "sign").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ reverses or negates the base action.

The etymology is exact: ~zeihen~ is "to accuse," and ~ver-~ negates it, so ~verzeihen~ is literally to un-accuse, to drop the charge, and hence to forgive.
en.verzichten:
An 18th-century denominal verb derived from the noun ~Verzicht~ ("renunciation, waiver") + the verb-forming suffix ~-en~. ~Verzicht~ itself derives from Middle High German ~verziht~, from ~ver-~ + a derivative of ~zeihen~ ("to accuse, blame"). The root ~zeihen~ descends from OHG ~zīhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tīhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~tīhaną~, from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point out").

• ~zeihen~: From OHG ~zīhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~tīhaną~ ("to show, point out; to blame, accuse"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show"). Cognate with Latin ~dīcō~ ("to speak, say"), Ancient Greek ~δείκνυμι~ (~deíknumi~, "to show, point out"), and English ~token~ (from the related *~taikną~, "sign").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix moves the sense from accusation to abdication, declaring against oneself.

The semantic journey of ~verzichten~ is a three-act drama. Act one: PIE *~deyḱ-~ means "to show, point out." Act two: ~zeihen~ means "to accuse", pointing a finger at someone to declare their guilt. Act three: ~ver-~ inverts the direction, making it a declaration against oneself, "to formally renounce, to waive." Formal legal and ecclesiastical language crystallized this meaning: ~auf etwas verzichten~ is to make a public declaration of giving something up. The root *~tīhaną~ is extinct as a simplex in modern German; only ~zeihen~ (highly archaic) and compounds like ~verzichten~ and the noun ~Verzicht~ preserve it. Cognate with Middle Low German ~vortichten~, Middle Dutch ~vertichten~.
en.verziehen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

In this sense ~verziehen~ is to pull something out of true: ~den Mund verziehen~, to twist the mouth; ~das Holz verzieht sich~, the wood warps. The same spelling also carries the unrelated senses "to move house" and, of a child, "to spoil."
en.verzählen:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~zählen~:

• ~zählen~: From MHG ~zel(e)n~, ~zellen~, from OHG ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~ ("to enumerate, count; to recount, tell"). German split this dual sense: ~zählen~ kept "to count," ~erzählen~ took "to narrate." Cognate with Dutch ~tellen~, English ~tell~ and ~tale~, Danish ~tælle~, Gothic ~talzjan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ marks the action as going wrong, astray, or amiss.

~Verzählen~ is used reflexively: ~sich verzählen~ means to lose one's count and arrive at the wrong number, the counting gone astray.
en.verändern:
From ~ver-~ + ~ändern~:

• ~ändern~: From MHG ~endern~, a denominative from ~ander~ ("other, different"), from Proto-Germanic *~anþeraz~, from PIE *~h₂énteros~ ("the other of two"). Cognate with English ~other~, Dutch ~ander~, Gothic ~anþar~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). Here the prefix adds a completive or transformative sense, changing something thoroughly, bringing it into a wholly different state.

The doubled sense of transformation (~ver-~ ("completion, away") applied to a verb already built on the concept of "making other") produces one of German's most precise words for change. Unlike ~ändern~ alone (which can mean merely to adjust or tweak), ~verändern~ implies a more thoroughgoing alteration. The reflexive ~sich verändern~ ("to change oneself") is culturally ubiquitous, used for everything from personal growth to career changes. Cognate with Dutch ~veranderen~, Yiddish ~farendern~.
en.verärgern:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~ärgern~:

• ~ärgern~: From MHG ~argern~ ("to worsen"), from OHG ~argerōn~, from the adjective ~arg~ ("bad, wicked"), from OHG ~arg~, Proto-West Germanic *~arg~, Proto-Germanic *~argaz~, from PIE *~h₃erǵʰ-~ ("to copulate; ardent"). The sense softened to "to annoy, to irritate." Cognate with English ~eerie~, Dutch ~erg~ ("bad, severe"), Lithuanian ~eržùs~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Ärgern~ irritates; ~verärgern~ intensifies it into lasting displeasure; one is left verärgert, put out.
en.veräußern:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~äußern~:

• ~äußern~: From MHG ~ūzeren~ ("to bring out, express"), deadjectival from ~äußer~ ("outer"), the comparative of ~aus~ / ~außen~, from MHG ~ūȥ~, OHG ~ūȥ~, Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, Proto-Germanic *~ūt~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"), bringing the inner outward. A doublet of English ~out~; related to English ~utter~, Dutch ~uit~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.

~Äußern~ properly means "to bring outward"; ~veräußern~ is the legal term for parting with a possession, transferring it out of one's own estate.
en.veröffentlichen:
From ~ver-~ + ~öffentlich~ + ~-en~. Compound of:

• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~, from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, first"). This prefix often adds a sense of completion or bringing into a state.
• ~öffentlich~: From MHG [unattested as compound], from OHG ~offanlīh~ ("open, public"), itself from ~offen~ + ~-lich~. ~Offen~ derives from MHG ~offen~, OHG ~offan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~opan~, from Proto-Germanic *~upanaz~, the past participle of a hypothetical verb *~ūpaną~ ("to open, to put up"), from *~upp~ ("up"). The literal sense was "lying on top" > "clear, open." Cognate with Dutch ~open~, English ~open~, Swedish ~öppen~.
• ~-en~: Standard verbal suffix converting the adjective ~öffentlich~ into a verb.

The verb ~veröffentlichen~ (literally "to make (completely) public/open") follows the productive German pattern of ~ver-~ + adjective + ~-en~ for causative verbs (compare ~verdeutlichen~, "to make clear"; ~vereinfachen~, "to simplify"). The chain from PIE *~upp~ ("up") → PGmc *~upanaz~ ("open") → OHG ~offan~ → ~öffentlich~ → ~veröffentlichen~ traces an ancient directional concept ("upward, above") all the way to the modern act of publication. Cognate with Dutch ~publiceren~ (different root, same semantic niche).
en.verüben:
An inseparable compound of ~ver-~ + ~üben~:

• ~üben~: From MHG ~üeben~, ~uoben~, from OHG ~uoben~, from Proto-Germanic *~ōbijaną~ ("to do, practice"), the causative-iterative formation of a lost strong verb *~afaną~, from PIE *~h₃ep-~ ("to labor, work, toil"), which also gives Latin ~opus~ and ~opera~. Cognate with Dutch ~oefenen~, Old Saxon ~ōbian~, Old Norse *~œfa~ (Icelandic ~æfa~).
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.

~Verüben~ preserves the older sense of ~üben~: to carry out, to put into effect, rather than to rehearse; today it is used almost only of misdeeds: to perpetrate an outrage, a murder, an assassination.
en.vollbringen:
An inseparable compound of ~voll-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~voll-~: From the adjective ~voll~, from MHG ~vol~, from OHG ~fol~, from Proto-West Germanic *~full~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~plh₁nós~ ("full"), from the root *~pleh₁-~ ("to fill"). Cognate with English ~full~ and, through the same root, Latin ~plēnus~, whence English ~plenty~ and ~replenish~. ~voll-~, as an inseparable prefix, conveys carrying an action through to full completion.

Being inseparable, ~voll-~ never splits from the stem here (one says ~er vollbringt eine Tat~, not ~er bringt voll~), and the compound means to bring a deed fully to pass, to accomplish it.
en.vollenden:
An inseparable compound of ~voll-~ + ~enden~:

• ~enden~: From MHG ~enden~, from OHG ~entōn~ ("to end, to complete, to die"), a denominative from ~Ende~ (OHG ~enti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~andī~, from Proto-Germanic *~andijaz~, from PIE *~h₂entíos~ "front, forehead," from *~h₂ent-~ "face, front"). Cognate with English ~end~, the prefix ~ent-~ and Latin ~ante~ ("before").
• ~voll-~: From the adjective ~voll~, from MHG ~vol~, from OHG ~fol~, from Proto-West Germanic *~full~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~plh₁nós~ ("full"), from the root *~pleh₁-~ ("to fill"). Cognate with English ~full~ and, through the same root, Latin ~plēnus~, whence English ~plenty~ and ~replenish~. ~voll-~, as an inseparable prefix, conveys carrying an action through to full completion.

The compound means to carry something wholly to its ~Ende~ (to complete or perfect it), and as an inseparable verb it forms its participle without ~-ge-~: ~vollendet~, not ~vollgeendet~.
en.vollführen:
An inseparable compound of ~voll-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~voll-~: From the adjective ~voll~, from MHG ~vol~, from OHG ~fol~, from Proto-West Germanic *~full~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~plh₁nós~ ("full"), from the root *~pleh₁-~ ("to fill"). Cognate with English ~full~ and, through the same root, Latin ~plēnus~, whence English ~plenty~ and ~replenish~. ~voll-~ conveys the formal execution or accomplishment of an act.

~Vollführen~ names the formal carrying-out of an act (one ~vollführt~ a leap, a maneuver, a gesture), where the plain ~führen~ would merely "lead" it.
en.vollfüllen:
A separable compound of ~voll~ + ~füllen~:

• ~füllen~: From MHG ~vüllen~, from OHG ~fullen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fullijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullijaną~ ("to make full"), the causative of *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pl̥h₁nós~ ("full"). English ~fill~ and ~füllen~ are exact cognates, each the causative of its native word for "full." Cognate with English ~fill~, Dutch ~vullen~, Danish ~fylde~, Swedish ~fylla~.
• ~voll~: From MHG ~vol~, from OHG ~fol~, from Proto-West Germanic *~foll~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pleh₁-~ ("to fill"). Cognate with English ~full~, Dutch ~vol~, Gothic ~fulls~; Latin ~plēnus~ ("full") is from the same root, whence English ~plenty~ and ~replenish~. The separable particle ~voll-~ is resultative (~vollmachen~, ~volltanken~), and it should not be confused with the homophonous inseparable ~voll-~ of ~vollenden~ and ~vollbringen~, which means "completely" and never separates. The sense of ~voll~ here is: completely full, filled to capacity.

Here ~voll~ is the free adjective and the verb separates (~sie füllt den Krug voll~), so the particle states the result: the vessel ends up full.
en.vollladen:
A separable compound of ~voll~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two historically distinct verbs under one infinitive. ~laden~ (strong, "to load"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"); cognate with English ~lade~ and ~laden~, Lithuanian ~klṓti~. ~laden~ (weak, "to invite, summon"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root found only in Germanic and Anatolian (Hittite ~halzai~).
• ~voll~: From MHG ~vol~, from OHG ~fol~, from Proto-West Germanic *~foll~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pleh₁-~ ("to fill"). Cognate with English ~full~, Dutch ~vol~, Gothic ~fulls~; Latin ~plēnus~ ("full") is from the same root, whence English ~plenty~ and ~replenish~. The separable particle ~voll-~ is resultative (~vollmachen~, ~volltanken~), and it should not be confused with the homophonous inseparable ~voll-~ of ~vollenden~ and ~vollbringen~, which means "completely" and never separates. The sense of ~voll~ here is: filling something up as the result of the action.

The root here is the strong ~laden~ "to load" (the weak ~laden~ "to invite" is a separate verb), and the resultative particle gives ~vollladen~ its sense: to load a thing until it is full.
en.volllaufen:
A separable compound of ~voll~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~voll~: From MHG ~vol~, from OHG ~fol~, from Proto-West Germanic *~foll~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pleh₁-~ ("to fill"). Cognate with English ~full~, Dutch ~vol~, Gothic ~fulls~; Latin ~plēnus~ ("full") is from the same root, whence English ~plenty~ and ~replenish~. The separable particle ~voll-~ is resultative (~vollmachen~, ~volltanken~), and it should not be confused with the homophonous inseparable ~voll-~ of ~vollenden~ and ~vollbringen~, which means "completely" and never separates. The sense of ~voll~ here is: completely full, filled to capacity.

Intransitive and taking ~sein~, ~volllaufen~ is said of a vessel or space filling of itself (~die Wanne läuft voll~), the liquid running in until it is full.
en.vollmachen:
A separable compound of ~voll~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~voll~: From MHG ~vol~, from OHG ~fol~, from Proto-West Germanic *~foll~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pleh₁-~ ("to fill"). Cognate with English ~full~, Dutch ~vol~, Gothic ~fulls~; Latin ~plēnus~ ("full") is from the same root, whence English ~plenty~ and ~replenish~. The separable particle ~voll-~ is resultative (~vollmachen~, ~volltanken~), and it should not be confused with the homophonous inseparable ~voll-~ of ~vollenden~ and ~vollbringen~, which means "completely" and never separates. The sense of ~voll~ here is: filling something up as the result of the action.

Colloquial ~vollmachen~ is simply to make something full (~den Tank vollmachen~), the particle naming the state the object reaches.
en.vollziehen:
Compound of ~voll-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). Cognate with English ~tow~ (from OE ~togian~), Latin ~dūcere~ ("to lead," whence ~duke~, ~conduct~, ~educate~).
• ~voll-~: From MHG ~vol~, from OHG ~fol~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pleh₁-~ ("to fill"). Cognate with English ~full~, Latin ~plēnus~ ("full," whence English ~plenty~, ~replenish~).

~Vollziehen~ means "to carry out, to execute, to consummate." Literally "to pull to fullness," it conveys completion of an official act: ~ein Urteil vollziehen~ ("to execute a sentence"), ~die Ehe vollziehen~ ("to consummate a marriage"), ~eine Maßnahme vollziehen~ ("to implement a measure"). The derived noun ~Vollzug~ ("execution, enforcement") appears in the compound ~Strafvollzug~ ("penal enforcement"). Latin ~dūcere~, from the same root as ~ziehen~, produced an astonishing family of English words: ~duke~, ~duct~, ~deduce~, ~produce~, ~reduce~, ~educate~, ~conduct~, all from the simple idea of pulling or leading.
en.vonstattengehen:
A separable compound of ~vonstatten-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~vonstatten-~: A fossilized prepositional phrase, ~von~ + ~statten~, in which ~statten~ is the old dative plural of MHG ~state~ ("place, opportunity, favourable position"), the same noun as ~Statt~ and ~Stätte~, ultimately from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). It survives only in ~vonstattengehen~, "to proceed, to come off", beside the parallel fossil ~zustattenkommen~ ("to come in useful"). English keeps that noun alive in ~stead~ and ~instead~. The sense of ~vonstatten-~ here is in ~vonstattengehen~: to proceed, to go off, to take place.

The verb takes ~sein~ and describes how an event unfolds or comes off, usually with a manner adverb (~reibungslos~, ~zügig~), as when something ~vonstattengeht~: goes smoothly, proceeds apace.
en.vorangehen:
A separable compound of ~voran-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~voran-~: A transparent compound of ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~) and ~an~ ("on, at"), together "out in front and pressing on," hence "ahead, forward, onward." It differs from bare ~vor-~ in adding the sense of continued progress. ~voran-~ marks position at the head of something, going first (~vorangehen~).

~Vorangehen~ is to walk at the head, going before the rest, and figuratively to set an example, as one who ~mit gutem Beispiel vorangeht~.
en.vorankommen:
A separable compound of ~voran-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~voran-~: A transparent compound of ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~) and ~an~ ("on, at"), together "out in front and pressing on," hence "ahead, forward, onward." It differs from bare ~vor-~ in adding the sense of continued progress. ~voran-~ marks progress, the thing advancing rather than merely being in front (~vorankommen~, ~vorantreiben~).

~Vorankommen~ is rarely meant spatially: one makes headway with a task, a plan, a country: it is about getting on, not about the place at the front.
en.voranmachen:
A separable compound of ~voran-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~voran-~: A transparent compound of ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~) and ~an~ ("on, at"), together "out in front and pressing on," hence "ahead, forward, onward." It differs from bare ~vor-~ in adding the sense of continued progress. ~voran-~ marks progress, the thing advancing rather than merely being in front (~vorankommen~, ~vorantreiben~).

Colloquial and mostly heard as the imperative ~mach voran!~, ~voranmachen~ means to get a move on, the ~voran~ urging the action onward rather than marking a place in front.
en.voranschieben:
A separable compound of ~voran-~ + ~schieben~:

• ~schieben~: From MHG ~schieben~, from OHG ~skioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeubaną~, from PIE *~skewbʰ-~ ("to push, to shove, to thrust"). A class II strong verb (~schieben~, ~schob~, ~geschoben~). Cognate with English ~shove~, Dutch ~schuiven~, Danish ~skubbe~.
• ~voran-~: A transparent compound of ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~) and ~an~ ("on, at"), together "out in front and pressing on," hence "ahead, forward, onward." It differs from bare ~vor-~ in adding the sense of continued progress. ~voran-~ marks progress, the thing advancing rather than merely being in front (~vorankommen~, ~vorantreiben~).

~Voranschieben~ is to shove something forward (a cart, a chess pawn, or figuratively a project), the ~voran~ giving ~schieben~ its onward direction.
en.voranschreiten:
A separable compound of ~voran-~ + ~schreiten~:

• ~schreiten~: From MHG ~schrīten~, from OHG ~skrītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīþan~ ("to step, stride"), from Proto-Germanic *~skrīþaną~ ("to walk, glide, crawl"), from PIE *~(s)kreyt-~ ("to stride"), an extension of *~(s)krey-~ ("to go about"). Cognate with Lithuanian ~skrìsti~ ("to rush, run"), Latvian ~skrìet~ ("to run, fly"). Related to ~Schritt~ ("step").
• ~voran-~: A transparent compound of ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~) and ~an~ ("on, at"), together "out in front and pressing on," hence "ahead, forward, onward." It differs from bare ~vor-~ in adding the sense of continued progress. ~voran-~ marks progress, the thing advancing rather than merely being in front (~vorankommen~, ~vorantreiben~).

~Voranschreiten~ is used above all of abstract advance (technology, digitalization, a process ~schreitet voran~), the stately ~schreiten~ "to stride" lending progress a measured, inexorable gait.
en.voranstellen:
A separable compound of ~voran-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~voran-~: A transparent compound of ~vor~ ("before, in front," from OHG ~fora~, from PIE *~per-~) and ~an~ ("on, at"), together "out in front and pressing on," hence "ahead, forward, onward." It differs from bare ~vor-~ in adding the sense of continued progress. ~voran-~ marks position at the head of something, going first (~vorangehen~).

~Voranstellen~ is to place one thing in front of another (a word before a clause, a remark before a speech), setting it at the head where it comes first.
en.vorantreiben:
Compound of ~voran-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~, from PIE *~dʰreybʰ-~ ("to drive, push"). Cognate with Dutch ~drijven~, English ~drive~, Danish ~drive~, Swedish ~driva~.
• ~voran-~: Compound separable prefix from ~vor-~ (from PIE *~preh₂~ "before, in front") + ~an-~ (from PIE *~h₂en~ "on, onto"). Together they mean "ahead, forward, onward."

~Vorantreiben~ means "to push forward, to advance, to drive on", literally "to drive something ahead." It is the quintessential verb of progress and ambition: ~ein Projekt vorantreiben~ ("to push a project forward"), ~die Forschung vorantreiben~ ("to advance research"). The English cognate ~drive~ is a perfect semantic match in many contexts: to "drive" progress forward, to "drive" a project.
en.vorausahnen:
A separable compound of ~voraus-~ + ~ahnen~:

• ~ahnen~: From MHG ~anen~, from OHG *~anōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~anōn~, from the preposition *~ana~ ("on"), from Proto-Germanic *~an~ ("on"). Cognate with Middle Low German ~ānen~, dialectal Dutch ~anen~ ("to conjecture"), Saterland Frisian ~oanje~ ("to suspect").
• ~voraus-~: The compound adverb ~vor~ ("before, in front of") + ~aus~ ("out"); see those entries for their separate histories. Together they mean "ahead, in advance." More often it is temporal: doing something in advance, before the fact.

~Vorausahnen~ is to sense a thing before it happens (to have a foreboding of it in advance), the ~voraus~ setting the intuition ahead of the event.
en.vorausberechnen:
A separable compound of ~voraus-~ + ~be-~ + ~rechnen~:

• ~rechnen~: From MHG ~rechenen~, from OHG ~rehhanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rekanōn~ ("to count, explain"), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to make straight or right"), the same root as German ~recht~ and Latin ~rectus~. Cognate with English ~reckon~, Dutch ~rekenen~, Low German ~rekenen~, Danish ~regne~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~voraus-~: The compound adverb ~vor~ ("before, in front of") + ~aus~ ("out"); see those entries for their separate histories. Together they mean "ahead, in advance." More often it is temporal: doing something in advance, before the fact.

~Vorausberechnen~ is to compute a value ahead of time (to project a figure before the fact), with ~be-~ making ~rechnen~ transitive and ~voraus~ throwing the reckoning forward into the future.
en.vorausgehen:
A separable compound of ~voraus-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~voraus-~: The compound adverb ~vor~ ("before, in front of") + ~aus~ ("out"); see those entries for their separate histories. Together they mean "ahead, in advance." ~voraus-~ means going on ahead of others in space.

~Vorausgehen~ is to go on ahead of the rest, in space or time: the scout out in front, or the event that precedes another and leads up to it.
en.voraushaben:
A separable compound of ~voraus-~ + ~haben~:
