Sense 1 ("to weigh"): a northwestern variant of ~wegen~ that generalized the present-singular stem vowel ~i~, from OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, move"); the original ~e~-form survives in the doublet ~wägen~. Sense 2 ("to rock, cradle"): from ~wige~ ("cradle," modern ~Wiege~), from OHG ~wīga~, likely related to Proto-West Germanic *~waggjan~ ("to cause to move"), from the same PIE root. Cognate with English ~weigh~, Dutch ~wegen~, Danish ~veje~.
• ~vor-~: From MHG ~vor~, ~vore~, from OHG ~fora~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fura~, from Proto-Germanic *~furai~, from PIE *~pr̥h₂-éy~, a case form of the root *~preh₂-~ ("before, in front"). Cognate with English ~fore~ and ~before~, Dutch ~voor~, Gothic ~faura~, and, from the same root, Latin ~prae~ and ~prō~. The prefix conveys precedence: putting one thing ahead of another.

The root here is ~wiegen~ "to weigh" (the strong verb), not the weak ~wiegen~ "to rock": what ~vorwiegt~ weighs more than the rest and so predominates.
en.vorzeigen:
A separable compound of ~vor-~ + ~zeigen~:

• ~zeigen~: From MHG ~zeigen~, from OHG ~zeigōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taigōn~, possibly from Proto-Germanic *~taikōną~ (iterative), an intensive derivative of OHG ~zīhan~ ("to accuse"), ultimately from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to point out, show"), whence also ~Zeichen~ ("sign") and English ~teach~. In Modern German it absorbed the unrelated MHG ~zöugen~.
• ~vor-~: From MHG ~vor~, ~vore~, from OHG ~fora~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fura~, from Proto-Germanic *~furai~, from PIE *~pr̥h₂-éy~, a case form of the root *~preh₂-~ ("before, in front"). Cognate with English ~fore~ and ~before~, Dutch ~voor~, Gothic ~faura~, and, from the same root, Latin ~prae~ and ~prō~. The prefix conveys presenting or performing something for an audience.

To ~vorzeigen~ is to hold something out openly for viewing: a ticket, a picture, a proof.
en.vorziehen:
A separable compound of ~vor-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~vor-~: From MHG ~vor~, ~vore~, from OHG ~fora~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fura~, from Proto-Germanic *~furai~, from PIE *~pr̥h₂-éy~, a case form of the root *~preh₂-~ ("before, in front"). Cognate with English ~fore~ and ~before~, Dutch ~voor~, Gothic ~faura~, and, from the same root, Latin ~prae~ and ~prō~. The prefix conveys forward motion or position in front.

Literally one draws something to the front: here the curtains; alongside stands the figurative sense "to prefer," to ~vorziehen~ one person over another.
en.vorüberfahren:
A separable compound of ~vorüber-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~vorüber-~: The adverb ~vor~ ("before, in front") compounded with ~über~ ("over, across"): past a point and beyond it. Transparently compositional and close in sense to ~vorbei~; the etymology belongs to the two component entries. The sense of ~vorüber-~ here is: directional, "past, by", of moving alongside something and on beyond it.

To ~vorüberfahren~ is to come driving past something and carry on beyond it.
en.vorübergehen:
A separable compound of ~vorüber-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~vorüber-~: The adverb ~vor~ ("before, in front") compounded with ~über~ ("over, across"): past a point and beyond it. Transparently compositional and close in sense to ~vorbei~; the etymology belongs to the two component entries. The sense of ~vorüber-~ here is: temporally, "over, at an end".

~Vorübergehen~ means spatially to walk past, but figuratively to elapse: an opportunity or a pain ~geht vorüber~ ("passes, comes to an end").
en.wachhalten:
A separable compound of ~wach~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~wach~: The adjective ~wach~ ("awake") is young: a sixteenth-century back-formation from the noun ~Wache~ ("watch, guard"), taking the place of older ~wacker~. Its family is ~wachen~, from OHG ~wahhēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wakāną~, from PIE *~weǵ-~ ("to be lively, vigorous"). Cognate with Old English ~wacian~ (English ~wake~), Dutch ~waken~, Old Norse ~vaka~, Gothic ~gawaknan~; through Latin ~vigil~ and ~vigēre~ the same root gives English ~vigil~ and ~vigour~. The sense of ~wach~ here is as a resultative adjective, "awake": the verb brings someone into wakefulness.

To ~wachhalten~ here is literally to keep someone from falling asleep; figuratively one also keeps a memory or an issue ~wach~ ("alive, current").
en.wachrufen:
A separable compound of ~wach~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. A parallel weak form in Middle High German explains why the modern present lacks the expected umlaut (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~wach~: The adjective ~wach~ ("awake") is young: a sixteenth-century back-formation from the noun ~Wache~ ("watch, guard"), taking the place of older ~wacker~. Its family is ~wachen~, from OHG ~wahhēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wakāną~, from PIE *~weǵ-~ ("to be lively, vigorous"). Cognate with Old English ~wacian~ (English ~wake~), Dutch ~waken~, Old Norse ~vaka~, Gothic ~gawaknan~; through Latin ~vigil~ and ~vigēre~ the same root gives English ~vigil~ and ~vigour~. The sense of ~wach~ here is: figuratively, "alert, alive", of keeping a memory or an issue current.

Thus ~wachrufen~ is to call a memory, a feeling, or an image into consciousness, to rouse it, as it were, back into wakefulness.
en.wachsen:
From Middle High German ~wahsen~, from Old High German ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb. Cognate with Low German ~wassen~, Dutch ~wassen~, West Frisian ~waakse~, English ~wax~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~. Non-Germanic cognates include Ancient Greek ~aéxein~ ("to increase") and Latin ~auxilium~ ("help," from a sense of "increase of strength").

English preserves the same verb as the literary and poetic ~wax~ ("the moon waxes"), enshrined in the phrase ~wax and wane~. In everyday modern English the verb ~wax~ (to grow) is archaic except in that fixed phrase and in expressions like "to wax poetic." German ~wachsen~ has remained the ordinary word for growing throughout: of plants, of children, of economies. The PIE root *~h₂weg-~ is also the ancestor of Latin ~augēre~ ("to increase"), giving English ~augment~, ~auction~ (from "increase by bidding"), and the imperial title ~Augustus~ ("the increased, the revered one"). The ablaut series ~wächst~/~wuchs~/~gewachsen~ follows class VI. The compound ~entwachsen~ ("to outgrow") and the noun ~Wuchs~ ("growth, stature") preserve the root's productive legacy.
en.wagen: From Middle High German ~wāgen~ ("to risk, to dare"), ultimately derived from Old High German ~wāga~ ("scales, balance; weight"), the modern word ~Waage~ ("scales"). The underlying metaphor is vivid: to ~wagen~ is to place something on the scales without knowing where the balance will fall. The OHG noun ~wāga~ descends from Proto-West Germanic *~wāgu~ ("scales"), from Proto-Germanic *~wēgō~, related to *~weganą~ ("to move, to weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to move, to transport, to carry"). This root is spectacularly productive: it gave Latin ~vehere~ ("to carry") and its derivatives ~vehicle~, ~convex~, ~invective~; English ~way~, ~weigh~, ~wain~ ("wagon"); and German ~Weg~ ("way"), ~bewegen~ ("to move"), ~wiegen~ ("to weigh"), and ~Wagen~ ("car, wagon"). The noun ~Wagen~ and the verb ~wagen~ are thus false friends in disguise: ~Wagen~ comes from the "vehicle" branch of the root, while ~wagen~ comes from the "scales" branch; yet both trace back to the same PIE notion of weighing and moving. Cognate with Dutch ~wagen~ ("to dare").
en.wahrnehmen: From Middle High German ~war nemen~, from Old High German ~wara neman~, literally "to take attention." A compound of ~wahr-~ (not the adjective ~wahr~ "true," but a separate word meaning "heed, attention, care") + ~nehmen~ ("to take"). The ~wahr-~ element derives from Proto-West Germanic *~warōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~warō~ ("care, attention, heed"), possibly from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, watch, guard, protect"). This *~warō~ also underlies ~wahren~ ("to safeguard, protect") and ~bewahren~ ("to preserve"), and, through a parallel Germanic branch, English ~wary~ and ~aware~. ~Nehmen~ derives from Old High German ~nëman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). The compound is a beautiful example of a metaphor now hidden beneath surface spelling: to perceive is literally "to take notice"; attention is grasped, not merely received. The homophony with ~wahr~ ("true") creates a productive ambiguity: ~wahrnehmen~ can feel as if it means "to take something as true," reinforcing the philosophical weight the verb carries in German. Cognate with Dutch ~waarnemen~, English ~wary~ and ~aware~ (via the *~warō~ root).
en.wahrsagen:
A separable compound of ~wahr-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~wahr-~: Two different words fall together in this spelling. In ~wahrsagen~ it is the adjective ~wahr~ ("true"), from MHG ~wār~, from OHG ~wār~, from Proto-Germanic *~wēraz~, from PIE *~weh₁ro-~ ("true, trustworthy"), cognate with Latin ~vērus~ (whence English ~very~, ~verify~, ~verdict~) and Old Irish ~fír~. In ~wahrnehmen~ it is instead the old feminine noun OHG ~wara~, MHG ~war(e)~ ("attention, heed, watchfulness"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to watch out for, to perceive"): OHG ~wara neman~ was "to take heed", and only in Middle High German did it narrow to sensory perception. That second root is the one English keeps in ~aware~, ~beware~, and ~wary~, so ~wahrnehmen~ is a closer relative of ~be aware~ than of ~true~. The sense of ~wahr-~ here is in ~wahrsagen~: the adjective ~wahr~: to speak true, to prophesy.

To ~wahrsagen~ is literally to "speak truth," and it converges in meaning with its near-synonym ~weissagen~, which, despite appearances, belongs not to ~weiß~ ("white") but to OHG ~wīzago~ ("seer," akin to ~wissen~ "to know"): two roads to prophecy from two different roots.
en.wandeln:
From Middle High German ~wandeln~, from Old High German ~wantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandōną~, from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). Cognate with Dutch ~wandelen~ ("to walk, stroll"), English ~wend~ (from OE ~wendan~, "to turn"), and ~wind~ (the verb, "to coil").

~Wandeln~ means both "to walk, to stroll" (an elevated, literary synonym for ~gehen~) and "to change, to transform" (~sich wandeln~). These senses seem unrelated, but both descend from the root idea of turning: to walk is to turn one's steps in a direction, and to change is to turn into something else. The same dual meaning survives in the related noun ~Wandel~ ("change, transformation") and the famous compound ~Wanderlust~, which passed into English unchanged. The tribal name ~Vandals~ (~Wandali~) may derive from the same root, possibly meaning "the wanderers."
en.wandern: From Middle High German ~wandern~, from Old High German *~wantarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandarōn~, itself formed from *~wandōn~ ("to turn, to change") with the frequentative suffix *~-rōn~, suggesting repeated or habitual turning or moving about. The root traces to Proto-Germanic *~wandōną~ ("to turn"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, to wind"). The frequentative formation captures the essential nature of wandering: not a single purposeful journey but a repeated, meandering motion. The word is attested since the 13th century and originally carried the sense of journeying on foot as a tradesman, the ~Wanderjahre~ ("years of wandering") were the years a journeyman spent traveling from workshop to workshop after completing his apprenticeship, a tradition formalized in the medieval guild system and still practiced by some German tradespeople today. Cognate with English ~wander~ (from the same Proto-West Germanic source), Dutch ~wandelen~ ("to stroll, to walk for pleasure"), Danish ~vandre~, Swedish ~vandra~. The PIE root *~wendʰ-~ also gives English ~wind~ (the verb, "to twist") and ~wend~, German ~wenden~ ("to turn"), and Latin ~ventus~ ("wind", air that turns and twists). The cultural concept of ~Wanderlust~ (that restless longing for the open road) was borrowed into English directly from German, one of those rare words that filled a gap no English term could.
en.warmhalten:
A separable compound of ~warm~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~warm~: From the adjective ~warm~, from MHG ~warm~, from OHG ~warm~, from Proto-West Germanic *~warm~, from Proto-Germanic *~warmaz~, of uncertain further origin: either PIE *~wer-~ ("to burn") or PIE *~gʷʰer-~ ("warm, hot"), the latter of which would make it a distant relative of Ancient Greek ~thermós~ and Latin ~formus~. Cognate with English ~warm~, Dutch ~warm~, Swedish ~varm~. As a separable particle it is resultative: the verb brings its object into a warm state. The sense of ~warm~ here is: figuratively, thawing a cold relation or keeping something hospitable.

~Warmhalten~ denotes not the heating but the preserving of warmth; in the figurative ~sich jemanden warmhalten~ it means keeping a contact or patron well-disposed toward oneself.
en.warnen: From Middle High German ~warnen~ ("to watch over, to protect"), from Old High German ~warnōn~ ("to deny, to refuse, to decline"), from Proto-West Germanic *~warnōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~warnōną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, to perceive, to watch out for"). The semantic evolution is noteworthy: in Old High German, ~warnōn~ meant "to refuse, to deny", an act of self-protection. By Middle High German, the sense had shifted to "to watch over, to guard, to caution", protecting others rather than oneself. In Modern German, ~warnen~ means specifically "to warn, to caution" (~vor etwas warnen~, "to warn against something"). The shift from refusal to warning follows a natural logic: one who refuses danger for oneself eventually tells others to do the same. Cognate with Old English ~wyrnan~ ("to refuse, to withhold"), Old Norse ~varna~ ("to refuse"), Old Saxon ~wernian~ ("to decline, to withhold"), and, most strikingly, English ~warn~, which underwent the same semantic shift independently. The PIE root *~wer-~ also yields Latin ~verēri~ ("to fear, to respect," whence English ~revere~), German ~wahren~ ("to safeguard"), and ~Wart~ ("watchman," as in ~Torwart~, "goalkeeper"). The derived noun ~Warnung~ ("warning") and the ~Warnweste~ ("high-visibility vest") both preserve the ancient watching-over sense.
en.warten:
From Middle High German ~warten~, from Old High German ~wartēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wardēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wardāną~ ("to guard, protect, watch over"), derived from *~warduz~ ("a guard"), ultimately from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, watch, guard").

The semantic shift from "to guard, watch over" to "to wait" reflects the experience of a sentinel: one who keeps watch necessarily also waits. This same shift occurred in English ~ward~ (from the same root) and in French ~garder~ ("to guard") and ~attendre~ ("to wait," literally "to attend to"). In Modern German, ~warten~ retains both senses in certain contexts, ~warte auf mich~ ("wait for me") and the older sense of tending/caring persists in ~warten~ as "to service, maintain" (as in ~ein Auto warten~, "to service a car"), a usage that connects back directly to the original "to watch over, tend." Cognate with Old Saxon ~wardōn~, Swedish ~vårda~ ("to tend, care for"), English ~ward~, Dutch ~bewaren~ ("to keep, preserve").
en.waschen:
From Middle High German ~waschen~, from Old High German ~wascan~, ~waskan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~waskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waskaną~ ("to wash"), from an earlier *~watskaną~, a ~ske~-present formation from PIE *~wed-~ ("wet, water"). The same PIE root gives English ~water~, ~wet~, and ~wash~ itself. Cognate with Dutch ~wassen~, English ~wash~, West Frisian ~waskje~, Danish ~vaske~.

The PIE derivation is revealing: ~waschen~ is built on a present-tense formation with the ~ske~-suffix (PIE *~wod-ske-~), a morphological pattern used to create iterative or inchoative presents. The basic meaning was "to make wet (repeatedly)", washing as the iterative application of water. German ~waschen~ and English ~wash~ descend from the same Proto-Germanic word and have maintained nearly identical meanings across a millennium of independent development. The verb is also notable as an anagram of ~wachsen~ ("to grow"), a coincidence with no etymological significance but one that generations of German schoolchildren have noticed. The reflexive ~sich die Hände waschen~ ("to wash one's hands") carries the same metaphorical meaning of moral disavowal as in English, both ultimately from the biblical account of Pontius Pilate.
en.weben: From MHG ~weben~, from OHG ~weban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~weban~, from Proto-Germanic *~webaną~, from PIE *~webʰ-~ ("to weave, braid"). Originally a class V strong verb (OHG ~weban~, ~wab~, ~giweban~); modern German conjugates it weak (~webte~, ~gewebt~) for the literal craft, while the strong ~wob~, ~gewoben~ (whose ~o~ is a later analogical remodelling on the pattern of ~heben~, ~hob~, ~gehoben~) belongs to elevated and figurative use (~um ihn wob sich eine Legende~). en.wechseln:
From Middle High German ~wëhseln~, from Old High German *~wehsalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wihslōną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~weyk-~, *~weyḱ-~ ("to change, bend, yield"). The connection between ~wechseln~ and English ~week~ runs through the Proto-Germanic root *~wikǭ~ ("sequence, turn"), itself from *~wīkaną~ ("to bend, yield, give way"). A week is a "turn" of days, a cycle that yields to the next. The same root produced Latin ~vicis~ ("change, alternation, turn"), found in ~vice versa~ ("with the turn reversed"), ~vicar~ (one who stands in another's turn or place), and ~vicious~ (originally relating to a flaw in the pattern). German ~Woche~ and English ~week~ are thus cognates of ~wechseln~, all sharing the sense of something that changes, turns, or yields its place. The notion of currency exchange (~Geldwechsel~) preserves the oldest concrete sense: money, like days, passes from hand to hand in alternating turns. Cognate with Dutch ~wisselen~, English ~week~, Latin ~vicis~ ("turn, change").
en.wecken:
From Middle High German ~wecken~, from Old High German ~wecchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wakkjan~ ("to wake up, to awaken"), from Proto-Germanic *~wakjaną~, a causative formation from *~wakaną~ ("to be awake"), from PIE *~weǵ-~ ("to be lively, to wake"). The causative relationship is transparent: *~wakaną~ means "to be awake" (intransitive), *~wakjaną~ means "to make awake" (transitive), and this is precisely the modern German distinction between ~wachen~ ("to be awake, to keep watch") and ~wecken~ ("to wake someone up"). Cognate with Dutch ~wekken~, English ~watch~ (from the same Proto-West Germanic source but with a different semantic development).

The English cognate ~watch~ reveals a surprising semantic drift: from "to wake, to be alert" (Old English ~wæccan~) to "to observe attentively" to "a timepiece used to mark the hours of wakefulness." German ~wecken~ stayed closer to the original causative meaning. The derived noun ~Wecker~ ("alarm clock") is transparently "the thing that wakes you", a straightforward agent noun. The compound ~aufwecken~ ("to wake up," with emphasis on the completion of the action) adds the ~auf-~ prefix for thoroughness. The related word ~erwecken~ ("to awaken, to arouse") has developed a strong figurative and religious sense: ~Erweckung~ ("awakening, revival") refers to spiritual renewal, as in the ~Erweckungsbewegung~ ("revival movement").
en.wegbefördern:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~be-~ + ~fördern~:

• ~fördern~: From MHG ~vürdern~, from OHG ~furdiren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~furþrijan~ ("to move forward"), a derivative of the comparative adverb ~fürder~ ("further, forward"), from Proto-West Germanic *~forþar~, from PIE *~per-~ ("before, in front, first"). The ~ö~ rather than the expected ~ü~ arose by conflation with ~vorder~ (whence ~fordern~). Cognate with English ~further~, Dutch ~vorderen~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ adds thoroughness or completeness to the base action.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Befördern~ means "to move forward, to transport," and ~weg-~ supplies the direction: to get something out of the way, often said jocularly of an irksome person or thing.

• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). • ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. en.wegerklären:

• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. ~Erklären~ is "to make clear, to expound"; with ~weg-~ the explaining becomes disposal: arguing an inconvenient fact out of existence rather than removing it in space.
en.wegfahren:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). • ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. en.wegfallen:

Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. en.wegfliegen:

• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. en.wegführen:

• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. en.weggeben:

• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. en.weggehen:

en.weghören:

en.wegjagen:

en.wegkommen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegkommen~ is "to get away, to escape" (intransitive, with ~sein~); "gut wegkommen" means to come off lightly, and "etwas kommt weg" means it goes missing.
en.weglaufen:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

In ~weglaufen~ the subject removes itself on foot, and the verb accordingly forms its perfect with ~sein~.

• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

Where ~legen~ merely sets something down, ~weglegen~ sets it aside: out of hand and out of use.
en.wegmachen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. ~Wegmachen~ is colloquial, meaning to make something disappear: a stain, a smudge.
en.wegnehmen:

en.wegräumen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~räumen~:

• ~räumen~: From Early New High German ~reumen~, a Central German umlaut variant of ~raumen~, from MHG ~rūmen~, from OHG ~rūmen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rūmijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rūmijaną~, a factitive verb from the adjective *~rūmaz~ ("roomy, spacious"), from PIE *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open"). • ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. en.wegschaffen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~schaffen~:

• ~schaffen~: Two historically distinct verbs have merged under a single infinitive, distinguished only by their conjugation. The strong ~schaffen~ (~schuf~, ~geschaffen~, "to create") descends from MHG ~schaffen~, OHG ~scaffan~, a byform of ~skephen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skappjan~; the ~-f-~ was chiefly back-formed from the participle ~giscaffan~. The weak ~schaffen~ (~schaffte~, ~geschafft~, "to manage, accomplish") descends from OHG ~skaffōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skapōn~, from the same root. Cognate with Dutch ~scheppen~, English ~shape~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

This is the weak ~schaffen~ in its sense "to convey, cart," not the strong "to create"; ~wegschaffen~ means to get something troublesome out of the way.
en.wegschauen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegschauen~ turns the gaze aside: often figuratively, a refusal to see.
en.wegschicken:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~schicken~:

• ~schicken~: From MHG ~schicken~ ("to outfit oneself, fit in, arrange appropriately"), from OHG *~skihhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skikkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skikkijaną~ ("to order, send"), the causative of the verb underlying MHG ~geschehen~ ("to happen, rush"). • ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegschicken~ sends someone or something off; the base sense "to send" becomes sending away from the speaker.
en.wegschieben:

• ~schieben~: From MHG ~schieben~, from OHG ~skioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeubaną~, from PIE *~skewbʰ-~ ("to push, to shove, to thrust"). A class II strong verb (~schieben~, ~schob~, ~geschoben~). Cognate with English ~shove~, Dutch ~schuiven~, Danish ~skubbe~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegschieben~ eases something aside with steady pressure, without the jolt of ~wegstoßen~.
en.wegschießen:

~Wegschießen~ severs or hurls something away with a shot.
en.wegschleifen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~schleifen~:

• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. This is the weak ~schleifen~ ("to drag"), not the strong ("to whet"): ~wegschleifen~ hauls something away across the ground.
en.wegschmeißen:

• ~schmeißen~: From MHG ~smīȥen~, from OHG ~smīȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~smītaną~, from PIE *~smeyd-~. • ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys disposal: getting rid of something for good.

en.wegschwimmen:

~Wegschwimmen~ describes a swimmer or flotsam moving off from a spot; the perfect takes ~sein~.
en.wegsehen:

• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. en.wegsetzen:

• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. ~Wegsetzen~ places something elsewhere; reflexively, ~sich wegsetzen~ can mean to move to another seat.
en.wegsperren:

• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. • ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. ~Wegstecken~ tucks something out of sight: into a pocket, away from view; figuratively also to take a loss in stride.
en.wegstehlen:

• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. en.wegsterben:

• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegsterben~ carries the directional sense into dying: people or species die off one by one until none remain.
en.wegstoßen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). Cognate with dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce, ricochet"), Dutch ~stoten~, Old Norse ~stauta~ and ~steyta~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegstoßen~ drives something off with a forceful shove: the vigor distinguishing it from the gentler ~wegschieben~.
en.wegtragen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb whose semantic range broadened from "to drag, pull" to "to carry, bear, wear." Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegtragen~ carries a load away from its place: the object is borne off, not moving on its own.
en.wegtreiben:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegtreiben~ has the two lives of ~treiben~ itself. With ~haben~ it drives people, cattle, or clouds off ahead of it, and the driving force lies with the subject. With ~sein~ the subject is the thing driven: a boat or a swimmer drifts away on wind and current (~das Boot ist weggetrieben~).
en.wegtreten:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

In military use ~wegtreten~ is the order to leave formation and move off.
en.wegwaschen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~waschen~:

• ~waschen~: From MHG ~waschen~, from OHG ~wascan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~waskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waskaną~, from an earlier *~watskaną~, a ~ske~-present formation from PIE *~wed-~ ("wet, water"), hence "to make wet (repeatedly)." Cognate with English ~wash~, ~water~, ~wet~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vaske~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegwaschen~ turns washing toward what it removes: dirt (or guilt) is carried off by water.
en.wegweisen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative verb from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from PIE *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know"). A class I strong verb; its senses "to show, point" and "to direct, expel" both direct knowledge or attention. Cognate with English ~wise~, ~wit~, ~wizard~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

Here ~weisen~ is not "to show" but "to direct, send off": ~wegweisen~ means to send someone away or turn them out.
en.wegwenden:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~wenden~:

• ~wenden~: From MHG ~wenden~, from OHG ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), the causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). It belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort (preterite ~wandte~, participle ~gewandt~) and has a doubled preterite: ~wandte~ for turning the self or one's attention, the regularized ~wendete~ for physical turning. Cognate with English ~wend~, Armenian ~gind~ ("ring").
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegwenden~ draws on the verb's ~wandte~ branch: turning one's gaze or oneself away from something.
en.wegwerfen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys disposal: getting rid of something for good.

~Wegwerfen~ is the everyday act of discarding; figuratively one can throw away one's worth or dignity too.
en.wegwünschen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~wünschen~:

• ~wünschen~: From MHG ~wünschen~, from OHG ~wunsken~ ("to choose, wish, desire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wunskijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wunskijaną~, from *~wunskaz~ ("wish, desire"), from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to wish, love"), which also underlies ~Wonne~ ("bliss") and English ~win~. Cognate with English ~wish~, Dutch ~wensen~, Danish ~ønske~, Sanskrit ~vāṃchati~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegwünschen~ moves the removal into the irrealis: one can only wish a person or thing gone, not make it so.
en.wegziehen:
A separable compound of ~weg-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~weg-~: Not a prefix but the adverb ~weg~ ("away"), shortened from MHG ~enwec~, from OHG ~in weg~ ("on the way"); the noun ~Weg~ descends from Proto-Germanic *~wegaz~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to go, to transport"), the root behind Latin ~vehere~ and English ~wagon~ and ~vehicle~. English built its equivalent from exactly the same parts: ~away~ is Old English ~onweg~, also literally "on the way." The adverb has since shortened its vowel, which is all that now distinguishes it from the noun ~Weg~. The particle conveys departure or removal from a place: going or taking away.

~Wegziehen~ is transitively to pull something away, intransitively to move house to another place.
en.wehren:
From MHG ~weren~, from OHG ~werien~, from Proto-West Germanic *~warjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~warjaną~ ("to defend, to ward off, to protect"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to close, to cover, to protect"). Cognate with English ~weir~ (a defensive barrier across a stream), ~ward~, ~warden~, ~guard~ (via Old French, from Frankish *~wardōn~), Dutch ~weren~, Old Norse ~verja~, Gothic ~warjan~.

~Wehren~ means "to defend, to ward off" and is most commonly used reflexively: ~sich wehren~ ("to defend oneself, to resist"). The noun ~Wehr~ gives rise to ~Bundeswehr~ ("Federal Defense", Germany's armed forces), ~Feuerwehr~ ("fire defense", the fire department), and ~Wehrmacht~ ("defense force", the name of Germany's armed forces from 1935 to 1945). The PIE root *~wer-~ ("to close, to cover, to protect") is enormously productive: it yielded Latin ~aperīre~ ("to open", literally "to un-cover," with privative ~a-~), whence English ~aperture~; Latin ~operīre~ ("to cover"), whence ~cover~ itself (via Old French); and Sanskrit ~vr̥ṇóti~ ("he covers, he closes"). The English words ~warn~, ~warrant~, ~garrison~, and ~guarantee~ all trace back through different paths to this same defensive root.
en.weichen:
From Middle High German ~wīchen~, from Old High German ~wīchan~ ("to yield, give way"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wīkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīkwaną~, from PIE *~h₃weyg-~ ("to start moving, to distance oneself, to bend, wind"). A class I strong verb. Cognate with Old English ~wīcan~ ("to yield, give way"), Old Norse ~vīkja~ ("to turn, retreat"), Swedish ~vika~ ("to give way, fold").

~Weichen~ means "to yield, to give way, to retreat." It is not to be confused with the weak verb ~weichen~ ("to soften, to soak"), which derives from a different source (~weich~ "soft"). The strong verb's PIE root *~h₃weyg-~ is also the ancestor of Old Norse ~vík~ ("bay, inlet", a place where the coastline bends), which gave us the word ~Viking~: people of the inlets, or perhaps people who turn aside (i.e., raiders who venture out). The connection between yielding and bending is preserved in the cognate Swedish ~vika~, which means both "to yield" and "to fold."
en.weichkochen:
A separable compound of ~weich~ + ~kochen~:

• ~kochen~: From MHG ~kochen~, from OHG ~kohhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kokōn~, borrowed from Late Latin ~cocō~, from Latin ~coquō~ ("I cook, I boil"), from PIE *~pekʷ-~ ("to cook, to ripen"). A loan early enough to have undergone the High German shift of ~k~ to ~ch~. Cognate with English ~cook~, Dutch ~koken~, Danish ~koge~.
• ~weich~: From the adjective ~weich~ ("soft"), from MHG ~weich~, from OHG ~weih~, from Proto-West Germanic *~waik~, from Proto-Germanic *~waikwaz~, a derivative of *~wīkaną~ ("to yield, to give way"), softness understood as the property of giving way, which is still the sense of ~weichen~. Cognate with Dutch ~week~, Old English ~wāc~, and Old Norse ~veikr~; English borrowed the Norse form as ~weak~ after its own ~wāc~ died out, so ~weich~ and ~weak~ are the same word by two routes. As a particle it is resultative: the verb softens its object. The sense of ~weich~ here is: of cooking, boiling or simmering until tender.

~Weichkochen~ is purely culinary: boiling potatoes or eggs until they are soft.
en.weinen:
From Middle High German ~weinen~, from Old High German ~weinōn~ ("to cry, lament, cry woe"), from Proto-Germanic *~wainōną~ ("to wail, weep"), from PIE *~wáy~ ("woe!"). Cognate with Gothic ~wainon~ ("to suffer"), Old Norse ~veina~ ("to wail"), Old English ~wānian~ ("to bewail"), and Dutch ~wenen~ ("to weep, to cry"). Related to ~Weh~ ("woe, pain"), from Proto-Germanic *~waiwô~, from the same exclamatory root.

The connection between ~weinen~ and English ~woe~ reveals that both descend from what was originally an exclamation of grief, a raw sound of pain that became grammaticalized into a verb ("to express woe") and a noun ("the state of grief"). The PIE exclamation *~wáy~ also produced Latin ~vae~ ("woe!," as in ~vae victis~ "woe to the vanquished") and Old Irish ~fáe~ ("woe"). The German noun ~Wein~ ("wine") is an unrelated homograph, borrowed from Latin ~vīnum~, a false-friend trap that has confused many a beginning German student. The distinction between ~weinen~ ("to cry, to weep") and ~heulen~ ("to howl, to bawl") mirrors the ~lächeln~/~lachen~ pair in reverse: ~weinen~ is dignified, quiet grief, while ~heulen~ is loud and unrestrained.
en.weisen:
From Middle High German ~wīsen~, from Old High German ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative verb derived from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know"). A class I strong verb.

The PIE root *~weyd-~ ("to see, know") is one of the most productive in the entire Indo-European family. It yields Latin ~videō~ ("I see"), Sanskrit ~veda~ ("I know"), and Ancient Greek ~eídō~ ("I see; I know"). In Germanic, the root produced both ~wissen~ ("to know") (a preterite-present verb) and the adjective ~weise~ ("wise"), whence ~weisen~. English ~wise~, ~wit~, and ~wizard~ all derive from the same PIE root, as does English ~vision~ (via Latin ~vidēre~). The two modern German senses of ~weisen~ ("to show, point" and "to direct, expel" (as in ~ausweisen~, "to expel or identify," and ~verweisen~, "to refer or rebuke")) both flow from the underlying idea of directing knowledge or attention: to point is to make someone see, and to expel is to direct away. The noun ~Beweis~ ("proof, evidence") is a nominalization of the same root, preserving the ancient link between seeing and knowing.
en.weismachen:
A separable compound of ~weis-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~weis-~: Neither ~weiß~ ("white") nor ~weise~ in its modern sense, but the older adjective ~weis~ ("knowing, informed"), from MHG ~wīs~, from OHG ~wīs~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīs~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsaz~, from PIE *~weyd-~ ("to see, to know"), the root of ~wissen~ and ~weisen~, of Latin ~vidēre~, and of English ~wise~, ~wit~, and ~wisdom~. MHG ~wīs machen~ meant "to make someone knowledgeable, to instruct", a sense that held into the eighteenth century; in the sixteenth it acquired the ironic reading "to make someone believe something untrue", which has since driven the honest one out. The particle now survives essentially only in ~weismachen~, a fossil of the older sense. ~weis-~ makes someone "knowing" of something, in modern use, of something false.

~Weismachen~ takes a dative for the deceived person and an accusative or ~dass~-clause for what is falsely put across.
en.weiterarbeiten:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. As a separable particle ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," marking the continuation of an action already under way.

Fitting ~arbeiten~'s descent from "toil," ~weiterarbeiten~ names the resumption of that very labor.
en.weiterentwickeln:
A transparent modern compound of ~weiter-~ + ~entwickeln~:

• ~entwickeln~: From ~ent-~ ("un-") + ~wickeln~ ("to wrap"), a calque of French ~développer~ (itself from Old French ~des-~ + ~voloper~ "to wrap"). ~Wickeln~ derives from MHG ~wickeln~, a denominative of ~wickel~, from OHG ~wickilī~ ("fibers wound around the distaff"), from Proto-Germanic *~wīkaną~ ("to bend"), from PIE *~weg-~ ("to weave"). The ~ent-~ prefix reverses the wrapping, yielding "to unwrap" and hence "to develop."
• ~weiter-~: From ~weit~ ("wide, far") + comparative suffix ~-er~. ~Weit~ descends from MHG ~wīt~, OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), from PIE *~wi-ito-~ ("gone apart"). As a verbal prefix, ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," indicating continuation or advancement.

The metaphor is vivid: to ~entwickeln~ is to "un-wrap," revealing what was concealed, and to ~weiterentwickeln~ is to carry that unfolding further. English ~wick~ (as in a candle wick) is a cognate of ~wickeln~, both descending from the same OHG root for fibers wound around a distaff. The word ~entwickeln~ as a calque of French ~développer~ is itself a remarkable cultural artifact, 18th-century German intellectuals systematically replaced French loanwords with native German equivalents, and this one stuck permanently. Its separable-prefix compound ~weiterentwickeln~ is a characteristically German formation that would require a whole phrase in English: "to develop further" or "to advance."
en.weiterfahren:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. It can also mark plain spatial advance: moving further in a direction already taken.

~Weiterfahren~ is continuing a journey in the literal sense; the vehicle keeps moving in the direction already taken.
en.weiterführen:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. As a separable particle ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," marking the continuation of an action already under way.

~Weiterführen~ is usually figurative: one continues a conversation, an office, or a proceeding, not a road.
en.weitergeben:
A transparent compound of ~weiter-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (via Old Norse ~gefa~, which displaced the native Old English ~giefan~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~ge~.
• ~weiter-~: From ~weit~ ("wide, far") + comparative suffix ~-er~. ~Weit~ from MHG ~wīt~, OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~, from PIE *~wi-ito-~ ("gone apart"). As a separable prefix, ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," indicating continuation or transmission.

The literal sense is "to give further": to pass something along. English ~give~ is the direct Germanic cognate, though modern English actually owes its form to Old Norse ~gefa~ rather than the native Old English ~giefan~ (which would have yielded something like *~yive~). Both ultimately trace back to PIE *~gʰebʰ-~, which also gave Latin ~habēre~ ("to have"), a fascinating semantic flip where "to give" and "to have" share a root, possibly through an original meaning of "to grasp, to take." The separable prefix makes for memorable word order in main clauses: ~Er gibt die Nachricht weiter~ ("He passes the message on"), with the prefix stranded at the end of the sentence, a feature that famously bewildered Mark Twain.
en.weitergehen:
Compound of ~weiter-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from OHG ~gān~, ~gēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave, to go"). Cognate with Dutch ~gaan~, English ~go~, Swedish ~gå~, and Danish ~gå~.
• ~weiter-~: From the comparative form of ~weit~ ("wide, far"), from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), from PIE *~wi-~ ("apart"). As a verbal prefix, it means "further, onward, continuing."

The compound means "to continue, to go on, to move forward"; ~Das Leben geht weiter~ ("Life goes on"), ~Bitte gehen Sie weiter~ ("Please move along"). The ~h~ in modern ~gehen~ was inserted by scribal analogy with ~sehen~ ("to see"), where the ~h~ had become silent but was retained in spelling; Old High German ~gān~ had no ~h~ at all. The PIE root *~ǵʰeh₁-~ is notable for being a suppletive verb in many daughter languages: English ~go~/~went~ borrows its past tense from ~wend~; German ~gehen~/~ging~ borrows from a different root entirely. The expression ~So geht das nicht weiter~ ("This can't go on like this") is a quintessential German complaint, while ~Weitergehen!~ as a one-word command from police or authorities ("Move along!") captures the authoritarian efficiency of the separable-prefix verb used as an imperative.
en.weiterhelfen:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~helfen~:

• ~helfen~: From MHG ~hëlfen~, from OHG ~hëlfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helpaną~, from PIE *~ḱelb-~, *~ḱelp-~. A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~e~-~a~-~o~ ablaut pattern (~helfen~, ~half~, ~geholfen~). Cognate with English ~help~, Dutch ~helpen~, Danish ~hjælpe~, Norwegian ~hjelpe~.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. As a separable particle ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," marking the continuation of an action already under way.

~Weiterhelfen~ narrows "to help" to advancing someone: helping them get a step further along.
en.weiterkämpfen:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~kämpfen~:

• ~kämpfen~: From MHG ~kempfen~, from OHG *~kempfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kampijan~, a denominal verb from *~kamp~ ("field, battlefield"), borrowed from Latin ~campus~ ("field, open plain"); the sense shifted early from the place of battle to the act of fighting. Latin ~campus~ also gives English ~camp~ and ~champion~.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. As a separable particle ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," marking the continuation of an action already under way.

~Weiterkämpfen~ resumes an interrupted fight, in the citation, the struggle of one woman who refuses to give up.
en.weiterleben:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. As a separable particle ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," marking the continuation of an action already under way.

~Weiterleben~ names the continuation of life, often past a loss or an ending.
en.weiterleiten:
From ~weiter-~ + ~leiten~. Compound of:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~laidijaną~, a causative of *~līþaną~ ("to pass, go by"), from PIE *~leyt-~ ("to go forth, depart"). Cognate with English ~lead~.
• ~weiter-~: From ~weiter~, the comparative form of ~weit~ ("wide, far"), from MHG ~wīter~, from OHG ~wītar~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), ultimately from PIE *~wéyh₁teros~, a comparative of *~wéyh₁-~ ("to pursue, go after"). The prefix conveys the sense of continuing further, passing onward.

The compound literally means "to lead further": to forward, redirect, or relay. In modern usage, ~weiterleiten~ is the standard word for forwarding an email or passing along a message, giving an ancient causative verb a thoroughly digital-age application. The base verb ~leiten~ as a causative of "to go" means literally "to cause to go", making ~weiterleiten~ "to cause to go further." Cognate with English ~lead~ (from Old English ~lǣdan~, the same Proto-West Germanic causative).
en.weiterlesen:
~Weiter-~ + ~lesen~. Compound of ~weiter-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lesan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather, collect"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather, collect").
• ~weiter-~: The comparative form of ~weit~ ("far, wide"), meaning "further, continuing." ~Weit~ derives from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~, from PIE *~h₁weydʰh₁-~ ("to divide, separate"), a univerbation from *~dwi-~ ("apart, asunder") + *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to do, place"). As a separable prefix, ~weiter-~ means "to continue doing (an action)."

~Weiterlesen~ means "to continue reading, to read on." The prefix ~weiter-~ is one of the most productive separable prefixes in modern German, attachable to almost any activity verb to express continuation: ~weiterarbeiten~ ("to keep working"), ~weitermachen~ ("to carry on"), ~weitersprechen~ ("to keep talking"). The underlying image is spatial: reading ~further~, progressing to a more distant point in a text. The root verb ~lesen~ has its own famous semantic shift: PIE *~les-~ meant "to gather, collect" (as in gathering scattered grains), and Latin ~legere~ underwent the identical evolution from "to gather" to "to read", presumably because reading was originally conceived as gathering letters or meanings from a surface, just as one gathered crops from a field. English ~wide~ is a direct cognate of ~weit~, sharing the PIE root.
en.weitermachen:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. As a separable particle ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," marking the continuation of an action already under way.

~Weitermachen~ is the most general of these continuations: simply to carry on, without needing to say with what.
en.weiterreden:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. As a separable particle ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," marking the continuation of an action already under way.

~Weiterreden~ is to go on speaking after being interrupted or after pausing oneself.
en.weiterreisen:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. It can also mark plain spatial advance: moving further in a direction already taken.

~Weiterreisen~ continues a journey, usually setting out again from a stopover.
en.weitersagen:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. With verbs of transfer it means "on to the next person," as in passing something along.

~Weitersagen~ passes a piece of news on to the next person: gossip, rumor, or a request to spread the word.
en.weiterschenken:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~schenken~:

• ~schenken~: From MHG ~schenken~, from OHG ~scenken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skankijan~ ("to pour, serve"). The sense "to give as a gift" grew out of pouring a drink for a guest, the paradigmatic act of generosity; the pouring sense retreated into ~Wein einschenken~ and ~Schenke~ ("tavern"). Cognate with Dutch ~schenken~ ("to pour; to give"), English ~skink~ (archaic) and ~shank~.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. With verbs of transfer it means "on to the next person," as in passing something along.

~Weiterschenken~ passes a received gift on to a third person instead of keeping it.
en.weiterverarbeiten:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~ver-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys using up, consuming, or wearing away.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. As a separable particle ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," marking the continuation of an action already under way.

~Weiterverarbeiten~ takes an already ~processed~ or semi-finished material and carries it a step further toward the finished product.
en.weiterverkaufen:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~ver-~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, a denominative verb from *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"), a loanword from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper"). Cognate with English ~cheap~, Dutch ~kopen~, Danish ~købe~, Icelandic ~kaupa~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. With verbs of transfer it means "on to the next person," as in passing something along.

~Weiterverkaufen~ sells on what one has bought to a next buyer, the essence of resale trade.
en.weiterverschenken:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~ver-~ + ~schenken~:

• ~schenken~: From MHG ~schenken~, from OHG ~scenken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skankijan~ ("to pour, serve"). The sense "to give as a gift" grew out of pouring a drink for a guest, the paradigmatic act of generosity; the pouring sense retreated into ~Wein einschenken~ and ~Schenke~ ("tavern"). Cognate with Dutch ~schenken~ ("to pour; to give"), English ~skink~ (archaic) and ~shank~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. With verbs of transfer it means "on to the next person," as in passing something along.

~Weiterverschenken~ gives a received gift away again, to a further recipient.
en.weiterzahlen:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. As a separable particle ~weiter-~ means "further, onward," marking the continuation of an action already under way.

~Weiterzahlen~ keeps ongoing payments going: wages, contributions, or installments that do not stop.
en.weiterziehen:
A separable compound of ~weiter-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~weiter-~: The comparative of the adjective ~weit~ ("wide, far"), hence "further, onward." ~Weit~ comes from MHG ~wīt~, from OHG ~wīt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīd~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīdaz~ ("wide"), most likely from PIE *~wi-itós~ ("gone apart"), from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two") + *~h₁ey-~ ("to go"). Cognate with English ~wide~, Dutch ~wijd~, Swedish ~vid~. It can also mark plain spatial advance: moving further in a direction already taken.

~Weiterziehen~ is the moving-on of people or groups; the party sets out and seeks the next place.
en.weißen: Derived from the adjective ~weiß~ ("white") with the verbal suffix ~-en~, meaning "to whiten, to whitewash." The adjective ~weiß~ descends from Middle High German ~wīz~, from Old High German ~wīz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hwīt~, from Proto-Germanic *~hwītaz~, from PIE *~ḱweytos~ ("bright, to shine"). Cognate with English ~white~, Dutch ~wit~, Swedish ~vit~, and Gothic ~hweits~, all from the same Germanic root. The initial ~hw-~ cluster, preserved in English spelling as ~wh-~, was lost in German (as in ~was~/~what~, ~wer~/~who~). The verb ~weißen~ specifically denotes the act of applying whitewash or lime-paint to walls, a practice so common in German-speaking lands that it gave rise to the surname ~Weißer~. The PIE root *~ḱweytos~ also produced Sanskrit ~sveta~ ("white, bright"), Lithuanian ~sviesti~ ("to shine"), and Old Church Slavonic ~svetŭ~ ("light"), revealing an ancient Indo-European association between whiteness and luminosity. In German, the same root branches into ~Weizen~ ("wheat," the pale grain), connecting agriculture and color in a single etymological thread.
en.wenden: From Middle High German ~wenden~, from Old High German ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), the causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap"), from Proto-Indo-European *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). English ~wend~ is a direct cognate, surviving in the fixed phrase "to wend one's way." Old English ~wendan~ ("to turn, go") gave Middle English ~wenden~ before it was gradually displaced by ~go~; only the idiom "wend one's way" endures.
