The causative relationship between *~windaną~ and *~wandijaną~ is the same pattern seen in German ~winden~ ("to wind") and ~wenden~ ("to turn something"), the a-grade vowel in ~wenden~ is the Indo-European causative ablaut grade, meaning "to cause to wind." Armenian ~gind~ ("ring") is a non-Germanic cognate preserving the original sense of circular turning. ~Wenden~ belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort (preterite ~wandte~, participle ~gewandt~), in which the preterite does not carry umlaut (see ~brennen~ for the phonological explanation). Like ~senden~, it has a doubled preterite: the historically strong form ~wandte~ is preferred today for turning the self or one's attention (~sich an jemanden wenden~ "to address someone," ~sich abwenden~ "to turn away"), while the regularized ~wendete~ is preferred for physical turning (~das Auto wendete~ "the car turned around").
en.werben: From Middle High German ~werben~, from Old High German ~werban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hwerban~, from Proto-Germanic *~hwerbaną~ ("to turn, move about, wander"). Cognate with Dutch ~werven~ ("to recruit"), English ~wharve~ ("to turn"), and Icelandic ~hverfa~ ("to turn, disappear"). The semantic evolution from "to turn, move about" to "to recruit, advertise, woo" followed a path through "to be busy, to go about doing something" to "to go about seeking" and finally "to solicit." This is remarkably parallel to the English word ~advertise~, which comes from Latin ~advertere~ ("to turn toward"). Both languages independently linked the concept of turning with the act of seeking attention. The related noun ~Werbung~ ("advertising") is ubiquitous in modern German, and ~Bewerber~ ("applicant") preserves the old sense of one who "goes about" seeking a position. English ~wharf~ is a distant cousin, from Old English ~hwearf~ ("heap, embankment"), related to the same root via the notion of a turning-place for ships. The Faroese cognate ~hvørva~ ("to disappear") preserves yet another semantic branch: turning away until one vanishes.
en.werden: From Middle High German ~wërden~, from Old High German ~werdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaną~, from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"), with semantic shift "to turn" > "to become (turn into)." The use as a passive auxiliary is old and found throughout West Germanic, but the use as a future auxiliary is a Middle High German innovation, originating in inchoative constructions with the present participle. Since the 14th century, the participle began to be replaced with the infinitive, probably by analogy with the older future auxiliaries ~wollen~ and ~sollen~, which ~werden~ has since displaced in Modern German. Also cognate with English ~weird~, from Old English ~wyrd~ ("fate, destiny"), literally "that which becomes", a noun derived from the same Proto-Germanic *~werþaną~. Shakespeare's Weird Sisters in ~Macbeth~ were originally the Fate Sisters; the sense shifted from "fate" → "supernatural" → "uncanny" → "strange." Other cognates include Dutch ~worden~, obsolete English ~worth~, Swedish ~varda~, Latin ~vertō~ ("to turn").
en.werfen:
From Middle High German ~wërfen~, from Old High German ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb. Cognate with Old Saxon ~werpan~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~, and English ~warp~.

The PIE root *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp") reflects the original sense of a rotational or twisting motion, the physical action of winding up before releasing a projectile. English ~warp~ preserves the root in a different semantic branch: the ~warp~ of a loom is the set of threads stretched lengthwise under tension, and the verb "to warp" means to bend or twist out of shape. German ~werfen~ has developed an exceptionally wide range of compound and idiomatic uses: ~verwerfen~ ("to reject," literally "to throw away"), ~entwerfen~ ("to design, draft," literally "to throw out a plan"), ~einwerfen~ ("to throw in, interject"), and the noun ~Wurf~ ("throw, litter of animals"). The ablaut series ~wirft~/~warf~/~geworfen~ follows the class III pattern shared with ~sterben~.
en.werten:
Derived from ~Wert~ ("value, worth"). ~Wert~ descends from MHG ~wert~, from OHG ~werd~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("worth, worthy"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"), related to Latin ~versus~ ("turned") and English ~worth~. The modern spelling with ~-t~ (rather than historical ~-d~) was generalized from the uninflected form.

~Werten~ means "to evaluate, to rate, to judge the value of", a denominal verb transparently formed from ~Wert~. It is common in sports commentary (~Die Jury wertet die Leistung~, "The judges rate the performance"), academic contexts, and legal language. The deeper etymology is striking: PIE *~wert-~ meant "to turn," and the connection to value is through the concept of exchange, turning goods over in a transaction. This same root produced Latin ~vertere~ ("to turn"), whence English ~verse~, ~version~, ~convert~, and ~controversy~. The Germanic branch took the "exchange" sense and solidified it into "worth", what something is valued at when turned over in trade. English ~worth~, ~worthy~, and ~worship~ (originally "worthship") all descend from this root.
en.wertschätzen:
A separable compound of ~wert~ + ~schätzen~:

• ~schätzen~: A denominal verb from ~Schatz~ ("treasure"), from MHG ~schaz~, OHG ~scaz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skatt~ ("cattle, treasure"), an early Germanic word in which cattle served as a measure of wealth. Cognate with Old Norse ~skattr~ (whence Danish ~skat~ and Swedish ~skatt~, both "tax"), Gothic ~skatts~, Old English ~sċeatt~.
• ~wert~: From the adjective ~wert~ ("worthy, worth"), from MHG ~wert~, from OHG ~werd~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werþ~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~; the PIE source is uncertain, possibly *~wert-~ ("to turn"). Cognate with English ~worth~, Dutch ~waard~, Swedish ~värd~, and the source of the noun ~Wert~ ("value"). As a particle it is evaluative: the verb treats its object as having worth. The sense of ~wert~ here is resultative: the action assigns or acknowledges worth.

Younger than its parts, ~wertschätzen~ has spread chiefly through the noun ~Wertschätzung~ ("esteem"), today more common than the verb itself.
en.wettmachen:
A separable compound of ~wett~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~wett~: From the adjective ~wett~ ("even, quits, square"), which is the MHG noun ~wette~ ("payment of a debt, compensation") frozen into a predicate: around 1300 ~wette werden~ meant "to be settled", hence "free of debt", hence "even", and the ending was gone by the seventeenth century. The noun survives as ~Wette~ ("wager") and ~wetten~ ("to bet"), from Proto-Germanic *~wadją~ ("pledge"), cognate with English ~wed~, a wedding being, etymologically, a pledge, and English ~wage~ and ~wager~ the same word again by way of Frankish and French. The particle keeps the accounting metaphor: the verb balances the books. ~wett~ marks a settling of accounts: making good a debt, loss, or fault.

~Wettmachen~ takes what is offset as its accusative object (a loss, a deficit, a disadvantage) and today is almost always figurative.
en.wichtigmachen:
A separable compound of ~wichtig~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~wichtig~: From the adjective ~wichtig~, borrowed in the sixteenth century from Middle Low German ~wichtich~ ("weighty, heavy"), a merchants' word built on ~wicht~ ("weight", modern ~Gewicht~) that spread from the northern trading cities southward. That noun belongs with ~wiegen~ and ~wägen~, from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to move, to convey"), the root behind English ~weigh~, ~wagon~, and ~way~ and Latin ~vehere~. The metaphor is still live and matches English exactly: what matters is what weighs, as in ~weighty~. The sense of ~wichtig~ here is: with a note of self-importance or puffery.

Almost always reflexive: ~sich wichtigmachen~ is to make oneself out to be more important than one is.
en.widerlegen:
An inseparable compound of ~wider-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~wider-~: From MHG ~wider-~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþrą~ ("against, back"), a comparative formation on PIE *~wi~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which meant "against" before it meant "alongside", a sense preserved in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. ~wider-~ conveys opposition, resistance, or contradiction.

Literally "to lay against": one lays a counter-proof against a claim and so brings it down.
en.widerreden:
An inseparable compound of ~wider-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~wider-~: From MHG ~wider-~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþrą~ ("against, back"), a comparative formation on PIE *~wi~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which meant "against" before it meant "alongside", a sense preserved in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. ~wider-~ conveys opposition, resistance, or contradiction.

Largely displaced today by ~widersprechen~, ~widerreden~ survives chiefly in the set phrase "ohne Widerrede" ("without protest").
en.widerrufen:
An inseparable compound of ~wider-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. A parallel weak form in Middle High German explains why the modern present lacks the expected umlaut (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~wider-~: From MHG ~wider-~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþrą~ ("against, back"), a comparative formation on PIE *~wi~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which meant "against" before it meant "alongside", a sense preserved in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. ~wider-~ conveys a motion back, as of something returning or reflected.

~Widerrufen~ is literally a "calling back" of a statement; that the particle here means "back" rather than "against" sets it right at the edge of the homophone ~wieder~ ("again").
en.widersagen:
An inseparable compound of ~wider-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~wider-~: From MHG ~wider-~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþrą~ ("against, back"), a comparative formation on PIE *~wi~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which meant "against" before it meant "alongside", a sense preserved in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. ~wider-~ conveys opposition, resistance, or contradiction.

~Widersagen~ ("to renounce") lives on chiefly in the baptismal formula of renouncing evil, and is otherwise elevated to archaic.
en.widersetzen:
An inseparable compound of ~wider-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~wider-~: From MHG ~wider-~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþrą~ ("against, back"), a comparative formation on PIE *~wi~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which meant "against" before it meant "alongside", a sense preserved in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. ~wider-~ conveys opposition, resistance, or contradiction.

Always reflexive and with the dative: ~sich einer Sache widersetzen~ is to set oneself against it.
en.widerspiegeln:
A separable compound of ~wider-~ + ~spiegeln~:

• ~spiegeln~: From MHG ~spiegeln~, a denominative verb from the noun ~Spiegel~ ("mirror"), from MHG ~spiegel~, OHG ~spiegal~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spēgl~, an early borrowing from Latin ~speculum~ ("mirror"), from ~specere~ ("to look at"), from PIE *~speḱ-~ ("to see, to observe"). The same root gave English ~spectacle~ and ~spy~, and German ~spähen~.
• ~wider-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþrą~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("further apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with Dutch ~weder~, Old Norse ~viðr~, and English ~with~, whose original sense was "against" and survives in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. Three things must be kept apart: separable stressed ~wider-~ (~widerhallen~, ~widerspiegeln~), which means "back"; inseparable unstressed ~wider-~ (~widersprechen~, ~widerstehen~), which means "against"; and ~wieder~ ("again"), which is the very same word, split off from ~wider~ by a purely orthographic convention that grammarians did not settle until the eighteenth century. The sense of ~wider-~ here is: in verbs of reflection and echo, the image or sound is cast back.

From the literal casting-back of an image, ~widerspiegeln~ has shifted to a predominantly figurative use: conditions, moods, and figures all "reflect" something.
en.widersprechen:
From Middle High German ~widersprechen~, from Old High German ~widarsprehhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~withrasprekan~. Compound of ~wider-~ + ~sprechen~:

• ~sprechen~: From MHG ~sprechen~, from OHG ~sprehhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sprekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sprekanan~, probably from PIE *~spregh-~ ("to crackle"). Cognate with Dutch ~spreken~ and English ~speak~.
• ~wider-~: From MHG ~wider-~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~withra~, from Proto-Germanic *~withra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("further apart, against"). This prefix adds the sense of opposition or contradiction. Not to be confused with ~wieder~ ("again"), though both descend from the same root.

The PIE root *~spregh-~ originally meant "to crackle" or "to make a sharp noise," and the semantic path from "crackling sounds" to "speaking" likely passed through the notion of rapid, animated vocal sounds. Lithuanian ~sprageti~ ("to crackle, to patter") preserves the original onomatopoeic sense. The compound ~widersprechen~ literally means "to speak against," and it is cognate with the archaic English ~withspeak~ (now obsolete but attested in Middle English). The distinction between ~wider~ ("against") and ~wieder~ ("again") is one of the classic pitfalls for German learners, though historically they are the same word that split into two spellings to differentiate two divergent meanings.
en.widerstehen:
An inseparable compound of ~wider-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~wider-~: From MHG ~wider-~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþrą~ ("against, back"), a comparative formation on PIE *~wi~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which meant "against" before it meant "alongside", a sense preserved in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. ~wider-~ conveys opposition, resistance, or contradiction.

~Widerstehen~ governs the dative (one withstands a temptation, an urge) and denotes holding firm against an outside pressure.
en.widerstreben:
An inseparable compound of ~wider-~ + ~streben~:

• ~streben~: From MHG ~strëben~, from OHG ~strëbēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stribēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~stribāną~ ("to strive, resist"). Cognate with Dutch ~streven~ ("to strive") and English ~strive~ (via Old French ~estriver~, itself borrowed from a Germanic source).
• ~wider-~: From MHG ~wider-~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþrą~ ("against, back"), a comparative formation on PIE *~wi~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which meant "against" before it meant "alongside", a sense preserved in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. ~wider-~ conveys opposition, resistance, or contradiction.

~Widerstreben~ governs the dative and often stands impersonally: "es widerstrebt mir" means something runs against one's own will.
en.widmen: From Middle High German ~widemen~, from Old High German ~widimen~ ("to gift, give as a gift"), from ~widimo~ ("dowry, gift"), from Proto-West Germanic *~weþmō~, from Proto-Germanic *~wetmô~ ("dowry, bride-price"). The noun ~Wittum~ (archaic for "dower, widow's portion") preserves this root in modern German. Note that despite the superficial resemblance, ~Wittum~ is not related to ~Witwe~ ("widow"), they are false friends at the etymological level. The semantic journey of ~widmen~ runs from "to give a bride-price" to "to assign, bestow, dedicate" to the modern sense of dedicating a book or composition to someone.
en.wiederaufleben:
A separable compound of ~wiederauf-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~wiederauf-~: A stacked particle: ~wieder~ ("again") + ~auf~ ("up"), as in ~wiederaufbauen~ ("to rebuild"). ~wieder~ is etymologically the same word as ~wider~ ("against"), separated from it only by spelling convention; ~auf~ goes back to Proto-Germanic *~upp~, cognate with English ~up~. See the ~wieder~ and ~auf~ entries for the components. The sense of ~wiederauf-~ here is: chiefly reconstruction and resumption: rebuilding, taking up, or starting anew.

Intransitive and taking ~sein~, ~wiederaufleben~ says of memories, customs, or friendships that they gather fresh strength after seeming to have died out.
en.wiederbeleben:
A separable compound of ~wieder-~ + ~be-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against", a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against." It also means "back," of returning something to its origin or to an earlier state.

Doubly layered, ~wiederbeleben~ means literally bringing back to life (resuscitation) and figuratively reviving an economy, a debate, or a custom.
en.wiederentdecken:
A separable compound of ~wieder-~ + ~ent-~ + ~decken~:

• ~decken~: From MHG ~decken~, from OHG ~decchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þakkjan~ ("to cover"), from Proto-Germanic *~þakjaną~, a causative formation from *~þaką~ ("roof, thatch"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to cover"); the verb is etymologically "to roof." Cognate with English ~thatch~, Dutch ~dekken~, Swedish ~täcka~; from the same root Latin ~tegere~, whence English ~protect~.
• ~ent-~: From MHG ~ent-~, from OHG ~int-~, ~ant-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~and-~, from Proto-Germanic *~anda-~ ("against, facing, away"), from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, forehead, front"). Cognate with English ~answer~, whose first element is the same morpheme. ~ent-~ reverses or undoes the base action.
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against", a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against." As a separable particle ~wieder-~ means "again": the action is repeated.

~Entdecken~ is the uncovering of what lay hidden; ~wieder-~ sets it going a second time: one finds one's way back to what had dropped out of view.
en.wiedererkennen:
A separable compound of ~wieder-~ + ~er-~ + ~kennen~:

• ~kennen~: From MHG ~kennen~, from OHG ~kennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kannijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~ ("to know"), a causative of *~kunnaną~, from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"). A member of the Rückumlaut cohort: the present shows umlaut (~ich kenne~), the preterite does not (~kannte~, ~gekannt~). Cognate with Dutch ~kennen~, Scots and English ~ken~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against", a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against." As a separable particle ~wieder-~ means "again": the action is repeated.

Like English ~recognize~ (re- + cognize), ~wiedererkennen~ is a knowing-again: grasping something as the very thing one already knew.
en.wiederfinden:
A separable compound of ~wieder-~ + ~finden~:

• ~finden~: From MHG ~vinden~, from OHG ~findan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~finþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to go, pass; path, bridge"). The development from "to go, pass" to "to find" parallels shifts in Slavic. Cognate with English ~find~, Dutch ~vinden~, Low German ~finden~, Danish ~finde~.
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against", a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against." It also means "back," of returning something to its origin or to an earlier state.

Beside recovering something lost stands the reflexive ~sich wiederfinden~: to find oneself, unexpectedly, in a place or a situation.
en.wiedergeben:
From Middle High German ~widergëben~, from Old High German ~widargeban~. Compound of ~wieder-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~ ("to bring, reach, give"), from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give").
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider-~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra-~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"), with an original sense of "in return."

The literal meaning "to give back, return" extends to "to reproduce, render, depict", giving back in the sense of representing faithfully. A translation ~gibt den Originaltext wieder~ ("renders the original text"); a recording ~gibt die Stimme wieder~ ("reproduces the voice"). Old High German ~widargeban~ already carried this dual sense over a thousand years ago. The PIE root *~gʰebʰ-~ also gave Irish ~gabhaim~ ("I take"), a reminder that "give" and "take" were once semantically closer, both involving the transfer of something between hands.
en.wiederhaben:
A separable compound of ~wieder-~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against", a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against." It also means "back," of returning something to its origin or to an earlier state.

A colloquial verb of possession: "etwas wiederhaben" is to get what was lost or lent back into one's own hand.
en.wiederholen:
From Middle High German ~widerholen~, from Old High German ~widarholōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþraholōn~. Compound of ~wieder-~ + ~holen~:

• ~holen~: From MHG ~holen~, ~holn~, from OHG ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, to get, to draw"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~. Cognate with English ~haul~.
• ~wieder-~: Meaning "again, back," from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative formation from *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). As an inseparable prefix (stress on ~-ho-~), ~wieder-~ conveys repetition.

~Wiederholen~ (inseparable, stress on ~-ho-~) means "to repeat, to review", literally "to fetch again." This is distinct from the separable ~wieder holen~ (stress on ~wie-~), which means "to fetch back, to retrieve": ~Hol dir das Buch wieder!~ ("Go get the book back!"). The stress difference creates a minimal pair: ~widerHOLen~ = "to repeat" vs. ~WIEderholen~ = "to retrieve." Cognate with Dutch ~wederhalen~, Saterland Frisian ~wierhoalje~, OHG ~widarhalōn~. The concept of learning through repetition is baked into the word: to learn is to fetch knowledge again and again, each time drawing it closer.
en.wiederkehren:
A separable compound of ~wieder-~ + ~kehren~:

• ~kehren~: A homograph concealing two distinct verbs. ~Kehren~ (1) "to turn": from MHG ~kēren~, from OHG ~kēran~, ~chēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kairijaną~ or *~kausijaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly connected to *~gers-~ ("to twist, bend, turn"). ~Kehren~ (2) "to sweep": from MHG ~kern~, ~keren~, from OHG ~kerian~, ~cherian~, from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~ ("to scrape, scratch"), from PIE *~ger-~ ("to scrape"). Etymologically unrelated, merged through phonological convergence.
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against", a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against." As a separable particle ~wieder-~ means "again": the action is repeated.

From ~kehren~ "to turn," not "to sweep": ~wiederkehren~ is a turning back. As a noun it carries Nietzsche's "ewige Wiederkehr," the eternal recurrence of the same.
en.wiederkommen:
A separable compound of ~wieder-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against", a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against." As a separable particle ~wieder-~ means "again": the action is repeated.

The everyday verb of return: literally of a person coming back, figuratively of a thought or an opportunity that comes round again.
en.wiedersehen:
A separable compound of ~wieder-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against", a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against." As a separable particle ~wieder-~ means "again": the action is repeated.

In the noun ~das Wiedersehen~ ("reunion") and the parting ~Auf Wiedersehen~ (literally "until we see each other again") this verb is woven deep into daily life.
en.wiederverwenden:
A separable compound of ~wieder-~ + ~ver-~ + ~wenden~:

• ~wenden~: From MHG ~wenden~, from OHG ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), the causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). It belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort (preterite ~wandte~, participle ~gewandt~) and has a doubled preterite: ~wandte~ for turning the self or one's attention, the regularized ~wendete~ for physical turning. Cognate with English ~wend~, Armenian ~gind~ ("ring").
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against", a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against." As a separable particle ~wieder-~ means "again": the action is repeated.

~Verwenden~ has hardened from "to turn away" (still heard in "den Blick nicht verwenden") to plain "to use"; ~wieder-~ makes of it a watchword of the circular economy: putting something to use a second time instead of discarding it.
en.wiederverwerten:
A separable compound of ~wieder-~ + ~ver-~ + ~werten~:

• ~werten~: Derived from ~Wert~ ("value, worth"), from MHG ~wert~, from OHG ~werd~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("worth, worthy"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"); the connection to value runs through exchange: turning goods over in a transaction. Related to Latin ~versus~ ("turned") and English ~worth~, ~worthy~, ~worship~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ derives a verb from a noun or adjective, meaning to make something into that.
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against", a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against." As a separable particle ~wieder-~ means "again": the action is repeated.

Through ~werten~ the noun ~Wert~ ("value") sits inside the verb: ~verwerten~ is to turn something to use and value, and ~wiederverwerten~ does so a second time, the ordinary German word for "to recycle."
en.wiederwählen:
A separable compound of ~wieder-~ + ~wählen~:

• ~wählen~: From MHG ~weln~, ~welen~, ~wellen~, from OHG ~wellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~walljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waljaną~, from PIE *~welh₁-~ ("to wish, choose"). The umlaut ~ä~ comes from the MHG second- and third-person singular; ~wählen~ and ~wollen~ share the same root. Cognate with English ~well~ (archaic "to wish well"), Dutch ~willen~.
• ~wieder-~: From MHG ~wider~, from OHG ~widar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wiþr~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiþra~ ("against, back"), from PIE *~wi-tero-~ ("more apart"), a comparative of *~wi-~ ("apart, in two"). Cognate with English ~with~, which originally meant "against", a sense English still preserves in ~withstand~ and ~withhold~. German keeps the two developments apart in spelling: ~wieder~ "again" beside ~wider~ "against." As a separable particle ~wieder-~ means "again": the action is repeated.

~Wählen~ joins "to choose" and "to elect by vote"; in ~wiederwählen~ it is the second that is meant: voting someone into office for a further term.
en.wiegen:
German has two distinct verbs spelled ~wiegen~, both from Middle High German ~wigen~:

Sense 1 ("to weigh"): From MHG ~wigen~, a northwestern variant of ~wegen~, which generalized the present-singular stem vowel ~i~ (from MHG ~wige~, ~wiges~, ~wiget~) across the whole paradigm. From OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, move"). Cognate with English ~weigh~, Dutch ~wegen~, Danish ~veje~, Icelandic ~vega~. The original ~e~-form survives in the doublet ~wägen~, now restricted to figurative senses and derivatives like ~abwägen~ ("to weigh up") and ~erwägen~ ("to consider").

Sense 2 ("to rock, cradle"): From MHG ~wigen~, derived from ~wige~ ("cradle," modern ~Wiege~), from OHG ~wīga~, ~wiega~, likely related to Proto-West Germanic *~waggjan~ ("to cause to move"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ (the same root as sense 1). The connection is movement: weighing involves the motion of a balance, and rocking involves the swaying of a cradle.

Both senses thus trace back to the same PIE notion of movement, though they arrived at their modern meanings by different paths. The PIE root *~weǵʰ-~ also gave Latin ~vehere~ ("to carry"), source of English ~vehicle~, ~vector~, and ~convey~.
en.winden: From MHG ~winden~, from OHG ~wintan~, from Proto-Germanic *~windaną~ ("to wind, to wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). Cognate with English ~wind~ (the verb, "to coil"), Dutch ~winden~, Danish ~vinde~.
en.winken: From MHG ~winken~, from OHG ~winken~ ("to nod, to blink"), from Proto-West Germanic *~winkōn~ (beside *~winkijan~), from PIE *~weng-~ ("to bend, to curve"), the same root as ~Winkel~ ("angle, corner") and, in ablaut, ~wanken~ ("to sway"). A weak verb, and already weak in OHG. Cognate with English ~wink~, Dutch ~wenken~, and, through the sense "bent thing," English ~winch~. The strong participle ~gewunken~ is a latecomer rather than a survival: Upper German dialects built strong forms on the model of ~sinken~/~gesunken~ in the MHG period, and over the last century ~gewunken~ has pushed the historically regular ~gewinkt~ toward the margins.
en.wirken: From Middle High German ~wirken~, from Old High German ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~, derived from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~wérǵom~, from PIE *~werǵ-~ ("to make, work"). This root also yields the English noun ~work~ and, via Greek ~ἔργον~ ("work", the direct reflex of PIE *~wérǵom~), the English loanword ~energy~. Early on, ~wirken~ merged with the dialectal ~würken~ (from OHG ~wurken~, PWGmc *~wurkijan~, PGmc *~wurkijaną~, a closely related form); the ~i~-form prevailed in Central German, the ~ü~-form in Upper German, with the ~ü~-form displaced from the written language in the 18th century. Cognate with English ~work~ and ~wrought~ (the archaic past tense of ~work~, from the same PGmc *~wurkijaną~), Dutch ~werken~.
en.wissen: From Middle High German ~wiȥȥen~, from Old High German ~wiȥȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~witan~, from Proto-Germanic *~witaną~, from PIE *~woyde~ ("to see, to know"), a stative perfect from the root *~weyd-~ ("to see"). A preterite-present verb: its present-tense conjugation (~weiß~, ~weißt~, ~weiß~) descends from an original perfect formation meaning "I have seen" and hence "I know," while its past tense ~wusste~ was built anew as a weak form. Cognate with Dutch ~weten~, Danish ~vide~, Swedish ~veta~, English ~wit~, and Latin ~video~ ("I see").
en.wohlfühlen:
A separable compound of ~wohl-~ + ~fühlen~:

• ~fühlen~: From northern MHG ~vüelen~, from OHG ~fuolen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōlijan~ ("to feel"); the further origin is uncertain, presumably related to Old Norse ~falma~ ("to grope"), and possibly a secondary causative of a strong *~falaną~, from PIE *~pelh₁-~ ("to stroke"). Cognate with English ~feel~, Dutch ~voelen~, Danish ~føle~.
• ~wohl-~: From the adverb ~wohl~ ("well"), from MHG ~wol~, ~wole~, from OHG ~wola~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wela~, from Proto-Germanic *~wela~, from PIE *~welh₁-~ ("to wish, to choose"). That is the same root as ~wollen~ ("to want") and Latin ~velle~: to be ~wohl~ is, etymologically, to be as one would wish. Cognate with English ~well~, Dutch ~wel~, Swedish ~väl~, Danish ~vel~, and the source of the noun ~Wohl~ ("welfare"). ~wohl-~, with reflexives, marks a state of comfort or ease.

The compound is almost always reflexive (~sich wohlfühlen~) and names bodily as much as emotional well-being; the spaced spelling ~sich wohl fühlen~ has counted as equally correct since the 1996 spelling reform.
en.wohnen:
From Middle High German ~wonen~, from Old High German ~wonēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wunēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wunāną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~wenh₁-~ ("to wish, love, strive for"). Cognate with Dutch ~wonen~, English ~wont~ ("accustomed"), Old English ~ġewunian~ ("to be accustomed to, dwell").

The PIE root *~wenh₁-~ connects dwelling with desiring: to inhabit a place is to love it enough to remain. The same root underlies German ~Wonne~ ("bliss, rapture"), ~wünschen~ ("to wish"), and ~gewinnen~ ("to win, gain"), in each case, the core sense is striving toward what one loves or desires. English ~wont~ (as in "as was his wont") descends from Old English ~ġewunian~ ("to be accustomed to, dwell"), the same verb as Proto-West Germanic *~wunēn~: to be ~wont~ is to be "dwelt," habituated into a place or practice. English ~win~ (from the same *~wenh₁-~ root via *~winnaną~) preserves the striving sense: to win was originally to labor, struggle toward the desired goal, not merely to come first. The cluster of ~wohnen~, ~Wonne~, ~wünschen~, ~gewinnen~, and English ~wont~ and ~win~ all radiate from the same ancient notion: the thing you love enough to reach for, dwell in, or be shaped by. Cognate with Dutch ~wonen~, Afrikaans ~woon~, English ~wont~, Gothic ~wunan~.
en.wollen: From Middle High German ~wollen~, ~wöllen~, ~wullen~, ~wellen~, from Old High German ~wollen~, ~wellen~, from a blend of Proto-West Germanic *~willjan~ and *~walljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wiljaną~ and *~waljaną~, ultimately from PIE *~welh₁-~ ("to wish, choose"). A preterite-present modal verb. Cognate with Low German ~willen~, Dutch ~willen~, English ~will~, West Frisian ~wolle~, Danish ~ville~, Swedish ~vilja~. Related to ~wählen~ ("to choose"), from the same PIE root.
en.wringen: Borrowed into standard German from Low German ~wringen~, from Middle Low German ~wringen~, from Old Saxon ~wringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wringaną~, from PIE *~wrengʰ-~ ("to turn, to twist"), a nasalized extension of *~wer-~ ("to turn, to bend"). A class III strong verb (~wringen~, ~wrang~, ~gewrungen~). Cognate with English ~wring~, Old English ~wringan~, Dutch ~wringen~; the inherited High German reflex of the very same verb is ~ringen~, which lost its initial ~w-~ before ~r~ and moved from "twist" to "wrestle, struggle"; the older sense survives in ~die Hände ringen~ ("to wring one's hands"). English ~wrong~ belongs to the same family by way of Old Norse ~rangr~ ("crooked, twisted"): what is wrong is what has been wrung out of true.
en.wundern:
From Middle High German ~wundern~, from Old High German ~wuntarōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wundrōną~, derived from the noun *~wundrą~ ("wonder, miracle"), whence German ~Wunder~. The noun *~wundrą~ may derive from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to desire, wish for, strive after, win, love") via a form *~wn̥h₁-tro-m~, suggesting the original sense was something "wished for" or "longed for", hence marvellous.

The verb's reflexive usage, ~sich wundern~ ("to be surprised, to wonder"), is the most common in modern German. The non-reflexive transitive ~das wundert mich~ ("that surprises me") places the wondering person as the object, not the subject, a grammatical pattern shared by several German verbs of emotion (~freuen~, ~ärgern~, ~langweilen~). English ~wonder~ is not a direct cognate; it derives from Old English ~wundrian~, from Proto-Germanic *~wundrōną~, making it in fact a sibling, both descend from the same Proto-Germanic verb, though their respective noun bases (~Wunder~ vs. ~wonder~) diverged phonetically through the High German consonant shift.
en.wundliegen:
A separable compound of ~wund~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~wund~: From MHG ~wunt~, from OHG ~wunt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wund~, from Proto-Germanic *~wundaz~ ("wounded"), beside the verb *~wundōną~ ("to wound"); the origin beyond Germanic is uncertain. Cognate with English ~wound~, Dutch ~wond~, Gothic ~wunds~. As a separable element it is resultative and almost always reflexive: the action is carried on until the body is raw from it. The sense of ~wund~ here is: reflexively, of rubbing, walking or lying until the skin is raw.

Used reflexively (~sich wundliegen~) it is the everyday word for the pressure ulcers (decubitus) that develop in bedridden patients.
en.wundreiben:
A separable compound of ~wund~ + ~reiben~:

• ~reiben~: From MHG ~rīben~, from OHG ~rīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrībaną~ ("to rub"); beyond Germanic uncertain, a PIE *~wreyp-~, labial extension of *~wer-~ ("to turn"), being proposed but not secure. A class I strong verb (~reiben~, ~rieb~, ~gerieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~wrijven~, Old Saxon ~wrīvan~; German dropped the initial ~w-~ before ~r~, as in ~ringen~.
• ~wund~: From MHG ~wunt~, from OHG ~wunt~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wund~, from Proto-Germanic *~wundaz~ ("wounded"), beside the verb *~wundōną~ ("to wound"); the origin beyond Germanic is uncertain. Cognate with English ~wound~, Dutch ~wond~, Gothic ~wunds~. As a separable element it is resultative and almost always reflexive: the action is carried on until the body is raw from it. The sense of ~wund~ here is: as a resultative adjective, "sore, chafed", from repeated action.

It is used reflexively or with a body part as object (~sich die Füße wundreiben~), with ~wund~ naming the outcome of the friction.
en.wägen: From MHG ~wegen~ ("to set in motion, to weigh, to be worth"), from OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, to move"). A class V strong verb whose modern principal parts are ~wägen~, ~wog~, ~gewogen~ (rarely weak ~wägte~, ~gewägt~), the ~o~-vocalism having prevailed from the fifteenth century onward. It is the doublet of ~wiegen~, which generalized the ~i~ of the old present singular and took over the literal business of weighing, leaving ~wägen~ the figurative one, chiefly in ~abwägen~ ("to weigh up") and ~erwägen~ ("to consider"). The ~ä~ spelling is a seventeenth-century refashioning after ~Waage~ ("scales"); the same PIE root gave ~Weg~, ~Wagen~, English ~way~, ~weigh~, and ~wain~, and Latin ~vehere~ ("to carry"), source of ~vehicle~.
en.wählen: From Middle High German ~weln~, from ~welen~, ~wellen~, from Old High German ~wellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~walljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waljaną~, ultimately from PIE *~welh₁-~ ("to wish, choose"). The modern umlaut vowel ~ä~ developed from the influence of the second- and third-person singular forms in Middle High German. As the ~wollen~ entry notes, ~wählen~ and ~wollen~ share the same PIE root, an elegant reminder that willing and choosing were once a single concept in Proto-Indo-European. Cognate with English ~well~ (in the archaic sense "to wish well"), Dutch ~willen~ (from the same root via a parallel path).
en.währen:
From Middle High German ~wëren~, ~wërn~, from Old High German ~wërēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~weʀēn~, related to OHG ~wesen~ ("to be, exist"). The deeper connection runs through Proto-Germanic *~wēraz~ ("true"), from PIE *~weh₁ros~ ("true"), from *~weh₁-~ ("true, trustworthy").

The semantic thread connecting "to last, endure" with "true" is the idea that what is true is what stands firm and persists. This same root gave German ~wahr~ ("true"), ~Wahrheit~ ("truth"), and the now-archaic ~Wesen~ ("being, essence"). The famous German proverb ~Was lange währt, wird endlich gut~ ("What lasts long turns out good in the end") captures the verb's core meaning. Latin ~vērus~ ("true"), Irish ~fíor~ ("true"), and Slavic *~vě̀ra~ ("faith") are all cognates from the same PIE root, showing that the ancient link between duration and truth runs across the entire Indo-European family.
en.wünschen: From Middle High German ~wünschen~, ~wunschen~, from Old High German ~wunsken~ ("to choose, wish, desire"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wunskijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wunskijaną~, derived from *~wunskaz~ ("wish, desire"), from PIE *~wenh₁-~ ("to wish, love"). The same PIE root underlies German ~Wonne~ ("bliss, rapture") and English ~win~, both preserving the old sense of "desired thing, pleasure." The connection between wishing and winning reflects a Proto-Germanic world in which what one wished for was what one strove to obtain. Cognate with Dutch ~wensen~, English ~wish~, Danish ~ønske~, and, across a vast linguistic distance, Sanskrit ~vāṃchati~ ("to wish, desire").
en.würdigen:
From ~würdig~ ("worthy") + ~-en~. ~Würdig~ derives from ~Würde~ ("dignity, worth") + ~-ig~. ~Würde~ descends from MHG ~wirde~, from OHG ~wirdī~, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~ ("valuable, worthy"), from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"). Cognate with English ~worth~ and ~worthy~.

~Würdigen~ means "to honor, to appreciate, to acknowledge the worth of", and, in a less common construction, ~keines Blickes würdigen~ ("to not deem worthy of a single glance"), which expresses withering contempt. The PIE root *~wert-~ ("to turn") connects ~Würde~ to Latin ~vertere~ ("to turn"), whence English ~convert~, ~divert~, and ~versus~; the Germanic branch produced ~werden~ ("to become," literally "to turn into"), ~-wärts~ ("-ward," as in ~vorwärts~), and English ~worth~. The development from "turning" to "exchanging" to "having value" to "being worthy" to "dignity" traces a beautiful arc across five millennia of semantic evolution.
en.zahlen:
From Middle High German ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from Old High German ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). Cognate with Bavarian ~zoin~, Dutch ~talen~, Swedish ~tala~, English ~tale~.

~Zahlen~ ("to pay") and ~zählen~ ("to count") are siblings from the same Proto-Germanic root *~talōną~. This root carried both counting and narrating from the beginning, a duality visible in English ~tell~ (to count: ~teller~ at a bank, ~telling beads~; to narrate: to tell a story) and ~tale~ (a story, but also archaic "a count, tally"). The semantic path from "to count" to "to pay" is natural: payment requires counting out the correct amount. In medieval German, ~zalen~ meant both to count and to pay, and the modern distinction between ~zahlen~ and ~zählen~ reflects the same productive split that gave English ~tell~ and ~tale~ their divergent senses. Cognate with Dutch ~betalen~ (via the same root), English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Danish ~tale~ ("to speak"), Swedish ~tala~ ("to speak").
en.zaubern:
From Middle High German ~zoubern~, from Old High German ~zouberōn~, ~zoubarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taubrōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taubrōną~, derived from *~taubrą~ ("magic, sorcery"). Cognate with English ~tiver~ (a red pigment, perhaps originally used in magical rituals) and Dutch ~toveren~ ("to do magic"), Old Norse ~taufr~ ("magic, sorcery").

The origin of Proto-Germanic *~taubrą~ is uncertain, but it may be linked to *~tawjaną~ ("to make, prepare"), suggesting that magic was originally understood as a kind of crafting or making. The Gothic Bible translator Wulfila used ~taujan~ for "to do, make," and the idea of magic as fabrication (making something appear from nothing) fits this connection. The noun ~Zauber~ ("magic, spell") and the fairy-tale figure ~Zauberer~ ("wizard, sorcerer") both stem from this root. Interestingly, the old Germanic word for magic survived where many other pagan-era terms did not, resisting replacement by Latin or Christian vocabulary.
en.zeichnen: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, symbol"), from Middle High German ~zeichen~, from Old High German ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~, *~taiknaz~ ("sign"), from Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point"). Cognate with Dutch ~teken~, English ~token~, Danish ~tegn~, Swedish ~tecken~. The PIE root *~deyḱ-~ is extraordinarily productive: it also underlies German ~zeigen~ ("to show"), Latin ~dīcere~ ("to say," giving English ~dictate~, ~judge~, ~index~), Greek ~deiknynai~ ("to show"), and Sanskrit ~diś-~ ("direction"). To draw (~zeichnen~) is etymologically to make a sign, and the sign itself descends from the same ancestral root as the act of pointing and showing. English ~token~ and German ~Zeichen~ are cognates across a millennium of linguistic divergence: both mean "a sign left behind to be read."
en.zeigen: From Middle High German ~zeigen~, from Old High German ~zeigōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taigōn~, possibly from Proto-Germanic *~taikōną~ (an iterative formation). An intensive derivative of Old High German ~zīhan~ ("to accuse"), whence modern ~zeihen~ ("to blame"). Ultimately from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to point out, show"), whence also ~Zeichen~ ("sign") and English ~teach~. In Modern German, ~zeigen~ absorbed the synonymous but entirely unrelated Middle High German ~zöugen~ (cognate with Gothic ~ataugjan~).
en.zeihen: From OHG ~zīhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~tīhaną~ ("to show, point out; to blame, accuse"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show"). Cognate with Latin ~dīcō~ ("to speak, say"), Ancient Greek ~δείκνυμι~ (~deíknumi~, "to show, point out"), and English ~token~ (from the related *~taikną~, "sign").
en.zerbeißen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~beißen~:

• ~beißen~: From MHG ~bīzen~, from OHG ~bīzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bītaną~, from PIE *~bʰeyd-~ ("to split"). A class I strong verb (~beißen~, ~biss~, ~gebissen~). Cognate with English ~bite~, Dutch ~bijten~, Swedish ~bita~; ~bitter~ is this verb's old participial adjective, literally "biting."
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

The prefix turns biting into severing: not merely to bite down, but to break what is bitten into pieces.
en.zerbersten:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~bersten~:

• ~bersten~: From MHG ~bresten~, from OHG ~brestan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brestan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brestaną~ ("to burst, break"); the deeper PIE ancestry is uncertain. A class IV strong verb (~bersten~, ~barst~, ~geborsten~). The modern ~-er-~ is a Middle Low German metathesis. Cognate with English ~burst~, Dutch ~barsten~, Old Norse ~bresta~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

~Bersten~ already denotes a sudden breaking open; ~zer-~ carries it to a complete shattering into fragments, and like the base verb it is conjugated with ~sein~.
en.zerbrechen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

~Zerbrechen~ is both transitive and intransitive: one breaks something, or something breaks (with ~sein~); figuratively ~an etwas zerbrechen~ is to be destroyed inwardly by a burden.
en.zerdrücken:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

With ~zer-~, ~drücken~ becomes crushing: everyday for mashing boiled potatoes, but also idiomatic in ~eine Träne zerdrücken~, to fight back a tear.
en.zerfallen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

Purely intransitive and built with ~sein~, ~zerfallen~ ranges from a crumbling building through a disintegrating state to the radioactive ~Zerfall~ (decay) of an atomic nucleus.
en.zerfließen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~fließen~:

• ~fließen~: From MHG ~vlieȥen~, from OHG ~flioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleutaną~ ("to float, stream, flow"), from PIE *~plewd-~ ("to flow, run, swim"). A class II strong verb (~fließen~, ~floss~, ~geflossen~); the zero grade *~flut-~ gave ~Flut~. Cognate with English ~fleet~, ~float~ and ~flood~, Dutch ~vlieten~, Swedish ~flyta~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys dispersal: scattering or dissolving in every direction.

Intransitive and with ~sein~: what ~zerfließt~ melts and spreads in every direction; figuratively one can ~in Tränen zerfließen~, dissolve into tears.
en.zergehen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys dispersal: scattering or dissolving in every direction.

Intransitive and with ~sein~, ~zergehen~ names melting or dissolving away; proverbially one lets something ~auf der Zunge zergehen~, melt on the tongue.
en.zerhauen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~hauen~:

• ~hauen~: From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). Originally a class VII strong verb (~hauen~, ~hieb~, ~gehauen~), partially weakened colloquially, where ~haute~ competes with ~hieb~. Cognate with English ~hew~, Latin ~cūdere~ ("to strike, forge").
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

~Zer-~ turns striking into severing: ~zerhauen~ is to split something into pieces with a strong blow, and the verb is today mostly weak.
en.zerkochen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~kochen~:

• ~kochen~: From MHG ~kochen~, from OHG ~kohhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kokōn~, borrowed from Late Latin ~cocō~, from Latin ~coquō~ ("I cook, I boil"), from PIE *~pekʷ-~ ("to cook, to ripen"). A loan early enough to have undergone the High German shift of ~k~ to ~ch~. Cognate with English ~cook~, Dutch ~koken~, Danish ~koge~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

A kitchen word: to ~zerkochen~ something is to cook it until it turns to mush; intransitively, vegetables ~zerkochen~ of their own accord.
en.zerlaufen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys dispersal: scattering or dissolving in every direction.

Said of butter, chocolate or ink: ~zerlaufen~ is to melt and lose shape in the warmth, and it is built with ~sein~.
en.zerleben:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~leben~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The development from "to cling" to "to remain alive" parallels ~bleiben~ ("to remain"). Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys complete destruction or ruin.

A rare, literary word: to ~zerleben~ a face or a life is to wear it out and mark it through hard living.
en.zerlegen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

~Zerlegen~ is methodical taking-apart: a carcass into cuts, a machine into components, or, in mathematics, a number into its factors.
en.zerlesen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys complete destruction or ruin.

Used almost only as a participial adjective: a ~zerlesenes~ book is one worn ragged and dog-eared by much reading.
en.zerreden:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys complete destruction or ruin.

Wholly figurative: to ~zerreden~ a good proposal is to talk it to pieces, draining it of all force through endless debate until nothing decisive remains.
en.zerreiben:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~reiben~:

• ~reiben~: From MHG ~rīben~, from OHG ~rīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrībaną~ ("to rub"); beyond Germanic uncertain, a PIE *~wreyp-~, labial extension of *~wer-~ ("to turn"), being proposed but not secure. A class I strong verb (~reiben~, ~rieb~, ~gerieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~wrijven~, Old Saxon ~wrīvan~; German dropped the initial ~w-~ before ~r~, as in ~ringen~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

Literally grinding to powder between two surfaces; figuratively a person is ~zerrieben~, ground down, between opposing forces like grain between millstones.
en.zerreißen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~reißen~:

• ~reißen~: From MHG ~rīȥen~, from OHG ~rīȥan~ ("to scratch"), from a conflation of two Proto-West Germanic verbs: *~wrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~, from PIE *~wer-~ ("to cut, scratch, tear, sketch an outline"), and *~hrītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrītaną~. The merger left an unusually broad semantic field, and *~wrītaną~ also gave English ~write~, originally "to scratch, carve." Cognate with Dutch ~rijten~, Low German ~rieten~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

Transitively one tears something in two; intransitively a thread ~zerreißt~ of itself; figuratively ~es zerreißt einem das Herz~, it tears one's heart apart with grief.
en.zerrinnen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~rinnen~:

• ~rinnen~: From MHG ~rinnen~, from OHG ~rinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~ ("to run, flow"); the PIE source is debated, most often given as *~h₃reyH-~ ("to churn, set in motion"). A class III strong verb (~rinnen~, ~rann~, ~geronnen~). German ~rennen~ is its causative, from *~rannijaną~. Cognate with English ~run~, Gothic ~rinnan~, Swedish ~rinna~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys dispersal: scattering or dissolving in every direction.

Said of liquids and, figuratively, of money and time: what ~zerrinnt~ slips away between one's fingers beyond holding, and it is built with ~sein~.
en.zerschellen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~schellen~:

• ~schellen~: Two Early New High German verbs merged here: a strong intransitive (MHG ~schellen~, OHG ~skellan~ "to resound", from Proto-West Germanic *~skellan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skellaną~) and its causative (OHG ~skellen~ "to make resound", from Proto-Germanic *~skallijaną~), both from PIE *~skel-~, an s-mobile variant of *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, sound"). Modern ~schellen~ ("to ring a bell") is weak (~schellte~, ~geschellt~), though the strong ~scholl~/~geschollen~ still surfaces in elevated and regional use. Cognate with Old Norse ~skjalla~, Old English ~sciellan~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

The root ~schellen~ originally means "to resound," and the sound survives in ~zerschellen~: the ship dashed against the rocks shatters with a loud crash. It is built with ~sein~.
en.zerschießen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb (~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~). Cognate with English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Old Norse ~skjóta~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

~Zer-~ drives shooting to the point of ruin: a ~zerschossenes~ building is one reduced to rubble by gunfire.
en.zerschlagen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

Transitively one smashes something to shards; reflexively ~sich zerschlagen~ means that a plan or hope falls through, and as an adjective ~zerschlagen~ means "worn out, exhausted."
en.zerschmeißen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~schmeißen~:

• ~schmeißen~: From MHG ~smīȥen~, from OHG ~smīȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~smītaną~, from PIE *~smeyd-~. A class I strong verb (~schmeißen~, ~schmiss~, ~geschmissen~). Cognate with English ~smite~, Dutch ~smijten~, Danish ~smide~, Gothic ~bismeitan~ ("to smear, to anoint").
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

"~zerschmeißen~" denotes smashing an object by hurling or striking it hard; it now sounds archaic, while ~schmeißen~ alone is colloquial for "to throw."
en.zerschmelzen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~schmelzen~:

• ~schmelzen~: From MHG ~smelzen~, from OHG ~smelzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~smeltan~, from Proto-Germanic *~smeltaną~ ("to melt"), from PIE *~(s)meld-~ ("to melt, to soften"). Intransitively a class III strong verb (~schmelzen~, ~schmolz~, ~geschmolzen~), beside a weak causative ~schmelzen~ ("to melt something down"). Cognate with English ~smelt~ and ~melt~ (the same root with and without the mobile ~s-~), and Dutch ~smelten~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys dispersal: scattering or dissolving in every direction.

Intransitively, ~zerschmelzen~ describes melting away entirely, a solid mass dissolving completely into liquid.
en.zerschneiden:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~schneiden~:

• ~schneiden~: From MHG ~snīden~, from OHG ~snīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~snīþan~ ("to cut"); no secure PIE root has been established, and the word may be a Germanic innovation. A class I strong verb (~schneiden~, ~schnitt~, ~geschnitten~). Cognate with archaic English ~snithe~ ("to cut"), Dutch ~snijden~, Icelandic ~sníða~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

The compound means cutting something into several pieces with a blade, and is used figuratively for severing ties.
en.zersetzen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys complete destruction or ruin.

"~zersetzen~" names the chemical breakdown of a substance into its components and, figuratively, the undermining of cohesion and order; the noun ~Zersetzung~ was a Stasi term of art.
en.zersingen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~singen~:

• ~singen~: From MHG ~singen~, from OHG ~singan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~singwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~singwaną~, from PIE *~sengʷʰ-~ ("to recite, intone, chant"), connected to Ancient Greek ~ὀμφή~ (omphḗ, "divine voice, oracle"). A class III strong verb (~singen~, ~sang~, ~gesungen~). Cognate with English ~sing~, Gothic ~𐍃𐌹𐌲𐌲𐍅𐌰𐌽~ (siggwan), Dutch ~zingen~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

The rare compound denotes shattering an object (a glass, say) through the vibration of song.
en.zerspringen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~springen~:

• ~springen~: From OHG ~springan~, from Proto-Germanic *~springaną~, from PIE *~sprenǵʰ-~, a nasalized form of *~sperǵʰ-~ ("to move energetically, to hasten, to spring"). A class III strong verb (~springen~, ~sprang~, ~gesprungen~). Cognate with English ~spring~, Dutch ~springen~, Danish ~springe~, Greek ~spérkhō~ ("to hasten").
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

Intransitive and built with ~sein~, ~zerspringen~ describes a sudden bursting under tension; figuratively the heart can burst with joy or grief.
en.zerstechen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~stechen~:

• ~stechen~: From MHG ~stëchen~, from OHG ~stëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stekaną~ ("to stab, prick"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to stick, poke"). Cognate with Dutch ~steken~ ("to stab, sting"), Old Norse ~stinga~, English ~stick~ (originally "to stab, pierce").
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys complete destruction or ruin.

"~zerstechen~" means rendering something useless by repeated stabbing (to slash a tire) as well as pricking skin all over with many separate stings.
en.zerstieben:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~stieben~:

• ~stieben~: From MHG ~stieben~, from OHG ~stioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~steuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~steubaną~ ("to fly about as dust"), with no secure cognates outside Germanic; a link to PIE *~dʰewbʰ-~ ("to whirl, smoke") has been proposed but is not established. A class II strong verb (~stieben~, ~stob~, ~gestoben~), with weak ~stiebte~, ~gestiebt~ also current. Rare and literary in modern German, surviving chiefly in ~Funken stieben~ and ~zerstieben~. Cognate with Dutch ~stuiven~ and ~stof~ ("dust").
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys dispersal: scattering or dissolving in every direction.

~Zerstieben~ paints a flying-apart into dust in every direction: sparks, spray, or a crowd bursting outward; the word is elevated and literary.
en.zerstoßen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). Cognate with dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce, ricochet"), Dutch ~stoten~, Old Norse ~stauta~ and ~steyta~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.
