~Zerstoßen~ means breaking something up by pounding or stamping, grinding a substance to powder in a mortar, for instance.
en.zerstreiten:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~streiten~:

• ~streiten~: From MHG ~strīten~, from OHG ~strītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~strīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~strīdaną~, probably from Pre-Germanic *~streydʰh₁-~, a compound of PIE *~strey-~ ("to resist") + *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, place"). Cognate with English ~stride~, Dutch ~strijden~ ("to fight, struggle"), Low German ~striden~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

Used reflexively (~sich zerstreiten~) the compound denotes a relationship breaking apart in quarrel until the parties have become estranged.
en.zerstören:
From Middle High German ~zerstœren~, equivalent to ~zer-~ + ~stören~:

• ~stören~: From MHG ~stören~, from OHG ~stōren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~staurijan~. Cognate with English ~stir~.
• ~zer-~: From PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, doubly, in two"). The prefix expresses shattering, breaking apart, or total destruction.

~Zerstören~ means "to destroy", etymologically, "to disturb to pieces." The ~zer-~ prefix is one of German's most violent: it takes the relatively mild ~stören~ ("to disturb") and escalates it to total annihilation. The same prefix appears in ~zerbrechen~ ("to shatter"), ~zerreißen~ ("to tear apart"), ~zerfallen~ ("to disintegrate"), and ~zerschlagen~ ("to smash"), in each case converting a moderate action into a catastrophic one. The derived noun ~Zerstörung~ ("destruction") and the agent noun ~Zerstörer~ ("destroyer", also the German word for the naval warship class) are transparently formed. The semantic distance between ~stören~ ("to disturb") and ~zerstören~ ("to destroy") (the difference between an annoying noise and total devastation) is carried entirely by the prefix ~zer-~, making it one of the most powerful morphological intensifiers in the German language. Cognate with Dutch ~verstoren~ (which uses ~ver-~ instead of ~zer-~).
en.zerteilen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~teilen~:

• ~teilen~: From MHG ~teilen~ and OHG ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~ ("to divide, part, deal"), from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, a denominative of *~dailiz~ ("part, share"), from PIE *~dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo-~, tentatively from *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, set, place"), though the precise PIE derivation is uncertain. Cognate with English ~deal~, Dutch ~delen~, Danish ~dele~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

~Zerteilen~ means splitting a whole into several parts, transitive or reflexive, as when a cloud or a crowd divides.
en.zertreiben:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys dispersal: scattering or dissolving in every direction.

~Zertreiben~ means driving apart, scattering and chasing a crowd or herd off in every direction.
en.zertrennen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~trennen~:

• ~trennen~: From MHG ~trennen~, from OHG ~trennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~trannijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trannijaną~. The deeper etymology is uncertain: the Proto-Germanic root is not securely connected to any PIE root. Cognate with Low German ~trennen~ and Dutch ~tornen~, which has narrowed to "to unpick stitches."
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

~Zertrennen~ means forcibly parting a joined thing, from undoing a seam to breaking up an alliance.
en.zertreten:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys complete destruction or ruin.

~Zertreten~ means crushing underfoot, destroying by treading, literally, as in the image of the serpent's crushed head.
en.zerwerfen:
An inseparable compound of ~zer-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~zer-~: From MHG ~zer-~, from OHG ~zi-~, ~za-~, ~zir-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ti-~, from Proto-Germanic *~te-~ ("apart, asunder"), from PIE *~dwís~ ("twice, in two"). Cognate with Old English ~tō-~ ("apart"), the prefix of ~tōbrecan~ ("to break to pieces"), and with Latin ~dis-~. ~zer-~ conveys breaking apart, shattering, or falling to pieces.

~Zerwerfen~ means smashing something by throwing it; reflexively (~sich mit jemandem zerwerfen~) it also names a falling-out, a rupture in a quarrel.
en.zeugen:
From Middle High German ~ziugen~, ~geziugen~, from Old High German ~giziugon~, from ~ziug~ ("equipment, gear"), ultimately from the root of ~ziehen~ ("to pull, draw, move"). The underlying noun ~Zeug~ comes from MHG ~ziuc~ ("stuff, gear"), from OHG ~giziug~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teug~, from Proto-Germanic *~teugą~, related to *~teuhaną~ ("to pull"), from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead").

The original meaning of ~zeugen~ was "to produce, bring forth through technical activity", literally to pull something into existence using tools (~Zeug~). From this developed two distinct modern senses: "to beget, procreate" (producing a child) and "to testify, bear witness" (producing evidence). The noun ~Zeuge~ ("witness") comes from the verb, as does ~Zeugnis~ ("testimony, certificate"). English ~tug~ descends from the same PIE root *~dewk-~. Cognate with Dutch ~tuig~ ("equipment, gear"), Old Norse ~tygi~ ("gear"). The semantic range of ~zeugen~ (from making things, to making children, to making a case in court) is a remarkable study in conceptual extension.
en.ziehen: From Middle High German ~ziehen~, from Old High German ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Low German ~tehn~, Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~. Cognate with obsolete English ~tee~ ("to draw, lead, proceed") and English ~tie~, from the same PIE root.
en.zielen:
From ~Ziel~ ("target, goal") + ~-en~. ~Ziel~ descends from MHG ~zil~, from OHG ~zil~, from Proto-West Germanic *~til~, from Proto-Germanic *~tilą~ ("aim, goal, fixed point"). Cognate with Old English ~til~ ("suitable, fitting"), whence English ~till~ (preposition: "up to a fixed point").

~Zielen~ means "to aim", both physically (~auf ein Ziel zielen~, "to aim at a target") and figuratively (~auf etwas zielen~, "to be directed at something"). The verb is a relatively transparent denominal formation: to aim is to direct oneself toward a fixed point (~Ziel~). The Proto-Germanic *~tilą~ connects to a semantic field of fitness and suitability rather than spatial targets; Old English ~til~ meant "suitable, good, apt," and the preposition ~till~ ("up to") preserves the sense of reaching a fixed endpoint. German ~Ziel~ narrowed to the spatial and aspirational senses: the place you aim for, the goal you strive toward. The noun ~Zielscheibe~ ("target disc") makes the archery metaphor explicit, while ~Ziellinie~ ("finish line") extends it to racing.
en.zitieren:
Borrowed from Latin ~citāre~ ("to summon, to call forth, to set in motion"), a frequentative of ~ciēre~ ("to move, stir"), from PIE *~keyh₂-~ ("to set in motion"). The Latin verb's primary sense was legal: to summon a person to appear before a court. The scholarly sense "to quote a text as evidence" developed as a metaphorical extension: calling a written authority to testify, as it were.

German borrowed ~zitieren~ with the ~-ieren~ suffix typical of Latin and French loan verbs. It retains both the quotation sense ("to cite a passage") and, more formally, the summoning sense ("to call someone to appear"). English ~cite~ arrived via Old French from the same Latin source, while ~excite~ and ~incite~ are formed from the same root with different prefixes.
en.zuarbeiten:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"); the sense runs from "orphan" through "hardship, toil" to "work." Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~, and, from the same root, English ~orphan~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

With a dative (~jemandem zuarbeiten~) the verb means doing the preparatory work for someone and supplying them with what they build on.
en.zubauen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~būwen~, from OHG ~būan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~būan~, from Proto-Germanic *~būaną~ ("to dwell, reside"), from PIE *~bʰuH-~ ("to be, become, grow"); one builds where one lives. Cognate with English ~be~, ~bower~ ("dwelling"), ~neighbor~ ("near-dweller"), Dutch ~bouwen~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

~Zubauen~ means filling or blocking an open space with buildings until the open area is closed off.
en.zubeißen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~beißen~:

• ~beißen~: From MHG ~bīzen~, from OHG ~bīzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bītaną~, from PIE *~bʰeyd-~ ("to split"). A class I strong verb (~beißen~, ~biss~, ~gebissen~). Cognate with English ~bite~, Dutch ~bijten~, Swedish ~bita~; ~bitter~ is this verb's old participial adjective, literally "biting."
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zubeißen~ means biting down hard, snapping the teeth shut on a target, whether in feeding or in an animal's attack.
en.zubereiten:
Compound of ~zu-~ + ~bereiten~:

• ~bereiten~: From MHG ~bereiten~, from OHG ~bireiten~, derived from the adjective ~bereit~ ("ready"), which descends from OHG ~bireiti~, ~reiti~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raidī~, from Proto-Germanic *~raidaz~ ("ready, arranged"), from PIE *~h₂reh₁dʰ-~ ("to put in order, arrange"). Cognate with English ~ready~, Dutch ~bereid~ ("prepared"), Gothic ~garaiþs~ ("arranged, ordered"), and Swedish ~redo~ ("ready").
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"). As a verbal prefix, it means "to, toward" and often conveys purposeful completion.

The compound means "to prepare", specifically food: ~eine Mahlzeit zubereiten~ ("to prepare a meal"), ~einen Cocktail zubereiten~ ("to mix a cocktail"). While ~vorbereiten~ means "to prepare" in a general sense (preparing for an exam, a trip), ~zubereiten~ is reserved almost exclusively for culinary preparation, making it one of the more semantically specialized ~zu-~ compounds. The underlying adjective ~bereit~ ("ready") connects German and English more closely than most speakers realize: English ~ready~ descends from the exact same Proto-Germanic root *~raidaz~. The Old English form ~ġerǣde~ still wore its Germanic prefix ~ge-~ openly, while German replaced it with ~be-~. Both prefixes carry a sense of collective completion, and both languages independently chose to prefix the same root to create their word for "prepared."
en.zubinden:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~binden~:

• ~binden~: From MHG ~binden~, from OHG ~bintan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bindan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bindaną~, from PIE *~bʰendʰ-~ ("to bind, tie"). A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~i~–~a~–~u~ ablaut (~binden~, ~band~, ~gebunden~). Cognate with English ~bind~, Dutch ~binden~, Gothic ~bindan~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

~Zubinden~ means closing something by tying it together: a sack, a shoelace, a pouch.
en.zubringen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

Today ~zubringen~ mostly means "to spend (time)"; the older sense attested here is "to bring or convey something to someone."
en.zudecken:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~decken~:

• ~decken~: From MHG ~decken~, from OHG ~decchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þakkjan~ ("to cover"), from Proto-Germanic *~þakjaną~, a causative formation from *~þaką~ ("roof, thatch"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to cover"); the verb is etymologically "to roof." Cognate with English ~thatch~, Dutch ~dekken~, Swedish ~täcka~; from the same root Latin ~tegere~, whence English ~protect~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

~Zudecken~ means covering from above (tucking someone in under a blanket) and, figuratively, concealing or hushing up.
en.zudrehen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). Cognate with English ~throw~ (a true cognate: Old English ~þrāwan~ meant "to twist," a sense that "throw a pot" still keeps) plus English ~thread~, Dutch ~draaien~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

~Zudrehen~ means closing by turning: to turn off the tap; reflexively, though, ~sich jemandem zudrehen~ means turning toward a person.
en.zudringen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~dringen~:

• ~dringen~: From MHG ~dringen~, from OHG ~dringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þringwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrinhwaną~, from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). A class III strong verb (~dringen~, ~drang~, ~gedrungen~); its causative ~drängen~ carries the expected umlaut. Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~ ("to press") and English ~throng~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zudringen~ means pressing forward toward someone or something; the related adjective ~zudringlich~ ("pushy, intrusive") preserves this sense of crowding too close.
en.zudrücken:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

~Zudrücken~ means closing something by pressing; the idiom ~ein Auge zudrücken~ means to turn a blind eye.
en.zueignen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~eignen~:

• ~eignen~: From MHG ~eigenen~, from OHG ~eiganen~, from Proto-Germanic *~aiginōną~, a denominative from *~aiganaz~ ("owned, one's own"), the past participle of *~aiganą~ ("to possess"), from PIE *~h₂eh₂óyḱe~, from *~h₂eyḱ-~ ("ability, possession"). Originally "to make one's own." Cognate with English ~own~, Dutch ~eigen~, Swedish ~ägna~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

~Zueignen~ means making something one's own (to appropriate it) and, in elevated usage, dedicating a work to someone.
en.zueinanderhalten:
A separable compound of ~zueinander-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~zueinander-~: A frozen adverb: ~zu~ ("to") + ~einander~ ("one another"), the latter itself ~ein~ + ~ander~, a reciprocal pronoun fused with its preposition and no longer inflected. The parallel with English ~to one another~ is exact, morpheme for morpheme; German simply writes it as one word and lets it behave as a separable particle. ~zueinander-~ marks reciprocity: the parties act toward each other.

~Zueinanderhalten~ means mutual loyalty: to keep firmly together through good times and bad and never leave one another in the lurch.
en.zuerkennen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~er-~ + ~kennen~:

• ~kennen~: From MHG ~kennen~, from OHG ~kennen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kannijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~kannijaną~ ("to know"), a causative of *~kunnaną~, from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ ("to know"). A member of the Rückumlaut cohort: the present shows umlaut (~ich kenne~), the preterite does not (~kannte~, ~gekannt~). Cognate with Dutch ~kennen~, Scots and English ~ken~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

In legal and official use ~zuerkennen~ means to formally adjudge a right, a title, or a status to someone.
en.zuerteilen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~er-~ + ~teilen~:

• ~teilen~: From MHG ~teilen~ and OHG ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~ ("to divide, part, deal"), from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, a denominative of *~dailiz~ ("part, share"), from PIE *~dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo-~, tentatively from *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, set, place"), though the precise PIE derivation is uncertain. Cognate with English ~deal~, Dutch ~delen~, Danish ~dele~.
• ~er-~: From MHG ~er-~, from OHG ~ir-~, ~ar-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uʀ-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uz-~ ("out, up"), from PIE *~ud~ ("up, out, away"). Doublet of the stressed prefix ~ur-~. ~er-~ marks the successful achievement or completion of the base action.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

~Zuerteilen~ means to bestow or confer, overlapping largely with ~zuerkennen~; it is used above all of awards and rights.
en.zufallen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

Literally ~zufallen~ means that something falls shut of its own accord, a door, say. The same formation also carries the figurative sense "to fall to someone, to accrue as one's share," which is what the quoted sentence shows.
en.zufassen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~fassen~:

• ~fassen~: From MHG ~vazzen~, from OHG ~fazzōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fatōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fatōną~ ("to hold, seize"), a weak class 2 verb, from PIE *~pod-néh₂-ti~, from *~pod-~ ("to fetch"). German kept the sense of grasping and holding, English that of going to retrieve. Cognate with English ~fetch~; the noun ~Fass~ ("barrel") shares the root.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zufassen~ means to grab hold decisively, to reach out and seize.
en.zufliegen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~fliegen~:

• ~fliegen~: From MHG ~vliegen~, from OHG ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"), an extension of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim") that also gave ~fließen~. The vowel path *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of class II strong verbs. Cognate with English ~fly~, Dutch ~vliegen~, Danish ~flyve~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zufliegen~ means to move through the air toward a target; in the quoted image the nails are drawn to the magnet mountain.
en.zufließen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~fließen~:

• ~fließen~: From MHG ~vlieȥen~, from OHG ~flioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleutaną~ ("to float, stream, flow"), from PIE *~plewd-~ ("to flow, run, swim"). A class II strong verb (~fließen~, ~floss~, ~geflossen~); the zero grade *~flut-~ gave ~Flut~. Cognate with English ~fleet~, ~float~ and ~flood~, Dutch ~vlieten~, Swedish ~flyta~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zufließen~ denotes flowing toward a destination; of money and revenue it means to accrue to someone, as in the quoted tax provision.
en.zufriedengeben:
A separable compound of ~zufrieden~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~zufrieden~: A frozen prepositional phrase written as one word: ~zu~ + the old dative of ~Friede~ ("peace"), MHG ~ze vride~ ("in peace, content"). The noun goes back to Proto-Germanic *~friþuz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, be dear"), the same root that gives English ~friend~ and ~free~. The modern one-word spelling hides a literal sense of being at peace. The sense of ~zufrieden~ here is: to settle for, to acquiesce in (~sich zufriedengeben~).

Reflexive ~sich zufriedengeben~ means to make do with what one has and demand no more.
en.zufriedenstellen:
A separable compound of ~zufrieden~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~zufrieden~: A frozen prepositional phrase written as one word: ~zu~ + the old dative of ~Friede~ ("peace"), MHG ~ze vride~ ("in peace, content"). The noun goes back to Proto-Germanic *~friþuz~, from PIE *~preyH-~ ("to love, be dear"), the same root that gives English ~friend~ and ~free~. The modern one-word spelling hides a literal sense of being at peace. The sense of ~zufrieden~ here is the resultative frame: bring someone into that state (~zufriedenstellen~).

~Zufriedenstellen~ is transitive and causative; the quoted Grimm example shows it in the stative passive ("war nicht zufriedengestellt").
en.zufrieren:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~frieren~:

• ~frieren~: From MHG ~vriesen~ (beside ~vrieren~), from OHG ~friosan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~freusan~, from Proto-Germanic *~freusaną~, from PIE *~prews-~ ("to freeze, frost"). A class II strong verb (~frieren~, ~fror~, ~gefroren~); the ~r~ arose by grammatischer Wechsel in the past forms and spread to the infinitive, as in ~verlieren~. Cognate with English ~freeze~ and ~frost~, Dutch ~vriezen~, Danish ~fryse~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

~Zufrieren~ is said of a body of water whose surface seals over with ice; the lake freezes over.
en.zufügen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~fügen~:

• ~fügen~: From MHG ~füegen~, ~fuogen~, from OHG ~fuogen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōgijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōgijaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to join, attach, fasten"). Reflexive ~sich fügen~ means "to submit": to join oneself to the arrangement of fate. Cognate with Dutch ~voegen~ and archaic English ~fay~ ("to fit closely," from Old English ~fēgan~).
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys addition or increase: adding to what is already there.

Literally ~zufügen~ means "to add to"; its main modern meaning, "to do harm or hurt to someone," adds the injury to the affected party, who always stands in the dative.
en.zuführen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zuführen~ means to bring something or someone up to a destination: to supply provisions, provide nourishment, or conduct a person somewhere.
en.zugeben:
Compound of ~zu-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~, displacing OE ~giefan~), Dutch ~geven~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys "to, toward" or "in addition."

~Zugeben~ means both "to admit, to confess" and "to add" (an ingredient). The confession sense is "to give to" the truth, to yield toward an admission. The culinary sense is more literal: giving something into the mixture. The duality mirrors the English verb ~concede~, from Latin ~concēdere~ ("to yield, to give way"), which likewise spans both "to admit a point" and "to grant, to hand over."
en.zugehen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

In the sense "to close," a door geht zu; alongside it stands the impersonal ~zugehen~ "to come about, to happen," which the quoted sentence shows.
en.zugehören:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~ge-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

In meaning ~zugehören~ today almost coincides with its simple base verb; the ~zu-~ only foregrounds the direction of belonging: to whom or what something belongs.
en.zugestehen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~ge-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

~Zugestehen~ means to grant someone a right or a claim; the sense of yielding has grown onto the base verb ~gestehen~ "to confess."
en.zugraben:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~graben~:

• ~graben~: From MHG ~graben~, from OHG ~graban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from PIE *~gʰrebʰ-~ ("to dig, scratch, bury"). A class VI strong verb (~graben~, ~grub~, ~gegraben~). Cognate with English ~grave~ as a verb (now only in ~engrave~ and ~graven image~), Gothic ~graban~, Dutch ~graven~, Old Norse ~grafa~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

~Zugraben~ means to close up a pit or ditch by shoveling earth back into it.
en.zugreifen:
Compound of ~zu-~ + ~greifen~:

• ~greifen~: From MHG ~grīfen~, from OHG ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~ ("to grab, grasp"), from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). Cognate with English ~gripe~ and ~grip~, Dutch ~grijpen~, Gothic ~greipan~. The Lithuanian cognate ~griebti~ ("to seize") confirms the PIE pedigree.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"). As a verbal prefix, it adds a sense of reaching toward and seizing.

The literal sense is "to grab toward": to reach out and take hold. ~Zugreifen~ means "to grab it, to help oneself" (as when food is offered: ~greifen Sie zu!~, "help yourself!"), "to seize an opportunity," or "to take decisive action." The English cognate ~grip~ preserves the physical sense most transparently, while ~gripe~ has narrowed to mean "to complain" (originally "to clutch, to cause a gripping pain"). The noun ~Zugriff~ ("access, grasp") is ubiquitous in computing and law alike. The PIE root *~gʰreyb-~ also appears in Lithuanian ~graibýti~ ("to seize"), confirming that the sense of grasping has been stable for over five thousand years.
en.zugutehalten:
A separable compound of ~zugute-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~zugute-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: ~zu~ + the old dative of the substantivized adjective ~gut~, MHG ~ze guote~ ("for the good, to the benefit"). It survives only in this fossilized adverbial shape, which is why it is written solid and why ~Gute~ here is no longer felt as a noun. The party benefited is the dative object of the verb. The sense of ~zugute-~ here is: to count something in someone's favor, to make allowance for it (~zugutehalten~).

In the quoted Luther passage ~zugutehalten~ still carries the older, concrete sense "to take in good part, to receive indulgently."
en.zugutekommen:
A separable compound of ~zugute-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~zugute-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: ~zu~ + the old dative of the substantivized adjective ~gut~, MHG ~ze guote~ ("for the good, to the benefit"). It survives only in this fossilized adverbial shape, which is why it is written solid and why ~Gute~ here is no longer felt as a noun. The party benefited is the dative object of the verb. The sense of ~zugute-~ here is: to accrue to, to be of use to (~zugutekommen~).

~Zugutekommen~ is intransitive and takes its beneficiary in the dative; in fiscal and political language it is the standard word for something conferring a benefit on someone.
en.zuhaben:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

Colloquially ~zuhaben~ means to have something shut: a shop hat zu, the door hat zu.
en.zuhalten:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

~Zuhalten~ means to hold something shut by hand or by force: to hold one's mouth, nose, or ears closed.
en.zuhauen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~hauen~:

• ~hauen~: From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). Originally a class VII strong verb (~hauen~, ~hieb~, ~gehauen~), partially weakened colloquially, where ~haute~ competes with ~hieb~. Cognate with English ~hew~, Latin ~cūdere~ ("to strike, forge").
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zuhauen~ is a blunt "to strike hard," landing a blow on a target; in the Grimm example the man raises his axe to strike.
en.zuhören:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zuhören~ directs one's hearing toward a source, to attend, listening, to someone or something.
en.zukaufen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, a denominative verb from *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"), a loanword from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper"). Cognate with English ~cheap~, Dutch ~kopen~, Danish ~købe~, Icelandic ~kaupa~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys addition or increase: adding to what is already there.

~Zukaufen~ means to buy something in addition to an existing stock, to acquire what is lacking as a supplement.
en.zukehren:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~kehren~:

• ~kehren~: A homograph concealing two distinct verbs. ~Kehren~ (1) "to turn": from MHG ~kēren~, from OHG ~kēran~, ~chēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kairijaną~ or *~kausijaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly connected to *~gers-~ ("to twist, bend, turn"). ~Kehren~ (2) "to sweep": from MHG ~kern~, ~keren~, from OHG ~kerian~, ~cherian~, from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~ ("to scrape, scratch"), from PIE *~ger-~ ("to scrape"). Etymologically unrelated, merged through phonological convergence.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

This is ~kehren~ (1) "to turn," not the identically spelled ~kehren~ (2) "to sweep": ~zukehren~ means to turn a side toward someone or a direction, one's back, for instance.
en.zuklappen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~klappen~:

• ~klappen~: From Middle Low German ~klappen~, from Old Saxon *~klappōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~klappōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klappōną~. The verb is onomatopoeic. Cognate with English ~clap~, Dutch ~klappen~, Old High German ~klapfō~ ("a clapping sound"); also related to ~klaffen~ ("to gape").
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

~Zuklappen~ means to shut something hinged with a folding motion: a book, a lid, a laptop.
en.zukleben:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~kleben~:

• ~kleben~: From MHG ~kleben~, from OHG ~klebēn~ ("to stick"), from Proto-West Germanic *~klibēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klibēną~, from PIE *~gleyb-~ ("to stick, adhere"), a durative formation from the strong root *~kleibēną~ ("to adhere, to climb"). Cognate with English ~cleave~ and ~climb~, Old Norse ~klīfa~ ("to climb").
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

The compound turns adhesion into closure: what is ~zugeklebt~ is sealed shut by sticking, an envelope, a wound, and in Nietzsche figuratively the ear stopped against false words.
en.zukommen:
Compound of ~zu-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~komen~, ~quemen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemanan~, from PIE *~gwem-~ ("to come, to go"). Cognate with English ~come~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo-~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"). This prefix adds a directional sense of motion toward something.

The initial ~qu-~ of Old High German ~queman~ (reflecting the original labio-velar *~gw-~) was gradually lost during the Middle High German period, yielding modern ~kommen~. This same PIE root *~gwem-~ also produced Latin ~venire~ ("to come"), showing how the labio-velar *~gw~ developed differently in ~Italic~ versus ~Germanic~ branches. The verb ~zukommen~ has two main modern senses: "to come toward someone" and "to be entitled to, to be due to" (~jemandem steht etwas zu~), the latter reflecting a metaphorical extension where something "comes to" a person by right.
en.zuladen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two historically distinct verbs under one infinitive. ~laden~ (strong, "to load"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"); cognate with English ~lade~ and ~laden~, Lithuanian ~klṓti~. ~laden~ (weak, "to invite, summon"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root found only in Germanic and Anatolian (Hittite ~halzai~).
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys addition or increase: adding to what is already there.

The base is the strong ~laden~ "to load," not the weak homograph "to invite"; ~zu-~ supplies the increment: to ~zuladen~ is to take on further cargo.
en.zulassen:
From Middle High German ~zuolāȥen~, equivalent to ~zu-~ + ~lassen~:

• ~lassen~: From MHG ~lāȥen~, from OHG ~lāȥȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lētan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lētaną~, from PIE *~leh₁d-~ ("to let, to leave, to be weary").
• ~zu-~: From PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"). The prefix adds the sense of granting access or permitting something toward a goal.

~Zulassen~ means "to allow, to permit, to admit", from allowing a possibility (~eine Ausnahme zulassen~, "to allow an exception") to admitting a person (~zum Studium zugelassen~, "admitted to study") to certifying a product (~ein zugelassenes Medikament~, "an approved medication"). The derived noun ~Zulassung~ is the standard word for official authorization: a vehicle registration (~Fahrzeugzulassung~), a professional license, or a university admission. The prefix ~zu-~ here implies opening a gate toward someone: what is ~zugelassen~ has been let through. Cognate with Dutch ~toelaten~.
en.zulaufen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

The compound is pure directed motion: to ~zulaufen~ is to run toward a goal, and, of a stray animal, to attach itself to a new owner.
en.zulegen:
From ~zu-~ + ~legen~. Compound of:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie"), from PIE *~logʰéyeti~, a causative formation from *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). Cognate with English ~lay~, Danish ~laegge~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo-~, from OHG ~zuo-~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~, from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"). As a verbal prefix, it indicates direction toward, addition, or closure.

The literal meaning "to lay toward, add to" generates several figurative senses: ~sich zulegen~ can mean "to acquire, get oneself" (laying something toward one's own pile), or "to pick up speed" (~zulegen~ in the sense of adding pace). The causative relationship between ~legen~ ("to lay," transitive) and ~liegen~ ("to lie," intransitive) mirrors exactly the English pair ~lay~/~lie~, both descending from the same PIE causative formation. English ~lay~ comes from Old English ~lecgan~, from the same Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~.
en.zuleiten:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~: the causative *~laidijaną~ of the strong verb *~līþaną~ ("to pass, go") with the suffix *~-janą~ ("to cause to go"), from PIE *~leyt-~ ("to go, depart, die"). ~leiten~ and ~leiden~ are a base-and-causative pair. Cognate with English ~lead~ (OE ~lǣdan~).
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

The compound conducts something to a designated recipient: a document is ~zugeleitet~ to a chamber, water to a channel, leiten's "guide, conduct" aimed at an addressee.
en.zuliefern:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~liefern~:

• ~liefern~: From MHG ~lieveren~ (attested before 1350), probably borrowed via Middle Dutch and Middle Low German ~lēveren~, from Old French ~livrer~, from Latin ~līberō~ ("I free, release, deliver"), from ~līber~ ("free"). The word belonged to the Hanseatic League's trade vocabulary. Cognate with Dutch ~leveren~, English ~deliver~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

The compound names the supplier's act: to ~zuliefern~ is to deliver components to a manufacturer, whence ~der Zulieferer~, the subcontractor of modern industry.
en.zumachen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

The compound is the everyday word for closing (the plain antonym of ~aufmachen~) from a door or an oven to a shop shutting for the night.
en.zunehmen:
Compound of ~zu-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due, to allot, to distribute"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Dutch ~nemen~, Danish ~nemme~ ("to learn, grasp"), and Swedish ~förnimma~ ("to perceive").
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys addition, increase, or closure.

The compound means "to increase, to grow, to gain weight"; the moon ~nimmt zu~ ("waxes"), a patient ~nimmt zu~ ("gains weight"), and traffic ~nimmt zu~ ("increases"). The image is of something "taking to itself," accumulating more. Its antonym ~abnehmen~ ("to decrease, to lose weight") uses the opposite prefix ~ab-~ ("away"). The PIE root *~nem-~ had the original sense of distributing or allotting; it also produced Greek ~nemein~ ("to distribute, to pasture"), whence ~Nemesis~ (the goddess who distributes what is due) and ~nemesis~ (one's deserved comeuppance). The semantic journey from "distributing fairly" (PIE) to "taking" (Germanic) to "increasing" (German compound) shows how a single root can travel through three thousand years of speakers who each nudged its meaning a little further from the original.
en.zunichtemachen:
A separable compound of ~zunichte-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~zunichte-~: A fossilized case form: ~zu~ + ~nichte~, the old dative of MHG ~niht~ ("nothing"), literally "to nothing". The dative ending is dead everywhere else in the modern language, so ~zunichte~ survives only in this phrase, chiefly ~zunichtemachen~ ("to bring to nothing, to destroy"). MHG ~niht~ is itself a contraction of ~ni~ + ~io~ + ~wiht~, "not ever a thing", and that ~wiht~ is the same word as English ~wight~ and German ~Wicht~. ~zunichte-~ reduces something to nothing: destruction, annulment, frustration.

What gets ~zunichtegemacht~ is almost always something abstract and hard-won (a plan, a hope, here a balanced budget) rather than a physical object broken.
en.zunähen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~nähen~:

• ~nähen~: From MHG ~nāian~, ~næjen~, from OHG ~nājen~, ~nāian~, from Proto-Germanic *~nēaną~ ("to sew"), from PIE *~(s)neh₁-~ ("to spin, to sew"), a root with an optional initial ~s-~ (~s-mobile~). The instrument noun *~neh₁-dleh₂~ gave, via *~nēþlō~, both ~Nadel~ and English ~needle~. Cognate with Dutch ~naaien~, Latin ~nēre~ ("to spin").
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

The compound is closure by needle and thread: a wound or a seam ~zugenäht~ shut, as the fairy-tale wolf's belly is stitched up again.
en.zuordnen:
From ~zu-~ + ~ordnen~. Compound of:

• ~ordnen~: From MHG ~ordenen~, from OHG ~ordinōn~, borrowed from Latin ~ōrdināre~ ("to put in order, arrange"), from ~ōrdō~ ("row, rank, order"). The Latin source also gave rise to German ~ordinieren~ (a learned doublet) and, via French, to English ~ordain~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo-~, from OHG ~zuo-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~, from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"). As a verbal prefix, it conveys direction toward or assignment.

~Zuordnen~ means "to assign, allocate, classify", to place something ~toward~ its proper order or category. It is the standard verb for mapping, assigning, or attributing in both everyday and technical German (~einer Kategorie zuordnen~ = "to assign to a category"). The fact that ~ordnen~ is a Latin loanword naturalized so thoroughly that it takes native Germanic prefixes (~zu-~, ~an-~, ~ein-~, ~unter-~) illustrates how deeply Latin administrative vocabulary penetrated German during the medieval period. The noun ~Zuordnung~ ("assignment, mapping") is ubiquitous in mathematics and data science, where it denotes any mapping from one set to another.
en.zupacken:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~packen~:

• ~packen~: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~packen~, from Old Saxon *~pakko~, from Proto-West Germanic *~pakkō~, from Proto-Germanic *~pakkô~ ("bundle, pack"), of debated ultimate origin. The absence of the High German consonant shift confirms it entered via Low German trade routes. Cognate with English ~pack~, Dutch ~pakken~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

The compound is a firm, energetic seizing: to ~zupacken~ is to grab hold with force, and figuratively to pitch in and get to work.
en.zupasskommen:
A separable compound of ~zupass-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~zupass-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: ~zu~ + ~Pass~ in its obsolete sense "fitting state, right measure". The noun is a Romance loan (MHG ~pas~ from Old French ~pas~, from Latin ~passus~ ("step, pace")) which acquired the figurative sense "suitability" under Middle Low German and Middle Dutch influence. By the sixteenth century ~zu paß~ meant "opportunely", and ~zupasskommen~ was built on it in the nineteenth, so this thoroughly German-looking particle is a cousin of English ~pace~, ~pass~, and ~passport~. ~zupass-~ marks timeliness: something arrives opportunely or suits the moment.

The living idiom is ~das kommt mir zupass~, "that comes at just the right moment for me", the fossilized particle surfacing only to mark good timing.
en.zurechnen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~rechnen~:

• ~rechnen~: From MHG ~rechenen~, from OHG ~rehhanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rekanōn~ ("to count, explain"), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to make straight or right"), the same root as German ~recht~ and Latin ~rectus~. Cognate with English ~reckon~, Dutch ~rekenen~, Low German ~rekenen~, Danish ~regne~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

The compound carries ~rechnen~ from the ledger to the conscience: to ~zurechnen~ is to charge a deed or a debt to someone's account, literal or moral.
en.zurechtfinden:
A separable compound of ~zurecht-~ + ~finden~:

• ~finden~: From MHG ~vinden~, from OHG ~findan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~finþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~finþaną~, from PIE *~pent-~ ("to go, pass; path, bridge"). The development from "to go, pass" to "to find" parallels shifts in Slavic. Cognate with English ~find~, Dutch ~vinden~, Low German ~finden~, Danish ~finde~.
• ~zurecht-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: MHG ~ze rehte~, the dative of ~reht~ ("right, what is proper") governed by ~ze~ ("to"). The phrase fused into a single adverb meaning "into proper order, rightly, as it should be," and the fusion is complete enough that modern speakers no longer hear the case ending inside it: ~zurechtlegen~ ("to lay out ready"), ~zurechtkommen~ ("to manage, get along"), ~zurechtweisen~ ("to reprimand"). ~Recht~ itself goes back to PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"), the root behind Latin ~rēctus~ and English ~right~. The sense of ~zurecht-~ here is: successfully, managing to cope with the circumstances.

The compound is reflexive: ~sich zurechtfinden~ is to get one's bearings, in a dark room, as in Kafka, or in the labyrinth of a new situation.
en.zurechtkommen:
A separable compound of ~zurecht-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~zurecht-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: MHG ~ze rehte~, the dative of ~reht~ ("right, what is proper") governed by ~ze~ ("to"). The phrase fused into a single adverb meaning "into proper order, rightly, as it should be," and the fusion is complete enough that modern speakers no longer hear the case ending inside it: ~zurechtlegen~ ("to lay out ready"), ~zurechtkommen~ ("to manage, get along"), ~zurechtweisen~ ("to reprimand"). ~Recht~ itself goes back to PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"), the root behind Latin ~rēctus~ and English ~right~. The sense of ~zurecht-~ here is: successfully, managing to cope with the circumstances.

The compound is the ordinary verb for managing: ~mit etwas zurechtkommen~ is to cope, to get along, as Luther's lost wanderer longs to come right again.
en.zurechtlegen:
A separable compound of ~zurecht-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~zurecht-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: MHG ~ze rehte~, the dative of ~reht~ ("right, what is proper") governed by ~ze~ ("to"). The phrase fused into a single adverb meaning "into proper order, rightly, as it should be," and the fusion is complete enough that modern speakers no longer hear the case ending inside it: ~zurechtlegen~ ("to lay out ready"), ~zurechtkommen~ ("to manage, get along"), ~zurechtweisen~ ("to reprimand"). ~Recht~ itself goes back to PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"), the root behind Latin ~rēctus~ and English ~right~. The sense of ~zurecht-~ here is: into proper order, into the right shape or arrangement.

The compound is laying something out ready: clothes ~zurechtgelegt~ for the morning, or, figuratively, an argument arranged in one's mind in advance.
en.zurechtmachen:
A separable compound of ~zurecht-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~zurecht-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: MHG ~ze rehte~, the dative of ~reht~ ("right, what is proper") governed by ~ze~ ("to"). The phrase fused into a single adverb meaning "into proper order, rightly, as it should be," and the fusion is complete enough that modern speakers no longer hear the case ending inside it: ~zurechtlegen~ ("to lay out ready"), ~zurechtkommen~ ("to manage, get along"), ~zurechtweisen~ ("to reprimand"). ~Recht~ itself goes back to PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"), the root behind Latin ~rēctus~ and English ~right~. The sense of ~zurecht-~ here is: into proper order, into the right shape or arrangement.

The compound spans preparing a thing (a bed made ~zurecht~ in the Grimm tale), and the reflexive ~sich zurechtmachen~, to do oneself up.
en.zurechtweisen:
A separable compound of ~zurecht-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative verb from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from PIE *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know"). A class I strong verb; its senses "to show, point" and "to direct, expel" both direct knowledge or attention. Cognate with English ~wise~, ~wit~, ~wizard~.
• ~zurecht-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: MHG ~ze rehte~, the dative of ~reht~ ("right, what is proper") governed by ~ze~ ("to"). The phrase fused into a single adverb meaning "into proper order, rightly, as it should be," and the fusion is complete enough that modern speakers no longer hear the case ending inside it: ~zurechtlegen~ ("to lay out ready"), ~zurechtkommen~ ("to manage, get along"), ~zurechtweisen~ ("to reprimand"). ~Recht~ itself goes back to PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to straighten, direct"), the root behind Latin ~rēctus~ and English ~right~. The sense of ~zurecht-~ here is: correcting something that was wrong or out of place.

The compound literally directs someone into right order (weisen's "point, direct" plus ~zurecht~) and so means to set right, to rebuke.
en.zureden:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

The compound aims speech at a person to move them: ~jemandem zureden~ is to urge or coax, the words directed at the listener as Kafka's warder directs his.
en.zureisen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

The compound is motion to a place that stays: to ~zureisen~ is to move to a town and settle there, whence ~der Zugereiste~, the not-quite-local newcomer.
en.zureiten:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~reiten~:

• ~reiten~: From MHG ~rīten~, from OHG ~rītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rīdan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rīdaną~, from PIE *~Hreydʰ-~ ("to set in motion, ride"), likely a suffixed form of *~h₃reyH-~ ("to move, churn"). German ~reiten~ narrowed to horseback riding, while English ~ride~ broadened to vehicles. Cognate with Dutch ~rijden~, Danish ~ride~, Swedish ~rida~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

The compound here is directed riding: to ~zureiten~ toward someone; a separate transitive ~zureiten~ "to break in a horse" shares the spelling but not this reading.
en.zurichten:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~richten~:

• ~richten~: From MHG ~richten~, from OHG ~rihten~ ("to straighten, set right, direct"), from Proto-West Germanic *~rihtijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rihtijaną~, a denominative from the adjective *~rehtaz~ ("straight, right"), from PIE *~h₃reǵtós~ ("right, straightened"), from *~h₃reǵ-~ ("to stretch out, straighten, direct"). Cognate with English ~right~, Dutch ~richten~, Gothic ~raihtjan~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

The base ~richten~ "to set right, prepare" gives ~zurichten~ its old sense "to dress, make ready" (leather, food); the reading glossed "hurt" is the figurative ~übel zurichten~, to maul, as in Nietzsche's shattered tightrope-walker.
en.zurufen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. A parallel weak form in Middle High German explains why the modern present lacks the expected umlaut (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zurufen~ aims the call at a recipient; one calls something out to someone across a distance.
en.zurückbauen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~bauen~:

• ~bauen~: From MHG ~būwen~, from OHG ~būan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~būan~, from Proto-Germanic *~būaną~ ("to dwell, reside"), from PIE *~bʰuH-~ ("to be, become, grow"); one builds where one lives. Cognate with English ~be~, ~bower~ ("dwelling"), ~neighbor~ ("near-dweller"), Dutch ~bouwen~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

The compound is undoing construction: to ~zurückbauen~ is to dismantle a building or scale an installation back toward an earlier, smaller state.
en.zurückbekommen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~be-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~be-~: From MHG ~be-~, from OHG ~bi-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bi-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bi-~ ("by, at, around"), from PIE *~h₁epi~ ("on, at, near"). The unstressed proclitic form of the preposition ~bei~. ~be-~ makes an intransitive verb transitive, directing the action at an object.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Stacked, the parts read "come back into possession": ~bekommen~ is itself an old ~be-~ + ~kommen~ that drifted from "come by" to plain "receive," and ~zurück-~ adds the return; to ~zurückbekommen~ is to get back what was yours.
en.zurückbilden:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~bilden~:

• ~bilden~: From MHG ~bilden~, a merger of two Old High German verbs: ~biliden~ ("to form into an image"), from Proto-West Germanic *~biliþijan~, and ~bilidōn~ ("to copy, represent"), from *~biliþōn~; both from the noun *~biliþī~ (whence ~Bild~), whose pre-Germanic origin is obscure, with no secure PIE etymology. Cognate with Dutch ~beelden~, Swedish ~bilda~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). en.zurückbleiben:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. en.zurückblicken:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. • ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The compound is the backward gaze, literal or in time: one ~blickt zurück~ over the shoulder, or, as in the report, a region ~blickt~ on a long history ~zurück~ in retrospect.
en.zurückbringen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). • ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

The literal sense of carrying something back to its place extends figuratively to recovering or restoring it.
en.zurückdenken:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~teng-~ ("to think, feel"). A mixed-conjugation verb of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~dachte~ pairs the vowel change ~e~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix and ~k~ > ~ch~. • ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). ~Zurückdenken~ governs ~an~ with the accusative and moves the return wholly into memory: one goes back not to a place but to a recollection.
en.zurückdrehen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~drehen~:

• ~drehen~: From MHG ~dræjen~, from OHG ~drāen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrāan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrēaną~ ("to twist, turn"), from PIE *~terh₁-~ ("to rub, rub by twisting, turn"). • ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Literally to reverse a rotation; figuratively to "turn back the clock," undoing a state already reached.
en.zurückdrängen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~drängen~:

• ~drängen~: From a merger of two Middle High German verbs: ~drengen~, from OHG ~drengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangwijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrangwijaną~ (a causative); and the now-obsolete ~drangen~, from OHG ~drangōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangōn~ (a denominative).
