• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

The sense runs from the military "push the enemy back" to the psychological "repress an urge."
en.zurückfallen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

Intransitive with ~sein~; beside the physical backward fall stands the figurative "to fall back on someone", guilt or deed returning to its author.
en.zurückfordern:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~fordern~:

• ~fordern~: From MHG ~vodern~, ~vordern~, from OHG ~fordarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ(a)rōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþą~, from PIE *~pŕ̥-to-~, from *~per-~ ("forward, through"); "to push forward" became "to advance a claim." Not to be confused with umlauted ~fördern~ from the same root. Cognate with English ~forth~, ~forward~ and ~further~, Dutch ~vorderen~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys withdrawal: taking back what was given or said.

The verb presupposes an earlier surrender: one reclaims only what was one's own.
en.zurückführen:
Compound of ~zurück-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, a causative of ~fahren~ ("to travel, go"). The verb ~fahren~ descends from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("to carry, bring forth"). Cognate with English ~fare~ and Dutch ~varen~.
• ~zurück-~: A compound prefix from ~zu~ + ~rück~, where ~zu~ derives from Proto-Germanic *~tō~, from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"), and ~rück~ from ~Rücken~ ("back"), ultimately related to PIE *~(s)krewk-~ ("heap, hill"). Together they convey "back, returning."

As a causative, ~führen~ originally meant "to cause to go," i.e., "to lead," while ~fahren~ simply meant "to go, travel." This causative pair is one of the clearest in German. The compound ~zurückführen~ means "to lead back, to trace back, to attribute to," and the intellectual sense of tracing an idea or phenomenon back to its origin is perhaps the most common usage today: ~Das lässt sich auf X zurückführen~ ("That can be traced back to X"). English ~fare~ preserves the intransitive root: a bus ~fare~ is the cost of going. The PIE root *~per-~ also produced Greek ~poros~ ("passage"), English ~ford~ (a crossing), and ~ferry~ (to carry across water). The noun ~Führer~ ("leader") is simply the agent noun of ~führen~, though its historical associations have made the word nearly unusable in modern German outside of compound forms like ~Reiseführer~ ("travel guide") or ~Führerschein~ ("driver's license").
en.zurückgeben:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Beyond concretely handing something back, ~zurückgeben~ also means to return in kind: a reply, a glance.
en.zurückgehen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Intransitive with ~sein~; figuratively "to go back to something" means to have one's origin in it.
en.zurückgreifen:
Compound of ~zurück-~ + ~greifen~:

• ~greifen~: From MHG ~grīfen~, from OHG ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~ ("to grab, grasp"), from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). Cognate with English ~grip~, ~gripe~, Dutch ~grijpen~.
• ~zurück-~: From PIE *~doh₁~ ("to") + *~(s)krewk~ ("heap, hill"); literally "to the back." The prefix means "back, returning."

The literal sense is "to grab back": to reach back for something already known or available. ~Zurückgreifen~ is typically used figuratively: ~auf etwas zurückgreifen~ means "to fall back on something, to resort to, to draw upon" (a resource, an experience, a method). Unlike ~zugreifen~ (which means to seize something present), ~zurückgreifen~ implies reaching into the past or into reserves. The spatial metaphor is vivid: one turns around and grasps something behind oneself. There is no single English equivalent: "fall back on," "resort to," "draw upon," and "have recourse to" all approximate its meaning. The prefix ~zurück-~ is itself a compound (from ~zu~ + an old form related to ~Rücken~, "back"), making ~zurückgreifen~ a triple-layered word: "to-back-grasp."
en.zurückhalten:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

~Zurückhalten~ names a keeping-back: not letting something advance; reflexively ~sich zurückhalten~ is to restrain oneself.
en.zurückholen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~holen~:

• ~holen~: From MHG ~holen~, ~holn~, from OHG ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, possibly from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, summon") via "to summon" → "to go and fetch"; the connection is uncertain. Cognate with Dutch ~halen~, Low German ~halen~, English ~haul~ (via French).
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Since ~holen~ means to actively fetch, ~zurückholen~ is to fetch back what had gone.
en.zurückkaufen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~kaufen~:

• ~kaufen~: From MHG ~koufen~, from OHG ~koufōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kaupōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaupōną~, a denominative verb from *~kaupô~ ("merchant, innkeeper"), a loanword from Latin ~caupō~ ("innkeeper, shopkeeper"). Cognate with English ~cheap~, Dutch ~kopen~, Danish ~købe~, Icelandic ~kaupa~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys withdrawal: taking back what was given or said.

The verb presupposes an earlier sale: one buys back what one had sold.
en.zurückkehren:
Compound of ~zurück-~ ("back") + ~kehren~ ("to turn"):

• ~kehren~: From MHG ~kēren~ ("to turn"), from OHG ~kēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kaizwijaną~ ("to turn, direct"), of uncertain PIE origin. Kroonen derives it from PIE *~geys-~ ("to turn, become"), comparing Hittite ~kīša(ri)~ ("to happen, occur, become"). Cognate with Danish ~køre~ ("to drive"), Swedish ~köra~ ("to drive"), Icelandic ~keyra~ ("to drive").
• ~zurück-~: From MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ + ~Rücken~ ("back"). Ultimately from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to") + *~(s)krewk~ ("heap, hill; back").

There are two homonymous verbs ~kehren~ in German: one meaning "to sweep" (from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~) and one meaning "to turn" (from *~kaizwijaną~). ~Zurückkehren~ uses the "turn" sense, to turn back, to return. The Scandinavian cognates evolved differently: Danish ~køre~ and Swedish ~köra~ now mean "to drive (a vehicle)," preserving only the sense of directing motion. The base verb ~kehren~ in the "turn" sense is largely archaic in Germany proper (replaced by ~umkehren~, ~umdrehen~, ~wenden~), but remains current in Swiss German. The derivative ~Rückkehr~ ("return") is the standard noun for returning from a journey or exile.
en.zurückkommen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Intransitive with ~sein~; figuratively "to come back to something" means to take a topic up again.
en.zurücklaufen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Intransitive with ~sein~; the strong ~laufen~ carries the concrete return on foot, and figuratively the reverting of a process.
en.zurücklegen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. • ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

~Zurücklegen~ ranges widely: to put a thing back, to set money aside, and to "cover a distance," leaving a stretch of road behind.
en.zurücklehnen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~lehnen~:

• ~lehnen~: A merger of two verbs: MHG ~linen~/~lenen~ (intransitive), from OHG ~hlinēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlinēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlināną~, from PIE *~k̂ley-~ ("to lean, incline"); and MHG ~leinen~ (causative), from OHG ~hleinen~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlainijaną~. A second, archaic ~lehnen~ ("to lend, borrow"), from OHG ~lēhanōn~, survives only in ~entlehnen~ and ~Lehnwort~. Cognate with English ~lean~, Latin ~clīnō~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

Usually reflexive; "to lean back" figuratively also means to relax and let things take their course.
en.zurückliegen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

Two readings: the competitive "to lie behind" and the temporal "to lie in the past."
en.zurücklächeln:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~lächeln~:

• ~lächeln~: From MHG ~lecheln~, from ~lachen~ ("to laugh") plus the diminutive suffix ~-eln~, literally "to laugh a little," the suffix triggering the umlaut ~a~ → ~ä~. ~lachen~ itself is from MHG ~lachen~, OHG ~lahhen~, Proto-West Germanic *~hlahhjan~, Proto-Germanic *~hlahjaną~. • ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Here ~zurück-~ carries the reciprocal sense "in return": to answer a smile with a smile.
en.zurückmachen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~machen~:

• ~machen~: From MHG ~machen~, from OHG ~mahhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~, from PIE *~mag-~ ("to knead, mix, make"). Cognate with Dutch ~maken~, Low German ~maken~, English ~make~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Colloquial for going back to a place; ~machen~ stands in as a general verb of motion.
en.zurückmelden:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~melden~:

• ~melden~: From MHG ~mëlden~, from OHG ~mëldōn~, ~mëldēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~melþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~melþōną~, from PIE *~meldʰ-~ ("to ask, pray, speak"). • ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Here ~zurück-~ means "as a reply": to answer with a report; reflexively ~sich zurückmelden~ is to check back in.
en.zurücknehmen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys withdrawal: taking back what was given or said.

Beside the physical taking-back stands the figurative "to take back a word or a promise": to retract.
en.zurückreichen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~reichen~:

• ~reichen~: From MHG ~reichen~, from OHG ~reihhen~, ~reichen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raikijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~raikijaną~, from PIE *~Hroyǵ-éye-ti~, a causative o-grade of *~Hreyǵ-~ ("to stretch out, reach"). The causative "to cause to stretch" broadened to "to reach," "to hand to," and "to suffice." Cognate with English ~reach~, Dutch ~reiken~, Danish ~række~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

Transitive "to hand something back," intransitive "to reach back to a time": to have one's origins far in the past.
en.zurückreisen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~reisen~:

• ~reisen~: From MHG ~reisen~ ("to set out on a campaign, to travel"), from OHG ~reisōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~raisōn~, from a form akin to Proto-Germanic *~raizijaną~ ("to cause to rise"); the root *~rīsaną~ ("to rise") also gives English ~rise~. The shift from "setting out" to "traveling" ran through the military sense: a ~Reise~ was originally a campaign.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Intransitive with ~sein~: to set out on the return journey, back to where one started.
en.zurückrennen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~rennen~:

• ~rennen~: From a merger of two Old High German verbs: the causative ~rennan~ ("to make something run or flow"), from Proto-Germanic *~rannijaną~, and the intransitive ~rinnan~ ("to run, to flow"), from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~, from PIE *~h₃reyH-~ ("to undulate, churn"). A member of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~ich renne~, ~rannte~, ~gerannt~; no umlaut in the preterite. Cognate with English ~run~, Dutch ~rennen~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Intransitive with ~sein~; mixed like ~rennen~ (~rannte zurück~, ~zurückgerannt~): to hurry back to where one started.
en.zurückrufen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~rufen~:

• ~rufen~: From MHG ~ruofen~, from OHG ~ruofan~/~hruofan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hrōpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrōpaną~, of uncertain further origin. A class VII strong verb. A parallel weak form in Middle High German explains why the modern present lacks the expected umlaut (~du rufst~, not *~du rüfst~). Cognate with Dutch ~roepen~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

From "to recall to mind" through summoning a person back to the telephone "call back."
en.zurückräumen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~räumen~:

• ~räumen~: From Early New High German ~reumen~, a Central German umlaut variant of ~raumen~, from MHG ~rūmen~, from OHG ~rūmen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rūmijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rūmijaną~, a factitive verb from the adjective *~rūmaz~ ("roomy, spacious"), from PIE *~(H)rewH-~ ("to tear open"). Etymologically, "to make room." Cognate with English ~room~, the noun ~Raum~, Bavarian ~rama~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Since ~räumen~ means "to clear space," ~zurückräumen~ is to put things back in their place.
en.zurückschicken:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~schicken~:

• ~schicken~: From MHG ~schicken~ ("to outfit oneself, fit in, arrange appropriately"), from OHG *~skihhen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skikkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skikkijaną~ ("to order, send"), the causative of the verb underlying MHG ~geschehen~ ("to happen, rush"). The sense "to send" grew from "to make ready to go." Related to English ~chic~ (via French), ~geschickt~, and ~Schicksal~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

The verb names sending a thing back to where it came from, a returned parcel to its sender, say.
en.zurückschieben:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~schieben~:

• ~schieben~: From MHG ~schieben~, from OHG ~skioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeubaną~, from PIE *~skewbʰ-~ ("to push, to shove, to thrust"). A class II strong verb (~schieben~, ~schob~, ~geschoben~). Cognate with English ~shove~, Dutch ~schuiven~, Danish ~skubbe~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

The prefix fixes the direction: the object is shoved not away but to the rear, back from the one acting.
en.zurückschlagen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

In the sense "retaliate," ~zurückschlagen~ is the answering blow, sent back at the attacker.
en.zurückschreiben:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Ordinarily ~zurückschreiben~ is answering in writing, a reply sent back to the sender; in the cited sentence it is the technical writing of data back onto a storage medium.
en.zurücksetzen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

In technical use ~zurücksetzen~ means putting a device back into its initial state, the "reset" to factory settings.
en.zurücksinken:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~sinken~:

• ~sinken~: From MHG ~sinken~, from OHG ~sinkan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sinkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sinkwaną~, from PIE *~sengʷ-~ ("to sink, to drop"). A class III strong verb (~sinken~, ~sank~, ~gesunken~); the weak causative ~senken~ is its transitive partner. Cognate with English ~sink~, Dutch ~zinken~, Danish ~synke~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

The intransitive verb describes a limp sinking backward: into a pillow, onto one's knees, into a former state.
en.zurückspringen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~springen~:

• ~springen~: From OHG ~springan~, from Proto-Germanic *~springaną~, from PIE *~sprenǵʰ-~, a nasalized form of *~sperǵʰ-~ ("to move energetically, to hasten, to spring"). A class III strong verb (~springen~, ~sprang~, ~gesprungen~). Cognate with English ~spring~, Dutch ~springen~, Danish ~springe~, Greek ~spérkhō~ ("to hasten").
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

Depending on context ~zurückspringen~ is a startled recoil or, as in the cited sentence, a leap back to a place just left.
en.zurückstecken:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~stecken~:

• ~stecken~: Modern ~stecken~ merges two verbs: the transitive weak one ("to put, stick something in") from MHG ~stecken~, OHG ~steckōn~, a geminate derivative of ~stëhhan~ (the ancestor of ~stechen~), and the strong intransitive one (archaic ~stak~/~gestocken~, "to be stuck"); the two fused in Early Modern German. Both trace to Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stikaną~, from PIE *~(s)teyg-~ ("to be sharp, stab, goad"). Cognate with English ~stick~ and ~steak~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

Literally one sticks an object back into its place; figuratively ~zurückstecken~ means lowering one's own demands and giving ground.
en.zurückstehen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

Usually ~zurückstehen~ is figurative: to remain behind someone or something, to be inferior to it, as here one market trails a larger one.
en.zurückstellen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

Figuratively ~zurückstellen~ means to postpone or subordinate something: it is moved to the back in time or in priority.
en.zurücktreten:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

Beyond the physical step backward, ~zurücktreten~ carries the political sense "to resign an office"; elsewhere in the corpus a Reich minister steps down from his post.
en.zurückverfolgen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~ver-~ + ~folgen~:

• ~folgen~: From MHG ~volgen~, from OHG ~folgēn~ ("to follow, serve faithfully, pursue," attested from the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *~folgēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fulgāną~; the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. Cognate with English ~follow~, Dutch ~volgen~, Danish ~følge~, Swedish ~följa~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ intensifies the base verb or carries its action through to completion.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

The verb names following a trail, line, or lineage backward to its source.
en.zurückversetzen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~ver-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~ver-~: From MHG ~ver-~, from OHG ~fir-~, ~far-~, ~fur-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fra-~, from Proto-Germanic *~fra-~ ("away, forth"), from PIE *~per~ ("before, in front, forward"). The single modern prefix continues three distinct Proto-Germanic prefixes, *~fra-~, *~fur-~ and *~fer-~, which fell together in Old High German. ~ver-~ conveys removal or motion away, from the prefix's older spatial sense.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

~Zurückversetzen~ means shifting back to an earlier place or time; one can mentally transport oneself back to childhood.
en.zurückweichen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~weichen~:

• ~weichen~: From MHG ~wīchen~, from OHG ~wīchan~ ("to yield, give way"), from Proto-West Germanic *~wīkwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīkwaną~, from PIE *~h₃weyg-~ ("to start moving, to distance oneself, to bend, wind"). A class I strong verb, "to yield, give way, retreat"; not to be confused with the weak ~weichen~ ("to soften, to soak"), which derives from ~weich~ ("soft"). Cognate with Old English ~wīcan~, Old Norse ~vīkja~, Swedish ~vika~ ("to give way, fold").
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

The strong verb means giving way backward: yielding before an opening door, a danger, or a superior force, and drawing back.
en.zurückweisen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative verb from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from PIE *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know"). A class I strong verb; its senses "to show, point" and "to direct, expel" both direct knowledge or attention. Cognate with English ~wise~, ~wit~, ~wizard~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

~Zurückweisen~ means to rebuff an objection, a petition, or a person; what is offered is not accepted but refused.
en.zurückwenden:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~wenden~:

• ~wenden~: From MHG ~wenden~, from OHG ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), the causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). It belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort (preterite ~wandte~, participle ~gewandt~) and has a doubled preterite: ~wandte~ for turning the self or one's attention, the regularized ~wendete~ for physical turning. Cognate with English ~wend~, Armenian ~gind~ ("ring").
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

Reflexively ~sich zurückwenden~ describes turning around to the rear; the weak preterite ~wendete~ (for physical turning, as in the citation), stands beside the ~wandte~ of attention.
en.zurückwirken:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~wirken~:

• ~wirken~: From MHG ~wirken~, from OHG ~wirken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wirkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wirkijaną~, from *~werką~ ("work"), from PIE *~wérǵom~, from *~werǵ-~ ("to make, work"). Early on it merged with the dialectal ~würken~ (from OHG ~wurken~), which left the written language in the 18th century. Cognate with English ~work~ and ~wrought~, Dutch ~werken~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys backward motion or retreat.

~Zurückwirken~ means that an effect reaches back to an earlier point in time, in law, the retroactivity of a statute.
en.zurückzahlen:
A separable compound of ~zurück-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~zurück-~: Not a single morpheme but a frozen phrase: MHG ~ze rücke~ ("to the back"), from ~zu~ plus the dative of ~rücke~, modern ~Rücken~ ("back"). The first element goes back to PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second to Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~ ("back, ridge"), whose further origin is uncertain. That second element is cognate with English ~ridge~: a spine and a ridge are the same picture. The particle conveys return to a former place or state.

~Zurückzahlen~ is refunding money lent or owed; the sum goes back to whoever provided it.
en.zurückziehen:
From ~zurück-~ + ~ziehen~. Compound of:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). Cognate with English ~tug~, Gothic ~tiuhan~, Dutch ~tijgen~.
• ~zurück-~: From MHG ~zerucke~, a compound of ~zuo~ ("to") + ~rücke~ ("back"), literally "to the back." The first element comes from Proto-Germanic *~tō~, from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"); the second from MHG ~rücke~, ~rugge~ ("back, ridge"), from Proto-Germanic *~hrugjaz~.

The literal "pull back" extends in two directions, and the auxiliary tells them apart. With ~haben~ the verb is transitive or reflexive: troops are pulled back (~Truppen zurückziehen~), what one revokes is a formal declaration (~einen Antrag~, ~eine Klage~, ~eine Bewerbung~, ~eine Kandidatur zurückziehen~), and one withdraws oneself, ~sich zurückziehen~ ("to withdraw, to retire"). English "withdraw" covers more ground than ~zurückziehen~ does: money comes out of an account with ~abheben~, never with ~zurückziehen~. With ~sein~ the verb is intransitive motion back to where one started: ~sie sind nach Leipzig zurückgezogen~ ("they moved back to Leipzig"). This is the ~ziehen~ of relocating rather than of pulling. The PIE root *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead") also gave Latin ~dūcere~ ("to lead"), source of English ~duke~, ~conduct~, ~produce~, and ~educate~, all words about pulling or leading in various directions. Cognate with Dutch ~terugtrekken~ ("to pull back").
en.zusagen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

~Zusagen~ means firmly promising something to a recipient; said of an invitation, it means confirming that one will come.
en.zusammenarbeiten:
Compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From OHG ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~ ("to toil, to labor"), ultimately from PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"). Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Old Saxon ~arvedian~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~.
• ~zusammen-~: From MHG ~zusamen~, from OHG ~zisamane~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ + *~samanē~ ("together"), ultimately from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to") + *~sem~ ("one, together"). As a separable prefix, it conveys the sense of doing something jointly.

~Zusammenarbeiten~ means "to collaborate, to work together." The noun ~Zusammenarbeit~ ("collaboration, cooperation") is indispensable in diplomatic, scientific, and corporate contexts. The etymology of ~arbeiten~ is one of the most poignant in all of Germanic: PIE *~h₃órbʰos~ meant "orphan", a child bereft of parents who must toil for others. This same root gave Greek ~orphanos~ ("orphaned"), Latin ~orbus~ ("deprived"), and English ~orphan~. The journey from "orphan's drudgery" to "work" in general reflects the social reality of the ancient Indo-European world, where the parentless child's lot defined the concept of hard labor. Old High German ~arabeit~ still meant "hardship, toil, suffering" rather than neutral "work"; the modern sense of productive activity is a relatively recent semantic elevation.
en.zusammenbinden:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~binden~:

• ~binden~: From MHG ~binden~, from OHG ~bintan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bindan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bindaną~, from PIE *~bʰendʰ-~ ("to bind, tie"). A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~i~–~a~–~u~ ablaut (~binden~, ~band~, ~gebunden~). Cognate with English ~bind~, Dutch ~binden~, Gothic ~bindan~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

~Zusammenbinden~ gathers several things into one by a tie: sheaves, hair, loose ends.
en.zusammenbleiben:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys acting jointly, together with others.

~Zusammenbleiben~ means staying together rather than parting.
en.zusammenbrechen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~brechen~:

• ~brechen~: From MHG ~brëchen~, from OHG ~brëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~brekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from PIE *~bʰreg-~ ("to break"), the same word as English ~break~, separated only by the High German consonant shift. The same root underlies Latin ~frangere~, whence English ~fracture~. Cognate with Dutch ~breken~, Danish ~brække~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys collapse: falling inward upon itself.

~Zusammenbrechen~ means caving inward, literally of structures, figuratively of people, systems, or a supply that gives way under strain.
en.zusammenbringen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

~Zusammenbringen~ means gathering and uniting what was apart in one place: herds, people, money.
en.zusammendrängen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~drängen~:

• ~drängen~: From a merger of two Middle High German verbs: ~drengen~, from OHG ~drengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangwijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrangwijaną~ (a causative); and the now-obsolete ~drangen~, from OHG ~drangōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrangōn~ (a denominative). Both from PIE *~trenkʷ-~ ("to beat, hew, press"). ~drängen~ took the transitive senses, the strong ~dringen~ the intransitive. Cognate with dialectal English ~thring~, English ~throng~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

~Zusammendrängen~ presses separate things into a tight space until they lie densely crowded.
en.zusammendrücken:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~drücken~:

• ~drücken~: From MHG ~drücken~, from OHG ~drucchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þrukkijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þrukkijaną~, from PIE *~trewk-~ ("to press on and break"). ~drücken~ ("to press") and ~drucken~ ("to print") are a doublet from the same Old High German verb. Cognate with Dutch ~drukken~, Old English ~þryċċan~, Welsh ~trychu~, Lithuanian ~trū́kti~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

The compound names pressing something in on itself until it grows smaller or denser.
en.zusammenfahren:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

Said of two moving bodies that meet; the same verb also means to flinch or start in fright, the body drawing suddenly together.
en.zusammenfallen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys collapse: falling inward upon itself.

The compound means the caving-in of a structure upon itself; figuratively a plan or a hope collapses in the same way.
en.zusammenfassen:
Compound of ~zusammen~ + ~fassen~:

• ~zusammen~: From MHG ~zesamen~, from OHG ~zisamane~, ultimately from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to give, put") + *~sem~ ("together, one").
• ~fassen~: From MHG ~vazzen~, from OHG ~fazzōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fatōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~fatōną~ ("to fetch, hold, seize"). Cognate with English ~fetch~, Dutch ~vatten~. The PIE root may be *~pod-~ ("to fetch"), though the connection to *~ped-~ ("to walk, stumble, fall") is semantically uncertain.

The literal image is of grasping things together into one bundle. From this concrete sense, ~zusammenfassen~ developed its primary modern meaning: "to summarize", gathering scattered ideas into a single coherent statement. The noun ~Zusammenfassung~ is the standard German word for "summary" or "abstract."
en.zusammenfließen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~fließen~:

• ~fließen~: From MHG ~vlieȥen~, from OHG ~flioȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleutaną~ ("to float, stream, flow"), from PIE *~plewd-~ ("to flow, run, swim"). A class II strong verb (~fließen~, ~floss~, ~geflossen~); the zero grade *~flut-~ gave ~Flut~. Cognate with English ~fleet~, ~float~ and ~flood~, Dutch ~vlieten~, Swedish ~flyta~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

Said of waters or currents that unite into a single flow.
en.zusammenfügen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~fügen~:

• ~fügen~: From MHG ~füegen~, ~fuogen~, from OHG ~fuogen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōgijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōgijaną~, from PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ ("to join, attach, fasten"). Reflexive ~sich fügen~ means "to submit": to join oneself to the arrangement of fate. Cognate with Dutch ~voegen~ and archaic English ~fay~ ("to fit closely," from Old English ~fēgan~).
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

The compound names the joining of individual parts into a whole, as in craftsmanship.
en.zusammenführen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

Unlike intransitive ~zusammenkommen~, ~zusammenführen~ is transitive: someone deliberately brings what was separate into one unit.
en.zusammengeben:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give"). Cognate with English ~give~ (from Old Norse ~gefa~), Dutch ~geven~, Swedish ~giva~/~ge~, Danish ~give~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

In the marriage rite the officiant gives two people together; ~geben~ keeps its old sense of solemn bestowal.
en.zusammengehen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From MHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from OHG ~gan~, ~gen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from PIE *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). The form ~gen~ is of Bavarian origin; the ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~. Cognate with English ~go~, Dutch ~gaan~, Low German ~gahn~, Swedish and Danish ~gå~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

Said of lines, edges, or paths that approach one another and meet.
en.zusammengehören:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~ge-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~ge-~: From MHG ~ge-~, from OHG ~gi-~, ~ga-~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ga-~, from Proto-Germanic *~ga-~ ("together, with"), from PIE *~ḱóm~ ("beside, near, by, with"). The same prefix that forms the Perfektpartizip and, as a noun prefix, collectives like ~Gebirge~ and ~Gebrüder~. ~ge-~ is no longer semantically distinct, having fused with the base verb.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

~Gehören~ has drifted far from ~hören~: from "to hearken to, to be subject to" came "to belong to." With ~zusammen-~ the verb names the mutual belonging of two things that form one unit.
en.zusammenhalten:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

Literally the holding of parts into one whole; figuratively the solidarity of people who stand by one another.
en.zusammenhauen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~hauen~:

• ~hauen~: From MHG ~houwen~, from OHG ~houwan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hauwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hawwaną~, from PIE *~kewh₂-~ ("to beat, hew, forge"). Originally a class VII strong verb (~hauen~, ~hieb~, ~gehauen~), partially weakened colloquially, where ~haute~ competes with ~hieb~. Cognate with English ~hew~, Latin ~cūdere~ ("to strike, forge").
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys collapse: falling inward upon itself.

Here ~zusammen-~ is resultative: to beat someone until they go down; colloquially also to knock something together in haste.
en.zusammenhängen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~hängen~:

• ~hängen~: The merger of three OHG verbs: ~hāhan~ (strong, transitive; past ~hieng~, participle ~gehangan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~hą̄han~, from Proto-Germanic *~hanhaną~; ~hangēn~ (weak, intransitive); and the causative ~hengen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hangijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hangijaną~. The distinction is upheld chiefly in the past tense: intransitive ~hing~/~gehangen~ versus transitive ~hängte~/~gehängt~. Cognate with Dutch ~hangen~, English ~hang~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

From two things physically hanging together, extended to the logical connection of cause and consequence.
en.zusammenkehren:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~kehren~:

• ~kehren~: A homograph concealing two distinct verbs. ~Kehren~ (1) "to turn": from MHG ~kēren~, from OHG ~kēran~, ~chēren~, from Proto-Germanic *~kairijaną~ or *~kausijaną~, of uncertain PIE origin, possibly connected to *~gers-~ ("to twist, bend, turn"). ~Kehren~ (2) "to sweep": from MHG ~kern~, ~keren~, from OHG ~kerian~, ~cherian~, from Proto-Germanic *~karjaną~ ("to scrape, scratch"), from PIE *~ger-~ ("to scrape"). Etymologically unrelated, merged through phonological convergence.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

Here ~kehren~ is "to sweep," not "to turn": the broom sweeps what is scattered into a single heap.
en.zusammenkleben:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~kleben~:

• ~kleben~: From MHG ~kleben~, from OHG ~klebēn~ ("to stick"), from Proto-West Germanic *~klibēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~klibēną~, from PIE *~gleyb-~ ("to stick, adhere"), a durative formation from the strong root *~kleibēną~ ("to adhere, to climb"). Cognate with English ~cleave~ and ~climb~, Old Norse ~klīfa~ ("to climb").
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

The verb runs both ways: transitively to bond torn pieces, intransitively to stick to one another.
en.zusammenkneifen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~kneifen~:

• ~kneifen~: An adaptation of the older ~kneipen~, from Middle Low German ~knīpen~, from Old Saxon *~knīpan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~knīpan~, from PIE *~gneybʰ-~ ("to pinch"). A class I strong verb (~kneifen~, ~kniff~, ~gekniffen~); the ~-f-~ is an artificial respelling that displaced ~kneipen~ only over the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Cognate with Dutch ~knijpen~, English ~knife~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

Most often said of eyes or lips pressed tightly shut.
en.zusammenkommen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

The verb describes drawing together into a tighter, smaller whole: clouds gathering, a muscle contracting, a text being condensed.
en.zusammenzählen:
A separable compound of ~zusammen-~ + ~zählen~:

• ~zählen~: From MHG ~zel(e)n~, ~zellen~, from OHG ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~ ("to enumerate, count; to recount, tell"). German split this dual sense: ~zählen~ kept "to count," ~erzählen~ took "to narrate." Cognate with Dutch ~tellen~, English ~tell~ and ~tale~, Danish ~tælle~, Gothic ~talzjan~.
• ~zusammen-~: The adverb ~zusammen~, from MHG ~zesamene~, from OHG ~zisamane~, which is ~zi~ ("to") plus ~samane~ ("together"), from Proto-Germanic *~samanē~, from PIE *~sem-~ ("one, together"). The second element is cognate with English ~same~ and, by way of Latin ~simul~ and ~similis~, with ~assemble~ and ~simultaneous~; Greek keeps it in ~homo-~. The particle conveys combining separate things into one.

The compound means adding individual numbers into a single total.
en.zuschauen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

The compound directs one's attention toward an event: one watches a process or person (with a dative object) without stepping in oneself.
en.zuscheißen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~scheißen~:

• ~scheißen~: From MHG ~schīzen~, from OHG *~skīzan~ (attested only in the compound ~biskīzan~), from Proto-West Germanic *~skītan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skītaną~, from PIE *~skeyd-~ ("to split, separate"); the root's basic sense is separation, not filth. A class I strong verb (~scheißen~, ~schiss~, ~geschissen~). Cognate with English ~shit~, Dutch ~schijten~, Old Norse ~skíta~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

Vulgar; here the particle means covering a surface completely, until it is "shut", sealed over.
en.zuschieben:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~schieben~:

• ~schieben~: From MHG ~schieben~, from OHG ~skioban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeuban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeubaną~, from PIE *~skewbʰ-~ ("to push, to shove, to thrust"). A class II strong verb (~schieben~, ~schob~, ~geschoben~). Cognate with English ~shove~, Dutch ~schuiven~, Danish ~skubbe~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

Literally one pushes a drawer or door ~zu~ until it is shut; figuratively one "pushes" something onto someone: blame, a task, the proverbial "Schwarzer Peter."
en.zuschießen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb (~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~). Cognate with English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Old Norse ~skjóta~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

The compound means passing: the ball is shot toward a teammate, driven in their direction.
en.zuschlagen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

Literally one strikes toward a target; the fixed idiom "zuschlagen" figuratively means to seize the moment decisively, to pounce when the chance comes.
en.zuschneiden:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~schneiden~:

• ~schneiden~: From MHG ~snīden~, from OHG ~snīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~snīþan~ ("to cut"); no secure PIE root has been established, and the word may be a Germanic innovation. A class I strong verb (~schneiden~, ~schnitt~, ~geschnitten~). Cognate with archaic English ~snithe~ ("to cut"), Dutch ~snijden~, Icelandic ~sníða~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

The verb means cutting toward a definite shape: cloth or leather is cut to a measure, a pattern, a target form.
en.zuschreiben:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

The verb assigns something to a person or thing: a quality, a cause, an authorship; the particle carries the allocation to a recipient.
en.zuschwellen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~schwellen~:

• ~schwellen~: From MHG ~swëllen~, from OHG ~swëllan~, from Proto-Germanic *~swellaną~ ("to swell"), perhaps from PIE *~swelH-~, though the root is not securely established. A class III strong verb (~schwellen~, ~schwoll~, ~geschwollen~), beside a weak causative ~schwellen~ ("to make swell") from Proto-Germanic *~swallijaną~. Cognate with English ~swell~, Dutch ~zwellen~, Old Norse ~svella~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

The verb means swelling until it closes: a throat or an eye swells ~zu~ until the passage is shut.
en.zusehen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zusehen~ directs one's sight toward an event one is present at without intervening; in the phrase ~zusehen, dass~ the sense shifts to "seeing to it that something happens."
en.zusenden:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~senden~:

• ~senden~: From MHG ~senden~, from OHG ~senten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sandijaną~, from PIE *~sont-eye-~, a causative of *~sent-~ ("to walk, travel"), originally "to cause to go." It has a double Präteritum: ~sendete~ for broadcasting, ~sandte~ (a Rückumlaut form) for sending a letter. Cognate with English ~send~, Dutch ~zenden~, Gothic ~sandjan~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

Beside plain ~senden~, ~zusenden~ foregrounds the recipient: something is sent expressly to someone.
en.zusetzen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~satjaną~ ("to set, to place down"), from PIE *~sodéyeti~, a causative derivation of *~sitjaną~ ("to sit") with the suffix *~-janą~, literally "to cause to sit." Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~, Yiddish ~zetsn~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys addition or increase: adding to what is already there.

Beside its additive core ("to add"), ~zusetzen~ carries the figurative ~jemandem zusetzen~: to press or harry someone.
en.zusichern:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~sichern~:

• ~sichern~: A denominative verb from the adjective ~sicher~ ("safe, secure"): OHG ~sihhurōn~ ("to justify, to vouch for"), whence MHG ~sichern~. ~sicher~ is itself a loanword: from OHG ~sihur~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sikur~, from Latin ~sēcūrus~ ("carefree"), from ~sē-~ ("without") + ~cūra~ ("care"); ~sē-~ from PIE *~sue-~ ("self, one's own"). English ~secure~ and ~sure~ descend from the same Latin root.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

~Zusichern~ directs a guarantee to a recipient: one assures something to someone, giving a firm pledge.
en.zusperren:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~sperren~:

• ~sperren~: From MHG ~sperren~, from OHG ~sperran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sparrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sparrijaną~ ("to bar, to block"), a denominative verb from *~sparrô~ ("wooden beam, log"), originally to bar a passage with a beam. Cognate with English ~spar~ ("to bolt, bar"; the noun for a wooden beam), Dutch ~sperren~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

In southern German and Austrian usage ~zusperren~ is the everyday word for closing up shop, where the north would sooner say ~schließen~.
en.zuspielen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward").
