Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

From the sporting pass (sending the ball to a teammate) ~zuspielen~ moved into the figurative: covertly getting information or documents to someone.
en.zusprechen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~sprechen~:

• ~sprechen~: From MHG ~sprëchen~, from OHG ~sprëhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sprekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sprekaną~, probably from PIE *~spregʰ-~ ("to crackle"). The sense developed from an onomatopoeic root meaning "to crackle, make noise" to "to speak." Cognate with Dutch ~spreken~, English ~speak~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

~Zusprechen~ forks: in legal use "to award something to someone" (a court awards damages), in everyday use "to speak encouragement or comfort to someone."
en.zustecken:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~stecken~:

• ~stecken~: Modern ~stecken~ merges two verbs: the transitive weak one ("to put, stick something in") from MHG ~stecken~, OHG ~steckōn~, a geminate derivative of ~stëhhan~ (the ancestor of ~stechen~), and the strong intransitive one (archaic ~stak~/~gestocken~, "to be stuck"); the two fused in Early Modern German. Both trace to Proto-West Germanic *~stekan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stikaną~, from PIE *~(s)teyg-~ ("to be sharp, stab, goad"). Cognate with English ~stick~ and ~steak~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

~Zustecken~ almost always carries a note of secrecy: one slips something to someone without others noticing.
en.zustehen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From MHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from OHG ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from PIE *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). The ~-h-~ entered the spelling by analogy with ~sehen~; the past-tense conjugations (~stand~, ~standen~) are suppletive, from Proto-West Germanic *~standan~. Cognate with Dutch ~staan~, English ~stand~, Danish ~stå~, Swedish ~stå~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

~Zustehen~ names not an act but a state: a right or claim ~is due~ to someone; it belongs to them by rights.
en.zustellen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

~Zustellen~ is two-edged: in officialese it means "to deliver, serve" (to serve a document), but colloquially "to block up with objects" (to clutter an entrance shut), the latter reading here.
en.zustimmen:
Compound of ~zu~ + ~stimmen~:

• ~stimmen~: From MHG ~stimmen~, from OHG *~stimmen~ (attested in the compound ~gistimmen~), derived from the noun ~Stimme~ ("voice, vote"). The noun descends from OHG ~stimma~, ~stimna~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stebnu~, from Proto-Germanic *~stebnō~ or *~stamnijō~, from PIE *~stomen-~ ("mouth, muzzle"). Cognate with Gothic ~stibna~ ("voice"), Old English ~stefn~, ~stemn~ ("voice"), Dutch ~stem~, and Greek ~stoma~ ("mouth," whence English ~stomach~).
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~ ("to"). As a verbal prefix, it means "to, toward."

The literal sense is "to voice toward," i.e., to add one's voice in support. The verb ~stimmen~ itself has a remarkable range of meanings: "to tune (an instrument)," "to be correct" (~das stimmt!~ "that's right!"), "to vote," and "to put in a mood" (~traurig stimmen~, "to make sad"). All trace back to the idea of a voice being in harmony or accord. The compound ~zustimmen~ narrows this to the specific act of expressing agreement. The related noun ~Zustimmung~ ("consent, approval") is a staple of legal and political German. The connection between ~Stimme~ ("voice") and Greek ~stoma~ ("mouth") reveals that the PIE speakers conceptualized the voice as emanating from the mouth-opening, a straightforward anatomical observation preserved in two wildly divergent word families across five millennia.
en.zustoßen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~stoßen~:

• ~stoßen~: From MHG ~stōzen~, from OHG ~stōzan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stautan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stautaną~, from PIE *~stówd-e-ti~, an o-grade intensive formation from *~(s)tewd-~ ("to hit, push"); the same root produced Latin ~tundere~ ("to beat, pound"). Cognate with dialectal English ~stot~ ("to bounce, ricochet"), Dutch ~stoten~, Old Norse ~stauta~ and ~steyta~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

From the spatial "to lunge at someone" ~zustoßen~ shifted into the fateful: a misfortune ~befalls~ someone.
en.zustreben:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~streben~:

• ~streben~: From MHG ~strëben~, from OHG ~strëbēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stribēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~stribāną~ ("to strive, resist"). Cognate with Dutch ~streven~ ("to strive") and English ~strive~ (via Old French ~estriver~, itself borrowed from a Germanic source).
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zustreben~ joins the prefix's directionality to the effort in ~streben~: to move toward a goal with exertion.
en.zuteilen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~teilen~:

• ~teilen~: From MHG ~teilen~ and OHG ~teilen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dailijan~ ("to divide, part, deal"), from Proto-Germanic *~dailijaną~, a denominative of *~dailiz~ ("part, share"), from PIE *~dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo-~, tentatively from *~dʰeh₁-~ ("to put, set, place"), though the precise PIE derivation is uncertain. Cognate with English ~deal~, Dutch ~delen~, Danish ~dele~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

~Zuteilen~ has an administrative ring: one allots rations, quotas, or tasks according to some formula.
en.zutragen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb whose semantic range broadened from "to drag, pull" to "to carry, bear, wear." Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

Beside the concrete "to carry to someone," ~zutragen~ took two side-paths: reflexive ~sich zutragen~ "to come to pass," and figurative "to carry tales."
en.zutrauen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~trauen~:

• ~trauen~: From MHG ~trūwen~, from OHG ~trūwēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~trūwēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~trūwāną~ ("to trust, believe"), from PIE *~deru-~ ("to be firm, hard, solid"). The same root gave ~treu~ ("faithful"), ~Trost~ ("comfort"), and ~Trauung~ ("wedding ceremony"), as well as English ~trust~, ~true~, and ~tree~. Cognate with Old Norse ~traust~ ("confidence").
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

~Zutrauen~ carries the trust in ~trauen~ over to ability: one credits someone with something, thinks them capable of it, and the noun ~Zutrauen~ is exactly that confidence.
en.zutreiben:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zutreiben~ joins the prefix's direction to the force in ~treiben~: to drive cattle or people toward a target, with ~haben~, or, with ~sein~, to drift toward it oneself (~das Boot trieb dem Ufer zu~).
en.zutreten:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zutreten~ is two-sided: "to step up to someone" (to approach) and "to kick out" (to strike with the foot), the same directedness, once of the step, once of the blow.
en.zutrinken:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~trinken~:

• ~trinken~: From MHG ~trinken~, from OHG ~trinkan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drinkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drinkaną~; no non-Germanic cognate has been securely identified, so the word may be a Germanic innovation. Cognate with English ~drink~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Old Norse ~drekka~ and Gothic ~𐌳𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌺𐌰𐌽~ (drigkan).
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zutrinken~ is a gesture aimed at someone: one raises the glass and drinks to another, in greeting or in honor.
en.zuvorkommen:
A separable compound of ~zuvor-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~zuvor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: ~zu~ + ~vor~ ("before"), MHG ~ze vor~, an adverb of temporal priority meaning "beforehand, previously." As a particle it contributes the idea of getting there first. ~Zuvorkommen~ ("to forestall, to anticipate") yielded the adjective ~zuvorkommend~, which has drifted from "anticipating" to "obliging, courteous": politeness reconceived as meeting a need before it is voiced. The sense of ~zuvor-~ here is: getting there first, forestalling another (~zuvorkommen~).

~Zuvorkommen~ governs the dative (one forestalls a wish or an opponent) and forms its perfect with ~sein~.
en.zuvorsagen:
A separable compound of ~zuvor-~ + ~sagen~:

• ~sagen~: From MHG ~sagen~, from OHG ~sagēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~saggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sagjaną~, ultimately from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to say, tell"). Cognate with English ~say~, Dutch ~zeggen~, Low German ~seggen~, Danish ~sige~, Swedish ~säga~.
• ~zuvor-~: A frozen prepositional phrase: ~zu~ + ~vor~ ("before"), MHG ~ze vor~, an adverb of temporal priority meaning "beforehand, previously." As a particle it contributes the idea of getting there first. ~Zuvorkommen~ ("to forestall, to anticipate") yielded the adjective ~zuvorkommend~, which has drifted from "anticipating" to "obliging, courteous": politeness reconceived as meeting a need before it is voiced. The sense of ~zuvor-~ here is: beforehand, previously, in advance.

~Zuvorsagen~ is "to say beforehand": to predict, to foretell; today largely displaced by ~voraussagen~ and ~vorhersagen~.
en.zuwachsen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from PIE *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Cognate with English ~wax~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix means "shut": closing something.

~Zuwachsen~ properly means "to close over by growing": a wound or a path grows shut; alongside stands the older legal usage in which a right ~accrues~ to someone.
en.zuwandern:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~wandern~:

• ~wandern~: From MHG ~wandern~, from OHG *~wantarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandarōn~, formed from *~wandōn~ ("to turn") with the frequentative suffix *~-rōn~ (not a single journey but repeated, meandering motion), from Proto-Germanic *~wandōną~, from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, to wind"). Cognate with English ~wander~, Danish ~vandre~, Swedish ~vandra~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zuwandern~ is movement from outside into a country; the noun ~Zuwanderung~ ("immigration") is the neutral counterpart to ~Auswanderung~ ("emigration") in German debate.
en.zuwarten:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~warten~:

• ~warten~: From MHG ~warten~, from OHG ~wartēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wardēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wardāną~ ("to guard, watch over"), from *~warduz~ ("a guard"), from PIE *~wer-~ ("to heed, watch, guard"): one who keeps watch also waits. The older sense persists in ~ein Auto warten~ ("to service a car"). Cognate with English ~ward~, Swedish ~vårda~, Dutch ~bewaren~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zuwarten~ intensifies ~warten~ with the idea of biding time toward an outcome, doing nothing until matters develop.
en.zuweisen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative verb from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from PIE *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know"). A class I strong verb; its senses "to show, point" and "to direct, expel" both direct knowledge or attention. Cognate with English ~wise~, ~wit~, ~wizard~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys allocation: assigning or granting something to a recipient.

~Zuweisen~ joins the pointing and directing in ~weisen~ to the prefix's recipient: one assigns someone a place, a task, or resources.
en.zuwenden:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~wenden~:

• ~wenden~: From MHG ~wenden~, from OHG ~wenten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wandijaną~ ("to turn"), the causative of *~windaną~ ("to wind, wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). It belongs to the Rückumlaut cohort (preterite ~wandte~, participle ~gewandt~) and has a doubled preterite: ~wandte~ for turning the self or one's attention, the regularized ~wendete~ for physical turning. Cognate with English ~wend~, Armenian ~gind~ ("ring").
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~Zuwenden~ turns the body, the gaze, or the heart toward another; hence the elevated "to bestow something on someone", to let a gift reach them.
en.zuwerfen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

With a personal dative ~zuwerfen~ means to throw something to someone (~jemandem den Ball zuwerfen~); with an inanimate object such as a door it shifts to "to slam shut," where ~zu-~ instead carries its "shut" sense.
en.zuwiderhandeln:
A separable compound of ~zuwider-~ + ~handeln~:

• ~handeln~: From MHG ~handeln~, from OHG ~hantalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~handulōn~, a denominative verb from Proto-Germanic *~handuz~ ("hand") with the frequentative suffix *~-lōną~; the sense broadened from "to handle" to "to act, deal, trade." Cognate with English ~handle~, Dutch ~handelen~, Danish ~handle~.
• ~zuwider-~: A frozen phrase: ~zu~ + ~wider~ ("against"), literally "contrary to", governing the dative. It lives on as an adjective ("repugnant") and as a separable particle in the legal-register verbs ~zuwiderhandeln~ ("to contravene") and ~zuwiderlaufen~ ("to run counter to"). For the ~wider~ half (Proto-Germanic *~wiþrą~, cognate with English ~with~ in its old sense "against") and for its confusability with ~wieder~ ("again"), see the ~wider~ entry. ~zuwider-~ marks contravention: acting against a rule, order, or law.

The verb governs the dative of whatever is being violated: one acts ~einem Verbot zuwider~ ("contrary to a prohibition"), with the particle ~zuwider~ stranded at the clause end.
en.zuwinken:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~winken~:

• ~winken~: From MHG ~winken~, from OHG ~winken~ ("to nod, to blink"), from Proto-West Germanic *~winkōn~ (beside *~winkijan~), from PIE *~weng-~ ("to bend, to curve"), the same root as ~Winkel~ ("angle, corner"). A weak verb, and already weak in OHG; the strong participle ~gewunken~ is a latecomer built on the model of ~sinken~/~gesunken~, not a survival. Cognate with English ~wink~ and ~winch~, Dutch ~wenken~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

With the dative of the person greeted, ~zuwinken~ names the friendly gesture of waving toward someone, the opposite of ~abwinken~, "to wave off in refusal."
en.zuzahlen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys addition or increase: adding to what is already there.

~Zuzahlen~ means to pay a further amount on top of one already paid; the related noun ~die Zuzahlung~ is, in health care, the patient's own copayment.
en.zuziehen:
A separable compound of ~zu-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~zu-~: From MHG ~zuo~, from OHG ~zuo~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tō~, from Proto-Germanic *~tō~ ("to"), from PIE *~doh₁~, the instrumental of *~de~ ("to, toward"). Cognate with English ~to~, Dutch ~toe~, Old Saxon ~tō~. The prefix conveys direction toward a goal or target.

~zuziehen~ (strong: ~zieht~, ~zog~, ~gezogen~) leads two lives, and the auxiliary tells them apart. With ~haben~, ~zu-~ means "shut" or "onto oneself": one draws a curtain shut, calls in an expert, or catches a cold (~sich eine Erkältung zuziehen~), as if pulling it in. With ~sein~, ~zu-~ means "toward here": a newcomer moves to the area (~wir sind erst kürzlich zugezogen~). That second life gave German the noun ~Zuzug~, an influx of residents, and the ~Zugezogene~, the incomer.
en.zwingen:
From Middle High German ~twingen~, from Old High German ~dwingan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þwinganą~, *~þwinhaną~. What appears to be a triple consonant shift (Germanic *~þ~ to OHG ~d~ to MHG ~t~ to modern ~z~) is actually a regular development that affected most words with OHG ~dw-~ and ~tw-~, compare ~Zwerg~ ("dwarf"). A class III strong verb with the ablaut pattern ~zwingen~, ~zwang~, ~gezwungen~. Cognate with Dutch ~dwingen~, Norwegian ~tvinge~, Swedish ~tvinga~, Icelandic ~þvinga~, and English ~twinge~.

The English cognate ~twinge~ (a sharp, sudden pain that grips or squeezes) preserves the original physical sense of the Proto-Germanic verb: to press, to squeeze, to constrain. German ~zwingen~ elevated this physical compression into abstract compulsion: "to force, to compel, to make someone do something." The noun ~Zwang~ ("compulsion, coercion") and the adjective ~zwingend~ ("compelling, cogent") carry the same force. The medieval ~Zwinger~ (the narrow space between inner and outer castle walls where attackers were "squeezed" and trapped) survives today as the name of Dresden's famous ~Zwinger~ palace complex, built on the site of such a fortification.
en.zwischenlagern:
A separable compound of ~zwischen-~ + ~lagern~:

• ~lagern~: Derived from the noun ~Lager~ ("camp, store, warehouse"), from MHG ~lëger~, from OHG ~lëgar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~legr~, from Proto-Germanic *~legrą~. The modern form with ~-a-~ is of East Central German origin, influenced by ~Lage~ ("position"). Cognate with English ~lair~, Dutch ~leger~, Danish ~lejr~, Swedish ~läger~.
• ~zwischen-~: From the preposition ~zwischen~, MHG ~zwischen~, a reduction of OHG ~in zwiskēn~, the dative plural of ~zwiski~ ("twofold"), built on the numeral ~zwei~ ("two"). English ~between~ is built the very same way, from Old English ~be tweonum~ ("by twos"), so both languages arrived at "in the middle" by way of "among two." Cognate with Dutch ~tussen~ and with the ~twi-~ of English ~twilight~ and ~twin~. The sense of ~zwischen-~ here is: provisional, done in the interval before the real thing.

~Zwischenlagern~ means to store something provisionally until it reaches its final place; the ~Zwischenlager~ for radioactive waste is the best-known instance.
en.zwischenspeichern:
A separable compound of ~zwischen-~ + ~speichern~:

• ~speichern~: A denominal verb from ~Speicher~ ("storehouse, granary"), from MHG ~spīcher~, OHG ~spīhhāri~, Proto-West Germanic *~spīkārī~, borrowed from Late Latin ~spīcārium~ ("granary"), from ~spīca~ ("ear of grain, spike"). The same Latin word also gives English ~spike~.
• ~zwischen-~: From the preposition ~zwischen~, MHG ~zwischen~, a reduction of OHG ~in zwiskēn~, the dative plural of ~zwiski~ ("twofold"), built on the numeral ~zwei~ ("two"). English ~between~ is built the very same way, from Old English ~be tweonum~ ("by twos"), so both languages arrived at "in the middle" by way of "among two." Cognate with Dutch ~tussen~ and with the ~twi-~ of English ~twilight~ and ~twin~. The sense of ~zwischen-~ here is: interposed, inserted into an ongoing sequence (~zwischenlanden~, ~zwischenspeichern~).

~Zwischenspeichern~ belongs to computing: data is held in a buffer for the duration of a process before being written out or discarded for good.
en.zählen:
From Middle High German ~zel(e)n~, ~zellen~, from Old High German ~zellan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talljan~, from Proto-Germanic *~taljaną~ ("to enumerate, count; to recount, tell"). The modern long vowel continues the second- and third-person singular of the present (where West Germanic gemination did not occur); it was reinforced by the lengthened vowel in ~Zahl~ (from MHG ~zale~, "number").

The Proto-Germanic root *~taljaną~ carried both senses ("to count" and "to recount, narrate") from the very beginning. Modern German split these into two verbs: ~zählen~ retained "to count," while ~erzählen~ (via the ~er-~ prefix) specialized in "to narrate." English underwent the same bifurcation: ~tell~ (from the same root) means both "to count" (as in ~teller~ at a bank, or ~telling beads~) and "to narrate." The word ~tale~ ("a story" but also archaic "a count, tally") shares this dual heritage. Cognate with Dutch ~tellen~, English ~tell~ and ~tale~, Danish ~tælle~, Gothic ~talzjan~.
en.ähneln:
A 17th-century alteration of the earlier verb ~ähnlichen~, from Middle High German ~anelīchen~, equivalent to ~ähnlich~ ("similar") + the verbal suffix ~-en~. The modern shortened conjugation in ~-eln~ may reflect a folk-etymological association with ~Ahn~ ("ancestor"), as if "to resemble" were derived from "to take after one's forebears", reanalyzed as ~Ahn~ + ~-eln~. Compare French ~s'apparenter à~ ("to be related to"), which shows a similar conceptual link between family resemblance and similarity.

The adjective ~ähnlich~ itself derives from OHG ~analīh~ ("similar"), literally "of one form" (~ana~ "on" + ~līh~ "body, form"), the same compound pattern that produced English ~alike~ and ~like~. The word ~Ahn~ ("ancestor"), despite the folk-etymological association, actually traces to Proto-Germanic *~anô~ ("forefather"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂en-~ ("ancestor"), cognate with Latin ~anus~ ("old woman"), a connection that would surely surprise speakers of both languages.
en.ähnlichschauen:
A separable compound of the adjective ~ähnlich~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~ähnlich~: From the adjective ~ähnlich~ ("similar"), MHG ~anelīch~, from OHG ~analīh~, literally "of one form": ~ana~ ("on") + ~līh~ ("body, form"). That second element is the Proto-Germanic *~-līkaz~ that also produced English ~-ly~ and ~like~, so ~ähnlich~ and ~alike~ are formed on the same principle. Cognate with Dutch ~aanlijk~ (dialectal) and Old English ~anlīc~ ("alike"). The sense of ~ähnlich~ here is the resultative or perceptual frame: to look like someone (~ähnlichsehen~).

The verb is the southern German and Austrian counterpart of northern ~ähnlichsehen~; the choice between ~schauen~ and ~sehen~ gives the region away. Idiomatically ~das schaut dir ähnlich~ is not about appearance but about behaviour: that is just like you.
en.ändern: From Middle High German ~endern~, a denominative verb derived from ~ander~ ("other, different"). ~Ander~ descends from MHG ~ander~, from OHG ~andar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~anþar~, from Proto-Germanic *~anþeraz~, from PIE *~h₂énteros~ ("other"). The PIE root *~h₂énteros~ is a comparative formation from *~h₂ent-~ ("front, forefront"), and its original sense was "the one opposite, the one facing" (i.e., the second of two) before broadening to "other." The semantic journey from "second" to "different" to "to change" completes in ~ändern~. Cognate with Hunsrik ~ennre~, English ~other~, Dutch ~ander~, Old Norse ~annarr~ (Swedish ~annan~, Danish ~anden~).
en.ärgern:
From Middle High German ~argern~ ("to worsen"), from Old High German ~argerōn~, derived from the adjective ~arg~ ("bad, wicked"). Cognate with English ~eerie~.

The adjective ~arg~ traces from MHG ~arc~, from OHG ~arg~, from Proto-West Germanic *~arg~, from Proto-Germanic *~argaz~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃erǵʰ-~ ("to copulate; ardent"). The semantic journey from "ardent, lustful" to "bad, wicked" reflects a moral judgment on excessive passion: what was once merely "passionate" became "wicked" as Germanic Christianity imposed new values on old vocabulary. Cognates include Lithuanian ~eržùs~ ("ardent, stubborn") and Hittite ~arkari~ ("to copulate"). The modern German meaning of ~ärgern~ has softened considerably from "to make worse" to "to annoy, to irritate," and the reflexive ~sich ärgern~ ("to be annoyed") is among the most common expressions of everyday frustration. Dutch ~erg~ ("bad, severe") preserves the older adjective sense.
en.äußern:
From MHG ~ūzeren~ ("to bring out, express"), deadjectival from ~äußer~ ("outer, external"), itself the comparative of ~aus~ / ~außen~ ("out, outside"). ~Aus~ derives from MHG ~ūȥ~, from OHG ~ūȥ~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ūt~, from Proto-Germanic *~ūt~, from PIE *~úd~ ("upwards, away, out"). A doublet of English ~out~; compare Dutch ~uit~, Low German ~ut~, Danish ~ud~.

The meaning of ~äußern~ is "to express, to utter (one's thoughts or feelings)", to bring something inner to the outside. The cognate English verb ~utter~ (as in "to utter a word") followed the same semantic path from the same root: PGmc *~ūtizô~ (comparative of *~ūt~) yielded both German ~äußer~ and English ~outer~ / ~utter~. The physical image of moving speech outward from within is thus embedded in the very shape of the word.
en.öffnen:
From Middle High German ~offenen~, from Old High German ~offanōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~opanōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~upanōną~ ("to open, to lift"). The underlying adjective *~upanaz~ ("open") was probably originally a past participle of a lost verb *~ūpaną~, derived from *~upp~ ("up"), with the original sense "lying on top" → "clear, unobstructed" → "open." The Modern German umlaut (~offen~ → ~öffnen~) arose from the verbal suffix, producing the standard denominal pattern of forming a verb from an adjective.

The directional metaphor ("open" as "lifted up") is shared across many cultures, as in English ~uplift~ (the door or lid is raised, revealing what was underneath). The adjective ~offen~ ("open") and the verb ~öffnen~ ("to open") remain distinct in German, as in the difference between ~das Fenster ist offen~ ("the window is open") and ~öffne das Fenster~ ("open the window"). Cognate with Dutch ~openen~, English ~open~, Danish ~åbne~.
en.übelnehmen:
A separable compound of ~übel~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~übel~: The adjective ~übel~ ("bad, ill, evil"), from MHG ~übel~, from OHG ~ubil~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubil~, from Proto-Germanic *~ubilaz~, probably from PIE *~upo-~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~evil~, Dutch ~euvel~, Gothic ~ubils~. Here it is adverbial rather than resultative: ~übelnehmen~ is to take a thing badly, hence to take offence, and ~übelwollen~ is to wish ill. The sense of ~übel~ here is in ~übelnehmen~: to take amiss, to hold against someone.

It is construed with a dative of the person and an accusative of the thing: ~jemandem etwas übelnehmen~, to hold something against someone.
en.üben:
From Middle High German ~üeben~, ~uoben~, from Old High German ~uoben~, from Proto-Germanic *~ōbijaną~ ("to do, practice"), the causative-iterative formation of a lost strong verb *~afaną~, from PIE *~h₃ep-~ ("to labor, work, toil"). The same PIE root gives Latin ~opus~ ("work") and ~opera~ ("effort, service"), whence English ~opera~, ~operate~, and ~opus~. Cognate with Dutch ~oefenen~ (with an ~n~-suffix extension), Old Saxon ~ōbian~, Old Norse *~œfa~ (Icelandic ~æfa~). The Swedish ~öva~ and Danish ~øve~ are borrowed from Middle Low German ~ôven~ rather than inherited.

The verb's core meaning, "to practice, to drill, to exercise," has remained remarkably stable across a thousand years of German. The reflexive ~sich üben in~ ("to practice at, to exercise in") preserves the iterative force of the original Proto-Germanic causative: not a one-time doing but repeated, deliberate effort. The derived noun ~Übung~ ("exercise, practice") and the adjective ~üblich~ ("usual, customary") both reflect this deep association between repeated action and established habit. German proverb: ~Übung macht den Meister~ ("Practice makes the master"), a direct calque of the Latin ~exercitium facit magistrum~.
en.überantworten:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~antworten~:

• ~antworten~: From MHG ~antwürten~, from OHG ~antwurten~, from Proto-Germanic *~andawurdijaną~, a denominative of *~andawurdiją~ ("answer"), from *~anda-~ ("against, in return") + *~wurdą~ ("word"); *~anda-~ from PIE *~h₂ent-~ ("face, front, opposite"); English ~answer~ is built the same way. Cognate with Dutch ~antwoorden~, Afrikaans ~antwoord~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys transfer or handing over to someone.

That ~antworten~ of all verbs should yield "hand over" is surprising: the older ~antwürten~ also meant "to present, deliver up," and ~überantworten~ preserves that sense, which the simple verb has long since lost.
en.überarbeiten:
Compound of ~über-~ + ~arbeiten~:

• ~arbeiten~: From Old High German ~arbeiten~, from Proto-Germanic *~arbaidijaną~, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃órbʰos~ ("orphan"), from which English ~orphan~ is also derived. Cognate with Dutch ~arbeiden~, Old Saxon ~arvedian~, Gothic ~arbaidjan~.
• ~über-~: From Middle High German ~über~, from Old High German ~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Indo-European *~upéri~ ("over, above"). In this compound, the prefix conveys the sense of "over again" or doing something excessively.

The verb has two distinct meanings depending on stress: ~UMarbeiten~ (separable, "to rework") versus ~überARbeiten~ (inseparable, "to revise" or reflexively "to overwork oneself"). The reflexive ~sich überarbeiten~ ("to work oneself to exhaustion") reflects the ~über-~ prefix in its "excessively" sense. The surprising PIE connection between "work" and "orphan" reflects an ancient reality: orphans were society's laborers, and the original sense of the Germanic root was "hardship, toil."
en.überbewerten:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~bewerten~:

• ~bewerten~: A denominal verb from ~Wert~ ("value, worth") with the prefix ~be-~ (from PIE *~h₁epi~, "on, at, near") and ~-en~. ~Wert~ is from MHG ~wert~, from OHG ~werd~, from Proto-Germanic *~werþaz~, from PIE *~wert-~ ("to turn"), the sense being something turned over in trade. Cognate with English ~worth~ and ~weird~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

The verb layers ~über-~ onto the already-prefixed ~bewerten~, assigning a thing more worth than it is due.
en.überbieten:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~bieten~:

• ~bieten~: From MHG ~bieten~, from OHG ~biotan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~beudan~, from Proto-Germanic *~beudaną~, from PIE *~bʰewdʰ-~ ("to be awake, aware"). A class II strong verb whose root conveys awareness and offering. Cognate with English ~bid~, Dutch ~bieden~, Danish ~byde~, Swedish ~bjuda~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

From the auction sense (to make a higher bid) came the figurative "to surpass"; the fixed phrase ~nicht zu überbieten~ simply means unsurpassable.
en.überbleiben:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. With verbs of pouring or spilling it means "over the edge," of a container running over.

~Überbleiben~ has today been largely displaced by ~übrigbleiben~ and means simply to be left behind as a remainder.
en.überblicken:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~blicken~:

• ~blicken~: From MHG ~blicken~, from OHG ~blicchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~blikk-~, from Proto-Germanic *~bliką~ / *~blikkaz~ ("shine, appearance, look"), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ ("to shine"); a ~Blick~ is a flash of light turned into a directed gaze. Cognate with English ~bleach~ and ~blank~, Dutch ~blik~, Old English ~blice~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys authority or vantage from above.

To ~überblicken~ is to let one's ~Blick~ ("gaze") range over a whole and grasp it at once: from surveying a landscape to taking in a situation.
en.überbringen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~bringen~:

• ~bringen~: From MHG ~bringen~, from OHG ~bringan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~bringan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~, probably from pre-Germanic *~bʰrenk-~, a compound root from PIE *~bʰer-~ ("to carry") + *~h₁nek-~ ("to bring"). Mixed conjugation: ~brachte~ pairs the vowel change ~i~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix. Cognate with English ~bring~, Dutch ~brengen~, Gothic ~briggan~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys transfer or handing over to someone.

Unlike plain ~bringen~, ~überbringen~ is reserved for solemn missives (greetings, news, a document) formally conveyed to their recipient.
en.überbuchen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~buchen~:

• ~buchen~: In its commercial sense ("to book, reserve"), a denominal verb from ~Buch~, modelled on English ~to book~. ~Buch~ is from MHG ~buoch~, OHG ~buoh~, Proto-West Germanic *~bōk~, Proto-Germanic *~bōks~, the same root as English ~beech~, early Germanic writing being scratched onto beech tablets. A separate older ~buchen~ is an adjective, "of the beech tree." Cognate with English ~book~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

~Buchen~ in its commercial sense was itself coined after English ~to book~; ~überbuchen~ is to sell more places than actually exist.
en.überdauern:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~dauern~:

• ~dauern~: Two separate verbs under one spelling. "To last, endure": from MHG ~dūren~, borrowed from Middle Low German ~dūren~, from Latin ~dūrō~, a denominative of ~dūrus~ ("hard, lasting"), from Proto-Italic *~dūros~, from PIE *~dweh₂-~ ("long, far"); cognate with Dutch ~duren~, English ~dure~. "To cause pity" (~er dauert mich~): from MHG ~tūren~, an ablaut variant of ~tiure~ ("dear, costly"), ancestor of ~teuer~, thus a doublet of ~teuer~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

The base here is ~dauern~ "to last, endure," not the pity-verb ~er dauert mich~: to ~überdauern~ is to outlast a span of time or its adversities.
en.überdecken:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~decken~:

• ~decken~: From MHG ~decken~, from OHG ~decchen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þakkjan~ ("to cover"), from Proto-Germanic *~þakjaną~, a causative formation from *~þaką~ ("roof, thatch"), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ ("to cover"); the verb is etymologically "to roof." Cognate with English ~thatch~, Dutch ~dekken~, Swedish ~täcka~; from the same root Latin ~tegere~, whence English ~protect~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Stressed and separable, ~über-~ is literal and spatial: something moves over, across, or on top of something else.

Separable and stressed (~über+decken~), it means to lay something over as a cover; the inseparable doublet ~überdécken~ stresses complete covering instead.
en.überdenken:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~denken~:

• ~denken~: From MHG ~denken~, from OHG ~denken~, from Proto-West Germanic *~þankijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~þankijaną~, from PIE *~teng-~ ("to think, feel"). A mixed-conjugation verb of the Rückumlaut cohort: ~dachte~ pairs the vowel change ~e~ > ~a~ with a weak dental suffix and ~k~ > ~ch~. Cognate with English ~think~, Dutch ~denken~, Icelandic ~þekkja~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys going over something thoroughly or covering it completely.

~Überdenken~ takes its object directly in the accusative (~etwas überdenken~) where ~nachdenken~ requires the preposition ~über~; one runs the whole matter through the mind once more.
en.übereignen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~eignen~:

• ~eignen~: From MHG ~eigenen~, from OHG ~eiganen~, from Proto-Germanic *~aiginōną~, a denominative from *~aiganaz~ ("owned, one's own"), the past participle of *~aiganą~ ("to possess"), from PIE *~h₂eh₂óyḱe~, from *~h₂eyḱ-~ ("ability, possession"). Originally "to make one's own." Cognate with English ~own~, Dutch ~eigen~, Swedish ~ägna~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys transfer or handing over to someone.

~Eignen~ belongs to ~eigen~ ("own"); to ~übereignen~ is thus to make a thing pass legally into another's ~Eigentum~ ("ownership"), a term of property law.
en.übereinanderhalten:
A separable compound of ~übereinander-~ + ~halten~:

• ~halten~: From MHG ~halten~, from OHG ~haltan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~haldan~, from Proto-Germanic *~haldaną~. Cognate with English ~hold~, Dutch ~houden~, Low German ~holden~, Danish ~holde~, Icelandic ~halda~, Swedish ~hålla~.
• ~übereinander-~: The preposition ~über~ ("over") + the reciprocal pronoun ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ + ~ander~ and the exact counterpart of English ~one another~. The whole means "one on top of the other," and it is transparently compositional; see the entry for ~über~. In ~übereinanderlegen~ and ~übereinanderschlagen~ it describes stacking or crossing, and in verbs of speech it means "about one another." ~übereinander-~ crosses one thing over another, as with legs or arms.

~Übereinanderhalten~ is to hold two things so that one lies over the other, two sheets held up to the light, say.
en.übereinanderlegen:
A separable compound of ~übereinander-~ + ~legen~:

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~, a causative of *~ligjaną~ ("to lie") with the suffix *~-janą~, from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. The verb is thus the causative partner of ~liegen~: to ~legen~ is to "cause to lie," i.e., to lay. Cognate with Dutch ~leggen~, English ~lay~, Danish ~lægge~.
• ~übereinander-~: The preposition ~über~ ("over") + the reciprocal pronoun ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ + ~ander~ and the exact counterpart of English ~one another~. The whole means "one on top of the other," and it is transparently compositional; see the entry for ~über~. In ~übereinanderlegen~ and ~übereinanderschlagen~ it describes stacking or crossing, and in verbs of speech it means "about one another." ~übereinander-~ stacks or layers things one on top of another.

~Legen~ is the causative of ~liegen~; ~übereinanderlegen~ accordingly names the active layering, the stacking of things one on another.
en.übereinanderliegen:
A separable compound of ~übereinander-~ + ~liegen~:

• ~liegen~: From MHG ~ligen~, from OHG ~ligen~ (from earlier ~liggen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~liggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~ligjaną~, from PIE *~legʰ-~ ("to lie down"). A class V strong verb. The weak causative ~legen~ comes from the same root via *~-janą~ (*~lagjaną~). Cognate with English ~lie~, Dutch ~liggen~, Gothic ~ligan~.
• ~übereinander-~: The preposition ~über~ ("over") + the reciprocal pronoun ~einander~ ("one another"), itself ~ein~ + ~ander~ and the exact counterpart of English ~one another~. The whole means "one on top of the other," and it is transparently compositional; see the entry for ~über~. In ~übereinanderlegen~ and ~übereinanderschlagen~ it describes stacking or crossing, and in verbs of speech it means "about one another." ~übereinander-~ stacks or layers things one on top of another.

~Liegen~ is the resting counterpart to setting and laying; ~übereinanderliegen~ describes the state of stacked things, not the act of stacking.
en.übereinkommen:
A separable compound of ~überein-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~überein-~: A fossilized prepositional phrase, MHG ~über ein~ ("into one, as one"), over into unity, that is, into agreement. It attached early to a small set of verbs, of which ~kommen~, ~stimmen~, and ~treffen~ survive; older German also had ~überein tragen~. The particle is no longer productive, and ~ein~ here is the numeral "one", not the particle ~ein-~ ("in, into"). The sense of ~überein-~ here is: into agreement, into accord.

From ~übereinkommen~ comes the noun ~Übereinkunft~ ("agreement, convention"), the formal pact, a coming-together in a shared will.
en.übereinstimmen:
A separable compound of ~überein-~ + ~stimmen~:

• ~stimmen~: From MHG ~stimmen~, from OHG *~stimmen~, a denominative of ~Stimme~ ("voice, vote": OHG ~stimma~, Proto-West Germanic *~stebnu~, Proto-Germanic *~stebnō~, from PIE *~stomen-~ "mouth, muzzle"). Hence the senses "to tune" (an instrument), "to be correct," and "to vote." Cognate with archaic English ~steven~ ("voice"), Dutch ~stem~, Gothic ~stibna~, Ancient Greek ~stóma~ ("mouth").
• ~überein-~: A fossilized prepositional phrase, MHG ~über ein~ ("into one, as one"), over into unity, that is, into agreement. It attached early to a small set of verbs, of which ~kommen~, ~stimmen~, and ~treffen~ survive; older German also had ~überein tragen~. The particle is no longer productive, and ~ein~ here is the numeral "one", not the particle ~ein-~ ("in, into"). The sense of ~überein-~ here is: to one and the same result, matching, corresponding.

~Stimmen~ derives from ~Stimme~ ("voice"); ~übereinstimmen~ draws the picture of several voices sounding as one: hence both "to agree" and "to be congruent."
en.übereintreffen:
A separable compound of ~überein-~ + ~treffen~:

• ~treffen~: From MHG ~treffen~, from OHG ~treffan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drepan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drepaną~ ("to strike, push, beat"), from PIE *~dʰrebʰ-~, *~dʰreb-~ ("to crack, crush, strike, kill"). The High German consonant shift from *~dr-~ to ~tr-~ obscures the cognate relationship with Old English ~drepan~ ("to strike"). Cognate with Old Norse ~drepa~ ("to kill, strike").
• ~überein-~: A fossilized prepositional phrase, MHG ~über ein~ ("into one, as one"), over into unity, that is, into agreement. It attached early to a small set of verbs, of which ~kommen~, ~stimmen~, and ~treffen~ survive; older German also had ~überein tragen~. The particle is no longer productive, and ~ein~ here is the numeral "one", not the particle ~ein-~ ("in, into"). The sense of ~überein-~ here is no longer productive: bound to ~kommen~, ~stimmen~, ~treffen~.

~Übereintreffen~ is today the rarest of the three surviving formations, meaning the coming-together of several parties in a shared decision, usually replaced by more current verbs of the same pattern.
en.überfahren:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~fahren~:

• ~fahren~: From MHG ~varn~, from OHG ~faran~, from Proto-West Germanic *~faran~, from Proto-Germanic *~faraną~, from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). A class VI strong verb whose old sense "to go, travel" narrowed to vehicular travel; the causative ~führen~ (*~fōrijaną~) is its transitive counterpart. Cognate with English ~fare~, Dutch ~varen~, Danish ~fare~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

As a separable verb ~überfahren~ means "to ferry across," as an inseparable one "to run down with a vehicle"; the stress alone tells them apart.
en.überfallen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~fallen~:

• ~fallen~: From MHG ~vallen~, from OHG ~fallan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fallan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fallaną~; the PIE origin is uncertain, one proposal being *~h₂peh₃lH-~ ("to fall away, be destroyed"). A class VII strong verb, reduplicating in the Proto-Germanic past; the weak causative ~fällen~ (*~fallijaną~) shows the umlaut as its trace. Cognate with English ~fall~, Dutch ~vallen~, Danish ~falde~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

The spatial sense is "to fall upon someone," from which came the sudden assault and, figuratively, being overcome by a feeling.
en.überfinanzieren:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~finanzieren~:

• ~finanzieren~: From ~Finanz~ + ~-ieren~. ~Finanz~ derives from French ~finance(s)~, from Middle French ~finer~ ("to pay a ransom, settle a debt"), from ~fin~ ("end"), from Latin ~fīnis~ ("end, boundary"): a debt is "ended" by payment. Cognate with English ~finance~, French ~financer~, Italian ~finanziare~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

A young word of financial jargon: to provide more capital than a project can absorb.
en.überfliegen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~fliegen~:

• ~fliegen~: From MHG ~vliegen~, from OHG ~fliogan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fleugan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fleuganą~, from PIE *~plewk-~ ("to flow, fly"), an extension of *~plew-~ ("to flow, float, swim") that also gave ~fließen~. The vowel path *eu to OHG *io to MHG *ie is characteristic of class II strong verbs. Cognate with English ~fly~, Dutch ~vliegen~, Danish ~flyve~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

Beyond literal flight, ~überfliegen~ also means skimming a text: glancing rather than reading closely.
en.überfordern:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~fordern~:

• ~fordern~: From MHG ~vodern~, ~vordern~, from OHG ~fordarōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~forþ(a)rōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~furþą~, from PIE *~pŕ̥-to-~, from *~per-~ ("forward, through"); "to push forward" became "to advance a claim." Not to be confused with umlauted ~fördern~ from the same root. Cognate with English ~forth~, ~forward~ and ~further~, Dutch ~vorderen~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

~Überfordern~ is "to demand more than someone can deliver"; its counterpart ~unterfordern~ demands too little.
en.überführen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~führen~:

• ~führen~: From MHG ~vüeren~, from OHG ~fuoren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fōrijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fōrijaną~, the causative of *~faraną~ ("to go, travel"), from PIE *~per-~ ("going, passage"). To ~führen~ is thus "to make go," the transitive counterpart of strong ~fahren~. Cognate with Dutch ~voeren~, English ~fare~ (from the base verb).
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys transfer or handing over to someone.

The same verb also means "to convict someone": to bring a deed home to an offender beyond doubt.
en.überfüllen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~füllen~:

• ~füllen~: From MHG ~vüllen~, from OHG ~fullen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~fullijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~fullijaną~ ("to make full"), the causative of *~fullaz~ ("full"), from PIE *~pl̥h₁nós~ ("full"). English ~fill~ and ~füllen~ are exact cognates, each the causative of its native word for "full." Cognate with English ~fill~, Dutch ~vullen~, Danish ~fylde~, Swedish ~fylla~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

Where ~füllen~ reaches the brim, ~überfüllen~ goes past it.
en.übergeben:
~Über-~ + ~geben~. Compound of ~über-~ + ~geben~:

• ~geben~: From MHG ~gëben~, from OHG ~gëban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~geban~, from Proto-Germanic *~gebaną~, from PIE *~gʰebʰ-~ ("to give").
• ~über-~: From PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). The inseparable prefix adds a sense of transfer across a boundary.

~Übergeben~ means "to hand over, to deliver, to transfer", and, colloquially, "to vomit." The formal sense is transparent: to give ~over~, to pass something across from one person to another. The colloquial meaning follows the same spatial metaphor (to ~give over~ the contents of one's stomach) and is shared by Dutch ~overgeven~, which means both "to surrender" and "to throw up." The inseparable prefix ~über-~ creates a fixed, non-literal meaning; contrast the separable ~übergeben~ (stressed on ~über~), which would mean "to give excessively" but is rarely used. The noun ~Übergabe~ ("handover, transfer") is common in legal and military contexts. English ~overgive~ existed in Middle English with the same sense of "to surrender" but has since fallen out of use, replaced by the French-derived ~surrender~. Cognate with Dutch ~overgeven~, English ~overgive~ (archaic).
en.übergehen:
Compound of ~über-~ + ~gehen~:

• ~gehen~: From Middle High German ~gān~, ~gēn~, from Old High German ~gān~, from Proto-West Germanic *~gān~, from Proto-Germanic *~gāną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰeh₁-~ ("to leave"). Cognate with Dutch ~gaan~, English ~go~, Swedish ~gå~.
• ~über-~: From Middle High German ~über~, from Old High German ~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Indo-European *~upéri~ ("over, above"). As an inseparable prefix it conveys "passing over" or "skipping."

Like many ~über-~ verbs, ~übergehen~ splits into two distinct words depending on stress. The separable ~ÜBERgehen~ means "to go over, to pass into" (as in ~in eine neue Phase übergehen~, "to transition into a new phase"). The inseparable ~überGEHen~ means "to skip over, to ignore" (as in ~jemanden übergehen~, "to pass someone over"). This stress-based semantic distinction is a hallmark of German prefix verbs that challenges learners and delights linguists.
en.übergreifen:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~greifen~:

• ~greifen~: From MHG ~grîfen~, from OHG ~grīfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ ("to grab, grasp"). A class I strong verb (~greift~, ~griff~, ~gegriffen~), like ~reiten~ and ~schneiden~. Cognate with English ~gripe~, Dutch ~grijpen~, Low German ~griepen~, Old Norse ~gripa~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Stressed and separable, ~über-~ is literal and spatial: something moves over, across, or on top of something else.

From the spatial "reach across" came the figurative "spread": a fire or a crisis reaches over onto its neighbors.
en.überhandnehmen:
A separable compound of ~überhand-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due"). A class IV strong verb. Cognate with Dutch ~nemen~, English ~nim~ ("to take, filch"), Danish ~nemme~.
• ~überhand-~: A frozen noun phrase: MHG ~überhant~ ("superiority, the upper hand"), from ~über~ + ~Hand~, with ~überhant nemen~ attested from the 15th century. The metaphor is the one English preserves in ~gain the upper hand~; the grasping hand stands for control. The fossilization is complete: ~Überhand~ survives in no construction other than ~überhandnehmen~, "to proliferate past all bounds". The sense of ~überhand-~ here is in ~überhandnehmen~: to get out of hand, to proliferate, to become rampant.

Object and verb have fused orthographically into a single word, a rare case of univerbation in German.
en.überheben:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~heben~:

• ~heben~: From MHG ~heben~, ~heven~, from OHG ~heffen~, ~heven~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to seize, take hold of"). A class VI strong verb: the past ~hob~ and participle ~gehoben~ continue the strong ablaut paradigm. Cognate with English ~heave~, Dutch ~heffen~, Danish ~hæve~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

Reflexive "sich überheben" covers both straining oneself lifting a load and the moral raising of oneself above others, arrogance.
en.überhelfen:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~helfen~:

• ~helfen~: From MHG ~hëlfen~, from OHG ~hëlfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~helpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~helpaną~, from PIE *~ḱelb-~, *~ḱelp-~. A class III strong verb with the characteristic ~e~-~a~-~o~ ablaut pattern (~helfen~, ~half~, ~geholfen~). Cognate with English ~help~, Dutch ~helpen~, Danish ~hjælpe~, Norwegian ~hjelpe~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Stressed and separable, ~über-~ is literal and spatial: something moves over, across, or on top of something else.

Rare and mostly spatial: to help someone over an obstacle or into a garment.
en.überholen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~holen~:

• ~holen~: From MHG ~holen~, ~holn~, from OHG ~holōn~, ~holēn~ ("to fetch, get"), from Proto-West Germanic *~holōn~, possibly from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, summon") via "to summon" → "to go and fetch"; the connection is uncertain. Cognate with Dutch ~halen~, Low German ~halen~, English ~haul~ (via French).
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

The participle ~überholt~ lives on as the adjective "outdated", what has been overtaken is left behind.
en.überhören:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~hören~:

• ~hören~: From MHG ~hœren~, from OHG ~hōren~, from Proto-Germanic *~hauzijaną~, from PIE *~h₂ḱh₂owsyéti~ ("to be sharp-eared"), from *~h₂eḱ-~ ("sharp") + *~h₂ows-~ ("ear"). Cognate with English ~hear~, Dutch ~horen~, Danish ~høre~, Gothic ~hausjan~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys passing over, skipping, or overlooking.

~Überhören~ hovers between the accidental "failing to catch" and the deliberate "choosing not to hear."
en.überkochen:
~Über-~ + ~kochen~, in two different compounds that share a spelling:

• ~kochen~: From MHG ~kochen~, from OHG ~kohhōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~kokōn~, borrowed from Late Latin ~cocō~, from Latin ~coquō~ ("I cook, I boil"), from PIE *~pekʷ-~ ("to cook, to ripen"). A loan early enough to have undergone the High German shift of ~k~ to ~ch~. Cognate with English ~cook~, Dutch ~koken~, Danish ~koge~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words.

~Über-~ is why this verb has two readings, because the prefix does different work depending on whether it is separable. Separable ~überkochen~ (stress on ~über-~, perfect with ~sein~) is spatial and literal: the boiling goes over the rim of the pot, as in ~die Milch kocht über~. It is also the ordinary German metaphor for losing one's temper, exactly as English boils over: ~vor Zorn überkochen~, ~die Emotionen kochten über~.

Inseparable ~überkochen~ (stress on ~koch-~, perfect with ~haben~) is neither spatial nor excessive. It belongs to the ~über-~ of ~überarbeiten~ ("to revise"), ~überdenken~ ("to think over"), and ~überprüfen~ ("to check over"); it is the prefix of doing a thing a second time, of going back over it. So the verb means cooking something again, as in ~die Marmelade muss überkocht werden~, and it is regional, chiefly Austrian. German does not use ~über-~ for excess here at all: cooking something too long is ~verkochen~.

The PIE root *~pekʷ-~ supplies a fitting footnote. Through Latin ~coctus~ ("cooked") it gives Old French ~bescuit~, from ~bis coctus~, meaning "twice-cooked," and so English ~biscuit~ and German ~Biskuit~. The inseparable ~überkochen~ says in one German word what ~biscuit~ has been quietly saying in Latin all along.
en.überkommen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~kommen~:

• ~kommen~: From MHG ~quemen~, ~komen~, ~kumen~, from OHG ~queman~ (rarer ~cuman~, ~chuman~), from Proto-West Germanic *~kweman~, from Proto-Germanic *~kwemaną~, from PIE *~gʷem-~. Cognate with English ~come~, Low German ~kamen~, Dutch ~komen~, Danish ~komme~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

A feeling ~überkommt~ someone as if from without; as a participle ~überkommen~ also means "inherited, handed down."
en.überladen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~laden~:

• ~laden~: Two historically distinct verbs under one infinitive. ~laden~ (strong, "to load"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~hladan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaþan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaþaną~, from PIE *~kleh₂-~ ("to put, lay out"); cognate with English ~lade~ and ~laden~, Lithuanian ~klṓti~. ~laden~ (weak, "to invite, summon"): from MHG ~laden~, from OHG ~ladon~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laþōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~laþōną~, from *~laþō~ ("invitation"), from PIE *~h₂lot-eh₂~, a root found only in Germanic and Anatolian (Hittite ~halzai~).
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

Here ~laden~ is the strong "to load," not the weak "to invite"; ~überladen~ means "to load with too much," also figuratively of an overwrought style.
en.überlassen:
Compound of ~über-~ + ~lassen~:

• ~lassen~: From MHG ~lāzen~, ~lān~, from OHG ~lāȥan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lātan~ ("to let, allow"), from Proto-Germanic *~lētaną~ ("to leave behind, allow"), from PIE *~leh₁d-~ ("to let, leave behind"). Cognate with English ~let~, Dutch ~laten~. Related to Latin ~lassus~ ("tired"), the connection being the sense of "letting go" from weariness.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über-~, from OHG ~ubar-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber-~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). As an inseparable prefix (stressed on ~-lassen~), it conveys "over to someone."

Like ~übersetzen~, ~überlassen~ splits by stress. As an inseparable verb (stress on ~-lassen~: ~er überlässt~), it means "to relinquish, leave to someone, leave up to someone." As a separable verb (stress on ~über-~: ~er lässt über~), it is an informal alternative to ~übriglassen~ ("to leave over, spare"). The inseparable sense captures a deliberate act of ceding control, one "leaves something over" to another person's judgment or possession. The PIE root *~leh₁d-~ connects ~lassen~ not only to English ~let~ but also to Latin ~lassus~ ("weary"), suggesting that the original Proto-Indo-European concept involved the weariness of releasing one's grip.
en.überlaufen:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~laufen~:

• ~laufen~: From MHG ~loufen~, from OHG ~hloufan~, ~loufan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~hlaupan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hlaupaną~. A class VII strong verb. The initial ~hl-~ cluster was lost during the Old High German period. Cognate with English ~leap~ and ~lope~, Dutch ~lopen~, Danish ~løbe~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. With verbs of pouring or spilling it means "over the edge," of a container running over.

Separable and intransitive it means "to overflow" (das Wasser läuft über); inseparable and transitive it means "to overrun, come over" instead, one spelling, two verbs.
en.überleben:
Compound of ~über-~ + ~leben~, calqued from Latin ~supervīvō~:

• ~leben~: From MHG ~lëben~, from OHG ~lebēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~libbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~libjaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to leave, cling, linger"). The semantic path from "cling, remain" to "be alive" reflects a view of life as persistence. Cognate with English ~live~, Dutch ~leven~, Swedish ~leva~, Gothic ~liban~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above").

The fact that ~überleben~ is a calque of Latin ~supervīvō~ (itself from ~super-~ + ~vīvō~) makes it a structural parallel to English ~survive~ (from Old French, ultimately from the same Latin source). Three languages, three different root verbs for "live," but the same metaphorical prefix meaning "over, beyond."
en.überlegen:
From Middle High German ~überlegen~, past participle of ~überligen~. By surface analysis, ~über-~ + ~legen~.

• ~legen~: From MHG ~legen~, from OHG ~leggen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laggjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lagjaną~ ("to lay, cause to lie"), from PIE *~logʰéyeti~. A causative denominative: "to cause to lie." Cognate with English ~lay~, Dutch ~leggen~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubiri~, ~ubari~, from Proto-Germanic *~ubiri~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). As an inseparable prefix in the "to ponder" sense, ~über-~ lends the sense of turning something over in the mind, laying thought upon thought.

~Überlegen~ has two distinct existences in Modern German, distinguished only by stress and separability. The inseparable verb (stress on ~-legen~) means "to reflect, consider, ponder"; one lays thoughts over a problem. The adjective ~überlegen~ (also stress on ~-legen~, but derived differently) means "superior, dominant." The two arose independently: the verb from the idea of placing something mentally "over" a problem, the adjective from the literal sense of lying over or on top of someone (as in a wrestling hold). The MHG past participle ~überlegen~ from ~überligen~ ("to lie over, overpower") gave rise to the adjective; the thoughtful verb derives from ~Überlegung~ ("reflection, consideration"). The noun ~Überlegung~ is the standard German word for deliberate, careful consideration; "after much ~Überlegung~" is a formula in formal prose. Cognate with Dutch ~overleggen~.
en.überleiten:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~leiten~:

• ~leiten~: From MHG ~leiten~, from OHG ~leiten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~laidijan~: the causative *~laidijaną~ of the strong verb *~līþaną~ ("to pass, go") with the suffix *~-janą~ ("to cause to go"), from PIE *~leyt-~ ("to go, depart, die"). ~leiten~ and ~leiden~ are a base-and-causative pair. Cognate with English ~lead~ (OE ~lǣdan~).
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. It covers crossing to the other side: of a river, a street, a border.

~Überleiten~ leads across from one section or thought to the next, in music and speech, the smooth transition.
en.überlesen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~lesen~:

• ~lesen~: From MHG ~lësen~, from OHG ~lësan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~lesan~, from Proto-Germanic *~lesaną~ ("to gather"), from PIE *~les-~ ("to gather"). The shift from "to gather" to "to read", paralleled in Latin ~legō~ ("I gather; I read"), construes reading as gathering letters. Cognate with Dutch ~lezen~, English ~lease~ (archaic).
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys passing over, skipping, or overlooking.

~Überlesen~ is the eye's slip: to pass over a word or an error while reading, or, in the opposite direction, to read a text over closely.
en.überliefern:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~liefern~:

• ~liefern~: From MHG ~lieveren~ (attested before 1350), probably borrowed via Middle Dutch and Middle Low German ~lēveren~, from Old French ~livrer~, from Latin ~līberō~ ("I free, release, deliver"), from ~līber~ ("free"). The word belonged to the Hanseatic League's trade vocabulary. Cognate with Dutch ~leveren~, English ~deliver~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys transfer or handing over to someone.

~Überliefern~ is handing on across the generations: texts, customs, tales passed from one age to the next.
en.übermitteln:
A relatively modern formation, coined in the early twentieth century. Compound of ~über-~ + ~mitteln~:

• ~mitteln~: A denominative verb from ~Mittel~ ("means, medium"), from MHG ~mittel~, from OHG ~mittil~, from Proto-Germanic *~midlą~ or *~midilą~ ("middle"), cognate with English ~middle~ and Dutch ~middel~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über-~, from OHG ~ubar-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uberi-~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). This prefix adds the sense of transmitting across a distance or barrier.

The verb means "to convey, to transmit, to communicate," literally "to mediate (something) across." It is related to the older verb ~vermitteln~ ("to mediate, to arrange"), which uses the ~ver-~ prefix instead. The noun ~Mittel~ also gives rise to ~Mittelalter~ ("Middle Ages"), ~Mittelpunkt~ ("center"), and ~Lebensmittel~ ("groceries," literally "means of life"). Despite its recent coinage, ~übermitteln~ filled a genuine lexical gap, providing a formal verb for the transmission of messages, data, or information across channels. English speakers might use "to transmit" or "to convey" in the same contexts.
en.übernehmen:
Compound of ~über-~ + ~nehmen~:

• ~nehmen~: From MHG ~nëmen~, from OHG ~nëman~, from Proto-West Germanic *~neman~, from Proto-Germanic *~nemaną~, from PIE *~nem-~ ("to give or take one's due").
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubiri~, ~ubari~, from Proto-Germanic *~ubiri~, from PIE *~upéri~, ultimately from *~upo~ + *~-i~. Meaning "over, across, above." Cognate with Ancient Greek ~hupér~ ("above"), Latin ~super~ ("above"), Sanskrit ~upári~, Dutch ~over~, English ~over~, Swedish ~över~.

The semantic range of ~übernehmen~ illustrates how "taking over" can mean taking on responsibility (~eine Aufgabe übernehmen~), assuming control (~ein Unternehmen übernehmen~), or adopting something (~eine Idee übernehmen~). The verb can also be reflexive: ~sich übernehmen~ means "to overextend oneself," a sense that turns the completive force of ~über-~ against the subject. Cognate with Dutch ~overnemen~.
en.überordnen:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~ordnen~:

• ~ordnen~: From MHG ~ordenen~, from OHG ~ordinōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ordinōn~ ("to put in order"), borrowed from Latin ~ōrdināre~ ("to arrange"), from ~ōrdō~ ("row, rank, order"), from Proto-Italic *~ordō~, probably from PIE *~h₂er-~ ("to fit together"). Doublet of ~ordinieren~. Cognate with English ~order~, Italian ~ordinare~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Unstressed and inseparable, the same particle takes abstract senses instead (excess, transfer, overlooking) and moves the verb's stress off the particle.

Its counterpart ~unterordnen~ places below; ~überordnen~ assigns the higher rank.
en.überprüfen:
From ~über-~ + ~prüfen~:
