• ~prüfen~: From MHG ~prüeven~, ultimately from Latin ~probāre~ ("to test, approve"), a denominative of ~probus~ ("good, upright"), from PIE *~pro-bʰuH-wó-s~ ("being foremost"). Entered German before the ~-ieren~ suffix was productive, fully assimilated into the native weak-verb system. Cognate with English ~prove~ and ~probe~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubiri~, ~ubari~, from Proto-Germanic *~ubiri~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Here the prefix adds thoroughness and coverage, to check something over, to go over it comprehensively.

~Überprüfen~ ("to check over, verify, review, audit") extends ~prüfen~'s sense of testing with the thoroughness of ~über-~: where ~prüfen~ tests a student or a hypothesis, ~überprüfen~ reviews a complete file, audits an account, or re-examines a decision from above. The verb is ubiquitous in administrative and legal German. That its root ~prüfen~ derives ultimately from Latin ~probus~ ("upright, good") means that every act of ~überprüfen~ is etymologically an inquiry into whether something meets the standard of uprightness. Compare Dutch ~controleren~ (parallel function, different root).
en.überraschen:
~Über-~ + ~raschen~. Compound of ~über-~ + ~raschen~:

• ~raschen~: A now-rare verb derived from the adjective ~rasch~ ("quick, swift"), from MHG ~rasch~, ~rasche~, from OHG ~rask~, ~rasc~ ("quick, prompt, powerful"), from Proto-Germanic *~raskuz~, possibly from PIE *~Hreth₂-~ ("to run, roll").
• ~über-~: From PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). As an inseparable prefix here, ~über-~ conveys the sense of coming upon someone from above or beyond expectation.

~Überraschen~ means "to surprise", literally "to rush over someone quickly," capturing the sudden, overwhelming quality of surprise. The adjective ~rasch~ ("quick, swift") survives independently in modern German, but the verb ~raschen~ from which ~überraschen~ was formed is essentially extinct outside this compound. The noun ~Überraschung~ ("surprise") is one of the most common German nouns. English ~rash~ (meaning "hasty, impetuous") is a cognate of ~rasch~, borrowed into English from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch; so when someone acts ~rashly~, they are being etymologically ~rasch~. The underlying image of surprise as speed (something happening too fast to anticipate) is preserved intact in this compound.
en.überreagieren:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~reagieren~:

• ~reagieren~: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ~reagō~ ("to act back, react"), from ~re-~ ("back, again") + ~agō~ ("to drive, act"), from Proto-Italic *~agō~, from PIE *~h₂eǵ-~ ("to drive"). German took it from Neo-Latin scientific vocabulary with the ~-ieren~ suffix that naturalizes Latin verbs as German weak verbs. Cognate with English ~react~, French ~réagir~, Dutch ~reageren~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

A calque on English ~overreact~: to react more strongly than the situation warrants.
en.überreden:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~reden~:

• ~reden~: From MHG ~reden~, from OHG ~redōn~, ~rediōn~ ("to speak"), a denominal verb from ~reda~, ~redia~ ("speech, word, opinion"), from Proto-Germanic *~raþjǭ~ ("accountability, speech"). The shared PIE root carried the sense of organized, accountable speech. Cognate with Latin ~ratiō~ (whence English ~ratio~, ~reason~), English ~rede~ ("counsel"), and German ~Rat~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys going over something thoroughly or covering it completely.

~Überreden~ wins by talking where ~überzeugen~ wins by reasons; the one aims at the will, the other at understanding.
en.überreichen:
Compound of ~über-~ + ~reichen~:

• ~reichen~: From Middle High German ~reichen~, from Old High German ~reihhen~, related to the adjective ~reich~ ("rich, powerful"). The adjective traces to Old High German ~rīhhi~, from Proto-Germanic *~rīkijaz~, a borrowing from Celtic *~rīgos~ ("king"), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃rēǵs~ ("king, ruler"), also the source of Latin ~rēx~. The verb's original sense was "to make powerful, to extend," hence "to reach, to hand over."
• ~über-~: From Middle High German ~über~, from Old High German ~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Indo-European *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Here the prefix conveys the sense of handing something across or over to someone.

~Überreichen~ is always inseparable and carries a formal, ceremonial tone: one ~überreicht~ an award, a gift, or a document. The more casual equivalent is simply ~geben~ ("to give"). Cognate with Dutch ~overhandigen~, which uses a different metaphor ("over-handing") for the same formal concept.
en.überrinnen:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~rinnen~:

• ~rinnen~: From MHG ~rinnen~, from OHG ~rinnan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~rinnan~, from Proto-Germanic *~rinnaną~ ("to run, flow"); the PIE source is debated, most often given as *~h₃reyH-~ ("to churn, set in motion"). A class III strong verb (~rinnen~, ~rann~, ~geronnen~). German ~rennen~ is its causative, from *~rannijaną~. Cognate with English ~run~, Gothic ~rinnan~, Swedish ~rinna~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. With verbs of pouring or spilling it means "over the edge," of a container running over.

A loftier, older word for overflowing: liquid that runs over the rim and is no longer contained.
en.überrollen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~rollen~:

• ~rollen~: From MHG ~rollen~, borrowed from Old French ~roeler~, from Medieval Latin ~rotulāre~ ("to roll"), from Latin ~rotula~ ("small wheel"), diminutive of ~rota~ ("wheel"), from PIE *~ret-~ ("to run, to roll"). Cognate with English ~roll~ (also borrowed from Old French), Dutch ~rollen~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

Literally something rolls over something else; figuratively a wave or an event ~überrollt~ whoever cannot withstand it.
en.überrunden:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~runden~:

• ~runden~: From ~rund~ + ~-en~. ~Rund~ descends from MHG ~runt~, borrowed from Old French ~ront~, from Latin ~rotundus~ ("round"), from ~rota~ ("wheel, disk"), from PIE *~Hróth₂o~ (from *~ret-~ "to run, to roll"), one of the few everyday German adjectives that arrived via Latin and French rather than directly from Proto-Germanic. English ~round~ took the same detour.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

Despite the formal decomposition, ~überrunden~ is denominal from ~die Runde~ ("lap, round"), not built on ~runden~ ("to make round"): to ~überrunden~ a rival is to be a full lap ahead of them.
en.überschallen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~schallen~:

• ~schallen~: From MHG ~schallen~, a denominal formation on ~Schall~ ("sound"); the Grimms took it instead as a reshaping of the older strong MHG ~schellen~ ("to resound"), from Proto-West Germanic *~skellan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skellaną~, from PIE *~kelh₁-~ ("to call, shout") with s-mobile. Normally weak today (~schallte~, ~geschallt~), it keeps the strong Präteritum ~scholl~ as an elevated variant. Cognate with Old Norse ~skjalla~, Old English ~sciellan~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys going over something thoroughly or covering it completely.

~Überschallen~ names a louder sound that completely covers a quieter one and drowns it out.
en.überschauen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~schauen~:

• ~schauen~: From MHG ~schouwen~, from OHG ~scouwōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~skawwōną~ ("to look, see, watch"), from PIE *~(s)kewh₁-~ ("to heed, look, take note of"). The same root gives English ~show~, the Germanic descendants dividing between intransitive "to look" and transitive "to make visible." The verb is characteristic of southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage. Cognate with English ~show~, Dutch ~schouwen~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys authority or vantage from above.

~Überschauen~ means taking in an entire scene or situation at a single glance from a raised vantage; "overlook" here is this comprehensive taking-in, not the missing sense.
en.überschießen:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~schießen~:

• ~schießen~: From MHG ~schiezen~, from OHG ~sciozan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skeotan~, from Proto-Germanic *~skeutaną~ ("to shoot, to shove"), possibly from PIE *~(s)kewd-~ ("to throw, shoot, pursue"). A class II strong verb (~schießen~, ~schoss~, ~geschossen~). Cognate with English ~shoot~, Dutch ~schieten~, Old Norse ~skjóta~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Stressed and separable, ~über-~ is literal and spatial: something moves over, across, or on top of something else.

In the separable reading, ~überschießen~ names shooting or projecting something over an obstacle.
en.überschlagen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~schlagen~:

• ~schlagen~: From MHG ~slahen~, from OHG ~slahan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~slahan~, from Proto-Germanic *~slahaną~, from PIE *~slak-~ ("to hit, strike, throw"), apparently onomatopoeic. The modern ~-g-~ is a secondary insertion by analogy with ~schlug~ and the noun ~Schlag~ (Grammatischer Wechsel). Cognate with English ~slay~ and ~slog~, Old English ~slēan~, Dutch ~slaan~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys passing over, skipping, or overlooking.

~Überschlagen~ in the "skip" sense means passing over something while reading or counting; the same verb also means "to reckon roughly" (die Kosten ~überschlagen~) and, reflexively, "to somersault, tumble."
en.überschneiden:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~schneiden~:

• ~schneiden~: From MHG ~snīden~, from OHG ~snīdan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~snīþan~ ("to cut"); no secure PIE root has been established, and the word may be a Germanic innovation. A class I strong verb (~schneiden~, ~schnitt~, ~geschnitten~). Cognate with archaic English ~snithe~ ("to cut"), Dutch ~snijden~, Icelandic ~sníða~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

Usually reflexive (~sich überschneiden~) the verb describes two lines, areas, or time spans that cross each other or partly coincide.
en.überschreiben:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~schreiben~:

• ~schreiben~: From MHG ~schrīben~, from OHG ~scrīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~skrībaną~, an early borrowing from Latin ~scrībō~ ("I write"), from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~, from PIE *~(s)kreybʰ-~ ("to scratch, incise"). Because the borrowing occurred in the Roman period, the verb was fully assimilated into the strong system (class I: ~schreiben~, ~schrieb~, ~geschrieben~). Cognate with Dutch ~schrijven~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Unstressed and inseparable, the same particle takes abstract senses instead (excess, transfer, overlooking) and moves the verb's stress off the particle.

~Überschreiben~ means transferring property or rights to someone; the verb also carries the senses "to give a heading to" and, in computing, "to overwrite existing data."
en.überschreiten:
Compound of ~über-~ + ~schreiten~. Cognate with Dutch ~overschrijden~, Swedish ~överskrida~, Danish ~overskride~:

• ~schreiten~: From MHG ~schrīten~, from OHG ~skrītan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skrīþan~ ("to step, stride"), from Proto-Germanic *~skrīþaną~ ("to walk, glide, crawl"), from PIE *~(s)kreyt-~ ("to stride"), an extension of *~(s)krey-~ ("to go about"). Cognate with Lithuanian ~skrìsti~ ("to rush, run"), Latvian ~skrìet~ ("to run, fly"). Related to ~Schritt~ ("step").
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über-~, from OHG ~ubar-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber-~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). As an inseparable prefix here, it conveys "across, beyond."

The semantic range of ~überschreiten~ mirrors the physical act of stepping beyond a boundary: "to cross" (a border, a threshold) and "to exceed" (a limit, a deadline). The verb preserves the formal, elevated register of its base verb ~schreiten~, which in modern German sounds literary compared to the everyday ~gehen~; one ~schreitet~ through a palace, one ~geht~ to the store. The Proto-Germanic ancestor *~skrīþaną~ originally meant "to walk, glide, crawl," a broad range of locomotion that narrowed to stately striding in German while Old Norse ~skríða~ retained the "crawl, slide" sense (whence Icelandic ~skríða~ "landslide").
en.überschätzen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~schätzen~:

• ~schätzen~: A denominal verb from ~Schatz~ ("treasure"), from MHG ~schaz~, OHG ~scaz~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skatt~ ("cattle, treasure"), an early Germanic word in which cattle served as a measure of wealth. Cognate with Old Norse ~skattr~ (whence Danish ~skat~ and Swedish ~skatt~, both "tax"), Gothic ~skatts~, Old English ~sċeatt~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

~Überschätzen~ sets a thing's value too high, the counterpart to ~unterschätzen~ ("to underestimate").
en.übersehen:
Compound of ~über-~ + ~sehen~:

• ~sehen~: From MHG ~sëhen~, from OHG ~sëhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sehwan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sehwaną~ ("to see"), from PIE *~sekʷ-~ ("to see, to notice"). Cognate with English ~see~, Dutch ~zien~, Danish ~se~, Gothic ~saihwan~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubari~, from Proto-Germanic *~ubiri~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). As an inseparable prefix here, it conveys "over" in the sense of looking past something.

~Übersehen~ means "to overlook, to miss", literally to see over something and thus past it. This is an inseparable compound (stress on ~-seh-~): ~Ich habe den Fehler übersehen~ ("I overlooked the error"). Contrast with the separable ~übersehen~ (stress on ~über-~), which means "to survey, to have an overview of": ~Man kann das ganze Tal übersehen~ ("One can survey the entire valley"). This stress-dependent meaning split is a hallmark of German prefix verbs: the same written form produces antonymic senses depending on whether the prefix is separable (stressed) or inseparable (unstressed).
en.übersenden:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~senden~:

• ~senden~: From MHG ~senden~, from OHG ~senten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~sandijaną~, from PIE *~sont-eye-~, a causative of *~sent-~ ("to walk, travel"), originally "to cause to go." It has a double Präteritum: ~sendete~ for broadcasting, ~sandte~ (a Rückumlaut form) for sending a letter. Cognate with English ~send~, Dutch ~zenden~, Gothic ~sandjan~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys transfer or handing over to someone.

~Übersenden~ is the elevated word for conveying a document or item to a recipient.
en.übersetzen:
Sixteenth-century formation, probably modeled on Latin ~trādūcere~ ("to lead across, translate"), perhaps through Middle Low German ~ōversetten~. Compound of ~über-~ + ~setzen~:

• ~setzen~: From MHG ~setzen~, from OHG ~sezzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sattjan~, a causative derived from Proto-Germanic *~sitjaną~ ("to sit"). Cognate with English ~set~, Dutch ~zetten~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über-~, from OHG ~ubar-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber-~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). As an inseparable prefix (stressed on the second syllable), it conveys "across" in an abstract sense.

German ~übersetzen~ is a fascinating case of stress distinguishing meaning. With stress on ~über-~ (separable prefix: ~er setzt über~), it means "to cross, ferry across", literally to set something over a body of water. With stress on ~-setzen~ (inseparable prefix: ~er übersetzt~), it means "to translate." The separable sense has Old High German roots (~ubarsezzen~), while the inseparable "translate" sense is a sixteenth-century calque of Latin ~trādūcere~, which similarly meant both "to lead across" physically and "to translate" metaphorically. This Latin-inspired semantic extension made German ~übersetzen~ part of a pan-European pattern: compare French ~traduire~, Italian ~tradurre~, all from the same Latin source. Cognate with Dutch ~overzetten~ (separable sense) and English ~overset~ (archaic).
en.überspielen:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~spielen~:

• ~spielen~: From MHG ~spil(e)n~, from OHG ~spilōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~spilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~spilōną~, a denominative verb from the noun *~spilą~ ("play, game, dance"); the pre-Germanic origin is uncertain. OHG ~spilōn~ was broader, covering dance and entertainment generally. Cognate with Dutch ~spelen~, Low German ~spelen~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Unstressed and inseparable, the same particle takes abstract senses instead (excess, transfer, overlooking) and moves the verb's stress off the particle.

~Überspielen~ means transferring a recording onto another medium and, figuratively, smoothly papering over a slip or an awkwardness.
en.überspringen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~springen~:

• ~springen~: From OHG ~springan~, from Proto-Germanic *~springaną~, from PIE *~sprenǵʰ-~, a nasalized form of *~sperǵʰ-~ ("to move energetically, to hasten, to spring"). A class III strong verb (~springen~, ~sprang~, ~gesprungen~). Cognate with English ~spring~, Dutch ~springen~, Danish ~springe~, Greek ~spérkhō~ ("to hasten").
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

~Überspringen~ is leaping over an obstacle and, figuratively, skipping a step or a section.
en.überstehen:
Compound of ~über-~ + ~stehen~:

• ~stehen~: From Middle High German ~stān~, ~stēn~, from Old High German ~stān~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stān~, from Proto-Germanic *~stāną~, from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stand~, Dutch ~staan~, Latin ~stāre~.
• ~über-~: From Middle High German ~über~, from Old High German ~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Indo-European *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Here the prefix conveys surviving through or getting past something.

The inseparable verb ~überSTEHen~ means "to survive, to endure, to get through", literally "to stand over" a difficulty. The separable ~ÜBERstehen~ means "to protrude, to jut out." The survival sense captures a vivid image: standing firm while hardship passes over you, still standing when it is done. The past participle ~überstanden~ appears frequently in the relieved exclamation ~Das wäre überstanden!~ ("That's over and done with!").
en.übersteigen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~steigen~:

• ~steigen~: From MHG ~stîgen~, from OHG ~stīgan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stīgan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stīganą~, from PIE *~steygʰ-~ ("to walk, climb"). A class I strong verb (~steigen~, ~stieg~, ~gestiegen~); the same root gave Ancient Greek ~steíkhō~ ("I go"). Cognate with archaic English ~sty~ ("to climb"), Dutch ~stijgen~, Gothic ~steigan~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

Literally "to climb over something," ~übersteigen~ developed the figurative sense "to exceed a measure", costs or deadlines that ~übersteigen~ a limit.
en.überstellen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~stellen~:

• ~stellen~: From MHG ~stellen~, from OHG ~stellen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stalljan~ ("to put, position"), from PIE *~stel-~ ("to place, put"). A causative weak verb, the transitive counterpart to ~stehen~ ("to stand"). Cognate with English ~stell~ ("to place, fix"), Dutch ~stellen~, Danish ~stille~, Yiddish ~shteln~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys transfer or handing over to someone.

~Überstellen~ is the official term for handing a person or item over to another authority or office.
en.übersteuern:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~steuern~:

• ~steuern~: From MHG ~stiuren~, from OHG ~stiuren~, from Proto-West Germanic *~stiurijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~stiurijaną~. The root noun ~Steuer~ carries two meanings sharing one ancestor: ~das Steuer~ ("rudder, helm") and ~die Steuer~ ("tax," via "supporting post" and "support"). ~Steuern~ thus means both "to steer, navigate, control" and, in archaic or Swiss usage, "to pay a tax." Cognate with English ~steer~, Dutch ~stuur~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

Taking the root verb's "to steer, control" sense, ~übersteuern~ means an excess of control: in a vehicle the rear breaking away, in electronics the overdriving of a signal.
en.überstimmen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~stimmen~:

• ~stimmen~: From MHG ~stimmen~, from OHG *~stimmen~, a denominative of ~Stimme~ ("voice, vote": OHG ~stimma~, Proto-West Germanic *~stebnu~, Proto-Germanic *~stebnō~, from PIE *~stomen-~ "mouth, muzzle"). Hence the senses "to tune" (an instrument), "to be correct," and "to vote." Cognate with archaic English ~steven~ ("voice"), Dutch ~stem~, Gothic ~stibna~, Ancient Greek ~stóma~ ("mouth").
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys authority or vantage from above.

From ~Stimme~ as "vote," ~überstimmen~ means overriding a minority by a majority of votes; from ~Stimme~ as "sound," it older means "to drown out."
en.überstürzen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~stürzen~:

• ~stürzen~: From MHG ~stürzen~, from OHG ~sturzen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~sturtijan~ ("to fall down, tumble"), of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly from PIE *~ster-~ ("to be stiff") via a dental extension *~sterd-~, though the derivation is debated. Cognate with English ~start~, a doublet from the same Proto-West Germanic source, from which the meanings have diverged radically.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

~Überstürzen~ means doing something headlong and rashly; reflexive ~sich überstürzen~ of events tumbling over one another.
en.übertauchen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~tauchen~:

• ~tauchen~: From MHG ~tūchen~, ~touchen~, from OHG *~tūhhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dūkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~dūkaną~ ("to duck, to dive under"), whose further etymology is uncertain. A class II strong verb that became weak in the early modern period: when it was reintroduced from Central and Low German, the strong conjugation was regularized to weak. Cognate with Dutch ~duiken~, Swedish ~dyka~; a Low German consonant variant of the same root is ~ducken~, cognate with English ~duck~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys motion across or over a boundary.

~Übertauchen~ is chiefly Austrian and means getting through a difficult time, figuratively diving under a wave and surfacing again on the other side.
en.übertragen:
From Middle High German ~übertragen~, at least in part a calque of Latin ~transferre~. Analyzable as ~über-~ + ~tragen~:

• ~tragen~: From MHG ~tragen~, from OHG ~tragan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~dragan~, from Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ ("to draw, drag, carry"), from PIE *~dʰregʰ-~ ("to pull, draw, drag"). A class VI strong verb. Cognate with English ~draw~ and ~drag~, Dutch ~dragen~, Icelandic ~draga~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubari~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Latin ~super~, Greek ~ὑπέρ~ (~hyper~).

~Übertragen~ is a Germanic calque of Latin ~transferre~ (~trans-~ + ~ferre~, "to carry across"), and the parallel is exact: ~über-~ ("over, across") + ~tragen~ ("to carry") = ~transferre~. English ~transfer~ is the Latin borrowing; ~übertragen~ is the native Germanic translation of the same concept. The verb's semantic range is wide: to transfer funds, to broadcast a signal, to transmit a disease, and (in the phrase ~im übertragenen Sinne~ ("in the figurative sense")) to carry a meaning metaphorically from one domain to another. That last usage is itself an act of ~übertragen~: figurative language carries a word across from its literal territory. Cognate with English ~carry over~ and Dutch ~overdragen~.
en.übertreffen:
From Middle High German ~übertreffen~. Compound of ~über-~ + ~treffen~:

• ~treffen~: From Middle High German ~treffen~, from Old High German ~treffan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drepan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drepaną~ ("to strike, hit"). Cognate with English ~drub~ ("to beat"). The semantic shift from "to hit, strike" to "to meet" (the primary modern sense of ~treffen~) happened because meeting someone was conceived as "striking upon" them.
• ~über-~: From Middle High German ~über~, from Old High German ~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Indo-European *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Here the prefix conveys exceeding or surpassing.

~Übertreffen~ is always inseparable and means "to surpass, to exceed, to outdo." The metaphor is hitting above or beyond the mark. The reflexive ~sich selbst übertreffen~ ("to surpass oneself") is common in both praise and ironic criticism.
en.übertreiben:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~treiben~:

• ~treiben~: From MHG ~trīben~, from OHG ~trīban~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drīban~, from Proto-Germanic *~drībaną~. A class I strong verb (~treiben~, ~trieb~, ~getrieben~) whose ablaut pattern directly reflects the Proto-Germanic vowel grades *ei / *ai / *i. Cognate with English ~drive~, separated only by the High German consonant shift, as well as Dutch ~drijven~, Danish ~drive~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

Literally "to drive too far" (like cattle driven excessively) ~übertreiben~ became the word for inflating an account beyond the truth.
en.übertreten:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~treten~:

• ~treten~: From MHG ~trëten~, from OHG ~trëtan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~tredan~, from Proto-Germanic *~trudaną~, from a possible pre-Germanic *~dret-~, perhaps an extension of PIE *~dr-~ ("to run"). A class V strong verb (~treten~, ~trat~, ~getreten~) whose Proto-Germanic root is probably a root aorist with alternating vocalism *~tred-~/*~trud-~. Cognate with English ~tread~, Dutch ~treden~, Old Norse ~troða~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. It covers crossing to the other side: of a river, a street, a border.

Separable (~ist übergetreten~), ~übertreten~ means "to go over to another party, faith, or side"; inseparable (~hat übertreten~), it means "to break a law or commandment"; stress alone distinguishes the two readings.
en.übertöten:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~töten~:

• ~töten~: From MHG ~tœten~, from OHG *~tōten~, from Proto-West Germanic *~daudijan~ ("to make dead, to kill"), from Proto-Germanic *~daudijaną~, a factitive of *~daudaz~ ("dead") + *~-janą~ ("to make X"), transparently ~tot~ + ~-en~. Compare English ~deaden~. Cognate with Dutch ~doden~, Old Norse ~deyða~, Gothic ~dauþjan~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

~Übertöten~ renders English "overkill": expending more means or force than the goal requires.
en.überwachen:
Compound of ~über-~ + ~wachen~:

• ~wachen~: From MHG ~wachen~, from OHG ~wahhēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wakēn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wakāną~ ("to be awake, to watch"), from PIE *~weǵ-~ ("to wake, to be strong, to be lively"). Cognate with English ~wake~ and ~watch~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über-~, from OHG ~ubar-~, from Proto-Germanic *~uberi-~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). The prefix adds the sense of watching over something from above, implying authority and control.

The PIE root *~weǵ-~ connects wakefulness with vigor and strength, reflecting the ancient understanding that being alert was itself a form of power. ~Überwachen~ means "to supervise, to monitor, to surveil," and its noun ~Überwachung~ ("surveillance") has acquired pointed political connotations in German, especially given the country's experiences with state surveillance under both the Nazi regime and the East German Stasi. The term ~Überwachungsstaat~ ("surveillance state") is a powerful compound that resonates deeply in German political discourse. English ~watch~ and ~wake~ are direct Germanic cousins, and the connection extends to Latin ~vigil~ ("watchful") and ~vigor~ ("liveliness"), both from the same PIE root. The related adjective ~wach~ ("awake") preserves the simplest form of this ancient word.
en.überwachsen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~wachsen~:

• ~wachsen~: From MHG ~wahsen~, from OHG ~wahsan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wahsan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wahsijaną~, from PIE *~h₂weg-~ ("to grow, increase"). A class VI strong verb (~wächst~, ~wuchs~, ~gewachsen~). Cognate with English ~wax~, Dutch ~wassen~, Danish ~vokse~, Swedish ~växa~, Gothic ~wahsjan~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys going over something thoroughly or covering it completely.

~Überwachsen~ describes plants spreading over a surface and covering it entirely; it forms its perfect with ~sein~ (~ist überwachsen~).
en.überwechseln:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~wechseln~:

• ~wechseln~: From MHG ~wëhseln~, from OHG *~wehsalōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~wihslōną~, from PIE *~weyk-~, *~weyḱ-~ ("to change, bend, yield"). Cognate with Dutch ~wisselen~, Luxembourgish ~wiesselen~, English ~week~, German ~Woche~, and Latin ~vicis~ ("change, turn, alternation").
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. It covers crossing to the other side: of a river, a street, a border.

~Überwechseln~ means moving from one side, lane, or group to another, also of game crossing a road.
en.überweisen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~weisen~:

• ~weisen~: From MHG ~wīsen~, from OHG ~wīsen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wīsijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsijaną~, a denominative verb from *~wīsaz~ ("wise, knowing"), from PIE *~weyd-so-s~ ("knowledgeable"), from *~weyd-~ ("to see, know"). A class I strong verb; its senses "to show, point" and "to direct, expel" both direct knowledge or attention. Cognate with English ~wise~, ~wit~, ~wizard~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys transfer or handing over to someone.

~Überweisen~ unites three handings-over: transferring money to an account, referring a patient to a specialist, and referring a bill to a committee.
en.überwerfen:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~werfen~:

• ~werfen~: From MHG ~wërfen~, from OHG ~werfan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~werpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~, from PIE *~wergʷ-~ ("to bend, spin, warp"). A class III strong verb (~wirft~, ~warf~, ~geworfen~). Cognate with English ~warp~, Dutch ~werpen~, Old Saxon ~werpan~, Old Norse ~verpa~, Gothic ~wairpan~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Stressed and separable, ~über-~ is literal and spatial: something moves over, across, or on top of something else.

Separable, ~überwerfen~ means throwing something quickly over one's shoulders; inseparable, ~sich überwerfen~ means "to fall out with someone."
en.überwiegen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~wiegen~:

• ~wiegen~: Two distinct verbs, both from MHG ~wigen~. Sense 1 ("to weigh"): a northwestern variant of ~wegen~ that generalized the present-singular stem vowel ~i~, from OHG ~wegan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~wegan~, from Proto-Germanic *~weganą~ ("to move, carry, weigh"), from PIE *~weǵʰ-~ ("to convey, move"); the original ~e~-form survives in the doublet ~wägen~. Sense 2 ("to rock, cradle"): from ~wige~ ("cradle," modern ~Wiege~), from OHG ~wīga~, likely related to Proto-West Germanic *~waggjan~ ("to cause to move"), from the same PIE root. Cognate with English ~weigh~, Dutch ~wegen~, Danish ~veje~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

From the root verb ~wiegen~ in the "to weigh" sense (not "to rock"), ~überwiegen~ means to weigh more and therefore to predominate.
en.überwinden:
From Middle High German ~überwinden~, from Old High German ~ubarwintan~, an originally Upper German form alongside Central German ~überwinnen~, ~ubarwinnan~. The ~nn~-form descends from Proto-West Germanic *~ubarwinnan~. Compound of ~über-~ + ~winden~ (or possibly ~winnen~):

• ~winden~: From MHG ~winden~, from OHG ~wintan~, from Proto-Germanic *~windaną~ ("to wind, to wrap"), from PIE *~wendʰ-~ ("to turn, wind, braid"). Cognate with English ~wind~ (the verb, "to coil"), Dutch ~winden~, Danish ~vinde~.
• ~über-~: From PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). The prefix conveys mastery and supremacy, to come over and above an obstacle.

Whether ~überwinden~ derives from ~winden~ ("to wind, twist") or from the now-lost simplex ~winnen~ ("to win," surviving only in the compound ~gewinnen~) is one of the more intriguing puzzles in German word history. The ~nd~ form may be a mere phonetic alteration of the ~nn~ form, or it may reflect a genuine reanalysis connecting the verb to ~winden~, twisting free from an opponent's grip as a metaphor for overcoming. Isolated MHG compounds like ~anewinden~ ("to attack") and ~widerwinden~ ("to repulse") support the fighting sense for ~winden~. Modern ~überwinden~ means "to overcome, to get over, to surmount": one overcomes fear (~Angst überwinden~), conquers obstacles (~Hindernisse überwinden~), and gets over grief (~Trauer überwinden~). The reflexive ~sich überwinden~ ("to bring oneself to, to force oneself") captures the internal struggle beautifully. Cognate with Dutch ~overwinnen~ ("to conquer, to defeat").
en.überzahlen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~zahlen~:

• ~zahlen~: From MHG ~zaln~, ~zalen~, from OHG ~zalōn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~talōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~talōną~ ("to tell, recount; to count, reckon"). ~Zahlen~ and ~zählen~ are siblings from the same root: payment requires counting out the correct amount. Cognate with English ~tale~ and ~tell~, Dutch ~betalen~, Swedish ~tala~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys transfer or handing over to someone.

In this reading ~überzahlen~ frames paying as a transfer: the sum passes over to a recipient. The more usual reading, though, is the excess one, "to overpay."
en.überzeichnen:
An inseparable compound of ~über-~ + ~zeichnen~:

• ~zeichnen~: Derived from the noun ~Zeichen~ ("sign, symbol"), from MHG ~zeichen~, from OHG ~zeihhan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~taikn~, from Proto-Germanic *~taikną~, *~taiknaz~ ("sign"), from PIE *~deyḱ-~ ("to show, point"); to ~zeichnen~ is etymologically to make a sign. Cognate with English ~token~, Dutch ~teken~, Danish ~tegn~, Swedish ~tecken~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, ~ubiri~, from Proto-West Germanic *~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). Cognate with English ~over~, Latin ~super~ and Ancient Greek ~hupér~, source of the ~hyper-~ of English learned words. ~über-~ conveys excess: doing something too much or past a limit.

~Überzeichnen~ is to render a picture past the right measure, until it tips into exaggeration or caricature.
en.überzeugen:
From ~über-~ + ~zeugen~:

• ~zeugen~: From MHG ~ziugen~, ~geziugen~, from OHG ~giziugon~, a denominative of ~Zeug~ ("stuff, gear, equipment, tools"). ~Zeug~ itself comes from MHG ~ziuc~, from OHG ~giziug~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teug~, from Proto-Germanic *~teugą~. This is the nominal derivative of *~teuhaną~ ("to pull, lead"), which also underlies ~ziehen~ ("to pull, draw"), from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead").
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubari~, ~ubar~, from Proto-Germanic *~ubar~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"). The prefix here carries the sense of mastery or going beyond, convincing someone by rising above their resistance.

The original sense of ~zeugen~ was "to bear witness, to attest", itself from the earlier meaning of producing or showing one's ~Zeug~ (one's evidence, one's gear). ~Überzeugen~ therefore literally means "to over-witness" or "to attest so thoroughly that one overcomes the other's doubt." The noun ~Zeuge~ ("witness") and the verb ~zeugen~ ("to beget, to produce") are related, all sharing the core idea of bringing something forth or pulling it into being. A curious English near-parallel: ~convince~ ultimately derives from Latin ~vincere~ ("to conquer"), reflecting the same metaphor of overcoming resistance through argument. Cognate with Dutch ~overtuigen~.
en.überziehen:
A separable compound of ~über-~ + ~ziehen~:

• ~ziehen~: From MHG ~ziehen~, from OHG ~ziohan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~teuhan~, from Proto-Germanic *~teuhaną~, from PIE *~dewk-~ ("to pull, lead"). A class II strong verb. Cognate with Gothic ~tiuhan~, Old English ~tēon~, Old Norse ~toga~, West Frisian ~tsjen~, and English ~tie~.
• ~über-~: From MHG ~über~, from OHG ~ubar~, from Proto-West Germanic *~uber~, from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upéri~ ("over, above"), an extension of *~upo~ ("under, up from under"). Cognate with English ~over~, Dutch ~over~, Swedish ~över~, Latin ~super~, Ancient Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~. Stressed and separable, ~über-~ is literal and spatial: something moves over, across, or on top of something else.

Stressed and separable, ~überziehen~ means to pull a garment on; unstressed and inseparable, the same spelling means to coat something or to overdraw an account.
en.übrigbleiben:
A separable compound of ~übrig~ + ~bleiben~:

• ~bleiben~: From MHG ~blīben~, ~belīben~, from OHG ~bilīban~ ("to remain"), from Proto-Germanic *~bilībaną~, a compound of *~bi-~ + *~lībaną~, from PIE *~leyp-~ ("to stick, adhere"); adhesion became a metaphor for staying in place. Cognate with Dutch ~blijven~, English ~belive~ ("to remain, stay").
• ~übrig~: The adjective ~übrig~ ("remaining, left over"), from MHG ~überic~, ~überec~, formed with the suffix ~-ig~ on the preposition ~über~ ("over, above"), from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upér~, the same root as English ~over~ and, through Greek and Latin, ~hyper-~ and ~super-~. The sense is what lies over and above the amount required. The sense of ~übrig~ here is: with ~bleiben~, "to remain, to be all that is left".

~Übrigbleiben~ names what stays behind once all else is gone, the remainder no one has taken away.
en.übrighaben:
A separable compound of ~übrig~ + ~haben~:

• ~haben~: From MHG ~haben~, from OHG ~habēn~, from Proto-West Germanic *~habbjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~, from PIE *~keh₂p-~ ("to grasp, seize"). Despite the resemblance it is not related to Latin ~habēō~, but it is to ~capiō~ ("I seize") and to German ~heben~. Cognate with English ~have~, Dutch ~hebben~, Danish ~have~, Gothic ~haban~.
• ~übrig~: The adjective ~übrig~ ("remaining, left over"), from MHG ~überic~, ~überec~, formed with the suffix ~-ig~ on the preposition ~über~ ("over, above"), from Proto-Germanic *~uber~, from PIE *~upér~, the same root as English ~over~ and, through Greek and Latin, ~hyper-~ and ~super-~. The sense is what lies over and above the amount required. The sense of ~übrig~ here is: predicatively, "left over, remaining".

Literally ~übrighaben~ is to have something to spare; the idiom "viel für jemanden übrighaben," the source of the "care for" gloss, extends having-to-spare to affection.
